If no plugin matches, the build stops with PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE and says why. There is no built-in fallback.

All inspection subcommands (search, versions, info, list, current, explain) take: Option Description --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store --refresh Update the verified catalog cache from permitted sources first. Installs no plugin --offline Never use the network. Read only the verified cached catalog search also takes --type <TYPE>, which shows only plugins that serve one capability. The only value today is build. update takes --dry-run, --store and --offline. The global options apply to all subcommands.

Lists the references the catalogs offer. $ oyzu plugins search --refreshCopy 14 plugin references in the catalog ​ Reference Package Latest stable Build selects Status docker/image oyzu/docker (build) — 0.1.0-preview.1 available dotnet/sdk oyzu/dotnet (build) — 0.1.0-preview.1 available go/app oyzu/go (build) 0.1.0 0.1.0 available go/library oyzu/go (build) 0.1.0 0.1.0 available helm/chart oyzu/helm (build) — 0.1.0-preview.1 available java/app oyzu/java (build) 0.1.0 0.1.0 available node/app oyzu/node (build) — 0.1.0-preview.3 available node/package oyzu/node (build) — 0.1.0-preview.3 available python/app oyzu/python (build) 0.1.1 0.1.1 available python/library oyzu/python (build) 0.1.1 0.1.1 available python/package oyzu/python (build) 0.1.1 0.1.1 available rust/app oyzu/rust (build) — 0.1.0-preview.4 available rust/library oyzu/rust (build) — 0.1.0-preview.4 available zig/project oyzu/zig (build) — 0.1.0-preview.3 available ​ … Output shortened. A reference that says "unavailable: preview only" has no eligible stable release and needs preview opt-in. Search covers the official catalog and your organization's catalog. It does not crawl OCI registries, so a plugin you reference explicitly can work without being listed. Eligibility is judged for this machine only.

versions lists a reference's known releases and why each can or cannot be selected on this machine. info shows one release in detail. The selector can be a major version (@v0) or an exact version (@0.1.0). $ oyzu plugins versions go/app --offlineCopy 3 known releases of go/app · oyzu/go (official default) ​ Locked here oyzu/go 0.1.0 (release sha256:a2b9a529…c989) ​ Version Labels Selectable here Release 0.1.0 latest-stable, latest-compatible, yes sha256:a2b9a529…c989 update-candidate, locked 0.1.0-preview.2 (preview) yes sha256:177c30e7…6d45 0.1.0-preview.1 (preview) yes sha256:25f830bd…f9bf ​ latest-stable is the newest stable release known, even if it cannot run here. latest-compatible is the newest that fits this engine, contracts and platform. update-candidate stays inside the adopted major; adoption-candidate is what oyzu build would adopt. ​ … Output shortened. latest-stable is the newest stable release even if it cannot run here. latest-compatible is the newest that fits your Oyzu version and platform. update-candidate is what plugins update would move to inside the adopted major version. adoption-candidate is what the next oyzu build would adopt. $ oyzu plugins info go/app --offlineCopy go/app 0.1.0 · oyzu/go (build) ​ Build, test and package Go modules and workspaces with the native go toolchain. ​ Release Publisher oyzu (maintainer Oyzu maintainers) Source official default · official catalog serial 49 Status selectable here Labels latest-stable, latest-compatible, update-candidate, locked Release sha256:a2b9a529697f8345158c13719cd8a2ab93371ec48c3c2fac305c45eb0b35c989 Contracts v1alpha1 Profiles app (builder), library (builder) Support supported ​ Platforms Platform Size Payload linux/amd64-musl 9.6 MiB sha256:161cac62…25f2 linux/arm64-musl 9.4 MiB sha256:843e0d2b…42b3 ​ Acquisition routes oci ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go@sha256:a2b9a529697f8345158c13719cd8a2ab93371ec48c3c2fac305c45eb0b35c989 ​ Verification Metadata verified signed catalog Snapshot serial 49 · content sha256:a00cc5a4…7995 The catalog metadata is verified. Package bytes are verified when installed; this view downloads none. ​ Locked here oyzu/go 0.1.0 (release sha256:a2b9a529…c989) ​ … Output shortened.

Lists the plugin releases installed in the plugin store: package, version, the references it serves, platforms, whether this project locks it, and its release digest. It lists the store only. The store keeps no record of which projects use a release.

oyzu plugins current [OPTIONS] oyzu plugins explain [OPTIONS] [TARGET] Argument Meaning [TARGET] A target, by name or path. Omit it for every plugin-backed target current shows each locked selection with its install state and whether it can run here. explain prints the same Builders record oyzu build prints: which release, why it was chosen and how to change it. $ oyzu plugins explain --offlineCopy -- Builders ----------------------------------------- official catalog serial 49 reused go/app project oyzu/go 0.1.0 (locked) · reused from oyzu.lock selected by go.mod module (rule go-module, official catalog serial 49) source official default · from the official catalog serial 49 package reused from the store · sha256:a2b9a529…c989 lock replayed from oyzu.lock tool deferred: the plugin reports its native tool requirements when it runs; oyzu build lists them not what you wanted? not a go/app target? Declare the targets you want in build.yaml; undeclared directories add none build.yaml: {builds: {project: {uses: <builder>, path: .}}} another implementation of go/app? Bind its package for this reference (or use your organization's catalog) and select again oyzu config set --global --json-value 'plugins.packages."go/app"' '{"archive":"<path>","sha256":"<digest>"}'; then oyzu plugins update go/app another version of a tool the build uses? Pin it in oyzu.toml oyzu pin <tool>@<version> ​ Nothing was installed, launched or written.

oyzu plugins update [OPTIONS] [REFERENCE[@SELECTOR]]... Argument / option Description [REFERENCE[@SELECTOR]]... References to update, each optionally with @v<major>, @<version> or @sha256:<digest>. Omit it to update every locked selection --dry-run Check everything and show the lock change without writing oyzu.lock --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store --offline Never use the network. Update from the cached catalog only oyzu plugins update # every locked selection, within its major version oyzu plugins update go/app@v2 # adopt major version 2 explicitly oyzu plugins update go/app@1.4.2 # select exactly 1.4.2 oyzu plugins update go/app@sha256:… # restore one exact release (the undo line a build prints) oyzu plugins update --dry-run A routine update moves to the newest eligible release inside the adopted major version. It never goes to an older release or to a preview. Each new release is installed and verified first, and oyzu.lock is rewritten only if every requested selection passes, in one step. A withdrawn or revoked release, or an unusable catalog, fails without changing the lock. With no plugin locked: $ oyzu plugins update --dry-run --offlineCopy oyzu.lock selects no plugin; nothing to update ​ Lock …\hello\oyzu.lock (unchanged) ​ Nothing was launched and no file changed.

oyzu plugins prune [--store DIR] [--apply] SHA256... When a release is revoked, Oyzu refuses to run it but leaves its files in the store. prune removes them. Copy exact sha256: release digests from plugins list or plugins info. Without --apply it only shows what it would do. --apply rechecks the cached catalog and the installation, then removes each selected revoked copy that no running Oyzu is using. It never refreshes the catalog or downloads anything. Run oyzu plugins list --refresh first if you need current revocations. An expired catalog, an ordinary withdrawal or an unavailable source cannot authorize deletion. Copies in use, and installations Oyzu cannot inspect, are kept. Project locks are not changed. A copy with no active user may still be locked by some project, so update that project with oyzu plugins update. Each release gets a state (eligible, retained, removed, absent or incomplete) with a reason. Preview exits 0. --apply exits 1 if anything was retained or removal was incomplete. If a filesystem error interrupts a removal, a partial copy can remain; check the reason and the leftover files before retrying. There is no option to remove everything or to force removal. $ oyzu plugins prune sha256:e6338a15… --store ~/storeCopy Plugin cleanup preview Release State Reason sha256:e6338a15a12b6442cf52… eligible Revoked release has no active cooperative use lease and is eligible for explicit removal. Store ~/store Catalog acme catalog serial 2 No installation was removed. Repeat the exact selected digests with --apply to recheck eligibility and remove revoked copies without active use leases. Output shortened.

You can bind a compiled plugin you built yourself to a profile that has no packaged plugin. Put the binding in user or machine configuration, never in the project, and select the same short id in build.yaml. The names and path here are examples. The executable must implement the builder operations for your project. User or machine configuration [plugins.development] "independent/app" = "/absolute/path/to/independent-plugin" build.yaml builds: app: uses: independent/app oyzu build app The build runs on the host and collects the artifacts the plugin declares. A bare executable can return no tool requirements or observations. If it needs tools, pack it with a manifest and bind that archive instead. Declare every potential tool, including conditional package managers and stage tools, by its fully qualified identity. Oyzu checks the selected requirements against that declaration and your normal configuration, lock, tool policy and offline rules. Each requested observation must also pass the target's tools.allowed policy before executable lookup or launch, including tools absent from the task's selected requirements. A local binding does not add zero-config detection, with options, dependency preparation or isolated execution. A target can also name an OCI package directly, for example uses: oci://registry.example/team/builder@sha256:<digest>#app. The package's manifest supplies its identity. Tags outside the official namespace need a user-level signer binding for the full URI. See direct OCI references and local plugin bindings.

An organization can publish its own signed tool index with a plugin catalog. Configure it in user or machine configuration, following the tool index reference. A company catalog replaces the official catalog. If it has no matching entry, or its selected release's route fails, Oyzu refuses the reference; it does not fall back to the official catalog. A typical workflow: oyzu plugins search --refresh oyzu tools check --catalog --json oyzu build --full # Keep the approved oyzu.lock and the installed tools and plugins for this user. oyzu build --offline --frozen --full --no-cache The online build installs the selected release. The frozen offline build replays exactly the locked installation and also needs the tool metadata prepared by the online build. If you use --store DIR, prepare that store too. Native Go builds also read the default user metadata store. Error Meaning Fix PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE A locked plugin is missing from the store and offline or frozen mode forbids downloading it Run an online, non-frozen build, or restore the store PLUGIN_LOCK_MISSING (exit 4) --frozen needs a plugin selection that oyzu.lock lacks Restore the complete approved lock PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE A new catalog selection has no usable download route, or the build is offline Run online, or bind the archive with plugins.packages PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN, PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED The catalog withdrew or revoked the release Run oyzu plugins update to adopt an eligible release PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE No plugin serves the reference Opt in to previews, or bind a package The 3600-second recent-catalog window does not extend a signed catalog's expiry. A locked, installed plugin can still replay against an expired catalog, with a warning that newer withdrawals may be missing. Retained withdrawals and revocations still block execution, and an expired catalog cannot authorize plugins prune. See catalog selection and lock selections for the full rules.

If your organization catalog serves plugins from an HTTPS mirror behind an inspecting proxy, use the standard environment variables for the proxy and your extra CA bundle: HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:8080 SSL_CERT_FILE=/absolute/company-ca.pem oyzu build --full The bundle adds trust for the proxy's certificate. It does not replace the official plugin signer or admit a new route, and it never selects a different release. Loopback addresses always bypass proxies. If a download fails, restore access to the mirror and check that the bundle contains your inspection CA. This works for HTTPS mirrors on Linux and Windows. macOS and OCI registry routes behind an inspecting proxy are not supported yet. See HTTPS package routes and proxy and trust settings.

Status When 0 Success, including "nothing to update" 1 An unknown target for explain (PLUGIN_TARGET_UNKNOWN), a refused or unusable catalog, or an update that failed verification 2 Invalid arguments 4 oyzu build --frozen found no plugin selection in oyzu.lock (PLUGIN_LOCK_MISSING)
Inspecting plugins, updating plugins and the plugin catalog. Go builder preview.

Publish a finished build's file artifacts. Without an account, oyzu publish reads named destinations from oyzu.toml, checks the build's existing signed provenance, signs exactly what it is about to publish, uploads the unchanged bytes to an OCI registry, and downloads them again to confirm. With --server, --account and --project, it instead registers the build with an Oyzu platform and requests governed publication. oyzu publish [OPTIONS] Note: Experimental. OCI registries are the supported destination. PyPI and mutable OCI tags are not implemented. Governed publication through a platform is not generally available yet.

Standalone publication: Option Description --destination <NAME> Named destination or publication set; repeat for several --manifest <FILE> The build manifest to publish. Repeat it to publish several bundles (one per platform) as one publication, checked for completeness together. Default dist/manifest.json --allow-incomplete <PLATFORM=REASON> Publish even though a declared platform has no artifact (repeatable), for example darwin/x86_64=no-intel-runner. Recorded in the signed publication evidence Governed publication through a platform: Option Description --server <URL> The platform's URL (or OYZU_URL); https unless it is localhost --account <ACCOUNT> The account to publish to (or OYZU_ACCOUNT) --project <PROJECT> The project to publish to (or OYZU_PROJECT) --provenance <FILE> Existing signed provenance bundle --policy-evidence <FILE> Original signed policy report bundle for central admission --version <VERSION> The build's version, when the pipeline names one --commit <SHA> The built commit; defaults to the CI system's --repository <OWNER/NAME> The repository as owner/name; defaults to the CI system's --audience <AUDIENCE> The audience to request OIDC tokens for (or OYZU_AUDIENCE; default oyzu) --token-env <NAME> Read the OIDC token from this environment variable instead of discovering one --no-upload Report artifacts without uploading them to the platform's registry (or OYZU_PUBLISH_UPLOAD=0) --destination and --allow-incomplete can't be combined with --server, --account, --project or --no-upload. The global options also apply.

Destinations go in the project root's oyzu.toml. A [publish] table in any other folder's file is a CONFIG_SCOPE error. An example OCI destination, with credentials read from environment variables and never written in the file: [publish] default = "sandbox" [publish.destinations.sandbox] kind = "oci" artifacts = ["app/archive"] # optional when the bundle has exactly one artifact registry = "https://registry.example.com" repository = "team/artifacts" usernameEnv = "REGISTRY_USERNAME" passwordEnv = "REGISTRY_PASSWORD" [publish.requirements.provenance] bundlePath = "evidence/build.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<base64 raw 32-byte Ed25519 public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/release" [publish.requirements.signing] keyEnv = "PUBLICATION_SIGNING_SEED" publicKey = "<base64 raw 32-byte Ed25519 publication public key>" For Rust, a plain development build may keep the declared Cargo version inside its binary. Rebuild with --full or --optimized before publishing to apply the inferred version; publication refuses unstamped development results.

oyzu build --full oyzu publish # the default destination oyzu publish --destination sandbox oyzu publish --manifest linux/dist/manifest.json --manifest windows/dist/manifest.json \ --allow-incomplete darwin/x86_64=no-intel-runner Every selected destination is required. Oyzu checks everything (selection, evidence, signatures) before the first upload. If a later destination fails, earlier ones stay published and the result names the unfinished ones. Running the same command again skips destinations that already have the exact bytes. Governed publication from CI: oyzu publish --server https://oyzu.example.com --account acme --project web --provenance evidence/build.sigstore.json

Each destination is reported as published, already-present, failed or unfinished, with the manifest, artifact and evidence digests that were checked. Outputs not selected for a destination are listed as unselected. --json returns the publication record with the same per-destination states. Publishing always needs the network.

Status When 0 Every selected destination published (or already had the exact bytes) 1 Refused before publishing: missing configuration or evidence, a wrong subject, a conflicting existing object, or a build that didn't succeed 2 A destination failed or is unfinished, or invalid arguments 3 Invalid configuration, such as an unknown destination kind or an artifact selector that names no build (CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN, CONFIG_SCOPE)

Code Fix PUBLISH_NOT_CONFIGURED Add [publish.destinations.NAME] (and optionally publish.default) to the root oyzu.toml, or pass --destination. PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED The manifest records a failed or interrupted build. Fix it and build again. PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID The bundle has several artifacts and the destination doesn't pick one, or a selector names an unknown output. Set artifacts = ["target/output"].

Publishing finalized artifacts: configuration, evidence, signing, incomplete platform sets and governed publication. Version inference for how Oyzu infers versions. oyzu release check to ask whether a build would ship before publishing.

Two platform commands. oyzu release check asks an Oyzu platform whether the build in dist/ would ship, environment by environment, before anything is published. oyzu secrets manages the account's secrets, whose values you can write but never read back. Both need a platform account: platform.url and platform.account in user configuration, and a credential from oyzu auth login (at a terminal) or the OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN environment variable. Note: Both commands are experimental, and release check isn't available on deployed platforms yet.

oyzu release check [OPTIONS] Option Description --project <PROJECT> The project to check in (or OYZU_PROJECT) --environment <ENVIRONMENT> Answer for this environment only; repeat for more. Default: every environment --manifest <FILE> The build manifest to check. Default dist/manifest.json --version <VERSION> Use this version for every component, instead of each artifact's own --commit <SHA> The built commit; defaults to the checkout's HEAD The global options also apply. Run it after oyzu build. It sends the manifest's artifacts to the platform, which works out the plan a release of them would get now and answers for each environment: would ship, would wait (naming each approval, gate or blocker), or refused (naming the policy). Nothing is published, saved or started. oyzu build oyzu release check --project web oyzu release check --project web --environment production oyzu release check --project web --json The answer has one line per environment (✓ qa would ship, … production would wait, ✗ eu would refuse it), each reason with its policy underneath, and, when a start policy covers the build, whether publishing would join an open batch or start a release. --json prints the platform's ship-check record with account added. Status When 0 No environment would refuse the build (waiting on a person or gate isn't a failure) 1 An environment would refuse it, or the check couldn't be made Code Fix RELEASE_CHECK_NOT_CONFIGURED Pass --project (or set OYZU_PROJECT) and set platform.url and platform.account. RELEASE_CHECK_UNAUTHENTICATED Run oyzu auth login from a terminal, or set OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. RELEASE_CHECK_NO_COMMIT This isn't a Git checkout with a commit. Pass --commit. RELEASE_CHECK_NOTHING_TO_SHIP The manifest lists no artifacts. PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED The manifest records a build that didn't succeed.

oyzu secrets [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Subcommand What it does list List a scope's secrets: names, exposure and value versions, never values create <NAME> Create a secret without a value; set one with oyzu secrets set set <NAME> Set or replace a value from standard input, a file, or a generated value shown once rm <NAME> Delete a secret and all its values, or end its overlap with --previous No command ever shows a stored value, and a value is never taken from the command line, where it would end up in your shell history.

Every subcommand takes a scope; without one it acts on the account: Option Description --org <ORG> An organization of the account, by identifier --project <PROJECT> A project of the account, by identifier create: Argument / option Description <NAME> Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens --exposure <EXPOSURE> Required. What may ever receive the value: a platform service (internal) or a job's runner (build) --type <TYPE> text (UTF-8, the default) or file (exact bytes) --description <DESCRIPTION> A short note shown in listings set: Argument / option Description <NAME> The secret's name (or ID) --file <PATH> Read the value's exact bytes from this file instead of standard input --generate Generate 32 random bytes (as 64 hex characters), set them and print them once --overlap <DURATION> Keep the replaced value valid this long, such as 24h (at most 168h) rm: Argument / option Description <NAME> The secret's name (or ID) --previous Retire only the previous value now, keeping the secret

oyzu secrets list # the account's secrets (never their values) oyzu secrets create release-webhook --exposure internal oyzu secrets set release-webhook --generate # make a webhook secret and show it once oyzu secrets set npm-token --project web < token.txt # set a value from standard input oyzu secrets set deploy-key --file key.pem --overlap 24h oyzu secrets rm release-webhook --previous # end an overlap now --overlap keeps the old value valid while consumers move to the new one; rm --previous ends the overlap early. A create, set or delete is sent once and never retried automatically. If one fails in transit, run oyzu secrets list to see what happened before you retry.

Exits 0 on success and non-zero on any failure; the error code names the cause. Code Fix SECRETS_NOT_CONFIGURED Set platform.url and platform.account. SECRETS_UNAUTHENTICATED Run oyzu auth login, or set a current OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. SECRETS_PERMISSION_DENIED You aren't allowed to manage secrets in that scope. SECRETS_NOT_FOUND No secret with that name in the scope. Create it first with oyzu secrets create. SECRETS_RESOURCE_CONFLICT The name is taken, there's no previous value to retire, or the platform manages the secret. SECRETS_VALUE_REQUIRED, SECRETS_VALUE_EMPTY, SECRETS_VALUE_TOO_LARGE Give a non-empty value on standard input, with --file or with --generate. SECRETS_OVERLAP_INVALID Use a duration such as 24h or 90m, at most 168h.
Checking whether a build would ship. Platform secrets. Platform sign-in.

List the development tasks in your project, or run one. Tasks come from your native files (such as Cargo.toml, go.mod or the scripts in package.json) and from oyzu.toml. A task runs with the project's locked tools, so oyzu run test behaves the same on every machine. oyzu run [OPTIONS] [TASK] [-- <ARGS>...] Argument Meaning [TASK] Task to run, such as test or cli:build. Omit it, or use list, to list tasks [ARGS]... Arguments passed to the task's own command, written after --

Option Description --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store --remote Run the task on a platform pool against the pushed HEAD and follow it here --worktree With --remote: run the working tree as it is on disk, including unpushed commits and local changes, instead of the pushed HEAD. Needs a standalone pool --isolated Run only this task, its prerequisites and hooks in the isolated executor, from a captured copy of the source --download <DIR> With --remote: download the run's outputs into this directory The global options also apply. --toolset NAME runs the task with a toolset's tools instead of [tools]. --remote is experimental and needs a platform account or access to a standalone pool (remote runs). Everything else on this page works without one.

$ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 6 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · go/app (6) project:build Inferred · go go build ./... project:format Inferred · go gofmt -w . project:format-check Inferred · go gofmt -l . project:install Inferred · go go mod download project:lint Inferred · go go vet ./... project:test Inferred · go go test ./... ​ Run one with: oyzu run <task> (extra arguments go after --) Commands show argv; task dependencies and hooks may also run. Use --json for full task records. Task IDs are target:task. When only one target has a task, the short name (test) is enough. With several, write api:test.

$ oyzu run testCopy · Setup Loading configuration and discovering tasks › project · Testing Running {"Time":"2026-10-20T23:04:08.2210781-04:00","Action":"start","Package":"example.com/oyzu/hello"} … · project · Testing TEST_EVIDENCE: Results 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped Coverage 50.0% of statements (1/2) ✓ project · Testing Succeeded (exit 0 after 3.17s) Output shortened. The native tool's output (here Go's test event stream) passes through unchanged between Oyzu's progress rows. Standard input stays connected, so interactive tasks work. A task that records a bundle also writes its full output to dist/logs.
Everything after -- goes to the task's command: oyzu run test -- -run TestGreeting -v
oyzu run test --remote This runs the task against the pushed HEAD on a pool and follows it in your terminal. Ctrl+C cancels the remote run.

oyzu --json run list returns one object keyed by task ID. Each task looks like this: $ oyzu --json run list { "project:test": { "argv": ["go", "test", "./..."], "availability": null, "build_stage": true, "cwd": "…\\hello", "depends_on": [], "env": {}, "mutates_source": false, "name": "test", "origin": { "kind": "inferred", "override": false, "source": null }, "provider": "go", "reports": [], "shell": false, "stdout_must_be_empty": false, "target": "project" } } oyzu --json run TASK captures the task's output to files and prints an outcome record, so standard output stays parseable: $ oyzu --json run test [ { "capture": { "encoding": "utf-8-lossy", "stderr": "file", "stdin": "inherited", "stdout": "file", "streaming": false, "tty": false }, "duration_ms": 1776, "evidence": { "acceptance": "accepted", "command": { "exitCode": 0, "status": "passed" }, "tests": { "failed": 0, "passed": 1, "skipped": 0 } }, "exit_code": 0, "invocationId": "56996-1792552225644301700-1", "status": "succeeded", "stderr": "", "task": "project:test" } ] Shortened: the full record also lists coverage and report paths under evidence, and stdout holds the captured output as one string. See JSON results.

oyzu run TASK exits with the task's own exit status, so oyzu run test && deploy works as you'd expect. Oyzu's own failures use the shared codes. With --remote, a non-zero exit on the pool is returned as is, a refused run exits 2 and an interrupt exits 130.

$ oyzu run nosuchCopy ✗ TASK_NOT_FOUND: no task "nosuch" in …\hello. Available tasks: build, format, format-check, install, lint, test. Run oyzu run to list tasks, or oyzu -C <project> run nosuch Next: Check the selected directory and name; use oyzu -C <project> to select a project. Code Fix TASK_NOT_FOUND (exit 5) Check the name with oyzu run list, or select the right project with -C. TASK_PROJECT_REQUIRED (exit 5) You're outside a project. There, oyzu run lists nearby projects by folder; cd into one or pass -C. TOOL_LOCK_STALE (exit 4) The lock doesn't cover a requirement. Run oyzu pin, then retry.
Build tasks: task sources, overrides, hooks, conditions and live output. Run native tasks guide. Remote runs.

Run the scanners your configuration or organization policy selects (Gitleaks, Trivy, Grype or SonarQube) against the exact source and artifacts a successful build recorded in dist/. scan doesn't rebuild, run tests or publish. It reads the build manifest's recorded source selection and scans that. oyzu scan [OPTIONS] Note: Experimental. Native Gitleaks scanning works on Windows; other scanners and project layouts have more limited support. See the scan reference.
Option Description --offline Use local inputs and tools only; download and analyze nothing online --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store The global options also apply.

scan works on an existing build's inputs, so run oyzu build first. With no scanner selected, it stops before doing anything: $ oyzu scan --offlineCopy ✗ SCAN_SELECTION_REQUIRED: no scanner selected; add [scan.gitleaks] with enabled = true to oyzu.toml Turn on Gitleaks for the project in oyzu.toml: [scan.gitleaks] enabled = true failOnFindings = true # optional: any finding fails the scan Oyzu installs Gitleaks through its tool store like any other tool (a [tools] entry for it wins when present), without editing oyzu.lock. Other scanners and SonarQube are selected by organization policy (scan.policy), which a project file can't set. Then run: oyzu scan Each run is recorded under .oyzu/scans/<run-id>/ (manifest.json, plan.json, events.jsonl and each scanner's report). The output shows a Preflight phase, a Scan phase and a final table with each scanner, subject, result and duration.

Status When 0 Every selected check ran and the result is accepted 1 A scanner failed to run, the result was rejected (for example, a finding with failOnFindings), no scanner is selected, or the recorded source doesn't match (SCAN_SOURCE_MISMATCH) 2 Invalid arguments 3 Invalid configuration or policy

Code Fix SCAN_SELECTION_REQUIRED Enable a scanner, such as [scan.gitleaks] enabled = true. SCAN_SOURCE_MISMATCH The source changed since the build. Build again, then scan. SCAN_SOURCE_SELECTION_INVALID Files that affect source selection changed after the build (for example, a new Cargo workspace member or a release file that was ignored). Fix the source or workspace membership, build again, then scan. TOOL_OFFLINE --offline and a scanner image isn't available locally. Run once online. SCAN_OFFLINE SonarQube is selected and --offline is set. SonarQube needs the network. Checks are never skipped to make an offline run pass.
Scan command: inputs, policy, results, Trivy, Gitleaks and Grype.

Shell integration puts the right tool versions on PATH as you cd between projects, like a version manager, so you don't have to wrap every command in oyzu exec. Command What it does oyzu activate SHELL Print shell activation code for this session oyzu deactivate [SHELL] Print code to restore this shell session oyzu shell install [SHELL] With no shell, set up every supported shell found and keep oyzu and the shims on your PATH; with one, add its activation block to its startup file oyzu shell remove [SHELL] Undo that, for every shell or the one named oyzu trust [PATH] Allow this project's environment and PATH settings without prompting Supported shells are bash, zsh and pwsh (PowerShell 7 or newer for automatic directory switching): PowerShell on Windows, and Bash and Zsh on Linux and macOS. Note: Shell activation is experimental.
documents.s: oyzu activate, deactivate, shell and trust

documents.t: oyzu activate [OPTIONS] <SHELL> Argument / option Description <SHELL> Shell to generate code for: bash, zsh or pwsh --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store --shims Put the shims folder on PATH instead of activating this shell The global options also apply. activate prints code; evaluate it to apply it: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" # Bash; use zsh for Zsh oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression The code adds a prompt and directory-change hook. Before each prompt, the hook applies the current project's locked tools and trusted [env] values, and undoes the previous project's changes when you leave it. Hooks never install tools, run tasks or use the network, so install tools first with oyzu install.

--shims puts the shims folder on PATH instead. There's no prompt hook; each shim works out the project it runs in. Use it for login profiles, IDEs, CI and other non-interactive shells. With --json, activate returns {"shell": "bash", "script": "…"}. Evaluate the raw script, never the JSON.
documents.s: Shims for IDEs, CI and login shells

documents.t: oyzu deactivate [OPTIONS] [SHELL] Argument Meaning [SHELL] Shell to generate code for (defaults to the shell that ran activate) In an activated shell, oyzu deactivate restores the environment the session started with. Oyzu's PATH entries are removed, variables go back to their earlier values, and changes you made yourself are kept. The oyzu shell function that activation defines evaluates the output for you. Outside an activated session it fails with Oyzu shell session is not active.

oyzu shell install [OPTIONS] [SHELL] oyzu shell remove [OPTIONS] [SHELL] Argument / option Description [SHELL] bash, zsh or pwsh. Leave it out to set up every supported shell found, plus PATH --rc-file <PATH> Shell startup file; defaults to the selected shell's user profile. Needs a shell --shims (install only) Put the shims folder on PATH instead of activating the shell, for login profiles that non-interactive shells read. Needs a shell oyzu shell install # every shell found, plus PATH oyzu shell install bash # ~/.bashrc oyzu shell install zsh --rc-file ~/.zshrc oyzu shell install pwsh --rc-file $PROFILE oyzu shell install bash --shims --rc-file ~/.profile oyzu shell remove # undo the no-argument install oyzu shell remove bash With no shell, oyzu shell install is what the install scripts run. It adds the activation block to each supported shell it finds (bash, zsh, PowerShell 7) and puts the shims folder and the folder holding oyzu first on your persistent PATH, so IDEs, GUI programs and scripts find oyzu and your installed tools without activating a shell or running oyzu exec. On Windows that is your user Path in the registry (running programs keep their old Path; restart them). On Linux and macOS it is a PATH block in your login profile (~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login or ~/.profile, whichever exists first, and ~/.zprofile for zsh). Repeating it moves an unmodified login PATH block after later startup lines; oyzu shell remove removes it, but entries added by an oyzu installed in another location stay. fish and Windows PowerShell 5.1 are not set up. See tool shell environment. The default files are ~/.bashrc, $ZDOTDIR/.zshrc (or ~/.zshrc), and PowerShell 7's current-user console profile. Open a new terminal afterwards, or evaluate oyzu activate <shell> in the current one. remove only affects new shells; run oyzu deactivate to undo the current session.
documents.s: oyzu shell install and oyzu shell remove

documents.t: oyzu shell check reports commands that win over shims and how to fix them. It is read-only, uses no network and exits 1 when shadowed, 0 otherwise. --json returns shadowed; shell install also reports findings but still succeeds when setup succeeds. Windows checks both machine-plus-user new-process PATH and current PATH; Unix checks current PATH only. Windows machine Path precedes user Path. On a single-user machine, use elevated oyzu shell install --machine to put the per-user shims and Oyzu folders first on machine Path. Elevated oyzu shell remove --machine removes entries it added. On shared machines remove or reorder the system tool instead. There is no auto-elevation, and Unix hosts have no machine Path. Rerun shell install to move an unmodified login PATH block after later PATH-prepending startup lines; modified blocks are refused and preserved. Services, scheduled tasks, launchd jobs and systemd units need an absolute shim path (<shims folder>/node, or <shims folder>\\node.exe on Windows) or the shims first on the job's own PATH. Verify with oyzu shell check in that environment. Oyzu installs none. See PATH checks and limits.

oyzu trust [OPTIONS] [PATH] Argument / option Description [PATH] Project folder (defaults to the current project's root) --revoke Remove this folder's trust record --list List explicitly trusted project folders Environment variables can run code (PATH, loader and interpreter variables), so Oyzu applies a checkout's own [env] values and env._.path entries in shells, shims, oyzu exec and oyzu env --shell only after you trust the folder. Until then nothing prompts or blocks: tools still appear, those values are skipped, and a short hint mentions oyzu trust. oyzu run, oyzu build and build planning always use the project's environment settings, so they match CI. oyzu trust # trust this project's root oyzu trust --list oyzu trust --revoke Trust is recorded per folder, survives edits to oyzu.toml, never writes into the checkout and never contacts a service. In user configuration you can trust every project under chosen folders ([trust] parents = ["/home/you/src"]) or turn the check off ([trust] enabled = false). Project files can't. CI is trusted automatically.
Status When 0 Code printed, profile changed or trust record updated 1 deactivate outside an active session; a startup file that can't be written 2 An unsupported shell or other invalid arguments
Shell activation: activation, restoration, trust and running without a shell. Tool shell environment, including profile installation. oyzu exec, which and env for one-off use without activation.

Look up tool records without running any tool. Use it to answer "which Go does this project use?", "what's taking space in my tool store?", "which versions could I install?" and "would my organization's catalog allow this?". To change what a project uses, see pin, install, update and uninstall. oyzu tools [OPTIONS] <COMMAND> Subcommand What it does current Show the tools in effect here: requested and selected versions, source and status list List the installations in the tool store, and what references each prune Preview unreferenced store content; remove eligible entries only with --apply versions List the versions of a tool that could be installed, and why others are excluded info Show a tool's provider, source, verification and eligibility check Check the tools declared here against the signed tool index request Ask your organization's administrators to approve a tool version in its catalog requests List the approval requests made from here, with their current state migrate Move mise.toml tools and aqua: ids to Oyzu names in oyzu.toml (dry run by default) trust status, trust refresh Show or refresh the Sigstore trusted root the tool index is verified against inspect-lock Check that an oyzu.lock file is well formed (not that its tools are installed) inspect-backend Validate a tool-backend descriptor file (an advanced diagnostic) inspect-tree Look at an installed tool's file tree (an advanced diagnostic) resolve Evaluate community recipe data offline into per-platform artifact sets evidence Download an artifact set's files from their publishers and record and compare their digests Every subcommand accepts the global options, including --json. Inspection commands install nothing and don't re-hash installed tools: a tool is verified once, when it is installed. prune --apply removes store content, request and --cancel change catalog requests, migrate --write edits configuration, trust refresh updates cached trust data, and evidence downloads publisher files. Note: current, list, versions and info are stable. The tool index client (check, migrate, trust), the organization catalog (request, requests) and recipe resolution (resolve, evidence) are experimental. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

oyzu tools current [OPTIONS] Option Description -g, --global Show only your global declarations --all Include declarations that a more specific scope overrides --details Include full installation paths, identities and cross-compilation targets --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store $ oyzu tools currentCopy 1 tool ready ​ Tool Requested Selected Source Status go 1.22 1.22.12 project ok ​ Use --details for paths and identities, --all for overridden declarations. ​ Store: C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\Oyzu\tools Installed state comes from stored receipts; payloads are not re-hashed. Status Meaning ok Locked and installed not installed Locked but not in the store. Run oyzu install blocked Refused by tools.allowed; the row names the rule stale lock The lock doesn't match the request. Run oyzu pin ambiguous The lock can't be used because more than one entry could match the request; the details say why In a project with nothing declared, it says No tools are declared here and suggests oyzu install <tool>@<version>. With --json, each entry in tools has tool, request, version, scope, source, lock, status, platform, location and the installation identity.

oyzu tools list [OPTIONS] Option Description --details Include full installation paths and identities --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store $ oyzu tools listCopy 98 installations of 24 tools · 97 unreferenced · 35.2 GB on disk ​ go (core) · 2 installations · 503.6 MB Version Platform Size Used by ID 1.23.12 windows/amd64/msvc 243.9 MB unreferenced ec8ec2a4 1.24.13 windows/amd64/msvc 259.7 MB unreferenced dd5f9b80 … Used by is global, project or unreferenced. Other projects aren't indexed, so an installation shown as unreferenced here may still be used by another project. ID is the start of the installation digest; two installs of one version can differ by recipe or platform ABI.

oyzu tools prune [OPTIONS] Option Description --apply Remove the entries that can safely be reclaimed. Without it, nothing is removed --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store Lists the tool installations, downloaded archives and plugin installations that nothing references, with their size and the reason for each. It runs offline. Anything named by this project's lock, your global lock or a recorded developer selection stays, and other projects are never scanned, so review the preview before you apply it. See reclaiming unreferenced content.

oyzu tools versions [OPTIONS] <TOOL> Argument Meaning <TOOL> The tool, as [provider:]name Option Description --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store --offline Read only the last verified tool index and organization catalog; never fetch Versions are listed newest first, from the publisher's catalog or from the tool index when it lists the package. The tool index also works offline from its cached copy. A publisher catalog needs the network, so --offline fails for those tools with TOOL_OFFLINE. Rust and the Cargo helpers have no version catalog (TOOL_VERSIONS_UNSUPPORTED).

oyzu tools info [OPTIONS] <TOOL> Argument Meaning <TOOL> The tool, as [provider:]name, or oyzu:name@version with --artifact-set Option Description --artifact-set <FILE> Resolved artifact set to evaluate for a registry tool; repeatable --artifact-set-digest <sha256:DIGEST> Pin a set record by its digests.full; repeatable (provisional flag) --connector-bindings <CONNECTOR_BINDINGS> Host-owned connector endpoints and authorization environment references --details Include every check, route and note of a set evaluation --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store $ oyzu tools info goCopy oyzu:go · eligible ​ Provider Property Value Provider oyzu Source go-releases Accepted names core:go, go, oyzu:go Commands go, gofmt Platforms darwin/arm64/native, linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, windows/amd64/msvc Verification SHA-256 from the publisher's checksum manifest, locked and verified at install (no publisher signature) ​ Declared Scope Requested Source project 1.22 …\hello\oyzu.toml ​ Here Selected 1.22.12 · ok An unknown name fails with TOOL_ALIAS_UNSUPPORTED and lists every supported tool and the registry name forms (oyzu:<name>, oyzu:<owner>/<repo>, github:<owner>/<repo>).

oyzu tools check [OPTIONS] --catalog Option Description --catalog Check against the tool index and any organization catalog (the only check today; required) --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store --offline Read only the last verified tool index and organization catalog; never fetch $ oyzu tools check --catalog --offlineCopy ✓ All 1 declared tools can be installed ​ Tool Request Source Reason oyzu:go 1.22 direct resolved by Oyzu's built-in provider for this tool ​ Checked against the tool index at https://github.com/oyzuai/tool-index/releases/latest/download/ (version 23, expires 2026-11-03T10:25:02Z). using the last verified copy because a newer index could not be used: offline For each declared tool it reports whether it installs from the tool index, would be evaluated locally from its registry recipe (standalone only), or is refused. With toolCatalog.url set, each tool is judged as an install would judge it: approved by the organization catalog, refused with its reason, or not in the catalog. It installs and writes nothing, and exits 1 when any tool would be refused, so it fits in CI.

oyzu tools request [OPTIONS] [TOOL@VERSION] oyzu tools requests [OPTIONS] Argument / option Description [TOOL@VERSION] The tool and version, as <tool>@<version>; the version may be a prefix such as 1.7 --reason <REASON> Why you need it, shown to the administrators --status <ID> Show whether request ID has been decided, instead of asking for a tool --cancel <ID> Cancel your pending request ID, instead of asking for a tool oyzu tools request kubectl@1.31 --reason "cluster upgrade" oyzu tools request --status 7 oyzu tools requests These need an organization tool catalog: toolCatalog.url and OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN. Asking and cancelling go to the catalog's admin API (toolCatalog.adminUrl or OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL) as the person signed in with oyzu auth login, who needs the catalog.request permission. Asking again for the same tool and version returns the request that's already pending. The organization's auto-approve rules may approve a request at once. A pending request expires after 30 days unless the organization sets another limit. Only the person who asked can cancel it. requests lists the newest 50 requests made from this machine with the current organization token.

oyzu tools migrate [OPTIONS] Option Description --write Write oyzu.toml instead of only showing the result --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store --offline Read only the last verified tool index; never fetch Reads [tools] from mise.toml (or .mise.toml) and oyzu.toml. aqua: ids become their tool index names, core: prefixes are dropped and github: stays. asdf and vfox plugins and unsupported backends are listed and left out. mise.toml is never changed. With nothing to move, it fails with TOOL_MIGRATE_NOTHING.

oyzu tools trust status [OPTIONS] oyzu tools trust refresh [OPTIONS] Option Description --from <DIR|URL> (refresh) A TUF repository mirror: a directory, or an HTTPS URL. Default: Sigstore's public repository --store <DIR> Use this tool store instead of the shared user store status shows the trusted root built into oyzu, its digest and version, and which root is in use. refresh runs the standard TUF checks starting from the root built into oyzu and keeps the verified trusted_root.json in the tool store, where it replaces the built-in root while it is newer. To refresh an offline machine, carry a copy of the repository and run oyzu tools trust refresh --from /media/sigstore.

oyzu tools inspect-lock [OPTIONS] [LOCK_FILE] oyzu tools inspect-backend [OPTIONS] <DESCRIPTOR_FILE> oyzu tools inspect-tree [OPTIONS] <DIRECTORY> Argument Meaning [LOCK_FILE] Lock file to check; defaults to oyzu.lock in the current directory <DESCRIPTOR_FILE> Path to the backend descriptor file <DIRECTORY> Directory to look at, usually an installation's payload inspect-lock checks structure and identities only, not that the tools are installed. inspect-tree expects a directory (find installation paths with oyzu tools list --details). inspect-backend expects a descriptor file, not a tool name. They exit 0 on success and 2 for malformed, oversized or unreadable input.

These build and check the data behind the tool index. oyzu tools resolve [OPTIONS] --registry <FILE> oyzu tools evidence [OPTIONS] resolve options: Option Description --registry <FILE> Registry snapshot: the merged registry.yaml file --registry-digest <DIGEST> Reject the snapshot unless its SHA-256 equals this value (sha256:HEX) --snapshot-tag <TAG> Record the snapshot's release tag (a label you assert) --snapshot-commit <SHA> Record the snapshot's commit (a label you assert) --tool <NAME> Registry package name such as hashicorp/terraform (repeatable) --tools-file <FILE> File with one package name per line --version <VERSION> Exact upstream version as the recipe sees it, such as v1.16.5 (repeatable) --platform <OS/ARCH/ABI> Platform (repeatable); defaults to the three default platforms --limit <NAME=VALUE> Lower a counted limit (repeatable); limits can't be raised evidence options: Option Description --set <FILE> The tools resolve document to verify; - reads standard input --provider <PROVIDER> Build and verify provider records: java, node, go, python, maven, gradle, helm, kubectl, k3d, liquibase, tailscale, npm, pnpm or rust --version <VERSION> Exact provider release to record, such as 21.0.8 (repeatable; with --provider) --platform <PLATFORM> Platform to record (repeatable; with --provider). Default: every platform the provider installs --allow-host <HOST> Allow a host besides those named by the set's own URLs (repeatable) --verify <METHOD> Run only these verification methods (repeatable); others are reported as not run oyzu --json tools resolve --registry ./registry.yaml --tool hashicorp/terraform --version v1.16.5 > set.json oyzu --json tools evidence --set set.json resolve reads only the registry file you name and never downloads one. evidence downloads each artifact and its checksum file and verifies attestations where they exist. Both exit 0 when complete, 2 on an input problem, and 3 when the document is complete but some item couldn't be decided or verified.

Status When 0 Success 1 check --catalog found a refused tool; a network or catalog failure; nothing to migrate 2 Invalid arguments or an unknown tool name; malformed input to inspect-*, resolve or evidence 3 resolve or evidence: complete, but some item undecided or unverified
Tool commands, tool index, tool catalog. Recipe resolution and evidence, artifact sets. Lock inspection, store inspection.

Oyzu is one command, oyzu, that looks at a repository, works out what it can build, installs the exact tools it needs, runs the native commands your ecosystem already uses, and leaves a record you can check later. You don't write a pipeline. You keep your go.mod, Cargo.toml, package.json or pyproject.toml, and Oyzu works from them. This page is a map. Each step links to the page that explains it.

your repository what Oyzu decides what you get ─────────────── ───────────────── ──────────── native files (go.mod, Cargo.toml …) ─┐ build.yaml (optional) ─┼─► targets and builders ─┐ │ (discovery) │ oyzu.toml cascade, oyzu.local.toml ─┼─► settings per folder ──┼─► plan: stages and ─► actions ─► dist/ bundle user configuration, policy ─┘ (configuration) │ actions per target │ manifest, plan, │ │ artifacts, reports oyzu.lock ───► exact tool versions ──┘ │ (tools) ▼ action cache ◄──── reuse or run on the host, in a container, or remotely Discovery reads your native files and finds targets, one buildable unit each, such as a Go module or a Cargo package. A builder (go/app, rust/app, node/app …) knows how to build each one. An optional build.yaml makes the list explicit. See How Oyzu sees a project. Configuration decides how strictly and where to build: which checks run, how many jobs, which executor. It comes from oyzu.toml files, your personal overrides and any organization policy. See Configuration layers. Tools are resolved to exact versions, recorded in oyzu.lock, installed and verified once. See Tools and toolchains and The lock file. Planning turns targets into stages (format-check, lint, test, build, package) and actions, the units of real work, ordered by the dependencies between targets. See The build graph and Tasks and builds. Execution runs each action on your machine, in an isolated container, or on a remote pool. See Execution modes and Platforms and matrices. The action cache skips actions whose inputs haven't changed, and says so. --affected narrows a build to what changed since a Git commit. See The action cache and affected builds. The bundle in dist/ records what happened: the manifest, the plan, artifacts with digests, test and coverage reports, and logs. Earlier bundles move to history. See Artifacts, bundles and evidence.

Each concept has a command that shows it. None of these change your project. Concept See it with What it shows Targets and builders oyzu discover Each target, its builder, and whether detection or build.yaml chose it Tasks oyzu run list Every task and the native command it runs The plan oyzu build --plan Stages per target, tool requirements, and what is still unknown Configuration oyzu config explain <setting> The effective value and every file that set it, in order Tools oyzu tools current Requested and selected versions and where each came from The lock oyzu pin --dry-run What would be locked, for which platforms, without writing The cache oyzu cache explain <target> Why a target's cache key last changed Results oyzu inspect dist, oyzu history Whether recorded files match their digests; past builds Every command also accepts --json. See CLI output.

Most projects start with neither. When you need them, each has one job: File Says Organized by Example build.yaml What the project produces and how builds connect Build name; the same for everyone builds: {api: {uses: go/app, path: api}} oyzu.toml How, where and how strictly: tools, checks, tasks, environment Folder; can vary by context and person [tools] go = "1.27" You can request an exact version in a native pin or [tools]. Oyzu records the resolved version and download identity in oyzu.lock. See which file a setting belongs in.
documents.s: The two files you might write

documents.t: Native files first. If a native file already says something (a Go minimum in go.mod, a Rust channel in rust-toolchain.toml), Oyzu reads it there instead of asking you to repeat it. A plan does nothing. oyzu build --plan installs, downloads and runs nothing. Only a real build produces results, and it records what ran, what was reused and what failed. Plain labels. A reused test result says "reused from an earlier run, not run now". An action that never ran because something before it failed is "blocked", not "failed". oyzu inspect says it checks file integrity, not who built the files. No account needed. Everything here works on its own. Platform features such as oyzu build --remote are optional and say so. Policy overrides are shown. When an organization rule changes a value, Oyzu shows the override and where it came from. Oyzu hasn't had a stable release yet. Where something is experimental or limited to some platforms, the page says so. See Current capabilities.

New to Oyzu: follow the tutorial, then come back here. Adopting Oyzu in an existing repository: read How Oyzu sees a project and Configuration layers. Setting up CI: read Execution modes, Platforms and matrices and the CI guide.

When you run oyzu build, Oyzu doesn't run one big script. It turns each selected target into stages, turns stages into actions, and connects them in a graph, so independent work runs in parallel and dependent work waits. The graph explains why something ran, why it waited, and why it was skipped.

Level What it is Example Target One buildable unit, found by discovery or declared in build.yaml api Stage A step every builder understands: format-check, lint, test, build, package api:test Action One unit of work with a fixed command, environment, inputs and outputs go test -json -coverprofile=… ./... A builder supplies the stages for its ecosystem and the native commands behind them. One stage can have several actions (a Node package, for example, has separate version, build and package actions). The plan records every action as it will run, and the bundle records how each one ended.

Inside a target, the builder's stage order applies. A test stage runs after the build it tests, and hooks such as pre_test or post_build attach to the stage they name. See Tasks and builds. Between targets, links come from what you declare: Declared in Effect depends_on: [api] in build.yaml Ordering only: api finishes before this target starts. No files move materialize in build.yaml An artifact api produces is placed into this target's inputs; the ordering follows depends_on = ["schema:verify"] on a task in oyzu.toml That task runs first, in its own target's folder Oyzu relies on the declared graph. If one target's build script quietly reads another target's folder without a declared link, the cache and --affected can't know. Declare the relationship. See what the cache relies on.

oyzu build with no arguments builds every target. Name targets to build fewer. Oyzu adds everything those targets need, and each added target gets its full set of stages: $ oyzu build worker --planCopy … api · go/app · windows/x86_64 Executor: host Stage Selection Details build selected Native commands and report bindings resolve during preparation … ​ worker · go/app · windows/x86_64 Executor: host After targets: api Stage Selection Details build selected Native commands and report bindings resolve during preparation … Targets outside the selection get no tools, no dependency downloads and no actions. Target names must match exactly; an unknown name fails before anything starts. oyzu build --affected <git-ref> selects targets another way: the ones whose files changed since that commit, plus the targets that depend on them. See affected builds.

oyzu build --plan shows the graph without doing anything. It installs no tools, downloads no dependencies, runs no project code and leaves dist/ alone. Some details, such as exact commands, artifact names and report locations, are only known once the build prepares, and the preview lists them under Unresolved until preparation. A real build shows the graph as a table before it starts: $ oyzu build --fullCopy … ── Plan ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 2 targets format lint test build api/ project-api run run run run worker/ project-worker run run run run … Each cell is run, skip (with a note giving the reason, such as fast local build) or - when the stage doesn't apply. Which stages run depends on the build's check settings and context; see Configuration layers.

An action starts as soon as everything it depends on has finished, up to the job limit (build.jobs, or oyzu build -j N). Two targets with no link between them build at the same time: $ oyzu build --fullCopy … 00:10 .. project-api build started 00:10 .. project-worker build started 00:12 ✓ project-api build go build -trimpath -buildv… executed 1.7s 00:12 ✓ project-worker build go build -trimpath -buildv… executed 1.7s …

When an action fails, Oyzu keeps the outcomes apart: Failed: the action's own command ran and exited non-zero. Its log path and exit code appear in a failure section. Blocked: the action never ran because something it depends on failed. It isn't reported as a failure of its own. Independent work continues: a target that doesn't depend on the failure can still succeed. A cycle, whether through task prerequisites, hooks, stage order, target dependencies or materialized artifacts, fails before any action runs. Reordering the YAML doesn't fix a cycle; removing one of the links does.

The plan (dist/plan.json) and manifest (dist/manifest.json) record which targets were requested, which were selected, and which were left out and why. oyzu inspect dist rejects a bundle whose manifest disagrees with its plan. Targets left out are never reported as built. See Artifacts, bundles and evidence.
Selecting targets Read-only build preview Affected builds

Most builds change very little. Oyzu notices which targets' inputs haven't changed since an earlier successful build and restores their results instead of running them again. There's nothing to configure: you never write cache keys or per-language cache paths. Separately, --affected narrows a build to the targets a Git change touches. Both rely on the declared build graph. Note: The action cache is experimental. It works on Linux and Windows, and results are reused only on the same machine and user account unless you set up the remote cache.
documents.s: The action cache and affected builds

documents.t: Build a two-target project, edit a source file in worker/, and build again. Eligible unchanged stages in api/ can reuse their results; stages whose inputs changed in worker/ run again. Native Go tests still execute because their runtime reads and outputs are unbounded. See the current Go example. Reused tests, where admitted, are never counted as "tests run now", and the output names the run that originally produced them. Unchanged source cannot make an incomplete native stage eligible. oyzu build --explain gives its refusal reason; adding a known input or clearing the cache cannot establish complete arbitrary runtime reads. See native read coverage.

A target's key is a SHA-256 hash over its planned actions and inputs: Input Notes The target's actions Command, environment, working directory, platform, limits, required reports and the configuration digest Source it reads Complete admitted reads for eligible stages; declared inputs and relevant configuration and locks also count. Incomplete native reads refuse reuse, including whole-target restoration Tools Admitted locked-tool identities and the host platform or execution-image digest. Incomplete tool declarations retain the whole-lock fallback. Typed external locked-tool inputs, such as the Java formatter's JDK, also bind their current admitted identity Dependencies The content of the prepared dependencies, not where or when they were prepared Builder The Oyzu engine and the selected builder plugin release Consumed artifacts Digests of artifacts placed from other targets Executor Any executor other than your own machine Known checkout and temporary paths are normalized, so moving an unchanged checkout does not itself change action keys. Paths outside those roots can still matter. Tool, plugin, profile and platform identities must agree. Compiler-state reuse has stricter path requirements than action-result reuse. Native TEMP, TMP and TMPDIR values are replaced with private paths and do not enter action keys, even when configured or declared by a builder. Changing only those overwritten values preserves eligible reuse. Passed home/profile values remain keyed; configuration read as program data remains an input.

The cache errs on the side of running. A target runs, and the output says why, when: it contains a task you wrote that doesn't ask to be cached (cache = true with outputs), or a hook without declared outputs, because Oyzu can't see what they do; it uses secret environment values; a native stage lacks complete admitted reads or bounded outputs. It runs again even with unchanged source, and whole-target restoration cannot skip it; you pass --no-cache or set cache.local = false. Failed, blocked and cancelled targets are never stored as complete results. Eligible actions that completed successfully can still be reused after a later action fails. A complete target is stored only after all its actions succeeded and its reports were collected. oyzu run task runs are never cached.

A reused action keeps its original artifacts byte for byte (each checked against its recorded digest), its original reports, and a record naming the original run. Every report is checked again against the current rules: if you raised your coverage minimum and the old report no longer passes, the cached result is rejected and the target runs normally. Policy and required checks apply exactly as they would to fresh work.
documents.s: A reused result still passes every check

documents.t: The cache relies on the declared target graph. If a build script reads another target's folder without a declared link (depends_on, materialize or a task dependency), an edit there doesn't invalidate it. Declare the relationship, or use --no-cache, for builds that read across folders. On your machine, a tool that isn't in oyzu.lock, such as a system C compiler used by cgo, isn't part of the key either. Use --no-cache after changing one.

Two read-only views name the first part of the key that changed since the last build of the same thing: $ oyzu cache explain project-workerCopy Cache key explanation project-worker ​ project-worker (whole target) Key d2ffb95e8f68 · since run 43340-1792553125626099300 · last seen run 43340-1792553125626099300 (2026-10-21T03:25:25Z) Result stored · the next build with these inputs reuses it Changed since run 60260-1792553111917879400: source files in scope changed (also: action definition: project-worker:build argv, project-worker:build extensions and 3 more) oyzu build --explain prints the same reasoning for every stage after a build. See explaining reuse.

Builders can give each stage its own key. A stage with complete admitted reads can reuse its result after an edit to a file it does not read, provided the other key inputs still match. An incomplete native stage runs again and cannot be skipped by restoring a whole target. Arbitrary native npm scripts retain that refusal. Isolated Linux crun admits supported Node workspace members, Go application, Helm and .NET stages, and coupled Maven/Gradle lifecycles. Eligible .NET solutions can reuse per project; unsupported shapes retain solution-wide stages. Preparation and current report checks still apply on a hit. Compatible Java plugins reuse eligible Maven modules and Gradle projects independently and couple Ant's selected targets. Python complete-read reuse is not yet available. See stage reuse and the caching guide.

An action hit skips the command. On a miss, native compilers can still reuse their own incremental state while the command runs. --no-cache turns off action-result reuse; it keeps native compiler caches. Development and optimized results have different keys when the builder produces different output. Shared-cache writers normally request optimized builds, while ordinary local readers request development builds. Use --optimized to match an optimized result. Builders whose two profiles use the same commands share their results. See optimized builds.

The local cache belongs to your user account: %LocalAppData%\Oyzu\cache\actions on Windows and $XDG_CACHE_HOME/oyzu/actions on Linux, with a 10 GiB size budget. Set cache.dir in user configuration to move it. oyzu cache status shows its size; oyzu cache clear removes every cached result and never touches build bundles.

An experimental remote OCI cache shares results through an ordinary container registry. Set cache.remote (an oci:// URL) in user, machine or administrative configuration, or the OYZU_CACHE_REMOTE variable; a project file can't set it. Credentials come from OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or a CI job's ID tokens. cache.ciRemote names a repository that only CI writes and everyone reads first. Remote entries aren't signed. Digest checks protect content integrity; access control on the registry determines who can supply results. See remote OCI cache. REAPI action-cache servers are another option, using grpc:// on loopback or grpcs:// with TLS. Provider and platform limits still apply; see REAPI servers. Captured Rust can also consume compiler-state seeds from an OCI CI cache. Seeds do not replace actions or checks, require matching compiler-visible paths, and are never published by this client. See compiler-state seeds.

oyzu build --affected <git-ref> compares your working tree with a local Git commit, selects the targets whose files changed, adds the targets that depend on them, then adds what those need. Every selected target gets its normal checks. $ oyzu build --affected HEADCopy … ── Scope ───────────────────────────────────────── compared with HEAD at 2f721a7 changed 1 target project-api · 1 changed path unaffected 1 target not built · -v lists them ​ ── Plan ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 1 of 2 targets format lint test build why project-api skip skip skip run changed … --affected and the cache work together: --affected decides which targets to consider, and the cache can still reuse unchanged results among them. Oyzu falls back to building every target, and says why, when it can't be precise: the commit isn't available locally, a file is new, a changed file belongs to no target, or build, configuration or lock files changed. It never fetches the commit for you. Changes to tools or the environment outside Git aren't detected; run a full build after those. See affected builds.

Command Use it to oyzu build Reuse unchanged results automatically oyzu build --no-cache Run every action; read and write nothing oyzu build --explain See why each stage ran or was reused oyzu cache explain <target> See why a target's key last changed oyzu cache status / oyzu cache clear Inspect or empty the local cache oyzu build --affected <ref> Build only what changed since a commit See also the caching guide and the action cache reference.

Oyzu configuration is split by one question: does this setting change what ships, or only how it's built? What ships goes in build.yaml and is the same for everyone. How, where and how strictly go in the oyzu.toml cascade, which can vary by folder, build context and person, within limits an organization can set. Tool requests, including exact pins, belong in native files or [tools] in oyzu.toml; Oyzu records their resolutions in oyzu.lock. Many projects need no configuration at all. Add a file only when you have a reason. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

File Committed Holds Native files (go.mod, Cargo.toml, rust-toolchain.toml, package.json …) yes What your ecosystem already says: modules, dependencies, toolchain pins build.yaml yes Which builds exist, their builders, platforms and connections oyzu.toml yes Tools, checks, tasks, environment, executors and caching for its folder and below oyzu.local.toml no Your personal overrides for that folder User configuration (config.toml) no Your defaults for every project, and machine-only settings such as cache locations Machine and administrative files managed Organization defaults and limits oyzu.lock yes Exact tool versions and archive digests, written by Oyzu The user configuration file is %AppData%\Oyzu\config.toml on Windows and ~/.config/oyzu/config.toml (or under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME) on Linux. OYZU_USER_CONFIG points at another file. See files and persistent state.

Ask, in order: Does changing it change what ships (the artifact, its name, its platform or ABI, or how builds connect)? Put it in the native file if that file can say it, otherwise in build.yaml. Otherwise, could it differ by folder, context or person, or need an organizational limit? Put it in the cascade: oyzu.toml for the team, oyzu.local.toml or user configuration for you, and policy or [constraints] for limits. You want to Write it in Ship cli for Linux and Windows x86_64 build.yaml: platforms: [linux/x86_64, windows/x86_64] Make worker wait for api build.yaml: depends_on: [api] Use Go 1.27 oyzu.toml: [tools] go = "1.27" (or the native go.mod) Turn off format checks under legacy/ legacy/oyzu.toml: [checks] format = "off" Require tests in release builds oyzu.toml: [context.release.checks] tests = "required" Use two build jobs on your laptop oyzu.local.toml: [build] jobs = 2 Stop any folder lowering release tests root oyzu.toml: [constraints."checks.tests"] When one file names something another declares, such as a task key naming a build, Oyzu checks the name before anything runs and reports the file, line and nearest valid name.
documents.s: Which file a setting belongs in

documents.t: Later sources win: Built-in defaults Organization defaults Machine configuration User configuration oyzu.toml files from the project root down to the target's folder, nearest last oyzu.local.toml files on the same path Flags and environment variables such as OYZU_BUILD_JOBS Then constraints apply on top, first the project's own [constraints], then organization policy. A constraint is a limit, so a nearer file can't get around it. Within a file, [context.<name>] values beat base values when that context applies, and a profile you choose explicitly beats both. Arrays replace rather than merge. Most settings resolve per target, from that target's folder chain: a value in docs/oyzu.toml applies to the targets under docs/. A few apply to the whole run (such as build.jobs and the cache.* settings), a few may only be set in the root oyzu.toml (publish.* and [constraints]), and a few can never come from a project file, so a cloned repository can't redirect them (such as cache.dir, cache.remote and platform.url). See registered settings for every key. oyzu config explain <setting> shows the effective value and every source that set it, in order.

oyzu.local.toml is for you: a smaller job count, a personal cluster to load images into. Keep it out of version control. In a detected CI context, Oyzu ignores local files and user build settings, so a CI run doesn't depend on whoever set up the runner. --local-overrides includes them anyway.

Every build has one context: local, pr, ci or release. Oyzu detects it from CI variables (GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TF_BUILD, Jenkins, Buildkite and others), using pr for a pull or merge request and release for a tag. With no CI signal it is local. oyzu build --context <name> or OYZU_CONTEXT sets it; in detected CI you can raise the context but not lower it. The context is only a hint: it never grants credentials, cache access or permission to publish. The context matters mostly for checks. Each check (tests, coverage, lint, format) has a level: Level Runs in A failure off never; its tools aren't even installed nothing advisory builds that run every check a CHECK_ADVISORY warning; the build still succeeds enforce (default) builds that run every check fails the build required every build, including fast local builds fails the build Local builds are fast builds that run only required checks. Builds in pr, ci and release, and oyzu build --full, run every check that isn't off. # oyzu.toml [checks] lint = "advisory" coverageMinimum = 50 [context.release.checks] tests = "required" coverageMinimum = 90 See check levels and per-context values.

A profile is a named set of settings, chosen with --profile <name>, OYZU_PROFILE or profile.default. The built-in ci profile runs every check. A profile grants no extra permissions and can't change tools. To also test on another runtime version, such as Node 24, use a toolset.

A constraint limits a setting after every ordinary value is applied. It can lock a value, set a minimum or maximum, add required members, or restrict allowed values (anything else is refused with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED). A project can make a rule hold in every folder with a [constraints] table in its root oyzu.toml: # root oyzu.toml only [constraints."checks.tests"] minimum = "required" when = { context = ["release"] } A folder that sets tests = "advisory" still runs required tests in a release build, and Oyzu prints a CONFIG_CONSTRAINT_OVERRIDE warning. Organization policy works the same way and always wins over project constraints. A tool version outside an allowed set is refused, not quietly swapped. Every override shows in oyzu config explain, the plan and the bundle. See policy constraints and selectors and project constraints.

Project configuration never holds secret values. [env] values are plain strings and can end up in build inputs and records. Credentials for caches, registries and the platform come from environment variables or sign-in. See trusted environment and credential destinations.

Command Use it to oyzu config show See every effective value, the selected profile and diagnostics oyzu config explain <key> See the value, every source that set it, and any constraint oyzu config validate --strict Fail CI on configuration errors and warnings oyzu config set --project <key> <value> Edit one file safely, keeping comments oyzu config schema oyzu.toml Print the JSON Schema for editor completion See oyzu config for every subcommand.
Configuration reference Shell activation and [env] The lock file

A build should still be explainable after the terminal scrollback is gone. Every oyzu build ends by writing a bundle to dist/: the artifacts it produced, the reports its checks collected, and machine-readable records of what was planned and what happened. The previous bundle moves to history. oyzu inspect checks a bundle, and oyzu history finds older ones.

Term Meaning Artifact An output identified by its digest: a binary, a package, an image archive, a chart Report A collected test (JUnit) or coverage result, linked to the action that produced it Bundle The dist/ folder: manifest, plan, envelope, logs, artifacts and reports Manifest dist/manifest.json, the record of what happened, including failures and reused results Plan dist/plan.json, the exact plan the build ran Summary The end of a build's output: outputs, tests, coverage, result and where the records are Invocation One run of the CLI, with its own ID. A reused result keeps the ID of the run that first produced it

dist/ manifest.json plan.json envelope.json logs/ project-api/windows/x86_64/project-api-0.0.0-dev.g638adc2c9cc7.exe project-api/windows/x86_64/reports/junit.xml project-api/windows/x86_64/reports/coverage.out project-worker/windows/x86_64/project-worker-0.0.0-dev.geac6053bbe02.exe project-worker/windows/x86_64/reports/junit.xml project-worker/windows/x86_64/reports/coverage.out Each target's artifacts and reports go under dist/<target>/<platform>/, with the platform written as os/arch.
