The layout is the same for local, multi-platform and CI builds, so bundles from different machines merge without collisions. Platform-independent output goes under any. Everything that reads a bundle (oyzu inspect, publishing, the cache) uses the paths recorded in the manifest rather than assuming a layout. See the bundle layout. Each artifact also records the build profile it was built with, development or optimized. A native executable, such as a Rust or Go binary, is checked when it's collected: it must be a valid ELF, Mach-O or PE file for its target platform and architecture. It's never run, so cross-built binaries are checked too. Oyzu never overwrites a dist/ it didn't create; if your application already uses dist, move it first. While a build writes, it holds .oyzu/build.lock, so two builds in one workspace can't interleave.

The end of a build's output summarizes what happened: $ oyzu build --fullCopy … Checks selected 6 actions · 6 succeeded ​ Tests run now 2 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (2 collected reports) Coverage project-worker: 50.0% (1/2 statements) Coverage project-api: 50.0% (1/2 statements) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 2 targets · 8 executed · 18.1s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 16812-1792553089481901600-1 It follows a few rules: Fresh and reused are separate. Tests from a restored result appear under "Reused test evidence … not run now", never under "Tests run now". No coverage isn't good coverage. A report with nothing measurable isn't shown as a percentage. Blocked isn't failed. An action that never ran because something before it failed is reported as blocked. A failed build still leaves a record. The manifest records what failed, its exit code and log path, alongside what succeeded.

$ oyzu inspect distCopy ✓ Bundle contents verified · build succeeded Run 11832-1792553204327373000 · source sha256:9b1d7b5a1e76 · uncommitted changes ​ Reports Report Path Status project-api:test project-api/windows/x86_64/reports/junit.xml collected project-api:coverage project-api/windows/x86_64/reports/coverage.out collected … ​ Verified: every recorded file matches its digest. This does not show who produced the build or that it may be released. Output shortened. inspect does more than compare digests. It checks that every planned artifact and every required action and report is present, that the manifest agrees with the plan, and it reads each report again with the same rules the build used, so an edited or failing report fails inspection. The last line matters: intact files don't prove who built them, that they came from trusted CI, or that they may be released. For that, verify signed provenance with oyzu inspect --provenance.

When a new bundle is finished, the previous dist/ moves to .oyzu/history/<run-id> and the new one takes its place. $ oyzu historyCopy Invocation evidence Invocation / run Outcome Scope Started 11832-1792553201084382300-1 succeeded 2 targets · 8 actions 2026-10-21T03:26:44.327373+00:00 25368-1792553132239941800-1 succeeded 1 target · 1 action 2026-10-21T03:25:36.268291100+00:00 … oyzu history <id> summarizes one run: action counts, fresh and reused test totals, warnings, unusual actions, the selection, why each action ran or was reused, and where its files are. History reads what was recorded; a later source change or oyzu cache clear never rewrites it. The list shows at most twenty entries. History stays on your machine. Nothing is uploaded or shared.

File Contains manifest.json Targets, actions and their outcomes (succeeded, failed, blocked, or reused with a record of the original run), artifacts with digests and profiles, reports, selection, policy overrides plan.json The exact plan: actions, commands, inputs, outputs, platforms and executors envelope.json The execution details for the run logs/ Each action's standard output and error, and events.jsonl, the structured event log Use oyzu inspect dist --json or oyzu build --json to read them from scripts; see CLI output.

Bundles are written with two renames, so a power loss at the wrong moment can leave a partial bundle. History has no size limit or automatic cleanup yet. Bundles stay until you remove them. Remote runs aren't part of local history. See verification and limits.

Command Use it to oyzu inspect or oyzu inspect dist Check a bundle's files, plan agreement and reports oyzu inspect <bundle-dir> Inspect a bundle from history or elsewhere oyzu history List past builds oyzu history <id> Summarize one build and where its files are oyzu build --explain See why each stage ran or was reused, after a build
Build bundles and retention Understand your build results The action cache

The same build can run in different places. Oyzu calls the place an action runs its executor. The executor affects speed, isolation and how far you can trust the result, so Oyzu always shows the choice before work starts and records it in the bundle. Mode Selected by Runs Needs Host (native) Default for supported targets Native commands as normal processes, each target in its own view of the source The pinned tools, plus native prerequisites such as a linker Isolated (captured) --isolated, --all-platforms, or a target the host path doesn't support A captured copy of source and dependencies, inside a container or sandbox Docker and the execution image, or the daemonless sandbox on Linux Remote --remote A pushed commit or working-tree snapshot on a pool, with full checks in isolation A configured platform or standalone pool; experimental

A plain oyzu build runs on your machine when every selected target supports it: Rust, Go, Gradle, Maven, npm node/app and pip Python targets, plus supported image builds. This is the fast development path, and the one the tutorial uses. $ oyzu build --planCopy … project-api · go/app · windows/x86_64 Executor: host Placement: runs on windows/x86_64 · no Docker engine needed · Runs as host processes without a container engine … Host builds are native, with some guard rails: Each target compiles in its own view of the source: its folder plus any inputs it declares. Declare cross-target inputs explicitly. This view organizes inputs; host processes still have your normal filesystem access, so it is not an access-control boundary. Tools come from the lock, set up per action. A compiler that happens to be on your PATH isn't used for managed tools. Compiler state worth keeping between builds, such as Cargo's target directory, lives under .oyzu/native/, within a size budget (cache.nativeMaxMiB). Built binaries are collected into dist/ and also linked at .oyzu/bin/, which keeps the last successful build if a later one fails. Host execution isn't a sandbox. The processes have your normal access, native package managers use their own registries and credentials, and a host build doesn't by itself qualify for publication. The plan, manifest and logs record that the build ran on the host. Some builders check the environment before compiling. Rust, for example, compiles and links a tiny program first; a missing linker or SDK fails in under a second with EXECUTOR_PREREQUISITE_UNAVAILABLE and setup instructions instead of a raw compiler error. Oyzu doesn't install operating-system components.

oyzu build --isolated captures the source and the dependencies a build needs, then runs each target's actions in a private workspace inside a container, using that captured copy rather than your live checkout. Toolchain images are identified by content digest, not by tag. Use it for builds that shouldn't depend on the machine they run on. --all-platforms uses it to build platforms your machine can't. $ oyzu build api --plan --isolatedCopy Planning shop Windows x86_64 (host) · Isolated · context local · Fast build requested … api · go/app · unresolved until executor selection Executor: captured-worker Placement: runs on any platform · Docker engine required · Isolated steps run in the captured worker on a Docker engine Stage Selection Details build selected Native commands and report bindings resolve during preparation … prepare unresolved Target environment setup is determined by native dependency preparation package unresolved Artifact packaging is determined by native metadata Note the extra prepare and package stages, and that the executor, not your machine, decides the platform.

On Linux, eligible isolated targets can run under crun, a rootless container runtime, instead of Docker. The sandbox is the same either way: no network, a read-only image, no extra privileges, a seccomp filter and a user namespace. build.isolation chooses: auto (the default) uses Docker when an engine answers and crun otherwise; docker and crun force one. Both produce the same cache keys, so a result cached by one serves the other. See the daemonless sandbox and, for the external Go plugin, plugin packages.

oyzu build --no-docker (or OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1) never contacts a Docker engine. Before anything runs, it works out where each target would run; if a selected target needs Docker, it stops with exit status 3 and NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON. Exit 3 means "wrong kind of runner", distinct from a failed build (1) or a bad command (2), so CI can retry the job on a runner with Docker.

oyzu build --remote asks a configured pool to build the pushed HEAD, always with full checks in isolation, and streams the output back. A snapshot-capable standalone pool also accepts unpushed work with --remote --worktree; snapshot results cannot be published or written to shared caches. The CLI exits with the remote exit code, and Ctrl+C cancels the run. oyzu build --remote --plan previews what the pool would run, with each target's platform and executor needs, without contacting the platform. Remote runs are optional and experimental. Platform pools need an account; standalone pools use their own configured authentication. Local builds work without either. See remote runs.

A plain build uses the host when every selected target supports it, and the isolated path otherwise. --isolated (and --image) always use the isolated path; --all-platforms uses the container executor for every declared platform. If a target needs a platform other than your machine's, such as a Linux container image that packages a Go binary built on Windows, the build uses the isolated path so the binary is built for the right platform. --affected works out its selection first, then follows the same rules. A failed build never retries on another executor, and detecting CI doesn't change the choice. What the plan says is what runs.

The executor is recorded on every target in the plan and manifest, and any executor other than your own machine is part of the cache key. A container-built or cross-compiled result never stands in for a host build of the same platform, or the other way round. A project can also name the only executor allowed for a platform with build.executors; see Platforms and matrices.
documents.s: The executor is part of the result

documents.t: Separately from where it runs, each target is built with a development profile (for a fast edit-build loop) or an optimized one. A build is optimized when its artifacts leave your machine (a release context, a write to a shared remote cache, a split-build slice, or packaging by another selected target), and development otherwise. oyzu build --optimized and --no-optimized choose for one run, and build.optimized in oyzu.toml chooses per folder. Rust runs cargo build --release when optimized; builders where optimization changes nothing stay development. Optimized and development results never stand in for each other in the cache. See optimized builds.

Host execution is the most mature path. Isolated execution needs Docker, which pulls the base execution image on first use, or the Linux daemonless sandbox. Which builders support it varies. See Native local builds and Current capabilities.
Native local builds Building without Docker Isolated builds guide

oyzu.lock records the exact tools a project uses: which version each request resolved to, on each platform, and which archive (with its digest) provides it. Oyzu writes it and you commit it. Everyone who checks out the repository, and every CI runner, then installs exactly the same bytes, instead of whatever "latest" means that day.

Configuration says what you asked for. The lock says what that resolved to. Lives in Example Request [tools] in oyzu.toml, native files such as go.mod go = "1.24", go 1.22 Resolution oyzu.lock oyzu:go 1.24.13, go1.24.13.windows-amd64.zip, sha256:40b1… Tool requests, including exact pins, belong in native files or [tools] in oyzu.toml. build.yaml does not hold tool versions. The lock records the resolved version and archive identity.

The lock is TOML. A shortened example for a Go project after oyzu install go@1.24: format = 1 environment = [] tool = [] [[resolved_environment]] required_capabilities = [] request_digest = "sha256:5197…" roots = ["sha256:1deb…", "sha256:8a42…", "sha256:dfd4…", "sha256:ff28…"] [resolved_environment.requests] "oyzu:go" = "1.24" [resolved_environment.native_constraints] "oyzu:go" = ["go-minimum:>=1.22"] [resolution."sha256:8a42…"] tool = "oyzu:go" version = "1.24.13" execution_platform = "windows/amd64/msvc" components = [] [resolution."sha256:8a42…".inputs.archive] url = "https://dl.google.com/go/go1.24.13.windows-amd64.zip" digest = "sha256:40b16bc8f00540a2cb02dff4de72b73e966fdd8d65f95e33d8e4080b48a2459a" resolved_environment is one set of requests (here "oyzu:go" = "1.24"), the native constraints that applied (go.mod asked for at least 1.22), and the resolutions that satisfy them. resolution entries are one per tool, version and platform: the exact version, the archive URL and its digest. Each platform gets its own. environment and tool entries describe installation details where a provider records them. A resolution doesn't mean anything is installed. An entry locked for a toolset has toolset = "NAME". The lock holds no machine paths, profiles or scopes, so it moves between machines unchanged. oyzu tools inspect-lock checks its structure without downloading or running anything.

When a tool is resolved, Oyzu locks it for every platform any build declares, plus the current machine, and installs only this machine's archive. Set tools.lockPlatforms to list the exact platforms instead (the current machine is always kept), for example to prepare for another build environment. See tool lock coverage.

Command Effect on the lock First oyzu build with no lock Resolves what the builders need and writes the lock, without editing your TOML oyzu pin Locks requirements and installs nothing. --dry-run previews oyzu install <tool>@<version> Declares the tool in oyzu.toml and locks it, together oyzu update [tool] Moves to the newest version within each existing request; never edits configuration oyzu uninstall <tool> Removes the declaration and its lock entries oyzu pin --refresh Refreshes install recipes, keeping the selected versions Configuration and lock change together: a failure leaves both files as they were, a simultaneous edit fails with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT, and an interrupted write is recovered the next time you run install, update, uninstall or pin.

Once a lock exists, builds and installs use it as written and never quietly re-resolve. If you change a request so the lock no longer covers it, Oyzu stops and tells you what to run. For example, after changing go = "1.24" to "1.23": $ oyzu install --frozenCopy ✗ TOOL_LOCK_STALE: configured tool request is not pinned; run oyzu pin, then oyzu install Next: Run oyzu pin --refresh to refresh the lock, then oyzu install. Two flags make this explicit: oyzu install --frozen needs an existing matching lock and never resolves a new version. Use it in CI. oyzu install --offline uses no network. It needs the lock plus either an installed copy or a cached archive, which it checks against the locked digest before using. A cached archive that doesn't match its locked digest fails instead of being replaced by a fresh download.
documents.s: The lock stays as written until you change it

documents.t: Organization policy can allow or lock tool versions. The lock is checked against those rules before anything is installed or used, so a hand-edited lock that maps an allowed 22 to 26.1.0 is refused, naming the rule and the lock file. When a policy applies only in some contexts (say, an exact Rust version for release), the lock keeps one entry per request, so local and release entries sit side by side. See policy constraints.

For stages with complete admitted tool requirements, the action cache keys the selected tool identities. Other stages conservatively key the whole lock. Changing a tool used by a stage reruns that work; changing it back can reuse earlier results. A tool that isn't in the lock, such as a system C compiler, isn't part of the cache key, so use oyzu build --no-cache after changing one. See The action cache.

Commit oyzu.lock. It's what makes other machines match yours. Don't edit it by hand. Change requests in oyzu.toml or with oyzu install, and let Oyzu rewrite the lock. One lock per project root. A nested project with its own build.yaml has its own lock. Your user-level defaults (oyzu install -g) use the lock beside your user configuration file. Review lock changes like dependency updates. A changed version or digest is a changed toolchain.
Lock inspection Pin declarations without installing Requirement discovery and pinning

"Build it for Linux and macOS" and "test it on Node 22 and Node 24" sound alike, but they're different requests. The first changes what ships: there are two artifacts. The second changes only how the build is checked: there's still one artifact, tested twice. Oyzu keeps them apart. Platforms are declared in build.yaml; extra runtime versions to test against are toolsets in oyzu.toml. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Every platform is written os/arch[/abi]: Platform Meaning linux/x86_64 Linux on Intel/AMD 64-bit darwin/x86_64 macOS on Intel windows/x86_64 64-bit Windows linux/x86_64/musl, windows/x86_64/msvc With an explicit ABI You can also type amd64 for x86_64; output, records and dist/ folders use x86_64. ARM64 targets remain unsupported. The ABI is optional and only matters where an OS has several (gnu or musl on Linux; msvc, gnu or gnullvm on Windows). Without one, the builder picks its default. Rust cross builds for Linux default to musl, which can break code that relies on glibc features such as dlopen or NSS name lookup; declare linux/<arch>/gnu where that matters.

Two terms stay separate: The target platform is what an artifact is built for. The executor is where its build actions run: your machine, a cross toolchain on your machine, the container executor, or a remote pool. A Linux x86-64 binary can be built natively on a Linux machine or in a Linux container. The executor is recorded on every target and is part of its cache key, so these results never stand in for each other. See Execution modes.

A build lists the platforms it ships for in build.yaml: builds: cli: uses: rust/app platforms: [linux/x86_64, darwin/x86_64, windows/x86_64] A build with one platform keeps its name. With several, each instance gets a platform-qualified ID, and each platform's output goes in its own folder, dist/<target>/<platform>/, so bundles from different machines merge without collisions. A build that declares nothing builds for your machine.

Command Builds oyzu build Your machine's platform. If a target declares platforms but not yours, it builds the one declared platform your machine can build, asks for --platform if there are several, or is skipped with the reason if there are none oyzu build --platform

(repeatable) Exactly those. A declared platform that can't be built here fails before anything runs, with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE oyzu build --all-platforms Every declared platform, through the container executor; fails if any can't be built The plan says how each platform would be built. Platforms your machine could build are listed with the flag to use, and the rest are listed with the reason, such as "needs a macOS runner (Apple SDK and linker)". Today only Rust has a native cross toolchain. Go, Node, Python, Java, .NET and Helm build only for your own platform natively.

By default, a platform is built on your machine if it matches, otherwise with a cross toolchain when the builder has one. You can instead set the executor per platform in oyzu.toml, per folder and per context: [build.executors] "windows/x86_64" = "cross-toolchain" # use the available Rust cross toolchain "darwin/x86_64" = "host" # only on an Intel macOS runner [context.release.build.executors] "linux/x86_64" = "container" # release builds use the container executor A declared executor is the only one used for that platform. When it's unavailable, the platform isn't built here and the plan says why; asking for it explicitly fails with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE. Nothing falls back to another executor, so a release builds each platform exactly as its plan says. See declaring a platform's executor.

You don't have to hand-write your CI matrix. oyzu build --plan --json includes a matrix with one entry per declared platform of every selected target: the runner that can build it natively (os as CI providers name it, and arch), the declared executor, and the targets that declare it. The matrix doesn't depend on what the planning machine can build, and with --affected <ref> it holds only the affected targets. Feed it to your workflow's matrix and run, in each job: oyzu build <targets> --platform <platform> Mapping each runner to your provider's runner labels is up to your workflow. When the artifacts are published, Oyzu checks that every declared platform is present. See a CI matrix from the plan for a complete GitHub Actions example.
documents.s: A CI matrix from the plan

documents.t: To check that an application also works on another runtime version, define a toolset in oyzu.toml. The shipped build is built and tested once, with the [tools] versions. Each toolset adds a verification run that repeats the build and test stages with its tools and records the result. A verification run never produces an artifact, so publishing still sees one artifact. # build.yaml: nothing about runtime versions builds: app: uses: node/app # oyzu.toml [tools] node = "22.14.0" # builds, tests and ships the app [toolsets.node24.tools] node = "24.14.1" # also tested on Node 24 Command Runs oyzu pin Locks Node 22.14.0 and the node24 toolset's 24.14.1 oyzu build Locally: the app alone oyzu build --verify-with node24 Locally: the app and its Node 24 run oyzu build --context ci In CI: the app and its Node 24 run A toolset runs in every context except local, unless it lists contexts = [...]. Each run is its own target in the plan (app-verify-node24). It skips lint and format checks, which don't depend on the runtime, and never packages or publishes. A failing test in a run fails the build. Runs are listed under .verify in the plan JSON, so CI can give each its own job. The global --toolset <name> option uses a toolset's tools for exec, run, env, activate, which and install, so you can reproduce a run's environment by hand. A build can require passing verification on certain tool versions before publishing with verification.<tool> (for example verification.node = ["22", "24"]), and policy or [constraints] can make versions required. A version no toolset covers adds a run, and oyzu publish refuses a release without a passing result for each. A version outside the project's own range, such as below the go line in go.mod, is recorded as not applicable instead of failing the build. See verification toolsets. Runtime versions never go in build.yaml: the old matrix.<runtime> field is refused with a message showing the toolset form. Profiles can't hold tools either. A toolset is the one place to define an alternative set of tools.
Native cross toolchains exist only for Rust so far. Isolated execution needs Docker or, for eligible Linux targets, the daemonless sandbox. See platform requirements and platforms and executors.
Platforms and executors Verification toolsets and platform matrices Build bundle layout CI guide

Oyzu starts from the files your ecosystem already has. A go.mod is a Go module, a Cargo.toml is a Rust package, a package.json with a lockfile is a Node project. You don't have to describe your repository before Oyzu can build it. When you want the list of builds to be explicit and reviewed, add a small build.yaml; from then on that file decides. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Term Meaning Example Project root The folder Oyzu treats as the top of your project The Git worktree root Target (also called a build) One buildable unit with a name api, a Go module in api/ Builder The ecosystem support that finds, plans and builds one kind of target go/app, rust/app, node/app, python/app Discovery Reading native files to find targets and pick their builders, without running project code oyzu discover Inventory The list of builds in build.yaml builds: {api: {uses: go/app, path: api}}

Inside a Git repository, configuration is inherited from the worktree root, and the nearest build.yaml above you decides the builds. Outside Git, the outermost folder with Oyzu configuration or a build.yaml is the project; failing that, the folder you ran the command in. --root <dir> sets the root explicitly, and -C <dir> runs from another folder as if you'd changed into it. A nested project with its own build.yaml is independent: running Oyzu inside it uses that project, with its own oyzu.lock and dist/. Parent inventories aren't merged. See inspection and selection for the exact rules.

Without a build.yaml, Oyzu walks the tree from the root. When a builder recognizes a folder, that folder becomes a target and the walk doesn't go deeper there, because the builder owns everything below it. Dependency and output folders, nested Git repositories and folders with their own build.yaml are skipped. A small repository with two Go modules and no Oyzu files: shop/ api/ go.mod main.go main_test.go worker/ go.mod main.go main_test.go $ oyzu discoverCopy 2 targets · 12 tasks discovered without running project code Project root: …\shop ​ project-api · go/app Chosen by detected from project files Location api … ​ project-worker · go/app Chosen by detected from project files Location worker … Without configuration, names follow the folder: a target at the root is project, and one below it is project-<path>, here project-api and project-worker.

Inside a target, a builder still has choices to make: which package manager, test runner or formatter. Each option comes with evidence, and the strongest evidence wins: Strength Examples declared a test script that runs exactly one recognized test runner native a lockfile, packageManager in package.json, a [tool.*] table in pyproject.toml conventional a declared dependency, a uv.lock that locks no packages default the documented default when nothing else applies, such as npm or Ruff If two options have equally strong evidence, Oyzu doesn't guess. Discovery fails, names both, and prints the build.yaml line that settles it: $ oyzu discoverCopy ✗ COMMAND_FAILED: conflicting Python formatter candidates black, ruff: black via pyproject.toml tool.black; ruff via pyproject.toml tool.ruff; declare the intended one for this target in build.yaml with `with: {formatter: black}` or `with: {formatter: ruff}` oyzu build --plan shows every choice and its reason in a Discovered table. Each builder's options are listed in discovery decisions and build.yaml selectors.
documents.s: How a builder makes its choices

documents.t: A build.yaml at the root turns discovery into an explicit list you can review. With one present, only its builds exist. Discovery never adds a build on its own. builds: api: uses: go/app path: api worker: uses: go/app path: worker depends_on: [api] Field Purpose uses The builder. Optional when exactly one builder recognizes the folder path The folder, relative to the root depends_on Builds that must finish first (ordering only) materialize Artifacts from another build to place in this build's inputs platforms The platforms this build ships for, such as [linux/x86_64, windows/x86_64] inputs Extra source paths the build reads with Options for the selected builder, such as formatter: ruff With that file, oyzu discover reports the names you chose (api, worker), shows Chosen by build.yaml, and confirms that build.yaml declares every folder where a build was discovered. build.yaml holds only what changes what ships. Tool versions, check levels, tasks and environment variables go in oyzu.toml; see Configuration layers. A build.yaml that belongs to another tool (Dart's build_runner uses the same name) is recognized by its keys and skipped.

Once you have a build.yaml, a folder someone adds later won't build unless it's listed. Oyzu helps you notice: oyzu discover lists folders a builder recognizes that no entry covers, with the line to add for each. oyzu build --plan names up to five of them under Not in build.yaml. A real build never builds them. oyzu discover --check exits 1 with INVENTORY_UNDECLARED while such a folder exists. Add it to CI. oyzu discover --write adds an entry, with uses written out, for every folder exactly one builder recognizes. It keeps your comments and order and adds an editor-schema comment. exclude: lists folders that are deliberately not builds, for example exclude: [tools/scratch, tooling/**]. Folders that a declared build's native workspace already includes (Cargo members, go.work use, npm, Yarn or pnpm workspaces) are covered by that build. Inside Git, only folders with tracked files count, so files a CI job creates can't fail the check. See builds build.yaml leaves out.

If a native file already says something, Oyzu reads it there: The go and toolchain lines in go.mod set the minimum Go version. rust-toolchain.toml selects the Rust channel and components. Lockfiles decide the Node package manager. Native workspace manifests decide which folders belong to one build. Oyzu configuration only adds what native files can't say, and when both mention the same thing they must agree. See Tools and toolchains.

Command Use it to oyzu discover See targets, builders and how each was chosen oyzu discover --json Get the full discovery record, including each task's environment oyzu discover --check Fail CI when a recognized folder is missing from build.yaml oyzu discover --write Add every undeclared folder to build.yaml oyzu config schema build.yaml Print the JSON Schema for build.yaml oyzu run list See the tasks each target offers
Discovery decisions and build.yaml selectors Build inventory fields and errors Set up projects guide The build graph: what happens once targets are known

Oyzu has two ways to do work: oyzu run <task> runs one named task now, with live output, the way you'd run go test or npm run lint yourself, but with the project's pinned tools. oyzu build produces the project's outputs. It runs stages across every selected target in dependency order, reuses unchanged results, and leaves a bundle in dist/. Both use the same tasks. The difference is what happens around them.

A task is a named operation on a target, written target:task, such as api:test. Builders infer the common ones from your native files, so most projects need no task configuration: Task Purpose Part of builds build Compile or package the target yes test Run the tests and collect JUnit and coverage where supported yes lint Run the ecosystem's linter yes format-check Check formatting without changing files yes format Rewrite files to the formatter's style no, development only install Fetch dependencies no, development only $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 13 across 2 targets ​ Task Source Command api · go/app (7) api:build Inferred · go go build ./... api:smoke oyzu.toml go run . api:test Inferred · go go test ./... … The Source column shows where each task came from: inferred by a builder, or written in oyzu.toml.

$ oyzu run api:smokeCopy · Setup Loading configuration and discovering tasks › api:smoke Running · native tool output follows Hello, Oyzu! ✓ api:smoke Succeeded (exit 0 after 1.16s) oyzu run runs in the target's folder with the project's tools on PATH, streams native output as it happens, and uses your terminal's input. A bare task name works when only one target has it; otherwise write api:test. Arguments after -- are passed on: oyzu run api:test -- -run TestPrice. Task runs are never cached. They're for the edit-run loop.

oyzu build runs the same tasks as stages, with more around them: oyzu run <task> oyzu build Scope One task (plus its prerequisites and hooks) Every stage of every selected target Ordering That task's prerequisites The whole build graph Reuse Never cached Unchanged actions are reused Output Live native output Live progress, then a summary of outputs, tests and coverage Record Test runs can write a test bundle Always a bundle in dist/ Checks You choose the task Chosen by check levels and context

A plain local oyzu build is a fast build: it runs the build and package stages and only the checks set to required, and shows the rest as skip · fast local build. A full build runs every check that isn't off. You get one: with oyzu build --full on any machine; automatically in the pr, ci and release contexts, which Oyzu detects from CI variables, so CI needs no extra flags; with oyzu --profile ci build. Each check (tests, coverage, lint, format) has a level in oyzu.toml: off, advisory (a failure is a warning), enforce (the default; fails full builds) or required (runs in every build and fails it). No flag skips a check the project chose; turning one off is a committed change. See check levels.

Tasks go in oyzu.toml under [tasks]. Each one is either argv (an argument list, recommended) or run (a shell command): [tasks."api:smoke"] argv = ["go", "run", "."] A task with the same name as a builder stage replaces that stage's command. The stage's requirements still apply: a replacement test stage must still produce the reports its builder needs. Which builds a task applies to depends on its name: Key Applies to [tasks."api:smoke"] Build api only [tasks.post_build] (a hook) Every build below that file's folder that has a build stage [tasks.test] (a stage name) Replaces test in every build the file reaches; refused if those builds use different builders [tasks.lint-docs] (any other name) At the root, a workspace task: oyzu run lint-docs Names are checked before anything runs. A misspelled build or hook target is an error naming the file and line and suggesting the nearest name. See which build a task belongs to.

A hook is a task named pre_<task> or post_<task>. It runs with that task, both in task runs and in builds. Prerequisites use depends_on: [tasks."api:pre_test"] argv = ["node", "scripts/check-api-inputs.mjs"] depends_on = ["schema:verify"] [tasks."schema:verify"] argv = ["node", "scripts/verify-schema.mjs"] schema:verify runs once per command even if several tasks need it, in the schema target's folder with that target's tools. A custom command never installs a new tool by itself: the tools it calls must be ones the project already uses.

A hook can say when it applies with when and unless, using facts such as the build context, platform, whether the build is optimized, and for post_build hooks the artifact. It can receive values through placeholders like {artifact.path}: [tasks."cli:post_build"] argv = ["{artifact.path}", "--version"] when = { optimized = true, platform = ["linux/x86_64"] } Conditions choose behavior; they aren't a security control. Use check levels and constraints for checks that must run. See task and hook conditions.

Files that ship belong on the build in build.yaml, even when an authored task produces them. Use artifacts to name the qualified producer, exact relative file path and media type; keep the command and conditions in oyzu.toml. A release-only or skipped producer records not-produced with a reason and does not fail the build. Publication requires the file only when it is selected. See named file artifacts. Builder stages are cached without any setup. Oyzu can't see inside a task you wrote, so a target containing one runs every time, unless the task sets cache = true with outputs, or the hook declares outputs. See authored tasks cached on request.
Build tasks Task settings Run native tasks guide

A build is only as reproducible as the compiler that ran it. Oyzu manages toolchains itself, so your laptop, a teammate's machine and CI use the same Go, Node or Rust without anyone installing it by hand. You say what you need, Oyzu picks an exact version, verifies the download once, records it in oyzu.lock, and puts it on PATH for builds, tasks and your shell. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Oyzu collects tool requirements from three places and combines them, keeping track of each source: Source Example What it adds Native files go 1.22 in go.mod; rust-toolchain.toml Minimums, channels and components the project already declares The builder Go's builder needs a Go compiler; Rust's test stage needs nextest and cargo-llvm-cov Tools for the stages that will run [tools] in oyzu.toml go = "1.24" Explicit requests, for tools with no native pin or to pick within a range Tools follow checks: when a check is off, its tools aren't installed. With [checks] format = "off", the Rust builder no longer adds rustfmt. oyzu build --plan shows the combined list without checking or installing anything: $ oyzu build --planCopy … Tool requirements · availability not checked Requirement Kind Constraint Targets Source oyzu:go minimum-version >=1.22 all 2 targets go.mod go oyzu:go request 1.22 all 2 targets api/go.mod (native pin); worker/go.mod (native pin) …

If a native file already pins a tool, that file is the request, and Oyzu configuration either adds nothing or must agree: a [tools] value in the pin's folder, or nearer the build, must name the same version line, or preparation fails naming both files; a [tools] value farther away loses to the pin and is shown as overridden; native ranges, such as npm devEngines, stay constraints. Today Oyzu reads the Rust toolchain files and the go and toolchain lines in Go's go.mod and go.work. Go's lines count as a minimum, not an exact pin, because Go treats the toolchain line as a suggestion. Oyzu requests that minimum when no [tools] go is set, and a configured version below it fails with TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT. Support for other native pin files, such as global.json, Gradle and Maven wrapper properties and packageManager, varies by ecosystem; the build guide for your ecosystem says which it reads. See Go version selection and Rust toolchain files.

Installing a tool takes the same steps whichever command starts it: Resolve the request ("1.24") to an exact version (1.24.13) for every platform in the lock, from the publisher's catalog or Oyzu's signed public tool index. Download the archive for this machine. Verify it: the archive digest against the publisher's checksum, the publisher's signature where available, and the unpacked layout. Store it in the shared tool store with an install record, and write oyzu.lock. After that, the tool is trusted. Running a command doesn't re-hash the installed files, and a damaged installation may simply fail when run. Checking happens once, at install, which keeps every command fast. $ oyzu install go@1.24Copy Installing requested tools Resolving every platform, then installing this one ✓ Installed (reused existing installation) go 1.24.13 Declared "1.24" in …\shop\oyzu.toml (project) Locked in …\shop\oyzu.lock for 4 platforms (darwin/arm64/native, linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, windows/amd64/msvc) ​ Store: C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\Oyzu\tools The ARM64 records shown in this output do not imply installation support; ARM64 installation is unsupported. Current default host metadata covers x64 Linux, Intel macOS and Windows, with installation support varying by tool. See native tool hosts. Configuration keeps what you typed ("1.24"). The lock records the exact version and an archive for each platform. Only this machine's archive is installed; here Go 1.24.13 was already in the store, so nothing was downloaded. go@1.26 is a prefix, go@1.26.8 is exact, go@latest is the newest eligible version, and plain go keeps an existing declaration. Several tools in one command are applied together or not at all.

Installed tools live in one store per user, shared by every project: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\tools on Windows and ${XDG_DATA_HOME:-~/.local/share}/oyzu/tools on Linux. Two projects that lock the same Go version share one installation. oyzu uninstall never deletes shared files; oyzu tools list shows what uses each installation.

The selected tools reach every place you run commands: Where How Builds The build installs any missing pinned tool and uses the exact selection for each action Tasks oyzu run <task> puts the selected tools on PATH Your shell oyzu shell install (the install script runs it) adds the selection to PATH as you change directories, so plain go version works One command without activation oyzu exec -- go version Lookup oyzu which go prints the selected executable $ go versionCopy go version go1.24.13 windows/amd64 oyzu which and oyzu exec never fall back to a program elsewhere on your PATH when the selected tool is missing; they fail and tell you to install it. Shell activation applies a project's environment variables only after you trust the folder, because environment variables can run code in shells and interpreters.

Command Declares in Locks in oyzu install go@1.24 project oyzu.toml project oyzu.lock oyzu install -g node@22 your user configuration the oyzu.lock beside it oyzu install --local go@1.24 oyzu.local.toml project oyzu.lock Outside a project, a command without -g fails with TOOL_NO_PROJECT instead of guessing.

Oyzu installs supported tools from their publishers: Node, Go, Python, Java, Maven, Gradle, Helm, kubectl, k3d, npm, pnpm, Rust and the Cargo helpers it needs, among others, plus experimental registry packages (aqua: and github:). It doesn't install operating-system components. A Windows Rust build that needs the MSVC build tools and SDK, or a system linker, reports it as an executor prerequisite with setup instructions; oyzu pin --dry-run lists these separately from managed tools. Tool commands are supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64); support for individual tools varies. See tool commands.

Command Use it to oyzu install <tool>@<version> Declare, lock and install a tool oyzu install Install everything declared; --frozen never changes the lock, --offline never uses the network oyzu update [tool] Move to the newest version within each requirement; never edits configuration oyzu uninstall <tool> Remove a declaration and its lock entries oyzu pin Lock requirements without installing oyzu tools current / list / versions / info See what is selected, stored, available and why oyzu which <command>, oyzu exec -- <command> Find or run a command with the selected tools
Tool commands The lock file Manage your first tool guide Shell activation

Oyzu builds container images from ordinary Dockerfiles and packages Helm charts from ordinary chart folders. Neither needs configuration. With a little build.yaml, the pieces connect: a binary built by one target is copied into an image, and the image's exact digest is written into the chart that deploys it. Image builds produce an OCI archive in dist/ and never push. Chart builds produce a packaged .tgz and a rendered manifest, and never contact a cluster. Publishing is a separate, explicit step (publishing). Note: The Docker and Helm builders are experimental. They run as the oyzu/docker and oyzu/helm plugins. Supported image targets are Linux x86-64 only (linux/x86_64). Builds that need an engine use Docker with a Linux engine, on Linux or Windows x64. macOS and ARM64 are not supported. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Files Builder Tasks Dockerfile docker/image build, lint (Hadolint), format-check and format (dockerfmt) Chart.yaml or chart/Chart.yaml helm/chart build (helm package), test, lint (helm lint), format-check and format (yamlfmt), install (helm dependency build) If both chart locations exist, discovery fails as ambiguous, so declare the path in build.yaml. If a folder with a Dockerfile also looks like an application (a package.json or pyproject.toml), select the Docker builder with uses: docker/image.

Oyzu looks at the Dockerfile and picks the cheapest safe path for each target. You don't set anything. Daemonless assembly. If the final stage only copies files onto one base and edits image settings (COPY, WORKDIR, USER, ENV, LABEL, EXPOSE, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, STOPSIGNAL), and the base is scratch or pinned by @sha256: digest, Oyzu writes the image itself, like ko or Jib. This build needs no Docker engine. Base images are fetched by digest and cached; private registries use your native Docker login store during preparation. BuildKit in an isolated worker. Anything else (a RUN in the final stage, ARG, ADD, a tag-only base, .dockerignore) runs in Oyzu's rootless BuildKit worker with no network. Oyzu uses local base images first and captures missing digest-pinned bases into verified OCI inputs during preparation, using your native Docker login for private registries. Floating tags need local provisioning. The worker itself never reads registry credentials. No separate base-image bootstrap pull is needed for pinned bases. # Daemonless: a digest-pinned base and only COPY and settings FROM gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12:nonroot@sha256:7f0c72cd138b442ae0deeb69c08b1acf5525439ba251a49ad93c320a061567e5 COPY bin/server /server USER 65532:65532 ENTRYPOINT ["/server"] The full list of instructions daemonless assembly accepts is in daemonless assembly.
documents.s: Two ways an image is built

documents.t: A Linux Docker engine for BuildKit builds and for the quality checks. You also need the base execution image and, for RUN steps, the pinned rootless BuildKit worker (published execution images). Oyzu pulls both by pinned digest the first time it needs them. Set OYZU_NO_TOOLCHAIN_PULL=1 to forbid pulls on an offline host. For builds, dockerfmt ships in the Docker plugin package and Hadolint is downloaded (pinned release, checked SHA-256) when the lint stage runs. To run oyzu run lint and oyzu run format on your machine, they must be on PATH. oyzu build --no-docker builds a daemonless target without contacting Docker. A target that needs the engine stops with exit status 3 before anything runs.

lint runs hadolint --no-color Dockerfile and honors a .hadolint.yaml next to the Dockerfile. format-check runs dockerfmt with --check and honors a nearby .editorconfig. Both are build gates with --full and in CI. See Dockerfile linting and formatting. A successful image build records: Output Contents <target>-<version>.oci.tar The image as an OCI layout archive, with its digest in manifest.json JUnit report Integrity and platform checks on the archive Dependency record Each base image's requested reference and verified digests, the Dockerfile digest and the build path used Every image is checked against its target platform, and an image for the wrong architecture fails. The supported target is linux/x86_64 (linux/amd64 is also accepted). ARM64 image targets and multi-architecture images are unsupported. A Dockerfile with RUN in a target-platform stage needs the worker and target platforms to match.

with.repository names the image's eventual registry repository, such as registry.example.com/team/app. Building never contacts it. A chart binding reads it (below). To load a built image into Docker or a k3d cluster without a registry, set docker.load and run oyzu run load. See loading the image locally.

oyzu build packages the chart and renders it with helm template --dry-run=client and an empty kubeconfig, so you get both a .tgz and a rendered.yaml. With --full or in CI it also runs: Validation. Rendering plus values.schema.json checks for an application chart, or strict lint for a library chart. Reported as junit.xml. helm-unittest, when a chart or subchart has flat tests/*_test.yaml suites or recursive unittests/**/*.yaml suites. Reported separately as unittest.xml. Rendering alone doesn't count as a passing unit test. Snapshot baselines are inputs, so creating or changing one during a build fails it. helm lint and a read-only yamlfmt check of the chart's YAML. Templates aren't formatted. Coverage is recorded as not applicable instead of as an invented percentage.

Charts build in the isolated worker with the Helm in your lock; the base image has none. Declare the version and install it, which records the exact archive in oyzu.lock: # oyzu.toml [tools] helm = "4.3.0" oyzu install helm@4.3.0 Helm takes an exact version only. yamlfmt comes from the lock too. When a chart has unit test suites, Oyzu fetches its pinned helm-unittest release and restores it for the test stage, so a pinned Helm must be able to run that plugin. Isolated chart builds are supported on Linux amd64. See pinned Helm.

On Linux, oyzu build chart --isolated --no-docker --full --explain uses crun's complete input boundary. Packaging/rendering, lint, validation and helm-unittest can reuse when admitted inputs and retained outputs match. Preparation and current report validation still apply; reused tests are labelled as earlier evidence, not tests run now. Helm and helm-unittest identities from the lock remain inputs. Outputs remain location sensitive unless declared relocatable. Native chart predictions alone do not establish complete runtime reads, so incomplete native stages rerun. Docker does not inherit crun's complete-read guarantee. See Helm isolated reuse.

A chart can use the identity of an image built in the same oyzu build, so nobody passes --set image.digest=… at deploy time: builds: image: uses: docker/image with: repository: registry.example.com/team/greeting chart: uses: helm/chart path: chart bindings: - from: image artifact: image type: image-reference repository: /image/repository digest: /image/digest The destinations are JSON Pointers into the chart's values.yaml, and each must already be a string there (an empty digest: "" is the usual shape). Oyzu writes the repository and the image's real manifest digest into a private copy of the chart before packaging. The packaged defaults and rendered.yaml carry the produced reference, and your checked-in chart is never edited. A changed image rebuilds the chart, and a failed image blocks it. See image bindings for the reference form and the limits. For private OCI chart dependencies, use helm registry login and commit the native Chart.lock with exact dependency versions. Preparation reads the native login store; the worker receives verified chart archives and stays offline. See OCI dependencies for store precedence and authentication limits. Keep login files outside project source.
documents.s: Bind an image into a chart

documents.t: This example is examples/builds/image-and-chart/project in the Oyzu repository. Copy it to a new folder and run git init. It has a Go command in app/, a Dockerfile at the root and a chart in chart/: FROM scratch COPY bin/server /server ENTRYPOINT ["/server"] build.yaml connects them. materialize copies the Go target's binary to bin/server in the image's build context, and the chart binds the image: builds: app: uses: go/app path: app image: uses: docker/image with: repository: registry.example.invalid/team/greeting materialize: - from: app to: bin/server platforms: - linux/amd64 chart: uses: helm/chart path: chart bindings: - from: image artifact: image type: image-reference repository: /image/repository digest: /image/digest The chart's values.yaml holds the placeholders the binding fills: replicaCount: 1 image: repository: registry.example.invalid/team/greeting tag: development digest: "" oyzu build --plan shows how the three targets depend on each other: $ oyzu build --planCopy Declared task ordering Task After app-platform-linux_x86_64-a7b09986ced7:build image:build app-platform-linux_x86_64-a7b09986ced7:build chart:build image:build Output shortened. Read the plan this way: The image's platforms: [linux/amd64] makes the Go binary a linux/amd64 build too, so the copied file matches the image. Oyzu names those variants app-platform-linux_x86_64-…. The image needs no Docker engine: FROM scratch plus COPY is assembled in process. The chart waits for the image and receives its OCI archive as .oyzu-bindings/0.oci.tar, the data its binding reads. The Go binary and the chart still run in the isolated worker, which needs Docker. With --full, the image also runs lint and format-check, and its placement changes to Docker engine required, because Hadolint and dockerfmt run in a container from the Docker plugin package. oyzu build then produces the Linux binary, a versioned .oci.tar image archive with its JUnit report, and the chart .tgz plus a rendered.yaml whose image.digest is the image's real manifest digest.
documents.s: Worked example: binary, image and chart

documents.t: You see Cause Fix Preparation names a missing base image (BuildKit path) The base isn't in your local Docker image store Pull or provision it your usual way. Or pin it by digest and keep the final stage free of RUN, so the daemonless path fetches it A private base fails on the daemonless path Missing/rejected native Docker credentials, an unavailable helper, or a token service on another origin Check docker login, DOCKER_CONFIG and helper availability. For a separate token-service origin, provision the base with native docker pull A foreign-platform RUN fails before any action RUN in a target-platform stage that differs from the worker Build on a matching worker. Or compile in a FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM stage and only COPY into the target stage Hadolint or dockerfmt fails A lint or format finding Fix it, or run oyzu run format and review the change helm lint reports missing dependencies A vendored subchart under charts/ isn't declared in the parent Chart.yaml Declare it (name and version, no repository URL) A unittest snapshot fails the build A baseline under __snapshot__ would be created or changed Update baselines deliberately with helm-unittest, review and commit them A binding fails during configuration The destination is missing from values.yaml, the image has no with.repository, or both binding forms are set Add the string field, set with.repository, or use one form NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON with --no-docker (exit 3) A selected target needs Docker, such as lint or format checks under --full Run with Docker, or select only daemonless work

Images are Linux x86-64 only (linux/x86_64). Native Windows images and emulated RUN aren't supported. Remote ADD and secret and SSH mounts aren't supported. The BuildKit worker never reads registry credentials; private bases are fetched during preparation with your native Docker login. Binding a multi-platform image (an OCI index) into a chart is refused. Go-template formatting is unsupported. For supported remote chart dependencies and their limits, see Helm dependencies. See capabilities and known limitations for the whole product.

Docker image inputs and offline builds, including offline dependency contexts for pip, npm, Yarn, pnpm, Go modules and Cargo Oyzu's BuildKit frontend and declared fetches Helm charts and chart tests Publishing finalized artifacts, including OCI destinations

Oyzu builds an SDK-style .NET solution or project with no configuration. It honors global.json for SDK selection and uses the managed SDK to restore, build, test, publish and pack. Native Linux and Windows builds use your NuGet configuration; isolated builds restore through a controlled mirror and run offline. Test results become JUnit, VSTest runs collect Cobertura coverage, and the dist/ bundle contains framework-dependent application folders and NuGet packages for packable projects. Note: The .NET builder is experimental. It runs as the oyzu/dotnet plugin and supports Linux and Windows x64 native builds and isolated Linux containers with Docker or crun. The default SDK is 10.0.401. macOS builds are unsupported. The build flow requires a compatible .NET plugin declaring dotnet-lock-admission. Updating the CLI does not replace an installed plugin; use oyzu plugins update dotnet/sdk to select a compatible package. The .NET reference has the full details.

For a native Linux or Windows x64 build, run oyzu install to provision the managed SDK, then oyzu build --full. Native restore uses your NuGet/MSBuild configuration and package cache. Native offline builds and build-task overrides are unsupported; use the isolated path for those. See native host builds. For an isolated build, you need: Docker with a Linux engine, or crun on Linux with --isolated --no-docker. See isolated builds. The base execution image. Oyzu pulls it on first use. The SDK in oyzu.lock. Run oyzu pin. Without a [tools] dotnet setting it locks the default SDK, 10.0.401, and restores it into every action. See provisioning. A compatible .NET plugin. Its builder role must declare dotnet-lock-admission. An older exact package selection is refused before private restore preparation; explicitly select an admitted capable package with oyzu plugins update dotnet/sdk. See isolated restore. To run on an image of your own, pass --image dotnet=<image>. The locked SDK is still used. You don't need a separately installed .NET SDK for an isolated build.

On Linux or Windows x64, oyzu build --full restores, builds, tests, publishes application folders and packs using the managed SDK on the host. Native NuGet configuration and package source mapping select private feeds. Keep credentials in user-level configuration, credential providers or %ENVIRONMENT_VARIABLE% references in NuGet.config; no Oyzu registry setting is needed. Tracked literal credentials are refused before source projection. Private captured/isolated builds are refused before actions; use host mode. See the private-feed reference for configuration, credential handling and limitations.

A folder is a .NET target when it directly contains a solution (.sln, .slnx) or an SDK-style project (.csproj, .fsproj, .vbproj whose root names an MSBuild SDK). Legacy non-SDK projects aren't claimed. The version comes from a literal <Version> in the root Directory.Build.props. A literal Version or VersionPrefix in the entry project works too. The tasks are native dotnet commands: $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 5 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · dotnet/sdk (5) project:build Inferred · dotnet dotnet build project:format Inferred · dotnet — Unavailable: No native configuration or registered integration was discovered project:install Inferred · dotnet dotnet restore project:lint Inferred · dotnet — Unavailable: No native configuration or registered integration was discovered project:test Inferred · dotnet dotnet test That capture shows the older plugin. With a compatible current plugin, lint runs dotnet format analyzers and the format check runs dotnet format whitespace --verify-no-changes, using your .editorconfig. See the reference.

Every native command gets one entry: the single solution, otherwise the single SDK-style project. If a folder has more than one candidate, the build fails and names them. Pick one in build.yaml: builds: app: uses: dotnet/sdk with: project: Greeting.slnx with.project is the only option. Any other key is refused (invalid .NET with options: unknown field …, expected project).

global.json in the target folder selects the SDK the way the dotnet host does: sdk.version, sdk.rollForward (default patch with a version, latestMajor without one) and sdk.allowPrerelease. Without global.json, the locked SDK is used. global.json must be strict JSON, so comments are refused. Oyzu doesn't predict the result. During isolated preparation it lists the SDKs in the container and asks dotnet --version which one your folder selects. If nothing installed satisfies the request, preparation fails before restore. The message names the request, the available SDKs and oyzu pin as the remedy. --plan shows the request. Current versions list the SDK requirement as oyzu:dotnet; the output below may show an older image default. $ oyzu build --planCopy Tool requirements · availability not checked Requirement Kind Constraint Targets Source dotnet-sdk tool 10.0.400 rollForward latestFeature; default image SDK project global.json /sdk 10.0.401

Command What runs oyzu build --plan Nothing. Shows the SDK request and the stages oyzu build On Linux or Windows x64: native restore, build, publish and pack (Debug by default, Release with --optimized) oyzu build --isolated Restore, build, publish and pack in a Linux container oyzu build --full Also tests, analyzer lint and whitespace checks, with test results converted to JUnit In CI the test stage runs without --full. Inside the container: Restore runs once during preparation with no network, through a loopback mirror. The mirror reaches only the public https://api.nuget.org/ flat container (and its vulnerability data) through Oyzu's scoped broker. Feeds and credentials from NuGet.Config, user settings or RestoreSources aren't used. If any packages.lock.json exists, restore uses --locked-mode. Build runs dotnet build <entry> --configuration Debug --no-restore (Release for an optimized build) with -p:Version=<snapshot version>. Test, when selected, runs dotnet test --no-build --no-restore with TRX output (VSTest, or Microsoft.Testing.Platform when global.json selects it). All TRX files become one JUnit report. A test run that produces no TRX fails instead of reporting an empty suite. Publish runs dotnet publish --no-restore --no-build for selected applications. Each application becomes a <project-name>-<version>-portable directory, runnable with dotnet <app>.dll on a compatible runtime. This needs a plugin and engine declaring dotnet-publish. Pack runs dotnet pack --no-build --no-restore for packable projects. An app-only selection without packable projects omits the NuGet artifact. A library selection with no packages still fails. See build, test and package.

On Linux, oyzu build --isolated --no-docker --full --explain uses crun to enforce a complete input view. Conventional deterministic compile, test and pack stages can reuse on unchanged builds, including another clean checkout when retained bytes contain no checkout paths. Restore regenerates local assets. Publish and unknown or unbounded MSBuild customizations rerun. The SDK identity, dependency content and consumed producer outputs remain inputs. With a compatible plugin, solutions with literal ProjectReference edges and separate, non-nested project folders can reuse compile, test and pack per project. Editing a shared library also reruns its dependents; an untouched library can keep its package when only consuming tests change. Solutions with applications, shared/nested folders or unknown customizations retain the solution-wide path. Native Linux and Windows stages still rerun because their reads are incomplete. See .NET read boundaries and stage reuse.

Preparation restores with NuGet audit on and reports what it finds as a NuGet audit step (for example known vulnerabilities: 1 high), as NUGET_AUDIT warnings and in the dependency record. Findings never fail the build, and they can't turn into compile errors under TreatWarningsAsErrors.

This is the .NET fixture from the Oyzu source tree (tooling/fixtures/dotnet-app): a solution with a packable Greeting library and an xUnit test project. global.json: { "sdk": { "version": "10.0.400", "rollForward": "latestFeature" } } Directory.Build.props: <Project> <PropertyGroup> <Version>1.2.0</Version> <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework> <Nullable>enable</Nullable> <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors> </PropertyGroup> </Project> Greeting.slnx lists src/Greeting/Greeting.csproj (with RestorePackagesWithLockFile and a checked-in packages.lock.json) and test/Greeting.Tests/Greeting.Tests.csproj (IsPackable false, referencing Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk, xunit and xunit.runner.visualstudio). oyzu build --isolated --plan --full previews the Linux container path: $ oyzu build --isolated --plan --fullCopy project · dotnet/sdk · unresolved until executor selection Executor: captured-worker Profile: development · local dist only (--configuration Debug) Placement: runs on any platform · Docker engine required · Isolated steps run in the captured worker on a Docker engine Discovered Selection Reason sdk 10.0.400 rollForward latestFeature native global.json /sdk Output shortened. The request 10.0.400 with latestFeature admits 10.0.401. Now build with oyzu build --isolated --full. The retained Windows capture below shows that container path: $ oyzu build --fullCopy Building dotnet-app windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ NuGet audit no known vulnerabilities 22.5s ✓ Version 1.2.0-dev.gb0a8e2fc937d · 1 package 0.4s … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ project prepare dotnet/sdk restore executed 14.7s ✓ project build dotnet build Greeting.slnx --configura… executed 9.7s ✓ project test dotnet/sdk test executed 3.6s ✓ project package dotnet/sdk pack executed 6.3s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/linux/x86_64/nuget-packages-1.2.0-dev.gb0a8e2fc937d 3.4 KB development ​ Tests run now 2 passed · 0 failed · 1 skipped (1 collected reports) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 4 executed · 61.9s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 46700-1792554997213667400-1 Output shortened. The artifact is under linux/x86_64 because the build ran in the Linux container.
documents.s: Worked example: a library with tests

documents.t: Output Contents nuget-packages-<version>/ One directory artifact with every packable project's .nupkg reports/junit.xml All TRX results converted to JUnit, keeping class names, failures and skips Dependency record SDK version used, lock digests, each restored package's digest and audit findings The version is a snapshot from your declared version and Git history, passed to restore, build and pack as -p:Version. See version inference.

You see Cause Fix Several entry candidates named More than one solution or project in the folder Set with.project in build.yaml No installed SDK satisfies the request global.json asks for an SDK the locked one doesn't satisfy Change global.json, or set a matching [tools] dotnet and run oyzu pin Restore fails under --locked-mode packages.lock.json no longer matches the project's dependencies Update the lock with dotnet restore and commit it NU1503 or an MSBuild SDK not found A NuGet-supplied MSBuild SDK whose version is a property, range or wildcard Write a literal version (Sdk="Name/1.2.3" or msbuild-sdks in global.json) so Oyzu can restore it in preparation Pack fails: no packable project A selection without an application has no packable projects Make the library packable, or build a different target A test fails The test run failed JUnit is kept and the package isn't exported

Linux and Windows x64 native hosts, and Linux x64 containers. macOS builds are unsupported. Isolated restore does not support private feeds, credentials, package source mapping or workloads. Native restore uses your host configuration. Isolated builds do not copy global.json or Directory.Build.* files from above the target folder. VSTest collects coverage; Microsoft.Testing.Platform does not. RID-specific or self-contained publishing, single-file apps, trimming and NativeAOT are unsupported. A repository without a root solution needs with.project. The default SDK, memory and timeout limits and the builder name may still change. See the reference.
.NET reference NuGet sessions: managed NuGet for oyzu exec, separate from builds Build bundles

Oyzu builds Go modules and workspaces from go.mod and go.work alone. It picks the Go version your module asks for, installs it, and runs the native go build, go test, go vet and gofmt commands. It collects the binary, JUnit results and statement coverage into a verified dist/ bundle. Note: The Go builder is experimental. It runs as the oyzu/go plugin, which has stable releases in the official catalog. Applications build on your machine. Libraries and workspaces build in the isolated executor and need Docker. Supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS is not supported yet. The Go reference has the full details. The tutorial walks through a Go project step by step, including a failing test and reuse.

Project Builder Where it builds A module with a main package (go.mod) go/app On your machine A module with no main package go/app, packaged as a module In the isolated executor (Docker) A workspace (go.work) One target for the workspace In the isolated executor (Docker) Discovery reads files and runs nothing. Go itself decides workspace members, which packages are main, dependencies and cgo during preparation. To package a module as a library even when it also has commands, set uses: go/library in build.yaml. The inferred tasks are plain Go commands: $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 6 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · go/app (6) project:build Inferred · go go build ./... project:format Inferred · go gofmt -w . project:format-check Inferred · go gofmt -l . project:install Inferred · go go mod download project:lint Inferred · go go vet ./... project:test Inferred · go go test ./... format rewrites your files and never runs inside a build. The build uses format-check, which fails when gofmt -l lists anything.

Command What runs oyzu build --plan Nothing. Shows the stages and the Go minimum read from go.mod oyzu build go build with -trimpath and VCS stamping off, then collects the binary oyzu build --full Also go test -json with a coverage profile, go vet and gofmt -l oyzu run test Only the tests, on your machine, writing a test-only dist/ bundle In CI the checks run without --full. Arguments after -- go to the task's command, so you can select tests the Go way: $ oyzu run test -- -run TestGreetingCopy · project · Testing TEST_EVIDENCE: Test evidence project:test Command passed Results 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped Coverage 50.0% of statements (1/2) Acceptance accepted ✓ project · Testing Succeeded (exit 0 after 2.30s) Output shortened. Oyzu adds -json, a fresh -coverprofile and -count=1 to the implicit go test ./..., converts the events to JUnit and keeps Go's coverage profile. Coverage is statement coverage, as Go measures it. If checks.coverageMinimum is above zero, the test action supplies the target's coverage report, and the build fails if that report is missing or below the minimum. See build check requirements.

Native build, vet and format checks can reuse when their admitted reads are complete. Native runtime tests remain unbounded and run again. An incomplete stage also prevents a whole-target shortcut. For eligible isolated go/app stages on Linux, use oyzu build --isolated --no-docker --full --explain. With crun, the execution image and locked tools available, compilation, generated test preparation, tests and exports can reuse. Tests include the whole admitted source view, so a source edit can rerun more than one test stage. Generated manifests and compiled tests are identified handoffs; changed bytes invalidate consumers. Windows and macOS have no complete Go runtime-read backend. See Go stage reads and stage reuse.

Go's own files decide. Oyzu runs Go with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, so Go never downloads a toolchain behind your back. Oyzu selects and installs it instead. The go line in go.mod (or go.work in a workspace) is a minimum. With go 1.22 and nothing else, Oyzu locks the newest stable release of that line. A toolchain line is honored too. The newer of the two lines is the minimum. [tools] go = "1.24" in oyzu.toml picks a release at or above that minimum. The exact choice goes in oyzu.lock with the minimum recorded beside it (for example go-minimum:>=1.22). Commit the lock. The Tools row of each build says what ran: go 1.22.12 already installed detected from go.mod. If you change [tools] go (say to 1.23), the next build refuses to guess and tells you to update the lock: $ oyzu buildCopy ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✗ Tools failed: preparation did not complete <0.1s ✗ TOOL_LOCK_STALE: oyzu:go 1.23; run oyzu pin Next: Run oyzu pin --refresh to refresh the lock, then oyzu install. A request below the module's minimum (here [tools] go = "1.21" with go 1.22) is refused before any work, naming both files: $ oyzu pinCopy ✗ TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT: project: [tools] go = "1.21" in oyzu.toml is below the go minimum 1.22 that go.mod declares (go line); set [tools] go to 1.22 or later in oyzu.toml, or remove it so the native file decides The Go reference has the complete rule, including toolchain lines, workspace files and oyzu.toml values in different folders.

Everything lands in the dist/ bundle. The Outputs section prints each artifact's path, and manifest.json records it with its digest. The bundle layout describes the directories. Output Contents <target>-<version>[.exe] The application binary, or one per named command module-<n>-<version>.zip, .mod, .info For a library: the module archive, its go.mod and proxy metadata reports/junit.xml Test results converted from go test -json reports/coverage.out Go's coverage profile manifest.json Every file with its digest, plus the plan and build evidence Versions are snapshots: 0.0.0-dev.g<source> without a tag, or a tag-derived base with the same suffix. For a /v2 module the snapshot is v2.0.0-dev.g…, so it satisfies Go's module path rules. A snapshot isn't a release; see version inference.

This is the same program as the tutorial: a go.mod with go 1.22, a main.go that prints a greeting, and one test. It lives in examples/builds/go-app/project in the Oyzu repository. Copy it to a new folder outside any other repository and run git init. Preview the build: $ oyzu build --planCopy project · go/app · windows/x86_64 Executor: host Profile: development · local dist only (no difference: the Go compiler always optimizes) Placement: runs on windows/x86_64 · no Docker engine needed · Runs as host processes without a container engine Stage Selection Details build selected Native commands and report bindings resolve during preparation format-check skipped fast local build lint skipped fast local build test skipped fast local build ​ Tool requirements · availability not checked Requirement Kind Constraint Targets Source oyzu:go minimum-version >=1.22 project go.mod go oyzu:go request 1.22 project go.mod (native pin) Output shortened. The application runs as host processes, so no Docker engine is involved. Now build with every check: $ oyzu build --fullCopy Building go-app windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ Tool versions Resolved and locked 3.5s ✓ Tools 1 tool pinned · 0 installed now 0.2s go 1.22.12 already installed detected from go.mod … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ project build go build -trimpath -buildvcs=fals… executed 1.2s ✓ project test go test -json -coverprofile=C:\Us… executed 1.8s ✓ project lint go vet ./... executed 1.1s ✓ project format-check gofmt -l . executed <0.1s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/windows/x86_64/project-0.0.0-dev.g933478b85fef.exe 2.0 MB development ​ Checks selected 3 actions · 3 succeeded ​ Tests run now 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports) Coverage project: 50.0% (1/2 statements) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 4 executed · 9.0s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 60212-1792553348765929400-1 Output shortened. Go 1.22.12 was already in the shared tool store. On a fresh machine the Tools row says it was installed now. Check the result with oyzu inspect dist, as in the tutorial.

A module with no main package, or a go.work workspace, builds in the isolated executor. The plan says so before anything runs: $ oyzu build --planCopy project · go/app · unresolved until executor selection Executor: captured-worker Placement: runs on any platform · Docker engine required · Isolated steps run in the captured worker on a Docker engine Output shortened. Isolated builds download public modules through Oyzu's scoped Go proxy, verify them against go.sum, then build, test, vet and package with no network. They run on the base execution image, which Oyzu pulls on first use. The image has no Go: the Go in oyzu.lock is restored into each action. See the Go reference.

You see Cause Fix TOOL_LOCK_STALE: oyzu:go …; run oyzu pin (exit 4) [tools] go or the module's go or toolchain line changed since oyzu.lock was written. go get and go mod tidy can rewrite them Run oyzu pin and commit oyzu.lock cannot select oyzu:go for request "…"; declared requirements: >=… from go.mod go The configured Go is below the module's minimum Raise [tools] go, or remove it so go.mod decides format-check fails gofmt -l listed files Run oyzu run format, review the changes, rebuild A test or go vet fails The Go command failed The failure section names the log under dist/logs/ and the command to rerun one target. The previous good binary is kept A library or workspace build can't start its worker The isolated executor needs a running Docker engine, the execution image and Go in oyzu.lock Start Docker, make sure the execution image is available, and run oyzu pin

Private module sources, direct VCS fetches and module publication aren't supported. Cross-compiling with GOOS and GOARCH as a build option isn't supported. Platform matrices select matching provisioned toolchains (toolchain platforms). cgo builds work only through the coarse isolated plan. Full cgo portability isn't supported. Libraries and workspaces need Docker. See capabilities and known limitations for the whole product.
Go reference and Go installation Direct tests: what oyzu run test records Build bundles

Oyzu builds Maven reactors and Gradle builds from pom.xml and build.gradle alone. It provisions the JDK and Maven or Gradle itself, runs your normal lifecycle, collects JUnit and JaCoCo reports and records the jars it produced. You don't need Java installed, and you don't write an Oyzu build file. Note: The Java builder is experimental. It runs as the oyzu/java plugin, whose one build kind, java/app, covers Maven, Gradle and Ant. Maven and Gradle build on your machine with the tools Oyzu provisions. Ant builds on your machine once you provide Ant and its reporting libraries, or in the isolated executor. Supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS is not supported yet.

Signal in your project What it decides pom.xml A java/app target built with Maven.
