A reactor (parent POM with <modules>) is one target, and Maven owns module order, inheritance and profiles build.gradle or build.gradle.kts A java/app target built with Gradle. A multi-project build, including includeBuild composites, is one target, and Gradle owns membership and task dependencies build.xml A java/app target built with Ant, natively with Ant provisioned by you or in the isolated executor mvnw or gradlew committed Oyzu runs the wrapper instead of mvn or gradle and provisions only the JDK Literal root Maven compiler-plugin release/source/target or corresponding maven.compiler.* properties The compiler JDK floor; java.version alone is only a default hint JavaLanguageVersion.of(…) or sourceCompatibility in the root Gradle build script The static startup JDK minimum; nested compilers are checked through Gradle during native preparation toolchainVersion in gradle/gradle-daemon-jvm.properties The exact daemon Java feature release; unrelated sibling scripts do not contribute requirements Discovery reads files only. It doesn't start Maven or Gradle. Gradle also supports Kotlin JVM single and multi-project builds applying org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm, with Kotlin DSL scripts, JUnit 5 and JaCoCo coverage of Kotlin classes. Java lint and format tools skip Kotlin-only targets with an explicit reason and check Java files in mixed targets. Kapt/KSP, Kotlin Multiplatform and Android are outside this support. Use a matching Java plugin release with the gradle-kotlin-jvm capability; see Kotlin JVM projects.

A folder with build files for two tools, such as a pom.xml beside a build.xml, stops discovery and asks you to choose. Declare the target and name the build tool: builds: app: uses: java/app with: build-tool: maven build-tool takes maven, gradle or ant, and it's the only with option for java/app. oyzu build --plan shows the decision as the build-tool row of the target's Discovered table.

The example is examples/builds/java-maven-reactor from the Oyzu repository. Copy it to an empty folder and run git init. It's a reactor with two modules, library and app, each with a JUnit 5 test. The root POM declares <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release>. $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 6 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · java/app (6) project:build Inferred · maven mvn -B verify project:format Inferred · maven java OyzuJavaQuality.java format project:format-check Inferred · maven java OyzuJavaQuality.java format-check project:install Inferred · maven mvn -B dependency:go-offline project:lint Inferred · maven java OyzuJavaQuality.java lint project:test Inferred · maven mvn -B test test is a development task, not a build stage, because mvn verify already runs your tests. oyzu build --plan shows Executor: host, so Maven runs directly on your machine with no Docker, and names where the JDK floor came from: $ oyzu build --planCopy Tool requirements · availability not checked Requirement Kind Constraint Targets Source oyzu:java minimum-version >=17.0.0 project pom.xml properties.maven.compiler.release oyzu:java tool from configuration / native project JDK for the selected Maven build stages oyzu:maven tool from configuration / native project Apache Maven for the selected build stages Output shortened. Now build: $ oyzu buildCopy Building java-maven-reactor windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · fast ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ Tools 2 tools pinned · 0 installed now 0.2s java 17.0.20 already installed detected from pom.xml maven 3.9.16 already installed detected from pom.xml … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ project build mvn -B -ntp org.jacoco:jacoco-maven-plug… executed 19.0s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/windows/x86_64/library-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar 1.8 KB development project dist/project/windows/x86_64/app-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar 1.9 KB development ​ Tests run now 2 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (2 collected reports) Coverage project: 50.0% (1/2 lines) Coverage project: 66.7% (2/3 lines) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 1 executed · 22.0s Output shortened. Oyzu selected JDK 17 from the POM and Maven 3.9, locked them in oyzu.lock, and ran one Maven verify with JaCoCo around it. Each module's Surefire XML and JaCoCo report were collected (one coverage line per module), and both jars were published to dist/ because every test passed. Your checkout isn't modified, because the build runs in a private workspace. On a fresh machine, the first build downloads the JDK and Maven first.

The example is examples/builds/java-gradle-multi-project: an app and a library subproject plus an included support build. rootProject.name = "oyzu-gradle-example" include("app", "library") includeBuild("support") $ oyzu buildCopy ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Tools 2 tools pinned · 0 installed now 0.4s gradle 8.14.6 already installed detected from build.gradle java 17.0.20 already installed detected from build.gradle … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ project build gradle -I C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\T… executed 16.4s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/windows/x86_64/app.jar 820 B development project dist/project/windows/x86_64/library.jar 729 B development project dist/project/windows/x86_64/support-0.1.0.jar 717 B development ​ Tests run now 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports) Coverage project: 50.0% (1/2 lines) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 1 executed · 55.9s Output shortened. Oyzu reads Gradle's own model through an Oyzu-supplied init script, which reports each project's archive and test tasks. It then runs gradle --no-daemon build with an init script (-I) that applies JaCoCo, and publishes the jars the model reported, including the included build's support-0.1.0.jar. Only library has tests, so there's one report.

You don't configure tests or reports. Maven. verify runs Surefire and, where a module declares maven-failsafe-plugin and has IT*, *IT or *ITCase classes, Failsafe. Each module with test sources must produce JUnit XML in target/surefire-reports (and target/failsafe-reports). JaCoCo 0.8.13 runs around verify, and each module's target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml is collected. Gradle. build runs your Test tasks. Oyzu collects each tested project's JUnit results and the JaCoCo report its init script writes under build/reports/oyzu/<test task>/jacoco.xml. A failing test fails the build with the native output and publishes no jars. A module with test sources but no XML (for example because tests were skipped) fails its report requirement. Oyzu never invents a passing report. To run only the tests on your machine and collect the same reports into a test-only bundle, use oyzu run test and then oyzu inspect dist. That path needs Maven or Gradle and the JDK already provisioned, and it runs them offline. See Maven and Gradle.

lint and format-check are build stages, selected by --full or a CI context. The defaults are Checkstyle 10.26.1 (unused and redundant imports, empty statements, equals and hashCode consistency) and google-java-format 1.28.0. They check .java files under the target and skip target, build, .gradle, out, dist and similar directories. format rewrites files and runs only when you ask: oyzu run format. Run oyzu pin to record the exact quality set in oyzu.lock. Preparation installs it in the shared tool store for local tasks and full builds; isolated builds restore the same installation read-only. No separate quality-tool home or provisioning script is needed. Offline runs need those locked tools already available in the same store. An existing lock keeps its checker versions and default rules after you update Oyzu. Use oyzu pin --refresh or a whole-project oyzu update to adopt the defaults shipped by the current CLI. Downloads are verified at installation, and installed tools are trusted on reuse. If the project already uses Checkstyle or Spotless, replace the defaults in oyzu.toml. The native tasks must exist in your project: [tasks.lint] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "checkstyleMain", "checkstyleTest"] [tasks.format-check] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "spotlessCheck"] Oyzu doesn't infer Maven quality-plugin bindings or Gradle quality tasks, read your own Checkstyle XML, or run Kotlin or Groovy linters. See Java quality.

Native files come first, then oyzu.toml. The result is always recorded in oyzu.lock. Tool Default request Override JDK The root Maven compiler floor or Gradle Java level, raised to 17 if lower. Maven java.version alone is a default hint; otherwise Maven uses lts [tools] java Maven 3.9 [tools] maven Gradle Gradle 8, or 9 when the project declares a Java level above 24 [tools] gradle The declared level is a floor. A project declaring release 21 gets JDK 21, not the newest JDK. A project declaring 8 or 11 gets JDK 17, the oldest JDK that Maven, Gradle and Oyzu's Java support run on. JDK 17 compiles the older level correctly with --release. Maven configuration wins over its corresponding root property, then release overrides both source and target. Without release, the higher source/target floor chooses the default. Canonical same-parameter references to literal root properties work without general interpolation. Literal release configuration requires a canonical compiler-plugin 3.x declaration at version 3.6 or newer. Relevant managed/profile/execution/test/toolchain overrides stop with a precise inference limitation; discovery does not evaluate parent or module POMs. See the full selection rules. To choose explicitly: [tools] java = "21" # latest 21.x, "lts", or an exact "21.0.8" maven = "3.9" # or gradle = "8" oyzu pin --dry-run previews what would be locked, and in an activated shell mvn -version runs the locked Maven. JDKs are Eclipse Temurin, checked against the SHA-256 the Adoptium API declares. Maven comes from the Apache distribution server and Gradle from services.gradle.org, each checked against its published digest. A build sees JAVA_HOME, MAVEN_HOME and GRADLE_HOME from these tools only. It never inherits a machine-wide JDK. See Java, Maven and Gradle installation. Wrappers. With a committed mvnw or gradlew, Oyzu runs the wrapper and provisions only the JDK. The wrapper downloads its own Maven or Gradle outside Oyzu's checks, so pin distributionSha256Sum in maven-wrapper.properties or gradle-wrapper.properties. The Maven wrapper's only-script form also needs curl or wget on PATH.
documents.s: Choose the JDK, Maven and Gradle

documents.t: Project What lands in dist/ Maven reactor (native build) Each module's jar under its own name, such as library-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar Gradle build (native build) Each archive Gradle's model reports, such as app.jar and support-0.1.0.jar. Same-named archives are prefixed with the project path Isolated Maven or Gradle build pom, jar and war (Maven) or JAR, WAR, EAR, ZIP and TAR archives (Gradle), with snapshot versions from version inference written into private copies of your build files dist/manifest.json records every artifact with its digest, the tests and coverage, and the logs. oyzu inspect dist verifies them. A build artifact isn't a publication or release approval.

oyzu build runs Maven and Gradle on your machine when the project fits: Maven. A reactor whose jar names can be read from the POMs (literal or inherited versions, jar packaging, no finalName or classifier). Gradle. Any build whose archives Gradle's model reports. Request captured execution with oyzu build --isolated --full. On Linux, --no-docker selects crun, a container runtime that needs no Docker daemon. Docker is the other executor. Both need the base execution image. The JDK and Maven or Gradle come from oyzu.lock; the image has no JDK. A selected JDK older than 17 is refused with TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION. Ant's pinned integration files are fetched and restored for captured builds. Ant also supports native builds with the Ant prerequisites. Oyzu locks and installs Ant itself, so ANT_HOME is only needed when you run Ant outside oyzu.

On Linux, oyzu build --isolated --no-docker --explain uses crun to restrict the lifecycle to identified source, dependencies, locked tools and earlier outputs. An unchanged Maven verify or Gradle coupled lifecycle can reuse its compilation, archives and test/coverage evidence together. Bounded archive exports follow their producers. Preparation and current report checks still apply, and restored tests are labelled as earlier evidence. With a compatible Java plugin, eligible Maven modules and Gradle projects reuse independently along native dependency edges. An unchanged rebuild reuses every module; editing a leaf reruns that module, while editing a base reruns its dependents. Shared build definitions invalidate all modules, and unbounded module views retain the whole lifecycle. Ant keeps its selected targets together. Native lifecycle reads remain incomplete and run again, including on Windows. Docker does not inherit crun's complete-read guarantee. See Maven reuse, Gradle reuse and stage reuse.

Symptom Cause Fix QUALITY_LOCK_REQUIRED The project has no locked default quality set Run oyzu pin, then retry; see Java quality Build fails with a JUnit failure and no jars in Outputs A test failed, and jars are never published from a failing build Fix the test. The Surefire output and log path are in the failure section A module fails its report requirement Test sources exist but no JUnit XML was produced (skipped tests, disabled reporting, or a custom report directory) Let the tests run, or move reports to the default directory. Custom report directories aren't collected on the native path Dependency or JaCoCo download fails Maven Central was throttled or unreachable. Coverage tooling is fetched by Maven or Gradle Retry. --offline builds need those artifacts already in the local repository TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION An isolated build selected a JDK below 17 Remove the low [tools] java pin. JDK 17 compiles older --release levels Native Ant preparation says Ant metadata needs ANT_HOME The command ran outside Oyzu's tool selection, so no Ant was set up Run it through oyzu (or an activated shell), or set ANT_HOME; provide the reporting libraries for tests Gradle refuses the daemon JDK vendor gradle-daemon-jvm.properties names a vendor other than Adoptium (isolated builds) Use Temurin, or provision a matching runtime yourself For anything else, start with the Log path in the failure section and Troubleshooting.

Native Maven/Gradle lifecycle and Checkstyle stages rerun because their complete reads are not reported; whole-target reuse cannot skip them. The default google-java-format check can reuse independently with a compatible plugin/CLI. Its managed JDK identity is bound from oyzu.lock: changing that identity invalidates formatter reuse even with unchanged Java source. This does not make lifecycle reads complete. Use oyzu build --explain; see Java cache limits. Default Java quality tools must be locked with oyzu pin before use. Private dependency and plugin repositories use oyzu build --full in host mode with native Maven settings or Gradle credentials. Standalone credentials are unsupported in captured and isolated builds. See Maven private repositories and Gradle private repositories. Custom JaCoCo destinations, aggregate reactor coverage and custom test report directories aren't collected. Isolated lifecycle reuse requires Linux crun and a compatible plugin. Shared controls or source links can retain the whole Maven/Gradle lifecycle. A green build shows that the stages passed on this source. It isn't a release approval.
Maven · Gradle · Ant · Java quality Java, Maven and Gradle installation · Native host builds · Version inference Recipes: Maven application · Maven reactor · Gradle application · Ant application

Oyzu finds Node packages and workspaces from package.json, the lockfile and your native configuration, so you don't need an Oyzu build file. It installs the Node version your project asks for, runs your build, tests, lint and format checks, and collects JUnit and LCOV reports and the packed or built output in a verified dist/ bundle. Note: The Node builder is experimental. It runs as the oyzu/node plugin. It supports npm, pnpm and Yarn (Classic 1.22.22 and Berry 4.17.1 with nodeLinker: node-modules), with different limits for each (see Limits). Supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS is not supported yet.

Discovery reads files only. It never runs npm, project scripts or configuration code. Signal in your project What it decides package.json A Node target. Packages are discovered as node/app. Set uses: node/package in build.yaml to force package behavior package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock The package manager: npm, pnpm or Yarn packageManager in package.json The manager and, for an exact npm or pnpm release, the version to pin workspaces in package.json, or pnpm-workspace.yaml A workspace, built as one target scripts.build, scripts.test, scripts.lint, format-check or format:check The commands for those stages. Root scripts always win over Oyzu's defaults A node --test, Jest, Vitest or Mocha script, configuration or dependency The test framework, which decides how JUnit and coverage are collected eslint.config.*, .prettierrc*, biome.json The linter and formatter. ESLint and Prettier are the defaults, and biome.json selects Biome for both A vite build script A Vite application, whose dist/ output becomes a directory artifact engines.node A constraint every Node version Oyzu selects must satisfy Dependency preparation does not require Node test files in every package. An explicit test script can report zero tests; required report checks still apply. Implicit workspace Node suites without owned files are omitted with an informational “no tests” note in human output and JSON diagnostic events (not a warning). Explicit framework selection still requires owned files; neither path recursively discovers another member's tests. See workspace test bundles. When two equally strong signals disagree (for example two test frameworks), discovery fails and the error names the with: setting to add in build.yaml, such as with: {test-framework: mocha}. See discovery and selection.

The example is examples/builds/node-package/project from the Oyzu repository. Copy it to an empty folder and run git init. It's a package with a build script and node:test tests: { "name": "oyzu-example-package", "version": "0.1.0", "private": false, "type": "module", "scripts": { "build": "node build.mjs", "test": "node --test" }, "engines": { "node": ">=22" }, "files": ["dist"], "exports": "./dist/greeting.mjs" } oyzu run list shows what Oyzu will run: $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 6 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · node/app (6) project:build Inferred · npm npm run build project:format Inferred · npm prettier --write . project:format-check Inferred · npm prettier --check . project:install Inferred · npm npm ci project:lint Inferred · npm eslint . project:test Inferred · npm npm run test oyzu run <task> runs one of these on your machine with your installed dependencies. oyzu build also records artifacts and reports. This single-root npm package builds natively by default; --isolated selects the offline worker. oyzu build --plan lists every decision Oyzu made and why: $ oyzu build --planCopy Discovered Selection Reason formatter prettier default, no stronger evidence linter eslint default, no stronger evidence output-profile native-package default, no stronger evidence package-manager npm native package-lock.json lockfile test-framework node-test declared package.json /scripts/test Output shortened. A plain local oyzu build skips checks unless they are required. It projects the version in a private copy, builds and packs the package: $ oyzu buildCopy -- Outputs --------------------------------------------------------------------- project dist/project/linux/x86_64/oyzu-example-package-0.1.0-dev.g25bee662058d.tgz 353 B development Checks not requested project: format-check, lint, test ​ ok Build succeeded 1 target · 3 executed · 4.6s Output shortened. oyzu inspect dist verifies the archive against its recorded digest. Commit oyzu.lock and keep dist/ out of version control.

oyzu build --full selects tests, lint and formatting. A failed check blocks packaging and keeps its reports. Required checks also apply to a fast build; omitting --full does not waive them. Project-installed checkers take precedence over the managed defaults. A declared checker that is missing fails instead of silently selecting another version. The Node quality reference describes tool selection and configuration.

The plan's Executor: line tells you. For an isolated build it is captured-worker: Oyzu copies your source, downloads the locked dependencies through its broker, then runs every action in a sandbox with no network. Windows x64 needs a running Docker engine for this. macOS is unsupported. Linux uses Docker when an engine answers. Otherwise it uses the daemonless crun sandbox, which needs unprivileged user namespaces. --no-docker (or OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1) forces crun. The build.isolation setting in oyzu.toml chooses between them; see configuration. Image. Every manager runs on the base execution image, which Oyzu pulls on first use. Node and npm, pnpm or Yarn come from oyzu.lock, and the pnpm and Yarn lockfile parsers ship in the Node plugin. To run on your own image instead, pass --image npm=<image> (or pnpm=, yarn=). Some applications build directly on your machine and need no Docker: npm and pnpm applications whose build writes the conventional dist/ directory (for example a Vite app), single-root Yarn applications, and explicitly declared single-root npm packages. Oyzu installs Node itself for these. See native host builds and Node applications. Native lifecycle scripts can read arbitrary files without a complete read report, so these stages run again even with unchanged source. Whole-target cache reuse cannot bypass them. oyzu build --explain names the refusal; download caches remain available. Captured actions have separate confinement and reuse rules. See native npm caching.

On Linux, oyzu build app --isolated --no-docker --full --explain uses crun, a rootless container runtime, to enforce a complete input boundary. Eligible npm install, build and test stages can reuse outputs and reports. A bounded script-free install can survive a source edit; install scripts or uncertain environment reads require installation again. Build and test version inputs remain keyed. You need the execution image, locked tools and prepared dependencies even on a hit. Package-local npm, pnpm and Yarn Classic workspaces can reuse member build/test actions independently on Linux crun. Native dependency edges determine which members rerun after source edits. A metadata-only package.json edit behaves differently by manager: npm and Yarn Classic can keep an untouched leaf's build/test keys if shared installation output stays byte-identical; the edited member and dependents rerun. pnpm bookkeeping can instead rerun every member, even with unchanged module bytes. Shared root configuration and opaque root scripts retain workspace-wide reads. Other executors refuse member reuse. See workspace reuse for supported links, configuration and plugin requirements.

On Linux you can ask a plain oyzu build to run Node applications in the crun sandbox, so eligible install, build and test stages can reuse. This is a preview: set it only where you want to try it. Set it in oyzu.toml: [build] isolation = "crun" Oyzu moves the build to the sandbox only when all of these hold; otherwise the build stays native and nothing changes: every selected target is an npm application (node/app). pnpm and Yarn single-root applications stay native: under crun they build but never reuse; the root package.json declares none of the install scripts npm runs (predependencies, dependencies, postdependencies, preinstall, install, postinstall, prepublish, preprepare, prepare, postprepare), there is no binding.gyp, no .pnpmfile.cjs, and the project is neither a workspace nor a workspace member (a workspaces field or pnpm-workspace.yaml in the project or a parent directory up to the repository root; a project that is itself the repository root has no parents to check); oyzu.lock does not pin an Oyzu engine, which only oyzu build --isolated installs (a missing lock counts as unpinned); crun works on this host. A missing, unreadable, malformed or oversized (over 16 MiB) package.json, the same for a parent package.json in the workspace check, or an unreadable or malformed oyzu.lock, also keeps the build native. The check covers install scripts in the root package.json only: Yarn plugins, an .npmrc that needs a private registry and similar network needs are not detected, and such a build fails in the sandbox because it has no network. Remove the setting for those projects. The sandbox has no network, so a build step that downloads anything fails there where the native build would have succeeded; remove the setting for such projects. Dependency install scripts are only known after install, so they run in the sandbox without reuse. A selection that mixes in other ecosystems stays native. Check with oyzu build --explain: an isolated run names crun as its executor. When the setting is on but a build stays native, Oyzu prints NODE_CRUN_NOT_APPLIED with the conditions above. This is opt-in; plain builds are native unless you set it. Native Windows Vite builds have no merged complete-read backend. Incomplete script reads make stages run again, and clearing the cache cannot change that. The Linux command above requires a Linux host. See stage reuse and Node read boundaries.
documents.s: Reuse on a plain oyzu build

documents.t: An npm workspace root is one target, and each member becomes its own versioned package. examples/builds/node-workspace has a private root and two members, @oyzu-example/shared and @oyzu-example/app, where app depends on shared: { "name": "oyzu-workspace", "version": "0.1.0", "private": true, "workspaces": ["packages/*"] } $ oyzu build --fullCopy ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project 367 B development dist/project/linux/x86_64/oyzu-example-shared-0.1.0-dev.gfe03e51cecc5.tgz project 346 B development dist/project/linux/x86_64/oyzu-example-app-0.1.0-dev.gfe03e51cecc5.tgz ​ Checks selected 3 actions · 3 succeeded ​ Tests run now 2 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (2 collected reports) Coverage project: 100.0% (1/1 lines) Coverage project: 100.0% (1/1 lines) Output shortened. Each member got its own archive and its own JUnit and LCOV pair. Inside the archives, app's dependency on shared points at shared's snapshot version. The private root produced no package. How the work is divided: Stage Root script present No root script build Runs once with npm's lifecycle hooks Each member's build script, in dependency order test Runs once and owns one report pair Each member's script or detected test framework, with its own reports lint, format-check Runs once Root-owned files are checked by default. Each member uses its script or the default tool A failed member build stops its dependents. Test and quality failures continue through the other members so you see every problem, then fail the build. Every member needs a distinct package name and a real version (see member names). pnpm workspaces (pnpm-workspace.yaml with packages) and Yarn workspaces use the same planner with their own installation and packing. Their isolated builds use the same execution image. See npm workspaces, pnpm and Yarn.

You don't configure reporting. Oyzu instruments the detected framework and collects JUnit and LCOV for every package: Framework Detected from Notes Node's test runner A node --test script, or the default Oyzu passes Node 22 flags, so pin Node 22 or later when tests run Jest Script, configuration or dependency Jest 29 is supported Vitest Script, configuration or dependency Needs its matching coverage provider installed. Runs with one worker Mocha mocha script, .mocharc*, package.json section or dependency Mocha with c8 for coverage. See Mocha Reports land under dist/<target>/<platform>/reports/, with digests and summaries in dist/manifest.json. A failed test blocks packaging but keeps its reports. For a native npm, pnpm 10 or Yarn Classic root workspace application, declare uses: node/app in build.yaml and run oyzu build --full. The root build produces one application directory; without a root test script, each member's Vitest or Jest suite contributes distinct JUnit and LCOV reports. A root test script keeps aggregate ownership. Missing required reports fail the build. Native lifecycle stages with incomplete reads execute again on unchanged builds. Windows workspace application tests remain unverified. See full workspace application builds. To get the same reports without a full build, run the tests directly on your machine: oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist This writes a test-only dist/ bundle from your installed dependencies. It packages nothing and doesn't isolate the run. See direct tests and workspace test bundles.

lint and format-check are build stages, selected by --full or a CI context. format writes files, so it's never part of a build. Run it yourself with oyzu run format. Tool Default version Behavior ESLint 10.13.0 Uses your configuration when present, recommended JS/TS rules otherwise. Never fixes Prettier 3.9.10 Uses your configuration, .editorconfig and ignore files Biome 2.5.15 Selected by biome.json or biome.jsonc for both roles A tool your project installs wins over the default. A tool you declare but haven't installed fails instead of silently using another version. The defaults check JavaScript and TypeScript sources only and skip node_modules, dist, build and coverage output. To pass your own flags, write a script ("lint": "eslint . --max-warnings 0"), because the defaults reject extra arguments. See Node quality.

oyzu build --plan ends each Node target with a Static analysis section. For each stage it lists the files the stage is predicted to read and write, the tools it needs and anything it couldn't bound, each with a confidence level and a file:line source. It parses files and runs no project code. An excerpt: $ oyzu build --planCopy project:build · confidence: over-approximate · scope: predicted 9 exact, 1 over-approximate, 0 unknown Reads Path or name Confidence Source Why package-lock.json exact package-lock.json lockfile package.json exact package.json manifest src/greeting.mjs exact build.mjs:3 file-read · copyFileSync Writes Path or name Confidence Source Why dist/greeting.mjs exact build.mjs:3 file-write · copyFileSync Narrow the view with --stage <name>, ask about one file with --why <path>, list only the uncertain facts with --unknown, or skip the analysis with --no-analysis. All of these need --plan. The analysis also runs rules that catch problems visible only across files: phantom-dependency, escaping-reference, undeclared-env, public-env-secret-name, exports-target-missing, lockfile-manifest-drift and others. They're advisory by default. oyzu build --check applies them without preparing or running anything: $ oyzu build --checkCopy ✓ Check passed: no blocking findings Static analysis only: nothing was installed, downloaded or executed. To make a rule fail builds, set its level in oyzu.toml: [analysis.rules] phantom-dependency = "enforce" # off | advisory (default) | enforce [[analysis.suppress]] rule = "escaping-reference" path = "legacy/**" reason = "vendored fork, tracked in the migration plan" Only a warning backed entirely by exact facts can block. See Node static analysis for every rule and its limits.

Native files come first. Oyzu reads them in this order: packageManager in package.json. An exact stable npm or pnpm release ("packageManager": "pnpm@10.20.0") becomes a tool requirement and is locked beside Node. A Corepack +sha512.… suffix is accepted and ignored. Ranges and tags select nothing. Yarn is pinned the same way with an exact yarn@1.22.22 or yarn@4.17.1; see managed Yarn. engines.node limits every Node selection. It doesn't pick one. No pin. The default is lts: the newest LTS release that satisfies every engine constraint, or the newest stable release if no LTS release does. In the run above, >=22 selected 24.22.0. oyzu.toml, to choose explicitly. It must agree with packageManager and satisfy engines.node: [tools] node = "22.12" npm = "11.6.2" # or pnpm = "10.20.0" The nearest .nvmrc or .node-version up to the project root supplies an explicit version request. Without either file, an exact devEngines.runtime version is used. Aliases such as lts/* are refused; [tools] node must agree with a native pin. The first build writes the exact choices to oyzu.lock, and later builds reuse them, including offline. oyzu pin --dry-run previews what would be locked, and oyzu install node@22.12 declares, locks and installs in one step. The isolated worker restores the locked Node and npm, pnpm or Yarn. The execution image has no copies of its own. See Manage your first tool, Node selection and npm and pnpm installation.
documents.s: Pin Node and the package manager

documents.t: Project Artifact Package (npm, pnpm, Yarn) An npm pack-style .tgz named <name>-<version>-dev.g<source>.tgz. The embedded package.json carries the same version Workspace One .tgz per member, plus one for a publishable (non-private) root node/app with Vite or a dist/ build script A directory artifact application-<version> holding the built output. A configured Vite build also records the resolved output metadata Versions come from your version field, Git tags and commits; see version inference. Artifacts appear only when every required stage passed. Creating an artifact never publishes it.

A test fails. If you change the greeting in the example and rebuild, the other checks still run so you see every problem, but package is blocked because no artifact comes from a failing build: $ oyzu build --fullCopy ✗ project test npm run test -- --experi… failed 1.5s · 1 warning ✓ project lint node /oyzu/node-quality.mjs lint executed 4.3s ✓ project format-check node /oyzu/node-quality.mjs forma… executed 1.1s ⊘ project package needs project · test ​ ── Failure: project · test ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── actual: 'Hi, world!', expected: 'Hello, world!', Exit 1 Log dist/logs/0003.stderr Next oyzu build project re-run only this target ​ ✗ Build failed 1 failed · 1 blocked · 5 succeeded · 17.8s Output shortened. The exit status is 1, and the full log is at the path shown. Symptom Cause Fix NPM_WORKSPACE_MEMBER_NAMES Two members (or a publishable root and a member) share a package name, or a member's version is latest Rename them so each name is used once, or mark the root "private": true. Give each member a real semver version. "private": true on a member doesn't exclude it. See member names npm, pnpm or Yarn rejects the lock during preparation The lockfile no longer matches package.json Regenerate the lock with your package manager, commit it and rebuild. The lockfile-manifest-drift rule in --plan often shows the exact entry pnpm capture does not yet support configuration <key> in <file> A pnpm setting outside the supported list, such as hoistPattern or nodeLinker. .npmrc and .pnpmfile.cjs aren't supported either Remove the setting. catalog, catalogs, overrides, patchedDependencies, minimumReleaseAge, allowBuilds and trustPolicy are supported. See pnpm workspace settings Yarn capture does not yet support <file> setting <key> A setting outside the supported subset. .yarnrc.yml is Yarn Berry configuration Use a supported Yarn Classic setting, or use a Berry project that meets the Berry limits. There is no automatic PnP conversion Lint fails with a missing tool Your package.json declares ESLint, Prettier or Biome but it isn't installed Install the project's dependencies with its package manager and retry Discovery fails on conflicting evidence Two linters, formatters or test frameworks claim the same role Remove one configuration, or select one in build.yaml with with: {linter: <name>}, with: {formatter: <name>} or with: {test-framework: <name>} Test stage fails with bad option Node is pinned below 22, and Oyzu's reporting passes Node 22 flags Pin Node 22 or later NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON (exit 3) No Docker engine for the isolated worker Start Docker. On Linux, use the crun sandbox NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES (exit 3) crun can't create user namespaces on this Linux host Allow unprivileged user namespaces, or use a host with Docker TOOL_LTS_METADATA_UNAVAILABLE An organization catalog has no LTS markers for the lts default Pin an approved exact version or a named line such as lts/krypton For anything else, start with the Log path in the failure section and Troubleshooting.

Yarn Berry support is for exact 4.17.1 with a literal nodeLinker: node-modules. Single-root applications work natively and in the isolated executor. Workspace packages work natively only (publishable root, app and shared members, or a named private root). Pack hooks are limited to analyzed local copy and helper scripts. PnP, aggregates, project plugins, yarnPath and custom or non-registry sources aren't supported. Yarn Classic 1.22.22 supports single-root applications natively and in the isolated executor. Classic workspace packages work natively only, with a private root and members. Project plugins, custom registries and extra rc settings aren't supported. pnpm isolated builds support pnpm 10.11.0. Vite builds need one written Vite 8 client environment. SSR, library, watch, multiple-environment and no-write modes fail with an explicit message. npm TypeScript workspaces work natively on Linux (x86-64) with a literal tsc -p tsconfig.json and noEmitOnError. Native version files need explicit versions; aliases such as lts/* are unsupported. Cyclic workspace graphs, affected selection inside a workspace and member task groups aren't supported. Default lint and formatting cover JavaScript and TypeScript only, not JSON, CSS or other files. A green build shows that the stages passed on this source. It isn't a release approval.

Node applications · npm workspaces · pnpm · Yarn Node quality · Mocha · Workspace test bundles · Node static analysis npm and pnpm installation · Native host builds · Build bundles Recipes: npm application · npm package · pnpm application · pnpm workspace · Yarn Classic application · all Node examples

Static PEP 621 python/app projects using pip can build natively on Windows x64 with a matching native plugin and managed CPython. Core prepares the original wheel closure through its broker; pip has no socket transport. The build then installs and uses that closure offline to produce a .pyz, wheel and sdist, and tests the extracted application. Native closure reuse is not yet supported, so this build path currently refuses --offline. See the application reference. Oyzu builds Python distributions from pyproject.toml, uv.lock, poetry.lock or requirements.txt. It selects and installs CPython for you, builds wheels with your own backend, runs pytest with JUnit and Cobertura coverage, and checks your code with Ruff. You don't write an Oyzu build file for a package. Note: The Python builder is experimental. It runs as the oyzu/python plugin. If no release of it is available to your installation, the build stops with PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE. Supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS is not supported yet. Which of two paths your project takes matters: Native (on your machine): pip projects with a pyproject.toml, and Linux uv package projects with uv.lock. Oyzu installs CPython and builds the distribution. No Docker. Isolated (in a Linux container): Poetry, requirements-only and legacy projects, uv applications or projects without uv.lock, and anything you request with --isolated. Dependencies are downloaded first, and every action runs offline. This needs Docker and the base execution image, with CPython in oyzu.lock. uv is restored from oyzu.lock; Poetry builds need an image of your own with Poetry installed, passed with --image poetry=<ref>. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Native pip and uv package builds also use private indexes through the native tool's configuration. pip supports pip.conf, PIP_INDEX_URL, PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL and user .netrc; uv supports uv.toml or [[tool.uv.index]] with named-index username/password environment variables. Keep credentials in user configuration or environment variables. Tracked native config files containing literal credentials are refused before source is copied; environment references are kept unchanged. Captured and isolated Python builds refuse unsupported private-index preparation before actions run. See private indexes in host builds for prerequisites and limits. Signal in your project What it decides pyproject.toml with [build-system] A python/package target built with pip through your declared PEP 517 backend uv.lock uv manages the project, and the lock's hashed export owns the dependency set poetry.lock Poetry manages the project requirements.txt only A requirements-only application, with no invented distribution metadata uses: python/app in build.yaml with one [project.scripts] entry An application. Native static pip and isolated builds produce a runnable .pyz requires-python A constraint every selected CPython must satisfy .python-version The default CPython request pytest.ini, [tool.pytest.ini_options], [pytest] in tox.ini, [tool:pytest] in setup.cfg pytest configuration (pytest is the default either way) Discovery reads files only. It never imports conftest.py, runs Python or collects tests.

The example is examples/builds/python-api from the Oyzu repository. Copy it to an empty folder and run git init. It's a small setuptools project with one console script and two unittest tests that pytest runs: [project] name = "oyzu-api-example" version = "0.1.0" requires-python = ">=3.10" dependencies = [] [project.scripts] oyzu-example-api = "api:main" [build-system] requires = ["setuptools==80.9.0"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" Its build.yaml contains only uses: python/app for the api target. $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 5 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command api · python/app (5) api:build Inferred · pip python -m build api:format Inferred · pip ruff format . api:format-check Inferred · pip ruff format --check . api:lint Inferred · pip ruff check . --no-fix api:test Inferred · pip python -m pytest oyzu build --plan shows Executor: host, which means the native pip path. The only tool requirement is CPython, constrained by requires-python: $ oyzu build --planCopy Discovered Selection Reason formatter ruff default, no stronger evidence linter ruff default, no stronger evidence package-manager pip default, no stronger evidence test-framework pytest default, no stronger evidence ​ Tool requirements · availability not checked Requirement Kind Constraint Targets Source oyzu:python minimum-version >=3.10.0 api pyproject.toml project.requires-python Output shortened. Now build: $ oyzu buildCopy Building python-api windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · fast ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ Tools 1 tool pinned · 0 installed now 0.2s python 3.15.0 already installed detected from pyproject.toml … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ api build python -m pip wheel --no-deps --wheel-dir \\… executed 16.7s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── api dist/api/windows/x86_64/wheels-0.1.0 1.8 KB development Checks not requested api: format-check, lint, test ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 1 executed · 19.5s Output shortened. Look at the selected interpreter: CPython 3.15.0. With only requires-python = ">=3.10" and no pin, Oyzu picks the newest stable CPython, which can be a very recent release. Pin a version for predictable builds (below). pip then ran its PEP 517 wheel build, downloading the setuptools backend from the package index, and the wheel was published as the directory artifact wheels-0.1.0. The native path produces a wheel only. It doesn't assemble the runnable .pyz application. That's part of the isolated path.
documents.s: Your first build: a pip project

documents.t: oyzu build --full adds test (pytest) and lint and format-check (Ruff). On the native path, Oyzu doesn't install pytest, pytest-cov or Ruff for you, so on a fresh machine the checks fail: $ oyzu build --fullCopy ── Failure: api · test ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pytest' Exit 1 Log dist/logs/0001.stderr Next oyzu build api re-run only this target ​ ── Failure: api · lint ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── cannot execute ruff: program not found ​ ✗ Build failed 3 failed · 1 succeeded · 13.2s Note Local binaries were not updated; existing binaries are from the previous successful build. Output shortened. The wheel built, but required test evidence is missing, so the build fails and Oyzu keeps the previous good outputs. To fix this, create a .venv in the target folder from the Python Oyzu selected, install your dependencies, pytest, pytest-cov, coverage and your quality tools into it, and build again: python -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install pytest pytest-cov coverage ruff # .venv\Scripts\python on Windows # also install your project's own dependencies the usual way oyzu build --full Oyzu checks that the .venv was made from exactly the Python it selected. A .venv made from another Python, or with system site packages, is refused: recreate it from the selected base. Activation, VIRTUAL_ENV and PYTHONPATH don't select the environment. You can also replace a stage's command in oyzu.toml with [tasks.lint] and similar. A replacement test task must still produce the JUnit and coverage reports. See native preparation.
documents.s: Tests and checks on the native path

documents.t: Use oyzu build --isolated --full to follow this example in the isolated executor. A locked uv package otherwise builds natively on Linux x86-64, or Windows x64 with a Python plugin release after 0.1.3 (it reruns every stage there); Poetry and requirements-only projects always use the isolated executor. The example is examples/builds/python-uv-library: a setuptools package with a committed uv.lock and a dev dependency group that holds pytest and pytest-cov. $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 6 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · python/package (6) project:build Inferred · uv uv build project:format Inferred · uv ruff format . project:format-check Inferred · uv ruff format --check . project:install Inferred · uv uv sync --locked project:lint Inferred · uv ruff check . --no-fix project:test Inferred · uv uv run --locked pytest oyzu build --isolated --plan shows Docker engine required. The isolated Python path restores CPython and uv from oyzu.lock into the base execution image. Poetry still needs an image that provides it (--image poetry=<ref>). See manager runtimes. The following excerpt shows isolated placement. $ oyzu build --planCopy project · python/package · unresolved until executor selection Executor: captured-worker Placement: runs on any platform · Docker engine required · Isolated steps run in the captured worker on a Docker engine Discovered Selection Reason package-manager uv native uv.lock lockfile test-framework pytest default, no stronger evidence Output shortened. A full build goes through these stages: prepare downloads binary wheels for the uv export --locked closure, the build backend and the test and quality tools, through Oyzu's broker to public PyPI. Each wheel's digest is recorded. build runs the backend once in a private workspace, with a PEP 440 snapshot version of the form 0.1.0.dev0+g<source>. Your pyproject.toml isn't edited. test installs the built wheel offline and runs pytest against it, so coverage measures the installed package, not your checkout. lint and format-check run Ruff read-only. package publishes the wheel and source distribution once every gate has passed. The example folder contains a .python-version file with 3.12. Without it, requires-python = ">=3.10" selects the newest CPython, and prepare fails with coverage-… is not a supported wheel on this platform, because the lock holds wheels built for Python 3.12. See Choose the Python version.
documents.s: Your first build: a uv project (isolated)

documents.t: Ordinary local captured tests of supported pip packages with flat declarative setuptools layouts use project source through a genuine native editable install. Mark tests and coverage required in oyzu.toml to run them locally without selecting full checks. --full, CI, pull-request and release checks test the built wheel; development-source evidence does not validate that wheel. The supported Linux development route has demonstrated selective case reuse. See test subjects and local invocation for the supported layout, configuration and limits. Host oyzu run test tasks retain the behavior below. pytest is the supported runner, and it also runs unittest.TestCase suites, as in the pip example. Oyzu records JUnit and Cobertura for every build and stores them under dist/, with digests in dist/manifest.json. You don't configure reporting. Manager Development command (oyzu run test) pip python -m pytest uv uv run --locked pytest Poetry poetry run pytest oyzu run test runs on your machine with your installed environment and writes a test-only dist/ bundle. Pass pytest arguments after --, as in oyzu run test -- -k health. pytest, pytest-cov and coverage must already be installed there, because Oyzu doesn't install them for development tasks. pytest owns test collection: testpaths, file patterns, markers and conftest behavior. Your coverage settings, including fail_under, are kept. Expect this behavior: An empty suite keeps pytest's exit code 5 and fails the build. Add tests or fix collection, because an empty directory isn't a passing result. A failed coverage threshold fails the build even when every test passed. Assertion failures keep their reports and block packaging. See Python testing.

Ruff runs ruff check . --no-fix for lint and ruff format --check . for format-check, reading its own configuration as usual. Both are selected by --full or a CI context and never modify files during a build. oyzu run format runs ruff format . and does write files. In the isolated path Ruff is downloaded during preparation. On the native path it must already be installed, as shown above.

Oyzu uses the nearest .python-version up to the project root, or your oyzu.toml request when no native pin applies. The choice must satisfy project.requires-python and native tool.poetry.dependencies.python comparisons when present. Without a request, it selects the newest stable CPython satisfying every constraint. Source Role .python-version (one release such as 3.12 or 3.12.4) The native request; nearby oyzu.toml settings must agree [tools] python in oyzu.toml The request when no native pin applies requires-python in pyproject.toml A constraint every selection must satisfy tool.poetry.dependencies.python in pyproject.toml An additional constraint, using supported PEP 440 comparisons None of these The greatest stable release available Set it in oyzu.toml: [tools] python = "3.12" # latest 3.12.x; ranges such as ">=3.11 <3.14" also work Run oyzu pin --dry-run to preview the choice, or oyzu pin to write oyzu.lock (the next oyzu build also does it). Commit the lock. Pre-releases, free-threaded and debug builds are never selected. A requires-python specifier that uses !=, === or pre-release versions can't be turned into a tool range and fails with the specifier named. Use a supported native range; a configured tool pin does not bypass an unsupported declaration. For Poetry, use a native declaration such as python = ">=3.12,<3.13". Both native ranges apply if you also declare requires-python. Poetry-only caret, tilde, bare wildcard and union forms fail with guidance to use equivalent supported comparisons. A tool pin never overrides those native constraints. Interpreters come from Python Build Standalone for Linux (amd64, arm64), macOS (arm64, amd64) and Windows (amd64), checked against the publisher's checksum manifest. In an activated shell, python --version runs the locked interpreter, and pip runs it with -m pip. Oyzu provisions uv for supported Linux projects and restores its locked release into isolated builds. Poetry still comes from your image. Isolated builds use the locked CPython selected by these same requirements. On Intel macOS you can install Python 3.11 and run pip with it, but wheel builds there aren't supported yet. See Python installation.

Project Artifacts pip with pyproject.toml (native) A wheels-<version> directory holding the built wheel Package (isolated) Wheel and source distribution, named with the PEP 440 snapshot version such as 0.1.0.dev0+g<source> python/app (isolated) Wheel, source distribution and a runnable <target>-<version>.pyz containing the wheel's files and runtime dependencies Requirements-only application (isolated) A .pyz built from app.py or __main__.py, versioned 0.0.0-dev.g<source> Versions come from your static version, Git tags and Conventional Commits; see version inference. A .pyz needs a compatible Python to run, requires pure-Python wheels, and isn't a release approval.

Symptom Cause Fix No module named 'pytest' or cannot execute ruff: program not found in a native --full build The native path doesn't install test or quality tools Create the .venv described above Wheel build fails on Windows with [WinError 3] The system cannot find the path specified under build\bdist.win-amd64 The project is in a very deeply nested folder Move the checkout to a shorter path The build picked a brand-new CPython Nothing pins Python, so the newest stable release wins Add .python-version or [tools] python Poetry lock is missing or stale; update it with poetry lock poetry.lock doesn't match pyproject.toml Run poetry lock and commit the result Direct URL requirements need an approved source adapter A dependency points at a URL or Git source outside uv.lock Use a registry release, or a public GitHub Git source locked by full commit in uv.lock Source package NAME needs build requirement maturin... A dependency must be built from Rust source Not supported. Use a project or version that publishes wheels Dependency group NAME is not defined A [dependency-groups] include names a group that doesn't exist Fix the include. Only the dev group is selected The build fails with no tests run pytest collected nothing (exit 5) Check testpaths and file patterns. Run the manager's test command to see collection --offline build fails fetching the build backend pip downloads the backend during the wheel build Build once online so pip has the backend cached NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON or a missing image The isolated path needs Docker, the execution image and, for Poetry, an image of your own Start Docker, make sure the execution image is available, and pass --image poetry=<ref> for Poetry The full list of preparation errors is in Python preparation. For anything else, start with the Log path in the failure section and Troubleshooting. requirements.txt accepts trailing comments after whitespace and backslash continuations with LF or CRLF line endings. For example, idna==3.10 # runtime keeps the requirement and discards the comment. Includes (-r), constraint files (-c) and alternate-index directives remain unsupported; see Python preparation.

Complete-read Python stage reuse is not yet available. Existing captured preparation and upstream packaging have bounded contracts, but application assembly still embeds the whole-target identity. Do not expect every stage to reuse on an unchanged application build. The supported test-case selection described above is separate from whole-lifecycle reuse. Windows has no merged complete-read backend for native uv builds, and the published Python plugin currently refuses Windows uv before execution. Clearing the cache cannot enable it. See Python reuse limits and the stage-reuse table.

Native pip projects with pyproject.toml produce wheels. Locked uv packages also build natively on Linux x86-64 (and Windows x64 with a plugin release after 0.1.3) and produce wheels and source distributions. The isolated path needs Docker and the base execution image (plus your own image for Poetry). CPython and uv come from the lock. Private package indexes are supported only on the native path; isolated builds take dependencies from public PyPI. On a Windows host, the package stage of isolated builds doesn't export the wheel and source distribution (it stops with No such file or directory or environment variable not found). The checks before it run normally. Source builds of Git, sdist-only and local dependencies work only for uv projects. Poetry and pip Git or path sources are refused. Only the dev dependency group is selected. A green build shows that the stages passed on this source. It isn't a release approval.
Python applications · Python testing · Python preparation · Python containers Python installation · Native host builds · Version inference Recipes: pip package · uv package · Poetry package

Point oyzu build at a folder with a Cargo.toml and it compiles with Cargo, runs your tests with coverage, checks Clippy and rustfmt, and writes a verified dist/ bundle. You don't write any Oyzu configuration for a normal Cargo project. Note: The Rust builder is experimental. It runs as the oyzu/rust plugin, which Oyzu selects and records in oyzu.lock. If no release of it is available to your installation, the build stops with PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE. Supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS is not supported yet. The Rust reference has the full details.

Oyzu treats any folder with a Cargo.toml as a Rust target. It reads manifests without running Cargo or any of your code. Project Target A single package, binary or library One rust/app target A Cargo workspace ([workspace] in the root manifest) One rust/app target for the whole workspace. Cargo decides the members The target delivers every enabled binary. A package that is publishable also gets a .crate archive when you build in the isolated executor. A library-only package gets its .crate and no executable. You need a checked-in Cargo.lock, because Oyzu runs Cargo with --locked and a stale lock fails instead of being rewritten. oyzu run list shows the tasks Oyzu infers. They are plain Cargo commands: $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 8 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · rust/app (8) project:archive Inferred · cargo cargo package --workspace --locked --offline project:build Inferred · cargo cargo build --locked --workspace project:fetch Inferred · cargo cargo fetch --locked project:format Inferred · cargo cargo fmt --all project:format-check Inferred · cargo cargo fmt --all --check project:install Inferred · cargo cargo install --path . --locked project:lint Inferred · cargo cargo clippy --locked --workspace -- -D warnings project:test Inferred · cargo cargo test --locked --workspace oyzu run <task> runs one on your machine. build, test, lint and format-check are also the stages of oyzu build. format edits your source and is never part of a build. fetch and install are development tasks only, and oyzu run install -- --root <dir> passes its arguments to cargo install.

Command What runs oyzu build --plan Nothing. Shows the stages and the tools Oyzu read from your files oyzu build Compiles the workspace and collects the binaries. Checks are skipped locally oyzu build --full Also runs tests with coverage, doctests, Clippy and cargo fmt --check oyzu build --isolated The same build in a Linux container (needs Docker; see Isolated builds) In CI the checks run without --full. See build selection and checks. Tests run through cargo llvm-cov nextest, so the test stage needs cargo-nextest, cargo-llvm-cov and the llvm-tools-preview Rust component. Oyzu pins and installs the first two for you. Doctests run in the same stage, because nextest doesn't run them.

Oyzu reads the files Rust developers already use, in this order: rust-toolchain.toml (or the older rust-toolchain file). Everything rustup accepts is read, including components. A channel such as 1.99.1 is an exact pin. package.rust-version in Cargo.toml is a minimum. [tools] rust = "…" in oyzu.toml, only when you have no native file or want a different value in one folder. A native pin file wins over a farther oyzu.toml. With none of these, Oyzu locks the newest stable Rust on the first build. Either way the exact choice goes in oyzu.lock, so commit it. After you change a pin, run oyzu pin to update the lock and oyzu install to download what it names. oyzu pin --dry-run previews the change. The Tools row of every build says which compiler ran and why, for example rust 1.99.1 already installed compilation (detected from rust-toolchain.toml). You never install Rust yourself. You do need the platform's linker: on Windows, Microsoft Build Tools with the Windows SDK (MSVC) or LLVM-MinGW; on Linux, the system C toolchain. Oyzu checks the linker with a tiny test build before compiling.

A successful build writes one dist/ bundle. The Outputs section prints each artifact's path, and manifest.json records it with its digest. The bundle layout describes the directories. Output Contents <binary>[.exe] Each enabled Cargo binary <package>-<version>.crate Crate archive for each publishable package (isolated builds) reports/junit.xml Test results from nextest (with --full or in CI) reports/coverage.xml Line coverage in Cobertura format reports/doctest.xml One case per package that has doctests manifest.json Every file with its digest, plus the plan and build evidence Packages with publish = false get no .crate, but their binaries are still delivered. A binary that needs required-features is delivered only when that feature is enabled. Versions are snapshots from your declared version and Git, such as 1.2.3-dev.g<source>. A snapshot isn't a release; see version inference.

You need a build.yaml only to change something Cargo can't express. The Rust builder accepts these options under with: Option Values Default Meaning features List of Cargo feature names none (default features stay on) Applied to build, test, lint, doctests and packaging packages List of unique Cargo package names none (the whole workspace) Limits the build, checks and packaging to these workspace members. features must then be plain feature names test-packages List of unique Cargo package names inherits packages Overrides only which packages are tested. [] tests the whole workspace. See the Rust reference artifacts all, binaries all binaries delivers only enabled binaries and skips crate packaging; the build fails if no binary is enabled builds: greeting: uses: rust/app with: features: [loud] Unknown with keys are refused. To build for other platforms, declare platforms on the build; see cross-compiling.

In a workspace you can make chosen packages share one version number, using the same release metadata cargo-release reads. Oyzu only reads it and never runs cargo-release. shared-version = true joins the workspace's shared group. A string such as "suite" joins that named group. false leaves a group. Matching version strings, or version.workspace = true alone, don't group packages. tag-prefix sets the Git tag namespace used to find each group's last release, for example suite/. # Workspace root Cargo.toml [workspace.metadata.release] shared-version = "suite" tag-prefix = "suite/" # A package that versions on its own [package.metadata.release] shared-version = false tag-prefix = "helper/" Every member of a group must have the same native version and tag mapping. Private or unselected members count too. Conflicting versions or overlapping tag namespaces make the build fail. This applies to Cargo workspaces only. The Rust reference lists every inheritance rule and refusal.
documents.s: Keep selected packages on one version

documents.t: This is a tiny binary crate with one unit test, from examples/builds/rust-app/project in the Oyzu repository. Create these files in a new folder and run git init there. Cargo.toml: [package] name = "oyzu-greeting-example" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2021" Cargo.lock: version = 3 [[package]] name = "oyzu-greeting-example" version = "0.1.0" src/main.rs: fn greeting(name: &str) -> String { format!("Hello, {name}!") } fn main() { println!("{}", greeting("Oyzu")); } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn greets() { assert_eq!(greeting("Oyzu"), "Hello, Oyzu!"); } } rust-toolchain.toml: [toolchain] channel = "1.99.1" components = ["rustfmt", "clippy"] Run oyzu build for a fast build. The first build also writes oyzu.lock, which you should commit. The binary is under dist/: $ dist/project/windows/x86_64/oyzu-greeting-example.exeCopy Hello, Oyzu!

The first build locks only what a fast build needs. If you then ask for --full, Oyzu names the missing lock entry instead of guessing: $ oyzu build --fullCopy Building rust-app windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✗ Tools failed: preparation did not complete <0.1s ✗ TOOL_LOCK_STALE: cargo:cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1; run oyzu pin Next: Run oyzu pin --refresh to refresh the lock, then oyzu install. Run oyzu pin to lock every tool the project's builds can need, including the test-stage tools, then build again: $ oyzu build --fullCopy Building rust-app windows/x86_64 (host) · local · context local · full ​ ── Prepare ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Configuration Loaded and validated <0.1s ✓ Tools 3 tools pinned · 0 installed now 1.7s cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1 already installed coverage, if enabled cargo-nextest 0.9.146 already installed testing, if enabled rust 1.99.1 already installed compilation (detected from rust-toolchain.toml) … ​ ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ project build rust/app build-host executed 0.6s ✓ project test rust/app test executed 2.1s ✓ project lint cargo clippy --locked --workspace… executed 0.4s ✓ project format-check cargo fmt --all --check executed 0.2s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── project dist/project/windows/x86_64/oyzu-greeting-example.exe 143.9 KB development ​ Checks selected 3 actions · 3 succeeded ​ Tests run now 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports) Coverage project: 66.7% (6/9 lines) ​ ✓ Build succeeded 1 target · 4 executed · 7.1s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 53896-1792554065729458000-1 Output shortened. Running the same command again without changes can reuse compilation and bounded checks. The test stage still runs; eligible test units may reuse their earlier reports, labelled as not run now. Arbitrary tests execute again. See test reuse. Compile reuse requires complete native Cargo read observations. On Windows x64/MSVC, compile reads can currently remain incomplete on unchanged builds, so compilation reruns; rustfmt checks, Cargo incremental state and eligible individual compiler results remain separate. oyzu build --explain names the refusal. See native Rust caching.

$ oyzu inspect distCopy ✓ Bundle contents verified · build succeeded ​ Actions Action Status Exit Gate project:build succeeded 0 required project:test succeeded 0 required project:lint succeeded 0 required project:format-check succeeded 0 required ​ Reports Report Path Status project:test project/windows/x86_64/reports/junit.xml collected project:coverage project/windows/x86_64/reports/coverage.xml collected ​ Verified: every recorded file matches its digest. This does not show who produced the build or that it may be released. Output shortened.

oyzu build --isolated runs the same stages in a Linux container with no network. Oyzu first downloads every locked crates.io dependency and checks each archive against the SHA-256 in Cargo.lock, then builds offline. Isolated builds also package publishable crates with cargo package and verify them. You need Docker and the base execution image, which Oyzu pulls on first use. Rust and its test tools come from oyzu.lock, and cross builds fetch pinned linkers. See the isolated-build image.

You see Cause Fix TOOL_LOCK_STALE: cargo:cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1; run oyzu pin (exit 4) oyzu.lock came from a fast build and lacks the test-stage tools, or a pin changed Run oyzu pin, commit oyzu.lock, build again COMMAND_FAILED: provision llvm-tools-preview before Rust tests: missing llvm-cov The Rust installation used for tests has no llvm-cov Set LLVM_COV and LLVM_PROFDATA to the tools from a toolchain with the llvm-tools-preview component (under lib/rustlib/<host>/bin), or delete oyzu.lock, run oyzu pin and rebuild LINK : fatal error LNK1104: cannot open file '…\linker-arguments' (Windows) The project path is too long for the MSVC linker. Compiler state lives under .oyzu/native/rust/ in the project Move the project to a shorter path invalid Rust with options: unknown field … A with key the Rust builder doesn't accept Use features, packages, test-packages or artifacts, or remove the key A test fails The Cargo test failed The failure section names the test, the log under dist/logs/ and the command to rerun one target. The previous good binaries are kept Formatting and Clippy findings are build gates too. Fix them with oyzu run format and oyzu run lint, then rebuild.

Private or alternate registries, private Git dependencies and credentials aren't supported. Locked crates.io dependencies and public GitHub sources pinned to a full commit are. Coverage is line coverage from nextest. Doctests aren't measured, and the doctest report counts packages, not individual examples. Isolated builds need Docker and the base execution image.
Rust reference Native local builds Tool commands: pin, install and tools Build bundles Capabilities and known limitations

Use the zig/project plugin to build a Zig project with its own build.zig and collect what the build installs: programs, libraries and resources. Zig keeps full control of the build graph. Oyzu selects the compiler, runs zig build with a private install prefix and caches, and records the installed files in a verified dist/ bundle. Note: The Zig builder is experimental and uses the signed oyzu/zig plugin. Zig 0.15.2 is supported. Dependency-free native builds work on Linux x86-64 and Intel macOS; the Windows x86-64 path has limited support. Native builds with dependencies work on Intel macOS, and isolated builds with dependencies run on Linux x86-64. ARM64 is unsupported. The Zig reference has the full details. Managed compiler acquisition supports Intel macOS and Linux x86-64 GNU; Windows acquisition currently fails with TOOL_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED. Native Debug artifacts also retain absolute workspace and cache roots in DWARF, with no Zig 0.15.2 remapping flag, so independent clean roots can produce different artifact digests even with --no-cache. This upstream limitation does not change release modes or captured builds; local Debug builds continue to run natively.

Oyzu doesn't detect Zig projects automatically. Declare the build in build.yaml beside your build.zig: builds: hello: uses: zig/project Choose the compiler in oyzu.toml: [tools] zig = "0.15.2" The signed oyzu/zig package is in the official plugin catalog. Enable preview selection in your user configuration, then build: oyzu config set --global plugins.preview true oyzu build The first build installs the package and records its exact release in oyzu.lock. Commit that lock. See plugin selection.

oyzu build runs: zig build --prefix <output>/install --cache-dir <output>/cache --global-cache-dir <output>/global-cache Oyzu collects the install directory as the build's artifact and keeps both Zig caches out of it. The path of the collected files is in dist/manifest.json (for example hello/darwin/x86_64/install), so run your program from there: install/bin/hello. Discovery never evaluates build.zig or downloads anything. Oyzu reads build.zig.zon for the package identity, the compiler minimum and the declared dependencies. .minimum_zig_version limits which compiler Oyzu selects. It doesn't pin one. Task Command Notes build zig build Installs into the private prefix test zig build test --summary all Dependency-free native builds collect one JUnit case for the test step format zig fmt . Rewrites files. Never part of a build format-check zig fmt --check . Native format check If you replace the build task in oyzu.toml, your command runs exactly as written. It must produce the install directory itself and doesn't get the options below.

Put these under with in the build: Option Values Default Meaning steps 1 to 16 step names (letters, digits, _, -; start with a letter; up to 64 characters) the native default install Run these build.zig steps. Flags, paths and shell text are refused definitions Map of up to 16 option names to strings, booleans or integers none Each entry becomes one -Dname=value argument. Compiler, target, cache and fetch options are reserved and refused install-format directory, tar.gz directory tar.gz packs the install tree into one install.tar.gz, keeping relative links and executable bits String values can be up to 1,024 bytes with no control characters. All arguments together are limited to 4,096 bytes. Values are never evaluated by a shell. Other option names are passed to your build.zig, and its failures show up normally. You can keep build.zig and a tracked dist/ folder in place and send Oyzu's own bundle elsewhere: # oyzu.toml [tools] zig = "0.15.2" [build] bundleDirectory = ".oyzu/bundle" # build.yaml builds: ghostty: uses: zig/project inputs: [dist] with: steps: [lib-vt] install-format: tar.gz inputs: [dist] adds your tracked dist folder as a source input. oyzu inspect then reads .oyzu/bundle by default. See bundle placement. definitions selects project options the same way, for example definitions: {xcframework-target: native}.

Declared packages in build.zig.zon (URL, transitive, path and lazy dependencies) are prepared before build.zig runs. Oyzu downloads each archive through its scoped broker, checks it against the native package hash, and gives Zig only local files through --system. Native macOS (Intel). Preparation needs network access on every invocation. It supports archives and GitHub repositories pinned to a full 40-character commit, within size and metadata limits. Nested Xcode projects are limited to the exact Xcode and Swift versions in the reference. Isolated Linux (x86-64, GNU). The build runs with no network, -j1 and the install prefix described above. After one online build, the prepared packages let an offline build reuse them. This path needs a plugin package that includes the Linux executable, as the catalog package does. See the reference. Native host builds that declare dependencies are refused unless they take one of these paths.

If your build.zig runs other tools, such as Pandoc for documentation, pin them in oyzu.toml next to the compiler. Pins apply to every build in that folder. The compiler stays first on PATH, and the other tools follow. [tools] zig = "0.15.2" "github:jgm/pandoc" = "3.12.1" oyzu pin zig@0.15.2 oyzu pin 'github:jgm/pandoc@3.12.1' oyzu install --frozen oyzu build --isolated Pandoc 3.12.1 works on Linux (x86-64, GNU). Oyzu accepts complete publisher tar.gz and tar.xz packages whose commands match their file names. Archives that need an interpreter, command aliases or missing executables are refused. Offline builds need the publisher archives cached by an earlier online build. The tools run during the build and aren't part of the collected install tree. See native documentation installation tree.

The isolated build reserves 4,096 MiB of memory plus virtual machine overhead. The default Docker Desktop memory limit is too small, so raise it (6 GiB worked on an 8 GiB Mac) and keep at least 2 GiB of free disk. Native JUnit reports require a plugin declaring zig-native-test-report; the catalog's 0.1.0-preview.3 does not yet declare it. See native test reports.

You see Cause Fix Metadata error with a file, line and column Invalid build.zig.zon (duplicate field, expression or unsupported escape) Fix it at the reported location A build that installs nothing fails artifact collection build.zig installs nothing Add an install step, or select the right steps Refusal about a required test report The selected execution path cannot produce the required report Use a supported test path; required checks still apply Dependency or hash refusal An archive doesn't match its package hash, or the source form isn't supported Correct the hash, or use a supported source Options refused next to a build task replacement with options need the standard build command Remove the replacement or the options Native failures from build.zig are passed through as they are. A failed build never produces a successful artifact.

Dependency-free native tests and isolated Linux tests collect JUnit for the whole test step, not individual test functions. Isolated tests with dependencies use the build's prepared package tree and remain offline during execution. Run oyzu build --isolated --full with checks.coverage = "off" for test reports. Dependent native Linux builds, dependent native macOS test reports and coverage remain unavailable. Only Zig 0.15.2 is supported. Other compiler versions and other platforms are not supported yet. Isolated builds need Docker, the Linux plugin executable and the memory above. Native macOS dependency preparation needs the network each time. There is no offline reuse. Git dependencies other than a full-commit GitHub repository are refused. Native dependency packages can't contain links other than a direct link to a sibling regular file. An install tree with links fails the directory format. Use install-format: tar.gz, which keeps links that stay inside the tree.

use std::{env,fs,path::PathBuf}; fn main() { println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed=../channel.txt"); let channel=fs::read_to_string("../channel.txt").unwrap(); let generated=format!("pub const CHANNEL: &str = {:?};",channel.trim()); fs::write(PathBuf::from(env::var_os("OUT_DIR").unwrap()).join("channel.rs"),generated).unwrap(); }

Run the delivered codebook executable and expect Release channel: stable. Change channel.txt to preview, rebuild, inspect the new bundle, and run its delivered executable: expect Release channel: preview. This is illustrative configuration requiring real evidence and roots. Keep it in the normal configuration owner; destination maps replace atomically across the cascade. Secret settings are environment references. Required managed controls still apply. The artifact and accepted evidence must already exist. Inspect each destination's receipt; independent destinations are not an atomic transaction.
