The Rust build guide walks through a Cargo application with real output: discovery, toolchain pinning, oyzu build --full, the output bundle and common failures. For more projects, use the first build recipe and the catalog for workspaces, features and generated sources. The Rust reference covers every Rust builder setting.

Oyzu builds, tests and runs tasks for your existing projects using the conventions they already follow. It installs the exact compilers and runtimes each project needs, so the same project builds the same way on every machine. You need no account and no configuration file to start. Early release Oyzu is in early development. Support varies by ecosystem and platform; check what works today before you rely on a particular combination.

Install Oyzu, then open a new terminal so shell activation and tool shims are on PATH. Follow the tutorial to build, test, inspect, rebuild and debug a small Go program, or use the four-command version on your own project. Manage your tools: lock exact versions for your whole team. Read your build results: what ran, what was reused and what was recorded.

Run these from your project root: oyzu discover # what Oyzu found: targets, builders and tasks oyzu run list # the tasks it found and the native command each runs oyzu build --plan # preview the build; runs and downloads nothing oyzu build # fast local build oyzu build --full # build plus tests, lint and format checks oyzu history # past builds

No configuration to start. Oyzu reads Cargo.toml, go.mod, package.json, pom.xml, pyproject.toml and other native files. You add a small build.yaml only for the exceptions. The same tools everywhere. Exact tool versions are recorded in oyzu.lock, checked against their published digests when installed, and used the same way on every machine and in CI. Clear results. Output says what ran now and what was reused from an earlier build. Reused test results are never shown as a fresh run. One interface for every ecosystem. Rust, Go, Node, Java, Python, .NET, Docker and Helm builds use the same commands and produce the same kind of output bundle.

Guides for everyday workflows: adopting Oyzu in a repository, CI, monorepos, caching. CLI reference for every command and flag. Concepts to understand how a build is planned and run. Known limitations before you commit to Oyzu for a project.

Run these four commands from the root of an existing Rust, Go, Node, Java, Python, .NET, Docker or Helm project. You don't need a configuration file. For a step-by-step walkthrough with full output, see the tutorial. oyzu discover # 1. what Oyzu found oyzu build --plan # 2. what a build would do oyzu build --full # 3. build, test, lint and format-check oyzu inspect dist # 4. check the output

$ oyzu discoverCopy 1 target · 6 tasks discovered without running project code Project root: ~/hello ​ project · go/app Chosen by detected from project files Location . Manager go Version 0.0.0 Part of builds build, format-check, lint, test Development tasks format, install ​ Target names are what `oyzu build <target>` accepts. Next steps: oyzu run list every task and the command it runs oyzu build --plan preview the build stages without running them Use --json for the complete discovery record, including each task's environment and dependencies. Oyzu reads your native files (Cargo.toml, go.mod, package.json, pom.xml, pyproject.toml and so on) and lists each target (a buildable unit, here project), the builder that handles it and its tasks. It runs none of your code to do this. oyzu run list shows the exact command behind each task.
oyzu build --plan shows which stages run for each target (build, test, lint, format check) and which tool versions they need. It installs, downloads and runs nothing.

oyzu build # fast local build: build stages only oyzu build --full # also run tests, lint and format checks The first build picks tool versions, writes them to oyzu.lock and downloads any tools that are missing. The output has the same sections every time: Prepare, Plan, Build (one row per action) and Outputs, then a result line. A failed action gets its own section with the error, the exit code, the log file and a command to re-run just that target. oyzu build exits with 0 on success and non-zero on failure, so it works in scripts and CI. Add --json for machine-readable output. Commit oyzu.lock and add dist/ and .oyzu/ to .gitignore.

oyzu history # past builds oyzu inspect dist # check the output bundle against its recorded digests Build again without changes and eligible stages reuse earlier results, labelled as reused. Native stages without complete reads run again. Use oyzu build --explain to see why. See Read your build results.

Problem Where to look A tool is missing or can't be installed Manage your tools The build fails The failure section and the log it names, then Troubleshooting A target is missing or uses the wrong builder Add a small build.yaml: Adopt Oyzu in an existing repository
Run your project's tasks. Adopt Oyzu in a larger repository. Command details: CLI reference, local builds, build tasks.

Oyzu is a single executable, oyzu. It needs no account, agent, daemon or desktop app, and no administrator rights to install. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

On Linux or macOS: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh | sh On Windows, in PowerShell: irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1 | iex The script: Picks the newest release on your channel that has an executable for your platform. The default channel is stable. Downloads it and refuses it unless its SHA-256 digest matches the one GitHub reports. Installs oyzu into ~/.oyzu/bin (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\bin on Windows) and runs oyzu --version. Enables first-party preview plugins if plugins.preview is unset in your user configuration; preserves an existing true or false. Runs oyzu shell install to set up your shells and PATH (see What it sets up). It prints the release it chose, one line with the tag, asset, digest and install location, and the installed version. For an existing Windows install, prefer oyzu self update, then check oyzu --version in PowerShell, cmd or Git Bash. If a project reports FILE_READER_TOO_OLD, install at least the version named in the error before retrying; keep the project's minimum-version marker. A successful self-update keeps the previous binary for oyzu self rollback. Re-running the installer does not create rollback history. See Windows upgrade and recovery for disposable candidate installs and reader recovery for pinned versions and PATH checks. Preview releases Every release is a preview. Releases are binaries and notices published on the public oyzuai/oyzu-releases repository, so you need no account or token. The scripts don't check release provenance yet. Some first-party builders are previews, so the installer opts in for a new user. To undo this, run oyzu config set --global plugins.preview false. If you already turned previews off, the installer leaves that choice in place; enable them with oyzu config set --global plugins.preview true before your first build. Configuration setup failures are warnings; the CLI stays installed. A GitHub token is optional. It lifts the anonymous API limit of 60 requests an hour: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh | GH_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) sh $env:GH_TOKEN = (gh auth token); irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1 | iex

To read the script before you run it, download it first: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh -o install.sh less install.sh sh install.sh --version oyzu/v0.3.1 --version (or OYZU_VERSION) installs one release tag instead of the newest. In PowerShell, pass parameters like this: & ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1))) -Version oyzu/v0.3.1 The install script reference lists every option, the exit codes and the errors.
documents.s: Read it first, or pin a version

documents.t: Your shells need to activate oyzu, and programs that never start a shell (IDEs, GUI apps, scheduled jobs) need to find oyzu and your tools. oyzu shell install handles both: Shell activation goes into ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc and the PowerShell 7 profile, for each of those shells you use. oyzu and the shims folder go on your PATH, so node, go or cargo run at the project's locked version everywhere, without oyzu exec --. On Windows this is your user Path in the registry. On Linux and macOS it is your login profile. Open a new terminal, and restart any IDE, afterwards. You can run oyzu shell install again at any time. To install the file only, pass --no-modify-path (-NoModifyPath in PowerShell). With fish or Windows PowerShell 5.1, the installer prints what to run or which folders to add yourself.

An installed oyzu keeps itself up to date. About once a day, a command you run in a terminal checks its release channel in the background, verifies the newest release's signatures and swaps it in; the next command tells you, and oyzu self rollback undoes it. If rollback restores a local build, oyzu self update returns to the recorded channel's newest release. With no recorded channel, start with oyzu self channel stable. Status names the previous local build so you can see what rollback restores. The useful commands: oyzu self # installed version, channel and update mode oyzu self update # update now oyzu self versions # newest version in stable, beta and nightly oyzu self versions --all --channel beta # recent beta versions only oyzu self channel beta # follow release candidates too oyzu self install 0.2.0 # install one exact version and pin it oyzu self channel --manual # notices only, no automatic updates oyzu self shows named Download and Install steps, then the outcome and a runnable Next: command. Warnings explain non-fatal engine or shim failures; -v keeps full digests and child details. --json retains the machine-readable records. Use --all --channel stable, beta or nightly to filter version history by exact kind. This leaves your followed channel and pin unchanged. An empty history succeeds when that kind has no release in the recent list. Install from a channel other than stable with --channel beta (-Channel beta in PowerShell). Set OYZU_SELF_UPDATE=off to turn the automatic check off; CI runs never check. Updating oyzu itself covers channels, verification and rollback. To uninstall, run oyzu shell remove to undo the shell and PATH setup, then delete oyzu, oyzu-shim, any *.previous files and .oyzu-install.json from the install folder.

oyzu --version oyzu --help The version shows the release (or source revision) and platform of your build. A source build says local. oyzu --help groups commands by job: develop and build, project tools, environment and configuration, platform, and diagnostics. The platform group (auth, release, secrets) needs an Oyzu platform account. Everything else works without one. oyzu <command> --help works offline with no project open. Then run it on a project. The tutorial builds a real program step by step, and Your first build is the short version. Something wrong? See troubleshooting. You don't need to install Go, Node, Java or any other ecosystem toolchain first. Oyzu acquires the tools a project asks for. See Manage your first tool.

The install scripts are tested on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS and musl Linux installation are not fully supported yet; musl release binaries are not available. Support for builds differs by ecosystem and tool provider. See what works today and known limits.

This is for contributors, or when you need an unreleased change or a platform with no release executable. You need a checkout of the Oyzu repository and either an existing Oyzu, which provides the repository's managed Rust, or the Rust toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml. The first run needs network access unless the managed Rust and the locked Cargo dependencies are already cached; the build uses --locked. On macOS, native builds also need Apple's Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install). tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh --source export PATH="$PWD/.oyzu/bin:$PATH" oyzu build cli Unless an oyzu that can read the checkout is already on your PATH or in .oyzu/bin, the script builds the CLI, the native shim and the Rust and Node plugins, copies them to .oyzu/bin and restores the repository's own locked tools. Without --source it downloads the newest release's oyzu instead and builds only when no release executable works on your machine. The source bootstrap section covers the user configuration it writes, when it refuses to run, and CARGO_TARGET_DIR. Later, run oyzu run bootstrap from the checkout to build and install its host CLI. Add -- --development-plugins to rebuild development plugins, or -- --isolated to also prepare a Linux engine. To install a release instead, run oyzu run bootstrap -- --channel stable. See Refreshing the oyzu on your PATH. The source task checks actual plugin capabilities and keeps an absolute CLI path, so an older project-local build cannot hide a compatible installed CLI. If none qualifies, it uses Oyzu-managed Cargo to build a temporary seed CLI first. A version label alone does not establish compatibility; existing plugin admission and your configuration choices still apply.

Isolated builds (oyzu build --isolated) run a Linux oyzu inside the container. On Windows and macOS the install scripts set this up from the release. For an oyzu you built yourself, pass the Linux oyzu built from the same source: oyzu engine install --linux ./oyzu-linux-x86_64 If you have a compatible development engine archive with its identity and digest, you can install it for your user: oyzu engine install --identity <BUILD_ID> --archive ./engine.tar.gz --sha256 sha256:<HEX> This doesn't change your PATH or pin a project. The installed executable, and any byte-identical copy of it such as the oyzu on your PATH, supplies its own isolated-build workers without an engines.packages entry. Explicit project pins and administrator pin requirements still take precedence. Add --json for a machine-readable record. The engine staging reference covers package requirements, offline use and recovery.
Every build ends by telling you what ran now, what was reused from an earlier build, what the tests reported and where the full record is.

The tutorial shows a complete build transcript. Prepare sets up configuration, tools and workspaces. Plan shows which stages run for each target. Build has one row per action with its native command, executed or reused, and the time. Outputs lists the artifacts. The summary gives tests, coverage, the result and where the details are. A failed action gets its own section with the cause, exit code, log file and a command to re-run just that target. CI logs show the same sections without live progress. Add -q for less output or -v for more. Every section is explained in Read output, receipts and history.
documents.s: Read the output top to bottom

documents.t: Wording Meaning executed The command ran in this build reused Inputs are unchanged, so Oyzu restored an earlier result. The row shows how long the original run took blocked Not run, because something it depends on failed unknown Oyzu couldn't confirm a final result for the action Tests run now Tests that ran in this build Reused test evidence Test results from an earlier run with the same inputs. The tests did not run now Oyzu never presents reused tests as a fresh run, and it never shows a coverage percentage it didn't measure. Unchanged source does not guarantee reuse. Native stages need complete admitted reads and bounded outputs. oyzu build --explain names a refusal such as native stage has no complete observed reads; the stage runs again and cannot be skipped by restoring the whole target. oyzu cache explain <target> reads the recorded lookup reason between builds. Clearing the cache or adding a known inputs path cannot prove arbitrary runtime reads complete. See reuse explanations and current native coverage. Here is the same build repeated with nothing changed. Change a source file and only the affected actions run again. See Cache build results.

Each build writes an output bundle to dist/: the artifacts, test and coverage reports, logs, and manifest.json, which lists everything that was built with its digest. The previous bundle moves to .oyzu/history/. oyzu history # past builds, newest first oyzu history <id> # one build: outcome, why each stage ran, file paths oyzu history <id> --json # the same, as JSON oyzu inspect dist # check every recorded file against its digest oyzu inspect tells you the bundle is intact. It doesn't tell you who produced it or whether it may be released, and its output says so.
Every command accepts --json. Standard output then holds only the JSON result. The exit code is 0 on success and non-zero on failure either way.
Read output, receipts and history CLI output, build bundles, action cache, affected builds Build evidence

Oyzu treats the tools a project needs (compilers, runtimes, package managers) as part of the project. It records exact versions in oyzu.lock, installs them and runs your commands with them, so your team and CI get the same versions without installing anything by hand.

Native files your ecosystem already has: rust-toolchain.toml, the go and toolchain lines in go.mod, global.json, the packageManager field in package.json, Gradle and Maven wrapper properties. oyzu.toml, under [tools], for anything a native file can't say. oyzu.lock, which records the exact version and download digest Oyzu picked. Write each version in one place only. If a native file already says it, leave it out of oyzu.toml.

$ oyzu pin --dry-runCopy Build requirements · preview ​ Consolidated across 1 build target(s). ​ Tool requirements Requirement Requested version Needed for Installation support Applies to oyzu:go 1.22.12 Declared requirement Oyzu All targets ​ Executor prerequisites Requirement Needed for Availability Applies to ​ Check tools are required when their checks are enabled by the build or policy. ​ Tool execution platform coverage OS Architecture ABI linux amd64 gnu Metadata coverage only; native installation support varies. ​ No files changed. Tool resolution complete. Installed availability was not checked. Nothing was installed. Use --json for sources, constraints and discovery limitations. --dry-run writes and installs nothing. Add --json to see where each requirement came from.

oyzu pin # pick exact versions and write oyzu.lock oyzu install # install the tools declared in oyzu.toml $ oyzu installCopy Installing tools Checking pinned tools and verifying reusable installations Oyzu checks each download against its recorded digest and publisher information before using it, and trusts the installed tool after that. You often don't need either command: oyzu build locks and installs what it needs. Commit oyzu.lock. Command What it does oyzu install go@1.26 Adds Go 1.26 to oyzu.toml, locks it and installs it oyzu update Moves locked versions forward within what oyzu.toml allows; never edits oyzu.toml oyzu uninstall go Removes the declaration and its lock entries; the installed copy stays in the shared store

$ oyzu which go && go version /home/you/.local/share/oyzu/tools/installs/d966a600…/payload/bin/go go version go1.22.12 linux/amd64 oyzu which shows the exact executable a command would run, and plain go runs it because your shell is activated: the install script set that up unless you passed --no-modify-path. To set it up yourself: oyzu shell install # every shell found, plus oyzu and the shims on your PATH oyzu shell install bash # or only one shell Open a new terminal afterwards. With the shims on PATH, plain go or node use the project's locked version in shells, IDEs and scripts alike. oyzu exec -- <command> runs one command with the project's tools where nothing is activated, such as a bare container.

oyzu tools current shows the versions in effect here and where each came from. oyzu tools list, oyzu tools versions <tool> and oyzu tools info <tool> show the shared store, the available versions and where a tool comes from. Not every tool installs automatically on every platform; when one can't, the command says what is missing.
Pin tools for your team: exact versions, updates and scopes. Tool commands, shell activation, configuration.

In about ten minutes you build a tiny Go program with Oyzu: you see what Oyzu detects, preview the build, build and test it, check the result, rebuild it from cache and read a failure. The output on this page comes from a real run on Linux; your times, hashes and paths will differ. You need the oyzu executable (Install Oyzu) and network access for the first build, so Oyzu can download Go. You don't need to install Go yourself.

mkdir hello && cd hello git init Create go.mod: module example.com/oyzu/hello go 1.22 Create main.go: package main import "fmt" func greeting(name string) string { return "Hello, " + name + "!" } func main() { fmt.Println(greeting("Oyzu")) } Create main_test.go: package main import "testing" func TestGreeting(t *testing.T) { if got := greeting("Oyzu"); got != "Hello, Oyzu!" { t.Fatalf("unexpected greeting: %q", got) } } That's the whole project. There is no Oyzu configuration file: Oyzu works from the files Go already uses. Known limitation: Resolving the unpinned go 1.22 requirement can fail with TOOL_RELEASE_AGE_UNAVAILABLE when release publication dates are unavailable. If you encounter this error, an exact native toolchain go1.22.12 line in go.mod selects the compiler used in the successful output below. That output includes this workaround; it does not show a successful unpinned build.

$ oyzu discoverCopy 1 target · 6 tasks discovered without running project code Project root: ~/hello ​ project · go/app Chosen by detected from project files Location . Manager go Version 0.0.0 Part of builds build, format-check, lint, test Development tasks format, install ​ Target names are what `oyzu build <target>` accepts. Next steps: oyzu run list every task and the command it runs oyzu build --plan preview the build stages without running them Use --json for the complete discovery record, including each task's environment and dependencies. Oyzu found one Go application, which it calls project. It only read files; it ran nothing. To see the commands behind each task: $ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 6 across 1 target ​ Task Source Command project · go/app (6) project:build Inferred · go go build ./... project:format Inferred · go gofmt -w . project:format-check Inferred · go gofmt -l . project:install Inferred · go go mod download project:lint Inferred · go go vet ./... project:test Inferred · go go test ./... ​ Run one with: oyzu run <task> (extra arguments go after --) Commands show argv; task dependencies and hooks may also run. Use --json for full task records. These are ordinary Go commands. You can run any of them with oyzu run, for example oyzu run test.

Tests, lint and format checks are skipped to keep local builds fast. --full turns them on.

Read it from the top: Prepare loads configuration, picks the Go version and installs it. Here Go 1.22.12 was already installed. A missing compiler is downloaded and checked against its recorded digest before use. Plan shows which stages run for each target. Build has one row per action, with the command or plugin operation, the result and the time. Export copies the built program to its versioned artifact path. Outputs lists that path. The last lines summarize the tests that ran, coverage and the overall result. The build added two things to your project: Path What it is Commit it? oyzu.lock The exact Go version and download digest Oyzu used Yes, so everyone gets the same Go dist/ The output bundle: the program, test reports, logs and a manifest No, add it to .gitignore

Every build keeps a record. oyzu history lists them: $ oyzu historyCopy Invocation evidence Invocation / run Outcome Scope Started 566674-1793485015732001339-1 succeeded 1 target · 5 actions 2026-10-31T22:16:57.695913939+00:00 561934-1793484985021011907-1 succeeded 1 target · 5 actions 2026-10-31T22:16:28.395324552+00:00 0 older entries omitted · 0 incomplete bundles Next: oyzu history <ID> for a bounded summary and evidence paths Recorded observations; this summary does not verify artifact contents. oyzu inspect checks the bundle in dist/: $ oyzu inspect distCopy ✓ Bundle contents verified · build succeeded Run 566674-1793485017695913939 · source sha256:e52ee6b61ade · uncommitted changes ​ Targets Target Builder Platform Path project go/app linux/x86_64 . ​ Actions Action Status Exit Gate project:build succeeded 0 required project:lint succeeded 0 required project:format-check succeeded 0 required project:export succeeded 0 required project:test succeeded 0 required ​ Artifacts Path (under dist/) Kind Size Platform Digest project/linux/x86_64/ file 1.9 MB linux/x86_64 sha256:bc329b1b6748 project-0.0.0-dev.gcfac4fb0ec55 ​ Reports Report Path Status project:test project/linux/x86_64/reports/junit.xml collected project:coverage project/linux/x86_64/reports/coverage.out collected ​ Verified: every recorded file matches its digest. Content integrity alone does not identify a producer or grant release authority. Use --json for the full inspection result, including the plan and execution envelope. inspect confirms that every file in dist/ is exactly the file the build recorded, by comparing digests. It tells you the bundle is intact. It doesn't tell you who built it, and the last line says so.

Native Go tests ran again: their runtime file reads are unbounded. The output keeps executed work separate from reused results. Other builders and execution paths can reuse test reports when their cache contracts permit it; those reports are labelled as not run now. See Read your build results.
