$ oyzu run listCopy Available tasks · 13 across 2 targets ​ Task Source Command api · go/app (7) api:build Inferred · go go build ./... api:format Inferred · go gofmt -w . api:format-check Inferred · go gofmt -l . api:install Inferred · go go mod download api:lint Inferred · go go vet ./... api:smoke oyzu.toml go run . api:test Inferred · go go test ./... ​ worker · go/app (6) worker:build Inferred · go go build ./... worker:format Inferred · go gofmt -w . worker:format-check Inferred · go gofmt -l . worker:install Inferred · go go mod download worker:lint Inferred · go go vet ./... worker:test Inferred · go go test ./... ​ Run one with: oyzu run <task> (extra arguments go after --) Commands show argv; task dependencies and hooks may also run. Use --json for full task records. Tasks come from two places, shown in the Source column: Inferred: the builder reads native files (go.mod, Cargo.toml, package.json scripts and so on). oyzu.toml: tasks you add yourself. There is no fixed task list for every project, so start from what oyzu run list shows.

In a project with one target, the bare name works: oyzu run test. With several targets, add the target name: To capture source and run the selected task in its builder's isolated image, use oyzu run --isolated api:test. Its prerequisites and hooks run too; other build and package stages are not added. The run collects logs, isolation evidence and required reports into the usual bundle, and never falls back to running the task on the host. See isolated tasks for supported ownership, outputs and current limits. $ oyzu run api:testCopy · Setup Loading configuration and discovering tasks · Skipped api · Compiling · Not included in the selected action graph · Skipped api · Checking formatting, api · Linting · fast local build · Actions 1 known; counts do not estimate time remaining › Build Running selected work › api · Testing Running {"Time":"2026-10-20T23:18:57.3274085-04:00","Action":"start","Package":"example.com/shop/api"} … {"Time":"2026-10-20T23:18:57.5269071-04:00","Action":"pass","Package":"example.com/shop/api","Elapsed":0.199} · api · Testing TEST_EVIDENCE: Test evidence api:test Command passed Results 1 passed · 0 failed · 0 skipped Coverage 50.0% of statements (1/2) Acceptance accepted ✓ api · Testing Succeeded (exit 0 after 2.24s) The native tool's own output appears unchanged (here, go test -json), with a few lines from Oyzu around it. If several targets define the same task, an unqualified name is refused rather than guessed: $ oyzu run testCopy · Setup Loading configuration and discovering tasks ✗ COMMAND_FAILED: ambiguous task test; choose api:test, worker:test Next: Correct the reported cause and retry the command. To run from another folder, use -C: oyzu -C services/api run test.
Everything after -- goes to the task's command: oyzu run api:test -- -run TestGreeting
documents.s: 3. Pass arguments to the native command

documents.t: Add a table under [tasks] in oyzu.toml. The command is an argv list and never goes through a shell. # oyzu.toml at the repository root [tasks."api:smoke"] # belongs to build api, runs in api/ argv = ["go", "run", "."] $ oyzu run api:smokeCopy · Setup Loading configuration and discovering tasks › api:smoke Running · native tool output follows Hello, Oyzu! ✓ api:smoke Succeeded (exit 0 after 1.16s) A task runs with its build's tools, environment and folder. cwd changes the folder, relative to the file that declares the task. Adding a task never installs a new tool: a task that runs node needs a target whose tools include Node. Where a task applies depends on its key and file: Key Applies to [tasks."api:smoke"] Build api only [tasks.lint-docs] in the root oyzu.toml The whole repository: oyzu run lint-docs [tasks.lint-docs] in a subfolder's oyzu.toml Every build below that folder [tasks.test] (a stage name) Replaces that stage in every build the file reaches. Qualify it when those builds use different builders A misspelled build name, or a task key in a file outside its build's folder, is an error naming the file and line.

A task named pre_<stage> or post_<stage> runs before or after that stage in oyzu build: [tasks."worker:pre_build"] argv = ["go", "vet", "./..."] $ oyzu buildCopy … ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 00:03 .. api build started 00:04 ✓ api build go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -o… executed 1.2s 00:04 .. worker pre_build started 00:05 ✓ worker pre_build go vet ./... executed 1.2s 00:05 .. worker build started 00:07 ✓ worker build go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -o… executed 1.1s ​ ── Outputs ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── api/ api dist/api/windows/x86_64/api-0.0.0-dev.g638adc2c9cc7.exe 2.0 MB development worker/ worker dist/worker/windows/x86_64/worker-0.0.0-dev.ge3334bd9de96.exe 2.0 MB development Checks not requested api: format-check, lint, test Checks not requested worker: format-check, lint, test ​ ✓ Build succeeded 2 targets · 3 executed · 7.3s api/ ✓ 1 target 1.2s worker/ ✓ 1 target 2.3s Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 58428-1792552742079235600-1 Output shortened. Tasks and hooks can depend on other tasks with depends_on = ["schema:verify"]. A prerequisite runs once per command, even when several tasks need it. Two things to know: Hooks run on every build. A hook without declared outputs means its target can't be reused from the cache, because Oyzu can't see what the hook changed. oyzu history <id> says so: contains authored tasks or hooks without declared outputs, which are never cached by default. See Cache build results. Conditions choose when a hook runs; they don't make it mandatory. when and unless limit a hook to certain contexts, platforms, profiles or artifacts: [tasks."cli:post_build"] argv = ["{artifact.path}", "--version"] # smoke-test each built binary when = { optimized = true, platform = ["linux/x86_64"] } For checks that must run, use check levels instead.

oyzu --json run list # the task list as JSON oyzu --json run api:test # a structured result; the exit status is kept When a task fails, oyzu run exits with the task's own exit code. Tasks run with oyzu run run on your machine and are never cached; use oyzu build for cached, recorded results. oyzu run <task> --remote runs a task on a platform pool (Remote builds).

Message Fix ambiguous task test; choose api:test, worker:test Add the target name to the task. TASK_NOT_FOUND: no task "nope" … (exit 5) Check oyzu run list and the folder you're in; use oyzu -C <project> run <task>. CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN A task key names a build or hook target that doesn't exist. The message suggests the nearest name. CONFIG_TASK_AMBIGUOUS An unqualified stage replacement reaches builds with different builders. Qualify it per build. A format task is refused in a build Tasks that change files, such as format, are for oyzu run only. Builds use the read-only format-check. Reference: build tasks (hooks, conditions, placeholders), CLI output.

Set up a project so every developer and CI job uses the same compiler, runtime and package-manager versions, with nothing installed by hand. You need: a project Oyzu discovers and network access for the first download. No account. Note: Tool management is fully tested on Linux x86-64; Windows x86-64 works with less test coverage, and macOS isn't supported yet. Automatic installation isn't available for every tool on every platform. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

File Holds Who edits it Native pin files What your ecosystem already says: rust-toolchain.toml, go.mod (the go line is a minimum), global.json, packageManager in package.json, Gradle and Maven wrapper properties You, as today oyzu.toml [tools] What a native file can't say, such as an exact Go version or a tool no native file names oyzu install, oyzu uninstall, or you oyzu.lock The exact version, download and digest of every tool, for every platform your team uses Only Oyzu (pin, install, update) Commit all three. Write each version in one place: if a native file pins it, leave it out of oyzu.toml.

$ oyzu pin --dry-runCopy Build requirements · preview ​ Consolidated across 2 build target(s). ​ Tool requirements Requirement Requested version Needed for Installation support Applies to oyzu:go 1.22 Declared requirement Oyzu All targets ​ Executor prerequisites Requirement Needed for Availability Applies to ​ Check tools are required when their checks are enabled by the build or policy. ​ Tool execution platform coverage OS Architecture ABI darwin arm64 native linux amd64 gnu linux arm64 gnu windows amd64 msvc Metadata coverage only; native installation support varies. ​ No files changed. Tool resolution complete. Installed availability was not checked. Nothing was installed. Use --json for sources, constraints and discovery limitations. --dry-run writes and installs nothing. Add --json to see each requirement's source and constraint.

If your native files already say everything (for example rust-toolchain.toml with an exact version), you only need a lock: oyzu pin # pick exact versions and write oyzu.lock; installs nothing The first oyzu build writes a lock if there isn't one. After that, builds never pick new versions on their own. If a native minimum moves past the lock (for example go get raised go.mod), the build fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE; run oyzu pin again.
documents.s: 2. Lock what the native files ask for

documents.t: Native files often give only a minimum or a release line. For Go, a toolchain go1.24.5 line selects exactly 1.24.5, while go 1.22 with no patch number selects the newest stable 1.22.x (Go version selection). To move the team to a newer version, declare it: oyzu install --dry-run go@1.24 # show what would be declared, locked and installed oyzu install go@1.24 # declare, lock for every platform, install for this one $ oyzu install go@1.24Copy Installing requested tools Resolving every platform, then installing this one ✓ Installed (reused existing installation) go 1.24.13 Declared "1.24" in …\shop\oyzu.toml (project) Locked in …\shop\oyzu.lock for 4 platforms (darwin/arm64/native, linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, windows/amd64/msvc) ​ Store: C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\Oyzu\tools oyzu.toml now holds what you typed, and oyzu.lock holds the exact version: [tools] go = "1.24" Spec Meaning go@1.24 Newest 1.24.x go@1.24.13 Exactly 1.24.13 go@latest Newest available version go Keep the existing declaration Several specs in one command are applied together or not at all. Tools Oyzu can install: node, go, python, java, maven, gradle, helm, kubectl, k3d, liquibase, tailscale, npm, pnpm, rust, cargo-nextest, cargo-llvm-cov, plus aqua:<owner>/<repo> and github:<owner>/<repo> packages (experimental). Zig 0.15.2 can be installed on Intel Macs (experimental); see Zig installation. The full list is in tool commands. The lock covers other platforms too, so teammates and CI runners get a matching download. Platforms the publisher doesn't build for are left out and reported.

Commit oyzu.toml and oyzu.lock. Teammates and CI then run: $ oyzu install --frozenCopy Installing tools Checking pinned tools and verifying reusable installations Tool installation ​ Tool Version Result go 1.24.13 reused ​ Selected installations verified. Use oyzu tools current to inspect availability. --frozen fails instead of changing the lock when it doesn't match the configuration. Each download is checked against its locked digest; installed tools are trusted after that. oyzu install installs tools declared in oyzu.toml. When every requirement comes from native files, it says so: $ oyzu installCopy Installing tools Checking pinned tools and verifying reusable installations ✗ COMMAND_FAILED: configure a tool before running oyzu install Next: Correct the reported cause and retry the command. That's fine: oyzu build installs every pinned tool it needs on its own.
documents.s: 4. Commit, and let everyone else install

documents.t: $ oyzu tools currentCopy 1 tool ready ​ Tool Requested Selected Source Status go 1.24 1.24.13 project ok ​ Use --details for paths and identities, --all for overridden declarations. ​ Store: C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\Oyzu\tools Installed state comes from stored receipts; payloads are not re-hashed. Command Shows oyzu tools list Installations in the shared store, their size, and whether this project or your global configuration uses them oyzu tools versions go Versions you could install, newest first oyzu tools info go Where the tool comes from, accepted names, platforms and how it is verified oyzu which go The exact executable a command would run oyzu tools current statuses: Status Meaning Fix ok Ready not installed Locked but not in the store oyzu install stale lock No matching lock entry oyzu pin blocked Not allowed by tools.allowed Ask the policy owner ambiguous Conflicting lock entries or tool names Use the exact tool name the message lists

go version # an activated shell has the locked tools on PATH oyzu run test # tasks always use the locked tools To have your normal terminal pick up the tools inside the project, set up shell integration once with oyzu shell install bash (or zsh or pwsh). See shell activation.
documents.s: 6. Run commands with the pinned tools

documents.t: oyzu update go # newest version within the declared request ("1.24" -> latest 1.24.x) oyzu update # every declared tool oyzu install go@1.25 # change the request itself oyzu pin --refresh # refresh download details, keep the selected versions oyzu uninstall go # remove the declaration and its lock entries update never edits oyzu.toml. Commit the lock change like any dependency update.

Flag Writes to Use for (none) Project oyzu.toml and oyzu.lock The team's tools --local oyzu.local.toml (the project lock is still used) A personal override you don't commit -g, --global Your user configuration and the lock next to it Tools you want in every project Outside a project, a command without -g fails with TOOL_NO_PROJECT instead of guessing.
An administrator can limit which tools are allowed with tools.allowed. Other requests fail with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED, naming the rule. See configuration.

Preview with oyzu tools prune, then run oyzu tools prune --apply to remove eligible tool installations, archive blobs and plugins. Use the same --store DIR on both commands for a custom store. Entries referenced by recorded locks or receipts, recent use, active leases or processes stay; uncertainty also keeps them. See store reclamation for retention rules and Windows, macOS and Linux limits.

Code Meaning Fix TOOL_LOCK_STALE The lock has no entry for a request, or a native minimum changed oyzu pin, then commit the lock TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT (exit 3) A configured version is below what a native file requires Raise the request, or lower the native minimum TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT Specs combined with --frozen, --offline or --update Run two separate commands TOOL_NOT_DECLARED uninstall or update of a tool this scope doesn't declare The message names the scope that does PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT / PIN_RECOVERY_REQUIRED Another or an interrupted lock edit Run oyzu install, update, uninstall or pin again; they recover first TOOL_LOCK_MISSING install --frozen with no lock Run oyzu pin or oyzu install online once Reference: tool commands, configuration. Offline and proxy setups: Work offline or behind a proxy.
Find your symptom below. Every Oyzu failure starts with a code (such as TOOL_LOCK_STALE) or a plain cause, then a Next: line with the fix. Read those two lines first.

oyzu --version # the exact Oyzu you are running oyzu build --plan # what Oyzu will do; runs nothing oyzu -v build # debug detail; -vv for trace oyzu history # past builds, with invocation IDs oyzu history <invocation-id> # result, why each stage ran, file paths Every failure also prints the invocation ID, the Oyzu version, the executable and the directory: $ oyzu build nopeCopy … ✗ COMMAND_FAILED: unknown build target nope; available targets: api, worker Next: Correct the reported cause and retry the command. Invocation: 36620-1792552675147666000-1 oyzu … · windows/x86_64 Executable: …\oyzu.exe Directory: . With --json, the failure is an object with code, error, exitCode and nextStep. For detail from one area, set for example OYZU_LOG=warn,oyzu::tools=debug. Areas: commands, config, discovery, tools, acquisition, executor, builders, reports.

A project folder is missing from oyzu discover. Discovery stops at the first folder a builder recognizes and skips nested Git repositories, folders with their own build.yaml, and dependency and output folders. With a root build.yaml, only listed builds exist. Add the folder: builds: web: uses: node/app path: web oyzu discover --write adds such folders for you (builds build.yaml leaves out). Oyzu picked the wrong package manager, test runner, linter or formatter. oyzu build --plan shows each choice and why. Override it in build.yaml with the with key the plan names, such as with: {package-manager: pnpm} (selecting a role). conflicting … candidates …; declare the intended one … with: {…} Two native files disagree equally. Add the suggested with: setting to that build, or remove the stale file (for example an old lockfile from another package manager). … is recognized by docker/image and node/app, so discovery cannot choose Name the builder: both: {uses: docker/image, path: both}. Another tool's build.yaml (for example Dart's) is in the way. Oyzu only treats a build.yaml with a builds, members or exclude root key as its own. Others are listed as skipped.
documents.s: Discovery: Oyzu doesn't see my project as expected

documents.t: Message Cause Fix CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming a build.yaml field Unknown field or root key, or builds not under builds: Put builds under builds:. Each build accepts only uses, path, default, platforms, depends_on, inputs, materialize, bindings, fetches, artifacts, with CONFIG_SCOPE A setting in a file that can't hold it: cache.remote, cache.ciRemote, cache.dir, platform.url or platform.account in a project file, or [publish] outside the root oyzu.toml Move it to user configuration (oyzu config set --global …), the environment, or the root file CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN A task key, depends_on or publish setting names a build, task or output that doesn't exist (the message suggests the nearest name) Fix the name CONFIG_REFERENCE_MISPLACED A task key for a build sits in an oyzu.toml outside that build's folder Move it to the root or the build's folder CONFIG_TASK_AMBIGUOUS An unqualified stage replacement such as [tasks.test] reaches builds with different builders Qualify it per build: [tasks."cli:test"] build.yaml changed between discovery and source capture The file was edited during a build Finish the edit and run again Run oyzu config validate after every edit, and oyzu config explain <key> to see where a value comes from. CONTEXT_INVALID: an unknown --context or OYZU_CONTEXT value. It fails every command that reads configuration, including install and exec: $ oyzu build --context nightlyCopy ✗ CONTEXT_INVALID: --context has unknown context "nightly"; use one of local, pr, ci, release Next: Correct the reported cause and retry the command.

unknown build target nope; available targets: api, worker: build arguments are exact target names from oyzu discover, not task names, paths or patterns. ambiguous task test; choose api:test, worker:test: several targets define the task. Add the target name: oyzu run api:test. TASK_NOT_FOUND (exit 5): the task doesn't exist in this folder. The message lists the tasks it found; pick another project with oyzu -C <dir> run <task>: $ oyzu run nopeCopy · Setup Loading configuration and discovering tasks ✗ TASK_NOT_FOUND: no task "nope" in …\shop. Available tasks: build, format, format-check, install, lint, pre_build, smoke, test. Run oyzu run to list tasks, or oyzu -C <project> run nope Next: Check the selected directory and name; use oyzu -C <project> to select a project. --affected builds everything. The JSON plan says why: oyzu build --affected origin/main --plan --json selection.affected.fallback Fix baseline-unavailable The ref isn't in the local clone. Run git fetch origin main, or use fetch-depth: 0 in CI. configuration-or-lock-change build.yaml, oyzu.toml, oyzu.lock or a native manifest changed. Commit it and later builds narrow again. If changedPaths lists files you didn't edit, line endings differ between your files and Git; fix them with .gitattributes. SOURCE_TRACKED_IGNORED: tracked source .oyzu-tool-lock-edit.lock is excluded …: an ignored file was committed. For Oyzu's coordination file, untrack it with git rm --cached .oyzu-tool-lock-edit.lock and keep it in .gitignore. If the build really needs the file, list it in the build's inputs.
documents.s: Selection: the wrong things are built

documents.t: Message Cause Fix TOOL_LOCK_STALE The lock has no entry for a request, or a native minimum moved (for example go get changed go.mod) oyzu pin, then commit oyzu.lock TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT (exit 3) A configured version is below the minimum a native file sets Raise [tools], or remove it so the native file decides configure a tool before running oyzu install Nothing is declared in [tools]; all requirements come from native files Nothing to fix: oyzu build installs those itself. Use oyzu install <tool>@<version> to declare one TOOL_LOCK_MISSING install --frozen or --offline with no lock Run oyzu pin or oyzu install online once TOOL_NO_PROJECT A tool command outside a project without -g Run it inside the project, or add --global PIN_RECOVERY_REQUIRED / PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT An interrupted or simultaneous lock edit Run oyzu install, update, uninstall or pin again; they recover first CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED The tools.allowed policy excludes the tool Ask the policy owner, or choose an allowed tool tools current shows not installed Locked but not in the store oyzu install --frozen tools current shows stale lock No lock entry for this platform or tool oyzu pin The tool store is shared per user: Platform Location Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\tools macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/tools Linux ~/.local/share/oyzu/tools Tools are checked when installed and trusted after that, so a damaged tool simply fails when it runs. Reinstall it.

Read the Failure section, not just the last line. It names the failing action, the native error, the exit code, the full log and the narrowest re-run command. Here a failing test in api blocked worker, which depends on it (the tutorial shows a single-target failure): $ oyzu build --fullCopy … ── Build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 00:03 .. api build started 00:10 still running: api build 6s · 8 waiting 00:11 ✓ api build go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false… executed 8.6s 00:11 .. api test started 00:20 still running: api test 8s · 7 waiting 00:21 ✗ api test go test -json -coverprofile=C:\Use… failed 9.3s 00:21 .. api lint started 00:22 ✓ api lint go vet ./... executed 1.1s 00:22 .. api format-check started 00:22 ✓ api format-check gofmt -l . executed 0.2s 00:22 ⊘ worker pre_build needs api · test 00:22 ⊘ worker build needs api · test, worker · pre_build 00:22 ⊘ worker test needs api · test, worker · build ⊘ + 2 more blocked · -v lists them ​ ── Failure: api · test ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── --- FAIL: TestGreeting (0.00s) FAIL example.com/shop/api · TestGreeting FAIL coverage: 50.0% of statements FAIL\texample.com/shop/api\t0.613s FAIL example.com/shop/api Exit 1 Log dist/logs/0001.stderr Next oyzu build api re-run only this target ​ Checks selected 6 actions · 2 succeeded · 1 failed · 3 blocked ​ Tests run now 0 passed · 1 failed · 0 skipped (1 collected reports) Coverage api: 50.0% (1/2 statements) ​ Test evidence api:test Command failed (exit 1) Results 0 passed · 1 failed · 0 skipped Coverage 50.0% of statements (1/2) Acceptance rejected · required evidence is absent, invalid or failing ​ Test evidence worker:test Command blocked (exit 1) Results missing · required Coverage missing · required Acceptance rejected · required evidence is absent, invalid or failing ​ ✗ Build failed 1 failed · 5 blocked · 3 succeeded · 22.7s api/ ✗ 1 target 19.2s worker/ ✗ 1 target Details dist/manifest.json · dist/logs/events.jsonl · invocation 40716-1792553002522238800-1 Note Local binaries were not updated; existing binaries are from the previous successful build. Output shortened. blocked actions didn't run because something they depend on failed. Fix the first failure. After a failure, .oyzu/bin still holds the programs from the last successful build. Passes locally, fails in CI: CI runs every check. Reproduce with oyzu build --full. CHECK_ADVISORY warning: an advisory check failed, but the project set it to warn only, so the build succeeded. Another build is running in this folder. A second build in the same folder fails before running anything. Wait for the first one. Don't delete .oyzu/build.lock; the lock is released when the build exits. An existing dist/ blocks the build. Oyzu only replaces a dist/ that contains an Oyzu manifest. If your project writes its own dist/, move that output, or set [build] bundleDirectory (bundle destination). Oyzu never deletes it. An error names a .oyzu/bundle-… folder. dist/ couldn't be written, so the results were kept there. Inspect that path with oyzu inspect, fix the disk space or permission problem, and rebuild.

Symptom Check Fix A result was reused that you didn't expect oyzu build --explain, oyzu cache explain <target> Oyzu doesn't see changes outside the key, such as an environment variable a tool reads. Run once with oyzu build --no-cache Nothing is ever reused oyzu build --explain or oyzu cache explain <target> names the refusal or changed input Incomplete native reads, hooks without outputs, secret environment values, or changed computation settings. Missing complete reads require builder support; cache clearing cannot fix them oyzu cache clear says the cache is busy A build is using it Retry when it finishes A test row says reused The result is from an earlier run, labelled as such Use --no-cache to run the tests now Details: Cache build results.

Code Meaning PROXY_INVALID A proxy variable is set but isn't a valid URL. Oyzu never falls back to a direct connection TRUST_BUNDLE_UNREADABLE / TRUST_BUNDLE_INVALID SSL_CERT_FILE is missing, unreadable, empty or not PEM SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE The download failed after two retries. Check your connection and the proxy SOURCE_TIMEOUT The 45-second download deadline passed SOURCE_DENIED No approved source allows the request or redirect BYTE_LIMIT / REQUEST_LIMIT A download or session went over its size or request limit TOOL_OFFLINE The command needs the network and --offline forbids it With --offline, a missing tool or dependency stops the build instead of being downloaded. Go online once and run the same build. See Work offline or behind a proxy.

Code (exit 3) Fix NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON Use a runner with Docker, or the host path for builders that support it NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES The Linux crun sandbox can't run here. Allow unprivileged user namespaces, or use Docker PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE This platform's executor isn't available on this machine. The plan names the runner it needs See Isolated builds.
See the failure tables in Remote builds and Publish artifacts.

A new PATH entry isn't picked up. An open terminal keeps the PATH it started with. Update the session ($env:Path = "C:\path\to\bin;$env:Path") or open a new terminal. Line endings. With core.autocrlf, files on disk can differ from what Git stored, and --affected counts that as a change. Set explicit eol rules in .gitattributes. Paths in messages may start with \\?\. It's the same path.

Collect oyzu --version, your platform, the full failing command, its output with -v, and oyzu history <invocation-id> --json. Oyzu hides credentials in URLs, headers and key=value text, but native tool output is passed through unchanged, so check it for secrets before you share it. Reference: CLI output, build logging, build bundles, tool commands, acquisition transport.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/acquisition-transport.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. When Oyzu downloads tools, helper archives and container-build dependencies, the requests go through one HTTP client with fixed rules: which sources may be contacted, how credentials are used, how retries work and how large downloads may be. This page explains those rules, how to use a corporate proxy, and what the download errors mean. Native package managers still read their own lockfiles, resolve dependencies and check package integrity. Oyzu only fetches bytes from allowed sources; it doesn't resolve dependencies. Note: The download client is experimental.

Each builder supplies the sources it may use. A source is an HTTPS origin and path prefix, with an optional authorization header held on your machine. Every request and every redirect must match an allowed source, or it fails with SOURCE_DENIED. A redirect uses the destination source's credentials. A token is never forwarded to another source. Some sources only accept redirects. For example, Go's proxy.golang.org sends large module zips to https://storage.googleapis.com/proxy-golang-org-prod/; a request that starts there is refused. go.sum still pins every zip. Plain HTTP is only allowed for local loopback endpoints. Base URLs with credentials, a query or a fragment, and encoded path escapes, are refused. Downloads happen while the build prepares, before the plan is frozen. Build actions then run with networking off. A missing input or integrity failure during an offline build never falls back to downloading. oyzu run tasks such as oyzu run install run on your host with normal network access.

The download client reads the standard environment variables of the process that runs oyzu. They apply to tool metadata and archives, helper archives and container-build dependency downloads. Variable Effect HTTPS_PROXY / https_proxy Proxy for HTTPS sources (CONNECT tunnel). HTTP_PROXY / http_proxy Proxy for HTTP sources. ALL_PROXY / all_proxy Used when the scheme-specific variable isn't set. NO_PROXY / no_proxy Hosts, domains and CIDR ranges that skip the proxy. SSL_CERT_FILE A PEM bundle of extra trusted certificates, for corporate TLS inspection. The built-in public roots stay trusted. Loopback addresses (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1) always skip the proxy, so local endpoints and their credentials never go through it. Proxy URLs may include credentials. They are never printed. An invalid proxy URL fails with PROXY_INVALID. An unreadable or empty SSL_CERT_FILE fails with TRUST_BUNDLE_UNREADABLE or TRUST_BUNDLE_INVALID. Oyzu never silently connects directly instead. A proxy doesn't widen the allowed sources; it's only a route. A TLS-inspecting proxy can see request headers, including source credentials. Only use a proxy you trust with them. Extra trusted certificates don't replace signature checks: a tool's publisher signature is still verified against its own trust root. Not supported: proxy authentication other than credentials in the URL, PAC files, system proxy settings and per-source proxies. Proxy support is tested on Linux and Windows. macOS isn't supported yet.

Rule Value Retries per download 2, after the first attempt Network deadline per download 45 seconds, shared across redirects and retries Redirects per download 5 Requests per session 4096, counting retries and redirects Backoff 200 ms, then 400 ms, or longer if the server sends Retry-After Statuses 408, 429, 502, 503 and 504, and connection or transfer failures, are retried. A partial download is discarded before retrying. Statuses such as 401, 403, 404 and 500 fail at once. So do denied sources, invalid redirects and size limits. If Retry-After asks for a wait longer than the remaining deadline, Oyzu returns the failure instead of retrying early. These limits can't be configured. A package manager may make its own further requests; its own retry behavior applies to those. Delivery edges still filling. An organization's delivery edge that is still fetching an artifact from its publisher answers 503 with Oyzu-Fill: pending and Retry-After. Oyzu waits the Retry-After seconds (1 to 30, default 5) and asks again with a fresh deadline, for up to 15 minutes, without counting it as a retry. Without that header, a 503 is an ordinary retryable status.

Each successful response may be up to 256 MiB, and one session may read up to 1 GiB in total, including failed attempts. Pinned tool archives (Rust, Node, Go, Python, JDK and Maven) download in sequential 8 MiB ranges, up to 512 MiB in total. Each range has its own 45-second deadline, so a large archive can take longer overall while a stalled request still times out. Ranges must line up exactly; an inconsistent server response fails with SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, and a total over the cap with BYTE_LIMIT. The archive's SHA-256 is checked before use. Up to eight downloads run at once, sharing the session limits. Error response bodies from servers are discarded. You get a fixed message with the HTTP status.

Errors Oyzu generates include a code and a fixed message, without the URL, query, token or server error text: Status Code Meaning and next step 400 REQUEST_INVALID A malformed request from a builder. Report it as a bug. 403 SOURCE_DENIED No allowed source matches the request or redirect. Check the source configuration. 413 BYTE_LIMIT A size limit was exceeded. Check the dependency's size. 429 REQUEST_LIMIT The session ran out of requests. Check how many dependencies are being resolved. 502 SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE The download failed after retries. Check the source and your connection, then rerun. 502 REDIRECT_INVALID, REDIRECT_LIMIT An invalid or too long redirect chain. Fix the source endpoint. 504 SOURCE_TIMEOUT The network deadline expired. Check the source and your connection, then rerun. For BYTE_LIMIT, the error also reports which limit was hit (response, session or artifact), the bytes observed and the limit. The pnpm adapter includes these in its failure message. When a server itself returns an error, its real status is kept with a redacted body, and the package manager shows it its own way. Maven runs with -e so nested resolution causes appear in failed builds. A failed preparation produces no dependency snapshot or build plan. The next build prepares fresh inputs.

Container npm builds fill npm's cache with npm cache add, 16 archives or 16 MiB at a time. When that fails, the message names the batch, archive count and size, the exit status and signal, and any recognized OS error code, errno and system call, for example: npm cache seed batch 1 (16 archives; 4066624 bytes): npm cache add failed (244): status=244; signal=none Oyzu may read the end of npm's debug log for these codes. Raw log text, arguments, configuration and URLs aren't included, and the log isn't kept in the bundle. An exit status like 244 alone doesn't mean the worker ran out of memory; use the reported cause to decide.

Artifact set installs use the same client, with one source per host route, and two differences: A source with redirects = "server" treats any 3xx response as ROUTE_REDIRECT_UNEXPECTED and doesn't follow it. A redirect to a host that no route allows fails with ROUTE_REDIRECT_UNROUTABLE. A redirect to a host with its own rule is fetched from that rule's destination. With no tools route configured, redirects may reach any HTTPS host. Redirect targets and their query strings are never stored or reported.

Rust helper archives (nextest and cargo-llvm-cov) download through this client. Public downloads use GitHub and its release-asset redirect host. A configured tool connector replaces that public source, with no fallback to the public one. The recipe is checked against its metadata before download, and the archive digest before extraction. See helper installation.

Downloads in progress can't be interrupted immediately when a session ends. Private registries other than those builders support, and automatic credential refresh, aren't supported. A successful retry doesn't authenticate a dependency or make it eligible for release.
Declared fetches for pinned downloads in build.yaml. Artifact sets for routed tool installs.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/action-cache.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A repeat oyzu build skips targets whose inputs haven't changed and restores their earlier results. You configure nothing: you never write cache keys or per-language cache paths. This page covers what is reused, what invalidates it, how to see why a stage ran, and how to share results through a registry. Note: The action cache is experimental. The remote cache is unsigned, so a remote hit tells you which run produced a result, not that the result was verified. See stage reuse for builder and execution-path admission rules.

Cache explanations accept additional descriptive JSON fields. Updating an explanation preserves annotations on its envelope, subject and retained observations, including component annotations when the action key is unchanged. History still retains only the latest and previous observations. Explanations never authorize reuse: action keys, content digests and trust checks remain binding. Annotations on test-unit and case-history envelopes are retained only while their identity key and subject remain unchanged. A new key starts a new record; facts from an earlier identity do not carry over. Annotation-only lookup data does not replace the current explanation or its version-scope fallback. oyzu history reads recorded build and test summaries without rewriting their files. It locates logs/events.jsonl as an opaque journal; additional event kinds or descriptive fields do not affect that lookup or establish verification. Paths remain confined to the bundle. Installation lease journals and interrupted configuration-edit journals remain strict because recovery can remove locks or replace files.

oyzu build # first build runs and stores; repeats reuse oyzu build --affected HEAD # Git-selected targets also reuse unchanged results oyzu build --full # quality stages and their reports are reused too oyzu build --no-cache # run every action; read and write nothing oyzu cache status # where the store is, how large, how many entries oyzu cache clear # remove every cached result (bundles are untouched) oyzu build --explain # after the build, why each stage was reused or ran oyzu cache explain api # why target api's key (and its stages' keys) last changed Every oyzu cache command supports the global --json flag before or after the subcommand. status and clear inspect the configured store; explain reads its recorded key history. Output shortened. A project with four targets, one run each: $ oyzu build # cold ✓ Build succeeded 4 targets · 4 executed · 9.4s $ oyzu build # unchanged repeat ↺ api build reused was 1.2s ✓ Build succeeded 4 targets · 4 reused · 1.8s $ echo "// edit" >> api/src/greeting.mjs && oyzu build ✓ Build succeeded 4 targets · 3 reused · 1 executed · 3.1s Reuse is local to one user on one machine unless you configure a remote cache. Every output says plainly that a restored result was not executed now: Receipts keep reused test evidence apart from fresh tests. When known, reuse.source records whether the local or remote store served the result. Compile-stage cache misses annotate the existing action row with missed: <reason>. The same reason appears on the running task event in events.jsonl and in cache explanation history, including builder identity changed when that component changes. Development plugins report plugin.source_digest through describe. First-party plugins embed the digest of their Cargo package source and local build/runtime dependency closure at compilation, including the dependency lock and runtime assets. Private per-invocation plugin executable locations and frozen invocation tokens use that verified identity in output-location keys and native-read definitions; checkout and native compiler-cache locations remain significant. Replacing linked executables from the same inputs does not invalidate reuse, including when a self-host build installs its newly built CLI. A plugin without this identity can still build, but its development results are not reused. Published packages keep their admitted release digest in the key. Executable verification, private invocation copies and package admission remain required independently of cache identity. Moving an unchanged checkout on the same platform preserves keys only for stages whose builder declares every retained output relocatable. Before hashing, Oyzu replaces known checkout, private-workspace and per-run scratch locations in command arguments, environment values and declared paths with stable relative locations. This includes paths inside native JSON arguments and Windows drive, separator and verbatim-prefix forms. Paths to inputs outside those known roots still affect the key; resolved tool and plugin identities remain part of it. Source bytes, build profiles and platforms must still agree. Root matches require the end of the value or a directory separator. A sibling such as C:\ws)external\input.rs stays distinct from the root C:\ws. This also applies inside command text: punctuation alone does not establish containment, so ambiguous text retains its original identity. Entries written by versions that retained checkout-specific paths can miss once after upgrading; the existing cache need not be cleared. An unavailable cache is different from --no-cache. If the store can't be used, permitted native builds continue with a warning and run everything.

The builder's relocatable_outputs command promise covers intermediate trees and reports as well as delivered artifacts. Without that promise, the key also binds the actual checkout, execution working directory, arguments and environment before location normalization. Moving the checkout or changing those native locations causes recomputation instead of restoring files that refer to the old location. The location input is stored as a digest. This is automatic; there is no project setting to override the builder's promise. Core-allocated temporary report directories do not change this digest between invocations; checkout, working-directory and native compiler-cache paths still do. On Windows, leased tool locations use the on-disk spelling captured from the already-pinned store-root handle. Case aliases (including drive-letter case), 8.3 short names and \\?\ paths for that same store do not change the tool location or its command-derived extension digests. This does not lowercase paths: different case-sensitive directories keep different location keys. Store roots and ancestors still refuse reparse points: junction aliases fail closed, even when their target is another store directory. Publication locks and installation leases continue to protect the same pinned store entries through admitted aliases. If handle-path retrieval or lexical normalization fails, normalization changes the drive prefix, or the path has a different number of components from the pinned ancestor chain, the existing exact path spelling remains significant and an alias may miss. In particular, subst and mapped drives keep their drive spelling rather than expanding to a longer path or UNC location. No path is reopened or resolved to obtain this identity after pinning. Builder Outputs eligible for cross-location action reuse Rust Native copy/export operations and rustfmt checks. Compilation, package verification and arbitrary tests remain location-sensitive: debug information, dep-info and build-script products are not a portable tree. Go Conventional application compilation with frozen ordinary compiler controls uses native -trimpath and -buildvcs=false. The validated native export copy is relocatable, with its producer's content digest still binding. Unknown controls, custom flags/commands, preparation and other stages remain location-sensitive. Node Native single-package archive packing (with lifecycle scripts disabled) and entry verification are relocatable; reuse still requires complete-read admission. Installation, workspace operations and authored build/test tasks remain location-sensitive, including executable shims and generated source maps. Python Native package export is relocatable; reuse still requires complete-read admission. Preparation, backend execution, tests and quality tools remain location-sensitive, including interpreter paths and bytecode. .NET Linux crun builds reuse compile, test and pack results across roots for audited deterministic SDK projects with complete admitted inputs. Offline restore always reruns and regenerates local NuGet assets; publish and unknown MSBuild customizations retain conservative contracts. Linux/Windows native stages have incomplete reads and rerun. Other isolated backends do not provide this complete-read guarantee; macOS execution is unsupported. See .NET stage reads. Java Maven and Gradle archive-copy exports preserve producer bytes and can reuse across locations. Linux crun execution can reuse the lifecycle under its enforced input boundary and stable container paths. Native-host lifecycle trees remain location-sensitive and have incomplete reads. Helm, Docker, Zig Location-sensitive unless their command explicitly declares all retained outputs relocatable. Artifact portability alone does not grant intermediate-tree reuse. Zig 0.15.2 native Debug artifacts embed absolute workspace and cache roots in DWARF, and the compiler has no remapping flag. Identical sources built from independent clean roots can therefore produce different artifact digests even with --no-cache. Conformance retains an explicit Debug exception for this documented upstream limitation. This does not change release modes or captured builds, which retain their existing fixed worker placement; neither artifact equality nor release optimization grants cross-location intermediate reuse. See Zig Debug artifact reproducibility. Portable consumers still depend on the content identity of their upstream outputs. Declaring a copy or archive operation portable never makes its producer portable. Location-sensitive stages can miss even in an unchanged checkout when their native arguments contain newly allocated scratch paths; native compiler incremental state remains independently available. This does not rewrite cached outputs or weaken artifact validation, cache admission or required checks.

There is no merged Windows complete-read backend for Vite or uv lifecycles. Native stages with incomplete reads must execute again; copying the source into a private workspace does not change that. Python 0.1.3 refuses Windows uv before actions start; later releases admit it and run it again each time. Supported isolated Linux reuse requires a Linux crun host; it does not enable native Windows reuse. On native Windows, Maven/Gradle lifecycles and arbitrary npm scripts have incomplete runtime reads. They run again on unchanged builds; a whole-target cache hit cannot skip them. Independently admitted complete-read stages and native tool/download caches may still reuse their own results. Use oyzu build --explain or oyzu cache explain app (replace app with your build target) to see the named refusal: native reads are incomplete on this host. For a whole-target refusal, query the target name rather than an action name; the refusal is recorded even though no reusable result is stored. This is a safe execution decision, not a damaged cache. Clearing the cache or adding known inputs cannot establish complete runtime reads. For Maven/Gradle and npm stage reuse, use the isolated Linux crun path: oyzu build --isolated --no-docker. Windows does not provide that boundary. --no-cache runs the same native commands without reading or writing action-cache results; changed external inputs must affect both cached and uncached execution.

Native host builds preserve the compiler/runtime controls declared by their builder and freeze their inherited values into the action environment before cache lookup. Changing one of these values invalidates both whole-target and individual-stage reuse. Explicit project/task environment settings still take precedence; configuration removals and environment policy validation still apply. Human output and --json report the same executed/reused actions. The Rust builder declares Cargo/rustc flags (including encoded flags), compiler and documentation executables, compiler wrappers, toolchain/build-target controls, Cargo/Rustup home locations, the selected target's Cargo flags/linker/runner, native C/C++ compiler and linker controls, and reproducible-build stamps. The Node builder declares NODE_ENV, NODE_OPTIONS, NODE_PATH, NODE_ICU_DATA, OPENSSL_CONF, TZ, native C/C++ compiler and linker controls, and SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH. The lists live beside each builder's stage declarations. npm installation also retains its existing binding of discovered npm_config_* controls. Native build actions receive their frozen declared and configured environment, plus shared launch, home and Windows machine-discovery controls. HOME, USERPROFILE, APPDATA and LOCALAPPDATA are passed through when set and keyed with their exact values, alongside PATH, SYSTEMROOT, SYSTEMDRIVE, PROGRAMDATA, WINDIR, COMSPEC, PATHEXT, ProgramFiles, ProgramFiles(x86), ALLUSERSPROFILE, OS, PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE and PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432. Explicit configuration overrides inherited values. Changing a passed home/profile value between shells changes the action key, even if the native tool ultimately does not use it. This preserves native Go, .NET and Helm home-directory defaults without guessing which tools read home. Home inputs are a single set: HOME, USERPROFILE, APPDATA and LOCALAPPDATA. Go, .NET/NuGet, Helm, Cargo/Rust and npm/Node all retain this set, including formatting commands. Other builders and commands with no home declaration retain the same default. Home values identify the environment; they do not establish complete filesystem reads or authorize reuse of files discovered through passwd, Windows known folders, registry or JVM properties. The SDK also retains home for pnpm/Yarn, pip/uv/Poetry, Maven/Gradle/Ant, Zig and Docker contracts. Their tool-specific cache and configuration variables keep their existing environment and key semantics. Builder source contracts may declare home: "required" or home: "none". Missing declarations mean required. An unqualified none claim retains the home environment and prevents native action, whole-target and shared-cache reuse. Fixed source rules and compiler read reports alone do not cover home discovery or descendants. Explicit home environment settings or declared home names cancel the claim and retain ordinary home-required behavior. Replacement commands and hooks use their own contracts. On Windows the declaration recognizes these four names without regard to case. Existing environment precedence and policy validation remain binding; case-colliding aliases are refused with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Configure one spelling per name and retry. No native host scope omits home on Linux, Windows or macOS. This requires no new user setting or network access. The scoped exception is first-party packaged Rust format-check under the Linux crun executor (oyzu build --full --isolated --no-docker). Core admits the package identity and bounded Cargo formatter command separately from the claim, then freezes an enforced boundary in the action identity. The formatter and its descendants can read only admitted image, tool and source inputs and private outputs; ambient host home is not mounted. Passwd/account fallback sees keyed image facts, not the host account database. Image defaults cannot restore the omitted variables. Explicit CARGO_HOME and RUSTUP_HOME remain inputs. Only that action loses home; a compilation or other receiving sibling retains its own home values in its key and the enclosing target key. Native hosts, development plugins and third-party declarations do not acquire this exception. Windows shell lookup uses these frozen launch inputs, including a configured Path, rather than consulting the host environment again. The corrected lookup advances Oyzu's internal cache identity, so older action results are rebuilt. TEMP, TMP and TMPDIR are executor-owned: native actions always receive private temporary paths in place of inherited, configured or builder-declared values. These overwritten values are omitted from native host action keys, declared environment reads and command-derived extension digests, including when supplied by configuration or a builder. Changing only those values preserves reuse. Authored inputs and the final allocated environment still undergo policy validation. Configuration files read as ordinary program data remain source inputs; editing their bytes can still invalidate those reads. The private paths never enter keys or extension digests. Other undeclared shell variables are absent, even with --no-cache; declare project-specific inputs in configuration. Complete read admission remains required: removing an unused ambient variable never makes incomplete reads reusable. Native .NET stages still run on every build because their reads are incomplete. Native Helm packaging and archive normalization also rerun without complete observed reads. Development tasks retain host inheritance. Ordinary host stages do not provide filesystem or network isolation; admitted authored tasks use the per-action boundary described below.

On Unix, source and output inventories record ordinary regular-file permission bits as unixMode (0 through 511, the octal 0777 mask), retaining the existing executable fact. Mode-only changes participate in both coarse target and selected-content action keys. Listing-only selectors still identify names and entry kinds; source-version scopes remain permission-independent. This is conservative invalidation for captured source too: raw observed modes can change a key even when the selected captured execution view normalizes its permissions. That execution behavior is unchanged. Prepared-file copy provenance requires mode equality as well as bytes and executable intent. Cached group and workspace-delta files carry the admitted mode from the same file handle as their bytes. Verification rejects absent, out-of-range or executable-inconsistent Unix mode evidence before accepting a restore; older records follow normal cache refusal/recompute behavior. It never substitutes a canonical 0644 or 0755. Verified bytes remain readable during cross-device staging, and the final mode is applied before atomic publication. A failed file restore preserves its existing destination. On hosts that cannot observe Unix modes, the optional fact is absent. Directory output modes, ACLs, ownership and special bits are not added to the cache contract. Use --no-cache when those properties affect the required output. Directory output trees retain empty roots and nested empty directories as well as regular files. Restore verifies the complete directory inventory against the artifact record; missing directories are corruption, even when no file bytes are missing. Directory artifacts reject symbolic links, including links to directories and linked artifact roots. Cache capture does not follow them. Private action-output collection converts native relative path components to portable /-separated names before validation. Nested files and empty directories retain their layout; nonportable names, links and special files are rejected. Unix executable permission bits are preserved where the host supports them.

The test-attempt controller can retry genuine test failures within a build. Rust case reruns use exact nextest selection and retain native retry attempts without adding Oyzu retries on top. A recovered case is reported as flaky, and its unit is never stored as a clean reusable result, including when nextest performs the retries. Native pytest reruns exact failed node IDs; detected pytest native retries have unknown attempts, prevent storage and receive no additional Oyzu retry. Missing requested cases stay failed. --no-cache preserves the same retry and completeness rules. Eligible test units also retain actual executed outcomes in local cache history. An exact unit input key and test identity with both a pass and a failure proves flakiness. Named native cases are compared individually. A legacy report with unnamed cases uses the whole unit when it declares a dedicated assertion exit and retries are disabled. Findings retain both outcomes, run IDs and machine names. Machine names come from the operating system on Unix and Windows, independently of ambient environment variables such as COMPUTERNAME, including in native build actions with a cleared environment. A cache hit adds no execution evidence. Different keys, skipped cases, missing reports, setup failures and executor/resource errors do not prove a flaky test. By default every current failure still fails under its configured check level. Opt in explicitly with [checks] quarantineFlaky = true in the configuration cascade. Policy can forbid it. Quarantine executes tests freshly, keeps their failures and required native reports, and makes only a proven same-key flaky assertion failure non-blocking. Release context and governed main CI always ignore quarantine, including an explicit true value under [context.ci.checks] on a main-CI run in ci context. Coverage, required reports and the existing order-dependence guard remain binding. Separate native test and doctest reports are matched to the complete contributions of their named units; unknown or missing contributions still fail. Human and no-color receipts list Flaky tests and Quarantined failures. JSON and retained manifests include unit executions, flaky, quarantined, nativeExitCode and nativeCases; each unit's native outcome remains failed when quarantine changes its step disposition. The build's tests section also collects executions, sameInputFlaky, sameInputFlakyCount, quarantinedFailures and quarantinedCount. flakyCount continues to count attempt flakes; sameInputFlakyCount counts historical same-input findings separately and defaults to zero when absent in an older record. Native JUnit failures remain failures. History requires an already admitted input key and the existing local cache store; quarantine grants no missing read bounds or cache authority. It works offline with installed tools and needs no account. --no-cache retains visible retries but reads/writes no cross-build outcome history and applies no history quarantine. History is local: another machine or an evicted store may lack earlier outcomes. There is no platform quarantine integration. A known conflict revokes clean-pass reuse for that key even after a later pass; healthy siblings retain normal reuse. See quarantine configuration.

Control Effect oyzu build --no-cache No lookup and no storage for this build. The summary shows disabled (--no-cache). cache.local = false Same, from configuration (default true). cache.dir Absolute directory that replaces the default store location. User or system scope only. A project oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml that sets it is rejected with CONFIG_SCOPE. User-scope configuration is ignored in CI. oyzu cache status / clear Show or empty the store. status also reports the Docker image budget. oyzu build --explain, oyzu cache explain <target> Explain why stages were reused or ran. Read-only. cache.remote, cache.read, cache.write The remote OCI cache: destination, lookup (default on) and publishing (default off). cache.ciRemote, cache.immutableTags The CI repository, and whether the registry refuses to replace tags (default off). build.host-workspaces-dir Absolute directory where native builds park private copies of your source. User or machine configuration only. Changed execution locations invalidate location-sensitive stages. See configuration. Keys and cache paths are never user-authored. Native builds work from a private copy of each target's source, kept in a host-workspaces folder next to the action store. It follows the platform cache location, not cache.dir. If that folder is on a different drive than your checkout (for example the cache on C: and the repository on E:), Oyzu parks the copy in the repository's Git directory instead (.git/oyzu/host-workspaces, or the linked worktree's Git directory), so parking stays a rename rather than a full copy. The first such build moves a copy parked at the old location. Use build.host-workspaces-dir to choose the folder yourself. It must be outside the source tree; the Git directory counts as outside. The path must not pass through a symbolic link, except root-owned top-level links in a root-owned filesystem root that is not writable by group or others, such as macOS /tmp and /var. Oyzu renames the copy into place when it can, and otherwise copies only the pruned source, keeping file times and permissions so native tools such as Cargo still see unchanged files as fresh. A real source edit still invalidates native compilation. Oyzu never copies compiler, dependency or tool caches. Changing the setting doesn't move existing parked workspaces. For disposable native projects, set both cache.dir and build.host-workspaces-dir in a private user configuration selected with OYZU_USER_CONFIG. Setting only cache.dir does not isolate source parking. On Windows, changing HOME does not redirect the native cache location. The Git fallback requires an existing repository, recognized by the same metadata checks as project discovery. Outside Git, parking stays in the native cache even across filesystems, unless you set build.host-workspaces-dir. Empty .git markers and directories holding only Oyzu state do not expand the host source boundary or select the fallback. Oyzu never creates a .git directory for host-workspace state. If a configured parking path would require one, the build fails with host workspace storage cannot create a Git directory; select a cache folder outside the source tree.

Host Default store Linux $XDG_CACHE_HOME/oyzu/actions (fallback ~/.cache/oyzu/actions) macOS ~/Library/Caches/Oyzu/actions Windows %LocalAppData%\Oyzu\cache\actions The store is per user and shared across projects. It holds blobs/sha256/ (file bytes), results/<key>.json (result descriptors), history/, pushed/ (remote publication markers), quarantine/ (rejected data), preparation-locks/ and tmp/. Output trees are stored as a manifest plus one file per blob, not as a compressed archive. Workspace changes and merge-back from private native or confined views are detected against a content baseline. The tracker compares size, modification time, executable status and link target. On Unix it also compares change time (ctime), device and inode; on Windows it reads ChangeTime and the volume/file ID through attribute-only handles without following links. These native facts detect same-length rewrites even when a tool restores an old modification time. Each baseline starts with a temporary probe in the workspace, removed before scanning, whose modification time supplies the filesystem clock. An otherwise unchanged regular file is content-compared if either its modification time or native change time is not strictly older than that stamp. This includes equal clock ticks and future timestamps. Unchanged older files keep the stat-only fast path. If native change information or a timestamp is unavailable, regular files are conservatively content-compared: the modification-time rule alone cannot detect a rewrite that restores an old timestamp. Views keep baseline digests only for regular files with racy or unavailable clocks. An equal-size, equal-mtime write is merged back before delta capture; unchanged older files require no content read. Identical content produces no delta. Symbolic links, special files and executable changes retain their existing handling; a delta containing links or special files is not restorable. Serial confined actions may share files with their private target workspace through hard links. Creating and removing those views changes native metadata without changing content, so those files still require hashing. Before staging a candidate, the tracker compares its digest, executable status and link kind with the content baseline. An identical entry produces no delta or staging copy. An executable-only change still stores its bytes so it can be restored. Changed files use the digest and size returned by verified store admission, which may read the file again after the preliminary hash. This avoids unnecessary staging; it does not remove link-induced hashing. Preserved-mtime writes and racy or unavailable clocks retain their content-comparison rules. Workspace restores verify every cached file into private staging before accepting a hit. Deferred restores retain those staged files without keeping a file handle open per file, so large results such as Python virtual environments do not require raising the process file-descriptor limit. Staged files are removed after restore or when the pending restore is discarded. A corrupt blob rejects reuse before the workspace is changed.

At the end of a build, if the store is over 10 GiB, Oyzu removes the least recently used results until it fits, then removes blobs no result references. A hit refreshes an entry. Eviction touches only the cache. Bundles in dist hold their own copies. The budget is fixed. Cache history metadata, including definition-keyed native observations, has a separate 64 MiB ceiling (bounded further by a smaller maintenance budget). Every retention pass prunes its least recently used records, even when result bytes are below budget. Pruned observations discard narrowed lookup shapes. Native stages can still discover stored complete-prediction results; otherwise they return to whole-target keys. The same pass bounds the store's other expendable state, so a long-lived laptop or runner cache doesn't grow without limit: State Kept quarantine/ (rejected data) 7 days, and at most 256 MiB; the oldest goes first. pushed/ (remote publication markers) 7 days. A missing marker only makes the next push recheck the remote. tmp/ (staging) Files older than 24 hours are abandoned leftovers and are removed. Active staging is newer and protected by the build lease. preparation-locks/ Removed when no process holds them. A held lock is never unlinked. oyzu cache status reports these together with history as auxiliary bytes (auxiliaryBytes in --json), separately from the result budget, and oyzu cache clear removes them too. store.lock and history.lock are never removed. Installed tools and bundles in dist are outside the store and are never touched. Builds hold a shared lock on store.lock while they read or write the cache. Preparation publishers and history writers release their operation locks when they finish, including on failure. Unrelated child processes do not extend those locks' lifetimes. An unused store isn't created. Runs with the cache disabled, or with nothing cacheable, leave it alone. oyzu cache clear needs exclusive access. While a build uses the cache it fails with a retry message and leaves active staging alone. Retry when the build finishes. If end-of-build eviction hits contention it warns, and the store may briefly exceed its budget. A later build retries. If a store is busy with maintenance, builds proceed without it and cache commands return an error. Don't delete store.lock to clear contention. The lock protects cooperating Oyzu processes, not external deletion or filesystems without working locks.

Oyzu hashes file bytes while copying them into the cache and again when restoring them. It checks every file of a restored action before accepting the hit, and it replaces each destination file only after its copy succeeded, so a missing or corrupt blob leaves the previous file in place. Corrupt cache data is rejected, quarantined and recomputed (see Failures and recovery). A restore that touches several files isn't rolled back if a later file operation fails. Artifact and report gates still run after a restore.

The unit of reuse depends on what Oyzu knows about the target: Per action for targets whose actions all carry a stage contract (including captured node/package and node/app), or which contain an independently admitted native authored cached action. Each eligible action (for example api:version, api:build, api:package) has its own key and result. A companion without a stage contract always executes; its output digest still keys actions that follow it, and it blocks storing or restoring a whole-target group. See Per-action reuse. Per target where individual actions are not admitted: one key per target, restoring all its actions together or none. Native whole-target reuse requires every stage to have complete admitted reads and bounded outputs; it cannot bypass a stage that must run. A reused target or action keeps: its artifacts, byte for byte (each is checked against its recorded digest); its original JUnit, coverage and other reports and their producer evidence; the original run ID, key and completion time, in a reuse record. Oyzu stores a target only after all its actions succeeded and its reports were collected. Failed, blocked and cancelled targets aren't stored. Built-in builders declare their own actions; no user-authored cache key is needed. Reuse still requires admitted reads, bounded outputs and valid results. Declared source inputs are included in the target's key on both native and captured paths. Targets with a builder-selected source projection are cacheable too. A projection narrows the target's own folder to selected target-relative files; it does not declare additional source outside that folder. Whole-target keys include the projection definition and the captured identities of its selected entries (paths, types, content digests and executable bits). For native captures, whole-target fallback keys retain both the frozen selection rules and the captured content digest, even when the caller's source scope is unchanged. A workspace member edit therefore invalidates the fallback key. Native capture keys use the existing engine cache contract; invalidation follows the captured inputs. A stage with an admitted read set keys only its selected reads, including directory listings used for discovery. The whole candidate projection is not a second input to that stage. Native reuse first finds observations for the same command, engine and prediction, then validates a complete observation against the current admitted source and computes the result key from those reads. Successful admitted native results are also stored under a key covering the complete current prediction. A remote reader with empty local result and observation history can derive that key without receiving or trusting a remote read list. It uses the same tool, environment, profile, platform, upstream, artifact and report checks as other action results. A valid narrow hit also offers a result for its current complete prediction, so an edit to a predicted but unread input does not leave subsequent empty readers without a lookup. This discovery key matches only the current prediction's inputs; it does not provide observation history across different source snapshots. Existing remote scope and producer trust limits still apply. Missing, incomplete or out-of-prediction observations cannot authorize new prediction or narrowed results. Without an existing admitted result, the native stage runs without restoring or storing a coarse result. A whole-source key cannot cover files read outside the source root. Confined captured actions use the files available in their view. Key construction reuses captured entry digests; it does not walk or hash source files again. The same rule applies to an export or copy stage without a stage contract: the target still runs, but cannot fall back to caching the whole target. With complete contracts, eligible stages can retain their separate cache entries. Explicit builder reads and writes are scoped from the target folder on both captured and native paths. Parent traversal (two dots) is refused for paths, globs and listings. Declared workspace inputs remain a separate source-admission mechanism. Conventional native Go compilation writes a stable intermediate executable. A final export copies it to the inferred-version filename. An unread README content edit can reuse build, vet and format-check; a commit with unchanged source reuses those stages. If version metadata changes without source changes, only the versioned export runs again. A plain empty commit leaves the source-content snapshot version unchanged, so export can reuse too. Artifact metadata and receipts retain the current inferred version. Go does not inject a version variable into the program. Authored version-bearing commands and environment values remain inputs, and other builders need their own final-stage version boundary.

These targets simply run, and the output says why: Targets with authored tasks or task overrides that don't ask to be cached, and targets whose hooks ([tasks."api:pre_build"]) declare no outputs. An authored task with cache = true and outputs is eligible only with complete read admission (see Authored tasks). A hook that declares outputs is followed on targets reused action by action (see Hooks). Targets with hooks on a path that reuses a target only whole (native host targets with hooks, and captured targets without stage contracts). Restoring them would skip hooks that must run on every build. Targets that use secret environment values ({ secret = "…" }).

Linux crun npm stages use complete-read enforcement through the existing isolated/container selection (oyzu build --isolated --no-docker). Successful stages can reuse their workspace changes, artifacts and required reports on unchanged runs. Their keys include admitted source reads, prepared dependency identities, the locked Node runtime, other tool/runtime identities, command, environment and producer outputs. A source edit invalidates the stages that read it and their consumers. Script-free installation omits only the generated OYZU_VERSION default when the admitted model proves it is unread, allowing reuse across shipping edits. Lockfile, npm config, tool identity and other execution inputs remain keyed. Explicit version environment values remain keyed, and every build/test stage keeps its version input. Root/dependency install scripts (including scripts with reviewed file reads), implicit native compilation, incomplete facts and runtime loaders retain the variable and refuse install reuse. Arbitrary lifecycle scripts conservatively read the entire admitted source view. Lock/dependency and locked tool changes invalidate the affected stages. These actions share the enforced boundary with the captured Maven experiment: live proc/sys and undeclared host paths are hidden, network is denied, and each lifecycle starts with private output state. Fixed core retirement/export helpers retain their existing bounded contracts. Failed unsupported reads cannot publish reusable success. A handled absence is stable within this view. The closed non-keying device allowance below also applies; entropy must not affect retained outputs. --no-cache runs under the same boundary and report gates. No extra setting is needed. Native npm on Linux, Windows and macOS still refuses incomplete reads; Docker and other Node package managers retain their existing captured rules. For native npm applications with dependencies, the target includes the install action (npm ci) in the private target workspace before pre-build hooks. Arbitrary build and package lifecycle scripts have no complete native read report, so their results cannot be reused, even with unchanged source. An incomplete native stage also prevents whole-target restoration. Bounded install declarations alone do not enable native per-action admission. This does not disable the separate tool and dependency download caches, or the admitted captured actions described below. Nothing needs clearing after a CLI update.

Before looking up actions, the captured npm path validates native metadata and downloads locked dependency bytes with lifecycle scripts turned off. That script-free step can be reused from the local store. The key covers the full source and target tree, the worker image and platform, the admitted tools, the command and environment, configuration and the download routes. Any change to the source, lock, tools, routes or configuration needs a new download. Tools are checked before lookup, and restored files are verified before use. This download entry does not cache later offline install or lifecycle work. Those stages can reuse separately under the Linux crun boundary described above. The journal records a reused step as not executed now, with its original time and key. These entries share the local store, lock and 10 GiB budget. They are never uploaded to a remote cache. A missing or damaged entry falls back to a fresh download. Partly restored trees are discarded. --no-cache, cache.local = false and --verify-contract turn this reuse off. Builds with managed configuration, secret environment values or authenticated routes don't use it. Offline builds can reuse earlier captures.

Native builder actions can bind exact prepared-resource files. The plan records those files and their content digest, and execution mounts the same selection even with --no-cache. Captured Go tests run in confined workspaces with fresh report folders. Validated reports are captured into the build bundle; restored reports keep their producer evidence. Test manifests and compiled tests are explicit build outputs consumed through producer relationships. See Go. Go compile actions and exports retain separate captured source/dependency keys. Source, module/lockfile, prepared dependency and selected Go identity changes invalidate consuming actions. On Linux crun, isolated go/app builds reuse complete-read stages, including generated test preparation and unit results. Generated manifests and compiled tests enter the observed read set and stage key; changed manifest bytes miss, and undeclared carried files are refused. Every invocation gets fresh writable /out, with only selected phase inputs and identified unit contributions mounted read-only. --no-cache executes every stage with these same boundaries and required report gates. Incomplete native-host reads continue to refuse stage and whole-target reuse on Linux, Windows and macOS. There is no complete Go runtime-read enforcement backend on Windows or macOS. See Go.

Captured path: oyzu build and oyzu build --affected on targets that use the Docker executor and its toolchain images (for example node/package). Native host path: builds that run on the host with Oyzu-provisioned tools reuse only stages with complete admitted reads and bounded outputs. Unchanged source alone does not guarantee reuse. See Native host builds and current native read coverage. Targets built by a host-coordinated image worker aren't cached yet and say so. oyzu run executions are never cached. No account is needed. Ephemeral CI runners start with an empty local store. With a remote cache they reuse results other checkouts pushed. Tested mainly on Linux.
