On a Windows host, shared edits conservatively re-run unrelated work. macOS isn't supported yet. On Windows, action tracking records native symbolic links and the Linux links Docker creates in a captured workspace without following them, so pnpm links stay usable by later native actions. A change that contains links can't be restored from the cache. Other Windows reparse formats fail with an error.

In the live Build section, restored actions show ↺ (the word reused without color) in place of executed. The summary counts them apart from executed work (2 targets · 3 reused · 1 executed). With -v and in JSON you also get each target's reuse origin and the Cache line. The final receipt marks test and coverage lines from restored reports as reused from an earlier run, not run now. In the build bundle a reused action keeps status: "succeeded", so every gate applies unchanged, and gains: "actionKey": "sha256:…", "reuse": { "actionKey": "sha256:…", "originalRunId": "…", "originalCompletedAt": "2026-10-07T08:43:02Z", "originalDurationMs": 812 } manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"] records the mode, whether the cache was active or disabled (and why) and each target's outcome: reused, executed (with stored, and rejected if a damaged entry was replaced) or not-cached with the reason. Journal events in logs/events.jsonl use the finish status reused. Logs for reused actions aren't recreated. A hit never skips a gate. On restore, every report is parsed again from its stored bytes and judged by the current contract (for example the coverage minimum). A report that fails there rejects the entry, and the target runs normally. Preflight, policy and required-check enforcement are unchanged.

oyzu build --explain explains decisions after running the build; oyzu cache explain <target> reads recorded history without running anything. They report reuse refusals as well as the first key component that changed. A stage can be refused reuse even when its key is unchanged. Native action explanations include skipped history discovery and candidates in nativeCandidates, with basis: "history", lookup: "skipped" and a reason. Reasons cover disabled observation, a missing HISTORY subject or unreadable record, missing or malformed reports, the four-report history limit, incomplete observations, reads outside the current prediction, missing source snapshots, and unavailable admission or key derivation. Outside-prediction reasons show the first five sorted paths, listings or external inputs and count any remainder. History is also skipped for an uncacheable action, a missing stage contract, unbounded outputs, or an authored replacement without admitted observation. A missing-record reason names the current HISTORY subject digest. Reports under another subject are not considered; a record can also be absent, unreadable or invalid. Skipped entries describe why no lookup occurred and never admit a hit. nativeHistory includes the lookup subject, sorted storedSubjects for the same action ID, and unattributedRecords for older native records without action and subject metadata. Human output names these alongside the gate reasons; other subjects remain diagnostic only and never supply candidates. A native action restored through a whole-target hit still has an actionExplain entry with its current nativeHistory.subject. Its winning nativeCandidates entry has basis: "whole-target" and lookup: "hit"; no independent action candidate was probed on that shortcut. Set OYZU_DEBUG_NATIVE_SUBJECT=<dir> to write best-effort lookup-<pid>-<random>.json and store-<pid>-<random>.json receipts with action ID, frozen HISTORY digest and pre-digest payload structure (scalar values hashed to protect secrets); disabled by default, with no cache behavior change. For example (illustrative): {"basis":"history","candidate":1,"lookup":"skipped","reason":"observation outside prediction: extra.rs"} Each key is made of named components, compared in this order: Component What it covers Parts named on a change builder The builder ID, engine cache contract, and declared plugin source/package identity profile The applied build profile, development or optimized profile development vs optimized platform, variant The target platform and variant toolchain The toolchain: image content digest or resolved tool lock, host platform dependencies The prepared dependencies (for Node, node_modules) projection Frozen source selection rules and captured content digest for whole-target fallback keys source The source digest in scope: the whole target scope, or a confined action's predicted reads definition The frozen action definitions, field by field and environment variable by variable: argv, env.<NAME>, cwd, limits, report contracts, configuration digest, input mounts api:build env.MODE (group key) or env.MODE (action key) materialized Digests of artifacts consumed from producer targets The artifact ID upstream Output digests of the earlier actions an action follows The action ID When several components differ, the first is the reason and the rest are listed after it. A matching key permits reuse only after admission and result validation; components explain key changes. source comes before definition because an action's environment can carry values derived from source, such as the development version. Every lookup also records the subject's latest key in history/ under the store: the run that first and last used it, and the distinct key before it. A subject is a target or, for targets reused action by action, each action. History is written even when nothing is stored (a failed build, an always-run target), is a few kilobytes per subject and is removed by oyzu cache clear. A cold native lookup can use a conservative source scope. Complete read observations from its execution can produce a narrower stored result key; cache explain --json continues to describe the lookup in subjects[].actionKey. On a later hit, the action's actionKey and reuse.actionKey identify the reused result, and reuse.originalRunId identifies its producer. Use those reuse fields to compare completed results across builds. Key-history persistence is best-effort. A lookup continues if recording its history fails, and its action or target explanation includes historyWarning with the cause. Fix the backing-store permissions or filesystem issue, then build again to record history.

After the receipt, it shows at most eight action decisions, with a count of the rest. The manifest has complete detail. A blocked or failed action keeps its failure cause. An expanded entry looks like this: Why each stage ran or was reused api:build — Executed Recorded selection: api (requested) Reuse: source files in scope changed Source comparison: run previous-observation changed: shared/greeting.mjs (reads-source) Native provenance: applications/api/build.mjs:2 (path, exact) Other reasons you may see: profile development vs optimized (the recorded build used a different applied profile) source projection changed (its selection definition or selected content changed) no earlier build of it is recorded in this cache (first build, or after cache clear) no result stored for this key in the ci remote cache; no local build history either (a fresh CI container whose remote cache was asked and had nothing), or no local build history, and the ci remote cache was unavailable (denied|unreachable); a stored result could not be looked up when the remote could not be asked (the class only, never a host or token) inputs unchanged since run …, but no result is stored (not stored, evicted or cleared) the stored result was rejected: … (damaged entry) a hook runs on every build… native reads are incomplete on this host; this stage must run, with the builder-specific reason and the isolated Linux crun command for Maven/Gradle and npm stage reuse a builder-specific incomplete-read reason, followed by whole-target reuse is disabled; this stage must run until the builder supplies complete reads and bounded outputs a note that the result came from a remote A stage of a target that is reused or run whole shares the target's reason. A target that isn't cacheable shows its not-cached reason. An incomplete-read refusal means the native command runs again; it is not a failed test or damaged cache entry. Read the named stage and reason. Adding a known source input can cover that file, but cannot prove that arbitrary tests, plugins or build scripts read nothing else. Clearing the cache cannot fix missing read admission. Update the builder when compatible support is available, or keep running the stage. --no-cache forces execution too; it does not make the stage eligible for reuse. --explain conflicts with --plan and --remote. It changes only the human output. The reasons are always in the manifest, under manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"].targets.<target> as explain ({reason, changed?, previousRunId?, sourceChanges?, historyWarning?}) and, per action, actionExplain.<action>, so --json carries them without the flag. A failed local lookup is recorded as lookup: unavailable with the cause, which is different from a stored result that failed validation.

Oyzu keeps a source inventory per captured context in the cache history. sourceChanges compares the previous build's file identities with the current ones under the action's read scope (or the whole target scope), including added and removed files. Exact reads are labeled reads-source, approximate bounds bounded-read, and unmodeled relationships scope-input. sourceChanges.status is available, unavailable or scope-changed. Oyzu never guesses file names when the inventory is missing or the boundary changed. These inventories follow the history rules: --no-cache writes none, and cache clear removes them. Windows has no confined actions, but captured whole-scope comparison works. Native builds without captured context explain at target level only.

Reads the key history for a target ID (its group key and every recorded action) or one action ID such as api:build. For each it shows the latest key, the runs that first and last used it, whether a result is stored and the first component that differs from the previous key. It reads no project and runs nothing, so it works between builds and on another checkout that shares the store. An unknown name exits non-zero with no key history for <name> in this cache. A build cached only as a whole target records that target ID. If its builder supplies no bounded action contract, use the target ID rather than an action ID; whole-target caching does not create per-action history. $ oyzu cache explain api Cache key explanation api api (whole target) Key 3608cd663130 · since run 26520-… · last seen run 26520-… (2026-10-10T10:04:22Z) Result stored · the next build with these inputs reuses it Changed since run 25996-…: source files in scope changed (also: action definition: api:build env.OYZU_VERSION, api:build env.PROOF_VALUE added and 7 more) api:build (stage) Key f700515a6d9c · since run 26520-… · last seen run 26520-… (2026-10-10T10:04:23Z) Result stored · the next build with these inputs reuses it Changed since run 23970-…: source files in scope changed (also: action definition: env.OYZU_VERSION, env.PROOF_VALUE added and 1 more; output of an earlier action: api:version) --json returns kind: "action-cache-explain" with subjects[] (id, kind, target, actionKey, firstRunId, lastRunId, lastSeenAt, stored, previous, reason, changed). Builder identity differences name the changed semantic field, such as engine.identity or plugin.sourceDigest. JSON exposes these names in changed[].parts[].part; arbitrary input values are not retained. Executable digests remain admission and provenance facts and do not invalidate a result when the semantic identity is unchanged. The Lookup row reports the most recent action lookup's hit, miss or refusal reason, even when its key has not changed. JSON exposes this as lastLookup (reason, lookup and, when applicable, native candidate diagnostics). Restricted targets still record a diagnostic key when their frozen inputs can form one; recording it does not permit reuse or store their outputs. Explicit --no-cache builds do not write cache history. Whole-target hits refresh the histories of their referenced action results too, so their last-seen run identifies the invocation that reused the group. Limits: History keeps two distinct keys per subject, so cache explain compares the latest keys, not an arbitrary older build. To look at a finished build, use history. Whole-target entries without per-action result references have only target history. Builds that share one store at the same time can interleave history writes. Each write is atomic and the later one wins.

Every builder operation declares source reads, an explicit unbounded reason, or explicit upstream-only output consumption. A bounded captured stage keys on its declared read selection. Native source selection also conservatively includes unowned workspace entries. Configuration, tool and prepared-input identities remain separate key components. A directory read includes its listing: adding a source or test file changes the key. An unbounded stage retains the whole-target source key for identity and explanation. On the native path, incomplete reads prevent reuse rather than enabling a coarse fallback. Analyzed native builders include Rust and Zig. Zig's format-check declares fixed .zig/.zon file reads and recursive directory listings. Its build and test stages remain unbounded because build.zig and runtime tests can read arbitrary files without a complete tool-reported read set. See Zig stage reads. Zig opts its fixed-read formatter into a private workspace with no retained files and order-only build/test edges, allowing independent formatter reuse. Build and test retain whole-target source keys for explanation, but their incomplete native reads prevent result reuse. A whole-target source key covers captured project files, not arbitrary files outside the project. Native configuration and scripts can read such files even when a builder does not declare them. When diagnosing suspected stale reuse, compare the edited build with oyzu build --no-cache; matching source keys alone do not establish that an external native input stayed unchanged. Native stages with incomplete reads execute again instead of restoring a result; see native external reads. The Helm plugin also declares per-stage chart read bounds, including conservative chart and formatter scan trees and specific reasons for image bindings and helm-unittest suites. Its captured execution path retains whole-target caching; declaring reads alone does not admit individual stages to the action cache. An admitted upstream_only export reads no source files. Its key uses its own definition, tool/configuration identity and declared upstream output digests, without the target source scope or implicit source inputs. Native admission requires complete observations or fixed command semantics; an empty read list alone never authorizes this. Native Rust binary exports use core-admitted typed copies from the producer's indexed binaries, with stable export paths in each fresh private workspace. Equal producer bytes therefore give equal export output identities despite per-run temporary allocations. Later unconfined checks retain their conservative dependency edges, including the export. Older published plugins may omit this declaration. Oyzu accepts their results and treats each undeclared operation as unbounded, with the reason plugin <reference> <version> declared no reads. The build reports it once the plugin answers, with one PLUGIN_READS_UNDECLARED warning per plugin per build that asks you to update the plugin. oyzu build --plan never invokes a builder. Its Why column (JSON sourceReason) describes stage contracts recorded in that target's last retained build plan, across current, legacy and historical bundles. Reasons are language-neutral and marked as facts from the last build; they do not establish current source completeness or cache admission. Stages without a recorded contract say reported when the builder answers. A later build of another target does not replace this target's recorded reasons. These operations retain whole-target key definitions; native stages still require complete read admission before reuse. The SDK and conformance suite require declarations from new and updated plugins. Read-only preview distinguishes a stage without a retained declaration from a plugin that answered without one in the last build. The former says reported when the builder answers; the latter names the plugin and missing stage contract as a fact from the last build. Node lifecycle fallbacks name arbitrary project/package reads, while script-free single-root npm installs can declare their manifest, lock and manager controls. Rust's final declarations come from Cargo read facts, with specific reasons when native inputs cannot be bounded. These explanations do not relax confinement or native-observation requirements. A target's key is a SHA-256 over these inputs and nothing else: Input Notes The target's actions Command, environment, working directory, platforms, limits, report contracts and configuration digest. Scheduling settings such as build.jobs aren't part of it. Source in scope The target's own directory, the directories of every target it declares as a prerequisite (depends_on, materialize, task dependencies, the same edges --affected uses) and every file no target owns (root build.yaml, oyzu.toml, locks). Complete admitted tool contracts can replace tool-control bytes with their semantic non-tool content; dependency locks, plugin selections and other settings remain inputs. Source projection The builder's selection definition and captured selected-entry digest for fallback keys; admitted narrow actions key their selected reads Toolchain The resolved image's content digest, not its tag, plus the canonical locked tool identities for a complete admitted stage. The target's prepared primary tool and manager stay keyed even if the builder omits their names. Missing declarations or missing admitted records retain the whole-lock fallback. Prepared dependencies The dependency snapshot's content (lock digests, prepared tree, manager identity), not where or when it was prepared Builder Builder ID, deliberately bumped engine cache contract, plugin reference/protocol/runtime and package release digest or compiled development source-closure digest. CLI and development executable bytes, paths and mtimes are provenance, not key inputs. Materialized inputs Digests of artifacts consumed from producer targets, known once producers finish When a build pins missing tools or quality sets, planning uses the validated, newly published lock capture. Its tool inputs therefore match later builds that reuse the unchanged lock. Incomplete tool declarations continue to bind the captured lock bytes; a real lock-file edit changes that conservative identity. Host paths, run IDs, timestamps, credentials and the number of parallel jobs never enter a key. A serial build, a --jobs N build and a host with a different core count share hits, and so do different checkouts, worktrees and branches. Source ownership comes from the full static build inventory, even when a named build resolves only the builders it needs. Unselected builds keep ownership of their folders without loading their plugins. Changing one target's inputs re-runs exactly that target. One thing to know: execution-only settings such as --full are part of the configuration digest, so changing them re-keys every action. Prepared dependency identity excludes whole-source provenance, version decision evidence and the frozen plugin planner request/answer. The frozen action definition still keys version-bearing arguments and OYZU_VERSION; source reads have their own key component. Dependency locks, manager/tool identities and prepared content remain in the dependency identity. A changed lock or prepared payload therefore remains a prepared-dependency cause in oyzu cache explain. This exclusion does not remove a version written into a prepared file: those bytes remain prepared content. Helm retains the authored Chart.yaml version during preparation and projects the resolved version into its private stage workspace. Its bounded captured stages use their admitted read contracts; a root README outside those reads can change without invalidating the shipping actions. A README inside the chart ships unless .helmignore excludes it, so editing it normally invalidates the build. Prepared capture can record source provenance using the copy roots supplied by preparation. A nonempty regular file is copied source only when its prepared root-relative path maps to the same source root-relative path, and its captured bytes, size and executable mode match. Empty files, dependency locks, files outside the declared roots and rewritten files (including stamped chart metadata) remain generated. Equal names or bytes elsewhere never establish a copy coordinate. Helm keeps dependency-build charts/ directories acquired, including committed subcharts reproduced byte-for-byte. If preparation has no workspace-relative source inventory, it declares no copied files rather than using target-relative coordinates that could hide a nested chart's templates. Provenance is computed from inventories already produced during capture and is stored with the dependency record. Reuse reads that record; it adds no prepared tree scan or source-byte hashing. Planning decodes it once per prepared target. If an action hides no copied files, it retains its ordinary dependency input and mount: no extra file list, view, rehash or copy is introduced. When a confined captured action must hide a copy outside its source reads, dependency identity covers the generated/acquired entries and all (prepared path, source path) names. Visible copied bytes and modes remain in the bound physical view digest. Each action carries hidden-copy paths and a digest reference to a shared table of read-copy diagnostics, not an inventory per action; an explicit prepared-file selection still applies. Opening a filtered view verifies its selected content, copies it and verifies the resulting tree, even with --no-cache. This cost applies only to actions that actually hide copies (or already request an explicit prepared-file view). Upstream-only actions that consume prepared resources retain the whole prepared input and its whole-content identity. An empty source-read set does not mean those actions can run with copied files removed from their dependency payload. oyzu cache explain lists copied source paths as added, removed or changed, showing up to three and an and N more count. Whole prepared inputs, including upstream-only staging, also separate verified copies from generated dependencies in the explanation: for example, copied source chart/templates/pod.yaml changed (whole prepared input). This diagnostic split uses the captured inventory once per target; it does not narrow the input, materialize a view, or change its key. Locks, acquired files and rewritten bytes still report prepared dependencies. Unbounded actions, native host actions and prepared trees containing links retain whole-tree behavior. Native observed reads do not yet map prepared copies back to source coordinates.
documents.s: Inputs and what invalidates a target

documents.t: The native path has no plan of captured inputs, so its key is built from what the host build actually saw: Input Notes The target's actions Each eligible builder action, otherwise the whole group: command line (per-invocation locations such as temporary output folders become fixed tokens), environment variable names, working directory, report contracts and configuration identity Source The digest of the target's private source copy: its own directory plus declared inputs. Mandatory oyzu.lock source/version identity retains the build's selected tool recipes, plugin pins and tool dependency records, instead of unrelated sections. Raw bytes remain binding for authored inputs and explicit or unknown program-data reads. Only complete-tool admission permits projection of tool requests in oyzu.toml. Native tools are host processes, so ambient reads outside this are not in the key. Tools Each completely declared stage keys the locked commands it admits. Opaque native stages key their entire prepared selected environment: tool version, platform, backend, recipe, installation and artifact identity, including component and dependency closures. Managed quality sets have their own identity. Missing preparation retains the whole-lock fallback. The host platform remains binding. Builder The engine cache contract and the external builder plugin's semantic source/package identity. Executable digests remain admission/provenance facts. Materialized inputs Digests of artifacts consumed from producer targets An unrelated toolset or unused plugin pin in oyzu.lock does not change a prepared native stage's toolchain identity. Changing a selected tool version, recipe, component closure or artifact changes an opaque stage's key. Changing the selected builder plugin's release changes the builder identity. Reinstalling identical locked inputs keeps their identity. Source-read and configuration rules still apply independently: opaque reads can retain whole-file source identity and cause a source miss even when the selected tools are unchanged. For observed native stages, a package-wide prediction alone does not make the whole lock a data input. Completed command observations retain raw lock bytes when the command actually reads the lock, including from a build script. A reader without local observation history still uses raw lock bytes for its prediction candidate, so unrelated lock edits can miss until that reader has retained complete observations. An unrelated edit does not itself establish which files the command reads. A valid unused current-format tool resolution does not block preparation or require a legacy-ID migration. The complete lock still undergoes structural and identity validation; real legacy IDs retain their migration checks. Selected lock projection is computed once per declared native build closure from frozen locks and retained tool selections. It keeps selected tool acquisition inputs and transitive tool dependencies, and the selected plugin pins. The selected portable request's declared platforms stay together so snapshot versions retain the same identity across hosts. Changing any retained entry invalidates its consumers. Ordinary ecosystem dependency locks and prepared dependency inputs retain their existing keys. A tool that isn't in the lock (a system C compiler used by cgo, or sh) isn't part of the key. Use --no-cache after changing such a tool. Tool identities come from retained verified installations and invocation-captured locks, frozen before execution. Key calculation does not resolve tools, reopen the lock or rehash installed payloads. A quality-set refresh therefore need not invalidate an unrelated admitted Rust stage. Custom commands without retained preparation keep conservative misses. Bundled commands such as pip and npm contribute their supplying runtime's installation identity; they do not require a separate installation lease. A complete builder stage contract keys its named, admitted tools; sibling stages' leases do not enter that key. Rust compilation names Cargo and rustc; lint names Clippy and formatting names rustfmt. Configured RUSTC_WRAPPER and RUSTC_WORKSPACE_WRAPPER settings retain the whole admitted tool environment and managed PATH for compiler stages: a wrapper may launch another runtime even in a manifest-only project. Core checks the frozen action's configured environment names, including redacted values; it conservatively retains this fallback even for an empty authored setting. Arbitrary Rust tests and coverage also retain the whole admitted environment and managed PATH: test code can launch tools such as Node even without build scripts, proc macros or Cargo configuration. Refreshing an admitted user-level runtime lock can invalidate wrapped compilation or test reports even when its configured selector stays the same. Unknown build-script, proc-macro or authored Cargo configuration tools also keep the whole-target fallback. Physical installation locations are normalized, and sibling managed PATH entries are omitted only for complete tool contracts; an explicit PATH read retains its complete value as data. A complete stage's computation configuration omits checks.run and plugins.packages: the former selects work, while the selected builder package release and executable remain independently bound in every key. Other computation, execution, environment and policy values stay binding. Rust tool identity uses the admitted publisher channel-manifest digest, version, backend and platform, rather than an installation key that also names optional components. A missing publisher record retains the installation identity. Tool policy such as tools.minimumReleaseAgeDays remains configuration identity; it is not removed as a tool-version request. A control file explicitly read as program data keeps its original bytes in the source key. Unknown read contracts do too. A same-named TOML fixture is ordinary source, rather than a configuration control, unless configuration capture actually consumed it. Current complete declarations cover ordinary Rust compilation without build scripts, proc macros or authored Cargo configuration, source-free Rust exports, and the owned default Node quality adapter without project plugins or configuration. Other stages keep their existing fallback. Default Node quality reports have bounded outputs and can be reused independently while following the recorded outputs of preceding work. oyzu cache explain names changed tools and their previous and current versions. JSON differences carry the same names and from/to versions. An artifact or backend change with an unchanged version still changes the tool identity. A restored native target keeps its materialization receipts, and promoted local binaries (.oyzu/bin) are refreshed from the restored artifact as after a run. Eligible native host targets try configured remote whole-target results before executing individual actions. Incomplete native stages prevent that shortcut. Per-action cache workspaces are selected once for the target; a target without a private root uses whole-target caching. Profile-dependent shared-cache writers (Rust and .NET) produce both development and optimized compile stages when the selected output is optimized. A plain reader looks up compile-development; an optimized reader looks up compile-optimized. Each stage records its actual profile and never substitutes the other profile's binaries. Both use one preparation and build plan. Rust uses host-native stages; .NET uses captured stages with separate Debug and Release commands and requires a compatible package declaring dotnet-compile-stages. Profile-independent builders (Java/Maven/Gradle/Ant, Go, Zig, Node and Python) keep one entry. Stage reuse also requires matching admitted tool environments and computation settings. Full CI writers and plain readers can still differ in those inputs, even when their compile profiles match. Publishing both profiles does not by itself guarantee a shared-cache hit. Rust test, lint and format stages use declared Cargo manifests and locks, without consuming final binary exports. Their applied profile reflects the actual native command: Cargo's development/test profile for checks, independently of the exported binary's profile. Final native compilation applies inferred controls only for that operation, validates them around Cargo, then restores and revalidates declared controls before later checks. This also applies when hooks require stages to share one workspace. A failed native guard remains a failure after restoration; restoring controls never legitimizes a changed manifest or lock. Rust compile-stage keys bind declared Cargo versions. Plain local development readers export the declared-version compile result directly, recording compiledVersion separately from the inferred artifact version. Stamped paths (full, CI, optimized, shared-cache writer, packaged, handed-off and release) require a separate final Cargo stage binding the inferred version map and projected manifests/lock. Development results cannot satisfy that stage or stamped packaging/publication gates. The final projection is absent from compile-stage payloads. The engine-injected OYZU_VERSION default (inferred or tagged) is not passed to host compile, test, lint and format-check commands, so env!("OYZU_VERSION") fails to compile there and option_env! is unset; use CARGO_PKG_VERSION. The final stage still receives it. Explicit environment values remain keyed (oyzu#2364). Stage restores do not transfer Cargo compiler state; the final stage can still recompile affected crates. Conventional native Rust stages have independent results. Adding --full to an unchanged development build may reuse compilation, but also requires the inferred-version final stage and selected checks, and a repeat full build may restore bounded checks with their original reports and compiler warnings (labeled as reused). Arbitrary tests always execute and produce fresh required reports. A compile that succeeded stays reusable if a later check fails. Stdout and stderr logs stay available after reuse. Rust test stages can reuse individual test executables. See test-unit evidence for keys, reports and the native runtime-read limit. Builders can opt individual native stages into private source copies by declaring a finite output-file handoff. Core admits private execution when outputs are bounded and producers are admitted. An observed or fixed native read basis separately enables narrow keying. Source-free exports use upstream_only and retain their producer dependencies. A private copy still contains the full target; narrow keys require the separate native read admission described below. This is host execution, not a sandbox. Private branches start from the frozen pre-run source projection plus the finite outputs of their admitted producers. They never copy later shared-stage changes, even inside their declared reads. The prepared source projection stays immutable while shared stages and deferred cache restores use a separate retained execution root. Private branches are populated only on execution and carry the projection's admitted digests without hashing copied source again. Reused private stages do not populate their forks; reused producer bytes are handed off only when a consumer executes. Producer files come from their executed fork or verified cached bytes, not from the live shared root. Native artifacts are collected from the workspace of their declared producing stage, including shared execution roots beside private checks. A target can mix private and shared stages. Cached shared-stage changes are captured from and restored into the shared execution root. If a later stage fails, retrying can reuse a successful producer and restore its files before the consumer executes, without changing the source of later private forks. Editing a check's declared reads reruns that check. Shared, unconfined native actions follow every dependsOn edge, including order-only edges. Private branches retain the existing order-only non-observation rule and follow real producer dependencies. Cargo declares these neutral facts for its host stages and indexed binary exports. Compilation and Clippy need complete observations before reusing results; rustfmt uses its fixed tool rule. The separately lowered test has no complete native read basis. Its unbounded outputs keep it on the shared execution path with AlwaysRun; unit results require the explicit native Rust trust opt-in described below. By default, it retains conservative action configuration and whole-target source identity. Hooks, task replacements and materialized inputs keep their separate restrictions. Maven and Gradle formatter admission additionally requires their plugin's fixed-read declarations; a private-stage request alone grants no reusable key. Native compile, test and package stages cannot fall back to whole-target reuse when their read or output contracts do not qualify. A fixed-read formatter can reuse independently of unbounded build and test stages when its builder opts into a private workspace. Its default pipeline edges are order-only; explicit data dependencies still invalidate it when their outputs change. An unrelated file edit can still change inferred version or whole-target projection identity and cause a conservative miss. The same mechanism admits Go build and vet with complete observed reads and gofmt with fixed reads once their plugin opts in. A successful completion binds its own complete observation before publication, so the next unchanged build can reuse that narrow result. Admitted test-unit plans can expose independent results; see test-unit evidence. Unit reuse remains subject to the stage's native read and cache admission. Cargo integration-test scratch is removed before native compiler cache retention, even under budget. Compiler state remains available for incremental work, and action results retain their normal reuse rules. The pinned tools must include the selected check helpers. An incomplete lock reports TOOL_LOCK_STALE; run oyzu pin and retry.

Oyzu's own main CI keeps test-result reuse disabled pending independent OVH execution-binding security acceptance. Main executes the full suite with cache reuse disabled, including when using an older released driver. The guarded consumer additionally refuses whole-target, whole-test-stage and per-case hits that would bypass unit admission. Ordinary project caching keeps the rules below. The CLI captures this policy once for Oyzu's own main, scheduled and release jobs and retains it for that invocation. The private build worker captures it from GITHUB_* at startup. The library's build::run convenience entry also captures this policy when it creates build options. Lower-level library cache operations use explicit invocation inputs, including the consumer checkout used for ancestry; ambient CI variables do not change their test-reuse policy or the behavior of unit-test fixtures. Remote-write trust separately reads CI variables, including GITHUB_*, by design to restrict cache publication to trusted pushes. After security acceptance, the guarded path requires an original signed actual execution from a main-push or main-line nightly run, within 24 hours of startedAt, plus fresh independent mismatch state. The execution commit must be an ancestor of both the consumer checkout and its fetched origin/main; missing history runs the tests. Execution and mismatch-state keys have separate purposes. A controller nonce binds state to the current journal view, so an older clean state cannot override a later mismatch within the same attempt. The host supplies state and nonce through a read-only /run/oyzu mount. PR, dev, manual, failed, cancelled and stale evidence cannot satisfy it. Every required unit is validated before any reuse; an input or evidence mismatch runs the full enclosing suite. Reuse preserves the original execution receipt under sourceRecord.ovhExecution and never refreshes its age. Missing evidence, offline state or unavailable trust data causes execution. Main admission refuses trust-native-test-reads keys even when local or user configuration enables package trust. It requires captured bounded reads or a key covering the whole target scope. There is no user setting that can enable this internal policy. Exact-commit green main CI and the full native Windows release-like suite remain release gates. A plugin can declare native test units through the optional test-unit plan. Captured Python package tests use one pytest file per unit and can select cases inside a changed file; see Python cases inside a bounded unit. Rust stages declare Cargo test executables as units and preserve native coverage and fresh doctest reporting during finalization. Cargo-supplied companion executables (CARGO_BIN_EXE_*) are keyed by variable name and digest. Core owns unit keys, lookup and passing-result storage. A failed unit is never stored. The native adapter prepares its inventory, runs the selected units and combines fresh and reused evidence into the operation's existing required reports. Cancelled preparation preserves the executor's cancellation status and stops before unit execution or report finalization. An unbounded AlwaysRun stage does not gain reusable result storage merely by exposing a unit plan. An enclosing stage with unbounded outputs still runs on every invocation. Its test units may reuse results independently only when core admits the stage's frozen tool, dependency, environment, materialized-input and predecessor facts and enforces each unit's bounded runtime view, or the native Rust trust opt-in below explicitly admits package-file reads. This does not admit a reusable whole-stage result. Missing predecessor or materialized-input bindings keep the ordinary stage path. Under an unbounded stage, units without proven runtime bounds run without reuse. A newly stored test-unit result also records the producing run's wall time in milliseconds (durationMs) as optional timing history for later shard planning. Readers that don't know the field ignore it, and a missing or malformed value means no history; it never affects keys, reuse or result validity. Test-unit execution stays sequential by default. OYZU_TEST_SHARDS=N explicitly requests concurrent shards when N is an integer above one. The effective count is at most the unit count, four, and the worker CPU budget divided by the existing per-step CPU allocation (with a minimum of one). Each shard retains that CPU allocation. A diagnostic reports any reduction from the requested count; an invalid value runs sequentially. This override never changes cache keys. Concurrency requires every unit to have an enforced, private confined runtime view. If any unit lacks one, including units with unbounded outputs, the entire step runs sequentially in manifest order using the ordinary workspace for non-confined units, preserving hard-link aliases and in-place writes. Main-CI governed runs remain sequential. Shard view storage is created beside the actual execution workspace, including temporary native-tool-control workspaces. Confined views copy their files, without hard links to the workspace. Creation failures are reported without falling back to a different filesystem. Results and failure selection retain manifest order; the step's duration measures elapsed wall time across preparation, units and finalization. Cargo integration-test targets (kind = "test") retain a conservative runtime contract: Cargo target metadata does not establish their complete runtime reads or nested helper compilation and writes. They use the ordinary test stage's admitted workspace, tools, materializations and scratch, retaining whole-source and upstream key inputs. Without the native trust opt-in below, they are not independently stored or reused under an unbounded enclosing stage. Captured library and binary unit tests keep their bounded runtime contracts and remain eligible for independent reuse. Declared inputs add reads; they do not establish a missing integration-test write closure. The combined report retains each unit's contribution. Summary totals put cases from executed units under Tests run now and reused cases under Reused test evidence, marked not run now. JSON build reports retain each contribution in reports[].summary.units. Invocation summaries (oyzu history <id> --json) use tests.fresh and tests.reused for the same counts. Even when all units reuse results, the action still executes preparation and finalization. It counts in actions.succeededNow; only whole-action reuse counts in actions.reused. Each unit's key includes the stage's non-source inputs, the native artifact's digest, its runtime-read digest and the declared companion executable digests. Runtime reads narrow the key only when the captured-path view enforces them. Declared inputs widen reads without enforcing a boundary. Runtime listing selectors conservatively include the selected directory's contents in unit keys and views. Captured unit views also include preparation's finite version-control inputs. Core checks their original identities against the admitted source and their projected identities against the private workspace. Keys cover the actual projected bytes and observed absence; the worker's version-control guard remains binding inside the unit view. These paths are resolved from the prepared context root, independently of an individual test's working directory. On the native host path, runtime reads remain unbounded. By default, unbounded Rust test stages do not reuse unit results. oyzu cache explain <target> records the refusal and names cache.trustNativeTestReads. To opt in, set this in project, user or local oyzu.toml: [cache] trustNativeTestReads = true This explicitly trusts native Rust tests to read only the owning crate's full Cargo package file set, its resolved local dependency package files, and the declared environment. Cargo's package include/exclude rules apply; tests/, fixtures, build.rs and README files participate when packaged. Undeclared host files, excluded files, network state and undeclared environment are outside this trust contract. Policy can lock the setting to false; profiles cannot grant it. It does not enforce isolation or relax acquisition or report validation. A Rust adapter supplying Cargo package identities is required. Each unit key binds its package closure and lockfile, compiled test executable, companion executables, declared environment, toolchain and prepared dependencies. An unchanged repeat can reuse every successful unit; a packaged fixture edit reruns the owning crate and units depending on it. Unrelated builds retain their keys when their admitted environment and stage definition remain unchanged. A shared workspace stage can invalidate multiple crates when those common facts change. For example, a library test and an independent integration test in the same crate both rerun after a packaged README or source edit: their admitted package file identity changes even if an executable's bytes stay identical. An unchanged repeat can report 0 ran, 2 reused (trusted native reads). To check selective reuse, use independent Cargo packages declared as separate builds with no local dependency between them. Run oyzu build --full twice with native-read trust enabled, then edit a packaged source file in one package and repeat. The unchanged run should reuse both test units; the edit should rerun only the edited package's unit. Keep required doctests and coverage enabled: reused executable results do not replace those report obligations. On MSVC targets, instrumented test compilation requests reproducible linking (/Brepro) and disables incremental codegen for those instrumented tests so clean builds can retain the same executable identity. Executable digests remain mandatory; this does not make Rust outputs portable across paths. Only unit reports are restored. Finalization still combines JUnit and coverage and runs required doctests. Receipts and cache explanations name trust-native-test-reads; human build output identifies reused trusted native reads. Hooks always run; authored tasks still require complete reads of their own command. Native test-read trust does not admit an authored replacement's reads. The isolated execution path continues to require its enforced runtime views. Without an individually enforced view or explicit native trust admission, unbounded unit keys retain whole-target source and upstream output identities. Executor support alone does not narrow an unbounded or nonconfinable unit. Per-run inventory paths and coverage environment are not bounded key inputs. Targets with hooks or authored tasks follow their complete-read reuse rules. Their outputs are never narrowed to unit identities. If per-action cache facts are unavailable, the ordinary test stage runs instead. The native inventory determines what runs: undeclared units execute without reuse, known units retain their own entries, and missing predicted units do not fail an otherwise valid native inventory. The existing test action row shows N ran, M reused, including in redirected and no-color output. Its JSON action record lists units, each with name, key and outcome (ran, reused or failed). An operation without a unit plan retains its existing whole-stage behavior.

The cache trusts the declared target graph, like --affected. An action that reads another target's directory without a declared edge is invisible to the key. For example, if api and web copy ../shared but declare no relationship to it, editing shared/ reuses their old results, while oyzu build --no-cache rebuilds them. Native cross-root dependency discovery isn't implemented. Declare relationships in build.yaml (depends_on: [shared]), or use --no-cache, for builds that read across target directories.

A target built by an external builder plugin (plugins.development or plugins.packages) is reused like a built-in target. Oyzu records the selected binding as extensions["oyzu.dev/builder-plugin"]. Cache keys use its semantic identity alongside the engine cache contract; executable digests remain in the binding record for admission and provenance: {"reference":"go/app","source":"package","protocol":"plugins-v1alpha1","package":"oyzu/go","version":"0.1.0", "release":"sha256:…","executableDigest":"sha256:…","runtime":{"os":"linux","arch":"amd64","abi":null}} {"reference":"go/app","source":"local-development","protocol":"plugins-v1alpha1","sourceDigest":"sha256:…", "executableDigest":"sha256:…","runtime":{"os":"linux","arch":"amd64","abi":null}} runtime uses the plugin package names (linux/darwin/windows, amd64/arm64, gnu/musl/msvc). A development executable's ABI is unknown and recorded as null. Changing the compiled development source closure, admitted package release/version, runtime or reference causes builder identity changed. Reverting can reuse the earlier result. Replacing linked development executable bytes alone does not invalidate it. For self-host builds, replacing the CLI or relinking a development builder preserves reusable results when the declared builder identity, compiled source closure and engine cache contract stay the same. A source change still invalidates the affected builder's results; rebuilding an executable is not a cache reset. Selection provenance (resolved now or locked) does not change a key. A plugin-built target never shares a key with the built-in builder it replaces. Reuse also requires matching source projection, action definition and other key inputs. If an unchanged self-host build runs again, use oyzu cache explain <action> to distinguish a builder identity change from a miss in another component. Native private executable locations, worker-location tokens and read-history subjects use the same semantic identity when deriving cache inputs. Admission still uses the full frozen binding, and each shared-executable reference keeps its own identity. Private copies and fresh output staging remain required. Development reuse requires a native executable and a compiled source-closure digest from describe. Scripts and undeclared producers are not-cached with an actionable reason. A native wrapper's declared closure must cover the code it starts; rebuild it when that closure changes. Installed package results can use cache.remote and cache.ciRemote: the key binds the admitted package release digest. Development bindings remain local except for an invocation's explicit --handoff repository. Existing exclusions remain: --no-cache, cache.local = false, --verify-contract, secret environment values and hooks without declared outputs prevent reuse.

If an action carries a stage contract that Oyzu cannot decode, external-input admission and cache key computation reject it with the action ID and decoding reason. Oyzu never treats that contract as absent or keys the action without its declared inputs. Correct the contract in the producing builder before retrying. Native ancestor-file inputs are resolved from the canonical target directory, including targets reached through directory symlinks. If an ancestor cannot be keyed (for example, it is a directory, a symlink or larger than 4 MiB), native execution continues without cache reuse. ANCESTOR_INPUT_UNKEYABLE reports the action and cause as a warning, also retained in the build manifest's diagnostics when no invocation logger is supplied. Planning attaches a stage contract to each action of an analyzed target: the reads, writes, environment names and tools the static analysis found for the stage, the actions it follows, and whether its outputs are bounded. A target whose actions all have a contract is reused action by action. Captured node/package and node/app operations use these contracts when the final command matches the analyzed script or builder-owned command. Ordinary SDK-style dotnet/sdk projects also declare stage reads on the captured path. See .NET stage reads for the SDK audit, resolved-package checks and conservative MSBuild fallbacks. Captured .NET targets cannot see ancestor configuration files above their target folder; future native admission must treat those files as unbounded until covered by read evidence. Fixed core-owned stages can supply a contract alongside analyzed builder stages. Docker also declares per-stage reads for its captured operations. Projection-aware caching and captured version rebinding require a supporting core release before the updated Docker plugin. Source projections retain conservative version scope, and copied source in prepared dependencies can still prevent reuse after an unread edit. Host-coordinated image workers remain excluded from caching. Step Behavior Lookup The target's group record is tried first when every native stage permits whole-target restoration (unchanged target: one step). Native stages with unbounded outputs prevent this shortcut, including remote fetches. Eligible actions are looked up separately when ready. Action key The action's frozen definition, the target scope, toolchain, builder, variant, platform, prepared dependencies (only if the action reads them), materialized artifacts and the output digests of the earlier actions it follows Action result The files the action published to the bundle (artifacts, reports), their records and the workspace changes it made (files created, modified and deleted, new folders) Reuse Records enter the manifest as succeeded with a reuse record. Reports are parsed again and gated by the current contract. Workspace changes are restored before the next action that has to run, so later actions see what running it would have left. A fully reused target never touches its workspace. Early cutoff A re-run action that produces the same workspace changes leaves its dependents' keys unchanged, so they are still reused. Always runs An action without bounded outputs never gets reused on its own. It runs every time, and what it produces still feeds what follows. A target holding such an action isn't restored whole. Storing Eligible actions are saved after their own outputs and required reports pass validation, even if a later action fails. A complete target result requires every action to succeed. Captured .NET planning admits a fixed set of literal package metadata and project-local None/Content file additions. The project XML and included file bytes are keyed for prepare, compile and pack; changing metadata or a packed license invalidates those inputs. Unknown or dynamic MSBuild constructs retain named unbounded reasons. See .NET stage reads for the exact bounded set and conservative fallbacks. This does not change native-host admission or the requirement to regenerate offline restore assets. Without a confining contract (see below), an action's key uses the whole target scope. Targets with an authored task or override that doesn't set cache = true with outputs, or a hook without declared outputs, are not cached. On Unix, relative workspace symbolic links can restore when their targets stay inside the workspace and point directly to ordinary files or directories. The cache rejects escaping links, link chains, writes through link ancestors and special files; it rechecks target containment before recreating a link. Link targets are identified as link text, without reading their contents. Windows link-containing changes remain nonrestorable. The manifest records each action's outcome (reused, executed, always-run) under manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"].targets.<target>.actions. Rust test and coverage stages, including native Cargo test commands under another stage name, run whenever scheduled. Arbitrary test code can write outside the captured workspace, so these stages declare unbounded outputs and use the always-run outcome instead of storing reusable action results. Required test and coverage reports are still collected and checked. Compilation and other stages with bounded outputs retain their separate cache eligibility.

Core's prepare-dependencies action can carry a source-free stage contract when its provider declares every destination written by its fixed staging command. The Cargo overlay copies manifests and lock data into those declared paths; Helm declares .oyzu-build, including its prepared chart copy and the parent directory it creates. These copies read no workspace source and have bounded outputs; the prepared-input selection remains keyed, so changing a staged manifest or lock invalidates staging. A source-only edit can reuse staging independently of compilation when the prepared bytes are unchanged. With a Rust package declaring captured-cargo-projection, dependency staging copies declared manifests and the original lock from its exact prepared-file view. Frozen projected controls are applied in a separate project-version action before every Cargo consumer. A source edit changing only the inferred version can therefore reuse staging; manifest and lock changes still invalidate it. Staging excludes the engine-injected OYZU_VERSION default, while explicit user environment values retain their normal precedence and remain keyed. Unmarked Rust packages keep the projected overlay, so edits changing the projected version still rerun their staging. Local verification of a source package does not establish public package adoption. Other provider setup commands keep their existing behavior unless they declare an equivalent bounded, source-free staging contract. This does not turn staging into a network fetch or vendor operation.

A hook ([tasks."api:pre_build"], post_<stage>) that declares outputs doesn't make a per-action target uncacheable: [tasks."api:pre_build"] argv = ["node", "hook.mjs"] outputs = ["generated"] # workspace paths, folders or globs the hook writes Aspect Behavior The hook Runs on every build. It is never restored and its record never has reuse. The action record shows always-run. Its output The files it changed are recorded, and their digest enters the key of every later action of the target. A hook that writes something else re-runs what follows. A hook that writes the same bytes leaves it reused. Target outcome reused when every other action was reused. Otherwise executed. The target's group record isn't stored. Undeclared effects A hook that changes a file outside its declared outputs isn't followed. Nothing of the target is stored, and the outcome carries a rejected note naming the files, so the next build runs it again. No outputs The target is not-cached ("hooks without declared outputs"). Whole-target path On the native host path and on captured targets without stage contracts, a target is only restored whole, which would skip its hooks. It is not-cached and its hooks run every build. outputs paths are relative to the hook's working directory (the target, unless cwd says otherwise). Use / or \. Editing a hook script counts as a source edit, so it re-runs actions keyed on the target scope and any confined action that reads the script. On Windows no action is confined, so any source edit re-runs the whole target, though an unchanged repeat is still reused. Whether a script edit also changes the development version, which is in every action's environment, depends on the hook: Hook Development version Comment-only edit of its script pre_build with outputs, on a builder that finalizes versions (Node) Finalized after the hook (below) Keeps the version. A confined api:build is reused. Any other hook (pre_test, post_build, …) or another builder The script stays in the version scope Changes the version, which re-keys every action of the target

On captured Node targets, Oyzu moves the version action after the followed pre_build hooks, so nothing that writes the version runs before them: Planning records every action in plan.json with the pre-hook source version (the version scope without the hook's script). The target record carries extensions["oyzu.dev/version-finalization"]. The actions before the hook run with the pre-hook version. When the hooks succeed, the files under their declared outputs are digested from the workspace (so --no-cache gives the same result) and folded into the version. The target is planned again, and the remaining actions run from that post-hook plan, written to plans/<target>.post-hooks.json. plan.json itself isn't changed. The manifest's target record is the post-hook one. manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/version-finalization"].<target> gives preHookVersion, version, hookOutputs, planPath and planDigest. A hook edit that changes what it writes changes the version and the package. A script stays in the version scope if it isn't named as an argument of the hook's command (for example run = "node hook.mjs" through a shell) or if a builder stage reads or writes it. Other builders, other hook phases and the native host path aren't finalized. Effects outside the workspace (network, global state) are invisible to Oyzu, so declare them away yourself.

An authored task or task override isn't cached by default, because Oyzu can't see its effects. Request reuse with the cache and outputs task fields: [tasks."api:test"] run = "node --test" cache = true inputs = ["src/**", "test/**"] # optional; may only add to the target scope outputs = [".events"] # workspace paths, folders or globs the task writes Reuse requires complete reads of the authored action itself. On Linux, ordinary native Node application/package builds can select the existing crun boundary for an authored task without making the whole build isolated. Oyzu freezes selected target source and bounded predecessor outputs, retains the locked native Node payload, and probes it against an admitted Linux runtime root before lookup. The action sees those identified bytes read-only, empty private output/report and temporary roots, and no host home, package cache, network or general proc/sys view. The closed startup allowance remains subject to the ambient output-independence rule. cache = true asserts that clocks, entropy and permitted startup values do not influence retained outputs; the boundary does not detect semantic nondeterminism. The first native slice supports the retained Node command and an equivalent runtime-root sh/bash, literal directory output roots, and the existing Node report adapters. A shell is admitted only when its selected native bytes match the identified runtime shell. File/glob output allocation, other tool payloads, worker plugins and unbounded dependency/generated trees have no native binding in this slice. Their optional boundary is unavailable; they execute ordinarily with NATIVE_AUTHORED_BOUNDARY_UNAVAILABLE and remain nonreusable. Windows and macOS have no native authored backend and follow that same explained-rerun rule. Offline admission requires an already unpacked runtime root and retained tools. Captured Node targets also retain oyzu build --isolated --no-docker support. After selecting the boundary, a required outside read fails with the native path or endpoint diagnostic, action name and Remove cache = true guidance for ordinary nonreusable execution where policy permits. Oyzu never retries that failure unrestricted. --no-cache keeps the same view and report gates; it only disables lookup, result storage and history. Removing cache = true does not relax separately required isolation or policy controls. Selected tracked and nonignored untracked source is visible and keyed. Ignored .env and local configuration remain hidden; supported explicit source inputs can admit nonsecret ignored files, subject to fixed exclusions and containment. The live checkout is never a fallback. Declared bounded hook outputs are frozen only after their writers retire, and their consumed bytes enter the key. Completed actions record the selected/enforced executor and boundary/runtime/tool digests in extensions["oyzu.dev/ambient-reads"].execution. Only successful execution, retirement, contained collection and current report gates can publish a result. Hits preserve the original producer's completion facts and reports; they do not claim a new crun launch. Old unrestricted entries and inherited builder read contracts cannot admit an authored replacement. Incomplete reads still block whole-target and whole-source fallback, following the complete-read decision and its authored-task correction. Aspect Behavior Opt-in cache = true and at least one outputs entry. The plan marks the action cacheable: true and records the declaration in extensions["oyzu.dev/authored-cache"]. cache on a hook is ignored: hooks always run. Key The task's frozen definition (command, environment names, working directory, report contracts, configuration digest) and the target scope, as for a builder stage. Editing a file in the target, or the task, re-runs it. inputs Relative to the task's directory. Entries inside the target are already covered. An entry outside the target isn't supported yet: the target is not-cached ("declares inputs outside its target …"). Per-action Node targets (admitted native or captured isolated Linux crun) With complete read admission, the task is a reusable action. Its workspace changes must lie inside its declared outputs, otherwise nothing is stored and the outcome carries a rejected note. Around a hook it is reused while the hook's output is unchanged. Restored reports are gated again. Native hosts/actions without complete-read admission The task reruns with an explanation. A whole-target key cannot replace complete reads, and whole-target restoration stays blocked when any stage lacks them. cache = true without outputs not-cached: "<task> sets cache = true but declares no outputs, so it is not cached" --no-cache, cache.local = false Nothing is reused or stored. A task that leaves nothing in the workspace must still name an output (for example the folder its tool writes logs to). Reusing a task around hooks needs per-action reuse, which captured Node package and application targets support. A command the builder doesn't recognize for report instrumentation keeps today's reporting behavior. An independently admitted native authored action can reuse even if a companion has no stage contract. That companion still executes on every build and prevents a whole-target restore; no group result is stored for this mixed target. Only separately bounded, frozen producer outputs can enter the authored view. A test hit can therefore appear beside an executed build and a target outcome other than reused. Hooks always execute; equal produced bytes can preserve a hit, while changed consumed bytes force execution.

A narrow key is only sound if the action can't see anything the key left out. So Oyzu keys a captured action on the files its contract reads only when the action also runs confined to them. This needs the captured path and a Unix host. Linux is tested. macOS isn't supported yet. Windows doesn't support captured confinement. Native stages on every host instead require complete fixed or observed reads; incomplete native stages run every time. Step Behavior Eligible The stage's own command was modeled by the analysis, none of its facts is an unbounded unknown (a bounded one adds its bound to the reads, see bounded unknowns), and its outputs are bounded. For an analyzed Node package that covers build and test from its scripts, plus the builder's own commands: version, the npm install (prepare), npm pack (package) and the default ESLint and Prettier checks (lint, format-check) of a package without such scripts. pnpm and Yarn installs and packs, workspace plans, application packages, Biome and authored replacements keep the whole-target key. See builder-owned stages. Key The digest of the source files the contract reads, the output digests of every earlier action of the target (except a check ordered before it only to share the workspace, see checks that run at once), the frozen action, toolchain, prepared dependencies and materialized artifacts. Editing a file the stage doesn't read leaves its key alone only if the edit also leaves the development version unchanged. Any other edit changes the version, which is in every action's environment, and re-keys every action. View Before the action runs, the executor builds a private view of the workspace with only the declared reads, what the earlier actions created, and the artifacts materialized for it, and mounts it as /workspace. Other files don't exist for the action. Merge When the action ends, what it created, changed or deleted in the view is merged back into the workspace. Not confined Any action without a contract, with an unbounded unknown fact or write, on a builder without analysis, on the native host path and on hosts without view support. Captured actions keep the whole-target key. Native stages require complete read admission before reuse. Example: oyzu build --full on a Node api target after appending a comment to api/test/greeting.test.mjs: · api:build Reused from an earlier run · not executed now · originally ran … (key 0452eeca9fb2) › api:test Running Cache active · 3 targets reused The same edit also reuses api:version, api:prepare and api:package (it packs only files: ["dist"]) and re-runs api:lint and api:format-check, which read every JavaScript file of the target. manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"].targets.<target>.confined lists the confined actions. --no-cache and cache.local = false turn off lookup and storage, but eligible actions keep the same private views, so a fresh run sees exactly the files a reusable run would.

Static analysis sometimes meets a construct it can't resolve, an unknown fact. An unknown can carry a bound: the files, globs, task environment or installed packages the construct can't read outside of. A stage whose unknowns are all bounded has scope widened. Its reads gain each bound, and it still runs confined with a narrow key. One unbounded unknown keeps the whole stage on the whole-target key, unconfined. Bound Covers Example Hard What the tool's own rules allow npm pack files entries (the package folder), an unexpanded test pattern (the runner's root), a computed environment mode (<envDir>/.env*), a missing relative import (the files resolution probes), a tsconfig extending a package (installed packages and the config's folder), computed process.env access (the task's environment) Heuristic Where a tool usually stays A command with no tool profile (prettier, biome, oxlint, tsup) or an unmodeled subcommand or flag (next lint, ng test, vitest --coverage): its folder, the files directly in each folder above it, and installed packages. Task runners (turbo, nx, lerna, ultra, wireit) are never bounded. A bound that relies on installed packages counts only for an action that reads the prepared dependencies. If a confined widened action reads outside its bound, it fails with the path and the inputs fix (see below). Declared inputs add to a bound but never bound an unbounded unknown. oyzu build --plan shows scope: widened and each bound in the Why column. --why <path> answers covered-by-bound for a path only a bound covers. Test units can also receive package-level bounds directly from their builder; see inferred test-input bounds. Their layer explanations are advisory; the sandbox enforces the declared selectors.

The check stages of one target (test, lint, format-check, scheduled by --full or CI) don't produce anything another check consumes, so the plan marks the edge between two consecutive checks as order-only. A hook between them, or a declared depends_on, keeps the edge a real dependency. When build.jobs is above 1, a check starts as soon as what it really needs (for example build) has finished, beside the checks ordered before it, if all of these hold: the check runs confined (and --verify-contract isn't set); every action of its target already running is a confined check; no two of them declare writes that could meet (a glob counts as its literal folder). Otherwise it waits its turn. Serial and parallel runs give the same keys and outputs: Behavior View A check's view leaves out what the checks ordered before it left, and checks that may overlap get copied files instead of hard links, so one check's in-place write can't reach another. Key A check's key follows the actions its view shows, not the checks ordered before it. package still follows every check. Failure A failed check doesn't block the next check. It still blocks package and everything after it. A check that finishes early is recorded after the checks ordered ahead of it. Different targets still run one action at a time per branch. The native host path and Windows have no views, and oyzu run stays serial. Native sequence edges after a check with a complete empty workspace-write bound are order-only. The consumer follows the check's data predecessors instead, so an export after read-only lint still consumes the build output without importing lint's source reads or result identity. Checks with declared writes or incomplete write bounds keep their data edges. Explicit produced-output dependencies and authored task dependencies also retain their data semantics.

Version narrowing follows the execution admission: all selected actions must have contracts, and every shipping action must actually run confined. Non-check steps that can feed shipping reads join the version read closure. Source-free shipping exports also include their transitive producers. Every omitted check needs a complete write bound proving its effects cannot feed shipping. Unconfined checks are checked against their observed workspace changes when the target has a narrowed version scope; a write outside the declared bound fails that build, including when cache storage is disabled. Whole-target version scopes retain ordinary check behavior. An unbounded generator therefore retains the whole-target version even if build and package are bounded. Prepared charts retain their native version; runtime staging projects the final version. Narrowed reuse also requires dependency views that hide unselected prepared files; narrowing source alone cannot hide copies in a dependency mount. A development snapshot version (1.2.3-dev.g<digest>) is written into package.json by the version action, so it feeds every later action. Oyzu derives it from the target's source scope, minus files that only a quality stage (test, lint, format-check) is known to read exactly. A test-only edit changes neither the version nor the artifact names. A new test file, which only a glob finds, does. An unknown fact of a shipping stage (build, package) counts as reading its bound, or every file if it has none, so a test-only file that a computed import of build may reach stays in the version. If several targets share the folder holding a file, the file is left out only if every one of them reads it only from a quality stage. The script of a followed pre_build hook leaves its own target's scope, and what the hook wrote is folded in after it runs (version finalization). For a captured target whose version-carrying commands (build, package, export, or artifact producers) are bounded, cacheable and confinable, the suffix uses the files those commands read, plus configuration, lock files and declared inputs. Unbounded quality stages retain their own whole-target keys without widening this suffix. This needs Unix view support and per-action eligibility, with the same confinement predicate used by execution. Targets with hooks, authored replacements, source projections, materialized inputs or cross-target prerequisites keep the wider scope. See version inference. Captured Cargo builds retain the whole-target version scope. Preparation admits projected manifests, lock coordinates and Cargo metadata together; command-only version refinement cannot change those native facts. Executable test caching still applies, but an unread source edit can change the projected version and invalidate otherwise unchanged executables. Tagged and history-derived versions don't change. The version reaches every action as OYZU_VERSION, except host Rust compile, test, lint and format-check stages, which use the declared Cargo versions. The core rebinds supported captured commands, native payloads and artifact paths with the decisions before computing keys, so an action that embeds the version still keys on the version it executes. Textual rebinding requires the old core version's recorded per-build hash component. An unmarked plain version such as 1.0.0 keeps the whole-target version and plan, so equal dependency versions and path fragments remain untouched. oyzu cache explain and build --explain include this fallback reason. This diagnostic does not change the action key.

If a confined action fails and its output names a file that exists in the target but not in the view, the build reports the stage, the path, the missing fact and the smallest fix, in human, NO_COLOR and --json output (diagnostic confined-read-outside-contract, with details in manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/contract-violations"]): ERROR api:build read extra.txt, which its stage contract does not declare, so the confined view hid it. Missing fact: reads-path extra.txt Fix: declare it as an input of api in build.yaml: inputs: ["api/extra.txt"] (Or make the reference static so the analysis sees it.) Declare the path as an input. The declaration is relative to build.yaml, while the read path is shown as the target's own files write it. --json carries the same declaration as fix.declare.inputs. Oyzu finds the file by scanning the action's output for paths, so a tool that fails without printing the path is reported only as a failed action. The builder's node --test stage also runs the spec reporter on stderr, so a test file that reads an undeclared file is explained like any other stage. The behavior is the same when targets run in parallel.
documents.s: When a confined action reads something undeclared

documents.t: Native execution can read host files outside the captured source tree. A whole-target source key does not track changes to those files. Native stages without complete admitted reads execute on every build, including Rust build scripts with external reads and arbitrary Node, Maven or Gradle lifecycle code. This applies on plain Linux as well as Windows and macOS. Native Python application preparation, assembly and packaging also run when their native read admission is incomplete.
