Captured Python preparation, upstream packaging and generated distribution-application assembly declare their own source-view contracts; requirements applications and authored application build tasks still run assembly with the whole target as its read set. Neither local nor remote whole-target entries can bypass this rule, including entries saved by an older CLI. --no-cache executes these stages too. Independently bounded stages still reuse their results. Complete native reads retain stage and whole-target reuse where all other cache requirements hold. Restoring a check does not release dependent work while an earlier required parallel check is still pending; its success or failure remains a gate. Rerunning a native stage preserves its compiler's incremental cache: an unchanged Rust build can run Cargo without recompiling unchanged crates. --explain names the incomplete read admission; an unchanged source digest alone does not prove that native inputs are unchanged. For Rust, missing active build-script records and unassessed proc-macro reads remain incomplete even when the compiler and linker are pinned. Tool identity binds the selected tool; it does not establish which other files a build script or macro can read. oyzu build <target> --explain reports these refusals separately from a changed toolchain key. Host Cargo finalize keys include the final package versions, compilation identity, and the digest of each projected manifest and lockfile in the native build command. Narrowing the source key to observed reads retains those command inputs: changing any projected control changes the final action key even when dep-info is unchanged. Finalize observes the shared compiler target with final metadata. Earlier declared-version dep-info can widen the observed source set, but cannot replace the keyed final controls. Missing observations or reads outside the prediction prevent publication; editing an observed source invalidates the final result. With complete native read admission and unchanged keyed inputs, finalize can reuse its result whether lint and compilation executed or reused their results. Its key retains the compiler, plugin, dependency and environment identities alongside source reads and projected controls. The target source digest alone cannot admit a native result with incomplete reads, because files outside that target can still affect Cargo or its build scripts. A build-script record restored from earlier compiler state can name a file in a toolchain install that is no longer on this machine. Planning does not count that vanished path as an uncovered read, because Cargo re-runs the script for this build. Observation after the build never ignores it: a vanished path recorded by a stage with no executed-script list (such as lint), or any other path outside the source root keeps the stage always-run. A build-script or dep-info record that names a file in another install that still exists is covered only when the file is a regular, non-symlinked file in that install's payload and has exactly the same bytes as the same relative file in the active sysroot, which the toolchain identity already binds. A differing, missing, symlinked or ..-escaping file keeps the stage always-run. Only the file the record names is compared; other files the script reads in that install are not, the same limit the active sysroot has. Restored dep-info can retain absolute paths to compiler libraries used by proc macros. It uses the same verification as build-script records before a complete compile or lint observation can be saved; a matching install-shaped path alone does not authorize reuse. A record can also name a file in an earlier run's private copy of the checkout (<checkout>/.oyzu/native/host-actions/<hash>/...). That copy was the source snapshot, so the read maps to the same relative path of the current source, but only when the old copy is gone (Cargo then re-runs the script) or the file there (or, for a watched directory, its whole tree: same entries, no links, bounded) has exactly the current bytes. A surviving copy with different bytes, a nested copy, a .oyzu remainder, a lookalike elsewhere or a .. escape stays an uncovered read.

Rust library and binary test units infer a runtime bound from their package folder. On Linux crun (oyzu build --full --isolated --no-docker), a fixture beside the package is visible and participates in its test-unit key without an inputs declaration. An edit inside that bound reruns the unit; an edit outside it preserves reuse when its executable and other keyed inputs are unchanged. Dependency and build-output directories are excluded from the source bound; prepared dependencies and compiled artifacts retain their own identities. The bound also includes ancestor Cargo manifests, lockfiles, toolchain pins and Cargo configuration, plus package and ancestor .config/nextest.toml locations. The framework layer extracts no extra paths from nextest configuration contents. Ordinary and raw relative path strings reaching outside the package can add workspace files with over-approximate confidence. Detection reads configuration and source bytes; it does not execute project code. Computed paths, including env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR") joined with .., need inputs when they reach beyond the detected bound. oyzu build --plan lists static package candidates under Test input bounds, with a Why column identifying convention, shared configuration, framework configuration, literal paths and exclusions. Cargo resolves actual executable units during preparation; unexpanded workspace member patterns are labelled unresolved in the preview. An unparseable nextest configuration retains its known paths, the package folder and other detected inputs, and adds a plan note. Fixing that configuration changes the keyed input. Native framework validation still applies when the tests run. Source-read failures (including non-UTF-8 Rust source), unsupported string tokens and paths that cannot safely be represented leave that package unbounded with a named reason; they do not fail planning for other packages. This includes glob-character literals, overlaps with excluded output, and ../ literals that leave the workspace. An outside literal never grants access beyond the captured workspace. The preview shows the fallback reason in its note. Integration tests and doctests retain their conservative contracts. Native host runs gain no confinement or complete-read guarantee from the inferred bound; Windows keeps rerunning these tests and macOS is unsupported. A confined test that reads outside its bound still fails. When its output prints the missing path, Oyzu reports confined-read-outside-contract with the exact target-level inputs declaration below. The sandbox hides undeclared files even when a test tolerates their absence. Pure-Go package test units also infer their package folder, including testdata and embed discovery membership. Their bounds retain ancestor go.mod, go.sum, go.work and go.work.sum locations, workspace vendor trees, and native EmbedFiles, TestEmbedFiles and XTestEmbedFiles. Ordinary and raw parent-path strings in selected test and production GoFiles, including reachable checkout helpers, widen the bound within the workspace; literal os.Getenv and os.LookupEnv names join the keyed environment. Bare parent elements in joins, such as filepath.Join("..", "shared", "x.json"), use the same parent-path rule and retain refusal when that bound is unsafe. Absolute literals retain refusal on every planning host, including uncertain route-like strings such as /healthz; detection never probes the host filesystem to distinguish routes from files. Windows drive-rooted and backslash-rooted paths also retain refusal. URLs and colon data such as k:v add no filesystem evidence. Changing, adding or deleting a fixture invalidates every unit whose bound contains that path. Independent sibling package bounds can retain reuse. On the captured pure-Go lane, preparation compiles each test executable once. Execution runs that admitted executable in its package directory through Go's test2json, retaining case filters, retries, JUnit and coverage reports. Each executable invocation uses Go's default 10-minute timeout. The current test-unit contract has no configurable timeout field. Core hashes the executable, its package-directory metadata and prepared manifest as generated runtime artifacts. Prepared package executions must leave workspace bytes and membership unchanged; workspace writes fail before a successful attempt is reported. Write temporary test files through Go's t.TempDir or the sandbox's scratch directory instead. This is a confined runtime contract, not a claim that go list -test observes runtime I/O. Native host tests remain unbounded. The static plan shows source package candidates and their inferred layers; native package identities, selected sources, workspace/vendor/embed facts and flags remain unresolved until preparation. The preview never runs Go or project code and supplies no cache-admission authority. Missing package/source facts, unsafe source links, unsupported strings, outside-workspace or excluded-output literals, computed environment lookups, cgo and unsupported flags retain conservative execution. A package whose detector refuses a bound also refuses test-result reuse; a healthy sibling can remain bounded. The admitted flag subset is empty GOFLAGS or combinations of -mod=readonly, -mod=vendor and -p=2. Computed file paths within the confined view work normally; paths beyond that view require the existing target inputs. Custom subprocesses retain the complete existing tool/environment identity rather than claiming a complete statically detected tool list. Static scanning is limited to native checkout source inventories: missing nonstandard helper sources, runtime imports (including runtime.Caller roots), and aliased or dot-imported os retain refusal rather than infer their reads.

A target's inputs in build.yaml name extra source paths it reads (files or folders, relative to build.yaml; see target workspaces). On captured and bounded native paths each one: joins the target's source scope, so the whole-target key and the development version cover it; joins the reads of every stage contract of the target, so a confined action sees it and its narrow key covers it. A target-level input re-keys test too when the file changes, even if only build reads it; only adds. It never removes an inferred read, and it never makes an action confinable. An input that leaves the workspace (the folder holding build.yaml) or names no captured file is a CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE error before anything runs, so a typo can't silently declare nothing. Globs aren't accepted. A folder covers everything beneath it. --affected doesn't yet treat a change under another target's declared input as affecting the declaring target.

The Go builder predicts conventional native build and vet reads from preparation's Go package file lists and writes observed-read reports after successful execution. format-check uses fixed gofmt rules, content globs and directory listings. Native runtime tests and authored build invocations stay unbounded. Incomplete package facts, overlays, cgo headers and unsupported embed discovery retain explicit fallbacks. Conventional native contracts must cover core's prepared file and listing facts; missing coverage is rejected. A main-module manifest outside the target root makes prediction incomplete. Conventional build and vet also require matching resolved task environments before sharing frozen predictions. Conventional native builds use -buildvcs=false; Git commits do not add compiler stamping reads. The compiler output path is stable and its injected version default is omitted. The final export alone carries the inferred version in its filename and receipt. Complete native reads allow build, vet and format-check reuse across unread README content edits. Captured per-package actions keep confined reads; source-free exports and grouping gates use upstream_only.

The Java builder declares the default Maven and Gradle format-check file inventory: each selected Java file and each scanned directory's listing. google-java-format's fixed explicit-file rule establishes this boundary. Existing documentation-file content edits do not change those reads; Java source edits and new source files do. Configuration, declared inputs, command definitions and producer results also contribute to the complete key. Native Maven verify includes runtime tests and lifecycle plugins without a complete read report, so it stays unbounded. Gradle configuration scripts and Ant build files are programs whose complete reads are not reported. Runtime tests and Checkstyle retain specific unbounded reasons. Captured Gradle and Ant exports consume their producer's archives; Maven packaging reads its explicit POM and archive copy inputs and depends on its build producer. Native Maven and Gradle formatting uses a private stage with no retained outputs and order-only lifecycle edges. Private execution alone does not admit narrow keys. Inferred versions or whole-target projection identity can still cause conservative misses after an unread edit. Unbounded lifecycle and lint outputs prevent whole-target restoration, so unchanged builds can still rerun those stages. Fast builds also rerun an unbounded lifecycle when format and lint are omitted: dropping those checks does not make the lifecycle safe to cache. Native whole-target lookup and remote fetching cannot bypass the stage's output bounds, including entries saved by an older CLI. Captured execution is unchanged. oyzu build --explain identifies the stage and its incomplete read report. The stage stays uncached until the builder can establish complete reads and bounded outputs. Adding declared inputs covers those files but cannot bound arbitrary runtime reads by tests, plugins or build scripts. --no-cache also executes the lifecycle; required tests and reports apply in both cases. Use a Java plugin that supplies these declarations and a CLI with compatible private native-stage support. Older plugin declarations do not acquire complete reads by running on a newer CLI. See Maven, Gradle, Ant and Java quality.

A builder's source contract can declare native_reads: {kind: observed} or native_reads: {kind: fixed, rule: "…"}. Omission prevents native stage reuse. Fixed admission names the tool rule that establishes the complete boundary; a prediction alone is insufficient. When a builder supplies bounded source predictions but omits native read admission, --explain says it declares source read predictions but no complete native read observation or fixed read rule. Native Helm packaging and archive normalization use this conservative refusal: their predictions exist and retain home, but neither stage declares complete native reads or stores a reusable native result. Native lifecycle programs can read external files through tests, scripts, plugins or child processes. A whole-source digest covers captured source; it cannot detect changes to files outside that boundary. Declared paths and tool identities establish known inputs but do not prove a lifecycle's reads are complete. A private working directory or read-only root also does not establish complete observations of every mounted filesystem. Isolated Linux Maven and Gradle lifecycles use an enforced complete input boundary under crun. It keys the admitted source and dependency inputs, locked tools, runtime and boundary facts. It hides live proc/sys data and starts each lifecycle with private output state. Unsupported ambient input requirements fail within that restricted view and cannot publish a successful reusable result. An unchanged compatible lifecycle reuses its compilation, archive and test evidence together. With a compatible Java plugin, multi-module Maven and single-build Gradle projects use one coupled lifecycle action per module/project, including its declared producers. Compile and test-class results stay coupled inside that unit. Reports retain the producer's identity and are validated again on reuse. Source, dependency and locked JDK identity changes invalidate the affected action. Fixed archive-copy exports follow their producer's content identity. Use the existing oyzu build --isolated --no-docker selection, or select crun with build.isolation and run oyzu build --isolated. No internal environment gate or new setting is needed. Preparation and tool/input admission still run before a lifecycle hit. Other executors and Windows/macOS do not supply this complete Java boundary. Native-host Maven/Gradle lifecycles keep refusing reuse when their reads are incomplete, including with unchanged sources. Plain Java builds still select native execution; making isolation the Java default is a later product decision. See Maven and Gradle. The .NET consumer uses the same boundary automatically on Linux crun, without a new gate or user option; see .NET stage reads. The closed ambient allowance is /dev/random, /dev/urandom, /dev/null, /dev/zero, and the startup files /proc/self/maps, /proc/self/status, /proc/self/stat, /proc/self/cgroup, /proc/self/limits and /proc/self/mountinfo, plus readlink of /proc/self/exe for executable discovery/identity checks. Opening the executable through proc is not allowed. Other processes' proc entries and all other proc/sys entries stay inaccessible. Self-proc files are supplied as read-only descriptors for the requesting process; the proc tree stays hidden. Successful enforced actions retain that allowance as non-keying facts under extensions["oyzu.dev/ambient-reads"]; the device bytes are never sampled for cache lookup. Self-proc facts record presence only, never contents. Ambient values must not influence retained outputs. Workloads whose outputs depend on entropy remain outside this reuse contract. Other ambient reads receive no allowance. Linux crun Helm stages use the same enforced boundary. Packaging/rendering, lint, validation and helm-unittest can reuse unchanged successful actions with valid reports. The plugin's bounded chart reads are retained; suites without complete observations key the full admitted source view. Helm and helm-unittest are typed locked-tool inputs. The latter uses its normal github:helm-unittest/helm-unittest recipe in oyzu.lock, including publisher archive and resolution identities. A changed selected tool misses; a legacy fixed download is not lock admission. Native-host chart stages still refuse incomplete reads. Helm outputs remain location sensitive unless explicitly declared relocatable. Ordinary source selectors and observed paths must stay within the source root; absolute paths and parent traversal are rejected. They cannot bind ambient JDK or SDK directories, dependency caches outside the workspace, or external test data by naming their paths. Locked tools have separately admitted identities. The Java formatter declares its JDK as an external locked-tool input. Core binds it to the current admitted oyzu.lock identity before cache lookup and publication: changing that identity invalidates reuse even with unchanged source. An unchanged identity permits reuse subject to the other cache inputs. Missing admitted tool identity stops the build with external input <tool> has no admitted oyzu.lock tool identity; run oyzu pin and oyzu install for the required tool, then retry. Do not supply an external path or digest. This does not make arbitrary Java lifecycle or test reads bounded. Only locked-tool external inputs are supported; arbitrary external files and directories have no typed content binding. The tool identity participates in stage and whole-target keys and read-history identity. A changed version, artifact or lock binding invalidates reuse even with unchanged source; the declaration alone does not establish a complete tool set or complete reads. Adding a known input does not establish completeness for arbitrary reads by tests, build scripts or plugins; those stages remain unbounded without a complete read record or fixed tool rule. For observed stages, core allocates an action-specific report path inside the invocation's scratch directory, beside its report directories, in OYZU_OBSERVED_READS. The exact file is cleared before every process attempt, including retries. The action writes a JSON report with complete, paths, listings and reasons, relative to its working directory. Core retains up to four recent complete observations within the prediction in local action-cache metadata, keyed by the structural action definition and core engine identity. Environment names belong to that history subject; their current values remain bound to each result key. This lets branches share observation history when a source-derived value such as OYZU_VERSION changes, without reusing a result built with a different value. Known per-invocation argv and environment paths are normalized before deriving those identities. A subsequent run can use a narrow native key only when that structural definition has an admitted observation. Planning declares observed-read intent before compiler records exist; missing or malformed completion records never authorize reuse. When an execution completes a valid observation and passes the ordinary result-storage checks, core also stores its result under the narrow key computed from the pre-execution snapshot and that report. The next unchanged run can hit that key immediately, including after the first cold compilation. A native key covers the reported files and directory listings, required configuration and declared inputs, shared source inputs, and the declared environment and resolved tool identities. An edit outside those inputs keeps the observation and narrow key. A changed read or listing produces a narrow miss, then successful execution records its new observation and result; the next unchanged run can hit again. Each execution is stored only under narrow keys computed from its own completed report. A lookup key based on an older report is not populated when the execution reads a different set, even if another build changes the shared observation history concurrently. Whole-source results retain their complete source boundary. On Windows, read coverage matches paths without case sensitivity, including literal paths, globs and directory listings. A reported DATA.TXT read binds the captured data.txt file, so changing its contents invalidates reuse. Directory membership changes likewise invalidate a differently cased listing. Snapshot capture rejects case-colliding paths. Linux and macOS read coverage remains case-sensitive. History tries observations in most recently used order, checking each against the current prediction, files, listings, environment and tools through the same narrow lookup gates. The first valid result wins. Switching between branches with different read sets can therefore reuse either branch's result after each has built once. Each lookup hashes at most four observed sets; a hit or valid completion moves its observation to the front, deduplicated by observation digest. Adding a fifth evicts the least recently used observation. Concurrent updates merge atomically, preserving different observations within this bound. When no observed candidate hits, one complete-prediction candidate can discover a stored result without local observation history. oyzu cache explain <action> summarizes each candidate's skip, miss or rejection and names the candidate that hit. JSON also includes nativeCandidates and nativeLookupMicros (elapsed candidate lookup time, including result admission and restore preparation). Candidate probes do not advance key history. Only the selected hit key, or the ordinary request key when every candidate misses, is observed. The comparison baseline comes from an earlier invocation, never another candidate of this lookup. The same choice owns the invocation's execution and publication state. A cache hit preserves admission without requiring a new report. A missing, invalid, empty or incomplete report, or a report with reasons, cannot add an observation or authorize narrow publication; other complete observations remain available. The prediction remains the admission boundary for every report, and required report, artifact and policy checks still apply. Core rebases cwd-relative reports by the action cwd and target before checking the prediction, including configuration files and declared inputs. On a narrowed run, an observed read outside prediction refuses result storage with confined-read-outside-contract. An incomplete native report cannot publish a coarse whole-source result instead. These reports grant no isolation or authority. Current native read coverage​ Read completeness is per stage and invocation, not a property of an entire language. These rules apply to compatible current CLI and builder contracts; an older plugin without them cannot enable reuse. Other inputs and output bounds must still qualify. macOS native action reuse is not supported. Builder and host Complete-read stages and current limits Rust, Linux x64 Compilation and Clippy can reuse with complete Cargo dep-info/build-script observations inside the prediction. Unknown macros, outside-source reads or incomplete reports prevent reuse. rustfmt uses fixed reads. Rust, Windows x64/MSVC Compile observations can currently remain incomplete on unchanged builds, so compilation reruns rather than restoring a coarse result. rustfmt's fixed-read admission and eligible individual compiler-result reuse remain separate. Do not assume a warm build has zero compilation. Maven/Gradle, Linux and Windows x64 The default google-java-format check has fixed file/listing reads and a bound locked JDK. Lifecycle builds, runtime tests and Checkstyle have incomplete reads and rerun. Ant's authored build/quality stages remain unbounded. Node/npm, Linux isolated crun Complete enforced views admit stage reuse. Script-free installation excludes the unread generated version default and can reuse across shipping edits. Installation with lifecycle/environment uncertainty retains the version and reruns. Shipping build/package versions and explicit test environment values remain keyed. Node, native host (Linux, Windows, macOS) Arbitrary project/package lifecycle scripts do not have complete native reads and rerun. Bounded npm install source selectors alone do not admit native stage reuse. Helm, Linux isolated crun Complete enforced views admit packaging/rendering, lint, validation and helm-unittest reuse. Suites retain the full source boundary; selected Helm and helm-unittest lock identities remain keyed. Helm, native host Chart read predictions do not establish complete native observations; incomplete stages rerun. Go, Linux and Windows x64 Build and vet can use complete observed package reads; gofmt has fixed reads. Native runtime tests remain unbounded. cgo and other unresolved inputs can prevent complete admission. Zig, Linux x64 The formatter has fixed .zig/.zon reads and directory listings. build.zig and runtime tests remain unbounded and run again. Node check commands, including captured npm aggregate tests and conventional workspace quality tasks, omit the generated version default. Stable command inputs do not establish complete reads: arbitrary lifecycle code can still read any file or listing in its admitted view. Captured whole-target fallback keys retain that inventory, and incomplete native observations still make the stage run. Shipping Vite workers also retain their version and source-path inventory for output metadata and source/output overlap validation. A listing selector keys the names and kinds of entries directly in a directory. Adding, removing or renaming an entry changes the key; changing its contents alone does not. Nested entries are excluded. Captured views expose empty file placeholders and empty directories for listing-only entries, so undeclared file contents remain hidden. A path on the directory or an ancestor also predicts its listing. A glob must provably match every direct child, such as dir/*, dir/**, or an ancestor's **; merely matching the directory name (for example * matching src) is insufficient. Ordinary file reads still require a covering path or glob.

The Python plugin analyzes captured setuptools package builds, pip preparation and pytest, with output-only packaging. Quality task binding, unknown backends, executable configuration and native operations retain specific unbounded reasons. See what each Python stage reads. Python package snapshot versions still use the whole-target source digest, so an unread edit can change build/package definitions even with a narrow read list. Supported development-source case tests use their separate native editable subject rather than that unused inferred wheel-version default. Captured Python prepare and build record their environment and normalized distributions in .oyzu-build/python inside the private workspace. Cache hits restore these outputs; built-package tests and packaging depend on the built wheel bytes, including package data. Development-source tests inventory their own editable environment instead. Wheel member timestamps and sdist timestamps are normalized before capture so native mtimes do not change downstream output keys. Additional setuptools build requirements keep the build unbounded because they may install backend plugins.

Learned build-script file and environment names remain admission inputs, while the native definition and history subject contain only base/configured facts. Observed native source keys bind base env names plus ObservedReads.env, with values from the environment the process actually received; an absent name binds None. Bound build actions do not inherit undeclared host values. The narrow action recipe omits learned prediction metadata; whole-target and group keys continue to bind effective environments and output locations. The observedEnv payload marker prevents reuse of older path-only observations. Prediction candidates are published or backfilled only when their frozen env declarations cover every name in the admitted report, including names whose values were unset. An uncovered name prevents both local and remote prediction aliases; the complete observed result remains reusable with matching observed inputs. The same rule applies when a history hit could backfill a new prediction after an unread file changes. A reader without native history must execute if that prediction alias is unavailable. Per-run TMP, TEMP and TMPDIR reads are excluded. With learned names unset on the host, an unchanged second run can reuse the first result. If a learned name is set, the cold process did not receive it, while a later planned process does: that environment change requires a miss before reuse can converge. cache explain lists names (never values) in nativeHistory.learnedEnvSetOnHost and in its text reason. Output-location identity still binds compiler flags, tool homes, the checkout and the effective environment. Unset, empty-string and nonempty values are distinct inputs. Removing local Cargo records cannot authorize restoring a result that requires an environment name missing from the new prediction. Scripts must declare their env dependencies through cargo:rerun-if-env-changed or cargo::rerun-if-env-changed; undeclared script reads remain outside this guarantee. Missing, malformed or incomplete observations refuse result storage; they do not become empty successful read sets. Rust predicts each stage's reads from Cargo workspace manifests and target source folders, Cargo and Rust configuration, build scripts, and literal include_str!, include_bytes!, include! and #[path] references. Manifest-relative concat!(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"), ...) references with literal suffixes are resolved too. Source and discovery directories remain conservative directory reads. Cargo metadata paths are resolved against the preparation workspace. Compiler and build-script records instead use Cargo's actual execution workspace, recorded beside each build or Clippy target directory before execution. These projections can differ: preparation uses a source-only workspace while actions use retained private source trees. Manifests, source files, build-script watches and dep-info map to target-relative read selectors; projection locations do not become part of those paths. Records without an execution-workspace record use the metadata workspace conservatively; an unmappable source makes reads incomplete. Unbounded source diagnostics show a bounded sample and the omitted count within the plugin protocol's message limit. Shortening a diagnostic never admits an incomplete observation. On Windows, dep-info drive, UNC and verbatim (\\?\) paths retain their prefixes when mapped to source selectors. Unparseable dep-info paths or unreadable records make the observation incomplete with a reason; they cannot silently authorize a narrow key. Rust native compiling stages declare observed admission. The Rust plugin writes the neutral read report from complete Cargo dep-info and build-script records, plus Cargo manifests and configuration controls that dep-info does not list. Until a previous run of the same action definition has an admitted report, they can discover a stored complete-prediction result; otherwise they keep the whole-target key and execute without restoring a coarse stage result. After execution, a read outside the prediction prevents result storage and reports confined-read-outside-contract, naming the path and the inputs declaration that adds it. Human, no-color and JSON diagnostics carry the same fix. A missing or incomplete observation never authorizes stage result storage, under either a narrow or a whole-source key. format-check uses rustfmt's fixed module-tree and configuration rules and does not need a runtime observation. Native Rust tests and coverage remain unbounded: tests may read files at run time. They retain the current native stage's conservative execution and cache admission. Independently bounded Rust executables can reuse results under the test-unit contract; the enclosing unbounded stage still executes. Cargo dep-info does not record a proc macro's runtime file reads. Native Rust builds assess registry proc macros and registry build scripts as identity-bound: the exact registry package name, version, source and checksum must match Cargo.lock, and the action also binds its selected toolchain and target. This assessment applies to registry implementations without a version allowlist. Workspace/path macros, Git macros, local source replacements and implementations without an identifiable locked registry checksum remain unassessed and refuse stage reuse. Compiler and Cargo locator environment selectors remain keyed. Native target-scoped read names such as CC_x86_64-pc-windows-msvc and CFLAGS_x86_64-pc-windows-msvc are keyed without renaming their hyphens. The managed Rust installation is also bound through the typed locked-tool external-input class; this declaration does not admit arbitrary external paths. Residual risk: a registry proc macro can read ambient files without reporting them to Cargo. The identity-bound assessment trusts that implementation; it is not a complete operating-system read trace or native filesystem confinement. Changing an unreported ambient file can therefore leave a registry macro result reusable. --no-cache bypasses action-result reuse; Cargo's own freshness rules still apply. Workspace/path macros do not inherit this registry assessment, even if they have the same name. Active-unit membership comes from Cargo's successful execution message stream, including fresh units, for the selected target, features and profile. Units excluded by feature or fixture gates do not require build-script records. Before each execution, the old membership is cleared; a failed or incomplete execution cannot publish replacement membership. Active build scripts still need their Cargo records. Existing registry script records contribute environment reads; package-local registry files are covered by the lock checksum, and explicit reads outside the source or admitted tool roots retain an incomplete reason. Missing records during planning request observation rather than claiming completeness. The current execution's report remains the admission decision. Before script records exist, the native prediction covers the local package directory so discovery of package-owned assets does not fail a cold build. Completed observations can still narrow the key to the actual script watches. Native Clippy also records compiled-unit membership from Cargo's JSON messages. An uncompiled fixture package therefore needs no build-script record for lint. Lint still checks every retained script record for each compiled package; a compiled package's build script with no matching record leaves reads incomplete. Lint does not record which script directories ran, so a retained record can mask a missing current record. Membership matches by manifest path. If any compiled manifest matches no metadata package, membership cannot narrow reads: every package is checked and reuse remains blocked. The macro prediction uses Cargo's target-filtered resolved graph, following reachable dependencies rather than every downloaded package. Missing or mismatched target resolution remains unbounded. Other unresolved include expressions still name their source file and line. An OUT_DIR include is generated output: its source inputs are the build script and its rerun-if-changed paths. A watched directory includes all its contents. Without any rerun-if-changed, a workspace/path script keeps the stage unbounded because Cargo uses package changes as the default. rerun-if-env-changed names contribute their effective environment values to the key without publishing those values. Acquired compiler and dependency inputs retain their separately admitted identities. Git metadata watched by a build script is a real input, including in linked worktrees. A script that watches .git/HEAD or its branch reference prevents compiling-stage reuse when that identity changes, even for a documentation-only commit. Unstaged edits outside predicted reads can still reuse a bounded stage. Changing build identity is a project decision; Oyzu does not remove those watches.

oyzu build --verify-contract # also: --json, --full This can't be combined with --no-cache or --plan. A normal build runs. In addition, for every confined action: The action starts from a copy of its target workspace and runs confined, as usual. The same action runs again from an identical copy with the whole target visible. Oyzu compares the results: exit code, every workspace file created, changed or deleted, and the artifacts collected. Test and coverage report files aren't compared, because they carry timing. Equal results pass. If they differ, Oyzu re-runs the action with subsets of the hidden files (at most twelve extra runs) to find a minimal set that explains the difference, and names those files and the declaration that fixes them: Contract check failed · 8 confined actions run again with their whole target visible · 7 equal · 1 diverged · 20 not confined (not checked) api:build Diverged · also reads optional.json · declare inputs: ["api/optional.json"] A divergence fails the build, including when independent targets run in parallel (diagnostic contract-diverged; manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/contract-verification"] has status, counts and one record per action). The check uses a throwaway store, so it reuses and stores nothing. It doesn't run on the native path. Each confined action runs at least twice with copies of the workspace, so it is slow on large installed trees. Actions that aren't confined are counted, not checked. If the search stops at its budget, the record says minimal: false.

You can share action results through any OCI registry. Share them from CI to developers, or between a team's machines. Targets built by an installed plugin package participate in cache.remote and cache.ciRemote. Keys include the verified package release digest, protocol and runtime; changing the plugin identity causes a miss. Remote hits pass the same digest, artifact and report checks as local hits. plugins.development bindings never read or write these shared remotes, including bindings to native executables or package archives. Their reusable results stay local. A slice's --handoff repository has its separate handoff contract. # user or machine configuration: where results are shared [cache] remote = "oci://registry.example.com/team/oyzu-cache" # user configuration: this machine also publishes what it builds [cache] write = true Supported registries: zot, CNCF Distribution behind a token service, and a Harbor proxy-cache project, on Linux. Other registries (Artifactory, Nexus, Docker Hub, GHCR) aren't supported yet, and neither are Windows and macOS clients.

Setting Default Meaning cache.remote unset The OCI repository to share results. Accepted only in user/global, machine or administrative scope. cache.read true once cache.remote is set Look results up. cache.write false Publish results. cache.ciRemote unset The CI repository, see CI and development repositories. Same scope rule as cache.remote. cache.immutableTags false The registry never replaces a tag. See CI and development repositories. A project or local file that sets cache.remote or cache.ciRemote fails with a scope error, even in trusted project folders. Use the environment variables OYZU_CACHE_REMOTE and OYZU_CACHE_CI_REMOTE for one invocation or CI. They override ordinary files and stay subject to administrative constraints. cache.read and cache.write are per-machine preferences and don't change action keys, so readers and writers share entries. A loopback host (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1) is reached over plain HTTP. Every other host uses HTTPS with the shared proxy and trust settings. The remote is used only while the local cache is active. --no-cache, cache.local = false and --verify-contract use no remote.

Per-action results, for targets reused action by action (captured node/package and node/app targets with stage contracts). Whole-target results, for targets reused only whole (the native host path, other builders). These appear under the target's ID in the build record where an action ID would be. A per-action target's group record is never pushed. A client rebuilds it from the action results, so an unchanged repeat after a remote hit makes no registry request.

Step Behavior Lookup After a local miss, one GET of the manifest under the action's tag. On a hit, two blob GETs (config and layer). No HEAD requests, no tag listing. Verify Manifest shape, media types, key annotation, config and layer size and SHA-256, the uncompressed archive's SHA-256, every archive entry against its name, and the entries against the blobs the config references. Only then is the result committed to the local store. Push After an action's result is committed locally and cache.write is true: one GET of the tag (to check for a racing writer), config and layer uploads, then the manifest PUT, which is the only write that makes the entry visible. Offering a reused result A build can offer a result this machine produced when writing is enabled. A completed offer (written, converged or conflicted) suppresses another offer to that remote for 24 hours. After expiry, a later local reuse reads the tag again, even with immutable tags, and refills a missing entry through the normal push path. Results that came from a remote aren't offered. Racing writers Equal output identity (artifact digests and workspace changes; reports are excluded because they carry timing) converges and writes nothing. A different one is a conflict: recorded, never replaced.

A registry that requires sign-in is supported through the registry token flow. The credential is an environment variable, never a setting: export OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN=… # the token your registry's token endpoint accepts In a CI job that offers OIDC ID tokens the way GitHub Actions does (OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL and OYZU_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN, which the Oyzu runner sets), leave OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN unset. The client signs in with the job's ID tokens and asks for a new one when needed. The credential is first sent as a bearer token. A 401 with a Bearer challenge names the registry's token endpoint. Oyzu uses it only if it is on the registry's own origin (scheme, host and port). Otherwise the request is denied and the credential is never sent elsewhere. The client then asks that endpoint for one token per repository, with OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN as the Basic password (user name oyzu), or with no credential if the variable is unset or empty. Tokens ask for pull, plus push when cache.write is true. A rejected or expired token is fetched again once. A second refusal is a denial. With ID tokens, the Basic password is the job's ID token: GET $OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL with ?audience=<registry origin> and the request token as a bearer, answered with {"value": "<jwt>"}. It is reused until 30 seconds before it expires. The request token goes only to that URL, and neither token is recorded. A blob response can redirect to another host (for example a separate blobs host with short-lived signed links). Redirects are followed without the Authorization header when they change origin, at most 5 times, and never from HTTPS to HTTP. A manifest lookup for an entry in the cache carries an advisory X-Oyzu-Cache-Rung header: target for a whole-target entry, action for a single action's entry. A cache gate may count the two apart, because a whole-target key moves with any source change and its 404 is routine. Registries ignore the header, and lookups from other clients or for other purposes (plugin and bundle reads) send none. The build record's remote (and ciRemote) section reports lookups as {target: {hits, misses}, action: {hits, misses}}, counted the way a cache gate counts them (a 404 is a miss; an answered entry, even one rejected after verification, is a hit), so a CI summary matches the gate. A lookup during which the remote went off counts as neither, even if the gate already saw a 200, and REAPI lookups are counted by the client only because there is no OCI gate in front of them. An entry fetched from an OCI registry records its rung in its origin, and oyzu cache explain says whether it came as a whole-target or a stage entry.

Repository <prefix>/v1alpha1/<first two key hex>, tag lookup-<64-hex key>. An OCI image manifest with artifactType application/vnd.oyzu.action-result.v1alpha1. The action-result descriptor as config (application/vnd.oyzu.action-result.config.v1alpha1+json) and one layer (application/vnd.oyzu.tree.v1alpha1.tar+zstd) holding every blob the descriptor references, named sha256/<hex>. Annotations: dev.oyzu.action.key, dev.oyzu.action.output and, on the layer, dev.oyzu.tree.uncompressed-digest.

The build record gains manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"].remote: location, read, write, status (active, unavailable with reason, or unusable for a cache.remote the client can't use), counts of hits, pushed, converged, conflicts and rejected, the requests sent by kind, and per target the actions in each list. A result materialized from the remote carries extensions["oyzu.dev/remote-origin"] in the local store. The summary line adds the remote part, for example remote 7 reused · 0 pushed.

Use a stock Remote Execution API action cache in place of the OCI registry: [cache] remote = "grpc://127.0.0.1:9092/oyzu" write = true grpcs://host[:port]/<instance> uses TLS (default port 443). Plaintext grpc://host[:port]/<instance> is accepted only on loopback (default port 80). The instance can be empty or contain /. Credentials, queries and fragments are forbidden in locations. Standard proxy variables, loopback bypass and SSL_CERT_FILE additional trust follow the shared outbound transport settings. The user/machine scope restrictions, CI/development selection, offer behavior, local verification and report gates are unchanged. cache.immutableTags is ignored for REAPI; every push checks for an existing result first. Supported server and client combinations: Provider Client platform Limits bazel-remote 2.6.4 Linux x86_64 Node package and native Rust results; TLS with an additional CA bundle, HTTP CONNECT proxying and mTLS. API-key header authentication is not supported for this provider yet. Buildbarn bb-storage ae61334 Linux x86_64 Node package and native Rust results, read-only instances, TLS with an additional CA bundle, HTTP CONNECT proxying, mTLS and API-key header authentication. bazel-remote / Buildbarn Windows x86_64 Uploads work; native Rust reuse in a fresh checkout is not supported yet. bazel-remote / Buildbarn macOS Not supported yet. BuildBuddy, NativeLink, EngFlow and other REAPI implementations All Not supported yet. Self-hosted servers need no Oyzu account. Configure authentication before exposing a server to untrusted clients. CI ID-token delivery to these providers is not supported yet. Platform, builder, toolchain and source identities (including line endings) can change a key; identical keys across operating systems are not promised. This client uses the servers for cache storage, not remote execution. REAPI object Oyzu mapping Command Arguments ["oyzu-action-result"], no environment, output path oyzu. Action Command digest, empty Directory input root, 32 raw SHA-256 key bytes as salt, platform property oyzu.dev/key-domain = action-result.v1alpha1. Its serialized SHA-256 and size address the AC entry. ActionResult Exit code zero, regular output files only; no output directories or symlinks. Pushes label the worker oyzu; fetch accepts server-modified or omitted worker metadata. oyzu/result.json Existing result descriptor, including keyComponents, stored in CAS. oyzu/blobs/sha256/<hex> Each blob referenced by that descriptor, stored in CAS. The client requires advertised SHA256 support. It uploads the Command and Action before updating the action cache. Empty blobs are already present by protocol. CAS batches account for the encoded request and gRPC framing within the server's size limit (4 MiB when unset). Read batches also reserve encoded response headroom. Blobs that do not fit use ByteStream. Entries are limited to 256 MiB. Every digest, size, descriptor and referenced blob set is checked before local publication. Corrupt content is quarantined and the action runs normally. CAS eviction is an ordinary miss, including when the action-cache record remains: it is not counted as a rejection or quarantined. A later push repairs that entry when its descriptor or any output blob is missing. Readable, valid entries with equal output identities converge without writes; different identities are conflicts and stay in place. Worker metadata is not an identity or trust check; the output layout and verified descriptor/key identify an entry. REAPI has no atomic create-only AC update, so this check does not provide an immutable-tag server guarantee against simultaneous writers. Concurrent uploads of the same valid output can both write or converge. A writer that sees a different output records a conflict, but racing updates can still replace one another after that check. Every read verifies the result's embedded action key, shape, CAS digests, sizes and complete blob set before committing it locally; normal restore and report checks still apply. A conflicting AC update that fails those checks is rejected, including during concurrent reads. A valid but nondeterministic result for the same key can be last-writer-wins: integrity checks do not authenticate a producer or prove that a computation was honest. The credential is an environment variable, never a setting. OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN, when set, is sent as authorization: Bearer <token> metadata. A server requiring an API-key header can select its non-secret name with cache.remoteHeader; the same token value is then sent verbatim, without a bearer prefix. This setting applies only to REAPI and accepts a lowercase application metadata header, not reserved grpc-*, binary *-bin, host, content-type or te headers. Without that token, OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL and OYZU_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN use the same CI sign-in flow as OCI. The requested audience is the cache endpoint's origin (scheme, host and port), excluding the instance path. ID tokens always use bearer authorization, regardless of cache.remoteHeader. They are reused until within 30 seconds of expiry, then fetched again. A denial never triggers an anonymous retry. GET id token appears separately in request counts. For mutual TLS, set both cache.remoteClientCert and cache.remoteClientKey to absolute PEM file paths and use grpcs://. The key must be unencrypted and readable by the build account; restrict access to that file. These paths and the header name belong only in user, machine or administrative configuration, not project files or profiles, and resolve once per build. They apply to all configured REAPI remotes; OCI is unchanged. The certificate authenticates to the cache server, not to a CONNECT proxy. SSL_CERT_FILE still supplies additional server trust. Client identity setup errors name the relevant setting and file path and retain the filesystem or PEM parsing cause. Correct the path, file permissions or PEM contents before trying again; private-key contents are not included in the error. Illustrative user configuration for a header-based server with mTLS: [cache] remote = "grpcs://cache.example.com/team" remoteHeader = "x-api-key" remoteClientCert = "/home/developer/.config/cache/client.pem" remoteClientKey = "/home/developer/.config/cache/client.key" Set OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN through the shell or CI secret facility. No token value, request token or private-key bytes are written to configuration, logs or build records. Server messages are omitted from failure records to protect secrets. Do not interpret a successful build as proof that credentials were accepted: check the remote status and the build's Warnings section. Remote failures never fail a build. NOT_FOUND on lookup is a miss. UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, ABORTED, timeouts and connection failures get at most three attempts with exponential backoff and jitter, then disable this remote for the invocation. UNAUTHENTICATED and PERMISSION_DENIED disable it without retry. FAILED_PRECONDITION on update records a push failure and computation continues. When capabilities report update_enabled = false, writes are skipped with a read-only reason; reads remain available. Authentication denial appears in the remote build record as status: unavailable with a denied reason while the build computes normally. One warning names the location, gRPC status and credential inputs or permissions to fix. Transient outages also warn and compute locally. A read-only capability skips uploads without disabling reads; a write permission denial disables that remote for the build. Fix permissions, provide a fresh token or correct the certificate paths, then start a new invocation. Denial does not fail the build. TLS handshake failures can surface as gRPC Unknown rather than an authentication status. They also disable the remote and warn; check the CA and client certificate configuration rather than assuming the token was rejected.

User, machine or administrative configuration can name a second repository that only CI writes. In CI, use machine configuration or environment variables because user configuration is ignored: # machine configuration [cache] ciRemote = "oci://registry.example.com/team/oyzu-cache/ci" # CI writes, everyone reads remote = "oci://registry.example.com/team/oyzu-cache/dev" # optional: developers share here immutableTags = true # the registry never replaces a tag write = true # CI ignores user configuration Build Reads (after a local miss) Writes (with cache.write) CI (the execution context detects a CI provider or CI) cache.ciRemote only. cache.remote is recorded as skipped. cache.ciRemote, for an upstream branch push authorized by the registry gate Anywhere else cache.ciRemote, then cache.remote cache.remote only, never cache.ciRemote No cache.ciRemote cache.remote cache.remote On an upstream CI branch push with cache.write enabled, the client requests pull and push scope for the configured CI repository. The registry's cache gate authorizes the job and the ref it is building; it alone decides which refs may write. Upstream feature-branch pushes request the same scopes as other branch pushes, regardless of branch protection. Pull-request and merge-request jobs (including fork requests) remain read-only even with a write credential. Unknown providers, missing ref facts, tags and non-push events also remain read-only. Reads and all existing cache verification checks stay enabled. The same remote-cache ref rule restricts action results and compiler-state publication; compiler-state publication remains disabled independently. Ref facts are caller hints that restrict the client, not authenticated authority. Configure the registry to restrict write credentials to trusted upstream jobs and refs; never expose them to fork jobs. A changed client or forged environment cannot be made trustworthy by this client-side guard. Supported CI facts are: Provider Required facts to request push scope GitHub Actions GITHUB_EVENT_NAME=push, GITHUB_REF=refs/heads/<branch>, and GITHUB_EVENT_PATH containing repository.fork=false GitLab CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE=push and a nonempty CI_COMMIT_BRANCH; fork and merge-request detection must identify an upstream push Provider detection uses the existing execution-context markers. Conflicting provider markers refuse writes. Context and profile overrides never grant write permission. There is no Oyzu branch allowlist. Other providers can read the CI repository but cannot publish until their branch/event facts are supported. If the OCI gate refuses push scope (401/403), the client requests pull-only scope once with the same credential. It disables writes for that CI cache client for the rest of the invocation, preserves admitted reads and explains the fallback. It never tries another credential or falls back to anonymous access. A refused upload also disables further writes while preserving reads. If pull is refused too, the remote is disabled and the build continues locally. Artifact publication retains its separate failure behavior. The build record's ciRemote.write is false when the event guard or registry refuses writes, and ciRemote.writeSkippedReason explains why. Human output shows the same reason as writes skipped: ...; JSON retains the structured fields. This also covers reused local results and the native compiler-result tier. A build that sets CI without the credential is refused (403), keeps building and writes nothing. A CI build never reuses a developer's upload. It doesn't read cache.remote, and a result in its local store that came from a development remote is looked up again in the CI repository. A remote hit is recorded with its scope (ci or development). Nothing is signed, so a hit from the CI repository says where it was read, not who produced it. The registry credential is OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or, without it, the CI job's ID tokens. It is never a setting, and it is never written to a record or log. OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN is sent as a bearer token on every request to the configured registry host (over HTTPS or to a loopback host), and dropped when a redirect leads elsewhere. Immutable tags. cache.immutableTags = true says every configured cache repository refuses to replace a tag. A push then skips the racing-writer read, so a pushed action costs 6 requests instead of 7, and a refused manifest PUT (409 or 412) counts as the conflict. Don't set it for a registry that replaces tags, or the last writer silently wins. Either way, a hit is used only after the digests its manifest names verify.

Counted from the registry's own log for a project with one node/app target and seven cacheable actions (oyzu build --full): Build Manifest GET Blob GET Upload POST Blob PUT Manifest PUT Total Cold push (7 executed, 7 pushed) 14 0 14 14 7 49 Warm hit, second checkout, empty store (7 reused) 7 14 0 0 0 21 Partial hit, test-only edit (1 reused, 6 executed and pushed) 13 2 12 12 6 45 Unchanged repeat after a warm hit 0 0 0 0 0 0 A hit costs 3 requests per action. A miss that pushes costs 7. Signing in adds one token request per repository the build touches. With a storage-backed registry, a push can cost many more storage operations than the 3 objects an entry consists of (about 25 write-class operations per entry on CNCF Distribution's S3 driver), which matters if your object store bills per operation. Harbor's proxy cache revalidates every manifest with the upstream registry, so it saves blob traffic, not manifest requests. For legitimate local producer results, a fresh publication marker suppresses offer requests for 24 hours across invocations. Each completed offer explicitly refreshes the marker timestamp, including on Windows; an expired or future-dated marker allows revalidation. After expiry, an OCI offer costs one manifest GET when the key remains occupied, or six requests when it is missing (one manifest read, two uploads and the manifest write). This is eventual refill on eligible local reuse, not immediate eviction detection. Missing, unreadable, non-file or future-dated markers permit re-offer; failed/skipped offers do not refresh the marker. Marker updates are best effort. A completed conflict also refreshes suppression: the marker records a recent offer, not proof that our result is remotely available. REAPI counts use RPC names in the same build record's remote.requests. For entries fitting one read/update batch, the expected request shapes below exclude retries and ByteStream transfers; these are formulas, not measured stock-server build results. H is the number of remote hits and M the number of misses subsequently pushed. Capabilities are queried once per invocation. REAPI build GetCapabilities GetActionResult BatchReadBlobs FindMissingBlobs BatchUpdateBlobs UpdateActionResult Cold push (M actions) 1 2M 0 M up to M M Second checkout, empty store (H hits) 1 H H 0 0 0 Partial (H hits, M misses) 1 H + 2M H M up to M M Unchanged local reuse, offered within 24 hours 0 0 0 0 0 0 After marker expiry, REAPI offers use the existing push path, including its remote result/CAS validation, convergence and missing-CAS repair. They can read CAS bytes as well as query the action cache; the one-manifest OCI revalidation cost does not describe REAPI.

Remote failures never fail a build: Situation Behavior 404 under the tag A miss. The action runs (and is pushed when writing). 5xx, 408, 429, timeout, connection failure Retried up to 3 times with exponential backoff and jitter. Then the remote is off for the rest of the build and everything is computed. 401 / 403 After sign-in (one token renewal), not retried. The remote is off for the build and no other route is tried. A wrong OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN, no credential where one is required, and a read-only credential with cache.write = true all end here. The build computes and succeeds. 409 / 412 on the manifest PUT The registry refused to replace the tag: a conflict. Not retried. The entry there is kept and not read back. The remote stays on. Digest, size or shape mismatch, missing blob, conflicting config The entry is rejected and its bytes are quarantined in the local store (quarantine/remote-<key>-<part>). The action runs. The remote entry isn't repaired. Push failure The build succeeds. The record says why the entry wasn't pushed. Push interrupted before the manifest PUT Uploaded blobs stay unreferenced. Nothing is visible under the tag.

Sign-in uses only OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN (bearer or the OCI registry token flow; verbatim API-key metadata when REAPI cache.remoteHeader is selected) or the CI job's ID-token flow. REAPI can additionally use mTLS through the two client certificate/key file-path settings. There are no credential helpers, Docker configuration, login command or OAuth2 POST token form; Basic auth to an OCI registry itself remains unsupported. Immutable tags are declared, not detected. Results aren't signed and producers aren't verified. Lookups aren't batched. Transfers are sequential. Entries above 256 MiB aren't pushed. There is no client-managed remote retention or pruning. An evicted OCI tag can be refilled by an authorized local producer after its offer marker expires. A present damaged OCI entry is rejected by readers but never repaired or replaced; the offer preflight checks manifest shape/key/output identity rather than verifying its blobs. An entry pushed by an older Oyzu without keyComponents in its config is rejected like a damaged one.

Situation Behavior No entry The target runs; eligible successful results are stored. Incomplete native reads or unbounded outputs The affected stage runs without result reuse or storage; whole-target restore cannot bypass it. Read the --explain reason. Cache clearing and extra inputs do not establish missing completeness. Missing admitted external locked tool Preparation fails; pin and install the named tool, then retry. A filesystem path or plugin-supplied digest cannot replace admission. Damaged blob or descriptor, mismatched key, unreadable entry Rejected and quarantined. The target runs and replaces it. The summary notes the rejection. Report gate fails on restore The entry is rejected and the target runs normally. Cache location missing, unwritable or unusable The build runs normally and stores nothing. cache.local = false / --no-cache Everything runs. Cancelled or failed build Completed actions that are valid on their own can still be reused. Failed or interrupted actions and failed targets have no stored result. Writes are atomic (stage, then rename), and a descriptor is published only after every blob it references. After a failed build, an eligible action's outputs, workspace changes and reports are sealed when it completes, so a later writer or target failure can't change them. An action whose required reports are missing or malformed isn't stored. Changing the engine cache contract or the declared builder source/package identity invalidates entries; replacing CLI or development-plugin executable bytes alone does not. Nothing is migrated, and old entries age out through retention. Python application archives record their planned version and runtime package identities, not a dependency or source digest; dependency, source and version changes remain separate key inputs.

The cache trusts the declared target graph (see Trust model). Targets built by a host-coordinated image worker aren't cached. Native authored tasks without complete observation of their own reads rerun, with or without hooks; cache = true and an inherited builder contract cannot admit them. The admitted Linux slice is described under authored tasks. Version finalization after hooks covers only pre_build hooks on captured Node targets. Narrow keys require a confined action or an admitted native read contract. Captured stages with an unbounded reason retain the whole-target key; incomplete native reads prevent stage reuse. cache.local and cache.nativeMaxMiB control reuse and native-cache retention, not computation identity. Changing their resolved values does not change configuration-derived action keys; cache.local = false still disables lookup and storage. Source files explicitly read by an action remain normal key inputs. Windows has no confined actions. macOS isn't supported yet.

Build bundles for what reuse records in the manifest, and build logging for the live view. Affected builds for Git-based selection, and native Node static analysis for stage contracts. Configuration for the cache.* settings.

Eligible passing test units and supported Python cases use the same OCI and REAPI remotes as action results. Core computes each key from current inputs; the remote transports its immutable descriptor and referenced report bytes. Unit restores validate exact key facts and components, stage only that unit's files, and require a passing JUnit report before accepting the hit. Unit JSON records include the original execution producer in sourceRecord when known. Report timings and producer metadata are evidence, not racing-writer outputs. CI/development origin restrictions and ordinary outage fallback apply to these entries too. Failed units are never reusable as successful units. Passing cases can still be reused independently when another case in the same unchanged unit fails. A reader without history looks up a reference using the full locally computed unit key and current native case ID, then validates the separate immutable passing record and current components. References contain no input or coverage lists. Failed, new, missing or incompatible cases execute; latest local failure and order-dependence records take precedence over remote successes. Combined reports preserve original case producers and distinguish reused evidence from work executed now. Incomplete local executions also refuse older remote successes. Case outcomes remain recorded when coverage is incomplete. A unit assembled from remote case contributions is not stored as a new locally produced unit, preserving its contributors' remote-origin restrictions. This discovery is deliberately conservative. A remotely discovered trace stays bound to the full unit input key even after it is recorded locally. When that key changes, its historical coverage cannot authorize omitting current inputs. For a deliberately smaller plain-Python subset, a reader can instead compute a complete current native function closure before lookup. It hashes the current case and every transitively referenced function locally, retaining all module setup, file membership, non-code inputs, environment, tools, locks and configuration. The exact resulting key finds the immutable passing record; remote coverage never determines that closure. An unrelated body edit can then reuse an independent case even with no local history. Existing guarded traces remain guarded. This path accepts direct calls, primitive expressions and immutable literal constants in plain top-level functions. Native import facts carry actual loaded origins and aliases, including relative package imports. Rust resolves only origins in the current admitted source inventory. Fixtures, marks, decorators, dynamic calls, introspection, mutable setup, unresolved origins or custom pytest plugins retain conservative execution. Native plugin registrations are observed historically, so unregistering a custom plugin cannot make the run eligible. Fresh records require complete native coverage within the computed closure and matching prepared/runtime observations. The core and normally admitted Python package must have matching native runtime identities; an older package is rejected rather than treated as compatible. If execution adds reads or invalidates the current native facts after a partial selection, the existing unit runner retries the complete unit once in a fresh view. It retains the initial native case/JUnit contributions and logs. An initial failure remains a failure even if the full selection fallback passes; combined reports explain both observations. Only validated complete conservative results can be stored. Local coverage-based selection continues for its existing supported shapes. This transport does not add Rust executable discovery, test sharding or quarantine, or qualify new test subjects or platforms.

Captured pip/pytest package tests can keep passing case results inside a changed file-level unit. Native collection supplies each full node ID, including parameters. Only the selected cases run, in their original relative order. The step combines native IDs, outcomes, durations and failure reasons with reused evidence in one JUnit report. Fresh native JUnit contributions are also retained with their configured output capture; the combined report does not add captured passing output. The action row shows, for example, 12 of 140 cases ran, 128 reused. A case key compares five inputs: shared unit configuration and tool/dependency identities; non-code runtime inputs; code executed during import and collection; the case's executed code; and its native ID. Shared-input changes rerun every case. A changed import-time input reruns the whole unit. Within the bounded source shape below, a function-body edit reruns cases that executed that function. For supported captured development-source tests, the shared identity names that test subject and its genuine editable environment, including native metadata, RECORD and import mapping. It does not inventory the separate inferred-version wheel environment or inject its unused version default. Built-package tests keep actual wheel-installed facts; subject identities never share passing records. Required runtime-read confinement and the guards below apply to both subjects. Unsupported source layouts retain built-package testing. New cases and cases whose last result did not pass always run. Missing input or coverage facts also run the case. The stored passing record, rather than diagnostic history, authorizes reuse. Its case ID and all current key components must match the requested case. A history pointer to a different existing record is a miss, so the requested case runs instead of borrowing unrelated passing evidence. Coverage facts come from an Oyzu-supplied pytest adapter using coverage.py's test_function contexts. For parameterized tests, a static native node-ID context keeps parameter identities separate. Core hashes admitted source bytes; the Python adapter never chooses cases or keys. Python's AST supplies current UTF-8 byte ranges and stable names for plain top-level functions. Rust hashes each executed function's entire definition from the admitted runtime view, including branches the previous run did not take. It resolves names against the current collection instead of reusing old line offsets. An unchanged function can move when another body grows or a new case is inserted; reused line/arc evidence is relocated to its current position for the combined coverage report. This separation currently accepts modules consisting of imports, literal constant assignments, docstrings and plain top-level functions. Import statements and whole literal assignments, including multiline values, remain shared. Merely creating a function during collection does not make its body shared; executing it outside a case does. Modules with classes, computed module setup, colliding top-level bindings (including native import aliases, constants and function names), one-line definitions, decorators, defaults, annotations or unsupported source encoding retain whole-file identity. Python's native encoding detection honors coding cookies; only UTF-8 without a BOM supports function ranges. Other encodings stay opaque and execute with their native interpretation, even when their raw bytes also happen to decode as UTF-8. Missing location facts and case execution outside located functions also retain whole-file identity. Syntactic references to namespace inspection or evaluation (globals, locals, vars, dir, eval, exec, __globals__, __dict__ or __builtins__), including imported aliases and qualified attributes, keep every source in the bounded unit opaque. The adapter does not attempt to resolve which module an observer can inspect. For example, an unchanged assert 'test_added' not in globals() can fail when a new function is added; an unchanged assert 'added' not in vars(api) can likewise observe a new function in api without executing it. Both retain whole-file import/collection identities. Explicit source reads such as inspect.getsource remain shared runtime reads. This is a bounded native source contract, not general Python dependency analysis. Shared tool, environment and runtime-artifact changes remain binding, including the actual installed package version and all .dist-info bytes (METADATA and RECORD included). A source edit that changes those inputs still reruns the whole unit; function regions do not normalize or discard them. File membership, kinds, executable facts and frozen non-code inputs stay shared; only inventoried code bytes move into the coverage components. Selective function-level reuse is limited to the supported Linux development flow. Full, CI, package and release validation retain their broader inputs; other platforms do not support this selective flow. Selection currently requires Linux crun (--isolated --no-docker), enforced captured runtime-read bounds and coverage.py in the project environment. Coverage.py is not currently an independently acquired Oyzu tool. Missing or incomplete coverage runs the entire unit and gives a one-line reason. Native host tests and authored test tasks retain their existing whole-unit or whole-stage behavior. Python application archives and other languages do not use case selection. The release context runs every case when its unit key changes. If fresh selective and full executions disagree on an identical case key, the result is reported as order-dependent, with both run IDs and which run was selective. Selection stays disabled for that unit key. A disagreement blocks the unit even if the selective child passed; the next build runs it fully. Native outcomes remain in the report. Detection does not turn a failure into a pass or run an automatic retry through case-selection fallback. The separate in-build test-attempt controller may retry a genuine native test failure, reporting a pass on retry as flaky and refusing unit storage. oyzu cache explain <target> lists each case's deciding component or the original run record used for reuse. JSON action records add caseSelection inside each unit, including fresh/reused counts, decisions and any order-dependence finding. Reused cases remain evidence not run now in test summaries. Existing v1alpha1 records are extended in place; records without case facts continue to use unit-level behavior.

documents.t: The experimental native Linux and Windows compiler tier reuses individual already non-incremental library compilations beneath a Cargo build. Linux also supports build-script and admitted application binary compilation reuse. Use the normal oyzu build entry point and existing cache settings. --no-cache disables this tier too. Action records include localReasons alongside compiler outcome totals in extensions["oyzu.dev/rustc-invocations"]. Local receipts distinguish unsupported arguments, incremental state, unresolved inputs/linkers and cache/input rejection. These reasons explain native fallback without treating it as reuse. The tier also reuses Cargo's exact empty-stdin capability query for the native Linux x86-64 toolchain. The supported request prints file names, sysroot, split-debuginfo modes, crate name and target cfg, with Cargo's conventional crate types and optional x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu target. Its exact arguments, empty source, compiler identity, compiler environment and physical compiler/workspace placements are keyed. Successful stdout is restored byte for byte through the verified store. Failed queries or queries producing diagnostics are not stored. Other flags, custom targets and nonempty stdin retain native execution; a nonempty source is forwarded intact and reported as nonempty-capability-query-source. Cargo still creates consumer-local bookkeeping and decides whether an invocation is needed; its freshness messages do not count as compiler-cache hits. Compiler admission uses the exact canonical managed rustc retained by native preparation, independently of whole-stage tool completeness.
