Build scripts still execute locally; their presence and proc macros do not prevent invocation reuse. Whole-stage caching retains its existing tool-completeness checks. Opaque native stages bind the full selected tool environment without gaining source or PATH narrowing; missing preparation retains the whole-lock fallback. Cargo configuration may supply rustflags and target settings; effective rustc arguments and encoded rustflags remain keyed. Compiler or wrapper substitutions in the environment or .cargo/config* keep the stage's compiler invocations local. Proc-macro and build-script compilation keys also bind resolved linker file contents and linker arguments. Unresolved linkers and explicit linkers outside retained managed tools stay local; rlib/rmeta invocations do not require a linker identity. Proc-macro and build-script compiler invocations also stay local if PATH contains any empty or relative entry, including .:/usr/bin on Unix. Rustc's linker subprocess receives that PATH unchanged and can search its working directory; filtering entries only during key generation would bind a different linker. Use only absolute entries to allow reuse of these compiler outputs. On Windows, .dll proc-macro extern inputs are keyed by content. Proc-macro and build-script compilation and native -l library closures remain local with unresolved-windows-linker-closure or unresolved-windows-native-library: MSVC linker discovery, SDK libraries and auxiliary inputs are not yet admitted. Windows support covers native x64/MSVC library invocations. Locally rebuilt proc-macro DLLs can change bytes between builds, including PE timestamps and CodeView/PDB identity or age fields. Those bytes remain part of the extern digest: changed DLLs invalidate dependent library results even when their Rust sources are unchanged. Oyzu does not strip or normalize them to force a cache hit. A candidate must use supported library, proc-macro, build-script or application binary arguments and admitted workspace or lock/archive-bound crates.io inputs. Fresh local rustc dep-info supplies source and environment dependencies before lookup. Keys bind file/extern contents, compiler/profile/lock controls, actual consumed environment values and the invocation's admitted Unix creation mask. Builds under masks 0022 and 0077 cannot share compiler results. Cache descriptors retain environment digests rather than their raw values. Windows has no Unix creation mask; its not-applicable value is keyed with the host platform. Missing Unix mask evidence still prevents admission. Windows compiler invocations use rustc response files so large registry remap lists fit within the native process command-line limit. The native owner's explicit RUSTC is accepted only when it is the exact canonical selected managed compiler path. Custom compilers, aliases and alternate path spellings retain local execution. Frozen source facts come from the immutable projection; reads are bound to the core-reserved executing action fork, including any nested workspace prefix. Only those verified RUSTC, RUSTDOC and RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN placements use tool role identities in the compiler-control digest, so the same admitted tool can be installed in different user stores. Other compiler environment values and actual consumed env! values retain their data semantics and path fallback. The private worker removes its injected wrapper/binding variables before invoking rustc, including native fallback. Authored wrappers outside this hook are unchanged. Native Cargo preparation freezes Cargo.lock and Cargo metadata without inventorying registry archives. When a native action misses the finished-result cache and is admitted for compiler reuse, Oyzu can admit crates.io source files from a cached .crate archive only after verifying its checksum against the frozen lock. Task listing, finished-result hits, builds with --no-cache and actions that cannot use the compiler cache do not compute this inventory. The inventory covers regular archive entries; the extracted cache directory and .cargo-checksum.json never grant authority. The package manifest and each consumed file must match those frozen facts before reuse. Every compiler-cache binding still reads each compressed archive and verifies its SHA-256 against the lock checksum, including when file facts are cached. A changed or corrupted archive cannot use cached facts. After that verification, Oyzu reuses the decompressed file inventory from the local action-cache store, keyed by the lock checksum. Only relative file paths and digests are retained; the current Cargo metadata supplies the physical source root. The same facts can serve copied trees and different registry locations. Concurrent bindings use the store's existing per-key lock and atomic publication. Evicted or invalid records are rebuilt from verified archive bytes. If the store is busy or unavailable, Oyzu inventories the already-verified archive buffer instead. A failed cache write keeps those computed facts usable. When a compiler consumer detects mismatched or missing registry facts, it refuses reuse and quarantines that archive's facts record. A later binding rebuilds the facts from verified archive bytes and checks consumed files again. These records remain local; no registry or toolchain bytes are uploaded. Missing archives, unsupported entries or changed consumed files retain local compilation. Archive admission remains bounded to 64 MiB compressed, 128 MiB of files and 20,000 files per package; it does not scan the extracted source tree. For a non-empty registry inventory, the compiler binding records elapsed time as Registry compiler inputs. JSON diagnostics and event logs retain the timer; use -v to show fast steps that ordinary human output may collapse. Registry admission compares canonical filesystem paths, including Windows verbatim paths and registry roots reached through symbolic links. Only the exact admitted package manifest qualifies; similarly named directories do not. Admission resolves registry roots before launching Cargo and freezes those physical paths in the compiler binding. Absolute source arguments must use the physical spelling; an unresolved source alias keeps the invocation local. Only expected rlib/rmeta files, host proc-macro dylibs and compiled build-script executables and admitted application binaries pass through the existing verified result store. Metadata-only library invocations restore rmeta outputs; linked library invocations restore both rlib and rmeta. Build-script invocations restore their executable; proc macros restore their dylib. Extern inputs retain their exact file kind and content identity. Their modes are preserved. A CI reader treats development-origin local results as misses before probing its CI remote. Existing read/write permissions, remote scope, integrity checks and failed-output/report gates still apply; a compiler hit is not successful test or target evidence. An exact admitted workspace prefix produces logical /oyzu/source debug and compiler metadata paths. Admitted absolute registry source arguments map to /oyzu/registry/<archive-sha256> in compiler paths, including file!() output. Workspace and registry containment use canonical filesystem paths, including Windows verbatim spellings and registry roots reached through symlinks. This does not authorize sibling paths with a shared text prefix. Compiler source arguments retain their original spelling. Relative source filenames remain unchanged; relative and absolute source spellings have distinct keys. Oyzu does not rewrite CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR, environment values or source text. A consumed absolute environment path stays local, except admitted OUT_DIR under the physical location contract below. Dep-info is freshly generated on the consumer and never restored from the producer. Only typed artifact notifications may replay with consumer output paths; diagnostics prevent publication. Sources containing declarative macros, proc-macro declarations outside a proc-macro crate, absolute path literals or standalone env!("OUT_DIR") use an explicit physical location contract alongside the native source remapping. Their keys additionally bind the layout of the working directory, target root and generated-output directory relative to the source root, and the admitted registry archives. Moving a whole checkout keeps the key, because the native source remapping already names those roots logically; changing the layout selects a different key. Standalone OUT_DIR observations retain their exact value and keep the physical generated-output directory in the key. Restored bytes are never rewritten. Receipt reasons name keyed-physical-location-contract; localReasons includes that contract count for compiled and reused invocations as well as reasons for local execution. Cargo runs build scripts itself. A library consuming its own build-script output can reuse compiler results when generated file reads appear in fresh dep-info under its contained OUT_DIR. Those files are keyed by content and an OUT_DIR-relative name. Consumed cargo:rustc-env values are keyed through rustc's environment dependencies. --cfg, --check-cfg and --env-set arguments remain key inputs. Native -l inputs must resolve to exactly one regular file in admitted -L directories inside the target tree; unresolved, ambiguous or unsupported libraries retain local execution. Search-directory and generated output placements use logical paths. Dependencies of build-script and proc-macro packages are admitted independently; extern contents bind their compiled inputs. Build-script binary compilation can reuse its executable, preserving its bytes and executable permissions; Cargo still runs that script and owns its generated outputs. Editing build.rs invalidates its compilation key. The physical location contract also applies when the script source needs it, so same-path repeats can hit. Application binary links can reuse on the same physical paths with the native Linux x86-64 GNU cc driver and Rust-provided lld. Their keys bind every candidate rlib/rmeta in the Rust dependency search directories and native sysroot by content, including transitive dependencies. This conservative inventory can invalidate a link when an unused candidate changes; only application links pay this cost. The compiler's actual linker arguments supply a discovery hint. Successful links publish it through the same local and remote result caches as compiler outputs, so an empty local store and history can discover a remotely cached link. Before lookup, the native linker resolves libraries again and reports the files it opens, including ordered -L/-l choices, linker scripts and crt objects. Changing a native library or adding a library that shadows an earlier choice changes the key. The resolved driver, linker, support programs and their ELF runtime libraries, built-in driver specifications, link arguments and native search environment also enter the key by content or value. The full physical location contract applies to every application link. A crate whose dependency closure holds a proc-macro target, directly or through a re-exporting dependency, also keeps the full physical location contract: expansion can read CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR or another path and emit it without a dep-info env-dep line, so the key must not omit the checkout and cache directories. The closure comes from the Cargo resolve graph (normal, build and development edges), not from build state, so identical runs agree. Results are reused only where those directories match. The contract covers checkout and cache roots only; a macro that emits another unobserved variable such as HOME is not keyed. A first link, or a missing discovery hint, executes locally before publishing its result and hint. Failed links publish neither. Discovery hints use the same read/write and CI-origin admission as compiler outputs; they do not restore outputs. Native inputs are checked before and after linking. Successful repeat hits restore the executable's verified bytes and permissions, then regenerate local dep-info; the executable is never rewritten. Existing compiler-cache read/write, artifact validation and report requirements remain binding. Unknown driver specifications, linker controls, nonempty generated raw-dylib search paths, thin archives, native autolink/GNU LTO inputs and unresolved libraries keep the application local with a specific refusal reason. Custom shell linker wrappers, ambiguous parent traversal through directory symlinks, parent-traversing linker scripts, other linker families, cross targets and other host platforms are not admitted. Conventional supported linker flags remain keyed; unknown arguments retain native execution. Cargo capability queries outside the exact empty-source request above remain local (cargo-capability-probe). Build-script feature probes such as autocfg remain local (unfrozen-stdin-source): their generated stdin source and LLVM IR outputs are outside the frozen source and compiler-artifact contract. autocfg also generates a fresh crate name for each probe; the name and LLVM IR output identity cannot be erased or rewritten to manufacture a hit. Incremental invocations, active/unknown Cargo configuration, authored wrappers, unknown compiler arguments and inputs outside the admitted source or generated-output roots retain native execution. Incremental arguments are never removed. This repository sets CARGO_INCREMENTAL = "0" in [context.ci.env] through normal configuration resolution so CI dev-profile compilations can qualify. Local development keeps Cargo's incremental default; it trades cross-checkout compiler reuse for local incremental compilation. Frozen Cargo configuration containing only exact target tables for neither the selected target nor compiler host may be admitted: those tables have no compilation effect, and their captured digests remain keyed. Conditional cfg(...) tables and other settings retain local execution. Linux x86-64 OCI consumers can reuse admitted compiler results across checkout roots. After a source edit, unchanged dependency compilations can reuse their results while changed crates compile locally. Development readers restore only their matching profile, even when the writer also stores optimized entries. Registry reuse follows the same location contract and retains local fallback for other consumed absolute environment paths. Registry support does not establish reuse for every crate, REAPI compiler-result transport or another host platform. The compiler summary reports reused, compiled and local invocation counts separately from whole-action reuse. Both compiled and local execute rustc; local means the invocation did not qualify for shared compiler reuse. Action receipts retain these counts under extensions.oyzu.dev/rustc-invocations, including in the JSON build manifest. The receipt also includes timingsMs for source-compilation invocations, summed separately for compiled, reused and local, plus up to eight slowest invocations with their phase timings. Capability-query outcomes remain counted without source-compilation phase timings. Phases separate binding preparation, argument/extern classification, the fresh dep-info probe, input admission, lookup, verified restore, output installation, compilation and publication/rechecks. Native compilation includes linker work. These are elapsed times per compiler process: concurrent invocations overlap, so their sums are not the build's wall time. Store lookups use a nonblocking maintenance lease; contention refuses reuse rather than waiting for a lock. A whole-action hit retains its original receipt; those original counts and timings do not represent new compiler work.

Contributors can run tooling/key-stability-sweep.sh --reinstall-toolchain NAME PROJECT_DIR from a Bash shell with oyzu and Python 3 on PATH. It copies the fixture into scratch, builds twice with one private tool store, then rebuilds with a second store and the same action cache. This needs network access and space for two toolchain installations. Both stores must list the same non-empty set of installed tool identities. REINSTALL_STAGES selects space-separated stage names, defaulting to compile-development lint. Every selected action in the second build must retain its non-empty actionKey after reinstall and be reused. Missing actions and missing, empty or changed keys always fail. Extra new actions are ignored: the sweep guards the baseline actions, rather than requiring identical action inventories. Unrelated optional manifest fields are tolerated. The sweep judges reuse misses against NAME-reinstall in tooling/key-stability-known-leaks.json: recorded misses print XFAIL, new misses print FAIL, and resolved recorded misses print XPASS until the entry is removed. Exit 0 means PASS or XFAIL; exit 1 means a key failure, unexpected reuse miss or XPASS. Exit 2 means a failed build or missing comparison prerequisite, including a selected stage absent from the baseline. SDK_PIN rewrites only the scratch copy's global.json, materializing a private regular file if it was a symlink. The source fixture stays untouched. Scratch and logs are removed on exit unless KEEP=1 is set. SWEEP_BUILD_ARGS replaces the default --full; BUILD_ARGS appends execution options.

Captured Rust compilation can start from a compiler-state seed in an OCI cache.ciRemote repository. REAPI remotes do not supply or publish compiler seeds: they skip seed filesystem work and requests while ordinary action-result caching remains available. This is native compiler state, not a successful action result: Cargo still runs, artifacts are validated and the selected checks still execute. It does not enable cross-path reuse for host-native builds or change their compiler-cache retention. Seed keys include the compiler archive digest, native Cargo lockfile digest, target triple, absolute compiler-visible workspace and Cargo home, selected worker and command, effective-environment digest, tool-lock identity and tool archives. Workspace and Cargo home paths must be canonical and absolute. Dot and parent aliases are refused, including slash-separated aliases inside Windows verbatim path components. Raw environment values are not stored in the seed inventory. A path mismatch selects a different lookup before any compiler-state download. When native read completeness is unknown, the key also binds the complete final staged source and preparation identity: changed inputs then build cold, even at matching paths. There are no fingerprint edits, filesystem aliases or new sandbox mappings. The seed is an OCI manifest with content-addressed inventory and archive blobs, under the configured CI repository's compiler-state/v1alpha1 segment. For example, a CI repository prefix of oyzu-cache/ci keeps seed manifests and blobs under oyzu-cache/ci/compiler-state/v1alpha1/<key-shard>. Seed publication is disabled in this client, including CI and pool jobs with write credentials. There is no configuration or environment switch to enable it. Enabling publication and qualifying a trusted producer require a separate change; client environment hints cannot authenticate that producer. Developer remote repositories are never seed sources. The registry owner manages retention. Restoration verifies the key, blob sizes and digests, archive member inventory, file contents and containment before committing compiler state. Symlinks, hard links and special files refuse the seed. An existing local directory is never overwritten. A refusal or unavailable remote causes a cold build; offline builds do not contact the seed remote. A seed manifest or blob request that fails after transport retries, or is denied, disables that remote for the rest of the invocation, including subsequent action-result lookups. A missing manifest is an ordinary miss; a missing blob rejects that seed. Neither missing response disables the remote. A seed does not provide missing tool or dependency archives. The inventory preserves native compiler metadata and records source contents and times. Identical source contents regain their recorded times; changed inputs remain newer than restored compiler work. Compiler fingerprints and dep-info retain their original bytes. Capture and restore read the compiler tree to verify it and inspect source contents to bind freshness; this work happens only for an active, readable OCI CI seed consumer. REAPI-only remotes skip it, and installed-tool use does not trigger it. Archive bounds are 1 GiB compressed, 12 GiB expanded and 32 MiB for the inventory; an oversized seed is refused. Windows native actions freeze platform installation, home/profile and architecture inputs used by SDK discovery, alongside the declared compiler controls. They remain explicit action inputs; native launches do not recover undeclared values from the parent environment.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/affected-builds.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build --affected <git-ref> builds only the targets that changed since a Git commit, plus the targets that consume them and whatever those need to build. Use it in pull requests and CI to skip unchanged parts of a monorepo. Status: experimental. oyzu build --affected HEAD --plan oyzu build --affected origin/main oyzu inspect dist The ref must already exist locally; Oyzu doesn't fetch it. Git must be on PATH. --affected can't be combined with target names. No project configuration is needed. Without --affected, every target builds as usual.

Oyzu compares your current source with the committed files at the ref, including deleted files and executable-bit changes. A project nested inside a repository is compared with its own subtree. The usual source exclusions apply to both sides, so changes in dist, .oyzu, dependency folders and other excluded folders don't trigger builds. Checkout filters and line-ending conversion can make working files differ from committed ones; such differences count as changes. A changed file selects targets whose bounded stage read sets or declared build.yaml inputs include it. Declared inputs are relative to build.yaml, including paths outside the target folder. Selection uses the same analysis contracts as action-cache source keys. If any stage has no complete read contract, every change inside its target folder selects that target. Selection then follows consumers through depends_on, materialize.from and cross-target task prerequisites, transitively. The producers and task dependencies those targets need are added. Each selected target runs its normal checks and packaging. A native workspace (for example a Cargo workspace) is one target; individual members aren't selected separately. Declare cross-project file reads with inputs and build relationships with the normal dependency fields. Build inputs are literal file or directory paths relative to build.yaml; a directory includes its descendants. For example, docs with path: docs-site and inputs: [docs/reference] is selected when a tracked file under docs/reference changes or is deleted. Task inputs also support globs, relative to the task's working directory. A change matched only by an independent root task selects that task without adding a build target; a genuinely unowned change retains the full-build fallback below. Unbounded stages can keep a root target selected for every repository edit; selection never assumes unknown reads are empty. Execution follows the plain-build rules: native when every selected target supports it, otherwise the container executor.

--plan returns an empty preview and leaves dist alone. A build writes an empty, inspectable bundle with no tools, actions or artifacts. Old artifacts aren't copied into it, and unselected targets aren't reported as successful.

The plan and manifest record oyzu.dev/selection with mode: "affected", the impacted targets, the final selection and the excluded targets. Its affected object records the ref, the resolved commit, the source digest, changed paths, the reason each target was selected, and any fallback to a full build. affected.inputModel: "stage-reads" identifies read-set-aware selection. affected.tasks lists affected root tasks, including consumers of other affected tasks. Root tasks use their declared inputs (paths or globs relative to their working directory); a task with no declared inputs is conservatively selected. When an affected root task feeds a target hook, selection also includes that target and its consumers, including through intermediate task dependencies. This records which repository checks to run without executing them during preview. Older CLIs without this input model must not be used to skip CI jobs. Affected selection compares available declared inputs before requiring inputs for execution. Generated, ignored inputs need not be prepared just to select work, in either a preview or a build. The JSON facts list absent inputs by build in affected.absentDeclaredInputs. The human Scope section, including with --explain, says when no selected action needs a build's inputs; selected builds mark their absent inputs as required for execution. Absence alone adds no change; deleting a tracked input still selects its consumer, even when a later ignore rule also matches it. The comparison retains its committed bytes without adding it to the live inventory. Changes to a preparation task's declared inputs select that task and its consumers as usual. Before preparing actions, execution still requires every input of the final selected builds and their dependencies. A fallback to a full selection requires all those builds' inputs. Previews without --affected also require selected inputs; prepare the input before running the build. For this repository's documentation source checks on a fresh checkout, use oyzu --toolset checks run check-docs followed by git diff --check. These checks run against source and do not need generated website inputs. An affected build that leaves the website unselected does not require those inputs either, including with --full. Reference edits declared as website inputs still select the website. A selected docs target renders it and requires its prepared inputs; the docs-site job generates and validates the examples before building. --full enables checks without generating those inputs. Use the affected preview to inspect selection before preparation. The human output shows a Scope section: counts of changed, dependent and unaffected targets, the base and its short commit, or a Not narrowed notice with the fallback reason. The JSON plan and manifest selection record retain that reason in affected.fallback; full-selection fallbacks leave directlyAffected and dependents null. Changed paths, selected targets and per-target reasons have deterministic ordering. A missing base, including one absent from shallow history, records baseline-unavailable; an unowned change records unowned-input. Renaming to a new path still selects everything and records new-or-untracked-input, even if the old path was a declared input. Fetch missing history before retrying a missing-base selection. See result output. These records describe the selection. They aren't release or CI evidence.

Oyzu builds everything when it can't safely narrow the selection: the ref can't be read locally; a file is new compared with the ref; a changed file belongs to no target; build, configuration or lock files changed; inputs of a root task with cross-target prerequisites changed; the configuration is managed by policy; the source read analysis cannot be completed; Git object limits or unsupported entries prevent comparison. The recorded fallback says which. If the ref was missing, fetch it and run again. A fallback may need tools that a no-change build wouldn't.
documents.s: Falling back to a full build

documents.t: --affected works in a clone made with git clone --filter=blob:none, which has full history but only the file contents a checkout needs. Git fetches the contents of changed files from the remote on demand, so the clone needs read access to the repository. If that fetch fails, Oyzu falls back to a full build. Git fetches these one file at a time, so a very large change takes longer to plan. This is how a platform pool plans a remote run.

Changes to external configuration, tools or environment aren't seen by Git. Run a full build when those change. Reuse of cached actions isn't part of --affected itself; see the action cache. Discovery and validation still cover the whole workspace. Reading the baseline needs no network, but preparing selected targets may download dependencies. Git metadata never grants signing or publication rights.
Build tasks for target selection. Native local builds for the CI matrix from --plan --json --affected. Action cache for reusing unchanged results.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/ant.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The java/app builder, for a folder with build.xml, builds conventional and custom Ant projects on your machine or in a container and exports versioned JARs. oyzu run test produces test and coverage reports without packaging a JAR. Both use the same Ant reporting integration. Status: experimental. Native host builds support Linux x64 and Windows x64; Windows qualification is pending. Captured builds run on Linux with Docker or crun. The oyzu/java plugin selects Ant for a folder with build.xml (or with.build-tool: ant); see plugin catalog and selecting a role.

With the native prerequisites provisioned, run: oyzu build --full oyzu inspect dist Oyzu uses the managed JDK to evaluate your Ant project on the host, discovers its JAR targets and outputs, then runs the build, test, archive and quality stages. It copies versioned JARs into a fresh core-owned output directory and collects them with JUnit and JaCoCo reports into dist/. A model evaluation error fails preparation with Ant's diagnostic; it does not silently select a container. On Windows, Ant model evaluation, JAR packaging and reporting receive ordinary drive or UNC paths that the JDK accepts, including classpath and report paths. Oyzu keeps extended paths for its own filesystem operations and passes the complete path to Java, including paths longer than 260 characters. This requires the managed JDK; it does not enable long paths for other native tools used by your build. The JDK and Ant come from your native tool selection and [tools] configuration. With nothing configured, oyzu build locks the latest LTS JDK and Ant 1.10.18 in oyzu.lock, downloads them into the shared tool store and sets JAVA_HOME and ANT_HOME for the build, so no Ant needs to be installed. Select another Ant release with an exact version such as [tools] ant = "1.10.17". Ranges such as "1.10" resolve only once the signed tool index carries Ant records. Ant is downloaded from archive.apache.org; Oyzu checks the archive against Apache's SHA-512 sidecar, which comes from the same server as the archive, so no publisher signature is checked, and records the archive's SHA-256 in the lock. For 1.10.18, the release the isolated builds pin, the SHA-256 must also equal the one pinned in Oyzu, both when resolving and when restoring from oyzu.lock; other releases have only the same-server sidecar. The JUnit and JaCoCo reporting libraries described below are not downloaded by the native path. Native builds clear ANT_OPTS and set ANT_ARGS themselves, so JVM options and arguments from your account's environment don't reach Ant; On Linux and macOS, Oyzu's own Ant tasks run ant --noconfig -nouserlib <target>, so the launcher doesn't read ~/.ant/ant.conf or ~/.antrc (it already skips /etc/ant.conf because Oyzu sets ANT_HOME) and jars in ~/.ant/lib stay off Ant's classpath. Windows' ant.bat has no --noconfig, and Ant rejects it, so Windows tasks run ant -nouserlib <target>: ant.bat hands -nouserlib to Ant's Java launcher, which is where ~/.ant/lib is added, but ant.bat still runs antrc_pre.bat and antrc_post.bat from your home folder. An Ant command you write yourself, such as [tasks.test] argv = ["ant", "verify-contract"], reads host configuration and ~/.ant/lib unless you add --noconfig -nouserlib on Linux or macOS, or -nouserlib on Windows. Native execution uses your machine's network and environment, including any effects of Ant's project configuration. Use --isolated when you need container isolation. ivy.xml remains unsupported. A build run outside Oyzu's tool selection, with no ANT_HOME set, still fails with Ant metadata needs ANT_HOME before build actions or artifacts are produced. Run it through oyzu so the locked Ant is used, or set ANT_HOME to your own installation.

On the native host, Ant build, archive and check operations stay unbounded: build.xml, imported build files and custom tasks are programs whose complete reads are not reported. Native tests may read files at run time. The package operation consumes only its archive producer's JARs through an upstream-only contract. No conventional source layout is assumed. Native build, test, archive and quality actions currently run again on unchanged inputs because their output sets are unbounded. Packaging can reuse a result only when the upstream archive workspace is unchanged.

With a compatible Java plugin and the base execution image available, use the existing Linux crun executor: oyzu build --isolated --no-docker --explain oyzu inspect dist Literal Ant build and test commands and the discovered JAR targets run in native order as one coupled build action. Compilation, selected tests, coverage and JAR creation reuse together on an unchanged rebuild. Editing an admitted source file reruns that lifecycle. The package action exports its producer's archives. Compound authored commands keep their separate actions and conservative reads. Separate quality actions retain their incomplete-read refusal and rerun when selected. Retained Ant workspaces and reports use conservative output-location keys. Moving an unchanged project to a different root can rerun the lifecycle. The shared boundary keys the admitted source view, locked JDK, prepared Ant and reporting libraries, command, environment and producer outputs. It hides undeclared host files, denies network access and restricts ambient runtime reads as described in stage reuse. An unsupported read can fail the lifecycle; failed execution is never reused. Reused actions record their original run, identifying the retained test/coverage reports as reused evidence. Required reports and artifacts still pass current validation. Preparation still evaluates the model and admits dependencies on a hit. Offline builds need those inputs already acquired. --no-cache executes with the same isolation and report gates. Native host execution, Docker, Windows and macOS do not gain complete Ant reads; build --explain names the incomplete native-read refusal. Clearing the cache does not supply missing read admission.

oyzu build --isolated --full oyzu inspect dist For literal Ant build and test commands, captured fast mode intentionally runs the selected test target and coverage: oyzu build --isolated includes them without --full, on both Docker and crun. A failing test blocks the JAR. Compilation, tests, coverage and discovered JAR targets run together in the captured build action, followed by package and export actions. Change from 0.3.x: Captured Ant previously planned build, test and archive as separate actions. The coupled lifecycle now matches Maven and Gradle in 0.4.0: fast captured builds run the selected tests, and failing tests block the JAR. To retain separate build, test and archive planning, run oyzu build --full without --isolated on the native host, with the native prerequisites. Plain oyzu build keeps native fast-mode check selection. There is no switch to restore split planning on the captured path. Native host execution runs with your account's file and network access and retains the incomplete-read limits above. If the selected literal test target is absent from the evaluated Ant project, the captured lifecycle builds and packages the JAR without tests or test reports. Set [checks] tests = "off" in oyzu.toml to omit the test target and coverage even when the project defines it. Tests and coverage marked required still need their reports; a project without tests cannot satisfy those requirements. You need Docker or Linux crun and the base execution image. Oyzu pulls the image when it's missing. Ant 1.10.18, JUnit 4.13.2, Hamcrest 1.3, JaCoCo 0.8.13 and the Java quality tools are pinned upstream files. Preparation fetches them, checks them and restores them read-only at /scratch/java-integration, so there is nothing to build or install yourself for this mode. --isolated selects captured execution. --full adds separate lint and format checks to the coupled lifecycle and package/export actions. Checks you marked required still run. Plain oyzu build uses the native host's fast defaults. Oyzu chooses the archive targets and JAR paths from what Ant reports for your project. It doesn't assume a layout. Ant projects with ivy.xml are refused, and arbitrary downloads from Ant aren't supported. The bundle contains the versioned JARs and the reports from the checks that ran. A failed check or a missing required report blocks the JARs and keeps the available reports in the failed bundle. A custom task that exits zero without writing its reports counts as incomplete reporting. To make the reports mandatory, add a [checks] section with tests = "required" and coverage = "required" (check levels). See direct reporting for how command success differs from verified results.

The JDK comes from oyzu.lock; the base image has none. It is used to evaluate the project and for every build action. For example: [tools] java = "21" Run oyzu pin, then oyzu build --isolated --full --frozen. The locked archive is restored read-only, and JAVA_HOME and PATH are fixed in the plan. Oyzu's Java integration needs JDK 17 or newer. Offline runs need the archives already captured. A missing or incompatible pin is refused before any action runs.

Builds use version inference over the native version property and your Git history. Core evaluates Ant again with the chosen version and oyzu.version user properties before planning. ANT_ARGS and OYZU_VERSION carry that version into the build and checks. The artifact name, the bundle version and the JAR's Implementation-Version agree. Qualifiers that can't take part in SemVer inference are kept. An exact tag produces a snapshot, not a release.

An Ant project with a conventional test target can run oyzu run test to write native test and coverage reports to a test-only dist/ bundle. It needs no Oyzu configuration. oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist To use a different Ant target, replace the task: [tasks.test] argv = ["ant", "verify-contract"] One literal ant <target> command is instrumented, including the equivalent literal shell form and ant --noconfig -nouserlib <target>, which Oyzu's own tasks use outside Windows (ant -nouserlib <target> on Windows). Compound shell commands and other replacements run unchanged and must write the required JUnit and JaCoCo reports themselves, at the paths in OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT. Extra arguments forwarded to the automatic reporting aren't supported and fail with an error. Target-qualified names and pre and post hooks work as in the common task engine. A failed test skips its success-only post hook. Discovery always provides an implicit test task. Without a test target in build.xml or a replacement, running it fails with Ant's missing-target error. Oyzu doesn't invent a test suite.

Install these before running: a JDK with java and javac, with JAVA_HOME set (or both on PATH); Ant, which oyzu provides from the tool store unless you run Ant yourself with ANT_HOME set to its folder; JaCoCo, with JACOCO_HOME set to a folder containing jacocoant.jar and jacocoagent.jar; your test libraries. JUnit projects need JUnit and Hamcrest in Ant's lib folder. Oyzu compiles its own Java integration into a temporary folder and starts Ant with your platform's classpath separator. It doesn't install tools or download dependencies.

The manifest links JUnit results and JaCoCo coverage for your application. JUnit suites keep individual tests and skipped cases. Forked Java assertion programs produce one case per run. They need fork="true" and failonerror="true". Coverage follows the src folder convention and the javac output that Oyzu observes. Test classes are excluded. Builds without line debug data keep the instruction counters they have instead of inventing line coverage. Other source layouts, alternate task implementations and the JUnit Platform need explicit reports. Direct tests keep your project's version properties, run the target's compile prerequisites, and can update your build output. They don't package snapshots or run lint and format checks. oyzu build --full applies versions, runs the quality checks and collects JARs; add --isolated to run in a container. A missing tool, a compile error, a failed test, a missing or invalid report, or an unmet coverage constraint fails the command. The reports available at that point stay in the failed bundle. Fix the cause and rerun. See direct tests for output handling and provenance. Direct tests run on your machine with your network and environment, so they aren't isolated.

Run oyzu inspect dist after a build or a direct test run to check the bundle. A failed check, or a required report that is missing or invalid, fails the command, and the bundle keeps the reports that exist so you can see what happened.
Captured builds run on Linux only. Other source layouts and test frameworks need explicit reports.
Java quality tasks, direct tests, version inference.

Recognized Ant test targets emit one unit for the complete target through the public plugin protocol. tests.retries reruns that target in a fresh native process, including its prerequisite targets and passing test classes. Class or method selection remains a later milestone. Custom compound task commands retain their existing generic report handling. With Oyzu-managed attempts, the owned AntJUnit adapter disables JUnit halt-on-failure/error so the first target attempt can produce its complete failed set. A target that stops during compilation, setup, another Ant task, or report and coverage production is incomplete and cannot recover through retries. JUnit failures, errors, native class timeouts and forked-JVM crashes remain distinct; native error types and messages are retained. A failed case that disappears on a later target run stays failed even if that run exits zero. Every attempt is kept; a consistently failing target keeps its original failure exit. A recovered target is flaky and cannot be stored as a reusable pass. --no-cache has the same retry and completeness rules. Ant's built-in <retry> task is recognized at execution time. Its hidden native attempts are declared unknown: Oyzu adds no retries and refuses test result storage. Native halt behavior is preserved when such retries are active. Retries implemented inside arbitrary custom tasks or test code cannot be inferred from Ant XML reports and remain a detection limit. Direct oyzu run test retains its native single-target invocation.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/artifact-sets.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A resolved artifact set is a JSON file that lists, for each tool, version and platform, the download URLs, archive facts and verification evidence for a community-recipe tool. oyzu install --artifact-set reads such a file, decides which platforms are usable, writes their entries to oyzu.lock, and downloads and verifies the host artifact. Later installs replay the lock without the set file. Note: Experimental. Flags and error codes may change. Installing from the signed tool index is the normal path; use artifact sets only when you have a set file to install from directly. Supported on Linux x86-64; Windows and macOS are not supported yet. Installed recipe tools are not runnable yet (see Limitations). You can produce a set with oyzu tools resolve followed by oyzu tools evidence. No account is needed, and install and tools info never evaluate recipes themselves. # Check eligibility only: nothing is written or downloaded oyzu install --dry-run --artifact-set terraform.verified.json oyzu:terraform@1.16.5 oyzu --json tools info --artifact-set gh.verified.json aqua:cli/cli@2.102.0 --details # Pin a record by its digests.full, lock its platforms, download and verify the host artifact oyzu install --artifact-set go-task.verified.json --artifact-set-digest sha256:<digests.full> \ oyzu:go-task/task@3.54.0 # Replay from the lock alone (the set file can be gone); --offline reuses the verified cache oyzu install --frozen

Flag Meaning --artifact-set FILE A set file (JSON, format: 1, kind: "artifact-sets"). Repeatable. Accepted by install SPEC and tools info. With --frozen it is checked against the lock. --artifact-set-digest sha256:D Trusts one record by its digests.full. Repeatable. Without it, each file is a local set that you vouch for. --connector-bindings FILE Connector endpoints for routes. --details (tools info) Show every check and route. The spec can be oyzu:<name>@version, oyzu:owner/name@version, aqua:owner/name@version or recipe:owner/name@version. It matches records whose tool.id is aqua:owner/name or recipe:owner/name. The version matches either the upstream form (v1.16.5) or the normalized form (1.16.5). core: records (Oyzu's own providers) can't be installed from a set (LOCK_ID_UNREPRESENTABLE). Sets work in the project scope only; -g and --local aren't supported.

The whole file is rejected, and nothing is written, if: it is over 16 MiB, is malformed JSON or has a duplicate key; format isn't the integer 1 or kind is wrong (SET_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED); it has unknown top-level fields, more than 4096 records, a duplicate record, or records not sorted by tool ID, version and platform (SET_SCHEMA_INVALID). A single record is unusable (other records still count) if it has unknown fields or values, a URL that isn't plain https (no user info, fragment, backslash or dot segments), evidence that doesn't match its URLs, is over 1 MiB, or its recorded digests don't match its content (SET_DIGEST_MISMATCH). A set doesn't vouch for itself. Each record needs an anchor: a --artifact-set-digest pin, or your choice to use a local set.
documents.s: What a set file must look like

documents.t: You get one result per platform. Checks run in this order: Check What it checks Codes tool-admitted tools.allowed CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED set-integrity record is valid, anchored and not expired SET_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED, SET_SCHEMA_INVALID, SET_DIGEST_MISMATCH, SET_UNANCHORED, SET_ANCHOR_EXPIRED, SET_DISAGREEMENT record-status resolved passes; unsupported means unavailable; error means invalid the record's own reason code evidence-floor verification tier and evidence TIER_BELOW_FLOOR, EVIDENCE_BELOW_FLOOR, EVIDENCE_VERIFIER_UNAVAILABLE, EVIDENCE_ORIGIN_NOT_ACCEPTED routes every download and evidence host can be reached through your routes ROUTE_UNROUTABLE, ROUTE_EGRESS_UNROUTABLE lock-representable (install only) the record fits in oyzu.lock LOCK_ID_UNREPRESENTABLE, DIGEST_NOT_SHA256, ARCHIVE_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED, PLATFORM_ABI_UNSUPPORTED Outcomes: Outcome Meaning eligible Usable. denied A rule blocks it; someone can change the rule. unavailable The set says there is no asset for this platform. It is left out of the lock and listed in unavailablePlatforms. Selecting that platform later fails with TOOL_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE. invalid The record can't be used. If set-integrity or record-status fails, later checks show skipped. The exit status is 1 for denied, invalid or an unavailable host platform, and 2 for argument errors. Human output starts with the outcome, then platforms, reasons and a "Denied by" table (rule, scope, reason, fix). --json prints the same result (outcome, results[].checks, denials, routes, code, written). Secrets, query strings and redirect targets are never shown. The minimum tier is verified and there is no evidence minimum. You can't change these yet.

Oyzu uses the lock first, then an anchored set, then a local set. It never falls back to evaluating a recipe. A record that matches a --artifact-set-digest is anchored. Without any digest, every record is local. When you pass digests, only matching records are used. The host platform must match; other unmatched platforms are left out of the lock. Two anchored records for the same registry snapshot with different content fail with SET_DISAGREEMENT, and neither is used. In managed mode, local sets are refused (SET_UNANCHORED; use the catalog instead), and installs from sets are rejected.

Artifact sets and recipe tools use the shared tool acquisition route contract. Administrative tools routes select a connector by exact host or tool family; a family wins over a host, and any configured route makes acquisition closed-world. The caller supplies the connector binding file with --connector-bindings. The shared contract owns destination path/query mapping, duplicate-scope errors, client/server redirects, credential handling and offline behavior. Artifact-set eligibility checks all declared URL and evidence hosts before acquisition; routing does not replace anchoring, tier, evidence or digest checks.

Each accepted record becomes a normal oyzu.lock entry: id is recipe:<owner>/<name>, whether the record said aqua: or recipe:. version is the normalized version; digest and size come from the verified artifact. The entry records the download URL and digest. Direct and mirrored installs produce identical lock entries. Digests must be lowercase sha256:<64 hex>. oyzu install --frozen downloads (or reuses the cached copy of) each locked recipe: tool and checks its size and digest. With --artifact-set, it fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE if an anchored record disagrees with the lock.

Installing downloads and verifies the artifact into the tool store cache, but doesn't extract it, create shims or write [tools]. A recipe tool isn't runnable yet. Signatures and attestations aren't re-checked at install; only the digest is compared. oyzu tools evidence verifies GitHub attestations when the set is produced. No organization catalog source, no update for sets, and no settings for the minimum tier or evidence. Supported on Linux x86-64 only.
Resolving recipes into artifact sets Tool commands Tool index and tool catalog

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/auth.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu auth signs you in to an Oyzu platform account and keeps the session in your operating system's credential store. Remote builds and runs (--remote), oyzu secrets and oyzu release check then use it. Everything else Oyzu does is local and needs no account. Note: Platform sign-in is experimental. It needs a platform that publishes the sign-in endpoints described below; until it does, login reports discovery as unsupported. It hasn't been tested yet against a real identity provider or each operating system's credential store. oyzu config set --global platform.url https://platform.example.com oyzu config set --global platform.account payments oyzu auth login oyzu auth status

Command What it does oyzu auth login Shows a web address and a short code. Approve the code in any browser, on any device. Oyzu then checks that you're an active member of platform.account and stores the session. oyzu auth status Shows the platform, account and local session state: absent, active, refreshing, reauthentication-required or logged-out. Reads local state only; contacts no server. oyzu auth logout Deletes this account's local session, then asks the issuer to revoke it and reports that result separately. oyzu auth conformance Checks the client against a built-in fake issuer on your machine. Needs no account. Exits 1 if any scenario fails.

platform.url and platform.account set in user, machine or administrator configuration. Project and local files can't set them, so a checkout can't choose where your credentials go. For login, a terminal where you can read the code. A credential store: macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or a running Linux Secret Service provider (GNOME Keyring, KWallet). There is no plaintext fallback. Without a store, login stops before asking you to approve anything. A platform that publishes OAuth protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728) naming one issuer that supports the device authorization grant (RFC 8628) for the public client oyzu-cli.

Oyzu reads /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource from platform.url (with the URL's path appended, if it has one). Its resource must equal platform.url, and it must list exactly one authorization server. Oyzu reads the issuer's metadata. The issuer must match, and its device and token endpoints (and revocation endpoint, if any) must use HTTPS on the issuer's own origin, with no credentials, query or fragment. Plain HTTP is accepted only for a loopback host. Redirects aren't followed and no token is sent. Oyzu starts the device grant for oyzu-cli, with no client secret and no scope (it never asks for offline_access). A verification address on a different origin isn't shown. Oyzu polls at the issuer's interval for up to 15 minutes. Oyzu calls GET /api/v1/access-context?account=<platform.account>. The answer must show an active membership of exactly that account; another membership is never used instead. If the account requires stronger sign-in, you get AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED; without a membership, AUTH_NOT_A_MEMBER. In both cases the new sign-in is revoked and nothing is stored. The session is stored only after every step succeeds, so a cancelled, denied, expired or failed login leaves nothing behind. The device code is never shown or logged.

Every command that talks to the platform gets its credential the same way. The rule is fixed, and a failure never falls back to a different identity. Situation Credential platform.authentication.provider is environment OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. Without it: AUTH_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE. platform.authentication.provider is session The stored session. If OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN is also set: AUTH_PROVIDER_CONFLICT. platform.authentication.provider is network No Authorization header. The server identifies the caller through its trusted network. A supplied OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN is ignored. platform.authentication.provider is workload A fresh GitHub Actions OIDC token for every request attempt. A supplied OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN is ignored. Outside Actions: AUTH_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE. platform.authentication.provider is private-key or execution AUTH_PROVIDER_UNSUPPORTED (not available). No provider set, OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN set That token, as given. It's never stored, refreshed or replaced. No provider set, at a terminal (stdin and stderr) The stored session. No provider set, unattended (CI, scripts, agents) AUTH_PROVIDER_REQUIRED. A stored session is never used implicitly. If the platform rejects a token, the command reports *_UNAUTHENTICATED; it doesn't try your stored session instead. The credential is sent only to the origin of platform.url, never to a redirect or any other address.

Setting Values Default Meaning platform.authentication.provider session, environment, network, workload (private-key, execution are reserved) unset Chooses the credential source, as above. Environment variable OYZU_PLATFORM_AUTH_PROVIDER. User, machine or administrator configuration only. OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN holds a credential. It isn't a setting and doesn't belong in a configuration file.

Use network only with a server that authenticates its callers through the network, such as a pool behind a trusted tailnet proxy. platform.url still requires HTTPS or loopback HTTP. The client never adds an identity header. workload requires GITHUB_ACTIONS=true and a job with id-token: write. The client requests a token from ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL, using ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN only at that endpoint. The audience is platform.url with trailing slashes removed, including any path prefix. The endpoint must use HTTPS or loopback HTTP, without user information or a fragment. Redirects are refused. Neither request secrets nor returned tokens are stored; each API attempt, including retries and cancellation, requests anew. See Actions usage. These providers don't create a login session; auth status and auth logout still describe the stored session. They cannot authenticate a separate service host through the catalog administration client. Workload runs require network access to both the Actions token endpoint and the configured pool.

The refresh credential and the cached access token are stored as separate entries in the credential store. A small non-secret file under the user data directory (auth/) records the issuer, subject, state and expiry. On Windows, session-file reads and replacements retry transient access-denied or sharing conflicts for up to 500 ms. Replacements keep the destination present for concurrent readers using Windows POSIX rename semantics; open readers retain their previous record while new opens see the replacement. If the filesystem rejects POSIX rename as unsupported (Windows errors 1, 50 or 87), Oyzu falls back to the standard in-place rename without first removing the destination. Both paths retain the same sharing-conflict retry limit and support long Windows paths. Readers see a complete old or new record. Windows reads also retry a missing file for up to 20 ms from the first missing-file error because a pathname open can race replacement, including POSIX rename. At least one retry is guaranteed even if the first read was delayed or encountered sharing conflicts. A genuinely absent record returns absent after that short retry; Unix reads return absent immediately. Persistent failures retain the underlying operating-system error; permissions are never bypassed. When several commands need to renew at once, only one renews; the others wait and reuse the result. If a renewal answer is lost (timeout, crash, failed store write), the session ends with AUTH_REFRESH_AMBIGUOUS or AUTH_STORE_FAILED and you sign in again. A rejected renewal ends it with AUTH_REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED. An issuer outage or lost network leaves the session as it is. logout wins over a renewal already in progress, which can't bring the session back. Local logout can succeed while remote revocation can't. The result says so with remote: refused, unreachable or not-advertised. Access tokens already issued stay valid until they expire. A separately supplied OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN isn't affected.

Human output leads with the outcome. With --json, each command prints one record (auth-login, auth-status, auth-logout or auth-conformance) with session facts only. The login address and code go to standard error, and only when it's a terminal, so JSON on standard output stays clean. Without a terminal, login fails with AUTH_INTERACTION_REQUIRED before contacting anything.

Failures exit 1. If a session can't be renewed, run oyzu auth login again. Code Cause Fix AUTH_NOT_CONFIGURED platform.url or platform.account is missing. Set them with oyzu config set --global. AUTH_INTERACTION_REQUIRED login isn't running at a terminal. Run it in a terminal. AUTH_STORE_UNAVAILABLE, AUTH_STORE_FAILED The credential store is missing, locked or failed. Start or unlock the store. AUTH_DISCOVERY_UNSUPPORTED, AUTH_DISCOVERY_UNAVAILABLE, AUTH_DISCOVERY_INVALID, AUTH_DISCOVERY_AMBIGUOUS The platform's sign-in metadata is missing, unreachable, invalid or lists more than one issuer. Check platform.url; ask your platform administrator. AUTH_ISSUER_MISMATCH, AUTH_ISSUER_UNTRUSTED, AUTH_ISSUER_CHANGED, AUTH_REDIRECT_REFUSED, AUTH_GRANT_UNSUPPORTED, AUTH_DEVICE_UNTRUSTED The issuer's metadata or endpoints failed a safety check. Ask your platform administrator. AUTH_DEVICE_EXPIRED, AUTH_LOGIN_DENIED, AUTH_LOGIN_CANCELLED The code expired, was denied or you cancelled. Run oyzu auth login again. AUTH_NOT_A_MEMBER, AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED You aren't an active member of the account, or it needs stronger sign-in. Check the account, or complete the stronger sign-in. AUTH_CONTEXT_UNAVAILABLE, AUTH_ISSUER_UNREACHABLE The platform or issuer couldn't be reached. Retry later. AUTH_LOGIN_REQUIRED, AUTH_REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED, AUTH_REFRESH_AMBIGUOUS No usable session. Run oyzu auth login. AUTH_DESTINATION_MISMATCH, AUTH_AUDIENCE_UNSUPPORTED A credential would have gone to the wrong place. Check platform.url. AUTH_PROVIDER_* See which credential a command uses. Set the provider or token. AUTH_WORKLOAD_ENDPOINT_INVALID Unsafe Actions token endpoint. Use the endpoint supplied by GitHub Actions over HTTPS. AUTH_WORKLOAD_UNAVAILABLE, AUTH_WORKLOAD_REJECTED, AUTH_WORKLOAD_RESPONSE_INVALID Actions token request failed, was refused or returned an invalid response. Check id-token: write and endpoint connectivity; no other credential is tried.

Tokens, device codes and refresh credentials never appear in output, logs, configuration, command arguments, error text or the metadata file. There is no plaintext credential file. Coding agents and unattended jobs don't inherit your session. Don't give an agent your OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN: a copied token still identifies you.

Supported credential stores are macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager and the Linux Secret Service, but none has been tested with real sign-ins yet. Workload identity supports GitHub Actions only. The private-key and execution providers, browser-redirect (PKCE) login and a background agent aren't available. To switch accounts, change platform.account and run login again.
Remote runs Secrets Checking whether a build would ship

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/build-bundles.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Every oyzu build writes its results to a bundle, in dist/ by default. The bundle holds the manifest, the plan, the execution record, logs, reports and the artifacts themselves. Use oyzu inspect to check a bundle and oyzu history to look up earlier builds. oyzu build oyzu inspect # check this project's bundle oyzu history # recent builds A failed build still writes a bundle. Read manifest.json for what actually happened. A target's artifacts are delivered only when its required actions and report gates succeed. If a later required check or hook fails, Oyzu removes that target's collected artifacts from the bundle and manifest, while retaining its logs and reports. Successful independent targets keep their artifacts; advisory check failures alone do not withhold them. Test evidence distinguishes the native command's exit status from report acceptance. A command that exits zero without its required test or coverage reports is recorded as passed at the command level, with missing reports and rejected acceptance; the task and build still fail.

Build and test evidence readers tolerate inert descriptive additions. They still check required outcomes, source and artifact subjects, report obligations and digest relationships. oyzu inspect hashes the original retained files; removing an unfamiliar field from a digest-covered record changes its identity. A newer min_oyzu_version produces the shared compatibility notice when the content is understood. Rewriting a newer-marked record must retain unknown data and its higher marker, or fail with FILE_READER_TOO_OLD before replacing it. Keep the bundle and update Oyzu when a required feature is unsupported. Published 0.3.8 still refuses higher markers; baseline-compatible writers omit the marker when no newer semantics are required. See file compatibility. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

If your project already uses dist/ for its own files, put the Oyzu bundle somewhere else in the root oyzu.toml: [build] bundleDirectory = ".oyzu/bundle" Setting Values Default Where build.bundleDirectory dist, .oyzu/bundle dist Root oyzu.toml only (including root context and profile sections, and policy). Component, local and per-folder values are refused. Other paths aren't supported, and Oyzu doesn't pick a destination for you. The destination doesn't change artifact names or identities. Artifact paths in the manifest are relative to the bundle. .oyzu/bundle is never treated as source. If a build reads your own dist/, declare it with inputs: [dist] in that build's build.yaml entry. Being tracked in Git isn't enough. oyzu inspect (with no argument), history, scan, publish and local image loading all use the chosen destination. They never fall back to an old dist/. oyzu inspect <path> with an explicit path reads that bundle directly, without opening project configuration. Connected publishing (oyzu publish --server ...) and oyzu release check read dist/manifest.json by default. Pass --manifest .oyzu/bundle/manifest.json if you moved the bundle. The manifest records the destination in extensions["oyzu.dev/bundle-directory"]. To inspect a bundle you moved by hand, pass its path.

Each target's artifacts and reports go under <bundle>/<target>/<platform>/: dist/ manifest.json plan.json envelope.json logs/ cli/windows/x86_64/oyzu.exe cli/windows/x86_64/oyzu-shim.exe cli/windows/x86_64/reports/junit.xml docs/windows/x86_64/application-0.1.0/ The layout is the same for host, isolated, multi-platform and CI builds, so bundles from different platforms merge without collisions. For a named build, the target folder is its declared build name, such as cli, rather than an internal platform-expanded execution ID. Rust binary artifacts retain their native executable names (oyzu and oyzu-shim on Linux; .exe on Windows) in both host and isolated builds. Package archives retain their builder-declared, versioned names. Named files from authored tasks join builder artifacts in the manifest with their own producer, media type, digest and size. They use their producing target's folder, including when an individual file declares platform-independent compatibility.

The platform folder is os/arch, such as linux/x86_64, windows/x86_64 or darwin/x86_64. An ABI is added to the architecture only when you declared or requested one that isn't the OS default: --platform linux/x86_64/musl writes linux/x86_64-musl/, while linux/x86_64/gnu writes linux/x86_64/. A platform-independent target uses any. Build Platform folder Native host build The host, such as windows/x86_64. Isolated build The platform of the execution image the action runs on (such as linux/x86_64), or the target's single declared platform. Docker image target under a native build The worker's platform. Output a builder declares platform-independent any. No current builder does this for a whole target yet. OCI image index any, since it covers several platforms. Node applications, including static dist/ and Vite sites, are kept per platform. The folder follows the platform you declared or requested, not the ABI the toolchain picked. If a target declares linux/x86_64 and is cross-built to musl, it lands in linux/x86_64/ even though the asset is -musl. Declare the ABI (linux/x86_64/musl) to keep GNU and musl builds apart.

Each target's path names its declared build folder relative to the project root. Its optional contextRoot names the native source context relative to that same root; when omitted, consumers use path. For example, a Go command at cmd/api can use contextRoot: "." for its enclosing module. Both fields follow the record's existing relative-path constraints. This context belongs to the target, rather than to individual artifact intents. Build and task evidence bundles use the same target fields. The manifest and plan record each artifact's path relative to the bundle (for example cli/windows/x86_64/oyzu.exe). oyzu inspect, oyzu publish and the action cache read that path; they never assume a layout. reports is reserved for a target's reports. No artifact can be named reports. Builder-internal files, such as Docker's container/image.tar, also live in the platform folder. Vite's vite-state.json stays in dist/<target>/.
documents.s: Paths in the manifest and plan

documents.t: An action record in manifest.json can include observedReads, an array of strings containing its reported source read paths. The field is optional and is omitted when the action did not report an observation. Consumers must accept records with or without it.

Each artifact records profile: development or optimized, the profile its build actually used. It's shown on its Outputs row. Which profile a target uses depends on where its output goes, build.optimized and --optimized / --no-optimized; see optimized builds. optimized is recorded only where the profile changes the output: Rust binaries (cargo build --release) and .NET packages (--configuration Release). Rust .crate archives and other builders' output stay development. Output from a custom task that replaces the builder's command is development.

Each target records the platform it was built for (os/arch[/abi]), including the ABI when the OS has several, for example "linux/x86_64/musl" (recorded for Rust today). Canonical platform identities in plans, manifests, dependencies, cache records and execution envelopes use JSON strings, with x86_64 and arm64 architecture names. Native OCI descriptors and plugin execution descriptors retain their separate structured contracts. The unreleased v1alpha1 contract accepts only this string form. Rebuild older bundles and engine packages that recorded canonical platforms as objects; an old object is a decoding error, rather than a second supported representation. extensions["oyzu.dev/platforms"] records how the target was built: Field Meaning target The logical target all platform variants share. declared The platforms the target declares. declaredExecutors The executors declared. platform, executor What this record was built for and with: {"kind":"host"}, {"kind":"cross-toolchain","toolchain":"rust-lld","target":"x86_64-unknown-linux-musl"} or {"kind":"container"}. rows One entry per declared or requested platform with selected, executor or reason, and the runner that builds it. oyzu publish uses declared to refuse an incomplete platform set. See platforms and executors.

When Oyzu collects a native executable (Rust and Go binaries), it checks the file without running it, so cross-built binaries are checked too. It must be a valid ELF, Mach-O (including the matching slice of a universal binary) or PE file for the target platform and architecture, and must not be empty or truncated. The record gets extensions["oyzu.dev/executable"] with platform and, once checked, verified.format (elf, mach-o, pe) and verified.architecture. A failure stops the build with EXECUTABLE_INVALID: artifact <id> is not a valid <platform> executable: <cause>. Known architectures: x86_64, arm64, 386, arm, riscv64, ppc64le, s390x. A plugin's executable flag only places a file in .oyzu/bin; it isn't checked.

In an isolated build, explicitly selecting a producer without declared platforms together with a consumer that materializes it for a declared platform can retain two producer instances for the same platform. If their artifact paths coincide, collection refuses the second file instead of overwriting it. Select the consumer alone to build its producer dependency once. A Python wheel that turns out to be py3-none-any still stays in the platform folder. oyzu run <target>:test puts reports under the host platform.

oyzu history oyzu history <invocation-id> oyzu history <run-id> --json oyzu inspect <bundle-directory> --json oyzu history reads the current bundle and earlier ones kept under .oyzu/history/. It doesn't load project configuration, so old builds stay readable even if your configuration is broken or the bundle moved. It doesn't install, use the network, run anything or hash artifacts. Look up a build by the invocation ID or run ID from its summary. Old bundles without an invocation ID can be found by run ID. An invalid ID fails with INVOCATION_ID_INVALID; an unknown one with INVOCATION_NOT_FOUND.

A listing shows up to 20 builds, newest first, with counts of what was left out and up to 8 notices about incomplete bundles. A summary of one build shows: action counts, test totals (fresh, reused, unknown origin), warnings, and up to 8 failed or unusual actions and 8 diagnostics, with short excerpts; up to 8 recorded action decisions (why each ran or was reused), the selection, and cache status; unavailable cache tiers (cacheLimitations) and selection fallbacks (selectionFallback); paths to the full records. Lists are capped at 8 entries, with a *Omitted count beside each. The full manifest has everything. oyzu build --explain shows the same summary.
documents.s: What a listing and a summary contain

documents.t: Native log bodies and environments aren't included. Open the returned paths for the full records. A summary isn't artifact verification. Use oyzu inspect for that. Later source or configuration changes, or oyzu cache clear, don't rewrite a past build's recorded decisions. Older records without file-comparison detail say it's unavailable.

checks shows which checks each target ran, from the build's recorded oyzu.dev/build-checks facts. Up to 8 targets are listed; totals count all of them. Each target's tests is selected, not-requested or unknown. Missing or malformed records stay unknown; current configuration never fills the gap. checks.status is recorded when every target has a record, partial for a mix, and unknown when none do. unknownTargets gives the count.

Totals are split into fresh, reused and unknown origin. Each also counts zeroTestReports: reports that say they ran 0 tests. If passed, failed or skipped is missing, that total is null (shown as unavailable). Zero tests, skipped tests, missing required reports and missing records are always reported separately.

When a policy constraint changed a target's setting, the plan and manifest record extensions["oyzu.dev/policy-overrides"], one entry per override: setting and the effective value; constraint: source, kind (lock, minimum, maximum or required), bound, selector, and label (org policy, admin policy or project constraint); replaced: the value, source and scope it replaced; a human note. See policy constraints and selectors and project constraints. In a release build, when a nearer folder lowered a check below a farther [context.release] value, the target records extensions["oyzu.dev/release-lowerings"]: the setting, the value used and its source (such as app/oyzu.toml:2), and the releaseValue and its releaseSource (such as oyzu.toml:5). See per-context values.

History is local. Nothing is uploaded or shared. Nothing expires automatically and there's no delete command. Remove old bundles yourself when you no longer need them. A command that stops before the bundle is created leaves no history entry. Crashes, write failures and full disks can leave partial or missing records. Remote runs don't appear in history. Use the platform's run link.

oyzu inspect checks a bundle against its own records. It confirms the files match what was recorded; it doesn't prove who produced them. To check a downloaded artifact against signed GitHub provenance, see release provenance verification. Manifest and plan readers retain optional descriptive additions as JSON data. These additions grant no execution, replay or publication authority. Plan annotations remain inside the plan's semantic digest, so changing them after the manifest binds that digest fails inspection. Paths, artifact membership, file sizes, content digests and cross-record identities are still checked. Rewriting a newer-marked manifest or plan must retain unknown fields, including fields nested in arrays, or refuse with FILE_READER_TOO_OLD before replacement. Frozen publication plans are security-strict throughout: unknown fields in artifact compatibility (including kind: independent), coordinates, signing requirements or effects refuse before publication. Descriptive tolerance in a build bundle does not open those records.

Published executables keep their historical behavior. Writers omit the marker for baseline content; adding an inert annotation alone does not raise it. Input / operation Released 0.3.8 Current reader Candidate-written manifest and plan with an optional display field, bound by the matching plan digest Reads successfully Reads successfully Unchanged JSON manifest emitted by released oyzu --json inspect Reads successfully Reads successfully Manifest or plan carrying a marker newer than 0.3.8 Refuses with FILE_READER_TOO_OLD Reads understood content with one FILE_READER_NEWER notice Plan annotation changed after its digest was recorded Refuses Refuses Artifact digest tampered or artifact path escaping the bundle Refuses Refuses Newer-marked record rewritten without its unknown fields No preservation guarantee Refuses before replacement The same release supports ordinary optional oyzu.toml settings but refuses unknown lock fields and higher markers in oyzu.lock. Even an explicit 0.3.8 configuration marker is too new for that release's hidden development suffix. See configuration compatibility and tool locks. Plan and manifest agree. Target records and artifact identities must match the plan. Named authored-file availability is completed from collected artifacts and action outcomes using the same rules as the build; targets without such declarations stay unchanged. Relabeling a variant or inventing an availability status or reason in the manifest alone fails. Generated versions. A target whose version was set by declared hooks must match its recorded post-hook plan; only the declared version fields may differ. Successful bundles are complete. Every planned artifact, required action and required report must be there. Reports are re-parsed and checked against the plan's rules (including coverage), rather than trusting stored summaries. OCI images. The image's OS and architecture must match the target. See Docker target selection. Plugins. See plugin provenance. Reports for runtime variants are tied to their own target records; see runtime matrices. Preserved native output. Unclaimed host files keep their recorded bytes and, on Unix, ordinary permission bits, including restrictive file modes. A later change to either fails inspection. See existing application output.

A build holds an OS file lock on .oyzu/build.lock until it finishes. A second build in the same workspace fails before running anything. The lock file existing on disk doesn't mean a build is running; the lock is released when the process exits. Staging happens in .oyzu/bundle-* on the same filesystem as the destination. An isolated build only replaces an existing destination that contains an Oyzu manifest. Any other existing folder, even an empty one, is refused. Oyzu never deletes files it doesn't own. Use .oyzu/bundle if your project writes its own dist/. With .oyzu/bundle, native builds and direct tests also require Oyzu ownership. Your native dist/ stays where it is and isn't copied into the bundle. Symlinks (including broken ones) and Windows reparse points are refused for the lock, state, bundle and history paths.
