Just before replacing the bundle, Oyzu checks that the destination hasn't changed since the build started. A new destination, changed manifest or existing history slot stops it rather than overwrite anything.

When a build finishes, the previous bundle moves to .oyzu/history/<new-run-id> and the staged one becomes current. Nothing is appended to the old manifest. This step is local and never uses the network. Paths inside the current bundle have that bundle's lifetime. If automation needs a built executable after another build, retain its platform directory outside the bundle first. The repository's candidate-build action copies the CLI and its sibling files to a unique directory under the runner's temporary directory before exporting OYZU_CANDIDATE; a later quality-tools build can then replace dist/ without removing the executable used by subsequent commands. If the second step fails, Oyzu tries to put the previous bundle back. If that fails too, the error names the history folder holding it. oyzu build --plan is a read-only preview and never replaces the bundle.

The previous bundle's artifacts move to history even when the new build fails. They aren't copied back into dist/, which would block a later retry. Unrelated native files are kept. .oyzu/bin stays at the last successful build. If an older bundle recorded old binaries as unclaimed output, move that bundle aside before rebuilding. A matching file name alone doesn't allow replacing them.

The new staging folder is kept and its path is in the error. If its records are complete, inspect it directly: oyzu inspect .oyzu/bundle-EXAMPLE Use the path from the error message. Keep the conflicting destination and fix the filesystem problem before rebuilding. A kept staging folder is never treated as a successful build or reused. Abandoned staging folders are cleaned up normally.

When a build uses an external builder (see plugin packages), the plan, execution record and manifest each carry extensions["oyzu.dev/plugins"]: one entry per plugin with its source (package or local-development), identity and executableDigest. oyzu inspect fails with plugin records differ from plan or ... from envelope if the manifest's or execution record's copy is missing or edited.

Note: Slice handoff is experimental and is mainly used by platform pools. oyzu build --slice --handoff oci://host/path builds only the named targets and, on success, uploads the complete bundle (plan, execution record, logs, artifacts and reports) to the OCI repository before writing it locally. Ordinary builds never need a registry. Part Value Repository and tag <handoff>/v1alpha1/<first two manifest-digest hex>:bundle-<64 hex> Artifact type application/vnd.oyzu.build-bundle.v1alpha1 Config The manifest.json bytes, application/vnd.oyzu.build-manifest.v1alpha1+json. Its SHA-256 is the tag. Layer One application/vnd.oyzu.build-bundle.v1alpha1.tar+zstd archive with the other bundle files Annotations dev.oyzu.build.manifest (config digest), dev.oyzu.bundle.uncompressed-digest (raw tar digest) The archive is reproducible: sorted paths, zero owner and timestamps, and folders 0755. On Unix, regular files retain their observed ordinary permission bits (0000–0777), including restrictive modes such as 0600, so restored directory artifacts agree with their recorded inventory and digest. Capture on non-Unix hosts uses 0644 or 0755 without inventing Unix permission facts. Links are refused; ownership, ACLs, special bits and directory permissions are not retained. The config plus layer, and the unpacked tar, are each limited to 256 MiB. Your normal registry credentials and proxy settings are used. Uploading the same bundle again is harmless; a different bundle at the same tag fails. The plan records each target's oyzu.dev/execution (needsDaemon, executionPlatform) and oyzu.dev/slice (transferable, repeatable, reason, detail) facts. transferable doesn't mean a cache hit. If the upload still fails after retries, the build ends with HANDOFF_PUSH_FAILED and exit status 5. The actions' real outcomes are kept, along with the exact upload bytes, so the upload can be retried without rebuilding.

Replacing the bundle is two renames, not a crash-safe transaction. If the process or machine stops in between, there's no automatic recovery; the error or history folder tells you where the previous bundle is. The path checks and lock protect against other Oyzu commands, not against a hostile process that can replace folders. Bundles aren't stored remotely, and there are no automatic retention limits.

Direct Node, Python and Go tests use the same process. With the default dist destination, a test run can copy your existing native dist/ output into the new test bundle and keep the original in history. Those copies are listed separately and aren't build artifacts. With .oyzu/bundle, your native dist/ is left alone. Earlier reports in the current bundle move to history.
Local builds and build tasks for what fills the bundle. Action cache for reuse recorded in the manifest. Publishing for what uses a finished bundle.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/build-logging.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build shows its work as it happens: preparation steps, parallel targets, commands, live output and a final receipt. It also saves complete logs and an event journal in the bundle. How output is shown never changes what is built or which checks run. oyzu build oyzu build api web worker oyzu build --output plain oyzu build --output interactive oyzu build --plan oyzu build --json > result.json 2> events.jsonl For the section-by-section layout of the default view (Prepare, Builders, Scope, Plan, Build, Failure, Outputs, Warnings, summary), see build transcript. This page covers the output modes, the interactive dashboard, CI output, saved logs and interruption.

A build-failing action stops further work by default. The first failure leads the human receipt; only real failures appear in its Failure sections. Stopped work is summarized once, for example Stopped 3 actions after cli:lint failed. An advisory check failure remains a warning. Use oyzu build --keep-going for a full failure sweep; only dependents are then blocked. The same behavior is selected per target with build.failFast = false; --fail-fast forces the stop policy. See configuration and precedence. Each target's existing extensions["oyzu.dev/build-checks"] includes failFast: {value, source} in both the plan and build record. Execution uses that frozen value, including platform splits. The manifest and --json use the same records: Action state Status Reason Not admitted before the stop not-started Stopped after <action id> failed Terminated while running cancelled The same reason The build-failing action failed Its actual failure The build stays failed, with the first failure's exit code. The manifest's extensions.oyzu.dev/fail-fast records that action and exitCode, independently of plan order. Stopped actions' outputs are not collected or cached. Successful actions retain their normal cache commits. A real user interrupt still produces interrupted and its existing Ctrl-C behavior. An in-flight action that finishes on its own keeps its actual success or failure, even after another action requests a stop. An automatic build stop allows cleanup, report collection and build-record writes to finish; it does not start the user cancellation grace period.

Option Behavior --output auto (default) Compact linear view: named preparation steps, one row per action and one final receipt. --output plain The same linear view. Never uses an alternate screen, fixed panes, key input or full-screen redraws. --output interactive The full-screen dashboard. Needs a terminal on stdin and stderr. Works in CI too. --json Stdout holds the final manifest or plan JSON; stderr holds JSON-line events only. Takes precedence over --output. -q Quiet output. Takes precedence over --output. On a capable terminal, each active step shows a header and its last eight output lines. Routine successes collapse; slow steps and problems stay in scrollback. Redirected output is append-only, never redrawn. Color is separate from interactivity: ui.color = auto | always | never. A nonempty NO_COLOR wins, and CLICOLOR_FORCE can color a pipe without turning on redraws. GitHub Actions gets the same linear view, wrapped in collapsible groups.

--output interactive opens a dashboard that stays in place while the build runs. The header shows the project, elapsed time, phases (Prepare, Build, Collect) and the selected platforms with readable OS and architecture names. During preparation it shows how many tools are verified or pending, and up to two pending tools. Finished setup collapses when the build starts. Each row shows its current operation, elapsed time and, for active rows, how long the output has been quiet. One live pane shows the selected step's last seven output lines. New parallel work doesn't steal focus from the step you're watching. Warnings and failures stay pinned above the pane. Reused actions show Reused · not executed now. After a process exits, a step may show Checking outputs until its reports and artifacts pass validation; a clean exit alone isn't success. Blocked tasks show which prerequisite they're waiting for. Resizing recalculates the layout; very small terminals show a resize hint. Long lines are clipped, and you can pan to see them. Scrollback is kept in a temporary file on disk, deleted when the view closes. The saved build logs are the permanent record. When the build ends (or fails), your previous screen is restored and the permanent receipt is printed. Key Action Up / Down Select the previous or next step. Enter Expand or collapse the live output pane. a Follow active work automatically. p Show or hide preparation details, requested versions and the selected work's stages and outputs (up to eight setup rows; see oyzu build --plan --json for the rest). d / l Show or hide the full combined log. Escape Return to the compact live pane. Page Up / Page Down Scroll the log. Left / Right Pan long lines. f / End Follow new output again. n Select the next failed task. Failures only raise a notice; they never move your selection. q Close the dashboard and continue the build with plain output. Doesn't cancel anything. Ctrl+C Restore the terminal and interrupt the build. The dashboard never needs input to finish.

When output is redirected, or the build runs in a detected CI system, the view is append-only: Each action prints a start line (00:12 .. api build started) and an end line with its outcome and duration, both led by the elapsed time since the build began. In builds with more than twelve actions, only end lines and the final tally are printed. Every ten seconds a heartbeat line names what's still running: 00:31 still running: api build 10s · auth-lib test 12s · 6 waiting (up to three actions, then + N more). A heartbeat shows the build is alive, not that a tool is making progress. Output is laid out at 100 columns on every host. Terminal width comes from the console, so COLUMNS doesn't change it. Without color, marks are padded words (ok, reused, warn, FAIL) and rules use dashes. Terminal controls in every value are escaped. Redirected files never contain cursor movement. Recognized CI systems: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Buildkite, Jenkins and TeamCity, with a generic CI fallback. Detection only affects presentation (and the build context); it never grants any permission. GitHub Actions. Preparation, dependency and planning phases are wrapped in collapsible groups, closed before actions run. When GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY is set, Oyzu appends an HTML-escaped receipt to it; if that write fails you get a warning and the build result doesn't change. In JSON mode, no group commands are printed. Oyzu doesn't upload artifacts or add source annotations. The sectioned view described in build transcript applies to local oyzu build runs. --plan, --check, remote runs, oyzu run, oyzu scan and the dashboard use their own layouts.

The heading names the project, the host or platform selection, the execution mode and the requested checks. Which targets were selected, and why, is in the Scope section; stage status is in the plan table. Preparation runs as named steps: configuration, tools, dependencies, output bundle, compiler cache, source snapshot, CLI identity and report setup. › running, ✓ done, ✗ stopped by an error. A step that's still running when an error stops the build is shown as stopped, not done. Fast successful steps collapse. Steps that take ten seconds or more, and failures, stay visible. A slow step that succeeds is still a success. Tool installation shows the requested version. A reused tool collapses to one Ready line; a real download stays visible. Host prerequisites say they're checked during compilation. Optional tools that aren't used aren't listed. Each running subprocess (formatting, linting, tests, compilation, hooks, tool installation) gets a short preview under its row, showing its latest eight lines in dim text. Each parallel task has its own preview. The preview area is limited by the terminal height and says when activity is hidden. On success, the preview collapses into the totals. On failure, the first useful eight lines of error context are kept (or the last eight lines if no error marker is found), with the exit code. The receipt names the saved log. -v shows the full captured output, including successful preparation.

A finished step shows a mark, a name, a short result and its duration. Durations read <0.1s, 5.9s, 149s and 10m 06s. ✓ Source captured 2781 files · sha256:668b3844b9d7 13.0s ✓ Rust compiler 1.95.0 · reused the packaged copy from an earlier build 0.8s ✓ Compiler in container restored into a read-only volume 19.5s ✓ Cargo crates 371 locked · all from the cache 5.6s ✓ Project metadata 8 container runs · slowest `cargo metadata` 9.0s 25.0s ✓ Build inputs ready compiler, crates and project metadata 60.8s On a terminal, a running step shows in the live pane (› name detail). Redirected output prints a step when it finishes, with heartbeats while it's slow. With several targets, each step names its target (Cargo crates · cli · linux/x86_64). While Cargo compiles, individual Compiling lines aren't printed. The running status shows the count and latest crate (Running · 60s elapsed · 271 crates compiled · latest oxc_ast_visit), and the finished line shows the total (Succeeded · 276 crates compiled). Warnings and errors still print in full. -v prints every crate. With -v, a finished build also shows where the time went (Preflight 71s · Build 174s · Collect 4s). After the last action finishes, Collect does its own work: it saves the private source copies for the next build (Source workspaces), records results and verification evidence (Build records), and writes the local bundle (Output bundle). Each is a step like the ones above. It shows in the live pane while it runs, a redirected run prints › Source workspaces saving private copies for the next build · 10s every ten seconds while it is slow, and a finished step appears only if it took ten seconds or more, failed or warned. Generated platform IDs such as cli-platform-windows_x86_64-157f0d1f6adb are shown as cli · windows/x86_64. The event journal has the same steps and durations (Step events with duration_ms).

An isolated (container) build prepares these steps for each target: Step What it does Rust compiler Unpacks the locked Rust installation once per build and packages it for the container. The package is cached under cache/rust-packaged in the Oyzu user data directory. Compiler in container Restores the package into a read-only Docker volume named oyzu-tools-<hash> (the hash covers the worker image, compiler archive and format). The volume is kept between builds, so a repeat build reuses it in under a second instead of about 20 seconds. Cargo crates Captures every crate in Cargo.lock into an offline registry for the container, which has no network. Archives are checked against the lock's checksums and cached under cache/cargo-crates; registry index entries are cached for seven days. Project metadata A few short container runs (cargo metadata, rustc -vV, lock file generation). Shown as one step naming the slowest run; -v lists them all. Source snapshot, Dependency snapshot Private, hashed copies the offline build uses. Version The version stamped into the artifacts. About the compiler volumes: A companion volume, oyzu-tools-<hash>-ok, marks a finished restore. A volume without it is rebuilt. A lock file under cache/ in the user data directory stops concurrent builds from restoring the same volume twice. Each new compiler or worker image adds a volume of about a gigabyte. After each build, Oyzu removes older oyzu-tools-* pairs, keeping the current one and the three most recent others. Volumes in use by a running container are skipped and retried next time. Other Docker storage is limited by the Docker storage budget. A native (non-isolated) build shows Source workspaces (a private copy of the sources) and one step per executor prerequisite (a small compile-and-link check of the linker). The › Tools determining… line is a placeholder while this runs.

Native output is shown as it arrives. Oyzu can't show output a tool hasn't written yet, and Cargo can be quiet for a long time while compiling or linking. Silent tasks show elapsed time every ten seconds. Each excerpt names its task once and keeps the tool's own indentation and carets. Color codes from tools are removed in the human view; other terminal controls are escaped. The saved logs keep the original output. Parallel tasks never interleave within a line. Lines from one stream stay in order; the order between different tasks or between stdout and stderr isn't a strict cause-and-effect order. Cargo JSON is shown as short compiled-target and status lines. go test -json shows native output and failed test names instead of JSON. A single record over 1 MiB isn't shown; read the saved log instead. Native warnings appear once, in the receipt's Warnings section, and as NATIVE_WARNING diagnostics in JSON. Cargo warnings keep their source location, and Cargo's repeated summary line doesn't add another warning. npm and Node warnings are recognized too. Oyzu never decides an action's result from warning or error text. Warning and error excerpts have separate budgets, so warnings can't hide a later failure. Installer messages from rustup go through the same view. Its advice to add a temporary folder to PATH is hidden, because Oyzu activates the installed tools itself; JSON and saved events keep it. Rust doctests stream live; see Rust direct test evidence. The command shown for an action is redacted for display. It isn't a portable shell script.

The receipt is the summary at the end of a build. See receipts and history for what it counts. A build that fails during preparation says Build failed during preparation and No build actions started, and keeps the count of selected targets. Fresh tests and reused test results are counted separately. Reused results name where they came from and never count as tests run now. Missing reports never mean zero failures or 100% coverage. Coverage isn't averaged across unrelated measures. Receipt sections show up to eight entries and say how many were left out. -v adds the manifest and report paths. An empty result says No artifacts produced. Error and recovery paragraphs wrap at word boundaries (100 columns if the terminal width is unknown).

Every build saves these files in its bundle (dist/ by default): Path Contents logs/events.jsonl The event journal, including preparation output. logs/<target>/… Numbered stdout and stderr files for each action. manifest.json, plan.json The build's result and plan. plans/ Sealed plans for independent branches. If setup fails before the bundle exists, no journal is saved. The terminal, JSON and redirected output still have the error. oyzu run test and other bundled tasks also save their full stdout and stderr, in text and JSON modes. A task marked interactive = true uses your terminal directly, so its log files are empty. See task output. oyzu build --plan creates no bundle; see read-only build preview. See build bundles for how bundles are kept.

Each line of events.jsonl (and each JSON event on stderr) has schemaVersion, sequence, elapsedMs, scope, severity, target, invocationId, operationId, parentOperationId and an event: event Contents diagnostic A warning, error or other message, with code. heading, fact, inventory The build heading, context facts, and the selected targets, platforms, check mode and color preference. preparation, phase, task, progress Lifecycle changes. plan Target IDs and builders, action IDs, dependencies and artifact versions. Never action environments. command The redacted command. output stream, text and continued. finished status, and optional exit_code and duration_ms. Every warning and error is saved, whatever the console showed. Debug and trace messages are saved only when enabled. Environment maps are never included. New event types may be added; ignore ones you don't recognize. The format is experimental and separate from the plan's identity and from release records.

Logging uses no network. Your project's commands can print sensitive values, and Oyzu doesn't try to detect secrets in arbitrary output. Credentials Oyzu uses for downloads are never passed in a command's arguments or environment. A failure to write a log never changes a tool's result.

Builds use the global diagnostic controls. Event Level Routine lifecycle info Command details debug Failed step error Blocked task warn Native stdout and stderr are always saved, whatever the threshold. A line on a tool's stderr isn't an Oyzu error.

The first Ctrl+C (or SIGTERM, or SIGHUP when the terminal closes) asks the build to stop. No new work starts and running container steps are removed. A signal that was already ignored when the build started (such as SIGHUP under nohup) stays ignored. Steps blocked inside a native tool or Docker call can't respond right away, so Oyzu prints a notice ending waiting up to 10s for running steps. Press Ctrl-C again to force exit. The notice goes through the normal log, so it's a JSON line with --json. After an interrupt: Actions that never started are not-started, and the build is interrupted. Native tasks asked to stop by the executor report cancelled when they exit unsuccessfully, including a signal handler or shutdown hook exiting with code 143. A successful exit remains successful. Tasks that finish before a stop is requested keep their actual success or failure. In the dashboard, Ctrl+C restores your terminal first.

A second Ctrl+C, or 10 seconds after the first user interrupt, forces exit: Oyzu removes the containers this build started (named oyzu-* or the build worker names). On Windows it also ends tracked child process trees. All of this shares one five-second deadline; cleanup that doesn't finish in time is abandoned. It names any container or process tree it couldn't remove, then exits with status 130, even if Docker isn't responding. These time limits are fixed. Forced exit is best effort. It can leave containers, processes and partial staging behind, and there may be no failure bundle. Once Docker is responsive again, remove the named leftovers before retrying, and see bundle recovery. Cleanup messages go to stderr even with --json and aren't a JSON result. Limits: On Unix, forced exit doesn't kill native child processes in other process groups. Containers left by an earlier hard kill (for example kill -9) aren't cleaned up.
CLI output for the section layout, JSON and diagnostic controls. Build bundles for inspect and history. Local builds

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/build-tasks.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build runs each selected builder's stages (format, lint, test, build, package), together with your own tasks, prerequisites and hooks, and collects the results into a bundle. Use this page to choose which targets and checks run, to add or replace tasks in oyzu.toml, and to understand how oyzu run tasks behave. Builds show live progress and command output. Add --json to get the final manifest and plan as JSON.

oyzu build # fast local build oyzu build --full # run every check that isn't off oyzu build api web --plan # preview two targets oyzu build --jobs 4 # limit concurrency for this run oyzu run list # list discovered tasks oyzu tasks list # alias for oyzu run list oyzu run test # run a development task oyzu run --isolated test # run just this task in its builder's isolated image Choose which checks run, per context, in oyzu.toml: [checks] format = "off" # never run; rustfmt isn't prepared for it lint = "advisory" # failures are warnings; the build still succeeds [context.release.checks] tests = "required"

A plain local oyzu build is a fast build. It runs the build and package stages and only the checks set to required. Other test, lint and format-check stages are skipped (skip · fast local build in Plan). Every check that isn't off runs in the pr, ci and release build contexts, and with --full, the ci profile or --remote. You change these defaults per context with checks.run, and set each check's level in oyzu.toml (check levels): Level Behavior off Never runs. Plan shows off and where it was turned off. The builder doesn't prepare the check's tools. advisory Runs where checks run. A failure is a CHECK_ADVISORY warning. enforce, required See check levels. Required checks and report validation always apply to stages that run. Test and coverage requirements apply to each target as a whole. The compile step doesn't need to produce coverage when the test step does. A positive checks.coverageMinimum needs a selected step that produces coverage and a valid report that meets the minimum. Missing coverage, a disabled test with no other coverage source, or a replacement task that omits required reports fails the build. oyzu run tasks have their own report rules; see direct test reports. On the native Rust path, --full can reuse an unchanged build while format, lint and test run at the same time, within --jobs. A failed required check still fails the build. See native cache behavior. A native build command may run tests itself. For example, Maven runs tests in verify. Skipping the separate test stage doesn't turn those off.
documents.s: Local fast builds and CI checks

documents.t: A local build that only writes its own dist/ uses each builder's development profile. A build is optimized when its artifacts leave the machine: handed off (--slice), written to a shared remote cache, packaged by another selected target, or published (the release context). A development plugin binding's results are handed off but never written to a remote cache (action cache), so a remote cache alone does not optimize them; a plugin package's results are written like a built-in builder's. --optimized and --no-optimized choose for one run. build.optimized in a folder's oyzu.toml (optionally per context) chooses for the targets under it. Policy wins over both. Optimized Rust runs cargo build --release; optimized .NET uses --configuration Release. Builders where it makes no difference stay development. Plan shows each target's profile and why (profile cli · optimized · --optimized), and Outputs labels each artifact. Optimized and development results never reuse each other from the action cache. For Rust and .NET, a CI build that writes the remote cache (optimized) doesn't serve a local development build; build with --optimized to reuse it. See optimized builds. Platform selection is covered in platforms and executors.

oyzu build oyzu build api oyzu build api web --plan With no arguments, every discovered target builds, except a build that sets default: false in build.yaml. default is an optional boolean (true or false); omitting it selects the build by default. Use that for builds you only want on request, such as release-only packaging: oyzu build <name> builds it, and a selected build that lists it in depends_on or materialize still pulls it in. Arguments are exact target IDs, not task names, globs or paths. Duplicates are ignored. An unknown ID fails before anything is prepared. Use oyzu discover to see target IDs and oyzu run list to see task names. Only the plugins of the selected builds and the builds they need are installed and run; see only the plugins your selected builds need.

The targets you name, plus their depends_on and materialize.from producers, transitively. The owners of prerequisites and hooks reached from those targets' stages. Each added target runs its full set of build, check and package stages, not just the task that was needed. A custom task that no build stage reaches doesn't select its dependencies. Unselected targets get no tools, downloads, actions or artifacts. Concurrency uses the smallest build.jobs among the root configuration and the selected targets. Selection doesn't change which build a task belongs to: an unqualified root hook belongs to every build it reaches, selected or not. Discovery, configuration checks and source capture still cover the whole workspace. Broken metadata in an unrelated project can stop a build of another target.

The plan and manifest record oyzu.dev/selection: requested and selected IDs, the mode (all, explicit or affected), and excluded targets with reason outside-selection. Excluded targets aren't reported as successful. oyzu inspect dist fails if the manifest's selection doesn't match its plan. Runtime toolsets and affected builds also change the selection.

Oyzu reads build.yaml once per run and uses that copy for selection, ordering, platforms and artifact passing. If the file changes between discovery and source capture, the build fails with build.yaml changed between discovery and source capture. Finish the edit and run again. Changes after capture don't affect the running build.

Most projects need no task configuration. Builders supply build, test, lint and read-only format-check tasks. oyzu run list shows them. A format task that rewrites files is for running by hand. It is refused inside a container build. You can replace a builder stage with your own command. The replacement runs instead of the original. It keeps the stage's hooks, required reports and policy, so it must write the required reports to their assigned paths. Oyzu adds native reporting only to commands it recognizes.

A prerequisite uses the normal TOML task syntax: [tasks."api:pre_test"] argv = ["node", "scripts/check-api-inputs.mjs"] depends_on = ["schema:verify"] [tasks."schema:verify"] argv = ["node", "scripts/verify-schema.mjs"] Here api and schema are targets. Each script path is relative to its target's folder. Both tasks need Node available; a custom command doesn't install new tools. schema:verify runs once per build, even if several tasks need it. It runs with schema's folder, tools, configuration, environment and report paths. Its own dependencies and schema:pre_verify / schema:post_verify hooks follow the same rules. api:pre_test waits for the prerequisite and its post-hook before api:test starts. Hooks don't get hooks of their own.

Builder stage order always applies. A stage that already ran as an earlier prerequisite doesn't run again. A target's own prerequisites run in the order listed, after the previous stage. Another target's prerequisites follow that target's order. A cycle between prerequisites, hooks, stages, target dependencies or artifact passing fails before anything runs. Fix the relationship; reordering YAML entries doesn't help. A root workspace task (neither a hook nor a stage) reached through a prerequisite uses that prerequisite's target and tools, but keeps its own working folder. In a build with several targets, a root workspace task needed by more than one target is refused as ambiguous. Qualify it with the target that should run it.

A task key in any oyzu.toml belongs to builds by these rules. They are checked when configuration is read, before anything runs. Key Belongs to Errors [tasks."api:pre_test"] (qualified) Build api only. Wins over an unqualified definition of the same name for api. Unknown build (CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN); file outside api's folder chain (CONFIG_REFERENCE_MISPLACED); a hook of a task api doesn't have (CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN, with the nearest name). [tasks.post_build] (unqualified hook, pre_* or post_*) Every build whose folder chain reads the file and that has the hooked task (package always counts). A root hook reaches every build, including the root's own. At the root it is also the hook of a workspace task with that name. A hook of a task none of those builds has (CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN). [tasks.test] at the root (any name that isn't a hook) A workspace task (oyzu run test), run once at the root. It never replaces a build's stage, even where builds run a stage with that name. — [tasks.test] in a subfolder (unqualified builder stage) Replaces that stage in every build below the folder that runs it. Reaching builds with different builders: CONFIG_TASK_AMBIGUOUS. Qualify it per build. [tasks.lint-docs] in a subfolder (any other name) A task of every build below it. — To replace a stage of a build at the project root, qualify the key with the build's name, such as [tasks."app:test"]; oyzu run list shows the name. Because a root name is always the workspace's own task, oyzu run <name> for a task the root defines only selects the plugins of the builds that task depends on, often none. See only the plugins your selected builds need. A nearer folder's definition, or a qualified key, replaces a farther one for that build. Hooks can be narrowed further with when/unless. Stage replacements take no conditions. A task runs in its build's folder unless cwd says otherwise, relative to the file that declares it. Every depends_on entry must name an existing task, by id (schema:verify) or name (verify). # root oyzu.toml, with builds cli (rust/app), docs (node/app) and the root's own [tasks.post_build] # every build, the root's included argv = ["scripts/attest.sh", "{artifact.path}"] [tasks."docs:test"] # one build's stage: docs only argv = ["npm", "run", "test:ci"] [tasks.lint-docs] # a workspace task: oyzu run lint-docs argv = ["node", "tooling/check-docs.mjs"] Writing that docs:test replacement as [tasks.test] would also reach cli, a Rust build, and is refused: CONFIG_TASK_AMBIGUOUS: oyzu.toml:5:1: [tasks.test] replaces the test stage of builds with different builders: cli (rust/app), docs (node/app); one command cannot replace stages of different builders. Qualify it for each build instead, such as [tasks."cli:test"] In a single-build project, [tasks.test] works as before. Its task id is the build's own (project:test), and oyzu run test still finds it. oyzu config validate checks task keys' build names and placement. Hook targets and depends_on need the discovered tasks, so oyzu build (including --plan), oyzu run and other commands that discover the project check them. See names that cross files.
documents.s: Which build a task belongs to

documents.t: Declare non-executable files to ship in the build's bundle under artifacts on that build in build.yaml. This inventory is the same in every context; the producing command and its conditions stay in oyzu.toml. builds: app: uses: rust/app artifacts: notices: task: app:post_build path: generated/NOTICE.txt mediaType: text/plain schema: task: app:post_package path: generated/schema.json mediaType: application/schema+json platformIndependent: true [tasks."app:post_build"] argv = ["scripts/notices", "generated/NOTICE.txt"] [context.release.tasks."app:post_package"] argv = ["scripts/schema", "generated/schema.json"] Each map key is a unique artifact name of at most 64 ASCII letters, digits, periods, underscores or hyphens. task, path and mediaType are required; platformIndependent defaults to false. task names an authored task or hook of this build, qualified as <build>:<task>. Naming a different build is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE when build.yaml is read, even if that build and task exist. Use the declaring build's name before the colon. The cross-file name is checked against definitions in every context before any action runs; an unknown name is CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN at build.yaml:line:column. oyzu build collects the files when their producing tasks succeed; oyzu run executes development tasks without creating a build bundle. A producer defined only in another context, or excluded by when/unless, does not fail a build. The target's extensions["oyzu.dev/task-output"] in the plan records the declaration and its availability (planned or not-produced, with a reason). The build record finishes each declaration as produced or not-produced, with a reason for absent output. Only collected files enter artifacts. Publication fails if a selected artifact was not produced; an unselected absent artifact does not block publication. Keep destination and provenance selectors in the base configuration rather than copying them per context. path names one regular file relative to the task's working directory. It accepts no globs, placeholders, absolute paths, parent traversal or symlinks. The file must exist when the task succeeds; a missing or unsafe file fails collection. The manifest records its target, platform, producer, media type, digest and size, and the bundle stores it beside the builder's artifacts. Names and bundle paths cannot collide with another task's or a builder's artifact (TASK_ARTIFACT_COLLISION). A per-artifact hook may produce files, but repeated instances cannot claim the same output name. The file retains its target's platform by default. Set platformIndependent = true only for data with the same meaning across platforms, such as a JSON Schema. This also keeps its filename unchanged when publishing to GitHub; platform-bound .txt files gain the platform slug before their extension. outputs continues to declare cache paths; it does not add manifest artifacts. Named artifacts do not make an otherwise uncached task cacheable. A custom task still needs its tools prepared (for example by activating a pinned toolset). These files use the same provenance, signing and publication requirements as builder outputs. They do not authorize extra processes, network or policy access.
documents.s: Named file artifacts from authored tasks

documents.t: A task or hook in oyzu.toml can say when it applies (when, unless) and receive build values through {namespace.name} placeholders. Both are plain data from a fixed vocabulary. Anything that needs logic belongs in the program argv runs. For example, a post_build hook that runs the built binary: [tasks."cli:post_build"] argv = ["{artifact.path}", "--version"] when = { optimized = true, platform = ["linux/x86_64"] } unless = { artifact = ["bin-oyzu-shim"] }

when and unless are tables over these facts. They use the same form as policy constraint selectors. Fact Values Notes context local, pr, ci, release The context the build runs as (--context, OYZU_CONTEXT or detection). provider CI provider names (github-actions, gitlab, …) fork true, false false outside a pull request. Read from GitHub Actions and GitLab; using fork where the provider doesn't report it is an error. target Target names Matches the target's id and, for a platform variant (cli-platform-linux-x86_64), its declared target (cli). An unknown name is an error that lists valid names. platform os/arch[/abi], with the usual aliases A value without an ABI matches every ABI. optimized true, false The target's build profile. artifact Logical artifact names (bin-oyzu, as Outputs and the manifest show them, not file names) Only on post_build and post_package hooks. An unknown name is an error, except for a target with several platforms, where it may be built elsewhere. Every when key must match; a list matches when any value does. One matching unless key excludes the task. A task with neither always applies. Unknown keys, wrong value types, artifact on other tasks, and conditions on a stage replacement fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE when configuration is read. Put conditions on the stage's pre_ or post_ hook instead. A task under [context.release.tasks."cli:post_build"] already applies only in release; it needs no condition. Note: Conditions aren't a security control. A job with only the generic CI variable can lower its context with --context local. Use check levels and policy for checks that must run. Conditions are decided when the build is planned. A task that doesn't apply isn't scheduled, and anything that waited on it keeps its order. Plan shows one task note per conditional task: task pre_build · skip · unless context = local post_build · run for bin-oyzu · unless artifact = bin-oyzu-shim The plan and manifest record each conditional task under oyzu.dev/task-conditions: the conditions as written, run or skip and why, and for each run its action id, artifact and resolved argv. oyzu build --plan shows the same notes and taskConditions records; a per-artifact hook shows once per matching artifact there.

A placeholder is {namespace.name}. It is replaced with plain text inside one argv element at a time, and in the task's own env values. Nothing goes through a shell. Placeholder Value {build.context}, {build.provider}, {build.optimized}, {build.version} The context, comma-separated providers, true/false, and the version this build gives the target. In oyzu run, the version the project declares. Not available in container builds for builders that set versions after hooks, such as Node. {build.root} The build root, relative to the task's working folder. {target.name}, {target.dir}, {target.builder} The task's target. dir is relative to the working folder. {platform.platform}, {platform.os}, {platform.arch}, {platform.abi} The target's platform (abi only when it has one). {artifact.path}, {artifact.name}, {artifact.kind}, {artifact.platform}, {artifact.os}, {artifact.arch} In a post_build/post_package hook, the artifact it runs for. path is the packaged file, relative to the working folder. {env.NAME} A literal value from [env] in oyzu.toml. In argv, only when it doesn't look sensitive. {build.<target>.artifact.<field>} Another target's artifact, only along a declared depends_on or materialize edge. A producer with several artifacts needs materialize.artifact. What counts as a placeholder: Only {word.word…}. Everything else is left as written: {.Dir}, {a,b}, a lone brace. Go and Docker templates such as {{.Id}} or {{json .}} pass through unchanged. To write a literal placeholder, double the braces: {{env.HOME}} gives {env.HOME}. This applies only to the namespaces build, target, platform, artifact, env and tool. Doubled braces in other namespaces are ordinary text, so Jinja, Ansible and GitHub expressions ({{item.name}}, ${{github.sha}}) pass through. A single-brace {item.name} is still PLACEHOLDER_UNKNOWN. There are no functions, defaults or filters, and a substituted value is never expanded again. A run script can't use placeholders, because it goes through a shell. Use argv. Per-artifact hooks. A hook that uses the artifact fact or an {artifact.*} placeholder runs once per matching artifact, as actions such as cli:post_build[bin-oyzu], one after another. post_build runs for the artifacts the build produced; post_package for every artifact packaged into dist/. A target with no package stage (such as a native Rust build) still runs a declared post_package hook, after all its other actions. Before each run, the artifact is copied to .oyzu/artifacts/<target>/<platform>/<file> in the target's private workspace; {artifact.path} points there. A hook with no matching artifact is skipped, with the reason. Every run executes even if an earlier one failed; then any failure fails the build. Oyzu never runs an artifact unless you declare a hook that does. A per-artifact hook can't declare outputs (CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE). Sensitive values. argv is recorded as written in the plan, manifest and command log, while task env values are recorded as [REDACTED]. So an {env.NAME} whose name or value looks sensitive (names containing TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, API_KEY, CREDENTIAL, AUTH and similar, or a value that looks like a credential) is refused in argv with PLACEHOLDER_SENSITIVE. Pass it through the task's env instead (TOKEN = "{env.API_TOKEN}"), or use the tool's own credential mechanism. Path values are relative to the task's working folder, in the platform's path form, and never expose your checkout path. That way the same build resolves the same argv on every machine, and cache keys match. Placeholder errors. Placeholders are resolved when the build is planned. Errors name the task and argv element: Code Cause PLACEHOLDER_UNKNOWN Unknown name. Lists valid names and the nearest one. PLACEHOLDER_UNDECLARED An {env.NAME} not declared in [env] or the environment. PLACEHOLDER_UNAVAILABLE An [env] entry that is a secret reference, path list or table; or a value that doesn't exist where it's used, such as {artifact.path} outside a post_build/post_package hook. PLACEHOLDER_UNREACHABLE Another target's artifact without a declared edge. PLACEHOLDER_SENSITIVE A sensitive-looking {env.NAME} in argv.

Command Conditions Placeholders oyzu build (native) Evaluated per target All, including per-artifact hooks oyzu build --isolated Evaluated per target All but artifacts: a hook that reads artifacts fails with PLACEHOLDER_UNAVAILABLE oyzu build --plan Evaluated; per-artifact hooks pending Rendered for decided tasks. {build.version} shows (resolved during the build) oyzu run Evaluated with the host platform and development profile A hook that reads artifacts is skipped (TASK_SKIPPED). A requested task that doesn't apply fails with TASK_NOT_APPLICABLE Limits: {build.dist}, {artifact.digest} and {tool.NAME.*} aren't available (PLACEHOLDER_UNAVAILABLE). Placeholders in cwd are refused. Artifacts built by an image worker aren't staged for hooks. Per-artifact runs of one hook run one after another. when/unless on [context.*] setting tables isn't supported.

Limit how many workers run at once for one build, without editing configuration. Remote and CI runners use this to fit a build into a fixed amount of memory: oyzu build --jobs 4 # or -j 4 oyzu build --keep-going # finish independent work after a failure OYZU_BUILD_JOBS=4 oyzu build Source (highest first) Notes --jobs / -j Accepts 1–65535. --keep-going / --fail-fast Override every target's build.failFast with false / true; mutually exclusive. Flags outrank OYZU_BUILD_FAIL_FAST and files, subject to constraints. Default true stops new and running actions on a build-failing failure. OYZU_BUILD_JOBS A value outside 1–65535, or not an integer, fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. An empty value is ignored. build.jobs From configuration files and profiles. CPU count The default. --jobs and OYZU_BUILD_JOBS replace every build.jobs value, so the whole build shares one limit. Policy constraints on build.jobs still apply, and available memory can lower it further. The build prints the worker count, the plan records it in oyzu.dev/execution.jobs, and oyzu config explain build.jobs shows where it came from. oyzu run has no --jobs, because tasks run one at a time. The limit doesn't affect threads a compiler starts inside one action.

build.jobs limits both dependency preparation and build actions. In container builds, each worker reserves memory, and Oyzu runs only as many as fit in three quarters of the container engine's memory (docker info MemTotal). With default 2 GiB workers, a 16 GiB engine runs at most six at once. Dependency download workers reserve 4 GiB each and may run for up to 30 minutes. Native host builds have no engine to ask, so build.jobs alone applies. Each long-running container action gets an even share of the engine's CPUs, at most one CPU per 512 MiB of its memory reservation and never fewer than two. The chosen share is printed. Cargo sizes itself from it.

Free slots are refilled as soon as an action finishes and its reports and artifacts check out. Two actions never write to the same target's workspace at once. A target's check stages (test, lint, format-check) can overlap only when each runs in its own private view (see checks that run at once). A failed check doesn't block the next check, but it blocks packaging. A failed prerequisite blocks the actions that depend on it. Independent targets can prepare, run and package while others are still preparing. Each target's plan is saved in plans/ in the bundle, and oyzu inspect checks it against the final plan. Container execution uses the inputs captured during preparation. Task dependencies don't grant network, credential or host access. oyzu run uses your host environment.

Diagnostic When What it tells you worker-out-of-memory An action or preparation worker exits with 137, or its output ends with ENOMEM, cannot allocate memory or a heap-limit message. The action, its memory reservation (memoryMiB) and how many ran at once (jobs). Lower build.jobs or give the engine more memory. worker-file-sharing-error Windows only: an action's output ends with an I/O error. Docker Desktop file sharing failed a read. Build from a checkout inside WSL. On Windows, the out-of-memory message also notes that Docker Desktop file sharing can fail large writes with the same error, and that building inside WSL avoids it. Oyzu doesn't retry these.

oyzu run --isolated <task> resolves the same task names, depends_on, and pre_<task> / post_<task> hooks as an ordinary task run. It captures source and configuration, prepares the owning builder's dependencies and toolchain image, and runs that task graph through the isolated executor. It does not add the builder's other build, check or package stages. A native task can still require a producer through its builder's declared data dependencies. The run writes the usual bundle with its plan, action logs, isolation evidence and required reports. Test/report failures fail the run; a native command's nonzero exit code is returned. --json prints the final manifest. Only outputs whose artifact producers actually ran are collected; arbitrary files written inside the captured workspace are not copied into your checkout. The task gets no interactive stdin. An unavailable isolation backend fails without executing the task on the host. As with ordinary task runs, an artifact-reading hook is skipped because the task invocation does not stage build artifacts. Other selected hooks and dependencies still run. A full isolated build continues to refuse hooks that read artifacts. Successful actions record their enforced sandbox controls. A failed or interrupted action currently omits those fields, so its manifest alone cannot establish that action's isolation. Keep the execution logs when diagnosing interruption or cancellation; the failed action's manifest does not record all runtime controls. A qualified target task uses that target's existing builder/image. An unqualified root task needs exactly one target, or must be reached from a qualified task whose owner it can inherit. Missing or ambiguous ownership is refused before task execution. Unlike a native root task, an unqualified isolated task keeps the project's full target inventory for this ownership check, even when its task dependencies name no builds. This first version refuses extra task arguments (-- args), platform/runtime matrices that change the task's owner, and owners with build-level depends_on or materialize artifact inputs. Use oyzu build --isolated for those artifact pipelines. It adds no separate task image setting. Configured report obligations, disabled checks and administrative check requirements remain binding; unrelated stages are never added to satisfy them. Native tasks also need an explicit captured operation from their builder. A conventional placeholder that only supplies the host-discovered command is refused with TASK_CAPTURED_OPERATION_UNSUPPORTED, including authored replacements of native check slots whose report obligations are unavailable. The selected package must supply the captured task contract. Maven and Gradle require admitted native JVM model preparation before they can provide native test commands and JUnit/coverage duties; legacy metadata or a placeholder is insufficient. Windows wrapper commands such as mvnw.cmd and gradlew.bat are never substituted into a Linux captured task. The current Node provider supplies captured test and build operations; report collection and authored task behavior still depend on the selected operation and isolation backend. Use oyzu build --isolated for the full captured build lifecycle. Ordinary host tasks are unchanged.

oyzu run tasks get the project's pinned tool folders on PATH, plus tool variables such as GOROOT and JAVA_HOME. For example, argv = ["bash", "scripts/test-database.sh"] can call the pinned go by name. The tools must already be installed. oyzu run doesn't install them; run oyzu install first (or install --frozen --offline when cached). On Windows, a bare bash or sh skips the WSL launchers in System32 and WindowsApps. Oyzu looks for a native shell on PATH, then Git for Windows' shell next to git.exe, then standard Git install folders. If none is found, the task fails with the places searched; it never silently enters WSL. Git Bash converts the Windows PATH itself, so pinned tools work in scripts. shell = "bash" or shell = "sh" tasks use the same lookup. The default shell is PowerShell on Windows and sh elsewhere.

oyzu run <task> reports configuration, the selected task, tool verification and execution as they happen. Silent preparation shows an activity update every ten seconds, and a running task shows a heartbeat. Task kind Output Text mode, no bundle Uses your terminal's stdout and stderr directly. Records a bundle (oyzu run test, with its prerequisites and hooks) Shows output live and also saves it in the bundle's numbered dist/logs/*.stdout and *.stderr files. Bundled task with interactive = true Uses your terminal directly. Its output can't also be saved, so its bundle logs are empty. --json Stdout is one final result including captured output. Diagnostics stream on stderr. The task's streams aren't terminals, so prompts appear only at the end; use text mode for interactive prompts. Tasks receive your stdin, including piped input, in text and JSON mode. Container builds get no stdin. -q hides Oyzu's progress and keeps the task's output and logs. When output is saved, the task's stdout and stderr are pipes, which can change its buffering, color and terminal detection. PowerShell shell tasks need interactive = true to drop -NonInteractive. The task's own color handling, including NO_COLOR, is unchanged. For example, a task with argv = ["sh", "-c", "read x; printf 'got:%s\\n' \"$x\""] prints got:hello for printf 'hello\n' | oyzu run ask -q.

On Windows, each oyzu run command, prerequisite and hook runs in its own job object that is killed when closed. Child processes stay in the job. If Oyzu is killed, the whole task tree stops and releases the ports it held. When a task finishes, any processes it left behind are stopped. Don't leave background services running after a task returns; run a service in the foreground instead. stdin, arguments, exit codes and Ctrl-C behave as usual. This is process cleanup, not file or network isolation. If the job can't be created or the task's main thread can't be found or resumed, the task doesn't start and you get a TASK_JOB_* or TASK_PRIMARY_THREAD_* error. An enclosing job that doesn't allow nesting, or denied OS access, must be fixed first. If leftover processes don't exit within ten seconds, the task fails with TASK_JOB_CLEANUP_FAILED.

Native builds use the same task planner as container builds. Independent targets run in parallel up to build.jobs. depends_on: [api] under builds.web makes web wait for api's stages to succeed. A failed dependency blocks its consumers, not unrelated targets. Use materialize to pass files between targets; see target workspaces.
Container builds run each target in its own private workspace.

Prerequisites order tasks; they don't pass files between targets. When a consumer needs a producer's files, declare artifacts and use materialize (see directory artifacts). dist/plan.json records each action's owner, tools, dependencies, environment and required reports. The manifest records results, reports and artifacts. See build bundles. Packaging waits for every selected task of that target. Direct test runs collect each native report once, after the post-test hook. The hook can read or transform the evidence at its assigned paths; it does not inherit a second set of native report obligations. A hook may still declare its own reports. A failed prerequisite, post-hook or required report blocks dependent actions and packaging. Whatever evidence exists stays in the failure bundle, and independent targets can still succeed. oyzu inspect dist checks the bundle's integrity, not whether it may be released.

Container builds capture your source once and give each target its own copy from that capture. Capture follows in-tree .gitignore rules (case-sensitive), including rules above a nested build root. Untracked files that aren't ignored are included. Tracked files that are ignored are left out with a SOURCE_TRACKED_IGNORED warning. To include an ignored file, list it in the target's inputs. This never includes Oyzu state, Git metadata or a nested repository. Listing a file includes its ignored parent folders but not their other contents; listing a folder includes everything ordinary inside it. Global Git excludes and tool-specific ignore files don't affect capture. Source selection is limited to 100,000 paths. The source walk also keeps its 100,000-entry bound, including directories. It stops at the first admitted entry over that bound with source exceeds 100000 captured entries (walk stopped at 100001), before reading or copying that entry. The refusal lists up to five top-level folders by regular-file count, largest first, with folder-name ordering for ties. Counts include the overflow file when it is regular; directories and links don't contribute. These are counts from the visited part of the tree, not totals for the whole checkout. Files directly in the capture root appear as (root files). Ignore unnecessary folders with in-tree .gitignore rules or narrow the target's inputs, then rerun. The same walk limit and diagnostics apply to native source copies. A builder can further narrow its own folder with a source projection. Whole-target fallback keys include the projection definition and its captured selected entries. Admitted narrow action keys use only their selected reads, including discovery listings, so unread projection-membership changes can reuse results. Projections do not declare source outside the target folder. Authored inputs separately control admission of ignored and additional paths; a projection does not bypass source exclusions or containment checks. See the action cache. Replaying captured source in Oyzu-owned scratch uses the recorded source rules. A Git repository above that scratch cannot supply tracked-file warnings or other repository evidence for it. Each copy is checked against the capture (size, digest, executable bit). A changed or missing file, a symlink or reparse point, or a copy failure stops the build; fix the problem and rerun. The plan and manifest record the selection in source.selection (container builds) or source.projections (native builds), so it can be replayed later. Compare the result with source.treeDigest to confirm the bytes are the same. When oyzu.lock is part of a container build's source, it is recorded with the source and tool evidence but hidden from the builder's view of the project, so license scanners don't treat it as project source. Listing it in a target's inputs keeps it visible.

Captured plugin actions default to a 30-minute timeout, including cold native compilation and tests within the same action. A builder can supply its own execution deadline; the plan records the selected limit. A timeout fails the action with exit 124 and blocks dependent artifact export. There is currently no user setting for this action timeout. Docker preparation commands have fixed time limits, separate from action timeouts: Operation Limit per command Image and platform inspection, daemon checks, tagging, worker control and volume operations 30 seconds Image pulls and exports, worker file copies and tool restoration 30 minutes Removing a failed restoration or a running worker 5 seconds They can't be configured. When one expires, the command fails with a deadline error and the Docker client is killed. Failed pulls keep Docker's error message. Before retrying, check the daemon, registry access and free disk space. Killing the client doesn't stop work inside the daemon. After the daemon recovers, look for and remove leftover Oyzu containers. Cancelling a build has its own cleanup budget; see forced cancellation.

oyzu build --frozen uses the plugin selections pinned in oyzu.lock and fails with PLUGIN_LOCK_MISSING instead of resolving or rewriting the lock. --store picks the store that holds installed plugins. See plugin packages.
Error messages for cycles don't yet show the shortest cycle path. Oyzu doesn't infer a task's generated outputs; declare them. Long-running interactive services aren't supported as tasks.

Native local builds for the host path, platforms and slices. Action cache for reuse, affected builds for selection by Git history, and build logging for live output. Configuration for check levels, contexts and names that cross files.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/cargo-sessions.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Standalone oyzu build uses native Cargo configuration and credentials in host mode, without a credential agent; see Rust builds. The optional agent protocol below applies to direct Cargo commands through Oyzu. Use this when your crates come from a private sparse Cargo registry and you want Cargo to get its token without cargo login or a credentials file. Each time you run Cargo through oyzu, oyzu asks a local credential agent for a session and hands Cargo the token in memory through Cargo's own credential-provider protocol. Note: Experimental. You need a credential agent running on the same machine; oyzu doesn't include one. Supported on Linux with Bash (Cargo 1.95). Isolated oyzu build runs don't use this yet.

Add the agent's address to your user or administrator configuration (not the project's oyzu.toml): [cargo] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43199/session" Setting Values Default Meaning cargo.sessionEndpoint http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<path>, no user name, password, query or fragment Not set The local agent to ask for sessions. Remove it to go back to plain Cargo Project, local and command-line configuration and profiles can't set this value. User configuration isn't read in CI, so this doesn't work there. In your project, depend on the registry by name as usual: [dependencies] example = { version = "=0.1.0", registry = "internal" }

Run Cargo through oyzu exec, or in an activated shell: oyzu exec -- /absolute/path/to/cargo build --locked eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" cargo fetch --locked Supported commands are build, check, test, fetch and generate-lockfile. --help and --version run without asking the agent.

Sends the agent a POST with {"directory": "<working dir>", "tool": "cargo", "arguments": [...]}. Reads the agent's answer: { "credentialEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:43199/credential", "name": "internal", "index": "sparse+https://packages.example.com/index/" } name uses lowercase letters, digits, _ or - and can't be crates-io. index is sparse+ followed by an HTTP(S) URL ending in /, with no credentials, query or fragment. credentialEndpoint must also be on 127.0.0.1. Starts Cargo with CARGO_REGISTRIES_<NAME>_INDEX and CARGO_REGISTRIES_<NAME>_CREDENTIAL_PROVIDER set for that registry, and CARGO_REGISTRIES_<NAME>_TOKEN removed. The provider is oyzu itself, run as cargo-credential-oyzu. When Cargo asks for a token, oyzu accepts only a read request for that exact index. It POSTs {"ecosystem": "cargo", "request": <Cargo's request>} to credentialEndpoint, which must answer {"token": "..."}. Cargo may reuse the token for the rest of that one Cargo run, but not for other operations. Your CARGO_HOME, caches, Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock and other Cargo configuration are left alone. Any provider you've configured for the same registry is overridden for that run only. The agent is asked every time, even for a warm offline build. Requests to the agent time out after 10 seconds and don't go through a proxy.

The token never goes into a file, a command argument or an environment variable. It's in Cargo's memory, so anything with access to that process (for example an administrator) can read it. Read-only access has to be enforced by the registry account the agent uses. If the agent fails, Cargo gets a generic error; the agent's response isn't shown. Denial or an unreachable agent stops the command. oyzu never falls back to running Cargo without a session.
Cargo's output and exit code pass through unchanged. With --json, they're captured in the usual oyzu exec result.

Code Cause Fix NATIVE_SESSION_CONFIG The endpoint is set in project or local configuration Move it to user or administrator configuration NATIVE_SESSION_UNAVAILABLE The agent can't be reached Start the agent and retry NATIVE_SESSION_DENIED The agent refused the request Get access granted; don't work around the agent NATIVE_SESSION_INVALID The endpoint isn't 127.0.0.1 HTTP, or the agent's response is too large or malformed Fix the endpoint or the agent CARGO_SESSION_INVALID The registry name or index in the response isn't valid Fix the agent's response CARGO_OPERATION_UNSUPPORTED The Cargo command isn't one of the supported ones. cargo publish isn't supported Use a supported command. Publish with oyzu publish CARGO_ROUTING_CONFLICT You passed --config, --token, --registry, --manifest-path, -C or -- Remove the override

One named registry per run. Other registries, Git and path dependencies, crates.io replacement, source replacement and Cargo aliases aren't covered. Arguments after -- aren't supported. Linux and Bash only. Windows, macOS and other shells aren't supported yet.
Cargo credential-provider protocol Cargo registry configuration Rust installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/cli-help.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu --help lists every public command, grouped by workflow: Develop & build, Project tools, Environment & configuration, Platform and Diagnostics. Common examples follow the options. For one command's arguments and options, run oyzu <command> --help or oyzu help <command>. This works for nested commands too. oyzu --help oyzu build --help oyzu help config oyzu config set --help oyzu --json --help Help works offline, outside a project and without a platform account. It never runs the examples, installs tools or changes files.

On a color-capable terminal, help shows cyan headings, green command and option names and yellow placeholders. Redirected help is plain text. Variable Effect NO_COLOR=1 Turn help color off. CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 Turn help color on, even when redirected. Don't set both. The project ui.color setting doesn't apply to help, because help prints before any project configuration is read.

With --json, help and version requests return the unstyled text in output with exitCode: 0. Put --json before the command or after the command's --help. For oyzu help <command>, put --json before help. The human help layout can change between releases. Don't parse it; use --json.
CLI output for result and error formats.
CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/cli-output.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them.

Builds list same-input test disagreements in a Flaky tests section, after failures and before outputs. Each row names the test and its attempts. The test action row appends the flaky count; a successful build names flakes in its warning summary. Redirected and no-color output retain the same information. JSON build results expose tests.flakyCases, tests.flakyCount, fresh units and observations. Each observation names its unit, test, input key, evidence kind and ordered attempts. Reused units add no observations. Invocation summaries retain tests.flakyCount alongside fresh and reused counts. It continues to count attempt flakes. Historical same-input findings use the separate tests.sameInputFlakyCount, defaulting to zero in older records, and appear separately in the human receipt's warning summary. Combined JUnit uses flakyFailure for failed attempts of a flaky case and failure plus rerunFailure for consistent failures. Per-attempt reports remain separate. A flaky pass defaults to exit zero with a warning; tests.flaky="fail" blocks enforced/required checks. See test retries. Diagnostic Meaning and recovery TEST_FLAKY Attempts disagree; inspect the case and its attempt logs. TEST_RETRY_UNIT The plugin lacks rerun-cases; Oyzu retried the whole failed unit, including passing siblings. Update the plugin for exact case selection. TEST_ATTEMPTS_UNKNOWN Native retries lack visible history; remove native retries to use Oyzu retries. The unit is not stored. TEST_REPORT_INCOMPLETE The attempt lacks fresh, complete, consistent evidence or ended abnormally. Inspect retained stdout/stderr and the declared report path for sanitizer/data-race findings, malformed or truncated reports, or exit-code mismatches; correct the native failure or reporting, then rerun. No retry. TEST_RETRY_CAP More than ten cases and five percent failed; fix the wider failure before retrying. TEST_RERUN_INCOMPLETE A retry lacks a requested case or trustworthy completion; failure stands. Fix selection or reporting. TEST_IDENTITY_UNMATCHED Reserved for an unmatched connected-platform identity; standalone retries do not consume platform decisions. Every public command prints readable text for people by default and accepts the global --json flag for machine-readable output. This page shows what each kind of output looks like, which flags and environment variables control it, and what scripts can rely on. Choosing an output mode never changes policy, configuration, lock contents or exit codes.

Control Effect --json (before or after the subcommand) One machine-readable result on stdout; diagnostics on stderr as JSON Lines. See JSON results and errors. -v, -vv Debug and trace diagnostics; more detail in build output. -q, --quiet Hide routine progress. Results, warnings and errors stay. --log-level error|warn|info|debug|trace Set the threshold explicitly. See Diagnostic controls. OYZU_LOG Per-area log levels. NO_COLOR Turn color off. CLICOLOR_FORCE Force color (any nonzero value). NO_COLOR wins over it. ui.color Project or user setting: always, never or auto. Doesn't apply to help.
Run oyzu or oyzu --help for an overview of every command. Bare oyzu prints the same help and exits 0. See CLI help for nested help, help color and JSON help.

oyzu reshim (under Project tools) refreshes the shims folder and existing activation launchers. Human output shows the shims folder and the commands it holds; --json returns directory and commands. See the shims folder. oyzu shell install and oyzu shell remove manage shell startup profiles. oyzu shell check leads with the precedence outcome, followed by an aligned attention table of commands, winning executables, PATH sources and shims, plus fixes. It exits 1 when shadowed, 0 otherwise. JSON returns shims and shadowed; install adds the same shadowed array to its setup result without changing its success status. See PATH checks.

oyzu tools prune leads with eligible entry count and reclaimable logical bytes; --apply reports completed removals and bytes reclaimed. The entry table shows kind, path, size, state and reason, including retained and incomplete entries. Unknown sizes are shown explicitly. --json returns the same facts without prose. See store reclamation for retention rules, fields and exit statuses.

oyzu --version prints the compiled display label. A development build is independent of the checkout's commit, dirty state and wall-clock time: oyzu 0.2.2-dev (development; x86_64-pc-windows-gnu) Part Meaning 0.2.2-dev Development display label based on the compiled package version. x86_64-pc-windows-gnu Target triple. Development includes optimized local and CI builds unless release stamping is explicitly supplied. Their engine pin/admission identity is a separate content fingerprint; see engine identity. Release compilation supplies a full OYZU_RELEASE_COMMIT and Unix seconds in SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH. Its existing form is preserved, for example 0.2.2-local.8aee8560a0ca (release; x86_64-pc-windows-gnu; build 1791211857). Missing or malformed release inputs fail compilation. A timestamp alone does not turn a development build into a release build. Clean matching beta/nightly tags preserve their full prerelease label, such as 0.4.0-rc.1 or 0.4.0-alpha.0.nightly.20261104010101, in the display version and engine identity. An appended dev.g<source-digest> snapshot suffix is removed only after matching the release tag. A stamped release compilation from a clean checkout of the release tag oyzu/v<version> that matches the package version reports just that version, for example oyzu 0.2.4 (release; x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu; build 1793100000). Every platform built from that tag reports the same version, whichever oyzu built it, so a Windows install and the Linux engine it installs agree. The tag is read from Git at compile time; it isn't a signature, and release provenance remains the trusted evidence. --version never opens project configuration, runs Git or contacts a service. It does not hash the executable or source tree. Development compilation also reads no Git state; its embedded original notices omit the source revision. --version --json returns the text in the usual JSON envelope.

Pulling new source doesn't replace an installed oyzu. To see which one your shell runs, use command -v oyzu (POSIX shells) or Get-Command oyzu -All (PowerShell), then compare versions: oyzu --version ./.oyzu/bin/oyzu --version On Windows, use .\.oyzu\bin\oyzu.exe. oyzu build copies executable artifacts into the project's .oyzu/bin only after a successful native build. A failed build keeps the previous binaries. Compiling with Cargo through oyzu exec writes Cargo's own target/ output and doesn't update .oyzu/bin. Don't assume target/debug/oyzu is the one your shell runs. In an activated shell, ordinary commands run the first oyzu on PATH, so a project-local .oyzu/bin on PATH takes over. See shell activation.

Ordinary builds show a Facts section after preparation and before Builders, Scope, Plan and the actions. It needs no flag, login or network. Fact Meaning Branch / Commit The local branch and the commits recorded for versioning. Different targets keep their own commit. This doesn't prove that Git HEAD matches the files that were built. Git state Always shown as not verified. Source digest Content identity of the build inputs. Shortened by default; -v and JSON show it in full. Version / Basis Each target's or package's planned version and why. Packages in a target that share a version and basis are grouped: by count, or by name with -v. When some differ, each differing package gets its own row, the rest are grouped as others, and a basis they all share is shown once; -v lists every package with its own Version and Basis rows. Distinct native artifact versions get their own Artifact row. Kind The version kind; currently snapshots. A release context alone doesn't make a release. Context The build context (local, pr, ci, release) and where it came from. Protection unknown · not queried. Oyzu doesn't ask your Git host. Release Whether the build is eligible for release, or unknown. Version facts never allow publishing on their own. When independent targets prepare at different times, each new plan shows only new or changed facts before its actions. A version set by a hook shows pending post-hook finalization; the final version appears under Build. --quiet hides this section. In JSON, each plan event carries the facts in buildFacts. Environments, credentials and arbitrary extensions are never included. Uncertain Git or protection facts don't change the exit status, cache identity or release rules.

A default build shows compact linear progress, with one plan table before work starts. Sections always appear in the same order, and any section with nothing to say is left out. Every row, the title and the section rules share one width (80 columns, or less on a narrower terminal). Routine successes are collapsed; -v, --plan, oyzu inspect, oyzu history and --json keep the detail. Section What it shows Title line Project name and, right-aligned, the facts under Title line. ── Prepare ── One row per preparation step, then the pinned tools. ── Builders ── Which builder each target uses, why, and whether it was adopted, installed or reused. ── Scope ── Why the build isn't every declared target, or why narrowing fell back to all targets. ── Plan ── A table of targets by stages, with reason lines. ── Build ── One row per finished action. ── Flaky tests ── Actual same-key conflicting test executions, with complete identity, key, run IDs, machines and both outcomes. ── Quarantined failures ── Every admitted flaky assertion failure waived by the opt-in cascade setting. Native failures remain recorded. ── Failure: <target> · <stage> ── The native cause of a failed action. ── Outputs ── Artifacts with sizes and build profile. ── Warnings (N) ── Each distinct warning once, with its owner. Summary The outcome and counts, then a dim Details line. These test evidence sections appear in both successful and failed build receipts, including no-color output. They do not retry a test or imply its failure passed. --json carries the same findings and actual failed outcomes under action units; see flaky tests and quarantine. Title line​ The title line names the project and, right-aligned, shows: the host platform; local or the CI provider; the build context (context pr, context local). Where it came from is shown in Facts and by oyzu config explain context; see build context; fast or full, then optimized or development when you passed --optimized or --no-optimized. Under a CI provider the right-hand side may wrap onto the next line. If you pin a lower context while a CI provider marker is present, you get a CONTEXT_OVERRIDE_IGNORED warning. Prepare​ ── Prepare ── shows each preparation step as a row: mark, name, detail, duration and warning count. The Tools row summarizes the tools (2 tools pinned · 0 installed now) and lists each one with its version, already installed or installed now, and why it's needed (the detected requirement, or pinned in oyzu.toml). Toolchain components and host prerequisites follow. With several targets, the tool list prints once and each tool appears once. If the reason differs by target, each reason is shown (detected from …; pinned in … · not detected for <target>).
