A marker counts when it is set to a nonempty value other than false, 0, no or off (case-insensitive). Provider Marker pr signal release signal GitHub Actions GITHUB_ACTIONS GITHUB_BASE_REF set GITHUB_REF_TYPE=tag GitLab GITLAB_CI CI_MERGE_REQUEST_ID CI_COMMIT_TAG Azure Pipelines TF_BUILD BUILD_REASON=PullRequest BUILD_SOURCEBRANCH starts with refs/tags/ CircleCI CIRCLECI CIRCLE_PULL_REQUEST CIRCLE_TAG Buildkite BUILDKITE BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST is not false BUILDKITE_TAG Travis CI TRAVIS TRAVIS_PULL_REQUEST is not false TRAVIS_TAG Bitbucket Pipelines BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER BITBUCKET_PR_ID BITBUCKET_TAG Drone DRONE DRONE_BUILD_EVENT=pull_request DRONE_BUILD_EVENT=tag AppVeyor APPVEYOR none APPVEYOR_REPO_TAG=true Jenkins JENKINS_URL CHANGE_ID none These providers are detected as CI without a pull request or release signal: Gitea Actions (GITEA_ACTIONS), TeamCity (TEAMCITY_VERSION), Bamboo (bamboo_planKey), Bitrise (BITRISE_IO), Google Cloud Build (BUILDER_OUTPUT), AWS CodeBuild (CODEBUILD_BUILD_ARN), Harness (HARNESS_BUILD_ID), Codefresh (CF_BUILD_ID), GoCD (GO_PIPELINE_LABEL), Prow (PROW_JOB_ID), Cirrus (CIRRUS_CI), Semaphore (SEMAPHORE), Netlify (NETLIFY), Vercel (VERCEL) and Xcode Cloud (CI_XCODE_PROJECT). TaskCluster needs both TASK_ID and RUN_ID (RUN_ID=0 counts). CI=woodpecker, CI_NAME=sourcehut and CI_NAME=codeship identify those providers. Any enabled CI value selects CI behavior even for an unknown provider. CI=false disables only that generic hint, not a vendor marker. A system with no recognized marker must set CI=true. A variable such as BUILD_ID alone is not enough. Several matching providers are kept in sorted order. With no signal the context is local. oyzu config explain shows executionContext with ci, the sorted providers and the matched variable names in signals. Values and private runner URLs are not recorded. Build plans keep the same context.

A plain oyzu build builds and packages artifacts and runs any check at level required. In the pr, ci and release contexts it also runs every check that is not off (see check levels). oyzu build --full runs every check that is not off in any context. oyzu --profile ci build does too, because the built-in ci profile sets checks.run = "all". A different profile or --no-profile does not turn off the checks of a detected CI context. To change that, edit oyzu.toml. See build context behavior.

Every build resolves one context: local, pr, ci or release. With no CI signal the context is local. Any CI marker gives at least ci. A pull request or tag signal of a matched provider raises it to pr or release. When signals conflict the more demanding one wins (release over pr over ci). Detection never fails a build. Only fixed literals (such as =tag) are ever recorded as signals, never values. Overrides. oyzu build --context <name> or OYZU_CONTEXT=<name> pins the context. The flag wins. An unknown name is the only context error (CONTEXT_INVALID), and because every command that opens a configuration session resolves the context, a bad OYZU_CONTEXT also fails install, exec and config get. Under a vendor CI marker a pin can raise the context but not lower it. The pin is ignored with a CONTEXT_OVERRIDE_IGNORED warning. With only the generic CI hint, or no signal, a pin can also lower it. Set OYZU_CONTEXT=release once in a manually triggered release workflow, which carries no tag signal. Where the context is recorded. Build plans (--plan, --plan --json) and manifests record it in extensions["oyzu.dev/execution-context"].context: detected, requested, effective, policy (the stricter of detected and requested, which policy constraints evaluate) and a note. oyzu config explain context shows the value, source and deciding signal. The same record has fork for task conditions. It is false outside a detected pull request. Inside one it says whether the pull request comes from a fork, read from the GitHub Actions event payload (GITHUB_EVENT_PATH) or from GitLab's CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_PROJECT_ID and CI_MERGE_REQUEST_PROJECT_ID. It is absent when the provider does not say.

Any setting can take a value that applies only in one context. Write it in the same oyzu.toml as the base value: [checks] coverageMinimum = 50 [context.release.checks] coverageMinimum = 90 [context.pr] checks.coverageMinimum = 70 The table is [context.<name>] with <name> exactly local, pr, ci or release. Inside it, tables and dotted keys are written as for the base value. Context tables are valid wherever the setting is valid (user, project root, component folder, oyzu.local.toml) and follow its scope rules. A project file still cannot set cache.remote or trust.enabled under a context.

Within one file, lowest first: the base value the ci profile, when CI detection (not you) selected it the value for the effective context a profile you chose (--profile, OYZU_PROFILE, a task's inherited profile or profile.default) So an inferred [profiles.ci] loses to the same file's [context.ci.*], while --profile ci beats it. Between files, the nearer scope wins as for any setting. A component folder's base value beats the root's [context.release] value. To vary a component by context, write a [context.release] table in the component's own file. A context table never applies when its context is not the effective one. Project constraints, then administrative constraints, apply after every ordinary value, including context values and chosen profiles. See policy constraints and selectors.

In a release build, if a nearer folder's value leaves a check level (checks.tests, checks.coverage, checks.lint or checks.format) below what a farther folder's [context.release] table asked for, every command that resolves it reports CONFIG_RELEASE_LOWERED, naming both files and lines: checks.tests = advisory from app/oyzu.toml:2 lowers required from oyzu.toml:5 [context.release] in this release build The nearer value still wins. The warning only makes the lowering visible. A nearer folder's own [context.release] value is deliberate and never warns. oyzu config validate --strict fails on this warning. Plans show it as a lowered note (oyzu build --plan prints Lowered:, --plan --json has releaseLowerings), and plan and manifest targets record it under extensions["oyzu.dev/release-lowerings"]. To make lowering impossible, use a project constraint.

Most settings (checks, tasks, environment, build.failFast) resolve per target from the target's folder chain, like tool pins. A root value applies to every target, a value in docs-site/oyzu.toml applies to targets under docs-site/, and targets in one folder share settings. There are no target-keyed sections. Some settings are decided once for the whole build: scheduling, presentation and selector settings: build.jobs, build.isolation, ui.color, profile.default, config.* the whole cache.* family For these, [context.<name>] values are accepted in the user file, the project root oyzu.toml and oyzu.local.toml. In a component folder they are a configuration error. profile.default and config.* cannot vary by context at all, and cache.remote, cache.ciRemote and cache.dir are accepted only from user scope. scan.jobs is per target. A component folder's base value for a once-per-build setting is still read for its targets, and the build combines them. build.jobs is the minimum over the build root and every selected target. explain reports that minimum and lists the folders with their own value under targetValues. Root-only settings (publish.* and build.bundleDirectory) go further: no file outside the project root folder may hold a value at all, in a base, context or profile table. The [constraints] table follows the same rule.
documents.s: Per target or once per build

documents.t: These are configuration errors with file:line:column: an unknown context name ([context.relese]), reported as CONFIG_CONTEXT_UNKNOWN a context table that is not a table, an invalid value, a setting that cannot vary by profile or context, compatibility or overrides inside a context, a once-per-build setting in a component folder, and tool pins ([context.<name>.tools] is not supported), reported as CONFIG_CONTEXT_INVALID A setting a project may never set (such as cache.remote) keeps its CONFIG_SCOPE refusal, now naming the full key (context.release.cache.remote). An unknown setting under a context table is an inert warning, as in the base.

oyzu config explain <setting> [--context <name>] [--target <name>] resolves the setting as that context (default: the detected or pinned one) for that build.yaml target (default: the current folder). It prints the value, every scope that set it with the table's context, the contextValues considered (applied, overridden or not this context in the human view), and resolution (perTarget, perBuild or projectRoot). A once-per-build or root-only setting is read at the project root whatever --target names. --context and --target cannot be combined with --global, --project or --local. An unknown target fails with CONFIG_TARGET_UNKNOWN and lists the declared targets. oyzu build --plan --json (per target as contextValues) and the plan and manifest targets of a bundle (extensions["oyzu.dev/context-values"]) list the settings whose effective value came from a context table, so a build can be reproduced under --context. Docker image builds do not record this yet.

Each check a builder offers has one level. The checks are tests, coverage, lint and format. An old checks.required line is an unknown-setting warning with no effect. [checks] format = "off" lint = "advisory" coverage = "required" [context.release.checks] tests = "required" Level Runs in A failure off never: the stage is not planned and its tools are not prepared not applicable advisory builds that run every check a CHECK_ADVISORY warning; the build still succeeds enforce (default) builds that run every check fails the build required every build, including a fast local build fails the build; its report is mandatory checks.run decides which builds run every check: required runs only required checks, all runs every check that is not off. The defaults: Context checks.run Checks that run local required required only (fast build) pr, ci, release all (built-in context values) every check that is not off any, with --full not applicable every check that is not off You can change these like any value, per context and per folder, for example [context.ci.checks] run = "required" for pushes to a main branch, or [checks] run = "all" to run everything locally. No flag skips a check the project chose. Turning a check off is a committed change in oyzu.toml.

The test stage serves tests and coverage. Tests collect coverage, so tests = "off" also turns coverage off. lint serves lint, and format-check serves format. A stage runs when any check it serves runs, and is off when every check it serves is off. Each report is judged by its own check. With tests = "advisory", a failing test report is a warning, but the coverage report follows checks.coverage, so required or enforced coverage (including a shortfall below checks.coverageMinimum) still fails the build. Builders derive tool requirements from the stages that run. With format = "off" the Rust builder no longer adds rustfmt. A component you declare yourself, such as components = ["rustfmt"] in rust-toolchain.toml, stays a requirement. Coverage off only turns off judging. Builders collect coverage with the test command, which does not change with the level. With checks.coverage = "off" and tests running, coverage is still collected and its tools are still prepared, but it is never judged: no minimum, the report is not required, and a missing or invalid coverage report is a warning. Plans say Collected with test; not judged (checks.coverage = off). Running tests without coverage collection is not available yet. Levels resolve per target from the folder chain: the nearest folder wins, and a context value beats the base value in the same file. An administrative constraint still wins. A lock or minimum replaces a project value below it and the plan says so (format enforce · admin policy minimum in pr, release (project oyzu.toml sets off)). An allowed set such as ["enforce", "required"] refuses a project value outside it with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED.

checks.quarantineFlaky is a per-folder boolean in the existing oyzu.toml cascade, defaulting to false. Context and profile values use ordinary precedence; protected policy constraints remain binding. It controls how an actual same-input flaky assertion failure affects the step, while keeping the failed native outcome, report, input key, original runs and machines visible. When true, admitted test units and cases execute freshly while retaining their existing local observation history; passing test results do not skip execution. A known same-key pass/fail conflict removes the corresponding passing result from reuse, including after a later native pass. Default healthy-test reuse and --no-cache (no result or observation reads/writes) retain their ordinary meaning. This setting does not grant missing input/output bounds or create a history store for an ineligible unit. [checks] quarantineFlaky = true An administrator can forbid opt-in through the existing policy setting "checks.quarantineFlaky": {"allowed": [false]}. A conflicting project, local, context or profile value is refused with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED. A protected {"locked": true, "value": false} instead resolves the setting to false and records the policy override. No separate quarantine policy channel exists. Native framework configuration cannot express a cross-run, cross-language input-key comparison with machine attribution or apply the organization's Oyzu policy. This setting changes execution judgment by folder/context rather than what ships, so it belongs in this cascade rather than build.yaml or builder with options. Routine projects need no new configuration. Its frozen plan value records the choice but does not change the executed test's input key; it cannot make a failed result eligible for immutable cache reuse. Release context and governed main CI always ignore quarantine, even when explicitly enabled. This includes [context.ci.checks] quarantineFlaky = true on main-CI runs whose effective context is ci. Main-CI and required release gates retain their ordinary failure behavior. A quarantined test still runs. Only admitted assertion failures with a recorded opposite execution on the same key and exact identity can be waived. Setup, compilation, required reports, coverage, contract/resource/refusal failures and the active order-dependence safeguard retain their ordinary gates. advisory continues to apply to a whole check independently. See flaky tests and quarantine for native evidence requirements, output fields and current producer limitations.

Code Cause Fix CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE A level other than the four; or a positive checks.coverageMinimum with checks.coverage or checks.tests off (the message names both sources); or an authored task that depends on the stage of an off check Use a valid level, or turn the check back on CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED In the plan: a required check, or a positive coverage minimum, that the builder cannot run (<target> cannot satisfy required <check> check); or a policy lock or minimum of enforce or above on a check the builder has no action for Lower the requirement, or narrow the policy constraint with a path selector

The plan shows an off cell with its source (format · disabled in oyzu.toml), a skip cell with its reason (fast local build, or only required checks run in ci (checks.run)), and an advisory note for advisory stages that run. --plan --json reports stage status off with the same reason. Plan and manifest targets record extensions["oyzu.dev/build-checks"] (the mode, each check's level, and each off stage with its source). A failing advisory check is recorded with status failed and one CHECK_ADVISORY warning with the native cause. The target's artifacts are still collected, the manifest status stays succeeded, the exit code is 0 and oyzu inspect dist accepts the bundle.

Each target is built with the development profile (a fast edit-build loop) or the optimized profile. By default optimization follows where the output goes. The build Optimized because is a slice (oyzu build --slice, with or without --handoff) artifacts are handed off (--slice) writes results to a shared remote cache (cache.remote, or cache.ciRemote in CI, with cache.write = true, not with --no-cache), for a target whose results can be cached remotely (not a development plugin binding, a host image worker or a target with secret environment values) configured to write results to a shared remote cache selects a target that packages this one: a materialize input with usage runtime or data, or the target's own container image artifacts are packaged by image runs in the release context release builds are published does none of these development: local dist only build.optimized decides instead whenever it is set. It is a per-target setting: a folder's oyzu.toml sets it for the targets under that folder, optionally per context, and policy can set or lock it. # cli/oyzu.toml: the self-installed CLI is always fast [build] optimized = true # oyzu.toml: never optimize release builds of this folder [context.release.build] optimized = false oyzu build --optimized and --no-optimized set it for one invocation, above every file. Giving both is a usage error (CLI_USAGE, exit 2). A locked build.optimized replaces a flag or file that contradicts it, and the override is shown. A build.optimized in user configuration is ignored in CI.

Builder Optimized Development Rust (rust/app) cargo build --release cargo build .NET --configuration Release for build, test and pack --configuration Debug Go (go/app) no difference: the Go compiler always optimizes and builds use -trimpath Node, Python, Java (Gradle, Maven, Ant), Helm, Docker and other plugins no difference A builder with no difference always applies development, so its artifacts are labeled development and its cache entries are shared. Test stages keep each builder's own test mode in both profiles. The profile is resolved once per target and recorded on the plan and manifest target as extensions["oyzu.dev/optimization"] (requested, applied, reason, builder). --plan prints it as Profile: optimized · --optimized (cargo build --release), and --plan --json reports it as each target's optimization. An artifact's profile is optimized only when the builder's own optimizing commands produced it, so an authored replacement of the build stays development (see build bundles). An optimized build is not automatically publishable. The profile does not imply reproducible output or publication eligibility.

A toolset is a named set of tool versions for testing builds on other tools than the ones they ship with, and for running commands with them. oyzu build adds a toolset's verification run for each build whose builder uses one of its tools: in every context but local unless the toolset lists contexts, and locally with oyzu build --verify-with NAME. A run repeats the build and test stages with the toolset's tools and never ships an artifact. See verification toolsets. Define a toolset in a project's oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml: [tools] rust = "1.99.1" [toolsets.go-test.tools] go = "1.24.13" [toolsets.node24] contexts = ["ci", "release"] # optional; default: every context but local platforms = ["linux/x86_64"] # optional; default: one run, on the build's first declared platform or the host tools.node = "24" Select it for one invocation with the global --toolset NAME option: oyzu --toolset go-test install --frozen oyzu --toolset go-test exec -- go version A profile cannot change tools. [profiles.<name>.tools] (or a tools key in a profile table) is refused in every file with CONFIG_PROFILE_TOOLS, which shows the toolset that replaces it: CONFIG_PROFILE_TOOLS: oyzu.toml:4:1: [profiles.x.tools] is not allowed: a profile cannot change tools, so the tools a build uses never depend on the selected profile. Move the table to a toolset: [toolsets.x.tools] go = "1.24.13" and select it with `oyzu --toolset x exec -- …` (also run, env, activate, which, install, update and uninstall)

--toolset works with exec, run, env, activate (an activated shell keeps the toolset on every prompt), which, pin (locks only that toolset's tools), and the project-scoped install (without specs it installs, and locks when needed, the toolset's tools; with specs it declares them in [toolsets.NAME.tools]), update and uninstall (both act on that toolset's declarations and lock sets only). Every other command refuses it with TOOLSET_UNSUPPORTED, as do activate --shims and --global installs, updates and removals. oyzu build refuses it with TOOLSET_BUILD_REFUSED and points to oyzu build --verify-with NAME: a build always uses the [tools] versions, so a toolset never changes what ships.

contexts lists the contexts (local, pr, ci, release) whose builds run the toolset's verification runs. Without it a toolset runs in pr, ci and release, never local. contexts = [] turns it (or an inherited definition) off. platforms lists the os/arch[/abi] platforms to make one run each for. Without it there is one run, assigned to the build's first declared platform (the host's when the build declares none). A toolset applies only to builds whose builder uses one of its tools, so a Go toolset adds nothing to a Node build in the same folder.

The toolset's tool requests replace the cascade's, above every file (a nearer folder's [tools] value included) and below policy. Administrative and project constraints still bind a toolset's tools, and a value outside a policy lock fails with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED. Tools the toolset does not name keep their cascade value. A toolset is exempt from native pin agreement. A toolset Go below the go.mod minimum is used as written. oyzu tools current --all lists toolset declarations with their toolset.

One definition of a name applies, whole, as tasks do: the last one in source order, which is every oyzu.toml from the root to the folder, then every included oyzu.local.toml from the root to the folder. A nearer oyzu.toml replaces a farther one, and any included oyzu.local.toml that defines the name replaces every oyzu.toml. The folder you run from must have the name in its chain, or the command fails with CONFIG_TOOLSET_UNKNOWN and lists the toolsets defined there. A build target in another folder chain keeps its cascade tools.

A toolset holds its tools table and optionally contexts and platforms. Unknown optional fields warn and are ignored. These are CONFIG_TOOLSET_INVALID errors: unknown contexts, repeated or empty platform lists, and non-tool keys such as platforms or ignore under tools. Toolsets are refused in user, machine and administrative configuration and inside [profiles.*] or [context.*] tables (CONFIG_SCOPE).

The tools a toolset declares itself are locked in oyzu.lock as their own request sets, labelled toolset = "NAME", beside the unlabelled [tools] sets. Tools it inherits from [tools] stay in the [tools] sets. A toolset's install, update, uninstall, install SPEC and the automatic install of exec and run change only that toolset's sets. The [tools] commands never rewrite a toolset's. oyzu --toolset NAME update re-resolves only the tools that toolset declares. One request string resolves to one version in the whole lock, so a request a toolset shares with [tools] uses the same pin, and updating it updates it everywhere. uninstall in one scope never removes a pin another scope uses, and tells you where the tool is still declared. oyzu pin locks, for each build, the tools each toolset in that folder supplies. oyzu --toolset NAME pin locks only that toolset's tools. Plain oyzu update re-resolves [tools] and then each toolset. oyzu install --frozen writes nothing and replays the pins its requests need. A task run with oyzu --toolset NAME run sets OYZU_INHERITED_TOOLSET (@none when the task runs without one), so a nested exec, run, env, activate, which, install, update or uninstall keeps the task's toolset. Every other nested command, oyzu build included, removes the variable, so plans and cache keys never depend on a toolset they do not record. Toolsets in nested folders are not locked. Only a toolset defined in the project root's oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml is locked. For one defined (or redefined) in a nested folder's file, --toolset NAME install, install SPEC, update, uninstall, pin, and any exec, run or verification run that would install or lock its tools, fail with TOOLSET_NESTED_LOCK, name the file and change nothing. exec, run, env and which still work when the tools are already locked. Plain oyzu pin and oyzu update leave such a toolset out, list it under Toolsets not locked (toolsetsNotLocked in JSON) with the reason, and still succeed. They do the same for a toolset whose tools policy refuses.

A tool version your project already writes in its ecosystem's own file is a complete tool request, so such a project needs no [tools] entry for that tool. [tools] is for tools with no native pin (Helm, kubectl, Node in a project with no .nvmrc) and for folders outside a native project. Policy still constrains the selected version. Ecosystem Native pin Found by Kind Rust rust-toolchain.toml toolchain.channel, or the legacy rust-toolchain file The nearest file upward from the build folder, like rustup Pin file Go The newer of the go and toolchain lines of go.work, else go.mod The build folder A minimum, not an exact pin (see Go version selection) Node .nvmrc or .node-version holding an explicit version (22, v22.14.0) The nearest file upward, like nvm and fnm Version-manager file npm, pnpm package.json packageManager naming the build's own manager (pnpm@10.20.0) The nearest package.json upward that declares it, like Corepack Pin file Node, npm, pnpm package.json devEngines.runtime / devEngines.packageManager with an exact version or line and onFail error (npm's default) The build folder's package.json A range that is also the request when no other pin names the tool Python .python-version holding one CPython release (3.12, 3.12.4) The nearest file upward, like pyenv and uv Version-manager file Upward searches start in the build's folder and stop at the project root, so a file above the root (a home-directory .python-version) never pins a build. A native pin applies only to builds of its own ecosystem. A .nvmrc pins Node for Node builds, never for a Rust build in the same folder, and does not make other builds prepare that tool. The Tools block and oyzu.lock name the pin file as the request's origin (detected from rust-toolchain.toml; in the lock, facts such as "oyzu:node" = ["node-version-file:22.14.0"]).

A pin is accepted when [tools] accepts the same value, and it is resolved and locked the same way. Anything else is refused before any work, naming the file and a fix: File Refused Fix in the message rust-toolchain.toml A channel other than stable or an exact stable release (nightly, beta, 1.99, a host-qualified or dated channel) Write an exact release such as 1.99.1, or stable, or remove the channel and set [tools] rust rust-toolchain.toml toolchain.path, a local toolchain directory Set toolchain.channel to a release .nvmrc, .node-version An alias or range (lts/*, lts/iron, node, latest, system, >=22) or several lines Write an explicit version such as 22 or 22.14.0, or delete the file and set [tools] node .python-version Anything but one CPython release (system, pypy3.10, 3.13t, 3.12-dev) or several versions Write one release such as 3.12, or delete the file and set [tools] python packageManager (npm, pnpm) A range, tag, major only, pre-release or URL (pnpm@10, pnpm@latest) Write an exact stable release such as pnpm@10.20.0, or remove it and set [tools] pnpm Blank lines and # comments in .nvmrc, .node-version and .python-version are ignored, and a UTF-8 byte-order mark at the start of any pin file is skipped. When one folder holds both .nvmrc and .node-version they must name the same version line, and the more specific is used. A Corepack hash suffix (pnpm@10.20.0+sha512.…) is accepted but not compared.

Agreeing means naming the same version line: 22, 22.14 and 22.14.0 agree; 1.99.1 and 1.85.0 do not; stable agrees only with stable. A committed [tools] value that also applies to the build is compared with the pin by where it is written: [tools] value Result none The pin is the request On the same version line as the pin, in any folder The more specific of the two is used Another line, in a folder farther from the build than the pin file (the project root for a pin in app/, or user configuration) The pin wins. The Tools row shows detected from .nvmrc · overrides 20 from oyzu.toml Another line, in the pin file's folder or nearer the build Refused before any work with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_CONFLICT (exit status 3), naming both files Another line, in oyzu.local.toml Used for that personal experiment, with a TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_OVERRIDDEN warning. oyzu pin locks the pin, not the override. oyzu install --local node@20 declares the override and locks it as a set of its own beside the pin's set, and a build without oyzu.local.toml (CI) still uses the pin. Without that lock entry, a build with the override stops before any action naming the missing version Another line, from a source that is not a file Refused with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_CONFLICT A toolset's value Used: a toolset exists to differ A policy value Refused with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_CONFLICT: the project cannot change policy With .nvmrc holding 22.14.0 in web/ and [tools] node = "20" in web/oyzu.toml, oyzu pin stops with exit status 3: ✗ TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_CONFLICT: web: [tools] node = "20" in web/oyzu.toml does not agree with node 22.14.0 that web/.nvmrc pins (version); both apply to this build, so set [tools] node to 22.14.0 (or its version line) in web/oyzu.toml, remove it so the native file decides, or change the native file Next: Make the configured tool version agree with the native pin file, or remove it, then retry. A refused pin file also exits with status 3: ✗ TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_INVALID: hello: crates/rust-toolchain.toml toolchain.channel "nightly" is not a Rust release Oyzu can request (Oyzu installs stable Rust releases); write an exact release such as 1.99.1, or stable, in crates/rust-toolchain.toml, or remove the channel and set [tools] rust in oyzu.toml If a pin file changes after oyzu pin, the build stops with TOOL_LOCK_STALE, naming the file, the pinned version and the one in the lock, until you run oyzu pin again. oyzu build, oyzu build --plan and oyzu pin refuse alike. A build that runs in a captured worker (a Node or .NET build in a container) stops before any action and keeps the code in its bundle diagnostics. oyzu build --plan lists each pin's version as a request row with its file and any override.

.NET's global.json is the SDK request, but Oyzu does not acquire the .NET SDK. It is checked against the image or host SDK (see .NET SDK selection) and read from the target folder only. Gradle and Maven wrapper properties are not tool requests. Yarn has no Oyzu provider, so packageManager: yarn@… selects nothing. .tool-versions is not read. devEngines entries with onFail warn are not read. oyzu config explain tools.<name> does not show the native pin. The Tools block, build --plan and oyzu.lock do. The Node plugin builder reads packageManager from the build folder only and does not read .nvmrc or .node-version. A plugin builder's native default counts as a pin only when it is a plain exact release (10.20.0). Any other value (lts, a range) is the request only when nothing is configured.

oyzu publish reads these settings. See publishing for a complete example, the evidence profile and current limits. publish.default selects a named destination or set when oyzu publish has no --destination. publish.destinations maps names to registry, repository and optional paired usernameEnv / passwordEnv credential references. publish.sets maps names to nonempty destination lists. Destination and set names must differ. Every selected destination is required. publish.requirements holds provenance (bundlePath, an accepted Ed25519 publicKey, builderId) and signing (keyEnv, publicKey). Public keys are base64 raw 32-byte keys. keyEnv names a separately provisioned variable holding a base64 32-byte signing seed. Never store secret values in project configuration. Evidence paths resolve relative to the file that declares the requirements. An optional signing.subject table (signer = "sigstore", identity, issuer) also signs each OCI subject keylessly in CI; see subject signatures. Configure it once, at the project root. Only the project root folder's oyzu.toml and oyzu.local.toml may set publish.*, in a base, [context.<name>] or profile table. A [publish] table anywhere else is a configuration error, for every command that reads configuration: CONFIG_SCOPE: <root>/api/oyzu.toml:1:1: [publish] is allowed only in the root oyzu.toml (<root>/oyzu.toml); move it there: publishing is configured once, for the whole project oyzu config explain publish.default reports resolution: projectRoot. Independently released packages still publish separately, because destinations select artifacts by build. Otherwise these settings use the normal cascade (user, root project and root local files), selected profiles and constraints. The destinations map, sets map and requirements object are replaced whole by a later source, not merged. They set standalone safeguards only and cannot grant managed publication authority. The builds, outputs and platforms their selectors name are checked before any build action runs (see names that cross files).

When oyzu.toml names something that build.yaml or a builder declares, one validator checks the name against the build inventory before any action runs. An unknown or misplaced name is an error (exit code 3, including a build refused at Prepare) that names the file, line and column, lists the valid names and suggests the nearest one. Name Example Checked by A task key's build [tasks."api:test"]: api exists, and the file is the root or in api's folder chain oyzu config validate and every command that opens the project (oyzu build, --plan, oyzu run) A publish selector's or evidence key's build publish.destinations.<name>.artifacts and publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact keys: cli in cli/bin-oyzu The same A selector's platform @linux/arm64 is one of the build's declared platforms (unchecked for a build that declares none) The same A bound chart's image A publication that publishes a chart with bindings also pushes each bound image to its with.repository. Checked for publish.default and each publish.sets entry (CONFIG_BINDING_UNPUSHED), and by oyzu publish for the destinations it selects (PUBLISH_BINDING_UNPUSHED) The same, and oyzu publish A hook's task and depends_on [tasks.post_biuld], depends_on = ["schema:verfy"] (see task binding) Every command that discovers the project's tasks, not config validate A selector's output bin-oyzu in cli/bin-oyzu is an output of cli Each build's Prepare, once the outputs are known and before the first action. oyzu publish keeps its final check against the bundle CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN: oyzu.toml:13:13: publish.destinations.github.artifacts names "clii/bin-oyzu", but there is no build clii; builds: cli, docs; did you mean cli/bin-oyzu? CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN: oyzu.toml:13:13: publish.destinations.github.artifacts names "cli/bin-oyz", but build cli has no output bin-oyz; outputs of cli: cli/bin-oyzu, cli/bin-oyzu-shim; did you mean cli/bin-oyzu? Limits: Only files that some build's (or the invocation folder's) chain reads are checked. A stray oyzu.toml in a folder with no build below it is not read. A selector for a build this invocation does not prepare has its output checked by oyzu publish.

build.yaml says what is built. A builds mapping holds one entry per build with these fields: uses, path, default, platforms, depends_on, inputs, materialize, bindings, fetches, artifacts and with. Any other field fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming it. default: false leaves a build out of a plain oyzu build; naming it builds it (select targets). depends_on orders builds only; it does not transfer artifacts. inputs names extra source paths a build reads (declared inputs). fetches declares pinned downloads (declared fetches). artifacts declares named files produced by authored tasks, with a producing task, exact path and media type (named file artifacts). bindings writes a produced image's reference into a chart's values during the build (image bindings). with holds builder-specific options, validated by the selected builder (for Rust, see build options). Tool requirements stay in TOML, and resolved tool identities stay in oyzu.lock. Configuration normalizes the inventory and freezes all declared platforms. The root keys are builds, members and exclude, plus the optional min_oyzu_version. Any other root key fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming it. members is not supported yet and is refused. exclude lists folders where discovery recognizes a build that is deliberately not one.

uses is optional. web: {path: web} is a complete entry when exactly one builder recognizes web, and discovery freezes that builder into the inventory before planning. A folder that no builder or several builders recognize fails, naming the candidates and the line to write. Folders discovery recognizes but the inventory leaves out are listed by oyzu discover and oyzu build --plan, and never built. oyzu discover --write declares them, and oyzu discover --check fails on them in CI. A folder that a declared build's native workspace manifest lists as a member (Cargo members, go.work use, npm, Yarn or pnpm workspaces) is covered by that build and needs no entry. See discovery. oyzu config validate checks chart bindings (unknown producers, repository and values fields) without discovery. Checks that depend on an omitted uses (the build's with options, bindings only on helm/chart builds, a docker/image producer) wait until discovery infers the builder, as oyzu discover and oyzu build --plan do.

builds: is the only shape. The former flat shape, with build entries at the top level, is refused with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. The message shows the file's own lines indented under builds:, which is the whole fix: # Refused: builds at the top level cli: uses: rust/app # Accepted: the same entries, indented two spaces under builds: builds: cli: uses: rust/app Fields the flat shape once carried have new homes, and the old spellings fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming the new location: Old New matrix Toolsets in oyzu.toml (see verification toolsets) platform: <os/arch>, matrix.platform platforms: [<os/arch[/abi]>, ...] The rust object (features, targets) with.features, and cross-compilation targets as platforms entries container (python/app) with.container (Python application containers) dependencies (docker/image) with.dependencies (Docker dependency contexts) with.load (docker/image) The docker.load setting A build that declares one platform keeps its name. Several platforms give each instance a platform-qualified ID (see platform requirements). Builders check their static with options when the inventory is read, so oyzu config validate reports those errors. Plugin builders keep runtime capability negotiation and plugin-owned option-value validation in the normal build path.

Other tools use the same file name. Dart's build_runner reads a build.yaml with targets:, builders: and global_options:. A build.yaml is an Oyzu inventory only when its root has builds, members or exclude, or the refused flat shape (a top-level entry whose mapping has uses). A file that is not valid YAML also counts, so its syntax error is reported instead of the file being skipped. A misspelled envelope counts too, and fails naming the root keys (found build (did you mean builds:?)). That covers a root key equal to builds, members or exclude ignoring case, the key build, or any root key with uses two levels below it (buildz: {web: {uses: node/app}}). A leading UTF-8 byte order mark is ignored. Any other build.yaml, including an empty one, belongs to another tool: It never makes its folder a build root, a project root or a configuration boundary. Discovery and oyzu discover --check continue below its folder as if it were absent, so a Flutter package in a monorepo no longer hides the builds under it. At the project root, zero-config discovery decides the builds, and every discovering command (oyzu build, --plan, discover, run) warns CONFIG_BUILD_FILE_IGNORED: build.yaml: ignored, not an Oyzu inventory … naming its root keys (a JSON diagnostic event on stderr with --json). oyzu discover lists it under Skipped with its root keys. JSON records it in skipped_build_files (plain oyzu discover without an inventory) or skippedBuildFiles (the inventory record), each entry {path, keys}. oyzu discover --write never edits another tool's build.yaml at the project root. It fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming the file's root keys and leaves it unchanged. An Oyzu inventory cannot share that file, so such a folder can only use zero-config discovery.

Every refusal of a build.yaml names the place to fix it as build.yaml:LINE:COLUMN: after the code. Lines and columns start at 1. This covers YAML syntax errors (CONFIG_SYNTAX), anchors, aliases, tags, merge keys and duplicate keys (an inventory uses none of them; CONFIG_SYNTAX or CONFIG_DUPLICATE), the flat shape and wrong root keys, unknown, moved or retired build fields, bad uses, platforms, materialize, bindings and fetches values, unknown dependencies, a builder discovery cannot infer, and with options a builder refuses (at the option when the message names it, otherwise at with). ✗ CONFIG_SYNTAX: build.yaml:3:6: invalid YAML: while parsing a flow mapping, did not find expected ',' or '}' ✗ CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE: build.yaml:5:7: docker/image with.repository must be a repository name without scheme, tag or digest With --json the same text is the error record's error. YAML follows the 1.2 core schema: true, ~, 12 and 1.5 are a boolean, null, integer and float, while yes, on and 1.2.3 stay strings.

Rust targets take Cargo features from with.features and cross-compilation targets from platforms entries, built by the native cross toolchain or the executor build.executors declares (see Rust platforms). The python/app builder's optional with.container is a boolean or an object with base, user, workdir and entrypoint. See Python application containers for types and defaults. The builder validates it when the inventory is read, so oyzu config validate rejects malformed values without resolving images or running a build.

Oyzu generates a JSON Schema for each of its two files, so an editor can complete keys and flag a wrong value or a key in the wrong file while you type. The build.yaml schema covers the root keys and every build field. The oyzu.toml schema covers every registered setting and the sections the reader accepts (profiles, context, toolsets, constraints, overrides, compatibility). Builder with options and settings a plugin registers are left open. Defaults that depend on the host (the CPU count for build.jobs, the Docker AppArmor profile) are described, not written into the schema's default. The schemas flag what the CLI refuses, with two deliberate differences: In build.yaml, paths (path, inputs, materialize to and into) may not contain \ or :, so a file stays portable across Windows, macOS and Linux. The CLI decides such a path where it is used. In oyzu.toml, a build.yaml key such as [builds.web], exclude or a top-level uses is refused by the schema, while the CLI only warns (CONFIG_UNKNOWN_OPTIONAL). Other unknown keys stay open in the schema because the CLI warns about them and oyzu config validate --strict refuses them. The CLI's own checks stay the authority, including rules a schema cannot express (a value accepted only from user configuration, a root-only section, which ABIs an OS has). File Published at (every release, unversioned) build.yaml https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu-releases/releases/latest/download/build.yaml.schema.json oyzu.toml https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu-releases/releases/latest/download/oyzu.toml.schema.json oyzu config schema prints them without a project, configuration session or network, so you can keep a saved copy for offline machines: oyzu config schema # both files, their URLs and how to print each oyzu config schema build.yaml > build.yaml.schema.json oyzu config schema oyzu.toml > oyzu.toml.schema.json oyzu --json config schema build.yaml # {"kind": "config-schema", "file", "asset", "url", "print", "schema"} With a file named, the schema itself is the output, printed as JSON in both modes (--json wraps it in the record above). Without one, --json prints {"kind": "config-schemas", "schemas": [...]}. To point an editor at them: build.yaml: the YAML language server (VS Code's YAML extension and others) reads a first-line comment, # yaml-language-server: $schema=https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu-releases/releases/latest/download/build.yaml.schema.json. oyzu discover --write adds it when it creates or edits build.yaml and the file has no such comment. Add it by hand to a file you write yourself. build.yaml is not registered with SchemaStore, because SchemaStore already lists Dart's build configuration for that name. oyzu.toml: point Taplo or Even Better TOML at the URL, using Taplo's [[schema]] setting or a #:schema <URL> first line. Oyzu's schema is not registered with SchemaStore, so editors do not find it by file name.

oyzu --root path/to/project config set build.jobs 8 --project oyzu --root path/to/project config set checks.tests required --local oyzu --root path/to/project --profile dev config set ui.color never --global oyzu --root path/to/project config unset build.jobs --project Exactly one of --global (the user configuration file), --project or --local is required. --directory can select a nested project scope. unset removes the assignment from that file and exposes inherited values. It does not leave a removal marker. Edits keep unrelated comments and unknown syntax, validate known types and scopes, and compare the original bytes before an atomic replace. A concurrent change gives CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT. A small .oyzu-config-edit.lock file coordinates Oyzu writers. The lock is released when the edit finishes, including on failure; unrelated child processes do not extend its lifetime. Edits work even when resolution is blocked, so you can repair invalid values. They cannot repair malformed TOML (fix the syntax in an editor first) and cannot change administrative or enrollment records. Only an explicit --profile NAME writes into that profile. Without it the edit goes to the base section, even when a profile is inferred or defaulted. A profile cannot hold tools: config set tools.NAME VALUE --profile P fails with CONFIG_PROFILE_TOOLS. Use oyzu --toolset P install NAME@VERSION. Booleans and numbers are parsed by type and strings are literal. Use --json-value for arrays or objects.

All config commands print readable text by default. Add the global --json for structured results and errors. The JSON shapes may change. Command Result show Effective values, selected profile, digest, diagnostics and resolution status get KEY One effective value (a JSON value with --json); fails if the key has no effective value explain [KEY] Where each value came from, optionally for one key, including origins and constraints profiles Available profiles, the selected one and why validate [--strict] [--all-profiles] valid: true on success; nonzero exit on failure status Standalone or enrolled state and managed cache health; does not refresh over the network refresh Explicit online policy refresh; returns the revision and offline deadline; needs protected enrollment set / unset Changes one ordinary file and reports its destination schema Prints the JSON Schema (see editor schemas) show, get and explain accept the mutually exclusive --global, --project and --local, which inspect only that file: user configuration, oyzu.toml in the selected directory, or oyzu.local.toml there. Without a flag you get the merged result. Scoped reads add no defaults, read no other source, contact no policy service and keep redaction. --profile NAME overlays only that profile from the file. get fails when the key is not declared there. These show declarations, not whether policy would allow the values. show and explain print resolved status and profile first, then setting tables grouped by namespace and the computation digest. Keys keep their exact spelling, booleans print true or false, and empty lists print []. Human explain groups keys with effective values and their last source. Several origins appear as an ordered history. Nonempty policy restrictions, exclusions and diagnostics are expanded. explain <key> narrows the view. --json keeps the complete metadata. TOML syntax errors give file:line:column (one-based) and the parser's reason, without a source snippet so configuration values stay out of diagnostics. --strict keeps every warning's key, source, line and column, message and fix. Human errors list them, and JSON errors have a diagnostics array. show and explain can exit 0 with status: "unresolved", and status can exit 0 for an unhealthy managed state. Scripts should inspect those fields or use validate as the gate. Execution errors go to stderr with a nonzero exit.

Before a build copies project source, Oyzu checks Git-tracked pip.conf, pip.ini, uv.toml, .yarnrc.yml, .cargo/config.toml, .cargo/credentials.toml, .npmrc, .pypirc, .netrc, settings.xml, gradle.properties and NuGet.config files, including files in subdirectories. Literal passwords, tokens, authorization values and credential-bearing URLs are refused with NATIVE_CONFIG_CREDENTIAL (SOURCE_CREDENTIAL_DENIED for npm auth settings). The diagnostic identifies the file without echoing the value. Move credentials to user-level native configuration or a supported native environment reference such as ${VAR}, ${env.X} or %VAR%. Reference-bearing files pass credential admission without expansion. Python configuration is copied unchanged; the existing Node source projection omits registry and authentication lines, retaining them only for native preparation and host execution. Oyzu adds no reference syntax to a native tool. Ordinary registry URLs without credentials are allowed. This check covers tracked native configuration; it is not a general secret scanner. Native source selection, authentication and build execution constraints still apply to each ecosystem.

Some settings decide trust or where credentials go. Project and local files (including profiles) may not set trust.enabled, trust.parents, platform.url, platform.account, platform.authentication.provider, cache.remote or cache.ciRemote. Set them in user, machine or administrative configuration. trust.enabled (boolean, default true) and trust.parents (absolute folder paths, default []) control folder trust. These invocation environment variables override ordinary files and remain subject to administrative constraints: OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST (true/false, on/off, yes/no or 1/0), OYZU_PLATFORM_URL, OYZU_PLATFORM_ACCOUNT, OYZU_PLATFORM_AUTH_PROVIDER, OYZU_CACHE_REMOTE and OYZU_CACHE_CI_REMOTE. The plugin and engine settings are in the same group (see plugins and engines). In CI, PR and release contexts the engine development override is not available.

Administrators can add limits that ordinary files cannot override. They live in protected files that must be owned and writable only by an administrator: Windows uses ACL checks, Unix checks root ownership and write permissions, and macOS also rejects non-root ACL grants. An insecure, unreadable or malformed enrollment never turns into standalone mode. admin-settings.json uses the same constraint evaluator as organization policy. Locks, allowed values, numeric and ordered bounds and required sets combine independently of ordinary precedence. An empty ordinary array cannot remove a required check. The planner requires every configured check to have a real action and report, and report collection enforces the coverage minimum, including missing or zero-denominator coverage failures.

Central policy has two forms. A default ("default": …) is an ordinary inherited value that a project can override. A constraint is a limit applied after every ordinary value (base, context and profile values, flags) that a project cannot go past. Constraint Applies to When the ordinary value is outside it "locked": true, "value": v Any setting The lock replaces it. Shown as an override "minimum" / "maximum" Numbers (build.jobs, checks.coverageMinimum, cache sizes) and ordered levels (checks.tests, checks.coverage, checks.lint, checks.format: off < advisory < enforce < required) The bound replaces it. Shown as an override "required": [...] Sets The members are added. Shown as an override "allowed": [...] Any setting Refused with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED naming the setting and the policy source Tool versions​ A tool request (tools.<name>) under a lock or allowed set is refused, not replaced, because a requested version is never silently substituted. A constraint binds every spelling of the tool. A lock on tools.rust also refuses [tools] "oyzu:rust" = "1.90" or "core:rust". A tool lock supplies the request and binds every target whose builder needs or detects the tool, whether or not the project pins it. Deleting [tools] rust cannot avoid a release lock on Rust. If the locked version cannot be resolved, the build fails. The version a builder needs (a pin, the builder's default such as lts, a detected tool's latest, or a verification run's request) is checked against every tool constraint wherever tools are prepared. A violation is refused with the constraint named (CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED: tools.node violates administrative constraints: 24 is outside allowed ["20","22"] in release (local-administration); pin an allowed version …). A tool a builder only detected can be silenced with tools.ignore. The version oyzu.lock resolves a request to is checked too, before anything is installed or activated (--frozen included). A stale lock mapping an allowed 22 to 26.1.0 is refused, naming the constraint and the lock file. Versions match by components: 22 admits 22, 22.14 and 22.14.0 (not 220.1). Any other value (lts, latest) matches only itself. Write allowed sets as majors or exact versions: an allowed lts or latest cannot vouch for what it resolves to, so a locked version under such a set is refused. A tool constraint never affects a target whose builder does not use the tool. A version supplied by a context-scoped lock is locked per context. oyzu.lock keeps one entry per tool request, so a local build (rust = stable) and a release build (rust = 1.95.0 from the lock) need one entry each. A build in a context whose entry is missing fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE. Run oyzu pin and OYZU_CONTEXT=release oyzu pin once, on a machine with the same policy, and commit the lock. For a lock limited by provider or path, pin from a build that has them (in that CI job or folder). A build does not add such an entry while other tools are already locked, and --frozen never does. Not bound by tool constraints: custom tasks that run tools through argv; plugin builders that run host tools without declaring them; oyzu exec, which activates only requested tools; a tool the isolated worker image supplies with no declared requirement (Helm, npm without packageManager, Yarn) or whose default request is missing from oyzu.lock, which runs the image's copy unchecked; and tool recipe artifacts (recipe:* entries in oyzu.lock), which oyzu install replays without tools.allowed or tool constraints. Otherwise a project's configuration never breaks a build merely because policy tightened. Policy wins and the CLI says so. Check levels under policy​ A policy lock or minimum of enforce or above on a check makes the check run wherever the constraint applies, whatever checks.run says. A project's [context.pr.checks] run = "required" does not skip a check policy requires in pr. The override is recorded (runs although checks.run = required) and changes the configuration digest. required also makes the check run in every build and its report mandatory. A minimum on checks.coverage also lifts checks.tests to at least the same level, because tests collect coverage. A policy minimum on checks.coverageMinimum lifts an off checks.tests or checks.coverage to enforce (or advisory where a policy maximum or allowed set caps it). An advisory level is not lifted. A lift never overrides another policy constraint. A coverage percentage with a policy lock that keeps coverage off, or a coverage level with a lower tests lock, is CONFIG_POLICY_CONFLICT naming both, raised when the policy is read if both are unconditional, otherwise when a build meets both. Selectors​ A constraint can be limited with when and unless tables. Every key in when must match (a list matches when any listed value does), and any matching key in unless excludes. Facts available when policy applies: context: local, pr, ci or release provider: detected CI providers such as github-actions path: the target's folder, matched as a /-separated glob A setting can carry one entry or a list of entries with different selectors: { "schemaVersion": 1, "kind": "local-admin-policy", "settings": { "checks.format": {"minimum": "enforce", "when": {"context": ["pr", "release"]}}, "checks.tests": [ {"minimum": "required", "when": {"path": "services/**"}, "unless": {"context": "local"}}, {"minimum": "enforce", "when": {"context": "release"}} ] }, "profiles": {}, "requiredCapabilities": [] } Contexts cannot be avoided. A build counts as every context it detected, runs as or requested (the detected context, the effective one and the stricter of the two). A when context matches when it names any of them, and an unless context excludes only when it names all of them. So a pull request job under GitHub Actions run with --context local or --context release still meets when context = pr. explain reports these as policyFacts (contexts, providers, path). Folders. path is the target's folder relative to the repository boundary: the nearest Git boundary above the build root, climbing from a submodule to its superproject. A linked worktree, a nested clone and any other repository are their own root, and the boundary is never the user's home folder or above. Without Git it is the nearest folder holding oyzu.toml, oyzu.local.toml or build.yaml, else the build root. --root and the current folder never move it. A target folder outside the boundary (reached through a link) is a CONFIG_SCOPE error. Patterns are normalized (./services/ is services) and compared without case. services/** matches services and every folder below it, and * matches one folder level. The repository root (.) is matched only by . and **. Path selectors are not containment. They select by repository layout. A git init in a subfolder makes it its own root, and a when path services/** constraint no longer matches it. Write rules that must hold everywhere as unconditional constraints, or limit them by context or provider. Conflicts. Constraints on one setting that can apply to the same folder in the same context are compared when the policy is read. An unconditional lock off with minimum required when context = release, or two constraints for a shared context that cannot both hold, fail the policy with POLICY_INVALID naming both. Constraints for different contexts load. When one build counts as several contexts and they cannot all hold, the strictest context wins (local < ci < pr < release): its lock, minimum or maximum, and the intersection of its allowed sets. Allowed sets that agree pairwise but share no value for one build fail closed with CONFIG_POLICY_CONFLICT. Errors. These fail with POLICY_INVALID naming the setting: an unknown fact, a fact with no value at this point (fork is not detected yet; target, platform, artifact and optimized are decided after settings), an unknown context, a non-string value, an empty table, an absolute, .., .-segment or // path pattern, an unknown entry field, and when or unless on a default. A bound that is not a valid value of the setting is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. A minimum or maximum on a setting that is neither a number nor an ordered level, a non-integer bound, reversed bounds, and unconditional constraints that cannot hold together are CONFIG_POLICY_CONFLICT. Policy errors stop the session before a build starts. When a constraint replaces your value​ oyzu config explain <setting> lists it under Policy overrides (checks.format enforce admin policy minimum in pr, release (project oyzu.toml sets off)), adds a policy-<kind> step to the history, and marks each constraint with applies. --json has policyOverrides (with the replaced value, its origin and a label) and policyFacts. The label is org policy for enrolled organization policy and admin policy for the machine's admin-settings.json. The plan prints one policy note per distinct override. oyzu build --plan prints Policy: lines (Constraint: for a project constraint) per target, and --plan --json has policyOverrides per target. Plan and manifest targets record extensions["oyzu.dev/policy-overrides"]: the setting, value, constraint (source, label, kind, bound, selector), replaced (value, source, scope) and a note. Every command that resolved an overridden setting reports a CONFIG_POLICY_OVERRIDE warning once per override, naming the setting, the policy source and the value that lost (checks.format = enforce by admin policy minimum in pr (local-administration) instead of off from oyzu.toml). The shell prompt hook does not repeat it. config validate --strict reports it without failing. A value a task passes on as written (a task's own env) is checked without being replaced, so a locked environment value a task contradicts is refused with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED. A policy lock or minimum of enforce or above on a check the builder cannot run fails in the plan, naming the constraint (see check levels). Signed, cached organization policy carries the same entries and keeps working offline within its expiry.

config status reports enrollment and cached-policy status. config refresh asks the enrolled platform's public configuration endpoint for current policy. Enrollment is done by your administrator; there is no enrollment command in the CLI. Signed responses use pinned Ed25519 keys, canonical JSON, identity and context binding, increasing sequence numbers, expiry and explicit offline permission. Cache entries are content-addressed and flushed before an operating system credential-store pointer commits them. Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain and Linux Secret Service hold integrity state. If that service is unavailable, managed execution fails. Standalone use does not need it. A corrupt entry can be repaired only by a newly verified online response. Retry backoff never extends signed deadlines, and a server denial never becomes offline permission. Offline execution needs explicit signed permission and is bounded by the signed expiry and a maximum offline age of 24 hours. CI requires online policy. Changing the protected bootstrap pins invalidates the previous cache binding. Recovery needs an online response verified against the current pins with a strictly newer policy sequence. Do not delete credential-store state to rotate keys. Policy is not a login session and grants no publishing or signing authority. Platform sign-in is the separate oyzu auth.

A project without central policy can make a rule hold in every folder with a [constraints] table in its root oyzu.toml. It uses the constraint and selector vocabulary and is applied after every ordinary value and before central policy, so a component folder cannot undercut it: # root oyzu.toml only [constraints."checks.tests"] minimum = "required" when = { context = ["release"] } With services/oyzu.toml setting [checks] tests = "advisory", a release build of services runs its tests as required, and a local build keeps advisory. Vocabulary. Each entry is a table, or a list of tables ([[constraints."checks.tests"]]), with locked = true with value, minimum, maximum, allowed, required, when and unless. They mean what they mean in policy, including ordered check levels, tool version matching and the rule that tools are refused, not replaced. Name the setting by its whole path in quotes. A default is refused, because a project default is an ordinary value written in the setting's own table. Only settings a project file can set may be constrained, and not env.* or tasks.*. Credential destinations, trust controls and administrative settings are refused naming the setting. Selectors. context and provider behave as in policy. path is the target's folder relative to the folder of the root oyzu.toml (the Git top level, else the outermost folder with oyzu.toml, oyzu.local.toml or build.yaml, or --root), not the repository boundary that policy paths use. So a project's own rules keep matching when it sits inside a larger repository. explain --json reports it as policyFacts.projectPath. Only the root file. A [constraints] table in any other file is an error naming the file: a component folder's oyzu.toml (CONFIG_SCOPE: app/oyzu.toml:1:1: [constraints] is allowed only in the root oyzu.toml), oyzu.local.toml, user or machine configuration, and a [context.<name>] or [profiles.<name>] table. A misspelled section ([Constraints], [constraint], [constriants]) is ignored with a warning and a hint, and config validate --strict rejects it. An invalid entry is CONFIG_CONSTRAINT_INVALID naming the file, line and setting. Entries that cannot hold together in one context fail as policy entries do. Policy always wins. A project can never loosen policy. A project constraint that cannot hold together with the policy constraints that apply is set aside for that build: A floor or ceiling of an ordered or numeric setting is clamped to what policy allows. A project minimum = "required" under a policy maximum = "enforce" becomes minimum = "enforce" and still raises a lower folder value to enforce. A project maximum = "off" under a policy minimum = "enforce" becomes maximum = "enforce", and policy raises the value. A lock, an allowed set or a required set that policy rejects, or any project constraint where policy limits the setting with an allowed set, is dropped. A coverage floor that would lift another check level is resolved the same way. A policy coverage percentage lifts tests over a project lock of off (the project lock is dropped). A project coverage floor that needs tests above a policy cap is dropped and lifts nothing. Every command reports each case as a CONFIG_PROJECT_CONSTRAINT_SET_ASIDE warning naming the project constraint, the policy constraint and the value the build uses (checks.tests: project constraint minimum required in release (oyzu.toml [constraints]) is clamped to minimum enforce by admin policy maximum enforce (local-administration); checks.tests = enforce). When both layers apply and hold together, the project constraint replaces the folder value first and policy then replaces the project's value. Each step is recorded. What you see. Project constraint overrides are shown like policy overrides, labelled project constraint with source oyzu.toml [constraints]. oyzu config explain lists them under Constraint overrides (checks.tests required project constraint minimum in release (project services/oyzu.toml sets advisory)). The plan prints a project note and oyzu build --plan a Constraint: line. Plan and manifest targets record them in extensions["oyzu.dev/policy-overrides"] with constraint.label. Every command reports a CONFIG_CONSTRAINT_OVERRIDE warning. A project minimum of enforce or above on a check makes it run whatever checks.run says, as a policy one does. oyzu config validate --strict does not fail on CONFIG_CONSTRAINT_OVERRIDE or CONFIG_PROJECT_CONSTRAINT_SET_ASIDE, since tightening a folder value is not a configuration error. It does fail on CONFIG_RELEASE_LOWERED, which asks for a deliberate [context.release] value or a fix. Limit. --root selects the configuration root. oyzu --root app build reads app/oyzu.toml as the root file, and the repository root's [constraints] does not apply to that build.

How resolved settings reach a build: Builders register their own settings (docker.apparmorProfile, docker.frontends, docker.load). A builder reads the target's resolved snapshot, never the files. A frozen build configuration contributes its digest to target and action records. Formatting, profile names and presentation preferences do not change it. A policy snapshot grants no signing, publishing or credential authority. Planning needs the resolved snapshot of the invocation and of each selected target, including targets inferred without configuration files. A missing snapshot fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE and never disables policy checks. Edits to configuration files after a plan is frozen apply to the next invocation. Each target keeps serial mutation and hook order and has private workspaces and output roots. A failed dependency blocks its consumers while independent targets can finish. Explicit tool requests that cannot be bound to a verified installation are rejected before builds. Enforced registry routes or catalogs that need unavailable bindings fail before any download. Managed host tasks stay blocked because the host runner cannot enforce managed network routing. Task and native-adapter environment additions must satisfy administrative environment restrictions. Connector credentials and shell secret consumers are not available. The remote action cache is experimental and signs in only with a token from OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or a CI job's ID tokens (see the action cache).

[tools] declarations can be written, replaced and removed with oyzu install SPEC, oyzu uninstall and -g / --local, and in a toolset with oyzu --toolset NAME install SPEC. These keep comments and lock the result. See tool commands. A declaration is a version string, or mise's option table with only a version key (node = { version = "22" }), which validation turns into that string. Edits change only the table's version. Unknown option keys warn and are ignored. They do not install hooks, select platforms or change acquisition. A table without a valid version string fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE (see option tables). tools.lockPlatforms is an optional list of execution platforms, set in the normal folder cascade. It cannot vary by profile or context. Without it, lock coverage comes from the declared platforms of every build in the complete inventory, plus this host. Selecting fewer builds, a profile, a context or host-only execution does not narrow that default. With no declared platforms, coverage is this host. An explicit nonempty list replaces the inferred candidates and still includes this host. Use it to prelock tools for another executor even when no build declares that output platform, or to check its approved catalog coverage. Values are exact execution tuples such as linux/arm64/gnu and darwin/amd64/native, unlike the artifact platform names in build.yaml. Linux musl output maps to GNU execution metadata. Windows GNU and LLVM compiler recipes keep their ABI, while native helper and archive tools use MSVC. Platforms the provider supports bound the inferred coverage. Unavailable foreign auxiliary recipes appear in pin's platformsNotLocked warnings. An unsupported host or explicit platform fails without writing a partial lock. Catalog checks need the host plus the explicit platforms, while foreign inferred candidates stay optional. It selects lock metadata only, not output platforms or install authority. tools.platforms was removed. Rename it to tools.lockPlatforms, or remove it to use the inventory default. The old key gives a configuration error, never a silent alias.

Config commands resolve plugin builder references from the catalog metadata, configured bindings and oyzu.lock. They read installed package metadata without refreshing the catalog, installing or adopting a package, or launching a plugin. The selected package must contain the builder profile, satisfy the required engine features and have a usable payload for this host. Condition Result and fix Bound package has no adopted lock selection PLUGIN_NOT_ADOPTED. Run a normal build to adopt it Locked package is not installed PLUGIN_NOT_INSTALLED or PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE. Restore the approved binding and install it through a normal build Selected development executable has no admitted package metadata Warning PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_UNVERIFIED; inspection succeeds without launching the plugin or checking source freshness. Plugin-owned option validation is deferred to a normal build. Rebuild/rebind a stale plugin before execution; in this repository use oyzu run bootstrap -- --source --development-plugins An authored builder id is unregistered CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE at uses. Correct the id or configure its package Catalog, profile, engine or lock requirements refuse selection The usual plugin refusal stays. Inspection does not replace the selection or bypass policy The generic with object is checked, but plugin-owned option values and runtime capabilities are checked only by a normal build. An expired catalog's permitted locked replay is a warning in show, explain and validate, and validate --strict refuses it without refreshing metadata. Source-scoped commands such as config show --project inspect only the chosen file.

Code or symptom Fix CONFIG_SYNTAX, duplicate keys Correct the syntax or the duplicate declaration, then validate CONFIG_UNREADABLE A configuration file exists but your account can't read it (usually its permissions). Grant read access to the named file, then retry CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, CONFIG_SCOPE Use the setting's type and permitted file. set / unset can repair invalid values CONFIG_PROFILE_UNKNOWN Run oyzu config profiles and select an existing name. Use --no-profile only if policy allows it CONFIG_PROFILE_TOOLS Move [profiles.NAME.tools] to [toolsets.NAME.tools] and select it with --toolset NAME (see toolsets) CONFIG_TOOLSET_UNKNOWN, CONFIG_TOOLSET_INVALID Define the toolset in a project oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml in this folder chain, holding only a tools table plus optional contexts and platforms TOOLSET_BUILD_REFUSED, TOOLSET_UNSUPPORTED Use --toolset only with exec, run, env, activate, which, or project-scoped install, update and uninstall. Build with the [tools] versions, or use --verify-with TOOLSET_NESTED_LOCK Define the toolset in the project root's oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml to lock it, or use it with tools already locked Optional-setting warning, or a --strict failure Fix the spelling or remove the inert setting Unsupported schema major or required capability Use a compatible CLI. Remove a requirement only if the project no longer needs it CONFIG_POLICY_CONFLICT, CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED Reconcile conflicting administrative constraints or choose an allowed value. A missing execution binding must be provisioned first CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT Re-read the file and retry the edit. Do not overwrite another writer's changes CONFIG_LIMIT Reduce file size, nesting or the number of entries, including data in inactive profiles POLICY_INVALID Check enrollment protection and the policy cache. An administrator may need to repair bootstrap permissions or signing configuration POLICY_EXPIRED, POLICY_UNAVAILABLE Restore the endpoint and the native credential store, then run oyzu config refresh. A failure never turns an enrolled machine into a standalone one POLICY_CLOCK_UNCERTAIN Correct the clock and reconcile online. Do not erase rollback-protection state to get past the error An explicit config refresh can fail while an older valid cache stays stored. Refresh rechecks the time after I/O, so a request that finishes after a deadline does not extend authorization. Damaged credential-store state can need an administrator.

Global verbosity flags and OYZU_LOG are invocation-only presentation inputs, resolved before any project session. They are not project keys and never enter resolved configuration or its digest. Explicit CLI controls override the whole environment filter, and help and version do not resolve them. See CLI diagnostic controls.

oyzu.toml reference: every section and key with examples. Shell activation: env._.path, folder trust and shims. Tool commands: installing, pinning and updating tools. Build tasks: tasks, hooks and local versus CI builds. CLI output: human and JSON output. Publishing: destinations and evidence.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/declared-fetches.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A declared fetch names one file by HTTPS URL and SHA-256 digest in build.yaml. Oyzu downloads it while preparing the build, checks the digest and hands it to the build, which then runs offline. Use it to replace a RUN curl or a download in a script with a pinned input. Note: Declared fetches are experimental. Field names and messages may still change.

builds: image: uses: docker/image fetches: - name: migrate url: https://github.com/golang-migrate/migrate/releases/download/v4.18.1/migrate.linux-amd64.tar.gz sha256: <64 lowercase hex characters> unpack: tar Field Required Meaning name yes Target-unique name: a letter, then up to 63 letters, digits, _ or - url yes An https:// URL without user information, query or fragment sha256 yes Expected digest of the downloaded bytes, 64 lowercase hex characters unpack no tar (plain or gzip, detected from the bytes) or zip. Without it the file is delivered as is A target can declare at most 64 fetches. Two names that give the same environment variable, such as migrate-cli and migrate_cli, are refused. An invalid declaration fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE when build.yaml is read, before any preparation. Without unpack, the file keeps the last segment of its URL as its name. That segment may contain only letters, digits, ., _, + and -.

In a Dockerfile, copy from the named context oyzu-fetch-<name>: COPY --from=oyzu-fetch-migrate migrate /usr/local/bin/migrate The context holds the unpacked tree, or the single downloaded file. A Dockerfile that reads oyzu-fetch-<name> without a matching declaration fails during preparation. These context names are reserved and are never treated as images. On the isolated lane, fetches are captured before the Docker plugin plans the build. The planner receives each context's declared name and verified tree digest; the same captured inputs are mounted read-only for the image build. The worker receives only each declared subtree. Its private context copies and their container parent are readable by rootless BuildKit even when the host uses umask 077; permissions on the prepared fetches and their store stay unchanged. Command actions (prepare, task and package commands) get OYZU_FETCH_<NAME>, the name upper-cased with - replaced by _. It points to the file, such as /dependencies/fetches/migrate-cli/migrate, or to the unpacked directory, such as /dependencies/fetches/migrate. Content is read-only. Declared fetches are delivered only to container workers: oyzu build --isolated, and builders that use a container worker even in a native build, such as Docker images. A native host build of a target with fetches fails and asks you to run oyzu build --isolated. A builder that captures no dependency inputs cannot receive fetches and fails with a message naming the target.
