Without an administrator restriction, any HTTPS URL is allowed and HTTPS redirects are followed. No credentials are sent, and every redirect must stay on HTTPS. An administrator can restrict fetches with fetches.sources, a list of HTTPS URL prefixes ending in / (see configuration). Then: A URL outside every prefix fails with SOURCE_DENIED before anything is downloaded. The prefix is matched by path segment, so /tools/ does not admit /toolsets/. Every redirect must stay inside the listed prefixes, or the fetch fails with REDIRECT_DENIED. Project configuration cannot set fetches.sources, so a project cannot widen it. Setting it there fails with CONFIG_SCOPE.

Verified bytes are stored by digest under <user data>/cache/fetches/sha256-<hex>. Bytes are checked before they are stored or unpacked. A mismatch stores nothing, and a damaged store entry is replaced rather than trusted. A later build reuses the stored file without downloading. For builders that support offline preparation, --offline refuses a fetch that is not stored with DEPENDENCY_INPUT_MISSING. Run one online build to capture it. Docker image builds with declared fetches still require online preparation, even when every fetch is stored. Repeating oyzu build --isolated reuses those bytes; adding --offline fails before any action because captured Docker preparation does not support that flag. The isolated image build actions themselves run without network access. When unpacking archives, Oyzu refuses path traversal, links that point outside the tree and oversized expansion.

Each fetch is recorded as a package in the target's dependency snapshot: Field Value id fetch:<target>/<name> version, digest sha256:<hex> sourceId fetch:<host> standalone, or fetches.sources/<index> under an allowlist size Downloaded size in bytes purpose build verification digest-only: the digest matched, but no publisher signature was checked The snapshot extension oyzu.dev/fetches records each fetch's environment variable, path, build context name and tree digest. Both are part of the snapshot digest, so the plan records exactly what was fetched. Building the same declaration again records the same package identity.

Each message starts with its code and names <target>: declared fetch <name>. Code Cause Recovery CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE Missing digest, non-HTTPS URL, or a URL with user information, a query or a fragment Fix the declaration INTEGRITY_MISMATCH The downloaded bytes do not match sha256. The message shows both digests Check the URL and the upstream release before updating the digest. The observed digest has not been independently verified SOURCE_DENIED The URL is outside fetches.sources Use an admitted source, or ask an administrator to admit it REDIRECT_DENIED A redirect left the admitted sources Pin the final URL, or ask an administrator to admit its source SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE The server answered with a status other than 200 Check the URL DEPENDENCY_INPUT_MISSING An offline build needs a fetch that is not stored Run one online build

Only SHA-256 digests are accepted. sha512, Subresource Integrity strings and a command that prints a URL's digest aren't available. Builder recipes for common downloads, such as Puppeteer's browsers, reuse this engine; see installer-asset recipes. Credentialed sources are not supported. Dockerfile ADD <url> with --checksum is still refused. Use a declared fetch and COPY --from=oyzu-fetch-<name>. Native host builds do not receive fetches. docker/image targets with declared fetches cannot build with --offline, because captured Docker preparation does not support it yet. Their fetches are still stored and reused by later online or --isolated builds without downloading again. Only tar (plain or gzip) and zip can be unpacked. An offline RUN curl fails when it runs, and the error doesn't suggest a declared fetch. An npm install in a container build whose lifecycle script tries the network does: see downloads without a recipe. Windows and macOS builds with declared fetches aren't supported yet.
Installer-asset recipes for common downloads. Docker images for Dockerfile builds. Acquisition transport for how downloads are made.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/deploy.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu deploy <target> makes a verified directory artifact live on a GitHub Pages branch. It signs the planned change, pushes one commit, reads every file back, and signs a deployment record. No platform account is required. Use oyzu deploy for a static site and oyzu publish for finalized release artifacts and packages. Both consume build evidence; neither creates missing build provenance. Audit the built site before supplying its provenance to deploy. Status: experimental. This branch protocol uses system Git. Build provenance must already be signed by your accepted builder; deploying does not create historical build provenance. The GitHub Pages deployment API, SSH remotes and Git-hosted build commands are unsupported.

The following configuration is illustrative. Replace both public keys with base64-encoded raw Ed25519 public keys. Supply the corresponding deployment signing seed and repository token through the named environment variables. [deploy.targets.docs] kind = "github-pages" artifact = "docs/primary" repository = "example/docs" branch = "gh-pages" domain = "docs.example.com" tokenEnv = "DOCS_DEPLOY_TOKEN" [deploy.requirements.provenance] bundlePath = ".oyzu/evidence/docs.sigstore.json" publicKey = "BASE64_BUILDER_PUBLIC_KEY" builderId = "https://example.com/builders/docs" [deploy.requirements.signing] keyEnv = "DEPLOY_SIGNING_SEED" publicKey = "BASE64_DEPLOYER_PUBLIC_KEY" oyzu build docs oyzu inspect dist # Run the site's independent content/notice audit and obtain signed build # provenance for the recorded directory tree before the next command. oyzu deploy docs oyzu deploy docs --status The Node application builder records its static output as docs/primary, a directory artifact with a tree digest and per-file inventory. The native Windows build places it at docs/windows/x86_64/application-<version>; the recorded path and compatibility remain the builder's facts. Use the output name and path in your manifest. Deploy never reinterprets a loose native output folder as a bundle.

The repository's docs target produces exactly one docs/primary directory in dist/manifest.json. Deploy consumes that original bundle, not the docs-site/dist export used by the independent public-content and notice audits. The export must contain the same bytes as the selected artifact; changing it does not change what deploy reads. Rebuild and repeat the audit after any change. CNAME and .nojekyll are build inputs under docs-site/static, so they are covered by the recorded tree digest rather than added during deployment. The static-site audit accepts these exact site-root hosting paths and requires .nojekyll to be empty. A nested marker or another unqualified file is refused; the deployment domain check still validates CNAME. The destination is oyzuai/oyzu-docs, branch gh-pages, domain docs.oyzu.ai. Before applying it, retain all previously published release catalog identities and fingerprints, pass the public-output and original-notice audits, and supply accepted provenance whose subject is the exact docs/primary tree digest. The configured evidence path is .oyzu/docs-evidence/linux/x86_64/docs.sigstore.json for the Linux x64 docs workflow. Deploy treats the selected site tree as platform-independent, so this target uses an explicit evidence path rather than {artifact.platform}. The witness's producer platform determines its output subdirectory; use the matching explicit path on another host. A local witness is an observation under the configured builder identity, not protected hosted-build provenance. tooling/release-witness.mjs sign --artifact docs --manifest dist/manifest.json --out .oyzu/docs-evidence verifies the bundle through oyzu inspect and witnesses the recorded tree digest. A changed manifest, inventory or tree is refused. A signature over one file or an exported archive cannot satisfy the tree subject. This self-managed witness does not establish protected hosted provenance or a SLSA level. Actions supplies secrets.DOCS_DEPLOY_TOKEN as DOCS_DEPLOY_TOKEN only to the deployment step. It must select only the destination repository, with Contents read/write and Metadata read. A builder using the configured witness identity requires secrets.OYZU_RELEASE_BUILDER_SEED in its provenance-producing step; that secret is not supplied to the deployer. The existing deployment signer seed is secrets.OYZU_RELEASE_PUBLISHER_SEED, bound as OYZU_RELEASE_PUBLICATION_SEED. No token or seed belongs in configuration, artifacts, logs or local fixtures. Success requires oyzu deploy docs --bundle dist, followed by oyzu deploy docs --status reporting unchanged. Core independently reads the destination Git revision and every served file after apply. A separate fresh consumer must retrieve the serving branch and compare its site files and public evidence with the selected bundle. For a live rollout, also fetch the homepage, command-reference route, catalog and notices from https://docs.oyzu.ai and verify their bytes after Pages has deployed that revision. A successful Git push alone does not establish that Pages is serving it. Local acceptance uses an absolute path to a task-owned bare Git repository in place of repository, omits tokenEnv, and uses independent test-only evidence and deployment identities. Build a small real site through the compiled CLI, audit its output, deploy the resulting bundle, clone the branch into a fresh consumer and verify all files and provenance. Repeat unchanged to require no extra commit; changed bytes or invalid provenance must fail before a push. This exercises the Git branch protocol offline with installed tools. It does not establish HTTPS credentials, DNS, TLS or live Pages propagation.

Input Default Meaning <target> Required One named entry in deploy.targets. --bundle <directory> build.bundleDirectory (dist) Existing successful build bundle. --status Off Compare live revision and complete file inventory with the last signed record. --rollback Off Resolve the previous deployment's subject locally and deploy it under current requirements. --json Off Return structured facts or a structured failure on stdout. --status, --rollback and --bundle cannot be combined. The configuration cascade accepts deploy.targets and deploy.requirements in root project, user and machine configuration, with policy constraints remaining binding. Component-folder settings fail with CONFIG_SCOPE. Target setting Accepted values Meaning kind Deployer name Resolves <kind>/site; github-pages/site can use an embedded signed package when the CLI contains one. artifact Build/output name, or build for its primary output Select exactly one directory artifact. uses Optional plugin reference Overrides <kind>/site through the ordinary admitted package/development binding and profile contract. repository owner/repository, HTTPS Git URL, absolute local bare repository path Target repository. URL credentials, SSH and hosted build integration are refused. branch Valid Git branch name Serving branch; required. domain Optional domain Require the build's CNAME to contain this domain. tokenEnv Environment variable name Repository-scoped token for HTTPS Git; no token is needed for a local bare repository. Only kind, artifact, tokenEnv and uses are shared keys. Other target settings, including nested tables, numbers and booleans, pass unchanged to the selected deployer's target-plan for validation. repository, branch and domain above are specific to GitHub Pages. That plugin expands repository shorthand and enforces HTTPS and the build's CNAME. deploy.requirements.provenance uses the same accepted self-managed-key profile as publication evidence: a Sigstore v0.3 DSSE bundle with SLSA v1 provenance, the accepted public key and exact builder identity. Its subject must match the directory's tree digest. bundlePath is relative to the configuration file that declares the requirements. byArtifact profiles use the configured artifact selector. Current required verification lines and build report gates apply before the deployer can access the target. deploy.requirements and publish.requirements are configured separately; publication requirements do not supply deployment defaults.

Deployment does not search the plugin catalog. A catalog listing alone does not make github-pages/site available. After checking trusted development bindings, deploy uses an explicit plugins.packages binding, or, for github-pages/site only, the signed archive embedded in the CLI when no explicit binding exists. An explicit package binding takes precedence; an invalid or mismatched binding does not fall back to the embedded archive. Release builds can carry that archive, but a release version alone does not guarantee it is present. The archive is verified and installed offline through the ordinary official signature, complete-graph, identity, role and host-runtime checks. Neither an embedded archive nor a configured package bypasses these checks. For a CLI without the embedded archive, configure the exact approved package in machine/administrative configuration for CI. User configuration is excluded in CI, and project-scoped package or development bindings are refused. The following machine configuration is illustrative; replace the placeholder with the actual approved OCI release-root digest, not an archive checksum or executable digest: [plugins.packages] "github-pages/site" = { oci = "ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/github-pages@sha256:<approved-root>" } The first non-frozen deploy can adopt a supplied package and write its exact selection and all declared runtime payload identities to oyzu.lock after host validation. A frozen invocation refuses a missing selection. Existing locks reuse the exact installed root; a cold store also needs a matching explicit binding or embedded archive to reacquire it. A lock alone cannot populate a cold store, and a different bound or embedded root fails PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH without rewriting the lock. A warm developer store does not prove cold-runner availability. Trusted user/machine plugins.development."github-pages/site" bindings remain available for development under their ordinary scope and freshness rules. They do not demonstrate resolution through a released package. Package reuse never substitutes for fresh destination planning and independent read-back. The deployment signer is the self-managed Ed25519 signer configured by deploy.requirements.signing.keyEnv and publicKey. The key environment variable contains a base64-encoded 32-byte seed. Both intent and record use this signer. Registry subject signing does not apply to deployment.

Core verifies the recorded directory inventory and provenance, stages the exact files, and supplies them read-only to the deployer process. The site's own output must leave /.well-known/oyzu/ free. Core serves two evidence files: manifest.json: a public projection with schemaVersion = "v1alpha1", kind = "deployment-manifest" and one artifact object. Its fields are id, name, target, kind, digest, size and entries when recorded. Each entry contains only path, kind, digest, size, executable and unixMode when recorded. The observed Unix regular-file mode participates in the directory tree digest; retaining it lets readers verify that identity. Hosts without Unix mode observations omit it. Paths are relative to the served tree. Bundle locations, other artifacts, actions, environments, runner facts and extensions are omitted. provenance.sigstore.json: the accepted signed build provenance, byte for byte. Its signature and subject tree digest can be checked against the public inventory. Provenance is public too; use a builder whose signed statements contain only information suitable for publication. The deployer creates an orphan commit when the serving branch is absent. Authentication and network failures always fail; they never mean the branch is absent. Existing branches receive one normal fast-forward commit. A concurrent update fails with instructions to replan; there is no force push. An unchanged tree creates no commit. Core compares every read-back file digest and the applied revision before recording success. Symlinks, .git, .env files, package manifests and package-manager locks are refused at every depth. CNAME and .nojekyll must come from the docs build output. The deployer does not synthesize them or run a site build. HTTPS Git uses core's reverse credential proxy. The plugin and native Git receive a host-bound loopback URL; core alone loads tokenEnv and attaches authentication to the admitted upstream. The GitHub Pages package declares only https://github.com as a credential origin, bound to the target's repository setting. Owner/repository shorthand uses that origin. An explicit repository URL must have the same origin, including its port; a different HTTPS host needs a deployer package declaring that host. Core checks the planned URL against the package's describe.output.credential_hosts and the explicit setting before reading tokenEnv. Credential URLs must use HTTPS and contain no userinfo, query or fragment. A refusal sends no credential. An empty or unset reference fails; there is no OIDC fallback. Writes are permitted only during target-apply. Core verifies read-back using observations made after write authority closes, and independently compares the fetched Git files with the plugin inventory. Credentials never appear in plugin environments, arguments or files. The proxy limits request and response bodies to 64 MiB and refuses redirects and requests outside the declared destination. Use a GitHub App installation token or a fine-grained token restricted to the repository and necessary content writes. Native host execution provides best-effort process/network separation.

Local state lives under .oyzu/deploy/<target>/: signed intent, signed record, receipt, and signed subject history. The record names the subject digest, target, previous subject, signer, policy/verification facts, plugin identity and digest, applied revision and read-back inventory. A failed read-back leaves the prior successful record in place even though a remote commit may already exist; inspect the branch before retrying. Accepted provenance is retained with each local subject record. Rollback searches the recorded bundle, current bundle locations and .oyzu/history, then re-verifies the exact tree and retained provenance against current trust. --status returns unchanged or drift. Drift means the revision or any served file differs from the last record. GitHub Pages has no runtime signature gate: whatever lands on its serving branch may be served. Restrict writes to the deployer identity through repository permissions and branch protection, and run drift checks. A valid deployment record cannot prevent another authorized writer from changing the branch. Rollback requires the previous subject's local bundle and accepted provenance to remain available. It repeats current evidence checks and produces a new commit and record. Local state is not a remote archive or a retention service. Fresh CI containers have no deployment history unless .oyzu/deploy/<target> is restored from trusted persistent storage. With no last record, --status and --rollback fail, and a new record has no previousSubject. Deploying an identical live tree still creates no commit and writes a new local record. Remote record discovery and previous-subject retention are not implemented.

Diagnostic Cause Recovery DEPLOY_NOT_CONFIGURED Missing or unknown target. Configure root deploy.targets. DEPLOY_SUBJECT_AMBIGUOUS Selector finds zero or several outputs. Inspect the bundle and name one directory output. DEPLOY_SITE_REFUSED Forbidden content or reserved evidence namespace. Correct the build output and rebuild. DEPLOY_DOMAIN_MISMATCH Built CNAME does not match domain. Correct the native site configuration and rebuild. PUBLISH_HOST_REFUSED Planned credential URL has an undeclared origin, mismatches the explicit repository URL, or is not a valid HTTPS endpoint. Correct repository or select a deployer declaring that origin. No credential was resolved or sent. DEPLOY_PLUGIN_INVALID Invalid declared credential origin or credential host setting. Correct the deployer description and the named target setting. PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE HTTPS token variable unset, empty or invalid. Supply the repository-scoped token in the invoking environment. DEPLOY_PLUGIN_MISSING No package route or installed locked deployer, and no trusted development binding. Use a CLI containing the signed deployer or an admitted plugins.packages binding in machine/administrative scope for CI. A catalog listing alone is insufficient. PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE Locked deployer root is absent from the store and has no acquisition route. Supply a binding or embedded archive for that exact root; keep the approved lock. PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH Explicit or embedded package root differs from the lock. Restore the matching route or deliberately update the approved selection; deploy never silently replaces it. DEPLOY_PLUGIN_FAILED Git, target race, auth/network or plugin operation failed. Follow the nested diagnostic; check the branch before retrying. DEPLOY_READ_BACK_MISMATCH Live bytes or revision differ after apply. Inspect remote changes; no new successful record was written. DEPLOY_ROLLBACK_UNAVAILABLE Previous bundle/digest unavailable. Restore the exact retained bundle and its accepted provenance. Provenance and policy refusals retain their existing PUBLISH_, CONFIG_ or POLICY_ diagnostic. They do not authorize bypassing a gate. Local bare repositories work offline with installed tools/plugins and local signing material; HTTPS targets require network access.
Build bundles and artifact inspection Publishing CLI output Reference index

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/direct-tests.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu run test runs your project's tests on your machine and writes a test-only dist/ bundle with JUnit results, coverage and logs. Use it for a quick test run that still produces the same reports a full build would. Native cases.json attempt files may contain additional descriptive fields at the report, case, JUnit identity and individual-attempt levels. Oyzu ignores those annotations and retains the original attempt files. Known field types, outcomes, attempt identities and agreement with JUnit remain mandatory. Native retry declarations remain strict because they control retry eligibility. Fresh case-results.json files likewise accept descriptive additions on the report and individual cases. Runtime-read collections, source coverage bindings and digest-covered cached case records remain strict. The cache stores a canonical copy of accepted fresh case facts, so descriptive annotations do not prevent a later cache hit. The original native report is retained; cached copies still undergo strict decoding and digest validation. Reading these files does not convert annotations into test evidence or permit reuse. Invalid or contradictory facts still prevent a trustworthy result. oyzu run list oyzu pin oyzu install --frozen oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist oyzu run test -- --test-name-pattern=greeting It needs no Docker or account. Pin the project before a direct Node test and use oyzu install --frozen to install its selected runtime (see Node selection). Task preparation installs the locked Node quality set in the shared store when needed, including fallback reporting tools. Install your project's own dependencies and reporters first; the task does not install missing declared packages. Source admission and offline rules apply to managed preparation. See locked quality tools.

Project Test runner and reports Node, single package or npm/pnpm/Yarn workspace node:test, Jest, Vitest or Mocha, with JUnit and LCOV coverage. See npm workspaces and native workspace tests. Python with pip, uv or Poetry pytest, with JUnit and Cobertura coverage. See Python test reporting. Go module or workspace go test, with JUnit and Go coverage profiles. See Go testing. Rust app or workspace nextest JUnit, Cobertura coverage and doctests. See Rust test reports. Helm chart Local validation and optional helm-unittest suites. Coverage is recorded as not applicable. See Helm. Ant Assertion and JUnit targets. See Ant. Maven reactor Native tests and JaCoCo. See Maven. Gradle multi-project or composite build Native test reports. See Gradle. Docker targets don't produce test-only bundles. A supported test that depends on an unsupported one fails before running. The examples on this page use Node.

The builder recognizes the usual test runner, or an exact supported test command, and adds JUnit and coverage reporting. npm pretest and posttest scripts run as usual. A qualified name such as api:test uses that target's configuration and folder. A Go command-folder build such as path: cmd/api tests that selected package with native JUnit and Go coverage reporting; see Go direct tests. Your pre_/post_ hooks and prerequisites run in the usual task order. Arguments after -- go only to the requested task. Hooks and commands get OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT, the paths to write reports to. Each run uses a fresh private report folder. Test runs don't run packaging, lint or formatting. Use oyzu build for those and for artifacts.

oyzu build and oyzu run <target>:test pick the same test command: your Oyzu task if you defined one, else the package.json test script, else the builder's default. The command runs in one of three modes, shown in the summary and in the manifest's oyzu.dev/report-integration extension: Mode When What Oyzu does builder-default No test script or task. Runs node --test with JUnit and LCOV reporters. No extra packages needed. native-runner The script is exactly node --test plus plain --flag options. Runs the script through npm (so pretest/posttest still run, once) and appends reporter and coverage options after --. Scripts that name paths, reporters, coverage or watch options aren't changed, because Node ignores flags after paths. opaque Any other command. Runs it exactly as written. Reports are collected only if the command writes them to OYZU_TEST_REPORT / OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT (or a declared reports path). Missing reports are recorded as status: missing. Each test also gets a test-evidence record (oyzu.dev/test-evidence in the manifest, the Test evidence block in the output, evidence in oyzu run --json) with the status of the command, test results and coverage, and a verdict: Case Verdict Builder default or native runner, reports collected accepted Opaque command passed, reports missing, not required incomplete ("command passed; test results missing; coverage missing"); the run still succeeds Test command failed (any mode) rejected; the command fails and partial reports are kept A required report is missing (checks.tests = "required", checks.coverage = "required", checks.coverageMinimum, or a reports entry on the task) rejected with a report-missing error Builder default, but a report is missing The command fails Only reports written during this run count; older files are rejected. Oyzu never edits package.json or your configuration. An opaque task replacement has the same report rules as an opaque package.json script. Replacing node --test with a command such as argv = ["node", "-e", "process.exit(0)"] can succeed with incomplete evidence; it does not prove tests ran. Set checks.tests = "required" or checks.coverage = "required" to reject missing results. A positive coverage minimum or a task's declared reports entry also remains binding. You can also declare where a supported command writes a report: [tasks."project:test"] argv = ["node", "--test"] reports = [{ kind = "test", format = "junit", path = "reports/junit.xml" }] The path is relative to the task's folder. Missing parent folders are created. A recognized native Node command with one test owner writes to the declared destination, including when it runs through the workspace-test adapter. Redirecting JUnit leaves the coverage destination unchanged unless you declare that too. The assigned host paths preserve Windows drive and UNC forms. Declaring one report doesn't remove the other required kinds. No file may already match a declared path or glob before the run. Move or delete old files first. For a glob, your command must produce the matching files. A missing declared report fails the task even when the command exits zero. For a collected JUnit report, the copy in dist/ retains the bytes written to your declared destination.

dist/manifest.json links the JUnit and coverage reports (LCOV for Node, Cobertura for Python and Rust, Go coverage profiles for Go), their summaries, the plan and the logs. It lists no new artifacts. The command fails when tests fail, a required report is missing or malformed, or coverage is below the configured minimum. Failed test reports are kept when available. Native Node JUnit and coverage are copied independently. If one is missing, the available report stays in the bundle; the missing required report still rejects the command. No earlier report substitutes for a missing current one. A failing pre-hook blocks its test. A failing test skips its post-hook. A failing post-hook keeps the test's reports. Reports are collected after the post-hook, so a hook can transform them. A test that can't start is recorded as failed. Actions that never ran are marked blocked. Output is shown live and also saved in the bundle's numbered log files, including when tests fail. A task with interactive = true uses your terminal directly, so its output isn't saved. See task output. Only one oyzu run test can write a bundle at a time; a second one fails with a workspace-lock error.

Host tasks often build into dist/ before testing. A direct test keeps those files next to its reports and records their paths, sizes and digests under oyzu.dev/host-outputs. On Unix, regular files also keep their observed ordinary permission bits, including restrictive modes such as 0600 and 0700. These files aren't listed as artifacts of the test run. oyzu inspect checks the recorded bytes and file modes. Earlier Oyzu reports and logs move to history. The previous dist folder moves to .oyzu/history/<run-id>. Native output must be ordinary files and folders. Links, reparse points and files that collide with new reports fail. manifest.json, plan.json, envelope.json and logs are reserved names in dist. Move an application file with one of these names before running. If the command fails early, the earlier bundle may still be in place. Check the command's result and run ID rather than assuming dist belongs to the last attempt. A later full build can keep a preserved file at an artifact's destination only when it matches the new artifact exactly (kind, digest, size, executable flag and observed Unix mode). Different content or ordinary file permissions at the same path fail. See bundle retention and recovery.

A direct test run is local development evidence. The plan, envelope and manifest record oyzu.dev/invocation with: Field Value Meaning kind test A test-only run. execution host Ran on your machine. isolation none No sandbox; tests have your network and file access. source observed-before-run Source was hashed before the run; later changes aren't captured. toolIdentity unverified Ambient tools weren't verified. Actions declare network: host and aren't cached. Environment values are redacted in the plan. The tests' own output isn't scanned for secrets. In CI the producer is recorded as ci-unverified. A test run doesn't satisfy full-build checks and grants no publishing or signing rights. oyzu inspect checks integrity, not authenticity.

No test configuration is needed. Detection picks the runner, and the exact scripts jest, jest --ci, vitest, vitest run and mocha keep npm's pretest/posttest while Oyzu adds JUnit and LCOV. Your framework configuration still decides which tests run, reporters and coverage scope. Framework Tested version Also needs Jest 29.7.0 — Vitest 5.0.3 @vitest/coverage-v8 of the same version Mocha 11.8.0 c8 10.x in the project, or the locked default in Oyzu's managed quality set. See Mocha reporting. Single-package implicit Mocha tests use the reporter staged by the selected Node plugin. See Mocha support and limits. Install project dependencies before oyzu run test. Missing reporters aren't installed for you. Other major versions aren't tested. On Windows, npm is called through its JavaScript entry point, not a .cmd file. Scripted pnpm and Yarn combinations on the host aren't tested yet.

With no Node pin, oyzu build picks the latest LTS release that satisfies every engines.node range. If no LTS release does, it picks the latest matching stable release, and the plan explains why. For example, with 24.x as LTS and 26.x as Current, >=22 selects 24.x and >=26 selects 26.x. Pins in configuration (latest, 26, exact versions, lts/<name>) work as usual and must satisfy engines. The build writes oyzu.lock and installs Node before any action runs. It doesn't run tests at this point. Explicit versions in the nearest .nvmrc or .node-version up to the project root are read; without either, an exact devEngines.runtime version can supply the request. See native version selection. oyzu build --connector-bindings <file> supplies host bindings for tool sources routed by an administrator. See Node selection.

Direct tests are supported on Windows, Linux and macOS for Node frameworks and Rust (Rust on Windows needs MSVC; the windows-gnu toolchain lacks the profiler runtime). Helm direct tests are tested on Windows only. Docker targets have no test-only bundle. Framework and workspace support depends on the selected Node plugin. Use a compatible package and the versions listed in each framework's reference. Host tests aren't hermetic.
Build tasks for task order, hooks and output. Build bundles for bundle layout and history. Configuration for check levels and coverage minimums.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/directory-artifacts.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A directory artifact is a build output that is a whole folder, such as a static website in dist/, rather than a single file. Oyzu records every file and folder in it, lets you check the bundle later with oyzu inspect, and can copy it into another build with materialize. Note: Directory artifacts are experimental. Today they come from the Node application builder: conventional Vite builds and explicit node/app custom builds that write to dist/. Oyzu doesn't guess directory outputs for other build scripts.

In the build manifest, a directory artifact has the usual artifact fields (identity, target, producing action, version and bundle path) plus: Field Meaning kind directory. entries Every file and folder inside, sorted by relative path, including hidden files and empty folders. The root itself is left out. entries[].path, kind, size, executable Present on every entry. Folders have size 0 and executable: false. entries[].digest SHA-256 of the file's bytes. Files only. entries[].unixMode Observed ordinary Unix permission bits (0000–0777) for regular files captured on Unix. Included in tree identity when present; absent on non-Unix hosts. size Total bytes of all files. digest SHA-256 identity of the whole tree, computed from the sorted entries. It is not the checksum of an archive. Timestamps, absolute paths and user or group IDs don't affect the digest. Everything in the folder is collected, so names like dist, target or .hidden inside it are part of the artifact.

oyzu inspect <bundle> reads the folder without changing it and compares it with the manifest. Inspection fails when bytes changed, entries were added or removed, an empty folder is missing, entry metadata doesn't match, or a path is invalid. Inspection runs no tools or project scripts and uses no network. A passing check means the files match what the build recorded. It doesn't prove who produced them.

When a consumer build lists a directory output under materialize, the folder's contents land directly under the destination. An artifact containing index.html copied to site becomes site/index.html. The producing build must have succeeded. Oyzu checks the recorded content before copying and checks the copy afterward. Each consumer gets its own copy, so editing it never changes the producer's bundle. The copy fails if the destination already exists, two mappings overlap, or it collides with a source file. Producer and consumer must target the same OS and architecture. A consumer's platform requirement selects the matching producer variant; see matrix selection and Docker target selection. A directory output is never treated as platform-independent automatically.

Symlinks, special files, names that aren't portable and paths that differ only by case are rejected. To ship a tree with symlinks, produce a regular archive file instead. A tree can hold at most 100,000 entries and 10 GiB of file content. If a file changes while Oyzu is collecting or copying it, the operation fails. On Unix, regular-file permission bits, including restrictive modes such as 0600, are recorded and preserved when copied into a consumer or restored from a bundle handoff. A mode-only change fails inspection. Directory permissions, ownership, ACLs and special bits aren't retained. Unix executable bits are recorded and copied. On Windows every file is recorded with executable: false, so moving Unix executables through a directory artifact to Windows doesn't keep them executable. Static data folders aren't affected. Supported on Linux and Windows.
A failed collection can leave partial output on disk. It isn't a valid artifact and isn't reused. Fix the reported error, then rerun the producing build or restore an intact bundle.
Node applications Build bundles Host workspaces

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/discovery-selection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Discovery works out each Node or Python target's tools, such as its package manager or formatter, from your project files. When the files settle the question, you need no Oyzu configuration. When they don't, discovery stops and tells you which line to add to build.yaml. This page also covers how build.yaml and discovery decide which builds exist, and how Rust toolchain files are read. Discovery only reads files. It never runs a tool, script or configuration file, and it never picks a winner silently. oyzu build --plan shows every decision with its reason. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

If discovery reports a conflict, add the selector the error names under with and run again: builds: pytest: uses: python/package with: formatter: ruff conflicting Python formatter candidates black, ruff: black via pyproject.toml tool.black; ruff via pyproject.toml tool.ruff; declare the intended one for this target in build.yaml with `with: {formatter: black}` or `with: {formatter: ruff}` Then check the result with oyzu build --plan; see decisions in the build preview.

A role is one tool choice a target needs, such as its package manager, test framework, linter or formatter. Each candidate comes with evidence of a certain strength, and the strongest wins: Strength Examples declared A test script that runs exactly one recognized test runner. native A lockfile, package.json packageManager, a framework configuration file, a pyproject.toml tool table. conventional A declared dependency, a settings-only pnpm-workspace.yaml, a uv.lock that locks no packages. default The default when nothing else applies: npm, ESLint, Prettier, pip or Ruff. Two different candidates tied at the strongest level are a conflict. A candidate Oyzu has no support for, such as packageManager: nub@0.8.3, is unsupported. Both stop discovery; file order never decides.

A lockfile beats a settings-only pnpm-workspace.yaml. pnpm can write this file just to store settings; only its packages list declares a workspace. Without packages, the file is conventional evidence, so package-lock.json (npm) wins. With no lockfile it still picks pnpm over the npm default. A file with packages, or one that isn't a YAML mapping, is native evidence and conflicts with another manager's lockfile. The runner a compound test script names. If the test script isn't exactly a recognized command (jest, vitest run, mocha, …), but its &&, ||, ; and | parts name exactly one of jest, vitest, mocha or node --test, that runner wins. Parts such as pnpm lint, npm run unit or yarn unit are followed into the referenced script. Leading NAME=value assignments, cross-env, npx and <manager> exec are skipped. A script with quotes, $, backticks, parentheses, redirection or flags such as --filter isn't read; other evidence decides. The script still runs as written. Oyzu adds test reporting only to an exact recognized command. A uv.lock that locks no packages. uv records the project itself in uv.lock, so a lock with no [[package]] entries is conventional evidence and yields to poetry.lock or [tool.poetry]. A uv.lock that locks packages is native evidence.
documents.s: Native rules that settle a role without configuration

documents.t: With a build.yaml, its builds are the full list. Discovery only fills in an omitted uses and reports folders the file leaves out (see builds build.yaml leaves out). Without a build.yaml, discovery uses a project at the root, or searches below the root for projects. The search stops going deeper once it finds a project; that project's builder handles everything inside it. Nested Git repositories and folders with their own build.yaml also stop the search. A build.yaml that belongs to another tool (its root has none of builds, members and exclude, such as Dart build_runner's file) doesn't stop the search. oyzu discover lists it under Skipped with its root keys (which build.yaml files are Oyzu's). If such a file is at the root, discovery works as if there were no build.yaml. The search skips generated and dependency folders, goes at most 32 levels deep and finds at most 1,024 targets.

Discovery stays inside the configuration boundary of the command. An empty or broken .git marker in a parent folder doesn't make that folder the workspace. For sibling projects with no shared Oyzu configuration, oyzu -C first run list lists only first's tasks. In a real Git workspace, discovery includes all its projects, and an unqualified task that several targets have is ambiguous. Use the qualified task name from the error, or --root first to choose a narrower root. Linked worktrees and .git pointer files follow the same rules.

When discovery stops, declare the target and add the selector the error names under with (see the quick start). If the files match more than one builder, choose uses first. For example, a root with both package.json and Dockerfile needs builds: {app: {uses: node/app}} before the Node test runner can be decided. Builder with key Values node/app, node/package package-manager npm, pnpm, yarn test-framework node-test, jest, vitest, mocha, custom linter eslint, biome formatter prettier, biome python/app, python/package, python/library package-manager pip, uv, poetry linter ruff, flake8 formatter ruff, black java/app build-tool maven, gradle, ant The keys match the role names shown by --plan. Your selection always wins. Discovery still records what it saw. Any other value, a non-string value or any other with key fails. A selection applies only to the target's own folder. It doesn't change packages inside a Node workspace. Tool versions don't go here; set them in oyzu.toml. Another example error: conflicting Node package manager candidates nub, pnpm (nub unsupported): nub via package.json /packageManager; pnpm via pnpm-lock.yaml lockfile; declare the intended one for this target in build.yaml with `with: {package-manager: pnpm}` The suggestions list the supported candidates that were seen, or every supported value if none was. Choosing a tool your project doesn't actually use can still fail later, when that tool runs.

oyzu build --plan shows a Discovered table per target with each role, the chosen tool and the reason. With --json, each target has a discovery object mapping the role to selected and reason: package-manager npm native package-lock.json lockfile; outranks pnpm (conventional pnpm-workspace.yaml settings without packages) formatter ruff build.yaml with.formatter; discovery also observed black A reason names the winner's evidence and every candidate it beat (other than defaults). A real build keeps all observations and any selector in the plan's oyzu.dev/discovery extension.

The Rust builder reads rust-toolchain.toml and rust-toolchain in every form rustup accepts. Like rustup, it uses the nearest one, searching upward from the build folder and stopping at the project root. Form Meaning Legacy rust-toolchain holding only a name, such as stable, 1.95.0 or nightly-2020-07-10 The toolchain name. [toolchain] table, in either file channel (stable, beta, nightly, <major.minor>, <major.minor.patch>, optionally dated or with a host triple), components, targets and profile. A table without channel Oyzu uses its own default ([tools] rust in oyzu.toml, else Oyzu's default Rust) and keeps the declared components, targets and profile. path, a local toolchain folder Not supported. oyzu pin, oyzu build and build --plan fail with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_INVALID; set toolchain.channel to a release instead. A [tools] rust value doesn't override it.

A channel acts as a native pin only when [tools] rust would accept it: stable or an exact stable release such as 1.99.1. Any other channel (nightly, beta, 1.99, a dated or host-qualified name) makes builds, build --plan and oyzu pin fail with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_INVALID and a fix. oyzu discover still lists it.

An empty [toolchain] table, channel together with path, or an empty channel or one containing whitespace fails. Having both files fails with both rust-toolchain.toml and rust-toolchain exist, even though rustup itself would prefer rust-toolchain.
With a build.yaml, only its builds exist; discovery never adds one. It does two things instead: it fills in an omitted uses, and it reports folders the file doesn't mention.

A build may leave out uses. When exactly one builder recognizes the build's folder, discovery uses it. oyzu discover shows the build as build.yaml; builder detected from project files (builder_selection: inferred in --json). Builds that name uses show as explicit. builds: web: {path: web} # discovery supplies uses: node/app cli: uses: rust/app # written out: reviewers see exactly what was chosen platforms: [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64] exclude: [tools/scratch, tooling/**] If no builder or several builders recognize the folder, discovery, planning and builds fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, naming the candidates and the line to write: build both: both is recognized by docker/image and node/app, so discovery cannot choose; write the one you want in build.yaml, for example both: {uses: docker/image, path: both}

A folder that a builder recognizes but no entry covers is listed, never built. Command What it does oyzu discover Lists each such folder, the builders that recognize it, and the line to add (web: {path: web} when one builder matches). A folder several builders match gets an example: line with a placeholder, such as both: {uses: <docker/image or node/app>, path: both}. oyzu build --plan Names up to five under Not in build.yaml, then a count of the rest. A real build doesn't look for them or fail because of them. oyzu discover --check Writes nothing. Exits 1 with error[INVENTORY_UNDECLARED] and a table of folders while any folder is neither declared nor excluded; otherwise exits 0 with Build inventory is current. Without a build.yaml, every discovered build counts as undeclared. Add it to CI to catch new folders that would silently not build. oyzu discover --write Declares every undeclared folder that exactly one builder recognizes. --check and --write can't be combined. --write details: Each folder is added as one line with uses written out (web: {uses: node/app, path: web}), at the end of the builds: block. Comments, order and your own entries stay as they were. It creates build.yaml if there is none. It refuses a file whose builds: isn't a block mapping at the start of a line, a symlinked file, a file changed meanwhile, or another tool's build.yaml. A folder several builders match isn't written. It's listed under Needs a choice and the command exits 1 (outcome incomplete). If nothing else was written, the first line says A choice is needed: …; nothing was written. When it writes, it adds # yaml-language-server: $schema=https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu-releases/releases/latest/download/build.yaml.schema.json as the first line unless a schema comment is already there, so editors can validate the file (editor schemas). With --json, oyzu discover adds an inventory object with tracked, undeclared and excluded lists (or inventory.error, which never fails discovery). Plan JSON has undeclared: {total, folders, tracked}.

--write and --check print a build-inventory record with --json: Field Meaning mode The command mode. outcome current, undeclared, written or incomplete. path, tracked The build.yaml path and how files were counted. undeclared / added / needsChoice, excluded Folder lists. Each folder has path, builders, name, entry and, when excluded, glob. workspaceMembers Folders covered as workspace members, each with path, builders and the owning build. warnings Workspace manifests that couldn't be read, and one summary of unreadable folders encountered by the inventory walk. skippedBuildFiles Other tools' build.yaml files, each with its path and root keys. Plain oyzu discover --json lists them as skipped_build_files.

A folder listed as a member by the workspace manifest in a declared build's folder belongs to that build. It's never reported as undeclared, and --write never declares it. Builder Manifest in the build's folder Members rust/* Cargo.toml [workspace] members paths and globs (*, ?, […]), minus each exclude path and its subtree. A member listed by literal path stays a member even below an excluded path, as in Cargo. go/* go.work Each use folder (one module each, not its subfolders). node/* package.json workspaces (npm, Yarn; an array or {packages: [...]}) and pnpm-workspace.yaml packages The folder globs, minus those starting with !. A crate under crates/ that members doesn't list isn't a member (Cargo wouldn't build it), so it's still reported. Only the build's own builder counts: a docker/image build at the root doesn't own a Cargo workspace there. A build without uses asks every builder that recognizes its folder. A member covers only its own folder; the search continues below it. A manifest that can't be read owns nothing and never fails the check, plan or build. Its members stay reported, with a warning such as warning: build web: cannot read the workspace manifest package.json: …. Fix the file and run the check again. Human output counts members: Build inventory is current · 2 builds declared, 10 workspace members.

The walk starts at the build root and skips dependency and output folders, nested Git repositories and folders with their own build.yaml. It stops below a folder a builder recognizes. A declared folder owns everything below it, whether or not a builder recognizes it. The root never owns the whole tree while a build.yaml exists. A build declared at the root (path omitted or .) covers the root folder only; its workspace members are covered, and any other project below is listed until declared or excluded. Without a build.yaml, a recognized root is the only build, so --write declares just that. The walk continues below an excluded folder.

Zero-config discovery and the inventory walk skip folders they cannot read because access is denied or the folder disappeared. One Could not read folders: summary names up to five root-relative paths with their OS reasons, followed by and N more when needed. With a discovered project, the build reports this summary in its existing Warnings section; JSON diagnostics carry it on stderr. Before build discovery, oyzu build checks the same project boundary as oyzu run: Oyzu configuration, an Oyzu build inventory, a Git boundary or a recognized native manifest. If the root is not a project, the same bounded lookup used by oyzu run searches within three directory levels without opening child configuration; unreadable folders are skipped. Static markers are checked first. If none are found, eligible detections from the configured plugin catalog also count as project markers, at the root or within that same bounded lookup. This uses normal catalog verification and refresh rules; --plan and --offline use cached metadata. Configuration and catalog metadata may be loaded or refreshed before refusing. When either check finds a project, build discovery proceeds normally, supporting a zero-config workspace over child projects. A root build.yaml always passes the boundary check. If neither the root nor the nearby lookup finds a project, build refuses with PROJECT_NOT_FOUND (exit 5), before deeper build discovery, preparing a workspace or printing Building … or Prepare output. This applies with a target, --plan, --full and --json. Next: suggests oyzu -C <project> build. oyzu run keeps its navigation behavior: outside a project it refuses and lists nearby projects instead of running their tasks. Inside a recognized project, the discovery summaries described above still apply. If discovery finds no readable native project or declared build target, its PROJECT_NOT_FOUND error retains any unreadable-folder summary in human and JSON output. Select the intended project, or restore folder access and retry. This does not change which folders count as projects. Errors reading required files still fail, and skipping a folder during discovery does not exempt it from source capture or build input validation when a build needs that path.

Without a build.yaml, --write keeps the existing zero-config names (project at the root, project-<path> below it, such as project-web), so dist/ paths and cache identity don't change. With a build.yaml, a new folder is named after the folder, then its path joined with -, then a numbered variant if needed.

exclude: lists folder globs relative to the build root. It silences the listing and the check; it never changes which builds exist. Use / on every platform. Matching is case-sensitive, as in Git. * stays within one folder, tooling/** covers everything below tooling, and . is the build root. Absolute paths, .., backslashes and drive letters are refused. The key is exclude, not ignore, so it isn't confused with tools.ignore.

Inside a Git work tree only tracked files count, so a file a CI job creates can't fail the check. A folder is considered when Git tracks a file directly in it (read with git ls-files, no network, no index writes). Outside Git, or without git, every file counts and the output says so (tracked: all-files).

Selections are read once from build.yaml. When npm workspace tests and checks run on the host, each package (including the root) is detected again without them, so a root that needed a selection fails there. Node output profiles and the Python test framework have no selector. Undeclared-folder detection works per folder: an untracked manifest next to tracked files still counts. The catalog detection budget applies to the whole walk. Going over it fails --check and --write (with a fix) and is reported, not fatal, in the plan. Workspace members come from the manifests listed above only. Cargo path dependencies that are automatically members, Maven modules, Gradle include, .NET solutions and uv workspaces aren't read, so those folders are reported until you declare or exclude them. npm doesn't document ! in workspaces; Oyzu reads a leading ! as pnpm does. Discovery is tested on Windows. The walk uses no platform-specific paths.
Configuration for build.yaml, native pin files and editor schemas. Local builds and build tasks for what builds do. CLI output for the oyzu discover output.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/docker-frontend.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. docker/image builds run every Dockerfile through oyzu-buildkit-frontend, a BuildKit frontend that ships in the Docker plugin package. It runs the standard Dockerfile frontend of BuildKit v0.34.1 (the version its Go module pins) unchanged and adds two things: an approved list for Dockerfiles that request their own frontend with # syntax=, and a way to inject files into RUN steps. You normally only meet it when a Dockerfile starts with # syntax=. Oyzu loads the frontend from an OCI layout in the plugin package (share/buildkit-frontend), never from a registry. Preparation copies the layout into the prepared dependencies, which the BuildKit worker mounts at /oyzu-docker. A different plugin package changes the frontend and therefore the build plan.

A Dockerfile whose first line is # syntax=<reference> builds only if that reference is on the docker.frontends list (see configuration). Every entry must be pinned by digest: # oyzu.toml, user or managed configuration [docker] frontends = ["docker/dockerfile:1.17@sha256:<index digest>"] A request matches an entry when it has the same repository (docker/dockerfile and docker.io/docker/dockerfile are the same) and either the same digest, or the same tag if the request names no digest. An untagged request means latest. Oyzu copies the approved frontend image from your local Docker engine, for the build's platform, and loads it by digest. It never resolves the tag again. Anything else fails during preparation, before a worker starts: FRONTEND_NOT_APPROVED: Dockerfile requests frontend docker/dockerfile:1, which is not on the approved list; approved: docker/dockerfile:1.17@sha256:... An entry without a digest fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Oyzu never ignores the # syntax= line or substitutes its own frontend. Oyzu still parses the Dockerfile with the plugin's pinned BuildKit parser during preparation. Syntax that parser does not understand fails even if the frontend you requested would accept it.

When a build plan carries injection files, the frontend gives every RUN step: a read-only mount of those files at /oyzu-inject, and APT_CONFIG and SSL_CERT_FILE set to the named files inside it (a RUN's own value for either variable is replaced). The mount and variables exist only while that step runs. No layer, image configuration entry or history line carries them, and the base image keeps its digest. Your Dockerfile is not edited. A RUN that mounts something at /oyzu-inject fails because the path is reserved. Nothing in Oyzu supplies injection files yet, so builds currently run without injection and RUN steps are unchanged.

Injection reaches only RUN steps. A requested frontend's own planning steps (for example, reading a file from a stage) run before Oyzu rewrites its graph and do not see the mount. The frontend follows the Dockerfile frontend of the BuildKit release its Go module pins. Updating it means releasing the Docker plugin again. Generated image recipes (such as Python containers) use BuildKit's built-in dockerfile.v0, not this frontend. A Docker plugin package built without its Linux helpers has no frontend and fails preparation.
Docker image inputs and offline builds Configuration for docker.frontends

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/docker-images.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The docker/image builder turns a Dockerfile into a verified OCI image archive. Simple Dockerfiles that only add files to a base image build without any container engine. Everything else builds in an isolated, offline BuildKit worker. This page covers what the builder accepts, how base images and dependencies reach the build, and what a build records. Note: Image builds are experimental. The builder supports scratch, earlier stages in the same Dockerfile, provisioned local base images and public registry bases pinned by digest. Image build actions run without network access. On the captured lane, --offline also forbids network acquisition during preparation. That lane does not support offline Docker preparation yet and refuses before any action, even with cached declared fetches. Repeat an online oyzu build --isolated to reuse verified fetch bytes. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.
documents.s: Docker image inputs and offline builds

documents.t: The Docker plugin declares the following source contracts for captured builds: Stage Reads build (daemonless assembly) Dockerfile, .dockerignore, Dockerfile.dockerignore, and admitted COPY source roots, including directory descendants and newly added files. build (BuildKit) The same Docker controls and the native frontend's frozen context inventory after Docker ignore filtering. The worker receives only that inventory; a changed inventory changes the operation. lint Dockerfile, .hadolint.yaml, .hadolint.yml. format-check Dockerfile, .editorconfig when the target's own file declares root = true; otherwise unbounded because ancestor EditorConfig files may apply. test The upstream image archive. Validation inspects OCI structure; it does not execute image code. package The upstream image archive copied into the published artifact. To describe source reads, oyzu build --plan uses stage contracts from the target's last retained build plan, without preparing inputs or invoking the plugin or native frontend. Recorded reasons are marked as facts from the last build and do not admit cache reuse. Stages without a retained contract say reported when the builder answers. BuildKit's frozen context inventory is available only after native preparation. The typed image build embeds core's supplied version, not a separately computed source identity. Its source reads are bounded by the admitted context. Core can bind a development version and its frozen image name to the admitted shipping reads; a README outside those reads then leaves that version unchanged. For BuildKit, the reads include the whole context after ignore filtering. A README is therefore an input even when no COPY instruction names it, unless an ignore rule excludes it. Add README.md to .dockerignore if it is not an image input (or to the Dockerfile-specific ignore file when one takes precedence). Daemonless assembly instead selects only its admitted COPY source roots and Docker controls. An arbitrary host file outside the captured context is unavailable to RUN. Use COPY for project files that a RUN command needs; changing those files changes the build input. An edit to an unrelated host file does not make it visible in the image worker or change the captured source. dockerfmt keeps native EditorConfig support. A target-local .editorconfig with root = true stops the ancestor search, so format-check can use a bounded contract. Captured plugin planning receives a target source view without the project's ancestor view or project-root boundary. Without a locally provable root = true, it conservatively reports EditorConfig reads an unknown path above the target; captured planning does not expose project ancestors and keeps format-check unbounded, even if no ancestor file is visible. An unreadable file or an unsupported root declaration also keeps that fallback; no EditorConfig option is disabled or rewritten. The projected context's file list is also a version input. Adding or removing a selected file changes the snapshot version even if the shipping read declarations have not changed. An ignored file outside the shipping reads changes neither the version nor the version-bearing image operation. The Dockerfile and ignore files remain control reads, so changing a selection rule still changes the version. Image validation and packaging may consume a build artifact when its producer is included in the same confined shipping-read closure. Core retains a conservative whole-target version when it cannot admit that boundary: hooks or authored tasks, artifact inputs from producers outside the shipping closure, cross-target prerequisites, unbounded outputs, unsupported confinement, and versions without a safely replaceable source hash. A changed supplied version still changes the image operation and its cache key. Declaring bounded context reads does not bypass these fallbacks. Absent configuration candidates remain reads, so creating one invalidates the stage. Base images, frontend, captured dependency/fetch contexts and OS package snapshots remain explicit prepared inputs with their captured identities. Remote ADD, dynamic sources and unsupported capabilities still fail admission rather than acquiring undeclared inputs. The builder exposes no native-host build operation, so it does not produce host observed-read records. Context inventories exceeding the wire contract's 65,536 selectors retain a whole-target key with an explicit reason. Selective reuse needs a core release with projection-aware caching and captured version rebinding, followed by a Docker plugin release with these declarations. Older cores retain their conservative behavior. A checker with unbounded outputs still prevents narrowing, including format-check when its captured contract cannot bound those outputs. Prepared dependencies that include copied source can still miss after an unread edit. The package operation still copies to a version-bearing published filename; a changed version changes its argv. These declarations do not remove the action-cache limitation for host-coordinated image workers: those builds still run every action.

FROM alpine:3.22 COPY greeting.txt /greeting.txt RUN test -f /etc/alpine-release oyzu run list oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist No extra project configuration is needed. oyzu build prepares the inputs. The floating alpine:3.22 reference above must already be provisioned; to permit automatic acquisition, use a public base pinned as alpine:3.22@sha256:<verified-manifest-or-index-digest>. The base execution image must also be available. oyzu build --plan only previews the build. The output is dist/<target>/<platform>/<target>-<version>.oci.tar, with its digest in dist/manifest.json. For an image with a Helm chart, run oyzu install, then oyzu build. An online, non-frozen install records captured tool recipes as well as installing Helm. A frozen install consumes an already complete lock. A missing captured recipe stops build preparation with TOOL_LOCK_MISSING and the recovery command oyzu pin; no build action runs. oyzu run build is a native development command. It does not give you the isolated, verified build that oyzu build does. The Docker plugin never takes the native host path. A workspace that selects an image target, including an image that packages a host-platform binary, takes the captured path along with its producers. That path needs a supported engine. Without one the build stops with ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH (see plugin development).

The Docker builder ships as an external plugin package (oyzu-plugin-docker). It reads your Dockerfile and tells Oyzu what to run: assemble an image, run BuildKit, validate the result and copy outputs. Oyzu itself still fetches base images and OS packages, selects source files, runs the isolated steps, enforces policy and records artifacts. A plugin cannot grant itself credentials, mounts, frontends or publishing rights. A preview release needs user-level opt-in (oyzu config set --global plugins.preview true); a stable catalog release does not. A project cannot opt you into previews. Oyzu selects the signed catalog release and records its version and digest in oyzu.lock, without a package or development binding. See plugin catalog. The small compiled Go helpers that read Dockerfiles and image metadata, serve OS package snapshots and carry the BuildKit frontend ship inside the plugin package. Oyzu mounts them at /oyzu-plugin, so your machine needs no Go installation.

For BuildKit builds you need a Linux Docker engine. Docker Desktop on Windows and macOS works if it runs a Linux engine. Windows containers are not supported. Preparation and the quality checks run on the base execution image. The plugin package carries the metadata helpers, Oyzu's BuildKit frontend and the lint and format tools. RUN steps run in the rootless BuildKit worker oyzu-execution/buildkit:0.34.0, the upstream moby/buildkit 0.34.0 rootless image. Oyzu pulls it by its pinned digest when it is missing (see Published execution images). Oyzu uses provisioned local base images first. When Docker explicitly reports a digest-pinned base missing, preparation captures it from its registry into an immutable OCI input store, using your native Docker login for private registries. It does not load that base into the daemon. Floating tags must already be provisioned; they are never acquired silently. No separate base-image bootstrap task or manual pull is needed for pinned bases. Daemonless builds need none of this. After a BuildKit action succeeds, Oyzu waits up to 30 seconds for Docker to confirm that the worker container is gone. If Docker does not, the build fails and its output is not accepted. Check the Docker daemon and build again. If a build stops with cannot verify the BuildKit worker's AppArmor boundary, Docker did not report its security options in the expected form (docker info --format '{{json .SecurityOptions}}' should return a list of strings). Wait until the Docker engine is fully running and try again.

Image targets currently support linux/x86_64 only (linux/amd64 is an alias). ARM64 targets and multi-architecture images are unsupported. Do not use retained ARM64 identifiers or metadata as a supported build configuration. builds: image: uses: docker/image platforms: [linux/x86_64] Oyzu installs no image or emulator for you. A base image must match the platform of the stage that uses it: the target platform, or the worker's platform for a FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM stage. A base with the wrong architecture fails before export, even if the tag matches. A target built from another target's output (see target workspaces) must have the same OS and architecture as its consumer. Setting the image's platform sets the producers' platforms too. Every image is checked against its target platform when it is tested, collected and inspected, so a valid image for the wrong architecture is never kept as a success. RUN and the target platform. Oyzu cannot run foreign-platform code. A Dockerfile with RUN in a target-platform stage needs the worker and target platforms to match. If they differ, preparation fails before any action runs, even if your machine has an emulator. RUN in a FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM stage is fine.

If the final stage of a Dockerfile only adds files to one base and edits image settings, Oyzu builds the image itself without Docker, BuildKit or any container engine. Earlier stages may contain RUN if the final stage does not depend on them. They are skipped and not part of the image. Oyzu fetches the final base from its registry, adds each COPY as a layer and edits the image configuration. This is the approach ko, Jib and crane append use. Nothing selects it: the Dockerfile's content decides, per target. FROM gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12:nonroot@sha256:7f0c72cd138b442ae0deeb69c08b1acf5525439ba251a49ad93c320a061567e5 COPY bin/server /server USER 65532:65532 EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]

Instruction Supported form FROM The final base is scratch or a reference pinned by @sha256: digest (a tag may also be present), with optional AS name. No --platform. Earlier stages must also use scratch or digest-pinned bases. COPY Files or directories from the build context (no wildcards), plain shell operands or JSON form, --chown=user[:group] (names or ids) and --chmod=<octal>. Shell operands with quotes or backslashes use BuildKit. Relative destinations resolve against WORKDIR. WORKDIR, USER, STOPSIGNAL One literal value. ENV, LABEL key=value pairs with shell quoting, or legacy ENV KEY value. EXPOSE Ports with optional /tcp, /udp or /sctp; no ranges. CMD, ENTRYPOINT JSON (exec) form with any admitted base. Shell form with scratch becomes /bin/sh -c; shell form with an inherited base uses BuildKit. Use JSON COPY when a source or destination needs quoting, for example COPY ["greeting.txt", "/greeting.txt"]. Shell-form COPY greeting.txt "/greeting.txt" selects BuildKit so its native frontend handles quotes and escapes; they never become literal image-path characters. Use JSON exec form to specify the command and its arguments explicitly when inheriting a base image. It does not depend on that base's configured shell. Oyzu cannot assume an inherited base uses /bin/sh, so shell-form CMD or ENTRYPOINT selects BuildKit even when the base is pinned by digest. An explicit WORKDIR does not change this shell rule. With scratch, /bin/sh is only a configured command: your image still needs that executable if you intend to run it. When using a digest-pinned base, set an absolute WORKDIR before relative COPY destinations or relative WORKDIR instructions. This makes their location explicit instead of depending on the base image's inherited working directory. Without it, those relative paths select BuildKit. scratch starts at /, so relative paths there can use daemonless assembly immediately. Absolute COPY destinations alone do not change the working directory. In an unused earlier stage the same instructions are read, but its RUN instructions are skipped. For example, FROM scratch AS unused, RUN exit 99, FROM scratch, COPY greeting.txt /greeting.txt builds only the last COPY. These use the BuildKit worker instead: a RUN in the final stage, stage references such as FROM unused or COPY --from=unused, ADD, ARG, HEALTHCHECK, VOLUME, SHELL and ONBUILD, unsupported COPY flags, heredocs and variable expansion, a # syntax= or non-default # escape= line, a base pinned only by tag, and a .dockerignore or Dockerfile.dockerignore file.

Oyzu first looks for the exact digest-pinned reference in your local Docker image store. A matching OCI index or manifest is exported and checked: the index must contain the requested platform exactly once, and the manifest, config and every layer must verify. A local image that fails the identity, platform or export checks is an error. Oyzu does not go and pull a different image. Classic Docker stores that expose only a config ID cannot be used for local capture. If Docker is missing or not running, you pass --no-docker, or the image is not in the local store, Oyzu pulls from the registry instead. Registry pulls use the OCI Distribution API by digest, so a moved tag can never change the content. For an index, Oyzu uses the entry for the target platform (linux/amd64). Verified content is kept in your image cache: %LocalAppData%\Oyzu\cache\images on Windows, ~/Library/Caches/Oyzu/images on macOS, $XDG_CACHE_HOME/oyzu/images or ~/.cache/oyzu/images on Linux. The project's cache.dir does not move it. Later builds trust content already in the cache. Offline registry builds need it cached. Local images can be used offline. Under managed configuration, builds never contact a public registry. Any non-empty OYZU_NO_TOOLCHAIN_PULL also forbids fetching base-image content. Verified cached content can still be reused; uncached content fails with the requested image, digest and control in the diagnostic. Registry preparation reads your native Docker login from $DOCKER_CONFIG/config.json, or ~/.docker/config.json by default. Registry-specific credHelpers take precedence over credsStore and inline auths. Helpers must be available on PATH. When a helper reports that it has no credentials for the registry, Oyzu continues anonymously, as the Docker CLI does; any other helper failure stops preparation. Use docker login <registry> before building a private base; Oyzu adds no registry setting. Credentials stay in preparation and are scoped to the registry authority, including its port. They are never supplied as build arguments, copied into the image, or written into the dependency inventory. A credentialed token exchange must stay on the registry's own origin. The one exception is Docker Hub: credentials for docker.io, index.docker.io or registry-1.docker.io may go to https://auth.docker.io on the default port, a pairing Oyzu decides from its own registry resolution, never from the challenge. Any other separate authentication origin requires native docker pull provisioning instead. Error messages never repeat the registry's authentication challenge. Denials fail preparation with guidance to check native login; there is no public fallback. Native identity-token refresh (identitytoken or a helper's <token> username) is not supported by registry preparation. Provision these bases with native docker pull instead. Keep native login files outside the project. Source capture refuses literal credentials in recognized native registry configuration files; use user-level configuration or authored environment references instead. Environment references are captured as written, never expanded into source evidence. This also covers project-contained files selected through DOCKER_CONFIG, even when the directory is not named .docker. BuildKit consumes local daemon images and verified OCI inputs captured during preparation. Pin a private base by digest, or provision a tag-only private base with native docker pull. This does not add a BuildKit registry pull path. HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY and SSL_CERT_FILE apply as for other Oyzu downloads. A loopback registry (localhost:5000/...) is contacted over plain HTTP. A base with ONBUILD triggers, zstd or foreign layers, or a different platform from the target fails.

Base layers are copied byte for byte. Docker schema 2 bases are written with the equivalent OCI media types. Each COPY becomes one gzip layer, and so does a WORKDIR that creates a directory. Entries are sorted, stamped with 1980-01-01 UTC and carry numeric ownership only. Files are 0644, or 0755 when they are executable on a Unix host or start with an ELF header or #!. Directories are 0755. --chmod overrides both. New files and directories that COPY creates belong to --chown, or root. Names are looked up in the base image's /etc/passwd and /etc/group, and an unknown name fails the build. Without a group, the user id is also the group id, as in Docker. Directories already in the base keep their owner. The configuration comes from the base, with Env, Labels, User, WorkingDir, ExposedPorts, Cmd, Entrypoint and StopSignal edited as Docker does. An ENTRYPOINT drops an inherited CMD unless the Dockerfile sets one. An image without PATH gets Docker's default. COPY can read the files under each source in the target folder, plus artifacts you materialize into it. Nothing else in the workspace is visible.
