The output has the same layout, name annotations, checks and reports as a BuildKit build. Rebuilding the same inputs gives the same image digest on any machine. It is not byte-identical to what BuildKit would build from the same Dockerfile.

dist/dependencies/<target>.json names the adapter docker/oci-assembly and records: imageSource: registry or provisioned-local. The base's requested reference, manifest digest, config digest and content-tree digest (under images). The files selected from the context and the Dockerfile digest. The selected context is a source projection, which is eligible for the action cache. Its definition and captured file identities enter the target key. Bounded stages key the projected files they read; other stages retain the whole-target key. A changed projected input invalidates its readers, and oyzu cache explain names a changed projection. This does not expand Docker's supported context or COPY paths. Oyzu checks the Dockerfile and base against those identities before it writes anything. The build action records oci-assembly as its execution mode and that it used no container engine and ran no project code.

If Docker cannot provide the execution image (for example on a host or pod with no engine), a daemonless target still builds. Oyzu's own executable acts as the worker. Captured plugin planning still runs in isolation, with read-only source and no network. It uses the base execution image as an unpacked Linux root filesystem through the daemonless sandbox. The image is selected by its published digest and reused after installation. A compatible Linux engine member, plugin package and working crun/user namespaces are required, including for FROM scratch. If that runtime is unavailable, preparation refuses; the planner never runs directly on the host. Build and packaging retain their separate in-process identity, and the frozen preparation records the planning runtime and its asset placements. In-process assembly does not stage Dockerfile lint or format tools. Its planner still requires the admitted plugin package and runtime described above. oyzu build --isolated --no-docker accepts such a target when its selected work is just the build and packaging. The plan shows needsDaemon: false and isolation: in-process. Tasks that need the execution image still need Docker. --full adds Dockerfile lint (hadolint) and format checks (dockerfmt), so the build stops with NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON (exit 3) before preparation. Dockerfiles that are not daemonless have the same refusal. A digest-pinned base with ONBUILD triggers fails. Oyzu does not run the triggers or fall back to BuildKit.

Image selection can use ordinary Dockerfile ARG defaults, with no Oyzu configuration: ARG REGISTRY=docker.io/library ARG VERSION=3.22 ARG BASE=${REGISTRY}/alpine:${VERSION} FROM ${BASE} RUN test -f /etc/alpine-release Only ARG lines before the first FROM take part in choosing the base and platform. Defaults expand in order using BuildKit's own quoting, escaping and expansion rules. A later declaration with a value replaces an earlier one. A declaration without a value keeps the existing default. You can use expressions such as ${BASE:-alpine:3.22}. An empty base or empty explicit platform fails preparation. ARG inside a stage is not a global default, and host environment variables are never read. If an argument resolves to scratch or an earlier stage, it adds no external image. A stage's platform must be the target platform or the worker's (FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM). Anything else fails. A base for a worker-platform stage is captured for the worker's platform and bound as the BuildKit context <name>::<platform>, so one reference can serve both a build stage and the target stage.

Arguments Value TARGETPLATFORM, TARGETOS, TARGETOSVERSION, TARGETARCH, TARGETVARIANT The target platform. TARGETSTAGE The final stage name, or default if it has none. BUILDPLATFORM, BUILDOS, BUILDOSVERSION, BUILDARCH, BUILDVARIANT The Docker toolchain worker's platform. It is checked against the worker during planning. The target platform is never assumed to describe the worker. SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH Set by Oyzu. A global ARG SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH makes it available to image selection and overrides the Dockerfile's default. Without that declaration it is not part of global selection. A declaration inside a stage can expose it to RUN commands separately. A global declaration can replace the target defaults. For example, ARG BASE=registry.example/runtime:${TARGETARCH} selects an architecture-specific image without reading the host architecture. These values do not let you run foreign-platform code. RUN still needs matching target and worker platforms. The common cross-compile pattern works: FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang AS build, then COPY --from=build into a target-platform stage with no RUN. Foreign ARM64 image targets remain unsupported. RUN in the target-platform stage still fails before any action runs. Hadolint's rules about explicit FROM --platform flags still apply. You cannot override build arguments on the command line, and variables in stage-level mounts are not expanded.

with.repository names the image's registry repository (no scheme, tag or digest), such as registry.example.com/team/app. Building never publishes to it or contacts it. A helm/chart image binding reads it to name the image it uses. with option Values Meaning repository A repository name without scheme, tag or digest The image's repository. dependencies A provider name Selects the offline dependency provider. docker/image accepts only these two with options. oyzu config validate and every command that reads the build inventory reject others. Where a built image is loaded locally is set by docker.load, not by with.

The docker.load setting lists where oyzu run load puts an image you already built, so a local cluster can run it without a custom docker load step. # build.yaml builds: image: uses: docker/image with: repository: registry.example.com/team/app # names the loaded image # oyzu.local.toml (Git-ignored), or oyzu.toml for a team default [docker] load = ["docker", "k3d:dev"] oyzu build oyzu run load # or: oyzu run image:load when several targets exist oyzu config explain docker.load --target image # where the list came from Which cluster you use is personal, so the list lives in configuration and not in build.yaml. Put a team default in oyzu.toml and your own cluster in oyzu.local.toml or user configuration. Like other per-target settings, it applies to the docker/image builds in its folder and below. The nearest file wins, and [context.<name>] and profile tables can vary it. The image is named by the build's with.repository. oyzu.local.toml is ignored in CI unless you pass --local-overrides (inspection and selection). Changing it does not rebuild anything. Destination What happens Needs docker docker load of the archive, docker tag as <repository>:<version>, then docker image inspect <repository>@<digest> must succeed. Docker Desktop Kubernetes shares this engine. docker on PATH, using Docker's containerd image store (which keeps OCI manifest digests). Another store fails the inspect with an explanation. k3d:<cluster> k3d image import of the archive, then on every server and agent node ctr -n k8s.io images tag names the image <repository>@<digest> and <repository>:<version>. docker and k3d on PATH (install k3d with oyzu install k3d) and a running cluster. The task never builds, pushes or contacts a registry. It reads the latest dist/manifest.json (the build must have succeeded and the archive must still match its recorded digest), picks the single OCI archive for this target, and makes the image available as <repository>@<manifest digest>. A bound chart uses that reference, so a deploy pulls nothing. Loading is a compiled core task, including when an external Docker builder package produced the image. It does not require the package to implement a native task-command operation. Rules and failures: A list holds zero to eight distinct destinations. load = [] in a nearer file turns off a default from a farther one. If docker.load reaches a build without with.repository, the load task is listed as unavailable with that reason. Other commands are not affected. An unknown or repeated destination is rejected when the value is read. oyzu config validate reports it and every command that reads that configuration fails. The old with.load key is rejected with a message that points here. A platform matrix with several image variants is refused. Loading one chosen variant is not supported. Pushing to a registry is not part of loading. Use oyzu publish.

When a build needs one of Oyzu's execution images and your Docker engine doesn't have it, Oyzu pulls it by the digest pinned in src/executor/published_images.json and tags it with the name the build expects. The registry verifies the content, so a moved tag can't swap in a different image. No login or credentials are involved. Pinned today: the base execution image oyzu-execution/base:1, from ghcr.io/oyzuai/oyzu-execution/base (linux/amd64 supported), and the BuildKit worker oyzu-execution/buildkit:0.34.0, from docker.io/moby/buildkit (0.34.0 rootless). Dockerfile bases are acquired only by digest into prepared OCI stores, as described below. Execution images you supply with --image still require explicit provisioning. An image already on your machine is used as is, never replaced. Set OYZU_NO_TOOLCHAIN_PULL=1 to forbid execution-image pulls and base-image acquisition, for example on an air-gapped host. An uncached base then fails with a message that names the image, digest and control; locally provisioned images and verified cached base content remain usable. Limits: The pinned digests are not yet recorded in oyzu.lock. A pulled image is trusted by its pin and not re-checked on later runs. Pulls cannot go through a tool broker or private mirror.

Isolated builds add Docker resources, so Oyzu limits the ones it creates. It never touches anything it did not create. A resource is Oyzu's only if it carries the label dev.oyzu.owner=oyzu or is recorded in the per-user ledger docker-storage.json (in the cache folder of Oyzu's user data directory). Containers and volumes are labelled when created. Docker cannot label an image after a pull, so images are recorded instead: an execution image Oyzu pulled by its pin (images in ghcr.io/oyzuai/oyzu-execution/ that an earlier run pulled are adopted on the first pass) and container tools Oyzu installed. A locally built base image, Dockerfile base images and anything you pulled yourself are never listed, measured or removed. Setting Values Default Meaning cache.dockerMaxMiB 1 to 1048576 MiB 20 GiB The budget for recorded images. Set it in the ordinary configuration cascade. It is not part of any action key. After an isolated build that used a Docker image, Oyzu cleans up under a lock shared by builds: Images. Recorded images that lost their tag to a newer pinned image, and those unused for 60 days, are removed. Then the least recently used are removed until the recorded images fit in cache.dockerMaxMiB. Images used by the build that just finished are never removed, and Docker refuses to remove an image a container uses. Containers. Labelled containers that exited over an hour ago are removed along with their anonymous volumes. This includes the BuildKit worker's private store, so BuildKit's cache cannot outlive its worker. Volumes. Unused labelled volumes are removed. Persistent oyzu-tools-* volumes follow their own retention (see build logging). Cleanup is best effort. A failure leaves the work to the next isolated build and never changes a build's result. Host builds add no Docker resources and run no cleanup. The 60-day and one-hour ages are fixed. oyzu cache status shows the recorded image count, size and budget on its Docker line (and under docker in --json). It leaves the line out if Oyzu has recorded no image or cannot query Docker. oyzu cache clear empties the action cache only.

A native parser reads your Dockerfile to find the images it needs, without running any Dockerfile command. Global ARG defaults are expanded with BuildKit's own expansion library. Dynamic mount references, remote ADD, secret and SSH mounts and host networking are rejected. A # syntax= line builds only if it is on the digest-pinned docker.frontends list (see Oyzu's BuildKit frontend). To bring in a pinned download instead of remote ADD or RUN curl, declare a fetch and copy from the named context oyzu-fetch-<name>. Oyzu inspects each local image and exports it by its immutable identity, so a tag change in between cannot substitute another image. An explicit local miss permits registry acquisition only for a digest-pinned reference. A daemon permission refusal, transport failure or invalid local image remains an error. Oyzu never starts a base during capture and never gives project code the host Docker socket. An offline Go adapter verifies a daemon export and writes its OCI content store. Registry capture uses the existing anonymous OCI Distribution client and content cache, preserving the requested manifest or index digest and verifying every acquired blob. Both paths check the selected platform and layer identities. Registry-captured inputs support plain or gzip layers; unsupported encodings fail. Images containing ONBUILD fail, because their hidden inputs are not part of discovery. Oyzu freezes the stores and records the reference, config digest, manifest digest and store digest for each image. Before the worker starts, it copies each store to private storage and checks it against the plan. BuildKit receives the stores as OCI named contexts. The worker and RUN steps stay offline. The stores are read-only inputs to the worker and are not mounted into RUN containers. No shared build cache is imported. The identities are recorded under extensions.oyzu.dev/docker.images in dist/dependencies/<target>.json, and they feed the dependency and build plan digests. For these captures, imageSources maps each prepared store (such as images/base-0) to provisioned-daemon or registry; a single build may use both. This replaces the single imageSource label for BuildKit preparation. metadata.selection records the target platform and the export epoch. Planning rejects values that disagree with the selected target. The manifest digest of a daemon-captured image can differ from the registry's original manifest, because docker save does not keep every registry representation. Oyzu verifies the config identity and captured content without inventing registry provenance. Registry capture keeps the requested digest in reference, the selected platform manifest in manifest, and the verified config and store digests; it never resolves a floating tag to choose content. These facts enter the dependency record and plan, not a new oyzu.lock image section. A successful build keeps the versioned <target>-<snapshot-version>.oci.tar archive and its OCI digest in dist/manifest.json, plus integrity and platform JUnit results and lint and format results. These checks do not measure application code coverage. Producers you materialize into the image keep their own test and coverage reports. Version inference supplies a tag-derived base version and a source-derived snapshot suffix. The image reference uses the same version. A changed base image changes the plan and content digests even if the version string is the same.

Before the worker starts, Oyzu sets the file and directory access and modification times of its private copies of the source, Dockerfile, materialized artifacts and dependency contexts to the export epoch (1980-01-01 UTC). This makes identical inputs behave identically. Your originals and the prepared stores are unchanged. On Unix, file modes are also normalized, keeping executable bits and dropping umask differences. If a timestamp cannot be set, the worker does not start. Oyzu passes the same fixed epoch explicitly to both the Dockerfile frontend (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH) and the OCI exporter (source-date-epoch), with BuildKit layer timestamp rewriting enabled. The exporter uses it for image creation metadata, layer timestamps and the OCI descriptor creation annotation, including when a frontend returns only platform-scoped epoch metadata. No image post-processing is performed. This does not freeze application clocks, randomness or other file metadata. Installers keep their normal metadata, and the Dockerfile needs no change. Images built by an older Oyzu need to be rebuilt.

Within one oyzu build, each distinct base is exported with docker image save and converted once. Other targets that need the same base (same reference, Docker image ID, target platform and converter image) wait for it and get a verified copy. This keeps several targets on one large base from holding several copies in Docker's memory. Captures are kept in the system temporary directory and deleted when the build finishes. A failed capture is not reused, and separate oyzu build processes do not share captures. Oyzu gives the BuildKit worker each captured base as a private copy made with docker cp before the worker starts, not as a bind mount. The source context, definition and output folders are still bind-mounted. The copy is checked against its planned digest, owned by root inside the worker, and removed with it. A Dockerfile that changes while it is being copied is rejected rather than run. Python application packaging with container: true uses this path (see Python containers).
documents.s: Sharing base images and copying them in

documents.t: A dependency context is a read-only package store that Oyzu prepares before the offline build. A Dockerfile reads it through an external context named dependencies. The sections below each give a complete example. Dockerfile RUN instructions own the reproducibility of files they create. Oyzu does not rewrite user-authored layers. A stable plan and verified offline dependency archives do not make timestamp-bearing installer state or runtime caches reproducible; remove unnecessary state in the Dockerfile or use the native tool's controls. Provider Native inputs The base image must already contain python/pip requirements.txt Python 3.11 or later and pip python/uv pyproject.toml and uv.lock Python, pip and uv python/poetry pyproject.toml and poetry.lock Python, pip, Poetry and its export plugin node/npm package.json and a v2 or v3 package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json Node and npm node/yarn package.json and a Yarn Classic yarn.lock Node, Yarn Classic 1.22.22 and @yarnpkg/lockfile 1.1.0 node/pnpm package.json and a single-project v9 pnpm-lock.yaml Node, pnpm 10.11.0 and yaml 2.8.1 go/modules go.mod or go.work Go and a POSIX shell (plus a C compiler for cgo) rust/cargo Cargo.toml and a checked-in Cargo.lock Rust/Cargo 1.94.0, a POSIX shell and the project's native compiler and linker All providers: Oyzu installs none of the tools. A missing tool in the base fails preparation. Preparation downloads from the public registry for that ecosystem, then the build runs offline. Private registries, direct URL or VCS dependencies, managed connector authorization and a persistent download cache are not supported. Oyzu puts no registry token in the image, build arguments or Dockerfile. Stale lock files, failed integrity checks and unsupported inputs fail preparation, before any action runs. Fix the inputs or the base and build again. The dependency record (dist/dependencies/<target>.json) keeps package identities and digests, source and lock identities, the observed tool versions and the base image identity. Package integrity is not a release approval. One matching provider is picked automatically. If several match, set with.dependencies (see Selecting a provider).

For a Docker target, an external context named dependencies asks for a prepared package store. With one Python ecosystem and a requirements.txt, you do not need to select a provider. Choose the Docker builder explicitly if the project also looks like an application: builds: image: uses: docker/image FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ pip install --no-index --no-cache-dir --no-compile --find-links=/dependencies -r requirements.txt COPY app.py . CMD ["python", "app.py"] Add application files with ordinary COPY. --no-compile avoids bytecode timestamps in the example. Use python -B for import checks during the build. A requirement such as six==1.17.0 is resolved by pip inside the exact base image, with its Python, pip, ABI and platform. Preparation downloads binary wheels through Oyzu's public-PyPI proxy. It adds no build, test or quality tools to the store and runs no project code or source builds. The Docker build then installs from the store with no network. Oyzu does not rewrite your RUN commands.

If other ecosystems' manifests make automatic selection ambiguous, name the provider with with.dependencies: builds: image: uses: docker/image with: dependencies: python/pip The value must be one provider name. oyzu config validate rejects anything else. The old top-level dependencies: build field is rejected with a message pointing at with.dependencies. Several matching managers need an explicit with.dependencies, even within Python. Unknown providers and missing native manifests fail. with.dependencies without an external dependencies reference also fails. A Dockerfile stage that is actually named dependencies stays a normal stage. Other external names are treated as image references.

uv uses its locked, offline export with --no-default-groups. Poetry uses its export plugin for the main group, with project plugins off. Stores exclude development groups and optional extras. A stale lock or hash mismatch fails. Local, path and VCS dependencies and extra indexes are not supported. uv and Poetry projects use their own lock, not a nearby requirements file. All three Python providers add a generated requirements.txt next to the wheels, pinning the whole selected closure with SHA-256 hashes. A uv or Poetry project can install from it without copying its lock into the image: RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ pip install --no-index --no-deps --require-hashes --no-cache-dir --no-compile --find-links=/dependencies -r /dependencies/requirements.txt uv's uv pip install can use the same file. uv sync and poetry install are not supported inside the build.

The base image must already be local and provide Python 3.11 or later with pip. The worker and target platforms must match for package preparation, even if the Dockerfile only copies files. With earlier named stages, the consumer is the stage's original base. Several different consuming bases, a scratch consumer or mismatched platforms fail instead of sharing an unchecked set of packages. Preparation uses the base's captured config, not a tag that may have moved. If later commands change the interpreter or libraries in the stage, compatibility is up to you. The dependency record keeps wheel identities and digests, source and lock identities, the interpreter and manager versions and a digest of the store. Only the wheels and the generated requirements enter BuildKit's context. Direct URL requirements, alternate-index directives and source distributions are rejected. Remote syntax frontends and secret mounts are not supported.

node/npm exports verified registry tarballs using the Node builder's locked acquisition. A Docker target with package.json and a v2 or v3 package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json picks this provider automatically (shrinkwrap wins, as in npm). With several ecosystems, set with.dependencies: node/npm. FROM registry.example.com/build/node:22-npm11 WORKDIR /app COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ export NODE_DISABLE_COMPILE_CACHE=1 \ && for archive in /dependencies/*.tgz; do npm cache add "$archive" --offline --cache /tmp/npm-cache --ignore-scripts; done \ && npm ci --offline --cache /tmp/npm-cache --ignore-scripts --omit=dev --no-audit --no-fund \ && rm -rf /tmp/npm-cache COPY app.js . CMD ["node", "app.js"] The example base is one you provision that contains Node and npm. npm enables Node's module compile cache. The example uses Node's native NODE_DISABLE_COMPILE_CACHE=1 control for the install RUN, so this execution-time optimization is not shipped in the application image. It leaves the installed packages and application runtime unchanged. Copy all workspace manifests and sources for a workspace install. Copy npm-shrinkwrap.json instead when you use shrinkwrap. The glob needs at least one captured package. A project with no dependencies can run npm offline with no store. A declared packageManager must match the base image's npm version, and npm checks engines. A package npm records as bundled inside its parent (inBundle, with no resolved URL or integrity of its own) is not fetched separately. It ships in the parent's tarball, whose integrity is verified. Any other inBundle entry is refused, naming the package. Packages outside the public registry, such as a package pinned to a public GitHub commit tarball (an HTTPS tarball URL in package.json and the lockfile, not a git spec), are fetched only from locations the project declares in npm.sources. Their locked integrity is still checked. The store contains only <sha256>.tgz files. Oyzu fetches every locked registry tarball, verifies the SHA-512 lock integrity and runs npm offline with lifecycle scripts off, which rejects stale locks and incompatible installs. Workspace links stay in the source. Development and optional packages are fetched too (the example omits development packages with --omit=dev). npm's cache, logs, configuration and Oyzu's own state are not exported. The example seeds a throwaway cache and deletes it in the same RUN, so no cache layer is left. Oyzu does not run project lifecycle scripts while preparing. Packages that need a compile step need a compiler in the base and an explicit offline command in your Dockerfile. Failures and limits: Missing or stale locks, unsupported lock versions, failed integrity checks, incompatible engines or a mismatched package manager fail preparation. The registry is https://registry.npmjs.org/. Private registries, VCS or direct non-registry sources and managed connector authorization are not supported. There is no persistent download cache or internet fallback during the build.

node/yarn exports a Yarn offline mirror after Oyzu validates the locked dependency graph. With package.json and yarn.lock and no competing ecosystem, it is selected automatically. With several native locks, set with.dependencies: node/yarn. A modern Yarn lock is not treated as Classic. FROM registry.example.com/build/node:22-yarn1 WORKDIR /app COPY package.json yarn.lock ./ RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ --mount=type=tmpfs,target=/tmp \ export DISABLE_V8_COMPILE_CACHE=1 \ && printf 'yarn-offline-mirror "/dependencies"\ndisable-self-update-check true\n' >/tmp/oyzu.yarnrc \ && yarn install --offline --non-interactive --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts --use-yarnrc /tmp/oyzu.yarnrc --cache-folder /tmp/yarn-cache \ && yarn cache clean --offline --non-interactive --cache-folder /tmp/yarn-cache \ && rm -rf /tmp/yarn-cache /tmp/oyzu.yarnrc COPY app.js . CMD ["node", "app.js"] The image must already have Node and Yarn Classic 1.22.22. Oyzu installs neither. The @yarnpkg/lockfile 1.1.0 parser that reads yarn.lock ships in the Node plugin package, so the image doesn't need it. An OYZU_YARN_LOCKFILE path set in the image takes precedence. Yarn Classic bundles v8-compile-cache. The example disables it with its native DISABLE_V8_COMPILE_CACHE=1 control for both Yarn commands. The temporary /tmp mount keeps install scratch out of the image layer. Only the verified mirror archives enter dependencies. The temporary configuration in the example lives inside the RUN and is removed there. Lifecycle scripts stay off. Preparation uses the base's Node and Yarn, checks engines and package-manager constraints and rejects a graph that changed. Yarn applies registry-only resolutions. Oyzu records every locked input with purpose build. It does not prune to runtime-only packages. Supported: a single project, Classic v1 locks, SHA-512 or legacy SHA-1 lock integrity, scoped and transitive registry packages, registry version-range resolutions, and the root .yarnrc and .npmrc settings listed in Yarn project settings. Copy those files into the consumer stage too if Yarn should apply them there. Not supported: workspaces, other .yarnrc and .npmrc settings, .yarnrc.yml, path and VCS dependencies, modern Yarn, private registries and managed connectors. Missing tools, stale locks, changed integrity or a changed base fail before any artifact is built. The build cannot fetch missing packages, and there is no persistent download cache.

node/pnpm prepares a pnpm store in the exact base image, using the Node builder's registry downloads and frozen-lock checks. package.json and a single-project v9 pnpm-lock.yaml select it if unambiguous. Otherwise set with.dependencies: node/pnpm. FROM registry.example.com/build/node:22-pnpm10.11 WORKDIR /app COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./ RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ cp -r /dependencies /tmp/pnpm-store \ && pnpm --config.manage-package-manager-versions=false install --offline --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts --ignore-pnpmfile --config.verify-store-integrity=true --config.side-effects-cache=false --store-dir /tmp/pnpm-store \ && rm -rf /tmp/pnpm-store \ && rm node_modules/.modules.yaml node_modules/.pnpm-workspace-state.json COPY app.js . CMD ["node", "app.js"] The image must already have Node and pnpm 10.11.0. The yaml 2.9.1 parser that reads pnpm-lock.yaml ships in the Node plugin package. An OYZU_PNPM_YAML path set in the image takes precedence. Other pnpm versions fail at export, because the store format is tied to this version. The example produces a runtime-only image: it removes pnpm's timestamp-bearing install bookkeeping (.modules.yaml and .pnpm-workspace-state.json) in the same authored RUN. Native Node imports and pnpm exec node work without those files. Keep the files if the image must support later installs; their timestamps can change image digests. The context is read-only. Copy it so pnpm has a private writable store, and delete the copy in the same RUN. Installed packages keep working after the store is gone. Oyzu exports only pnpm's v10/files and v10/index records, sets each index file's checkedAt to zero and writes index keys in a fixed order. Package bytes and integrity values are unchanged, and pnpm rechecks the copied content. Links, special files, unknown store paths and side-effect caches are rejected, with limits of 100,000 files, 10 GiB and 16 MiB per index. An empty lock exports an empty store. User configuration and Oyzu's own state are not included. For a patched project, copy pnpm-workspace.yaml and patches/ before installing, or use the package.json patch declaration. pnpm applies and verifies the patches, and the record keeps the original package integrity and patch digests. Lifecycle scripts and side-effect caching are off. Every locked registry input is captured and recorded with purpose build. Not supported: workspaces, .npmrc, .pnpmfile.cjs, unsupported overrides, direct, path and VCS dependencies, other pnpm versions and private or managed registries. Stale locks, changed integrity, missing tools or unrecognized store data fail preparation. The build has no registry access, so an incomplete store fails and is never topped up from the internet. If pnpm reports a native-mirror HTTP 502 during preparation, check the build diagnostic for the original acquisition cause. A SHA-512 integrity mismatch means the downloaded archive differs from the lock's publisher checksum; no build action or artifact is produced. Verify the lock and registry source before retrying. Do not disable integrity verification to accept different bytes.

go/modules gives the build Go's checksum-verified module download cache through dependencies. A Docker target with go.mod or go.work picks it automatically. With mixed ecosystems, set with.dependencies: go/modules. For a pure-Go command with a complete go.sum: FROM golang:1.24-bookworm AS build WORKDIR /src COPY . . RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ GOMODCACHE=/tmp/gomodcache GOPROXY=file:///dependencies/cache/download GOSUMDB=off GOTOOLCHAIN=local CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -mod=readonly -trimpath -buildvcs=false -o /app . FROM scratch COPY --from=build /app /app ENTRYPOINT ["/app"] Go resolves workspace members, local replacements and test imports from your source and checksum files. Oyzu fetches the required modules through the public Go proxy, and Go verifies go.sum. Preparation does not change your manifests or checksum files. The base must already have Go and a POSIX shell, plus a C compiler for cgo. The example uses the standard golang:1.24-bookworm image. Preparation compiles a small metadata helper with that Go using only the standard library. It does not need oyzu-go-modulezip, version projection or module packaging, which belong to ordinary go/app and go/library builds. Toolchain download, VCS access and user Go configuration are off during preparation. The store is Go's download cache (module zips with their .mod and .info files), mounted read-only. The build uses it as a file proxy and extracts what it needs into its own writable GOMODCACHE, and Go verifies each zip against go.sum. Extracted trees are not stored, because many small files on a Docker Desktop bind mount were slow. No broker, credentials or acquisition metadata are in the store. Compiler output stays in the build stage, and the final scratch stage holds only the binary. Use a real runtime image instead of scratch for cgo or other runtime libraries. The record keeps the Go version and platform, lock and source digests and the module archives used. Its module-artifact list is empty because preparing dependencies does not publish your own module. The image's JUnit report checks the image, not your source. Build a separate Go target if you need source tests and coverage. Failures: missing checksums, stale manifests, workspace or replacement paths that escape the project, or an incompatible base fail preparation. Update and commit your Go files, or fix the base, and build again. Private modules, direct VCS sources, checksum database integration and a persistent cache are not supported.

rust/cargo gives the build a Cargo local registry. A Docker target with Cargo.toml and a checked-in Cargo.lock picks it automatically when no other ecosystem is present. Otherwise set with.dependencies: rust/cargo. The lock file is required even for a local-only workspace. FROM rust:1.94.0-slim-bookworm AS build WORKDIR /src COPY . . RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ CARGO_HOME=/tmp/cargo-home CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/cargo-target CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 cargo \ --config 'source.crates-io.replace-with="oyzu-captured"' \ --config 'source.oyzu-captured.local-registry="/dependencies"' \ build --release --locked --offline \ && cp /tmp/cargo-target/release/oyzu-registry-example /app RUN test "$(/app)" = "Answer: 42" FROM debian:bookworm-slim COPY --from=build /app /app ENTRYPOINT ["/app"] The base must already have Rust/Cargo 1.94.0, a POSIX shell and the compiler and linker your project needs. The example uses rust:1.94.0-slim-bookworm. Preparation does not need Python, nextest or llvm-cov. Oyzu checks the whole lock before downloading, using only crates.io registry sources whose index and archive SHA-256 checksums match. Cargo then validates the workspace and lock offline inside the exact base image. Preparation runs no build scripts, does not rewrite your lock and does not produce your crates' artifacts. Only *.crate archives and their index/ entries enter the read-only context. It uses Cargo's local-registry source replacement. Cargo unpacks into a fresh private home. The example's final stage copies the binary onto a Debian runtime that has the dynamic libraries it needs. A workspace with no dependencies needs no source replacement. Local workspace packages remain source inputs. The record keeps Cargo's metadata, the compiler and manager versions, the base identity, source and lock digests and the verified packages. It has no nextest or coverage evidence. The image's JUnit report checks the image, not your Rust tests. Build a separate Rust target if you need tests and coverage. Failures: a missing or stale lock, mismatched checksums, Git or alternate-registry sources, local paths that escape the project or missing tools fail before any artifact is built. Managed or private registries, a persistent download cache and other Rust versions are not supported.

For a dependencies context, Oyzu checks that the base image still has the captured OCI config digest, then runs it by its immutable Docker image ID. The consumer runtime must already be provisioned in the Docker daemon. This is checked before base acquisition. Capturing a base into an OCI input store does not make it runnable in the daemon and does not satisfy with.dependencies. With Docker's containerd image store, a single-platform image's ID is its manifest digest. Oyzu then exports the image, checks the manifest bytes against the ID and reads the config digest from it. Classic storage reports the config digest as the ID. If the base reference changed, the build fails before the dependencies run. Oyzu never silently switches to a newer base. The dependency record keeps runtime_config separate from runtime.digest (the execution ID).

The Python and Cargo providers run Oyzu's compiled Linux worker inside the base image, so the image's own interpreter or compiler resolves the packages. Go and Node providers run only native tools and use no worker. Your base image does not contain the worker, and Oyzu never changes it. Oyzu mounts the invocation's engine read-only into the preparation containers, as in every other container action (see What runs in a container action). The selected engine member is recorded with the dependency record, so a different engine changes the plan. Requirements: An engine must be available for the base image's platform. Without an engine package, a Linux CLI of the same architecture mounts its own executable. Otherwise preparation stops with ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE. An engine package's static Linux member runs on glibc and musl bases alike. When a Linux CLI mounts its own executable instead, the base needs that executable's glibc (2.39 or newer for release builds).
documents.s: Compiled worker in the base image

documents.t: Oyzu can use a base whose OCI index carries attestations. It selects and exports the runnable manifest for the requested platform, verifies its digest and config, and keeps the index identity for execution. This needs Docker image inspect and export to support --platform (Docker 29.8 is known to work). It does not verify signatures or trust the attestations. If selection or export is unsupported, the build fails and no image is substituted.

A missing floating-tag image fails preparation with a provisioning message. A missing digest-pinned public base can be captured during preparation when acquisition is permitted. --offline, managed configuration and the existing no-pull control prevent registry acquisition; they do not grant a different execution boundary. The captured lane's separate offline-preparation limitation still applies. A Docker permission refusal, unavailable daemon or other inspection failure is reported as an inspection error with Docker's diagnostic; it does not establish that the requested base is missing. Restore daemon access before retrying. Registry failures name the requested image and digest. A network failure or anonymous-access denial is distinct from registry digest not found. A denial explains that a private image requires login; run docker login for that registry and retry, or provision the image locally. A rejected login is terminal, with no fallback to anonymous access and no login loop. A platform mismatch, malformed export, config mismatch, hidden ONBUILD, a modified frozen store or a native worker failure blocks artifacts. Fix the input or base image and build again. Lint and format failures still block the build (see Dockerfile linting and formatting). Limits: At most 64 distinct image references per build, 100,000 entries per image export and 10 GiB for an export or captured tree. Unsafe archive paths, duplicate member names and links are rejected without extracting layers on your machine. Unsupported archive forms fail. Equivalent references such as alpine:3.22 and docker.io/library/alpine:3.22 share one BuildKit context when their identities agree. Both requested references stay in the record. Conflicting identities fail planning, and reference order never picks between different images. Managed registry access, secret mounts, other package managers and a Dockerfile-free application image profile are not supported. An image in your local Docker daemon is not a statement that it is trusted or approved for release. Upgrading: Captures and plans made by older tools must be regenerated. They fail rather than assume defaults for missing platform or frontend facts. No project file changes are needed.

Check a build's result with oyzu inspect dist. For an image it confirms that the archive's digests and platform match what the build recorded. The build itself checks every image against its target platform, so an image for the wrong architecture is never kept as a success, and a valid archive hash is not enough. An image archive also carries a JUnit report with its integrity and platform assertions. These do not run the image or replace your application tests. Related: Dockerfile linting and formatting, Oyzu's BuildKit frontend, OCI indices, publishing an image, Helm charts.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/docker-quality.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Dockerfile projects get lint, a read-only format check and an explicit format task with no Oyzu configuration. Linting uses Hadolint 2.15.1 and formatting uses dockerfmt 0.5.4. Neither builds or runs your application. Status: experimental. Managed defaults require a published tool pair for the execution platform; see Tools and platforms. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

oyzu run list oyzu pin oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format oyzu build Task What it runs Changes files lint hadolint --no-color Dockerfile No format-check dockerfmt with --check No format dockerfmt with --write Yes. Only runs when you ask for it, and is not a build stage. Hadolint's rules, severities, configuration and inline suppressions decide whether lint passes. It reads a target-local .hadolint.yaml or .hadolint.yml. dockerfmt reads a target-local .editorconfig. With no .editorconfig, Oyzu adds --newline so formatted files keep a final newline. With one, dockerfmt's own defaults and your settings apply, including the end-of-file rule. Oyzu does not parse these files itself. Invalid native configuration is a native failure. Task listing needs neither checker. Before a selected task runs, Oyzu prepares its exact locked tools in the shared store. A missing pin or unavailable platform fails preparation; no checker is silently skipped. Task overrides and pre/post hooks work as for other tasks. A task you replace owns its own behavior.

In an isolated oyzu build, lint and format-check are required gates before the image archive is collected. If either fails, the diagnostics are kept and no image artifact is produced. Your source and checkout are unchanged. Fix the findings, run oyzu run format if you want the formatter to rewrite the file, and build again. Lint results are not counted as application tests or coverage. The image's JUnit report comes from the OCI checks, and coverage is recorded as not applicable. .dockerignore controls what goes into the image, not what the checkers see. Oyzu keeps .hadolint.yaml, .hadolint.yml and .editorconfig available to the checkers even if .dockerignore excludes them from COPY. Configuration from folders above the target is not imported in a build. Keep required checker configuration inside the target folder so isolated and local runs agree. Local development runs also see configuration from your machine. Isolated builds do not mount any. dockerfmt defaults to four-space continuation indentation. If your repository has an .editorconfig in a parent folder, copy a Dockerfile example elsewhere before comparing native defaults.

oyzu pin records Hadolint and dockerfmt under quality.docker in oyzu.lock, with exact versions, upstream URLs, upstream integrity and SHA-256 values. The first quality task installs the pair in the shared tool store. Host tasks and isolated builds consume the same selection; neither checker needs to be on PATH or in a custom execution image. Downloads use the normal source-admission rules and are verified before installation. Hadolint's upstream license and source pointers are retained, as are notices inside the unchanged dockerfmt archive. Installed payloads are trusted on reuse. Isolated actions restore a read-only archive and run with networking disabled on the base execution image. The managed pair has upstream assets for Linux x86-64, Linux arm64 and macOS arm64. Hadolint also publishes other assets, but no complete managed pair is available for Windows or macOS x86-64 because dockerfmt does not publish matching binaries. Selecting either host fails with QUALITY_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE; a tool found on ambient PATH does not fill the gap. Use a supported Linux executor or an explicit project task with its own tools. Asset availability does not imply that every platform has been qualified through a full image build. Ordinary runs, builds and oyzu pin retain the exact project lock. Use oyzu pin --refresh or a whole-project oyzu update to adopt the defaults shipped by your current CLI. The next task prepares the new selection. Offline checks need the lock and bundle already available in the same store. If fetches.sources is restricted, permit the locked GitHub release and license URLs; source restrictions apply on reuse too. See locked quality tools.

Hadolint is a static linter. It is not a vulnerability scanner and does not prove policy compliance. Inline suppressions change its result. dockerfmt has documented syntax limits, including escape directives and some shell grouping forms. See Hadolint and dockerfmt for their configuration.
Docker image inputs and offline builds

Docker image checks validate OCI structure and declared image properties. They are deterministic validations, so tests.retries does not retry them or report them as flaky. A failed image check remains failed, including with --no-cache.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/dotnet.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu builds a directory that has a solution (.sln, .slnx) or an SDK-style project (.csproj, .fsproj, .vbproj) without any Oyzu configuration. The dotnet/sdk builder runs restore, build, test, publish and pack on a Linux or Windows x64 host or in a network-denied container. It delivers framework-dependent application folders and a versioned NuGet package directory for packable projects. Note: The .NET builder is experimental. It supports Linux and Windows x64 native host builds and Linux amd64 isolated builds with Docker or crun. macOS builds are unsupported. See the SDK 10.0.400 versus 10.0.401 audit. This build flow requires a compatible plugin package declaring dotnet-lock-admission. Updating the CLI alone does not replace an installed plugin; use the normal plugin update flow or rebuild and rebind a development plugin.

The dotnet/sdk builder is supplied by the oyzu-plugin-dotnet plugin. The plugin finds your projects, plans the build and runs the restore, test and pack steps. Oyzu itself still provides the SDK and source, the NuGet mirror, version resolution, credentials, and the checks on artifacts and reports. The plugin gets the NuGet mirror address from Oyzu and never sees your credentials. The plugin uses the shared SDK to ignore inert annotations only in designated stdio containers and check required request features before family dispatch. Native commands, acquisition and lock-facts inputs remain strict, including nested MSBuild SDK identities. A missing request capability directs you to oyzu plugins update dotnet/sdk; a manifest capability unsupported by the CLI directs you to oyzu self update. Unknown required reply fields and undeclared reply capabilities are plugin contract violations. See the plugin compatibility contract.

oyzu run list oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Plain oyzu build selects the fast build and package path with Debug compilation. --optimized selects Release. An optimized shared-cache writer also publishes the separate Debug compile stage; each reader reuses only its selected profile. Both stages share one restore and require a compatible plugin declaring dotnet-compile-stages. oyzu build --isolated --full also runs the native tests. --isolated alone doesn't select tests. On Linux or Windows x64, plain builds run natively. Use --isolated for captured SDK/NuGet preparation. Docker execution needs Docker; daemonless Linux execution uses crun with --isolated --no-docker. Both use the locked SDK described under Provisioning.

On Linux or Windows x64, oyzu install provisions the managed SDK and oyzu build --full runs restore, build, test, lint, format-check, publish and pack on the host. The result is one directory per app, a NuGet package directory when projects are packable, JUnit test results and VSTest Cobertura coverage. oyzu build --full --optimized selects Release instead of Debug for build, test, publish and pack. Native restore uses the host's NuGet/MSBuild configuration and package cache. An existing packages.lock.json or packages.<Name>.lock.json in the selected projects enables --locked-mode. Offline native builds are refused; use isolated execution with prepared dependencies. Authored build-task overrides also require isolated execution; authored test tasks run as given. Every native stage has incomplete reads because NuGet/MSBuild can read user state and ancestor files outside the target. The rerun reason recorded for each stage names the ancestor files, relative to the target (such as Directory.Build.targets, .editorconfig, global.json or NuGet.Config above the target) that are actually present. Core keys those ancestor files by content, but these stages still run again on every build, because user NuGet/MSBuild state is not yet bounded; whole-target reuse cannot bypass incomplete-read refusal. Captured read-set guarantees below apply only to isolated builds. Ancestor declarations count parents from the canonical target directory, so a target beneath a directory symlink declares the same probes as its physical location. An unresolvable target directory fails native planning with its cause. Native planning also refuses a target with more than 21 physical parents: all 12 configuration filenames must be declared in every parent up to the filesystem root, within the protocol's 256 external-input budget. It never silently drops these inputs. Move the checkout to a shallower physical path or use isolated execution; a directory symlink does not reduce physical depth. An ancestor that cannot be keyed produces ANCESTOR_INPUT_UNKEYABLE; the build manifest retains the reason and cache reuse is disabled for that action. Stage read declarations and observed paths stay within the source root. External locked-tool inputs can bind an SDK's admitted identity, but cannot bind ancestor configuration, user NuGet configuration or external fallback-package folders. Declaring a folder's location in the environment does not include its file contents in the cache key. Compiler PathMap does not make the intermediate tree portable. obj/project.assets.json records absolute project, output, package-cache and NuGet configuration paths. Those paths must remain valid for later MSBuild operations; portable DLL or NuGet bytes alone do not authorize restoring the intermediate tree in another checkout. Native builds do not supply the captured NuGet dependency inventory or broker audit. The managed SDK provider admits Linux x64 GNU and Windows x64 MSVC archives; macOS native builds are unsupported.

In host mode on Linux or Windows x64, builds use native NuGet.config packageSources, packageSourceCredentials, packageSourceMapping, user configuration and NuGet credential providers. Oyzu adds no registry setting or source overlay. NuGet owns configuration precedence and mapping; a mapping failure remains a restore failure, with no Oyzu fallback to a public source. Keep credentials in user configuration or environment references, for example: <configuration> <packageSources> <clear /> <add key="company" value="https://packages.example.com/v3/index.json" /> </packageSources> <packageSourceCredentials> <company> <add key="Username" value="reader" /> <add key="ClearTextPassword" value="%COMPANY_NUGET_PASSWORD%" /> </company> </packageSourceCredentials> <packageSourceMapping> <packageSource key="company"><package pattern="Company.*" /></packageSource> </packageSourceMapping> </configuration> Export COMPANY_NUGET_PASSWORD in your shell or CI secret environment, then run oyzu build --full. Native NuGetPackageSourceCredentials_<source> and NUGET_* variables are supplied at process launch, outside the action identity. Environment references in native NuGet XML attributes are passed without writing expanded configuration. Known credential values are redacted before native output capture. Secret registration covers Password and ClearTextPassword values in packageSourceCredentials, apikeys values and native credential environment values, including VSS endpoint secrets. References such as %USERPROFILE% or %HOME% in globalPackagesFolder are forwarded without registering their values as secrets. Output admission rejects known credential bytes. Authenticated or custom-source host builds do not reuse action cache entries. Do not put credentials in source URLs or project outputs. Before source projection, tracked native configuration containing literal credentials is refused. Move those values to environment references or user configuration; the diagnostic identifies the file without its contents. Private feeds and mappings are refused in captured/isolated builds before actions run; use host mode. Isolated support remains tracked in #1440. Host mode uses native networking and is not an offline or isolated credential boundary. Missing credentials and HTTP 401/403 remain native restore failures: check the named source and the corresponding user configuration, environment reference or credential provider. Providers must keep their own diagnostics free of secrets.
documents.s: Private NuGet feeds in host mode

documents.t: Isolated builds run on the base execution image, which has no .NET SDK. The SDK comes from oyzu.lock and is restored read-only into every action (see Capturing a selected SDK). Without a [tools] dotnet setting, oyzu pin locks the default SDK, 10.0.401. The base image carries the shared libraries the official SDK loads (OpenSSL, ICU, Kerberos and zlib) and a C toolchain. Only Linux x64 GNU SDKs are supported, so .NET builds run on linux/amd64. Pass --image dotnet=<ref> to run on your own image, for example one with OS packages a project links against. It must meet the bring-your-own requirements, and the locked SDK is still the one restored. No image carries an Oyzu worker. Restore, test and pack run the engine and the .NET plugin that Oyzu mounts into the container, so updating the CLI never needs an image rebuild. If a compiled operation reports a likely CLI/.NET plugin version mismatch, inspect the selected package with oyzu plugins explain, select compatible CLI and .NET plugin versions, and run oyzu pin before retrying. The error retains the unknown operation and argument count to help identify the incompatible request.

A directory is claimed when it directly contains a solution, or a project whose root element names an MSBuild SDK (Sdk="...", an <Sdk> element or an SDK import). Legacy non-SDK projects are not claimed. Discovery adds install, build and test tasks that run dotnet restore, dotnet build and dotnet test. A literal SemVer Version or unsuffixed VersionPrefix in the entry project or its nearest in-target Directory.Build.props becomes the native version. For a selected project, lookup starts in that project's folder and stops at the target root; a nearer props file shadows the root file. Solution entries retain only the target-root props scope. The last assignment wins, with the selected props read before the project; an explicit Version takes precedence over a prefix. A later computed, invalid or conditional assignment keeps the value unresolved instead of reviving an earlier literal. A nonempty or conditional VersionSuffix likewise keeps a prefix unresolved, because the version fact records only one source property. MSBuild retains evaluation of these unresolved values. Build, test and pack select one entry file: a single solution, otherwise a single SDK-style project. The complete-read path can expand its reference graph into per-project actions. Publish receives each app project selected by that entry. If there is more than one entry candidate, the build fails and lists them. Choose one: builds: app: uses: dotnet/sdk with: project: src/App.slnx Option Values Default Meaning with.project A solution or project file, relative to the target The single solution, otherwise the single SDK-style project The entry for build, test and pack, and project selection for publish. Other with keys are rejected. An explicit with.project also selects the native entry for captured dependency admission, including a nested project when the target root has no solution or project file. Missing, nonportable or wrongly typed selections fail; they do not fall back to another root entry.

Setting Where Values Default Meaning [tools] dotnet oyzu.toml An exact stable SDK version, such as 10.0.402 10.0.401, locked by oyzu pin Downloads and uses that SDK (see below). lockPlatforms oyzu.toml [tools] ["linux/amd64/gnu"] The platform of the SDK archive to lock. sdk.version global.json in the target root An exact SDK version The build's native pin (native pin files). A configured SDK must also satisfy it. sdk.rollForward global.json Native roll-forward policies patch with a version, latestMajor without one Native SDK selection. sdk.allowPrerelease global.json true or false true Native SDK selection. test.runner global.json Microsoft.Testing.Platform Runs tests with Microsoft.Testing.Platform. Without it, tests use VSTest. msbuild-sdks global.json Literal versions NuGet-supplied MSBuild SDKs to restore (see MSBuild project SDKs).

By default the build uses the default SDK (10.0.401). To use another one, name an exact stable Linux x64 GNU SDK. Oyzu downloads it from Microsoft's builds.dotnet.microsoft.com release metadata and archives. This is experimental. [tools] dotnet = "10.0.402" lockPlatforms = ["linux/amd64/gnu"] Run oyzu pin, then oyzu build --isolated --full --frozen. Oyzu checks Microsoft's SHA-512 for the archive and records its SHA-256 in oyzu.lock. The archive is restored read-only and unchanged. Installation keeps all archive notices. DOTNET_ROOT, PATH and the exact version are fixed for restore, build, test, publish and pack. The dotnet --version seen inside the container must equal your selection and satisfy global.json. Another SDK is never picked silently instead. Warm frozen or offline runs need the existing lock, the SDK archive and the NuGet inputs. They don't consult release metadata. Limits: The execution image provides the OS, linker and library prerequisites. An image of your own must provide them too. Oyzu doesn't provide an OS, a separate runtime, Windows, macOS or ARM SDKs, or a GNU fallback for musl. Prereleases and older SDK download layouts aren't supported. If the build is refused, the cause is one of these: Problem What to do Checksum mismatch, unsupported platform or archive layout Don't edit the lock digest to accept unexpected bytes. Restore the missing inputs online and rerun. global.json conflicts with the selected SDK Make the two agree, run oyzu pin, and retry the frozen build. You need a different SDK Change [tools] dotnet and run oyzu pin. Changing only the image doesn't override a locked SDK archive.

global.json in the target root selects the SDK the way the .NET host does: sdk.version, sdk.rollForward and sdk.allowPrerelease. patch can keep an exact installed SDK even when a newer patch is available. latestPatch takes the latest available patch. Oyzu runs dotnet --version in the target directory to see what the host would pick, instead of predicting it. Without global.json, the .NET host chooses the SDK supplied to the build, which is the locked SDK. A value that isn't an exact SDK version (10.0) is refused, with a hint naming an exact version such as 10.0.100. Only the target root's global.json is read. The .NET host's upward search for a global.json in parent folders isn't followed. global.json must be strict JSON. Comments are rejected. Custom SDK search roots (sdk.paths) aren't supported. oyzu build --plan lists the oyzu:dotnet tool requirement, with the global.json sdk.version as its constraint when there is one. The discovery record shows the request under sdk. Before restoring, preparation lists the SDKs installed in the container and checks which one the host would select in the target directory. Each check has a 30-second timeout. If no installed SDK is allowed, the build fails before restore. The message names the request, the SDKs provided and oyzu pin. The selected version must be installed and allowed by the request. The dependency record and the .NET SDK evidence record that version. Offline restore checks the selection again and requires the same answer. A failed or timed-out check, or an invalid answer, fails preparation.

Build actions run with the network denied: A prepare action restores offline from the prepared packages into /workspace/.oyzu-dotnet/packages (also NUGET_PACKAGES). It keeps --locked-mode when preparation used it. build runs dotnet build <entry> --configuration Debug --no-restore --disable-build-servers -p:Version=<version>; optimized builds use Release. Compilation also sets MSBuild PathMap to map the temporary build workspace to ./. Source and embedded PDB paths retain their relative project layout, including nested projects, so relocating a clean workspace does not change package bytes solely because of its path. Debug information and the selected configuration are preserved. Debuggers may need a source mapping from ./ to your checkout; CallerFilePath values also use the mapped paths, relative to the folder the process runs in. Project inputs outside the build workspace are not mapped. Isolated builds still map to /_/. When tests are selected (for example by --full), test runs dotnet test --no-build --no-restore and writes TRX results: VSTest uses --logger trx and collects Microsoft Code Coverage with --collect "Code Coverage;Format=cobertura". The collector comes with Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk, so test projects need nothing extra. Microsoft.Testing.Platform uses --report-trx and --solution or --project. Set test.runner: Microsoft.Testing.Platform in global.json to use it. All TRX files are converted into one JUnit report that keeps class names, failures and skipped tests. A passing run with no TRX results fails instead of reporting an empty suite. A custom test task must still produce the required JUnit report, or the action fails and no package is exported. After a passing VSTest run, the per-project Cobertura files are merged by source file and line into one coverage.cobertura.xml, so a library that several test projects exercise is counted once. The build summary shows line coverage, and a coverage check in oyzu.toml can require it. Microsoft.Testing.Platform runs report no coverage yet. When lint is selected, lint runs dotnet format analyzers <entry> --verify-no-changes --no-restore after build. It reports the SDK's code-analysis (CA) rules and any analyzer packages your projects reference, at warning severity and above, using your .editorconfig settings. Code-style (IDE) rules are enforced only through the build, with EnforceCodeStyleInBuild. When format checks are selected, format-check runs dotnet format whitespace <entry> --verify-no-changes, which fails on whitespace that differs from your .editorconfig. Run dotnet format whitespace <entry> locally to fix it. publish runs dotnet publish <project> --configuration Debug --no-restore --no-build -p:Version=<version> -o <destination> for each selected app; optimized builds use Release. Each app produces a directory artifact named <project-name>-<version>-portable. The app's .dll runs with dotnet <app>.dll on a compatible runtime. This requires a plugin and engine declaring dotnet-publish. dotnet pack --no-build --no-restore writes one directory artifact, nuget-packages-<version>. An app-only selection with no packable projects omits that artifact; otherwise the existing no-packages error remains. App selection reads literal OutputType=Exe/WinExe or the Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web/Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Worker SDK from selected projects and their nearest Directory.Build.props. IsTestProject=true excludes a project from publishing. Solution members and project references select the projects; unrelated apps under the target are not exported. Conditional or computed output-selection properties cannot currently be resolved and fail planning. This is static interpretation, not full MSBuild evaluation of imports. No additional with option is needed. Publish remains conservatively unbounded and reruns because native content items can read files beyond compilation inputs. Environment: The version comes from version inference over the native version and your Git history. It is passed to restore, build, publish and pack as -p:Version. CI is removed from the action environment, because ContinuousIntegrationBuild source mapping needs a .git directory that the captured source leaves out. Telemetry, first-run output, workload notices, MSBuild node reuse and online certificate revocation checks are off. Actions reserve 4096 MiB and time out after 30 minutes.

Native-host stages on Linux and Windows have incomplete reads and rerun even on an unchanged build. Linux crun builds use an enforced read boundary automatically, without another setting. Select it with oyzu build --isolated --no-docker or the existing build.isolation = "crun" setting. Ordinary deterministic SDK projects can reuse compile, test and pack results on unchanged builds and in another clean checkout. The SDK's admitted identity and prepared dependency content are stage inputs. Changing configuration visible inside the target, package content or SDK identity invalidates the affected results. Tests retain the ordinary retry and report gates. For multi-project solutions with literal ProjectReference edges and separate, non-nested project folders, compile, test and pack results reuse per project. Editing a terminal test project reruns that project; editing a shared library also reruns its dependents. Each project consumes the compiled outputs of its reference closure. Shared configuration, SDK and NuGet identities remain inputs. For a chain Tests -> Library -> Shared, an unchanged rebuild reuses all three projects. Editing Tests reruns its compile and test actions while both libraries reuse compile and pack; editing Library reruns it and Tests; editing Shared reruns all three. Editing shared Directory.Build.props also reruns all three. Failed compilation or tests never supply a reusable result: repeating the same failing input executes the failed action again and still blocks delivery. The target's resolved version base stays common; each project's snapshot source suffix covers that project's admitted reads and reference closure. Restore regenerates assets per project with the same stamp used by its compile and pack actions. This avoids changing an untouched library's assembly version when only its consumer changes. Packing declares writes to that project's obj metadata and its dedicated package output directory; writes outside the declared boundary fail the build. SDK analyzer and whitespace checks can update selected projects' obj metadata; their write declarations exclude source files. Test projects declare IsTestProject; their runtime source view contains their own project and admitted upstream outputs. Runtime files outside the test project folder (for example ../../testdata/x.json) are not visible in project mode; include test data inside the test project folder. A test that requires a missing file fails. A test that tolerates its absence can still pass, and that successful result may be reused within this restricted view. Reused tests and reports are labelled reused, rather than counted as freshly executed tests. A library can reuse its package when only consuming tests change; selected checks still gate the final bundle. Project actions include the project path in their native-unit facts and use stable action names such as compile-development:project-<path-digest>. Use oyzu build --explain to see each decision. Packable projects each export a nuget-packages-<project>-<version> directory. This needs a compatible .NET plugin package; an older package retains its whole-solution stages. The CLI sends the optional complete_reads fact only when the admitted plugin executable describes dotnet-project-reads. This is an optional request capability, not a package-wide engine requirement. If describe fails, the CLI omits the fact and retains whole-solution stages. A new plugin with the 0.4.0 CLI also retains whole-solution stages because that CLI omits the fact. Solutions containing an application retain whole-solution stages so publish receives all restore and compiler outputs and the common target version. Shared/nested project folders, references declared through imported props/targets, cyclic references (including a project referencing itself), legacy solution evaluation and unknown MSBuild customizations retain the conservative solution-wide path. Unsupported reads keep a named refusal in oyzu build --explain; declaring a reference does not admit arbitrary reads. Single-project tests conservatively read the whole target. Offline restore always reruns from prepared packages. project.assets.json and other local NuGet metadata are regenerated, rather than treated as a portable result. Each project restore currently keeps a full private package copy, so project mode can use more disk than whole-solution restore. Compiler PathMap and the deterministic SDK default normalize source/PDB locations; native-host intermediate trees remain location-sensitive. Unknown MSBuild reads and unsupported SDK/package customizations retain their conservative contracts. Publish still reruns. The crun view hides the proc/sys trees and permits only the closed startup allowance. Its self-proc facts record presence only, never contents, and are non-keying. Other processes' proc entries and undeclared external files stay inaccessible. Each action starts with private output; test phases share only their own preparation metadata and selected unit state. Other isolated backends retain the conservative predictions below; they do not establish this complete-read or clean-root test-reuse guarantee. macOS execution remains unsupported. For ordinary Microsoft.NET.Sdk projects using an audited SDK (10.0.401, and 10.0.400, whose audited MSBuild files are byte-identical) on the captured path, prepare (offline restore) and package (pack --no-build) read solution/project files, props/targets and project .user imports, global.json, NuGet configuration, default and packages.<ProjectName>.lock.json package locks, .editorconfig, .globalconfig and *.globalconfig, app.config, testconfig.json and runtimeconfig.template.json. build also reads C#, F# and Visual Basic source files, and so do lint and format-check. Test settings (*.runsettings) are covered by the whole-target test boundary. Default SDK item discovery records directory listings. Only each project's own bin and obj folders are excluded; Data/obj/Seed.cs remains a source input. Hidden folders such as .github and .vs are not scanned. Editing an existing default None item such as a README does not itself change the content key. On isolated backends without the complete-read crun guarantee, unchanged builds can reuse bounded stages while tests run again. Native-host stages on Linux and Windows still rerun because their reads are incomplete; bounded source predictions do not authorize native reuse. Packaging follows the test's workspace changes, so changed test effects invalidate its key even when source inputs are unchanged. An unread edit can also rerun those stages: the whole-target test read/write boundary keeps the development version scoped to the whole target. A committed README edit therefore changes the version passed to prepare, build, package and publish, even though the bounded source input is unchanged. Restore retains the version because MSBuild conditions and NuGet restore outputs can depend on Version; preparation cannot be reused across inferred version changes. lint and format-check omit the default OYZU_VERSION; an explicitly authored OYZU_VERSION still keys them. Omitting the inferred version does not enable native-host stage reuse. Lint also depends on restore and compilation outputs, so a change to those outputs can still rerun lint even when its own command and source reads match. oyzu cache explain reports the changed action definition. Narrow source reads alone do not promise reuse across these version changes. Prediction conservatively covers all projects under the target. Literal imports inside analyzed target folders are followed recursively; references into skipped hidden or output folders keep the stage unbounded. Project-owned None and Content additions can be bounded when Include names one existing literal file inside that project's folder. Their allowed metadata is Pack (true/false), PackagePath (empty or a literal relative package path), and CopyToOutputDirectory (Never, Always, PreserveNewest). Metadata can use attributes or child elements. The project XML and included file contents are byte inputs to prepare, compile and pack, including pack --no-build. Changing a packed license or copied data file therefore changes the source key. Default None items without an explicit declaration remain listing-only. The literal project properties PackageLicenseExpression, PackageId, Authors, Description, PackageTags, RepositoryUrl, PackageProjectUrl and Copyright are also bounded. Their values remain keyed through the complete project XML; package metadata is never ignored. This allowance does not extend to new properties or items in imported props/targets. Admitted property values and item-metadata child values must contain only text: comments, processing instructions and nested elements keep named refusals, even around literal text. Unknown metadata, Update/Remove, conditions, computed or escaped values, wildcard/list includes, missing files, parent traversal, external paths and links keep named refusals. Properties that select other files or revision identity, including EnableDefaultCompileItems, SourceRevisionId, InformationalVersion and SourceLink controls, remain unbounded, as do explicit Compile items. Legacy .sln solutions, unresolved imports, custom SDKs/tasks, computed values, conditional evaluation, custom items/properties, response files and potentially custom resource readers retain a whole-target key with a reason naming the file. This includes SourceLink and revision-identity properties. Other SDK versions, such as 10.0.399 or 10.0.402, remain unbounded until audited. Preparation examines restored project.assets.json inventories, including transitive packages. Packages supplying props/targets from build, buildTransitive, buildMultiTargeting or deprecated buildCrossTargeting make the stages unbounded, except for the exact test-package identities and NuGet sha512 payload hashes vetted by the plugin. The vetted set covers the xUnit and Coverlet packages and these parts of the MSTest 3.10.2 stack: MSTest adapter, framework and analyzers, Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk and TestHost 17.13.0, and Microsoft.Testing.Platform plus its MSBuild, Telemetry and TrxReport extensions 1.8.2. Microsoft.CodeCoverage 17.13.0 and Microsoft.Testing.Extensions.CodeCoverage 17.14.2 remain unbounded until referenced-project changes are proven to invalidate their source-root mapping consumer. A stack containing either deferred package therefore still reruns compile, pack and lint. Restore still reruns on every build, and other versions stay unbounded until audited. A missing or mismatching hash does not receive an exception. Missing resolved inventories or inventories predating payload-hash checks also keep the stages unbounded. Setting NuGetLockFilePath likewise keeps the stages unbounded. Ordinary library, reference, runtime and analyzer assets do not by themselves widen source reads. On the conventional solution-wide path, test retains a whole-target boundary because tests may read files at run time. Its native result files live in disposable scratch and are converted to the required JUnit report. Tests can also change workspace files, including compiled DLLs. package therefore consumes the workspace changes from restore, build and test, and its key includes those changes. Authored pre/post hooks and task replacements retain their workspace data dependencies too. Pack still evaluates project configuration, so it is not an upstream-only export. Package ZIP timestamps, random core-property part names and relationship IDs are normalized for repeatable package bytes. Already signed packages are refused without modification; signing must follow packing. Legacy ZIP entry names retain their decoded spelling and payload bytes during normalization. Invalid Unicode extra fields are rejected without modifying the package. Files above the target—including Directory.Build.props, Directory.Build.targets, .editorconfig, .globalconfig, global.json and NuGet.config—are not visible on the captured path, even when the target is a workspace subfolder. Host-native stages remain unbounded because they can read ancestor files and user NuGet/MSBuild state; the captured SDK audit does not bound native reads. Compiler response files do not establish every read of MSBuild or arbitrary tasks. These contracts reach users with the next .NET plugin release after a core release containing observed-read and listing-selector support.

The selected .NET package must declare the builder-role feature dotnet-lock-admission, and the engine must support it. Preparation refuses an unmarked package with PLUGIN_FEATURE_UNSUPPORTED before mounting the native worker or running private lock-facts/acquisition.
