To replace an older locked package, explicitly select an admitted capable release with oyzu plugins update dotnet/sdk; frozen and offline replay do not upgrade it. This requirement does not identify a minimum package version or establish capability support for an existing published Preview binary. Preparation asks the admitted SDK for its native restore graph, freezes the lock selection, and rechecks the graph under the final restore properties before running dotnet restore <entry> once. Native commands run with the network denied, through a local mirror that forwards only the NuGet V3 flat container and vulnerability data of https://api.nuget.org/ to Oyzu's download broker. Restore reads only a generated NuGet.Config. Oyzu clears project RestoreSources, additional sources and fallback folders, so repository and user feeds, package source mappings and credentials are not used. If any packages.lock.json or packages.<ProjectName>.lock.json exists in the target, restore runs with --locked-mode. NuGet applies each lock to its own project, and projects without a lock restore normally. The lock files are recorded. Existing custom NuGetLockFilePath files also select locked mode, using the native SDK's effective project properties, including imported or computed values. Core admits each project and custom path inside the captured target before restore, refuses redirected/outside paths, and records existing lock paths and digests. Relative custom paths resolve from their project folder. An explicit RestorePackagesWithLockFile=false does not enable a custom lock; missing locks retain native generation behavior. Authored RestoreLockedMode remains native-owned. Acquisition and offline restore use the same frozen automatic lock decision; a mismatching plan is refused. If final locked-mode evaluation changes a project or effective lock path, preparation refuses before project restore. Keep lock paths independent of RestoreLockedMode. The actual private workspace's admitted locks must remain regular, contained files with their original bytes before restore and before capture acceptance; unchanged originals in the source tree do not excuse a changed private copy. Restored packages go into a NuGet global packages folder in the prepared tree. Each package's .nupkg digest and size is recorded. The recorded package source is the public index, so the prepared tree doesn't depend on the mirror's port. For a project-relative custom lock, use native project properties and commit the lock file generated by NuGet: <PropertyGroup> <RestorePackagesWithLockFile>true</RestorePackagesWithLockFile> <NuGetLockFilePath>locks/deps.json</NuGetLockFilePath> </PropertyGroup> An existing file selects Oyzu's automatic locked mode without requiring an explicit RestoreLockedMode property. A stale lock fails native restore with NU1004 instead of being rewritten. Graph observation preserves native restore parallelism and uses the acquisition's source, package, audit and warning inputs; changing lock paths under the final locked-mode properties is refused.

Preparation restores with NuGetAudit=true and keeps warnings NU1900 to NU1905 as warnings, even under TreatWarningsAsErrors or WarningsAsErrors. The findings come from NuGet's own logs. Oyzu: shows a NuGet audit step with a summary, for example known vulnerabilities: 1 high; logs each finding as a NUGET_AUDIT warning; records them in the dependency record under oyzu.dev/nuget-audit, with complete: false when NuGet couldn't read vulnerability data. Audit findings never fail preparation. Build actions restore with NuGetAudit=false, so audit warnings can't turn into later compile errors.

Some MSBuild SDKs come from NuGet, such as Aspire.AppHost.Sdk or Microsoft.Build.NoTargets. A project names them with Sdk="Id/Version", an <Sdk Name Version> element, or msbuild-sdks in the root global.json. MSBuild restores them itself while it evaluates a project and ignores the generated NuGet configuration, so with the network denied the evaluation failed and restore skipped the project (NU1503). To avoid that, preparation scans the root global.json and every project, props and targets file for literal versions. It restores each SDK package through the broker into the prepared packages before restoring the entry, and the offline build restores them from there. The ids and versions are recorded under msbuildSdks in oyzu.dev/dotnet, and each package appears in the dependency record. SDKs bundled with .NET (Microsoft.NET.Sdk*) are never restored. A version written as a property, range or wildcard isn't restored and fails in MSBuild.

Every build checks its own results: A test failure keeps the JUnit report and blocks the package. A test run that exits successfully without a report fails. Analyzer findings fail lint, and whitespace differences fail format-check. A changed dependency that doesn't match an existing lock fails restore. A SDK request nothing satisfies fails before restore. Run oyzu inspect dist to check the bundle, including the SDK, lock and package records and the test results.

These choices may change: the builder id dotnet/sdk; the default SDK; audit is reported but never enforced; CI is removed; the action memory and timeout limits; packing each packable project into a directory artifact; failing on an ambiguous entry, an unsatisfiable SDK request or missing TRX results. Not supported: private feeds, credentials, package source mapping and nuget.sessionEndpoint in captured builds; workloads, and MSBuild project SDKs whose versions MSBuild computes or a range names; global.json and Directory.Build.* files above the target directory in isolated builds; coverage for Microsoft.Testing.Platform runs; per-package file artifacts, RID-specific or self-contained publishing, single-file apps, trimming and NativeAOT; macOS builds; repositories with several projects and no root solution, unless with.project selects one. Resource limits: The download broker allows 1 GiB and 4096 requests per session, and 256 MiB per response. The prepared tree is limited to 100,000 entries and 10 GiB. NuGet's HTTP cache and extraction scratch use /scratch/nuget, which can grow with the action's 4 GiB memory reservation instead of being limited by the 512 MiB /tmp mount. Large packages such as Microsoft.Playwright fit. For managed NuGet sessions with oyzu exec, see NuGet sessions.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/ecosystem-support.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Use this page to see what Oyzu builds today, which reports it produces, and where each build runs. Oyzu is experimental. Support is for the project shapes and platforms listed here. A language or tool not listed on this page isn't supported yet, and neither is an unlisted combination.

Native builds run on your machine with the tools Oyzu installs for you. They have your account's access to files and the network. See native local builds. Isolated builds (oyzu build --isolated) run in a Linux container. They need Docker, collect dependencies first, and then build offline. The container is Linux (amd64). The host can be Linux or Windows (x86-64). Plain oyzu build is native when every selected target has a native build, and isolated otherwise. See which builds are native.

ARM64 hosts and build targets are unsupported across tools, builders, plugins, containers and releases. Use a supported x64 host and target. Platform Support Linux x86-64 Supported for native and isolated builds Windows x86-64 Supported for native builds. Isolated builds run Linux containers through Docker macOS Intel (x86-64) Zig native builds only macOS Apple silicon (ARM64) Not supported yet Linux ARM64 Not supported yet Windows ARM64 Not supported yet Rust can also build for other platforms from a supported host. See Rust cross-compiling.

Oyzu doesn't deploy to a cluster Docker OCI images OCI validation JUnit Runs in a BuildKit container, so it needs Docker Yes Zig The installation tree of a build.zig project JUnit: one case per test step for dependency-free native and isolated Linux builds, including dependencies. Coverage not available Intel macOS; dependency-free Linux x86-64 (GNU). Dependency-free Windows x86-64 admitted, unverified Yes, on Linux x86-64 (GNU), including JUnit test reports Builder capabilities also depend on the selected plugin package. The current .NET catalog release lacks a feature required by this CLI; native Zig JUnit requires a newer package capability. See .NET and Zig before using those flows. Each build produces the reports its checks select. A successful --full build doesn't create reports for checks that are off or not available for that ecosystem.

The right Node setup depends on the package manager and the project shape. This table shows what works for each combination. Project shape npm pnpm Yarn Classic 1.22.22 Yarn Berry 4.17.1 Single-root application (a dist/ directory, Node test runner reports) Native and isolated Native and isolated (pnpm 10.11.0 only in isolated builds) Native and isolated Native and isolated. node-modules linker only Single-root package (.tgz) Native and isolated Isolated, for projects with no dependencies Not supported yet Not supported yet Workspace packages (several .tgz files) Native and isolated Isolated Native Native Workspace application Isolated, with a private root Not supported yet Not supported yet Not supported yet Package-local workspace (node/app, member archives and tests) Linux crun, member reuse Linux crun, member reuse Linux crun, member reuse Not supported yet Native Node builds are supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64), except where noted. Isolated builds use a Linux (amd64) container. Single-root npm builds with dependencies accept package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json; see npm lock requirements. A native npm single-root package is built when you declare it explicitly with uses: node/app. Native workspace packages: npm on Windows (plus TypeScript workspaces on Linux), Yarn Classic on Linux, Yarn Berry on Windows. Yarn Plug'n'Play and per-member application directories aren't supported. Yarn node/package workspaces use native execution; isolated package-local node/app workspaces follow the separate row above. See npm workspaces, pnpm and Yarn for workspace details. Captured npm aggregate tests support explicit report-owner redirection to contained literal files. Other owners retain their default report pairs; missing required reports still block artifact export. oyzu run test can run workspace tests for npm, pnpm 10 and Yarn Classic on Windows. Aggregate root scripts retain workspace scope; native host lifecycle reads remain incomplete.

The Node test runner is supported in the shapes above. These also work for npm applications: Tool Support Vitest 5.0.3 with V8 coverage Native single-package builds on Linux and Windows; native npm/pnpm 10/Yarn Classic workspace application tests through build --full (Windows workspace builds unverified). CMake and C/C++ builds, SwiftPM, Xcode and Android aren't supported. You can run their tools with oyzu exec or a task, but Oyzu doesn't discover those projects, collect their artifacts or check their reports. Windows ARM64 and macOS Apple silicon hosts aren't supported. On Windows, Oyzu doesn't run Windows containers or use Windows SDKs for isolated builds.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/engine-staging.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The engine is the oyzu executable that runs a build. A project can pin an exact engine in oyzu.lock. When the oyzu you run is a different build, it hands the build to the pinned engine, which you supply as a local engine package. Note: Engine packages are local archives that you build and verify yourself, or that the install scripts compose from a release's own executables. There is no separate release channel, public catalog or automatic upgrade for engines. Engine staging works on Linux x86-64 and Windows x64 (MSVC). macOS is not supported yet. Isolated builds (--isolated) run the engine's Linux member inside the container. A Linux oyzu mounts itself. On Windows and macOS, oyzu needs an installed package that pairs it with the Linux oyzu built from the same source; see Installing this oyzu with its Linux member. The install scripts do this for releases. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Install a package you built and verified: oyzu engine install --identity <BUILD_ID> --archive ./engine.tar.gz --sha256 sha256:<HEX> Run the executable the command prints. It reports identity, release, executable, registration and admission; add --json for machine-readable output. To make a project use a different engine, pin it in oyzu.lock and admit the archive in your user configuration: # oyzu.lock [engine] identity = "0.1.0-local.0123456789ab" # user configuration [engines.packages] "0.1.0-local.0123456789ab" = { archive = "/path/to/engine.tar.gz", sha256 = "sha256:<64 lowercase hex>" }

A release engine identity is the first version token that oyzu --version prints. A development engine instead uses the complete content fingerprint shown as Engine in build output and inventory, independently of the development display label. See engine identity for its inputs. The archive digest binds the package's exact member bytes. Without a pin, the running oyzu is the engine. Every build records the engine identity it used and whether it was pinned. On Linux, this includes a CLI built from source: run that executable with build --isolated and no --engine-development. The engines.development setting only permits that flag; it does not select an engine for isolated execution. Administrative pin requirements remain binding. With a pin that differs from the running oyzu: oyzu looks for an admitted archive for that identity in engines.packages. It installs the engine beside your oyzu and hands the build to it before configuration is read, tools are resolved or plugins load. Your oyzu and the project lock do not change. oyzu build --plan and oyzu plugins update do the same, so the update check runs under the pinned engine's capabilities. A compatible engine change doesn't update plugin or tool selections, and a plugin update keeps the engine pin. If no admitted archive supplies the pin, the build stops with ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH before doing any work. The project's oyzu.lock must be readable, even for build --plan. Captured builds (--isolated or an explicit --image) with a pin always need the admitted archive, even when the running oyzu already has the pinned identity. The archive supplies the Linux worker that runs inside the container. If the archive has no member for the platform, the build fails instead of using the worker built into the image. A build with no pin that you start from an installed engine (see below) uses that engine's package the same way.

engines.packages maps exact build identities to archives: Field Meaning key The exact engine identity archive Absolute path to the archive sha256 Archive digest, sha256: plus 64 lowercase hex digits The map holds at most 64 entries. There is no default source, tag lookup, newest cache lookup or network fallback. Set it in user or system configuration, never in a project file, local override or profile, so a project can't authorize its own engine. User configuration doesn't apply in CI. Edit it with oyzu config set --global (with --json-value) and oyzu config unset. The build's --store option selects the tool store. Engines live in engines/<archive-sha256>/ inside it.

When a Linux invocation uses its own executable as a captured worker, Oyzu keeps a stable copy under $XDG_STATE_HOME/oyzu/engine-copies (by default ~/.local/state/oyzu/engine-copies), rather than in /tmp. The private directory contains oyzu-engine-* copies keyed by engine identity, executable digest and platform. Overlapping invocations reuse the same copy. A hard link is used when the executable and state directory share a filesystem; otherwise Oyzu copies the executable. Replacing the original executable does not change a selected worker. Private-state validation refuses unsafe ownership, unsafe ancestor permissions and non-system symlinks. If the normal state path is shared, set XDG_STATE_HOME to a private, user-owned location with safe ancestors. Normal completion and unwinding release the invocation's owner record and remove the copy when no live owner remains. After a forced exit, the next invocation that selects a worker reuses a complete matching copy and reclaims other unused copies. Only a confirmed-dead process is reclaimed: inaccessible or reused live PIDs are retained, and live owners never expire by age. A failed deletion is retried on a later selection. The small coordination lock file remains. Copies left by older versions in /tmp are not automatically removed. Windows and macOS hosts still use admitted engine packages with Linux members; they do not create this fallback copy. Their package storage and leases are unchanged. The copy cleanup also tolerates Windows executable sharing failures by leaving the unused directory for a later retry.

oyzu engine install --identity <BUILD_ID> --archive ./engine.tar.gz --sha256 sha256:<HEX> oyzu engine install --identity <BUILD_ID> --archive ./engine.tar.gz --sha256 sha256:<HEX> --json Option Meaning --identity The exact build identity declared by the package's engine.json --archive Local archive, with its platform members and notices --sha256 The archive digest you trust, with the sha256: prefix Each runtime's platform in engine.json is a canonical JSON string, for example "windows/x86_64/msvc" or "linux/x86_64/gnu". Recompose older local packages whose runtime platforms were objects; that unreleased form is no longer accepted. The command checks the archive digest, every executable listed in the manifest, and that the package has a member for this machine's exact OS, architecture and ABI. It needs no network. It doesn't change PATH, install system-wide or touch project locks. Payloads go in your per-user data directory under tools/engines/<archive-sha256>/. A separate registration file, tools/engine-installations/<archive-sha256>.json, binds the package to its installed executable. Only oyzu engine install creates it. Admitting an archive through engines.packages doesn't. Registrations also store runtime platforms as strings. If an older local registration contains a platform object, Oyzu reports ENGINE_INSTALLATION_INVALID, names the file and retains it unchanged. Move only that named registration to a backup outside engine-installations, then repeat oyzu engine install with a current package and its trusted digest. If the installed engine.json also contains platform objects, first recompose the package with string platforms as described above. Reinstalling the same archive without moving an invalid registration does not overwrite it. Keep the backup for diagnosis; do not edit authenticated manifests or registrations to make a package appear compatible. The engine manifest, its runtime members and the installation registration have closed field sets. Unknown fields are rejected, including descriptive additions. The archive digest authenticates the original manifest and executable members; editing a manifest or copying a registration cannot make another package compatible. Keep package bytes and registrations intact when updating Oyzu. An unpinned build uses an installed package only when the running executable is that registered, installed member with the matching identity and platform. For isolated builds on Windows and macOS, a copy of that member counts too when its bytes are identical (same executable digest, identity and platform), such as the oyzu the install scripts, oyzu self and oyzu run bootstrap put on your PATH. Any other copy, and every copy on Linux, doesn't inherit the registration. Warm use doesn't need the original archive, and installed files aren't re-hashed on each command. --store changes the tool store but not where registrations live. A registered engine can supply its own Linux worker for captured builds without any engines.packages setting. engines.requirePin and [engine] pins are still checked first, and engines.development doesn't affect registered packages.

From the Oyzu source checkout, build a static Linux x86-64 member with: oyzu build cli --platform linux/x86_64/musl Use the resulting oyzu executable under dist/cli/linux/x86_64-musl/ as the --linux input below. Explicit /musl selects the static ABI even on a Linux x86-64 host; an unqualified linux/x86_64 selects that host's default ABI when it matches the host. Plain oyzu build cli retains the native host build. The pinned Rust toolchain needs the target standard library. C dependencies such as ring use Oyzu's pinned Zig and cargo-zigbuild through the Rust cross-compiler environment, with rust-lld linking the result. System clang and musl-gcc are not prerequisites. No additional tool pin in build.yaml or oyzu.toml is needed for this compiler. Rust's native host linker and C runtime are still required for build scripts and procedural macros; the managed cross compiler handles the target's C dependencies. Check the resulting member before packaging it: file dist/cli/linux/x86_64-musl/oyzu ldd dist/cli/linux/x86_64-musl/oyzu file should report a statically linked or static-PIE ELF executable for x86-64. ldd should report statically linked or not a dynamic executable rather than a list of shared libraries; the latter message can return a nonzero status. The first build needs online access to the pinned compiler archives at https://ziglang.org/download/0.15.2/ and https://github.com/rust-cross/cargo-zigbuild/releases/download/v0.21.2/. Offline builds need those archives already cached. If source access is denied or unavailable, or an archive is missing offline, preparation stops before compilation with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE, names the compiler asset and prints the online retry command using the selected platform's canonical spelling (arm64, not aarch64). The underlying access failure remains in the diagnostic. An administrative source denial requires an administrator to admit the source; retrying does not bypass that control. Integrity, archive and filesystem failures retain their original diagnostics instead of source-admission or online-retry advice. oyzu engine install --linux ./oyzu-linux-x86_64 oyzu engine install --linux ./oyzu-linux-x86_64 --linux ./oyzu-linux-arm64 --json This packs the oyzu you run together with the Linux oyzu executables you name into one engine package, then installs and registers it exactly like an archive (see above). Afterwards, isolated builds on this machine run the Linux member from the package, whether you start the installed executable or the oyzu on your PATH with the same bytes. Rule Detail Members 1 to 4 --linux files; can't be combined with --archive Platform Read from the file: a 64-bit ELF for x86-64 or arm64. With a dynamic loader it is gnu (musl for musl's loader); statically linked it is musl Same source Each file must carry this engine's identity, independently of the development --version display label, or the command stops with ENGINE_IDENTITY_MISMATCH before installing anything Result The same fields as an archive install, plus platforms, every member of the package The development identity covers engine sources and the lock, transitive local runtime/build dependency package inputs, enabled features, shared profile facts (optimization, debug information, debug assertions, overflow checks and panic strategy) and the rustc release. It leaves out the host triple and target-only rustflags, linker and C toolchain. Shared RUSTFLAGS, CARGO_BUILD_RUSTFLAGS and project build.rustflags are included; only explicitly identified target.<triple>.rustflags selections are excluded from Cargo's effective flags. Build members from the same source state, features, shared profile settings and compiler release. The identity does not cover user [patch] overrides or source replacement, or C toolchain inputs; it is not a source attestation. Each member's executable digest separately binds its bytes. Release members use their shared explicit release stamp. Local package inventories retain native Cargo manifest path spelling and the compiling invocation's working directory/configuration. Captured file identities remain canonical, including on Windows. Development package composition checks Cargo's aggregate binary dep-info against the actual files hashed by the identity capture. That record covers the binary and its linked workspace crates. Compiler/sysroot and Cargo registry sources have separate toolchain/lock identities; the capture also identifies its own generated identity and notice files. Other compiled reads must be in the captured file set. An ignored include_str! input, an include outside its package, or an omitted nested package file stops composition with ENGINE_INPUTS_UNCOVERED, naming the file. Add the file to the package/source inputs and rebuild; packaging does not silently add it to the identity. Retain the original Cargo output while composing a development engine. The compiled capture names its original oyzu.d; alternatively copy that record beside a relocated member with the .d extension. Missing source capture or dep-info stops with ENGINE_INPUTS_UNVERIFIED. This check runs during explicit development engine composition, not ordinary startup or installed-tool use. Ordinary test and coverage builds do not produce an engine package and do not need an aggregate oyzu.d. Installing an already composed archive uses archive admission rather than repeating the compilation coverage check. Explicitly producing a development package still requires every member's compiler records. Cargo package membership depends on Git ignore state. A Git archive without its Git directory, or a worktree whose Git directory is not mounted, can include files that Cargo excluded in the Git checkout. Build all members with the same available Git/ignore context. Otherwise their identities can differ and composition fails closed with ENGINE_IDENTITY_MISMATCH; a non-Git tree is not guaranteed to match an otherwise identical Git checkout. The Linux worker checks its exact identity and platform again before each isolated build. Run the command again after you replace oyzu: the new executable has different bytes, so the old package no longer applies.

documents.t: An administrator can require every build in some contexts to have an exact engine pin and a complete lock, using the protected setting engines.requirePin. It is administrative-only, defaults to false, and can't be set in machine, user, project, local, invocation or profile settings. A nonbinding policy default doesn't require anything. For example, in a protected policy: { "engines.requirePin": { "locked": true, "value": true, "when": { "context": ["ci", "pr", "release"] } } } Put this in the administrative policy file, not in oyzu.toml. The build root and the stricter of the detected and requested contexts decide whether it applies. A weaker --context, a profile or an ordinary override can't waive it. Without an applicable requirement, local, CI and release builds can be unpinned. A build that requires a pin: Stops with ENGINE_PIN_REQUIRED if oyzu.lock has no [engine].identity, before discovery, plugin roles or preparation. Can't use --engine-development to skip the pin. Replays existing plugin selections and refuses unpinned local development plugin bindings. Checks that each selected tool has a portable lock entry before preparing tools. Never adopts or writes a missing plugin or tool selection. Prepare the whole lock before running the governed build. Removing --frozen doesn't remove the requirement. For a missing plugin selection, restore an approved complete lock, or run oyzu build in an approved context where policy allows adoption. Otherwise ask your policy administrator for a context where you can prepare the lock. oyzu plugins update replaces existing selections but doesn't adopt a missing first one, and oyzu pin and oyzu install don't repair a missing plugin selection. The requirement carries over when the build is handed to another engine. An older engine that doesn't understand it refuses the handoff.

To test a CLI you built from source while keeping the shared pin, first allow the override in user configuration (or ask your administrator to): oyzu config set --global engines.development true Then run that executable with --engine-development on each build: ./dist/cli/artifacts/oyzu -C ~/projects/app build app --engine-development Rule Detail Setting engines.development, boolean, default false. Not allowed in project or local files or profiles. Administrative constraints apply. Per build The setting only permits the flag; you pass the flag for every build. Where it works Local development only. Detected CI and requested CI, PR or release contexts refuse it, even with --context local. Combinations Not allowed with remote, isolated, image, all-platform or slice builds. Undo oyzu config unset --global engines.development The flag keeps the executable you started. It doesn't look for another executable, install the pinned engine, change the pin, or change PATH. Build inventory and local preview JSON record developmentOverride: true, pinned: false, the actual identity and executableDigest, and the requestedPin. The Context section of the human output names the override, its digest and the bypassed pin. Two builds with the same version label can have different content, so this record identifies bytes and is not a publisher attestation. Captured builds with external builders need an admitted engine archive and refuse this override.

For a captured build, --image go=<reference> picks the execution image for that ecosystem, separately from the engine, plugin and tool pins. Oyzu resolves the image to its immutable digest and platform once per build. Changing a tag later affects new builds, not one already running. To use the exact images of an earlier build again, keep that build's bundle outside the source tree and run: oyzu build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --frozen \ --execution-images-from /retained/build-a This reuses the images only. It doesn't re-run the old plan. Oyzu checks the bundle's integrity (not who produced it), then checks that the source, the target, variant and builder selection, the lock bytes and the engine selection match. It then prepares and plans as usual under your current policy and checks. The new plan records which earlier build it took its images from. Rule Detail Required --isolated and --frozen Not allowed with --image, remote execution, previews, affected selection, slices, handoff, --engine-development, contract verification Supported Captured builds with an admitted engine archive, for built-in and external builders Not supported Derived application containers, in-process image assembly, and bundles recorded without the comparison facts (you can still inspect them) --offline Ordinary offline rules apply. It never permits missing tools or dependencies. Errors: Code Cause and recovery EXECUTION_IMAGES_SOURCE_CHANGED, EXECUTION_IMAGES_SELECTION_CHANGED The source or pins differ from the earlier build. Restore them, or run an ordinary new build. EXECUTION_IMAGE_UNAVAILABLE The recorded image isn't available, or your executor refuses it. The error names the target, digest and platform. Provide that exact image and retry. Oyzu never substitutes the current tag. On Windows, the frontend oyzu stays attached during Ctrl+C until the staged engine finishes cleanup and returns its exit status. The engine reports the interruption and keeps the failed build bundle. oyzu install --store <directory> and oyzu exec --store <directory> -- <command> use the same store when they read requirements from an already installed, locked external builder. Neither adopts a missing plugin; prepare it with a build first. On Windows, install oyzu.exe and oyzu-shim.exe together.

Captured builds run the engine, plugin and locked tools inside a Linux image. There are two ways they can get there: mounted: Oyzu mounts them read-only into the container. This is the default. image-installed: the exact files are already installed in the image, so Oyzu uses them in place without mounting or restoring anything. Image labels and PATH never choose versions. The engine archive, the plugin lock and the locked tool distribution do. When you install a package, the store keeps a record of its verified contents next to it. If that record is missing (older installs, or an interrupted install), builds use mounted placement. Reinstalling a removed package renews the record. Before a build, Oyzu compares the selected files with the image's filesystem once and caches the result for that image in your user cache. Only regular files and directories can be image-installed. A tree that contains links stays mounted. Anything that doesn't match stays mounted. Docker volumes, scratch paths and explicit overlays can't hide admitted files. An overlay that conflicts with one stops the build with ENGINE_CONTROL_CONFLICT. Evidence in the build records the selected engine member (identity, archive digest, platform and executable digest) separately from the engine baked into the image. Oyzu never runs the baked executable to observe it. The baked observation is for information only and never changes which engine is selected. An image from the classic Docker store can lack an OCI Descriptor. Then placement can't be observed, the baked engine shows as unavailable, and builds use mounted placement. A descriptor that is present but invalid is an error, not a fallback.

After a build has installed the exact engine, plugin and tools and filled the ecosystem's dependency cache, you can repeat it without the network. For Go: oyzu -C <project> install --frozen --offline --store <store> oyzu -C <project> exec --offline --store <store> -- go mod download oyzu -C <project> build app --frozen --offline --no-docker --no-cache --store <store> Keep the same GOMODCACHE, GOCACHE and GOPATH you used for preparation. To make Go itself refuse the network, also set GOENV=off, GOWORK=off, GOTOOLCHAIN=local, GOPROXY=off, GOSUMDB=off and GOVCS=*:off. --offline and these variables control the clients Oyzu and Go use. They don't block the network at the operating-system level, so an arbitrary project command could still reach it. Missing engine or plugin installations are restored from their admitted local archives, and a cached tool archive can restore a missing tool. If neither an installation nor an archive exists, the command stops. A missing Go module reports module lookup disabled by GOPROXY=off. Restore the content with an online build first. Don't edit the lock to match whatever is cached. Replaying means running the same command again with the same executable, arguments, directory, source, lock and package selections. There is no command that replays history. Current admission still applies: removing the engine's admission makes the build fail with ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH, even if the bytes are cached. Matching evidence doesn't guarantee byte-identical output. If you cancel a build, the staged engine records it as interrupted, prints BUILD_INTERRUPTED, keeps no artifact from the run and exits with status 130. Other builds that share the installed engine are not affected.

An engine package is a gzip tar or ZIP archive with engine.json at its root and one executable per platform at the path the manifest gives. One admitted archive covers every platform member of the engine build. { "contract": "oyzu.engine.v1alpha1", "identity": "0.1.0-local.0123456789ab", "runtimes": [{ "platform": "windows/x86_64/msvc", "entrypoint": "bin/windows/oyzu.exe", "executableDigest": "sha256:<64 lowercase hex>" }] } Rule Detail Members 1 to 16 platform members with unique platforms and entrypoints Executables Each must be a regular file whose digest matches the manifest Platform match OS, architecture and ABI must match the running engine exactly. Oyzu doesn't infer ABI compatibility. Identity The running engine's compiled identity must match the manifest, so a manifest can't relabel a different build The digest you supply covers the whole archive, including the manifest. Oyzu verifies the archive before extracting it, extracts it without following links, checks the manifest and executables, then publishes the installation atomically. Installed files are trusted afterward. Admitting an archive by digest is not a publisher signature check and says nothing about official provenance.

Code Cause and recovery ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH No admitted archive supplies the pinned engine. Run the pinned engine, or admit its archive in user or system configuration. ENGINE_PIN_REQUIRED Policy requires an engine pin and oyzu.lock has none. Pin the engine and prepare the full lock. ENGINE_DEVELOPMENT_DENIED --engine-development isn't permitted here: the setting is off, the context isn't local, or policy requires the pin. Drop the flag or get permission. ENGINE_DEVELOPMENT_UNAVAILABLE The development executable couldn't be read. Make it readable and retry. CONFIG_SCOPE A project, local or profile source tried to admit an engine. Move the setting to user configuration or the administrator. ENGINE_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE The archive can't be read. Restore it. ENGINE_PACKAGE_DIGEST The archive doesn't match the digest. Get the expected archive; don't just change the digest. ENGINE_PACKAGE_INVALID The manifest or executables don't match the package rules above. Rebuild the package. ENGINE_INCOMPATIBLE The package's contract or platform isn't supported by this engine. Supply a matching build. ENGINE_IDENTITY_MISMATCH, ENGINE_HANDOFF_MISMATCH The manifest or the running build doesn't match the requested identity or entrypoint. Fix the package. No second handoff happens. ENGINE_HANDOFF_CHANGED The pin or the admitted release changed during the handoff. Retry with consistent settings. ENGINE_HANDOFF_INVALID The receiving engine can't take this handoff, for example an older engine that only supports builds, not updates. Run that engine directly or pick one that supports the operation. ENGINE_INSTALLATION_INVALID The registration and the installed executable disagree. Reinstall the package. Don't copy registrations between installations. ENGINE_START_FAILED The verified executable wouldn't start. Check host prerequisites and the package layout. ENGINE_CONTROL_CONFLICT An overlay or volume conflicts with an admitted engine file in a container. Remove the overlay. ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE An isolated build on Windows or macOS found no package with a Linux member for this oyzu. Run oyzu engine install --linux with the Linux oyzu built from the same source, or reinstall the release with the install script. A failure at this stage happens before the build does anything. Oyzu doesn't adopt plugins or tools or change selections. Complete engine installations stay in the store for reuse.

Engine packages are local archives. No separate release channel, catalog or automatic upgrade exists. On Windows and macOS, oyzu run bootstrap -- --isolated cross-compiles the Linux member for the host's architecture only; pass others with --linux <file>. Plain bootstrap builds and installs only the host CLI. A nested build uses its own lock, not the parent's. Native (non-container) builds have no filesystem or network isolation from this feature. Updating plugins through an engine handoff works only when both the frontend and the receiving engine support it. macOS isn't supported yet.
Configuration Plugin packages Plugin updates

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/execution-image.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build --isolated runs every container action on one small Linux image, the base execution image oyzu-execution/base:1. It holds operating system pieces and a C toolchain and nothing else. Oyzu mounts everything a build needs into it: the invocation's own engine, the builder's plugin package and the tools oyzu.lock selects. Native builds (plain oyzu build on a host that has a native build for the project) don't use it. This page lists what the image contains, how Oyzu gets it, and what an image of your own must provide when you pass --image. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.
oyzu build --isolated # every builder runs on the base image, pulled on first use oyzu build --isolated --image npm=node:22-trixie-slim # one manager on your own image

Each action is assembled the same way, whichever builder it belongs to: Image. An explicit --image <manager>=<ref> for that manager, otherwise the base image for the action's architecture. Engine. The invocation's engine is mounted read-only. With an installed engine package (oyzu engine install, which the Windows and macOS install scripts run for you, or an [engine].identity pin in oyzu.lock), Oyzu mounts its Linux member for the image's architecture (the static musl one when the package has several). Without one, a Linux CLI of the same architecture mounts its own executable. On Windows and macOS hosts an engine package is required; without it the build stops with ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE before any work. No image carries an Oyzu worker, so a new CLI release never needs a new image. Tools. Every language toolchain and stage tool comes from oyzu.lock and is restored read-only into the action: Rust and its components, cargo-nextest, cargo-llvm-cov, Go, Node with npm, pnpm or Yarn, CPython, the .NET SDK, the JDK with Maven, Gradle or Ant, Helm, helm-unittest and yamlfmt, and Zig. A builder whose tool isn't locked for the platform stops with the oyzu pin command that fixes it; the image has no copy to fall back to. Plugin. The selected builder plugin package is mounted read-only at /oyzu-plugin, with any helpers it ships: the Docker plugin's metadata, image and snapshot helpers, BuildKit frontend and dockerfmt, and the Node plugin's pnpm and Yarn lockfile parsers. Pinned integration files. A few upstream files that aren't tools in the lock are fetched once, checked against a SHA-256 pinned in Oyzu, stored with your declared fetches and restored read-only: the default Node lint, format and coverage packages (Node quality), Checkstyle, google-java-format, JaCoCo, JUnit and Ant for Java builds (Java quality), and the cross linkers of a Rust cross build (Rust). The plan and the build evidence record the image digest, the engine member, the plugin release and each tool's locked identity. In the daemonless Linux executor, each invocation has a fresh private /tmp. When its declared HOME is a directory beneath /tmp, that directory is also created as a private temporary filesystem owned by the action's user, with mode 0700. This applies separately to compilation and each test invocation; a home created by an earlier phase is not reused. The executor keeps the declared HOME value, imports no host home contents, and discards the temporary home when the sandbox ends. Homes outside /tmp retain the image's existing behavior. Docker image builds that run RUN steps use a second image, the rootless BuildKit worker oyzu-execution/buildkit:0.34.0. It is the upstream moby/buildkit 0.34.0 rootless image pinned by digest, with nothing of Oyzu's added. See Docker image inputs.
documents.s: What runs in a container action

documents.t: The image is Ubuntu 24.04 (ubuntu:24.04, pinned by digest) with these packages, built for the supported linux/amd64 platform: Package Why it is there gcc, g++, libc6-dev, make, cmake, ninja-build, pkg-config C and C++ compilers and build tools for Rust build scripts, cgo, native npm and Python extensions and Zig's C interop. Rust links with cc. musl-tools musl-gcc, for C code in a static musl build. git Native tools that read Git metadata, such as Go VCS stamping and Cargo Git dependencies. ca-certificates, tzdata TLS roots and time zones for tools and tests. libssl3t64, libgssapi-krb5-2, libicu74, zlib1g, libatomic1 Shared libraries the locked .NET SDK and Node releases load. bzip2, xz-utils, zstd, zip, unzip, patch, file Archive and patch tools native builds call, and .tar.xz restoration of locked tools. Oyzu builds and publishes the Linux amd64 image itself from tooling/images/build.yaml, installing the packages from an OS package lock that lists every version, including the dependencies apt pulled in; tooling/images/base/debs.lock.yaml is the committed copy, and each publishing run uploads the lock it actually built from. Publication uses the single image's manifest digest, without composing a multi-platform index. See Dogfooding in workflows. The source lock selects libbrotli1 1.1.0-2ubuntu0.1 for amd64, Ubuntu's fix for CVE-2026-111497. This applies to images rebuilt from that lock. Updating it does not replace the CLI's published image pin, existing local images or running containers. The source lock and required image-build matrix use amd64. ARM64 image builds are unsupported. There is no language runtime, package manager, Oyzu engine or Oyzu plugin in it. PATH is the standard Ubuntu one; each action prepends the restored tools.

Ubuntu 24.04 ships glibc 2.39. Anything a build links against glibc in the container needs glibc 2.39 or newer wherever it later runs. A Rust or Go binary built for linux/* with the GNU target won't start on an older distribution such as Debian bookworm (glibc 2.36) or Ubuntu 22.04 (glibc 2.35). If your binaries must run on older Linux systems, build them statically: target musl in Rust (x86_64-unknown-linux-musl; Oyzu's isolated cross builds already link those with rust-lld), or build Go with CGO_ENABLED=0. A Docker image's own base decides its libc at run time; this note is about binaries built in the execution image and copied elsewhere.

When the image isn't in the local Docker engine, Oyzu pulls it from ghcr.io/oyzuai/oyzu-execution/base by the digest pinned in the CLI, so a moved tag can't substitute another image. The package is public and needs no login. An image already present locally is used as it is. To use an image built from source instead, build it under the same name before the first isolated build: docker build -t oyzu-execution/base:1 tooling/images/base from a checkout of the Oyzu repository. A local image of that name is used as it is, without a digest check. Set OYZU_NO_TOOLCHAIN_PULL=1 to forbid every pull, for example on an air-gapped host that preloads the image. The BuildKit worker is pulled the same way from docker.io/moby/buildkit by its pinned digest. Oyzu records pulled images and keeps them within the Docker storage budget. An organization registry allow-list and mirror for Oyzu-published images is designed in the platform repository and not implemented in the CLI yet.

--image <manager>=<ref> runs that manager's isolated actions on an image you choose, for example one with OS packages your native build links against: oyzu build --isolated --image cargo=registry.example.com/build/rust-base:2026-10 The manager is the one the target's builder uses, for example cargo, go, npm, pnpm, yarn, pip, uv or poetry. The reference must already be in the local Docker engine; Oyzu never pulls a bring-your-own image. The image's immutable identity is recorded in the plan and evidence. The image must provide: Linux x86-64. ARM64 workers and targets are unsupported. A C runtime the engine can start on. An engine package's static Linux member runs on any libc. When a Linux CLI mounts its own executable instead, that executable's glibc requirement applies; release builds need glibc 2.39 or newer. A C runtime the locked tools can start on. The official Node, .NET, JDK and Rust releases need glibc, and Rust and cgo need a working cc. Alpine and other musl images only suit tools that are static. tar that extracts .tar.gz and .tar.xz archives with --strip-components, and sleep: Oyzu restores locked tools with the image's own tar and keeps tool volumes in use with sleep. Whatever OS packages the project's native build needs. Oyzu still mounts the engine, the plugin and the locked tools; an image's own copy of a tool is never used in place of the locked one.

Isolated uv builds restore uv from oyzu.lock. Poetry builds still need an image with Poetry installed, passed with --image poetry=<ref>. Rust builds for macOS link against Zig's libSystem stubs, with no Apple SDK in the image. Crates that link other Apple frameworks need an image that provides an SDK (SDKROOT). Only linux/amd64 workers are supported. ARM64 is unsupported. Remote pools don't use this image yet.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/go.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu builds Go modules and go.work workspaces without any Oyzu configuration. It finds go.mod and go.work, runs the native go tooling, and collects binaries, module archives, test reports and coverage into a build bundle. Use this page to see what the Go builder runs, how it picks the Go version and what it produces. Status: experimental. Single-main applications can build natively on the host. Captured builds use a Linux amd64 executor: Docker, or crun on Linux. Docker builds work from Linux and Windows hosts; complete runtime-read enforcement requires Linux crun. Captured macOS support is not available. The builder is supplied by the oyzu-plugin-go plugin; see plugin catalog.

Native oyzu build --full collects JUnit and coverage from the conventional Go test command. With a Go plugin that supplies JSON test events on stdout, Oyzu converts each process's events before checking attempt completeness; the final reports appear in the build bundle. These plugins retry the whole test step. Package and failed-case selection requires the matching plugin described below. Missing, malformed or truncated events still fail the build; inspect the test action's retained stdout and stderr before rerunning it. With a matching development engine and Go plugin, conventional build tests expose one test unit per package. Test retries rerun only failed cases through the public rerun-cases plugin feature. Local builds default to no retries; pr, ci and release default to two extra attempts. Each attempt runs a fresh go test -json -count=1 -failfast=false process. A retry adds -run with an escaped, anchored pattern for each subtest level, for example '^TestA$/^case_1$'. Each requested case gets its own invocation, avoiding cross-products between subtest names. Go runs matching parents too; aggregate parent results are containers, so passing siblings are not selected again. A fail-then-pass exits zero with TEST_FLAKY unless tests.flaky = "fail". Persistent failures retain Go's original exit status. Reports retain each attempt and distinguish assertions, package/setup errors, timeouts and crashes. A missing or skipped requested case remains failed with TEST_RERUN_INCOMPLETE, even if Go's filter exits zero. --no-cache uses the same attempt rules; flaky results are never reusable clean passes. Coverage retains the full first attempt. Go has no native retry setting. Oyzu forces -count=1 to disable Go's test-result cache and repetition, and disables fail-fast for complete first-attempt evidence. Build failures, incomplete reports, binary timeouts, and race/leak findings do not become flaky passes. Panics widen selection to the whole package, including init and TestMain; other package/setup failures remain incomplete. A parent's own failure without a failing subtest also prevents a case retry. Authored test commands and hooks keep their existing report integration and whole-step fallback. Runtime package reads remain conservative; the compiled test identity grants no narrower filesystem access. Retries need no account and work offline with installed tools and available native dependencies.

oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist oyzu run <task> runs a development task on your machine with your provisioned go and gofmt. oyzu build builds an admitted single-main application natively. Other module/workspace builds use the container executor (see Toolchain image); --isolated explicitly requests it. oyzu inspect dist checks the resulting bundle.

A Go build's path can name the folder containing go.mod or go.work. For go/app, it can also name a command package inside an enclosing module; native lookup stops at the project root. See multiple commands. A go.work workspace owns the modules it declares. Listing tasks (oyzu run list) does not run Go. A project with no main package produces module artifacts instead of failing as an unsupported library. Native application discovery ignores .go files whose names begin with . or _, as Go does. Generator or scratch files with those names do not add command packages or prevent a single-main host build. Source capture and gofmt checks keep their existing selection rules. Native application discovery skips leading line and block comments before reading the package clause. A package main example inside a documentation comment does not add a command package. Native application discovery excludes descendant folders with their own go.mod. Commands in those independent modules do not count toward the selected module's main packages. Selecting a nested module itself still discovers its own packages. uses: go/library selects module packaging even when the project has commands. go/app and go/library are the two Go builds. Oyzu reads the module and package facts from Go, picks the tools and versions, and runs the build, test and archive steps.

The selected engine and Go builder must support the same native inputs. Older engines that supply no prepared host facts use whole-source commands and versioned compilation outputs. Prepared host facts enable the typed commands, frozen environment checks and separate final export described below. Conventional native host build and lint (go vet) use per-stage source reads from Go's package file lists. Preparation runs go list -json -deps with the selected tool and resolved Go settings; vet's inventory also includes test packages. A declared command such as path: cmd/api predicts the selected main package and its dependencies within the module context, even when other commands exist in that module. The prediction covers module manifests, vendor inputs when present, selected source and resolved embed files, and package/asset directory listings. A README content edit outside those inputs does not change the predicted read set. Adding a Go file in a package directory or editing an embedded file does. The shared cache still keys action definitions and upstream outputs, so version or configuration changes can independently cause a miss. Native builds with complete admitted reads can reuse build, vet and format-check across unread README content edits. Compilation writes a stable intermediate executable; a final export copies it to the inferred-version filename. A commit with no source change reuses compile and quality stages. Core retains the exact output files of its validated native Go commands before selecting private stages, including with a compatible published plugin that does not declare private output files. Vet and format-check retain no workspace outputs. This output binding does not establish read completeness: missing or incomplete observations still prevent reuse. If version metadata changes, the final export runs for the new version. An empty commit alone leaves the source-content snapshot version unchanged and can reuse export too. The bundle and receipt name that current version. New files affecting discovery, changed source, authored flags and configured environment values still invalidate the stages that consume them. The plugin executes typed native Build/Vet commands and collects the same Go facts after successful execution. Complete observations permit a narrow key on a later run; missing or incomplete facts prevent native stage and whole-target reuse. Errors, overlays, cgo header dependencies, redirected sources and local dependencies outside the module/cache have explicit fallback reasons. Versioned module-cache sources are covered by go.sum. Root-level wildcard embeds that may include native output trees stay unbounded; a dedicated asset directory is supported. If the main module's go.mod is outside the target root, prediction is incomplete and the native stage reruns without result reuse. Core checks that each plugin build/vet contract covers every prepared content read and directory listing. A narrowed contract is rejected before execution; an explicitly unbounded fallback remains valid. Conventional native build and lint must have identical resolved task environments. Different overrides fail preparation with GO_NATIVE_ENVIRONMENT_CONFLICT; use matching environments or an authored lint invocation, which remains unbounded. The conventional build always uses -trimpath -buildvcs=false, so it does not stamp or read Git state. Authored build invocations remain raw, unchanged and unbounded. Preparation asks the selected Go tool for effective output-affecting settings, including GOFLAGS (and its -mod choice), GO111MODULE, cgo flags, platform/architecture settings, experiments and the enforced local toolchain. These values contribute to the action key as a snapshot, rather than overriding Go's settings during execution. Before a conventional build or vet, the plugin asks Go for those settings again. A changed value fails admission with GO_NATIVE_ENVIRONMENT_CHANGED, names the setting and asks you to rerun oyzu build. After a successful command and read collection, it checks again. A mismatch fails the action with the same diagnostic, even on whole-projection runs without a read report, so its output cannot be stored under the prepared key. A failed post-run observation makes the report incomplete, so it cannot justify narrow reuse. Diagnostics do not print values.

Private proxies and modules work in host mode using Go's native configuration, including user-level netrc and GOAUTH on Go versions that support it. Run oyzu build --context local --full for all enabled native checks. When private routing or GOAUTH is configured, the routing and credential variables are passed from the invoking environment to the host action, the action runs fresh instead of reusing the action cache, and credential values are redacted from captured native output and never written to Oyzu evidence or generated configuration. GOPROXY and GOPRIVATE URLs containing userinfo are refused before actions, including values in the native GOENV file. NATIVE_SOURCE_CREDENTIAL_REFUSED names the variable and setting origin; move the credential to netrc or GOAUTH. Captured and isolated private sources fail before actions with PRIVATE_GO_SOURCE_UNSUPPORTED; use host mode. There is no public fallback. Go's native checksum rules still apply in host mode: go.sum records module hashes, and GONOSUMDB (defaulting to GOPRIVATE when unset) controls which module paths bypass the public checksum database. GOPRIVATE also defaults GONOPROXY; using a private proxy may require an explicit GONOPROXY choice. Configure these through native Go configuration. Oyzu does not disable checksum verification to make a private dependency resolve. See Go's private-module reference. Native preparation, build, vet and post-run observations leave GOENV alone. Go reads its own configuration file, including GOPROXY, GOPRIVATE, GONOSUMDB, GOMODCACHE and other native settings. No Oyzu-specific routing configuration is needed. Standard Go environment-variable precedence applies; an explicit GOENV=off is still respected. Oyzu continues to enforce GOTOOLCHAIN=local, GOWORK=off for this single-module lane, and GOPROXY=off when offline mode is selected. Persisted routing and cache locations are excluded from the build-setting snapshot: changing only GOPROXY in that file leaves the key unchanged, while changing effective GOFLAGS changes it. The GOENV file's path is not a source read selector. Explicit task environment/configuration changes still follow the normal action-definition key rules. Keep output-affecting settings stable while a build runs; after editing them, rerun the build to refresh preparation. Native format-check has a fixed read contract, checked on Go 1.24.13: **/*.go contents (over-approximate) and listings of the directories gofmt walks within the workspace snapshot's source selection. Prediction and read reports use the same source exclusion rules as the snapshot: .oyzu/ state and conventionally excluded dist/ outputs do not add traversal listings. Native ignore rules can re-admit ordinary output defaults, as for other source reads; required state exclusions always apply. Admitted vendor, testdata, hidden and underscore directories are traversed. It ignores dot-prefixed file names and does not follow directory symlinks. A symlinked Go file stays unbounded. Native vet and format checks precede runtime tests so changing test reports cannot invalidate their results. Native test remains unbounded because tests may read files at run time. On the captured path, eligible per-package actions retain their confined read contracts. Source-free exports and grouping gates declare upstream_only; coarse stages keep their specific fallback reasons. See read contracts.

Declare one build per command folder. This illustrative layout shares module preparation and the module cache while producing one binary per build: go.mod go.sum internal/lib/lib.go cmd/a/main.go cmd/b/main.go build.yaml builds: a: {uses: go/app, path: cmd/a} b: {uses: go/app, path: cmd/b} Run oyzu build for the native host lane or oyzu build --isolated for the captured lane. Each build runs from the module root and compiles only its main package (go build ./cmd/a or go build ./cmd/b). Binary names follow the build names. Command subfolders use go/app; go/library selects the module root. The selected Go plugin package must declare target-path support; older packages are refused with an instruction to select a supporting package. This package feature also requires a supporting engine, including for root-module builds with no package path. Engines that predate target-path must retain a compatible older Go plugin release or update the engine. Captured compilation and exports keep their separate source/dependency keys. Changing a package source invalidates its consumers; changing go.mod, go.sum, the selected Go identity or prepared dependency content invalidates consuming stages. --no-cache executes stages instead of restoring their results. On Linux, oyzu build --isolated --no-docker --full uses crun's complete input boundary for eligible go/app stages. An unchanged warm build can restore compilation, test preparation, test results and exports separately. The input view contains identified source, tools and dependencies; live /proc and /sys are hidden. An undeclared host file stays inaccessible after its contents change. Runtime entropy must not influence retained outputs. Test preparation declares its generated manifests and compiled tests as build outputs. Test actions consume those identified outputs as reads in their stage keys. A changed manifest changes the key; an extra undeclared carried file is refused. Each invocation gets fresh writable /out; only explicit prior phase inputs and validated unit contributions are mounted there read-only, through the same shared mechanism used by Java. Other bundle files never become inputs. Required test and coverage report gates apply equally to executed and restored results. --no-cache keeps the same input boundary and executes every stage. Runtime test contracts conservatively include the whole admitted source view, so edits can invalidate tests beyond the package whose compiler inputs changed. Native-host stages with incomplete reads rerun on Linux, Windows and macOS; unchanged source does not establish complete runtime reads. Independently admitted native compiler and fixed-read stages retain their existing reuse. Windows and macOS have no complete Go runtime-read enforcement backend. For previews, a Go plugin declaring target-path requires an engine containing the module-context and target-path changes; manifest features are intentionally hard requirements. Go finds the enclosing go.mod, or go.work when there is no enclosing module, without searching above the project root. Separate modules in one workspace retain separate preparations. Module source, including internal/, is available; other builds' declared folders are excluded from each build's source scope. Observed package read sets narrow compilation inputs further: changing cmd/a invalidates a's compile, while changing a shared imported package invalidates both consumers. Module files remain inputs, so changing go.sum also invalidates module preparation. A native build at path: . still requires exactly one main package. For several mains, its error names the per-command path: cmd/<name> form. Captured builds at path: . retain one build action per main.

Development tasks use your provisioned go and gofmt. The implicit tasks install dependencies, compile, test, vet, format and check formatting. oyzu run format changes your source. Builds use format-check, which fails when gofmt -l prints anything. In a go.work workspace, the member modules supply the package patterns for the build, test and vet commands. oyzu run test writes the test bundle described under Direct test evidence. Other development tasks don't produce a bundle.

Captured builds need Docker and the base execution image, which has no Go of its own. Go comes from oyzu.lock (see Pinned Go in isolated builds), and Oyzu mounts its engine and the Go plugin into each action. When testing a local Go plugin with --isolated, bind go/app to a package archive, rather than the raw executable. The archive must declare captured-plan and contain a runtime for the execution platform. A raw development executable is deliberately refused with PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED; this does not mean conventional Go applications lack captured planning. The tooling/source-capture-proof.py harness needs this package binding too, including for its isolated refusal cases. The native host lane admits one module with exactly one main package. Use oyzu build --isolated for multiple binaries, libraries or workspaces. These shapes require a selected Go plugin package that declares captured-plan. If PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED says the selected package lacks that feature, select a package that provides it; updating the CLI alone does not update a separately selected or locked builder package. A host-admission note about the number of main packages does not mean captured Go rejects that shape. Preparation compiles the module archive adapter with the locked Go, against the golang.org/x/mod copy that the Go distribution vendors for its own go command. No image carries the adapter, and building it downloads nothing. Your own image (--image go=<image>) needs no adapter either. It must meet the bring-your-own requirements, and a locked Go takes the place of the image's own. Docker projects can also ask for an offline Go module context. It exports only the captured module cache, so the consuming image doesn't need the module archive adapter.

Oyzu runs Go with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, so Go never switches or downloads a toolchain itself. Oyzu picks the Go from your project files instead. Other ecosystems' exact pins are in native pin files. The Go minimum is the newer of the go and toolchain lines in the native context folder's go.work if there is one, otherwise in its go.mod. A command package uses its enclosing module as that context; workspace-root builds use go.work. Lookup stops at the project root. Go orders versions as 1.24 < 1.24rc1 < 1.24.0 < 1.24.5. A toolchain line is always honored. A suffixed name is read as Go reads it (go1.24.3-bigcorp and go1.24.3+auto mean 1.24.3). toolchain default and toolchain local are ignored. Any other value that isn't a Go release name is refused with a remedy. A go line from Go 1.21 on is a toolchain minimum. Before Go 1.21 it was a language level, so a line like go 1.16 only constrains the choice: with no toolchain line and no [tools] go, Oyzu uses the newest stable Go, and a configured value below the line fails resolution. In a workspace, the go.work lines decide. A go.mod beside the go.work keeps its go line as a constraint, and its toolchain line is ignored, as Go ignores it. Modules in subfolders are not read, because Go itself refuses a workspace whose go line is older than a module's. Project Go selected toolchain go1.24.5 (or go 1.24.5), no [tools] go Exactly 1.24.5 go 1.24 with no patch, or toolchain go1.25rc1 The newest stable release of that line (1.24.x, 1.25.x). Oyzu only installs stable releases, so a line that has only a release candidate fails resolution. [tools] go at or above the minimum, in any folder That value (1.25, 1.24 for a 1.24.5 minimum, latest). The minimum still binds its resolution. [tools] go below the minimum, in a folder above the module (the project root, or user configuration) The minimum. The farther value loses, and the Tools row shows overrides 1.23.4 from oyzu.toml. [tools] go below the minimum, in the module's folder or below it Refused before any work with TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT, naming both files. A command-line, environment or policy value below the minimum (a toolset value is exempt) Refused with TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT, naming its source and the native file. A policy value can't be changed in the project, so ask the policy owner or lower the minimum. For example, take toolchain go1.24.5 in app/go.mod, a root [tools] go = "1.25" and [tools] go = "1.24.0" in app/oyzu.toml. oyzu build stops after loading the configuration with exit status 3: ✗ TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT: hello: [tools] go = "1.24.0" in app/oyzu.toml is below the go minimum 1.24.5 that app/go.mod declares (toolchain line); set [tools] go to 1.24.5 or later in app/oyzu.toml, or remove it so the native file decides Next: Make the configured tool version reach the native minimum, or change the native file, then retry. With only a root [tools] go = "1.23.4", the build uses the minimum and says so in the Tools block: ✓ Tools 1 tool pinned · 0 installed now 1.9s go 1.24.5 already installed detected from go.mod · overrides 1.23.4 from oyzu.toml How requests are compared: Only plain releases and lines (1.23.4, 1.23) are compared with the minimum where they are written. Any other form, such as a range, is resolved against the minimum and fails when nothing satisfies it. Tool policy (a tools.go lock or allowed set) applies to the selected version, whichever file requested it, the minimum included. When policy refuses the minimum itself, TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT names the policy source. In a workspace that builds in the isolated executor, the same refusal stops the build during preparation with exit status 3, and the code appears in the bundle's diagnostics. oyzu config explain tools.go shows the configured value. The override appears only in the Tools block. Locking: The selection is locked in oyzu.lock like any request, with the minimum recorded as the constraint go-minimum:>=1.24.5. Changing [tools] go needs oyzu pin before the next build, as for any explicit request. So does a changed minimum. go get and go mod tidy rewrite the go and toolchain lines, and the next build stops and names the cause: ✗ TOOL_LOCK_STALE: oyzu:go 1.24.5; app/go.mod declares go 1.24.5 (toolchain line) but oyzu.lock pins 1.27.2; run oyzu pin Run oyzu pin and commit oyzu.lock. An oyzu.lock written before Oyzu read the Go minimum holds the request * and needs the same step once.

A project that pins Go (for example [tools] go = "1.23", locked with oyzu install go@1.23) builds with that exact Go inside the container. During preparation Oyzu: Reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) archive recorded for the pinned version in oyzu.lock. Downloads it through the tool broker, unless a copy in your user data directory still matches the locked SHA-256. Checks the bytes against the locked digest. Restores them read-only at /scratch/gotool. Puts that go first on PATH (and sets GOROOT) for preparation and every build action. The plan records the archive digest, so a different pin or archive changes the action identity. Without an explicit pin, the Go that preflight locked from the Go minimum is used the same way. The base image has no Go, so a captured build there needs Go in oyzu.lock. Run oyzu pin. Only your own image can supply its own Go when the lock has none. A lock with a changed digest is rejected, and a corrupted cached archive is replaced by a verified download. Offline builds need the archive already cached, or they fail with TOOL_OFFLINE.

oyzu run test runs the implicit go test ./... command with -json, a fresh -coverprofile and -count=1. Oyzu prepares the fresh JUnit and coverage report directories before execution. It does not create report files during setup; the native test adapter must produce them, and missing reports still fail collection. For a declared command folder, oyzu run a:test instruments that build's implicit go test ./cmd/a command with the same report flags. It tests only the selected command package; it does not expand the selection to the other commands or all module packages. Use one build per command as shown under multiple commands. Go owns test discovery and compilation. Oyzu converts Go's JSON events to JUnit and keeps the native coverage profile under dist/. The manifest records digests and summaries. Coverage is statement coverage, not branch or line coverage. A package with no tests gets an honest zero-test summary, and Go may succeed in that case. Missing or malformed reports, and configured coverage thresholds, can still fail the run.

For a go.work root, Oyzu uses the workspace's member packages and combines their test events and coverage. Members outside the task root fail. Forward selectors with oyzu run test -- -run TestGreeting. Forwarded arguments go only to the task you asked for. Go's cached test results are not reused, though Go may still reuse its compilation cache.

Hooks get OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT. The JUnit report is normalized before post_test runs and validated after it, so changes a hook makes are kept. An invalid event stream stays a failure even if a hook later writes valid XML. A failed test skips the success-only post hook and keeps the evidence it has. Exact argv = ["go", "test", "./..."] and run = "go test ./..." overrides get the same treatment. An exact argv = ["go", "test", "./cmd/a"] override also gets reporting when cmd/a is the selected build's command folder. Other package selectors or additional authored flags keep the custom-command behavior below. Other custom commands run unchanged and must write their own JUnit and Go coverage reports. An explicit coverage declaration redirects the native profile. An explicit JUnit declaration switches to file-based reporting, so your task or hook must produce that XML. The default Go command emits JSON, not JUnit. Declared paths must be fresh. See direct tests. This workflow needs a provisioned Go compiler and your dependencies. It needs no Docker and no account. It runs on your machine with your environment and network. For an offline run, use dependencies you already have and set GOPROXY=off, GOSUMDB=off and GOTOOLCHAIN=local. It is not an isolated build and produces no application artifacts. Direct tests covers provenance, output handling and recovery.

Go itself reports manifests, workspace members, main packages, dependencies and cgo use. Captured inputs must contain local modules, local replacement paths and workspace members. Missing paths, or paths that escape the project after resolving symlinks, fail. Prepared dependency observation accepts versioned modules inside Go's selected module cache, including its native @version and ! case-escaped paths. Public modules are downloaded through Oyzu's scoped Go proxy and verified against go.sum. A redirect from the proxy to its storage bucket is followed (acquisition transport). Private modules and direct VCS downloads are not supported. Oyzu records the compiler and ABI for cgo, and an environment override can't turn off required cgo support.

Preparation captures the dependency cache and the module artifact candidates. Library candidates come from captured source, before any build output exists. Go works in a module cache on a container tmpfs (/scratch/gomodcache). The prepared store keeps only the download cache: module zips with their .mod, .info and .ziphash files. Each build action serves that store to Go as a file:// module proxy and extracts what it needs into its own tmpfs cache. go.sum verifies every zip. Module downloads are reused across package-source edits. Their preparation key includes module and workspace manifests/checksums (including local module manifests), vendor inputs, the selected toolchain, configuration and acquisition controls. Changing go.sum or another module input invalidates that reuse. Preparation acquires the complete declared module graph, including modules not yet imported by a package. This can download and store more module archives than a capture of currently used packages, increasing cold-build network traffic and prepared-cache disk use. Capturing the declared graph makes acquisition independent of package imports and source edits. Module input selection uses the admitted source inventory, including its ignore rules and nested-repository boundaries. Only vendor/ directories beside an admitted go.mod or go.work contribute vendor inputs. Source-file symlinks, including symlinked manifests/checksums, retain the shared portable-source refusal; replace them with regular files before building. Package discovery, source archives and inferred versions are refreshed from current source. In dist/dependencies/<target>.json, extensions["oyzu.dev/go-module-preparation"] records the reusable component's key, inputDigest, inputs and preparedTree. The snapshot's top-level preparedTree also contains source-dependent planning and packaging files, so it can change after a source edit even when module preparation is reused.

Compile, test, vet and the read-only formatting check run with networking denied and the prepared module cache. Artifacts are collected only after the required checks pass. Applications build one primary binary or named multiple binaries, with -trimpath and without ambient VCS stamping. Libraries compile package patterns and produce no executable. Go's test JSON becomes JUnit, and Go coverage keeps its statement denominator. Both go under dist/, with paths, digests and summaries in dist/manifest.json. A failed test, vet, formatting check, missing report or compile error stops artifact collection. Your source is never changed. Read the task logs and reports, fix the problem and rebuild. Each scratch tmpfs has a 2 GiB minimum size and grows with the action's memory reservation. Go build actions reserve at least 4 GiB, so /scratch/gotmp holds large compiler and linker intermediates. The 512 MiB /tmp mount is separate.

For an application with pure-Go code, Oyzu plans one build action per main package and one test action per package. Only the actions whose inputs changed run again.
