Each test action gets the whole captured workspace and its own empty output and scratch directories. It can't see another action's reports or changes. Package tests run go test -json -count=1 and produce a separate JUnit report and statement coverage report per package. Binaries are written privately and exported with the module's current version in the file name after the required checks pass. A conflicting task environment fails validation before any result is reused. These targets run as one combined action instead: libraries, cgo, nested targets, native workers, targets with generated inputs, and configurations with any authored tasks or hooks. That keeps their command and hook order, including generated inputs and post-test report changes. This path runs the engine that Oyzu mounts into the execution image. Without one, the build stops with ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE. Direct oyzu exec -- gofmt uses the formatter bundled with the selected Go (Go installation).

Each library or workspace module produces three files: Artifact Contents module-<index>-<version>.zip The Go module archive, with the <module>@<version>/ prefix module-<index>-<version>.mod The exact go.mod included in that archive module-<index>-<version>.info Go proxy version metadata, with no invented release timestamp The index follows the sorted order of module directories. Manifest artifact names are module-<index>-zip, module-<index>-mod and module-<index>-info. dist/dependencies/<target>.json lists module paths and directories, file names, versions and the h1: zip and go.mod checksums, so other tools can map the files to registry identities. Oyzu does not publish the modules.

Versions come from version inference: a base from Git tags when there is one, plus the build's -dev.g... suffix from the source. With no applicable tags the base is 0.0.0. Go packaging maps that to the module path's major where needed, for example v2.0.0-dev.g... for a /v2 module. A version from a tag must satisfy Go's module path rules. v3.0.0 for an unchanged /v2 module fails instead of silently changing the version. These are snapshot prereleases, not Go pseudo-versions, and they don't authorize a release. An exact RC tag keeps its qualifier, for example v2.6.0-rc.2.dev.g.... Binary file names and manifest coordinates use their module's inferred version. Oyzu doesn't inject version variables into your program. A Conventional Commit that declares a breaking change in the tool minimum doesn't change the Go module path. Under the default auto strategy that still infers a major bump, and packaging refuses the mismatch. A project whose released tags define its development line can choose the tag strategy instead. Path-major checks, tool selection and the required build and report checks still apply.

Each module in a workspace gets its own version, based on the tags and changes that affect it. Directory-scoped tags such as math/v2.4.2 and api/v1.4.2 give each module its own baseline. A root tag applies only to a module at the Git root. It doesn't coordinate the other modules. Files outside module directories count as shared inputs for every module. Custom tag namespaces and special major-directory layouts aren't supported yet. Oyzu freezes the versions in version-plan.json, uses them when it creates each zip, mod and info file, and rewrites local requirements to match. Recreate older captures after updating Oyzu.

The archive tool uses Go's own module zip library for allowed files, nested-module and vendor exclusions, case collisions and size limits, and Go's dirhash for checksums. It doesn't apply its own zip rules. Workspace dependencies point at the matching snapshot versions. Local imports, including test imports, supply the links between members even without a require entry. A local replace to a workspace module is removed from the packaged go.mod. Your source go.mod is unchanged. The files follow the Go module proxy protocol, so you can serve them from a local file proxy.

When the build container can't fetch a module, its local proxy answers HTTP 502 with a fixed category, for example module acquisition failed: BROKER_RESPONSE_BODY (broker HTTP 200). The HTTP status shown is the broker's reply, not a successful download. Messages never include file paths, JSON errors, credentials or redirect URLs. Category Meaning and fix BROKER_REQUEST_ID The worker couldn't generate a request ID. Check the worker's runtime. BROKER_REQUEST_WRITE, BROKER_REQUEST_PUBLISH The worker couldn't write or publish its request. Check the spool mount and its permissions. BROKER_RESPONSE_READ, BROKER_RESPONSE_METADATA The worker couldn't read the broker's reply. Check the spool mount. BROKER_RESPONSE_BODY, BROKER_RESPONSE_LIMIT The reply body was unreadable or larger than the 256 MiB limit. Check broker delivery or the module's size. BROKER_TIMEOUT The broker didn't answer within 55 seconds. Check the broker on the host. Upstream HTTP errors and the broker's own source and authorization messages pass through unchanged.

Linux amd64 is the supported captured platform. Arm builds and general cross compilation are not supported yet. Captured and isolated builds do not support private module sources or direct VCS downloads. Other limits include replace directives that point outside the selected workspace, registry replacements that need different publishing rules, and module publishing. An unsupported replace fails preparation instead of producing a module that depends on a local path. Source archives claim no compiled ABI and no build provenance. Full cgo and sysroot portability is not available. A platform matrix can pick the matching Go toolchain for each platform (platform selection). Preparation checks the actual Go OS and architecture, and tests run in each selected runtime. Pinned Go in the worker supports only linux/amd64 workers and the go/-prefixed tar.gz Go archive layout. Embedded files (//go:embed) are captured with the source that Go reports for them.
Local builds and build tasks for the shared build model. Build bundles for the dist/ layout these builds produce. Direct tests, version inference and Go installation.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/gradle.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu detects build.gradle or build.gradle.kts without any build YAML, then builds, tests and packages the project with Gradle. A multi-project or composite build is one Oyzu target. Gradle still owns project membership, included builds, task dependencies and output paths, and Oyzu uses that model to plan artifacts and collect reports. The multi-project example has an application, a library and an included support build. Note: The Gradle builder is experimental. Captured builds run on Linux (Docker or Linux crun). It's the Gradle side of the java/app builder, supplied by the oyzu/java plugin, which selects Gradle for a folder with build.gradle or build.gradle.kts (or with.build-tool: gradle); see plugin catalog and selecting a role.

With the next Java plugin release and a compatible CLI supporting private stages, native host format-check reuses independently through its fixed reads and empty private-output declaration. Editing an existing README's contents does not change its source-read key, but a source-derived snapshot version can change the action definition and still cause a miss. Whole-target projection identity can also cause conservative misses. Editing a formatted Java file reruns it. Lifecycle builds (including tests) and Checkstyle currently have unbounded output contracts and rerun even on unchanged native builds. This mixed pipeline cannot restore a whole-target result. Fast builds rerun the lifecycle too, even when format and lint are omitted. Whole-target entries saved by an older CLI cannot bypass this rule. oyzu build --explain names the stage and the missing complete read report; reuse needs complete reads and bounded outputs from the builder. Declaring inputs alone does not bound arbitrary runtime reads. Required test and coverage reports still apply. Captured copy/export behavior is unchanged. See Java quality for the read boundary. Native-host Gradle build and test stages stay unbounded. settings.gradle, build.gradle and their Kotlin variants are programs; the current native integration does not report all configuration-script reads and task inputs. Tests can also read files at run time. Conventional source directories do not establish a complete boundary for those stages. The captured package operation consumes only its build producer's archives, using an upstream-only contract. Shared Java formatting and lint declare their own boundaries. These declarations reach users with the next release of the Java plugin.

Linux crun execution (oyzu build --isolated --no-docker, or the existing build.isolation = "crun" with --isolated) enforces the captured input boundary before admitting lifecycle reuse. No new flag, setting or internal gate is needed. The module's admitted source, shared native build definitions, identified dependency artifacts and read-only prepared repository, locked JDK/Gradle identities, runtime and upstream outputs remain keyed. An unchanged lifecycle can reuse its compilation, archives and test/coverage evidence together. With a compatible Java plugin, multi-project builds reuse one coupled lifecycle per project. Native settings and resolved component identities supply membership and dependency edges. In a chain where b depends on a and c depends on b, editing c reruns only c; editing a invalidates the chain. An unchanged rebuild can reuse every project. Gradle still owns task ordering; declared producers supply the dependency outputs without compiling them again inside a consumer's action. This does not cache individual Test classes or separate every task in the lifecycle. Archive tasks disable entry timestamps and use reproducible file ordering in the captured integration. Package exports copy the resulting producer bytes. Changed source, dependency or JDK identity causes a miss. Preparation and report validation still run for a hit; reused tests are labelled as not executed now. Each project retains its own JUnit and coverage evidence and producing action. Changing a shared build definition can invalidate several projects. Undeclared cross-project task dependencies fail with JVM_MODULE_UNDECLARED_READ; fix the native project dependencies before rebuilding. Source reads outside a project's admitted view fail instead of publishing a reusable success. Older native models without dependency facts retain the conservative whole-build lifecycle. Source links, an oversized inventory, or module-local controls such as x/version.txt also keep the whole lifecycle on every captured executor, including Docker, so configuration can share those controls. The selected project must still match its frozen native-version projection; only unrelated projects may be absent from that projection. Composite builds currently retain whole-build lifecycle reuse. Undeclared host files and live proc/sys data remain inaccessible. See the closed JVM device allowance and its requirement that entropy not influence retained outputs. Native-host Gradle still refuses lifecycle reuse when reads are incomplete. Other isolated executors and Windows/macOS do not provide this complete Java boundary. Plain Java builds remain native; changing that default is a later product decision.

oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Captured builds need Docker or Linux crun and the base execution image. The JDK and, for a project without a Gradle wrapper, Gradle itself are restored from oyzu.lock: oyzu -C examples/builds/java-gradle-multi-project/project build --isolated --full

oyzu run list doesn't run Gradle. It lists Gradle's build and test tasks and the shared Java lint and format tasks. Gradle's build already includes tests, so captured builds don't run a separate test stage. Qualified task names and TOML replacements work as in the common task engine. The default JVM test tasks need no report configuration. Kotlin JUnit 5 projects select useJUnitPlatform() in their own Gradle test task.

Command Runs Notes oyzu build Gradle on your machine Gradle's build lifecycle can run tests even in this fast mode. oyzu build --full Gradle on your machine Also runs Oyzu's quality checks. oyzu build --isolated --full In the container The captured path, with all checks. A custom Gradle JUnit directory doesn't change where JaCoCo coverage is read. Both are required evidence for a host build, and missing coverage blocks artifact export. On Windows, Oyzu supplies the native reporting adapter with a JVM-compatible workspace path, including when the workspace directory contains spaces. The default Java build needs no additional JaCoCo path configuration. When a test assertion fails, the build still retains its JUnit failure and JaCoCo coverage in the output bundle. This applies with caching enabled and with --no-cache; missing coverage remains a build failure.

Need Detail Gradle 8.14.3. Set GRADLE_HOME or put Gradle on PATH. A Gradle wrapper in the project is used if present, and its distribution must already be installed. JDK 17, with JAVA_HOME set. Dependencies Your project and test dependencies, including JaCoCo 0.8.13. Gradle's user home and your project's repositories stay in charge. Direct tests need these tools installed. oyzu build on your machine prepares tools through the shared tool management and records the versions in oyzu.lock. A tool on PATH alone doesn't pin the build. Host model observation can resolve plugins using Gradle's native repositories. With --offline, the model query requires cached plugins. Direct test commands remain offline. Automatic Java toolchain downloads are disabled. Offline resolution doesn't sandbox arbitrary build logic, and doesn't stop a wrapper from trying to install itself.

A JDK your project selects, through [tools] java or native requirements, is locked by build preflight. It is restored read-only at /scratch/jdktool from the verified Temurin archive in oyzu.lock, the same way as for Maven. Daemon JVM criteria​ An explicit toolchainVersion in gradle/gradle-daemon-jvm.properties selects the daemon JDK's feature release. For example, toolchainVersion=25 normally selects a stable Java 25. An explicit [tools] java must satisfy the same constraint. The declared vendor still applies when Gradle launches. Oyzu supplies Temurin. It refuses vendors other than ADOPTIUM or Eclipse Adoptium, and daemon requirements for a native-image-capable JDK, before downloading anything. The message gives the source path and field. Literal property names and whole-number feature releases are supported. Malformed or escaped criteria need to be corrected, or a matching JDK must already be installed. Without daemon criteria, Oyzu uses the highest literal Java level in the root build script (JavaLanguageVersion.of(21), sourceCompatibility) as the startup minimum, or Java 21 if none is declared. Adjacent or nested scripts do not prove native membership and do not contribute static startup requirements. oyzu pin does not execute Gradle to discover nested compiler requirements. With explicit daemon criteria, your compilation and toolchain declarations are left for Gradle to enforce. They don't replace the daemon JDK. The container restores one JDK. A build that needs a second JDK for some task can still fail, because automatic downloads are off. Compiler availability​ The Java package advertises the required gradle-compiler-facts engine capability for this preparation behavior. Catalog selection excludes it on an older engine; use an engine implementing that capability or an eligible earlier package. The core's prepared API digest must still equal the selected package's Gradle runtime digest. See package compatibility. selected JVM package and prepared native API differ means the CLI and selected Java package contain different native adapters. This can also happen on a fresh checkout without a lock or installed tools; installing a JDK or regenerating the Gradle wrapper does not resolve it. Use a CLI and Java package released with matching adapters. Preparation refuses the mismatch before build actions run. During native model preparation, Gradle resolves the effective compiler provider of enabled compileJava and compileTestJava tasks that have existing sources. This includes nested native member projects. The check runs after configuration and before metadata tasks collect dependencies or reports; it does not compile sources or substitute the daemon JVM for a task-specific compiler or vendor. The actual compiler must support the task's effective options.release, or both sourceCompatibility and targetCompatibility when no release is set. An explicit release takes precedence over the source and target defaults. If a compiler is unavailable, the native diagnostic contains OYZU_GRADLE_COMPILER_UNAVAILABLE, the build directory, project, task and known toolchain or target level, followed by Gradle's original cause. Provide the requested native compiler, or select a matching daemon JDK. For example, a single-JDK build needing a Java 25 compiler can declare: # gradle/gradle-daemon-jvm.properties toolchainVersion=25 Without daemon criteria, explicitly pin both a suitable [tools] java and a compatible [tools] gradle; Java 25 needs Gradle 9. A Java pin alone does not change the Gradle line inferred from the root script. A wrapper must itself support the chosen daemon JDK. Settings or plugin configuration can fail before this check. Custom compilation tasks, generated sources absent during preparation, conditional execution and compiler changes after the guard remain native execution concerns. This is not complete static inference of every compiler in a Gradle build. JDK installation and Gradle versions​ The selected JDK is always offered to Gradle through -Dorg.gradle.java.installations.paths, including before daemon JVM selection. Automatic toolchain downloads stay off. The image's Gradle 8.14.3 runs on the selected JDK when that is release 24 or older. For a newer JDK, the launcher keeps the image's bootstrap JDK and offers the selected one to Gradle. A newer Gradle can then use it for the daemon criterion, but Gradle 8.14.3 may not support the newer JDK. A project's own wrapper version isn't installed in the container yet. A selected JDK older than 17 is refused with TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION.

Single and multi-project builds applying org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm are supported, including Kotlin DSL build scripts, src/main/kotlin and src/test/kotlin. Kotlin JVM support is experimental on Linux x64. Windows Kotlin builds are not yet verified; macOS is unsupported. Gradle owns compilation, project dependencies and JAR packaging. Enabled Kotlin archive tasks, including sources JARs, run with the build so every declared archive can be collected. Oyzu attributes tests through the native Kotlin compilation tasks and source sets, and collects JUnit and JaCoCo XML, including Kotlin classes. Configure JUnit 5 normally: // build.gradle.kts in each JVM project plugins { kotlin("jvm") version "2.2.21" } repositories { mavenCentral() } kotlin { jvmToolchain(17) } dependencies { testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:5.11.4") testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher:1.11.4") } tasks.test { useJUnitPlatform() } For this example, select JDK 17 and Gradle 8.14.6 through the existing tool configuration: # oyzu.toml [tools] java = "17.0.21" gradle = "8.14.6" Use oyzu build --full for the native build, or oyzu build --isolated --full for captured execution. The Kotlin plugin resolves through the project's plugin management; captured preparation uses the existing admitted public Plugin Portal and Maven Central routes. No separate Kotlin installation is needed. Native model queries use native plugin resolution; with --offline, resolve the project's plugins and dependencies into Gradle's cache before building. Checkstyle and google-java-format apply only to Java files. A Kotlin-only target prints an explicit skipped reason for lint and format checks; mixed targets still check their Java files. These tools do not validate or format Kotlin, and Oyzu does not add ktlint or detekt. Kapt and KSP annotation-processing plugins are refused with a message naming the project and plugin. Kotlin Multiplatform and Android are outside this support. This runtime requires a Java plugin package advertising gradle-kotlin-jvm and a CLI implementing that capability with the same Gradle runtime digest. The matching Java plugin release must ship with the CLI; an older published package cannot interpret the changed prepared model. A source merge alone does not make that package available.

oyzu run test writes its reports to a bundle under dist/. After the usual task checks, Oyzu asks Gradle for the model of the root build and its included builds. The query runs only Oyzu's metadata tasks. It doesn't run your tests or compile your code on purpose. Gradle configuration, plugins and build logic still run normally. This is ordinary execution on your machine, not a security boundary.

Enabled test tasks that have test source files, with their JUnit destinations and JaCoCo destinations. Projects with no test sources don't create test obligations. A build with no tests fails instead of producing a passing empty suite. The implicit command runs the discovered tests across the composite, respecting task dependencies. Custom commands run unchanged and must produce the required reports. Forwarded extra arguments aren't supported by the default reporting.

Before each run, Oyzu removes previous XML from the selected test directories and the selected coverage XML. JaCoCo coverage is generated even after failed assertions. Each test task's suites are combined without dropping test cases, and fresh private JUnit and JaCoCo files are collected. dist/manifest.json links each report to its summary, plan and logs. Output stays in your project's build directories. Sources and versions are unchanged. Direct tests create no application artifact records and don't package, lint or format.

Pre and post hooks apply. A failed test skips its success-only post hook. Failed assertions, missing or malformed reports and unmet coverage thresholds fail the command and keep the evidence available. oyzu inspect dist checks the bundle. See direct tests for output handling, history, report overrides and provenance. Direct execution isn't isolated, and a passing local test grants no publishing or signing authority.

Preparation reads Gradle's models and downloads Maven-layout dependencies through Oyzu's scoped public repository adapter. The build then runs offline against the captured repository. Private and custom repositories aren't supported. Gradle plugins come from the plugin portal. Version inference resolves native versions, scoped tags and commit changes, and Oyzu applies the versions in a private copy of the source. Gradle's archive tasks supply the file names and archive versions. JAR, WAR, EAR, ZIP, TAR and gzip archives are supported, and the bundle records their planned versions and digests. JAR manifest attributes are not rewritten to add implementation-version metadata. Tests and checks: Java and Kotlin JVM tests supply JUnit and JaCoCo reports, including Kotlin classes. Projects without test sources are skipped. Each lifecycle's JUnit report combines its cases under a <testsuites> root. Read its path from dist/manifest.json; individual native suite files aren't separate bundle reports. Suite counters are optional, so consumers should count <testcase> elements and their <failure> or <error> children. JaCoCo coverage remains a separate required report. The shared Java quality checks run before artifacts are published to dist. Missing archives, unresolved dependencies and failed required stages or reports fail the build.

Oyzu reads the original versions first and freezes a version-plan.json for the project directories in the composite. Preparation checks the original versions and applies each decision, and the offline build uses the same result. A unique Gradle project name supplies the scoped tag name. Repeated names use directory paths. An unspecified version can take its version from a tag without adding a version to your build. Local project dependencies keep full build-tree identities, including substituted projects in included builds. Missing or unresolved graph facts fail preparation. Metadata-only queries on your machine don't resolve this graph. Changes in one project affect the projects that depend on it. Unrelated project directories keep independent bases.

Captured downloads come from two public sources: Maven Central and the Gradle plugin portal (https://plugins.gradle.org/m2/). The portal's artifact host, https://plugins-artifacts.gradle.org/, is also allowed so portal redirects for plugin JARs work. Redirects to Maven Central use the Central source. Plugins applied in settings.gradle or a project plugins {} block, and gradlePluginPortal() in pluginManagement, buildscript or project repositories, resolve through Oyzu during preparation: // settings.gradle plugins { id 'com.gradle.develocity' version '4.2' } How it works: An init script adds an Oyzu Central entry and an Oyzu portal entry to pluginManagement (replacing Gradle's implicit portal default) and routes each recognized repository to its own local path. Any other repository URL fails preparation with Gradle repository requires an approved source adapter. Files from both sources go into one Maven-layout repository that the offline build reads. repository-sources.json in the prepared tree records which source served each file, and the dependency snapshot lists each package under maven-central, gradle-plugin-portal or gradle-plugin-artifacts. A redirect to any other host fails with a source denial. Limits: Settings plugins resolve while Gradle evaluates the settings script, before Oyzu can reroute repositories that the script declares. Oyzu's own entries come first, so a plugin they serve is found. Plugin behavior that downloads at run time, such as Gradle toolchain provisioning, isn't covered.

oyzu build --full uses Gradle's own repository declarations and credentials, including pluginManagement repositories in settings.gradle.kts. Credentials can come from user gradle.properties, ORG_GRADLE_PROJECT_* environment properties, System.getenv("NAME") or providers.environmentVariable("NAME"). Native property precedence and repository selection remain Gradle-owned. Oyzu adds no repository setting or public fallback. For example, use the same repository in the dependency or plugin management repository block that already works in your native build: maven { url = uri("https://packages.example.com/maven/") credentials { username = "reader" password = System.getenv("COMPANY_GRADLE_PASSWORD") } } Keep literal passwords in user gradle.properties, outside project source. A tracked gradle.properties containing a literal credential fails with NATIVE_CONFIG_CREDENTIAL before the build; use an environment reference or user configuration. Build scripts are not scanned for literals, so do not write passwords into them. Observed native credential values are removed from captured process output and stay outside plans, action identities and evidence; credential-bearing JVM builds do not restore cached actions. Gradle's own user cache remains native state. A build counts as credentialed only when its scripts or your user init.d scripts declare a maven/ivy repository outside Maven Central, the Gradle Plugin Portal and Google (comments and publishing destinations are ignored); only then do user-wide properties and ORG_GRADLE_PROJECT_* credentials apply. A public project with a deploy password in user configuration stays uncredentialed, offline and capturable. Literal credentials in a repository credentials block of a project script, or in a project gradle.properties, are refused; user init.d literals are redacted. Unreadable or oversized unrelated files are skipped with a path-only note. Known limitations: only literal System.getenv/providers.environmentVariable names are redacted, a relocated Gradle user home passed with -g is not observed, and credential-like ORG_GRADLE_PROJECT_* names are matched conservatively by whole word. includeBuild projects outside the project root are not observed. User and installation init scripts, GRADLE_OPTS -I scripts and buildSrc/build-logic sources are scanned. Values under four characters are not redacted. The host model query can fetch plugins before the build lifecycle. --offline requires these plugins and dependencies to be cached already. Direct test commands remain offline. This online host observation requires a Java plugin containing the updated host adapter. Standalone credentials are unsupported in captured and isolated execution. Oyzu refuses them before build actions and directs you to host mode. Dynamically computed environment variable names and arbitrary credential-provider code cannot establish Oyzu's redaction boundary; use the native literal environment references or user properties described above.

Java and Kotlin JVM are supported. Groovy/Scala, custom coverage plugins, generated test sources and unusual plugin or composite setups may not work. Disabled tests and source-free tasks are skipped. Test tasks whose sources can't be attributed fail with an error. Standalone private repositories require host mode. Release authorization isn't supported. Daemon JVM selection for a Gradle build that needs a JDK newer than the image supports is limited by Gradle 8.14.3 itself (see JDK installation and Gradle versions).

On Windows, incomplete native reads require the lifecycle/scripts to run again. oyzu build --explain and oyzu cache explain app name this refusal and point to oyzu build --isolated --no-docker on Linux crun for complete-read stage reuse. Clearing the cache does not resolve it. --no-cache must agree with ordinary execution, including failures after external inputs change. Independently admitted complete-read stages and native download caches remain available. See native Windows refusal.
Java quality tasks, direct tests, version inference. Maven builds and Java installation.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/gradle-sessions.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Use this when a Gradle build should download from a private Maven-layout repository without storing a password in gradle.properties or init scripts. Each time you run gradle through oyzu, oyzu asks a local credential agent which repository to use, points every repository in the build at it and gives Gradle the password in memory. Note: Experimental. You need a credential agent running on the same machine; oyzu doesn't include one. Supported on Linux with Gradle 8.14.3, JDK 17 and Bash. Isolated oyzu build runs don't use this.

Add the agent's address to your user or administrator configuration (not the project's oyzu.toml): [gradle] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43199/session" Setting Values Default Meaning gradle.sessionEndpoint http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<path>, no user name, password, query or fragment Not set The local agent to ask for sessions. Remove it to go back to plain Gradle Project, local and command-line configuration and profiles can't set this value. User configuration isn't read in CI, so this doesn't work there.

With Gradle and a JDK installed: oyzu exec -- /opt/gradle-8.14.3/bin/gradle build # or, with Gradle on PATH: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" gradle build Use the real gradle executable; gradlew isn't supported. --help, --version, --status and --stop run without asking the agent.

Sends the agent a POST with {"directory": "<working dir>", "tool": "gradle", "arguments": [...]}. Reads the agent's answer: { "repository": "https://packages.example.com/maven/", "username": "reader", "credentialEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:43199/credential/session" } repository is an HTTP(S) URL with no credentials, query or fragment. credentialEndpoint must be on 127.0.0.1. Starts Gradle with a bundled init script and --no-configuration-cache. The script fetches the password with a GET to credentialEndpoint (the response body is the password, up to 64 KiB) on every run. The init script points plugin, settings, buildscript and project repositories at the one repository, with those credentials, and adds it where a build declares none. Existing Maven-layout repositories (including mavenLocal()) are redirected to it. Other repository types fail the build. Gradle downloads directly from the repository; oyzu doesn't proxy the traffic. Your build files, lock files and other options aren't changed. Gradle's dependency cache and daemon keep working as usual. The temporary files are removed when Gradle finishes or fails. The agent is asked every time, even with a warm cache.

The password never goes into project files, command arguments or environment variables. It's in Gradle's memory, so build code and plugins can read it. The init script doesn't keep the password between runs, even when the daemon is reused. Read-only access has to be enforced by the repository account the agent uses. Denial or an unreachable agent stops the command before Gradle starts. oyzu never falls back to running Gradle without a session.
Gradle's output and exit code pass through unchanged. With --json, they're captured in the usual oyzu exec result.

Code Cause Fix NATIVE_SESSION_CONFIG The endpoint is set in project or local configuration Move it to user or administrator configuration NATIVE_SESSION_UNAVAILABLE The agent can't be reached Start the agent and retry NATIVE_SESSION_DENIED The agent refused the request Get access granted; don't work around the agent NATIVE_SESSION_INVALID Bad endpoint, or the response has a bad repository or no user name Fix the endpoint or the agent GRADLE_SESSION_INVALID The agent's response couldn't be read, or an argument isn't valid UTF-8 Fix the agent's response GRADLE_SESSION_CONFLICT You passed --init-script/-I, asked for the configuration cache, or ran a task with publish in its name Remove the option. Publish with oyzu publish

One repository per run. Several repositories with different credentials aren't supported. Repository mode conflicts between settings and projects aren't resolved for you. Plugins that make their own HTTP calls aren't covered, and a build that changes repositories later isn't prevented from doing so. The configuration cache is turned off. Temporary files may be left behind if oyzu is killed. Linux and Bash only. Windows and macOS aren't supported yet.
Gradle builds Private Maven repositories Java installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/helm.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The helm/chart builder packages an application or library chart, renders it, lints it, checks its YAML formatting and runs your helm-unittest suites. It finds a chart at Chart.yaml or chart/Chart.yaml, so a basic chart needs no Oyzu configuration. If both locations exist, set the target paths in build.yaml, because ambiguous discovery fails. The chart example has a local library dependency and optional assertion suites. Use Helm's native apiVersion: v2 in Chart.yaml, including for library charts. Note: The Helm builder is experimental. It is supported on Linux (x86-64) and Windows. Builds never contact a cluster.
documents.s: Helm charts and native chart tests

documents.t: Plain oyzu build builds a chart natively on your machine with the locked Helm and yamlfmt, without Docker, when everything the chart needs is already in the source tree: either it declares no dependencies, or each dependency in Chart.yaml has a charts/<name> folder or a charts/<name>-*.tgz archive. A native build runs helm package with the build's version, normalizes the archive, and with --full also runs the test, format-check and lint stages. It collects the chart archive. The chart goes through the isolated path instead when a dependency isn't vendored yet (oyzu build --plan shows the reason; run oyzu run install to vendor it) or when the build has image bindings. A native build doesn't write rendered.yaml; the test stage still renders the chart. Charts with assertion suites select helm-unittest as a normal locked tool. oyzu install records and installs its publisher recipe in oyzu.lock; native builds use that installation. Existing installations and download caches are retained. An existing provisioned plugin folder can still be selected in user configuration; the shell's ambient HELM_PLUGINS alone is not carried into native build actions: [env] HELM_PLUGINS = "/absolute/helm-plugins" That folder contains unittest/plugin.yaml and its platform executable. Builds do not run the plugin's installation hooks. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist oyzu run list shows the tasks without launching Helm or reading assertion files. The tasks are: Task Runs Effect install helm dependency build May download dependencies and update locks build helm package Writes a chart archive lint helm lint None test Validation and helm-unittest Writes a test-only dist/ bundle format-check yamlfmt, read-only None format yamlfmt Rewrites your YAML files The group is named project. Explicit targets use their own names.

Direct tasks need Helm, helm-unittest for assertion suites, and yamlfmt for formatting. The native defaults are Helm 3.22.0, helm-unittest 1.2.0 and yamlfmt 0.21.0; explicit tool selections override them. Declared dependencies must already be prepared (for example with oyzu run install), because testing doesn't download them. Normal tool installation verifies the github:helm-unittest/helm-unittest distribution against its locked recipe. Builds never run Helm plugin installation hooks. Existing projects acquire the new requirement on their next oyzu install; commit the resulting lock. oyzu pin can update the lock separately. Isolated builds use Docker or Linux crun and the base execution image, which has no Helm of its own. Everything a chart build runs comes from the lock: helm must be in oyzu.lock for the worker's platform (see Pinned helm). Without it, preparation stops with a message that says how to lock it. yamlfmt, used by the format stages, is a locked stage tool. helm-unittest is required when the test stage is enabled and the chart has unit test suites. Preparation verifies the worker's selected release against oyzu.lock and restores the complete publisher archive read-only under /scratch/helm-plugins/unittest, including its license and plugin metadata. The build fixes HELM_PLUGINS to /scratch/helm-plugins so a task can't redirect it to project code. The image identity is recorded in the build's evidence. Offline builds require the locked tools, prepared dependencies and execution image to be available already; missing inputs fail without an execution-time download fallback.

The Helm builder comes from the compiled oyzu-plugin-helm package. The package finds your chart and declares the Helm commands, the image bindings and the report translation. Oyzu itself captures dependencies, admits the locked Helm, picks the package and image, decides the version and checks reports and artifacts. The Helm plugin uses the shared plugin compatibility contract. Only designated request/reply annotation containers tolerate added optional members. Native commands, prepared paths and digests, identities and manifests remain strict. Missing request support directs you to oyzu plugins update helm/chart; missing manifest support directs you to oyzu self update. An invalid plugin reply is a plugin contract violation and directs you to update the plugin. Development bindings need a rebuild and rebind. Source changes take effect for installed packages only after a compatible plugin release is published and adopted through normal admission. Build staging preserves files already admitted into the prepared chart, including payload directories named dist. It changes the private chart's version before packaging and rendering. Source admission and native .helmignore rules still determine which authored files can reach the package. Direct tests retain their generated-output exclusions described below. Test suites are recorded by the digest of their YAML or archive and their location inside it. Discovery never runs the assertions.

A README inside the chart directory is package content unless .helmignore excludes it. It is different from a README beside a nested chart at the project root. Captured charts without helm-unittest suites use these expectations when their read declarations are complete: Edit Development version Action reuse Chart README.md, stock .helmignore Changes Version-carrying actions rerun Chart README.md, .helmignore containing README.md Unchanged Every action reuses Project-root README.md outside the chart, in either setup Unchanged Every action reuses Chart source or .helmignore Changes when admitted inputs change Affected actions rerun With helm-unittest suites, the test action keeps the entire admitted source view and can rerun for an outside-chart edit while bounded chart actions reuse. Helm's source-scope owner refines positive literal ignore entries into a file inventory and retains .helmignore as a control. Wildcards, escapes and negations keep conservative bounds; this is not a replacement for Helm's native ignore parser. A new shipped file enters the next captured plan. The inventory reads metadata and the ignore control once per chart in each planning request; it does not hash source payloads again. The formatter uses its runtime's own inventory and validation, so README bytes are outside its reads while links and custom formatter configuration still fail explicitly. Preparation omits those proven exclusions from the private chart when there are no helm-unittest suites. Suites can read arbitrary values files, so their prepared view and unknown-read fallback remain conservative. These precision rules depend on the complete Helm read declarations; they do not admit native host execution or arbitrary custom commands.

Isolated chart builds need Helm in the lock. Pin the exact version: # oyzu.toml [tools] helm = "4.3.0" oyzu install helm@4.3.0 Helm takes an exact version only, and oyzu pin doesn't resolve it. Oyzu reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) archive recorded for that version in oyzu.lock. It downloads the archive through the tool broker unless a cached copy under the user data folder still matches the locked SHA-256, and verifies the bytes against that digest. It restores the archive read-only at /scratch/helmtool and puts that folder first on PATH for preparation and every build step. The pinned version and archive are part of the dependency record, so a different pin or archive changes the step's identity. A tampered lock is refused. Offline builds need the archive already cached, or they fail with TOOL_OFFLINE. A pinned Helm must be able to run the helm-unittest plugin.

The plugin declares these source bounds using the shared read contract: Stage Reads build, lint The chart directory, including metadata, locks, values, schema, templates, CRDs, .Files data and vendored charts; captured local file:// dependency trees are included normalize The package archive produced by build; the source prediction conservatively retains the chart tree test, without helm-unittest The same chart trees for local rendering/schema validation or library lint test, with helm-unittest Unbounded: suites may name values files outside the chart and helm-unittest does not report those reads format-check The target tree scanned for chart roots, YAML, links and unsupported formatter configuration bind The chart's values.yaml plus materialized OCI archives; unbounded until their read/write relationship with the prepared chart is admitted Helm's directory loader fixes the package/lint/template boundary. The declared bound conservatively retains .helmignore-excluded files rather than reproducing Helm's ignore matcher, so an ignored edit can cause an extra miss. Formatting also retains file contents beyond the selected YAML because its current read prediction uses tree selectors rather than separate directory listings. Adding a source file is covered by the tree selectors. No explicit external values files are passed by the implicit build commands; chart with options remain unsupported. If local dependency traversal needs preparation first (for example, a vendored archive has not yet been unpacked), chart-consuming stages stay unbounded with the metadata path and traversal failure. Read planning does not reject the build. Read analysis supplies the bounds before the captured-path confinement owner admits each stage. With captured per-action admission and hidden-copy dependency views, bounded build, lint and non-unittest test stages can reuse their own results when a file outside the chart changes. The formatter scans the whole target, so a root README edit may rerun format-check. A chart/README.md edit is inside the chart bound and invalidates chart-consuming stages. Image binding remains unbounded. Independent stage reuse requires both an engine that supports captured per-action reuse and a Helm plugin with complete read declarations. Native host builds use the same predictions but keep refusing reuse without complete native observations. oyzu run tasks are not cached. Native build and normalize intentionally declare neither observed reads nor a fixed native read rule (nativeReads is omitted); both retain home: required. Their chart predictions describe source bounds, not a complete record of host reads. The plugin does not emit complete native read reports for these commands, so neither stage stores a reusable native result, even on an unchanged build. When the chart's dependencies are bounded, --explain says the builder declares source read predictions but no complete native read observation or fixed read rule. Dependency traversal failures retain their specific reason. The prediction is present and home remains required. Native helm-unittest suites can name values files outside the chart, including absolute host paths. These files remain outside the captured source digest. Without complete native read observations, oyzu build --full still runs the assertions on an unchanged build. Changing an external values file affects both the ordinary full build and --full --no-cache. Repair that file after an assertion failure. Isolated builds retain the host-file confinement described below. The read-only --plan preview uses stage contracts from the target's last retained build, marked as facts from the last build. Stages without a retained contract say reported when the builder answers. Preview does not invoke Helm or the plugin and does not admit cache reuse.

On Linux, oyzu build --full --isolated --no-docker selects crun and its shared complete input boundary. Unchanged compatible chart builds reuse packaging and rendering (build), validation and helm-unittest reports (test), and lint. These native commands remain grouped within their existing actions. The chart read bounds above apply to bounded stages. For helm-unittest, core keys the entire admitted source view because suites do not report complete reads. The locked Helm and helm-unittest identities also enter the stage key. Changing a template, values, dependency lock or a selected tool invalidates affected actions. Required reports and artifacts are checked again on reuse. The enforced view hides host files and live proc/sys data and supplies private writable output state. Undeclared external values files cannot become cache inputs through a filename. A failed read cannot publish a successful result. The shared closed device allowance is non-keying; entropy must not affect retained outputs. See read admission. Captured preparation of an already-vendored file:// dependency can create duplicate subchart entries and fail archive validation. Use the declared local dependency and its Chart.lock without a generated vendored copy on this path; native builds retain their vendoring requirement. Preparation and tool admission still run before lookup. Outputs remain location sensitive unless explicitly declared relocatable. Other executors and native Windows/macOS execution do not gain this complete-read guarantee. Use oyzu build --explain to see reuse/refusal and --no-cache to execute afresh.

A chart can use the identity of an image built in the same oyzu build, so a deploy needs no --set image.digest=...: builds: image: uses: docker/image with: repository: registry.example.com/team/greeting # the image's eventual repository chart: uses: helm/chart path: chart bindings: - from: image artifact: image type: image-reference repository: /image/repository digest: /image/digest Field Meaning from, artifact The producer build and its output, as in materialize type image-reference is the only type reference Destination that receives repository@sha256:... repository and digest A pair of destinations, used instead of reference Use reference or the repository and digest pair, not both and not neither. Binding the same values field twice fails during configuration. Destinations are JSON Pointers into the chart's values.yaml, and each must already hold a string there. An empty digest: "" is the usual shape. Nothing is created or templated. The image must set with.repository: a repository name without scheme, tag or digest. Building doesn't publish. The bound reference names the intended repository and the real manifest digest of the local archive, so the chart isn't deployable until the image is pushed there. If you change the repository, rebuild the chart. How it runs: A binding makes the chart depend on the image and copies the image's OCI archive into the chart target (.oyzu-bindings/<n>.oci.tar, recorded in dist/inputs/<chart>.json). After the chart is copied to its private workspace and before it is packaged, linted or rendered, the bind step reads the archive's manifest digest and rewrites the destinations in that copy's values.yaml. The packaged default values and rendered.yaml carry the produced reference. Your checked-in chart is never edited. The rewrite re-serializes values.yaml in the private copy, so comments in the packaged defaults are lost. A new image digest reruns the chart's steps, and an unchanged one reuses them. A failed or blocked image blocks every chart step. Image bindings work on Windows with Docker Desktop. A multi-platform image (more than one manifest) is refused. Linux and macOS hosts, bindings through a platform matrix, publishing and deployed clusters are not supported yet.

Discovery adds a read-only format-check build stage and a format task that edits your files. Both use yamlfmt. Selected files: .yaml and .yml files directly in each chart root (the folder with Chart.yaml), plus YAML below tests/ and crds/. Unpacked subcharts and sibling charts inside the target root are included. Left out: Go templates in templates/, __snapshot__ baselines, packaged chart archives, Chart.lock, generated output and hidden folders. Dependency archives are never edited or repacked. Template formatting isn't supported, so a passing check says nothing about template style. Oyzu runs yamlfmt with its own private configuration: LF line endings, a final newline, and yamlfmt's basic formatter defaults. Configuration in parent folders or your home folder is ignored. A formatter file in the target (.yamlfmt, .yamlfmt.yaml, .yamlfmt.yml, yamlfmt.yaml, yamlfmt.yml) fails the implicit task with a message telling you to override the tasks. Use normal TOML task overrides for custom formatting. format-check lists the files that differ and exits non-zero without changing anything. Invalid YAML also fails, with yamlfmt's message. Run oyzu run format, review the changes and try again. format writes files as it goes, so if a later file fails, earlier edits stay. Neither task downloads dependencies or contacts a cluster. Links and non-regular files are rejected. Limits are 100,000 traversed entries, 4 MiB per file and 64 MiB in total, and each yamlfmt run has a 30-second timeout. Direct tasks run as host processes with no sandbox. Isolated builds use the executor's isolation. The chart is packaged and rendered in the build even when you don't select the test stage, so plain oyzu build still writes rendered.yaml.

Declare unpacked subcharts in the parent's native Chart.yaml dependencies. For a subchart inside the chart, give its name and version and leave repository empty. That selects the existing charts/<name> folder. If you skip this, strict lint fails, even when the subchart's assertions pass. Oyzu doesn't add the dependency for you or turn the lint gate off. Keep checksum files out of charts/, or list them in .helmignore (for example charts/*.tgz.sha256), because Helm reads non-chart files there as dependencies.

Without assertion suites, the implicit test checks that an application chart renders and passes its values schema. A library chart is checked with strict lint with subcharts, because it can't be rendered as an installable chart. In isolated builds, rendering uses helm template --dry-run=client with an empty kubeconfig and no cluster access. This checks the chart. It doesn't show that a deployed application works.

Oyzu finds helm-unittest suites in each chart, including unpacked subcharts and local charts/*.tgz subcharts, even when the parent has none: flat tests/*_test.yaml recursive unittests/**/*.yaml (any .yaml name) Packaged suite evidence binds the original binary .tgz bytes and the suite location inside the archive. Text suite files still require UTF-8; discovery retains its bounded reads, path containment and symlink refusal. .yml files, custom globs and recursive tests/ folders are not selected. Each subchart needs a regular Chart.yaml, and chart folders starting with a dot or underscore are ignored. Helm-unittest parses the YAML and runs the assertions, so malformed YAML is a native failure. For example, chart/tests/deployment_test.yaml: suite: deployment contract templates: - templates/deployment.yaml tests: - it: uses one replica asserts: - equal: path: spec.replicas value: 1 Oyzu passes both file patterns to helm-unittest explicitly, because helm-unittest 1.2.0 drops its defaults when you give it a pattern. Selected suites must produce at least one test case. You don't add a test section to build.yaml, and you don't set a glob. oyzu run test shows the logical task helm unittest --strict <chart>. It unpacks packaged subcharts in a private copy before calling the plugin. Isolated builds run both the render and schema validation and the unit tests, and ask the plugin for JUnit output. Suites are source files, so they go into the published chart archive unless you list tests/ in .helmignore. Oyzu doesn't change your packaging rules. Static discovery inspects archives without extracting them into your checkout. It stops at these limits: Limit Value Suites 128 Inspected entries 4,096 per scope Subchart levels 16 Archive nesting 16 Metadata file 4 MiB Expanded archive bytes 64 MiB per scope An archive needs one chart root with a Chart.yaml. Links, duplicate or case-alias paths, non-portable paths and mixed roots fail. Arbitrary tar layouts aren't accepted, only Helm-generated archives.

Preparation unpacks contained subcharts in its private workspace and captures the chart's local file:// dependencies. It rejects cycles and paths that escape, and runs dependency preparation offline. Existing locks are honored and stale locks fail. Lock timestamps and archive metadata are normalized. If a packed and an unpacked copy of a subchart both exist, the build fails instead of overwriting. Your source archives are never modified.

A captured chart can use up to two public, credential-free HTTPS chart repositories with distinct raw dependency names and non-overlapping HTTPS origin/path scopes. Declare them in native Chart.yaml, generate Chart.lock with native helm dependency update, and commit that lock. Native Helm validates lock consistency and selects versions; Oyzu does not resolve chart versions itself. For example, a dependency may name vault, version constraint ~0.30.0, and repository https://helm.releases.hashicorp.com with a lock selecting 0.30.1. The same repository can be used by a contained sibling file:// chart. Its acquired archives are expanded and validated at that local chart's own path. A single dependency can also set alias, for example name: vault with alias: secrets. Native Helm applies alias-scoped values under secrets and validates the native lock. The lock must uniquely match the raw chart name vault; captured index entries, archives, expanded paths and dependency records keep that raw identity. Repeated copies of one upstream chart under multiple aliases are outside this path's supported scope. For example, declare the dependency in Chart.yaml: dependencies: - name: vault alias: secrets version: ~0.30.0 repository: https://helm.releases.hashicorp.com Put its values under the alias in values.yaml: secrets: injector: enabled: false Generate the native lock normally; do not rename the locked chart or its archive to secrets. Each repository index, its selected archive URLs and every redirect must remain under that original repository's HTTPS origin and path prefix. Declaring a second repository does not let the first redirect to it: Oyzu refuses that hop before contacting the second repository. On the same origin, neither normalized repository path prefix may contain the other. For example, https://charts.example.test/ and https://charts.example.test/team-b/ cannot be captured together. This is checked before any capture lookup or upstream request. Each selected index entry needs a SHA-256 archive digest. Oyzu captures the original index and archive, checks the complete archive before supplying it to Helm, and validates the acquired chart names, versions and vendored dependency closure. Original chart and lock files remain unchanged. Dependency records distinguish original archive digests from the prepared chart bytes; a chart lock alone is not archive integrity evidence. Two repositories retain separate indexes, original archives and source-bound receipts. Both share one acquisition allowance of 4,096 requests, 1 GiB of response bytes and at most eight concurrent requests. Restoring a capture still requires current source and tool admission and the complete locked dependency set for each repository. An unchanged selection can reuse its verified acquisition snapshot. This reuses the recorded index, without claiming that the current upstream index is unchanged. Offline builds require that exact capture, locked tools and execution image to be available already. Missing inputs fail with a request to prepare the selection online; there is no network fallback during execution. Repository aliases (@repo or alias:repo in the repository field), authentication, managed connector routing, more than two remote repositories and archives hosted outside the repository prefix are not supported by this path. Remote archives must include their complete vendored closure; Oyzu does not acquire additional remote dependencies from those charts. Each index and compressed archive is limited to 4 MiB, with at most 4,096 archive URL slots per index. Existing archive expansion and source containment limits also apply. The direct native install task keeps its existing native behavior.

Captured builds accept public and authenticated OCI chart dependencies. Set an exact semantic version in Chart.yaml and commit the matching native Chart.lock, generated with helm dependency update: dependencies: - name: podinfo version: 6.7.1 repository: oci://ghcr.io/stefanprodan/charts Version ranges, latest and credentials in repository URLs are refused. The repository names a registry path; Oyzu appends the dependency name and exact version tag (Helm's _ encoding is used for semantic-version build metadata). The existing limit of two remote repositories applies across HTTPS and OCI. Run helm registry login <registry> before preparing private dependencies. Oyzu reads HELM_REGISTRY_CONFIG, then the native Helm configuration directory's registry/config.json (HELM_CONFIG_HOME or the platform default). Docker's native login store is the fallback when no Helm entry exists. Registry-specific credential helpers take precedence over the selected store's inline auths; helpers must be on PATH. A helper that reports no credentials for the registry leaves the request anonymous; any other helper failure stops preparation. No Oyzu registry setting is required. Oyzu uses its shared OCI Distribution client, including Bearer token exchange. Credentials remain in core preparation, scoped to the registry origin and port; they never enter the chart, dependency inventory or worker configuration. Credentialed token endpoints must share the registry origin, and redirects never receive credentials for another origin. A missing or rejected login fails preparation with HELM_OCI_AUTH_REQUIRED; check the selected native login store. There is no public fallback. Keep login configuration outside the project: source capture refuses recognized native configuration with literal credentials. This includes project-contained files selected by HELM_REGISTRY_CONFIG, regardless of the selected filename. Authored environment references remain unexpanded in captured source. Native identity-token refresh (identitytoken or a helper's <token> username) is unsupported in captured preparation; vendor those dependencies with native Helm before building instead. It captures the manifest, Helm config and chart content layer, and records both the manifest SHA-256 and chart layer SHA-256. Preparation and capture replay verify those digests, object sizes and chart identity before the existing archive and vendored-closure checks. A captured manifest binds the resolved tag; reuse does not query whether the tag moved. Each manifest, config and compressed chart layer is limited to 4 MiB, with at most 64 selected chart versions per OCI repository. Chart artifacts must contain one Helm chart content layer and include all transitive remote dependencies. The native chart and lock remain unchanged. The isolated preparation worker has no registry access: it receives the verified archive and replays it offline. Offline captured builds need the exact prepared capture, locked tools and image already available. Native host builds retain the existing vendored-dependency requirement: run oyzu run install online first, then oyzu build --full can package and validate the vendored chart offline. The direct native install task follows Helm's own acquisition behavior; core digest capture belongs to the captured build path. Chart publishing, OCI chart roots, chart signatures and provenance verification are outside this support. Chart signing/provenance verification remains a follow-up; digest verification alone does not establish publisher trust. Failure Meaning and recovery HELM_LOCK_REQUIRED / HELM_LOCK_INVALID Generate and review an authored native lock matching the declared repository HELM_SOURCE_UNSUPPORTED Use at most two public HTTPS or OCI repositories with distinct raw chart dependencies and non-overlapping origin/path scopes, or vendor the dependency locally SOURCE_DENIED An archive or redirect leaves the original repository prefix; use a supported source or vendor it HELM_INTEGRITY Captured archive bytes differ from the advertised SHA-256; inspect the repository rather than bypassing verification HELM_CAPTURE_INVALID / HELM_CLOSURE_INVALID Required native outputs, identity bindings or vendored dependencies are missing or inconsistent OFFLINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE Prepare the exact selection online before retrying offline The chart version comes from version inference over its native version and Git history, with a suffix from the source snapshot. appVersion and dependency versions keep their own meanings. A build packages the chart, runs the tests, strict lint and the read-only YAML format check, and collects the outputs if all pass. Application charts produce a versioned .tgz and rendered.yaml. Library charts produce the .tgz only. Building, generated files and the version change happen in private workspaces, so your checkout stays unchanged. The format check covers your source YAML, not the regenerated dependency chart. Reports are collected in dist/, and dist/manifest.json records their paths, digests and summaries: junit.xml is one render and schema check, or the library validation unittest.xml is required when suites are selected, and has the native test cases, failures and skips. A render success never covers a failed assertion Coverage is recorded as inapplicable in the target's extensions["oyzu.dev/coverage-applicability"]: chart assertions have no application-source coverage denominator. This applies to isolated builds and direct tests, including named targets and runs with hooks. No coverage percentage is made up, and a required coverage minimum still fails The manifest also lists framework discovery, step outcomes and artifacts. Testing fails for missing or invalid required reports, a plugin that won't launch, a native failure, a timeout, or a unittest run with zero test cases. Old report files are removed before each run, so an earlier success can't cover a failed launch. Validation and unit tests each time out after 120 seconds. Task replacements and hooks work as usual. A replacement keeps the required reports, and one that exits 0 without them fails collection. Direct tests collect validation and unittest reports once, after the post-test hook; a failing hook still fails the run and retains the test reports. A valid bundle isn't a release approval. If a build fails, read the retained logs and reports, fix the suite, tool, values or lock, and rebuild. A format difference needs oyzu run format or a task override.

Helm-unittest can create missing matchSnapshot baselines even without --update-snapshot. Oyzu compares the files under __snapshot__ folders before and after the run. Creating, changing or deleting a baseline fails the task and blocks artifacts. The native JUnit can still show a passing assertion, so read both the step status and the reports. Create or update baselines on purpose with native helm-unittest outside the build, review them and commit them with the suite. Then a matching baseline passes and a changed value fails normally. Direct oyzu run test applies the same rule and also rejects creation or changes. Direct tests run on a private copy of the chart that leaves out .git, .oyzu and dist, so the live bundle isn't visible to Helm. The copy holds the chart tree only, so relative references to files outside it don't work. It rejects links and is limited to 100,000 entries and 64 MiB. Baseline scanning has the same entry limit with 16 MiB per file and 64 MiB in total. Exceeding a limit fails the task. This checks baseline changes and is not a file write monitor. Direct tasks are not a sandbox. Isolated builds use the executor's isolation.

To check a chart before you commit, run oyzu build --full, or oyzu run test, oyzu run lint and oyzu run format-check for the quick version, and read the reports with oyzu inspect dist. Not supported yet: Custom suite globs, templated test charts, and suites in sibling file:// dependencies that aren't prepared are not discovered. Authenticated HTTPS chart repositories and managed chart repositories are not supported. HTTPS archives must stay within their repository prefix; OCI dependencies require exact versions and native registry login for private sources. See Locked HTTPS repositories and Locked public OCI dependencies. Go-template formatting and custom yamlfmt configuration aren't supported. Publishing and signing aren't part of the Helm builder. Image bindings: see Image bindings.

documents.t: Docker images Direct test reports Version inference Build bundles

Recognized Helm build tests emit units for helm-unittest files in the root chart and unpacked or packaged subcharts. With tests.retries enabled, Oyzu reruns a failing unit using --file, in a fresh native process from the root chart. Parent values, global values and native dependency conditions still apply. Helm-unittest matches --file relative to every recursively loaded chart. Files sharing that relative path form one unit: for example, tests/api_test.yaml and charts/child/tests/api_test.yaml run together as tests/api_test.yaml. All cases in a failing group run again, including its passing members. Other passing paths are left alone. A unique subchart path runs independently while retaining its root context. Native conditions can leave a subchart-only group empty; it runs once, with no test cases, only when native completion explicitly reports zero suites and zero tests. Malformed or empty suites fail even if Helm-unittest exits zero. Suite and case names must identify cases uniquely within a group; ambiguous native JUnit identities fail rather than recover. Local template/schema validation and library helm lint validation run once, before the file units. A validation failure never enters the test retry loop. Report-transforming hooks retain generic JUnit step handling; a failed validation is a suite-level error and still cannot recover through test retries. Each attempt's JUnit and failure kinds remain in the build bundle. A requested case missing from the next file report stays failed even if Helm exits zero. A consistent failure preserves the native failure exit. A recovered unit is reported as flaky and is not stored as a reusable pass. --no-cache disables result reuse without changing retry behavior. Configure retries in oyzu.toml, not in build.yaml. Helm-unittest 1.2.0 provides no native retry setting; Oyzu supplies the retries. This file selection path requires portable suite filenames without glob metacharacters (*, ?, [ or ]). Direct oyzu run test keeps its ordinary single-invocation behavior. Native builds require the provisioned Helm plugin; isolated builds use the prepared, pinned plugin as described above.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/how-oyzu-compares.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu gives teams one workflow for tools, tasks and builds across existing native projects. It runs ecosystem tools and collects artifacts and reports into a build bundle. Standalone builds, tool management and tasks need no Oyzu account. Status: experimental. Support depends on the builder, project shape, platform and installed plugin. Planned marks capabilities not shipped for the stated scope; check the ecosystem support matrix before adopting a workflow.

These are workflow tradeoffs, not performance rankings. No speedup or feature parity across these tools is promised. For supported isolated Linux builds, Oyzu can use crun, a container runtime that needs no Docker daemon. Alternative Where it is stronger or simpler Where Oyzu fits today Bazel / Buck2 Choose an explicit rule-based build graph when you need control over individual build actions and remote execution. Both Bazel and Buck2 support executing actions on remote workers. Oyzu discovers supported native projects and runs their own build tools. Its REAPI integration stores cache results. Planned: REAPI remote execution. Gradle / Maven Keep the native tool when your needs are inside its project model: Gradle caches eligible task outputs locally and remotely, and Maven provides a plugin-driven lifecycle. Oyzu wraps Gradle or Maven, selects tools and collects artifacts and reports. On Linux crun, compatible Java plugins reuse eligible module/project lifecycles independently, keeping compilation, archives and test evidence together. Unbounded module views retain the whole lifecycle. Native Java lifecycles with incomplete reads rerun. Nx / Turborepo Nx and Turborepo already cache task results. They are a more direct fit when your main requirement is scheduling and caching package tasks in a JavaScript workspace. Oyzu combines supported Node builds with other native targets, tools, artifacts and report requirements. Isolated npm stages and package-local npm/pnpm/Yarn Classic workspace members can reuse on Linux crun. Root aggregate scripts retain workspace-wide reads. Package-manager and workspace limits still apply, including unsupported Yarn Plug'n'Play and per-member workspace application artifacts. Cargo and other native tooling Cargo, Go, pip and other native tools remain the direct route to their own commands and configuration. For one ecosystem with an adequate existing workflow, using them directly avoids an orchestration layer. Native Oyzu builds invoke those tools and gather their outputs. Rust builds retain Cargo incremental state in private workspaces; Oyzu adds common selection, check and bundle handling. It does not replace Cargo dependency resolution or promise identical support for every native command. mise / asdf mise manages tools, environment variables and tasks; asdf offers plugin-based tool version switching. Keep them when those capabilities satisfy the requirement or a needed tool is outside Oyzu's supported providers. Oyzu offers tool installation and locking, shell activation and tasks, connected to supported builds and bundles. It does not support every tool-manager plugin. Planned: general macOS support; the Intel Zig exception is listed below. CI-only caching A CI cache that restores selected files, such as workflow dependency caching, can be enough when you only need to avoid repeated downloads in an existing pipeline. It requires less adoption than adding a build orchestrator. Oyzu's action cache derives keys from build inputs and restores eligible outputs and reports locally, with optional shared storage. It distinguishes reused checks from fresh execution. A hit does not prove a test ran now, and the experimental remote cache is unsigned.
documents.s: Choose by the problem you need to solve

documents.t: Oyzu's action identity includes source inputs, commands, configured environment, toolchain, prepared dependencies and builder identity. Cache keys and per-language cache paths are not user-authored. This is useful when you want the same reuse rules in local builds and CI, rather than maintaining archive keys in pipeline scripts. Oyzu reuses a stage only when it can account for all its inputs and bound its outputs. Rust has native stage and compiler-result reuse with documented limits. On isolated Linux crun, npm stages, supported Node workspace members, Helm, eligible Go application stages and Java lifecycles can reuse results. Compatible Java plugins reuse eligible Maven modules and Gradle projects independently and keep Ant's selected targets together. See stage reuse for each builder's limits and action caching for admission rules. The .NET implementation supports admitted compile/test/pack reuse, per project for eligible solutions, but the current catalog package lacks a capability required by this CLI. Use a compatible plugin as described in .NET builds. Delivery through the catalog is Planned. Full Python complete-read reuse is also Planned. An unchanged build can execute unbounded stages again. Moving a checkout can also invalidate stages whose retained outputs contain location-specific data. Native builds run with your account's file and network access; caching adds no sandbox. Choose isolated execution when that boundary is required. Native Windows stages with incomplete reads run again, including arbitrary Node scripts and Maven/Gradle lifecycles. Windows Vite/uv complete-read enforcement is Planned. Python 0.1.3 refuses Windows uv; later plugin releases admit it, rerunning each time. Clearing the cache cannot make those stages eligible. Native temporary-directory changes alone do not invalidate eligible actions: Oyzu replaces TEMP, TMP and TMPDIR with private paths. Home/profile values remain keyed. See temporary-directory keying.

Capability Availability Stage reuse Experimental for admitted stages and compatible plugins. Planned: full Python complete-read reuse and Windows Vite/uv complete-read enforcement. Node member invalidation depends on the package manager and shared installation bytes; see workspace reuse. Plugin delivery for implemented features Planned: a .NET catalog package compatible with this CLI, and independent native Maven/Gradle formatting reuse in the next Java plugin release. Updating the CLI alone does not update plugin declarations. See .NET requirements and Java formatting. Persistent Oyzu daemon Planned. Do not choose Oyzu expecting a resident build graph or file-watching service. Existing native incremental state is a separate capability. REAPI remote execution Planned. Current REAPI support is action-cache storage for the server/client combinations in remote caching. Additional publication support Publishing has an experimental built-in OCI destination and GitHub/npm publisher implementations; plugin destinations require an available catalog package or binding. Planned: signed catalog delivery of those publishers, PyPI and offline plugin bundling. OCI publishing uses digest coordinates; mutable tags are not supported. macOS support Planned for general use. The current exception is native Zig builds on Intel macOS. Apple silicon and other ARM64 hosts and targets are unsupported. Linux and Windows support is x64 and builder-specific. See platforms.

Check its exact project shape in ecosystem support, then follow native local builds or the owning ecosystem reference. Use tool commands if installation and version selection are all you need, or build tasks for a shared task workflow. Keep the native tool when it already meets your needs; adopt Oyzu where the common workflow removes work for your team.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/install-script.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. install.sh and install.ps1 install the oyzu executable from a GitHub release with one command. They pick the release asset for your platform, check its SHA-256 digest and put oyzu in a folder of your own. They need no administrator rights. They then run oyzu shell install, so your shells activate oyzu and both oyzu and its tool shims are on your PATH. Note: Every release is a preview. Releases are binaries and notices published on the public oyzuai/oyzu-releases repository, and both scripts default to it, so you need no account or token. The scripts check the digest but not release provenance (the *.sigstore.json files); oyzu self checks both on every later update. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

On Linux or macOS: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh | sh On Windows, in PowerShell: irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1 | iex A GitHub token is optional. It lifts the anonymous API limit, or lets you install from a private repository named in OYZU_RELEASE_REPO.
