With the GitHub CLI signed in: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh | GH_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) sh $env:GH_TOKEN = (gh auth token); irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1 | iex A successful run names the release, prints one summary line (tag, asset, SHA-256 digest, location), the installed oyzu --version and the result of oyzu shell install. Release values are placeholders here: Installing oyzu <tag> for linux/x86_64 from oyzuai/oyzu-releases Installed oyzu <tag> (oyzu-linux-x86_64, sha256:<digest>) to /home/you/.oyzu/bin/oyzu oyzu <version> (<build>; x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu; build <id>) Enabled first-party preview plugins. To undo: oyzu config set --global plugins.preview false Shells and PATH set up activation bash /home/you/.bashrc login-path bash /home/you/.profile Next Step: Open a new terminal (and restart IDEs) so they pick up the new PATH. To make preview builders available, the installer runs oyzu config set --global plugins.preview true if that setting is absent from your user configuration. This lets oyzu build select a preview builder immediately; a compatible stable release, when listed, needs no preview opt-in. An existing true or false is preserved. To turn previews off, run oyzu config set --global plugins.preview false. This user-level choice applies to all your projects; the CLI default remains off, and administrative controls still apply. A configuration read or write failure prints a warning and leaves the CLI installed; run the opt-in command yourself after resolving the cause.

Prefer oyzu self update for an existing installation: it verifies release provenance and keeps one previous version for oyzu self rollback. If the CLI is too old to provide self, download install.ps1 as shown below and run it again. FILE_READER_TOO_OLD means the project needs a newer CLI; install at least the version named in that error before retrying the build. For a disposable candidate install, use a separate folder and user configuration: $env:OYZU_USER_CONFIG = 'C:/throwaway/user.toml' # create this independent file first $env:HOME = $env:USERPROFILE = 'C:/throwaway/home' $env:LOCALAPPDATA = 'C:/throwaway/home/AppData/Local' $env:APPDATA = 'C:/throwaway/home/AppData/Roaming' New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $env:LOCALAPPDATA, $env:APPDATA | Out-Null pwsh -NoProfile -File ./install.ps1 -InstallDir C:/throwaway/bin -NoModifyPath & C:/throwaway/bin/oyzu.exe --version & C:/throwaway/bin/oyzu.exe reshim -NoModifyPath leaves shell profiles and the persistent PATH alone. The installer can still set plugins.preview in the selected user configuration. Use explicit executable paths in PowerShell, cmd and Git Bash to select the disposable install. Run this example in a separate PowerShell process so the profile variables apply only to the disposable session. Keep the same profile and user configuration through the upgrade. The installer retains existing configuration and tool state; it can enable preview plugins if that setting was absent. With -NoModifyPath, run reshim explicitly afterwards to refresh installed-tool launchers and remove orphaned shims for removed tools. This does not edit the persistent PATH. Close running managed tools before refreshing: Windows can retain a launcher in use until a later refresh. Check an installed tool through its refreshed shim and retry the project build after installation. For local candidate channels, OYZU_API_BASE can point to a loopback server serving GitHub-shaped release metadata and OYZU_DOWNLOAD_BASE to its asset download base. Serve oyzu-windows-x86_64.exe and its matching shim with their actual sha256: digests under an oyzu/v<version> tag. Remove GH_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN from that test process so it uses anonymous download URLs. Never point a personal installation at this test channel. This exercises the installer's digest verification, not release provenance. The installer replaces files without retaining oyzu.previous.exe and does not create rollback history. Back up the disposable binary pair and receipt before installing, and restore those backups to undo an installer replacement. Do not claim this proves self rollback; signed self-update and its rollback must be exercised separately when the candidate has admitted release evidence.

Piping a download into a shell runs whatever the server sent. You can read each script first: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh -o install.sh less install.sh sh install.sh irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1 -OutFile install.ps1 Get-Content install.ps1 powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\install.ps1 Both are served from the documentation site over HTTPS.
documents.s: Read it before you run it

documents.t: install.sh install.ps1 Environment variable Default Meaning --channel NAME -Channel NAME OYZU_CHANNEL stable Release channel to install from and follow: stable, beta or nightly (see channels) --version TAG -Version TAG OYZU_VERSION newest release of the channel with your platform's asset Install this release tag, for example oyzu/v0.2.0, and pin it so it is not updated automatically --dir DIR -InstallDir DIR OYZU_INSTALL_DIR ~/.oyzu/bin; Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\bin Folder that receives oyzu and oyzu-shim --no-modify-path -NoModifyPath OYZU_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 off Skip shell activation and PATH changes; preview plugin setup still runs (see Shell and PATH setup) --modify-path -ModifyPath Accepted and ignored. Shell and PATH setup is now the default --help -Help Print usage and exit An option wins over its environment variable. These variables have no option: Variable Default Meaning GH_TOKEN, then GITHUB_TOKEN none GitHub token for the API, for the rate limit or a private OYZU_RELEASE_REPO OYZU_RELEASE_REPO oyzuai/oyzu-releases Repository whose releases are read, for forks OYZU_API_BASE https://api.github.com GitHub API base, for GitHub Enterprise or a test server OYZU_DOWNLOAD_BASE https://github.com Base of anonymous release downloads To pass options through a pipe: curl -fsSL https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.sh | sh -s -- --version oyzu/v0.3.1 --dir "$HOME/bin" & ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://docs.oyzu.ai/install.ps1))) -Version oyzu/v0.3.1

Without a version, the script reads the newest 30 releases and takes the newest one of the channel that is not a draft and has an executable for your platform. The channel comes from the version string, as oyzu self decides it: stable takes only versions without a prerelease part, beta adds release candidates and betas, nightly adds nightly builds (-alpha.0.nightly.<date> after a release, -rc.1.nightly.<date> after a candidate). The scripts take the first matching release in GitHub's list, newest first, rather than comparing versions. GitHub's prerelease flag is ignored, so the 0.2.0 Preview counts as stable. Host Asset Linux x86_64 (glibc) oyzu-linux-x86_64 Linux x86_64 with musl (Alpine) oyzu-linux-x86_64-musl macOS Intel oyzu-darwin-x86_64 Windows x86_64 oyzu-windows-x86_64.exe If the release also has oyzu-shim-<platform>, it is installed beside oyzu as oyzu-shim. Releases so far publish no musl assets, so a musl host gets the no asset error. Keep the two executables together when moving an installation. On Windows the small shim launcher hands tool execution to the installed frontend; after replacing or moving the pair, run oyzu reshim to refresh the frontend pointers. Unix tool shims remain symbolic links to oyzu. On macOS and Windows the script also downloads the same release's Linux oyzu for your architecture (oyzu-linux-x86_64), checked the same way. Isolated builds (oyzu build --isolated) run that Linux oyzu inside the container. A Linux host doesn't need it: its own oyzu runs there.

Downloads the asset into a temporary folder and compares its SHA-256 with the digest GitHub reports for that asset. A mismatch or a missing digest stops the install. Runs the new oyzu --version from the temporary folder. An executable that can't run on this host leaves an existing install alone. Creates the install folder and replaces oyzu (and oyzu-shim) there, with the executable bit set. Running it again upgrades or reinstalls. On macOS and Windows, runs oyzu engine install --linux with the downloaded Linux oyzu. This installs the pair as the engine package of the new oyzu, so --isolated works. It prints Installed the Linux engine for isolated builds. If the release has no Linux oyzu for your architecture, or the step fails, oyzu stays installed and the script says so; only isolated builds are affected. Writes the install receipt .oyzu-install.json in the install folder: the channel, the pin when --version was given, the repository, and the tag and digest installed. oyzu self reads it to keep this install updated. Prints one line with the tag, asset, digest and location, then the version. Uses the installed CLI's scoped configuration reads to check your user file, then enables preview plugins only if plugins.preview is unset. Prints the undo command when enabled; configuration failures are warnings. Runs the installed oyzu shell install, unless you skipped it. The scripts never use sudo and never install toolchains.

The last step runs oyzu shell install with the new executable. It needs no network and edits only the files below. Running it again moves an unmodified login PATH block after later startup lines. What Where Shell activation: bash, zsh, PowerShell 7 (each one found) ~/.bashrc, $ZDOTDIR/.zshrc or ~/.zshrc, and the PowerShell 7 current-user profile oyzu and the tool shims on the persistent PATH, Windows your user Path in the registry (HKCU\Environment), with %VARIABLE% entries unexpanded, announced to running programs oyzu and the tool shims on the persistent PATH, Linux and macOS a marked block in your login profile (~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login or ~/.profile, whichever exists first; ~/.zprofile for zsh) With the shims first on their inherited PATH, IDEs, GUI programs and scripts can run node, go or cargo at the version the project locks, without oyzu exec --. Programs that are already open keep the PATH they started with, so restart them or open a new terminal. Run oyzu shell check to verify precedence (exit 1 means shadowing commands; --json returns shadowed). Windows machine Path precedes user Path; on a single-user machine use elevated oyzu shell install --machine to put the per-user folders first on machine Path, and elevated oyzu shell remove --machine to remove the entries it added. Shared machines should remove or reorder the system tool instead. No auto-elevation occurs; Unix hosts have no machine Path. Services, scheduled tasks, launchd jobs and systemd units must use absolute shim paths or prepend the shims on the job's own PATH; run oyzu shell check in that environment. Oyzu installs none. See PATH checks for startup-line repair and platform limits. If setup fails, the install still stands. The script says so on standard error and prints the command to run again. fish and Windows PowerShell 5.1 are not configured, so add the folders yourself. With --no-modify-path (-NoModifyPath, OYZU_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1) the script changes no profile or PATH. If the folder isn't on PATH, it prints how to set things up later: Shell Line any ~/.oyzu/bin/oyzu shell install (Windows: & "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Oyzu\bin\oyzu.exe" shell install) PowerShell, this session $env:Path = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Oyzu\bin;$env:Path" See oyzu shell for what each file receives and how to undo it.

An installed oyzu keeps itself updated on its channel; see Updating oyzu itself for oyzu self update, channels, pins, rollback and how to turn automatic updates off. Running the script again also moves to the newest release, or pass a version to switch to that one. To uninstall, run oyzu shell remove to undo the shell and PATH setup, then delete the files (and the folder if it is empty): rm -f ~/.oyzu/bin/oyzu ~/.oyzu/bin/oyzu-shim ~/.oyzu/bin/*.previous ~/.oyzu/bin/.oyzu-install.json Remove-Item "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Oyzu\bin\oyzu.exe", "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Oyzu\bin\oyzu-shim.exe", "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Oyzu\bin\*.previous", "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Oyzu\bin\.oyzu-install.json" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Tools that oyzu installed for projects live in its own store, not in this folder, so deleting these files doesn't remove them.

Integrity: the digest comes from the GitHub releases API over HTTPS, and the download must match it. This shows the bytes are the ones GitHub holds for that release asset. It doesn't show who built them, because the scripts don't check release provenance; oyzu self does for every update after this one. Transport: install.sh restricts curl to HTTPS, including redirects, unless OYZU_API_BASE or OYZU_DOWNLOAD_BASE names a plain http: test server. Tokens: a token is sent only in a request header to the GitHub API. install.sh gives it to curl on standard input, never on the command line, so it needs curl when you use a token (wget is used only without one). curl and PowerShell drop the header when GitHub redirects a download to its storage host. The scripts never print a token. Scope: files go to the install folder and a temporary folder that is removed afterwards. oyzu shell install then edits the profiles listed under Shell and PATH setup. --no-modify-path skips it.

Script Runs on Needs install.sh Linux, macOS; also Git Bash on Windows POSIX sh, awk, curl or wget, and sha256sum, shasum or openssl install.ps1 Windows x86_64 Windows PowerShell 5.1 or PowerShell 7 install.sh uses no bash features, jq or Python. Running install.ps1 under PowerShell on macOS or Linux stops and points you to install.sh. The scripts are tested on Linux and Windows (x86-64). macOS and musl are not tested yet. ARM64 hosts are unsupported; retained architecture detection does not establish support.

Status Meaning 0 Installed 1 Failed: network, HTTP error, no release or asset for this platform, the executable doesn't run, or the folder can't be written 2 Usage error (unknown option or missing value) 3 Integrity refusal: the digest differs, the release reports none, or no SHA-256 tool is available install.ps1 sets the process exit status when run with powershell -File install.ps1. Under irm ... | iex it doesn't exit, because that would close your window. It prints the error and sets $LASTEXITCODE.

Errors start with oyzu install: and leave an existing install unchanged. Message Cause Recovery GitHub answered 404 Not Found for the release list of <repo> ... private OYZU_RELEASE_REPO names a private repository and no token was given, or it doesn't exist Pass GH_TOKEN with access, for example GH_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) GitHub answered 404 Not Found ... with your token The token can't read the repository, or the tag or asset doesn't exist Check the tag and the token's repository access GitHub rejected the token ... (HTTP 401) Invalid or expired token Create a new token or run gh auth login GitHub refused ... (HTTP 403) Anonymous API rate limit (60 requests an hour) or missing permission Wait, or pass GH_TOKEN no published stable release of oyzuai/oyzu-releases has <asset> No release of the channel has an executable for this platform (musl, other CPUs), or none is published yet Build from source release <tag> ... has no <asset> That release lacks this platform Choose another --version <asset> ... has digest ..., but the release reports ... The download doesn't match the published digest Retry. If it repeats, don't use the file, and report it release <tag> reports no SHA-256 digest The release API returned no digest for the asset Choose another release could not connect to download ... Offline, DNS or proxy failure Check the network. curl, wget and PowerShell honor the usual proxy settings the downloaded <asset> does not run on this host Wrong ABI or a damaged download Build from source, or report the platform cannot write <path> No permission, or oyzu.exe is running on Windows Choose --dir, or close oyzu and retry
Getting started, including building from source. Shell setup for activating project tools.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/installer-recipes.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Some npm packages download extra files while they install or run: Puppeteer downloads a browser, node-gyp downloads Node.js headers. A captured build (oyzu build --isolated) runs without network, so those downloads would fail. For packages Oyzu recognizes, it downloads the matching file during preparation, checks it against a pinned SHA-256 and points the tool at it through the tool's own settings. Your project declares nothing. Note: Recipes cover Puppeteer and node-gyp on Linux x86-64 workers only, and there is no setting to turn one off yet. A native host build (without --isolated) has network access and downloads as the package intends.

After the package manager's captured install preparation, Oyzu reads the locked packages and the Node version. For each recognized package it looks up the pinned asset. If your version or platform has no pinned asset, Oyzu says so in the build log and guesses nothing (see When a package is recognized but not pinned). Oyzu downloads each asset the same way as a declared fetch, checks it against the pinned digest, stores it by digest under <user data>/cache/fetches/ and unpacks it under recipes/<recipe>/ in the prepared dependency tree. The build sees that tree read-only at /dependencies. Every command (install, tasks and package) gets the recipe's settings, so the install script skips its download and the tool finds the asset when it runs. If an administrator restricts downloads with fetches.sources, the asset's host must be allowed there, as for any declared fetch.

Recognized Every locked version of the registry package puppeteer, in npm, pnpm or Yarn locks Assets Chrome for Testing chrome and chrome-headless-shell for linux64, at the build Puppeteer pins for that release URL https://storage.googleapis.com/chrome-for-testing-public/<build>/linux64/<browser>-linux64.zip Layout recipes/puppeteer/<browser>/linux-<build>/<browser>-linux64/ (Puppeteer's cache layout) Settings PUPPETEER_CACHE_DIR=/dependencies/recipes/puppeteer, PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=true Pinned releases Puppeteer 24.0.0 to 25.13.0, and 25.16.0 Puppeteer's install script sees PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD and doesn't try the network. puppeteer.launch() and puppeteer.executablePath() read PUPPETEER_CACHE_DIR and find the browser for their own pinned build, so your project needs no change. Both browsers are delivered because Puppeteer downloads both by default. Firefox is skipped by default and has no recipe. Limits: Only linux/amd64 workers have pinned assets. Chrome for Testing has no Linux arm64 build before Chrome 153. On other platforms the log says the browser isn't pinned. If you select another browser build (PUPPETEER_CHROME_VERSION, chrome.version in .puppeteerrc) or another cache directory, your setting overrides the recipe for that value and the install fails offline. The base execution image doesn't include the system libraries Chrome needs to start (libnss3 and others). The recipe delivers the browser. To launch it, use an image that has those libraries (--image npm=<image>).

Recognized A locked registry package whose archive has a top-level binding.gyp, or a binding.gyp in the project root Asset node-v<version>-headers.tar.gz for the Node version in use URL https://nodejs.org/dist/v<version>/node-v<version>-headers.tar.gz Layout recipes/node-gyp/<version>/node-v<version>/include/node/ Settings npm_config_nodedir=/dependencies/recipes/node-gyp/<version>/node-v<version> Pinned releases Node.js 18.0.0 to 26.11.1, plus the 22.23.4 security-release headers node-gyp reads npm_config_nodedir and uses those headers instead of downloading them. The scripts that npm, pnpm and Yarn run inherit the variable. The headers alone don't compile an addon. You also need Python, make and a C++ compiler in the image. The base execution image has make and g++ but no Python, so a build that compiles an addon needs an image of its own: provide one with --image npm=<image>. Addons that download a prebuilt binary first (prebuild-install, node-pre-gyp) still fail offline unless they fall back to compiling.

Preparation continues and the build log shows one line for the recipe: Recipe puppeteer puppeteer@25.14.0 has no pinned Chrome for Testing build in this Oyzu release; its install script will try to download one Preparation doesn't fail here, because your project may already avoid the download with the tool's own settings. If it doesn't, the install fails as described next.
documents.s: When a package is recognized but not pinned

documents.t: When a captured npm install fails because a script couldn't reach the network, the error names the package, the URL and the fix, as far as npm's output shows them: DEPENDENCY_INPUT_MISSING: the install script of cypress@13.6.0 tried to download https://download.cypress.io/desktop.json, and captured execution has no network. Oyzu has no recipe for this asset. Declare it as a pinned fetch in build.yaml (name, url, sha256) and point the package at OYZU_FETCH_<NAME> through its own setting; see the declared fetches reference. The original npm output follows the message. If Oyzu can't find a URL it names the host instead, and if there was no network error it reports npm's failure unchanged. This diagnosis covers npm installs. pnpm and Yarn report their native error. For the root package, npm reports the build version that version inference applied, which can differ from the version in your manifest. To supply the asset yourself, add a declared fetch and set the tool's own variable to its path. For Puppeteer on an unpinned release, fetch the Chrome for Testing zip with unpack: zip and set PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=true and PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH=/dependencies/fetches/<name>/chrome-linux64/chrome.

Spotless steps backed by Eclipse formatters (<eclipse>, <greclipse>, <eclipseWtp> and <eclipseCdt> in the Maven plugin, and their Gradle equivalents) download Eclipse P2 bundles from download.eclipse.org at run time, into Spotless's own cache. There is no recipe for this, and a declared fetch can't be pointed at that cache. In a captured Maven build, spotless-maven-plugin:check fails during preparation with java.net.UnknownHostException: download.eclipse.org. To work around it, run that Spotless check outside the captured build, or keep the Eclipse step out of the captured lifecycle, for example with a Maven profile that sets spotless.check.skip=true.

Every recipe asset has a SHA-256 in a table inside Oyzu. A download whose bytes don't match fails with INTEGRITY_MISMATCH and nothing is stored. Oyzu never takes a digest from the network at build time. Chrome for Testing publishes no checksums. Oyzu's digests were computed from the downloaded zip after its bytes matched the checksum Google Cloud Storage reports for the file. Node.js header digests come from each release's SHASUMS256.txt. The signature of that file was not checked. The dependency snapshot records each asset with verification: digest-only: the bytes match the pinned digest, but no publisher signature was checked.

Each asset becomes a package in the target's dependency snapshot: Field Value id recipe:<target>/<recipe>/<asset>/<version>, for example recipe:web/puppeteer/chrome/136.0.7103.94 name, version The asset name (chrome, chrome-headless-shell, node-headers) and its upstream version sourceId fetch:<host> for a standalone build, or fetches.sources/<index> under an allowlist digest, size The verified bytes purpose, verification build, digest-only The extension oyzu.dev/recipes lists each applied recipe with the packages it serves, its settings and each asset's path and tree digest. Both are part of the snapshot digest, so the build plan is bound to the delivered assets.

Recipes apply automatically to every captured Node build that locks a recognized package. The digest tables cover a fixed range of releases. A newer release needs an Oyzu update. Recipe settings override the same variable from the builder plan. If a variable is delivered twice (for example by a recipe and a declared fetch), the build fails.

Recipe assets use the declared fetch errors. The message names the recipe, the asset and the package, for example web: puppeteer recipe asset chrome 136.0.7103.94 for puppeteer@24.9.0. Code Cause Recovery SOURCE_DENIED An administrative fetches.sources doesn't allow the asset's host Ask an administrator to allow it, such as https://storage.googleapis.com/chrome-for-testing-public/ INTEGRITY_MISMATCH The downloaded bytes differ from the pinned digest Report it. Don't change the digest without checking the upstream release. DEPENDENCY_INPUT_MISSING An offline build needs an asset that isn't stored, or an install script without a recipe tried the network Run one online build, or declare the asset as above
Declared fetches Version inference

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/java-quality.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Maven, Gradle and Ant projects get lint, format-check and format tasks without any configuration. They use Checkstyle 10.26.1 for linting and google-java-format 1.28.0 for formatting. Replace any of them with your own task if your project already has its own tooling. The same locked google-java-format 1.28.0 default applies on Java 21 and newer. The shared default stays below 1.29 to preserve Java 17 compatibility: newer formatter releases can require javac APIs unavailable on Java 17 even when their class files load there. Selecting a newer JDK does not silently replace the project lock. Use an explicit formatter task to select a different version. Status: experimental. The defaults use a managed JDK and locked quality tools; no platform account or separate provisioning script is needed. oyzu run list oyzu pin oyzu install --frozen oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format oyzu build --full In a workspace with several targets, qualify the task name, for example api:lint. oyzu run list needs no Java tools. It shows the linter and formatter that will be used. The first run prepares its locked quality bundle in the tool store. oyzu install --frozen prepares the selected JDK and build tool. lint and format-check are build stages. format changes your files, so it is never added to a build. A failed quality check blocks the artifacts. Test and coverage reports that were produced stay in dist/manifest.json. Lint and format output is in the action logs, not in JUnit or coverage reports.

The default native Maven/Gradle formatter binds its managed JDK as a typed external locked-tool input. Core admits the identity from oyzu.lock before cache lookup; changing it invalidates formatter reuse with unchanged Java source. The quality bundle remains covered by the toolchain lock. This does not bound arbitrary reads by lifecycle plugins or runtime tests. For Maven and Gradle builds, the default format-check reads the Java files selected by the shared source scanner and the direct entry names and kinds in every directory that scanner visits. Empty directories count too: adding a source file or a nested source directory changes the key. Editing only the contents of an existing README does not change these reads. google-java-format parses only the explicit files passed to it; it does not resolve imports, run build scripts or discover project configuration. This fixed native rule needs no runtime dependency report. Generated and dependency directories excluded by the scanner remain excluded. This uses one shared inventory for prediction and formatter arguments. lint stays unbounded because provisioned checks.xml can load checks that read additional files. Ant's authored targets and quality slots also stay unbounded. Authored task replacements retain ordinary task behavior. format changes source and is never a cached build stage. See action cache for lifecycle limits. Use a Java plugin supplying these declarations and a CLI with compatible private native-stage support; older declarations cannot admit the formatter merely because the CLI is newer. For native host Maven and Gradle builds, the default format-check runs in a private stage with no retained output files. Its order-only edges preserve build ordering without adding lifecycle or test results to its key. It reuses independently when its source, action definition and admitted tools remain unchanged. A README content edit leaves its source-read key unchanged, but a source-derived snapshot version or whole-target projection identity can still cause a miss. A formatted Java source edit reruns it. Native lifecycle builds (including tests) and Checkstyle have unbounded output contracts, so they currently rerun even on unchanged builds. Their presence prevents whole-target restoration for this mixed pipeline, even in fast builds that omit quality checks. oyzu build --explain names the incomplete-read reason; adding inputs or clearing the cache cannot bound arbitrary lifecycle reads. Captured execution has no private-stage opt-in from this declaration.

Use JDK 17 or newer, selected through Java installation. oyzu pin records the Checkstyle and google-java-format versions, upstream URLs, upstream integrity and SHA-256 values in quality.java in oyzu.lock. The same record freezes the default checks.xml and upstream notice text, so an older project lock keeps its exact rules after a CLI update. The first selected quality task installs the locked JARs in the shared tool store. Downloads go through source admission and SHA-256 verification before publication. Complete upstream JARs retain their embedded licenses and notices. Installed payloads are trusted on reuse; commands do not rehash them. Published Java builders receive this installation automatically; an old manual quality-home setting cannot replace the locked inputs. The repository provisioning script is no longer used. Local oyzu build --full, isolated builds and oyzu run lint, format-check and format consume that same installation. Isolated actions restore a read-only archive and run with networking disabled on the base execution image. They do not mount the live user tool store. Host tasks are ordinary development processes with the selected task environment. A build can record a missing default set during preparation, subject to its lock policy. Direct tasks require a pin first. A missing lock, denied source or unavailable locked input fails before quality actions run; no checker is silently skipped. Offline operation needs the lock and an already installed bundle or admitted cached inputs in the same store. Run one online check first. Ordinary pinning and builds preserve an existing quality selection. New defaults ship with Oyzu releases; use oyzu pin --refresh or a whole-project oyzu update to adopt the current CLI's defaults. New tools are installed when the next task needs them. See locked quality tools.

The lint defaults check for unused imports, redundant imports, empty statements and equals/hashCode consistency. Checkstyle does the parsing and rule checks. google-java-format formats and normalizes imports: format-check runs its dry-run mode, and format rewrites files. See the formatter CLI and Checkstyle CLI. Each task selects the .java files below its target, including custom source roots, reactor modules and included builds. It skips folders named .git, .oyzu, .oyzu-build, .oyzu-maven, .gradle, .idea, target, build, dist, out, node_modules and .venv, at any depth. It doesn't guess other output folders or tell generated files apart outside those names. If your authored source lives in a skipped folder, or you need a narrower scope or a different style, replace the task. Files are processed in sorted order. Up to 200,000 entries are visited and each Java file can be up to 16 MiB. Symbolic links aren't followed. Meeting a link outside the skipped names fails the task instead of reading outside the target. Files are passed to the tools in batches within a 16,000-character argument limit. If any batch fails, the task fails. With no .java files, the task reports that it doesn't apply. Build checks work on a private copy, so your checkout isn't modified. oyzu run format changes files in place and isn't transactional. A later malformed file can leave earlier files already formatted.

A native lint, format-check or format target in an Ant project wins over the default. Its format task remains marked as mutating source and stays out of build stages. TOML task replacements and hooks work as for any task. For example, a Gradle project that already has quality tasks can use them: [tasks.lint] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "checkstyleMain", "checkstyleTest"] [tasks.format-check] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "spotlessCheck"] [tasks.format] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "spotlessApply"] The tasks and plugins must exist in your project. These examples don't install them. Use ./gradlew or gradlew.bat if you use the wrapper. A replacement used in builds must work in the offline container. The default launcher rejects extra arguments, such as --replace on format-check. Put native flags in a replacement task.

Oyzu doesn't infer Maven quality-plugin bindings, Gradle quality tasks, custom Checkstyle XML or suppression files, Kotlin or Groovy tools, or per-module formatter differences. Checks you configured in your build still run through the native lifecycle and can coexist with the defaults. Replace the defaults if your rules differ.

A compatible CLI and Java builder with rerun-cases support apply the shared test retry settings to conventional Maven and Gradle build lifecycles. No test-framework retry library or platform account is required. Authored build replacements keep their existing behavior. [tests] retries = 2 flaky = "pass" Run oyzu build --context ci as usual. The first attempt runs Maven verify or Gradle build; later attempts run that same lifecycle with native filters for its remaining failed cases. Maven adds Surefire -Dtest=Class#method and Failsafe -Dit.test=Class#method. Gradle selects the native Test methods with --tests and reruns selected Test tasks. Module and task names remain part of case identities. A lifecycle is one retry unit so its native ordering and non-test failures remain visible. Passing cases are retained in the combined report, and each attempt is recorded separately. Assertion failures, setup errors, case timeouts and crashes retain distinct failure kinds. Class initialization errors, incomplete reports, process termination and non-test lifecycle failures cannot be repaired by case retries. A filter that returns no requested case leaves that case failed and reports TEST_RERUN_INCOMPLETE, including when the native command exits zero. Parameterized methods rerun all their parameters. A display name that cannot be expressed as a method filter reruns its class; every requested identity must still be present. Gradle fails natively when a selected Test filter matches no tests, and the completeness check also applies. Surefire/Failsafe rerunFailingTestsCount replaces Oyzu retries; each native attempt is read from its XML report. Gradle test-retry settings also replace Oyzu retries. Their attempts are visible only with reports.junitXml.mergeReruns = true; otherwise Oyzu reports TEST_ATTEMPTS_UNKNOWN, adds no retries and refuses cache storage. Native retries that a framework or custom runner does not expose remain undetectable. --no-cache uses the same attempts and completeness rules. A flaky or failed unit is never stored as a clean pass. Offline operation needs the locked JDK, build tool and native dependencies already available. Ant retains its existing retry tier; this lifecycle support covers Maven and Gradle.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/local-builds.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Plain oyzu build runs your project's own tools (Cargo, Go, npm, pip, Maven, Gradle) directly on your machine and collects the results into a build bundle. These builders need no Docker. This page covers which builds run natively, how to choose platforms and executors, how to preview a build, and how to split a build into separate jobs. Note: A native build runs with your user account's access to files and the network. It is not a sandbox. Use oyzu build --isolated when you need the container executor. Native build actions receive their declared and configured environment, rather than arbitrary inherited host variables. Builder-declared compiler/runtime controls and shared launch/home controls are frozen into the cache key. HOME, USERPROFILE, APPDATA and LOCALAPPDATA are passed through when set and keyed exactly; changing any of them changes the key. TEMP, TMP and TMPDIR are executor-owned and replaced by private temporary paths. Their overwritten values are omitted from native host keys, even when configured or declared by a builder; changing only those values preserves reuse. Authored values and the final allocated environment still undergo policy validation. Other undeclared shell variables stay absent. Windows machine-directory inputs include SystemDrive and ProgramData, which native MSVC discovery needs. Declare additional project inputs in configuration; see native environment inputs. Development tasks launched with oyzu run keep host inheritance. The Go, .NET/NuGet, Helm, Cargo/Rust and npm/Node builders declare that their native commands require the home set. Missing declarations keep that default. Native host commands retain home, including Rust formatting. The first scoped exception is the first-party packaged Rust format-check command under Linux crun (--isolated --no-docker): its enforced input view excludes ambient user home for the formatter and descendants. All four variables are absent from its frozen environment, launch and key; explicit Cargo/Rustup tool homes remain keyed. Image account information is an admitted image input. Other builders, replacement commands, hooks, Docker execution and native hosts gain no opt-out. An unqualified home: "none" claim retains home and disables native result reuse. Explicit home settings or declared home names cancel the claim. Windows home declarations recognize names without regard to case; existing case-collision and policy validation still apply to the resolved environment. See home inputs and cache admission. On Windows, native build shell lookup uses that same frozen environment, including PATH, SystemRoot, ProgramFiles, ProgramFiles(x86) and LOCALAPPDATA. A configured Path overrides inherited PATH for lookup as well as for the child process. Bare bash and sh require a native shell such as Git for Windows; System32 and WindowsApps WSL launchers are excluded. If the shell cannot be found in the frozen locations, configure its location or use an explicit executable path. Git fallback roots in ProgramFiles, ProgramFiles(x86) and LOCALAPPDATA must be absolute. Empty, relative, drive-relative (C:tools) and root-relative (\tools) values are ignored, so they cannot make shell lookup probe a working directory. When Oyzu resolves a bare native command, it searches only absolute PATH entries. Missing or empty PATH values and empty or relative entries (., tools, or an empty segment between separators) are ignored by Oyzu's lookup, so that lookup never searches the task or Oyzu working directory. A command absent from the remaining locations fails before launch with COMMAND_NOT_FOUND (or the native-shell diagnostic on Windows). Configure an absolute tool directory, or name an explicit command path such as ./tools/probe. The same rule applies when oyzu run removes env.PATH. Plugin tool observations and compiler-cache selection also use only the supplied absolute PATH entries, with the same environment-name precedence as the launched process. They never retry a missing tool through the host PATH or a bare name. Observation tool names must be single plain components; paths such as ./tool or tools/tool are rejected even if a plugin manifest declares them. These lookup rules apply to commands resolved by Oyzu. Child processes receive the original PATH and can honor its empty or relative entries. Native Rust compiler invocations that run a linker remain uncached whenever PATH contains any such entry, so the cache cannot record a different linker from the one rustc runs. Use only absolute PATH entries to allow compiler-output reuse. Each native host task action receives its own temporary directory through TMPDIR, TMP and TEMP, replacing inherited or authored values for those variables. Child processes of that action share it. Oyzu validates the resulting environment against configuration constraints before launch and removes the directory when the action completes, including command failure. On Unix it is created with mode 0700. Use a separate project-specific variable when a command needs an authored scratch location: these three names always select Oyzu's private allocation. Native capability probes, including the MSVC linker and Windows SDK check, also receive private temporary paths instead of authored values for these names. Oyzu first uses the operating system's temporary location. If that path is relative, missing or unusable, it creates private scratch under the Oyzu user data directory's tmp folder instead. Plugin copies, plugin launch scratch and log spools use the same fallback. If neither location is usable, the command fails before launch and reports both causes; restore access to temporary or Oyzu user storage and retry. No temporary-directory setting is required. This prevents unrelated actions from sharing ordinary temporary files; it does not add filesystem or network isolation, and programs that ignore these variables can still use other host paths. Temporary paths are execution allocations and do not enter action keys. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

oyzu build --plan # preview; installs and runs nothing oyzu build # host build with fast checks oyzu build --full # also run tests, lint and format checks oyzu build --platform linux/arm64 # build for one other platform oyzu build --isolated # use the container executor oyzu inspect dist # verify the bundle Run these commands from a project, or select one with oyzu -C <project> build. Build uses the same project-boundary check as oyzu run: Oyzu configuration, an Oyzu build.yaml, a Git boundary or a recognized native manifest identifies a project. A plain parent folder also builds as a zero-config workspace when the bounded lookup finds a project within three directory levels. Static markers are the fast path; eligible catalog detections also identify projects at the root or within that same lookup. The configured catalog uses normal verification and refresh rules (--plan and --offline use cached metadata), so configuration and catalog metadata may be loaded or refreshed before a refusal. If neither the root nor that lookup identifies a project, all build variants (including a named target, --plan, --full and --json) refuse with PROJECT_NOT_FOUND (exit 5) before deeper build discovery, workspace preparation, Prepare output or the Building … heading. Unreadable folders are skipped by the lookup. oyzu run still requires a project at the root and only suggests nearby projects. See missing projects and unreadable folders.

For a declared oyzu/plugin-package target, repeat --compose <bundle>/manifest.json to assemble already-built platform members instead of running the executable producer. Composition admits existing signed provenance and checks the target's declared platforms; deliberate gaps use --allow-incomplete <platform>=<reason>. See plugin packaging. Plain oyzu build runs natively when every selected target has a native host build (see the table below). Otherwise it uses the container executor. --isolated (or --image) always uses the container executor. --affected picks its targets first, then follows the same rule. --all-platforms builds every declared platform through the container executor and needs Docker. A failed build never retries with another executor. Running in CI doesn't change the choice. Native output is a runnable binary or package for this machine. Use --isolated when you need the packaging that the container executor produces. The bundle manifest still records each artifact's version: the builder's own version where it has one, otherwise the target's resolved version. When a consumer declares a platform other than the host, the build uses the container executor. For example, a docker/image with platforms: [linux/x86_64] that copies in a Go binary, built on Windows, gets a Linux Go binary built in the container. The container runs on the base execution image, and every tool comes from oyzu.lock there (see Go, Node and Helm). A tool that isn't locked for the platform is refused with the oyzu pin command that adds it.

These builders build on the host. Oyzu installs missing managed tool requirements into the shared tool store, then runs the ecosystem's own commands. Additional manual prerequisites, where required, are listed below. An admitted plugin runs from its installed host path. A tool store under a folder named /workspace, /out or /oyzu keeps that exact executable path; these names do not move the plugin into the build's private source workspace. This also applies to conventional check tasks, including Java lint and format checks. Project Native build Version chosen when you don't pin one Rust (Cargo) Yes Latest stable Rust that satisfies Cargo rust-version. A rust-toolchain.toml channel or an explicit pin wins. See Rust installation. Node node/app with npm and a dist/ output Yes Latest LTS release that satisfies every engines.node range, else the latest matching stable release. See Node selection. Inferred single-root npm package with a name and build script Yes (npm archive) Node from engines.node or the LTS default; npm from packageManager when declared. See Node output selection. Go go/app: one module, no go.work, exactly one package main Yes The Go minimum from the go.mod go and toolchain lines. See Go version selection. Python with pip and pyproject.toml Yes (wheel) Latest stable CPython that satisfies requires-python. See Python installation. Explicit python/app with pip, static PEP 621 name/version and one console script Yes (.pyz, wheel and sdist), including Windows x64 with a matching native plugin Selected managed CPython; core prepares the wheel closure and installs it offline. See Python applications. Java Maven reactor (a committed mvnw is used) Yes (jars; tests run in verify) JDK from the declared language level; Maven 3.9 unless the wrapper supplies one. See Java installation. Java Gradle build (a committed gradlew is used) Yes (jars; tests run in build) JDK from the declared language level; Gradle 8 or 9. Java Ant project with build.xml Yes (experimental; Linux x64; Windows x64 qualification pending) Managed JDK from native tool selection; Ant, JaCoCo and test libraries must be provisioned separately. Go libraries, Go workspaces, several Go binaries; other Java; Poetry or requirements-only Python; other Node projects No: container executor — When a builder without a native build is selected and Docker is unavailable, the build fails with a message that says so.

oyzu pin is optional for Rust, Go and Node. With no oyzu.lock, the first build resolves the tools, writes oyzu.lock and installs from it. Commit the lock to make later builds repeatable, or delete it to resolve again. Tools a builder detects on its own follow the same rule. For example, a Rust project whose Cargo.lock lists prost-build needs protoc. Its version is your folder pin, else the detection's hint, else the latest stable release in the catalog. The build locks and installs it with the other tools. oyzu pin records the same choice. A detected tool that has no catalog entry or checksum, or that can't be installed, is shown as an attention row and the build continues. Set tools.ignore to silence it. Only a tool you pinned in oyzu.toml fails the build when it can't be verified or installed.

[tools] go = "1.24" wins when it is at least the Go minimum. A module-folder value below the minimum is refused. The build runs go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, so only the locked Go compiles and none is downloaded mid-build. --offline adds GOPROXY=off. Compiler errors show their file and line, the exit status is kept, and no earlier binary is republished. The artifact is the executable <target>-<version>. --full adds go test -json with coverage, go vet and gofmt -l. Dependencies use Go's module cache from your Go environment. It isn't separate per project.

One oyzu build can build several native targets, such as a Python wheel and a Node dist/ directory, into one bundle. Oyzu selects the targets you named plus everything they depend on, prepares their tools, and runs one shared task graph. Independent targets run at the same time, up to build.jobs. A depends_on in build.yaml makes the consumer wait for the producer's stages. By default, a build-failing action stops the build, including unrelated work. With --keep-going, unrelated targets can finish and only dependents are blocked. Stages within one target run in order, because they share the target's files. Each target builds in its own private workspace. An ordering edge alone copies no files; use materialize to pass artifacts. Required reports must be produced and artifacts collected before a target counts as built. See build tasks. Two targets that would produce executables with the same file name are refused before anything runs. On Unix, native private source workspaces preserve ordinary file and selected directory permissions (0777) on cold population and later refreshes, including mode-only changes with unchanged file bytes and modification times. This includes selected nested and empty directories and target directories below the source boundary. Directory modes are applied after population; read-only directories are temporarily writable only in the private copy during refresh and pruning. The authored source tree is unchanged. The projection's engine-owned boundary root remains writable working storage; its mode does not reproduce the source boundary root. Captured execution views retain their existing directory behavior. ACLs, ownership and special bits are outside this native projection guarantee. Regular-file source observations include the ordinary Unix mode as well as executable intent. A mode-only change invalidates affected action keys, while source versions remain permission-independent. Cached regular files restore their verified ordinary mode; Unix admission refuses missing, invalid or inconsistent mode facts instead of assuming 0644 or 0755. Hosts without Unix mode observation leave that fact absent. Directory modes remain outside action-result cache identity and output metadata restoration. Use oyzu build --no-cache when directory permissions affect build outputs. ACLs, ownership and special bits remain outside this guarantee. See action caching for the current reuse limits. Linux native host action keys bind the file-creation mask inherited by child processes. A build launched with umask 0077 cannot reuse a result keyed under 0022, even when source files are unchanged. Oyzu reads the mask without changing it, freezes it once before cache lookup, and records the same bounded value in the host action's invocation and native command identity. If the mask cannot be read or validated on Linux, or cannot be observed on another Unix host, native host targets run without action-result reuse. Existing worker, builder and secret-environment restrictions retain their reasons. Image workers do not bind the coordinator's mask, and Windows has no Unix creation-mask fact. This does not establish full file/directory mode identity or output metadata restoration; the permission limits above still apply. Ecosystem notes: npm runs npm ci and needs a lockfile. Installation is the target's prepare step. It runs before pre_build hooks, is skipped on a full cache hit, and runs again with --no-cache. A failed install blocks the build and publishes nothing. npm lifecycle scripts run as usual. pip uses its own PEP 517 wheel build, including downloading the build backend. CPython is installed as a managed tool and pip is the one bundled with it. The output is a wheel, not a runnable application. Offline, npm runs in offline mode and pip uses --no-index. The build fails if what they need isn't already cached. Conventional native pip and uv package builds set SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=0, matching captured Python preparation, so supporting backends write stable archive timestamps. Authored replacement build commands keep their own environment. The default native Maven lifecycle uses the same fixed project.build.outputTimestamp as captured Maven builds (1980-01-01T00:00:02Z). These defaults stabilize archive timestamps; they do not establish reproducibility for every backend, authored task or compiler output. Plugin conformance compares collected artifact bytes.

Run oyzu build or oyzu build --plan in a nested folder that has its own build.yaml; you don't need --root. A source subfolder uses the nearest build.yaml above it. Repository configuration still applies, but the nested build has its own lock file and outputs. A parent build doesn't include nested builds. See configuration for how configuration is inherited.

oyzu build stops at the first build-failing action, locally and in CI. It starts no further actions and stops running actions through the same process-tree and worker cleanup used by Ctrl-C. The build is failed, with the first failure's exit code. An advisory check that only warns does not stop the build. Set build.failFast = false to finish independent actions and collect every failure in one run. Dependents of a failed required action remain blocked. Each target resolves this setting from its folder chain: the nearest folder wins, and a context value wins over the base value in the same file. A failure in a target with false blocks only its dependents; a build-failing failure in a target with true stops the whole build. For example, to keep going in CI: [context.ci.build] failFast = false oyzu build --keep-going sets false for every target; --fail-fast sets true. These mutually exclusive flags override OYZU_BUILD_FAIL_FAST=true|false, which overrides files. Ordinary policy constraints still apply. An empty environment value is ignored; other values fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. The flags also apply to --slice. The plan and build record show each target's resolved value and source beside its check levels. Inspect configuration with oyzu config get build.failFast or oyzu config explain build.failFast. Changing the setting does not change cache keys. Remote submission and oyzu run task DAGs retain their existing behavior. Actions that succeeded before the stop keep their normal action-cache entries. After fixing the failure, rerun the build to reuse them. Stopped actions export no outputs and are never cached. See stopped action records.

oyzu pin --dry-run previews tool requirements and lock changes without installing anything or changing files. oyzu pin writes the lock; conflicts or incomplete inputs fail and leave the lock unchanged. See the lock file. With no oyzu.lock, the first build resolves the tools, writes the lock (it never edits your TOML files) and installs them. You don't need a compiler already installed. An existing lock is never changed by a build. A missing or incompatible entry fails with a request to run oyzu pin. oyzu build --offline never resolves versions or writes a lock. It needs the metadata, archives or installations already cached. Pinning reads files only. It works offline and currently runs from the workspace root. For Rust, discovery reads: rust-toolchain.toml or rust-toolchain, in every form rustup accepts (see Rust toolchain files). Having both files is an error. Cargo rust-version minimums. Declared components, targets and profile. The tools each selected stage needs (rustfmt, Clippy, nextest, cargo-llvm-cov). With no toolchain file, Rust is listed without a version and the build locks the latest stable release. A file with no channel keeps its components and uses your configured or default Rust. A local path toolchain fails unless oyzu.toml selects a release. Node is resolved the same way. For pip wheels, CPython comes from requires-python or .python-version and is installed from Python Build Standalone. uv, Poetry and older Python tools are not installed for you.

Oyzu names the system linker and SDK a Rust toolchain needs, but doesn't install them: Toolchain channel Needs *-windows-gnullvm LLVM-MinGW (UCRT) with Clang linking *-windows-msvc Microsoft Build Tools and the Windows SDK *-windows-gnu A toolchain with the profiler runtime if you need coverage Unqualified, such as 1.95.0 GNU/LLVM or MSVC, listed as alternatives Discovery doesn't run rustup, search PATH or check whether these are installed. The build checks them when it runs (see executor readiness). Requirements of dependency build scripts and toolchain files in parent folders aren't detected.

Two ideas stay separate. The target platform is what an artifact is built for. The executor is where its build steps run: this host, for its own platform; a native cross toolchain on this host; the container executor (--isolated, --all-platforms); a remote pool (--remote). The executor is part of the build's identity. The plan and manifest record it on each target (oyzu.dev/platforms), and cache keys include it. A cross-compiled or container result never stands in for a host build of the same platform, or the reverse.

Write every platform as os/arch[/abi]: linux/x86_64, linux/arm64, darwin/arm64, windows/x86_64, windows/x86_64/msvc. Input also accepts amd64 for x86_64 and aarch64 for arm64, in build.yaml platforms, --platform and --allow-incomplete. Output, records and dist/ folders always use the canonical form. The ABI is optional: gnu or musl on Linux, msvc, gnu or gnullvm on Windows. Without one, the builder picks its default (see Rust). The resolved ABI is recorded in the target's platform. For Rust it is musl for a Linux cross build, msvc on Windows and gnu on a Linux host. Published names (dist/ folders, asset names) include the ABI only when it isn't the OS default (GNU on Linux, MSVC on Windows). See release asset names. Container engines and registries keep their own spelling (linux/amd64). Note: musl is the default for Linux cross builds. If your code depends on glibc (dlopen, NSS name lookup), declare linux/<arch>/gnu.

Command Platforms built oyzu build The host platform. A target that declares no platforms builds for the host. A target that declares platforms, but not the host, builds the one declared platform this machine can build. With several it asks for --platform; with none it is skipped, with the reason. oyzu build --platform

(repeatable) Exactly those. A target that doesn't declare

is skipped for it. A declared platform that can't be built here fails before anything runs (PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE), as does a run where no target builds anything. --platform linux/arm64/gnu narrows a declared linux/arm64. Native executors build one platform per target per run, so use one --platform per CI job, or add --isolated. oyzu build --all-platforms Every declared platform, through the container executor. One the container executor can't build here fails before anything runs. --platform and --all-platforms can't be combined with each other or with --remote. An invalid platform name is a usage error (exit status 2). A platform-independent target, such as a static site in dist//any/, is built once. When a build sends a platform off the host, or a target declares platforms this run doesn't build, the Plan names each row's platform and shows what builds it. other lists platforms this machine could build with --platform; not here lists the rest, with the reason: ── Plan ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── format lint test build package hello · linux/arm64 skip skip skip run skip other windows/x86_64 · host with --platform linux/x86_64 · cross toolchain (rust-lld) with --platform not here windows/arm64 · missing MSVC arm64 build tools (Visual Studio VC/Tools/MSVC//lib/arm64); --isolated builds it with the container executor darwin/arm64 · needs a macOS runner (Apple SDK and linker); --isolated builds it with the container executor built by hello · linux/arm64 · cross toolchain (rust-lld) Only Rust has a native cross toolchain. Go, Node, Python, Java, .NET and Helm build only for the host natively. For other platforms Plan names the runner they need (needs a Linux runner) and whether --isolated could build them.

By default, a platform builds on the host when it matches, otherwise with a native cross toolchain if the builder has one (or the container executor under --isolated). You can fix the executor per platform in oyzu.toml, per folder and per context: [build.executors] "linux/arm64" = "cross-toolchain" # always cross-compiled, never built on an arm64 host "darwin/arm64" = "host" # only on a macOS arm64 runner [context.release.build.executors] "linux/x86_64" = "container" # releases build it in the container executor Values: host, cross-toolchain, container. A declared executor is the only one used for that platform. Nothing falls back to another. When it isn't available here (no cross linker, the wrong host, container without --isolated, or host/cross-toolchain with --isolated), the platform isn't built and Plan says why. Asking for it explicitly fails with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE before anything runs. In the release context the host platform counts as asked for, so a release build fails instead of skipping it. Plan, the preview (declaredExecutor) and the CI matrix (executor) show the declaration.

oyzu build --plan --json includes a top-level matrix you can feed to a CI matrix strategy. It has one include entry per declared platform of every selected target, with: platform; runner: os (linux, windows, macos) and arch, the machine that builds it natively; executor: the declared executor, else host; targets: the targets that declare it. The matrix doesn't depend on what the planning machine can build: a target that declares only darwin/arm64 still gets its entry when planned on Linux. unconstrained lists targets that declare no platforms. With --affected <ref>, the matrix holds only affected targets. Each target in the preview also has a platforms record: declared, declaredExecutors, one row per platform (selected, executor, declaredExecutor, reason, refused, runner), and the platform and executor this run would use. jobs: plan: runs-on: ubuntu-latest outputs: matrix: ${{ steps.plan.outputs.matrix }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - id: plan run: echo "matrix=$(oyzu build --plan --json --affected origin/dev | jq -c .matrix)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT" build: needs: plan strategy: matrix: ${{ fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.matrix) }} runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner.os == 'macos' && 'macos-15' || matrix.runner.os == 'windows' && 'windows-2025' || 'ubuntu-24.04' }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: oyzu build ${{ join(matrix.targets, ' ') }} --platform ${{ matrix.platform }} Your workflow maps runner to real runner labels, including any arm64 runner. oyzu publish checks that every declared platform was built; see incomplete platform sets. Toolset verification runs are listed separately under .verify. Run them in the platform jobs, or pass --skip-verification to the platform jobs and run each .verify command in its own job. See fanning runs out in CI.
documents.s: A CI matrix from the plan

documents.t: oyzu build --plan shows what a build would do without doing it. It chooses native or container execution exactly as a build would. --isolated, --all-platforms, named targets, profiles and --full mean the same as in a build. You don't need Cargo or Docker installed to run it. The preview: reads configuration and project files, and shows each target's discovery decisions, stages (run or skipped), task order and tool requirements; doesn't install tools, download packages, run build tools or scripts, create a lock, or write a bundle; with --affected, reads local Git history and hashes local files, with no network access or writes. Some details are only known once a real build prepares: whether tools are installed, exact commands, artifact names and report paths. The preview marks these as unresolved. A stage marked run means configuration asks for it, not that its prerequisites will pass. A successful preview doesn't mean the build will succeed.

The Plan table shows targets by stage, with run, skip or - cells and one footnote per skip reason. A single target built for several platforms shows one row per platform. Above twelve rows, targets with identical stages share a counted row; -v lists every target. See result output. When every target needs the same tool, the requirements table shows "all N targets". --json still lists every target. Color follows your terminal (CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 forces it, NO_COLOR turns it off). --json returns a build-preview record with resolved: false, the selection, targets (each with a discovery map of role to selected and reason), tasks, requirements, unresolved details, effect flags and timings. The preview is not the executable plan. A real build writes that to dist/plan.json.

timings reports where the preview spent its time, in milliseconds: totalMs and phases, in this order: Phase What it measures discovery Configuration and target discovery. selection Selection, variants, task graph and requirements. source Listing the working tree from file metadata. Absent when analysis is off or fails. analysis Static analysis, with targets (one entry per target), finishMs and rulesMs. Absent when analysis is off or fails. planning Stage and task listing. Timings describe one run and aren't part of the analysis record.

Oyzu repository PRs also run the Initiative label check on OVH self-hosted runners independently of CI selection, skipping Dependabot and requiring at least one initiative:* label in the event payload from the shared taxonomy. Contributors to Oyzu itself should run the repository's presubmit before merging. Its default Linux mode reuses the main-CI candidate-build action and its --optimized --full --no-cache arguments in a disposable checkout in a private directory directly below /tmp (avoiding inherited configuration and excessive Unix socket path lengths), without .oyzu or prior action-cache results, including nextest, coverage and doctests. --changed-only omits this build and loudly reports that it is not main-equivalent. It reuses this selection mechanism, estimates cost up front, and distinguishes the default checks from the incomplete --changed-only iteration mode. Use oyzu build --plan --json --affected <base> after checking out the comparison history. The preview installs and runs nothing. Read the selected logical builds from selection.requested and the platform matrix, and repository-check tasks from selection.affected.tasks. See affected builds. Only use selection.affected.inputModel: "stage-reads" with an explicit fallback: null to skip jobs. A missing or malformed fallback field runs every job; a nonempty fallback reason also runs everything and explains why. A missing marker (including release v0.2.2), missing base, unsupported change or preview failure must run every job and retain the reason. Scheduled, release and explicit dispatch runs should build everything. A job-level if: can report an intentional skip while an aggregate required check still verifies that every selected job passed; a workflow path filter cannot provide that result. The repository's CI and docs-site workflows use the PR base, or the last successful run of that workflow on dev for a dev push. Main promotion pushes always select every job; they never use affected-only selection. Dev CI is a signal, while release requires successful full main CI on the exact release commit and the pre-tag Windows suite. Inputs belong to build.yaml and the tasks in oyzu.toml, including workflow/setup files read by the workflow checks. The released CLI remains the driver; a candidate built from the PR cannot qualify its own selection. A fresh affected preview records absent generated declared inputs in selection.affected.absentDeclaredInputs instead of requiring their preparation. Execution requires inputs only for the final selected builds and their dependencies; source docs/diff checks do not require generated website inputs when the website is unselected. Selection output explains which absent inputs no selected action needs. A selected website still requires its prepared inputs, including for reference edits declared as website inputs. The docs-site job keeps its examples generation and validation. The repository's unbounded root Rust stages currently keep the CLI job selected for docs-only edits; a source-only edit can leave docs unselected when no docs task inputs changed. Remote pool webhook/trigger integration remains a later, separate design. CI result records each job's selection and actual result in its run summary, including intentional skips and failures. These records describe that run; they do not authorize reusing test results across runs or at release. Selected jobs must pass, and an unexpected skip or cancellation fails the aggregate. Job execution limits are 10 minutes for CI and docs selection, 20 minutes for repository documentation/contracts checks, and 25 minutes for docs validation. The Rust producer retains 180 minutes; quality maintenance, feature-free CLI verification and each acceptance partition retain 60 minutes. CI result has 2 minutes and license inventory has 10 minutes. These limits exclude queueing; they bound execution rather than promising a completion time. The Linux CI gate builds one candidate with the released driver, then transfers that same executable and its companion files to parallel acceptance jobs. Quality-tool maintenance runs beside the candidate build. Feature-free CLI verification runs beside the acceptance partitions with its own compilation cache. Native-cache acceptance partitions its full default project inventory across three jobs; the smoke job also runs terminal, isolated-build and fresh-checkout checks. Main runs every partition. On PRs the Maven and Gradle/Python partitions run no native proofs, so they omit tool setup and candidate download/extraction; smoke checks still run. A missing candidate artifact, failed partition or unexpected skip fails CI result, which remains the single aggregate check. Artifact transfer requires available Actions artifact storage; it has no source-build fallback. A failed-only rerun can use the successful producer's artifact from an earlier attempt of the same workflow run. A full producer rerun replaces the artifact and its digest. Both consumers verify the producer's tar SHA-256 before extracting or running it; a missing digest or mismatch fails, including when an earlier extraction exists. An expired artifact requires rerunning the producer. Candidate and quality producers retain their bounded build-record/cache metadata in separate best-effort artifacts; failure to upload those diagnostics does not replace or overrule a gate result. The default-feature help comes from that candidate instead of a second ordinary Cargo build. The feature-free build still compiles both binaries and compares all command help. Each help header must match its executable's version stamp with the oyzu. help wordmark. The default and feature-free builds must report the same version; differing stamps fail the check. This repository retains up to 32 GiB of native compiler state in local and CI builds; the product default remains 8 GiB. Metadata-preserving copies use copy-on-write when the filesystem supports it and ordinary copies otherwise. The candidate and quality jobs seed from read-only compiler snapshots. Their exports replace only the directories each job built; the runner serializes the merge and atomically publishes it, so concurrent exports preserve both jobs' updates. Temporary publication links are removed on success or failure. A failed merge removes its partial version and export and still prunes expired retired states; cleanup failures do not replace the original error. Compiler state still passes the existing runner/toolchain and native-cache admission. Main retains --optimized --full --no-cache: all tests and reports execute again. The guarded test-result reuse and release-evidence admission switches are unchanged. The scheduled CLI acceptance workflow checks out main on Mondays and Thursdays at 06:17 UTC and runs full uncached verification with --full --no-cache, without restoring its compilation cache. Linux CLI compilation and crun reuse checks run on OVH; native task scenarios, the Docker worker contract and captured-build suites run on hosted Linux. Native Windows CLI and task scenarios run weekly on Wednesdays at 07:43 UTC. The $30/month Actions cap is shared organization-wide; schedules are budgeted with zero included minutes. Job timeouts bound scheduled hosted compute to $16.80/month: Linux scenarios 20m, worker contract 15m and all captured suites 202m combined (5–30m each); Windows CLI 60m and scenarios 20m. A timed-out job fails acceptance. These limits do not establish that every suite completes within its budget. Captured-build suites require Linux Docker/AppArmor; they are not Windows coverage. Dependent jobs use the same checked-out commit. There is no monthly macOS run: macOS runs only in the release workflow when darwin is declared. Releases retain their dedicated self-hosted runners and never read the shared action cache. Manual build.yml dispatch runs Linux on OVH and no longer accepts platforms. The tool-management, tool-worker and Python-constraint workflows also run only on OVH Linux for every event, without a platforms input. Leave OYZU_HOSTED_RUNNERS unset; it is no longer consulted. Hosted selection is restricted to the scheduled acceptance jobs. Dormant F4 workflows retain their existing placement; their hosting is decided at activation. Public visibility does not change ordinary workflow runner selection. Current OVH job containers have no engine socket or elevated capabilities, so they cannot run Docker or load the AppArmor profile. Captured-suite dispatch checks fail on these pools; a suitable executor must be separately qualified without weakening isolation.

oyzu build --remote --plan previews what oyzu build --remote would run on a platform pool. It doesn't contact the platform and needs no token. It uses the pool's settings: isolated execution, full checks and the normal platform selection. --remote doesn't imply --all-platforms. Named targets and --affected <base> work as in the remote run. --affected compares with the merge base of <base> and HEAD. The record's execution is remote. The preview reads your working tree, so it includes uncommitted changes, which a remote run never sends. --isolated, --all-platforms, --image, --check and --download can't be combined with --remote. Every preview target carries these placement facts: Field Meaning platform The artifact platform: from the target's variant, otherwise decided by the executor (unresolved until executor selection). platformSource variant, executor or host (a native host target). executionPlatform The platform the executor must run on, or null when any will do. A Rust cross-compile in the container runs on linux/x86_64 whatever it targets. A Docker image needs its own platform when its final stage uses RUN. needsDaemon, daemonReason Whether the work needs a Docker engine, and why. false for native host targets, for Node, Rust, supported external go/app and pip Python (python/package, python/app, python/library) targets that can use the daemonless sandbox, and for RUN-free image assembly. Selected quality checks or hooks can make an image target need Docker. isolation What the executor must provide: host, crun (Linux with unprivileged user namespaces, or Docker), in-process (Oyzu's own image assembly) or docker. id, logicalTarget, variant The concrete target ID, its logical name, and its variant axes. Use the returned id; don't construct one. dependsOnTargets The concrete targets this one depends on. sliceable Whether another slice could reuse this target's results. false means build it in the consumer's slice. sliceReason, sliceDetail Why it isn't sliceable, or null: ALWAYS_RUN_HOOK, UNCACHED_TASK, UNSCOPED_INPUTS, UNBOUNDED_OUTPUTS, SECRET_ENVIRONMENT, CACHE_DISABLED. platforms How each platform is built here; see a CI matrix from the plan. A target isn't sliceable when it has a hook (hooks always run), an authored task without cache = true and declared outputs, inputs outside its folder, stages with unbounded outputs, a secret environment, or local caching turned off. Image targets with source projections can be reused across slices under the same cache-key and artifact-verification rules. A build can still fail to reuse a sliceable target, for example when the producer failed. The top-level placement object says which facts can change. Each target's platform, executionPlatform and needsDaemon are final, as are tool requirements whose status is discovered. The target list, task graph, stages and unsupported requirements can grow when a real build discovers more targets. OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 doesn't change the preview.

oyzu build --no-docker, or OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1, is for executors with no Docker engine, such as a Kubernetes pool. Oyzu then runs no Docker command at all. Any value other than empty or 0 turns it on. Before preparing anything, the build works out the same placement as --plan. If any selected target has needsDaemon: true, it stops with exit status 3 and runs nothing: oyzu build --isolated --no-docker --json {"error":"NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON: cli need a Docker engine, which this executor does not provide (--no-docker); nothing was run","reason":"NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON","targets":["cli"],"exitCode":3} Exit status 3 means "wrong kind of executor", so a runner can tell it from a failed build (1) or a refused command (2) and requeue the job on a pool with Docker. What can still build without Docker: native host targets; Node, Rust, supported external go/app and pip Python (python/package, python/app, python/library) targets, in the daemonless sandbox; a RUN-free Dockerfile with FROM scratch or a digest-pinned base, with --isolated --no-docker (see Docker image assembly). --full adds Dockerfile lint and format checks, which need Docker, so the build refuses rather than skipping them. --no-docker can't be combined with --remote.

On Linux, the isolated steps of Node (node/app, node/package), Rust (rust/app, rust/library) and pip or uv Python (python/package, python/app, python/library) targets can run under crun, a rootless container runtime, instead of docker run. External targets still need an admitted execution engine, a packaged plugin with captured-plan, and a detected native dependency provider. Builder options also require the package's build-options feature. An unpackaged development executable does not qualify. Python packages using Poetry do not use this daemonless path; uv packages do.
