Each step gets the same sandbox as under Docker: no network, a read-only image root, no capabilities, no-new-privileges, a seccomp filter, Docker's masked /proc paths, the same mounts and tmpfs sizes, inside a user namespace that maps the workspace owner to itself. Each image's root filesystem is unpacked once per digest and shared by every build on the host. A root process gives unpacked files their archived owners. In a user namespace that does not map IDs 0–65535 (for example a planner sandboxed with unshare --user --map-current-user), a file whose archived owner is unmapped keeps the unpacking process's owner, as it would for a non-root process, and each step runs with only the workspace owner mapped, as for a non-root user. Such a root keeps its own copy of each image root rather than sharing the full-range one. Both backends produce the same cache keys and outputs, so a result cached by one serves the other. Unchanged npm builds can reuse earlier dependency downloads; see captured npm acquisition. Note: External Go and Rust plugin builds (go/app, rust/app) can also use crun on Linux x86-64. This is experimental. It needs a packaged plugin, a locked toolchain and a compatible Linux image; Go also needs a single application module. Commit the full oyzu.lock and build with --frozen; add --offline once everything is cached. On Linux, the locked Rust compiler is unpacked and checked by Oyzu itself, so a Rust build needs no Docker engine at any step.

build.isolation Behavior auto (default) Docker when an engine answers, otherwise crun. docker Always Docker. crun crun for eligible targets, even when Docker is present. --no-docker and OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 select crun for eligible targets whatever the setting says. oyzu install downloads a pinned crun release (1.24), checks its SHA-256 and keeps it in your user data folder. Set OYZU_CRUN to use a crun the executor already has. Images come from their digest-pinned published source, or from a running local Docker engine. A tag-only local image with no engine running fails before anything runs. crun runs without its own cgroup, so the executor pool's limits apply instead of per-step memory and CPU limits. Each action in the manifest records its sandbox in sandbox: backend (docker or crun), the crun runtime version, and resourceLimits (cgroup or pool).

Before dependency preparation or build actions run, a build that uses crun checks the runtime's actual namespace setup path. The cached check creates and deletes a stopped container with the same user, mount, network, PID, IPC and UTS namespaces as a real step; it starts no command. This applies to every ecosystem using isolated dependency preparation, including npm. If setup is refused, Oyzu stops with NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES (exit status 3). It reads host settings without changing them and names kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1 only for an EPERM / Operation not permitted setup error when that setting is enabled. Other causes include hybrid cgroups or a possible host/seccomp restriction. If the probe times out, the cause instead says that crun did not finish namespace setup within 30 seconds; a timeout does not establish an AppArmor refusal. A later unshare/clone permission failure reported in crun's own setup log keeps the same reason and exit status. A runtime executable that cannot be launched keeps its launch error; EPERM alone does not establish a namespace refusal. A command that starts inside the sandbox and exits nonzero remains an ordinary build failure (exit 1). Oyzu never runs the refused step without its sandbox. Inside a container (a CI job container, for example), the outer runtime must also leave /proc unmasked, because the kernel refuses a fresh /proc mount while parts of the outer one are covered, and its seccomp profile must allow unshare, clone, mount, umount2, pivot_root and sethostname without capabilities. Podman's and Docker's default profiles allow sethostname only with CAP_SYS_ADMIN, so a step under them fails with sethostname: Operation not permitted. {"code":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES","error":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES: the daemonless sandbox (crun) cannot run on this host: cgroups are mounted in hybrid mode, which crun does not support; the refused step was not run","exitCode":3,"nextStep":"Run on a Linux executor that allows unprivileged user namespaces and has crun, or on one with a Docker daemon.","reason":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES"}

You can split a build into jobs that follow the target graph, each reusing what earlier jobs built. Each job builds a slice: the targets you name. Every other target it needs must come from a cache; it is never built. oyzu build --slice --handoff oci://registry.example.com/acme/web/ci web Input Meaning Target arguments One or more logical target names or concrete targets[].id values from the preview. A logical name selects variants as a normal isolated build does. A concrete ID builds exactly that variant, even for a non-host platform. --slice Build only the named targets (at least one). Every other target they need is looked up in the local cache and remote caches. A missing result fails with UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED. Slices use the container executor. With --plan it prints the isolated preview of the slice. --slice-plan <target-id> Repeat once for every concrete ID in the original preview, including targets built in other slices. Pass the same set to every slice and retry. It lets a miss report whether the producer was in the original plan (inPlan). --handoff <oci-url> An OCI repository (oci://host/path, the same form as cache.remote). It is read first for upstream results, then cache.ciRemote and cache.remote, and every result this slice builds is written to it. It uses the same credential as a remote cache (OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or the job's ID token). An unusable URL is refused (exit 2) before anything runs. Plugin-built targets are handed off like any other: their results go to the --handoff repository, and their keys bind the plugin identity (action cache). For a development binding, cache.ciRemote and cache.remote are not read or written, so pass --handoff (or share one local cache) for a later slice to find its results. A plugin package's results also go to those shared remotes. Slices always run on the captured path. A plugin target that only builds on the native host lane is refused there with PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED; build it in a whole build instead. --slice can't be combined with --remote, --affected, --check, --no-cache or --verify-contract. It needs an active action cache when any upstream target isn't named. With cache.local = false, naming every target lets the slice run without reuse. With --no-docker, the same Docker check as an ordinary build applies. A slice builds the optimized profile, because its results leave the machine. Every upstream target's dependencies are still prepared, because its cache keys include them. Slices don't change cache keys. Per-target slices of a commit produce the same keys and artifact digests as one whole build. A producer that built something different shows up as a miss, never as a wrong reuse. A handoff hit is verified like any remote cache hit.
documents.s: Building a slice of a split run

documents.t: Reason Exit Raised when UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED 4 A result of a target the slice doesn't build wasn't found in any cache. Everything that needs it is blocked. HANDOFF_PUSH_FAILED 5 A result of a named target couldn't be written to the handoff repository. The build fails even when every action succeeded, because later jobs would miss. Exit status 1 is a failed build, 2 a refused command and 3 a missing executor capability (NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON, NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES). When both 4 and 5 apply, UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED wins. A failed slice prints one JSON line last on stderr, in human and --json mode, so an executor that keeps only the tail of the log can act on it: {"action":"app:package","error":"UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED: app:package of upstream target app (key sha256:…) is not in the local cache or oci://registry.example.com/acme/web/ci; a slice reuses upstream targets and never builds them","exitCode":4,"inPlan":true,"key":"sha256:…","reason":"UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED","repositories":[{"location":"oci://registry.example.com/acme/web/ci","status":"active"}],"target":"app","why":null}

The build record (dist/manifest.json, printed by --json) carries an oyzu.dev/slice extension: Field Meaning targets The concrete targets this slice built. upstream The other targets it reused. handoff The --handoff location, or null. written Each result written to the handoff repository: target, action, key and outcome (pushed; converged when an identical entry was already there; conflicts when a different entry held the key and was kept). misses Each upstream result not found: target, action, key, repositories (each remote asked, active or unavailable), inPlan, and why when it was never looked up (for example a task without declared outputs, which is never cached). notWritten Each result that didn't reach the handoff repository: target, action, key, repository and status. failure null, or the first miss (exit 4), else the first unwritten result (exit 5). inPlan: false means the missing producer wasn't in the original preview, for example a dependency added since. inPlan: true means an expected producer didn't leave a reusable result. Both exit 4, and neither lets the slice build the producer. The action cache summary gains a handoff section beside ciRemote and remote.

Name a sliceable: false upstream together with its consumer, for example oyzu build --slice --handoff oci://localhost:5000/demo/ci generate web. If several consumers need it, keep them in one slice. An unnamed unreusable upstream fails with UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED and its why.

Before compiling, a native Rust build runs a small Cargo compile-and-link check. It uses your Cargo linker settings and Rust flags, and asks for coverage instrumentation when tests are selected. Its temporary files are removed afterward. A failure reports EXECUTOR_PREREQUISITE_UNAVAILABLE with the cause. Install or fix the toolchain, linker or SDK and rerun. Oyzu doesn't install OS components. oyzu run runs the same check before a Rust task that compiles or links (cargo build, test, install, check, clippy, doc, run, rustc). Tasks like cargo fetch skip it. Without a linker, the task fails in under a second with guidance. For windows-gnullvm, the guidance is to put LLVM-MinGW's bin folder on PATH. Ready means the check passed. It doesn't check every library that dependency build scripts need. oyzu pin and discovery don't run this check; they report availability as not checked.

For an unchanged native Rust development build, Oyzu shares the Cargo metadata and target-filtered dependency resolution it captured during that invocation between compilation and final projection. It still compares manifest and lock contents before sharing those facts. Changed controls and stamped builds retain their separate Cargo reconciliation and metadata probes; action-cache admission and complete-read requirements still apply. A plain local build runs compilation and checks set to required. --full, the pr, ci and release contexts, or the CI profile also run tests (with JUnit, coverage and doctests), Clippy and a read-only format check, except checks set to off. See check levels. Required checks, hooks and task prerequisites always run. Binaries are collected only after the selected stages succeed. oyzu run test, oyzu run lint and oyzu run format-check run those tasks on their own. Replacing the native build task isn't supported yet and is refused with a message. Quality stages need their tools: rustfmt, Clippy, and for tests nextest, cargo-llvm-cov and the compiler's LLVM tools and profiler runtime. With a pinned Rust, the build installs nextest and cargo-llvm-cov automatically when tests are selected. See Rust test reports. On Windows, test coverage needs MSVC or windows-gnullvm (LLVM-MinGW UCRT). The windows-gnu toolchain lacks profiler_builtins, so coverage fails there. The native path builds the development profile unless the build is optimized: --optimized, build.optimized = true, or a build whose artifacts leave the machine (a slice, a shared remote cache write, a packaging target, the release context). Optimized Rust builds run cargo build --release. Tests keep Cargo's test profile. See optimized builds. Development and optimized artifacts use separate cache entries. An optimized result never satisfies a development build. Shared-cache writers for profile-dependent builders (Rust and .NET) also compile and publish the development stage when their selected output is optimized. The reader's default stays development; --optimized selects the separate optimized compile entry. Both stages use the same preparation. Rust uses host-native stages; .NET uses captured Debug and Release stages. Builders whose commands do not differ by profile keep one entry. Tool-environment and computation-setting differences can still prevent reuse; see native action caching.

Native Rust artifacts keep their inferred snapshot version. Their native compiled version depends on the build's use: Plain local development, including remote-cache readers: compilation keeps the declared Cargo versions. The version record includes compiledVersion beside the inferred artifact version; CARGO_PKG_VERSION is the declared version. A hit on compile-development can supply the exported binary directly. Full, CI, optimized, handed-off, shared-cache writer, packaged and release builds: a separate final Cargo stage projects inferred versions and produces the exported binary. Its actual CARGO_PKG_VERSION matches the artifact version. Explicit tag/history strategies also retain this final projection. Compile-stage keys bind declared versions, and final-stage keys bind the inferred version map and projected manifests/lock. Development results cannot satisfy that final stage or packaging, publication and release requirements: those consumers reject a compiledVersion marker with VERSION_STAMP_REQUIRED. Rebuild with --full or --optimized before packaging or publishing. Host compile, test, lint and format-check commands do not receive the engine-injected OYZU_VERSION default, so stamp-only changes and unrelated files do not miss the compile cache. Explicit environment overrides stay keyed, and the final stage still receives the default. Versions are written only into private source copies; your manifests and lock stay unchanged. Stage restores include indexed binaries, but do not transfer Cargo compiler state. A full build after a development build may recompile workspace crates because final projection changes their Cargo package versions. See version inference. Final compilation temporarily applies inferred manifests and the lock, checks their frozen identities around Cargo, then restores and revalidates the declared controls. Subsequent tests and quality checks use their exact declared-control guards, including when a hook makes stages share a workspace. The exported binary keeps its inferred native version; a guard failure is never suppressed by cleanup.

Before running builder commands, a native build installs any missing tool from your pins into the shared user store. It uses the same download, checksum and policy checks as oyzu install. A build never changes pinned versions. Run oyzu pin for missing or stale entries. --offline forbids downloads and needs the installers' cached inputs. An installation error stops the build before compiling. A denied or damaged tool is never replaced with an unverified one from PATH. System linkers and SDKs are not installed. See helper installation.

The Rust builder first tries Cargo metadata offline. If something is missing and the build is online, it runs cargo fetch --locked with live output, then continues offline. Cargo handles downloads, checksums and its own cache using your Cargo configuration, credentials and network settings. Oyzu doesn't rewrite Cargo.lock. Compilation always runs offline. --offline never fetches. It reports missing inputs and suggests an online build or a manifest fix. Failures keep a category and recovery hint even when details that might contain credentials are withheld.

A native build can include docker/image targets, which run in a BuildKit worker (see image workers). Oyzu watches both the docker exec client and the worker: Code Meaning BUILDKIT_BUILDCTL_FAILED The client exited with a nonzero status. BUILDKIT_WORKER_UNAVAILABLE The worker stopped, was killed for running out of memory, or stopped answering. The container and daemon are checked every five seconds. A stopped or OOM-killed container fails at once; probe failures need three in a row. Diagnostics keep the buildctl exit code, the container exit and the memory limit. Exit 137 alone is reported as a possible OOM or external kill. Restore the worker or give it more memory, then retry. Failed actions publish no artifacts.

Captured Rust builds can read a compiler-state seed from cache.ciRemote. The seed binds the locked compiler archive, Cargo lockfile, target triple, compiler-visible workspace path and CARGO_HOME, together with the selected command, tool archives and environment. The captured executor already uses /workspace and /scratch/cargo/home; a different checkout path on the host therefore does not change those in-sandbox paths. Host-native builds do not consume these seeds: their compiler-visible paths vary by checkout. A seed restores only into empty compiler state. Existing state is never replaced. Missing, mismatched, redirected, damaged or unavailable seeds leave Cargo to build normally. Successful restoration reports “compiler state restored from the team cache”. Fingerprints and dep-info are not rewritten. Incomplete native read information also binds the full source and preparation identity; changed inputs then build cold. Source modification times are retained only after comparing contents; changed inputs are newer than the restored compiler work. Seed publication is disabled for all builds, including CI and pool jobs with write credentials. Enabling a trusted producer is separate work; this client only consumes seeds. See compiler-state seeds for the trust boundary and limits. Native Rust builds keep Cargo's compiler state under .oyzu/native/rust/<host>/ in your project, so repeated builds stay incremental. Oyzu keeps Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock modification times unchanged when their contents didn't change, so Cargo doesn't rebuild for nothing. This also applies with --no-cache, which turns off Oyzu's action cache but keeps compiler caches. The experimental Linux compiler-output tier can reuse eligible already non-incremental workspace libraries through the existing action cache. It preserves Cargo's native incremental choices and keeps fingerprints/dep-info local. Unsupported inputs, configuration, diagnostics and path-sensitive invocations execute normally. Logical debug/metadata paths and the admitted creation mask are part of that compiler contract; this tier does not make opaque Cargo state portable or establish successful tests/reports. Cargo's integration-test scratch (CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR) is disposable. Before measuring retained caches at preparation and finalization, Oyzu removes tmp/ and <target-triple>/tmp/ from each Cargo target directory, including the coverage target. Installed tool symlinks inside that scratch are removed without following them. Symlinks or redirected directories in retained compiler state are still refused; a redirected scratch root or ancestor is also refused. Coverage scratch includes tests/coverage-target/tmp/ and tests/coverage-target/<target-triple>/tmp/. Preparation also discards scratch left by earlier builds, including builds run with an older engine that retained it; links inside that scratch recover automatically before the first size measurement. Cleanup runs even after a failed test, so links left inside disposable scratch do not block the next build. It does not relocate Cargo's scratch while tests are running; peak scratch usage still counts toward build-time disk needs. If scratch cleanup fails or its root/ancestor is redirected, the error names the exact scratch path, preserves the cause and gives a command to move the validated compiler cache aside. Stop other builds for the project and ensure the .quarantine destination does not exist before running that command, then retry oyzu build. This rebuilds compiler state without following scratch links or deleting their destinations. Correct permissions first if the move itself fails. Quarantined data remains on disk until you remove it safely; it is no longer part of the retained cache budget.

Initial retention enforces the compiler-cache size budget during preparation, before actions run. When any action executes or fails to start, final retention enforces the budget again after artifact and report collection, including after a fail-fast test failure. When every action is reused, no native command writes compiler state, so initial retention suffices and Oyzu omits final retention. Registry compiler-input archives are inventoried only after a Cargo stage misses the finished-result cache and is admitted for compiler reuse, before binding the compiler wrapper. Disabled caches and refused wrappers skip this work. Frozen lock checksums and actual consumed dependency bytes still govern compiler-result reuse. Reused results do not replace current dependency preparation or native-platform prerequisite checks. Those checks still run before selecting a cached result. Native cleanup commands share a 60-second budget within each initial or final retention pass, with bounded output and process-tree cleanup. The original build failure remains recorded through native build finalization. User cancellation stops cleanup before scratch removal as well as before native commands; a cleanup failure includes the cleaner's exit status and bounded standard output/error, without discarding collected artifacts and reports. Configure the retained size with: [cache] nativeMaxMiB = 8192 Setting Values Default Meaning cache.nativeMaxMiB 1–1048576 8192 (8 GiB) Total size kept across the host's Rust compiler caches. Works the same online and offline. Separate from remote cache settings. Progress shows the measured size and anything removed. With --json, these messages go to stderr.

When the caches are over budget: Oyzu runs cargo clean --workspace --offline on them, keeping compiled registry dependencies if that is enough. If still over budget, it removes whole cache folders with cargo clean, in this order: an old separate doctest target, the coverage target, the build target. Under budget, compiler state is kept; test scratch is still removed. Oyzu adds the standard CACHEDIR.TAG file before asking Cargo to clean a cache folder, because Cargo won't clean a folder without one. A budget smaller than your working set saves disk space but can cause a full recompile on every build. This repository sets cache.nativeMaxMiB = 32768 (32 GiB) for local and CI builds so optimized CLI, lint and instrumented test compilation can coexist. The product default remains 8 GiB. Retaining compilation does not reuse test verdicts: nextest still runs under coverage, followed by Cargo doctests, and required report gates still apply. Allow additional free disk space for test scratch and artifacts; the retention budget does not cap peak usage.

It limits what is kept after a build, not peak disk use. A crash or full disk can leave oversized caches until the next build. If cleanup fails at the end of a build, you get NATIVE_CACHE_RETENTION_FAILED but the build result stands. The next build retries before it starts, and a failure there stops it. Symlinked or redirected cache folders (including Windows reparse points) are refused. Use a normal folder. Only the Rust caches under .oyzu/native count. Installed tools, downloads, .oyzu/bin, dist, Cargo's own target folder and oyzu run tasks aren't touched.

Native actions keep independently writable source copies with retained native state. Unchanged builds preserve the paths and directory timestamps Cargo watches; action-cache hits leave these copies intact. A real source edit refreshes them before execution. A build that selects fewer targets keeps up to 32 copies of the unselected ones (newest by last top-level change), so selecting them again starts warm. Removing .oyzu/native clears both compiler outputs and these private copies; subsequent builds recreate them. Successful binaries go to dist/<target>/<platform>/ (for example dist/cli/windows/x86_64/; see the bundle layout) with their usual names, and, by default, are also copied to .oyzu/bin/<name>[.exe]. Set [build] installExecutables = false to leave executables only in the bundle. This setting follows the normal configuration cascade per target; it does not disable artifact validation or required checks. Oyzu’s own checkout sets it to false; opting back in requires build.installExecutables = true in your applicable configuration. Outputs labels each binary development or optimized. Each is checked to be an executable for the host before it is collected. The bundle keeps the manifest, plan, reports and action logs. They record that the build ran on the host, the source it saw and the tools it used. Rust state lives in .oyzu/native/rust/<host>/: target for compilation and tests for test and coverage builds. A build limited to some packages with with.packages keeps its own state in a p-<id> folder inside it. Cargo decides what to rebuild. The previous bundle's artifacts move to history on every build, successful or not. Other files in dist are left alone. See bundle finalization and recovery. A file in dist that no bundle owns causes a collision error instead of being overwritten. A failed build exits nonzero and leaves .oyzu/bin at the last successful build. The previous executable moves to a unique hidden .NAME.previous-<suffix> backup before the new one takes its place. On Windows, a running older generation can keep its backup locked without blocking another refresh. Later refreshes remove unlocked backups, including legacy .NAME.previous files. Locked backups remain until their processes exit and a later refresh can remove them. Refreshing .oyzu/bin happens after the successful output bundle is published. A refresh failure emits DEVELOPMENT_EXECUTABLE_REFRESH_FAILED as a warning; the build remains successful and its artifact stays available in the output bundle. The source Oyzu records is hashed from your working tree with the usual source exclusions. Native builds read your checkout directly; they don't freeze a copy.

Output starts with Building <folder> (or Planning for --plan), the platform, local or isolated execution, and fast or full mode. Then it follows Preflight → Build → summary. Preflight covers configuration, discovery, tool preparation, dependency metadata and planning. Each tool row shows the tool, the requested version and its status: downloaded and installed, then verified, or reused and verified. External SDKs and linkers show as not checked until native tools run. Formatting, lint and test tools are hidden in fast builds unless those stages run. Press p for more environment and source detail, and d for detailed logs on small terminals. Running tools and subprocesses show their last eight output lines on capable terminals. Success collapses them; failure keeps them. Terminal behavior: auto and plain output modes print a linear log that keeps your scrollback. --output interactive opens a dashboard instead. ui.color=auto colors terminal output unless NO_COLOR is set; always also colors redirected output; never turns color off. A terminal counts as capable when TERM isn't dumb and, on Windows, when the console accepts virtual terminal sequences. --json emits a structured heading event on stderr; -q hides it. See build logging.

oyzu build --store <path> uses the same store as oyzu install --store <path>. The default is the shared user store. A relative path resolves against the current folder (or --root). The store is used for native installs and container tool preparation. It never changes pins, checks or image policy. A missing or broken tool in that store doesn't fall back to another store. Use the same --store on install, build and tool inspection commands, especially with --offline.

Native execution has your user account's access. Cargo's offline mode doesn't stop a build script from using the network. A local build, even with --isolated, can't grant production publication rights. --require-release refuses the build unless it is an authenticated release-candidate or release tag build; ordinary local tags and --context release don't count. See release staging. Native builds support Windows and Linux x86-64, with builder-specific limits. Intel macOS supports the Zig native path; other macOS builders are unsupported.

These notes are for building the oyzu CLI itself from a source checkout. Build with cargo build --locked --release --bins, then copy target/release/oyzu[.exe] and target/release/oyzu-shim[.exe] together into a folder on your PATH outside the checkout. Check the build succeeded before copying, and keep a backup of the previous version. On Windows, rename the old executable pair to backup names before copying the new files into place. Windows can retain an executable's mapped image briefly after its command exits; overwriting that file can fail with error 1224. Keep the backup pair together for manual restoration. This explicit source promotion does not create oyzu self rollback history. Run oyzu reshim from that installed pair after replacing it. Windows tool launchers delegate to the frontend named in their adjacent .oyzu-frontend pointer, falling back to a sibling oyzu.exe when the pointer is absent. Unix tool shims remain symbolic links to oyzu; running oyzu-shim directly refuses with "launcher template, not a tool command". Both binaries support standalone --licenses output for their own dependencies. On Windows, updating your user PATH doesn't change terminals that are already open. Update the current PowerShell session: $fallbackBin = 'C:\path\to\oyzu-bootstrap\bin' $env:Path = "$fallbackBin;$env:Path" oyzu --version Keep your everyday oyzu outside this checkout. oyzu build cli leaves the new CLI at dist/cli/<os>/<arch>/oyzu[.exe] and does not install it into .oyzu/bin or change which oyzu drives your next build. The checkout no longer prepends .oyzu/bin to PATH. Remove an old checkout .oyzu/bin entry from your shell profile or current PATH; preserve the old executable by renaming it rather than deleting it. Activate from the checkout to define oyzu-dev, a separate command for the latest host dist build: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" # or zsh oyzu build cli oyzu-dev --version cd ../another-project oyzu-dev discover In PowerShell 7.5 or newer, use oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression from the checkout, then the same commands. Activation keeps the checkout’s absolute dist path, so oyzu-dev works in other projects too. It passes arguments and the current directory to that executable, and requires a successful host build first. Deactivating removes the function. oyzu-dev build refuses to build this checkout (DEVELOPMENT_CLI_BUILD_REFUSED); use the everyday oyzu build cli for that. A failed build leaves the everyday driver available to fix the next build. Dist outputs follow the normal bundle history rules, so rebuild successfully before testing them again. Windows cmd.exe does not support oyzu activate cmd or the activation-provided oyzu-dev command. Activation exits 2 with commands to run in a supported shell. Use PowerShell 7.5 or newer or Git Bash and activate from this checkout for the source loop. In cmd.exe, ordinary builds and explicit source promotion still use the external oyzu; to inspect the candidate version directly, run dist\cli\windows\x86_64\oyzu.exe --version from the checkout. Keep the external oyzu as the checkout's build driver. To opt in to checkout-local executable copies, put this in ignored oyzu.local.toml and run oyzu build cli --local-overrides: [build] installExecutables = true This copies the successful output to .oyzu/bin; it does not add that directory to PATH. Keep using the external driver for builds. Normal cascade precedence and administrative constraints still apply. Promote only when you intend to change your everyday driver: oyzu run bootstrap -- --source. To return to a release, use oyzu self update when a release channel is recorded, or oyzu self channel stable. The Windows task flow uses a pinned MSVC toolchain, which needs Visual Studio Build Tools (the C++ workload) installed first. Then run oyzu pin, oyzu install and oyzu run install. If an older oyzu.lock fails with TOOL_LOCK_AMBIGUOUS, delete it and run oyzu pin and oyzu install again. Keep machine-specific linker and CMake paths in an ignored oyzu.local.toml under [env].

Python fixture harnesses install uv, Maven 3.9.11, Gradle 8.14.3 and the Java 17 line through OYZU_RELEASED_DRIVER, falling back to OYZU_CANDIDATE. Set these to absolute Oyzu executable paths; a driver must support the requested tool on the host. The fresh-checkout harness uses its --cli executable as the candidate when OYZU_CANDIDATE is unset. Provisioning needs publisher network access and fails if neither driver can install it. Each tool uses a temporary harness-owned store removed at process exit. No harness store is activated or passed to fresh-checkout builds, whose tool-free environment and empty store remain independent. tooling/provision-maven.py --destination <directory> and tooling/provision-gradle.py --destination <directory> copy the complete managed distributions, including upstream licenses/notices, to apache-maven-3.9.11/ and gradle-8.14.3/ beneath that directory. Their pinned archive checksums and upstream.txt are retained; callers own these output directories. Fresh-checkout wrapper generation uses absolute managed Maven/Gradle executables and a private Java 17 JAVA_HOME. The Maven wrapper still selects Maven 3.9.9, and the Gradle wrapper still selects Gradle 8.14.3, independently of the harness tools. The oyzu-quality-tools Cargo tests provision Python from the repository's oyzu.lock into a temporary, test-owned store. They require network access for that fresh installation. Live native commands share the same frozen installation; dropping the last command removes its temporary store. These tests and the deploy_cli acceptance tests' Node provisioning neither install the full checks toolset nor use your personal tool store. Their subprocesses receive a private HOME, user config, and XDG data, config, cache and state roots, including XDG_STATE_HOME. OYZU_TEST_TMPDIR selects the parent directory for their disposable files; their state is removed with the temporary store. Other native-tool lookups retain their caller's environment. On Windows, the CI-selection, workflow-dogfood and release-workflow checks require Git for Windows with Bash and git on PATH. They use Bash from that Git installation so native test environment variables and temporary paths reach the workflow script. The System32 WSL Bash launcher does not preserve that environment. Linux and macOS use bash from PATH. On Windows, the wrapper prepends the private interpreter's directory to PATH so Bash subprocesses can find the same locked Python even with a disposable HOME. Shell fixture files and bootstrap pin updates retain LF line endings so their shebangs work in Git Bash. The build-record collector refuses inputs reached through symbolic links or Windows directory junctions. Its Windows link-rejection fixture uses a junction, which requires no symbolic-link privilege; the rejection check runs on every host. The deploy_cli acceptance tests provision their own locked checks Node in a temporary store for documentation audits and release-witness checks. They need network access for that installation and do not depend on another test installing Node, the full checks toolset, or a Node executable on PATH. The temporary store is removed when its last test command is dropped.

The host_environment e2e tests require provisioned plugins and managed native toolchains. Every test in this module is marked #[ignore] for those prerequisites; an ordinary Cargo test run does not execute them. On Linux, provision from the repository root with a compatible external oyzu, Git and a native linker on PATH. Use Oyzu's pinned Rust, not host Cargo. Cold plugin builds and managed tool installation require network access. The following Bash recipe builds source-verified plugins in an ignored directory. Go, .NET and Helm use archives carrying their plugin manifests; Rust and Node use executables. Keep this checkout available and rebuild after changing plugin sources. These commands describe manual provisioning, not a guarantee that the whole suite passes in every host environment. oyzu --toolset checks install --frozen eval "$(oyzu --toolset checks activate bash)" unset CARGO_BUILD_TARGET OYZU_PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_LOCATOR=1 cargo build --locked \ -p oyzu-plugin-rust --features plugin --bin oyzu-plugin-rust \ --target-dir .oyzu/host-environment-plugins for plugin in node go dotnet helm; do OYZU_PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_LOCATOR=1 cargo build --locked \ -p "oyzu-plugin-$plugin" --features plugin --bin "oyzu-plugin-$plugin" \ --target-dir .oyzu/host-environment-plugins done for plugin in go dotnet helm; do python tooling/package-plugin.py \ --executable ".oyzu/host-environment-plugins/debug/oyzu-plugin-$plugin" \ --manifest "docs/contracts/plugins-v1alpha1/examples/manifest.$plugin.json" \ --out ".oyzu/host-environment-plugins/$plugin.tar.gz" done export OYZU_RUST_PLUGIN="$PWD/.oyzu/host-environment-plugins/debug/oyzu-plugin-rust" export OYZU_NODE_PLUGIN="$PWD/.oyzu/host-environment-plugins/debug/oyzu-plugin-node" export OYZU_TEST_GO_PLUGIN="$PWD/.oyzu/host-environment-plugins/go.tar.gz" export OYZU_DOTNET_PLUGIN="$PWD/.oyzu/host-environment-plugins/dotnet.tar.gz" export OYZU_HELM_PLUGIN="$PWD/.oyzu/host-environment-plugins/helm.tar.gz" unset OYZU_CLI # Use the CLI built by Cargo for this test target. cargo test --locked --test e2e host_environment:: -- --ignored --nocapture \ --skip host_environment::node_inherited_options_never_restore_the_other_shells_output cargo test --locked --test e2e \ host_environment::node_inherited_options_never_restore_the_other_shells_output \ -- --ignored --exact --nocapture The two test commands mirror the split in .github/workflows/build.yml: the general ignored-e2e sweep excludes the Node case, and the task-scenario job builds the Node plugin and runs that case explicitly. The exclusion is job routing, not permission to omit the Node check from a complete manual run. To run all host-environment cases together after provisioning, use cargo test --locked --test e2e host_environment:: -- --ignored --nocapture. Fixture inputs are process environment variables, not normal user bindings: Variable Consumer and default OYZU_RUST_PLUGIN Required by the Rust fixtures; points to the source-verified Rust executable, including when a test repackages it. OYZU_NODE_PLUGIN Required by the Node fixture; points to its source-verified executable. OYZU_TEST_GO_PLUGIN Go home-defaults test override; the recipe supplies a development archive. Unset selects published-package resolution. This test does not read OYZU_GO_PLUGIN. OYZU_DOTNET_PLUGIN .NET home-defaults test override; the recipe supplies a development archive. Unset selects published-package resolution. OYZU_HELM_PLUGIN Helm home-defaults test override; the recipe supplies a development archive. Unset selects published-package resolution. OYZU_GO_PLUGIN, OYZU_PYTHON_PLUGIN Additional profile-specific inputs read by the shared Project::new helper; the host-environment module does not use that helper for Go or exercise Python. OYZU_CLI Optional CLI under test; defaults to Cargo's CARGO_BIN_EXE_oyzu. Set an absolute path only when deliberately testing another compatible CLI. OYZU_TEST_PROOF_ROOT Optional parent for Project::new fixtures; defaults to CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR. Package/home-defaults helpers use CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR directly. The fixture writes a private OYZU_USER_CONFIG with its selected development binding and an empty [plugins.packages] table. Binding tables replace the whole lower-precedence table, so normal user or machine packages cannot fill that empty table. Without the optional overrides, the Go, .NET and Helm home-defaults tests enable preview package resolution in a private store; a locked package absent from that store can fail with PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE when no plugins.packages binding supplies its archive. Use the overrides above for manual provisioning. In particular, dotnet_host_home_defaults_build_and_edit_preserve_read_refusal needs dotnet/sdk, and helm_host_home_defaults_build_and_edit_preserve_read_refusal needs helm/chart. An installed native SDK or Helm executable alone does not supply the builder package. The Go home-defaults test similarly needs go/app. CI's setup-oyzu action calls bootstrap with --ci-machine-binding, which writes [plugins.packages] OCI bindings for rust/app, node/app and github-release/publish from the repository's published pins. It does not supply dotnet/sdk or helm/chart bindings to these private fixtures. The shared plugin test helper separately builds this checkout's plugins with the locator and can generate archive/sha256 package bindings for all profiles, including .NET and Helm; that helper's USER file is not adopted by the home-defaults fixtures. All names below are under host_environment:: and require --ignored: Test Managed prerequisite behind #[ignore] main_ci_runs_native_units_despite_package_trust_and_warm_results Rust toolchain and Rust builder; uses the shared helper to build and package plugins. rust_observed_reads_bind_file_case_aliases Rust toolchain and Rust builder. rust_opaque_compile_keys_ignore_unused_lock_entries_and_bind_used_tools_and_plugin Rust toolchain and Rust builder; creates its own Rust package binding. rust_inherited_compiler_flags_never_restore_the_other_shells_output Rust toolchain and Rust builder. rust_cross_shell_environment_preserves_keys_and_extensions Rust toolchain and Rust builder; Linux and Windows only. rust_configured_temporary_paths_preserve_keys_and_reuse Rust toolchain and Rust builder; Linux and Windows only. rust_configured_home_reads_remain_keyed Rust toolchain and Rust builder. go_host_home_defaults_reuse_and_source_edit_reruns Go 1.24.13 and Go builder package. dotnet_host_home_defaults_build_and_edit_preserve_read_refusal .NET SDK 10.0.401 and .NET builder package; Linux and Windows only. helm_host_home_defaults_build_and_edit_preserve_read_refusal Helm 3.22.0 and Helm builder package. node_inherited_options_never_restore_the_other_shells_output Node 22.14.0 and Node builder; run separately in CI. The Rust fixtures pin Rust 1.99.1. Fixture pin/install operations acquire managed native tools in private stores; having those tools on the invoking shell's PATH does not populate those stores. Retain the recipe's plugin directory while tests use it; it can be removed after the run when no other task uses it. --features plugin alone does not capture the source location needed for development admission. PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_STALE with no compiled source location means rebuild the executable named by the fixture variable with OYZU_PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_LOCATOR=1 set at build time. Setting it only when running tests cannot repair an existing binary. Ordinary bootstrap refreshes the CLI; oyzu run bootstrap -- --source --development-plugins also rebuilds development plugins, but the fixture variables must still point to the rebuilt bytes. See development plugin freshness.

When changing Oyzu-owned file producers or readers, run the released-reader conformance check from an activated checkout on Linux or Windows x64: cargo test --locked --test e2e minimum_reader::released_038_file_reader_conformance -- --ignored --exact --nocapture This check needs network access. It uses the install script to download published 0.3.8 into a temporary directory, verifies the release asset digest, and invokes that executable by absolute path. It reads this checkout's project configuration and requires the ordinary reader-floor refusal for its 0.4.0 dogfood minimum. It exercises optional settings and required-feature refusals, checks lock strictness, and reads compatible edited configuration in both directions between the released and candidate drivers. Input files must remain unchanged by inspection; edits must preserve the unknown optional setting. The existing provisioned e2e CI sweep also includes this check. To exercise the updated reader's actual build flow, with a native linker and access to published Rust plugins and managed Rust inputs: cargo test --locked --test e2e minimum_reader::future_marker_builds_with_one_notice_and_required_feature_preserves_outputs -- --ignored --exact --nocapture This builds and runs a tiny Rust executable with newer TOML/YAML markers and an ignored optional setting. Human and JSON output must each carry one upgrade notice. A required-feature refusal must preserve the existing output manifest and lock. The test uses published plugins and task-local storage; it does not build plugin sources. Managed inputs may be acquired through the usual checks. Published Linux 0.3.8 refuses both a 0.3.8 marker and a future marker: its reader diagnostic reports 0.3.8-dev.gba8fb1a05b19 even though --version reports 0.3.8 (release). The check asserts these historical refusals rather than expecting an old executable to gain new behavior. It does not install tools or plugins or establish build execution compatibility. The temporary install skips shell and PATH changes and uses isolated user configuration. No self-update is performed.

Native development plugin bindings used by the selected builds are checked against their current source closure before use. Unused stale or unverifiable bindings do not block a selected build or a workspace repair task. PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_STALE means the bound executable or archive must be rebuilt, or its source checkout/build-time Cargo is unavailable. Run oyzu run bootstrap -- --source --development-plugins to rebuild repository plugins. See plugin development. Refresh checks the selected channel's available version before invoking a compatible self-updater and refuses releases older than this checkout. It uses this checkout's installer when an older installed updater cannot serve the checkout's plugin requirements, so an older updater cannot select an obsolete stable release through its old selection rules. If the selected release is still incompatible, refresh stops and suggests another channel or --source. An explicit version pin stays pinned. On Windows refresh also excludes releases older than the checkout's package version before downloading; if newer releases lack a Windows payload, it refuses instead of installing the last obsolete payload. The installer child rebuilds its PowerShell module path, so launching from PowerShell 7 does not hide PowerShell 5.1 modules such as Get-FileHash. Source refresh preserves verified host Cargo dep-info beside the installed oyzu before building the Linux member. Engine installation still verifies source coverage and refuses missing or uncovered inputs even if the native compiler cache was evicted during cross-compilation. Cargo's aggregate dep-info includes build-script inputs, including Rust distribution notices. Only the captured compiler sysroot is exempt as a toolchain input; other tool-store paths are not exempt, and a link inside the sysroot whose target resolves outside it is not exempt either. After changing Rust installations, rebuild with cargo build --locked --bin oyzu through the activated Oyzu shell before packaging a development engine. cargo test alone does not refresh oyzu.d, so an older sidecar can cause ENGINE_INPUTS_UNCOVERED even beside a rebuilt executable. oyzu run bootstrap builds this checkout's host CLI with oyzu build cli and installs oyzu and oyzu-shim on your PATH. Run it from the checkout. The default uses the selected plugins and does no separate plugin build, Linux build, plugin-binding setup or tool restore. --source remains an explicit spelling of this default. If the installed oyzu rejects this checkout's plugin output (an older driver paired with a newer plugin), bootstrap builds a driver from the checkout and retries once. Select a release explicitly with --channel: oyzu run bootstrap # host build and install oyzu run bootstrap -- --dest ~/bin # install into this folder instead oyzu run bootstrap -- --optimized # optimized host build oyzu run bootstrap -- --development-plugins # rebuild and bind host development plugins oyzu run bootstrap -- --isolated # also prepare the Linux engine oyzu run bootstrap -- --development-plugins --isolated # also build the Linux Rust plugin oyzu run bootstrap -- --linux <file> # install this source-matched Linux engine oyzu run bootstrap -- --channel stable # install the newest stable release oyzu run bootstrap -- --channel beta # follow beta (or nightly) For the default source refresh: It checks oyzu executables on PATH outside the checkout against the checkout's Rust and Node plugin manifests. The engine's compiled capabilities and source-loop probe decide compatibility, rather than its version label. The chosen absolute path drives the build, so a project-local executable cannot shadow it. If no candidate supports the required capabilities, an existing CLI runs cargo build --locked through Oyzu's managed execution contract, including configured Cargo session admission, to build a temporary seed CLI/shim. It checks the seed before selecting it; there is no direct or host Cargo fallback. The driver must resolve the checkout's Rust pin. A failed seed leaves installed executables unchanged. Temporary seed executables are removed on exit; Cargo output remains in CARGO_TARGET_DIR or target for reuse. Published locked plugins are used without a separate bootstrap installation pass. Existing Rust or Node development bindings require explicit --development-plugins; otherwise refresh stops before the build and names that flag. If the build reports PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_STALE, retry with oyzu run bootstrap -- --development-plugins. --development-plugins builds the host rust/app and node/app plugins and packs Rust as .oyzu/bin/oyzu-plugin-rust.tar.gz. Add --isolated (or --linux <file>) to also cross-compile the Linux Rust plugin. Binding setup and hints run only with this explicit plugin option. The checkout's .oyzu/bootstrap/config.toml is created or reused for this invocation when no personal choices exist. Existing checkout executable bindings move to the package; custom bindings stay user-owned. See Repository source bootstrap. It builds only the host CLI, then installs both executables into --dest or the folder holding the first oyzu on PATH outside the checkout (following links). With no such executable, it uses ~/.oyzu/bin or %LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\bin and runs oyzu shell install; open a new terminal afterwards. Each replaced file moves to NAME.previous, with one backup. Failed replacement restores the old file. Earlier CLI/shim copies in the checkout's .oyzu/bin are retired so they cannot hide the installed driver. With --development-plugins, it refreshes/rebinds plugins using the promoted CLI before further builds. A refresh failure stops bootstrap. --isolated prepares an engine for isolated builds. On Linux the installed CLI is its own engine. On Windows and macOS this option cross-compiles oyzu build cli --platform linux/<arch> and installs the Linux engine. To use source-matched Linux executables you already built, pass --linux <file> for each architecture instead. These explicit paths retain the host dep-info before cross-compilation. A Linux build failure leaves the host CLI installed and reports that isolated builds have no Linux engine. See engine installation. It prints the installed path and version. Source installs never update automatically. To return to a release, use oyzu self update if a channel is recorded, or oyzu run bootstrap -- --channel stable. With --channel stable|beta|nightly, bootstrap instead follows the selected verified release through oyzu self channel, or this checkout's install script when the installed CLI cannot update itself. Digest, provenance and publication checks remain required; failed replacement restores the old executable pair. Release refresh also installs published locked plugins, restores tools with oyzu install --frozen, and prepares the release's Linux engine where supported. --channel cannot be combined with source-build options. For the shell bootstrap, tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh --development-plugins is the corresponding explicit opt-in. Existing user [plugins.development] choices remain user-owned; remove those entries when returning to published packages. Neither helper deletes personal bindings. Either way it needs Node.js on PATH. If your installed oyzu is too old to read this repository's configuration (CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE), run tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh (Git Bash on Windows), which downloads the newest release into .oyzu/bin, and then .oyzu/bin/oyzu run bootstrap (which builds this checkout's CLI from source; add -- --channel stable to install the release instead).
documents.s: Refreshing the oyzu on your PATH

documents.t: Rust projects get an install task automatically. To update your installed CLI from the checkout: oyzu run install -- --bins --force --root "$env:LOCALAPPDATA/Oyzu/bootstrap" This runs cargo install, not the full build checks. It builds the release profile; add --debug after -- for a development build. CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT also sets the destination. On Windows with an explicit root, Oyzu installs into a staging folder first, so your current CLI keeps working while Cargo compiles. Only after Cargo succeeds are the files replaced, keeping one .NAME.previous backup each. Cancelling or a failed install leaves the installed CLI unchanged. A killed process may leave a .oyzu-install-* staging folder; don't remove one that belongs to a running install. Files are replaced one at a time, not atomically. If replacement fails, check the named file and its backup, close programs still using the old copy, and retry. If your installed CLI is too old to run this, use Cargo directly with the provisioned toolchain: cargo install --path . --bins --locked --force --root "$env:LOCALAPPDATA/Oyzu/bootstrap" oyzu run fetch downloads Cargo dependencies, oyzu run install installs project executables, and oyzu install installs development tools.
documents.s: Updating this repository's bootstrap with Cargo

documents.t: The coordinator approved the shared selection contract for #1863 on 2026-11-02. tooling/select-ci-jobs.py combines the existing affected preview with the Cargo-derived Rust test plan in the same selector. For a local comparison, activate the checks toolset and run: python tooling/select-ci-jobs.py --base origin/dev python tooling/select-ci-jobs.py --base origin/dev --build The JSON contains jobs with a selected boolean and reason for each job, rust with workspace/package scope and fallback reason, and rustTestCommand as an argument vector (null means no Rust test inputs changed). CI also exports this JSON as the selection step's selection output. A selector failure requests every check and reports the failure instead of granting a skip. Ownership comes from the deepest workspace member manifest directory in cargo metadata --locked --format-version 1 --all-features. Root src/ and tests/ belong to oyzu; unknown repository files do not acquire root ownership merely by being below its directory. Changed members select their transitive reverse dependents over normal, development and build edges. Selecting a member in the root package's dependency closure selects the root package, including its entire integration/e2e targets. Shared tests/support/ and tests/fixtures/ select root tests; member-local fixtures and build scripts select their member. The whole workspace is selected for root Cargo manifests/locks, workspace/build configuration, Rust toolchain configuration, .cargo/, tool configuration or locks, selection code/configuration, unknown non-documentation paths, and incomplete metadata. Added, deleted, copied or renamed Cargo.toml or Cargo.lock files anywhere, including fixtures and documentation examples, also require the compliance/license checks. Untracked manifests count as added. Existing compliance inputs cover all test fixtures. Outside-member includes and unresolved dynamic includes/build-script read sets retain the full-workspace fallback. A textual rerun-if-changed declaration alone cannot establish that an arbitrary build script has no other reads. This conservative implementation does not yet admit build scripts using closed read-set evidence; such packages can therefore keep ordinary Rust diffs at workspace scope. The fallback reason identifies that limitation. Documentation paths outside members can skip Rust tests when no required input is affected; member-local documentation remains a member input. Main always requests every job and uses optimized artifact compilation with full uncached checks while test reuse awaits OVH binding security acceptance. Nightly pins main and runs full uncached verification; it cannot refresh old test evidence by copying reports. Presubmit must keep documentation, contracts, compliance/license, selection tests, formatting and warnings-as-errors lint checks, independently of the Rust test plan. The JSON argument vector is the shared presubmit integration seam; it is not a new oyzu run presubmit task. With --build, the same selector runs oyzu build cli --full. It supplies --full only when the forwarded build arguments do not already include it; main and nightly keep their optimized, full, no-cache checks. It sets the Rust builder's with.test-packages for the candidate's test stage. CI passes its already emitted selection to the same consumer and provisions/invokes the locked checks Python through Oyzu. The artifact selection, formatting, warnings-as-errors lint, coverage, JUnit, doctests and report admission remain binding. Extra build arguments follow --, for example --build -- --no-cache. Main retains full workspace execution. The repository's marked with: {} slot in build.yaml is replaced only for a nonempty package decision and restored after the build, including native failure. An original-byte backup is printed under .oyzu/; after an uncatchable termination, restore that backup before another build. Do not edit the declaration concurrently; conflicting edits are preserved and the command fails with the backup location. Workspace fallback and malformed/missing evidence leave the declaration untouched and test the full workspace. A candidate requested with no Rust changes also keeps full tests rather than manufacturing an empty run. Narrow execution requires a core that freezes independent scope and a Rust plugin implementing with.test-packages. Older workers reject the unknown option; prepared facts that disagree with explicit test intent are refused rather than silently selecting artifact tests. Update core and worker together. CI consumes signed published packages and never compiles a replacement plugin. Update the admitted package before expecting narrowing. Existing workspace fallback works with older packages. Unclosed includes and build scripts can still force whole-workspace selection for this repository. Neither a selection plan nor a plain Cargo test vector establishes coverage or report admission.
documents.s: Rust test scope for CI and presubmit

documents.t: Tier Current obligation Main commit Every selected gate job, with full ordinary tests, coverage, doctests, format, lint and smoke checks; main selects all jobs. Nightly acceptance Full uncached ordinary verification and the explicitly provisioned toolchain, network and determinism suites on main; unavailable platform prerequisites remain visible. Additional nightly rollout Tool-management acceptance, default-off; existing weekly/monthly/push routes remain. Release Exact-commit green main CI and the full Windows desktop release-like suite before tagging; release legs retain their full verification. The repository's internal tooling/verification-tiers.json policy is off by default. It prepares advisory affected-job plans for main and additional nightly Linux runs of tool-management acceptance. Activation requires the same maintainer and Opus security acceptance as main test reuse; this policy does not enable the independent result-admission gate. Main's selection JSON includes a tieredPlan with advisoryOnly: true and the gate state. With the policy enabled, a missing, failed, cancelled, incomplete, future-dated or 24-hour-old comparison run keeps every job in that plan. A valid comparison uses the released driver's existing affected preview. These plans are diagnostics: main still selects every job and executes with --optimized --full --no-cache. Provider run metadata is not authenticated test-result evidence. The additional nightly route is scheduled at 06:41 UTC, separately from the Wednesday acceptance run at 06:37 UTC. It uses the existing suites and provisioning, with full uncached candidate verification and no restored Cargo target tree. Weekly, monthly and push routes continue to execute throughout rollout; unavailable selection also executes the suite. The ordinary acceptance workflow runs on its existing main schedule, fully and without outer result reuse. Hosted platform coverage remains subject to its existing gate and is not established by Linux. The additional nightly route always uses the existing self-hosted main pool, including when legacy hosted-runner overrides are set. Tier selection uses that pool for main and schedule runs; branch pushes use the existing PR pool expression. The daily route excludes quality-maintenance provisioning, builds, App-token minting, PR updates and advisory reporting; their weekly/monthly cadence remains unchanged. Activation also requires the daily route to consume the existing nightly CLI candidate without adding a source build. The prepared full uncached candidate build is dormant while the policy is off; the policy alone does not authorize an additional daily source producer. No test or release obligation moves out of main in this phase. Before any tag, green main CI for that exact commit and the full Windows desktop release-like suite remain mandatory. Release reuse, sharding and activation await their separate proofs.

Build tasks for stages, checks and tasks, and affected builds. Build bundles for the dist/ layout, and action cache for reuse. Rust, Go and Node applications for builder details. Target workspaces for passing artifacts between targets.

Captured pip/pytest package tests use native collection to define one test unit per Python test file. Collection follows pytest's configured paths and plugins; Oyzu's source inventory is only a conservative candidate list. Undeclared native units run without reuse. Preparing a unit exposes only its admitted source and runtime artifacts, and preserves the existing refusal of unsafe links. With coverage.py available in the project environment and enforced runtime-read bounds, a changed unit can reuse individual passing cases. See case selection for inputs, release behavior, reports and limits. A native host run has no enforced read boundary and runs the whole changed unit.

The focused reader-upgrade scenarios use a throwaway published v0.3.8 driver and the compiled candidate, with no development plugin bindings: $env:OYZU_UPGRADE_OLD_CLI = 'C:/throwaway/v0.3.8/oyzu.exe' $env:OYZU_CUSTOMER_CLI = 'C:/throwaway/candidate/oyzu.exe' $env:OYZU_CUSTOMER_BASH = 'C:/Program Files/Git/bin/bash.exe' cargo test --locked --test e2e customer_parity::windows_upgrade_reader_and_candidate_ -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1 cargo test --locked --test e2e customer_parity::windows_upgrade_local_channel_installer_and_trust_refusals -- --ignored --exact --nocapture cargo test --locked --test e2e customer_parity::windows_upgrade_signed_release_and_candidate_rollback -- --ignored --exact --nocapture These three #[ignore = "needs native Windows"] variants require PowerShell 7, cmd, Git Bash and online published Node plugin/tool acquisition. They check old reader refusal in human and JSON modes, candidate version and reader admission. Keep each executable's matching oyzu-shim.exe beside it. OYZU_CUSTOMER_CLI selects the candidate pair for all upgrade scenarios; without it they use the Cargo-built pair. The installer scenario first pins and installs tools with the released reader in one disposable profile. It checks that user configuration, the project lock, shell customization and cached customer data survive both refusals and installation, then explicitly refreshes the private shim farm. Removed-tool shims must disappear, retained tool shims must match the candidate launcher, and the refreshed tool and project must run in all three shells. The local-channel scenario owns the real Node build and repeat-build assertions: the locked plugin selection is reused, while the native Windows lifecycle runs again because its reads are incomplete. The cache explanation must name that refusal; restoring the lifecycle would violate its admission contract. The reader tests copy both drivers into task-owned storage; the source promotion step is explicit and is not a signed self-update. Obtain the old driver using a copy of tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh --release --require-release --no-plugins --no-install in an independent minimal bootstrap folder, and verify it reports 0.3.8. Before publication, exercise the local-channel installer route separately, including a wrong-digest refusal that leaves the old executable unchanged. An unsigned source candidate must be refused by self update; local API/download overrides do not replace the release signing keys. Record signed v0.3.8-to-candidate update, previous-version retention and self rollback as unverified until admitted candidate release evidence is available. Installer backup restoration and direct source promotion do not establish those claims. The local-channel test checks both self-install trust refusals and installer digest refusal before candidate installation. The signed rollback test starts from a candidate copy, installs the admitted published v0.3.8 release, and asks that old driver to roll back to the retained candidate. It checks the restored bytes and candidate version in all three shells. This proves the real swap and rollback direction it runs; it does not prove a signed upgrade to unpublished 0.4.0. Before tagging a release, exercise published-style customer projects separately from this repository's source bootstrap. Use a released or release-candidate CLI copied outside the checkout, an independent OYZU_USER_CONFIG with no development plugin bindings, and published plugin selections in each project's oyzu.lock. The customer fixtures must cover Rust, Node and Maven in PowerShell, cmd and Git Bash. Never use a personal installation as the self-update destination. The Rust e2e target owns the customer matrix: $env:OYZU_CUSTOMER_CLI = 'C:/throwaway/bin/oyzu.exe' $env:OYZU_CUSTOMER_BASH = 'C:/Program Files/Git/bin/bash.exe' cargo test --locked --test e2e customer_parity::windows_customer_matrix -- --ignored --exact --nocapture --test-threads=1 Run Cargo from an Oyzu-activated shell. OYZU_TEST_TMPDIR selects task-owned fixture storage. The Windows test is explicitly ignored in ordinary runs because it needs native Windows, PowerShell 7, cmd, Git Bash and online release/plugin/tool acquisition. The scheduled Linux e2e run includes customer_parity::linux_customer_matrix; it uses the built candidate unless OYZU_CUSTOMER_CLI supplies a release. The focused Windows Maven compatibility regressions cover pinning the published Java plugin, building a real Maven application, rejecting invalid Java source with cached and uncached builds, and rebuilding repaired source in each shell: cargo test --locked --test e2e customer_parity::windows_maven_published_compatibility_ -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1 The pre-tag desktop gate also runs the focused stage-reuse refusal regressions against the current worktree CLI (copied into each independent customer fixture): cargo test --locked --test e2e customer_parity::windows_stage_reuse_refusal_ -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1 Include the native Kotlin JVM Gradle flow in the desktop gate, using the same worktree CLI and a matching Java package: $env:OYZU_CLI = 'C:/throwaway/bin/oyzu.exe' cargo test --locked --test e2e kotlin_gradle::native_multi_project_archives_reports_freshness_and_failure -- --ignored --exact --nocapture --test-threads=1 This flow needs managed JDK 17.0.21 and Gradle 8.14.6 and access to the public Gradle Plugin Portal and Maven Central. It uses a project path containing spaces, two Kotlin DSL members, binary and sources JARs, JUnit 5 and Kotlin JaCoCo reports, an unchanged build, a source edit and a required-test failure. By default the fixture selects the published Java package. For a source CLI whose native API differs from the published package, set OYZU_TEST_JAVA_PACKAGE to the absolute path of a matching Java plugin archive built from the same checkout. The fixture admits it by digest for java/app through ordinary package admission, without a development binding. See the contributor instructions for packaging. A source-package run does not qualify the published package; unset the variable for that gate. Package/API mismatches still fail. Running the same test on Linux does not qualify Windows. The customer parity tests above use published Java/Node plugin admission with no development or package overrides. Each builds twice, checks human and JSON cache explanations, runs with --no-cache, then changes an external input without changing project source. Both ordinary and uncached builds must reach the native failure rather than restore a stale success. Published package admission failures block the gate; they do not count as stage-reuse proof. Use a short task-owned OYZU_TEST_TMPDIR for the disposable profiles and preserve the host's build/disk reserve. The three shell variants are marked #[ignore = "needs native Windows"] and use the same copied CLI and independent customer configuration as the matrix. Use CLI 0.4.0 (or its release candidate) with the existing published Java 0.1.1 Windows payload; the admission fix needs no Java plugin release. These focused tests cover compatibility and source rejection; native Maven stage reuse remains a separate limitation and is not required by this compatibility check. Verify first build, complete repeat reuse, reuse across shell/home/temp changes, failing source with cached and uncached builds and native tests, unrelated lock resolution edits, repaired source, self-update while its executable is running, rollback and a fully reused no-op under ten seconds. Self-update downloads and verifies an older release in disposable folders before exercising replacement; signing and publication admission stay enabled. A failed prerequisite leaves the remaining scenarios unverified. Record the complete scenario/shell/project table and linked defects in the PR, including failures and timings; passing this gate never replaces the full release suite.

Pushes to dev queue a CLI build (.github/workflows/dev-cli.yml, using the dev-cli profile, which runs only required checks). A build that has started finishes. Each workflow/ref/event concurrency group keeps only the newest pending push, so intermediate commits can be replaced before they start. The newest pending commit runs after the active build and stores its own workflow artifact. Dev CI, license and tool checks use the same queue behavior. PR runs cancel older runs for the same workflow and PR ref. Main, tag, scheduled, release and publishing runs remain non-cancelling. Replacing a pending run never supplies passing checks for the tip; its own run still executes the checks selected for that commit. Every push to dev builds a Linux x64 CLI artifact (dev-cli.yml). At 03:23 UTC each day, nightly-dev-cli.yml takes the current dev tip and builds Linux x64 on OVH. Windows x64 is opt-in: set the repository variable OYZU_NIGHTLY_WINDOWS to true once MICAH-DESKTOP's self-hosted runner labelled self-hosted, windows, x64 and oyzu-dev-win exists. When the variable is unset or has any other value, scheduled and manual runs skip Windows. Windows runs one job at a time with a 120-minute limit. Both platforms run independently from the same selected tip through the shared build action. The nightly uses oyzu build cli --full, including tests, lint, format and report requirements; push builds retain the dev-cli profile with required checks. The nightly attempts whatever is on dev, without waiting for other CI results. It is a scheduled check and does not gate pull-request merges. Schedules run from dev, the repository's default branch. Scheduling and queue delays can move the actual start time. For an approved manual timing run, dispatch the workflow with publication disabled (the default): gh workflow run nightly-dev-cli.yml --repo oyzuai/oyzu --ref dev -F publish=false This builds and tests Linux and, when enabled, Windows from the current dev tip. The Nightly job durations (OVH) job writes each job's result and elapsed seconds to its job summary, including failed jobs. A timing run skips release publication, pin changes and failure issues. Publication and failure reporting run only from dev in oyzuai/oyzu; use --ref dev -F publish=true when the manual run should have the same publication and issue behavior as the schedule. A dispatch on another branch still builds and times, even with publish=true, while the publication job and its release token stay unavailable. This also applies to dispatches from main. Scheduled and manual runs consume no GitHub-hosted minutes. Windows waits for the dedicated runner when it is busy or offline; there is no hosted fallback. The runner needs Git Bash and the ephemeral machine-binding setup described in self-hosted runner provisioning. The Windows job grants no repository permissions and receives no publication or signing secrets. Checkout credentials are not persisted in the worktree. Public Windows nightly assets are not published until the dedicated self-hosted Windows runner is provisioned. Windows currently uses authenticated push artifacts, when an opt-in push runner has produced an unexpired artifact; see the PowerShell instructions below. Nightly publication requires both platforms, so a missing Windows runner also prevents a new latest-green publication. Once both runners are available, only a green nightly publishes an internal, unsigned prerelease named dev-YYYYMMDD (the UTC date selected at build start) in the public oyzuai/oyzu-releases repository. These builds are for dogfooding and never qualify a tagged release or main's gate. The assets are oyzu-dev-linux-x86_64.zip and oyzu-dev-windows-x86_64.zip; ordinary release bootstrapping and self-update do not select these archive names. Each archive includes SOURCE_SHA, VERSION, binary checksums and notices. Windows also includes oyzu-shim.exe and its notices. macOS and other architectures are unsupported. After both platform build/test jobs succeed and the complete nightly is published, a metadata-only latest-green prerelease in the same repository points to its immutable date tag and source commit. A failed build/test run publishes nothing and leaves that pointer unchanged. Consecutive red nights keep using the last green build; there is no fallback to a newer unverified tip. With Windows disabled, publication is skipped and latest-green stays unchanged; the Linux build and job-duration summary still run. Once a nightly has been published, from a repository checkout fetch latest-green or select one for the day's dogfood version (illustrative date): tooling/fetch-dev-oyzu.sh tooling/fetch-dev-oyzu.sh --pin dev-20261107 OYZU_DEV_PIN=dev-20261107 tooling/fetch-dev-oyzu.sh The script requires Python 3, jq, SHA-256 tools, and either authenticated gh or curl. Public nightlies need no token when using curl; GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN optionally raises the API rate limit. The Bash script's Windows nightly path requires Git Bash with python3 on PATH and a published Windows nightly asset. Pass a destination directory as a positional argument; the default is ~/.oyzu/dev. The selected executable is installed at current/bin/oyzu (oyzu.exe on Windows), and the tag is recorded in PIN. Add current/bin to PATH in terminals that should use this build. --pin overrides OYZU_DEV_PIN; with neither set, the latest-green pointer selects the nightly. A missing pointer fails until the first green publication; the script does not guess from release dates. Set the repository variable OYZU_DEV_PIN=dev-YYYYMMDD to keep CI's enabled dev channel on that build. Leaving it empty follows latest-green; OYZU_DEV_CHANNEL=off keeps the released CLI. Setup falls back to the released CLI with a warning if a dev download or executable fails. Main, tags, merge groups and fork pull requests retain the released CLI. For an existing Linux push artifact, OYZU_DEV_RUN=<run id> remains supported; numeric OYZU_DEV_PIN values also select legacy run IDs. These need authenticated read access to oyzuai/oyzu (CI tokens need actions: read) and an unexpired artifact. Do not combine a nightly pin with OYZU_DEV_RUN. Legacy selections record RUN instead of PIN. The push workflow also builds Windows when OYZU_DEV_CLI_WINDOWS_RUNNER names an opt-in self-hosted Windows runner. To fetch these Windows push artifacts from PowerShell, use an authenticated gh with read access to oyzuai/oyzu: pwsh -NoProfile -File .github/actions/build-dev-cli/fetch-dev-oyzu.ps1 # Optional: select an unexpired push run; authentication is still required. $env:OYZU_DEV_RUN = '<run id>' pwsh -NoProfile -File .github/actions/build-dev-cli/fetch-dev-oyzu.ps1 -Dest C:\oyzu-dev Run it from a repository checkout. The PowerShell script selects the newest eligible push artifact by default, supports OYZU_DEV_RUN, and installs current\bin\oyzu.exe under ~/.oyzu/dev, retaining previous for rollback. It checks the run, artifact digest and source commit before replacing the installation. It requires authenticated gh even with OYZU_DEV_RUN; without it the script exits with an explanation and the gh auth login --hostname github.com recovery command before querying artifacts. It does not support latest-green, -Pin dev-YYYYMMDD or OYZU_DEV_PIN; clear OYZU_DEV_PIN to use push artifacts. An unavailable opt-in push runner or expired artifact fails without replacing the current installation. Before replacing current, the fetch script verifies the published prerelease and tag (or the successful dev workflow run), the archive's API-reported SHA-256, the recorded source commit, archive contents and every executable checksum. These are integrity checks, not signatures or release qualification. The published digests share a trust root with write access to oyzuai/oyzu-releases: they detect corruption and mix-ups, but cannot establish safety against a compromised publisher that can replace the bytes and digests. The previous installation is retained in previous for rollback. Missing pins, expired artifacts, mismatched metadata and failed downloads exit nonzero and leave current intact.
