Offline use requires an already downloaded installation. Publication requires the existing OYZU_RELEASES_TOKEN secret with Contents read/write on oyzuai/oyzu-releases; build jobs never receive it. Both platform builds and their full checks must succeed before publication. Assets upload to a draft, which becomes a prerelease only after both uploads succeed. Before creating a release, the workflow searches the paginated release listing, including drafts, for that date. An already published date keeps its artifacts. When its recorded source SHA matches the selected commit, a rerun repairs a missing or older latest-green pointer after a prior pointer-update failure. It preserves an already current or newer pointer. If the source SHA differs, it leaves the pointer unchanged. An identifiable leftover internal nightly draft with a valid run marker is deliberately deleted before creating a fresh draft. Failed uploads trigger cleanup of only this attempt's recorded, still-unpublished draft; cleanup verifies its release ID, tag and run marker. Cleanup also runs on cancellation; if no draft was created, it does nothing. Unmarked drafts and published releases are retained. No signing or release workflow runs for this channel. On failure, the workflow opens an issue in oyzuai/oyzu labelled nightly-failure, with the selected source commit, run link, attempt number and failing jobs. An open issue matching the failing tip or any failing job receives a comment instead, including matches in earlier comments. Issue reporting uses the workflow token with issues: write; it does not gate merges or change the pin. Publication failures are also reported. Cancellation or an unavailable cleanup API can leave a draft for the next attempt to retire. A completed daily release can remain without moving latest-green if pointer publication fails. The self-hosted Windows job has a 120-minute limit; a timeout is a red result, and no tests are skipped to fit that limit.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/maven.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu detects a pom.xml without any build YAML and treats a Maven reactor as one target. Maven still owns inheritance, active profiles, module order, dependency resolution and the lifecycle. Oyzu captures the inputs, assigns snapshot versions, runs the build in isolation and collects reports. The reactor example includes unit and integration test variations. Note: The Maven builder is experimental and runs captured builds on Linux (Docker or Linux crun). It's the Maven side of the java/app builder, supplied by the oyzu/java plugin, which selects Maven for a folder with a pom.xml (or with.build-tool: maven); see plugin catalog and selecting a role. It doesn't publish, sign or promote anything.

oyzu -C examples/builds/java-maven-reactor/project run list oyzu -C examples/builds/java-maven-reactor/project build Captured builds need the base execution image and Docker or Linux crun. Oyzu pulls the image when it's missing. The JDK and, for a project without a Maven wrapper, Maven itself are restored from oyzu.lock. See isolated stage reuse. Development tasks use your provisioned Maven or the project's Maven wrapper. oyzu run list doesn't run Maven. For native host builds, lifecycle metadata discovery uses the build's offline selection, Maven settings and execution policy. Online builds can resolve missing Maven plugin descriptors before tests start, including Failsafe and the plugins selected by a committed wrapper. --offline keeps discovery offline and requires those plugins in Maven's local repository. Captured builds use their prepared metadata and retain offline execution. Direct test discovery remains offline. JDK inference accepts literal root compiler-plugin release/source/target and testRelease facts and their corresponding root properties. Configuration wins for each parameter, then release overrides source and target; otherwise both production floors are retained. A separate testRelease floor is also retained: production release 17 and test release 25 select JDK 25 or newer. Literal release/testRelease configuration requires a canonical compiler-plugin 3.x declaration at version 3.6 or newer. Incompatible explicit Java selections stop before native compilation. This does not evaluate the effective reactor model: relevant managed, profile, execution, other test-compiler and toolchain overrides report an unsupported inference location. Parent-based projects retain partial root-property discovery. java.version alone supplies a default hint without asserting a compiler floor. See JDK selection and its limits for precedence, canonical property references and recovery. Task Runs Notes install (implicit) Dependency preparation build (implicit) mvn -B verify Checks bound to verify run under Maven. test (implicit) mvn -B test The test task isn't repeated during a build. The shared Java quality defaults add lint and read-only formatting checks. You can replace them with your own tasks.

The base image has no JDK or Maven. Both come from the lock. A project without a locked JDK stops with the oyzu pin command that fixes it. The Maven extension and the Oyzu worker come with the Maven plugin and the CLI, so no image supplies them. A custom --image maven=<image> only has to meet the bring-your-own contract. Linux crun builds use the admitted base execution image and locked tools.

The execution image has no JDK. Your project selects one, through [tools] java or the root POM's declared level (see how versions are chosen), and build preflight locks it. The container uses it. Preparation: Reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) Temurin archive recorded in oyzu.lock. Downloads it through the tool broker, unless a copy in your user data directory still matches the locked SHA-256. Verifies it. Restores it read-only at /scratch/jdktool. Then JAVA_HOME and the front of PATH point at it for preparation and every build action, so Maven and the compiler run on it. The plan records the archive, so a different JDK changes the action identity. A selected JDK older than 17 is refused with TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION. Maven and Oyzu's Java integration in the container need JDK 17. JDK 17 and newer can compile for older levels with --release. An oyzu.lock without a JDK entry stops the build with the oyzu pin command that fixes it.

Preparation captures the POMs and evaluates the reactor inside the container. Version inference combines native versions with scoped Git tags and relevant commit changes, and the Maven versions plugin applies each module's version, and local reactor references, in private copies of the POMs. Your checkout is unchanged. Supported packaging: pom, jar and war. Other types fail. Outputs keep their native final names, and the bundle records the planned snapshot versions.

Oyzu reads the Maven model first, decides each module's version, and freezes the result in version-plan.json. The final coordinates must match those decisions. If the facts change or the projection fails, the build stops. Maven evaluates version expressions. Oyzu never interprets POM expressions itself. A scoped tag uses the module's artifact ID when it is unique. A root tag doesn't coordinate a whole reactor. The reactor graph supplies each module's local upstream modules, including reactor parents. A library change therefore affects its consumers without advancing unrelated modules. Shared root inputs affect every module. A snapshot version never authorizes publishing. For a module with no version element of its own, preparation first writes the version Maven resolved into the private POM, so the versions plugin can set it independently of the parent. This may normalize the private POM's formatting. The POM in your checkout is never rewritten.

Maven downloads through a local mirror backed by Oyzu's scoped Maven Central broker. Upstream requests happen during acquisition. The captured repository is then copied into a private workspace for the offline build. Captured execution supports Maven Central and administrator-approved snapshot repositories. Use host mode for native private repositories. There is no Maven lockfile. The prepared repository records what was actually captured, which doesn't guarantee that a later download resolves identically. Maven resolves parent dependency management, BOMs and conflicts first. Dependencies on other reactor modules are not fetched, so preparation needs no prebuilt JARs and doesn't compile or test. project-dependencies.xml in the prepared tree lists the external coordinates that were fetched. Plugin and go-offline downloads may add more versions to the repository, so it is not a minimal repository or a complete dependency report. Missing required bytes fail preparation, before any plan is frozen. Transient download failures are retried within limits (acquisition transport). A failed download blocks the build.

One offline lifecycle runs verify and JaCoCo reporting. Your project's JaCoCo version and prepare-agent execution take precedence, including inherited configuration, phase, skip settings and property names. Oyzu adds an initialize preparation only when the project declares none. Inherited pluginManagement version, configuration and executions are respected. JaCoCo 0.8.13 is used when nothing manages a version. Preparation fetches every effective JaCoCo plugin version, because go-offline alone can leave one module's plugin dependencies incomplete in a reactor with mixed versions. If you disabled preparation, it stays disabled and no agent is added. After a failed lifecycle, Oyzu still tries to produce the coverage report without rerunning tests, and keeps the failure.

Required reports, logs and artifacts, with their digests, are listed in dist/manifest.json. A failed check, or an invalid or missing required report, blocks artifact collection. oyzu inspect dist checks the bundle's integrity. It doesn't say whether a build may be released.

After acquisition, Oyzu asks Maven for the effective verify plan and records the report directories of the bound Surefire test and Failsafe integration-test goals. Defaults, inherited and execution-specific configuration, and paths with spaces all follow Maven.

If a Surefire or Failsafe argLine is a literal string, Oyzu prefixes it with @{argLine} in the private model. The JaCoCo agent can then add its flags while your JVM flags and execution-specific overrides stay in place. Your POM is unchanged. Where Oyzu adds this, a missing default property keeps its native user or system value or is set empty. Existing values are never replaced. Property expressions, custom JaCoCo property names and non-forking tests keep Maven's behavior, and Oyzu can't promise coverage for them. Missing coverage still fails the required report check.

Before the run, Oyzu removes old TEST-*.xml files from the declared directories in the private workspace. After the lifecycle it copies the XML unchanged into .oyzu-maven/reports/<reactor-index>/, using hashes of the source path to avoid name collisions. Every XML file is validated and its results recorded. Duplicate directories are collected once. A Surefire or Failsafe directory can be empty. A module with only integration tests doesn't need unit-test XML. A module with test sources needs at least one JUnit file across both directories, plus a JaCoCo report. If tests are skipped or reporting is off and no XML exists, the check fails. Malformed XML fails too. If a custom reporter suppresses some output, Oyzu can't tell which engine's files are missing. It never invents a passing report. Limits: Report paths must stay inside the captured workspace, outside the reserved .oyzu-maven folder, and not be redirected. Different modules need different report directories. Shared paths fail planning rather than credit the same tests to several modules. One XML file can be up to 16 MiB, and one module's reports up to 64 MiB. If a test fails, its XML and any coverage are kept and no artifacts are produced. Fix the test, the report configuration or the missing evidence, and rebuild. Reports from both engines are combined. Use the report records in the manifest, not assumed Surefire paths. Each lifecycle's JUnit report uses a <testsuites> root with optional suite counters. Count its <testcase> elements and their <failure> or <error> children; each case's classname retains its module and native test class, including Failsafe integration tests. Individual native suite files aren't separate bundle reports. JaCoCo coverage is collected separately. JaCoCo reports are read from target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml under the module's build directory. Custom coverage destinations, aggregate reactor coverage and test source roots added only during the lifecycle aren't supported yet.

oyzu run test writes a test-only bundle to dist/. Each module with test sources gets named JUnit and JaCoCo reports, and oyzu inspect dist checks them. The implicit mvn -B test command (or the wrapper equivalent) is reported automatically, with no configuration. Qualified task names and hooks work as in the shared task engine. Custom task replacements keep their commands and must produce the required reports. Extra forwarded arguments and other lifecycle selections aren't supported for this automatic reporting.

Maven 3.9.11, a JDK 17 with java, javac and jar, and your project's plugins and test dependencies, including JaCoCo 0.8.13. MAVEN_HOME pointing at Maven and JAVA_HOME at the JDK, or the JDK executables on PATH. A wrapper must already have its distribution installed. Oyzu doesn't install wrapper distributions. Your Maven settings and environment apply. Oyzu runs Maven offline. A missing plugin or dependency fails instead of going online.

After task checks, a temporary Oyzu extension reads the effective reactor and the test plan in a dedicated Maven process, which exits before validate bindings or the default lifecycle run. Maven can load extensions while it builds its model, so this is ordinary execution on your machine. It is not a sandbox. oyzu run list stays static and doesn't run Maven. Captured builds look at the wider verify plan, which includes Failsafe integration tests. The run then clears old XML in the declared test directories and old JaCoCo execution and XML files, and runs prepare-agent, test and report. After a test failure it still tries to generate reports without rerunning tests. Native XML suites are wrapped into one JUnit document per module, and JaCoCo XML is copied to fresh private paths. Reports are validated and the bundle is finished after post hooks run. Empty suites and missing outputs never get invented passing reports. Limits: Direct tests don't run verify, package snapshots, run quality checks or run integration-only Failsafe suites. Use oyzu build for that. Missing tests or reports, failed tests and unmet coverage constraints fail the command and keep the current evidence. See direct tests for output handling and provenance. Custom JaCoCo destinations and aggregate reactor coverage aren't supported.

Captured preparation also fetches the dependencies declared on build plugins in Maven's effective model, in addition to dependency:go-offline. Oyzu gets the coordinates from the model and downloads them through the broker. It doesn't run the plugin to discover them. System-scoped plugin dependencies aren't supported. A dependency that a plugin chooses only while it runs is not found and can fail the offline build. Oyzu doesn't retry online. Spotless's Eclipse-based formatter steps are one such case: they download Eclipse P2 bundles from download.eclipse.org and fail with java.net.UnknownHostException. They aren't supported (Spotless Eclipse P2 artifacts). Standalone private repositories use host mode. The optional Maven session endpoint remains a separate managed acquisition path. Ordinary JAR plugin dependencies are supported. A plugin's overridden or excluded dependency graph may fetch more than needed, and plugin dependencies produced by the reactor itself aren't supported.

Some plugins download an artifact named in their own configuration while they run. Oyzu fetches these ahead of time for a short list of known plugin parameters, read from Maven's effective model after property expansion: Plugin Parameter Requested type org.codehaus.mojo:animal-sniffer-maven-plugin signature signature com.github.siom79.japicmp:japicmp-maven-plugin oldVersion/dependency Configured type, default jar Both plugin-level and execution-level configuration are read. Animal Sniffer accepts the structured form and the groupId:artifactId:version[:classifier] shorthand: <plugin> <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId> <artifactId>animal-sniffer-maven-plugin</artifactId> <executions> <execution> <goals><goal>check</goal></goals> <configuration> <signature> <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo.signature</groupId> <artifactId>java15</artifactId> <version>1.0</version> </signature> </configuration> </execution> </executions> </plugin> For japicmp, give an explicit old-version dependency inside the plugin's or execution's <configuration>: <oldVersion> <dependency> <groupId>org.jsoup</groupId> <artifactId>jsoup</artifactId> <version>1.23.2</version> <type>jar</type> </dependency> </oldVersion> An optional classifier and the artifact type are kept. A missing type means jar. Maven's artifact handler supplies a missing classifier (test-jar maps to jar:tests). An explicit classifier wins. The old artifact is fetched before the offline run so japicmp can compare it with the new one. A successful build alone doesn't prove the comparison happened: check japicmp's output for a warning that the old version was unavailable. File-based versions, newVersion, version ranges and versions japicmp computes aren't supported. The fetched signature file or old JAR is listed in the dependency snapshot's package inventory. A coordinate with a missing field, or an expression Maven didn't resolve, fails preparation and names the plugin. Fix the POM or its properties and rebuild. Other plugins, and parameters set only on the command line or computed by plugin code, aren't found and can fail the offline build.

Some projects inherit a parent that exists only as a snapshot. For example, jackson-core has a -SNAPSHOT jackson-base parent published to the Sonatype Central Portal snapshot repository and declared in the project's own <repositories>. Captured builds send every repository through one mirror to Maven Central, which serves no snapshots, so by default such a build fails preparation. Setting Values Default Meaning maven.snapshotRepositories A set of HTTPS repository base URLs ending in / Empty (off) The snapshot repositories Oyzu may use. Only corporate policy or the protected local admin-settings.json can set it. Project, local, user, machine and invocation configuration can't enable or widen it. For example, inside the settings object of admin-settings.json: "maven.snapshotRepositories": { "locked": true, "value": ["https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/"] } When the set isn't empty: Each URL becomes its own download source, maven-snapshots-<n>, numbered in sorted URL order. A URL with credentials, a query or a fragment, a plain HTTP URL, or one without a trailing / fails preparation. Admitted repositories can't carry credentials. The mirror and the repository identity stay the same, so the offline build reads snapshots from the captured repository exactly as it reads releases. Only snapshot version paths (group/.../artifact/<version>-SNAPSHOT/...) go to the approved repositories, which are tried in order until one returns the file. Every other path keeps the Central (or session-approved) route. The approved repositories, not the URLs your project declares, serve every snapshot. Maven only asks for snapshots when a declared repository enables them, so your project still declares its snapshot repository, as jackson-core does. The mirror replaces its URL. Each captured .pom, .jar, .module or .signature file under a snapshot version directory is listed in the dependency snapshot's package inventory with the maven-snapshots-<n> source that served it. The approved repositories are listed under extensions."oyzu.dev/maven".snapshotRepositories. Acquisition fails if one snapshot directory was served by two repositories. Release builds never use snapshot inputs. If any snapshot input was captured and any module's version decision isn't a development snapshot, or is production eligible, preparation fails with MAVEN_SNAPSHOT_RELEASE, even with the setting on. Today every captured build is a development snapshot build. A build without snapshot inputs is unaffected by the setting. Code or message Cause Fix Maven's "could not find artifact" error naming the snapshot The setting is off, and a snapshot parent or dependency can't be fetched Ask an administrator to admit its repository, or depend on a released version MAVEN_SNAPSHOT_REPOSITORY A captured snapshot package wasn't served by an approved repository. This applies whether or not the setting is on, so a snapshot served by a session-approved repository is refused too. The error names the file. Follow the approved-repository rules above MAVEN_SNAPSHOT_RELEASE A snapshot input was captured and a version decision isn't a development snapshot, or is production eligible The setting doesn't override this. Release builds never use snapshot inputs. CONFIG_SCOPE A project file sets maven.snapshotRepositories Remove it from the project file. Only corporate policy or the protected local admin-settings.json can set it.

Some POMs use os-maven-plugin properties to pick platform-specific artifacts, such as Netty's parent with <tcnative.classifier>${os.detected.classifier}</tcnative.classifier>. A project that only imports Netty's dependencies doesn't run the extension, so the expression is never resolved. Where the extension does run, it detects the machine Maven runs on. Captured preparation and execution therefore pass fixed Maven user properties taken from the job's target platform, not from the host or the execution image: Property linux/amd64 linux/arm64 darwin/arm64 windows/amd64 os.detected.name linux linux osx windows os.detected.arch x86_64 aarch_64 aarch_64 x86_64 os.detected.bitness 64 64 64 64 os.detected.classifier linux-x86_64 linux-aarch_64 osx-aarch_64 windows-x86_64 Names follow the plugin's own normalization (kr.motd.maven.os.Detector). Other platforms the plugin names, such as linux/ppc64le (ppcle_64) and linux/s390x (s390_64), map the same way. A target the plugin can't name fails preparation. os.detected.release* and kernel os.detected.version* aren't set, because a target platform has neither. A POM that needs them keeps Maven's behavior. Maven user properties win over the extension's detected values in interpolation, profile activation and plugin parameters, so ${os.detected.classifier} resolves the same way in every run, including in dependency POMs. A project that declares the extension still runs its own detection. Only these four properties are fixed. The properties are frozen in the prepared tree (properties.json) and listed in the dependency snapshot under extensions."oyzu.dev/maven".userProperties. Artifacts a plugin downloads from such a property while it runs, outside declared dependencies, aren't fetched ahead of time. Direct tests (oyzu run test) keep native detection.

On Linux, oyzu build --isolated --no-docker uses crun and admits lifecycle reuse through an enforced complete input boundary. The existing build.isolation = "crun" selection with --isolated is equivalent. No new flag, setting or internal environment gate is required. The captured source, admitted dependency artifacts and read-only prepared repository, locked JDK/Maven identities and execution runtime enter the key. An unchanged lifecycle can reuse its verify result, including compilation, archives and validated test/coverage evidence. With a compatible Java plugin, multi-module reactors keep the lifecycle coupled inside each module. Membership and dependency order come from Maven's evaluated reactor graph. For a chain where b depends on a and c depends on b, editing c reruns only c; editing a invalidates a, b and c. An unchanged rebuild can reuse all modules. Package exports are separately keyed on explicit POMs and producer archives. Changed source, dependencies or JDK identity cause a miss. Maven uses a fixed output timestamp for reproducible archive entries. Only the identified input view is available. Live proc/sys data and undeclared host files are inaccessible; failed actions publish no reusable result. The closed JVM device allowance and its output-independence requirement are described in native host read admission. Preparation and current report gates still apply to a hit; reused evidence is labelled as not executed now. Each module retains its own JUnit and JaCoCo evidence, attributed to its producing action. Reused reports describe the earlier execution. Native build definitions remain shared inputs; changing a POM can invalidate multiple modules. A module cannot read an undeclared sibling's source files. Missing producer archives or an invalid dependency graph refuse module reuse with JVM_MODULE_PRODUCER_MISSING or JVM_MODULE_GRAPH_INVALID; fix the native dependencies and rebuild. Planning retains the whole reactor if module reads cannot be bounded: source links, an oversized source inventory, or shared module controls such as build-tools/checkstyle.xml prevent splitting. This fallback applies to every captured executor, including Docker. It grants no native-host reuse. Older models without module dependency facts retain the conservative whole-reactor lifecycle. Native-host Maven still reruns the lifecycle because its runtime reads are incomplete. Other isolated executors and Windows/macOS do not establish this boundary. Plain oyzu build remains native; making isolated Java builds the default is a later product decision.

With the next Java plugin release and a compatible CLI supporting private stages, native host format-check reuses independently through its fixed reads and empty private-output declaration. Editing an existing README's contents does not change its source-read key, but a source-derived snapshot version can change the action definition and still cause a miss. Whole-target projection identity can also cause conservative misses. Editing a formatted Java file reruns it. Lifecycle builds (including tests) and Checkstyle currently have unbounded output contracts and rerun even on unchanged native builds. This mixed pipeline cannot restore a whole-target result. Fast builds rerun the lifecycle too, even when format and lint are omitted. Whole-target entries saved by an older CLI cannot bypass this rule. oyzu build --explain names the stage and the missing complete read report; reuse needs complete reads and bounded outputs from the builder. Declaring inputs alone does not bound arbitrary runtime reads. Required test and coverage reports still apply. Captured copy/export behavior is unchanged. See Java quality for the read boundary. The native-host Maven build action runs verify, including tests and lifecycle plugins. It stays unbounded: tests can read arbitrary files at run time, and Maven does not report a complete read set for the effective reactor's plugins. Conventional src/ directories alone cannot bound this lifecycle. Reactor POMs, configured source/resource roots, .mvn/ configuration and plugin-specific files contribute to source identity, but that identity cannot cover unobserved external reads or authorize native lifecycle reuse. The separate test action is also unbounded. Packaging reads only its explicit copy inputs: reactor POMs and generated archives. It also depends on the build producer's outputs. Since it copies POM bytes, it is not a source-free export. Shared Java formatting and lint have their own read boundaries. These declarations are supplied by the Java plugin; independent formatting reuse needs both a compatible CLI and the updated plugin.

Surefire tests using TestNG (including suiteXmlFiles pointing to a testng.xml suite) use the same TEST-*.xml collection as JUnit. Maven selects the provider and runs the suite. Oyzu requires genuine Surefire XML; providers or configuration that suppress these reports fail the required-report check. TestNG through Failsafe alone, JUnit 3 and Spock/Groovy are outside the supported scope. Whole-reactor lifecycles combine conventional per-module target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml reports into one reactor report. Its counters sum the tested modules, and module groups retain source/package ownership. It is a weighted total of covered and missed lines, not an average of module percentages. If every module lacks line debug metadata, the total uses instructions instead; mixed line/instruction reports fail with a request for consistent debug metadata. Oyzu does not add report-aggregate or measure cross-module execution that is absent from the individual module reports. The merged XML has the shared JaCoCo report limit of 16 MiB. Per-module captured lifecycles retain the individual JaCoCo reports and apply the configured coverage gate to each report. A project may already configure org.jacoco:jacoco-maven-plugin, including through its effective parent, profile or plugin management. Oyzu preserves an existing prepare-agent execution and its configuration instead of adding another agent. Otherwise it adds one preparation execution. The project's plugin version and report configuration remain Maven-owned; Oyzu requests the plugin's report goal after verify and reuses the conventional XML output. A disabled agent, a custom agent property that Surefire does not consume, a skipped XML report or a different output path does not waive required coverage: restore conventional XML output and agent wiring to build successfully. Literal Surefire JVM flags are retained through late argLine replacement. This behavior requires the next Java plugin release and a CLI supporting the maven-reactor-coverage feature. Existing plugin releases retain their previous native coverage behavior.

oyzu build --full uses Maven's native dependency and plugin repositories, servers and mirrors. Keep credentials in ~/.m2/settings.xml, or reference an environment variable from a project settings file selected through .mvn/maven.config. Oyzu adds no registry setting and does not replace the repository selection with a public mirror. For example, a native server entry can contain: <server> <id>company</id> <username>reader</username> <password>${env.COMPANY_MAVEN_PASSWORD}</password> </server> The server ID must match Maven's effective repository or mirror ID. Maven owns settings precedence and mirror matching. A project .mvn/settings.xml is used only when Maven selects it, for example with --settings followed by .mvn/settings.xml on separate lines in .mvn/maven.config. A target counts as credentialed only when a settings server id matches a repository or plugin repository declared in the project's POMs, an active settings profile, or a mirror. Unmatched servers, such as distributionManagement deploy servers, do not make a public project private, force fresh execution or block captured builds. Known limitations: repositories supplied only by remote parent POMs or command-line properties are not seen, parent POMs outside the project root, the global ${maven.home}/conf/settings.xml and -s/-gs supplied through MAVEN_ARGS are not observed. Every settings profile's repositories count, and httpHeaders tokens are treated as credentials. Credentials observed in native settings and referenced environment variables are supplied only to the native invocation and removed from its captured output. They never appear in plans, action keys or evidence, and credential-bearing JVM builds do not restore cached actions. A tracked settings.xml with a literal password fails with NATIVE_CONFIG_CREDENTIAL before the build; move it to user settings or use ${env.NAME}. Native user repository/cache state remains Maven-owned. Known limitation: a referenced ${env.X} value is redacted everywhere it appears in output, even if it also occurs in unrelated text. A settings file selected in .mvn/maven.config must be a regular file inside the project or user home. Captured and isolated execution do not support standalone credentials. They fail before build actions with guidance to use host mode. No public fallback is introduced. An explicit offline host build still requires Maven's native cache to contain the dependencies and plugins.

Not supported yet: test providers beyond JUnit through Surefire/Failsafe and TestNG through Surefire, custom coverage tools or custom/aggregate report layouts, test sources generated during the lifecycle, standalone private repositories in captured/isolated execution and release builds. Captured builds run on Linux. Conventional reactors can also build natively; see native Maven builds. Native Maven verify does not report complete runtime reads for tests and lifecycle plugins. Whole-target action-cache reuse remains disabled for that stage; a successful repeated build can execute again instead of reporting a complete target hit. A compatible CLI/plugin pair alone does not enable reuse. The published Windows CLI 0.3.8 cannot select a compatible published Java payload: older Java releases lack Windows payloads, while Java 0.1.1 needs newer engine capabilities. PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE stops pinning before Maven runs. Native Windows use needs a compatible CLI/plugin release pair; changing the POM or refreshing the same catalog cannot supply the missing compatibility. Java 0.1.1 requires the engine's gradle-kotlin-jvm capability for the whole package, including Maven projects. The compatibility fix ships with CLI 0.4.0, which implements that capability and admits the existing signed Java 0.1.1 Windows payload. No new Java plugin release is needed for this admission fix. Until CLI 0.4.0 is published, use a 0.4.0 release candidate for this combination. Removing requirements from catalog metadata or using a development binding does not make CLI 0.3.8 compatible. Native stage reuse is a separate limitation.

On Windows, incomplete native reads require the lifecycle/scripts to run again. oyzu build --explain and oyzu cache explain app name this refusal and point to oyzu build --isolated --no-docker on Linux crun for complete-read stage reuse. Clearing the cache does not resolve it. --no-cache must agree with ordinary execution, including failures after external inputs change. Independently admitted complete-read stages and native download caches remain available. See native Windows refusal.
Java quality tasks, direct tests, version inference. Maven sessions for private repositories, and Java installation for JDK selection.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/maven-sessions.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Use this when Maven should download from private repositories without passwords in settings.xml. A local credential agent tells oyzu which repositories are allowed and supplies the credentials. oyzu uses the same agent for two things: running mvn yourself through oyzu exec or an activated shell, where Maven gets the password in memory; oyzu build for Maven projects, where oyzu downloads the dependencies itself and Maven never sees the password (see Captured build acquisition). Note: Experimental. You need a credential agent running on the same machine; oyzu doesn't include one. Supported on Linux with Maven 3.9.11, JDK 17 and Bash.

Add the agent's address to your user or administrator configuration (not the project's oyzu.toml): [maven] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43199/session" Setting Values Default Meaning maven.sessionEndpoint http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<path>, no user name, password, query or fragment Not set The local agent to ask for sessions. Remove it to go back to plain Maven and Maven Central Project, local and command-line configuration and profiles can't set this value. User configuration isn't read in CI, so this doesn't work there.

You need Maven 3.9.11 and a JDK with java, javac and jar on PATH: oyzu exec -- /opt/maven/bin/mvn verify # or, with Maven on PATH: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" mvn verify Use the mvn from a Maven installation; mvnw and other wrappers aren't supported. --help and --version run without asking the agent. You don't need any authentication files or extensions in the project.

oyzu sends the agent a POST with {"directory": "<working dir>", "tool": "mvn", "arguments": [...]}. The agent answers with one or more mirror mappings: { "sources": [ { "id": "approved-libraries", "mirrorOf": "company-libraries", "access": { "repository": "https://packages.example.com/maven/", "username": "reader", "credentialEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:43199/credential/session" } } ] } Field Rules sources 1 to 64 entries, in Maven mirror order (exact matches before wildcards) id Unique. Letters, digits, -, _ or .. Can't be oyzu-source-denied mirrorOf A Maven mirror selector. Unique across entries access.repository HTTP(S) URL with no credentials, query or fragment access.username Not empty access.credentialEndpoint On 127.0.0.1. A GET returns the password as UTF-8 text Use "mirrorOf": "*" for one repository that serves everything, or separate entries for central, company-libraries, company-plugins and so on. Maven matches repository IDs, not group names.

Asks the agent before doing anything, even when Maven's cache is warm. Compiles a small bundled Maven extension against your Maven's libraries. Lets Maven read your normal settings.xml files (including -s and -gs). The extension then: keeps your blocking mirrors; adds the agent's mirrors, plus a catch-all that blocks every other repository, including ones declared in POMs; fetches each password into memory and authenticates only to that mirror's exact URL. Removes the temporary extension and files when Maven finishes or fails. An existing non-blocking mirror in your settings must match an agent mapping's URL, selector and layout (its ID may differ), or the run fails and names the settings file. <server> credentials in your settings are never used as a fallback. Profiles, properties, proxies and JVM settings work as usual. Maven downloads directly from the repositories; oyzu doesn't proxy the traffic.

With maven.sessionEndpoint set, oyzu build asks the agent for a session before it prepares a Maven project. The request has "tool": "mvn" and "arguments": ["oyzu-build-acquire"], a marker for the agent rather than a real Maven command. The agent answers with a single repository: { "repository": "https://packages.example.com/maven/", "username": "reader", "credentialEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:43199/credential/session" } The repository URL must end in /. oyzu fetches the password into memory and downloads the dependencies itself with Basic authentication. The build containers have no network access and never see the password; the build then runs offline from what was downloaded. Without the setting, dependencies come from Maven Central. If the agent denies or fails, the build stops. It never falls back to Maven Central. Snapshot versions are allowed only from administrator-listed snapshot repositories. If a plugin needs a dependency at build time that wasn't declared, the offline build fails. Declare it through the plugin's Maven configuration and build again. oyzu doesn't rerun the build online.

Passwords never go into settings files, command arguments or environment variables. When you run mvn yourself, the password is in Maven's memory, so plugins can read it. With oyzu build, Maven never receives it. The temporary files contain the credential endpoint, not the password, but treat them as sensitive. Read-only access has to be enforced by the repository account the agent uses. Denial or an unreachable agent stops the command before Maven starts, with no fallback.
Maven's output and exit code pass through unchanged. With --json, they're captured in the usual oyzu exec result.

Code Cause Fix NATIVE_SESSION_CONFIG The endpoint is set in project or local configuration Move it to user or administrator configuration NATIVE_SESSION_UNAVAILABLE The agent can't be reached Start the agent and retry NATIVE_SESSION_DENIED The agent refused the request Get access granted; don't work around the agent NATIVE_SESSION_INVALID Bad endpoint, or a mapping has a bad repository or no user name Fix the endpoint or the agent MAVEN_SESSION_INVALID The agent's response couldn't be read, or has no mappings or more than 64 Fix the agent's response MAVEN_SESSION_PREPARE The JDK tools couldn't compile the extension Install a working JDK and Maven MAVEN_SESSION_UNSUPPORTED mvn isn't inside a Maven installation (no lib directory), or the project has .mvn/extensions.xml Use Maven's own bin/mvn; remove .mvn/extensions.xml MAVEN_SESSION_CONFLICT A mirror in your settings doesn't match the agent; duplicate IDs or selectors; or maven.ext.class.path or deploy in the arguments, MAVEN_ARGS, MAVEN_OPTS, JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS or .mvn/maven.config/jvm.config Fix the setting or the mapping. Publish with oyzu publish

Plugins that make their own network calls aren't covered. Proxy authentication and custom TLS settings aren't supported yet. Credential rotation during a run, and cleanup after oyzu is killed, aren't handled. Linux and Bash only, with Maven 3.9.11. Windows, macOS and other Maven versions aren't supported yet.
Maven builds Private Gradle repositories Java installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/mocha.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The Node builder runs your Mocha tests with your own Mocha setup and collects a JUnit test report and an LCOV coverage report from them. Use it when your package already tests with Mocha and you want those reports in the build output. Note: This integration is experimental.

For a package that tests with npm and Mocha, add Mocha and c8 as dev dependencies and keep a plain mocha test script: { "scripts": {"test": "mocha"}, "devDependencies": {"mocha": "12.0.3", "c8": "10.1.3"} } Install dependencies with npm, then run the tests: oyzu run test oyzu build app --full --offline The test run writes junit.xml and coverage.lcov into the build's reports/ folder (see Reports). No Oyzu test or report section is needed in your configuration.

The builder detects Mocha from, strongest first: A test script that runs mocha, including a compound script that names only Mocha. A native .mocharc file or a mocha section in package.json. A mocha dependency. Oyzu reads configuration files without running them. If two frameworks have equally strong evidence, selection fails and names the with: {test-framework: <name>} selector in build.yaml. See discovery selectors. With no test script, a detected Mocha project gets an implicit test task that runs node node_modules/mocha/bin/mocha.js. oyzu run list shows it and oyzu run test runs it. Direct tests in single packages and npm workspaces also collect JUnit and LCOV into a test-only dist/ bundle. See direct tests and workspace test bundles.

Setup Mocha c8 Single npm package, implicit tests and host oyzu build 12.0.3 10.1.3 in your project Scripted direct tests, isolated builds and npm workspaces 11 (tried with 11.8.0) or 12.0.3 10.x or 12.x in your project, or Oyzu's locked default c8 The single-package setup is supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). For the platforms of isolated builds, see local builds. Other Mocha versions, pnpm and Yarn projects, and macOS are not supported yet.

This setup requires exactly mocha 12.0.3 and c8 10.1.3 in dependencies or devDependencies. It adapts an implicit Mocha test or a script that is exactly mocha, and keeps npm's script lifecycle and your configured Mocha reporter and options. Exact task overrides sh -c 'mocha' and sh -c 'npm run test', and their PowerShell equivalents, use the same reporting adapter. Oyzu normalizes these recognized bodies before adding reporter flags; npm run test keeps npm's script lifecycle. Other shell bodies run as authored. Tests run serially. Watch mode and parallel mode are not supported. You cannot override the CLI reporter, and Oyzu rejects authored c8 configuration (.c8rc.json and similar). c8 reports the sources your tests load, not every file in the repository. An authored c8 configuration fails with a message directing you to an authored test task with explicit reports. This rejection happens before tests run, so no JUnit report is expected; a missing-report manifest record has no file path. Keep required coverage minimums in that authored task rather than removing them to enable automatic reporting. Oyzu never downloads a reporting tool. The c8 in your project is always used. oyzu build app --full --offline uses your existing npm lock and cache and fails if a required input is not cached. Without --offline it prepares dependencies as usual.
documents.s: Single npm package: implicit tests and host builds

documents.t: Keep your existing project and native configuration: { "scripts": {"test": "mocha"}, "devDependencies": {"mocha": "11.8.0"} } Mocha must be a declared dependency that is captured with the build. c8 10.x or 12.x in your project is used when present. A declared but missing c8 fails. Without any c8 dependency, the locked Node quality set supplies the fallback. Run oyzu pin before a direct task; task preparation installs the selected set in the shared store. See Node quality for refresh and offline behavior. The test command runs under c8. Native thresholds, include and exclude rules and source-map handling in your c8 configuration apply. Only LCOV is exported, so additional coverage formats are not. No build action downloads reporting tools.
documents.s: Scripted direct tests, isolated builds and npm workspaces

documents.t: The engine collects the reports under dist/<target>/<platform>/reports/ and records their paths, digests and summaries in the manifest. Report File Test results (JUnit, from Mocha's XUnit reporter) junit.xml Coverage (LCOV, from c8) coverage.lcov Native suite and workspace report allocations include the suite's identity in their filenames, so members can share native report basenames. Read the bundle manifest for collected paths; see workspace test bundles. The adapter combines your configured Mocha reporter with Mocha's XUnit reporter, so your reporter options keep working. Oyzu supplies the reporting adapter itself; you do not need to copy a reporter into your project. The selected Node plugin stages the embedded mocha-native-reporter.cjs in its private runtime directory for the run, both for host tests and inside isolated builds. A failed assertion keeps the reports that exist and blocks packaging. A failed coverage threshold fails the build even when every test passed. Passing coverage never turns a failed test into a success. A configuration or startup failure never reuses an earlier run's reports. A command that exits zero without writing a required report fails the required-report gate. Read the action log to see why a report is missing, fix the cause and rerun. A successful build also produces the normal Node package artifact. Build, test, lint and read-only formatting stay separate stages. The default lint rules know Mocha globals in conventional test folders and in test and spec files. Your own lint configuration takes precedence. See Node lint and formatting.

Workspaces use the same adapter. Each member resolves Mocha, its configuration and c8 from its own folder, including hoisted installs. A publishable root without a test script gets its own test suite. It excludes workspace members and Oyzu's own state with Mocha's --ignore option, and keeps your existing exclusions. Its planned argv stays bound to the selected workspace command; native execution runs that root suite with Mocha, not another recursive workspace invocation. An explicit script keeps its native file selection, including --file entries, which Mocha does not filter through --ignore. An explicit root test script produces one combined report pair. Otherwise each package gets its own JUnit and LCOV files, and a failure in one package keeps its siblings' results and blocks packaging. See npm workspaces.

Isolated builds recognize a bare mocha, its direct Node entry point and equivalent exact task overrides. Other shell commands, and scripts with extra flags, run as written. They must write their own required reports, and Oyzu does not guess a rewrite. Configure recognized runs through your Mocha configuration. Watch mode is turned off. Parallel Mocha reporting is not supported and fails when Oyzu detects it. Browser runners and custom reporters are not supported. Mocha configuration is project code. Development tasks run it on your machine, and isolated builds run it in an offline sandbox. The reporting adapter gets no credentials and no network access. A passing report shows the tests ran. It does not make a build eligible for release.
Node lint and formatting Direct tests npm workspaces Discovery selectors c8 options and Mocha's XUnit reporter

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-applications.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The node/app builder builds a Node application and produces a directory artifact, normally the contents of its dist/ folder. Use it to ship a front-end site or another static application as a directory that other targets, such as a container image, can consume. Note: Node application builds are experimental. They support a single package root (npm, pnpm, or Yarn, see Yarn builds), Vite 8 projects, native npm, pnpm 10 and Yarn Classic root workspace applications, and isolated package-local workspaces. See Limits. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

If your package's native build script writes dist/, declare the build in build.yaml: builds: frontend: uses: node/app path: frontend oyzu run list oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Oyzu runs the native build script with your package manager, then stages the contents of frontend/dist/ as the primary directory artifact application-<snapshot-version>. A consumer that uses materialize: [{from: frontend, to: site}] receives site/index.html directly, without a nested dist directory. A package with a vite dependency and "scripts": {"build": "vite build"} needs no build.yaml. Package discovery selects node/app for it (see Vite projects). Builds use the Node builder plugin. See plugin packages for how plugins are installed and pinned in oyzu.lock. The plugin manifest declares oyzu:node, oyzu:npm, oyzu:pnpm and oyzu:yarn for the install, build, test, lint and format-check stages. Its runtime requirements select Node and, when package.json has an exact stable packageManager release for the selected npm, pnpm or Yarn manager, that manager. Without packageManager, the runtime requirements select Node alone.

For an npm, pnpm 10 or Yarn Classic workspace, declare the root node/app build and run oyzu build --full. The root build script still produces one dist/ application artifact. The package manager supplies membership; the same suite selection as oyzu run test runs each member's Vitest, Jest or other supported native tests and collects distinct JUnit and LCOV reports. A root test script keeps aggregate ownership. See workspace test bundles for prerequisites, report obligations and failures. This host flow does not enable isolated workspace tests, Yarn Berry/PnP or per-member artifacts. Windows workspace build tests remain unverified.

On Linux crun, npm lifecycle stages use complete read enforcement through the existing isolated/container selection, such as oyzu build --isolated --no-docker. An unchanged build can reuse successful script-free install, build and test stages, including their workspace changes and required reports. No extra setting is needed. Package-local npm, pnpm and Yarn Classic workspaces have separate reusable member actions; see workspace reuse. The key binds admitted source reads, prepared dependencies, locked Node/tool identities, runtime image, command, environment and producer outputs. An ordinary source edit reruns stages that read it and affected consumers while script-free installation can reuse. Its key retains the lockfile, npm configuration and tool identity. Only the generated OYZU_VERSION default is omitted when the admitted install model proves it is unread. Explicit environment values remain keyed. Build and package producers retain their version input. Owned test and quality commands omit the generated default: they consume source and producer outputs without stamping a shipping version. Explicit project or task OYZU_VERSION values still apply and remain keyed. If a check needs a version environment value, declare it explicitly. Root/dependency install scripts, implicit native compilation, incomplete install facts or runtime-loading hooks do not establish unread environment inputs. Installation then keeps OYZU_VERSION and runs every time, including on unchanged source. A reviewed dependency file-read allowance alone does not prove its environment reads. Arbitrary lifecycle scripts use the entire admitted source view, so any edit in that view can rerun them. Lockfile/dependency or locked runtime changes invalidate the corresponding stages. The executor hides undeclared host files and live /proc//sys data, denies network access and starts lifecycle stages with private output state. Fixed core retirement/export helpers retain their bounded contracts. An unsupported read that fails the command publishes no reusable success. --no-cache executes stages with the same isolation and report checks. Runtime entropy is permitted only when it does not affect retained outputs; scripts that embed random or other ambient values are outside this reuse contract. On the native host path, arbitrary project/package lifecycle scripts do not report complete reads. Their stages run again even with unchanged source, and whole-target cache restoration cannot skip them. Bounded npm install selectors alone do not enable native stage reuse. Tool and dependency download caches remain available. Use oyzu build --explain for the named refusal; adding inputs covers known files without proving all runtime reads complete. See native npm caching. Windows and macOS native builds retain this refusal; they do not gain the Linux crun boundary. Docker execution and other package managers retain their existing captured-cache rules.

Stage Source boundary Single-root npm install package.json, package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, .npmrc and binding.gyp, including missing-file probes. A v2/v3 lock must inventory dependency packages. Writes are limited to node_modules when the native install model can bound every lifecycle. Script-free workspace install Native member manifests, manager controls and lockfiles; admitted registry archive manifests must also be script-free. Workspace member build/test Own member source, native manager startup controls, installed dependencies and explicit workspace-dependency outputs. Root aggregate or opaque root dispatch keeps the whole workspace. Other installs Whole target; lifecycle or runtime-loading uncertainty refuses installation reuse. Build, test, lint and format check The selected command's existing static analysis supplies reads when modeled. Arbitrary project/package lifecycle code keeps the whole-target boundary. Version projection and package collection Package-owned operations retain the whole-target boundary unless an admitted command model supplies a narrower contract. Packaging can read metadata, ignore rules, notices and lifecycle inputs beyond the build script. An npm root lifecycle script, implicit node-gyp compilation, unmodeled dependency install script, local/Git/URL dependency, bundled dependency or unsupported .npmrc setting prevents a bounded install. The reason names the missing model rather than claiming the stage has not been analyzed. Existing reviewed dependency lifecycle models remain usable. Creating a previously absent control file invalidates its read set too. The install environment keys NODE_ENV, NODE_OPTIONS and noncredential npm_config_* values are frozen with the invocation. Install selection values enter the action key; delivery settings (registry, proxy and TLS credentials) reach execution without changing the install key. npm resolves user and global configuration paths; settings in those files that can change installation retain the whole-target boundary, with the file and key named in the reason. Registry, proxy and authentication settings alone do not make an external configuration unbounded. Configuration values are omitted from reasons. Declarations do not grant cache admission. Narrow keys still require confinement or complete admitted native observations. oyzu build --plan uses stage contracts from the target's last retained build, without invoking the plugin. Its stage Why says reported when the builder answers when no contract is retained; recorded reasons are marked as facts from the last build. The executed plan and oyzu cache explain describe the actual cache boundary; see action caching. On the native host, a bounded install declaration does not establish complete runtime reads or permit whole-target restoration across incomplete stages.

Selecting node/app is how you tell Oyzu that your build script follows the dist convention. Oyzu does not read your script to find out. The output must be a freshly produced directory inside the package: A missing output directory, a file where the directory should be, linked entries and special files fail the build. Contents left by an earlier build never count. Build, test, lint and read-only format checks still run. The default quality checks skip the generated dist. Dependency preparation accepts packages without Node test files. Test selection and required JUnit/coverage reports are checked separately; an explicit native test script may report zero tests. Implicit workspace Node suites without owned files are omitted with an informational “no tests” note in human output and JSON diagnostic events (not a warning); an explicit framework selection still requires owned files. Browser globals are not assumed from the application selection alone. The artifact keeps the platform it was built on. Reusing one artifact across platforms is not supported. How Oyzu picks a builder: Discovery reports builder_selection: explicit and the dist-application output profile. A recognized framework such as Vite has its own output rules and validation. uses: node/package always builds a package archive instead (see npm workspaces and plugin packages). If discovery infers a Node target whose script is unknown, it builds a package archive. Add uses: node/app only when the script writes dist/. A custom output directory other than dist is supported only for Vite (see below). An explicit node/package build of a single-root npm or pnpm package can pack its native files without a build script in the captured lane. An existing build script still requires its selected build task; workspace handling and explicit node/app build-task requirements are unchanged. The matching CLI and Node plugin must both accept this optional-task request. A published plugin embedding the older inferred-application-only validator requires a compatible signed package update through normal selection; changing the CLI alone does not update that consumer. This allowance applies to logical node/package references (including major pins); direct OCI package references retain their existing task requirement. A single-root npm project with a package name and build script can build this inferred package archive on the native host, without build.yaml or Docker. It keeps npm package output rather than assuming your script writes a static site. Run oyzu install and oyzu build, then consume the resulting .tgz as an ordinary npm package. Other inferred Node profiles retain their existing executor requirements. Dependency-bearing npm application and package builds require package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json. Generate the lock with npm before building; a missing lock fails before installation. Oyzu runs npm ci, which checks manifest/lock synchronization and prefers shrinkwrap when both files exist. Offline builds retain npm ci --offline and need the locked packages already available. An authored install task in oyzu.toml replaces the builder's install operation and runs before the application build. Oyzu prepares that task and its prerequisites under their own task owners before planning the native build; a workspace task does not borrow a target's tool environment. Pin tools in the task owner's configuration when it needs managed executables. A nonempty npm peerDependencies declaration also requires installation and a native lock, even when no other dependencies are declared. npm handles peer resolution and optional peers; Oyzu runs the same npm ci operation before the build and tests. An empty peer map alone does not add an install operation.
documents.s: How the output directory is chosen

documents.t: npm, pnpm 9+ and Yarn Classic use native project or user .npmrc registry settings. No Oyzu registry setting or platform account is needed. For example: registry=https://registry.npmjs.org/ @company:registry=https://packages.example.com/npm/ //packages.example.com/npm/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN} Set NPM_TOKEN in your shell or CI secret environment and generate the manager's native lock before running oyzu build --full. The scoped package must be locked to the selected registry. Unscoped packages keep the default registry. A default private registry can instead be selected with registry=.... Managed connector access remains separate; native tokens do not authorize a managed captured build. Project .npmrc credential values must be environment references such as ${NPM_TOKEN}. Source admission refuses a literal credential with SOURCE_CREDENTIAL_DENIED before build actions run, including when .npmrc is tracked by Git. Move literal credentials to your user-level native configuration or replace them with environment references. Registry settings and credential references are removed from captured source copies. Read analysis of an observed checkout verifies the same credential-free .npmrc content as a captured source copy. Install settings remain visible: an unsupported setting still makes the install boundary unknown, and changing an install setting invalidates its recorded read. Prepared dependency/output files are read as recorded rather than rewritten as source configuration. Host pnpm and Yarn application builds require an explicit profile selection and a build script that writes dist/: builds: project: uses: node/app Host npm packages can also use the inferred package profile described above. Host builds retain native manager configuration and inherited environment. Credentials are excluded from source identities, evidence and reusable results; authenticated host builds currently execute their actions without action-cache reuse. Project credentials omitted from the source projection are supplied in an invocation-owned temporary native config that is deleted after the run. Captured and isolated builds resolve native source settings during preparation. The host broker sends the token only to its configured origin and path. Tokens are excluded from worker configuration, dependency inventories and images. Execution installs the frozen, integrity-checked inventory offline. Captured acquisition supports origin-scoped _authToken, including ${ENV} interpolation, and native always-auth, with project settings taking precedence over user settings and native npm environment settings taking precedence over files. Use HTTPS; HTTP is accepted only for loopback registries. Basic authentication, multiple credentials for one origin, Yarn Berry private registries and arbitrary archive/CDN origins are outside this support. Other refused manager settings remain refused. A missing token, unmapped lock origin, HTTP 401 or HTTP 403 fails preparation; there is no fallback to the public registry. Check the named native setting and refresh the credential. Tokens are redacted from diagnostics. An output containing a known registry token is rejected before it can be exported or reused.

A docker/image target can take the application directory as input: builds: frontend: uses: node/app path: frontend image: uses: docker/image path: image materialize: - from: frontend to: site The image's Dockerfile can use COPY site/ /site/. It receives site/index.html and the generated assets with no extra dist layer. The image build uses the recorded artifact and the matching platform. The image build context is made from the selected source files plus the materialized directories: Directory inputs keep all their files, including empty directories and names like dist that source capture normally skips. Linked inputs, name collisions and paths outside the image target are rejected. The combined inputs may hold at most 100,000 entries and 10 GiB of file data. Oyzu checks that the copied content did not change during the copy. Source ignore rules do not filter materialized artifacts.
documents.s: Use the directory in an image

documents.t: Discovery recognizes a vite build script and selects node/app without a build.yaml. Native Windows x64 builds support Vite 5.4.21, 6.4.1 and 7.3.1 applications, and Vite 8.3.3 library directories, including test and coverage reports. Native npm stages rerun on unchanged builds when execution does not enforce complete runtime reads. Linux stage reuse requires the isolated crun path (oyzu build --isolated --no-docker); Windows native execution currently lacks complete-read enforcement. An unchanged output or stable staging allocation does not bypass that cache-admission requirement. SSR, multiple environments and isolated Windows execution remain outside this coverage.

To write somewhere other than dist/, use vite build --outDir public-site as the native script. The script must be exactly vite build, optionally followed by one literal --outDir <path>. The path must stay inside the project and use only ASCII letters, digits, /, _, - and .. Parent (..) segments, absolute paths, shell expansion, quoting and compound commands are not interpreted. Any other Vite flag fails planning with a diagnostic.

Oyzu uses Vite's own loader for vite.config.js, .ts, .mjs, .mts, .cjs and .cts. Your configuration can pick a mode, add plugins and emit extra assets. Discovery and dependency installation never run the configuration. During the build, Oyzu replaces the private copy's build script with a small wrapper. Your checkout is not changed. Your package manager still runs the prebuild, build and postbuild scripts. The wrapper calls the project's Vite 5–8 build API and records the resolved configuration and the directories written. A literal --outDir takes precedence over the configuration's output directory. Files that postbuild adds to the output directory are included. If your build script is replaced by something that writes no Vite output, the earlier site is not published.

For Vite 5–8, build.lib produces a directory artifact through the same node/app profile. Configure the library in your native Vite configuration: export default { build: { outDir: "library", lib: { entry: "src/main.js", formats: ["es", "cjs"], fileName: (format) => `library.${format === "es" ? "js" : "cjs"}`, }, }, }; Vite resolves entry, formats and fileName, including native defaults, multiple entry points and function-valued filenames. Oyzu collects the complete written directory, including all formats and assets. This is a directory build; use node/package for supported npm package archives. A matching Node plugin release is required; updating the CLI alone does not update the native adapter.

Select node/app with an installed Node plugin. No extra build option or helper file is needed. These commands build a Vite application: oyzu --json build app --full --no-cache oyzu --json build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --no-cache --image npm=<node-image> The second command runs the build in an isolated Linux amd64 worker with network access disabled during execution (see Isolated builds). The build checks that the resolved output path is inside the source, not linked, and was not left over from an earlier run. It then lets Vite write. After your npm command succeeds, Oyzu copies the output tree, including postbuild additions, into the planned artifact. A failed build leaves no usable artifact. Fix the command or configuration and rebuild. Before a build finishes, the implicit lint and format checks may evaluate your Vite configuration separately to find generated-output paths to skip. This does not run the build.

Artifact Name Notes Primary application-<snapshot-version> The output directory. Consumers that don't name an artifact get this one. build-metadata vite-output-<snapshot-version>.json Media type application/vnd.oyzu.vite-output.v1+json. Records the Vite version, snapshot version, project root, output directory and mode. Both artifacts are covered by the bundle's integrity checks.

One client environment and directory output only, for applications and library mode. SSR builds, multiple environments, watch mode and write: false fail with a message. The project root and output must stay inside the project, with no linked parent directories. Rollup (Vite 5–7) or Rolldown (Vite 8) output options must agree with the resolved directory. Vite 5–8 are supported. Vite 4 and older, and majors above 8, fail with a diagnostic naming the supported range. Your Vite plugins are project code. They run under the build sandbox but are not trusted release evidence. A failed build produces no output record. Missing, malformed or version-mismatched metadata fails the build. Fix the cause and rebuild.

With --isolated, Oyzu captures your dependencies first and then builds in a Linux worker with no network access. Use the usual build options. To use your own image instead of the base execution image, add --image npm=<node-image>: oyzu build app --full --no-cache --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --image npm=<node-image> The base execution image and Docker or the Linux daemonless sandbox are required. Tool versions belong in oyzu.toml, not in build.yaml. Isolated builds run on Linux amd64 workers, including from a Windows coordinator. A platform matrix can select matching images (see toolchain platforms). Captured npm, pnpm and Yarn registry archives use tarballs/<64 lowercase SHA-256 hex digits>.tgz in the shared raw archive store. Algorithm-qualified sha256:<hex> identities are validated before naming a file; inventory fields retain bare hex. Offline replay rejects malformed inventory digests rather than using them as paths. Yarn Classic's exported offline mirror retains Yarn's native package/version filenames, including scoped package names. Native-addon recipe recognition scans captured archives identified by SHA-256. Package records without a digest or with another digest algorithm are skipped by that scan; a malformed sha256: identity fails preparation. Captured npm tarballs must match the lockfile's publisher integrity before they are stored. Offline replay checks that integrity, the captured SHA-256 and the byte size again before seeding npm's cache. A mismatch stops dependency preparation before build actions run; restore or recapture the matching archive from the locked registry inputs rather than changing its verification metadata.

An isolated node/app workspace with package-local build scripts and member tests use separate reusable actions for each npm, pnpm or Yarn Classic member on Linux crun. Keep the root free of aggregate build/test scripts to use the manager's conventional member fan-out. Native membership and dependency edges are reused; Oyzu does not parse a second set of workspace patterns. oyzu build app --full --isolated --no-docker --explain An unchanged build reuses admitted member build and member test results. Script-free shared installation keys every member manifest and manager control; contained direct workspace links are restored without following external links. A leaf source edit reruns its build/tests; a shared member edit also reruns its native dependents. Member version projection and dependency output identities participate in these keys. Per-member JUnit/LCOV reports retain their producer's reused label and pass current validation. A metadata-only edit to a member's package.json reruns shared installation. Reuse then differs by package manager: npm: when installation output stays identical, the edited member and its native dependents rerun; an untouched leaf can reuse its build and tests. Yarn Classic: the same narrower reuse applies when installation output stays identical; an unrelated leaf keeps its matching action key. pnpm: installation bookkeeping changes the shared output, so every member's build and tests rerun, even when packaged module bytes stay identical. This is an accepted reuse-precision limit. --explain names a stored result matches this key for npm/Yarn leaf hits and the changed app:prepare-dependencies output for pnpm reruns. All readable installation bytes remain keyed. Any manager reruns all members when shared installation output changes. Shared root configuration, such as .browserslistrc, postcss.config.*, Babel, Prettier, tsconfig*.json, .editorconfig, biome.json(c), .swcrc or .env*, retains the whole workspace view and refuses member reuse with node-member-shared-configuration. pnpm hooks/patches and active Yarn rc settings refuse manifest-only install narrowing. Custom pnpmfile and global-pnpmfile settings in .npmrc or pnpm-workspace.yaml also refuse it. Docker and other executors refuse member reuse with node-member-reuse-requires-crun. Otherwise the enforced member view hides unrelated source. A failing command that prints a hidden path can report confined-read-outside-contract; successful optional missing-file probes are not diagnosed. This is not syscall read tracing, and member scripts must not depend on undeclared sibling/root inputs. A failed command never becomes a reusable success on retry. Aggregate root scripts and opaque root dispatch retain the existing workspace-wide contract. Changes outside declared workspace writes fail before a result can be published or restored. Native host workspaces gain no complete-read admission. See workspace test bundles.

Select node/app at the root of a private npm workspace that has a current package-lock.json. npm decides workspace membership and linking. For example, a root that depends on a shared member and builds it first: {"scripts":{"build":"npm run build --workspace @oyzu-example/shared && node build.mjs","test":"node --test"}} The member builds its module before the root imports it, and the root writes a self-contained dist/. oyzu build app --full --no-cache --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --image npm=<node-image> How it behaves: Your root build script runs once. Oyzu does not expand it into separate member builds. Recognized Node tests at the root produce one aggregate JUnit and one LCOV report. Member tests may run inside that invocation, but members get no reports or versions of their own. Before the build, Oyzu checks workspace membership, the lock and the installed links. Dependencies are replayed offline during execution. Lifecycle scripts run in the private workspace. If a member build fails, the rest of the root script and the artifact export are skipped. Read the native error and fix the member. This produces one directory artifact. It does not create a package archive per member (see npm workspaces). Supported: private npm root with one shared member, isolated on a Linux amd64 worker. Native root workspace applications use the separate workspace test flow. Package-local isolated workspace builds use the separate member reuse flow. Native per-member application artifacts remain unsupported.

The Node plugin builds a single-root pnpm application whose build script writes dist/. Declare an exact stable version in packageManager (for example pnpm@10.11.0), or configure pnpm under [tools] if there is no declaration. Keep a current pnpm-lock.yaml. Run oyzu build app --full. Oyzu runs pnpm install --frozen-lockfile before the build and checks. Node tests get JUnit and LCOV reporters. Your lint and format checks stay as package scripts. An offline build reuses pnpm's prepared store and fails if bytes are missing. Conflicting package managers and packageManager values that are ranges or prereleases are refused. Native pnpm 10 workspace applications follow workspace tests. Isolated pnpm builds are supported with pnpm 10.11.0 on Linux amd64 (see plugin packages). For pnpm settings and lock rules, see pnpm builds.
Single-root Yarn Classic 1.22.22 and Yarn Berry 4.17.1 applications are supported with node/app. See Yarn builds for requirements and commands.

Tasks: oyzu run list shows your native build and test scripts, inferred lint and read-only format checks, and explicit formatting. Listing runs nothing. oyzu build installs dependencies, runs the build, test, lint and format-check steps, then packages. Conventional workspace quality tasks and captured npm aggregate tests omit the generated version default, just like owned single-package checks. This does not narrow lifecycle source reads or make an incomplete native observation reusable. Shipping build, version projection and package commands keep their version inputs and published artifact names. For Vite projects, the fallback ESLint setup includes browser globals as well as Node globals. The output directory is excluded from implicit quality checks. Your own scripts and configuration are never overridden. After a build, implicit quality tasks use its recorded output directory. Before that, they resolve your Vite configuration in production mode. That can run your configuration code on the host for development tasks, or inside the sandbox for isolated tasks. See Node quality for the lint and format defaults. Reports and output: Native Node tests produce JUnit and LCOV. Built-in Node test reporting supports Windows project and temporary-directory paths containing spaces and Unicode. Recognized Jest, Vitest, Mocha and node --test commands support failed-case retries during builds, including --no-cache. The artifact is at dist/<target>/<platform>/application-<snapshot-version> in the build bundle. Read its path from the manifest instead of building the path yourself (see bundle layout). Only the selected output directory is staged. Source files, dependencies and tests are not copied into it. Failed tests or quality checks stop the artifact from being published. Their reports stay in the bundle. Integrity: The manifest records kind: directory, the version, the producing action, a full file inventory and a content digest. oyzu inspect dist checks them (see directory artifacts). materialize copies verified content into a fresh consumer context and keeps the producer's evidence references. A failed operation can leave partial output. It is not recorded as an artifact.

If your project pins Node ([tools] node = "22.12", locked with oyzu install node@22.12), isolated builds run on that exact Node instead of the image's copy.
