Oyzu: Reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) archive recorded for that version in oyzu.lock. Downloads it, unless a cached copy under the user data directory still matches the locked SHA-256. Verifies the bytes against the locked digest. Restores them read-only at /scratch/nodetool. How it is used: The locked runtime and package manager are placed on PATH before system directories. Preparation and every build action use that selection; the base image has no Node or package manager. A different pin or archive changes the action identity. Without a pin, the Node that build preflight locks is used the same way (see Default Node selection). If an engine range has no matching LTS release, a newer stable runtime can be selected without relying on an image-provided runtime. A missing locked Node entry stops preparation and names oyzu pin; the image does not supply a fallback. To test other Node versions, use verification toolsets, which run natively and never in the isolated worker. Limits: Oyzu's test reporting passes Node 22 flags such as --test-coverage-exclude. With a pin older than Node 22, the build works but the native test stage fails with bad option. Pin Node 22 or later if you run tests. Only linux/amd64 workers are supported, and offline builds need the archive already cached. Pinning was tried with the npm image only. How the pnpm and Yarn images handle the changed PATH has not been tried. A locked npm or pnpm release (from [tools] or an exact packageManager) replaces the image's manager the same way. See npm and pnpm installation.

Without a configuration pin, the default request is lts, whether or not engines.node is set. Oyzu picks the greatest stable release marked LTS in Node's index.json that satisfies every engine constraint. If no LTS release satisfies them, it picks the greatest stable release that does. Example: if 24.x is LTS and 26.x is Current, >=22 selects 24.x and >=26 selects 26.x. node = "latest", node = "26", exact pins and lts/<name> keep their usual meaning and must satisfy engines. The nearest .nvmrc or .node-version above the build folder (up to the project root) with an explicit version (22, v22.14.0) is used as the request instead. If neither file exists, an exact devEngines.runtime version is used. An alias such as lts/* is refused with a hint, and a [tools] node value must agree with the file (see native pin files). Explaining and locking: oyzu build --plan shows the LTS default and fallback rule as the requirement source. Pin previews and locks keep the lts request. A matching lock keeps its exact version, including a fallback, without checking today's LTS data. Engine constraints are still checked offline. A lock from the old default (*) does not match the lts default. Resolve it online once before building offline. Under an organization catalog, the signed index has no LTS markers. Use an approved exact version or a named line such as lts/krypton. The moving alias fails with TOOL_LTS_METADATA_UNAVAILABLE and does not contact a publisher outside the catalog.
The base execution image installs libatomic1, which newer Node binaries need. An image you pass with --image npm=<ref> (or pnpm=, yarn=) must provide it too.

Node and a supported npm or pnpm release, installed through tool management. Native builds need compatible tools and your project's dependencies already installed. Installing Node doesn't install your test or quality dependencies (see Node quality). Isolated builds need Docker or the Linux daemonless sandbox and the base execution image, with the locked Node and the pinned quality defaults. Dependencies are captured through your package manager before isolated execution, then replayed offline. No new download route or credential channel is added. For native builds on the host, see local builds.

Platforms: native builds are supported on Windows and Linux. Native Vite configuration output is supported on Windows only. Isolated builds run on Linux amd64 workers, including from a Windows coordinator. macOS, Windows ARM64 and Linux ARM64 are not supported yet. Vite SSR and library modes, compound Vite commands, per-member workspace application output and cross-platform reuse of one directory artifact are not supported. Project build scripts are project code. Isolated builds run them in the offline sandbox; native builds give them your account's access. Executable file modes in directory artifacts are not preserved when a Windows coordinator transfers them (see directory artifacts). The consumers tested read the output with a limited DOM, not a real browser. Browser behavior is not checked.

On Windows, incomplete native reads require the lifecycle/scripts to run again. oyzu build --explain and oyzu cache explain app name this refusal and point to oyzu build --isolated --no-docker on Linux crun for complete-read stage reuse. Clearing the cache does not resolve it. --no-cache must agree with ordinary execution, including failures after external inputs change. Independently admitted complete-read stages and native download caches remain available. See native Windows refusal.
npm workspace builds, pnpm builds and Yarn builds Directory artifacts and build bundles Node quality

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-quality.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Node packages get lint, format-check and format tasks without any Oyzu configuration. lint and format-check only read your files and run as build gates when selected by --full, CI or policy. format rewrites files and only runs when you ask for it. Status: experimental. It works for single packages using npm, pnpm or Yarn, and for npm workspaces. Other workspace forms are not supported yet.

From the package or npm workspace root: oyzu run list oyzu pin oyzu install --frozen oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format Your own scripts and oyzu.toml task replacements win. If package.json defines lint, format-check or format:check, Oyzu runs that script instead of the built-in check. A script named format:check is treated as the read-only formatting task. Owned quality commands do not receive the inferred build OYZU_VERSION default. An explicit project or task value still applies. Vite quality checks without that value resolve the output directory from native configuration; invocations that use versioned retained output metadata still validate its version.

Oyzu picks one linter and one formatter from your project's files: Role Default Chosen instead when Linter ESLint A biome.json or biome.jsonc selects Biome Formatter Prettier A biome.json or biome.jsonc selects Biome Your native ESLint or Prettier configuration counts as stronger evidence than the default. Oyzu reads configuration files without running JavaScript or launching tools. If your files point to two different tools for the same role, discovery fails instead of picking one. Resolve the conflict by removing one configuration, or choose in build.yaml: with: linter: eslint formatter: prettier Task overrides do not bypass this check. See discovery selectors.

Task What it does Changes files lint Runs ESLint or biome lint on your source files No format-check Runs prettier --check or biome format No format Rewrites files with Prettier or biome format --write Yes A build that selects lint and format-check runs them before collecting artifacts. A failure stops the build and no artifacts are collected. format is never part of a build. format is not transactional. If a later file or package fails, earlier edits stay. Conventional npm workspace lint, format-check and format tasks also omit the generated OYZU_VERSION default, including when they dispatch package scripts. Set a project or task environment value explicitly if a script needs it. Workspace build producers retain their version input. The built-in lint and format-check reject extra arguments, so an argument cannot turn a check into a write. To pass custom flags, write a package.json script or an argv task. Oyzu does not guess whether a custom script is read-only from its name. ESLint never applies automatic fixes. With no ESLint configuration, Oyzu uses recommended JavaScript and TypeScript rules. Prettier uses your options, EditorConfig and ignore files. Biome gets explicit file arguments and uses your Biome configuration and ignores. It does not read from stdin. Long file lists are split into batches, and a failure in any batch fails the task. Native diagnostics are shown as they are, with the tool's own exit status. Files a tool ignores can produce no check.

The built-in tasks check JavaScript and TypeScript files (.js, .jsx, .ts, .tsx, and their CommonJS and ESM variants). They do not format JSON, CSS or other files, even though Prettier and Biome can. To format those, write your own script. Source discovery skips dependency folders, .git, .oyzu, .oyzu-build, dist, build and coverage output. It never follows symlinks and stops at 100,000 files. In an npm workspace, the root checks skip member folders, and each member's checks skip nested members. See npm workspaces. For a Vite application, the build output folder is skipped and browser globals are enabled in the default ESLint rules. If the output folder is not known yet, the task reads your Vite configuration in production mode to find it, which can run your configuration code. Discovery and oyzu run list never do this. An invalid or uncontained output path fails the check. In a Mocha project, the default ESLint rules know Mocha globals in test and tests folders and in test and spec files. The default rules also know Jest globals in test files, and Node globals everywhere. A custom test location needs its own ESLint configuration.

Tool Version Oyzu provides Notes ESLint 10.13.0, with recommended JavaScript and TypeScript rules Uses your configuration when you have one. Legacy eslintrc needs a compatible ESLint 8 or 9 installed in your project, or a move to flat configuration. Prettier 3.9.10 Your configuration, EditorConfig and ignore files Biome 2.5.15 Biome 2 only. Other major versions are rejected. TypeScript 6.0.3 backs the default TypeScript parsing (typescript-eslint 8.72.0 supports TypeScript >=4.8.4 <6.1.0). TypeScript 7 is not supported by that parser. Your project can still compile with TypeScript 7. The listed versions are the ones Oyzu provides and uses by default. Other versions in the same major range can work but are not guaranteed.

Tools installed in your project win, including hoisted ones. If your package declares a tool that is missing from its installed dependencies, the task fails. Oyzu does not substitute a different version. Otherwise Oyzu uses the default. oyzu pin records the exact default set under quality.node in oyzu.lock: every package version, upstream URL, upstream integrity and SHA-256, plus the default package files. Commit that lock. pin selects metadata; install --frozen prepares the selected runtime. Host tasks, local full builds and isolated builds use the same locked set in the shared tool store. Preparation installs missing bundles and verifies downloaded bytes before publishing them. Installed tools are then trusted; reuse does not rehash their payloads. No manually provisioned checker directory is needed. Isolated actions restore a read-only archive from that installation without a Node quality image. npm lifecycle scripts never run while the default quality bundle is installed. No build action downloads checkers. New Oyzu releases ship new defaults. Ordinary builds, runs and oyzu pin retain an existing exact set. Use oyzu pin --refresh or a whole-project oyzu update to adopt the defaults shipped by your current CLI; the next task prepares the new installation. See tool commands. Offline tasks need the project lock, selected runtime and quality bundle already available in the same store. Run one online check first. Administrative tool eligibility and fetches.sources restrictions apply during preparation, including reuse. Biome's platform binary package is part of the locked bundle. A missing project-declared tool or unavailable platform fails preparation or execution; no stage is silently skipped. Supported on Linux and Windows. macOS is not supported yet.

Oyzu recognizes a Jest command in a single package or a native workspace member, either a jest script or the inferred test task, and asks Jest for JSON and LCOV output. Your Jest reporters, transforms and test selection stay as you configured them. The native JSON result is converted to JUnit. It is written next to the JUnit destination with .jest.json added to the name. Coverage goes to lcov.info beside the LCOV destination. Failed tests or loading errors, and missing required reports, fail the task. Oyzu refuses to overwrite an existing report file. Move or delete it, then retry. A script that is not a plain jest command keeps its own body and must write its own declared and required reports. If your test script is jest --ci and you want a different report location, declare the reports. An authored task needs run or argv; reports alone does not inherit a command. [tasks.test] argv = ["npm", "run", "test"] reports = [ {kind = "test", format = "junit", path = "reports/custom/junit.xml"}, {kind = "coverage", format = "lcov", path = "reports/custom/lcov.info"}, ] Jest 29.7.0 with npm is supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). Native npm, pnpm 10 and Yarn Classic workspace application builds use the same per-member adapter with oyzu build --full; see workspace tests. Windows workspace builds and other Jest versions remain unverified.

Oyzu runs Vitest through your own Vitest configuration (or your Vite configuration as a fallback) and adds JUnit and LCOV output while keeping your reporters. Scripts that are exactly vitest or vitest run keep their package manager lifecycle. For a project without such a script, Oyzu runs the installed Vitest CLI. Custom scripts are left alone and must meet their own report obligations. Oyzu requires Vitest 5 and a matching installed @vitest/coverage-v8 or @vitest/coverage-istanbul, whichever your configuration selects (V8 by default). A missing or mismatched provider fails before the tests run. Install your project's dependencies with its package manager and retry. Native coverage is always on for the required report, even when your configuration leaves coverage.enabled off. Vitest may read source files that no test imports, so the test action keeps the whole target's source. Your include and exclude rules, reporters and thresholds still apply, and Oyzu does not waive their result. Automatic Vitest commands skip .oyzu/** and .oyzu-build/**, so retained copies of your source do not add test suites. The Vitest reporting adapter runs one worker at a time. This does not change test selection, your timeouts, coverage, reports or gates, but a large suite can take longer within the 600-second action limit. Vitest 5 (tried with 5.0.3) and the V8 provider with npm are supported on Linux and Windows (x86-64). Native npm, pnpm 10 and Yarn Classic workspace application builds use the same per-member adapter with oyzu build --full; see workspace tests. Windows workspace builds, Istanbul, browser mode and other Vitest versions remain unverified.

Situation What to do A tool is declared in package.json but not installed Install your project's dependencies with your package manager, then retry. QUALITY_LOCK_REQUIRED Run oyzu pin, then retry with the same tool store. Offline preparation has no cached default bundle Run a check online with the same lock and store first. Two tools are indicated for the same role Remove one configuration, or set with: {linter: <name>} or with: {formatter: <name>} in build.yaml. Extra arguments rejected on lint or format-check Use a package.json script or an argv task for custom flags. An existing Jest report file is in the way Move or delete it and retry. Invalid configuration or failed rules Fix them as the tool reports. The native diagnostics are authoritative.

Native configurations and plugins can run their own code. Development tasks run on your machine with your task environment. Isolated builds run in the prepared offline environment. Preparation may acquire locked tools; isolated check actions run without network access. Global inherited configuration, some plugin forms and configuration inherited across package managers are not supported. Original-metadata formatting of files that a build rewrites is not supported. Built-in formatting does not cover JSON, CSS or other non-code files.
Mocha Node applications npm workspaces Discovery selectors Biome CLI

With a matching development CLI and Node plugin, oyzu build app --full uses package-owned test units for recognized Jest, Vitest, Mocha and node --test commands. Set [tests] retries = 2 in oyzu.toml to enable two extra attempts locally; CI, PR and release contexts default to two. See test retry settings for policy and check levels. The first attempt disables native fail-fast. A retry starts a fresh native process per selected file and selects only failing full titles with an escaped, anchored regular expression: Jest and Vitest -t, Mocha --grep, Node --test-name-pattern. Native configuration and npm script lifecycle still run. The supported framework versions and prerequisites above and in the Mocha reference continue to apply; this capability requires the matching plugin and has not expanded platform qualification. Case identities contain the package-relative file, native full title and its occurrence among identical titles. An identical-title match can rerun another case; every extra result is fresh evidence for that case. Missing, renamed or skipped requested cases never repair the original failure. Setup/import errors, including Mocha before all, incomplete reports and failed native report gates remain failures. Assertion failures, setup errors, case timeouts and process crashes remain distinct in attempt facts. Jest's native environment events preserve each attempt and its failure kind; JSON invocations and retryReasons provide additional consistency checks. The supplied Mocha reporter records native retry events and resolved retry limits. The supplied Vitest reporter reads retry counts and native errors, including multiple soft assertions in one attempt. Unknown native counts are declared unknown; known counts with ambiguous failure kinds fail report completeness. Native retry configurations suppress Oyzu retries. Unknown histories produce TEST_ATTEMPTS_UNKNOWN and cannot be cached. A native retry that leaves no observable configuration or result marker remains undetectable; no speculative source parsing replaces native configuration. Oyzu supplies its small native reporters, so projects install no Oyzu test library. Node's native event stream supplies file identity missing from its JUnit output; Mocha and Vitest expose retry and setup facts absent from their XML. Rust owns selection, execution and normalization. Native reports and coverage remain required, and complete first-attempt coverage is retained when later attempts select fewer cases. A recovered case reports TEST_FLAKY and follows tests.flaky; a persistent failure retains the original native exit code. Every attempt has its own JUnit and case report; combined JUnit keeps all attempts. Flaky or unknown-history units are never stored as clean results. --no-cache uses the same attempt rules. Offline runs require the native tools and package dependencies already available locally; no attempt downloads a reporting library.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-static-analysis.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu can read a Node package's source and scripts, without running anything, and predict what each build stage will read and write. Use it to see why a build depends on a file, to catch problems that only show up across files (an undeclared dependency, a secret in a browser variable), and to let the isolated build give each stage only the files it needs. Note: This feature is experimental. Names, output and rules can change.

Preview the analysis for a target: oyzu build --plan api Each Node target ends with a Static analysis section. This target never declares ../shared, but its build script copies a file from it, and the analysis reports that read with the script line that does it: api:build · confidence: over-approximate · scope: predicted 10 exact, 1 over-approximate, 0 unknown Reads Path or name Confidence Source Why package.json exact api/package.json manifest ../shared/src/greeting exact api/build.mjs:3 file-read · copyFileSync · outside the target directory .mjs build.mjs exact api/package.json:7 script-entry ! ../shared/src/greeting.mjs is outside api/. Declare it as a source input or a dependency, ... Output shortened. For each stage the section lists the files it is predicted to read, the paths it writes, the environment variable names it reads, the workspace targets it depends on, the tools it needs, and anything the analysis could not bound. Every line shows a confidence and a source (file:line). The analysis only reads and parses files. It never runs project code, scripts, package managers or the network.

oyzu build --plan api # analysis for every stage of the target oyzu build --plan api --stage build # one stage oyzu build --plan api --why ../shared/src/greeting.mjs oyzu build --plan api --unknown # only unknown and over-approximate facts oyzu build --plan api --facts # raw facts, one table row per fact oyzu build --plan api --no-analysis # skip analysis; whole-target scope oyzu build --plan api --json # everything, including the full analysis record oyzu build --check # apply the rule levels; runs nothing Flag Meaning --stage <name> Show one stage, for example build or test. Needs --plan. --why <path> Say, for each stage, whether the path is an input and why. The path is relative to the target or to the repository root. Needs --plan. --unknown Show only facts that are unknown or over-approximate. Needs --plan. --facts Also list every raw fact, grouped by kind. Needs --plan. --no-analysis Skip the analysis. Every stage uses the whole target. Needs --plan. --check Apply rule levels and exit non-zero on a blocking finding. The answer to --why is one of: Answer Meaning input A fact names the path. not-an-input No fact names it and nothing could cover it. covered-by-bound No fact names it, but the limit of an unknown fact covers it. covered-only-by-fallback No fact names it, but an unknown fact with no limit widens the stage to the whole target. --plan analyzes your working tree. A normal oyzu build analyzes the snapshot of the source it captured, before any action runs. Both give the same facts for the same files. When planning, Oyzu lists the tree from file names and sizes and opens only the files the analysis reads, so a large checkout costs a directory walk, not a read of every file.

Confidence Meaning exact Proven from literal text, for example copyFileSync("../shared/src/greeting.mjs", ...). over-approximate A superset that contains the truth: a glob, several resolution candidates, a dynamic import with a known directory. unknown Not pinned down: a computed require, a computed file path, a command the analysis does not model. An unknown only ever widens the result. If it has a limit (a relative import that is missing, a test pattern that is not expanded, a command with no tool profile), it widens its stage only by that limit. If it has none, the stage falls back to the whole target. See bounded unknowns.

Source What the analysis takes from it package.json, lockfiles, .npmrc Ancestor manifests, lockfiles, engines and packageManager tools, main, module, types, bin and exports entry points, files as outputs, and workspace:, file: and workspace-name dependencies Workspaces workspaces globs and pnpm-workspace.yaml members. A bare import of a member resolves to its exports or main. Scripts build, test and lint, with their pre and post hooks, using the script graph tsconfig The extends chain, include, exclude and files, paths aliases, references, and outDir and tsBuildInfoFile outputs Imports import, export ... from, require, literal import() and import x = require(), for relative, alias and workspace specifiers. Every resolution candidate is kept (all extensions, the TypeScript .js to .ts mapping, index files). File access fs read, write, copy, stat and readdir calls with constant paths, including path.join(__dirname, ...), import.meta.dirname, new URL(..., import.meta.url) and process.cwd(). Computed paths are unknown. Environment variables process.env.X, process.env["X"], import.meta.env.X and destructuring. Computed names and whole-object use are unknown. Dynamic access require(expr) and import(expr). A template with a literal directory prefix is limited to that directory (over-approximate). Anything else is unknown, and so is every child_process call. Paths in facts are snapshot-relative with forward slashes, so results are the same on every checkout path and host. Only the build, test and lint stages are modeled.

Human output leads with the outcome, uses aligned tables and reads fine without color. With --json, oyzu build --plan adds an analysis object to its document: Field Contents analyzedFrom working-tree or captured-snapshot snapshotDigest For the working tree, a digest of paths, kinds and sizes. It does not change when a file's bytes change at the same size. per-target stage views confidence, fallback (predicted or target-directory) and counts diagnostics The rule findings record The complete analysis record, with every fact A normal oyzu build reports unknown facts and analysis failures only in the debug log (--log-level debug), with the file, line, construct and what it widens.

Rules read the facts and report problems that are only visible across files and targets. They are advisory by default. A finding never fails oyzu build --plan. It fails oyzu build --check or oyzu build only when you set its rule to enforce. Warning (phantom-dependency): app:build imports `left-pad` at packages/app/build.mjs:2, but packages/app/package.json does not declare it; it resolves today only because package.json declares it and the package manager hoists it. Fix: add `left-pad` to the dependencies of packages/app/package.json. With --json, each finding has rule, severity, message and facts, the ids of the facts behind it. Messages name variables, never values. Severity is warning for a violation and note when the rule could not decide. A finding that rests on an over-approximate fact says so. Rule Reports phantom-dependency A bare package import that the importing file's own package.json does not declare (any dependency section, its own name, or the matching @types package). When the import works only through hoisting, the message names the ancestor manifest that declares it. escaping-reference An import, import glob, CSS reference or literal file read that leaves the target's directory, when the target has no workspace dependency on the package that holds the path. undeclared-env A literal process.env.X or import.meta.env.X read for a name that no task environment of that stage sets and no environment file the stage reads defines. NODE_ENV, MODE, BASE_URL, DEV, PROD, SSR and CI are never reported. A computed name is a note. public-env-secret-name A variable inlined into browser output (VITE_, NEXT_PUBLIC_, PUBLIC_, NUXT_PUBLIC_) whose name has a SECRET, TOKEN, PASSWORD or PRIVATE segment. A bare KEY is not reported, so publishable keys are left alone. exports-target-missing A main, module, types, bin or exports path that is neither in the source nor under anything the build is known to write. If the build's outputs are unknown, the finding is a note. Patterns containing * are not expanded. output-outside-declared A build script or source write to a path outside every output location the build is known to use (a compiler outDir, a framework output or generated directory, warm state). A target with no known output location is not judged. config-unreadable A configuration file (framework config, tsconfig, manifest, environment file, test-runner config such as next/jest) the analysis could not read statically. Always a note. The stage falls back to the whole target. script-wrapper-opaque A script step the closed shell grammar cannot resolve, for example a redirection. Always a note. lockfile-manifest-drift The nearest lockfile no longer matches the target's package.json: a declared range differs from or is missing in the lockfile, or the locked version does not satisfy the range. The fix names the package manager's command (npm install --package-lock-only, pnpm install --lockfile-only, yarn install). redundant-declaration A build.yaml inputs entry inside the target's own directory, which is always captured. An input outside the directory is never reported. lockfile-manifest-drift reads package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json (version 2 or 3), pnpm-lock.yaml (version 5 to 9) and both Yarn lockfile formats. If a directory has several lockfiles, it uses the one packageManager names. It skips what it cannot judge: non-semver specs (tags, git, URLs, file:, link:, workspace:, catalog:, npm: aliases), prerelease locked versions, and packages under overrides, resolutions or pnpm overrides. It does not check transitive entries. phantom-dependency compares manifests only. It cannot see installed node_modules, so it cannot confirm whether an import resolves through hoisting today. A file is judged against its nearest package.json. escaping-reference ignores authored inputs, so a path you already list there is still reported.

Set a level for each rule in the oyzu.toml cascade (see configuration): [analysis.rules] phantom-dependency = "enforce" # off | advisory (default) | enforce [[analysis.suppress]] rule = "escaping-reference" path = "legacy/**" # optional glob over the finding's file reason = "vendored fork, tracked in the migration plan" # required Level Meaning off The rule's findings are dropped from --check and from build logs. advisory Reported, never fails anything. This is the default for every rule. enforce A blocking finding fails oyzu build --check and oyzu build. A finding blocks only if its rule is enforce, it is a warning (never a note), and every fact it cites is exact. An enforced finding that rests on an over-approximate or unknown fact is reported as not blocking, with its confidence, and never fails a build. --check counts those so you can see how much enforcement is held back. A suppression needs a rule and a non-empty reason. path is a project-relative glob over the file the finding cites first (* stays within a directory, ** crosses directories). Without path, the suppression covers every file. A suppressed finding does not fail and is listed under Suppressed. With --json its reason is in suppressedBy. A suppression that matches no finding is reported as a stale note and never fails a build. Suppression changes reporting only, never a stage input or cache key.

oyzu build --check is static analysis only: it prepares, installs, downloads and executes nothing. It selects targets the way build --plan does (including --affected), and you cannot combine it with --plan or the analysis view flags. Exit status Meaning 0 No blocking finding. 1 At least one blocking finding, or the analysis could not complete (the error is shown, never a pass). 2 Usage error. ✗ Check failed: 1 blocking finding in enforced rules phantom-dependency · enforce Blocking packages/app/build.mjs:2 app:build imports `left-pad` at packages/app/build.mjs:2, but ... Fix: add `left-pad` to the dependencies of packages/app/package.json. With --json, the build --plan --json document gains a check object: Field Contents outcome passed or failed counts blocking, advisory, nonBlocking, suppressed, staleSuppressions findings rule, level, severity, status, target, path, line, message, fix, confidence, and suppressedBy when suppressed staleSuppressions Suppressions that matched nothing A normal oyzu build applies the same levels to the snapshot it captured (or, for native host builds, to the working tree) before any action runs. A blocking finding stops the build with the same file, line and fix, and the failed bundle records it. Advisory findings stay in the debug log. A native host build that enforces no rule skips the analysis. Limits: An unknown rule id, a level other than the three, an empty reason, an unknown suppression field or an invalid glob is a configuration error that names the valid ids. analysis.rules and analysis.suppress are whole-value settings. The nearest scope that sets one replaces the lower ones instead of merging per rule. A managed policy can pin a value. build --plan lists every finding and ignores levels and suppressions. Per-rule severity overrides and expiring suppressions are not available.

Each stage script (build, test, lint, with pre<name> and post<name>) is read with a closed shell grammar and resolved into a graph whose leaves are tool invocations. Scripts are read, never run. Every script it visits is reported as an exact fact at its line in package.json, with its command, the tools and unknown constructs it ends in, the scripts it calls, and the chain that led to it (build > build:compile > compile). Construct Handling &&, ||, ;, newline, | Every segment is analyzed, which is a superset of what runs. Comments, quotes and \ escapes are honored. $VAR, ${VAR} A read of that variable, except inside single quotes or after \$. NAME=value cmd, cross-env, env, npx, pnpx, time, command Stripped, and the real program is classified. Unknown flags of these wrappers are unknown. dotenv [-e file] -- cmd The env files are exact reads (default .env). -c cascades are unknown. cd dir Later commands in the same script use that directory. npm run, npm test, pnpm run, pnpm <script>, yarn <script>, node --run Delegation to the script of the same package, with hooks. --prefix, -C, --dir and --cwd select another package. --if-present tolerates a missing script. A missing script is unknown. -- and trailing arguments Appended to the last command of the delegated script. npm run s -w <name>, --workspaces, pnpm -r, pnpm --filter, yarn workspace, yarn workspaces foreach Fan out to the workspace members that define the script. A selector that matches nothing is unknown. A dependency or git-range selector selects every member, which is a superset. npm-run-all, run-s, run-p Script names and name:* patterns. A pattern that matches nothing is unknown. node, tsc Entry files, preloads (--require, --import, --env-file), --test, directories and extensionless names resolved like Node. For tsc: -p, -b, project lists, files on the command line, and --outDir, --declarationDir, --tsBuildInfoFile and --outFile as writes. node -e, node -p and watch modes are unknown. rimraf, del, rm, mkdir, touch, cp, copyfiles, mv, cat, echo, sleep, ... Known utilities. Deletes, creates and copies are writes (over-approximate), reads are reads, and echo-like commands have no effect. A glob or computed target of a write is unknown. Tools with a framework profile Run through the profile when the command runs in the analyzed target's directory. In another workspace member it is unknown. ./script.sh, bash file The file is an exact read. Its body is not analyzed, so it is also unknown. >, >>, < The command is still analyzed. Each target other than /dev/null is unknown. Subshells, $(...), backticks, &, eval, unterminated quotes, other programs unknown. Delegation deeper than 8 levels, or more than 256 script instances in a stage, stops with an unknown fact that names the chain. A cycle is an unknown fact that names the cycle. An unknown leaf widens only its own stage. The generated build command for npm, pnpm and Yarn workspaces runs the member builds, checks their public entries and packs them as one operation. Native packing also reads each package's files selection, ignore rules and lifecycle inputs, so the analysis treats this command as an unbounded read of the target source and keeps the whole target for confinement and cache inputs. An authored root build script keeps its own analyzed bounds. Not supported in scripts: if, for, while, case, functions, aliases, here-documents, glob expansion of shell arguments (an argument glob is unknown except for cp-like reads), concurrently, turbo, nx, lerna, bun and Yarn plug-and-play specifics. Arguments passed to a hook script and .npmrc settings that change scripts (script-shell, ignore-scripts) are not modeled. This is the build stage of a project that uses run-s build:*: Entry points, scripts and frameworks Path or name Confidence Source Why prebuild exact package.json:7 npm run clean build exact package.json:8 run-s build:* build:assets exact package.json:9 build > build:assets · cross-env NODE_ENV=production node scripts/assets.mjs --minify build:compile exact package.json:10 build > build:compile · npm run compile -- --pretty false compile exact package.json:11 build > build:compile > compile · node scripts/stamp.mjs && tsc -p tsconfig.build.json postbuild exact package.json:12 node scripts/report.mjs clean exact package.json:13 prebuild > clean · rimraf dist The entries these scripts reach (scripts/assets.mjs, scripts/stamp.mjs, scripts/report.mjs) are listed as well. In the same project, --stage lint lists redirection to or from "lint.log" is not analyzed as an unknown fact.

tsc -p, tsc -b, project lists and a bare tsc (which searches upward for tsconfig.json; tsc -b looks only in its own directory) predict the compiler's own file list from: The extends chain. This includes extends of a workspace-member package, read through the member's package.json. Any other package is unknown. files, include and exclude. The default exclude applies only when none is set. allowJs, and the priority between a.ts, a.d.ts and a.js. references, with each referenced project's own set. Build-info files for composite and incremental, as warm state. The imports reached from those files, plus the package.json of every directory above each program file and of every workspace member an import resolves to. Not predicted: extends of an installed package, types and typeRoots, lib files and anything under node_modules. Command-line compiler options other than -p, -b, the output flags and files are not applied to the file set. Oyzu does not run tsc --listFilesOnly to check its prediction.

A profile tells the analysis what a build tool reads and writes. It is used when a stage's script runs the tool's command. A value in your configuration beats the convention: an explicit Next.js distDir or Vite build.outDir replaces .next or dist. A value the analysis cannot read makes only the facts derived from it unknown. Script configs (.js, .mjs, .cjs, .ts, .mts, .cts) are evaluated by a small built-in interpreter, never by running your code. It understands object and array literals, string concatenation, path helpers, __dirname, import.meta.dirname and import.meta.url, new URL(...), spread, top-level const, defineConfig(...) wrappers, and relative imports of other config files and JSON. Anything else (another call, a loop, a function parameter, a binding changed after its declaration) is unknown for that value only. process.env.X is recorded as an environment read with an unknown value. Very large or deeply nested configs also become unknown and the message names the limit. Tool Recognized command Notes Vite vite build [--mode m] [--config f] Reads the config and what it imports, index.html (or build.rollupOptions.input or build.lib.entry) and the module graph from there, public/, tsconfig, PostCSS and Tailwind CSS v3. Writes build.outDir (default dist). resolve.alias, import.meta.glob, CSS @import and url(), and new URL(..., import.meta.url) are followed. A plugin other than the React plugins makes the stage unknown. Vitest vitest [run] Reads the config (vitest.config.*, else vite.config.*), files matching test.include minus test.exclude, setupFiles, globalSetup and their imports. test.workspace, projects, includeSource, typecheck, coverage and a workspace file are unknown. Next.js next build Reads the config, app/ route files and metadata files, pages/, src/ variants, root middleware, proxy and instrumentation, public/, and the file set of tsconfig (the type check). Writes distDir (default .next), out/ for output: "export", and the cache. webpack, turbopack, experimental.turbo, swcPlugins, images.loaderFile and cacheHandler make the stage unknown. See route handlers. SvelteKit vite build with sveltekit() in the Vite config (also under Vitest) Reads svelte.config.*, route files under kit.files.routes, static/, hooks, app.html, .env* from kit.env.dir, $lib and kit.alias, and the module graph through each component's <script> and <style>. Writes .svelte-kit (or kit.outDir) plus the adapter's output. Modeled adapters: adapter-static, adapter-node, adapter-vercel, adapter-netlify, adapter-cloudflare and adapter-auto. Any other adapter, a non-constant adapter option, a preprocessor other than vitePreprocess(), a component whose markup uses import( or import.meta, or a <style lang> other than CSS makes the stage unknown. Astro astro build [--mode m] [--config f] [--root d] Reads astro.config.*, src/pages, public/, middleware, actions, content collections loaded by glob() or file(), .env*, tsconfig, and the module graph through .astro frontmatter, scripts, styles and Markdown or MDX. Writes outDir (default dist) and .astro. Any adapter, an integration other than @astrojs/sitemap and mdx() without options, Vite options that can add files, Markdown plugins, a custom image service, experimental or legacy flags, and --outDir make the stage unknown. Nuxt nuxt build, nuxt generate (also nuxi) Reads nuxt.config.*, the source directory and its scanned directories, server/, shared/, public/, .env, css and plugins entries, the standard aliases, and the module graph through each .vue component. Writes .nuxt and .output (and dist for the static preset). modules, extends and layers, local layers/ and modules/ directories, nitro.config.*, .nuxtrc, a Nitro preset other than node-server, node, node-listener, node-cluster or static, and a CSS preprocessor make the stage unknown. React Router (framework mode) react-router build [--mode m] Reads the Vite config with reactRouter(), react-router.config.*, the app directory, every route module named by the route configuration, public/, .env*, tsconfig and aliases. Writes the build directory (default build) and .react-router. buildEnd, presets, serverBundles, a route list the evaluator cannot read, and a Vite plugin other than reactRouter() and vite-tsconfig-paths make the stage unknown. Remix v2 remix vite:build [--mode m] Reads the Vite config with vitePlugin(), the app directory, every route module, public/, .env* and tsconfig. Writes the build directory (default build). routes, presets, buildEnd, serverBundles, SPA mode and another Vite plugin make the stage unknown. The classic remix build is not modeled. Angular CLI ng build [project] [-c name] with the application builder (@angular/build or @angular-devkit/build-angular) or the webpack browser builder Reads angular.json, the build target's options merged with the selected configurations, the tsConfig program, browser or main, polyfills, index, styles, scripts, assets, fileReplacements and each component's template and style files. Writes outputPath (default dist/<project>) and .angular/cache. Other builders, ssr, prerender, serviceWorker, localize, Sass or Less styles, and a PostCSS or Tailwind CSS configuration make the stage unknown. ng test and ng serve are unknown. Nest nest build [--path p] [--config f] [--builder tsc|swc] Reads nest-cli.json, the selected tsconfig and its file set, compilerOptions.assets, and for swc the .swcrc and every source file under sourceRoot. Writes the tsconfig outDir (default dist) and each asset's own output. The webpack and rspack builders, compiler plugins (under swc only with a type check), watch modes and an @nestjs/cli major other than 11 or 12 make the stage unknown. nest start is not modeled. Jest jest Reads the config (jest.config.* or package.json jest), every file under roots, files matching testMatch, setup files, and Babel config for the default transform. preset, projects, moduleNameMapper, testRegex, custom transforms and configs built at runtime (such as next/jest) are unknown. ESLint eslint [paths] Reads the flat config found from the target directory upward, its imports, and the files and directories on the command line. Package presets and plugins, type-aware parsing and legacy eslintrc files are unknown. PostCSS and Tailwind CSS v3 (inside Vite and Next.js) n/a Reads the PostCSS config, tailwind.config.* and what it imports, every file the content globs match, and Browserslist files. Tailwind CSS v4 scans the whole project and is unknown. A test file under src/ is a build input in a Tailwind CSS project (the content scan reads it) and in a Next.js project whose tsconfig includes it (the type check reads it). Excluding tests in tsconfig or the Tailwind content globs makes them non-inputs. Jest lists every file under its roots, so its stage scope is the roots. Next.js next.config.* functions such as rewrites(), redirects(), headers() and generateBuildId are not executed. If one reads a file, that read is not predicted. Sass and Less @import, repeated extglobs, and inline <script type="module"> in HTML are not modeled.

From Next 15, app-router GET route handlers are dynamic unless the file opts into static generation. Environment reads inside a handler that runs only at request time are not build inputs. The analysis decides this per build and per route file, and records its decision as next-get-handler-default with the Next version it used and where that version came from. Input Effect Next version The version your nearest lockfile installs, else the lowest major your declared range allows. Tags such as latest and non-registry specs resolve nothing. Version below 15, or unknown Next 14 default: GET and HEAD reads are build inputs unless the file exports dynamic = "force-dynamic". next.config.* not readable, output: "export", or cacheComponents or dynamicIO set Next 14 default. Next 15 or later otherwise GET and HEAD reads are request-time unless the file opts in. Opt-in An exported dynamic other than "auto" or "force-dynamic", a revalidate other than 0, generateStaticParams, or export *. Metadata routes Routes such as robots, manifest, sitemap, icon and opengraph-image stay static. Reads inside POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and OPTIONS exports are always request-time. A handler defined in another module and re-exported is not recognized, so its reads stay exact. Partial prerendering is not modeled.

For the mode of the command (production for vite build and next build, test for Vitest, or the value of --mode), the candidate environment files are inputs whether they exist or not, because creating one changes the build. Tool Files read, lowest precedence first Vite, Vitest .env, .env.local, .env.<mode>, .env.<mode>.local in envDir (default: the project root) Next.js .env, .env.<mode>, .env.local, .env.<mode>.local (.env.local is skipped in mode test) Nuxt .env at the root, then Vite's .env, .env.local, .env.production, .env.production.local in srcDir Each file fact lists the variable names it defines. Values never enter facts. Names with a prefix the framework inlines into browser output (VITE_* or your envPrefix, NEXT_PUBLIC_*) are reported as public. A mode that is not a constant name, for example --mode $MODE, is unknown.

Facts belong to the stage that needs them. The test stage lists the runner's test files and setup files, and the build stage does not. A test-only edit therefore leaves every build fact unchanged: oyzu build --plan --why tests/extra.test.ts --stage build # not-an-input oyzu build --plan --why tests/extra.test.ts --stage test # input When the runner's configuration cannot be read statically (a computed test.include, a config built by next/jest), only the test stage falls back to the whole target. The build stage does not depend on test discovery and stays bounded. Vitest's test action always keeps the whole target view. Oyzu's reporting adapter turns on native coverage, which can read source files that no test imports. Your Vitest coverage settings and thresholds still apply.

On the isolated (captured) executor path, the analysis narrows the cache key and the source each action can see, for analyzed node/package and node/app operations whose final command it models: build, test and the builder-owned stages below. See confined actions. --affected and the native host path do not use it. Rule findings fail a build only when you enforce them.

Five stages of a Node package run commands the builder chooses instead of a project script. --plan lists their reads under these stages (for example oyzu build --plan --stage package). Stage Command version The version stamp prepare The npm install package npm pack lint, format-check The default ESLint and Prettier checks, for a package without such scripts The same analysis supplies contracts for plugin-planned operations. Oyzu matches the final native command to its model, so an operation named node-pack receives the npm pack reads and node-version receives the version-stamp reads. An authored replacement cannot inherit the original command's model. Unsupported commands and workspace operations retain their explicit whole-target reasons. A README edit can reuse stages that do not read it. npm pack always includes README and license files, even with an explicit files list, so changing a packed README reruns packaging. Default ESLint and Prettier checks read test sources too; a test-only edit can rerun those checks as well as tests. Bare node --test keeps a root-directory read for recursive discovery, so even unread documentation can rerun that test stage. Selecting explicit test files permits the narrower file/import closure. Reuse also requires unchanged version, command and prepared-dependency identities. Inferred-version or whole-target projection changes can still rerun stages after an unread edit; a bounded read contract alone does not guarantee a hit. Absent files are reads. A tool that looks for a file reads its absence. The version stamp probes npm-shrinkwrap.json, .npmrc and .npmignore. ESLint probes every eslint.config.* and .eslintrc* in and above the target. Prettier probes every configuration name and .editorconfig. Creating one changes the stage's cache key. Whole-package reads. npm pack without files (or with a glob in it) reads the whole package directory. The quality checks read every JavaScript and TypeScript file below the target. Implicit native install. If a package has a binding.gyp, gypfile is not false, and there is no install or preinstall script, npm defaults to node-gyp rebuild. The analysis treats this as an unbounded unknown, so preparation keeps the whole target. A postinstall script does not stop the native default. Locked npm preparation. A single-root npm install needs a v2/v3 package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json inventory before its outputs can be bounded. This also applies to dependency-free packages. Without that inventory, preparation runs every time and has no reusable action result; adding a lock does not admit unmodeled lifecycle scripts or native install effects. Not modeled. Workspace roots and members, pnpm and Yarn installs and packs, application package commands, Biome, legacy ESLint configuration, Prettier script configurations and plugins, install lifecycle scripts, dependency install scripts, and local, Git or URL dependencies. Each is unknown for its stage only, so that stage keeps the whole-target key and the others stay confined.

Supported on Linux and Windows. macOS is not supported yet. Profiles cover the tools in the table above. Other build tools, and commands or builders they do not model, are unknown. package.json exports conditions, packages in node_modules, .d.ts lookups in @types and tool installations are not analyzed. A bare import of an installed package yields no read fact, only evidence for phantom-dependency. Limits protect the analysis from hostile input: 1 MiB per file, 256 MiB and 20,000 files per snapshot, 400 open brackets (or an estimated 1,000 levels of nesting) per parse, and a 5,000-file import graph. A file that hits a limit makes its stage unknown and the message names the construct. The depth check over-estimates, so a very deep but legitimate file can lose precision. Non-UTF-8 files are treated as opaque. Symlinks are never followed. A specifier that differs from a file name only by case or Unicode normalization resolves to that file. Other lookups that miss only that way make the target unknown (case-variant-path). A leading byte order mark in a file is ignored, and CRLF files report the same lines and columns as LF files. The analysis is not a replacement for the tools themselves. A prediction is a superset, so a build may read fewer files than listed.

The Oyzu repository has a development script, tooling/measure-node-analysis.py, that compares predictions with what real builds read and checks that hiding every file a stage was not predicted to read changes nothing. It is not part of the oyzu CLI.

Action cache for how unknown reads and confined actions affect reuse Configuration for analysis.rules and analysis.suppress Node applications and npm workspaces Vite application lint and format-check stages that load vite.config.* remain unbounded. The native Vite API executes that configuration and its imports, so these stages keep the whole-target source view and report the Vite config as the reason. The ordinary owned quality-worker read model does not apply to them. For the captured-path reuse regression, developers can run python tooling/test-node-captured-reuse.py --cli <compiled-cli> --plugin-package <node-package.tar.gz> --workdir <new-directory>. It uses an isolated build with an admitted plugin archive, managed Node and the existing execution image. The default fixture selects its test file explicitly. It checks cold, unchanged, unpacked README, test-only and source edits, including cache explanations, delivered module contents and bundle inspection. Use --profile node/app for the application variant, or --test-discovery to keep bare node --test and verify its conservative README-triggered test rerun. Use --add-source to select a build script that copies the source tree, then check that adding a module reruns the build and delivers that module in the artifact. The following unchanged build must reuse every stage. The test requires the shared engine's narrow version and dependency identities; it does not qualify Windows and macOS.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-workspace-tests.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build --full runs native member tests in an npm, pnpm 10 or Yarn Classic workspace and collects each package's JUnit and LCOV reports alongside the application artifact. oyzu run test collects the same reports into a test-only dist/ bundle. Your package manager decides workspace membership. Oyzu picks each package's test runner and collects the reports. No build YAML or reporting section is needed. Status: experimental. Direct test bundles run on the native host. Native workspace application builds require an explicit node/app declaration; Windows workspace build tests remain unverified. Yarn Berry and PnP are unsupported. Package-local isolated builds use the separate member reuse flow. oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist

Declare the existing root application build, whose native build script writes dist/: builds: app: uses: node/app oyzu build --full oyzu inspect dist Run from the workspace root with a current native lockfile. Oyzu prepares dependencies using the selected package manager, runs the root build, and runs the selected tests and quality checks. Without a root test script, each member runs its own script or inferred runner. An explicit root test script remains one aggregate test invocation. No additional test configuration or per-member artifact declaration is needed. The ordinary install stage must be enabled; replacing it with an authored install command is unsupported. Each member gets distinct report filenames in the bundle. Native lifecycle scripts run again on an unchanged build when their reads are incomplete; the shared cache refuses whole-target restoration in that case. oyzu build --explain reports the reason. See native stage reads. Failed native tests fail the build and keep available reports; missing required JUnit or LCOV also fails. Install the framework and coverage provider, or make custom scripts write OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT, then retry. pnpm workspace application builds require an exact pnpm 10 packageManager declaration, such as pnpm@10.11.0. Yarn Classic requires yarn@1.22.22. Package archive builds retain their existing separate limits.

Install the project's dependencies and provide Node and your package manager first. Direct oyzu run test does not install tools or dependencies; full application builds use their normal installation stage. Manager Version tested npm 11.11.0 pnpm 10.11.0 Yarn Classic 1.22.22 Node 22 and 24 were used. pnpm must expose its native executable or JavaScript entry point on PATH; Yarn Classic requires its JavaScript entry point. Normal package installs, native executable links and Oyzu-managed pnpm are supported. Corepack acquisition is not invoked. A missing prerequisite or an unsupported manager major version fails with a message.

oyzu run list reads native markers and scripts without running a package manager. workspaces in package.json marks an npm or Yarn workspace. pnpm-workspace.yaml marks a pnpm workspace, even before a lock exists. Lockfiles and packageManager declarations take part in the normal manager conflict rules. Actual membership is read during test or build preparation. npm uses its installed dependency graph, pnpm uses its recursive JSON list (pnpm list), and Yarn Classic uses its workspace info output (yarn workspaces). Oyzu has no workspace glob parser of its own. pnpm runs with automatic manager-version management turned off. Yarn runs in offline mode and ignores yarn-path. Your other project settings still apply.

Without a root test script, oyzu run list shows the manager's recursive test command. When you run tests, Oyzu reads membership, fixes each package's scope and report files, then runs each member's script or inferred Node, Jest, Vitest or Mocha suite. An explicit root test script owns one aggregate report pair and runs once. A publishable root without a script also gets its own implicit suite, where the manager allows that layout. Its implicit Node suite is omitted if it has no owned tests. Yarn Classic needs a private workspace root. Package scripts keep their manager's argument and lifecycle behavior. Arguments reach each selected test command, and a root script receives them once. Inferred suites skip nested members. Explicit scripts keep their own selection. Dependency preparation may observe an empty test-file list for a root or member; it does not require every package to contain Node tests. An explicit test script keeps native zero-test behavior and must still produce any required reports. An implicit Node test suite for a root or member without owned files is omitted, with an informational “no tests” note in human output and JSON diagnostic events (not a warning) and no test action for that package. Explicitly selecting with.test-framework: node-test still fails if the suite has no owned files. Neither path falls back to recursive discovery of another member's tests. Test frameworks and reporters must already be installed (see native reporting prerequisites). Each package's current JUnit and LCOV files go into the bundle with the plan, logs and manifest summaries. Package names give stable report identities. Captured npm package builds that run a root aggregate test script also omit the generated OYZU_VERSION default from that test command. The selected argv, package-owned report paths and producer dependencies still apply. Declare an explicit project or task environment value if the aggregate script needs one.

The test-only oyzu run test flow above executes on the host. For an isolated workspace build, select node/app at the workspace root and run: oyzu build app --full --isolated --no-docker --explain On Linux crun, package-local npm, pnpm and Yarn Classic build producers and member suites have separate reusable actions. The package manager's existing native membership and dependency edges decide which members depend on one another. An unchanged rebuild reuses each admitted member's build and tests. Editing a leaf's source reruns that member; editing a shared member's source also reruns its native dependents. The key includes member sources, identified dependency outputs, locked registry dependencies and tools. Build producers retain the member version environment; owned test commands omit the inferred OYZU_VERSION default. Explicit project or task values still apply and remain keyed. Restored package JUnit and LCOV reports keep their named producer action, which is labelled reused. Current report validation still applies. A reused report does not mean its tests ran in this invocation. A member sees its own source, native manager startup controls, installed dependencies and explicit producer outputs. Shared root configuration (including Browserslist, Babel, PostCSS, Prettier, ESLint, Stylelint, TypeScript/JavaScript configs, .editorconfig, biome.json(c), .swcrc, .env* and config/.config directories) keeps the whole workspace visible and refuses member reuse with node-member-shared-configuration. A failed command that names a hidden source path can report confined-read-outside-contract; this is a failure diagnostic, not an observation of every read. An optional missing-file probe can succeed without that diagnostic. Member scripts must not rely on undeclared sibling/root inputs. Docker and other executors refuse member reuse with node-member-reuse-requires-crun. Root aggregate scripts and opaque root build dispatch retain their workspace-wide boundary. Native host lifecycle scripts retain the incomplete-read refusal; direct test bundles gain no isolated reuse. Script-free shared installation keys all members' manifests and manager controls. Even a metadata-only member package.json edit reruns installation: npm: identical installation output lets an untouched leaf reuse its build and tests; the edited member and its native dependents rerun. Yarn Classic: identical installation output also preserves unrelated leaf reuse with an unchanged action key. pnpm: shared installation bookkeeping changes, so every member's build and tests rerun even when packaged module bytes stay identical. This is an accepted reuse-precision limit. --explain names a stored result matches this key for npm/Yarn leaf hits and the changed app:prepare-dependencies output for pnpm reruns. All readable installation bytes remain keyed; changed shared installation output invalidates every member regardless of manager. pnpm hooks (.pnpmfile.cjs/.pnpmfile.mjs), patch directories or declared patchedDependencies, and active Yarn rc configuration refuse install narrowing; custom pnpmfile/global-pnpmfile settings in rc/workspace configuration also refuse it (including YAML globalPnpmfile). Their referenced files are not assumed to be covered by a manifest-only key. Isolated Yarn Classic actions use an Oyzu launcher for the locked Yarn JavaScript entry point, restored alongside the selected Node runtime. Relative workspace links can be restored on Linux when they stay inside the workspace and point directly to ordinary files or directories. Escaping, indirect or unsupported links refuse restoration. Install lifecycle scripts, implicit native compilation or runtime-loader uncertainty also keep installation conservative and can invalidate downstream reuse. See Node stage reads and stage reuse. A failing assertion fails the command but lets later suites run, and available reports are kept. A missing tool, malformed metadata or unresolved framework can stop the run before any suite starts. Missing or invalid required reports are errors, including under task overrides. Oyzu never invents a pass for a command that writes no reports. Hooks: Oyzu pre and post hooks use the common task engine. A failed test blocks its success-only post hook. Exact implicit commands get report instrumentation. Replacements in TOML keep their bodies and must write the required reports. Member commands receive OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT. Replacing a whole workspace task means providing each package's reports or explicit report collection paths.
documents.s: Reusing member results in isolated builds

documents.t: Direct test bundles don't rewrite package versions or locks, build archives, or run unrelated quality gates. Full builds retain their normal artifact and quality obligations. Test scripts can write host files and use the host environment and network. Offline manager flags only restrict the manager's own downloads. Installed dependencies are used as they are. Nothing records where they came from. Native workspace application builds produce one root directory artifact; per-member artifacts and native workspace package archives retain their separate builder limits. Modern Yarn workspace tests are not supported. A pnpm pnpm-workspace.yaml with a packages list selects workspace planning. Patch-only settings keep the single-project path. See direct tests for how existing output is preserved and how to inspect a failed bundle.
npm workspace builds, pnpm builds and Yarn builds for isolated builds and packaging Direct tests and Mocha

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/npm-workspaces.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu builds and tests an npm workspace using npm's own workspace membership and installed dependency graph. It handles private aggregation roots and publishable root packages, producing an independent package archive and test reports for each package. Run it from a conventional npm workspace root with no Oyzu configuration. Note: npm workspace support is experimental. Affected-only selection, member task groups and duplicate target selection are not available. See Limits. Builds use the Node builder plugin, which must be installed and selected (see plugin packages). There are three ways to build a workspace: Mode Where it runs Output Section Development tasks Your machine, with oyzu run Test-only bundle Direct test bundles Native workspace packages Your machine, with oyzu build One archive per package External native workspace packages Captured workspace packages Isolated Linux worker (Docker) One archive per package External captured workspace packages Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

From a workspace root that has package.json, its native lock and installed dependencies: oyzu run list oyzu run build oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format For an isolated build, which needs Docker and the base execution image: oyzu build oyzu inspect dist

Requirement Detail Node and npm Provide Node and npm and install the project's dependencies yourself. Oyzu does not install them for development tasks. Tested with Node 22 and 24 and npm 11. Oyzu configuration None required. Quality tools Default quality tasks need the ESLint and Prettier (or Biome) tools and their packages. Installed project packages take precedence. A declared but missing tool fails. If your project has no quality tools, oyzu pin records the defaults described in Node quality. Task preparation installs that exact set in the shared tool store. Project-installed tools win, and a declared but uninstalled dependency fails instead of falling back.

oyzu run list is static. It does not run Node, npm or any project script. Running a task reads the installed workspace using npm's own libraries, so missing dependencies or tools let you list tasks but stop you from running them. Install dependencies with your normal npm workflow, then retry. Before any member command runs, Oyzu checks that: Each installed workspace link resolves to its declared member directory. A link to another directory, or a copied package where a link belongs, fails. Repair the installation and retry. A root package's declared workspace dependency matches the member's actual version, using npm's own validator. An invalid required declaration fails even when a link exists. Optional dependencies keep npm's usual behavior.

Isolated builds version each member using scoped Git baselines and the local dependency graph. A change to an unrelated member does not advance a package's version. Shared root inputs affect all members. Local references in packaged members use each dependency's selected version.

Operation Root script exists No root script build Runs once with npm's lifecycle hooks Runs member build scripts in dependency order. Members without a script are reported as not requesting compilation test Runs once with npm's pretest and posttest hooks Runs each member's test script or detected Node, Jest, Vitest or Mocha runner. A publishable root also runs its own implicit suite lint Runs once Checks root-owned source. Uses each member's lint script or the selected ESLint or Biome format-check Runs format-check or format:check once Checks root-owned source. Uses each member's script or the selected Prettier or Biome check format Runs once, only when you ask Formats root-owned source. Uses each member's format script or the selected Prettier or Biome Native script names show up in task listings, including a root format:check. When that alias owns the operation, run oyzu run format:check. Oyzu does not add a second format-check task. Task replacements in your TOML configuration take precedence over inferred tasks (see configuration).

Each member's installed test framework is found, including hoisted dependencies. Jest, Vitest and Mocha entry points come from their package bin declarations. Implicit Node suites use native test filename patterns and skip nested members and engine state. Explicit scripts keep their own selection, so a script can deliberately cover other packages. A private root with no test script is just a container and gets no implicit suite. A failing assertion fails the run but lets later suites run. Discovery, missing-runner or selection errors can stop the run before later suites start. An implicit Node suite with no owned tests is omitted with an informational note. Explicit test scripts retain native zero-test behavior; required report checks still apply. An explicitly selected Node framework requires owned test files. Node test selection handles at most 4,096 files and 24,000 path characters. A publishable root without a test script joins the conventional workspace fan-out as an implicit suite. Its planned command retains the selected workspace invocation; the native adapter dispatches the root's detected framework without recursively running the workspace command. Member report collection remains required. Authored task replacements and explicit root scripts retain their original invocation and run once as an aggregate. Development test commands keep native console output and forward script arguments. Native scripts and framework configuration run on the host during oyzu run test. Only listing runs nothing.

Default root checks skip workspace members. Default member checks skip nested members, so a parent default cannot bypass a child's own script. The default file scope is JavaScript and TypeScript (including JSX, CommonJS and ESM extensions). Dependency directories, engine state, build output and coverage are excluded, and source symlinks are not followed. Native ESLint, Prettier and Biome configuration and ignore files are respected. Oyzu does not format other file types. Default checks are read-only. format writes files and is never run as an implicit build check. Your own scripts can do anything. A script named lint is not assumed to be read-only. A failed member build stops the builds that depend on it. A failed quality check lets the other members continue, so you see all diagnostics, then fails the run. Files already written by scripts or by format are not rolled back.

Arguments are forwarded to native scripts through npm. An operation that runs a default quality checker rejects extra arguments. Define a native script or an explicit argv task to pass options to a checker. A Biome configuration makes a member use Biome instead of ESLint and Prettier (see Node quality). A cycle in workspace build dependencies fails before any member build starts. A plan larger than 20,000 bytes fails with a host argument-limit error.

For a coarse root build, Oyzu checks the concrete JavaScript files your packages publish before packing: Files selected by Node's import and require conditions must exist. Declaration files selected by the types condition and literal legacy declaration paths must exist. Existence is checked, not TypeScript validity. A missing regular file fails the build. Null exclusions and conditional alternatives are left to Node. The check does not confirm npm put those files in the archive, and it skips browser or custom conditions and wildcard-only paths.

oyzu run test writes a test-only dist/ bundle with JUnit and LCOV for each package. No reporting configuration is needed. Run oyzu inspect dist to check the bundle. See direct tests for how existing output is preserved and what the bundle does and does not claim. For pnpm and Yarn Classic workspaces, see workspace test bundles. An explicit root test script owns one aggregate report pair. Otherwise each member has a pair, plus a pair for the root when it is publishable. Report names use the same package identity as isolated builds. Each suite's allocated filenames include its report identity, such as package-api-junit.xml and package-api-coverage.lcov, within that suite's report directory. Members can use the same native report basenames without colliding in the protocol. Bundle manifest paths identify the collected files; destinations remain unique ignoring ASCII case, including on Windows. A failing assertion fails the command but keeps the reports that exist, and Oyzu's success-only post hook is skipped. These bundles hold host test results. They are not versioned build artifacts. What it uses: Your installed dependencies. Oyzu does not download dependencies, update versions or rewrite the lock. Normal host network access and npm configuration apply. Install dependencies before running tests. The report contract is built before hooks and prerequisites run. Membership and installed links are read only after you ask for a test run. Listing still runs no native code. Jest, Vitest and Mocha read configuration from the package under test. Prerequisites match the single-package profiles. Vitest needs its matching coverage provider and Mocha needs c8. See Mocha.

A custom command keeps its body but must write the required reports. It receives per-package OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT paths when run by the workspace composition. Replacing the whole workspace test task means your task must write each package's reports or declare report collection paths. A command that exits successfully without writing reports now fails. Oyzu never invents a passing report. Report declarations on a root aggregate can redirect the single pair. Redirecting each member's report through configuration is not supported.

oyzu build runs isolated. It needs Docker and the base execution image, with Node (and any pinned npm) restored from oyzu.lock. It captures your source and locked dependencies, resolves the workspace graph and prepares versions in a private copy. oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Execution replays prepared dependencies offline. Acquisition uses your configured sources, and the build itself cannot download anything else. Development oyzu run tasks use the host environment and do not have this isolation. Isolated builds also recognize package-local lifecycles (pre, build, post), including literal copy outputs beside the manifest. Members and a publishable root are built in dependency order, even when npm's membership data doesn't name the root as a link target. Known protected or foreign writes are refused before any fallback. Opaque or fan-out root scripts keep the root-owned route with public-entry validation.

Each member produces its own npm archive. Its version contains the captured source identity. A root without "private": true also produces a root package. A private aggregation root does not. Local dependency references are rewritten to the members' snapshot versions. npm selects package contents. Engine state is excluded. Root staging rejects symlinks, inconsistent file lists and selections over 100,000 files or 1 GiB. Your manifests and lock are never edited in place. Making an archive, even for a private member, does not publish it. Members that share a package name, or are versioned latest, fail before acquisition (see Member names).

Every member needs a lock record, and its recorded name (if present) must match the member. A member's own version in the lock is left to npm ci, which reconciles it with package.json. Planning reads versions from package.json and writes them into the private copy's lock. A stale lock that npm itself rejects, such as a member version that no longer satisfies a sibling's dependency, fails during acquisition with npm's own error.

file: dependencies on local folders work in workspaces and single projects. npm records each as a link ("link": true) plus a lock record for the folder, for example "@oyzu-example/fixture-helper": "file:tools/fixture-helper" (see the npm-file-link example). The folder must be a relative path inside the captured source and outside node_modules. It needs its own lock record and package.json, with no symbolic link on the way. npm links it during installation. The folder is captured as source, never downloaded. Registry packages that npm locks under the folder (tools/fixture-helper/node_modules/...) are captured like a member's. A link to anything else fails with npm link is not a captured native workspace or local folder. The folder is not a workspace member. It gets no artifact, tests or version of its own, and root quality checks cover its source as root-owned files.

An explicit root test script runs once as one aggregate. Otherwise member suites run individually, and a publishable root needs its own tests too. Node, Jest, Vitest and Mocha produce JUnit and coverage automatically. Custom commands must write their reports. An implicit root Node suite with no owned tests is omitted; it never borrows a member's tests. Explicit framework selection still requires owned test files. Implicit suites use the same package-scoped test selection as development tests. A parent suite never rediscovers its nested members. Recognized framework commands expose one retry unit per package. Failed-case retries retain each package's complete first-attempt coverage and never borrow a sibling's passing result.
