Add the schema line at the top of the file and an editor with Taplo (for example VS Code's Even Better TOML) completes keys and flags wrong values: #:schema https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu-releases/releases/latest/download/oyzu.toml.schema.json oyzu config schema oyzu.toml prints the same schema offline. The CLI's own checks stay authoritative; see editor schemas.

Command Does oyzu config validate [--strict] [--all-profiles] Checks every file; --strict also fails on warnings. oyzu config get <key> Prints the effective value. oyzu config explain <key> Shows the value, every source that set it, and why it won. oyzu config show Prints the whole effective configuration. oyzu config set <key> <value> (--project | --local | --global) Writes a value to the project oyzu.toml, its oyzu.local.toml or the user file; exactly one is required. Add --profile NAME to write inside that profile. oyzu config unset <key> (--project | --local | --global) Removes it from that file, exposing inherited values. oyzu config profiles Lists profiles and which is selected. oyzu config schema oyzu.toml Prints the JSON Schema. None of them run project tasks. Add --json for machine-readable output.

Code Means Fix CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE A value has the wrong type or is out of range The message names the file, line and allowed values. CONFIG_SCOPE The setting isn't allowed in this file (a credential destination in a project file, [publish] in a folder, a trust setting in a profile) Move it where the message says. CONFIG_PROFILE_TOOLS [profiles.<name>.tools] Use [toolsets.<name>.tools]. CONFIG_TOOLSET_UNKNOWN --toolset names a toolset this folder doesn't see The message lists the toolsets defined here. CONFIG_TOOLSET_INVALID Bad contexts or platforms, or a non-tool key under a toolset's tools Fix the toolset fields. CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED A value contradicts a policy or project constraint Use an allowed value, or change the constraint. CONFIG_CONSTRAINT_INVALID A [constraints] entry is malformed or names a setting a project can't constrain Follow the message. CONFIG_UNKNOWN_OPTIONAL Unknown section or key (a warning) Check the spelling hint; --strict makes it an error.

Configuration concepts: the three files and why each exists. Configuration behavior in depth: precedence details, policy selectors, native pins, CI detection and migration. Tool commands and shell activation.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-catalog.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Every build target in Oyzu is built by a builder plugin. The plugin catalog tells oyzu which plugins exist, how to recognize a project they can build and where to download them. This page explains how oyzu finds the catalog, detects your project, chooses a builder, and shows you what it chose and how to change it. Note: Plugins are experimental. No builder is built into the CLI. Each target needs a plugin from a catalog, a package you bind yourself or a local development binding. When none is available, the build fails with advice; it never falls back to another builder. The official catalog lists Docker, .NET, Go, Helm, Java, Node, Python, Rust and Zig builders. Some releases require preview opt-in.

Go has a stable release and needs no preview opt-in. For builders that only offer previews, opt in through your user configuration (a project file cannot set this): [plugins] preview = true Run oyzu build in a Go module. Oyzu detects go/app from the catalog, downloads the selected oyzu/go release from ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go (anonymously, with its signature checked), records the release in oyzu.lock and builds with it. The build prints the choice in its Builders section with the source official default. You don't need a binding or an account. A plugins.packages binding still works and takes precedence if you want to supply the package yourself. A real oyzu build --isolated or oyzu build --no-docker adopts its selected plugins before checking executor placement. That first acquisition uses the same catalog verification and lock rules as an ordinary build. The placement preview then reads the installed selection offline. --offline still refuses a missing catalog package, and --frozen never adopts an unlocked selection. Plan-only commands remain offline and do not install plugins or write plugin selections.
documents.s: Quick start: build a Go project

documents.t: Setting Values Default Where it can be set plugins.preview true, false false User, machine or administrative configuration plugins.packages Table of builder reference to a package archive or OCI release (plugin packages) none User, machine or administrative configuration plugins.development Table of builder reference to a local executable (plugin development) none User, machine or administrative configuration toolIndex.* Which tool index, and so which catalog, to use (tool index) The official index User, machine or administrative configuration These settings select code that runs on your machine, so a project file, oyzu.local.toml or a profile can't set them (CONFIG_SCOPE).

Each command picks one catalog snapshot at the start and keeps it, so two lookups in one command never see different catalogs. The snapshot is the published catalog of your configured tool index: the official one, or your organization's. No catalog is built into the CLI. Tool index plugins.preview Catalog used A real build fetches it Official (default) on The official catalog, plus the preview supplement Yes. A copy fetched in the last 3600 seconds is reused Official off The official catalog; cached preview supplement for lock replay only. No new preview selection Yes, primary catalog only. A copy fetched in the last 3600 seconds is reused toolIndex.url = false any None No Organization (toolIndex.identity or toolIndex.trustedRoot set) any Your organization's catalog only Yes. A copy fetched in the last 3600 seconds is reused When a builder in the build came from a catalog, build output names that catalog on the Builders heading, for example official catalog serial 17 or acme catalog serial 3. The serial is the catalog's version number. A build whose builders are all local development executables or direct bindings names no catalog. The Builders section lists only the builders of the builds being built: oyzu build cli doesn't list the docs build's builder. How the catalog is verified. The catalog is plugins.json and plugins.json.sigstore.json, published next to index.json in the tool index release and signed with the same identity (tool index). Oyzu: verifies the signature with the index's trusted root and identity; checks the document's content digest, structure and size limits; refuses a catalog at or after its expires_at; refuses a rollback: a lower serial number, the same serial with different bytes, or a higher serial generated earlier. The last verified copy is kept in <store>/catalogs/plugins/ and the rollback floor in <store>/state/plugins/. If a newly fetched copy is refused, oyzu ignores it and keeps using the last verified copy, including its withdrawals. The 3600-second reuse window is separate from expires_at. A copy can expire sooner and still need a refresh. oyzu build --frozen refreshes catalog metadata the same way, so current withdrawals still apply, but it never changes the locked selection or downloads a missing package. --offline and read-only commands never fetch. Organization catalogs replace the official one. With an organization identity, oyzu never consults the official catalog. If that catalog selects a release and its bytes are unavailable, the build fails. If it has no matching entry, the reference is refused. Another catalog never supplies it.

When no catalog is usable, the reason decides what happens. It's the same for uses: references you write and for detected ones. Why there's no catalog Locked selection Reference not yet locked Refused: a fetched copy failed signature, decoding, expiry or rollback checks and no verified copy is cached, or the cached copy fails those checks Refused on every command, including --plan: PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE Refused: PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE Expired: the last verified copy has expired Replays oyzu.lock against that copy's withdrawals, with the warning PLUGIN_CATALOG_EXPIRED (newer withdrawals may be missing). JSON marks the catalog expired: true Refused Absent: nothing published, reachable or cached, and no catalog was ever verified in this store (a first run offline, or toolIndex.url = false) Replays from oyzu.lock Needs a package or development binding; otherwise PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE A plugins.development or plugins.packages binding for the reference works without a usable catalog, but never past a withdrawal or revocation that the last verified copy (even an expired one) lists for that release. If the network blocks the fetch on a machine that has never verified a catalog, the state is "Absent": a lock replays without any withdrawal check. When a refresh fails and the last verified copy decides, the Builders section shows note using the last verified <catalog>: <reason>, and JSON carries it as catalog.note.

The official catalog supplies signed first-party builder packages for Docker, .NET, Go, Helm, Java, Node, Python, Rust and Zig. Go, Java, Python and .NET have stable releases; the other builders currently require preview opt-in. The stable .NET 0.1.0 release declares the dotnet-lock-admission capability that .NET builds require. A stable plugin release does not expand the platforms or features supported by its builder. Use oyzu plugins search --refresh to see the current set, and oyzu plugins versions <reference> to check compatibility before adopting a release. Builds keep the exact selection in oyzu.lock. They refresh the primary catalog even with plugins.preview off, so stable releases and withdrawals can be discovered. Offline on a machine that has never obtained the catalog, a builder reference needs a lock entry or a binding.

With the default tool index and plugins.preview on, oyzu can also read a second signed document, plugins-preview.json, from the public plugins-preview release of oyzuai/tool-index. This supplement isn't available yet: no supplement is published, so it adds nothing today. Organization catalogs never fetch it. Once it's published, these rules apply: It can add official preview releases. It can't add stable releases or another publisher's packages, and it can't change or replace anything in the main catalog. Official withdrawals always win. A withdrawal in the supplement matches package, version and root digest together. Each document has its own serial, expiry and rollback state. A preview release found in it is signed by a person's identity (not the release workflow) under Sigstore's production roots. A release marked as a local preview but listed as stable is refused. New downloads need a current verified entry. An expired copy can still refuse a release but can't permit a download. Turning plugins.preview off stops new preview selection; a locked, installed release still replays unless a current refusal applies.

A catalog detection maps files in a directory to a builder reference. The matching is deliberately simple: exact marker file names, a few checks on JSON, TOML and go.mod fields (present, equals, prefix), and all, any and not. There are no globs, paths, expressions or commands. Only detections for references this build could actually use take part: a reference with an eligible release, a lock entry or a binding. Marker names match case-exactly. A symbolic link isn't a marker. A file that can't be parsed counts as having no field, not as an error. The work is bounded: 100,000 directories, 512 parsed files, 32 MiB parsed and 1,024 findings. Reaching a bound fails with PLUGIN_DETECTION_INCOMPLETE; declare your targets in build.yaml to avoid it. An explicit build.yaml is the full list of builds. Detection doesn't run, and an incidental file adds no target. Without one, a directory becomes a target when a catalog detection or a native convention recognizes it. Dependency and output directories are skipped, and nested repositories and build.yaml directories are boundaries. If one directory matches different references (two catalog detections, or a catalog go/app beside a native-convention rust/app), discovery stops with PLUGIN_DETECTION_CONFLICT. It names the evidence for each candidate and the build.yaml line that settles it. If exactly one candidate is already locked, the lock wins and the others become a note.

A reference gets its builder the same way whether you wrote it as uses: in build.yaml, the catalog detected it, or a native convention recognized it. Oyzu tries these in order: A plugins.development binding (plugin development). A plugins.packages binding. If its digest matches the catalog's selected release, it's that release's local archive route, and the package's publisher, name and version are checked against the catalog before installation. Any other digest is a local package binding. A binding for a withdrawn or revoked release is refused with PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN or PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED before it's recorded or launched. A binding that names a different release than oyzu.lock fails with PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH until you remove the lock entry. The release oyzu.lock already holds, replayed even if the catalog now lists a newer one. A locked release that a catalog has withdrawn or revoked is refused, naming the lock entry to remove so the next oyzu build can adopt an eligible release. If an organization catalog now binds the reference to a different package, the build fails with PLUGIN_BINDING_CHANGED so the change is adopted visibly, never silently. The catalog's newest eligible release of the reference's package and profile. A release is not eligible when it is withdrawn or revoked, is a preview and plugins.preview is off, is unsupported, doesn't support protocol generation v1alpha1 or the builder profile, or has no payload for this machine's OS, architecture and ABI. A release is a preview when its version has a prerelease part or the catalog marks it as a preview. A stable release needs no preview opt-in. Selection orders eligible versions semantically, so 0.1.0 outranks its 0.1.0-preview.N releases even with previews enabled. A missing host payload excludes that release and the refusal names the package, version and reason; it never enables a preview implicitly. A lock of a preview stays usable after opt-out until withdrawn or revoked. To adopt a stable replacement, run oyzu plugins update; builds never move a lock silently. These rules describe selection when such releases are listed, not a claim that a stable release is published. If nothing serves the reference, the build fails with PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE and the catalog's reason. Some packages need a supporting plugin. For example, a Python application container uses the Docker package, and a Docker dependency context uses its own ecosystem's package. Oyzu selects those through the same order and the same organization boundary before it writes the lock or starts any work. If selecting one fails, the lock isn't changed. A frozen or offline build needs the complete locked set.

A real oyzu build downloads a catalog-selected release from an OCI or HTTPS route in its catalog entry, using the same installer as an OCI binding. The download is anonymous, by the listed root digest, with the same package, platform and withdrawal checks. Oyzu records exactly that root in oyzu.lock. When both route types are listed, the first OCI route is used; otherwise the first HTTPS route. A failed route never falls back to another route or catalog. See HTTPS layout archives for the mirror format. With an existing lock and an empty plugin store, an online, non-frozen build downloads the exact locked digest from its entry in the current catalog, even when a newer release is listed. It doesn't rewrite the lock. A release already in the store is reused without a request. Routes only ever come from the verified catalog, never from project files. Only a real oyzu build adopts or installs a plugin. Every other command (build --plan, --check, run, discover) replays the lock and the store. An unadopted catalog selection there fails with PLUGIN_NOT_ADOPTED: nothing is downloaded, installed, launched or written. Help, --version, shell activation and oyzu exec never load a catalog or select a builder.

The signature rule follows the package's publisher, on whatever registry serves it. Package What oyzu requires Publisher oyzu (for example oyzu/go) A signature from the plugin-release.yml workflow of oyzuai/oyzu on refs/heads/main, from a GitHub-hosted or self-hosted runner, verified against Sigstore's production trusted root. This holds for the official ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/<name> route and for a company mirror. Nothing in a catalog or in configuration can name another signer or root Any other publisher (for example acme/go on a company registry) Trusted by digest: the signed catalog lists the root digest. No signature is requested A mirror of an official package must therefore serve the release's signature referrers as well as its root, manifests and blobs, and the root it serves must hash to the digest the catalog lists. A refused mirror reports one of: PLUGIN_SIGNATURE_MISSING: no signature referrer. PLUGIN_SIGNATURE_INVALID: no signature verifies for the official signer. PLUGIN_PACKAGE_DIGEST: other bytes under the listed root. Nothing is installed or recorded when a mirror is refused. A company catalog can't pass off its own build as oyzu/go; list it under its own package name instead.

plugins.preview = true makes preview releases eligible. Set it in user, machine or administrative configuration, never in a project file: oyzu config set --global plugins.preview true CI ignores user-scope plugin settings, including the opt-in above. In a disposable Linux job container, enable previews through machine scope instead: mkdir -p /etc/oyzu (set -C; printf '[plugins]\npreview = true\n' > /etc/oyzu/config.toml) CI=true oyzu plugins update rust/app@0.1.0-preview.6 This writes /etc/oyzu/config.toml, not a project file. Keep it in the job's container, never on a shared runner host. Exact preview versions still require this opt-in; routine and major-version updates do not select previews. Policy constraints and all catalog, signature and package checks still apply.

A build with plugin-backed targets shows the choice in a Builders section, after Prepare and before Scope (when present) and Plan. Scope separately explains --affected, Not narrowed fallbacks and requested/required targets. When the build adopted a selection or installed a package, each target gets a full record. Output shortened. -- Builders --- official catalog serial 18 ok go/app project oyzu/go 0.1.0-preview.1 (adopted) · adopted and installed now selected by go.mod module (rule go-module, official catalog serial 18) source official default · from official catalog serial 18 · preview release (plugins.preview) package installed now · sha256:0382c192…ee48 · 710.6 KiB · from /home/me/go-0.1.0-preview.1.tar.gz lock recorded in oyzu.lock now; review and commit the diff tool go 1.27.2 · installed now · go.mod requires go >=1.22; nothing pins it not what you wanted? not a go/app target? Declare the targets you want in build.yaml; undeclared directories add none build.yaml: {builds: {project: {uses: <builder>, path: .}}} another implementation of go/app? Bind its package for this reference (or use your organization's catalog) and select again oyzu config set --global --json-value 'plugins.packages."go/app"' '{"archive":"<path>","sha256":"<digest>"}' && rm oyzu.lock undo this adoption: revert oyzu.lock and this reference's settings (plugins.preview is the global preview opt-in) rm oyzu.lock && oyzu config unset --global 'plugins.packages."go/app"' && oyzu config set --global plugins.preview false another go version? Pin it in oyzu.toml oyzu pin go@<version> When nothing changed, each target is one line: -- Builders --- official catalog serial 18 reused go/app project oyzu/go 0.1.0-preview.1 (locked) · reused from oyzu.lock Field Meaning selected by uses in build.yaml, the catalog detection (evidence, rule and catalog), or the native convention source official default, company binding (organization catalog), local package binding, direct OCI source (an explicit URI), local development binding, or oyzu.lock (a locked release no current source explains). Followed by the catalog that listed it, and preview release (plugins.preview) or prerelease version where it applies package installed now with the release digest, archive size and route, or reused from the store lock Adopted now (a reviewable oyzu.lock diff), replayed, or not locked (development binding) tool Each tool this target needs, its version, whether it was installed now, and why not what you wanted? One copyable fix per case. For an earlier lock, the last line is oyzu plugins update <reference> Rows explain their glyphs: ↺ means reused from oyzu.lock (or reused development binding for an unlocked local executable), ✓ means adopted or installed now, and ! means not adopted or not installed. Without color, these marks are words (reused, ok, warn); the explanatory wording stays in the row. Notes follow the targets, for example a competing detection kept out by a lock, or why an expired catalog was used. With --json, the same record is in the build manifest under extensions["oyzu.dev/plugin-selection"]. There, state can also be not-adopted or not-installed.

Adoption happens only in a real build, always shows up as an oyzu.lock diff, and never prompts. What went wrong Fix A stray file added the wrong ecosystem Declare the targets you want in build.yaml (the printed line). The stray directory adds no target and its builder is never downloaded Right ecosystem, wrong implementation Run the printed oyzu config set --global --json-value 'plugins.packages."<reference>"' … line to bind another package, and remove the lock entry Right builder, wrong tool version oyzu pin <tool>@<version> writes the pin to oyzu.toml Ambiguous evidence (npm and pnpm lockfiles, two catalog detections) Discovery stops and names the smallest build.yaml selector. Nothing is guessed or installed Undo an adoption git checkout -- oyzu.lock (or rm oyzu.lock if this build created it), then remove the reference's plugins.packages entry if it supplied the bytes, and turn plugins.preview off for a catalog preview

Code Cause Recovery PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE No plugin serves the reference. The message gives the catalog's reason, for example "preview only" Turn on plugins.preview, or bind a package PLUGIN_DETECTION_CONFLICT Different references match one directory Declare the target with uses: in build.yaml PLUGIN_DETECTION_INCOMPLETE A detection work bound was reached Declare the targets in build.yaml PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN, PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED A catalog (an expired copy included) withdrew or revoked the locked release, or the release a plugins.packages binding names Run oyzu plugins update <reference> (it needs a binding or the store to supply the replacement), or remove the named [[plugin]] entry and build. For a binding, bind an eligible release or run the oyzu config unset --global … line the error prints. oyzu plugins list marks refused copies (withdrawn) or (revoked) and nothing can select them PLUGIN_BINDING_CHANGED The organization catalog binds the reference to a different package than the lock Remove the named [[plugin]] entry and build to adopt the new binding PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH A plugins.packages binding names a different release than the lock Remove the lock entry, or restore the binding PLUGIN_LOCK_MISSING build --frozen needs a plugin selection that's not in the lock Restore the complete lock PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE A locked release is missing and --frozen or --offline forbids downloading it, or no current catalog entry supplies it Run an online, non-frozen oyzu build that can reach the route PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE A new catalog selection has no usable download route, or this run forbids it Run online, or bind the archive with the release digest (plugins.packages) PLUGIN_ROUTE_FAILED The release's route can't be used (registry unreachable, release missing, or an unusable address). Nothing was installed or recorded Restore access to the route. Signature, digest and package failures have their own codes PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE No usable catalog and the catalog was refused, or an unlocked reference met an expired one Restore access to the catalog, or use a binding. Oyzu never falls back to another catalog PLUGIN_CATALOG_EXPIRED (warning) A lock replayed against an expired catalog's withdrawals Run an online oyzu build to refresh. If the refresh was refused, fix the catalog source PLUGIN_PACKAGE_MISMATCH The archive isn't the catalog's package and version Bind the right archive PLUGIN_NOT_ADOPTED A command other than oyzu build met an unadopted selection Run oyzu build

--frozen and --offline never download from a catalog route. A missing locked release needs an online build or a binding. Builds refresh the primary catalog independently of plugins.preview. Only the preview supplement requires the opt-in to refresh. Inspection commands have an explicit --refresh, which doesn't grant preview selection. A catalog entry lists the platforms a release was built for (macOS, Linux and Windows). Go builds through an HTTPS mirror have been tested on Linux x86-64 and Windows x86-64. Other platforms in a package aren't tested. A revocation refuses selection and launch of an installed release, even from an expired copy. The bytes stay in the store until you run oyzu plugins prune SHA256... --apply. @vN major selectors in uses aren't supported. Update with oyzu plugins update. oyzu config validate only replays what's already locked. It never adopts a release or installs a package.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-development.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Captured Go intent includes prepare-tests, with packages and a workspace directory under .oyzu-build/tests/. Its manifest and compiled tests are declared producer outputs. The test command's optional prepared_manifest consumes that output through a produced relationship and read declaration. The captured command binds OYZU_GO_TEST_MANIFEST to that same path; core rejects inconsistent intent or a missing producer. Core identifies current bytes before lookup and refuses undeclared carried files. Native-host tests omit the field and retain their existing admission. The plugin contract evolves in place; older engines refuse unknown commands.

Core admits execution history only for complete native test reports under an already admitted unit/case key. Builders keep native failures and report all cases, including setup/error facts. Optional compiled-manifest test_failure_exit_code constrains ordinary assertion exits; optional test_failure_report = "nextest-junit" additionally requires the native nextest failure type. Modern attempt reports supply validated completion and failure-kind facts without these legacy hints. Neither hints nor native retry facts authorize quarantine: the configuration cascade controls it, default off, and release and governed main CI ignore it. Unknown descriptive report fields remain tolerantly readable; unknown execution controls never grant authority. See quarantine configuration.

An optional builder describe feature, rerun-cases, advertises exact case selection through the existing JSON OYZU_TEST_CASE_IDS in the run phase. Core owns retry policy and cache admission. Without the feature, JUnit-reporting tasks use whole-unit or whole-step retries. The first-party Rust package template also lists rerun-cases as a required engine feature. Its signed release therefore needs a supporting driver (Oyzu 0.4.0 or newer); an older engine refuses it before running a plugin operation. The optional describe advertisement controls case filtering independently. Without it, a retried unit reports TEST_RETRY_UNIT and reruns all its cases. Core supplies OYZU_TEST_ATTEMPT (one-based) and OYZU_TEST_ATTEMPT_DIR, relative to the report root: units/<sha256-of-unit-name>/attempts/<n>. Each directory is fresh. The adapter writes junit.xml and cases.json with schema_version: "v1alpha1", unit, attempt, end, and a cases array. Each case carries its exact id, outcome (passed, failed, skipped), failure kind when failed (failure, error, timeout, crash), optional rerun_group, junit identity (classname, name), and optional native attempts. end distinguishes normal, crash, timeout, killed, and truncated. The SDK supplies shared directory, selection, JUnit parsing and writing helpers in native::test_attempts. Compiled units may declare native_retries with mechanism, max_attempts and attempts_visible. An attempt report may declare the same native_retries object when the runner exposes that fact only during execution. Runtime facts refine the prepare declaration and remain subject to the policy maximum. A visible declaration requires a complete, counted attempts history for every reported case, including the final outcome. Core never stacks its retries on native retries. Invisible attempts warn and prevent storage. A retry missing any requested ID stays failed. Core checks cases.json against JUnit before trusting it. The Go adapter uses the same phase and case-result contract: its typed native go command test carries packages and an allocated report_dir. Preparation uses Go's package inventory and compiled test executable digests; run translates case IDs into anchored, escaped -run patterns, one invocation per case. go test -json conversion retains repeated results and failure kinds. Go has no native retry mechanism to declare. No private retry callback is involved. Combined JUnit remains at the existing unit path; oyzu.outcome also accepts flaky, and the unit cannot be stored as a clean result. Python's existing ExecutedTestCase facts also carry optional kind, using the same failure vocabulary. Its selective-reuse report and attempt reports derive from the same pytest events; setup errors remain errors when reuse combines JUnit contributions. The pytest attempt example shows a parameterized node ID with a setup error and its native JUnit identity. Native-build requests may carry cache_dir, an absolute directory allocated by core for a plugin declaring native-cache. It is separate from the fresh output_dir: use it only for disposable native compiler state, never as an artifact source. Core owns admission, the retained-size budget and eviction. Captured requests omit it. The native Zig builder uses this directory to keep compiler caches across unchanged builds and source edits. A builder plugin is a separate program that tells oyzu how to build one kind of project: which tasks it has, which tools it needs, which command builds it and where the output lands. This page shows how to run a plugin from a local path while you develop it, how plugins work, what a plugin has to provide, and how to package it. It also covers the Node plugin's behavior, since it's the largest first-party plugin. Each operation's source contract accepts home: "required" (the default when absent) or home: "none". The requirement covers HOME, USERPROFILE, APPDATA and LOCALAPPDATA together, including child processes. Explicit tool homes remain separate environment inputs. The SDK source constructors declare required; older plugins may omit the field. The existing protocol evolves in place, with no version gate. This execution-affecting field is strict, rather than an optional display annotation: unsupported values are refused. A none declaration grants no isolation or cache authority. Core admits only the first-party packaged Rust formatter's bounded Cargo command under the Linux crun enforced read boundary. Its exact selected package and tools remain keyed; native hosts and other scopes retain home. Unqualified claims refuse native action and enclosing result reuse. Configured or declared home inputs cancel the claim. Package admission alone, fixed source rules and compiler observations cannot establish home independence. See the scoped home exception. Note: The plugin interface (plugins-v1alpha1) is experimental. It's edited in place and can change without a new version. The Rust crates in the oyzu repository that help write plugins are internal and not a supported SDK. You can write a plugin in any language that speaks the JSON contract below. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

The same plugins-v1alpha1 process envelope also defines a deployer role. Its target-plan, target-apply and target-read-back operations take frozen opaque JSON settings, core-resolved tool paths and a staged tree inventory. A target's kind resolves <kind>/site, or explicit uses selects its binding and profile. The selected deployer validates target-specific settings. Planning returns the current revision and added, changed and removed paths; read-back returns the complete observed file digests. Core owns evidence enforcement, signed intent and records, and the comparison with the subject. A deployer never decides that verification passed. Builder plugins return unsupported for these operations. A credential-free plan may return credential_url with an empty diff before reading live state. Deployer descriptions declare credential_hosts, for example [{"origin":"https://github.com","setting":"repository"}]. The setting field names a target setting, following the publisher host-to-setting binding. The description comes from the admitted package's executable, whose bytes are covered by package admission. An omitted or empty list authorizes no credential origin. Core validates each declared HTTPS origin and refuses any credential URL outside that list or inconsistent with an explicit URL in the named setting, before resolving tokenEnv. Shorthand is checked against the declared origin. Core admits the recipient, opens transport, and repeats planning; the intermediate plan is never signed or applied. Transport environments contain only the host-bound reverse proxy URL, never credential values. Git uses OYZU_DEPLOY_PROXY_URL; core attaches the tokenEnv credential upstream without an OIDC fallback. Only target-apply receives write authority. Read-back must use fresh core observations after writes close; core also fetches and compares the Git inventory independently. Requests outside the declared destination and bodies above 64 MiB are refused. See deployment limits. Bind your plugin archive to a builder reference in your user configuration (~/.config/oyzu/config.toml on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/config.toml on macOS, %APPDATA%\Oyzu\config.toml on Windows, or the file OYZU_USER_CONFIG names): [plugins.development] "go/app" = "/home/me/src/oyzu/oyzu-plugin-go.tar.gz" "node/app" = "/home/me/src/oyzu/oyzu-plugin-node.tar.gz" Use the packaging helper to include the manifest that admits the plugin's tools. A raw executable is sufficient only for a builder that returns no tool requirements and requests no observations. These USER bindings apply in a local execution context. CI, PR and release contexts exclude USER computation settings, even when OYZU_USER_CONFIG selects the file. CI=true or a provider marker such as GITHUB_ACTIONS=true activates that exclusion. In CI, use an authorized machine or administrative binding; see execution context. For the maintained tooling/test-fresh-checkout.py harness, set OYZU_TEST_JAVA_PLUGIN to the absolute path of your compiled Java plugin. Each fresh user configuration binds java/app through this same development admission path; its empty tool store and isolated build PATH remain in effect. Without the variable, the harness selects the signed catalog package. Then build as usual: oyzu build oyzu build --full oyzu run test Oyzu runs your executable for that reference instead of a catalog package. The build shows the plugin-owned output directory in its commands (for example go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -o .oyzu/native/plugin/…), the Context facts in dist/logs/events.jsonl include Plugins go/app → local development <path> (sha256:…), and the plan, envelope and manifest carry extensions["oyzu.dev/plugins"] (see plugin packages). For action-cache reuse, a native development executable must return its compiled source-closure digest as plugin.source_digest in describe (sha256: followed by 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits). This binds the plugin's source inputs and local build/runtime dependencies, rather than its linked executable bytes. Admission reads the supported role's describe contract, including publisher descriptions. First-party plugins embed this identity when compiled. The private source/Cargo locator is development-only: build with OYZU_PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_LOCATOR=1 to include it, regardless of Cargo profile. Repository source bootstrap and development refresh set this opt-in. Without it the locator file is empty, so published binaries do not contain build-host paths from this capture. Published package bindings never consult the locator. Before execution uses a native development executable or an archive's host member, core reads the compiled identity from its private copy and compares it with the current source closure. Cargo's package inventory includes added files and local build/runtime dependencies. Core runs the Cargo recorded in the locator when that file still exists. A binding made in another job or on another host (a transferred CI candidate, for example) may not have that managed install. Only then, core runs the absolute Cargo named by OYZU_PLUGIN_FRESHNESS_CARGO. This variable is internal CI plumbing, not a user setting: nothing else (PATH, CARGO, RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN) is consulted, a relative value is ignored, and the compiled digest is still compared with the inventory, so a different Cargo that lists different files makes the binding stale. With neither Cargo available the binding fails with PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_STALE and a message naming the recorded Cargo and the variable's state; rebuild and rebind the plugin on this host (oyzu run bootstrap -- --source --development-plugins). Inventory excludes Cargo's generated package lockfile and does not resolve registry dependencies; the existing workspace lockfile is captured separately. Freshness checks work offline with an empty Cargo home, including for coverage-built plugins. On adopting executions, core stores locator hints under .oyzu/plugin-freshness, keyed by the binding path, length/modification time and frozen executable digest. Task runs check freshness without persisting locator hints. Read-only commands (run list, tasks list, config validate, config show and inspect) do not compute source-closure digests or write this cache. A stale development binding alone cannot make these commands fail. Commands that select development bindings for metadata report PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_UNVERIFIED once per selected development binding, with the repair command. This warning means freshness has not been checked; it does not claim the plugin is stale. Help remains configuration-free and prints no binding warnings. build --plan checks selected builders' freshness and refuses stale or unverifiable development bindings with PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_STALE, without writing this cache. Preview and execution inventory source bytes once per admitted runtime; a persisted hint only avoids rescanning the executable for its locator and never substitutes for source validation. Removing the cache makes the next execution admission scan the executable again. The first selected execution therefore pays the cold source-inventory and digest cost; listing commands do not precompute it. A later invocation still inventories the selected plugin's source. The persisted locator hint is not a source-digest cache. The exact one-inventory-per-run count is tested on Linux only; other hosts are unverified. For builders, freshness admission also precedes native test preparation and tool selection from plugin requirements. oyzu pin refuses stale selected bindings before publishing tool selections. Explicit installation refuses; the shell hook warns and leaves the selection unavailable without installing from stale requirements. Development deployers and publishers follow the same freshness rule. After reading the copied executable's description, core verifies its source closure before deployment or destination planning, tool provisioning or credential access. Stale or unverifiable bindings fail with PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_STALE; rebuild and rebind the plugin before retrying. Published packages retain package admission and do not require an available source checkout. Only development bindings required by the selected builds or task are admitted. An unused stale or unverifiable binding does not block the selected work. Each invocation freezes its selected bindings; another discovery in the same process can select a different set without replacing the first invocation's plugins. A missing digest, missing source locator, unavailable checkout or build-time Cargo, or changed source fails at execution admission with PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_STALE, naming the binding and a refresh command. Rebuild the executable and any bound archive from current source, then retry. In this repository, run oyzu run bootstrap -- --source --development-plugins to refresh the plugins; unused stale bindings do not prevent that repair task from starting. Other plugin authors rebuild and rebind their own plugin; native plugins need the same private source capture as the first-party build scripts. Automatic rebuilding is not provided. Replacing the CLI does not itself change a plugin's source identity, but a newer CLI can enforce freshness checks that an older CLI did not enforce. Plugins built without the development locator must be rebuilt with the opt-in above. Scripts remain ineligible for reuse. The declaration grants no package trust and development results stay out of shared remote caches. Publisher and deployer package descriptions still match the admitted publisher/name/version coordinates; optional compiled source metadata is separate from package admission. Remove the entry to stop using the local executable. The next build then has to find the package some other way: the catalog, a plugins.packages binding or the lock. There's no built-in fallback. For Oyzu CLI development, keep the everyday build driver outside the checkout and use oyzu-dev for the CLI under test. Source promotion with oyzu run bootstrap builds and installs only the host CLI. Existing Rust/Node development bindings require --development-plugins to refresh the checkout payloads and bindings using the promoted CLI. Add --isolated to also build the Linux Rust plugin and prepare the Linux CLI engine. To return to published plugins, remove the relevant plugins.development entries from your user configuration (including a selected OYZU_USER_CONFIG file), then run oyzu run bootstrap to build the host CLI against the published locked packages (use -- --channel stable only to also replace your CLI with the newest release). Neither helper silently deletes personal choices. Windows still requires a published Rust host payload; that gap is tracked in #1679. This development loop does not supply that missing payload.

Key Type Default Where plugins.development Table of builder reference to absolute executable or package archive path none User, machine or administrative configuration Keys are short builder references without a major version (go/app, not go@1/app or an OCI reference). Values are absolute paths. At most 64 entries. The setting selects code to run, so a project oyzu.toml, oyzu.local.toml or a profile is refused with CONFIG_SCOPE: plugins.development is not permitted in this scope. In CI, user configuration is ignored as usual; a machine-level binding still applies. Pass --ci-machine-binding to the repository bootstrap to create one on an ephemeral runner (see CI machine binding). The table is replaced as a whole by a later source. Each command admits and freezes its selected bindings. A selected missing or unreadable executable fails with PLUGIN_BINDING_INVALID; a malformed or versioned key fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. A local binding has no download, signature check or oyzu.lock entry. An executable is recorded by file name and SHA-256 digest only, with no manifest check.

A development binding can also name a plugin package archive (a .tar.gz with plugin.json and its members). Use this when you want --isolated builds with your plugin: a raw executable has no Linux member or captured-plan manifest, so an isolated build refuses it with PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED. [plugins.development] "rust/app" = "/home/me/src/oyzu/.oyzu/bin/oyzu-plugin-rust.tar.gz" Oyzu recognizes the archive by its gzip header and installs it, with the manifest, layout and host-member checks a bound package gets, into a private folder that is removed when the command ends. Nothing goes into the shared package store or oyzu.lock, and no digest is pinned, so rebuilding the archive takes effect on the next command. The host member runs host builds; the member for the execution image's platform runs isolated ones. The binding is still recorded as local development, with the host member's digest. An archive that isn't a valid package for that reference fails with PLUGIN_BINDING_INVALID and the reason.

A binding key is <plugin>/<profile>, and the profile is not always app. Each first-party plugin declares its profiles in its manifest (docs/contracts/plugins-v1alpha1/examples/manifest.<plugin>.json). oyzu build prints the reference it selected (for example helm/chart) in its Builders section; if that line does not say local development, your binding used the wrong key and the published plugin ran instead. Plugin References Go go/app, go/library Java (Maven and Gradle) java/app .NET dotnet/sdk Python python/app, python/library, python/package Docker docker/image Helm helm/chart Node node/app Rust rust/app

Profiles that run isolated or captured (Helm and Python among them) refuse a raw executable with PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED. To exercise your build of such a plugin, pack it with the manifest for its plugin and bind the archive: cargo build -p oyzu-plugin-helm --features plugin --bin oyzu-plugin-helm python3 tooling/package-plugin.py \ --executable target/debug/oyzu-plugin-helm \ --manifest docs/contracts/plugins-v1alpha1/examples/manifest.helm.json \ --out /tmp/oyzu-plugin-helm.tar.gz oyzu config set --global plugins.development.helm/chart /tmp/oyzu-plugin-helm.tar.gz The helper ships only the host runtime member, so it covers builds that run on this machine. It requires Git and a clean source checkout: commit source changes before building and packing. It reads git rev-parse HEAD in the repository containing the helper, regardless of your current directory or the manifest's location, and writes that full 40-hex commit to provenance.source_revision for every package. It also refuses to pack a manifest whose provenance contains the text illustrative template (case-insensitive), so a packed release plugin.json cannot carry template wording; the example manifests use Oyzu maintainers. Inherited Git repository, worktree, index, object-store, namespace and discovery selectors are removed from every Git subprocess's environment; unrelated variables such as PATH and HOME remain available. The example manifest's revision is a placeholder and is always overwritten; other provenance fields, including unknown optional fields, are retained. Outside the existing host-runtime and optional version edits, other manifest fields retain their original JSON bytes. Duplicate JSON keys in templates are refused. The edited manifest is re-parsed to check the stamped revision and any requested --version before writing the archive. Use --revision <full-sha> to assert an expected commit. It must equal HEAD; abbreviated, malformed or mismatching revisions fail with a nonzero exit before an archive is written. Missing Git, an unavailable HEAD, or a dirty checkout also fails. Dirty means any staged, unstaged or untracked changes reported by git status --porcelain; ignored files are allowed. Put build and package output in ignored directories such as this repository's target/, dist/ or .oyzu/, or outside the checkout. The helper also checks git ls-files -v and refuses assume-unchanged and skip-worktree entries, including sparse checkouts, even when Git status reports a clean tree. Clear the index flags with git update-index --no-assume-unchanged -- <path> and git update-index --no-skip-worktree -- <path>, and use a full checkout before packing. You are responsible for rebuilding the executable from that same clean commit. The helper stamps the source checkout and does not verify a binary's build history or bind its development locator or source digest to the checkout. A stale binary or one built in another worktree can still be packaged with this checkout's HEAD. These checks run locally and require no network. Build with OYZU_PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_LOCATOR=1 set (as the repository bootstrap does) so Oyzu accepts the executable as current source. Remove the binding with oyzu config unset --global plugins.development.helm/chart to return to the published plugin.

A plugin doesn't have to match a built-in family. To develop a new profile such as independent/app, bind its id and name it in build.yaml. The names and path are illustrative: [plugins.development] "independent/app" = "/home/me/src/plugin/target/debug/independent-plugin" builds: app: uses: independent/app Run oyzu build app to build with it. An independent profile must be named in uses; the binding adds no detection, no with options, no dependency preparation and no isolated execution. Tool versions still come from your configuration or native files, and oyzu installs the tools the plugin's requirements answer names under the usual policy. Each returned tool must use a fully qualified identity, such as oyzu:go, and be declared in the builder descriptor, derived from the package manifest requirements. Declare conditional requirements too, including package managers and stage tools. Each declaration's stages should cover the stages for which the runtime requirements answer can return that tool. For example, the Node manifest declares oyzu:node, oyzu:npm, oyzu:pnpm and oyzu:yarn for install, build, test, lint and format-check; the runtime selects the manager declared by the project's package.json. The operation selects which of these tools the current project and stages need; tools.allowed checks that selection, rather than every potential manifest tool. Other providers retain their complete identity: for example, github:helm-unittest/helm-unittest or cargo:cargo-nextest. Declarations from another namespace or repository do not admit them. Bare names such as go and undeclared tools are refused, including in cached answers. Tool selection and installation still enforce provider and policy admission. A bare development executable has no declared tools; pack it with a manifest and bind the archive when it returns requirements or needs task-command observations (see below). When tools.allowed is set, oyzu run admits a task of a plugin-built target only if every tool the plugin's requirements declare for that task is on the list. A task whose binding declares no tool for it is refused with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED before anything launches. Registry routes and approved catalogs stay fail-closed for local bindings, as for any other builder.

For every operation, oyzu starts your executable once, with no arguments, a minimal environment and a fresh scratch directory as its working directory. It writes one JSON request to standard input and reads one JSON result from standard output. The process gets no credentials. Stream Content Standard input One request, then end of input Standard output One result and nothing else Standard error Diagnostic lines as JSON. Other lines are kept only for troubleshooting Documents use snake_case, schema_version: "v1alpha1" and a constant type. Duplicate keys, null members and numbers written with a fraction or exponent are invalid. Unknown members follow the compatibility rules. A request carries an operation_id, role (builder), operation, required_features, deadline_ms, the target (name, uses, whether the reference was inferred or explicit, absolute native-context source root, an optional relative path, and the base version) and the operation's input. Your result echoes operation_id and operation and has an outcome: completed (with output), failed (with error{code, message}), unsupported (with reason) or, for task-command, observe. target.root is the dependency owner's native context source view. target.path selects the declared target folder relative to it, using / separators and an empty string when they are equal. Core omits an empty path, preserving the existing request bytes for target-local contexts. Absolute paths, drive prefixes, backslashes, ./.. components and repeated or trailing separators are refused. A nonempty path requires the builder role's target-path feature in the selected package manifest and request. Captured planning also requires captured-plan. Core checks the manifest before sending the target. The SDK refuses nonempty paths by default; a builder opts in only when it implements this root/path distinction. Go supports command packages below a module root; other first-party builders retain their existing target-local behavior. Manifest role features are requirements on the engine for the entire package; they are not optional advertisements. Request required_features names what that individual call requires from the plugin. A package declaring target-path therefore needs an engine implementing it even for an empty target path. Older engines must use a compatible plugin release; omitting path preserves the request format but does not bypass package preflight. .NET packages using typed build commands and separate profile compile stages require dotnet-compile-stages in the manifest and describe builder features. The engine supplies development_compile only for an admitted optimized shared writer and requires that capability on its captured-plan request. Both profiles consume the same restore; the additional stage orders the selected compile without making the other profile's outputs a data prerequisite. Older engines exclude marked packages before invocation. Publish a compatible core before the marked .NET package; this feature grants no shared-cache or signing authority. .NET packages emitting typed publish { entry, version, optimized, destination } require dotnet-publish in both their manifest and describe builder features. The engine binds the project and output paths before native execution. The command exports already built framework-dependent apps without restoring or building. Older engines reject the package before invocation. Rust packages that emit native private_outputs require the builder role's native-private-outputs engine feature in both their manifest and describe response. The catalog and cold/warm package preflight use the same engine capability check, so an older engine excludes such a release before invoking a plugin role and can select an older compatible preview. This requirement identifies implemented wire/host-stage support; it grants no execution, source, cache or publishing authority. Release a core implementing the feature before publishing the marked Rust package. Oyzu accepts a result only if it's valid, the process exited with status 0 and the ids match. A valid result followed by a nonzero exit is a failure. Rust packages implementing deferred captured version projection require captured-cargo-projection in both their manifest and describe builder features. A compatible engine supplies the optional captured_projection control map and requires that feature on the captured-plan request. The package must copy those exact controls before every Cargo consumer, retaining mutation-carrying prerequisites. The engine validates the complete mapping and graph. Unmarked packages retain their existing projected-overlay preparation; they receive no optional projection facts. Publish a compatible core before publishing the marked package. This feature grants no acquisition or arbitrary filesystem-copy authority and changes no host finalization behavior. Limits: 16 MiB for a request or result, 1 MiB of kept diagnostics, at most 64 observations. Oyzu never truncates and accepts. Each operation has a deadline (60 seconds by default). At the deadline, or when the build is cancelled, oyzu terminates the whole process tree (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 2 seconds on Unix; the job object on Windows). Termination is a failure whatever the process wrote. Plugins keep no state between calls. Oyzu supplies every fact each time. Target-relative paths use /, never .. or spaces, and at most one leading dot per segment.

An operation you don't implement answers unsupported. Operation Called to Your answer describe Confirm identity and roles Protocol generations, plugin identity, roles with their profiles, operations and features tasks Discover conventional tasks The package manager, optional native package name and version (with the file they came from), and tasks (name, argv, build stage, whether it changes source, optional environment defaults) requirements Find the tools a target needs Tools (for example oyzu:go), stages, components, version constraints with their source files, and why. Read-only native-admission Decide whether the plugin can build this target on the host {admitted, reason}. Read-only native-build Plan a host build The build operations and the artifacts. Oyzu supplies the version, a fresh output_dir, offline and the execution platform native-test Plan the direct test run An optional test command, optional offline acquisition policy and the reports it must write, into a fresh report_dir task-command Adjust a task's command An optional replacement command, or observe to ask oyzu to run tool commands and call again once captured-plan Plan an isolated build Build and test intent, from read-only source. No observations or downloads The Zig adapter's zig-native-test-report capability covers one JUnit case for the conventional zig build test step. Its typed test command binds junit to the allocated report directory. Captured commands set prepared_packages to use the build's fixed read-only /dependencies/packages/p tree through --system and -j1; native commands leave it false. Core validates the mode, selected test task, working directory and report destination before lowering. The adapter never fetches dependencies or satisfies a coverage requirement. Native and captured test operations may declare test_units in the existing v1alpha1 contract. During preparation, report each compiled test executable with its digest and an executable_digests map from runtime executable name to digest. The native inventory is authoritative: core runs undeclared compiled units without reuse and keeps per-unit reuse for known compiled units. Malformed names, duplicate names and invalid digests still fail validation. The Rust native adapter may additionally report cargo_package_digest: the owning package's full Cargo package-file closure, resolved local dependencies (including workspace, dev and build dependencies), and workspace lockfile. Core requests this capture during native preparation through the private OYZU_TEST_UNITS_TRUST_NATIVE_READS=1 phase environment only when the resolved cache.trustNativeTestReads setting is on. It admits reuse with a visible trust-native-test-reads fact; this field never establishes confinement. Missing package identity keeps unbounded native units running. Bounded runtime reads require an enforced captured view; native units must give an unbounded reason. Shared setup reads belong to every affected unit. The combined JUnit report labels each suite with oyzu.unit and oyzu.outcome properties (ran, reused or failed) so its summary preserves each unit's counts. Core never stores failed units. Hooks and authored tasks keep the ordinary stage cache instead of per-unit reuse. See test-unit caching. What oyzu keeps for itself: the build version (the plugin must echo it), where output is written, scheduling, tool installation, running processes, collecting artifacts and the report gates. The plugin supplies intent: tasks, requirements, commands, artifact paths and report formats. Report formats are junit, cobertura, lcov, go-cover and jacoco; sources are file, go-test-events, jest-json and jest-lcov. A plugin that needs nonempty with options must declare the build-options feature. Captured intent permits textual version interpolation only when the complete core version contains its recorded per-build source hash. Core can narrow that hash after the final read contracts are known, then rebind command, environment, native payload and artifact strings with the decisions before computing action keys. An unmarked plain version such as 1.0.0 retains the whole-target version and plan: the same text may identify a dependency or be part of a path. oyzu cache explain records this fallback rather than treating those occurrences as interpolation sites. Plugins must keep native version projection in executable intent, so output bytes embed that same bound version. Helm's captured stage command carries the version it writes into its private chart; it never rewrites the source chart. A task-command observation names a core tool identity and its command line. Oyzu checks that the tool is one the builder may use and is eligible under the target's effective tools.allowed policy, that its command name is a single plain component without path separators or a drive prefix, and that argv[0] matches that name. Paths such as ./tool and tools/tool are rejected even when declared by a manifest. A manifest declaration does not override tool policy: even a tool omitted from the task's selected requirements is checked when an observation requests it. Policy exclusions fail with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED before executable lookup or launch. Observations require resolved target configuration. Oyzu runs the command once on the task's absolute PATH entries, with the task environment followed by observation overrides. The shared plugin host supervises its process tree with a 60-second deadline and a 2-second termination grace. Stdout up to 1 MiB and stderr up to 64 KiB are retained; exceeding either limit stops the tree while reading, rather than buffering unbounded output. Oyzu then calls task-command again in a new process with the results. One round only. A local development binding may not use observations. External builder host planning supports Linux, macOS and Windows on x86_64 and aarch64. Other hosts return a typed unsupported-host error with supported-host guidance. Artifacts must have unique names and sources (compared without regard to case). A default artifact lives inside output_dir. An artifact marked executable is promoted to .oyzu/bin after a successful build.

Some builds decide their own output location: npm run build writes dist, and the plugin can't steer it into output_dir. For those, the plugin marks the artifact "origin": "target" with a target-relative source, and the build operation runs the task's own command (oyzu sends it as input.task.argv): {"name": "primary", "producer": "build", "kind": "directory", "filename": "application-1.4.0", "media_type": "application/octet-stream", "source": "dist", "executable": false, "origin": "target"} Before any build action runs, oyzu checks the source and refuses it otherwise: Rule Refused with It names something below the target: not ., no segment that starts or ends with a dot (.git, .oyzu), is node_modules (any case) or is a Windows device name (con, nul, COM1.txt) PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED: … invalid result Sources are unique, ignoring case PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED: … invalid result It doesn't equal, contain or lie inside output_dir PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED: … overlaps the output directory It doesn't equal, contain or lie inside a file or directory of the target's source selection PLUGIN_ARTIFACT_REFUSED: … overlaps the frozen source selection at <path> No existing segment is a symbolic link or reparse point, and none above the last is a file PLUGIN_ARTIFACT_REFUSED: artifact … names … Oyzu then moves anything already at the path into a fresh directory beside the output (never deleting in place) and discards that directory after collection. The plan records moved paths under extensions["oyzu.dev/retired-outputs"]. A build whose script writes nothing fails with native artifact collection failed rather than republishing an old output. Collection then applies the usual rules: no links, no reserved names. On the native host lane the target directory is a private copy rebuilt from the selected source before each build, so nothing is ever moved there and previous is always false. In an isolated build, the output is moved aside in the private execution workspace, never in your project. To recover from a refusal, name a project output that isn't source, version control state or a dependency tree, and remove any link in its path.

A host native-build operation with neither command nor engine selects the target's existing task of that name. For build, this is the actual selected build task, including its working directory, environment and report obligations; it does not create a task or allow an unavailable task to run. Explicit plugin commands keep their existing native invocation bindings.

tasks can report native_package with an optional name and version and the file (origin{path,digest,location}) they came from. Oyzu checks that the file is inside the supplied source and that its digest matches. A missing declaration stays unknown, even when the target's version is 0.0.0. The Node plugin reports package.json; the Go plugin doesn't. See version inference.

Targets built by a plugin are reused from the local action cache like other targets. The key includes the compiled development source-closure digest (or admitted package release) and runtime. Changing those inputs reruns its targets; replacing linked development bytes alone does not. Scripts remain ineligible for reuse (see external builder targets). Preparing a native development binding queries describe for its compiled source identity. Other operations include tasks, requirements, native-admission, native-build and task-command, with another invocation when an operation asks for an observation. Launches depend on the selected targets and capabilities.

Every BuildOperation must carry contract, a SourceContract. Declare a complete locked command set with optional tools, including commands launched indirectly. A complete stage keys only these admitted commands, not sibling stages' tools. Managed sibling PATH entries are omitted from computation identity unless the stage explicitly declares a PATH data read. The selected builder's verified package identity always remains bound. Complete stages also omit sibling check selection (checks.run) and unrelated package bindings (plugins.packages) from computation configuration; execution and policy constraints stay binding. Omit tools when completeness is unknown; core retains whole-lock cache keys. An explicit empty array declares that no locked command is resolved. Core binds named commands to its own retained verified installations; a plugin cannot supply an installation identity or grant itself tool access. Missing admitted commands keep the fallback. The SDK's source::tools(contract, names) helper records this declaration. Source-read bounds remain a separate claim. Use external_inputs: [{kind: locked-tool, tool: java}] to bind an external tool read without claiming a complete command set. The SDK helper is source::external_tools(contract, names). Core resolves the identity from retained preparation and oyzu.lock; a missing identity is an error. The declaration supplies neither host paths nor plugin-chosen digests. Observed reports may name the same typed inputs, which must be declared in the contract. This field does not authorize filesystem access or establish read completeness. external_inputs: [{kind: ancestor-file, path: ../Directory.Build.props}] names a file above a host-native target: one to 32 ../ segments, then one portable file name (no separators, colons, control characters, trailing dot or space, or Windows device names such as NUL or COM1). Case is significant, so NuGet.Config and nuget.config are separate inputs. Core (not the plugin) reads each file beside the real target directory and keys its bytes, or its absence, in the action and target keys; a symlink, directory or file over 4 MiB refuses the key. A plugin that declares it requires the engine feature dotnet-ancestor-inputs (the SDK helper is source::ancestor_files(contract, paths)), so an older engine refuses the plugin rather than skipping the input. The declaration alone does not make a stage reusable: the stage must still be admitted by its other read claims. The input is must-understand: older readers fail to decode the contract rather than skip it, so update core before using a plugin that declares it. Other external-input kinds are unsupported. Declare a non-empty reads list, unbounded_reason with a non-empty explanation such as "not analyzed yet", or upstream_only: true for an operation that reads no source and only consumes declared upstream outputs. The SDK constructor source::upstream_only() sets empty reads and bounded outputs. This explicit form forbids source reads and an unbounded reason and requires bounded_outputs: true. An ordinary empty list without a reason remains invalid. The declaration grants no execution authority: native narrowing still requires complete observations or core-admitted fixed command semantics. An unbounded_reason must contain 1 to 4000 Unicode characters and must not be blank. Rust plugins can use source::unbounded_reason(reasons) to trim, deduplicate and sort explanations, supply a fallback for an empty or blank set, and summarize long sets with an (and N more) suffix. It keeps complete reasons where possible; a single oversized first reason gets a character-safe preview and also counts toward omitted reasons. source::unbounded(reason) uses the same formatter. Summarizing the explanation does not narrow the source boundary. For compatibility with older published plugins, core accepts results without a declaration and treats those operations as unbounded. Their whole-target source keys retain the existing conservative behavior. The build records plugin <reference> <version> declared no reads, and one PLUGIN_READS_UNDECLARED warning per plugin per build asks users to update it. oyzu build --plan never runs build actions. It reads plugin metadata and checks development-builder freshness first. Its source reasons describe the stage contracts in that target's last retained build plan, so a later preview can show the recorded reason. Without a recorded contract, it says reported when the builder answers. Historical reasons do not prove current source completeness or cache admission. This runtime fallback does not satisfy conformance for new or updated plugins. Each read selector has kind (path, glob or listing), a target-relative value, and confidence (exact or over-approximate). Paths cover their subtrees. A listing covers direct entry names and kinds, without file contents or descendants; listing-only captured entries are empty placeholders. Read and write selectors must remain target-relative: .. is refused for paths, globs and listings. A source projection narrows the target's own folder and does not admit parent traversal. Required writes, bounded_outputs, confinable and bound_dependencies fields retain their meanings. Optional env contains environment dependency names, never values. The internal Rust SDK supplies source::reads(selectors) and source::unbounded(reason) helpers; authors still declare output bounds and confinement explicitly. Native Cargo admission checks full-target input authority separately from output bounds. Compile and quality stages retain bounded outputs. The deferred test stage retains the same input authority with unbounded outputs, so arbitrary test effects use the existing always-run path rather than reusable results. Neither declaration permits narrower confinement or substituted native controls. A read prediction alone does not permit a narrow native key. A native stage needs complete observed reads after execution, unless its tool's own rules fix its read set. An observed path outside the prediction prevents storage and reports confined-read-outside-contract with the additive inputs fix. Unbounded stages retain the whole-target key. See action cache. For native host stages, use oyzu_plugin_sdk::source::observed(selectors) when the action reports its complete reads after each successful run. Core sets OYZU_OBSERVED_READS to a fresh output file path. Write this JSON there: {"complete": true, "paths": ["src/main.rs"], "listings": ["assets"], "env": ["FOO"], "reasons": []} ObservedReads.env lists environment names read by this execution, including unset names. It defaults to an empty list for older reports and is bounded to 65,536 names of 1-4,096 bytes each. Names cannot contain = or control characters. Core binds values from the effective task environment (absence is None); bound build actions clear ambient inheritance. The existing inheriting Node-install launch retains its environment rule. Per-run TMP, TEMP and TMPDIR names are excluded from observed env keys. Report names are dependencies, never permission to inject host values. Planning can tag a learned-only selector with source: "build-script-record" and list learned-only env names in SourceContract.learned_env (a subset of env). They remain in the admission set but leave the stable definition and history subject; base and configured names stay. The constant observedEnv: true payload marker separates current subjects from older path-only observations. A prediction candidate can be stored or backfilled only when its env covers every observed env name. These are in-place protocol additions, with no schema version change. Both path lists are relative to the action cwd; core rebases them to the target and captured workspace before prediction checks and evidence recording. Set complete: false and explain unknown reads in reasons when the tool cannot account for them. Missing, invalid, empty or incomplete reports, and nonempty reasons, keep whole-target behavior and retire prior admission. The protocol's ObservedReads type and report schema own this format. Core saves a complete report only within the declared prediction and only for the same action definition. Outside-prediction reads prevent sealing a narrowed result. On a whole-target run, they retire admission without failing that covered run. Use source::fixed(selectors, rule) for tools whose own rules fix their reads; name the rule in a short, nonblank string. This needs no runtime report. Without either basis, native predictions stay whole-target. A basis requires a native command and cannot accompany unbounded_reason or upstream_only. Source-free exports use the separately admitted upstream-output contract. For native host execution, set BuildOperation.private_outputs to the exact regular files the stage must retain in the target workspace for its consumers. Paths are target-relative; glob patterns and directory outputs are unsupported. Some(vec![]) opts in a check with no retained files; omission keeps the shared workspace. Reports and artifacts still use their existing collection contracts. This is a builder fact, not an execution capability: core requires a stage contract with bounded outputs and admitted producers. Private execution and narrow keying are separate: a stage without a native read basis can still run privately with its whole-target key and action configuration identity. Only observed or fixed reads without an unbounded reason admit a narrow key. Source-free copy/export stages instead declare upstream_only. Every producer must also be admitted; a consumer of an unadmitted producer remains shared. Declare all generated inputs through the existing action relations. Core validates portable file paths and retains files through the existing contained output collector. A producer feeding a private consumer must declare nonempty private_outputs, and its referenced output port must exist. Only that producer's named paths consumed by the consumer must be covered; the consumer's own source reads and another producer's paths need not be outputs of this producer. Multiple producers contribute their respective files. A source-free export consumes its producer's complete output port, so every named write must be covered. Uncovered paths or selectors whose complete coverage cannot be established keep the consumer shared. A source-free export still requires empty reads/writes, no confinement or dependency-bound authority, and no private-output or dependency-file command capability. The prepared source projection remains immutable throughout execution. Shared stages and cache restores use a separate retained root, so an executing private fork can be populated lazily from the pre-run source even after shared writers have run. Projection digests transfer with unchanged bytes and metadata; copied inode/ctime identities do not cause another content hash. A reused producer shares its verified staged bytes without copying output payloads; a consumer that executes requests the handoff. An unexecuted retained fork is never a fallback for a missing verified handoff. Private completion captures only its finite files, so concurrent shared writers cannot enter that action's result. Mixed targets retain each shared stage's whole-target source key while admitted private stages use their own native read keys after read admission, or retain the whole-target key without a read basis. Missing output declarations and unadmitted producers refuse private execution; unknown reads only refuse narrow keying. Hooks, replacements and materialized inputs keep the target-wide fallback. Shared native actions follow every dependsOn edge, including OrderOnly. Private branches with a native read basis do not inherit producers through order-only siblings; real producer edges still count. Private stages without a read basis preserve the existing whole-target dependency closure. For a bounded private stage with a native read basis, omitted relations refines the default mutable-workspace sequence to order-only edges. This lets a source-only formatter follow an unbounded build or test without importing their results or their producers into its key. Explicit Produced and Sequence relations, authored task dependencies, hooks and replacement boundaries retain their data dependencies; the private opt-in does not erase them. Declare generated inputs explicitly rather than relying on the default pipeline sequence. For example, a Zig formatter with fixed reads and no retained files opts in with operation.private_outputs = Some(vec![]); build and test can remain unbounded. The same opt-in works for source-only Go build and vet stages with observed reads, and gofmt with fixed reads.
