An observed stage needs a complete read report from its own successful execution before publishing a narrow result. The next unchanged build can reuse that result. These examples describe the core contract; each plugin must emit its own opt-in and read declarations. Release core support for private_outputs before plugins that emit it; older cores reject unknown wire fields. No new schema version is introduced. SourceSelectorKind::Listing declares only direct entry names and kinds in the named directory (. for the cwd). It reads neither contents nor descendants. Use a separate path or glob selector for contents. A captured listing exposes empty files and directories, preserving names and kinds while hiding contents. Observed listings require an exact listing selector, a path on the directory or an ancestor, or a glob that provably matches every direct child (dir/*, dir/**, or an ancestor **). A glob matching only the directory name does not predict its listing. These contract additions reach users with each plugin's next release. Release core first: older cores reject unknown native fields, including native_reads, Cargo final_projection and development_compile. The Rust core and plugin must both support the declared-version compile/final projection graph. A Rust plugin emitting it must follow a core release supporting it. On the native host path, core omits final_projection only for an admitted plain local development result. The plugin still names its stage compile-development and exports its indexed binary directly. Core records its actual compiledVersion separately from the inferred artifact version; stamped consumers reject that marker. When final_projection is present, the exported binary must follow the final stage. Plugins cannot choose development eligibility. The Rust plugin lists the engine-injected OYZU_VERSION default in excluded_default_env for its host compile, test, lint and format-check commands only; the final stage keeps it. Core allows this exclusion only for compile-development, compile-optimized, lint, format-check and test stages with Cargo build, quality or test commands. Package stages, renamed final stages and unknown stage names must retain the default. An empty exclusion list remains valid for older plugins. The existing experimental wire version evolves in place; there is no legacy empty-read format to preserve.

The Go adapter's private prepared test inventory uses the existing CompiledTestUnit.artifact_files: the executable, adjacent runtime.json containing its workspace-relative cwd, and the prepared manifest itself. The producer and runtime reader ship in the same plugin. Core hashes and admits these actual files before narrowing runtime visibility; a package-name/source inventory alone never establishes complete runtime reads. Execution validates the executable digest and contained package directory before invoking go tool test2json. Missing or unsafe runtime artifacts fail execution instead of falling back to an unkeyed recompilation. No plugin wire fields or schema versions change. NativeTestInput.offline is an optional boolean, defaulting to false. When true, native package acquisition must use local inputs and fail if they are missing. Full native builds pass their offline selection to test planning. Python's generated uv test invocation adds --offline; when the plugin receives offline=true, core refuses a uv plan that omits it. The admitted typed PoetryTest path consumes previously staged, hash-verified wheels offline, even when the field is absent. The Poetry fallback (poetry run -- python), pip/application test paths and authored commands cannot enforce this policy and emit a warning when it is requested. This is an acquisition policy, not a sandbox: network isolation for arbitrary test code remains the executor's responsibility. Plugins advertise native-test-offline in their builder describe features to accept this field. Host writers omit it for peers without that advertisement, including inside captured test input, so existing published readers keep their baseline messages, with a warning when a requested policy is omitted. The advertisement means the plugin accepts the policy and diagnoses unsupported paths; it does not promise enforcement on every path. Tolerant older readers can ignore the optional field; no schema version or minimum-reader change is required. Ignoring it does not grant an offline guarantee. Known values must still be booleans; execution records retain their validation. The policy is not separately hashed into action keys: it controls acquisition, not the identity of already admitted dependencies. Any changed executable invocation (such as uv's --offline) remains part of the ordinary command key. Typed PoetryTest generates the same offline command under either policy. Captured planning leaves the optional test field absent: its executor already denies network access, and its frozen input and existing record digests retain their baseline representation. Writers must omit optional annotations unless the peer advertises support. The SDK adds optional-annotations to the existing describe role features. The initial describe exchange is annotation-free. After seeing support from that exact admitted plugin, the host selects the feature in request required_features, advertising that it can read annotated replies. SDK writers omit annotations when selection is absent, so released 0.3.8 receives baseline messages it can read. Version numbers and min_oyzu_version do not select this feature. An absent advertisement preserves baseline messages; negotiation adds no mandatory describe operation for a peer that previously worked without one. A builder can return display-only text through BuilderPlugin::annotations and OptionalAnnotations. The SDK gates the envelope and tolerant payload maps, consumes the transport selection before semantic builder dispatch, and retains all other required features. A writer cannot use this helper to add metadata to strict payloads or nested identity, signing, digest, authority or execution records. Raw optional fields outside this helper follow the same advertise-before-emitting rule. The host request writer applies the peer's described support in the same way. The host retains negotiated envelope annotations for presentation. A tasks response can supply test-input-bounds as JSON text describing static package candidates: bounds contains unit, entries (path, why) and an optional note; notes explains unresolved candidates. Build previews render these entries in a Why column. Missing or unreadable advisory metadata is ignored. These annotations never supply source selectors or establish cache admission; the test unit's validated SourceContract remains authoritative. The Rust detector's framework layer retains package and ancestor .config/nextest.toml locations, including when parsing fails; it extracts no extra paths from their contents. Its literal layer scans ordinary and raw Rust strings without executing macros, build scripts or Cargo. Computed paths such as env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR") joined with .. need target inputs when they reach beyond the inferred bound. A detector failure must leave the affected package unbounded with its reason instead of failing the entire test plan. The Rust builder applies this fallback to source-read, string-scanning and SDK path-validation errors, including outside workspace literals and excluded-output overlaps. Preview notes show the same reason. Unparseable nextest contents add a note while retaining all known config paths and other inputs. An advisory note never substitutes for a conservative source contract, and ignoring an annotation never changes execution. Private continuation state is always refused, including inside tolerant query inputs, describe/tasks/requirements outputs and error records. Request and result envelopes tolerate unknown optional annotations. The same rule applies to the requirements query's input, describe output for every role, builder tasks and requirements outputs, and failure error records. On replies it also applies to SourceContract, SourceSelector, ActionRelation, OutputRef, NativeTooling and diagnostic records. These carry source/graph intent or descriptive facts; core still independently admits reads and effects. After validating the original reply, the runtime reader counts ignored members separately for each operation's contract (including read/write selectors) and relations. Any ignored member there retains the whole-target source key through an unbounded_reason that planning cannot replace with an analysis prediction, disables confinable and bounded_outputs, and clears native-read, upstream-only and narrowed tool-set claims. A clean sibling keeps its declaration. The same fallback applies independently to each TestUnit.contract, including units under build operations and captured plans. The reader preserves home; a downgraded action with explicit home: none fails planning when no-home execution is enforced; the error names the action, home: none and the reason, plugin source intent contains ignored optional fields. The accepted reply's single debug note describes this fallback without exposing unknown names or values. There is no exemption for unknown source-intent members. home is a known field in this reader: omission means required, and explicit none grants no core admission. Historical strict readers without home reject explicit none and need an upgrade; tolerance cannot be retrofitted into an installed executable. An annotation must be safe to omit: ignoring it cannot change execution, validation, admission or authority. It is discarded rather than echoed or included in an action's identity. All other typed records remain strict. This includes manifests, catalogs, OCI release records, plugin identities (also inside describe), role/capability records, digest-bearing source/prepared records, credential bindings, commands, artifacts, admission decisions and native/captured execution inputs and outputs. Nested NativeReadBasis, ExternalInput and ObservedReads remain strict: they bind native read admission and cache identity. Unknown relation, selector, confidence, home-policy and external-input kinds are refused even in a tolerant parent. The per-contract fallback prevents ignored source intent from authorizing a narrower cache key. TestUnitPlan and TestUnit records remain strict; their nested SourceContract uses the tolerant reader and fallback described above. Empty operation inputs remain empty. An unknown member in a strict record is refused. Known fields retain their required presence, types and validation; duplicate keys, unknown enum values and invalid digests are still errors. The Rust, Helm and Zig plugins use the shared SDK reader for their stdio requests, including the designated annotation containers above. The Rust plugin's separate --native Cargo command and --inspect inputs retain their typed decoding; annotation tolerance does not extend to those execution and inspection records. Updating the driver alone does not replace an already-installed plugin's reader. Helm's separate --native input uses the shared closed-record decoder for HelmCommand; command, path and prepared-digest records remain strict before native work. Zig's separate --native test command also uses the shared strict native decoder; it has no inspection or acquisition entry point. Core owns Zig acquisition and prepared closure admission. Go adoption uses the same stdio containers and shared SDK capability check. Its private --native Go command remains a strict execution record; Go has no --inspect entry point. Native Go tool output and acquisition metadata keep their existing ecosystem readers, outside the stdio annotation contract. Source adoption requires a new Go plugin release and normal package adoption; updating the driver alone does not replace an installed Go reader. The Java / JVM plugin uses the same SDK reader and capability preflight for stdio. Its Maven, Gradle and Ant --native commands and --acquisition-api assignments remain closed, including nested paths, digests and execution facts. Updating the driver alone does not replace an installed Java / JVM plugin; rebuild and rebind development packages after changing their source. The .NET plugin uses the same SDK reader and capability preflight. Its separate native helpers, --acquire and --lock-facts inputs remain strict, including nested MSBuild SDK package identities. Annotation tolerance does not extend to execution or acquisition records. Updating the driver alone does not replace an installed .NET reader. Node also uses the shared SDK reader for stdio. Its --native, --metadata-api and --validate-store inputs are closed execution, native metadata and acquisition-validation records, respectively. Empty native metadata queries such as errno-facts also reject extra members. Vite assignments also remain strict. Native metadata replies retain their existing fact validation; optional wire annotations grant no extra access or effects at these boundaries. Source adoption requires a Node plugin release and normal package adoption before an installed plugin gains the new reader behavior. The SDK writes one debug diagnostic with code plugin.unknown-optional when it ignores request annotations. The host retains the corresponding reply note in the operation's diagnostics; logged planning operations publish it through the normal diagnostic view. Notes report a count, never field names or values. Protocol users can retain these notes with decode_request_with_diagnostics, decode_result_with_diagnostics and accept_result_with_diagnostics. The simpler decode helpers return the same typed records without retaining diagnostics. Diagnostic parsing aggregates ignored stderr fields into one such debug note. Writer serialization and the JSON Schemas retain their existing shapes. Conformance/CI can demand exact result shapes with decode_result_exact and exact diagnostic shapes with Diagnostic::decode_exact; runtime hosts use the tolerant readers. The exact result reader also requires source declarations. Already-published readers keep their original decoding behavior. Core sends a new optional request field only when the plugin's describe advertises its feature; tolerance alone is not feature support. Package role features declare engine requirements before launch, and request required_features declare plugin requirements. This change introduces no new negotiated fields or driver floor. Sharing schema_version: "v1alpha1" alone does not establish compatibility. For an older reader's unknown field error, select an admitted driver/plugin combination that understands the field. Changing the schema label does not upgrade a decoder. Unpatched drivers, including affected 0.5.0-dev builds, cannot gain tolerant nested readers retroactively. If PLUGIN_PROTOCOL_REQUIRED_FIELD names an optional field such as /output/operations/0/contract/home, run oyzu self update to install a driver containing this reader fix, then retry. Until that driver is available on your update channel, use an admitted plugin that emits the baseline shape. Keep required semantics and trust checks intact; changing a schema label does not fix an installed decoder.

The Rust, Docker, Go, Helm, Java / JVM, .NET, Node, Python and Zig plugins check required capabilities through the shared SDK before family dispatch. A must-understand field changes what the operation does or how its safety is verified, so a reader cannot ignore it. The contract reuses request required_features for plugin-execution requirements and signed manifest roles[].features for requirements on Oyzu. Families adopt the shared check by implementing BuilderPlugin::request_features with their role/operation support; each adopted plugin uses one list for this method and its descriptions. Helm supports captured-plan and native-adapter; it has no with options or target-path capability. Unadopted families retain their existing checks. The shared execution check excludes host-permitted reply shapes such as optional-annotations and artifact-archive, preserving their separate transport and reply validation gates. There is no new reply requirement list, schema version or version gate. The directional message bodies are: Missing support Code Message template Plugin cannot satisfy an Oyzu request Keep PLUGIN_FEATURE_UNSUPPORTED, replace feature-refusal body Cannot safely continue: plugin "{plugin}" does not support request feature "{feature}" for "{operation}". No native work or writes were started. Run oyzu plugins update {plugin} and retry. Oyzu lacks a signed manifest's required feature Keep PLUGIN_ENGINE_REQUIREMENT, replace feature-refusal body only Cannot safely continue: plugin "{plugin}" requires feature "{feature}". No native work or writes were started. Run oyzu self update and retry. Plugin does not understand a required request field PLUGIN_PROTOCOL_REQUIRED_FIELD, pointer confirmed against the outgoing request Cannot safely continue: plugin "{plugin}" does not understand required request field "{pointer}" for "{operation}". No native work or writes were started. Run oyzu plugins update {plugin} and retry. Oyzu encounters an unknown manifest field PLUGIN_PROTOCOL_REQUIRED_FIELD, closed manifest refusal Cannot safely continue: plugin "{plugin}" requires understanding manifest field "{pointer}". No native work or writes were started. Run oyzu self update and retry. Reply contains undeclared required meaning after successful manifest preflight PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED, plugin contract violation Cannot safely continue: plugin "{plugin}" violated its contract by returning undeclared required feature "{feature}" for "{operation}". Run oyzu plugins update {plugin} and retry. Reply contains an unknown required security/execution field New agreed PLUGIN_PROTOCOL_REQUIRED_FIELD, plugin contract violation Cannot safely continue: plugin "{plugin}" violated its contract by returning unknown required field "{pointer}" for "{operation}". Run oyzu plugins update {plugin} and retry. The driver renders these bodies using its own admitted identity/binding: {plugin} is the update reference, such as rust/app, with the exact admitted release retained in diagnostic context. {operation} is its call; {pointer} comes from the decoder. For requests, {feature} is the lexicographically first outgoing execution requirement absent from the admitted peer's advertisement. The plugin's unstructured unsupported reason is untrusted secondary detail, never the source of identity, feature or remedy; without an independently established missing token, retain an operation-level unsupported failure. Rust's native/inspection helpers, .NET's native/acquisition/lock-facts helpers, Node's native, metadata and store-validation helpers, Python's native/acquisition helpers, and Zig's native test helper emit the field code and decoder pointer only; the host supplies the admitted identity and recovery message. Captured planning also checks refusal control output: pointers must be JSON pointers of at most 1,024 bytes with valid RFC 6901 escapes and no control characters. Request-field claims must name a member of a frozen outgoing request, and feature claims must be supported by the engine and absent from the signed role requirements. Invalid claims remain operation failures. Manifest features come from authenticated requirements; reply features come from the protocol crate's field-to-capability map next to strict records. Docker uses the shared stdio reader and advertises captured-plan and build-options from its SDK support list. Its typed OCI operations require captured-plan in the admitted manifest, including replies returned after successful preflight. Docker has no separate --native or --inspect stdio operation: captured metadata and acquisition helpers retain their closed records and existing core admission. Prepared paths/digests, nested OCI intent, commands, artifacts and plugin identities remain strict. Updating the driver alone does not replace an already-installed Docker plugin's reader. Use oyzu plugins update {plugin} through the authorized plugin update flow; rebuild and rebind development plugins. Updating Oyzu uses oyzu self update and its allowed release source. Neither remedy bypasses admission or changes a lock silently. Capability checks themselves need no network; updates may need the configured source or already available admitted assets. Unknown manifest members at any level use PLUGIN_PROTOCOL_REQUIRED_FIELD with manifest-specific Oyzu-update guidance. Role/contract mismatch and a missing requested contract retain their existing incompatibility diagnostics, even though they share PLUGIN_ENGINE_REQUIREMENT; they are not self-update cases. Existing plugin-failure status and config exit 3 stay unchanged. Config's declared_minimum, when present, remains attributed file guidance in next_step, not a version gate or proof of a feature's first supporting release. Required capabilities must be checked before native work or writes. Declare every new required reply/native meaning in the signed manifest so incompatible drivers refuse before plugin launch; a check after apply/publish is too late. Undeclared required reply meaning or an unknown reply security field after preflight is a plugin contract violation, never a reason to upgrade Oyzu. Stop further work; do not claim effects from a violating plugin were undone. Tampered signatures/digests and malformed known values retain their existing checks and concrete repairs; the new field code is only for unknown required meaning. Unknown optional fields remain accepted at the containers listed above; nested identity, command, digest, credential and authority records stay strict. Where an optional-field warning applies, retain CONFIG_WARNING, the CONFIG_UNKNOWN_OPTIONAL: message prefix, preflight scope/phase and no subcode or detail; wire annotations keep their existing debug note. Published readers retain their historical behavior, so producer omission and signed package eligibility must protect them until compatible packages are normally published and adopted. The protocol crate's capabilities module owns requirement classification, known reply-field capability mapping and directional message templates. The map covers Cargo native commands/private outputs; Go, Helm, Java / JVM, Node and Python native commands through native-adapter; .NET native/optimized/compile-stage/publish intent; Zig native test commands through zig-native-test-report; Jest report conversion; and shared artifact archive intent. Other families extend it with their existing owning capabilities as they adopt the SDK check. request_features derives requirements from the typed outgoing request; missing_request_feature chooses the first missing token in lexical order. Drivers compare with their admitted peer's advertisement and never infer a feature or remedy from an unsupported reason or a reply's claimed identity. An unsupported operation without an independently established missing token keeps its operation-level failure. New request/reply fields, including shared nested fields, must either be defaulted and documented informational-only, or mapped to a feature inferred by request_features / reply_features. A field that affects execution or safety needs the feature path. On strict records an informational field must also omit its default: #[serde(default)] alone does not prevent an older published plugin from rejecting a new key. Sending nondefault values to such a plugin still requires peer compatibility. oyzu --toolset checks run check-wire-fields, also included in checks and the protocol lib tests, checks these declarations; feature mappings need an executable classifier witness. Existing field exceptions are recorded individually without changing their wire behavior. Error::RequiredField retains a decoder-derived JSON Pointer, including array indices and escaped member names. decode_native_input applies the same bounded, duplicate-key and object-only decoding to native helpers. When request framing is readable but a strict child is unknown, the SDK echoes a failed result with error.code: "PLUGIN_PROTOCOL_REQUIRED_FIELD" and the pointer in error.message. Malformed framing, reserved continuation, invalid known values and tampering retain their existing failures. This code is the sole uppercase exception to the existing wire error-code syntax. Released 0.3.8 accepts baseline SDK messages but rejects unrecognized members in reply envelopes and describe/tasks outputs. A newer reader's annotation tolerance does not retrofit that release. Keep messages within the older reader's supported fields until compatible readers are deployed; advertising an unrelated feature does not make a new annotation safe to send. Project/user-file min_oyzu_version guidance uses the same minimum-reader policy as other commands. A higher marker alone warns once and does not prevent discovery when the files and plugin messages are understood. It cannot relax identity, execution or package admission checks. Plugin messages add no second marker or upgrade-warning mechanism; their optional-field debug notes remain distinct from the command's single compatibility notice. On Unix, a newly copied executable can briefly remain busy while an inherited writer closes. The host may wait up to one second before execution starts, within the original operation deadline. It never retries a plugin operation or accepts a failed result because of this startup handling.

A package is the archive described in plugin packages: plugin.json plus one executable per platform. The manifest (schema) requires: Field Meaning identity publisher, name and version. A builder reference is <name>/<profile>. The publisher oyzu is reserved for official releases (see below) protocol_generations Must include v1alpha1 profiles, roles The builder profiles you serve and, per role, the contract and features (for example go-test-events, captured-plan, build-options) runtimes One entry per platform: os (linux, darwin, windows), arch (amd64, arm64), optional abi (gnu, musl, msvc), entrypoint and its SHA-256 digest requirements Baseline tools needed whatever the project contains, with stages and a reason effects What the plugin needs: source-read, output-write, native-process, native-network. These limit what oyzu brokers; they don't remove a native executable's own operating system access provenance Source revision and maintainer Example manifests for each first-party plugin are in the repository. tooling/package-plugin.py in the oyzu repository packages one built executable for the host platform and prints the archive digest: python3 tooling/package-plugin.py --executable target/debug/oyzu-plugin-go --out target/go.tar.gz # prints sha256:<archive digest> The helper overwrites the example's provenance.source_revision with the clean checkout's full HEAD commit. See packing a source-built plugin for clean-tree requirements and the optional --revision assertion. To distribute your plugin through an OCI registry, publish a release root laid out as in the OCI package contract, with a Sigstore signature attached. Users then have two ways to trust it: Bind it by tag. A tag outside ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/ needs a plugins.packages entry with the exact signer identity to require. Binding by digest trusts the digest instead. See OCI sources. List it in an organization catalog. Your organization's tool index can list your package. For a publisher other than oyzu, the signed catalog's digest is the trust. A package named oyzu/* always needs the official signature, on any registry. You can't publish under that publisher yourself.

Before you ship a plugin, run it against the sample requests in the repository. oyzu-plugin-conformance <plugin-executable> docs/contracts/plugins-v1alpha1/examples (from the oyzu repository) sends every request.*.json through oyzu's real plugin launcher, so limits, deadlines and acceptance are the same as in a build. It checks that each result is valid and echoes its request, that the outcomes match the operations describe declares, and that the plugin is stateless (every request runs again in a new process in reverse order and must answer the same). It checks the protocol only. It runs no native tools, so it can't tell you whether your commands build anything. The examples include ecosystem-specific intent. Prepare a fixture directory for the plugin's supported profiles: retain the describe request, supply real source roots when the plugin reads source, and translate generic examples only where their intent applies. Preserve profile-specific facts and inferred/explicit selection; an inferred Node package may intentionally omit its build task. Do not translate another ecosystem's workspace or prepared facts by merely renaming its profile. describe must list itself among the builder's supported operations. To check all nine in-repository builder plugins, activate oyzu's shell and run cargo test --locked -p oyzu-plugin-conformance --test first_party -- --nocapture from the repository root. This builds their plugin executables, prepares temporary projects and native facts for the applicable canonical requests, and prints each plugin's verdict through the same harness. Go's native-context and multi-binary regressions stay with the Go fixtures; other ecosystems do not inherit Go-specific target-path requirements. It runs no native application builds. Python's translated test tasks use python -m pytest; the native and captured fixtures require its pytest adapter and mandatory JUnit/Cobertura report intent. Protocol reply equality does not establish reproducible build outputs. The conformance report's check_clean_builds check runs a fixture twice in distinct, empty directories and compares the complete map of artifact identities to collected digests. The native runner must disable action reuse and use fresh native build workspaces; acquisition still follows ordinary verification. Builds are separated by two seconds so archive timestamps cannot hide within one clock tick. A changed digest fails unless the fixture stage declares a nonblank nondeterminism reason identifying its native cause and tracked fix. The report prints that reason even when the digests match. Missing outputs, changed output identities and native build failures always fail, including stages with an exception. An exception affects conformance only; it grants no cache, trust or signing exemption. The compiled-CLI native fixture table covers Docker, .NET, Go, Helm, Java, Node, Python, Rust and Zig: cargo test --locked --test integration deterministic_conformance::all_first_party_outputs_are_deterministic -- --ignored --exact --nocapture The native table runs on Linux x64 and requires the applicable native tools, acquisition access, Docker and the base execution image for captured builders. The scheduled acceptance workflow runs the full table on its Linux path, with the base execution image and Docker payload provisioned before the test. Docker also needs OYZU_TEST_DOCKER_PAYLOAD pointing to the helpers and notices prepared by tooling/docker-plugin-payload.sh; the fixture packages those files through ordinary archive admission rather than substituting a bare executable. The comparison library itself is portable. Set OYZU_CONFORMANCE_BUILDER to one of docker, dotnet, go, helm, java, node, python, rust or zig to select one row. Each row invokes the compiled CLI with build --no-cache --json, using ordinary development plugin bindings and engine admission; Rust and the captured builders use package bindings. Rust also exercises installed plugin package admission and warm compilation reuse. The table compares artifact digests from the admitted build manifest, excluding per-run reports and evidence whose timestamps describe the run. A protocol-only pass does not imply a native determinism pass, and missing prerequisites are failures rather than exemptions. The native Rust Debug fixture requires equal artifact digests, retained debug information with a logical /oyzu/source compilation directory, a working binary and an action-cache hit on an unchanged warm build. The Zig Debug stage declares the upstream Debug path limitation. This documented exception remains visible in the report. The zig-release row selects ReleaseFast, runs both collected executables and compares their binary and installation-tree digests without an exception. Select that row alone with OYZU_CONFORMANCE_BUILDER=zig-release. All other fixture stages also require matching artifact digests. Then try the plugin in a real project through a local binding.

Error Cause Recovery CONFIG_SCOPE: plugins.development is not permitted in this scope The setting is in a project file or profile Move it to user or machine configuration PLUGIN_BINDING_INVALID: … cannot read plugin executable The path is missing or not a regular file Build the plugin or fix the path CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE: plugins.development A key isn't a short unversioned reference, or a path isn't absolute Use an id such as independent/app and an absolute path PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED: observation … which this builder does not admit The plugin asked for an observation with a tool it may not use. Local bindings may use none Return command intent without an observation PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED: <id> plugin <path> (<operation>) The plugin failed, answered unsupported, broke the protocol, exited nonzero, wrote no result or ran past its deadline. The cause and the plugin's diagnostics follow Fix the plugin PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED or ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE An isolated build lacks a package feature, platform member, supported profile or engine files. If the plugin also declined the target for the host build, the message ends with ; target <id> was not admitted to the native host lane: <reason> Fix what the reason names, or supply the isolated build prerequisites plugin … sets command env, which the native host lane does not carry yet A build operation or test command carried env Set the environment in the native-build output env. Per-command env isn't supported PLUGIN_ARTIFACT_REFUSED: artifact … names … A project-written artifact overlaps the source, passes through a link, lies below a file, or oyzu couldn't move the previous output aside Name a project output that isn't source and has no link in its path A failed operation fails the build or task. No partial plugin result is used.

A plain oyzu build tries the host build first. If the plugin declines a target, the build continues on the isolated path, as oyzu build --isolated would, with the engine that path mounts. Without an [engine] pin in oyzu.lock or an installed engine, a Linux oyzu mounts its own executable (see execution image); on Windows and macOS the build stops with ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE and how to install the Linux engine (oyzu engine install --linux). A pinned engine is installed only by an explicit isolated build, so a plain build with a pin stops with ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE naming the pin and oyzu build --isolated. If the isolated path can't take the target either (a raw executable binding has no isolated package, for example), the build fails during preparation, before any build action or tool installation, with the code above and the plugin's reason. The message lists every target the plugin kept off the host build, not only the first. A plugin that fails native-admission is named the same way. Human and --json output carry the same message. For fresh bindings, oyzu build --plan represents these placement refusals in its "Unresolved until preparation" list (unresolved in JSON), adding a Target <id> was not admitted to the native host lane: <reason> line for each one. With --isolated or --all-platforms, oyzu selects the engine first without launching plugins, so you see the engine's own refusal until an engine is available: ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH for a pin no admitted engine archive supplies, or ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE on a host that can't mount itself. After that, a target that can't be planned fails with its PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED message and the same clauses. This asks each selected plugin for native-admission once if it isn't cached, and a hanging plugin can cost its full 60-second deadline per target.

A binding runs the named executable with your user's permissions whenever oyzu discovers a workspace. Bind only executables you built or trust. The recorded digest says which bytes ran; it isn't a signature and grants nothing. The plugin gets no credentials and no inherited environment.

The Go plugin builds only go/app with one module and one package main on the host. go/library and workspaces keep task execution through the plugin, but oyzu build refuses them. Per-command env in native-build operations and the native-test command is refused. Observation commands are matched by tool short name (go for oyzu:go) on the task's PATH. Oyzu doesn't verify that the resolved file belongs to the locked tool. Ctrl-C (or SIGTERM and SIGHUP on Unix) stops a running plugin and its child processes. oyzu build reports a cancelled build. If oyzu run or oyzu build --plan ends from a signal, the private copy of the bound executable (an oyzu-plugin-* temporary directory) isn't removed. Diagnostics from successful operations aren't shown.

The Python plugin (python/package) builds pip and pyproject.toml projects into wheels with pytest and Ruff checks, using the same binding. It adds no installer, PATH change or PYTHONPATH bridge: dependencies, pytest, coverage and quality tools must already be in the project's environment, and a target-local .venv is used when present. A mismatched environment is refused. Direct oyzu run tasks don't use this binding. Tested on Linux amd64 (GNU). The official catalog supplies the Python plugin. See Python preparation and, for the isolated path, captured pip Python packages. Python uses the shared SDK's request-capability check before family dispatch and source inspection. Its describe advertises the same execution support list; the SDK adds optional-annotation support and keeps reply permissions separate. Other roles still undergo preflight with an empty execution-support list, so unknown required features are refused before dispatch, including describe. The stdio envelopes and designated operation payloads accept inert optional fields as described above. Targets, commands, prepared identities, digests and paths retain their strict contracts. --native uses the protocol's closed PythonCommand decoder; --acquisition-api (including stdin input with -) uses the same decoder for its closed operation/data/manager envelope. Its data retains the selected native API's operation-specific semantics; it is not an optional annotation container. Python has no separate --inspect entry point. Unknown strict helper fields return PLUGIN_PROTOCOL_REQUIRED_FIELD and the decoder pointer before dispatch. The driver supplies the admitted plugin name and directional recovery text. Source and embedded runtime identities, package release mappings and normal signed admission remain binding. Rebuild/rebind a development executable, or adopt a normally published compatible Python plugin; updating the source does not change an installed release.

The Node plugin serves node/app for npm, pnpm and Yarn (Classic and Berry). It's experimental and available from the official catalog. A package or local binding can select another compatible implementation. The host build takes a node/app target that is declared with uses: node/app, isn't a workspace root, and has a non-empty scripts.build that writes dist. Anything else is refused with the plugin's reason, and because a plugin-served id has no fallback, that target can't build until it's changed or the binding is removed. Workspace projects and package output are covered on npm workspaces, pnpm, Yarn and plugin packages. It builds on Windows and Linux x86-64. Windows ARM64, macOS and Linux ARM64 aren't tested.

Action Command When <target>:install npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, Yarn Classic yarn install --frozen-lockfile or Berry yarn install --immutable. Offline handling follows the manager The project has dependencies, devDependencies or optionalDependencies <target>:build The selected build task, normally <manager> run build Always <target>:test Your test script, or the detected default Tests are selected <target>:lint Your lint script, or the native ESLint or Biome adapter Lint is selected <target>:format-check or <target>:format:check Your check script, or the native Prettier or Biome adapter Format is selected. A script that changes files is never selected The shared check levels decide which checks run, and --full runs every check that isn't off. Your own scripts win over the defaults. format:check, build:prod and similar names are kept; unsupported names fail discovery with an explicit error. An authored install task in oyzu.toml replaces npm ci, and disabling the install stage drops it. Authored tasks run with your ambient environment, not oyzu's pinned tools, so an authored npm ci can fail where the plugin's own install works (on Linux without a global npm: cannot execute npm: No such file or directory). The artifact is the dist directory your build script writes (project-written outputs), named application-<version> from the version oyzu resolved (0.0.0-dev.g<source hash> for an unversioned checkout), not the version in package.json.

Dependencies need the manager's lock file, or planning fails before any action with a diagnostic like node.lock-file: host npm dependency preparation requires package-lock.json; create it with npm before building. npm: package-lock.json (an npm-shrinkwrap.json alone isn't enough). pnpm: pnpm-lock.yaml. A stale lock fails the install (--frozen-lockfile) and isn't rewritten. Update it with pnpm, then retry. Yarn: yarn.lock.

If packageManager is present it must be an exact stable release such as pnpm@10.11.0. Oyzu checks it against explicit tool configuration, and a conflicting release fails before any action. Ranges, tags and prereleases are refused. Without packageManager, select pnpm in [tools]. A pnpm-workspace.yaml that contains only settings is allowed. A packages key, or anything oyzu can't classify as settings, makes the project a workspace and it's refused. Competing manager evidence is also refused. pnpm owns install scripts and their policy. Oyzu adds no script approval. Offline builds add --offline and need the dependencies already in pnpm's own store. Missing bytes fail without going online. This is the host's ordinary pnpm configuration and store, not a hermetic replay, and --no-cache doesn't clear it.

Accepted exact releases: yarn@1.22.22 (Classic) and yarn@4.17.1 (Berry). Berry needs nodeLinker: node-modules in .yarnrc.yml (a quoted value is fine). Plug'n'Play is refused. See managed Yarn. Direct tests need dependencies installed in the source project. A full build installs into a private workspace. For Berry, run yarn install --immutable, then oyzu run test. Not supported: isolated Yarn builds, extra rc settings, workspaces on this path, project plugins, yarnPath, custom registries and non-registry sources.

An npm project whose build script is recognized vite build, with an optional literal --outDir, Vite as a dependency and a native Vite 8 configuration, builds as an application. Oyzu keeps the npm lifecycle around one Vite build and stages the output after the native postbuild step. Tested with Vite 8.3.3. Other Vite flags, pnpm or Yarn with Vite, SSR, library and multi-environment builds, and watch or no-write modes aren't supported. See Node applications. Node packages declaring node-workspace-complete-read require an engine that implements member read admission, non-crun/root-config refusal and contained installation restoration. Package preflight rejects engines missing this builder feature before any plugin role runs, independently of release version labels.

For non-workspace npm, pnpm and Yarn targets, oyzu run test adds JUnit and LCOV reporting to a default node --test, to flag-only test scripts it recognizes, and to exact vitest and vitest run commands. See Vitest and Jest for those frameworks (Vitest was tested with npm and Vitest 5.0.3; Jest with npm and Jest 29.7.0). The matching coverage provider must already be installed, because oyzu doesn't download it. pnpm and Yarn pass reporter flags directly after <manager> run test, with no npm-style -- separator. Other test commands run unchanged. They can write to OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT or to report paths you declare. A missing optional report makes the evidence incomplete. A missing required report, a malformed report or a failing test fails the command. Workspace tests and other managers fail with node.test-lane. Lint and format checks prefer your project's installed ESLint, Prettier or Biome. Otherwise they use the default set pinned in oyzu.lock, prepared by the shared tool store. A declared but uninstalled package fails instead of falling back. Native configuration and ignore files are authoritative. oyzu run format changes source; format-check doesn't. To run a named task such as format:check, use oyzu run app:format:check or [tasks."app:format:check"]. Environment defaults from native files go through the normal configuration and policy checks; reserved OYZU_* names stay unavailable.

Claude repository sessions keep the existing bootstrap hook and also run .claude/load-context.sh through .claude/settings.json. The context hook prints the committed shared constitution, INDEX and context commit <sha>. A load failure emits an ERROR: ... context load FAILED marker on both stderr and SessionStart stdout; it exits zero so offline work remains possible. Restore private context access or correct the sibling cache branch/origin and retry before relying on shared policy. It does not report a loaded SHA on failure. See the hook instructions for the offline shell test, skill-link behavior and the separately provisioned user-level cloud hook needed when the session starts outside a repository. These files do not install cloud user settings. This section is for people working on the oyzu repository itself. Releases use the shared package store instead. tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh tries the oyzu on PATH before .oyzu/bin, accepting the first compatible driver. It does not select the newest version among them. Its development setup can preserve complete existing bindings without rebuilding them; use oyzu run bootstrap -- --source --development-plugins to refresh stale repository plugins. Without a compatible driver it downloads the newest release's oyzu and oyzu-shim into .oyzu/bin, checking each against the digest the release reports, and builds from source only when no release executable can be used here (--source never downloads, so it builds whenever no usable oyzu is already there). An oyzu older than the required plugin driver contract (plugin_protocol_release at the top of the script) can't be used either. The current bootstrap minimum is 0.4.0, whose executables must publish for every required platform before adoption. The 0.4.0 driver owns same-build retries and Rust attempt evidence and supports native-private-outputs and captured-cargo-projection; repository dogfood adopts that driver floor after its executables publish for every required platform. This driver floor does not upgrade the pinned Rust preview.6 package, which still lacks exact case reruns. This version check does not publish or select a marked package; normal signed package and catalog admission still apply. --no-plugins, which runs no plugin, skips that check, so the released 0.2.5 driver can still provide the tools used to produce plugin packages. On a platform with no release that new yet, the script builds the CLI from source once, until such a release publishes an executable there. With --require-release (CI's setup action) it fails instead, before invoking a plugin. Raising the minimum does not provide a compatible executable: the checkout must remain buildable by the previous published driver until publication. The release workflow also uses --require-release and has no ordinary source-driver fallback. By default, on every host it then installs the published rust/app and node/app releases that oyzu.lock selects into the plugin store, reading the release digests directly from that lock, through a temporary user file that binds only them; your own configuration isn't changed. A failed install stops bootstrap. Missing Windows payloads must be published and pinned before a Windows build can use them. Development plugins require explicit --development-plugins; only that mode builds and binds the Rust and Node plugins from source. A CLI source fallback alone does not opt in. A warm plugin store returns before reading pins or selecting a TOML reader. Reading initial pins uses Python's standard TOML reader: bootstrap first checks PATH, then the already-installed checks Python. If neither can import tomllib, it explicitly reports and installs the existing checks toolset through Oyzu, then probes the pinned interpreter before reading the lock. On Windows it converts the complete native Python path, including spaces, for Git Bash. With --no-install, that toolset installation is forbidden: provision it first with oyzu --toolset checks install --frozen, or provide a capable Python on PATH, then retry. Ordinary provisioning may need network access before plugin acquisition starts. --ci-machine-binding continues to use published plugins exclusively (this repository declares both a cli and a docs build, so both builders must resolve before oyzu build cli). When an older CLI supplies the compiler, it resolves only the checkout's [tools] requests in a temporary project using its normal trusted tool resolver. The repository's oyzu.lock stays unchanged; newer build or plugin lock fields are not copied into that tool-only project. It compiles with the pinned Rust and Cargo's --locked dependency graph, and honors CARGO_TARGET_DIR and CARGO_BUILD_TARGET. It needs no Python, Node or jq just to read configuration; only the published plugin installation above and the read-back in the CI machine binding below use Python. With --development-plugins, on a machine with no user configuration file and no existing plugin choices, the script writes the two development bindings to .oyzu/bootstrap/config.toml and prints the OYZU_USER_CONFIG export (or records it through CLAUDE_ENV_FILE, or through GITHUB_ENV for later GitHub Actions steps). It doesn't touch your own user configuration, project or local files, or shell profiles. If any step fails, it removes the file it created. Running it again with the same unchanged file prints Reusing this checkout's unchanged bootstrap USER file and the same export. oyzu run bootstrap -- --source --development-plugins uses the same file, but once it has packed .oyzu/bin/oyzu-plugin-rust.tar.gz the file binds rust/app to that package archive. Add --isolated to include the Linux plugin and prepare the CLI engine for isolated builds (see refreshing the oyzu on your PATH). An earlier file with the executable binding is rewritten then; the script above keeps using whichever binding the file has. If you already have a user configuration file or other plugin choices, the script refuses instead of merging. Bind the two plugins yourself, then run it again; with both present it passes them through. From the checkout root: oyzu=.oyzu/bin/oyzu # .oyzu/bin/oyzu.exe on Windows bin="$(pwd -W 2>/dev/null || pwd)/.oyzu/bin" "$oyzu" config set --global plugins.development.rust/app "$bin/oyzu-plugin-rust" # add .exe on Windows "$oyzu" config set --global plugins.development.node/app "$bin/oyzu-plugin-node" # add .exe on Windows tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh Or edit the user file by hand: [plugins.development] "rust/app" = "/home/me/src/oyzu/.oyzu/bin/oyzu-plugin-rust" "node/app" = "/home/me/src/oyzu/.oyzu/bin/oyzu-plugin-node" In CI the user file is ignored, so the script refuses fresh user setup there; a CI job uses the machine binding below instead.

CI machine binding requires --release --require-release: a missing compatible driver fails before a source build. The one-time Windows bootstrap exception has been removed. Local source bootstrap remains available outside CI; without --development-plugins it builds only the CLI and shim, then installs the published locked plugins. Pass --ci-machine-binding (used by the repository's own setup action and release workflows) to bind the Rust and Node plugins in machine configuration on a GitHub Actions runner (GITHUB_ACTIONS=true; anywhere else the switch does nothing). Before the configuration check above, the script: Checks that the runner is ephemeral: a GitHub-hosted runner (RUNNER_ENVIRONMENT=github-hosted), or a runner image that declares itself ephemeral with a root-owned, read-only /etc/oyzu-runner-ephemeral and provides a machine directory owned by the runner user, as the repository's self-hosted runner image does with /etc/oyzu. Owning the machine directory alone isn't enough. Otherwise it fails and writes nothing. Refuses an existing machine config.toml. It never merges into or replaces machine configuration. Binds the published rust and node plugin releases on every platform: it creates the machine config.toml with only [plugins.packages] entries for rust/app and node/app, each an oci reference to ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/<name> pinned by release root digest read directly from oyzu.lock. The current builder pins carry Linux amd64 musl and Windows amd64 MSVC payloads. Other hosts need a compatible published payload before bootstrap can use them. Oyzu downloads each release on first use and checks its official signature. Nothing is built from source: a run with no recorded digest, or on a platform the release has no payload for, fails instead. The script then runs oyzu build for a target that does not exist, which installs the bound plugins during plugin selection and stops before building anything (a plan or task only replays installed plugins), and requires oyzu plugins current to report both installed. oyzu.lock must hold their selections. The automatic pin PR updates that lock after the new release appears in the signed catalog. The same file also binds github-release/publish to the signed GitHub release publisher (ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/github-release, Linux amd64 and arm64 musl), pinned by root digest, because the signed catalog has no publisher entries yet. Releases publish through it. It is installed when a publication first selects it. Reads the configuration back with oyzu --json config explain for plugins.packages (parsed with Python, which GitHub-hosted runners and the runner images provide) and requires exactly those three values, from machine scope only. The configuration check must then report the choices complete (unchanged), or the script fails. Machine configuration isn't personal configuration, so CI keeps it. The binding lasts as long as the runner, and a GitHub-hosted runner or runner container is discarded after its job. This applies only to these bindings on ephemeral runners.

Pass --no-plugins instead (it cannot be combined with --ci-machine-binding) when a job needs only the bootstrapped oyzu for oyzu install and oyzu exec and builds its own plugin payload, as the plugin release build does. The script then writes no machine configuration, creates no bootstrap USER file and builds no plugin from source, on any platform. Commands that select the Rust or Node plugins (oyzu build, oyzu run) fail in such a job until the plugins are bound.

Ant's typed test command accepts an optional ordered targets list for a captured coupled lifecycle. When omitted, it runs only target, preserving direct-test and native-host behavior. The listener attributes assertions to target; the complete selected target set, reports and workspace belong to one stage result. This evolves the existing v1alpha1 command in place. Java host preparation uses typed Maven, Gradle and Ant describe commands in the existing v1alpha1 native contract. Ant's command carries the core-owned model output path and an optional version projection. Core binds the model path before dispatch, runs the selected package with the managed task environment against the source root, and passes the resulting metadata through native-build.input.prepared. Plugin roles remain minimal-environment processes: Ant admission checks static project facts; a native evaluation failure is a build preparation error with Ant's diagnostic. The command does not grant acquisition authority or add a protocol generation.

The publisher role extends the existing plugins-v1alpha1 framing. The npm implementation is crates/oyzu-plugin-npm; bind its compiled executable from user, machine or administrative configuration, never project configuration: [plugins.development] "npm/publish" = "/absolute/path/to/oyzu-plugin-npm" This development binding records the actual executable digest in the native destination plan, signed publication intent and receipt. It does not confer the official oyzu package trust of a separately signed release. First-party publisher packages use the signed catalog and lock admission path used by builders; offline CLI bundling is deferred. See npm publishing for configuration and execution limits. Each of describe, destination-plan, destination-inspect, destination-publish and destination-read-back starts a fresh supervised process with a deadline, minimal environment and fresh scratch directory. describe declares destination settings, accepted artifact kinds, hosts, credential slots, tool requirements and pointer effects. Any non-built-in kind resolves <kind>/publish unless uses overrides it. Kind settings pass through opaque: core reads only shared destination keys and declared host settings. Tools declare a name, tool identity, command and optional default version; core provisions them through the ordinary admitted tool contract. Credential slots declare their scheme and optional provider (npm-trusted) and subject JSON pointer. Each plan entry has exactly one inspect and distribute on its native coordinate; pointer effects must be declared and bind readPath, jsonPointer and the expected value. Planning is read-only; inspection and read-back receive read-only proxies. Only a frozen publish effect allows the proxy to forward a write. The plugin uses admitted tool paths and local proxy URLs supplied by core; it never resolves credentials itself. The publisher schemas define the records. The conformance harness accepts a publisher-only fixture directory and uses the same core process host as builders.
Plugin packages, the store and lock selections Plugin catalog and builder selection Go builder preview Configuration

A publisher host declaration selects either a destination setting (setting) or a literal provider URL (url). credential_slot is optional: hosts without it are always anonymous. Core validates every URL and exposes only capability-bearing loopback proxy bases. It rewrites redirects only to declared bases, never follows them itself, and never adds authentication to anonymous hosts. GET/HEAD may run during planning, inspection and read-back; write permits exist only for publish. destination-plan receives core-selected native facts in context and read-only proxies when credentials do not depend on a not-yet-planned subject. Execution receives original signed evidence in evidence, staged read-only by digest after core signs the intent. An acknowledgement's optional receipt is not verification: destination-read-back.files binds each evidence/payload ID to a fresh proxy observation. Core compares every planned file and reconstructs verification from those observations. GitHub's repository visibility also requires its own observed metadata read. The plugin never receives a credential, signing key or authority. The GitHub publisher includes X-Oyzu-Publication-Target on proxy requests. Core accepts a read target only when it is the frozen release or one of its byte-bound assets, and reauthorizes that exact target. The proxy consumes this header locally; it is never forwarded to GitHub. Writes additionally match the frozen upload URL, filename and complete staged bytes before authorization. Protected workers plan from their frozen release facts with proxy requests denied until intent authorization. The admitted publisher identity and every native coordinate must match the frozen request before the worker can publish. Unit adapters write per-attempt completion facts even when they rerun whole units: rerun-cases describes filtering support. Core validates a supplied cases.json and its attempt history independently of that feature. Older JUnit-only units use the generic step safeguards, including an exit-zero final attempt with every originally failed testcase passing. Explicit non-normal native completion facts can accompany a suite-level termination error. A native unit crash retries the whole unit; a unit timeout, kill or incomplete setup remains failed. Ordinary JUnit steps still reject suite-level errors and signals without retrying.

Maven and Gradle native build commands accept an optional phase of compile, test or package in the existing v1alpha1 protocol. Omitting it keeps the single coupled module lifecycle. The jvm-phase-reuse builder feature advertises that a plugin understands the field; send it only to a plugin that describes the feature, and treat an unknown phase as a hard failure. The feature alone changes no planning or execution behavior. The step design is in OEP-0011 JVM phase reuse.

Java's optional rerun-cases description uses the same test-unit phases and cases.json format as other plugins. Maven/Gradle native build commands accept an optional attempt_reports allocation in the existing v1alpha1 protocol. A build operation can carry test_units when it supplies a command and JUnit report, as well as the existing test operation. When present, the package supplies a lifecycle test unit: prepare emits its manifest and native retry facts, run executes the ordinary lifecycle with native filters and completion facts, and finish exposes core's combined JUnit report. Omitting the allocation invokes the ordinary native command. The first attempt keeps the native lifecycle; compile, tool and other non-test failures mark the attempt incomplete. Core alone chooses retries and validates requested cases.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-inspection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu plugins shows which plugins the catalogs offer, which are installed, and which one each target in your project uses and why. Inspection never installs or runs anything and never changes a file. Note: Plugins are experimental. oyzu plugins search go oyzu plugins versions go/app oyzu plugins explain For catalogs, detection and the build's Builders section, see plugin catalog. For the store and oyzu.lock records, see plugin packages. To change a locked selection, use oyzu plugins update. To clean up revoked copies, use oyzu plugins prune.

Command Shows oyzu plugins search [QUERY] [--type build] The uses references the catalogs offer, with package, capability, description, newest stable version, the version oyzu build would pick, and status. oyzu plugins versions REFERENCE Every known release of a reference, labelled, with why each can or can't be selected here. oyzu plugins info REFERENCE[@VERSION] One release: package, publisher, contracts, profiles, platforms, payload digests, download routes and what is verified. oyzu plugins list Releases installed in the plugin store, with the references that name them. A release a catalog has withdrawn or revoked is marked (withdrawn) or (revoked) (JSON catalogStatus). oyzu plugins current This project's locked selections: installed or not, still eligible or not, the update candidate, and one line per plugin-backed target. oyzu plugins explain [TARGET] Why each target uses its plugin, and how to change it.

Option Meaning --json One JSON object on standard output. Before or after the subcommand. --store DIR The plugin store to read, as for oyzu build --store. --refresh Update the cached catalog first. Never downloads a plugin. --offline Never use the network. Can't be combined with --refresh. --type build Filter search by capability. build is the only value. The commands work in any folder. Outside a project, search, versions, info and list work as usual, and current and explain find no targets.

search, versions and info read the same catalog a build uses (see the catalog snapshot): the verified official catalog, or your organization's catalog, which replaces it. A version shown as selectable is one a build can select. Mode Behavior default Uses the cached catalog. Nothing is fetched. --refresh Updates the primary catalog cache even with previews off. Only the preview supplement needs plugins.preview. --offline Never fetches. Anything not cached is shown as unavailable, with the reason. An expired catalog is shown as history only: eligibility is reported as snapshot expired, and current shows it as unknown. Its withdrawals still apply. A catalog that failed verification isn't shown; you're told why no catalog is usable. Search covers the official and organization catalogs only; it doesn't crawl OCI registries. A plugin you name directly (in uses: or plugins.packages) can work without being listed. Under an organization catalog the official one isn't consulted, so a company replacement shows as its own package (for example acme/go for go/app).

oyzu plugins prune removes plugin releases from your local store after a catalog has revoked them. You name each release by its exact digest. Without --apply, it only previews. oyzu plugins list --refresh --store /path/to/store oyzu plugins prune sha256:<64-lowercase-hex-digits> --store /path/to/store oyzu plugins prune sha256:<64-lowercase-hex-digits> --apply --store /path/to/store Each argument must be sha256: and exactly 64 lowercase hex digits. Copy it from the list output. Only a current revocation of that exact release allows removal. A withdrawal, a release missing from the catalog, an expired catalog or unavailable metadata doesn't. Prune uses the cached catalog only. Run plugins list --refresh first if you need a newer one. --apply checks eligibility again; an earlier preview doesn't count. There's no whole-store scan, no force option, and builds, updates and inspection never prune on their own. A release in use by a running Oyzu command is kept. So is one with uncertain identity, malformed metadata or unreadable files. Project lock files aren't changed. If a project still locks a pruned release, Oyzu can install an eligible release again the normal way. See store maintenance. With --json, the result is kind: "plugin-prune" with apply, store, the catalog used, and releases (each with release, state and reason): State Meaning eligible Preview: revoked, identity matches and not in use. retained Not removed. The reason says why. removed The release and its metadata were removed (including leftovers from an interrupted earlier removal). absent Nothing of the release remains. incomplete Removal started but an operating-system error or an outside change stopped it. Some files may be gone. Fix the reported error; you may need to clean up the remaining files by hand. Preview exits 0 when it returns a result. --apply exits 1 if any release is retained or incomplete, otherwise 0. Invalid digests fail before anything is opened. Each release is handled independently.

Label Meaning latest-stable Newest release that isn't a prerelease or withdrawn. It may be incompatible or outside your adopted major version. latest-compatible Newest stable release that fits this engine and host: contract, builder profile, support status and platform. update-candidate Newest selectable release inside the major version your project has locked. adoption-candidate What oyzu build would adopt now, for a reference your project doesn't lock yet. locked The release oyzu.lock holds. A compatible major version 3 can be latest-stable and latest-compatible for a project locked to major 1; it shows outside the adopted major 1 and is never the update candidate. A prerelease shows preview only unless plugins.preview is on. With the opt-in, it can be the adoption candidate when no newer eligible stable release is available. Reasons (in JSON reasons): withdrawn, revoked, preview only, stable releases come from the official catalog, unsupported, no supported protocol generation, no such builder profile, no payload for this platform, outside the adopted major N, snapshot expired. Compatibility is checked for the running engine and this host only. A requested [engine] pin is shown separately (JSON requestedPin, human "Engine pin"), but its capabilities aren't guessed. Remote worker platforms aren't checked, and the output says so.

explain shows the same record oyzu build prints in its Builders section, for every plugin-backed target, followed by what it was checked against. With --json: { "kind": "plugin-explain", "target", "evaluation", "coverage", "lock", "selection" }. coverage.choice (also selection.catalogChoice) says which catalog was used: Value Meaning published The official catalog. organization Your organization's catalog. no-index toolIndex.url = false, so there is no catalog. official-unavailable The official catalog was never fetched, failed verification or expired. coverage.unavailable gives the reason. Two states appear only in inspection, because a build would act on them: state Meaning not-adopted A release is selected but oyzu.lock has no entry yet. The next oyzu build records it. not-installed oyzu.lock selects a release that isn't in the store, and a source for it is known. The next online, non-frozen oyzu build installs it without changing the lock. JSON route (and the explain human view) names the source. Where a build would fail, explain and current fail with the same error: Error Cause PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE The locked release isn't in the store and no binding or catalog entry supplies it. PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH A binding names a different release from the lock. PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE A catalog release isn't in the store and has no download route. PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE The catalog failed verification. PLUGIN_DETECTION_CONFLICT Two detections match the same folder. The error shows the smallest build.yaml selector that settles it. oyzu build --plan never downloads. With an empty store it stops with PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE; the message mentions --offline even if you didn't pass it. For a selection you disagree with, the output lists the same fixes as a build: declare the target in build.yaml (or set uses:), bind a different package, undo an adoption, or pin a tool in oyzu.toml. A plugin's tool requirements come from running the plugin, which inspection never does. So tools is absent from the JSON, the human view says deferred, and a generic oyzu pin <tool>@<version> suggestion appears instead. oyzu build lists the real tools. current returns { "kind": "plugin-current", "evaluation", "coverage", "lock", "locked", "selection" }. lock has path, exists, selections and enginePin. Each locked entry has the reference, package, major, version, release, installed, eligible (null when no usable catalog lists it), reasons, latestStable, latestCompatible and updateCandidate. A newer release in the store doesn't change what oyzu.lock selects. list shows both; current shows the locked one.

list reads <store>/plugins/* and shows package, version, release digest, profiles, platforms, the references that name each release, and whether this project locks it. It can't tell which other projects use a release; the store doesn't track that.

Human output leads with the outcome and uses aligned tables that wrap without losing text on narrow terminals. Meaning never depends on color. --json prints one object per command, and errors use the usual error shape. Human and JSON output always agree.

Code Cause PLUGIN_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN No catalog lists that reference. The error names what is listed. PLUGIN_VERSION_UNKNOWN No release matches the version you asked for. PLUGIN_TARGET_UNKNOWN No plugin-backed target has that name or path. Build resolution errors (PLUGIN_DETECTION_CONFLICT, PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE, PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED and others) are reported unchanged.

Inspection doesn't run the platform and package checks a build runs when it installs a plugin. A release already in the store that this host can't run shows as not-adopted, where a build would fail with PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED. A bound source that isn't installed isn't opened or checked. Only the host platform is evaluated, not remote workers. --type has one value, build. Organization policy beyond the catalog's own withdrawals isn't shown. --refresh refreshes the primary official catalog even with previews off. Only the preview supplement requires plugins.preview. Inspection is supported on Linux. prune is supported on Linux and Windows. macOS isn't supported yet.
Plugin catalog Plugin packages Updating plugins

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-packages.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A plugin package is the archive that holds a builder plugin: its manifest and one executable per platform. Oyzu verifies a package, installs it into a plugin store, pins the exact release in oyzu.lock and launches it for your builds. This page covers where packages come from, how they're verified, how they're locked and how builds record them. Note: Plugins are experimental. Builders are not built into the CLI, so every target needs a package. A package comes from the plugin catalog, from a plugins.packages binding, or from a direct oci:// reference. The official catalog supplies the first-party builders; use oyzu plugins search --refresh to list them. You can also use a development binding.
documents.s: Plugin packages, the plugin store and lock selections

documents.t: A package is a .tar.gz or .zip archive containing: plugin.json at the root, the plugin manifest (schema); the platform executables that the manifest's runtimes name by entrypoint. Installation refuses a package that: hashes to a different digest than the one configured (checked before extraction); exceeds the archive bounds (512 MiB archive; at most 4096 entries, 1 GiB extracted, 512 MiB per file, depth 16, expansion ratio 100), or contains path traversal, absolute paths, hard links, symbolic links that leave the payload, or non-portable names. Relative symbolic links inside the payload are allowed, but an entrypoint must be a regular file; has no valid plugin.json, or one with unknown fields. Fields that name another plugin (dependencies, preferences, successors) are unknown fields, so a plugin can't depend on another plugin; names an entrypoint that's missing, isn't a regular file, or whose SHA-256 differs from the manifest's runtimes[].digest; isn't the package the bound reference names (go/app needs package name go with builder profile app), or supports no protocol generation v1alpha1. Nothing in a package runs during installation. There are no install hooks. To build a package for development, see plugin development.

A binding tells oyzu which package serves a builder reference. Set it in user, machine or administrative configuration, never in a project file or profile (CONFIG_SCOPE): [plugins.packages] "go/app" = { archive = "/home/me/plugins/go-0.1.0.tar.gz", sha256 = "sha256:…" } # or "go/app" = { oci = "ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go:0.1.0" } Keys are short references without a major selector (go/app), or exact direct OCI target references. At most 64 entries. archive is an absolute path. sha256 is sha256: plus 64 lowercase hex digits and must match the archive. A reference can be bound by plugins.packages or by plugins.development, not both (PLUGIN_BINDING_INVALID). A binding applies only to the references your project's targets use. A Go binding never affects a Python or Rust project, and writes no lock entry for it. If the archive digest equals the release digest of the release the catalog selects, the binding is that release's local archive route, and the package must also be the catalog's package and version. Any other digest is a local package binding. Neither can bypass a catalog's withdrawal: a binding for a withdrawn or revoked release is refused with PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN or PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED before it's recorded or launched. Oyzu records how each OCI or HTTPS release was accepted (including whether it's a preview) alongside the installed release. A damaged record is an error; an older installation without one is treated as an ordinary release.

A uses entry in build.yaml can name an OCI release and builder profile directly: builds: app: uses: oci://registry.example/team/opaque@sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa#app The repository path says nothing about which package it is. Oyzu reads the package's own plugin.json, checks the requested profile, protocol and engine features, and records the original URI, the real package and version, and the release root in oyzu.lock. A digest must equal the bound and locked release. A tag is resolved once, when the selection is adopted. Later builds use the locked root and never resolve the tag again. A tag outside the official namespace needs a plugins.packages binding keyed by the complete URI, with the signer to require (see OCI sources). If you later remove that binding, an already installed release still replays without a registry request, but a missing one can't be downloaded until you restore the binding. A configured archive can supply a direct digest only when the archive's digest equals that release. A URI doesn't bypass a refused catalog, a withdrawal or the preview rules. A package named oyzu/* on any registry needs the official signature (below). HTTPS is a catalog route, not a uses syntax.

A binding can name a release in an OCI 1.1 registry, such as GHCR, a distribution registry or Harbor, whose token endpoint (if any) is on the registry's own origin. The release is laid out as the Oyzu OCI package contract defines: an immutable release root binding the plugin manifest and one manifest per platform payload, with a detached Sigstore signature attached to the root. [plugins.packages] # Official release by tag: signed by oyzuai/oyzu's plugin-release.yml. "go/app" = { oci = "ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go:0.1.0" } # Another registry by tag: say whose signature to require. "go/app" = { oci = "registry.example.com/team/go:1.2.0", identity = "https://github.com/acme/plugins/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main" } # By digest: the digest is the trust (no signature is checked unless identity is set # or the reference is in the official namespace). "go/app" = { oci = "registry.example.com/team/go@sha256:…" } Field Value Meaning oci registry/repository:tag or registry/repository@sha256:<hex>, no scheme The release root. A tag and a digest together are refused identity https:// certificate identity (SAN URI) The signer the root signature must come from: a GitHub Actions workflow identity. Signers other than the exact official identity require a GitHub-hosted runner, as with toolIndex.identity; the official identity also accepts self-hosted runners. Required for a tag outside ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/. Refused for an official reference trustedRoot Absolute path A Sigstore trusted_root.json that replaces the production root (for a private Sigstore deployment). Needs a signer.
