Refused for an official reference

A reference under ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/ (also written ghcr.io:443/…) is official. It must be signed by exactly https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu/.github/workflows/plugin-release.yml@refs/heads/main, issued by GitHub Actions OIDC on a GitHub-hosted or self-hosted runner and verified against Sigstore's production trusted root. A copy of the workflow on another branch signs as @refs/heads/<branch> and is refused. Only that exact official identity accepts self-hosted. Every other signer requires github-hosted; missing or unknown runner environments are refused. v0.2.1 is the first client release that trusts self-hosted official signatures. Earlier clients reject them. The certificate does not identify a particular self-hosted pool; pool rotation and revocation remain unresolved. An official binding with identity or trustedRoot is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Configuration can't replace the official signer or let a private CA vouch for it. Any other tag without identity is also CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, when configuration loads. A release found through a catalog (no binding) follows the package's publisher instead: publisher oyzu needs the same official signer on every route, a company mirror included, and any other publisher is trusted by the digest the signed catalog lists. See Who may sign a release. A package named oyzu/* needs the official signature and production root on any network OCI route, even on an arbitrary registry or digest.

On a glibc Linux host, when a release has no payload without an ABI or for gnu, oyzu uses the musl payload for that architecture. Musl payloads must be statically linked. A dynamically linked musl entrypoint is refused on a glibc host with PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED, naming the loader it needs. A package this machine can't run is refused before it's installed. The official Linux payloads are static musl.
documents.s: Choosing a payload for your machine

documents.t: Downloading runs only where an archive would be read: a real oyzu build adopting a selection, or installing a locked release that's missing from the store. It needs no Docker, ORAS, crane or login. Oyzu speaks the OCI Distribution API itself, anonymously, following a registry's Bearer challenge to its token endpoint without credentials, as public GHCR packages allow. A loopback registry (localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1) uses plain HTTP; every other registry uses HTTPS through your configured proxy and certificate trust. It fetches, in order: The release root, by the locked digest, the binding's digest, or (only at first selection) the tag. The digest is the SHA-256 of the bytes received, never a registry header. The signature, when one is required: referrers of the root, through the referrers API or the sha256-<hex> referrers tag. Each Sigstore bundle is verified against the root digest, the signer and the trusted root until one verifies. The metadata manifest and plugin manifest, checked against the bound reference. The manifest and payload for this platform only. Other platforms are never downloaded. Every object must hash to its descriptor before use, and the extracted entrypoint must match its manifest digest. Only then is the release published into the store. Moving a tag afterwards changes nothing, because later builds, --frozen replays and reinstalls into an empty store use the locked digest. An archive digest and a root digest never match, so switching a binding from an archive to OCI is an explicit re-adoption (PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH). Not supported: registries whose token endpoint is on another host (Docker Hub's auth.docker.io); credentials for private registries. A private package fails with PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE; payloads over 512 MiB (a payload is held in memory); organization route settings (list a mirror as a catalog route instead), a command that fills a mirror, and offline export or import.

A verified catalog release can list a route such as {"type":"https","url":"https://mirror.example/plugins/go.tar.gz"}. The URL serves a tar or gzip tar of a standard OCI image layout: oci-layout, index.json and blobs/sha256/<hex> at the archive root. The index names the catalog's exact release root and any detached signature manifests. See the layout contract. Unlike a local plugins.packages archive, the lock and the installed directory use the canonical OCI root digest, not the hash of the transport archive. Changing a release from an OCI route to an HTTPS mirror of the same root keeps the lock valid. Oyzu checks the layout, blob digests, descriptor sizes, metadata, the selected runtime and the extracted entrypoint before installing. Publisher oyzu still needs its fixed official release signer (GitHub-hosted or self-hosted) and the production Sigstore root. The mirror carries the original signature unchanged. Other publishers use the root digest the signed catalog lists. A catalog can't name another signer. The transport uses your configured proxy and SSL_CERT_FILE. HTTPS is required even for loopback. URLs can't carry credentials, a query or a fragment, and redirects must stay within the same origin and directory. Downloads are anonymous and limited to 256 MiB. The whole archive is downloaded, even if it includes other platforms; only your platform's payload is installed. Extraction uses the archive limits above and refuses links and unexpected paths. An installed release needs no archive request. --offline makes no request. --frozen can refresh catalog metadata but never downloads this route. Behind a TLS-inspecting proxy, set HTTPS_PROXY and SSL_CERT_FILE (a PEM file containing the inspection CA). This adds TLS trust only. It never changes the official signer, the production Sigstore root, the route or the locked release. Loopback destinations bypass proxies. Go builds through an inspecting proxy have been tested on Linux and Windows; see acquisition transport. A failed route is PLUGIN_ROUTE_FAILED. Invalid contents keep PLUGIN_PACKAGE_DIGEST or PLUGIN_PACKAGE_INVALID, and missing signatures keep their signature errors. Builds never choose a newer release to recover from unavailable content. Restore the route or the exact content.

Packages live in the tool store (--store, default the shared user store) under plugins/<hex>/, where <hex> is the release digest (the archive digest, or the OCI release root digest). Releases sit side by side, and a build uses the payload for your platform. Concurrent first builds extract once. A release is published with an atomic rename, so nobody sees a partial extraction. A shared lease on the release is held for the whole command to protect a running executable (this matters on Windows). An installed release is trusted. Later builds don't hash it again, and only a missing release needs the archive.

oyzu plugins prune removes a revoked release from your store. It previews by default and needs --apply to remove anything. It acts only on exact digests you name, and only when the current verified cached catalog revokes that release. It doesn't refresh the catalog. A withdrawal, or an expired or unverified revocation, never allows deletion. It takes the store's lock for the release, then an exclusive use lease, so a release in use by another oyzu command is kept. On Windows it also checks that no process has the executable open. Uncertain, malformed, linked or inaccessible content is kept. If the operating system interrupts removal, the result says incomplete, not retained. It touches only plugins/<hex> and the release's package-contents/plugin-<hex>.json. Other releases, catalogs, installed tools, the permanent locks/plugin-<hex> files and every project lock stay as they are. It doesn't check whether other projects' locks name the release. A normal build can download it again if a later selection allows it. To recover a project that still selects a revoked release, adopt an eligible one with oyzu plugins update. Pruning never changes a selection.

The first time oyzu resolves a plugin for a project, it appends the selection to oyzu.lock in the project root. Existing records, comments and ordering aren't touched. [[plugin]] reference = "go/app" profile = "app" package = "oyzu/go" major = 0 version = "0.1.0" release = "sha256:…" [[plugin.payloads]] os = "linux" arch = "amd64" digest = "sha256:…" Field Meaning reference, profile The builder reference and its profile package The publisher/name of the package major The major version of the manifest, set at first resolution version The exact release version release The archive digest, or the OCI release root digest payloads The executable digest per platform from the plugin manifest. For an OCI release, every platform the root lists The lock never records local paths, download times or the platform of the machine that wrote it. oyzu pin and other tool commands keep [[plugin]] entries. A lock that holds only a plugin selection doesn't count as pinned tools: your first oyzu build still pins the tools the builders need. Only a real oyzu build (not --plan or --check) can first install a bound package and record a selection. Only oyzu plugins update can install a release to replace a selection that's already locked. Every other command that discovers the project replays the lock and the store and writes nothing. Situation What happens Bound, not locked, real oyzu build Installs the package, records the selection, then builds Bound, not locked, any other discovery command (including oyzu pin) PLUGIN_NOT_ADOPTED. Nothing is installed or written. Run oyzu build Locked, release installed Reuses it. The archive isn't read Locked, release missing, binding present oyzu build installs it from the binding (an archive, or an OCI reference fetched by the locked digest), only if the binding names the locked release. Other commands report PLUGIN_NOT_INSTALLED Locked, release missing, no binding An online, non-frozen oyzu build downloads that exact release from its entry in the current verified catalog, without changing the lock. An unlisted release or an absent or expired catalog gives PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE. A refused catalog gives PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE. A listed release with no usable route gives PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE. A plugins.development binding for the reference still replaces the locked package Locked, release missing, no binding, --frozen or --offline PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE. Nothing is downloaded and the lock isn't rewritten. Prepare the release online first Binding names a different release than the lock PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH. Builds never change a selection. Use oyzu plugins update <reference> Installed release differs from the lock PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE oyzu build --frozen, selection missing PLUGIN_LOCK_MISSING. Nothing is resolved, installed or written. Restore a complete lock, or adopt with a normal oyzu build where your policy allows it. Removing --frozen never waives policy oyzu build --frozen, selection present Replays it. Missing content can still be installed from a bound local archive, but never from an OCI binding or a catalog route Two builds of one project at once The second is refused ("another oyzu build is using this workspace") Lock this oyzu can't parse, with [[plugin]] visible in it Discovery refuses with the lock error rather than guess tasks for a project whose package it can't know Lock with sections or fields this oyzu doesn't know Refused before anything changes ("use the oyzu release that wrote it")

oyzu build <name>..., plain oyzu build, oyzu build --plan, oyzu run <build>:<task> and oyzu run <task> for a task your root oyzu.toml defines select, install, replay and launch only the plugins of the builds they asked for and the builds those need. In a project with a cli build (rust/app) and a docs build (node/app), oyzu build docs never needs the Rust plugin installed, and a missing rust/app release doesn't stop it. A root task such as oyzu run check-docs that depends on no build needs no plugin at all, because a root task never replaces a build's stage (which build a task belongs to). oyzu decides which builds are needed before it selects any plugin, from build.yaml and your oyzu.toml files alone: the builds you named, or every build without default: false when you name none (none for a root task) each build they list in depends_on or materialize, and a chart's bound image each build named in the depends_on of a task those builds can reach, including unqualified tasks and hooks such as pre_test oyzu.lock keeps the selections of the builds left out exactly as they are; they're neither checked nor rewritten. --frozen only requires selections for the builds in play. The whole project is discovered, and every plugin it uses is selected, for oyzu build --affected, oyzu run with an unqualified name the root doesn't define (which may be a build's own task, such as oyzu run test in a one-build project), a root task whose depends_on names a task by its bare name that the root doesn't define or that has a qualified hook such as [tasks."api:pre_check"], oyzu discover, oyzu lock, tool commands, and a name that isn't a build (such as a platform variant id, or a typo, which is then reported with every build's name). Builds of different projects that share a store converge: a build that loses a race on the lock reuses the pins the other build published, or retries for up to 30 seconds, instead of failing with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT. Offline native builds also need their ordinary tool metadata in the same user context. oyzu tools check --catalog --json seeds the signed tool index into the default user metadata store; add --store DIR to target another store. An explicit plugin store doesn't replace the default metadata that native Go reads for its locked-version withdrawal check. Prepare both while online. A catalog revocation refuses installed releases, even when replaying against an expired catalog. Selection refusal doesn't delete bytes; use oyzu plugins prune. @vN major selectors in bindings aren't supported.
documents.s: Only the plugins your selected builds need

documents.t: Every build records the engine that ran it. A stamped release from a clean, matching oyzu/v<version> tag uses that release version, such as 0.2.4 or 0.4.0-rc.1, even when the building oyzu supplies a snapshot suffix. Beta and nightly identities preserve the full native prerelease part; only the appended dev.g<source-digest> snapshot part is removed. Other stamped builds use a token such as 0.2.2-local.36bdcec27267. A development engine uses <package-version>-dev.engine.<sha256>, independently of its short --version display label. Copy the complete Engine value from the build Context or retained inventory to pin it by hand: [engine] identity = "0.1.0-local.36bdcec27267" Compilation captures a deterministic inventory of engine source digests, the transitive local runtime/build dependency inputs, Cargo manifests/lock and the rustc release and shared profile facts (optimization, debug information, debug assertions, overflow checks and panic strategy), plus enabled features. Project Cargo profile tables and common CARGO_PROFILE_* overrides are bound too. Shared Rust flags (RUSTFLAGS, CARGO_BUILD_RUSTFLAGS and project build.rustflags) are bound; effective encoded flags are excluded only when identified as a declared target-only selection. Local dependency files follow Cargo's package include/exclude and ignore rules; ignored files and ignored symlinks do not change the identity, and packaged file symlinks are read through their targets. Development engine composition verifies compiled-file coverage from Cargo dep-info: consuming an omitted file fails with ENGINE_INPUTS_UNCOVERED, rather than silently widening that inventory. See engine staging for the required retained records and the non-Git-tree limit. The engine hashes that embedded inventory lazily on the first identity request and retains the result for the process. Development-only plugin dependencies do not enter this engine fingerprint. A docs-only commit keeps it stable; changed engine inputs change it. This is an input identity, not a signature or source attestation. Package admission separately binds every platform member's executable digest. Members packed together must carry the same engine identity. Development members need matching compiler releases, features and shared profile facts as well as source content. Host triples and target-only rustflags, linkers and C toolchains do not enter this shared identity. User [patch] overrides/source replacement and C toolchain inputs are not covered. Release members use the shared release stamp across targets. No source or executable hashing runs on public help, version or syntax-error paths. A protected administrative policy can require this pin and a complete lock (policy-required pins). CI alone doesn't make the pin mandatory. If the pinned engine isn't the one running, oyzu uses engine staging before discovering the project, when an allowed user or system source provides the archive. Otherwise it fails with ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH. A development override keeps the running executable and records its actual content and the bypassed pin. A package lists the engine features it needs (such as go-test-events or captured-plan). If the running oyzu lacks one, the build fails with PLUGIN_ENGINE_REQUIREMENT before any plugin operation, naming the missing feature and the running engine. Use an oyzu that supports it, or a compatible plugin release. The catalog skips releases whose required features oyzu doesn't support. Java packages using Gradle's compiler observations require gradle-compiler-facts. The engine must support that preparation contract as well as the package's exact native API. Kotlin JVM source attribution and reporting add the gradle-kotlin-jvm requirement; ship that Java plugin release with the matching CLI because their Gradle runtime digests must agree. Older engines skip that release and can keep selecting an eligible earlier package; a direct incompatible package binding fails before any plugin role runs. This does not waive preview opt-in, signature, withdrawal or platform checks. Python packages implementing per-test-case facts require python-test-case-facts on their builder role. The engine must implement those facts and use the package's exact native API; the strict prepared API/version check still rejects mixed runtimes. Older engines skip the newer release and retain an eligible earlier package. Direct incompatible bindings fail before a plugin operation. After a compatible signed release is available, use oyzu plugins update python/app (or the selected Python profile) to update an existing lock; a source merge or local engineering package does not update the published default. Python packages providing complete current case closures also require python-current-case-closure. Engines without this capability skip that release during catalog selection and reject a direct binding before any role runs. This marker does not relax the exact native runtime check or make an older package compatible with a new core. An existing lock remains exact until an explicit plugin update selects a compatible signed release. .NET lock preparation requires dotnet-lock-admission on the selected package's builder role. The engine checks that declaration before admitting its native worker for private lock-facts/acquisition. An older exact lock is replayed as recorded, then refused at that boundary if the capability is missing; it is never silently replaced. Use oyzu plugins update dotnet/sdk to explicitly select an admitted capable package. A newer version label alone does not prove support. Catalog eligibility still selects the newest eligible release under the existing preview and organization-catalog rules; execution failures never trigger a downgrade.

Windows plugin stores support executable paths longer than 260 characters. No shortened store path or additional launch flag is required; filesystem component and total path limits still apply. This applies to plugin protocol operations and native stage actions. Long absolute application paths use the Windows verbatim form at launch without resolving filesystem links; short paths retain their existing spelling and require no additional filesystem lookup. A package's entrypoint runs in place from the store, where its digest was verified at installation. A plugins.development executable is copied to a private per-command file and hashed as it's copied, so the recorded digest is that of the file as launched. Replacing the source afterwards changes nothing in the running command. The copy is removed when the command ends. If oyzu is killed by a signal, the copy stays in the temporary directory as oyzu-plugin-*; delete it by hand. Plans identify a host plugin command as <plugin-exec:sha256:…> using the admitted executable's digest, so a private copy's random directory does not change the plan. The owning target retains the full plugin identity. At launch, Oyzu resolves that identity through the current invocation's admitted handle and runs its verified copy; loading a plan cannot recreate plugin authority. Any planned program beginning with <plugin- without a matching admitted binding is refused with PLUGIN_SELECTION_MISMATCH before process launch. Cache-key normalization uses the separate <plugin-worker:…> semantic token; it is not a planned executable identity. For a wrapper script, the digest covers only the script, not the program it starts, so its targets are never reused from the action cache. Bind the plugin executable itself. Action cache keys include the plugin's semantic identity (reference, protocol, runtime and package release/version, or compiled development source-closure digest). The target's extensions["oyzu.dev/builder-plugin"] also retains executable digests for admission and provenance; those bytes are excluded only when deriving cache keys; see external builder targets. Every plan, execution envelope and manifest of a build or oyzu run carries extensions["oyzu.dev/plugins"] when a plugin is used, so plugin-built output is distinguishable from other output: {"reference":"go/app","source":"package","package":"oyzu/go","version":"0.1.0", "release":"sha256:…","executableDigest":"sha256:…","selection":"adopted"} {"reference":"go/app","source":"local-development", "executableName":"plugin","executableDigest":"sha256:…"} A development record keeps only the executable's file name, never your absolute path. Nothing refuses to publish plugin-built output; the record makes it visible. oyzu inspect requires the records in the plan, manifest and envelope to be identical (see build bundles). oyzu run --store DIR, oyzu scan --store DIR and oyzu lock --store DIR move the plugin store with the tool store, as oyzu build --store DIR does. Each discovery freezes its own selected bindings. A later discovery in the same process may select another executable, changed bytes or another reference without replacing the earlier discovery's plugins. Planning, execution and provenance for each discovered workspace use its own admitted bindings; clones share their lifetime. Read-only commands (oyzu run list, its oyzu tasks list alias and configuration inspection) do not compute development-plugin source digests. They emit one PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_UNVERIFIED warning per selected development binding, with a repair command. The binding may be stale; inspection does not establish freshness. Configuration inspection also defers plugin-owned option validation without launching the executable. Help opens no configuration and prints no binding warning; bundle inspection does not load project plugins. Before build --plan previews a selected development builder, or that builder supplies execution, core checks its compiled source identity against its checkout once per invocation runtime. A stale or unverifiable binding stops both preview and execution with PLUGIN_DEVELOPMENT_STALE. In this repository, repair it with oyzu run bootstrap -- --source --development-plugins; other plugin authors rebuild and rebind their executable or package archive from current source. Locator hints on disk never replace source validation. Direct test tasks check freshness before native model observation, including Maven/Gradle evaluation of project build scripts. Pinning and requirement-based tool selection also require fresh selected bindings before resolving or publishing tool selections. A stale binding leaves the tool lock unchanged. The shell hook reports an unavailable-selection warning and performs no installation from those requirements; rebuild and rebind the plugin before retrying. oyzu run <task> checks the selected task owners before preparing tools, including automatic installation from a portable project's pinned environment. oyzu run --isolated <task> also admits freshness before collecting requirements or installing tools. A stale selected binding supplies no requirements on either path and creates no tool installation. Tool auto-pinning can discover the workspace again before a build. If a selected target's builder or admitted core profile changed between those discoveries, both native and isolated builds stop with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT. Retry the build after finishing any concurrent plugin rebuild so routing, execution and provenance use the same selected plugin.
documents.s: Which bytes run, and how output records them

documents.t: --isolated builds run in a sandbox with no network, in Docker or the Linux daemonless sandbox. The plugin plans the build without running it (the captured-plan feature), and oyzu does everything that needs the network or a toolchain: it installs the locked tools and dependencies, then runs the plan offline. Note: Isolated builds with plugins are experimental and are limited to Linux amd64 targets. An isolated build with a plugin needs all of these: A package whose manifest declares captured-plan and has runtime members for both your host and the Linux execution platform. One member can serve both when the platforms match. For an isolated build, exactly one member must match the image's OS and architecture; none or several refuse selection. An accepted engine archive and a usable immutable Linux image. The locked tools for that platform. A raw development executable binding can't run an isolated build; a development binding to a package archive can (see plugin development). Any missing piece fails explicitly with PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED or ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE, and oyzu never falls back to another builder. The plugin supplies build, artifact and test report intent; it can't fetch dependencies in this role. JUnit and coverage reports stay required checks.

Supported: one conventional Go application module with one main package, with a Linux artifact and execution platform declared in build.yaml. oyzu build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full Add --no-docker to require the daemonless sandbox. On Linux amd64, a normal build adopts the package selection. Commit the complete oyzu.lock, then use --frozen to replay it, and add --offline when every exact input is retained. A missing input fails without using the network. --full produces the executable with native JUnit and Go coverage. This daemonless application path does not cover libraries or workspaces. Use the Go captured path for those shapes. Missing capabilities and unsupported settings fail explicitly.

Supported: python/package targets built with pip and PEP 517. The package must declare captured-plan. The official catalog supplies the Python plugin; a user or machine binding can select another compatible package. oyzu -C <fixture> --json build demo --isolated --full --frozen --no-cache --jobs 1 Oyzu freezes the selected CPython archive and the prepared dependencies, then lowers the plugin's intent to a wheel or sdist build. Put tool versions in native pin files or oyzu.toml, not in build.yaml. Installed-artifact tests and quality reports are required checks. Python builds with uv, Poetry or legacy distributions don't use this path. A refusal never falls back to another builder. See Python preparation.

Supported: npm node/app applications. The package must declare captured-plan. The official catalog supplies the Node plugin; enable preview selection if required by the selected release. oyzu build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --frozen --image npm=<node-image> Oyzu prepares the locked Node and npm archives and dependencies and runs an offline install before the plugin's build and check steps. JUnit and LCOV reports are required. A dist directory written by your project is moved aside in the private workspace before the build and exported with the usual containment checks. Select tools in oyzu.toml (they resolve into oyzu.lock). The image must be one your engine can run; a bare image without the right runtime fails explicitly. Yarn, workspaces and frameworks need their own pages (Yarn, npm workspaces, pnpm). pnpm applications use the same flow with --image pnpm=<node-image>. Export of the native pnpm store currently needs exactly pnpm 10.11.0, selected in packageManager or the tool configuration, with pnpm-lock.yaml and oyzu.lock up to date. The default base execution image is enough: the YAML parser the pnpm adapter needs (yaml 2.9.1, ISC license, shipped with its license) comes in the Node plugin package. An image you pass with --image pnpm=<ref> must meet the bring-your-own requirements.

Supported: a single-root npm project that produces a .tgz through npm pack. Oyzu uses this path when build.yaml has uses: node/package, or when there's no build.yaml and the project's output facts select a package: builds: package: {uses: node/package} oyzu build package --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --frozen --image npm=<node-image> oyzu inspect dist You need a package.json with a package name, a current npm lock, selected Node and npm tools, the required checks and a matching package that declares captured-plan. With no build.yaml, the command is oyzu -C <project> --json build --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --no-cache --image npm=<node-image>. Dependencies are installed offline. Oyzu applies the build's resolved version to a private copy of package.json and the lock, runs your build script and checks, then runs npm pack --json --ignore-scripts. Your checkout and its locks are not changed. A package with no build script skips the build step. Read the artifact's path, version and digest from its recorded manifest. Don't guess the file name npm produced. Failed tests or missing required reports block packing and export. Tested with Node 22.23.3 and npm 11.11.0 on a Linux amd64 worker. Failure Recovery Missing native lock, incompatible package or engine, or a workspace target Supply current inputs, or use a flow that supports your project Lock mismatch or install failure Regenerate the lock with npm, then update the frozen inputs. Nothing is projected or packed Build, required report or pack failure Fix the failure and rerun. No archive is exported Packed archive name or version doesn't match, or the path is unsafe Inspect the retained packing log and the package's name and version

An inferred single-root pnpm project produces a .tgz the same way, through pnpm pack --json --out. You need a real pnpm-lock.yaml, exactly pnpm 10.11.0 (tested with Node 22.23.3), the required checks, and a matching package that declares captured-plan. Vite projects and pnpm workspaces aren't covered here (see pnpm). oyzu -C <project> --json build --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --no-cache --image pnpm=<node-image> An explicit uses: node/package selects the same profile. A package with no scripts exports straight from the checked-in source with setup, checks and packing, and no build step.

Supported: an explicit single-root npm package built on your machine (no sandbox) with the Node plugin. Declare only the package intent and keep your npm lock: builds: package: {uses: node/package} oyzu --json build package --full --no-cache The first build records any missing selection in oyzu.lock. Lint and format checks prefer project-installed packages. Otherwise preparation installs the exact default quality set in oyzu.lock into the shared tool store. Missing pins or declared-but-uninstalled tools stop the build before export; see Node quality. Oyzu applies the version to a private copy, runs your checks and hooks, then runs npm pack --json --ignore-scripts into a fresh scratch directory. Read the artifact's path, digest and version from the manifest. Failed checks or missing reports prevent export. Tested on Windows x86-64 with Node 22.23.3 and npm 11.11.0. Inferred and Vite packages, pnpm and Yarn packages, and other platforms aren't supported on this path. For workspace packages, see npm workspaces and Yarn.

Code Cause Recovery PLUGIN_PACKAGE_DIGEST Archive bytes differ from the configured digest, or an OCI object differs from its descriptor Fix the digest or archive. For OCI, the registry or mirror is serving wrong bytes PLUGIN_PACKAGE_INVALID The manifest, entrypoint or archive broke a rule Rebuild the package PLUGIN_PACKAGE_MISMATCH The package doesn't provide the bound reference Bind the right package PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE The archive is missing and the release isn't installed, an OCI object is missing, or the registry refused anonymous access or is unreachable. The missing digest is named Restore the archive, complete the mirror or make the package public PLUGIN_SIGNATURE_MISSING No Sigstore signature is attached to the OCI release root. For an oyzu/* package on a catalog mirror, the message says the mirror must serve the official signature Publish the required signature. A package from another publisher can be bound by digest. For a mirror of an official package, copy the release's signature referrers (the sha256-<hex> tag or referrers entries, with the signature manifest and bundle) into the mirror unchanged PLUGIN_SIGNATURE_INVALID No attached signature verifies for the root digest, signer and trusted root Check identity and trustedRoot. For a mirror of an official package, serve the official release and its original signature. A company's own build can't stand in for oyzu/*; list it as the company's own package PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED No runtime for this OS, architecture and ABI. The message names your machine and what the package provides Use a package that has one PLUGIN_LOCK_MISSING, PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH, PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE, PLUGIN_NOT_ADOPTED, PLUGIN_NOT_INSTALLED See the lock table above PLUGIN_ENGINE_REQUIREMENT The package needs an engine feature this oyzu lacks Use an oyzu that supports it, or another release ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH The running engine isn't the pinned one Run the pinned oyzu
Plugin catalog and builder selection Inspecting plugins Updating plugins Go builder preview Writing and testing a plugin

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-preview.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu/go builds Go projects and is published as a signed OCI package on GHCR, listed in the official plugin catalog. It has stable and preview releases. This page says how to select it, what it supports, how long releases are supported, and what happens when a release is withdrawn. Note: The plugin interface (v1alpha1) is experimental and can still change. A later preview may behave differently; stable release selection does not expand the builder's documented platform or feature support. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

The install scripts enable preview plugins when you have no existing user-level choice, so preview builders are available. If you installed another way or turned previews off, enable them with: oyzu config set --global plugins.preview true Go now has a stable release, which a fresh build selects without preview opt-in. Build a Go module: oyzu build Oyzu downloads the eligible oyzu/go release from ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go, checks its signature, records the exact release in oyzu.lock and builds with it. A supported single-main application needs no account, login or Docker. Other project shapes have their own execution requirements. The build's Builders section shows the source as official default. To undo it, remove oyzu.lock, then run oyzu config unset --global 'plugins.packages."go/app"' and oyzu config set --global plugins.preview false. The build prints this line for you.

Immutable releases. A published version never changes. A fix, a changed payload or a new platform is a new version. Verified bytes. Oyzu accepts a release only when it's signed by the plugin-release.yml workflow on refs/heads/main from a GitHub-hosted or self-hosted runner, and it checks every object by digest (signature rules). No surprises. A lock never silently changes the implementation. A newer release, a newer preview or a new catalog serial changes nothing until you run oyzu plugins update. This includes a stable release replacing the locked preview; turning previews off also leaves the lock usable unless the release is withdrawn or revoked. Visible and reversible selection. The build shows which builder each target got and prints the line that undoes it. A preview does not promise that the plugin interface is stable, that a later preview behaves like this one, that every platform in the package is tested, or that it's supported after a newer release replaces it. Previews are left out of ordinary stable resolution and updates.

Selection is deliberate and per user. A project file can't select a preview (CONFIG_SCOPE), because the release is code that runs on your machine. Set it in user, machine or administrative configuration: [plugins] preview = true The installer preserves an explicit false as well as true. To opt out, run oyzu config set --global plugins.preview false. With previews disabled and a catalog offering only previews, builder selection reports PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE, explains that first-party plugins are preview releases, and names the opt-in command in both the message and next step. Offline, expired-catalog and fetch failures retain their own causes. Existing locked selections follow the normal replay rules. When you explicitly select a preview, the build downloads the release from the route in the verified catalog (ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go@sha256:25f830bd…f9bf). Optionally, a plugins.packages binding supplies the bytes instead and takes precedence: [plugins.packages] "go/app" = { oci = "ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go:0.1.0-preview.1" } A tag binding has these consequences: The tag can move. GHCR tags are mutable. Oyzu resolves the tag once, at first selection, so a fresh checkout without a committed oyzu.lock can resolve different releases at different times. The lock is what pins the release: it records the root digest, and later builds, --frozen replays and fresh stores fetch that digest. Commit oyzu.lock, or bind by digest (ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go@sha256:<root>). It's a local package binding. The catalog's supported, deprecated and unsupported statuses don't apply to a release a tag supplies. A withdrawal or revocation still refuses it. oyzu plugins update still never selects a preview you didn't name. A digest binding equal to the release the catalog would select counts as the official default. When a compatible stable release of the same package is listed, a fresh build selects it without the preview opt-in. Enabling previews still selects the newest eligible version: 0.1.0 outranks 0.1.0-preview.2. If only previews are eligible and the opt-in is off, the build fails with PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE and names the opt-in. A stable release without a payload for this host is excluded with that reason; it does not grant permission to use a preview. Existing locks keep their exact release. oyzu plugins update never moves a selection to a preview unless you name it (go/app@0.1.0-preview.2, which needs the opt-in). A routine update stays inside the adopted major version and skips previews.

Oyzu ignores the whole user configuration when it sees a CI marker (CI, GITHUB_ACTIONS and similar variables). A project file can't select a preview, so the settings above have no effect in a CI job. Instead, write them to the machine configuration before the build. On a GitHub-hosted Linux runner: - name: Select the Go preview run: | sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/oyzu sudo tee /etc/oyzu/config.toml > /dev/null <<'TOML' [plugins] preview = true TOML - run: oyzu build Keep the file owned by root and not writable by group or others. Oyzu doesn't check the owner or mode of the machine config.toml, so this is advice, not enforcement. The recipe replaces any machine configuration already on the runner, so use it on throwaway runners. The machine file is /Library/Application Support/Oyzu/config.toml on macOS and %ProgramData%\Oyzu\config.toml on Windows; those paths use the same rule but haven't been tested.

Support. Only the newest preview is supported. When a newer preview or a stable release replaces it, the catalog marks it deprecated for at least 30 days, with a message naming the successor, then unsupported. Fixes ship as a new preview. There are no backports. Withdrawal. A defective release is withdrawn at once, without waiting for the deprecation period. Retention. Release roots, platform payloads and signatures stay on GHCR for at least 12 months after the release is replaced. A withdrawn or revoked release's bytes and evidence are kept as long as its withdrawal is listed. Catalog entries. The catalog lists supported releases within their retention. Withdrawals are kept for good. A release removed from the catalog is unlisted, not withdrawn: new builds no longer offer it, but a lock that names it still replays while its bytes are in your store or on GHCR. Transparency log. Each signature is a public Sigstore (Rekor) entry. It can't be deleted, and withdrawing a release doesn't remove it. Freshness. The catalog is re-signed daily and is never valid for more than 31 days. Oyzu refreshes the primary catalog at most once an hour, even with previews off. Oyzu treats these cases differently. A deprecated or unsupported release still replays. Missing bytes fail with PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE. A withdrawn or revoked release is refused with PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN or PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED.

When the catalog selects the release (the usual path): Status New selection (an unlocked build) Adoption (oyzu plugins update) Replay of an existing lock supported Offered A candidate Replays. An online, non-frozen build with an empty plugin store downloads the exact locked digest again without rewriting the lock deprecated (even past its end date) Offered, with no build warning. oyzu plugins info shows the status and message, and --json also the end date A candidate Replays unsupported Not offered. The build fails with PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE unless you bind a digest, which still installs it Not a candidate ("up to date"). An explicit binding of the release still adopts it Replays preview, without plugins.preview Not offered Never chosen by a routine update (PLUGIN_PREVIEW_NOT_SELECTED) Replays preview, with plugins.preview Offered Only when named exactly (go/app@<version>) Replays unlisted (removed after retention) Not offered Not a candidate Replays from the store. A fresh store needs a binding of the locked digest, or fails with PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE withdrawn Not offered. A plugins.packages binding of it is refused (PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN) before it's recorded or run Refused by name or binding Refused on every command, including --plan and --frozen, naming the lock entry. The lock isn't rewritten revoked As withdrawn, with PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED As withdrawn As withdrawn With a plugins.packages binding (which takes precedence over the catalog's route), the catalog is consulted only for withdrawals: Binding New selection oyzu plugins update Lock replay Tag (oci = "…/go:<version>") Support status doesn't apply. Oyzu resolves the tag once and the lock pins the digest Never adopts a preview (PLUGIN_PREVIEW_NOT_SELECTED) Replays by the locked digest Digest (oci = "…@sha256:…", or archive with sha256) An unsupported release installs Adopts an unsupported release through the binding. Refuses a preview as above Replays Locked, no binding n/a n/a Replays A withdrawn or revoked release is refused for every kind of binding, before it's installed. Support is advice and withdrawal is authority: unsupported and deprecated never stop a lock, while withdrawn and revoked always do. Known limits: A passed end date doesn't change a status by itself. The catalog is re-published as unsupported. A build shows no deprecation warning. A revocation can't reach a machine that never verified a catalog, or stop an installed copy that isn't replayed through a lock.

A catalog change reaches you as the next serial of the tool index. Oyzu picks it up at its next refresh, at most an hour later, and applies its withdrawals on every command. Situation What you see What to do A release is defective and withdrawn Builds and --plan fail with PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN, naming the catalog serial and the lock entry Run oyzu plugins update go/app (it needs a binding or the store to supply the replacement). oyzu plugins versions go/app shows why a release is excluded A release is revoked (its content or signing is compromised) PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED ("it will not run") on every command. Installed copies outside a lock aren't removed Recover as above. Remove the copy with oyzu plugins prune The catalog is wrong and rolled back Oyzu ignores a lower serial, the same serial with other bytes, or a higher serial generated earlier, and keeps the last verified copy and its withdrawals Nothing to do The catalog is tampered with or its signature fails Oyzu refuses it and keeps the last verified copy. Unlocked references fail with PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE. A lock replays only against a verified copy. With no network or an expired copy, withdrawals still apply and a PLUGIN_CATALOG_EXPIRED warning appears Bind a package explicitly to continue without the catalog GHCR is unreachable or the package is private PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE naming the missing object or "refused anonymous access". A release already in your store keeps working with no network Retry when the registry is reachable A signed release can't be deleted: the signature log entry is permanent and the bytes stay for the retention period. It can only be withdrawn.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-updates.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu plugins update changes the plugin selections already recorded in oyzu.lock. Use it for a routine update within the major version you adopted, to move to a new major version on purpose, or to select one exact version or release (which is also how you undo an update). A ready-made GitHub workflow can run it on a schedule and open a pull request. Note: Plugins are experimental. oyzu plugins update # every locked selection, each within its adopted major oyzu plugins update go/app # only go/app oyzu plugins update go/app@v2 # move go/app to major 2 oyzu plugins update go/app@1.0.0 # exactly version 1.0.0 of go/app's package oyzu plugins update go/app@sha256:… # exactly this release (the printed undo) oyzu plugins update --dry-run # check and show the change without writing oyzu.lock For how a selection is first adopted, see plugin catalog. For the [[plugin]] lock record, see plugin packages. For read-only views, see inspecting plugins.

Option Meaning --dry-run Check everything and show the change, but don't write oyzu.lock. --offline Use the cached catalog only. --store DIR The plugin store, as for oyzu build --store. --json One JSON object on standard output. No account is needed. Publishing or caching a newer plugin release never changes your lock; builds keep using the locked release. Only this command (or deleting the entry) changes it.

You write Picks go/app, or nothing (every locked reference) The newest eligible release in the adopted major. Never an older one while the locked release can still be used. go/app@v2 or go/app@2 The newest eligible release of major 2. go/app@1.4.2 Exactly version 1.4.2 of the package the catalog binds, newer or older. go/app@sha256:… Exactly this release, which also fixes the package. The printed undo uses this form. "Eligible" means the same as for a build: listed by the catalog, not withdrawn or revoked, supported, on the current plugin contract, with the right builder profile and a payload for this host. A plugins.packages binding for the reference supplies the package instead, as it does for a build, and must still match the selector. Previews. Routine and @v<major> updates never pick a preview release (PLUGIN_PREVIEW_NOT_SELECTED). A release is a preview if its version is a prerelease or the catalog lists it as one. An exact @<version> or @sha256:… can pick a preview, but only with plugins.preview on. If it is off, the catalog refusal names the opt-in command and leaves the lock unchanged. Preview to stable. A routine update can replace a locked preview with a compatible stable release in the same adopted major, including major 0. For example, 0.1.0-preview.2 to 0.1.0 is a patch change: the major and minor numbers are unchanged. The report shows both versions and the lock changes only when the update succeeds. This also works after previews are turned off or the preview is withdrawn; the stable replacement must remain eligible. Package changes. A routine update never switches to a different package. If an organization catalog or a binding now points the reference at another package, you get PLUGIN_PACKAGE_CHANGE; adopt it with an explicit selector such as @v1.

If oyzu.toml pins an exact engine, that engine is set up first (see engine staging). Required features it doesn't support fail before anything changes. Then: Refresh the catalog. Unless you pass --offline, the verified catalog is refreshed first. If there's no current verified catalog (refused, expired or missing), the whole update fails with PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE. This is stricter than a build: a build continues with an older cached copy after a refused refresh; an update doesn't. Pick each candidate using the selector. Check it. Each new release is installed into the plugin store (from the store, a plugins.packages binding, or the OCI route in its catalog entry) and checked like a first adoption: digest, package and version, builder profile, protocol and a payload this host can run. It must also pass the build's lock rules: not withdrawn, not revoked, not rebound by an organization catalog. Write once. Only when every requested reference passes is oyzu.lock rewritten, replacing just those [[plugin]] entries (comments above them are kept). Other selections, tool records and the engine pin are untouched. If another process changed those entries in the meantime, nothing is written (PLUGIN_LOCK_CHANGED). Any failure leaves the lock exactly as it was. An update never runs a plugin and never edits configuration or other project files. Releases it installed stay in the store, even after a failed or --dry-run update.

Updated 1 plugin selection in oyzu.lock Changes Reference Before After Change Why go/app acme/go 1.0.0 acme/go 1.0.1 patch the plugins.packages binding supplies this release go/library acme/go 1.0.0 — unchanged newest eligible release in major 1 Releases go/app sha256:a9713fde…7583 → sha256:d660c518…06ca · installed now from /home/me/acme-go-1.0.1.tar.gz Undo oyzu plugins update go/app@sha256:a9713fde547a6353975dd14aad1c837a4c70b475961ec37563ae320fb32d7583 Restores the earlier releases while they remain eligible; reverting the oyzu.lock change does the same. Lock ./oyzu.lock (updated) Evaluated against Engine 0.1.0 (running engine) … Review and commit oyzu.lock to share the update. Nothing was launched and no configuration changed. Change Meaning patch, minor A newer release in the same major. major A new major, chosen explicitly. rollback An older release, chosen with @<version> or because the locked one can't be used anymore. package A different package now serves the reference, chosen explicitly. unchanged Nothing newer is eligible. With --dry-run, the heading says Would update … and the undo is labelled Undo (once adopted). Notes point out things like a binding that holds the locked release while a newer one is eligible. --json prints the same information: {"kind":"plugin-update","dryRun":false,"wrote":true,"lock":"/work/app/oyzu.lock", "changes":[{"reference":"go/app","selector":null, "from":{"package":"acme/go","major":1,"version":"1.0.0","release":"sha256:…"}, "to":{"package":"acme/go","major":1,"version":"1.0.1","release":"sha256:…"}, "level":"patch","reason":"…","installedNow":true,"route":"/home/me/acme-go-1.0.1.tar.gz"}], "undo":"oyzu plugins update go/app@sha256:…","notes":[], "evaluation":{"engine":"…","engineSource":"running engine","platforms":["linux/amd64"],"…":"…"}, "coverage":{"choice":"organization","snapshots":[{"label":"acme catalog serial 2","…":"…"}],"…":"…"}} evaluation and coverage match the inspection commands.

The undo line selects each changed reference's earlier release by digest, so it fixes the package as well as the version. It goes through the same checks, so it works only while that release is still available and allowed: A release the catalog has since withdrawn or revoked is refused with PLUGIN_UPDATE_UNAVAILABLE. If a catalog now binds the reference to another package, the earlier package is refused. The message names both packages and your options: ask the catalog's owner to bind the package you want, or update the bound one with an explicit selector. Under an organization catalog, builds refuse a lock of the other package too (PLUGIN_BINDING_CHANGED), including a reverted oyzu.lock. If a plugins.packages binding supplied the new release, the binding has to name the earlier release again (or be unset) before the undo works. The update's notes say so, and an undo against the binding fails with PLUGIN_UPDATE_CONFLICT and the oyzu config unset line to run. Reverting the oyzu.lock change in version control has the same effect; the next build checks it under the same rules.

Every failure says oyzu.lock was not changed. Code Cause and fix PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE No current verified catalog. Restore access and run again. PLUGIN_UPDATE_NOT_LOCKED The reference isn't in oyzu.lock. Run oyzu build to adopt it first. PLUGIN_SELECTOR_INVALID The selector isn't v<major>, an exact version or a sha256: digest, or a reference appears twice. PLUGIN_UPDATE_UNAVAILABLE No eligible release fits the selector. The reasons are listed (for example outside the adopted major 1, no payload for this platform). If the locked release is still fine, a routine update reports unchanged instead. PLUGIN_MAJOR_CHANGE A binding supplies a release outside the adopted major. Run the printed @v<major> update. PLUGIN_UPDATE_CONFLICT A plugins.packages binding supplies a different release from the one you asked for. PLUGIN_PREVIEW_NOT_SELECTED The release would be a preview. Use an exact selector with plugins.preview on. PLUGIN_PACKAGE_CHANGE A routine update would switch packages. Run the printed explicit selector. PLUGIN_UPDATE_REFUSED The new selection fails the build's lock rules (PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN, PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED or PLUGIN_BINDING_CHANGED). PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE The release isn't in the store, no binding supplies it and the catalog lists no OCI route (or --offline prevents using it). The message shows the plugins.packages line to add. PLUGIN_ROUTE_FAILED The catalog route couldn't be reached, doesn't hold the release, or has an unusable address. Nothing was installed. PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED, PLUGIN_PACKAGE_MISMATCH, PLUGIN_PACKAGE_INVALID, digest errors The downloaded package failed its checks. No other release is picked instead. PLUGIN_LOCK_CHANGED oyzu.lock changed while the update ran. Run it again. When a build fails with PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN, PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED, PLUGIN_BINDING_CHANGED or PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH, its suggested fix is oyzu plugins update <reference>.

workflows/oyzu-plugin-update.yml is a standard GitHub workflow. Copy it to .github/workflows/ in a repository whose oyzu.lock selects plugins. It runs weekly and on demand, in three jobs, so that nothing an unreviewed plugin does can change what gets proposed: update runs oyzu plugins update --json, which never runs a plugin. If oyzu.lock didn't change, it stops. Otherwise it uploads the new oyzu.lock, the JSON report, the change levels and the pull request text as one artifact. verify puts that oyzu.lock into a fresh checkout and runs BUILD_COMMAND (default oyzu build --frozen), which runs the new plugin. It has no repository write credential and uploads nothing. It's a pass/fail gate only. propose runs only if both passed. It downloads the update job's artifact, refuses it unless it contains exactly body.md, levels, oyzu.lock and report.json, commits only oyzu.lock to the oyzu/plugin-update branch, force-pushes it, and opens (or refreshes) a pull request listing each change, its level, the reason, notes and the undo line. It never merges directly. Setup: Item Meaning OYZU_UPDATE_TOKEN secret A GitHub App or fine-grained token with contents and pull-requests write access, used by the propose job only. The default GITHUB_TOKEN won't do: pull requests it opens don't trigger your required checks. Install oyzu steps Replace with your pinned, checksummed oyzu installation. AUTO_MERGE_PATCH: 'true' Optional. When every change is a patch, turn on GitHub auto-merge, which still waits for branch protection and required checks. jq Needed by the update job. GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners include it. When the workflow refreshes an open pull request with anything other than patch changes, it turns auto-merge off and confirms it's off before pushing, so an earlier auto-merge request never applies to the new proposal. If that check fails, the job stops without pushing.

Only this host's platform is checked for payloads. Other platforms you build for (a declared matrix, remote workers) aren't checked. Only a catalog's OCI route is used for downloads. A release whose catalog entry lists only an HTTPS archive route needs a plugins.packages binding. @vN works only on this command, not in uses:. The verify job runs an unreviewed plugin. It has no repository write token, but on a GitHub-hosted runner the plugin runs as the job's user (with passwordless sudo). It can read the job's ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN and use it to write Actions caches for the default branch, which other workflows may restore, or to upload artifacts. The propose job is protected because it checks the artifact it uses; other workflows that restore default-branch caches are not. Setting permissions: {} doesn't help, since that limits GITHUB_TOKEN, not the runtime token. Where you can, run verify on an ephemeral, isolated runner and key important caches so this workflow can't produce them. The workflow hasn't yet run on GitHub-hosted runners against a real plugin project. Supported on Linux. Windows and macOS aren't supported yet.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/pnpm.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Captured builds refuse .pnpmfile.cjs and .pnpmfile.mjs before invoking pnpm, including for version queries, because these project hooks can execute code. Oyzu builds Node projects that use pnpm and a pnpm-lock.yaml. Single projects and conventional pnpm workspaces need no Oyzu build configuration. Use it to build, test and package a pnpm project with dependencies captured from the public registry and checked against the lockfile's SHA-512 integrity values. Note: pnpm support is experimental. Oyzu captures and verifies the archives, then lets native pnpm validate the frozen lock and install. It is not full pnpm compatibility (see Limits). Builds use the Node builder plugin (profiles node/app and node/package), which must be installed and selected. See plugin packages. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Pin Node and pnpm (see Prerequisites and use), then run from the project: oyzu --root path/to/project run list oyzu --root path/to/project build oyzu --root path/to/project inspect dist oyzu run list shows your package scripts and the inferred test and quality tasks. oyzu build produces a snapshot-versioned .tgz under dist/ with its test and coverage reports. oyzu inspect dist checks the bundle's recorded content integrity.

Isolated builds run on the base execution image with Docker. Node and pnpm both come from oyzu.lock, so pin both: Node in [tools], pnpm with an exact packageManager (or pnpm in [tools]). The tested profile is pnpm 10.11.0 on Node 22. Setting Value Meaning Docker and the base image oyzu-execution/base:1 Required for isolated builds. See Execution image. --image pnpm=<image> An image name Runs pnpm's isolated actions on an image of your own. The locked Node and pnpm are still the ones that run. Lockfile parser yaml 2.9.1 Ships in the Node plugin package and reads pnpm-lock.yaml for planning. No image needs it. packageManager An exact stable release, such as pnpm@10.11.0 When present, must agree with the pnpm that runs. An exact stable release is pinned as a tool and locked as oyzu:pnpm, so pnpm never downloads itself in the worker. Corepack digest suffix pnpm@10.11.0+sha512.<hex> Accepted and ignored in that comparison. Node requirements Native strict engine validation Incompatible Node requirements are rejected. How tasks run: oyzu run <task> uses the tools installed on your machine. oyzu run list shows native package scripts and inferred test and quality tasks. oyzu build runs native build and test work plus read-only lint and format checks in the isolated worker. Node's built-in test runner gets JUnit and LCOV reporting. Other frameworks use their own adapters. Formatting during a build never rewrites your checkout. See Node quality for quality selection and defaults. To test other Node versions, use verification toolsets in oyzu.toml. matrix.node in build.yaml is refused. Verification runs execute on the native host executor, and pnpm builds use the isolated executor. A pnpm build that has verification runs fails with VERIFICATION_RUN_UNSUPPORTED. Private registries use the native .npmrc configuration, with environment references for project credentials.

A pnpm workspace has a private root, a native pnpm-workspace.yaml, a version 9 lock and locally linked packages (see the pnpm workspace example). Run oyzu build from the root with no Oyzu configuration file. oyzu run list shows build, test, lint and format-check. Development builds dispatch pnpm --recursive run build. Development tests use the workspace report collector.

Acquisition runs a frozen pnpm install with scripts disabled, then asks pnpm to list its members. Workspace commands use the first pnpm executable on PATH, including a standalone executable. They do not fall back to a lower-priority pnpm. Corepack pnpm shims are refused because they can download a package manager. JavaScript pnpm layouts run through the selected Node. Version projection reads the project lock with the yaml package the Node plugin ships (an OYZU_PNPM_YAML path takes precedence). Planning and execution: Local links come from the lock's importer records. They must point to captured members or to a named, publishable workspace root. A private root can't be a link target. Oyzu orders the root and members, fixes their snapshot versions and declares each package's JUnit and LCOV. In its private tree, Oyzu rewrites root and member versions, workspace dependency selectors and matching importer specifiers, then runs a fresh frozen install. pnpm pack turns workspace selectors into published snapshot dependencies. The publishable root is packed once, separately from member packages. Your source and lock are unchanged.

Select node/package to build a pnpm workspace into package archives in the isolated worker. Supported: pnpm 10.11.0 and Node 22.23.3, on a Windows x64 coordinator with a Linux amd64 worker. Three archives install in a fresh offline pnpm project with the source absent. Frozen reuse and failures in dependencies or package tests are caught. Not supported: private roots, other pnpm versions, native-host workspace packages, Linux coordinators, Linux ARM64, Windows ARM64 and macOS. It needs: A publishable root and publishable members. Native pnpm-workspace.yaml membership. A genuine version 9 lock. Recognized package-local build lifecycles and implicit Node tests. Aggregate or opaque root builds, explicit test scripts and replaced build or test tasks are not supported. How it works: Oyzu fixes versions and dependency decisions from native pnpm facts. In the private tree, it changes local workspace specifiers and importer specifiers but keeps link: resolutions and registry integrity data. pnpm builds each package and packs the archives. Each package must produce its JUnit and LCOV before anything is published. Your source and lock stay unchanged. Use the ordinary package binding and a matching coordinator and worker engine. Tool versions come from native pins or the configuration cascade. build.yaml only selects uses: node/package. The first build with a real, non-frozen run adopts the plugin and creates oyzu.lock. Later --frozen runs reuse it: oyzu -C <workspace> --json build workspace --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --no-cache --image pnpm=<image> Generate the lock with pnpm 10.11.0. For oyzu exec, select pnpm in the tool configuration, because packageManager alone doesn't select it.

A root script keeps ownership of its stage. Otherwise member build scripts run in dependency order, and member tests and quality use native scripts or inferred defaults. Required test or quality failures stop artifact collection. Available reports stay in the failed bundle. Overrides, prerequisites and hooks come from Oyzu's shared task scheduling. Format checks during a build are read-only. Registry inputs come from a local loopback server (see Acquisition and execution). pnpm's connection to it doesn't allow external downloads. An opaque root build keeps the native root script and runs it once. Oyzu does not guess which member scripts it covered. A root test script of the form tsc -p <relative-config> && vp test --run keeps its native pnpm script and TypeScript step, while Oyzu adds JUnit and LCOV reporters to the final vp test command. The Vitest and Vite configuration comes from your Vite+ package graph. The coverage provider must be a declared dependency matching the runner's version. Other custom root scripts must write their own reports. Oyzu adds no flags to them. A root format script that is only vp fmt --check with directory-prefixed operands can serve as the format check when you have no format-check, format:check, preformat or postformat script. An opaque or mutating format script does not become a check.

Before packing, Oyzu resolves each concrete public import and require entry from the package and requires the selected file to be a regular file. Declaration files selected by the types condition and a literal legacy declaration path must also exist. Existence is checked, not TypeScript validity. A missing declared JavaScript entry fails the build. Types-only and assets-only packages need no JavaScript entry. Null exclusions and conditional alternatives are left to Node. Wildcard-only entries without a concrete specifier can't be checked. One pnpm pack --json result records the archive's name, version, file name and files. An archive missing a selected public file is rejected before its artifact receipt is written. Browser or custom conditions, declaration validity and every wildcard path are not checked. Cyclic workspace graphs, affected selection, member task groups and full direct host build and quality composition are not supported. pnpm's own layout and peer rules stay in charge.

Checked-in patchedDependencies work in a single project's pnpm-workspace.yaml or in the pnpm object in package.json: patchedDependencies: is-number@6.0.0: patches/is-number@6.0.0.patch Create the patch with pnpm patch and pnpm patch-commit, and commit the patch, settings and updated lock together. No Oyzu setting is needed. A pnpm-workspace.yaml with patch settings doesn't make the project a workspace. A packages list turns on workspace discovery. Patch-only settings stay single-project. The workspace settings below are also accepted. Other configuration keys are not. Checks: Declared and locked patch paths must be regular files inside the project. Absolute paths, .. segments, backslashes, symlinks, missing files and patches over 4 MiB are refused. pnpm checks the lock and configuration agree and verifies patch hashes, then applies the patch in its private installation. Oyzu has no patch engine of its own. A changed patch with a stale lock fails before project lifecycle hooks run. Your source files and the registry archives stay unchanged. Recorded in the build output: The dependency inventory still identifies the original downloaded archives. The oyzu.dev/pnpm.sourcePatches extension records each patch's selector, captured relative path, SHA-256, size and the native lock hash. The source digest and dependency-snapshot digest include the patch inputs. Patched source is distinguished from the pristine upstream archive. This is not a full runtime SBOM.

Captured builds honor these pnpm-workspace.yaml settings as declared: catalog and catalogs, overrides, minimumReleaseAge, allowBuilds and trustPolicy. Each is either fixed by the committed lock or makes acquisition stricter, so none can widen what a build downloads or runs. No Oyzu configuration is needed. catalog: is-odd: 3.0.1 is-number: 6.0.0 overrides: is-number: 'catalog:' minimumReleaseAge: 1440 trustPolicy: no-downgrade allowBuilds: esbuild: false Oyzu never re-resolves dependencies for these settings. It checks them before any native invocation, then native pnpm applies its own --frozen-lockfile checks. See the settings example. Setting What Oyzu checks Effect with pnpm 10.11.0 catalog, catalogs Each catalog maps names to specifier strings. catalog is the default catalog, so also declaring catalogs.default fails. Every importer dependency whose specifier is catalog: or catalog:<name> needs a lock catalogs entry with the same specifier. pnpm compares the same entries and installs the locked versions. overrides The lock's overrides must equal the declared map after pnpm's normalization ($name takes the root package.json specifier, and catalog: takes the catalog entry for the target package). Overrides come from pnpm-workspace.yaml, or else from package.json pnpm.overrides merged over resolutions. Declaring them in both places fails. A mismatch fails with pnpm lock overrides differ from configuration for <selector>. pnpm makes the same comparison (LOCKFILE_CONFIG_MISMATCH). The locked graph already reflects the overrides. minimumReleaseAge Must be a whole number of minutes. Not read: pnpm 10.11.0 predates it (added in 10.16). A frozen lock resolves nothing new, and Oyzu fetches no registry metadata to check ages. trustPolicy no-downgrade or off. Not read: pnpm 10.11.0 predates it (added in 10.21). Newer releases apply it during resolution, which a frozen install doesn't do. allowBuilds Each value is true or false. A placeholder such as set this to true or false fails. When any entry is true, pnpm must be 10.26.0 or newer, the first release that reads it. Otherwise it fails with pnpm allowBuilds approves <selector>, but provisioned pnpm <version> predates allowBuilds. Denials are honored: pnpm 10 runs no dependency build scripts unless approved, and acquisition disables lifecycle scripts entirely. An approval needs a newer pnpm, which then runs only the approved packages' scripts during execution.

In package.json, the pnpm object may hold only patchedDependencies and overrides, because pnpm 10 reads other settings only from pnpm-workspace.yaml. Any other key in either file fails with pnpm capture does not yet support configuration <key> in <file>. The message names the key, not its value. That includes minimumReleaseAgeExclude, trustPolicyExclude, trustPolicyIgnoreAfter, onlyBuiltDependencies, ignoredBuiltDependencies and blockExoticSubdeps. Remove such keys to build.

After pnpm validates the lock, the oyzu.dev/pnpm.workspacePolicies extension records the declared minimumReleaseAge, trustPolicy and allowBuilds values, which leave no trace in the lock. The dependency-snapshot digest includes them. A recorded policy states what the project declared. It does not prove pnpm enforced it. Catalogs and overrides are covered by the recorded lock and source digests. If a catalog or override check fails, regenerate and commit the lock with the pnpm version the project declares. Newer pnpm releases can enforce minimumReleaseAge and trustPolicy during a frozen install, using publisher metadata. The captured adapter supplies the full publisher metadata and the attestation responses pnpm requests (see Acquisition and execution). pnpm makes the decision. Oyzu doesn't invent acceptance or treat a broker failure as missing metadata. With pnpm 12.6.0, a satisfiable release age passes and an unsatisfiable one fails with ERR_PNPM_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE_VIOLATION before any action or artifact. Projects that use these settings together with other unsupported keys (including non-registry .npmrc settings), or that pin a pnpm version that isn't provisioned (10.33, 11.9, 12.4), still fail.
This section explains what is downloaded, from where, and what is checked.

Oyzu reads lock format v9 with a root importer and, for workspaces, member importers. pnpm 12 can write the lock as two YAML documents: an environment document pinning pnpm itself under packageManagerDependencies, then the usual v9 project document. The project document is captured exactly like a single-document lock. The environment document is checked but not captured, because Oyzu provisions the package manager. It may hold only lockfileVersion, importers, packages and snapshots, one . importer, and only configDependencies and packageManagerDependencies in it. A non-empty configDependencies fails, because it would need its own captured inputs. Version projection rewrites only the project document and writes the environment document back unchanged. A lock with more than two documents fails. pnpm 10.11.0 can't read a two-document lock. An exact packageManager release is a locked tool requirement when the tool provider offers it, for both older and pnpm 12 packages. A full isolated build with pnpm 12.3.4 and a two-document lock works. Other pnpm 12 projects aren't supported yet.

Every registry package in the project document's packages section needs an exact SHA-512 integrity value. Native frozen pnpm install in the build image asks for the archives it needs. Oyzu captures only those requests, through the scoped npm-public route to https://registry.npmjs.org/. Optional archives for other platforms are fetched only if pnpm asks for them. Your lock is unchanged, and project lifecycle scripts are disabled during acquisition. Unsupported pnpm configuration and hook files are rejected before any native invocation, including the version query. Archive digests are verified before the bytes reach pnpm. An unknown route, or a failed broker or integrity check, fails preparation even if pnpm would tolerate a missing optional package. The snapshot holds content-addressed tarballs in lock order. It does not keep pnpm's mutable store. pnpm requests at most eight packages at once. Its loopback wait is 120 seconds during acquisition and 15 seconds when replaying captured bytes. Neither raises the broker's network deadline or byte allowance.

Oyzu creates a fresh private store and serves the captured archives to pnpm from a loopback port. The isolated worker has no external network. The server holds no registry credentials, forwards nothing, and fails unknown routes and methods. During execution it serves only the frozen subset. pnpm needs HTTP access to it, so pnpm's own --offline flag isn't used. For pnpm 12, Oyzu also captures full publisher metadata through the selected native registry's scoped broker route, and the attestation responses pnpm requests for locked name and version pairs. It records their bytes and digests in extensions["oyzu.dev/pnpm"].attestations and policyMetadata (source ID, URL, locked versions, SHA-256, size). A 404 from an admitted public or private source records absence. An empty or unavailable broker source is rejected; a broker denial or timeout never becomes absence. This is source and content data, not proof of authenticity or a runtime SBOM. pnpm evaluates its own attestation and supply-chain policy. Oyzu doesn't set trustLockfile. Execution mounts no broker, rechecks captured response identity, and turns native lifecycle behavior on. The private store lives in scratch space and is discarded. Lock and manifest checks run with --frozen-lockfile. Oyzu verifies the lock bytes are unchanged and that the pnpm and Node versions match between preparation and execution. oyzu build --offline is rejected for this builder before preparation. Capture online, then execute with no network. pnpm 10's dependency-script approval rules apply. Oyzu doesn't approve scripts for you. Credentials never enter the inventory or loopback endpoint. Private sources use the native registry configuration.

A successful build produces a snapshot-versioned .tgz under dist/. The package's embedded version matches the artifact version. The manifest records artifacts and the collected test and coverage reports. Native logs and the dependency snapshot are in the bundle. Failed tests keep their reports and block packaging. oyzu inspect dist checks content integrity. It doesn't check release eligibility or who produced the bundle. Dependency records use adapter layout 1. They list each captured archive with its name, version, source ID, size and SHA-256, and record lockfile-sha512 verification in oyzu.dev/pnpm. Every package counts as a build input. Runtime and test classification and registry dependency edges aren't recorded, so this is not a runtime SBOM. Workspace captures also keep local package edges for planning and version projection. Failure Recovery Stale lock Regenerate and commit the lock with the intended pnpm version, then rebuild. Digest mismatch, denied acquisition, missing captured archives, metadata or attestation responses, or changed runtime versions Fails instead of refetching during execution. Fix the cause and rebuild from acquisition. Your sources are never changed by an isolated build.

The Node plugin can build a single-root pnpm project into one native .tgz. You need an installed Node plugin package, Docker, a genuine pnpm-lock.yaml, and Node 22.23.3 and pnpm 10.11.0 in your tool configuration. No build.yaml is needed for the package fallback. An explicit node/app keeps its directory output (see Node applications). Vite projects are not supported here. See plugin packages for usage. Inferred, explicit node/package and scriptless packages each produce a versioned archive, Node test JUnit and LCOV, and install in a source-free, network-free consumer. A package with no build script has no build action. A failing assertion blocks packing and export. Supported: an empty dependency graph, a Windows x64 coordinator and Linux amd64 execution.
