Native-host single-package builds are npm only. Other versions, macOS, Windows ARM64 and publication are not supported.

This is incremental pnpm support, not full compatibility. Supported: single-project public registry packages with integrity-only lock resolutions, native dependency patches, the workspace settings above, and captured workspace packaging. pnpm 11 and later: Oyzu passes pmOnFail=ignore so pnpm doesn't download itself, and still checks the selected locked version. .npmrc registry, origin-scoped _authToken and always-auth settings support authenticated private registries; see private registry configuration. Other .npmrc keys remain refused in captured builds. Not supported yet: .pnpmfile.cjs, .pnpmfile.mjs, other configuration, packageExtensions, and explicit tarball, Git or file resolutions. hoistPattern and nodeLinker settings are refused. Workspace registry dependencies, peer and alias combinations, and framework variations beyond those above aren't covered. Yarn Classic has its own adapter.
Node quality, Yarn Classic, verification toolsets and the workspace report collector pnpm tool installation for the pinned packageManager tool

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/publish.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu publish sends files from a finished build to an OCI registry, an existing GitHub release or an npm registry. It needs no Oyzu account: you configure destinations in oyzu.toml, supply signed build provenance, and Oyzu uploads the files, signs a record of what it published and reads everything back to check it. If you use the Oyzu platform, oyzu publish can instead register the build there and follow a publication the platform runs (see Governed publication). Publishing is optional. Standalone builds, tool management and tasks work without an Oyzu account. Note: Publishing is experimental. The built-in destination is an OCI registry (files, single-platform images and composed plugin roots). GitHub releases and npm resolve first-party publisher packages. Their signed catalog publication is a separate release step; a development binding can be used before that release. Offline plugin bundling is deferred. PyPI and tag-based OCI publishing are not implemented. For plugin destinations, Oyzu checks reference availability in configured bindings and catalog metadata before loading provenance or looking up publication credentials. An unbound kind fails with PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE; configure its publisher binding or use an available catalog release. Package admission and publisher execution follow evidence validation. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Configure a destination and the evidence you accept, then publish a finished build: # oyzu.toml [publish] default = "sandbox" [publish.destinations.sandbox] kind = "oci" artifacts = ["app/archive"] # optional when the build has exactly one artifact registry = "https://registry.example.com" repository = "team/artifacts" usernameEnv = "REGISTRY_USERNAME" passwordEnv = "REGISTRY_PASSWORD" [publish.sets] release = ["sandbox"] [publish.requirements.provenance] bundlePath = "evidence/build.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<base64 raw 32-byte Ed25519 public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/release" [publish.requirements.signing] keyEnv = "PUBLICATION_SIGNING_SEED" publicKey = "<base64 raw 32-byte Ed25519 publication public key>" oyzu build oyzu publish --destination sandbox This is an example: use your own public keys, provenance bundle and credentials. Keep secret values out of the TOML. The file names environment variables that hold them. oyzu publish reads dist/manifest.json by default (or the configured build.bundleDirectory). Pass --manifest FILE to publish a different bundle.

Oyzu reads the build manifest, which must record a succeeded build, and selects the artifacts each destination asks for. It checks the selection and all evidence before it contacts any destination: the file's bytes and size, your signed provenance and the publication signature. It uploads the files and the evidence. It downloads what it uploaded and checks every digest and size. Upload acknowledgements alone never count as success. Publishing never builds, scans, repackages or runs project hooks, and it never creates missing provenance. It needs network access, and there is no offline mode. Native Rust development bundles can record a declared compiledVersion beside their inferred artifact version. They are for local use and cannot satisfy a stamped publication: VERSION_STAMP_REQUIRED refuses them before destination access. Rebuild with oyzu build --full or --optimized, preserving the required reports and provenance, before publishing.

Run oyzu publish --destination sandbox, or omit --destination to use publish.default. Repeat --destination to publish to several destinations, or name a set from publish.sets. All selected destinations are required. A later destination can fail without undoing earlier ones. Successful publications stay, and the receipt lists the unfinished destinations.

An OCI layout archive produced by oyzu build --compose publishes as its plugin release root, rather than as a wrapped file. Select its packaging output on an oci destination. Oyzu validates the complete graph before sending anything, pushes member blobs and manifests before the root index, then reads every object back and checks its bytes. The receipt's reference and manifestDigest name the root digest. The preexisting provenance and signed publication intent are referrers whose subject is that same root. Plugin signature policy still requires its separate subject signature; publishing does not create that signature. Other archived indexes remain unsupported; the existing image-index publication path is unchanged. This path needs network access only when publishing. A malformed or tampered graph fails before uploads with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED. Rebuild or compose again from unchanged, admitted members; do not repair individual archive blobs.

Publishing settings use the ordinary configuration cascade, but only in the project root's oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml. A [publish] table in any other folder's file is a CONFIG_SCOPE error naming the file and line (root-only settings). Setting Values Default Meaning publish.default A destination name The destination used when --destination is omitted. publish.destinations.<name>.kind oci, github-release, or a publisher kind oci The destination kind. publish.destinations.<name>.artifacts Build output IDs The outputs this destination publishes (see Selecting artifacts). You can omit it only when the manifest has one artifact. publish.destinations.<name>.registry An HTTPS URL The OCI registry. Plain HTTP is allowed only on loopback (for example a local test registry). publish.destinations.<name>.repository A repository name The OCI repository. publish.destinations.<name>.usernameEnv, passwordEnv Environment variable names Registry credentials. Set both or neither. Registries that use the same-origin bearer token challenge work. publish.sets Named lists of destinations Sets you can select with --destination. publish.requirements.provenance bundlePath, publicKey, builderId, or a byArtifact map The build provenance you accept (see Provenance evidence). publish.requirements.signing keyEnv, publicKey Signing for the publication record. keyEnv names an environment variable holding a base64 32-byte Ed25519 seed. Its public key must match publicKey. publish.requirements.signing.subject signer, identity, issuer, fulcioUrl, rekorUrl, trustedRoot unset Also sign each published OCI subject with a standard Sigstore signature (see Subject signatures). Rules: publish.destinations, publish.sets and publish.requirements each resolve as a whole. A later source in the cascade replaces the entire table and does not merge entries. Profiles and mandatory configuration constraints apply. An evidence path is relative to the file that declares the requirements. Artifact paths are relative to the bundle that holds the manifest.

kind defaults to oci, so older configurations need no change. github-release uses the adapter described in Existing GitHub release. npm uses the publisher plugin described in npm packages. pypi and unknown kinds fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE before Oyzu loads evidence, reads credentials or uses the network. Unknown destination fields are errors.

Each destination lists the build outputs it publishes in artifacts. An ID is target/name for the output called name, or just target for that target's primary output. It is not the file's name. artifacts = ["app/archive"] selects output archive of target app. artifacts = ["app"] selects the primary output of app. Each destination can name different files. Nothing fans out implicitly. Empty or duplicate entries fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Named file artifacts declared on a build in build.yaml use the same selectors and evidence rules as builder outputs. An inactive or conditionally skipped producer is recorded as not-produced with a reason on the target. Publication refuses a selected missing file with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID; unselected missing files do not block it. Keep the destination and provenance entries in base oyzu.toml when they are the same in every context. For GitHub releases, text/plain files publish before executables, followed by application/schema+json files. Each subject's evidence is uploaded and verified before its payload, and each payload is read back before the next subject. Platform-bound .txt files gain the platform slug; platform-independent files retain their filename. Oyzu checks selectors long before you publish (names that cross files): oyzu config validate, oyzu build --plan and every build refuse a selector (or byArtifact key) whose build does not exist, or whose @os/arch is not one of the build's platforms. The error is CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN, with the file, line, column and the nearest build name. Each build's Prepare step refuses an output name the build does not produce, and lists the outputs it does. At publish time, an unknown or ambiguous ID, or a missing selection in a bundle with several artifacts, fails with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID before any evidence loading, signing or upload. Platform selectors​ Add @os/arch to select one platform of an output, such as cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64. The platform is the one the builder recorded for the file, in the canonical spelling x86_64 or arm64. amd64 and aarch64 are accepted and normalized. An unqualified selector such as cli/bin-oyzu selects every platform of that output in the bundle. Each platform is a separate file with its own evidence. A qualified selector fails with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID, listing the platforms present, when the bundle lacks that platform or the output has no recorded platform. Two artifacts of one output and platform also fail. Listing an output both with and without a platform, or the same platform twice, fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. oyzu build writes one platform per bundle. To publish several platforms together, pass several bundles (see Incomplete platform sets). A bound chart needs its image​ A helm/chart build whose bindings write an image's with.repository into its values is published only when the same oyzu publish also pushes that image to that repository. That means an OCI destination whose registry host and repository equal with.repository, and whose artifacts select the image. Before building the image and chart together, run oyzu install to install the chart's pinned Helm and record the captured build requirements. With an existing complete lock, oyzu install --frozen restores the tools without changing the lock. If a captured recipe is missing, run oyzu pin online before retrying. Select chart/chart for publication; the Helm plugin also emits chart/rendered, which is a separate output. Otherwise publishing fails with PUBLISH_BINDING_UNPUSHED before any evidence, signing or upload. The message names the chart's destination and the destination to add. Mirrors elsewhere are still allowed. Publish the chart and image together, for example oyzu publish --destination charts --destination images. See Publishing an OCI image. Oyzu applies the same check to publish.default and each publish.sets entry when it reads the configuration (CONFIG_BINDING_UNPUSHED).

Oyzu publishes only files it can tie to signed build provenance that you supply. The file must be a regular file whose bytes and size match its recorded SHA-256 digest. Other outputs in the manifest are validated but their files are not read or published. Choose one of two provenance profiles. Both cover the exact SHA-256 digest of the selected file, and neither creates missing build evidence during publishing. Standard GitHub Actions provenance. Reuse the independent JSON profile accepted by release provenance verification: [publish.requirements.provenance] bundlePath = "evidence/build.sigstore.json" releaseProfile = "expected-build.json" The profile must match the expected source repository and commit, immutable repository IDs, signing and calling workflows, and build parameters. Oyzu verifies the public Sigstore certificate, signature and transparency evidence offline with its built-in trusted root. This profile accepts GitHub-hosted runners. It does not assess builder isolation, establish a SLSA level or grant publication authority. Any separate stagingBuilderWorkflow expectation remains outside the claims authenticated by standard provenance. Both paths are relative to the configuration file. Oyzu freezes the profile's values into the publication plan before effects; a worker never rereads the profile file. The same profile is accepted when oyzu build --compose verifies platform members. It cannot make a member's provenance cover the composed release. Self-managed Ed25519 provenance. The existing publicKey and builderId configuration accepts: a Sigstore v0.3 bundle with one DSSE application/vnd.in-toto+json envelope, holding an in-toto Statement v1 with SLSA build provenance v1, signed with the Ed25519 key in publicKey, from the exact builder in builderId, and covering the exact digest of the file being published. This profile uses keys you manage. It makes no transparency-log, trusted-time or keyless-identity claim and does not assert a SLSA level. Do not combine releaseProfile with publicKey or builderId in one entry. Standalone publishing rejects --no-upload, --provenance and --policy-evidence before reading configuration or using the network. It takes provenance only from publish.requirements.provenance. If different outputs have different provenance, replace the single form with a map keyed by output ID: [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."app/archive"] bundlePath = "evidence/app.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<accepted base64 raw Ed25519 builder public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/package" [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."cli"] bundlePath = "evidence/cli.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<accepted base64 raw Ed25519 builder public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/cli" Keys use the same IDs as artifacts. Only the selected output's entry is used and unselected bundles are not read. A selected output with no entry fails with PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_MISSING. Oyzu never substitutes another output's evidence. Combining byArtifact with the single form, an empty map or ID, or a malformed entry fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Provenance is one bundle per file, so an output published on several platforms needs one bundle per platform. Use a key per platform ("cli@linux/x86_64"), or one unqualified key whose bundlePath contains {artifact.platform}: [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."cli"] bundlePath = "evidence/{artifact.platform}/cli.sigstore.json" # evidence/linux/x86_64/cli.sigstore.json publicKey = "<accepted base64 raw Ed25519 builder public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/cli" {artifact.platform} is the only placeholder. Any other { or } in bundlePath fails validation. An unqualified key without the placeholder that would cover several platforms, or a placeholder on an output with no recorded platform, fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. A missing bundle for one platform fails the whole publish with PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_MISSING naming the key. Nothing is published. Hosted evidence failures report PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_INVALID, including a mismatched subject or release profile. The self-managed profile also reports PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_SUBJECT_MISMATCH (wrong file digest), PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_BUILDER_DENIED (unaccepted builder) and PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_UNSUPPORTED (certificate, transparency-log or timestamp material that this key profile does not accept).

Before uploading, Oyzu signs a publication intent with your publication key. The intent is a small signed record of exactly what this publish will do: the file's identity and media type, where it will go, the digest of your provenance, the digest of the whole plan and the operation publish. The intent cannot claim an earlier build origin or a finished upload. It does not contain the invocation ID, so publishing the same plan again reuses the same OCI coordinate. Oyzu verifies every signature before it uploads anything. A signing key that does not match publish.requirements.signing.publicKey fails with PUBLISH_SIGNING_INVALID. The OCI artifact holds the unchanged file, plus your provenance bundle and the publication-intent bundle as layers that anyone can download. The coordinate is registry/repository@sha256:<manifest-digest>. Tags are not supported. A mutable tag could be replaced by another writer between the check and the upload. Matching content already in the registry is reported as already-present. A different manifest, layer or digest at that coordinate is a PUBLISH_CONFLICT. Success requires Oyzu to fetch the manifest, config and every layer back from the registry and match their digests and sizes.

A docker/image build produces an OCI image archive (dist/<target>/<platform>/<target>-<version>.oci.tar). Select it by its output ID <build>/image, and Oyzu pushes it as an image rather than as a file: [publish.destinations.images] kind = "oci" registry = "https://registry.example.com" repository = "team/app" artifacts = ["image/image"] oyzu build oyzu publish --destination images docker pull registry.example.com/team/app@sha256:<image digest> Oyzu pushes the image's manifest, config and layers unchanged, by digest. The coordinate is the image digest the build recorded as ociDigest, which is also what a bound chart writes into its values. Before it touches evidence, signing or the network, Oyzu verifies the archive (every blob digest and layer diff ID) and checks that its image matches the recorded digest. If not, it fails with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED. An archive that holds a multi-platform image index, or an image selected by a github-release destination, fails with PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED. The image cannot carry evidence without changing its digest. Oyzu pushes the provenance and publication-intent bundles as a separate artifact in the same repository whose subject is the image (an OCI referrer with artifactType application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle.v0.3+json). Its reference is the entry's evidenceReference, and registries that support the OCI referrers API list it under the image. As for files, success means Oyzu fetched the image and the evidence back and matched every digest and size. In the receipt, reference and manifestDigest name the image, and verification.artifactDigest is the archive's SHA-256. An image already present without this publication's evidence gets the evidence pushed and counts as published. If the registry refuses a write, the entry fails with PUBLISH_UPLOAD_FAILED. If it cannot be reached, the entry fails with PUBLISH_REGISTRY_UNAVAILABLE. Both name the registry. Run the same publish again: content already pushed is matched by digest. When one OCI destination selects images of the same output for two or more platforms, oyzu publish also pushes an OCI image index of them, by digest. Each platform usually builds on its own host, so pass each build's manifest: ARM64 image builds are unsupported. Index composition does not add a supported multi-architecture build flow; use the single-platform publication above for current Linux x86-64 images. The index lists each image by digest, size and platform, sorted by platform, so the same images always give the same index digest. Images that share an OCI platform, such as glibc and musl builds for one architecture, form no index and are published alone, because the OCI platform has no ABI. The signed plan covers the index digest and its members. If a member changed since the plan, publishing fails with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED or PUBLISH_PLAN_CHANGED before anything is sent. Oyzu pushes the index only after every selected image succeeded, then reads it back. The receipt lists it under indexes, with output, artifactIds, manifestDigest, outcome and reference (or error). If an image failed, the index's outcome is unfinished. Governed publication doesn't compose an index yet. It pushes each image alone.

Add publish.requirements.signing.subject to sign every OCI subject you publish with a standard Sigstore signature, made keylessly from your CI job's identity. Anyone can then check what they pull with cosign verify or Oyzu's plugin verifier, without a key you distribute: [publish.requirements.signing.subject] signer = "sigstore" identity = "https://github.com/acme/app/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main" issuer = "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" # The publishing job in .github/workflows/release.yml permissions: id-token: write # the job's identity token, for the signing certificate packages: write Setting Default Meaning signer sigstore, the only signer implemented. identity The certificate identity the signature must carry: your publishing workflow and ref. issuer The OIDC issuer of that identity. runnerEnvironments ["github-hosted"] The runner environments the certificate may record: github-hosted, self-hosted or both. Oyzu's plugin verifier accepts self-hosted only for the official plugin release workflow. fulcioUrl, rekorUrl Sigstore's public instances (https://fulcio.sigstore.dev, https://rekor.sigstore.dev) A private Sigstore deployment. HTTPS, or HTTP on loopback. trustedRoot Sigstore's production trusted root A trusted_root.json for a private deployment, relative to the file that declares it. What happens: Signing starts only after every check of the whole plan has passed and the registry has answered, because a Rekor entry is public and permanent. If the subject already lists a signature that verifies for the configured signer (a retried publish), Oyzu reuses it and logs nothing new. Otherwise, for each OCI entry and before anything is pushed, Oyzu gets the job's OIDC token (GitHub Actions' token endpoint, or SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN) and checks that its issuer is issuer, makes an ephemeral key that is never written to disk, gets a short-lived certificate from Fulcio, signs an in-toto statement with predicate https://sigstore.dev/cosign/sign/v1 naming the subject's digest, and records it in Rekor. Oyzu then verifies the signature as a consumer would, against the trusted root, and requires the certificate to name exactly identity and issuer. A signature that fails is never published: PUBLISH_SIGNER_MISMATCH names the expected signer. The subject is the native content at the coordinate: the image manifest for an image archive, the release index for a composed plugin package, or the artifact manifest that wraps a file and its evidence. After the subject is pushed and read back, Oyzu pushes the signature bundle as a referrer of it (artifactType application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle.v0.3+json) and lists it in the subject's sha256-<hex> referrers tag, for registries without the referrers API such as GHCR. It reads both back. A repeated publish keeps the existing listing. In the receipt, the entry's signatureReference names the signature referrer and verification.signatureDigest is the bundle's digest. verification.signatureIdentity is the configured identity, and verification.transparencyLog has the Rekor url and the entry's logIndex. Errors: Code Cause and fix PUBLISH_SIGNING_UNAVAILABLE No identity token (grant the GitHub Actions job the id-token permission with the value write, or set SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN), or Fulcio or Rekor refused or could not be reached. Nothing was pushed. Run the publish again. PUBLISH_SIGNER_MISMATCH The certificate names another workflow, ref or issuer than configured. Publish from the configured workflow and ref, or correct identity. PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED Subject signing is configured and a selected destination is a GitHub release. Publish those through a separate run without subject signing. Limits: OCI destinations only. GitHub release assets don't get a subject signature yet. The certificate must come from GitHub Actions (it must record the runner environment). Other CI identities are refused by the verification step. Two publishes of the same subject at the same moment can each rewrite the referrers tag, and one listing can be lost. The signature referrer itself stays in the repository; publish again to relist it. The publication intent is still signed with publish.requirements.signing.keyEnv; keyless signing of the intent is not implemented. Governed (platform) publication doesn't use this setting.

Human output shows the operation, each selected output and each destination's result. Under each published entry it lists what was signed, attached and read back, with a row only for what applies (digests shortened here; real output prints them in full): Artifacts published and verified Operation 01jb2k7q4m8r3t6w9y0z1c5d7e Artifact web/image@linux/amd64 registry published web/image@linux/amd64 published Reference ghcr.io/acme/web@sha256:9f2c… Read back sha256:41ab… matches the built artifact Provenance sha256:c07e… signed · builder https://github.com/acme/web/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main Publish intent sha256:5d1a… signed Evidence ghcr.io/acme/web@sha256:a3f8… (referrer) Signature ghcr.io/acme/web@sha256:e61b… (Sigstore keyless, referrer) Signed by https://github.com/acme/web/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v1.4.0 Rekor entry 148201337 · https://search.sigstore.dev/?logIndex=148201337 Reference is the exact address to pull, by digest. Read back is the digest of the bytes Oyzu downloaded again from the destination, which match the build. Provenance and Publish intent are the digests of the signed bundles Oyzu checked after reading them back. Evidence says where they are: a referrer of an image, or layers of the artifact manifest for a file. GitHub releases list them as assets. Signature, Signed by and Rekor entry appear only with keyless subject signing. On a private Rekor the entry shows its log URL instead of the public search link. With --json, the receipt has operationId, status, planDigest, artifacts and destinations. Each destination has a kind and entries. An entry lists the artifact ID, coordinate, reference, payload outcome and how its evidence was stored and verified. An artifact's id is output-id@os/arch when the file has a recorded platform (cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64), and the output ID otherwise. Such artifacts also carry compatibility (kind target, native or independent, plus the canonical platform), which the signed intent covers. unselectedArtifacts lists, in sorted order, outputs you did not select. Human output lists them as unselected and not published. Each destination reports published, already-present, failed or unfinished, with the digests Oyzu verified. Outcome Exit code Published 0 A failed or unfinished destination in the receipt 2 A check failed before publishing (missing evidence, wrong subject, conflicting existing asset) 1 Invalid command syntax 2 After you fix a failure, run the same publish again. Successful destinations are matched by digest and not repeated.
Publishing needs network access. Each file and each response is held in memory, so very large files need that much memory. A destination's credentials come only from environment variables you name.

The npm publisher takes one finalized .tgz from a Node package build. It reads the native package name and version from package/package.json, verifies the archive digest, and invokes the Oyzu-managed npm client without lifecycle scripts. It does not pack, build or infer a new version during publication. [publish.destinations.npm] kind = "npm" registry = "https://registry.npmjs.org/" tokenEnv = "NPM_TOKEN" # optional with a CI OIDC identity distTag = "latest" # required, explicit mutable pointer access = "public" # optional: public or restricted artifacts = ["web/package"] # use "web" if its archive is primary # timeoutSeconds = 1800 # native publish deadline; 1..86400 Use the same signed build provenance and publication signing settings as OCI. The native registry does not receive separate evidence files: npm requires evidence.mode = "receipt" (the default for npm). Before uploading, core retains the original verified provenance and signed intent under .oyzu/publications/<operation-hash>/. The final receipt names that directory. Keep it with your release records; these files do not assert a transparency-log entry or trusted timestamp. The signed intent and receipt bind the publisher identity, version and digest, the package coordinate and tarball digest, and the set-dist-tag effect. Core checks downloaded tarball bytes independently of the plugin's reported digest and compares the tag in registry metadata with the signed pointer effect. An identical existing version is already-present. Different bytes at that version fail with PUBLISH_CONFLICT. An incorrect existing tag fails with PUBLISH_POINTER_VERIFICATION_FAILED; retrying does not authorize a tag repair. There is currently no separate tag-repair command.

Core reads the variable named by tokenEnv when configured. An unset variable fails with PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE; it never falls back to OIDC. Only when tokenEnv is omitted and the registry origin is exactly https://registry.npmjs.org does core use NPM_ID_TOKEN or request a CI identity through ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN, with audience npm:registry.npmjs.org. It exchanges that identity at the registry's package-scoped OIDC endpoint for an unexpired registry token. Configure the registry's trusted publisher for your job; prefer trusted publishing or a package-scoped token with the narrowest permissions. The exchange follows the npm registry API. Your registry must admit the configured CI identity before OIDC publishing can succeed. The plugin receives only an ephemeral http://127.0.0.1:PORT/<random-prefix>/ reverse-proxy URL and placeholder npm authentication. The per-run prefix has 128 random bits. Requests without the exact prefix are refused before authentication; core strips it before forwarding upstream. Each publication creates its own listener for the configured, plugin-declared registry and closes it after read-back or failure. Core connects upstream with verified TLS (plain HTTP is accepted only on loopback). It refuses foreign hosts, prefix escapes and redirects before forwarding credentials, and permits writes only during an authorized publish operation. Credential values stay out of plugin requests, environment, files, native arguments, plans and receipts; upstream responses that echo a credential are refused. Native error text is suppressed across this boundary. This implementation runs on the developer host: direct network connections by a plugin are best effort, not an isolated egress guarantee. Governed npm publication is refused. The proxy bounds credential forwarding even on this host lane.

npm/publish resolves through the same signed catalog, package store and lock admission as builder references. The npm publisher is not yet available from the official catalog. Use an explicit user, machine or administrative development binding. Project bindings fail with CONFIG_SCOPE. Offline CLI bundling is deferred. Core validates shared destination and declared-host settings. The npm plugin validates registry URLs, distTag, access and its one-package rule during planning; unsupported evidence settings fail core configuration validation. Missing or refused credentials fail with PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE; host substitutions fail with PUBLISH_HOST_REFUSED. Plugin failures and deadlines fail with PUBLISH_PLUGIN_FAILED. A missing or mismatched registry tarball fails with PUBLISH_READ_BACK_FAILED. A failure leaves retained evidence for investigation; an upload acknowledgement never counts as successful publication.

The first-party oyzu/github-release publisher uses the same configuration, evidence checks and signing as OCI. It uploads files to an existing release; it never creates tags or releases, changes release metadata or changes visibility. The package resolves through the publisher role. Until its signed catalog release, use an admitted development binding as described in Plugin development. Core supplies authenticated API and upload proxies, including authenticated reads for private repositories and draft releases. Writes are enabled only during the publish operation. Redirects are rewritten only to declared hosts; downloads from objects.githubusercontent.com and release-assets.githubusercontent.com are anonymous. An undeclared redirect is refused. The plugin receives no credential. Core stages the existing provenance and signed publication intent read-only, and compares every uploaded file with fresh proxy observations after writes close. Logical HTTPS endpoints are routed through core-provided HTTP loopback proxies. Core performs upstream TLS and credential attachment; the publisher's HTTP client does not need a TLS backend. Planning and execution reject HTTPS loopback proxy URLs, and a logical HTTPS endpoint without its declared core proxy is refused. The intent coordinate, effects and receipt record publisher with package, version, digest and source, using the same identity shape as npm. Existing GitHub configuration remains valid; the identity is bound into the signed plan. Payload and build-provenance bytes remain unchanged. Publication-intent signatures bind this added identity and therefore change. Replace the destination in the Quick start example with: [publish.destinations.sandbox] kind = "github-release" apiUrl = "https://api.github.com" repository = "your-owner/your-test-repository" tokenEnv = "GITHUB_SANDBOX_TOKEN" artifacts = ["app/archive", "cli"] [publish.destinations.sandbox.evidence] mode = "destination" Setting Values Default Meaning kind github-release oci Selects the GitHub Releases adapter. apiUrl An API origin The GitHub API root. repository owner/name The repository that holds the release. tokenEnv An environment variable name unset Holds a token with Contents read and write access to that repository. When omitted in GitHub Actions, core can use GITHUB_TOKEN as described below. artifacts Output IDs As for OCI. evidence.mode destination destination Where evidence is stored. destination (evidence next to the files, downloadable from the destination) is the only supported value for OCI and GitHub. receipt and managed are not accepted. Create the tag and release yourself first, and give Oyzu the token by environment variable. An explicit tokenEnv takes precedence: if that variable is unset or invalid, publication fails without falling back to GITHUB_TOKEN. With no tokenEnv, trusted mode requires GITHUB_ACTIONS=true and resolves GITHUB_TOKEN only for the exact HTTPS origins api.github.com and uploads.github.com. Other API origins require an explicit tokenEnv. The token stays in core's authenticated proxies; anonymous asset-download hosts receive no credential. Oyzu never creates refs or releases, publishes a draft, changes release metadata or deletes assets. It records the repository, release ID, tag commit, upload route, draft and prerelease state, and filenames, and stops before writing if any of them changes. A draft release can receive and verify assets. Publish the draft separately afterwards. If GitHub's tag endpoint returns 404, Oyzu looks for the exact tag in the release list. No match, or more than one, fails. Authentication and other HTTP errors are not treated as a missing tag.

A GitHub destination stores no tag in configuration. oyzu publish picks the release in this order: --tag <tag>, if given. It applies to every GitHub destination in that publish. Use it for manually started releases or tags version inference does not read. Otherwise the exact version tag that version inference recorded for the packages the destination publishes. A single-package repository tagged v1.4.0 at the built commit publishes to release v1.4.0. The api package of a workspace tagged api/v1.4.2 publishes to api/v1.4.2, even if another package has the same version. Oyzu decides the tag before any evidence loading, signing or network access, and the signed intent records it. --tag need not point at the built commit. If it replaces a different recorded tag, Oyzu warns with PUBLISH_TAG_OVERRIDDEN and continues. A tag key in a github-release destination is an error everywhere configuration is read: CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE: publish.destinations: PUBLISH_DESTINATION_TAG_REMOVED. Delete the key. Without --tag, Oyzu stops and sends nothing in these cases: Code Cause Fix PUBLISH_TAG_UNKNOWN A published package has no recorded version tag: the built commit has no version tag that applies to it. Tag the built commit (v1.4.0, or <package>/v1.4.0 for one workspace package), rebuild and publish again, or pass --tag. PUBLISH_TAG_CONFLICT The destination's packages have different tags, a package has several tags, or some have a tag and some do not. The message lists each tag and package. One release has one tag. Give each independently versioned package its own destination, delete a duplicate tag, or pass --tag. PUBLISH_TAG_AMBIGUOUS Several packages of a build share the artifact's version with different tags, and the build did not record which package made the artifact. Rebuild with this version of oyzu, or pass --tag. PUBLISH_TAG_COMMIT_MISMATCH The derived tag points at a different commit than the one built, in your checkout or on GitHub. Also when packages record the tag on different commits. Build the tagged commit and publish again, or pass --tag to publish to that release anyway. PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED --tag is given but no selected destination is a GitHub release, or the publication is governed. Drop --tag. The recorded tags are what the checkout looked like when you built. Oyzu does not authenticate them against source control. The tag is tied to the built commit, not to a clean tree: a build of the tagged commit with uncommitted changes still publishes to that tag.

Oyzu derives each asset's name when you publish, from the file's local name and the compatibility its builder recorded. This lets one release hold several platforms of one operating system. File bytes and local dist/ names do not change. Recorded compatibility Asset name Example target (built for one platform) <stem>-<os>-<arch><ext> oyzu for linux/x86_64 becomes oyzu-linux-x86_64. oyzu.exe for windows/x86_64 becomes oyzu-windows-x86_64.exe. app.tar.gz for linux/x86_64 becomes app-linux-x86_64.tar.gz. independent (no platform restriction) the filename site.tar.gz native (the package's own name encodes the platform, such as a wheel) the filename pkg-1.0-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl pending, unknown or missing refused with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID The builder must record what the file is for. Platforms use the canonical spelling (x86_64, arm64, never amd64). An ABI is added only when it differs from the OS default (GNU on Linux, MSVC on Windows, none elsewhere). A GNU Linux build is oyzu-linux-x86_64, a musl build is oyzu-linux-x86_64-musl, and a GNU Windows build is oyzu-windows-x86_64-gnu.exe. Evidence files follow the derived name. Qualified selectors (cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64/musl) and {artifact.platform} paths use the same form, so a GNU and a musl build of one output can sit in one release. In the evidence path the platform renders as linux/x86_64 for the default ABI and linux/x86_64-musl otherwise. A selector that names the default ABI (@linux/x86_64/gnu) never matches. Oyzu refuses it and shows the form to write. Two artifacts that publish to the same platform are refused with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID before any evidence loading or network access. Names carry no version, so releases/latest/download/oyzu-linux-x86_64 keeps working across releases. Assets uploaded earlier under unqualified names are left alone. They are never renamed or removed. Extension rule: the extension is the longest case-insensitive match from .tar.gz, .tar.xz, .tar.zst, .tgz, .zip, .exe, .msi, .dmg, .pkg, .deb, .rpm, .dll, .so, .dylib, keeping its original case. Without a match, the platform is appended. Name checks (all fail with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID before any evidence loading, signing or network access): Names use ASCII letters, digits, dot, underscore and dash only, at most 220 bytes, with no leading dot. A name must not end in a reserved evidence suffix. The evidence assets are <asset>.provenance.sigstore.json and <asset>.publication.sigstore.json. Two names that differ only in ASCII case collide. Executor records: each artifact also records how it was built (host, cross-toolchain with its target, or container). That record is part of the plan, the signed intent and the receipt. An unknown executor kind or field is PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID. A cross toolchain whose target does not match the artifact's platform is PUBLISH_EXECUTOR_INVALID. A release publication refuses a platform-specific (target or native) artifact that has no executor record, with PUBLISH_EXECUTOR_UNKNOWN. Rebuild it with this version of oyzu. Publishing does not otherwise judge how the artifact was built.

Before any upload, Oyzu checks the whole plan for name collisions and for assets that already exist on the release. Identical existing content is reused. Different bytes at the same name fail with PUBLISH_CONFLICT. Oyzu never overwrites or deletes. A GitHub API failure (an unexpected HTTP status, invalid JSON, or a release or asset list that is too large) fails with PUBLISH_GITHUB_API and the status. It uploads and re-downloads your provenance and the signed publication intent before the file they describe. Success requires downloading each asset and matching bytes, sizes, digests and evidence claims. An upload acknowledgement is not enough. An interrupted upload can leave an asset on the release. The receipt lists which assets were completed, failed or unfinished. Run the same publish again. Matching assets stay and only missing work is done. If the subject, coordinate or evidence changed, make a new plan. A same-name asset with different evidence is a conflict. Oyzu will not replace it. Other people can still edit release metadata, so a read-back is a check at that moment and not a permanent guarantee.

For GitHub.com, Oyzu talks to the configured API origin, the release's upload route on uploads.github.com and asset downloads on release-assets.githubusercontent.com. API path prefixes are preserved. Requests stay on the same origin, and upload routes are tied to the repository and release ID. Redirected downloads are anonymous. The token is never sent to a redirect target. GitHub Enterprise endpoints are supported only when all routes are on the API origin under its prefix. Translating /api/v3 to /api/uploads is not supported. GitHub Actions artifacts and GHCR are not supported destinations.

A build records the platforms each target declares (platforms: in build.yaml). When you publish, Oyzu compares them with the platforms of the artifacts you selected, combining the variants of one target. A declared platform with no selected artifact is a gap. It may never have been built (for example a build on only one runner) or you may not have selected it. In the release context a gap refuses the whole publish with PUBLISH_PLATFORMS_INCOMPLETE, naming each missing target and platform, before any evidence loading, signing or network access. In any other context it is a warning. A target that declares no platforms is not checked. A bundle with no platform records (built by an older oyzu) is refused in release with PUBLISH_PLATFORMS_UNKNOWN and warned about elsewhere. If you never ship a platform, remove it from the declared platforms. An allowance below covers one publication, not a standing exception. To publish anyway, name each missing platform with a reason: oyzu publish --destination github \ --allow-incomplete darwin/x86_64=no-intel-mac-runner \ --allow-incomplete windows/x86_64="Windows runner not available" Each value is <platform>=<reason> (aliases are accepted; the reason is 1 to 200 printable characters). A malformed value, a repeated platform, or a platform that no published target is missing fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, so the record never claims a gap that does not exist. Every gap, with the reason you gave (or null for a warned gap), is part of the plan digest, is recorded in every signed publication intent as incompletePlatforms, and appears in the receipt. Governed publication does not check completeness and refuses the flag (PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED). Several bundles as one publication. If you build one platform per job, publish every platform at once by repeating --manifest, one per bundle: oyzu publish --destination github \ --manifest bundles/linux-x86_64/dist/manifest.json \ --manifest bundles/darwin-x86_64/dist/manifest.json \ --allow-incomplete windows/x86_64=runner-unavailable The artifacts from all bundles are selected, checked for completeness together and published in one plan. Each artifact keeps its own bundle's files and executor record. Giving the same bundle twice is PUBLISH_REQUEST_INVALID. Governed publication takes one manifest (PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED).

If the build's configuration requires verification for certain tool versions (verification.<tool>, usually set by policy), standalone publishing checks each line against the verification the given bundles recorded. This happens after selection and the completeness check, and before any evidence loading, signing or network access. Each required line must be one of: outside the build's native version range (so it does not apply), covered by the build's own passing tests on a version in that line, or covered by a passing verification run of the same build, from any --manifest bundle, that verified its source or the published artifact. Otherwise publishing fails with PUBLISH_VERIFICATION_MISSING. The message names each uncovered line, why it is not covered and the commands of the runs the build left to other jobs. Oyzu resolves the requirement at publish time, in the build's folder and the publication's context. To cover a line, run a separate verification job (oyzu build --verify-only) and pass its bundle beside the platform bundles. That bundle is evidence only, and nothing is published from it. The receipt lists under verification how each line was settled. See required tool lines. Governed publication does not check verification evidence.

For 0.4.0, merge the version commit to dev before promoting it to main. Before tagging oyzu/v0.4.0, require successful full main CI and the full Windows release-like build on that exact final commit. Results from an earlier commit do not satisfy the release gate. Oyzu publishes its own releases with this same path. Each platform is built in its own job. One oyzu publish then runs in the release context with a --manifest per platform and a --tag, uploading binaries as assets of a release in the public oyzuai/oyzu-releases repository. Follow that repository's releases to download them. Releases are binary-only, and the source repository stays separate. Before 0.4.0 publishes, omit a redundant min_oyzu_version marker from the release checkout. Released v0.3.8 identifies its reader as a prerelease, so even "0.3.8" would refuse that driver. Bootstrap enforces the compatible driver floor. This workflow requires the newest released driver to support build.yaml authored artifacts (available in v0.2.4). Both building and publishing bootstrap a released CLI with --require-release, excluding the tag being built. A missing or older driver stops the job; there is no Cargo driver fallback and the publishing job does not use a binary built by the current run. The release checkout's configuration and bootstrap driver minimum must remain compatible with the previous published CLI. This checkout admits 0.4.0; new-reader dogfood is adopted only after the compatible release executables publish for every required platform. The 0.4.0 reader and retry features remain available in the released product. The shared release set in .github/release-platforms.sh currently requires linux/x86_64 and windows/x86_64. Every declared platform must build and audit successfully before publication; failed, skipped or cancelled legs block the release. The CLI plan also includes Darwin, which is recorded as omitted while it is outside this release set. Adding darwin/x86_64 to the shared declaration enables its native runner for CLI and plugin releases. Windows and Linux release builds require published drivers and builder plugins. The one-time Windows source-bootstrap input has been removed. CI machine bindings read the Rust and Node release roots directly from oyzu.lock; a pin PR updates that canonical selection without a second bootstrap-script digest. CLI release build and publish jobs, and plugin release build legs, use isolated home/data directories under RUNNER_TEMP before bootstrap and for the whole job. Each run attempt and platform gets fresh tool stores, so an older bootstrap CLI never reads receipts left by a newer CLI in another job. The runner's existing shared store is left untouched. This costs a cold tool install in every release job, including retries. The workflows use HOME (also honored by 0.2.2 on Windows and macOS) and XDG_DATA_HOME on Linux: OYZU_STORE alone is not a CLI environment override. Plugin producers pass their job-local store explicitly with --store. Before any job receives release secrets, release.yml resolves the supplied tag (including annotated tags) to its commit and requires a completed, successful push-to-main run of CI (ci.yml) on that exact commit. Missing, running, cancelled or failed runs block release; the error names the workflow, commit and available run URLs. Restore green main CI before retrying; there is no override. CLI and scenarios (build.yml) runs only on schedules or dispatch and is not a push-to-main prerequisite. GitHub API access is required; API failures block release. Unsigned audit_only=true runs explicitly log that they skip this gate. This check does not replace the required desktop Windows pre-tag release qualification. The desktop qualification includes the independent customer-project gate, using published plugins and disposable installs in PowerShell, cmd and Git Bash. Release test tool launches resolve managed Python, Node and Rust through the freshly built CLI, including when an older released build driver remains on PATH. The outer driver's tool shims are not used to select those test tools. The standalone repository-check target uses the explicitly activated OYZU_FRONTEND when no CLI is being built. When that variable is absent, it resolves the released oyzu driver on PATH, requiring an absolute file path. This supports older released drivers that do not forward OYZU_FRONTEND to build tasks. Tool launches explicitly select the test workspace with --root so root-only configuration stays scoped to that workspace in a nested source copy. Release-context tests still require the built CLI and refuse either fallback when it is missing. Repository checks install the frozen checks toolset before querying its executables; oyzu which only inspects installed tools and does not install them. To cut a release: Integrate the version commit (Cargo.toml says X.Y.Z) through a PR to dev, then fast-forward main to that chosen dev commit. Do not merge directly into main. Wait for full main CI on that exact commit and run the full Windows release-like suite on MICAH-DESKTOP from a fresh worktree: OYZU_CONTEXT=release oyzu build cli --output plain, with OYZU_RELEASE_COMMIT and SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH set for the promoted commit. A failed, cancelled or missing main run, or a failed desktop suite, blocks the tag. Fix on dev and promote again. Once both pass, tag that main commit oyzu/vX.Y.Z and push the tag to oyzuai/oyzu. Create and publish the release with the same tag in oyzuai/oyzu-releases. Start the release workflow: gh workflow run release.yml --ref main -f tag=oyzu/vX.Y.Z. The workflow attaches assets to that release. It never creates the release or the tag. It writes to oyzuai/oyzu-releases with the OYZU_RELEASES_TOKEN secret, a token with Contents read/write on that repository only, because the workflow's own token can't write to another repository. If OYZU_RELEASES_TOKEN is missing, or the release repository differs from the committed destination, the run stops before publishing. A fork sets the repository variable OYZU_RELEASE_REPO and edits the destination's repository. Beta and nightly releases​ Beta and nightly releases use the same manually started workflow and every release gate above. Choose a native Cargo version such as 0.4.0-rc.1 for beta or 0.4.0-alpha.0.nightly.20261104010101 for nightly, with the matching oyzu/v<version> tag. Integrate that version through dev and promote it to main before qualifying and tagging it. Create the matching public release as a prerelease before starting the workflow. A stable version uses X.Y.Z. Release preflight reads Cargo.toml at the tag's resolved commit and the existing public release metadata after checking exact-commit main CI. It requires the native package version to match the tag and the release to be published with that exact tag. Beta/nightly releases must have prerelease: true, so GitHub's latest-release endpoint is not advanced by them. Existing stable Preview releases remain valid. Missing metadata, API failures or mismatches stop before build or signing jobs receive secrets. Correct the native version or release metadata, then retry through the same manual path. Additional metadata fields are ignored. There is no scheduled signed nightly release: a maintainer must explicitly start each release after qualification. The separate internal dev channel can publish unsigned dev-YYYYMMDD Linux/Windows x64 archives in oyzuai/oyzu-releases and update latest-green only after both platform jobs succeed. Windows is opt-in; when disabled, neither archive is published and the pointer stays unchanged. These archives are not selected by oyzu self. Adding release-channel support or merging its code does not create tags, dispatch release jobs or publish assets. The release list is the channel index read by oyzu self versions; channel names come from version strings, rather than GitHub's prerelease flag. After assets are published, use oyzu self versions --all --channel beta or oyzu self versions --all --channel nightly --json to inspect the corresponding history. Presence in a list does not replace successful publication read-back or verification of every declared platform's assets. Unsigned native audits​ Set audit_only=true to build and audit the requested native platforms at the selected ref without a tag, provenance signing, release publication or schema attachment. An empty incomplete input requests all declared release platforms: linux/x86_64 and windows/x86_64. Darwin is automatically recorded as outside the declared release set, without waiting for its unavailable native runner. The incomplete input can name only undeclared canonical platforms with a nonempty reason, separated by semicolons or newlines. For example, incomplete=darwin/x86_64=Mac mini runner unavailable is accepted. incomplete=windows/x86_64=runner unavailable is refused. Aliases, combined names, missing reasons, repeated platforms and any declared omission fail before building. For example, these inputs audit the declared Linux and Windows set (illustrative): audit_only=true incomplete=darwin/x86_64=Mac mini runner unavailable Every requested platform retains its build, tests, notices/source audit and independent final companion verification. The job summary and retained bundle status record each omission as UNQUALIFIED / NOT RUN, with its reason. Missing bundles, mismatched omission reasons or a failed requested check fail the audit. A successful scoped audit covers only its requested checks. It does not qualify omitted platforms or satisfy a full-platform audit request. Production release completeness and --allow-incomplete controls remain separate; an audit omission is not a release allowance. Runner selection and any required hosted-runner approval still apply; an omission does not authorize running a platform elsewhere. The release build: Runs one job per platform. Each downloads the newest earlier release's oyzu for its platform, builds the release tag with it (oyzu build cli) and signs provenance with the witness. Audits the build for binary-only distribution, which refuses any shipped component that needs source delivery. The corresponding-source companion stays in the run's retained bundle and isn't uploaded. Runs Linux x86_64 and the publish job, which hold the signing seeds and the release token, on the dedicated Linux release runners (labels self-hosted, linux, x64 and oyzu-release), which no CI or pull request job uses, so a release never waits behind main's CI. The first job runs there too: while no Linux release runner is online, the run waits in it, before anything that holds a secret, rather than falling back to a hosted runner. macOS x86_64 and Windows x86_64 build natively on the maintainer's self-hosted ephemeral release runners (labels self-hosted, macOS or Windows, X64 and oyzu-release); ARM64 is excluded from the release matrix. A platform the incomplete input leaves out only records that it was skipped, so it runs on the self-hosted control pool (oyzu-control), needs no hosted runner and leaves the main runner free. Never reads a shared action cache, so every shipped output is built by the release job itself. Release and publishing jobs warm their isolated tool stores with lock-named download blobs from an Actions cache keyed by operating system, architecture, the tool lock and Rust toolchain file. Oyzu still verifies each input's digest and source admission and creates fresh installations and receipts. A cache miss downloads the required inputs normally. Older tags without the warming helper also acquire tools normally. Generated compiler archives, resolution mappings, installed tools, compiler state, test verdicts and release outputs are excluded. The checks toolset supplies both Python for compliance tasks and Node for the provenance witness, using their locked versions. Release bundles use fast compression while retaining every file. Publication refreshes signed plugin catalog metadata concurrently with the independent companion audit; both must succeed before publisher availability checks or uploads. Asset evidence, publication order and readback verification stay required. These setup and transfer optimizations do not replace the pre-tag gates or authorize reuse of a CI executable as a release bundle. The cli build declares notices, schema-build-yaml and schema-oyzu-toml once in build.yaml. Release-only task commands stay in oyzu.toml; the base GitHub destination and provenance entries select all five outputs once. Ordinary local builds record the three release-only files as not produced. Release tasks produce notices on every built platform and platform-independent schemas only on Linux x86_64, using Python from the pinned checks toolset. The independent compliance audit verifies the manifest's notices against the executable's exact audited notices. Build provenance covers every output. For each CLI release target, the licence review lists registry packages from the selected oyzu package's resolved normal/build graph, including proc macros. It reports every reviewed package's name and version in cli_license_review.packages. The package count and notice gaps refer to that same graph. An in-scope notice gap blocks release; gaps outside the target appear separately under out_of_scope_missing_notice_packages. The repository-wide inventory and original notice bundle remain complete, including inactive targets and development dependencies. Passing these technical checks is not legal approval. The publish job first runs oyzu plugins list --refresh in the release context with the same configuration and tool store as publication. It verifies and caches public signed catalog metadata without installing plugin packages or changing the tracked lockfile. Publication retains publisher admission and availability checks. One oyzu publish --destination github --tag "$TAG" consumes all platform bundles. It publishes and reads back notices before executables, then publishes schemas; each subject's evidence precedes its payload. An identical retry reuses assets. Names remain oyzu-notices-<os>-<arch>.txt, build.yaml.schema.json and oyzu.toml.schema.json; editor download URLs stay the same (see editor schemas). There is no separate companion or schema upload. Skipping an already-published platform still requires its notices on the release. Once any release asset exists, retries restore every selected platform's exact retained private bundle, including the Linux x86_64 schemas, audit inputs and witness evidence. Repeat the original omission reasons: every signed intent binds the whole plan. Published assets must match that plan; missing schemas are uploaded from its original outputs. Changing selected platforms or omission reasons requires a new release/tag in this workflow. The workflow keeps bundles for seven days and never overwrites original inputs with retry skips. If originals expired, are incomplete or fail validation, publication stops before uploads. Restore those exact accepted inputs before retrying; rebuilding cannot reconstruct the plan. oyzu's own CI jobs​ Every PR targets dev; its push CI is a latest-wins signal after local verification. Main promotion CI always selects all jobs and keeps running for the release gate. Dev and labelled PR runs use affected-only job selection and record each job's selection and result in the CI summary. Those records are not release evidence. The Monday/Thursday acceptance run checks out main and runs full uncached verification; it does not replace full successful main CI on the exact release commit or the pre-tag Windows suite. Release reads no results from the shared action cache. Trusted dev and main jobs use OYZU_MAIN_RUNNER when configured, sharing the CI cache; pull requests remain readers. Cache service admission must explicitly trust both branch identities. Publishing workflows and signatures remain main-only. Oyzu's own CI jobs start from the newest published release of oyzu and run Cargo with the Rust it pins, so the project builds itself with the tool it ships. Setup action. The setup step runs tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh --release --require-release --ci-machine-binding, reading releases from the public oyzuai/oyzu-releases (OYZU_RELEASE_REPO names another repository, for forks). It uses the downloaded executable only when its SHA-256 digest matches the one GitHub reports for the asset, as the install script does, then puts .oyzu/bin on PATH and writes one summary line naming the release tag, asset and digest of the oyzu used. After oyzu install --frozen it puts the installed tools on PATH for later steps (.github/actions/oyzu-env, CI's version of shell activation), so steps run cargo, node or python directly and never through oyzu exec. A job that installs into its own store or a toolset runs the same action after its install, with store or toolset. For a separately pinned source tree, root selects that tree's configuration and lock; the action fails if it cannot enter that root. CI ignores user configuration, so --ci-machine-binding binds the signed published Rust and Node plugins in a new machine configuration on the job's ephemeral runner, without building plugins from source (see CI machine binding). Node and Python. Repository checks and the CLI job's harness scripts get Node and Python from the checks toolset in oyzu.toml, pinned in oyzu.lock (oyzu --toolset checks install --frozen), so they don't use actions/setup-node or actions/setup-python. The repository checks are oyzu.toml tasks, and the job runs them with one oyzu --toolset checks run checks. A checks-deps task installs the checkers' Python packages into the ignored .oyzu/checks-site, outside the tool store, and each Python check's task reads them from PYTHONPATH. The docs site job does the same: its prepare, verify, export and audit steps are docs-* and test-docs tasks run with oyzu --toolset checks run, and it has no actions/setup-node. The task and build scenario jobs still use the setup-* actions, because those host tools are what the scenarios run the candidate against. No source build. The setup step never builds the oyzu CLI from source. If no release has an executable for the runner's platform, or the release's oyzu can't read this checkout's configuration or the pinned plugin protocol (currently requiring 0.4.0 or newer), the step fails with that reason; publish compatible CLI binaries to fix it. Run the bootstrap without --require-release locally to build from source. The setup action retains the verified released CLI and its shim outside the checkout's mutable .oyzu/bin, exports its exact path as OYZU_RELEASED_DRIVER (and the action's path output), and places that directory on PATH. A successful project build promotes its executables into .oyzu/bin; later producer builds, including repository quality maintenance, keep using the retained release. Candidate runs explicitly use OYZU_CANDIDATE. Plugin release jobs compile the plugin product being published with the released CLI and activated pinned tools. The dedicated publisher production step uses a separately pinned source tree and retains its independent artifact/source audit before publication. When a candidate build fails, its job log includes the retained bundle's report-admission diagnostics and the native command output. A successful test command can still fail the build when a required report is missing or invalid. The base execution image is published by a separate workflow using the released oyzu. With --root tooling/images, that folder is its own project root, so its configuration never mixes with the CLI's. Without --root, the repository root's configuration applies and refuses the folder's [publish] table with CONFIG_SCOPE. The supported Linux x64 image builds on its native runner, which runs: oyzu --root tooling/images lock --update base # re-lock the apt packages on this runner oyzu --root tooling/images build base # RUN installs them offline from the lock node tooling/release-witness.mjs sign --manifest tooling/images/dist/manifest.json \ --out tooling/images/.oyzu/release-evidence --artifact base/image@linux/x86_64 A publish job then downloads the x64 build and publishes its image: oyzu --root tooling/images --json publish --destination base \ --manifest base-amd64/dist/manifest.json The x64 image is pushed by digest to ghcr.io/oyzuai/oyzu-execution/base with the same release keys as the CLI, as in Publishing an OCI image. A single platform produces an image receipt, without a composed image index. The registry credential is the job's GITHUB_TOKEN. The lock is observed again on each run, because replaying debs.lock.yaml needs the signed apt metadata in the machine's own store (see OS package lock limits). The job summary shows how the lock changed against the committed one, and the run uploads the lock it built from. When it changed, the provenance records the source as dirty. The job needs a released oyzu that has the Docker plugin, pins the published base image and locks Ubuntu packages with epoch versions, plus a committed tooling/images/oyzu.lock that selects that release's Docker plugin. Until then, the job fails at its first oyzu step. Each runner locks its own architecture and keeps the committed lock's entries for the other. After a Dockerfile change, run oyzu lock on the supported amd64 host and commit the result. ARM64 observation is deferred. oyzu publish pushes by digest only, so a last step points the tag 1 at the image with docker buildx imagetools create --prefer-index=false, which copies its manifest unchanged, checks the tag's digest and prints the image digest. Image build and publication run on the isolated OVH release pool so signing seeds never reach pull request runners. A Docker engine and permission to load the BuildKit AppArmor profile are required; missing prerequisites fail the run. Public visibility does not select a hosted runner.

Every release build runs oyzu config validate with published builder bindings before building. The retired Windows source-bootstrap dispatch and its alternate development-binding validation path are unavailable. Bootstrap and compliance scripts are read from the release tag (the dispatch revision for audit-only runs). Release assets for the oyzu CLI are named per host. The install script and the repository bootstrap pick the one for your host and check the SHA-256 digest GitHub reports for it before installing: Host Asset Linux x86_64 oyzu-linux-x86_64 macOS x86_64 oyzu-darwin-x86_64 Windows x86_64 oyzu-windows-x86_64.exe On Windows, oyzu-shim-windows-<arch>.exe is installed beside oyzu.exe as oyzu-shim.exe. See the install script for how installation works.

With the Oyzu platform, oyzu publish registers the build, uploads its file, and asks the platform to run a publication. The platform decides which destinations and evidence requirements apply. Your command line cannot widen that authority. Choose it by giving a server, account and project: oyzu build oyzu publish --server https://oyzu.example.com --account acme --project web --provenance evidence/build.sigstore.json --provenance FILE is required. It is a signed provenance bundle you already have, sent unchanged. --destination cannot be combined with this mode. It publishes one staged file artifact. --no-upload does not work with it. Optionally pass --policy-evidence FILE, an existing signed policy report that the platform's policy may require. Oyzu sends the file unchanged as policyEvidence.bundle. It does not verify the report, evaluate policy or treat it as an approval. The platform decides whether to accept it. What the command does: Reads the manifest, uploads the artifact and registers the build with its components. Starts a publication operation: POST /publish/v1/accounts/{account}/projects/{project}/operations with the registration build, the artifact's identity and reference, and the provenance. Follows that operation (GET /operations/{operationId}) until it finishes and prints its decisions and receipts. Registering or staging a build is never reported as completed distribution. If following the operation times out, the CLI reports status: "unfinished" and a recovery message. The operation continues on the platform, so inspect it before you submit another request. Server URL path prefixes are preserved, with or without a trailing slash. Note: Governed publication needs an Oyzu platform that serves this API. It is separate from standalone publishing, which works on its own.

For governed publication: A finished oyzu build whose manifest records status: succeeded. A failed, cancelled or interrupted build is refused before anything is sent (PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED). The platform URL, account and project, as flags or environment variables. A credential the project accepts: the pipeline's OIDC token for a trusted CI connector, or a publish token from the project's CI connector. See Credentials. Commit, repository and ref come from the CI system's environment or from flags.

Flag Environment Default Meaning --server URL OYZU_URL required The platform's URL. Must be https, except http://localhost, http://127.0.0.1 or http://[::1] for local development, so a token never crosses a network unencrypted (PUBLISH_INSECURE_SERVER). --account ID OYZU_ACCOUNT required The account to publish to. --project ID OYZU_PROJECT required The project to publish to. --manifest FILE Standalone: the root's build.bundleDirectory. Governed: dist/manifest.json The build manifest, relative to -C. Repeat it to publish several bundles as one standalone publication. For governed publication, pass --manifest .oyzu/bundle/manifest.json if your bundle is elsewhere. --provenance FILE required for governed publication The signed provenance bundle, sent unchanged. --policy-evidence FILE none Optional signed policy report for the platform's policy. Governed only. --version VERSION none The build's version, if the pipeline names one. --commit SHA from CI The built commit. --repository OWNER/NAME from CI The repository the build came from. --audience AUDIENCE OYZU_AUDIENCE oyzu The audience to request for OIDC tokens the CLI gets from a CI system. --token-env NAME none Read the OIDC token from this environment variable instead of discovering one. --no-upload OYZU_PUBLISH_UPLOAD=0 upload Register the build without uploading artifacts. Governed publication needs the upload and refuses this. A flag wins over its environment variable. Account and project IDs use lowercase letters, digits and inner hyphens, 1 to 63 characters, starting and ending with a letter or digit. With --json, the CLI prints the final operation record, including registrationBuild. Transport errors use the usual {"error": ..., "exitCode": 2} shape.

jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 permissions: contents: read id-token: write # lets oyzu publish request an OIDC token steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: oyzu build - run: oyzu publish --server https://oyzu.example.com --account acme --project web --provenance evidence/build.sigstore.json

oyzu publish uses the first credential it finds, in this order: --token-env NAME, else OYZU_ID_TOKEN: an OIDC token the pipeline already has. A --token-env variable that is unset or empty is an error and does not fall through. GitHub Actions: when ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN are set (the job has permissions: id-token: write), the CLI requests a token for the audience and uses it. Bitbucket Pipelines: BITBUCKET_STEP_OIDC_TOKEN (a step with oidc: true). CircleCI: CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN_V2, then CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN. Buildkite: when BUILDKITE is set and buildkite-agent is on PATH, buildkite-agent oidc request-token --audience oyzu. OYZU_PUBLISH_TOKEN: a scoped, revocable publish token (oyzp_...) issued on the project's CI connector, for CI tools without OIDC. How each CI system provides its token: CI system How GitHub Actions Set permissions: id-token: write on the job. Oyzu finds the token automatically. GitLab CI/CD Add id_tokens: to the job, for example OYZU_ID_TOKEN: {aud: oyzu}. Oyzu reads OYZU_ID_TOKEN (or name another variable with --token-env). Bitbucket Pipelines Set oidc: true on the step. Bitbucket fixes the audience, and the project's trust must accept it. CircleCI Oyzu finds CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN_V2 or CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN, whose audience is the CircleCI organization. For an oyzu audience, run circleci run oidc get --claims '{"aud":"oyzu"}' and put the result in OYZU_ID_TOKEN. Buildkite Oyzu uses buildkite-agent oidc request-token. The pipeline's OIDC policy must allow it. Jenkins with the OIDC provider plugin Bind the plugin's credential to a variable and pass --token-env (or bind it as OYZU_ID_TOKEN). Jenkins without OIDC, TeamCity Use OYZU_PUBLISH_TOKEN from a credentials store or secure parameter. The platform decides which tokens a project accepts, based on the trusts on the project's CI connector. Oyzu sends the token only in the Authorization header of the publish request. It never prints, logs or writes it to disk. Progress output names only the source, for example "a GitHub Actions OIDC token". If a source is present but fails (GitHub refuses the token request, the Buildkite agent fails), the command stops with PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE and does not fall back to another credential. If none is found, it fails with PUBLISH_NO_CREDENTIAL. In GitHub Actions the message names the missing id-token permission.

The platform accepts a CI OIDC token once per privileged operation (build registration, upload grant, and publication create or retry). Reusing a token for the same operation is refused with HTTP 401. GitHub Actions and Buildkite can issue tokens on request, so Oyzu gets a new token for every attempt, including each retry after a connection failure or a 502, 503 or 504. Reads, such as polling an operation, use no token. Oyzu requests one token up front so a missing permission or failing agent stops the command before anything is sent. A failure to issue a later token stops the command with PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE. A fixed token (--token-env, OYZU_ID_TOKEN, Bitbucket, CircleCI, OYZU_PUBLISH_TOKEN) is sent as is on every attempt. If a retry is refused with a 401 (or the platform says replayed), the command fails with PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_REPLAYED. The earlier attempt may already have taken effect, so check the platform before you publish again with a new token. The Buildkite helper has a fixed 30-second deadline, including output capture. If it stalls, Oyzu tries to stop it and fails with PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE and external command deadline exceeded. Oyzu does not fall back to the publish token or wait on a process holding the output open. There is no timeout setting or automatic retry. Token output stays in memory and is not included in the timeout message. Check the Buildkite agent and its OIDC policy, then run oyzu publish again, or pass an already issued token with --token-env. Stopping the helper does not guarantee that remote work or child processes stopped.

Before registering the build, Oyzu uploads each artifact that is not an OCI image or index to the platform's registry as an OCI artifact. Pass --no-upload or set OYZU_PUBLISH_UPLOAD=0 to skip this. Images and indexes keep their oci_digest and are not uploaded this way. Only a regular file with its recorded size and SHA-256 digest is uploaded. A missing or changed file stops the publish with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED before Oyzu asks for any credential. A directory artifact is skipped with a warning and published without an oci_ref. Oyzu asks the platform for temporary registry access (POST .../builds/uploads, 1 to 1000 artifacts) and signs in to the registry with the standard token flow. The registry and its token endpoint must be on https and on the same origin (plain http only on loopback), so the grant token never goes elsewhere. It then pushes each file's bytes, skipping blobs the registry already has, and an OCI manifest addressed by digest (never a tag). The manifest carries the file's media type and name, and the output name in the annotation dev.oyzu.output.
