If the platform answers 404 (no artifact storage), Oyzu warns and publishes without upload. 401, 403 and 422 fail the publish with the platform's problem, and 502, 503 and 504 are retried like the publish request. Registry requests that fail with a server error or in transport are retried up to three times. Any other registry refusal fails with PUBLISH_UPLOAD_FAILED and nothing is published. Each uploaded artifact then carries "oci_ref": "<registry host[:port]>/<repository>@sha256:<manifest digest>".

POST {server}/publish/v1/accounts/{account}/projects/{project}/builds with Authorization: Bearer <credential> and a JSON body: { "version": "1.4.2", "commit": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567", "repository": "acme/web", "ref": "refs/heads/main", "run_url": "https://github.com/acme/web/actions/runs/42", "outputs": [ {"path": "dist/manifest.json", "kind": "manifest", "media_type": "application/vnd.oyzu.build-manifest.v1alpha1+json", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 2101}, {"path": "dist/api/linux/x86_64/server", "kind": "artifact", "media_type": "application/octet-stream", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 123, "target": "api", "name": "binary", "version": "0.1.0-dev.g111111111111", "oci_ref": "registry.example/acme/web/artifacts@sha256:…"} ] } outputs lists the manifest file and one artifact per artifact in the manifest, with its path, media type, digest, size, target, name and version. OCI images and indexes also carry oci_digest. Fields Oyzu cannot determine are left out. Paths are relative to the checkout root (the manifest's directory relative to -C, then the artifact's bundle path). Oyzu checks the platform's limits before sending (PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID): at most 1000 outputs, paths up to 1024 bytes, media types 255, targets 256, names 64 and versions 255. Every artifact needs a target, name, version, SHA-256 digest and safe relative path. Commit, repository, ref and run link come from the first CI system that announces itself: CI system commit repository ref run_url GitHub Actions GITHUB_SHA GITHUB_REPOSITORY GITHUB_REF $GITHUB_SERVER_URL/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/actions/runs/$GITHUB_RUN_ID GitLab CI_COMMIT_SHA CI_PROJECT_PATH refs/tags/$CI_COMMIT_TAG or refs/heads/$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH CI_PIPELINE_URL CircleCI CIRCLE_SHA1 CIRCLE_PROJECT_USERNAME/CIRCLE_PROJECT_REPONAME CIRCLE_TAG / CIRCLE_BRANCH CIRCLE_BUILD_URL Buildkite BUILDKITE_COMMIT (not HEAD) from BUILDKITE_REPO BUILDKITE_TAG / BUILDKITE_BRANCH BUILDKITE_BUILD_URL Bitbucket BITBUCKET_COMMIT BITBUCKET_REPO_FULL_NAME BITBUCKET_TAG / BITBUCKET_BRANCH https://bitbucket.org/<repo>/pipelines/results/$BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER Jenkins GIT_COMMIT from GIT_URL GIT_BRANCH without origin/ BUILD_URL TeamCity BUILD_VCS_NUMBER none (use --repository) none none

The platform answers 200 with the build, its eligibility (candidate or snapshot), one entry per component and the outputs that belong to no component: Build registered · 01jab7v3k9m2q8r4t6w0y1z5c7 (candidate) ✓ published api 1.4.2 (candidate) = already published web 2.0.0 ! skipped worker 0.3.0: the build did not publish [worker/config] Outputs in no component (never shipped) web/build-metadata This only records components. Nothing is distributed until the publication operation finishes, and its receipt controls success. A malformed response (missing build, eligibility or component fields) fails with PUBLISH_RESPONSE_INVALID. The server may already have published the build, so check its state and the platform and client versions. Retrying the same build is safe.

Publication receipts and build-manifest projections tolerate descriptive additions. Replacing a newer-marked receipt retains its unknown fields and higher marker, or refuses with FILE_READER_TOO_OLD before replacing the receipt. Retained provenance and publication bundles are immutable: retries require the same original bytes. Annotations inside signed evidence remain covered by the signature and content digest. Readers verify those bytes before interpreting claims. Frozen publication gaps, report obligations, publisher identities, subjects and independent release expectation profiles remain strict. A newer marker alone is advisory on an otherwise understood release profile; unknown profile fields and mismatched identity or digest still refuse. Updating Oyzu never substitutes for valid evidence or grants publication authority.

Governed publishing failures exit 2 and print one diagnostic. Nothing the platform refused is retried. Code Meaning PUBLISH_NOT_CONFIGURED A server, account or project is missing or malformed (or, standalone, destinations or requirements are not configured). PUBLISH_INSECURE_SERVER The server uses plain http and is not localhost. PUBLISH_MANIFEST_MISSING / PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID No manifest at the path, or it breaks a rule above. Nothing is sent and no token is requested. PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED The manifest records a build that did not succeed. PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED An artifact is missing, not a regular file, or no longer has its recorded size or digest. Nothing is sent. Build again. PUBLISH_UPLOAD_FAILED The registry refused or failed a sign-in, blob or manifest request after retries. Nothing is published. PUBLISH_RESPONSE_INVALID The platform's upload grant or answer is malformed, or names a registry that is not https. PUBLISH_NO_CREDENTIAL / PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE No credential was found, or a CI system did not issue one. PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_REPLAYED (401) The platform refused a fixed CI token on a retry, or said it was reused. The earlier attempt may have taken effect. Check the platform, then publish again with a new token. GitHub Actions and Buildkite send a new token per attempt. PUBLISH_UNAUTHENTICATED (401) The platform did not accept the credential: expired, wrong audience or revoked. 403 (PUBLISH_<code>) The token is valid, but no trust on the project's CI connector accepts this pipeline (repository, branch or workflow). other PUBLISH_<code> The platform's RFC 9457 problem: its detail, each errors[] entry as field: message, and the request ID. PUBLISH_UNREACHABLE The platform could not be reached after retries. Connection failures and 502, 503 and 504 answers are retried up to five attempts with backoff, honoring Retry-After (at most 30 seconds). Each retry carries its own token where the credential source can issue one. Standalone publishing codes are explained where they arise: Code See CONFIG_SCOPE, CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN Settings, Selecting artifacts PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID, PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_MISSING, PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_INVALID, PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_SUBJECT_MISMATCH, PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_BUILDER_DENIED, PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_UNSUPPORTED Selecting artifacts, Provenance evidence PUBLISH_SIGNING_INVALID What is published PUBLISH_BINDING_UNPUSHED, CONFIG_BINDING_UNPUSHED A bound chart needs its image PUBLISH_TAG_UNKNOWN, PUBLISH_TAG_CONFLICT, PUBLISH_TAG_AMBIGUOUS, PUBLISH_TAG_COMMIT_MISMATCH, PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED Which release: the release tag PUBLISH_CONFLICT, PUBLISH_GITHUB_API Uploads and conflicts PUBLISH_PLATFORMS_INCOMPLETE, PUBLISH_PLATFORMS_UNKNOWN, PUBLISH_REQUEST_INVALID Incomplete platform sets PUBLISH_VERIFICATION_MISSING Required verification evidence PUBLISH_EXECUTOR_INVALID, PUBLISH_EXECUTOR_UNKNOWN Asset names

Publishing needs network access, and each file is read into memory. Publisher credential proxies limit each request body and each response body to 64 MiB. npm's encoded upload request must fit this limit. For a newly published entry, both artifact and pointer read-back observations must be recorded after all write permits drop. Earlier reads can verify only an already-present entry. Standalone destinations include OCI registries, existing GitHub releases and publisher plugins (initially npm). PyPI publishing and mutable OCI tags are not implemented. Archived indexes are accepted only for composed plugin release roots; image indexes still use selected per-platform image outputs. Governed publication handles one staged file artifact and needs an Oyzu platform. A registry whose token endpoint is on another origin is refused. Commit, repository and ref are what the CI system reports. The platform decides what it trusts from the token's claims.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-applications.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A python/app target with static PEP 621 metadata and one console script produces a runnable, versioned .pyz application next to the usual wheel and source distribution. Use it to ship a Python service or tool as a single archive built from tested inputs. The application holds the built wheel's files and the runtime dependencies. It doesn't copy other files from your checkout. Note: Python applications are experimental. Isolated builds run in Linux containers, so they need the base execution image and either Docker or, for pip projects, the daemonless sandbox on a Linux host without an engine. See Compiled builder and provisioned images.

Declare the target in build.yaml: builds: api: uses: python/app Your pyproject.toml says what to build: [project] name = "example-api" version = "0.1.0" dependencies = [] [project.scripts] example-api = "api:main" [build-system] requires = ["setuptools==80.9.0"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [tool.setuptools] packages = ["api"] Build, inspect and run it: oyzu run list oyzu build oyzu inspect dist python <application-path-from-manifest> api.main is an ordinary console function. Oyzu doesn't add a server, port, health check or supervisor. Read the application artifact's path from dist/manifest.json.

Artifact Name Notes application <target>-<version>.pyz The runnable archive. The version is the package's PEP 440 build version, such as 0.1.0.dev0+g0123456789ab wheel Native wheel A separate artifact sdist Native source distribution A separate artifact Select artifacts by name, not by position: an application build produces more than two files. Version inference combines your metadata with exact tags, the nearest release tag and Conventional Commits. A v1.4.2 baseline plus a feature commit can give 1.5.0.dev0+g... for all three artifacts without editing your checkout. A local build or tag doesn't authorize a release. An unrelated source change no longer rekeys a Python target on its own: the .dev0+g<source> stamp follows only the files the shipping stages read, so a change elsewhere in the repository, such as documentation, keeps the version, the artifact names and the cache keys. The stamp stays a stamp: only the 12-character source hash moves, and only when a file that ships changes. This applies when the build runs confined (oyzu build --isolated); otherwise the whole target is still the source scope. Applications with only a requirements.txt use SemVer versions such as 0.0.0-dev.g<source>, and no distribution metadata is invented.

With several console scripts, or none, planning fails with a message. There is no setting yet to choose one. Auto-detected python/package projects may have several console scripts. A requirements-only application runs app.py or __main__.py.

Oyzu prepares the dependencies (Python dependency preparation). It runs your native build backend once. It assembles the application. It tests the sources extracted from that archive. It runs the lint and read-only format checks. Reports go to dist/ with their paths, digests and summaries in the manifest. See Python testing for overrides, empty suites and coverage thresholds. Direct tasks (oyzu run) run your native commands. They don't assemble archives or collect build reports.

Assembly: checks the wheel's name and console entry point against the plan installs the runtime wheels only (offline, without resolving dependencies) with pip. Build and test tools stay out removes installer-specific provenance and launchers tied to one interpreter generates a launcher from the package's entry point metadata records the source, version, project files, runtime packages, entry point and original wheel digest in oyzu-application.json inside the archive The archive has sorted paths and normalized ZIP metadata. Oyzu refuses unsafe paths, case collisions, symlinks and oversized payloads. Packaging confirms the archive is the one that was tested and that the wheel and sdist didn't change. If tests, quality checks or reports fail, or an artifact changed, the artifacts aren't collected. Read the logs and reports in dist/. These checks guard the build and are not a security boundary against malicious tests.

Complete-read reuse works for pip and uv python/app projects with a pyproject.toml and a declarative setuptools build, on the isolated Linux crun path with a plugin package that includes it (the published 0.1.2 package predates it). An unchanged rebuild reuses preparation, assembly, tests and packaging; a source edit reruns assembly, tests and packaging but not preparation; changing a dependency or build-requires pin reruns preparation too. Preparation does not receive the inferred version, so an edit that only changes its source suffix doesn't rerun it. Requirements applications, authored build tasks, Poetry preparation and native-host builds keep running those stages every time. Tests reuse only for the generated pytest task. See stage reuse. Windows has no merged complete-read backend for native uv builds. The Python plugin admits Windows uv from the first release after 0.1.3 (0.1.3 refuses it before execution), and those builds run every stage again. Clearing the action cache cannot add reuse. Existing Python test-case selection has its own supported scope; it does not establish complete-read reuse for the whole Python lifecycle.

Native pip applications with static PEP 621 name/version metadata build on the host, including Windows x64, without Docker. They produce the same .pyz, wheel and source distribution. Use a matching native Python plugin and managed CPython selected from requires-python or .python-version. Package and library profiles retain their native wheel output. Core prepares the native application's wheel closure through its scoped acquisition broker. pip resolves and verifies the original wheels through a socket-free native adapter; only core fetches upstream bytes. Installation into a fresh build environment, backend execution, assembly and archive testing use those local inputs offline. A changed or added prepared wheel is refused. Native closure reuse is not implemented: each invocation acquires its inputs, and --offline currently refuses this native app lane. Isolated builds also handle requirements-only, uv, Poetry and legacy projects. They use Linux containers through Docker with the locked CPython and pip, uv or Poetry. CPython comes from oyzu.lock, so installing CPython on your machine doesn't replace it. Isolated builds download dependencies during preparation. After that, assembly and tests run with the network off. If an input is missing, fix it during preparation. There is no network fallback in the build. The archive needs pure Python wheels and ZIP-compatible code and data. Native extensions, .pth startup files and libraries that need real files fail with an error. Test the app to check how it loads resources. Python is not bundled. Running the .pyz needs a compatible interpreter. Legacy setup.py applications, dynamic console metadata, editable installs, entry point overrides and native application layouts are not supported. To put the archive in an OCI image, see Python application containers.

Isolated builds run on the base execution image. Oyzu mounts its engine and the Python plugin into each action, so no image carries an Oyzu worker and none needs rebuilding when the CLI changes. CPython comes from oyzu.lock and is restored into each action. The base image has no Python. uv is restored from oyzu.lock on supported Linux builds. Poetry still needs an image that provides it: --image poetry=<ref>. See manager runtimes. An image you pass must meet the bring-your-own requirements. A locked CPython still takes the place of the image's own. The oyzu CLI itself doesn't need Python. Builds run Oyzu's own steps in compiled code. Small embedded Python helpers run inside the selected Python only to call the packaging, Poetry export, setuptools, pytest, coverage and quality-tool APIs. Ruff runs as a native program. The container that runs your finished application uses a plain python:3.12-slim-bookworm and doesn't need the Oyzu engine.
Python application containers Python testing Python dependency preparation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-containers.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Set with.container: true on a python/app build to package the tested application archive into an OCI image. You need no Dockerfile and no second application build. Note: Experimental. Supported for isolated builds on Linux. There is no startup smoke test of the application, and the image is built for CPython 3.12 only. builds: api: uses: python/app with: container: true Build with oyzu build --isolated. A native build refuses a container request with native build does not support these declared relationships; select --isolated explicitly. oyzu build runs the application's build, test, lint and format steps as usual, and then adds the image steps under a derived target named api-container in the plan and manifest. You can't run those derived steps directly with oyzu run or override them with hooks. If one of your own targets already has the derived name, the build fails instead of overwriting it. with.container belongs to python/app. oyzu config validate and every command that reads your builds check it. It is refused on any other builder, including python/library, and so is the older top-level container: field (the message names with.container).

The Python toolchain and dependencies described in Python applications python:3.12-slim-bookworm in your local Docker image store The base execution image. The image helpers ship in the Docker plugin package (Docker images) The right AppArmor profile, where your host needs one Oyzu doesn't pull any other missing image, install Docker or change host security settings.

The python-pure-zip-3.12-v1 profile needs a pure-Python, ZIP-compatible application and CPython 3.12. Oyzu checks the local base image's implementation and Python version without using the network and uses exactly that image content. If the image changes during the build, the build fails. Provision base images by a process you trust. Oyzu does not authenticate to registries, and a matching image is not an approval of its contents. Setting Default Archive path /app/application.pyz User and group 65532:65532 Working directory /app Entrypoint ["python", "/app/application.pyz"] CMD Cleared Oyzu doesn't add ports, health checks, a server lifecycle, deployment settings or secrets. Nothing is installed during image assembly. The archive already contains its runtime dependencies.

Use an object to change the defaults. Every field is optional, and {} behaves like true. builds: api: uses: python/app with: container: base: registry.example/python-runtime:3.12 user: "1000:1001" workdir: /srv/api entrypoint: [python, /app/application.pyz] Field Values Notes base An image reference, up to 512 bytes Must already be in your local store with CPython 3.12. It gets the same check as the default base. No pull and no public fallback user Numeric UID:GID, each up to 4294967295 Names and negative IDs fail. This identity also owns the copied archive workdir Absolute path, up to 1,024 bytes, using letters, digits and /._-, with no .. Doesn't move the archive from /app/application.pyz entrypoint 1 to 64 non-empty arguments, up to 4,096 bytes each, no control characters Used as given. No shell or variable expansion Unknown keys, wrong types and explicit null values fail validation. A custom entrypoint is recorded as launch metadata. It doesn't prove that the program exists or that your service starts. The runtime check still runs, and changing the entrypoint doesn't choose between several console scripts in the application. The overrides give no production approval. with.container: false means no container everywhere. The build counts as having no image.

The application, wheel and sdist artifacts are still produced. The derived target adds an image artifact, for example api-container/artifacts/api-0.1.0-dev.g<source>.oci.tar. The image version uses the SemVer spelling, not Python's PEP 440 version. The manifest records the file digest and the OCI digest. Image steps start after the application's tests, required reports and quality checks pass. A failure there blocks the image. Oyzu copies the exact tested archive into an empty private build context. Generated image files never enter your checkout. Assertions on the image's content and platform produce their own JUnit report. No application coverage is invented for the image. Failed image assertions block the image from reaching the bundle. Read the logs and reports, fix the error and rebuild. The configuration engine applies precedence and policy. Docker's eligibility is checked together with the application before preparation. docker.apparmorProfile comes from your resolved configuration and is fixed for the image step, and no environment variable overrides it. A profile name doesn't grant signing or publishing rights. In a managed setup, connector restrictions apply to application downloads, and there is no managed fallback.

The application's startup is not tested. Passing archive tests and image assertions doesn't show that it starts. Legacy and native Python application layouts, container matrices, other language runtimes and centrally configured runtime profiles are not supported. Discovery doesn't turn on containers for you. Related: Python applications, Docker images, configuration.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-preparation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Before an isolated Python build runs, Oyzu prepares your dependencies. A worker that can reach only PyPI downloads binary wheels, and every build, test and quality step then installs them offline. This page explains which inputs Oyzu reads and how it treats dependency-group includes, editable references to your own project, dynamic versions and packages that must be built from source. pip, uv and Poetry keep their own behavior; Oyzu reads only the declarations listed here. Note: Python builds are experimental. An isolated build needs Docker or, for eligible pip targets on Linux, the daemonless sandbox, and the base execution image, plus any system libraries your dependencies need. See Python applications.

Native python/app builds with static PEP 621 metadata use a core-owned host wheel closure. Native pip requests are translated over standard I/O; its socket transport is disabled. The scoped core broker admits each upstream request. Native pip retains dependency resolution and publisher hash checking; core freezes the downloaded bytes and verifies their hashes before offline installation. Build, test and quality tools remain outside the runtime closure embedded in the application. No project backend runs during acquisition. This path currently reacquires per invocation and refuses --offline. The python/package builder (also available as python/library) and python/app come from the oyzu/python plugin package. The plugin reads your project files, picks the package manager and quality tools you already use, and declares the commands, reports and artifacts. Oyzu itself downloads dependencies, runs the steps offline and checks the reports. If the plugin refuses a project, the build fails. There is no fallback to another builder. Python prepared native API/version differs from selected package means the prepared native adapter identity or resolved build version disagrees with the selected Python package. A fresh checkout without a lock can encounter this when the CLI and published plugin contain different adapters. Use a matching CLI and Python package; changing the interpreter or deleting downloaded wheels does not repair an adapter mismatch. The build refuses before executing actions. An isolated pip build needs a plugin package built for Linux, not a raw development executable. See plugin packages. A Linux environment image and its system libraries are also required; choosing a CPython version does not provide them.

The Python plugin declares source reads separately for each operation: Stage Captured source contract prepare Project metadata and dependency declarations for pip projects without local source references; other managers and local source dependencies remain unbounded. build Declarative setuptools.build_meta packages, modules, script files, metadata, uv.toml and discovery directories, only when build requirements contain setuptools and optionally wheel. A directory includes its listing, so adding a source file changes the key. Default flat discovery covers the whole target. test Python modules, test directories, pytest and coverage configuration, enforced by the private source view. Add root data folders outside tests/ or test/ with inputs in build.yaml; otherwise the captured view hides them. Absent pytest, coverage and uv configuration candidates are included so adding configuration invalidates the stage. lint, format-check Unbounded. The captured-plan request does not bind the finally selected Ruff task to its read prediction; Black and flake8 also lack a complete read contract. package Packages and applications copy only upstream outputs, with no source reads. The plan fixes the application layout. setup.py, project-defined backends, dynamic metadata, unknown backends (including Hatch), and unmodeled setuptools selection such as MANIFEST.in, setup.cfg, custom command classes or extension modules keep the build unbounded. Additional build requirements (such as setuptools-scm or setuptools-rust), extras and direct references also keep it unbounded, naming the requirement. Application assembly also retains the whole-target identity it embeds in its archive. Native PEP 517 builds, pytest and quality checks remain unbounded: they provide no complete observed-read record. Wheel RECORD and sdist membership show what was packaged, not everything the backend read. Native pytest may read files at run time. The read-only --plan preview does not invoke the plugin; its explanation may be generic until recorded contracts are available. Captured predictions are enforced by the source view even with caching off; declared inputs add files but never remove a required read. Read declarations alone do not guarantee reuse across an unrelated edit. Python snapshot versions currently include the whole-target source digest, which changes action environments and artifact names. The version identity is passed separately from dependency identity, including for post/dev, epoch and multi-part PEP 440 versions and declarative PDM version files. A source edit changes their snapshot version and wheel filename. Acquired packages.json stores only native version facts and a snapshot base; the shared version decision adds the source suffix during dependency preparation. That decision is kept outside the acquired tree and projected into action requests. An unrelated README edit therefore does not change the prepared dependency tree. Legacy setup.py metadata remains native and is compared again before building. The build projects the selected version into the wheel and sdist; dependency identity never supplies a version suffix. Preparation does not receive the version, so a source edit that only changes it does not rerun preparation. For supported development-source tests, preparation also retains the exact captured native pyproject.toml before that projection. The test preparation restores those bytes and installs the captured project through its selected backend's real PEP 660 path into a separate private environment. Its native version, METADATA, installer RECORD and import mapping are bound as observed runtime facts. The inferred wheel version and its separate environment are not inputs to this development test subject. They remain inputs to built-package testing, packaging and release validation. No native version or metadata is synthesized to make case keys stable. This route requires all declared backend and test dependencies to have been captured already; --no-index --no-deps --no-build-isolation never acquires a missing backend. Unsupported declarative layouts use built-package testing; an install or observed mapping failure is an error. The additional test venv is task-owned producer state under .oyzu-build/python/development-venv, separate from the build venv. Direct runs and application archive testing are unchanged. Captured prepare and build store their reusable environment and distributions at the fixed task-owned .oyzu-build/python path inside the private target workspace. The action cache records and restores these outputs, so consumers key on the built wheel bytes, including package data. Wheel member timestamps are normalized to the ZIP epoch, and sdist timestamps to zero, before producer outputs are recorded. Rebuilding the same inputs with different native member timestamps therefore preserves archive bytes. Dependency identity covers dependency declarations and local source dependencies, rather than unrelated target files. See action cache. Application assembly creates its own invocation-local scratch directory. A restored prepare supplies the environment without depending on scratch left by the original worker; that scratch is not part of the cached output. Generated tasks use the target-root environment even when their working directory is a subdirectory. An authored task replacement owns its interpreter and required report output; python alone selects the pinned base interpreter, not the prepared environment. Flake8, Black and Ruff explicitly exclude .oyzu-build before file discovery, retaining native default exclusions, project exclude and extend-exclude, and Black force-exclude configuration. Native flags precede path arguments, including an explicit --. This excludes producer state; ordinary source lint and format failures still fail. Ruff 0.11 formatting lacks --extend-exclude; its native --config override extends the exclusion list instead. Black resolves configuration before merging the producer-state regex into its selected extend-exclude expression. Captured PEP 517 builds run without a second build-isolation environment. Backend plugins installed as project dependencies are therefore visible too; a strict build-system.requires list cannot detect them. Projects relying on undeclared backend plugins fail an isolated native build and must declare their build inputs.

An isolated build uses the CPython version recorded in oyzu.lock. It comes from [tools].python and from your project's own requirements (requires-python, native Poetry Python comparisons, .python-version). Both Python range declarations apply when present; unsupported Poetry-only range syntax fails with guidance to use supported comparisons. See Python installation. oyzu pin records the choice, and oyzu build --isolated --full --frozen reads it without rewriting the lock. Oyzu checks the CPython archive against its locked digest and mounts it read-only in the worker. If the lock has no entry for the platform, the build stops and tells you how to fix it. It never falls back to the image's Python. Offline builds need the archive already cached. That one interpreter is used for environment markers, dependency inventory, pip downloads, wheel compatibility, the project version, virtual environments, source builds and tests. Your own task commands see it first on PATH. How each manager uses it: Manager Interpreter pip The selected CPython uv The selected CPython, passed explicitly. uv's managed Python and downloads are turned off Poetry The exporter runs in the image's own interpreter, where Poetry is installed. Your PATH is unchanged The image still supplies pip or Poetry and any compilers or system libraries you need. The default execution image does not include Poetry, so an isolated Poetry build needs a custom --image that does; without it, preparation fails with Poetry is not installed in the build image's Python. Poetry on your host PATH is not used. A uv project gets uv from oyzu.lock instead: Oyzu restores the locked uv beside the locked CPython, puts it first on PATH, and records it in the build's tool evidence, so the default execution image builds uv projects without a custom --image. oyzu pin locks uv for uv projects on Linux hosts; the restored archive is the Linux x86-64 release. A Docker image that asks for runtime-only dependencies uses its own interpreter, markers and compatibility, not the producer project's CPython. If a Python pin from your configuration or policy conflicts with that interpreter, the build fails. Runtime-only stores contain captured wheels and their hash manifest, not UV's installed environment. A Dockerfile choosing uv pip install creates its own installer metadata, which can embed Unix ctime even when input mtime and SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH are fixed. For byte-identical offline installed trees with uv 0.12.21, use its native --no-installer-metadata option alongside --require-hashes, --no-index and the captured wheel store. UV then omits optional installer files and their RECORD rows at installation. Oyzu preserves wheel bytes, native integrity checks and authored Dockerfile contents; it does not filter installed files or rewrite metadata after installation. Legacy setup.py projects with runtime dependencies are refused. A legacy package takes its version from the shared version decision, and planning fails if its metadata disagrees.

A native python/package pip build runs on your machine, not in a container. Supported on Linux x86-64 (glibc). Oyzu installs the managed CPython and, before copying your source, reads its runtime. You provide the dependencies: With no .venv in the target, Oyzu uses the managed CPython directly. With a .venv, it must be a standard virtual environment created from that exact managed interpreter, with system site packages off. A mismatch fails the build. A linked or shared environment root, or a source input inside .venv, fails the build. Ordinary interpreter symlinks inside a valid environment are fine. Each check has a 20-second limit. Install your project dependencies, pytest, pytest-cov, coverage and the quality tools you use into your own .venv by running the managed interpreter. Oyzu does not install them, copy the environment or repair it, and the source copy leaves .venv out. Missing packages fail as usual, and offline builds need them already present. The interpreter is used for the wheel build and for pytest and coverage reporting. Ruff runs from the environment's own entry point. Black and Flake8 run through the interpreter with -I -m. Task replacements and hooks keep their commands and still owe their reports. If the environment does not match, recreate it from the managed CPython. This applies to full native builds only. It does not apply to direct tasks, to VIRTUAL_ENV selection, to environments found in parent folders, or to uv and Poetry. See native uv builds.

A python/package uv project with pyproject.toml and a committed uv.lock builds natively too, with no container. Oyzu installs the managed CPython and uv (the [tools].uv version, otherwise the newest uv in the tool index), and oyzu pin locks both. build runs uv build --wheel --sdist --out-dir <output>, adding --offline for offline builds. uv uses the managed CPython only: UV_PYTHON_DOWNLOADS=never and UV_PYTHON_PREFERENCE=only-system keep it from downloading or picking another interpreter. The output folder holds the wheel and the source distribution. test runs pytest and coverage through uv run --locked, so pytest and pytest-cov belong in your locked dependencies or dependency groups. uv creates and syncs .venv from uv.lock as it normally does, so the first run needs network access unless uv's cache already has the packages. A replaced build task keeps its own command. For --full, selected quality tools such as Ruff must also be on your native PATH. With tools declared in your uv development group, run uv sync --locked and activate its .venv before invoking Oyzu. Tests still run through uv run --locked; Oyzu does not replace a missing quality executable with a different check. Supported on Linux x86-64 (glibc) and, with a Python plugin release after 0.1.3 that has a Windows payload, Windows x64 (pure-Python packages; stages always rerun because Windows has no complete-read backend yet). Without uv.lock, or for a python/app target, the build is isolated.

A python/package Poetry project with a committed, fresh poetry.lock builds natively on Linux x86-64 (CPython), with no container and without running Poetry. This needs a plugin and CLI that both know the python-poetry-native feature; older ones keep building Poetry projects isolated. Oyzu reads poetry.lock, checks its content hash against pyproject.toml as Poetry does, and installs the main and dev group closure with pip --require-hashes --no-deps. Wheels come through Oyzu's governed preparation and are kept in a content-addressed cache, so repeat builds install offline. OYZU_POETRY_WHEEL_CACHE moves that cache. Admission evaluates dependency markers for the selected managed CPython and compares each selected package's wheel interpreter, ABI and platform tags. A matching tag is admitted; a mismatch names the package and tag incompatibility and falls back to the container build. The selected interpreter's wheel tags also participate in native action cache keys. Source-only dependencies fall back too. Lock format labels do not restrict admission when the required fields and hashes remain readable. If the selected interpreter cannot be launched because it is missing, admission refuses with PYTHON_POETRY_NATIVE_NO_INTERPRETER. Oyzu reports it under PYTHON_POETRY_NATIVE_REFUSED and falls back to the container build. build caches the selected main and dev wheels, then runs the pinned poetry-core backend in an isolated environment and writes the wheel and source distribution to the build output. The metadata and contents match poetry build; the archives are not byte-identical. With --offline, a missing compatible cached wheel stops the build and names the first missing requirement; populate the cache with an online build before retrying. test runs pytest and coverage from the locked dev group, so pytest and pytest-cov belong there. Test preparation uses only verified compatible cached wheels and never downloads; missing wheels require an online build to populate the cache. A stale or missing lock is refused with Poetry lock is missing or stale; update it with poetry lock. Poetry plugins, Git, path and non-PyPI sources, other operating systems, and python/app targets fall back to the isolated container build.

Native pip and uv package builds use the native tool's configuration and credentials. No Oyzu registry setting or platform account is required. Use oyzu build --full on the supported Linux x86-64 host path: pip reads its native pip.conf, PIP_INDEX_URL, PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL and user .netrc. Keep credentials in user configuration or environment variables. The host pip path still requires your dependencies and test tools in the managed-interpreter virtual environment. uv reads uv.toml or [[tool.uv.index]] in pyproject.toml. For a named index, supply UV_INDEX_<NAME>_USERNAME and UV_INDEX_<NAME>_PASSWORD as uv documents. Commit uv.lock; its existing source and integrity checks apply. A private source distribution can obtain its PEP 517 backend from the same native private index. The host tool owns build isolation and index selection. An extra index retains native pip semantics; it is not a private-first priority rule. Use an aggregate index when you need one authoritative package source. Native Python registry, credential and transport environment values are supplied only to the host command. They are excluded from persisted action definitions and keys. When these invocation-only values or private-index configuration are present, Oyzu executes the target instead of restoring action-cache results; the native tools can still use their own caches. Frozen managed-interpreter controls, explicit environment removals and environment policy remain binding. Proxy settings (HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, ALL_PROXY, NO_PROXY) only route traffic, so on their own they neither enter keys nor stop results being reused. CI runners and sandboxes often set both spellings of a proxy variable, such as HTTPS_PROXY and https_proxy. Oyzu accepts the pair when both hold the same value. If they differ, the build fails and names the variable, never its value. Environment variables you author in configuration still reject case aliases. Do not commit literal registry credentials. Before copying source, Oyzu checks tracked native configuration and refuses literal credentials with instructions to use an environment reference or user-level configuration. In an index URL, the username and the password must each be a reference or absent. The one exception is a documented non-secret username (__token__, oauth2accesstoken, x-access-token, aws, _json_key or _json_key_base64), which may stay literal when the password is a reference. A token can sit in either slot (https://TOKEN:@host), so any other literal username is refused. Environment-reference files retain their bytes; Oyzu does not expand them. The selected native tool must itself support the reference syntax. See native configuration credentials. Private Python indexes are currently supported in host mode only. If captured or isolated preparation encounters private index configuration or named uv index credentials, it stops before dependency or build actions run, with guidance to use host mode. It does not replace the private index with public PyPI. This also applies to Python applications that require isolated execution. Correct the native configuration or use a supported native package build; switching to an anonymous public source is not an authentication repair.

Input Used for project.dependencies in pyproject.toml Runtime build-system.requires (or the locked legacy tools, with fixed defaults for tools not locked) Build The dev dependency group, with its includes Test requirements.txt Runtime Default test and quality tools you have not declared or locked Build or test How the closure is resolved: A uv project uses uv export --locked, and a Poetry project uses its lock export. That hashed export decides the closure for the project and its groups. Extra backend requirements, requirements.txt and injected tool requirements are resolved by pip, with your lock as constraints. They keep their extras and transitive dependencies. A pip project resolves all its declarations. uv writes its locked export to a private requirements file. Preparation reads that file separately from the plugin's JSON response. If export fails, preparation stops with uv's diagnostic; it does not accept an empty response or refresh the lock to hide the failure. Oyzu records every wheel's digest in the dependency snapshot. Requirements files accept an optional leading UTF-8 byte-order mark (BOM), LF or CRLF line endings, backslash continuations and comments beginning with # at the start of a line or after whitespace: idna==3.10 # runtime dependency httpx[http2]==0.28.1 \ ; python_version >= "3.10" # native marker The leading BOM is ignored for parsing; retained requirement records keep their original bytes when an editable project reference is removed. Continuations join before comments are removed. A URL fragment such as #sha256=... remains part of its URL; accepting comments does not approve a new download source. Requirements, extras and environment markers keep their native semantics. Includes (-r), constraint files (-c), alternate-index options and editable references to other projects remain unsupported. An authored build-system.requires is always authoritative, even when it conflicts with a lock. When it is missing, the default setuptools and wheel backend uses versions your lock already selects. For a tool the lock does not select, Oyzu falls back to setuptools==80.9.0 or wheel==0.45.1. Oyzu never refreshes a lock or drops one of your requirements to hide a conflict.

A package can provide its own quality tool, for example building Black and formatting with Black. The offline build installs your wheel before the quality checks, so the checks use that installed copy. Oyzu skips the default download of a quality tool whose name matches the current package. Explicit requirements, locked constraints and the report gates are unchanged.
documents.s: The current package as a quality tool

documents.t: [dependency-groups] follows PEP 735. An entry is a requirement string or an { include-group = "name" } table, and includes expand in place. Group names are compared after PEP 503 normalization, so Runtime_Checks and runtime-checks are the same group. [dependency-groups] dev = [{ include-group = "tests" }, "pytest-cov==6.0.0"] tests = [{ include-group = "runtime-checks" }, "pytest==8.3.5"] runtime-checks = ["packaging==24.2"] This captures packaging, pytest and pytest-cov as test inputs. Preparation fails, naming the group, for an include of an undefined group, two groups with equivalent names, a cyclic include, or any other table entry. Only the dev group is used, as in uv. For uv projects, the native export applies the same includes.

Requirements files often install the project itself (-e .[cli]), and dependency groups often reference it with extras (name[tests]). Oyzu builds the project from your source, so it never downloads it. It replaces the reference with what installing the project would add: project.dependencies plus the project.optional-dependencies for the extras you chose, following extras that reference the project again. Extra names are compared after normalization. An undefined extra fails preparation. A reference whose environment marker does not apply to the build interpreter is skipped, as pip skips it. In requirements.txt, the accepted editable forms are -e ., -e ./, --editable . and --editable=., each optionally followed by [extras]. The project needs a static project.name. Any other directive (-r, -c, an editable path to another folder, option lines) fails with Unsupported requirements directive; no alternate source fallback.
documents.s: The project itself as a requirement

documents.t: A dependency can require the project you are building, with extras. For example, a Litestar plugin requires litestar[cli]>=2.0.1. Oyzu satisfies that from your own source, without downloading it. Oyzu checks the declared requirements, the requested extras and their closure with native marker and extra rules. It fails on unknown extras, missing dependencies, unapproved direct URLs and a package that would be both downloaded and built from source. Dynamic dependency metadata can't be checked without running your build backend, so it is refused. Your source version can differ from the final version of the build. Before creating the virtual environment, Oyzu compares each constraint with the version it assigned to the build. It fails if there is no planned version, the project identity differs, or a constraint doesn't accept the version. This does not apply to apps or runtime-only dependency contexts.
documents.s: Dependencies that require the current project

documents.t: A project can list version in project.dynamic. For the pdm.backend, Oyzu reads the version from a file without running the backend or importing your code: [project] name = "example" dynamic = ["version"] [build-system] requires = ["pdm-backend"] build-backend = "pdm.backend" [tool.pdm.version] source = "file" path = "example/__init__.py" Oyzu reads that UTF-8 file with PDM's default rule: the first line that matches __version__ = "1.2.3" or VERSION = '1.2.3' wins, with an optional trailing comment. The value is validated as a PEP 440 version. Version inference then picks the build's version from it. The wheel and sdist metadata carry the build version, and the manifest keeps the original as nativeVersion. The path must be relative, inside your captured source, free of links, and name a regular file of at most 4 MiB. Bad paths, invalid UTF-8, a missing default literal and an invalid version fail preparation. Fix the declaration or the file and rebuild. Other dynamic forms use tag-based inference and are not executed: setuptools [tool.setuptools.dynamic] version = { attr = ... } Hatch file and VCS providers PDM call, SCM and custom-pattern providers PDM projects with backend-path, a tool.pdm.build.custom-hook, or a pdm_build.py Without applicable tags, the base is 0.0.0, which gives a version such as 0.0.0.dev0+g0123456789ab. The native strategy fails with version-needs-native when no native version exists. In its private build tree, Oyzu removes version from project.dynamic, removes tool.setuptools.dynamic.version if present and writes the build version as the static project.version. The wheel, sdist and their metadata then agree. Your checkout is unchanged. A pyproject.toml with neither a static nor a dynamic version fails with Python project version must be static or listed in project.dynamic.

Some locked packages have no wheel to download: a uv.lock package whose source is a Git repository pinned to a commit a uv workspace member or path dependency, which uv export lists as -e ./PATH or ./PATH a registry package that uv.lock locks with a source distribution (sdist) and no wheel Oyzu builds these from source, only inside the isolated worker that has no network, never during preparation. This works for uv projects only. Splitting. Oyzu separates these lines from the uv export and downloads only the registry wheels, with their hashes. A declaration that names such a package, including one that repeats the source as a direct URL such as advanced-alchemy @ git+https://github.com/..., is satisfied by the source build. A direct URL for a package that uv.lock doesn't build from source is still refused. Sdists. An sdist is downloaded from the files.pythonhosted.org route, checked against the SHA-256 in uv.lock and unpacked without running any of its code. A missing hash or a URL outside that route fails. Only regular files are written, names must be portable with one top-level folder, and archives are limited to 256 MiB. Git sources. Oyzu fetches the commit recorded in uv.lock with Git over a read-only route. Only public HTTPS GitHub repositories work. The checkout is stored without Git metadata, and no hooks, filters, submodules or credentials are used. Build requirements. Oyzu reads each source's build-system.requires (or the locked legacy tools for a setup.py package) and downloads them as build wheels, using the lock as constraints. No backend code runs. Build. In the worker, after the captured wheels are installed, each source is copied into the private build state and built with pip wheel --no-index --no-deps --no-build-isolation. A missing build requirement fails before the backend runs. The wheel must carry the locked name and version. Then all wheels are installed from a digest manifest with --require-hashes. For example, this declaration makes uv lock sampleproject at the commit: [project] dependencies = ["sampleproject"] [tool.uv.sources] sampleproject = { git = "https://github.com/pypa/sampleproject", rev = "621e4974ca25ce531773def586ba3ed8e736b3fc" } The dependency snapshot records each Git source with the digest of its captured tree and lists every source package in the oyzu.dev/python-sources extension, with its kind, path, commit, purpose and build requirements. An sdist source also records its URL and SHA-256. Workspace members belong to your project source and have no separate record. Because Git metadata is not captured, Oyzu sets SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION to the locked version during the source build, so setuptools-scm and hatch-vcs read it. A source that requires maturin or setuptools-rust needs Rust and Cargo crates, which Python preparation doesn't capture. Preparation fails naming the requirement, as it does for pydantic's pydantic-core member. A python/app whose runtime closure includes a package built from source fails at packaging, because application archives contain captured wheels only. Runtime dependency contexts for Docker refuse such packages.

Reusable producer outputs live under .oyzu-build/python in the private target workspace. Invocation-local scratch stays under /out/.oyzu-python: Location Contents .oyzu-build/python/venv/ The reusable build environment .oyzu-build/python/development-venv/ The separate editable environment for supported development-source tests .oyzu-build/python/dist/ The wheel and sdist before collection .oyzu-build/python/application.pyz The application archive, with its distribution and tested-application records beside it /out/.oyzu-python/ Invocation-local source-build and application staging scratch The private workspace is separate from your checkout. Quality tools exclude the producer-state directory before discovering source files. Backend output selection still needs to keep build state out of distributions. The action cache records declared reusable outputs; scratch is not a reusable contract. Packaging copies final artifacts and reports to /out/<target>/<platform>/, available as OYZU_OUTPUT. Read their collected paths from the bundle manifest.

Preparation failures stop the build before any action runs and keep the worker's message. Fix the input and start a new build. Message Cause and fix Dependency group NAME is not defined / includes itself Fix the include in [dependency-groups] Project extra NAME is not defined Declare the extra in project.optional-dependencies or fix the reference An editable project reference needs a static pyproject.toml project name Declare project.name statically Source package NAME needs build requirement maturin... The source builds Rust code, which isn't supported Source package NAME build requirement REQ is not in the captured dependency set A build requirement of a source package wasn't captured. The build stops before running its backend Isolated source build of NAME failed The backend failed offline with only captured inputs. pip's output is in the action log Locked path requirement PATH: only workspace members and path dependencies inside the captured project can be built The export names an absolute path, a parent folder or a file: URL Git sources currently require a public HTTPS GitHub repository / Git source must lock a full commit identity Pin a public GitHub repository by full commit Git source NAME uses submodules, which preparation does not fetch The locked commit has a .gitmodules file Git sources need the git client in the Python preparation image The base execution image includes git. An image you pass with --image must too Packages built from source are supported only for uv projects with uv.lock / ...not supported in runtime dependency contexts Source builds work for uv projects only, and not for a Docker runtime context uv.lock sdist-only package NAME: has no locked SHA-256... / ...outside the approved registry file route The sdist entry can't be trusted. Re-lock from PyPI The sdist of NAME does not match the SHA-256 recorded in uv.lock The download differs from the lock. Nothing is built Python applications cannot package runtime dependency NAME built from source yet A python/app runtime dependency is built from source Direct URL requirements need an approved source adapter A declaration or requirements file pins a direct URL or Git source outside uv.lock Current project dependency REQ is incompatible with planned version VERSION A dependency on your project doesn't accept the build's version Current project extra is not defined: NAME / Current project dependency closure requires static metadata The closure can't be worked out from static metadata Poetry lock is missing or stale; update it with poetry lock Run poetry lock and commit the result

Installed-artifact tests measure the installed package, not your checkout. A coverage setting such as omit = ["*/site-packages/*"] under [tool.coverage.report] can exclude every measured file. Then the tests may pass but coverage reports No data to report, the required Cobertura report is missing and packaging is blocked. Narrow or remove that exclusion in your coverage configuration so the installed package is measured, then rerun. See Python testing.

Source builds work only for uv. Poetry Git and path sources, and Git or path lines in a pip requirements file, are refused. Git sources need a public HTTPS GitHub repository and a full commit. Sdist-only packages need files.pythonhosted.org sdists in uv.lock. Submodules and Git LFS content are not fetched. Sources that build Rust (maturin, setuptools-rust) or need other non-Python toolchains beyond what the image provides are not supported. A source package that is itself a build requirement of another source is refused, environment markers on member lines are refused, and virtual members are skipped as uv skips them. Source-built wheels are not checked for reproducibility. Only the source tree and the captured build requirements are digest-recorded. A Poetry lock whose content hash no longer matches the project is rejected, as poetry install rejects it. Oyzu doesn't refresh it. Only the PDM default file form supplies a native dynamic version. Other computed versions use tags, and dynamic dependencies are not computed. Only the dev dependency group is used, and you can't select others.
Python testing Python applications Version inference Python installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-sessions.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Standalone native package builds can use your existing pip or uv configuration and credentials without a session agent. The optional session integration below is a separate way to obtain access. Use this when pip or uv should install from a private package index without a password in pip.conf, uv.toml, .netrc or environment variables. Each time you run pip or uv through oyzu, oyzu asks a local credential agent which index to use and gives the tool the password through its keyring support. You don't need the Python keyring package or any per-project authentication file. Note: Experimental. You need a credential agent running on the same machine; oyzu doesn't include one. Supported on Linux with Python 3.12, pip 25.0 and uv 0.12, using Bash. Isolated oyzu build runs don't use this yet.

Add the agent's address to your user or administrator configuration (not the project's oyzu.toml): [python] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43199/session" Setting Values Default Meaning python.sessionEndpoint http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<path>, no user name, password, query or fragment Not set The local agent to ask for sessions. Remove it to go back to plain pip and uv Project, local and command-line configuration and profiles can't set this value. User configuration isn't read in CI, so this doesn't work there.

With Python and pip, or uv, on PATH: oyzu exec -- python3 -m pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt oyzu exec -- uv lock oyzu exec -- uv sync --locked eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt An activated Bash shell routes python, python3, pip, pip3 and uv through oyzu when they're installed. oyzu exec also recognizes versioned names such as python3.12 and pip3.12. Running Python itself is unchanged; only python -m pip goes through the agent. Tool Supported commands pip install, download, wheel uv lock, sync, pip install, pip sync --help and --version run without asking the agent. Other commands, including uv run and uv publish, fail with PYTHON_OPERATION_UNSUPPORTED. Publish with oyzu publish.

Sends the agent a POST with {"directory": "<working dir>", "tool": "pip" or "uv", "arguments": [...]}. This happens on every run, including warm or offline installs. Reads the agent's answer: { "index": "https://packages.example.com/simple/", "username": "reader", "credentialEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:43199/credential/session" } index is HTTP(S) with no credentials, query or fragment. username can't be empty. credentialEndpoint must be on 127.0.0.1. Adds the user name to the index URL and puts oyzu itself on PATH as keyring. Replaces the tool's index configuration for that run: pip gets PIP_CONFIG_FILE set to the null device, PIP_INDEX_URL, PIP_KEYRING_PROVIDER=subprocess and no interactive prompts; uv gets UV_NO_CONFIG=1, UV_DEFAULT_INDEX and UV_KEYRING_PROVIDER=subprocess; extra-index and find-links variables and UV_CONFIG_FILE are removed. When the tool runs keyring get <service> <username>, oyzu POSTs {"ecosystem": "python", "service": "...", "username": "..."} to credentialEndpoint, which must answer {"password": "..."}. The agent should check the request against the index it approved. Because pip and uv configuration files are switched off for the run, other options in them are ignored too. Requirements files, pyproject.toml, uv.toml and lock files aren't changed. Package caches and installed packages work as usual.

The password never goes into generated configuration, command arguments or environment variables. It passes through the keyring helper into the tool's memory, so the process can read it. Read-only access has to be enforced by the index account the agent uses. Helper failures show a generic message. Denial or an unreachable agent stops the command before pip or uv starts, with no fallback to cached or direct access.
The tool's output and exit code pass through unchanged. With --json, they're captured in the usual oyzu exec result.

Code Cause Fix NATIVE_SESSION_CONFIG The endpoint is set in project or local configuration Move it to user or administrator configuration NATIVE_SESSION_UNAVAILABLE The agent can't be reached Start the agent and retry NATIVE_SESSION_DENIED The agent refused the request Get access granted; don't work around the agent NATIVE_SESSION_INVALID The endpoint or credential endpoint isn't 127.0.0.1 HTTP, or the response is too large Fix the endpoint or the agent PYTHON_SESSION_INVALID The response couldn't be read, or the index or user name isn't valid Fix the agent's response PYTHON_ROUTING_CONFLICT You passed an index, extra-index, find-links, keyring-provider, config-file, --isolated, --project or --directory option Remove the option PYTHON_OPERATION_UNSUPPORTED The command isn't in the supported list Use a supported command

One index per run, for ordinary named packages (including hash-pinned requirements and uv locks). Direct URL, VCS and path dependencies, source directives in requirements files, uv source and workspace overrides, and credentials in .netrc or other auth stores aren't covered. Poetry and scripts that run pip or uv internally aren't covered. Turning off pip and uv configuration isn't a network sandbox. Temporary files may be left behind if oyzu is killed. Linux and Bash only. Windows and macOS aren't supported yet.
pip documentation on configuration uv configuration files Python installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-testing.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Python projects built with pip, uv or Poetry get an implicit test task that runs pytest. The task exists even if your project has no tests/ or test/ folder. It runs when tests are selected, such as with --full or in CI; a fast local build skips it. Pytest decides at run time which tests exist. Oyzu never imports conftest.py, runs Python or collects tests while it discovers your project. Note: Python support is experimental. Direct oyzu run test is supported on Windows and Linux. Isolated builds run in Linux containers.
oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Pass extra arguments to pytest after --: oyzu run test -- -k smoke.

Conventional native pytest test steps in oyzu build participate in test retries. This requires the development CLI and Python builder containing native case reruns; older builder packages retain their previous whole-step behavior. Set [tests] retries = 2 to enable two extra attempts locally; pr, ci and release already default to two. Each test file is a unit. After a complete first run, only its failed pytest node IDs run again, including exact class and parameter IDs. Passing siblings do not run again. Pytest fail-fast (-x and --maxfail) is disabled so the first attempt can report every case. A failure followed by a pass produces TEST_FLAKY, passes by default and cannot be stored as a clean cache result. [tests] flaky = "fail" makes it block an enforced or required test check. Every attempt has separate JUnit and case reports; the combined JUnit retains the failed attempts. Assertion failures, fixture errors, case timeouts and crashes remain distinct. A missing requested case produces TEST_RERUN_INCOMPLETE and remains failed. Usage and collection errors, missing reports and incomplete shared-fixture setup do not qualify for a case retry. --no-cache uses the same retry rules. When pytest resolves pytest-rerunfailures, a --reruns option or a flaky marker, Oyzu reports TEST_ATTEMPTS_UNKNOWN, adds no retries and does not cache the unit: pytest's JUnit does not expose every native attempt. Remove the native retry configuration to use tests.retries. Undetectable retry plugins remain a limit. Authored test commands retain the generic JUnit step behavior. Native retries use the already provisioned project environment; they do not install pytest or require an account.

Oyzu looks for pytest settings in pytest.ini, .pytest.ini, [tool.pytest.ini_options] in pyproject.toml, [pytest] in tox.ini or [tool:pytest] in setup.cfg. With none of these, pytest is still the default. Several configuration files are not treated as competing frameworks. Detection only records your intent. Pytest owns testpaths, file name patterns, markers and collection errors. This configuration needs no Oyzu setting: [pytest] testpaths = checks python_files = spec_*.py The implicit command depends on the project's manager: Manager Command pip python -m pytest uv uv run --locked pytest Poetry poetry run pytest Install Python, the manager and your dependencies first. Direct runs use the manager's own environment and behavior, including any synchronization it does, and are not isolated. TOML task replacements and pre/post hooks work as for any task.

oyzu run test runs the pytest command and writes JUnit and Cobertura reports into a test-only bundle in dist/. Pytest still collects the tests, and your manager picks the environment. See direct test reports for hooks, overrides, retention and inspection. Requirements: Python 3.11 or newer in the selected environment. pytest and pytest-cov in that environment. Oyzu does not install them. It works with pytest 8.3.5 and 9.1.1 with pytest-cov 6.0.0. Other versions can fail with an error instead of producing partial reports.

A direct run measures your checkout, not an installed package. It keeps your coverage configuration (COVERAGE_RCFILE or the usual coverage files), including source settings, branches, exclusions and thresholds. Without source settings, it measures the task's working directory, including modules that no test imports. Collected tests, files matching pytest's name patterns, conventional test file names, conftest.py files and .oyzu and .venv folders are left out of application coverage. Helper modules that tests import are not guessed to be tests. Use coverage exclusions for them. Omissions apply below the measured source root. A project that Oyzu copied into .oyzu/host-workspaces is still measured. Each run uses its own temporary coverage configuration and data file. An existing .coverage file or COVERAGE_FILE can't add old results and isn't overwritten. pytest-cov source and output options on the command line don't override the report locations Oyzu sets. Selectors such as -k work normally. Pytest caches and Python bytecode can still be written.

Oyzu adds reporting to the exact python -m pytest, pytest, and the implicit manager commands. python -m pytest uses the python on PATH, even in a uv or Poetry project. Bare pytest also uses python from PATH. Any other command (a custom shell program, for example) runs as written and must write the required reports to the declared paths or the report environment variables. Assertion and collection errors, coverage thresholds and missing reports fail the run, and the reports that exist are kept. An empty suite keeps pytest's exit code 5 and a zero-test JUnit file. A zero-denominator coverage report is not rewritten to 100 percent.

Native pip python/app builds also test the sources extracted from the assembled archive. Core prepares pytest, coverage and the selected quality tools as part of the verified wheel closure, then installs them offline into a fresh build environment. Test and quality tools are not embedded in the runtime application. JUnit, Cobertura, coverage thresholds and failure withholding apply as described in Python applications. oyzu build runs tests in a Linux container after dependency preparation. Preparation adds pytest 8.3.5 and pytest-cov 6.0.0 unless your project or lock already selects them. Your versions win, and an incompatible integration fails instead of downloading a replacement. Dependencies come from PyPI. Packages in full, CI, pull-request and release contexts are tested as installed: pytest runs against the built wheel in importlib mode, and coverage measures the installed wheel's Python files. Your coverage settings, including thresholds, are kept. Ordinary local development package tests use captured project source through a genuine native editable installation for the supported layout below. This evidence describes development source, independently of the inferred-version wheel and source archive. It does not validate their installed behavior. Applications are tested from the sources extracted from the generated application archive. See Python applications. Testing an application that has not been built yet stops with an error naming the missing archive; run oyzu build <target> first. Pytest creates JUnit and Cobertura reports. Oyzu stores them in dist/ and records their paths, digests and summaries in dist/manifest.json. You don't configure test or output paths. Artifacts are collected only when tests and quality checks pass. An assertion failure, collection error or failed coverage threshold blocks the artifacts. An empty suite keeps pytest's exit code 5 and any zero-test JUnit file, and does not count as a pass. A suite with skipped tests keeps pytest's skip counts and exit code. A custom replacement that exits 0 can't satisfy a missing required report. If a project had no test folder before, the build now runs pytest and fails when it collects no tests. Add tests or fix your pytest configuration.

The development-source contract is selected from the resolved local context and ordinary check mode; it has no additional public flag. --full, CI, pull-request and release contexts retain built-package validation. Its initial supported layout is pip with static declarative setuptools.build_meta, an explicit list of flat regular packages and no backend plugins or source-built dependencies. Dynamic metadata, namespace roots, custom backends, setup.py, package-directory mappings, native extensions and authored test replacements retain the existing built-package path. A native editable installation or mapping failure fails the development test action rather than falling back to a host source path. To select tests and coverage in an ordinary local build, use the existing check levels in oyzu.toml: [checks] tests = "required" coverage = "required" Then run oyzu build --isolated --no-docker for the Linux crun case-selection path. Do not add --full or set checks.run = "all" when requesting the development-source subject: those select built-package checks instead. The selected backend produces real PEP 660 metadata and pip installs it offline in a separate captured test environment. Native direct_url.json, import specs, distribution metadata and installer RECORD remain evidence inputs. Coverage and tests read only admitted captured source and that environment. No ambient PYTHONPATH selects the package. Required JUnit, coverage thresholds, isolation, acquisition and artifact validation gates remain binding. Action and report metadata record oyzu.dev/python-test.subject as development-source or built-package; case keys bind this subject. The source subject omits the unused inferred wheel-version default and the wheel's separate installed environment from its case inputs. Explicit user environment values, native installed versions, metadata, backend/dependency/tool changes and editable mapping bytes remain binding. Full/package evidence continues to bind actual built-package version and wheel/RECORD facts. These identities cannot authorize reuse across the two guarantees. Native editable execution and selective captured reuse are limited to the supported Linux development flow. Full, CI, package and release validation retain their built-package inputs. Captured pip package builds collect one test unit per native pytest file. With coverage.py in the project environment and enforced runtime-read bounds, core can rerun affected cases and retain earlier passing evidence for the rest. New and previously failed cases always run. The step keeps one combined JUnit and coverage report, and the action row gives fresh and reused case counts. Import-time code, shared setup and runtime data changes rerun every case. Release builds run every case of a changed unit. Missing or incomplete coverage runs the whole unit with a one-line reason. Direct runs, native host builds, application archives and authored test replacements retain their existing behavior. See case selection for keys, explanations and order-dependence handling. When coverage.py cannot be imported, case collection prevents pytest-cov's unusable plugin from stopping the test run. Its supported coverage options still parse, including addopts = --cov=api in pytest.ini, so collection and the full test run can proceed. This does not supply a coverage report: a required coverage check still fails, and existing test failures remain failures. A run requesting coverage through --cov or --cov-fail-under also fails with an unavailable coverage message even when all cases pass. --no-cov disables that optional request, but cannot satisfy Oyzu's required report checks. Coverage.py currently comes from the prepared Python environment: pytest-cov depends on it, and a project requirement can select its version. This is Python dependency acquisition, with digest-only verification; it is not a separately managed tool with verified publisher provenance. oyzu tools info coverage and oyzu install pipx:coverage@<version> are unsupported. Oyzu has no admitted coverage.py tool provider or pipx: backend. Zero-setup acquisition with publisher evidence and a separate tool compliance record remains unavailable.

Package tests can import ordinary test helpers, including namespace folders such as docs_src and test packages with relative imports. Pytest keeps your working directory, collection paths and test resources. Built-package tests see your checkout's helper modules, but not the checkout's copy of the package being tested. Anything the installed wheel provides (modules, packages, namespace roots, native extension names, as listed in its RECORD) comes only from the install. A missing submodule never falls back to your source. Development-source tests retain the helper restrictions and obtain package imports exclusively through their native editable mapping into the capture. Configured pythonpath entries inside your project (relative or absolute) work. Entries outside the project, file or ZIP entries, and entries that enter an installed package fail with an error. Selected tests or conftest.py files inside a package that the wheel installs fail too. Move those tests into a separate test folder. Oyzu keeps importlib mode even if you pass another mode to pytest. These rules apply to package tests only, not to direct runs or application tests. Helpers are shared with shallow links (copies where Windows can't make symlinks). They don't grant network access, install packages or change your source.

Problem What to do No tests collected Check pytest's file name patterns and configuration, and run the same manager command to see what it collects Reporters missing Add pytest and pytest-cov to your declared dependencies or environment and prepare again Report or coverage failure Read the native logs and report records in dist/ Coverage says No data to report See Coverage reports no data Test configuration and plugins run during testing. In isolated builds they run offline. In direct runs they have your normal permissions.

Pytest is the only supported framework. It runs unittest.TestCase suites, but there is no dedicated unittest runner, other frameworks, distributed pytest or other pytest and pytest-cov versions. Coverage of native extensions is not measured. If no measurable Python source exists, that is a failure.

Oyzu runs the test steps itself. It chooses the command, creates private coverage files and starts the selected interpreter. Small pytest and pytest-cov hooks are built into the oyzu executable. They only read your pytest configuration, source metadata and framework events. Oyzu never searches your project for its own scripts. Python is required because you selected a Python build, not by the CLI. Pytest exit codes and report requirements are unchanged. For a full native pip build, Oyzu binds one explicit interpreter, either the managed CPython or your validated target .venv. It uses that interpreter with -I and fresh JUnit and Cobertura paths, and ambient PYTHONPATH or an activated environment doesn't select one. See native preparation. For package helpers, the pytest hook normalizes the resolved pythonpath list before pytest uses it, and guards conftest.py imports so that a protected package in your checkout is refused before either runs. Test selection stays with pytest. A pytest change that breaks this hook fails the run with an error. Related: direct test reports, Python applications, pytest configuration and pytest exit codes.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/release-check.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu release check asks the Oyzu platform, before you publish anything, what a release of your finished build would do in each of the project's environments. Run it after oyzu build. Note: This command is experimental. The Oyzu platform doesn't serve the would-ship check yet, so the command can't get an answer from a live platform today. oyzu build oyzu release check --project web oyzu release check --project web --environment production oyzu release check --project web --json For each environment the answer is one of: Verdict Meaning would ship Nothing waits on a person or a gate. would wait It would go out once the named approvals, gates or blockers clear. refused A policy or fact would refuse it.
