The reason is named. The platform works out the plan a release would get right now from the project's saved facts and policies. Nothing is published, saved or started.
documents.s: Checking whether a build would ship

documents.t: A finished oyzu build whose manifest says status: succeeded (dist/manifest.json by default). platform.url and platform.account in your configuration. A platform credential: an oyzu auth login session or a token in OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. See which credential a command uses. The check runs as you, so you need read access to the project. The project name, from --project or OYZU_PROJECT.

Flag Default Meaning --project OYZU_PROJECT The project to check in. --environment every environment Answer for this environment only. Repeat for more. --manifest dist/manifest.json The build manifest to check. --version each artifact's own Use this version for every component. --commit the checkout's HEAD The built commit.

The manifest's artifacts, named the way oyzu publish names them: each artifact's target, or target/name for an artifact that isn't the target's primary one. OCI images and indexes are identified by their OCI digest. The commit, the GitHub repository the checkout pushes to (if any), and the environments you asked about. The build is always checked as a candidate build.

Each environment gets one line, with its reasons and the policy behind each one underneath: Would this build ship? · web (checked as a candidate build) ✓ qa would ship … production would wait Approval from release-managers (1) (promotion policy prod-approval) ✗ eu would refuse it api has not been verified in staging (verification policy eu-staged-check) Once published (start policies) agents: joins the open batch of jobs (2 versions so far) and rides the release cut at 2026-10-11T15:02:00Z; 2 releases already wait in the queue ahead of it The Once published section appears when a start policy covers the build. It says whether publishing would join an open batch, open a new one or cut a release at once, and how many releases already wait ahead of it. With --json, the command prints the platform's ship-check record with account added.
The command exits 1 when any environment would refuse the build. Waiting on a person or a gate isn't a failure.

Code Cause Fix RELEASE_CHECK_NOT_CONFIGURED No project, or no platform.url / platform.account. Pass --project and set the platform settings. RELEASE_CHECK_UNAUTHENTICATED No credential, or the platform refused it. Run oyzu auth login in a terminal, or set OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. Unattended runs never use a stored session on their own. RELEASE_CHECK_NO_COMMIT Not a Git checkout with a commit. Run from a checkout or pass --commit. RELEASE_CHECK_NOTHING_TO_SHIP The manifest lists no artifacts. Build something first. RELEASE_CHECK_RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND The project doesn't exist, or you can't read it. Check the name and your access. RELEASE_CHECK_RESPONSE_INVALID The platform's answer is missing required fields or has an unknown verdict. Check that your CLI and the platform are compatible. An invalid answer never counts as "would ship". PUBLISH_MANIFEST_MISSING, PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID, PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED The manifest is read exactly as oyzu publish reads it. See publishing.
Authentication Publishing

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/release-provenance.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu inspect can check a downloaded artifact against its detached Sigstore provenance and a build profile you choose independently. Use it to confirm that a file was built by the exact GitHub repository, commit and workflow you expect. Verification runs offline and never runs the artifact or any project code. The same profile can admit provenance for publishing finalized artifacts and for platform members passed to oyzu build --compose. Set releaseProfile alongside bundlePath in publish.requirements.provenance; publication uses the built-in public Sigstore root and retains the profile values in its frozen plan. Note: This is experimental. Only one evidence format is supported: public GitHub Actions provenance (in-toto Statement v1, SLSA provenance v1, GitHub workflow/v1) in a Sigstore bundle v0.3. A passing check doesn't assess the producer's build controls or establish a SLSA level. oyzu inspect application.tar.gz --provenance application.sigstore.json \ --release-profile expected-build.json For a file inside an Oyzu build bundle, name its recorded path: oyzu inspect dist --artifact app/linux/x86_64/application \ --provenance application.sigstore.json --release-profile expected-build.json --json

Option Default Meaning --provenance <FILE> none The detached Sigstore bundle. Turns on provenance verification and requires --release-profile. --release-profile <FILE> none JSON file with the exact producer, source and build parameters you accept. Never read from the artifact. --artifact <PATH> none The recorded file path inside a bundle directory. Required for a bundle; not used for a plain file. --trusted-root <FILE> the built-in public Sigstore root A Sigstore trusted-root JSON file you supply. Never taken from the artifact or its evidence. Each input file can be at most 1 MiB. Keep profiles and trusted roots somewhere you control, separate from downloaded content. Oyzu never fetches or refreshes trust material over the network.

A release profile lists exact values. It isn't a policy language. Unknown fields and duplicate JSON keys are errors. Every field is required except stagingBuilderWorkflow. Field Meaning signer The signing workflow's certificate identity: https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/.github/workflows/FILE.yml@COMMIT, pinned to a full 40-character lowercase commit. signerRevision That same commit. stagingBuilderWorkflow Optional. A separate workflow URL, pinned to a full commit, that ran the build job. Used only by oyzu build --release-profile (see below). When absent, the signer is assumed to have built. null, empty or branch references are errors. builderId Exactly signer for workflow-identity provenance, or the legacy https://github.com/actions/runner/github-hosted. The predicate must equal the selected value. sourceRepository The application repository, as https://github.com/OWNER/REPO. sourceCommit, sourceRef The application commit and its full Git ref. repositoryId, repositoryOwnerId GitHub's numeric IDs, as decimal strings. workflowPath, workflowRevision The calling workflow under .github/workflows/ and its commit in the application repository. eventName The GitHub event, such as push. externalParameters The exact JSON object of build parameters you accept. Its workflow.repository, workflow.ref and workflow.path must agree with the source and workflow fields. The signer workflow's commit and the application's commit are different things. A valid signature from an unexpected repository, fork, workflow commit, builder or set of parameters fails. These are the only supported builder identities. The workflow URL is computed from the independently pinned signer, never from received evidence or the intermediate stagingBuilderWorkflow. Both forms still require the certificate's signer workflow ref and SHA to match signer and signerRevision, and its runner environment to be github-hosted. A builder identity alone grants no trust. The supported buildType values are exactly: https://slsa-framework.github.io/github-actions-buildtypes/workflow/v1 https://actions.github.io/buildtypes/workflow/v1 (modern GitHub attestation actions) All other values are refused, including other versions and URI suffixes. The profile cannot extend this list. Both forms require the same exact external parameters, source dependency, certificate identity, runner and subject checks. If your build job can mint its own OIDC token, the signer has to be a different workflow file. Separate jobs in one workflow don't give you that separation. Use stagingBuilderWorkflow for the build workflow and signer for the attesting one: { "stagingBuilderWorkflow": "https://github.com/example/builders/.github/workflows/build.yml@1111111111111111111111111111111111111111", "signer": "https://github.com/example/builders/.github/workflows/attest.yml@2222222222222222222222222222222222222222", "signerRevision": "2222222222222222222222222222222222222222" } These fields go alongside the other required fields.

For a bundle, ordinary bundle inspection and the required native report checks run first. A valid attestation can't rescue a failed build or a missing required report. The actual file is hashed. The certificate, issuer, signature and transparency-log or timestamp evidence are verified. The signed subject must match the file's digest. The signed source, repository IDs, calling and called workflows and build parameters must match the profile. Standard GitHub provenance doesn't name an intermediate build workflow. If stagingBuilderWorkflow differs from signer, the result reports that workflow as not-covered-by-standard-provenance, and human output says it wasn't authenticated. A plain file has no report inventory, so a passing check on one says nothing about tests or other reports.

With --json, the inspection result gains a releaseVerification object: Field Meaning passed All standard provenance checks passed. expectationsScope standard-provenance. signature, subject, expectations Each check's own result. Replaced bytes with genuine evidence show a verified signature and an unmatched subject. profileDigest, evidenceDigest, trustRootDigest Identify the exact inputs used. stagingBuilderWorkflow Present when a separate staging workflow was named; see above. builderAssurance Always unassessed. productionEligible Always false. Verification never changes manifests, versions, source, trust stores or publishing permissions. oyzu inspect without these options behaves as before.

A failed verification exits nonzero. Invalid input and ordinary bundle failures use the usual error output. Failure Fix Missing or invalid profile, unsafe --artifact path, unreadable file Correct the input. Nothing is rewritten. Replaced bytes or invalid signature Get the expected artifact and its genuine evidence. Don't edit the profile to accept the mismatch. Wrong source, signer, workflow, IDs, build type or parameters Check the profile against the producer you approved. A valid signature alone isn't enough. Missing or wrong trusted root Supply a complete trusted root. There is no network fallback. Failed build or missing required report Fix the producing build.

oyzu build --release-profile expected-build.json uses the same profile while building, for authenticated release staging. A reusable-workflow job must present signed job_workflow_ref and job_workflow_sha values that match stagingBuilderWorkflow (or signer when that field is absent). The calling source, tag, workflow and run checks still apply, and a job that doesn't match the profile is refused rather than built without it. --require-release still refuses a build when release evidence is missing. Profiles can't be forwarded to --remote builds.
documents.s: Staging a release build with a profile

documents.t: Only public GitHub Actions provenance is supported. GitHub Enterprise Server, private GitHub trust services, other CI providers and self-hosted runners are not supported. SLSA provenance doesn't authenticate each tool or test result recorded in the bundle. This doesn't sign anything, attest local builds or grant permission to publish.
Build bundles Version inference Publishing

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/remote-runs.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Add --remote to oyzu build or oyzu run <task> to run the same command on a platform or standalone pool instead of your machine. The pool checks out the exact commit you pushed, runs the build with full checks or the selected task in isolation, and streams the output back. Oyzu follows the run to the end and exits with the remote exit code. Note: Remote runs are experimental and have been run on Linux pools only. Everything else Oyzu does is local and works without an account. git push oyzu build --remote

A Git checkout whose HEAD is pushed to a github.com repository that the pool allows (or that is linked to a project in your platform account). git must be on PATH. The Actions flow can run without a checkout. platform.url and platform.account in user, machine or administrator configuration. Project and local files can't set them, so a checkout can't send your credential somewhere else. oyzu config set --global platform.url https://platform.example.com oyzu config set --global platform.account payments In CI you can set OYZU_PLATFORM_URL and OYZU_PLATFORM_ACCOUNT instead. A platform credential: an oyzu auth login session (used at a terminal, or when platform.authentication.provider is session) or a token in OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. See which credential a command uses. Unattended runs with neither fail with REMOTE_UNAUTHENTICATED. Standalone pools can instead use network or workload, as below.

Pool workers execute builds with oyzu build --isolated --full and tasks with oyzu run --isolated <task>. Task runs select only the requested task, its prerequisites and hooks, using their existing builders' images and report contracts. They never fall back to a host task. See isolated task limitations. A standalone pool serves the same runs API without a platform sign-in. Ask its operator for the URL, account and network access, then configure: oyzu config set --global platform.url https://pool.example.com oyzu config set --global platform.account example oyzu config set --global platform.authentication.provider network git push oyzu build --remote The network provider sends no authorization header. The pool authenticates you through its network access rules. HTTPS is required except on loopback. A rejected caller receives REMOTE_UNAUTHENTICATED; check access with the operator. The CLI never falls back to a local build. Standalone output downloads are not available; omit --download. With a configured shared cache, only pool runs created by GitHub Actions main push jobs from commits may write it; PR, terminal and working-tree snapshot runs only read it.

The internal shard planner is a pure, in-memory helper; remote runs do not yet dispatch its shards. It accepts unique unit IDs, optional last measured durations in milliseconds, and a shard count. Measured units use longest-processing-time-first placement on the least loaded shard, breaking duration ties by unit ID and load ties by shard index. Units without history use round-robin placement in stable ID order, starting at shard zero, independently of measured units. Planning returns exactly the requested number of shards, including empty shards. Zero shards is an error; one shard contains every unit in stable ID order. Duplicate input IDs are errors. Neither planning nor merging performs I/O or changes cache, execution or trust decisions. Report merging checks an expected unit inventory, sums executed and reused unit counts, and preserves each unit's existing result in ID order. Any failing shard makes the merged result fail. Missing, duplicate or unexpected unit results are errors rather than partial success, as is count overflow. If several shards fail, the merged exit status is the smallest nonzero code, independently of arrival order. Scheduler wiring and the build01 proof are follow-ups; there is no new CLI option or automatic remote sharding yet.

Use --worktree with a standalone pool to build the checkout as it is on disk: oyzu build --remote --worktree oyzu run app:test --remote --worktree The CLI captures the Git repository root in a source manifest, uploads missing file contents, then submits the manifest and starts the run. HEAD may be unpushed and files may be changed or untracked. The manifest includes every tracked file, even when it matches an ignore rule, and untracked files that Git does not ignore (git ls-files -z --cached --others --exclude-standard). Deleted tracked files stay absent. .git is never uploaded. File permissions and nanosecond modification times are retained. The limit is 512 MiB of logical file contents and 200,000 entries, checked before uploading. Repeated working-tree submissions send only missing file contents; unchanged files are not sent again. The Remote submission phase reports the transfer, for example Uploaded 1 of 812 files (4.1 KiB). At most eight file blobs transfer at once. The CLI reuses its existing source stat cache for unchanged file digests and rehashes recently modified files. If pool cleanup removes a blob before the manifest is accepted, the CLI uploads the missing contents and retries once. The transport carries regular files and relative symlinks whose targets stay inside the selected source tree. Outside, dangling and cyclic links are refused before upload. This does not extend the build engine's source-link support: snapshot builds apply the same source filtering and symlink refusals as local and commit builds. A link accepted by the upload may still be refused when the build captures its source. Both remote modes run at the repository root. -C <directory> locates the Git checkout; it does not change the remote working directory. Select a subproject by its existing target name or qualified task name. --worktree requires --remote and cannot be combined with --plan. Snapshot runs read shared caches when configured, never write them, and cannot be published. Their run and result include source.kind: snapshot, a source digest and, when available, the informational base commit. No files are downloaded to the caller. Servers without snapshot support reject the upload with REMOTE_SOURCE_KIND_UNSUPPORTED; the CLI does not create a commit-based run instead. Actions workload callers remain restricted to their signed commit and cannot submit snapshots to a standalone pool.

permissions: id-token: write contents: read steps: - uses: oyzuai/setup-oyzu@v1 - run: oyzu build --remote env: OYZU_PLATFORM_URL: https://pool.example.com OYZU_PLATFORM_ACCOUNT: example OYZU_PLATFORM_AUTH_PROVIDER: workload The job must be able to reach the pool. workload requests a fresh Actions OIDC token for each API attempt, with the normalized pool URL as audience. Outside GitHub Actions it fails with AUTH_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE; see authentication. Without a Git checkout, this provider reads GITHUB_REPOSITORY as an exact owner/repository, GITHUB_SHA as a full lowercase 40-character commit ID and GITHUB_REF as a full Git ref such as refs/heads/main or refs/pull/12/merge. Missing or invalid values fail with REMOTE_ACTIONS_SOURCE_INVALID before any token or run request. With a checkout, the normal pushed-HEAD checks still apply. --affected requires a checkout to compute its merge base. The pool validates the repository, commit and ref against the caller's identity. An Actions job may check out source to bootstrap its own CLI, then invoke that CLI from an empty directory outside the checkout. This exercises the checkout-less submission path; it does not mean the job has no checkout step.

Commit builds on a standalone pool can report a separate GitHub check for each target and stage, named oyzu / <target> / <stage>. The pool's GitHub App needs Checks write permission on the repository. A repository maintainer can mark an individual stage check as required in branch protection; Oyzu does not change those settings. Working-tree snapshot runs do not post checks. Each check starts while its stage runs and completes with that stage's result. JUnit failures from reports listed in the build manifest appear as file and line annotations when the report supplies a location; failures without a file appear in the check summary. Up to 200 failures are sent, with each message limited to 1 KiB. A stage that ends without a reported result fails its check, or is cancelled when the run is cancelled. Repositories without an installation of the pool's GitHub App receive no checks. A GitHub API outage can delay or prevent check updates; it does not change the remote build's exit code.

Command Runs remotely oyzu build --remote Every target. oyzu build --remote --worktree Every target from local disk contents. oyzu build cli web --remote Targets cli and web, plus what they depend on. oyzu build --affected origin/main --remote Targets affected since the merge base of origin/main and HEAD. oyzu run policy-check --remote Task policy-check (target:task also works). ... --remote --download out The same, then downloads every output into out/. To see what a pool would run without starting anything, use oyzu build --remote --plan; see planning a remote run. Oyzu sends the repository from the current branch's remote (or origin), the full HEAD commit and the branch. For --affected it sends the merge-base commit, not a local ref name. Without --worktree, uncommitted changes aren't part of the run; you get a warning.

The terminal view looks like a local build. Each streamed log line is attributed to the target or task that wrote it, and the pool's own lines (checkout, start, finish) appear under runner. At the end you get a summary: ✓ Remote build succeeded Run 01jab7v3k9m2q8r4t6w0y1z5c7 Commit 3f2a9c1d4b5e (main) Project oyzu/platform Oyzu 0.9.0 Outputs manifest dist/manifest.json 4.0 KiB sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaa report dist/cli/linux/x86_64/reports/junit.xml 2.0 KiB sha256:bbbbbbbbbbbb Use --download <DIR> to fetch outputs; nothing was written locally. With --json, standard error carries the same events a local build emits, and standard output carries one remote-run record: Field Meaning invocationId This invocation. submission What was sent: repository, commit and selection. run The final run resource. result State, exit code, reason and outputs. resultAvailable says whether the full result was fetched. downloads Each downloaded path, digest and local file. observation The last seen run state, time and log position, and any known log gaps. cancelled This invocation asked for cancellation. It doesn't mean the run stopped. cancellation requested, acknowledged and confirmed, as separate facts. If Oyzu loses track of a run after creating it, the outcome is unknown, with the last state it saw. That doesn't mean the run failed, and Oyzu never starts local work instead. Check the run in the platform (using the web link, if one was shown) before starting another.

Remote outcome Exit code Succeeded 0 Oyzu exited non-zero on the pool That exit code Failed before Oyzu ran, skipped, cancelled, timed out, or unknown 1 Refused before or while creating the run (configuration, Git or platform problem) 1 Interrupted with Ctrl-C 130

The first Ctrl-C asks the platform to cancel and keeps following the log while the pool stops the work. cancellation.confirmed is set once the run reports cancelled. A second Ctrl-C exits at once with 130. There's no confirmation prompt, so it behaves the same in CI. Cancelling a run that just finished is harmless; you see its real outcome. Closing the terminal (SIGHUP) doesn't cancel. It stops only the local follower; the run continues on the pool.

Outputs are listed by digest and never written into dist/. With --download <DIR>, Oyzu fetches each one through a short-lived download link (no platform credential is sent to it), checks its SHA-256 digest and writes it at its recorded path under DIR. A path that would land outside DIR is refused. Outputs are the manifest, artifacts and required reports. They aren't a complete local build bundle, so oyzu inspect can't check them as one. If the platform can't verify the work a pool sent back, the run fails with CONTRIBUTION_UNVERIFIED and no outputs, even if the native build succeeded. Check the run's diagnostics before retrying.

A refused remote run never falls back to a local build. Platform errors keep the platform's code with a REMOTE_ prefix, plus the platform request id. Code Cause Fix REMOTE_NOT_CONFIGURED platform.url or platform.account is missing or set in the wrong scope. Set them at user scope. REMOTE_NOT_A_CHECKOUT Not a Git checkout. Run from a checkout. REMOTE_REPOSITORY_UNSUPPORTED The remote isn't on github.com. Only github.com is supported. REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_PUSHED HEAD isn't on any branch of the remote. Push first. REMOTE_SOURCE_INVALID A snapshot contains an unsupported path, file type or outside link. Keep source files and relative links inside the checkout. REMOTE_SOURCE_TOO_LARGE The snapshot exceeds 512 MiB. Ignore untracked generated files, and stop tracking generated files that should not be uploaded. REMOTE_SOURCE_KIND_UNSUPPORTED The server does not accept snapshots. Use a snapshot-capable standalone pool or push and omit --worktree. REMOTE_AFFECTED_BASE_INVALID The --affected ref can't be resolved. Fetch the ref or pick another. REMOTE_UNAUTHENTICATED No credential, or it was refused. Run oyzu auth login, or set a current token. REMOTE_REPOSITORY_NOT_LINKED The repository isn't linked to a project. Link it in the platform. REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_FOUND The platform can't see the commit. Push first. REMOTE_VALIDATION_FAILED The platform rejected the request. Correct the named field. REMOTE_RESPONSE_INVALID The run result is missing output details. Check CLI and platform compatibility. The run isn't restarted. CONTRIBUTION_UNVERIFIED See Outputs. Check the run's diagnostics. Requests that fail on the network or get a 503 are retried up to five times with backoff, honoring Retry-After. Retried creation uses the same idempotency key, so it never starts a second run. Logs are followed with 30-second long polls over plain HTTPS, which works through proxies (HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY, SSL_CERT_FILE) with outbound access alone.

The credential is sent only to platform.url. platform.url must use HTTPS; plain HTTP is accepted only for a loopback host. Never put a token in command arguments, copy a browser session, or give a coding agent your personal token. Run ids and digests from the platform are checked before they're used in a URL or file name. Streamed log text is escaped before it reaches your terminal.
Only GitHub repositories on github.com. Task arguments (-- args) aren't supported remotely. There's no --detach, no way to list runs and no way to reattach to a run. Tested on Linux pools only.

A platform executor can hand private files, such as a signing key, to the native actions of a remote run. You don't configure this in your project, and ordinary local builds don't use it. The runtime-input contract describes the details. Files are mounted read-only at /oyzu-runtime, and an environment variable points to each file only while the action runs. The project can't name host files. The files never affect source, plans or cache keys. Affected targets skip the action cache so tests always see the current files. Where the executor provides an egress gateway, an HTTP client that can use a Unix socket can reach it through OYZU_HTTP_PROXY_SOCKET. Direct TCP networking stays off. Supported for Unix process actions on Linux x86-64 in Docker. Anything that doesn't match (unsupported host, missing or unsafe files, conflicting variables) is refused. Fix it and submit a new job. Removing the files afterward is cleanup, not secure erasure.
documents.s: Private files in isolated native actions

documents.t: Platform sign-in Local builds Build logging

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/runtime-matrices.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. To test a build on other runtime versions, add verification toolsets in oyzu.toml. To ship a build for several platforms, list platforms: in build.yaml. The two never mix: a toolset only changes how a build is checked, while a platform changes what ships. Runtime versions are never written in build.yaml; the old matrix.<runtime> axis is refused (see migration). Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

The build that ships is built and tested once, with the [tools] versions. Each toolset adds a verification run: the build's runtime-dependent stages, repeated with the toolset's tools. A run never produces an artifact, so a release always has one artifact per output, however many toolsets run. # build.yaml: nothing about runtime versions builds: app: uses: node/app # oyzu.toml [tools] node = "22.14.0" # builds, tests and ships the app [toolsets.node24.tools] node = "24.14.1" # also tested on Node 24, in pr, ci and release oyzu pin # locks Node 22.14.0 and the node24 toolset's 24.14.1 oyzu build # local: the app alone oyzu build --verify-with node24 # local: the app and its Node 24 run oyzu build --context ci # ci: the app and its Node 24 run Toolsets with contexts = [] also participate in oyzu pin and lock generation during a build. Lock generation does not itself request verification runs. A build with several platforms can keep qualified task dependencies such as app:verify depending on app:test: each platform's toolset instance keeps those dependencies within itself. Verification runs remain unavailable as artifact producers for other builds.

Question Rule In which contexts? Every context except local, unless the toolset lists contexts = [...] (local, pr, ci, release). contexts = [] turns it (or an inherited definition) off. --verify-with NAME (repeatable) adds a toolset's runs in any context. For which builds? Builds in the toolset's folder chain whose builder uses one of its tools in its build or test stages. A node toolset adds nothing to a Go build. The nearest definition of a name applies as a whole, as for --toolset. On which platform? One run per toolset, on the build's first declared platform (the host if it declares none). A toolset that lists platforms = [...] gets one run per listed platform. Runs aren't multiplied by the build's platforms. In which job? A job runs the runs assigned to the platform it builds: a plain local build runs the host's; a --platform job runs that platform's. Runs for other platforms are listed under Verification elsewhere and in the plan, never dropped. What runs? The build's build and test stages and its hooks, with the toolset's tools. Never lint, format, packaging or publication. Every check that isn't off in some context runs, as with --full. Test and coverage reports are collected; outputs aren't. What is verified? Each run records verifies: source (it rebuilt and tested the source). Every current builder does this. A builder that tested the built artifact instead would record verifies: artifact. Errors before anything runs: Code Cause CONFIG_TOOLSET_UNKNOWN A named toolset isn't defined in any selected build's folder. Lists the defined ones. TOOLSET_NOT_APPLICABLE No selected build uses the toolset's tools. VERIFICATION_RUN_NOT_HERE --verify-with or --verify-only named a toolset none of whose runs is on the platform this job builds. Names each run, its platform and command. TOOLSET_INVALID Policy refuses the toolset's tools. Only a build that would run it here fails; plans, --skip-verification jobs and jobs whose run is elsewhere list it and continue.

A run is its own target, <build>-verify-<toolset> (with the platform appended when the toolset lists several), and its own Plan row: -- Plan ------------------------------------------------------------------------ format lint test build app off off run run app-verify-node24 off off run run The Tools block lists each version once (node 22.14.0 and node 24.14.1). The run's target has no artifacts, and the manifest marks it with oyzu.dev/verification: {"build": "app", "toolset": "node24", "platform": "windows/x86_64", "verifies": "source", "reason": "context", "tools": {"node": "24.14.1"}} reason is context when the toolset runs in this context, and requested for --verify-with/--verify-only. tools are the toolset's requests as written; oyzu.lock resolves them. A failing test in a run fails the build, and the shipped build's evidence is kept. Verification evidence. Every native build's manifest records what its builds and runs verified, under oyzu.dev/verification-evidence. oyzu publish checks it: {"verifyOnly": false, "builds": [{"build": "app", "tests": "passed", "source": {"commit": "5f3b…", "tree": "9c1e…", "digest": "sha256:fc29…"}, "tools": [{"tool": "go", "id": "oyzu:go", "request": "1.24.13", "version": "1.24.13", "ranges": [{"dialect": "go-minimum", "expression": ">=1.24.0", "file": "go.mod", "field": "go"}]}], "notApplicable": [{"tool": "go", "line": "1.23", "native": "go.mod go >=1.24.0", "requiredBy": "project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints])"}]}], "runs": [{"id": "app-verify-go125", "build": "app", "toolset": "go125", "platform": "windows/x86_64", "verifies": "source", "status": "here", "command": "oyzu build app --verify-only go125", "subject": {"source": {"commit": "5f3b…", "tree": "9c1e…", "digest": "sha256:fc29…"}}, "stages": ["build", "test"], "result": "passed", "tools": [{"tool": "go", "id": "oyzu:go", "request": "1.25", "version": "1.25.14"}]}]} A build entry is each shipped build in this job: source is the source revision it built; tools are the tools its build and test stages use, with resolved versions and the native ranges that constrain them (package.json engines, go.mod go); tests is passed, failed or not-run (fast local builds skip tests); notApplicable lists required lines outside those ranges. A run entry is every run of the selected builds, with status here (ran in this job), other-platform or skipped (--skip-verification), and the command that runs it. A run that ran here adds its subject (the source revision), the tools it used, the stages that ran, and result: passed only when every action passed and its tests ran. verifyOnly is true for a --verify-only job; its bundle is evidence only. Source revisions​ verifies: source evidence is tied to a source revision: digest: always present. A SHA-256 over the selected files' paths and contents, with CRLF read as LF and executable bits ignored, taken before any action runs. commit and tree: present when the build's folder is in a Git work tree and none of its selected files differ from HEAD or are untracked. The HEAD commit and the Git tree of the build's folder. Two revisions are the same source when their digests match and, if both have a tree, their trees match. Because the digest is always compared, an edit hidden from Git's index (--assume-unchanged, --skip-worktree, a filter) still counts as different source. The commit is for reference only: another commit with the same tree and content is the same source. A Windows checkout with core.autocrlf and a Linux checkout of the same commit are the same source.

oyzu build --plan --json keeps .matrix for platform builds and lists runs under .verify. Each entry has id, build, toolset, platform, runner (OS and architecture), verifies, requested, source (the file defining the toolset), tools, status (here, other-platform, skipped) and the command for a dedicated job. The command includes --platform when the build declares platforms. "verify": [{"id": "app-verify-node24", "build": "app", "toolset": "node24", "platform": "linux/x86_64", "runner": {"os": "linux", "arch": "x86_64"}, "verifies": "source", "requested": false, "source": "oyzu.toml", "tools": {"node": "24.14.1"}, "status": "here", "command": "oyzu build app --verify-only node24"}] By default, one job builds and then runs every verification run for its platform. To give runs their own jobs, read .verify in a planning job (GitHub Actions: fromJSON) and: run each entry's command in a job on its runner. oyzu build app --verify-only node24 runs only that toolset's runs (the builds it depends on are still built); build the platform jobs with --skip-verification, which runs no verification and warns VERIFICATION_RUN_SKIPPED for each run, with its command. --verify-with and --verify-only can't be combined with --skip-verification, --isolated, --all-platforms, --image or --remote. Pass every job's bundle to oyzu publish (--manifest once per bundle). Platform jobs supply the artifacts and their builds' evidence; verification jobs supply the runs' evidence. Publication never takes an artifact from a --verify-only bundle, so the same output isn't offered twice.

Policy requires tool lines, not toolset names. The setting verification.<tool> lists the lines of a tool ("22", "3.12", "1.24": one to three numbers) that must have passing verification evidence before a build is published. Name the tool without a namespace (verification.node, not verification.oyzu:node). It's an ordinary per-folder setting: central policy and a root oyzu.toml [constraints] table can require lines with required, limited by when/unless, and a project can list its own. # root oyzu.toml [constraints."verification.go"] required = ["1.23", "1.24", "1.25", "1.26"] when = { context = ["pr", "ci", "release"] } # optional For each required line of a tool the build uses, in the build's folder and context: Not applicable. A line entirely outside the build's native range (package.json engines.node, the go.mod go minimum) is never run. The manifest records it under notApplicable with the native file and range (go.mod go >=1.24.0), and publication accepts it. Other native ranges (requires-python, rust-version) aren't evaluated: such a line runs, and tool resolution reports the conflict. To enforce a support floor, constrain tools.<name> instead. Covered. The build's own [tools] version in that line covers it in every context. A toolset with a version in the line covers it only in the contexts its runs run in: contexts = [] never does, contexts = ["release"] only in release (or when named with --verify-with/--verify-only). Otherwise, a run is added, as if the root oyzu.toml defined a toolset policy-<tool>-<line> (policy-go-1_26, dots become _). Its target is <build>-verify-policy-<tool>-<line>, listed in .verify with requiredBy and its command (oyzu build app --verify-only policy-go-1_26). It runs where toolset runs do: every context except local (unless the constraint's when names local), in contexts no toolset covers, on the build's first declared platform. --verify-with policy-go-1_26 adds it in any context. oyzu pin locks a policy run's tools in a set labelled toolset = "policy-go-1_26" when the requirement applies in pin's context and some context has no covering toolset. For a release-only requirement, run OYZU_CONTEXT=release oyzu pin. A build whose lock lacks the line fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE; run oyzu pin. oyzu build --plan shows the requirement as a CONFIG_CONSTRAINT_OVERRIDE (or policy override) note. oyzu config explain verification.go shows where each line comes from.

oyzu publish resolves verification.<tool> again at publish time, in each published build's folder and the publication's context, so a requirement added after the build still applies. Each required line must be settled by the bundles given with --manifest, in one of three ways: Not applicable: outside the recorded native range. The build's own tests: its bundle records tests passed with a version in the line. Fast local builds skip tests; build with --full, or in a ci or release context. A run: a run of the same build in any given bundle that ran here, passed, used a version in the line, and verified the published build. For verifies: source, its subject must be the build's source revision; for verifies: artifact, its artifact digests must include the published artifact. Otherwise publication fails before loading evidence, signing or any network access. The error lists every unsettled line, why, and the commands for runs left to other jobs: ✗ PUBLISH_VERIFICATION_MISSING: no passing verification evidence for app go 1.25 (required by project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints])): no run with go 1.25 was given. … Run what is missing (the runs this build left to other jobs: oyzu build app --verify-only go125) and pass every bundle with --manifest. Nothing was sent A bundle from the container executor has no verification evidence, so publication refuses its build when any verification.<tool> line applies in the build's folder. The publish receipt lists how each line was settled under verification, and the output shows it under Required verification: Required verification app go 1.23 not applicable: outside go.mod go >=1.24.0 · required by project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints]) app go 1.24 the build's own tests (1.24.13) · required by project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints]) app go 1.25 run app-verify-go125 (1.25.14) · required by project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints])

oyzu pin locks every toolset's tools beside the [tools] tools, each toolset in its own set labelled toolset = "NAME", whatever the context and whether or not a build uses them. oyzu --toolset NAME pin locks one toolset. oyzu update re-resolves [tools] and then every toolset. A build whose lock lacks a run's tools installs and locks them like any other tool. See toolset lock rules. A toolset that can't be locked (defined in a nested folder, TOOLSET_NESTED_LOCK, or refused by policy) is listed under Toolsets not locked (toolsetsNotLocked in JSON) with the reason. The rest is still locked and the command succeeds. A run that needs that toolset fails when it runs. Native ranges still apply: a toolset Node outside package.json engines fails when resolved, naming the constraint.

Runs execute only on the native host executor. A build that uses the container executor (--isolated, --image, --all-platforms, slices, remote pool builds, or builders without a native path such as pnpm and Yarn Node builds) and has runs fails with VERIFICATION_RUN_UNSUPPORTED, and so does its --plan. Build natively, or add --skip-verification. oyzu build --remote can't pass --skip-verification to the pool. A pool job runs as ci (or release), never local, so a toolset with default contexts makes a remote build fail. For remote builds, list contexts the pool doesn't use, such as contexts = ["local", "pr"]. oyzu build --remote --plan evaluates toolsets in your local context; pass --context ci to see what a pool job would refuse. No builder records verifies: artifact yet. Only native builds record verification evidence. The check that the work tree matches HEAD covers the build's folder only. An uncommitted change to an inputs file outside it doesn't stop the revision naming the commit. "Not applicable" is decided only for engines.node and the go.mod go minimum. Every builder repeats the same stages (build and test) in a run. When this job builds a platform with a cross toolchain, whether tests run follows the builder's cross-build rules.

build.yaml no longer accepts matrix. A runtime axis is refused with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE and the equivalent toolsets, built from the file's own values: CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE: app: matrix.node is no longer accepted: build.yaml says what ships, and tool versions belong in oyzu.toml. The build ships once, built with [tools]; each other version is a verification-only toolset that tests the build in pr, ci and release (add one locally with oyzu build --verify-with NAME). Remove matrix from build.yaml and add to oyzu.toml: [tools] node = "22.14.0" [toolsets.node24.tools] node = "24.14.1" See docs/reference/runtime-matrices.md The old axis built and kept one artifact per runtime. A toolset builds one artifact and verifies the other versions, so a release no longer holds two artifacts for one output. Shipping a separate artifact per runtime ABI isn't supported. matrix.platform is also refused; use platforms:.

builds: api: uses: go/app path: api image: uses: docker/image platforms: [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64] materialize: - from: api to: bin/server This expands into two image variants, each using an api variant built for the same platform. Platform requirements pass through materialize transitively, including named artifacts and directories. Ordering-only depends_on and other targets' task prerequisites don't pass them on. A producer's own platforms list limits what consumers can ask for. A conflict names the consumer's required platforms and the producer's allowed ones. platforms is the only way to declare artifact platforms. The old platform: <os/arch> and matrix.platform forms fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Aliases are accepted and stored in canonical form. Each builder checks the platforms against what it can actually run. Language builders need a toolchain that runs on the target platform, so the example fails before running if the only Go worker is x86-64. Cross-compiling a binary wouldn't prove its arm64 tests pass. See toolchain platforms. Docker can assemble x86-64 and arm64 scratch images on one x86-64 worker when no target code runs; see Docker platform admission. A complete set of image platforms also produces an OCI index. A partial selection keeps the individual images without an index.

A producer with no platforms keeps a standalone instance for commands like oyzu build api. Selecting image builds only the matching producer variants. A full workspace build skips the extra standalone instance when consumers already need platform variants, unless an ordering or task dependency requires it. Explicitly selecting both api and image can retain the standalone and demanded producer instances. The same OS and architecture do not make their computations interchangeable: native ABI, optimization profile and identity-sensitive tasks can differ. Coinciding artifact destinations are refused during collection; see layout limitations. If a standalone instance can't choose among a dependency's declared platform variants, selecting it fails with an ambiguity error before preparation. Resolve it with a platform declaration on the producer or consumer; Oyzu never guesses from the host.

A target that declares exactly one platform keeps its name. Several platforms give each instance a platform-qualified ID, and inferred producer variants always get one. IDs are deterministic and portable, derived from the name and platform, with a digest suffix when needed. Don't assume the logical name is the artifact's target ID; use the selection record and materialization receipts. Case-insensitive ID collisions are refused. A workspace can have at most 256 target instances and 16,384 copied tasks. Standalone instances count. Each instance gets its own copy of the build's tasks and hooks, including root hooks and stage replacements that reach it. Expansion never rewrites build.yaml.
Configuration for toolsets and constraints. Native local builds for the platform CI matrix. Publish for publication. Toolchain platforms for picking platform-specific images.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/rust.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu builds Cargo packages and workspaces with no Oyzu configuration. It finds Cargo.toml, runs Cargo, and collects binaries, crate archives, test reports and coverage into a build bundle. Use this page for what the Rust builder runs, the options it accepts, and how host builds differ from isolated (container) builds. Note: The Rust builder is experimental. Private Cargo registries, private Git sources and Git LFS aren't supported in isolated builds. See Limits. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Host builds use Cargo's native project and user registry configuration and credentials. Oyzu adds no registry setting or credential helper. When a private registry or a CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN, CARGO_REGISTRIES_*_TOKEN or CARGO_REGISTRIES_*_CREDENTIAL_PROVIDER variable is present, those variables and CARGO_HOME pass from the invoking environment to the host action, the action runs fresh instead of reusing the action cache, and token values are redacted from captured native output and never written to Oyzu evidence. Native user-level ~/.cargo/credentials.toml remains under Cargo's control. Private Cargo registries currently require host mode (oyzu build --context local, with --full for all enabled checks). Captured and isolated private-source builds fail before actions with PRIVATE_CARGO_SOURCE_UNSUPPORTED; use host mode. There is no public-registry fallback. oyzu build --plan # preview the stages and tool requirements oyzu build # build for this machine oyzu build --full # also run tests, doctests, Clippy and rustfmt oyzu inspect dist # check the bundle Plain oyzu build builds natively for the host. --platform <os/arch> cross-compiles one other platform. --all-platforms builds the declared matrix in the container executor. See build selection and checks. oyzu build --isolated runs the build in a Linux container. See Ordinary tasks and isolated build prerequisites. oyzu run <task> runs a development task such as build, test, lint or format-check with the Cargo you have installed. oyzu run list shows them. Cargo owns workspace membership, package metadata and dependency resolution. A checked-in Cargo.lock is required, and Oyzu runs Cargo with --locked.

Native Windows MSVC builds check the selected target's .rlib and .lib paths before compilation. Each ordinary absolute library path must be at most 259 UTF-16 units, leaving room for the terminating NUL. Windows long-path support and an extended path prefix do not remove this MSVC lookup limit. RUST_LIBRARY_PATH_TOO_LONG identifies the offending path and its length. Use a shorter absolute HOME, then run oyzu install and retry the build. The managed store follows HOME as described in configuration. Existing stores are retained. New Windows installs use compact installation directories; running oyzu install also populates that placement for an older installation. This admission check does not replace the compile-and-link prerequisite check: missing linkers and SDKs still fail their own probe.

The Rust builder is the oyzu-plugin-rust plugin. It reads your Cargo metadata, plans the build, and turns Cargo's output into binaries, crate archives and reports. Oyzu itself installs tools, downloads dependencies, projects versions, caches work and checks every artifact and report before it reaches dist/. Oyzu selects the plugin for rust/app and rust/library targets from its plugin sources (see plugin packages). There is no built-in fallback: if no Rust plugin is available, the build stops and says so. To use a locally built plugin, see local plugin bindings.

The marked Rust 0.1.0-preview.4 package requires Oyzu 0.3.0 or newer, including native-private-outputs and captured-cargo-projection support. Enable preview selection in user configuration to select it from the official catalog. This release covers the native Linux x86_64 flow; other platform combinations are not covered by this release. Existing projects retain their locked worker when the core or catalog changes. Before using the new core with a project locked to Rust preview.3, explicitly update the reference and then build: oyzu plugins update rust/app@0.1.0-preview.4 oyzu build Use rust/library@0.1.0-preview.4 for a locked library reference. Routine updates do not select previews, so this update names the exact published version. The older worker emits a different native Cargo operation graph and can fail with PLUGIN_CONTROL_CONFLICT on the new core. Updating uses normal signed package and engine admission; a build never silently changes a locked selection. The published 0.3.0 core cut does not bind inherited Unix file-creation masks to native cache identity. Keep that mask unchanged across cached builds with this core: after a mask change, cached outputs can retain stale permissions. It also does not preserve every authored directory mode in native source projections. Changed-mask reuse and custom directory-mode fidelity are unsupported by that release. Native builds retain Cargo compiler state for incremental work, but discard integration-test scratch under tmp/ and <target-triple>/tmp/ before measuring the retained cache. See native compiler cache retention for the budget and symlink checks. Building Rust needs no Python or other unrelated runtime. In isolated execution, Rust packages declaring captured-cargo-projection stage declared manifests and the original lock separately from inferred-version controls. The required project-version step then copies the exact frozen projected controls before compilation or checks. Source-only edits can reuse dependency staging without reusing stale version-bearing output. Authored manifests and locks remain unchanged. Older unmarked packages keep their projected staging overlay; native host finalization is unchanged. See prepared-input staging and plugin capabilities.

Stage Source boundary Build Cargo manifests, lock/config controls, selected package sources, reachable local path-dependency sources and predicted native inputs; compiler dep-info, build-script observations and macro resolution refine the boundary when available. Test, lint and coverage The same local source closure as build, including build and dev dependencies in Cargo's resolved graph, with stage-specific native observations. Unresolved build scripts or macros keep a specific conservative reason. Format check The selected crates' own source trees and module/include closures, without following Cargo dependency edges. Crate archive Cargo packaging inputs; an unbounded native packaging closure retains whole-target scope. Native binary export Declared producer outputs only, through the admitted typed binary copy. Local path dependencies include both workspace members and non-member packages under the build's source root. Their predicted reads include target source folders, build.rs and literal include closures. When the native read resolution is unavailable, compiling stages conservatively include every local package in the Cargo inventory. With resolution, unrelated members' source trees are excluded unless selected; workspace manifests remain declared. If a local path dependency is outside the target root, compiling stages remain unbounded with the reason local path dependency <name> is outside the target root. This does not block planning or change format-check's selected-crate boundary. On native hosts, build-script read record unavailable means Cargo's retained records do not establish an active script's reads. Feature-gated units that Cargo does not build need no record. After a successful build, observed reads cover only the build scripts Cargo reported running or finding fresh in that build, by package and <package>-<hash> directory. Records a reused target keeps from earlier toolchains, profiles or feature sets, and other packages' scripts, are ignored. Every reported script needs its own record; one without is unavailable, not zero reads. Planning cannot know what the coming build runs, so it still reads every exact <package>-<16 hex> record for compiled packages when membership is available. Native Clippy captures compiled-unit membership, including fresh units, from Cargo's JSON stream. Lint keeps every matching script record within that membership. If no matching record exists for a compiled package's build script, reads remain incomplete. Lint does not record which script directories ran, so a retained record can mask a missing current record. Membership matches by manifest path; if any compiled manifest matches no metadata package, membership cannot narrow reads and reuse remains blocked. Registry macros and build scripts use the locked checksum, toolchain and target identity assessment described in native Rust read admission, including its residual ambient-read risk. proc macro <name> may read files means a workspace/path or unidentified implementation cannot use that assessment. Neither reason identifies a missing compiler installation. Inspect oyzu build <target> --explain for the current build; these stages continue to execute until their read boundary can be established. Both native and isolated plugin planning attach Cargo read facts after the full operation graph is assembled. Intermediate construction defaults are never the final cache declaration. File-analysis facts are shared only within one planning request over the same source view; compilation and formatting still construct separate source closures. Later requests analyze their current source bytes. A read-only --plan uses stage contracts from the target's last retained build plan, marked as facts from the last build. Before a contract exists it says reported when the builder answers. It never runs Cargo or acquires tools to fill in that preview. An authored replacement cannot inherit a native command's narrow read contract. See action caching.

A host build runs Cargo on your machine and keeps Cargo's state under .oyzu/native/, so repeat builds stay incremental. oyzu build followed by oyzu build --full can reuse declared-version compilation when its complete native reads are admitted; the full build also requires inferred-version finalization and the extra checks. Each action uses a private source workspace and its own writable Cargo state. Clippy and tests use separate target directories, and coverage builds are kept apart from ordinary ones. Hooks and replaced tasks run without that reuse. See native action caching. Compilation and Clippy require complete Cargo observations; source prediction alone does not admit reuse. Missing dep-info, outside-source build-script reads and unresolved macro reads can keep a stage uncached. oyzu build --explain names the refusal, and oyzu cache explain <target> shows recorded lookup decisions. Declaring an extra inputs path cannot establish completeness for arbitrary reads. The stage runs again instead of restoring a whole-source result. On Windows x64/MSVC, compilation can currently report incomplete reads even on unchanged builds, so do not expect every warm build to reuse its compile stage. rustfmt's fixed-read check, Cargo's retained incremental state and eligible individual compiler results have separate admission and can still avoid work. Linux compilation can reuse when its reports are complete. See current native read coverage. Binary builds add a rustc source-path remap from the private compilation root to /oyzu/source. Development debug information stays enabled, so the ordinary Rust application fixture produces the same debug binary bytes from separate clean roots, including with oyzu build --no-cache. To locate sources in a debugger, substitute /oyzu/source with your project directory (for example, GDB's set substitute-path /oyzu/source /path/to/project). Cargo retains its normal configuration and environment flag precedence. The compiled Rust adapter adds the mapping through a compiler wrapper, chaining an inherited RUSTC_WRAPPER, including Oyzu's compiler-result cache. When Cargo configuration selects the wrapper instead, that configuration remains in control and automatic source remapping is unavailable. Build scripts, native linkers, absolute paths embedded by source code and other nondeterministic inputs can still affect artifact bytes. This remap does not declare retained Cargo state portable or change action-cache admission. Debug artifact equality is exercised on Linux x64; Windows PDB and macOS debug artifacts are not qualified. Shared-cache writers with optimized output run both compile-development and compile-optimized in one build plan. Readers reuse only the stage matching their requested profile. Check stages retain Cargo's development/test profile independently of the exported artifact. Compile, test, lint and format stages use declared Cargo versions. Plain local development readers may export the cached compile result directly; its compiledVersion is recorded separately from the inferred artifact version. Full, CI, optimized, packaged, handed-off, shared-cache writer and release paths require final projection so the exported binary's CARGO_PKG_VERSION matches the artifact version. Development results are rejected by stamped packaging, publication and release gates. Host compilation, tests and checks do not receive the engine-injected OYZU_VERSION default (inferred or tagged), so env!("OYZU_VERSION") fails there and option_env! is unset; read CARGO_PKG_VERSION instead. An unrelated file no longer re-runs compile, lint or format-check; tests keep whole-target source scope and still re-run. The final stage receives the default, and explicit environment values remain keyed. A final-stage receipt names its version map and projected-control digests; restoring compile binaries does not transfer Cargo compiler state. Checkouts below /workspace, /out or /oyzu use their original native Cargo cache and inventory paths when a stage runs from its private source workspace. Those checkout names do not turn native cache paths into executor mount paths. Tests, coverage, doctests and the other checks need their tools: rustfmt, Clippy, cargo-nextest, cargo-llvm-cov, and the compiler's LLVM tools and profiler runtime. See native execution for what Oyzu installs for you and what it checks first. Tests can also launch admitted tools through std::process::Command. Their cache keys conservatively retain the complete admitted tool environment and managed PATH, including user-level pins. A simple manifest does not prove that test subprocesses use only Cargo and Rust reporting helpers. Native Rust builds are supported on Linux (GNU) and Windows (x86-64, MSVC). macOS isn't supported yet.

A named build uses the shared fields in build inventory migration plus builder-owned with options. builds: cli: uses: rust/app platforms: [linux/x86_64] with: features: [integration] artifacts: binaries server: uses: rust/app with: packages: [my-server] Option Values Default Meaning with.features List of unique Cargo feature names none (Cargo's default features stay on) Applied to metadata, builds, lint, tests, doctests and package verification. with.packages List of unique Cargo package names none (the whole workspace) Limits the build to these workspace packages: cargo build --package …, and the same for lint, tests, doctests and package verification. Binaries and crate archives come only from them. with.features then belong to each of these packages, so they must be plain feature names (not package/feature or dep:). A name that is not a member of the workspace fails. with.artifacts all, binaries all all delivers the binaries and the crate archives of publishable workspace packages in isolated builds. binaries delivers only enabled Cargo binaries and never packages crates. with.test-packages List of unique Cargo package names inherits with.packages Overrides only the test scope, including nextest, coverage, doctests and test-unit discovery. [] explicitly selects the whole workspace. Every enabled test target of each selected package runs, including complete integration/e2e targets. Artifact packages, formatting, lint and archive verification retain their original scope. Unknown members fail. Unknown with keys fail. Options are never raw command strings. Use with.test-packages when the candidate artifact and test packages differ. For example, packages: [my-server] with test-packages: [my-library, my-server] still produces only the server's artifacts. A nonempty test selection also requires plain with.features names; Cargo applies them to the selected test packages. Metadata enables the union of artifact and test features. Coverage and report admission remain required for the selected scope. This option needs a core and Rust worker implementing independent test scope. An unrecognized option or mismatched prepared scope fails explicitly; update core and worker together rather than silently using artifact scope. Authenticated release staging requires the test scope to contain every artifact package. For example, packages: [server] with test-packages: [helper] fails with release-required-check; include server in the test scope or use test-packages: [] for the workspace. When artifact selection is the whole workspace, every workspace member must be tested. Authored non-Cargo test tasks keep their own invocation scope. Several builds can share one workspace root when each selects different packages. Two builds with the same selection fail with two targets own the same native build unit. The first-party plugins build this way: one build per plugin, each packages: [oyzu-plugin-<name>] with features: [plugin]. binaries fails if the build has no enabled binary. Feature-gated binaries need their Cargo features turned on. binaries still compiles, runs the selected checks and validates the executables. Conventional format and format-check tasks also honor with.packages, using cargo fmt --package for the selected members. Without a package selection they use --all. Formatting follows Cargo/rustfmt's native module traversal. Cargo can't package a publishable crate that depends on an unpublished path dependency. If you only need executables, select binaries. The old rust: object is no longer accepted. Cargo features go in with.features and cross-compilation targets go in platforms. Legacy language objects, tool versions, runtime matrices, unknown shared fields, and empty, repeated or suffixed platform entries are refused.

oyzu build builds for the host. oyzu build --all-platforms builds every declared platform in the container executor. Without platforms, a build targets the platform of the executor that runs it. The container executor needs the Linux Rust image described below and downloads crates.io inputs before it runs offline. Outputs and reports end up in the verified dist/ bundle. To pin the compiler, see Locked Rust compiler.

Name the platforms a Rust build ships in platforms, not Cargo target triples. builds: cli: uses: rust/app with: features: [mise-integration] platforms: [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64/musl, windows/x86_64, darwin/arm64] Cargo triple platforms entry x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu linux/x86_64 on a Linux x86-64 host, otherwise linux/x86_64/gnu aarch64-unknown-linux-musl linux/arm64 (musl is the cross default) or linux/arm64/musl x86_64-pc-windows-msvc windows/x86_64 on Windows, or windows/x86_64/msvc x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, -gnullvm windows/x86_64/gnu, windows/x86_64/gnullvm aarch64-apple-darwin darwin/arm64 oyzu build --platform <os/arch[/abi]> builds one of them on this host: the host platform as a host build, another one with the cross toolchain. oyzu build --plan --json lists every declared platform with the runner and executor it needs, so a CI matrix can build each on its own runner. A project that needs a particular executor declares it with build.executors. with.features applies to every platform. Outputs go to dist/<target>/<platform>/. Only x86_64 and arm64 on Linux, Windows and macOS have platform names. Other triples, such as riscv64gc-unknown-linux-gnu, can't be built yet. A build isn't a raw cargo build --target: Oyzu also applies tool requirements and artifact collection. A native executor builds one platform per target per run.
documents.s: Platforms instead of Cargo target triples

documents.t: oyzu build --platform <os/arch[/abi]> builds for another platform with your pinned toolchain: cargo build --target <triple> with the target's linker. Planning only looks at the host and the files it can see. It installs and runs nothing. Platforms and executors shows how the Plan reports each platform. Target platform Triple Linker Available when linux/<arch> (default, published as -musl), linux/<arch>/musl <arch>-unknown-linux-musl rust-lld (ships with Rust); C in build scripts uses zig cc (below) always linux/<arch>/gnu <arch>-unknown-linux-gnu <arch>-linux-gnu-gcc it is on PATH windows/<arch> on Windows, windows/<arch>/msvc <arch>-pc-windows-msvc MSVC Visual Studio's VC/Tools/MSVC/<version>/lib/<x64 or arm64> is installed windows/<arch> elsewhere, windows/<arch>/gnullvm <arch>-pc-windows-gnullvm <arch>-w64-mingw32-clang (LLVM MinGW) it is on PATH windows/<arch>/gnu <arch>-pc-windows-gnu <arch>-w64-mingw32-gcc it is on PATH darwin/<arch> <arch>-apple-darwin Apple clang the host is macOS; elsewhere the Plan says needs a macOS runner The defaults are musl for Linux, MSVC on a Windows host and LLVM MinGW elsewhere. An ABI in the platform name (linux/arm64/gnu) overrides them. The host's own machine and default ABI (GNU on Linux, MSVC on Windows) build as a host build. A musl build of the host's machine is a cross build. The target's standard library must be in the pinned toolchain. A cross build adds rust-std@<triple> to its tool requirements, and fails with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE if the toolchain has none. Output goes to dist/<target>/<platform>/ with the target's executable suffix. Oyzu checks the binary format and architecture against the target platform without running it. A Linux musl build whose dependencies include the cc crate (such as ring) compiles that C with zig cc, as an isolated build does: Oyzu fetches Zig 0.15.2 and cargo-zigbuild 0.21.2 built for your host (Linux, macOS or Windows, x86_64 or arm64), checks each against a SHA-256 pinned in Oyzu, and unpacks them once per machine in rust-cross beside the action cache (~/.cache/oyzu, ~/Library/Caches/Oyzu or %LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\cache). Downloads are admitted by your fetch sources, and an offline build needs one earlier online build. The Preflight shows a Cross C compiler step. CC_<triple>, CXX_<triple> and AR_<triple> run cargo-zigbuild's zig cc, which turns the cc crate's target into one Zig accepts, and CARGO_ZIGBUILD_ZIG_PATH names the fetched Zig. Zig's caches are kept in the target's native cache. The cc crate can't run a compiler whose path has a space, so a cache folder with one (a Windows user name with a space) stops the build with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE; use --isolated there. rust-lld still links. Cargo itself runs as cargo build, not cargo zigbuild. Pure-Rust builds fetch nothing. If compiler source access is denied or unavailable, or an archive is missing offline, preparation stops before compilation with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE. The diagnostic names the target C compiler, the missing archive and its URL, and an online oyzu build command to populate the cache. The original access error is retained. Integrity, corrupt-archive and filesystem failures keep their original diagnostics without this access recovery. Administrative fetches.sources denials require administrator approval; a host compiler does not replace the pinned compiler or bypass acquisition controls. Limits: C code for linux/<arch>/gnu, Windows and macOS targets needs that target's own C compiler on PATH (the linkers above). Otherwise use the container executor (--isolated, or "linux/arm64" = "container" under build.executors), which restores pinned cross linkers and C compilers for each target (details), or build on a runner of that platform. C built through something other than the cc crate (a hand-written build script calling cc, or CMake) gets no Zig compiler. Tests, coverage and doctests don't run for a cross-built platform. A project can require a cross build with build.executors. A release then cross-compiles that platform as declared or fails.

oyzu run list shows the Rust tasks without running Cargo: oyzu run list oyzu run build oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check Tasks use the Cargo, rustfmt and Clippy you already have. The implicit tasks are fetch (cargo fetch --locked), install (cargo install --path . --locked), build, test, lint, format, format-check and archive. oyzu run format changes your source. Builds only run the read-only format-check. oyzu build never runs fetch or install unless your tasks or hooks connect them. Test tasks write JUnit, Cobertura and doctest reports under dist/<target>/<platform>/reports/, not relative to the Cargo workspace. Required reports must be collected. Cobertura coverage allows 64 MiB per file and 2,000,000 XML nodes; JUnit and doctest reports retain their 16 MiB and 1,000,000-node limits. Older CLIs cap Cobertura at 32 MiB and reject a larger retained bundle. Path containment, freshness, digest verification and coverage acceptance remain enforced.
documents.s: Ordinary tasks and isolated build prerequisites

documents.t: Isolated builds need Docker and the base execution image, which has a C toolchain and no Rust. Host builds don't use it. Rust, rustfmt, Clippy and the LLVM tools come from oyzu.lock (see Locked Rust compiler). cargo-nextest and cargo-llvm-cov are locked stage tools for the test stage. If a tool the enabled stages need isn't in the lock, the build stops with a message that names oyzu pin. Oyzu mounts its engine and the Rust plugin into each action, so you never rebuild an image when the CLI changes. Python isn't needed. Cross builds add the pinned linkers described under cross-platform execution: Target Linker C code in build scripts Linux musl (linux/x86_64, linux/arm64) The compiler's own rust-lld zig cc, through cargo-zigbuild macOS (darwin/x86_64, darwin/arm64) cargo-zigbuild, against Zig's libSystem stubs zig cc, through cargo-zigbuild Windows gnullvm (windows/x86_64, windows/arm64) LLVM MinGW clang LLVM MinGW clang Zig 0.15.2, cargo-zigbuild 0.21.2 and LLVM MinGW 20260616 are each fetched once, checked against a SHA-256 pinned in Oyzu, stored with your declared fetches and restored read-only under /scratch/rust-cross-*. They're fetched only for a build that targets those platforms, and they run on linux/amd64 workers. The image has no Apple SDK. Crates that link Apple frameworks other than libSystem need your own image (--image cargo=<ref>) that provides one through SDKROOT. A custom --image cargo=<image> must meet the bring-your-own requirements, including a working cc. Oyzu still uses the locked tools. Docker dependency contexts use the narrower rust/cargo provider. Isolated Rust builds run on Linux with Docker.

oyzu run install -- --root /path/to/bootstrap --force oyzu run fetch -- --offline oyzu run install runs cargo install --path . --locked in the target's directory. With several Rust targets, qualify it (oyzu run cli:install). Arguments after -- go to Cargo. Installation uses Cargo's release profile. Use --bin to choose a binary and --force to replace an existing one. --root and CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT choose the install root. Otherwise Cargo's default applies, and its bin directory must be on PATH. Cargo reports its own errors for packages without installable binaries and for virtual workspace roots. A lock selects dependencies but doesn't make Cargo offline. Forward --offline when your caches are enough. Use oyzu run fetch for cargo fetch --locked. oyzu install provisions tools, not this task.
Isolated builds first collect everything Cargo needs, then build offline.

Oyzu reads the complete registry inventory from Cargo.lock before it makes any request. Only crates.io is supported: index entries from https://index.crates.io/ and archives from https://static.crates.io/crates/. Another registry or an unsupported Git host fails. Oyzu never falls back to Cargo's own network access. Every locked registry package needs a SHA-256 checksum. Oyzu requires the index metadata and archive bytes to match, then stores the archive and only the locked version's index entry in Cargo's local-registry format. If a cached index entry lacks the locked version, an online run fetches it once and checks it again. An offline run fails and tells you to run online. Duplicate matching entries and checksum disagreements are errors. Cargo extracts the archives, verifies checksums, resolves and compiles. No project code runs during acquisition. If the lock contains only local workspace packages, no registry replacement is written. Acquisition needs crates.io to be reachable on each fresh preparation. Once preparation succeeds, the build runs with the network denied.

Public GitHub sources need a full commit in Cargo.lock. Cargo fetches them through a repository-scoped broker inside a container with no network. The broker allows only Git smart-HTTP discovery and upload-pack requests, within size, redirect and request limits. Oyzu keeps the fetched object database and recreates the checkouts privately for the offline build. Repositories with Unix symlinks work on Windows hosts. Private Git, other hosts, submodule routing and Git LFS aren't supported.

Isolated builds archive only publishable workspace packages as .crate files. A package with publish = false (or an empty publish list) never gets a .crate. A private application delivers its executables instead. A private library is workspace internals. Private packages still build, lint and test. Publishable packages keep Cargo's own packaging and verification. One that depends on a private library fails with Cargo's own message.

For a workspace with local path dependencies and registry inputs, Oyzu packages members in dependency order. Each runs cargo package --locked --offline --allow-dirty --registry crates-io --package <name> with verification on. Each archive's name, version and SHA-256 are checked before dependent members can use it. Ordinary and build dependency cycles, and paths outside the workspace, fail planning. The captured registry stays unchanged. A temporary registry copy is removed when the action ends. An index over 4 MiB, an archive over 128 MiB, or an identity or checksum conflict fails packaging. Fix the manifest and rebuild. Native manifest publish restrictions still apply, and only the crates.io profile is supported. Development-dependency cycles between local members are supported when their ordinary and build edges are acyclic. Oyzu packages the cycle group together without verification, admits the results to a private registry, then packages and verifies every member separately and requires each final archive to match its provisional one byte for byte. Archives from a cycle group don't include Cargo.lock, so cargo install --locked doesn't work on them. If the original lock holds a different registry version of one of these members, Oyzu lets Cargo align its private lock with the verified workspace archives, offline, and restores the original lock afterward. Before packaging, Oyzu checks the original lock offline and writes workspace versions and local requirements into private manifests with a regenerated private lock. Your source files stay unchanged. Registry packages keep their locked versions and aren't delivered as artifacts.

Ordinary versions are snapshots with a source-derived suffix, such as 1.2.3-dev.g<source-prefix>. Workspace packages resolve independently unless they join a fixed version group. Snapshots are never marked eligible for release. A package's version follows its path-dependency closure. A relevant dependency commit changes the consumer's version, and an unrelated member's commit doesn't. Changes to root workspace inputs affect every member. Private manifests and packaged local requirements use each member's selected version. See version inference for strategies and tags. In a supported GitHub Actions tag job, release staging can select exact release coordinates. It's experimental and covers Linux x86-64 Cargo projects without repository hooks. --require-release refuses when the event or source evidence is insufficient. Cargo fixed version groups​ Workspace members can share one version using a subset of cargo-release's metadata. Oyzu reads the project-local settings and doesn't run cargo-release or its hooks. Fixed groups are supported on Linux x86-64. shared-version = true joins the workspace's shared group. A nonempty string such as "suite" names a group (case-sensitive; boolean true and the string "true" differ). shared-version = false opts a package out of an inherited group.
