Without effective membership, packages stay independent, even when their versions match or use version.workspace = true. Private and unselected members still count toward membership. This workspace groups App and Core and keeps Helper independent. Each package uses version.workspace = true. The root has: [workspace] members = ["app", "core", "helper"] resolver = "2" [workspace.package] version = "1.4.2" [workspace.metadata.release] shared-version = "suite" tag-prefix = "suite/" tag-name = "{{prefix}}v{{version}}" helper/Cargo.toml overrides both inherited fields: [package.metadata.release] shared-version = false tag-prefix = "helper/" With tags suite/v1.4.2 and helper/v1.4.2, an App-only feat: add API commit moves both App and Core to base 1.5.0. Helper stays at 1.4.2. All of them are still source snapshots. Each field merges separately, lowest to highest precedence: Workspace-root release.toml. Root Cargo.toml under [workspace.metadata.release]. Member-directory release.toml. Member Cargo.toml under [package.metadata.release]. A missing field inherits. An explicit false or empty prefix is a value. Home-directory configuration and cargo-release command-line overrides aren't read. Release, publish, signing and push settings don't control groups. For tag-based versions, every group member needs the same literal, slash-terminated tag-prefix (such as suite/). tag-name can be {{prefix}}v{{version}} (the default) or {{prefix}}{{version}}. An empty prefix means root tags and requires exactly one release subject at the Git root. Wildcards, crate-name templates and other tag formats are refused, as are partial prefixes, conflicting tags and unreadable controls. Fix the named declarations and rerun. --plan doesn't run Cargo or fetch history to fill in missing facts. Every member must declare the same normalized version, including qualifiers. Full builds write the common version and local requirements into private manifests and the private lock. Host builds first compile declared versions, then compile the final version in a separate Cargo stage. A registry backreference that needs a different member version is refused rather than splitting the group. The bundle records group membership, tag prefixes, where each setting came from and the resolved versions in oyzu.dev/version-subjects, beside each package's oyzu.dev/versioning entry. See Cargo groups in version inference for the strategy and conflict rules.

Native host tests, Clippy and formatting use the declared Cargo versions, while binary export follows the final inferred-version projection. Tests do not read the stamped binary export; assert shipped version strings against the final artifact and receipt rather than expecting a stamped CARGO_PKG_VERSION in tests. Cargo test, coverage and doctest commands also remove Oyzu's OYZU_RELEASE_COMMIT and SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH release-stamp environment variables. This keeps test subjects independent of tag presence and release-job time; the final shipped binary retains its separate release stamp. Compiler flags, features, instrumentation, dependencies and test arguments remain inputs. Matching source alone never establishes identical main/release test bytes. An isolated build runs release compilation of the workspace, native tests with reporting, Clippy, a rustfmt check, verified crate packaging and final collection. Commands use locked, offline inputs and the executor denies the network. Build scripts and proc macros run in that environment and must work with the collected inputs. The compiler's host target, the .oyzu-build/target output root, the private Cargo home and the offline setting are fixed by the plan. A task environment can't change them. Custom Cargo source replacement isn't supported and can fail offline resolution. Other Cargo settings in the project still apply. Compilation, tests, lint, formatting and archive verification are required. If one fails, no final artifacts are collected. The logs and any reports show which stage failed. Fix it and rerun. A bundle from an earlier successful build stays in .oyzu/history and isn't reused as this build's output.

Tests run through cargo llvm-cov nextest. JUnit and Cobertura reports land under dist/ and are indexed with paths, digests and summaries in dist/manifest.json. With Oyzu 0.4.0 or newer and a Rust plugin advertising rerun-cases, oyzu build --context ci retries failed nextest cases up to twice, using their exact native names. A recovered case is reported as flaky, with every attempt retained; it passes with a warning by default. A case that fails all three attempts still fails the build. Doctests retry at package granularity. These rules apply to native Windows MSVC and Linux builds; they do not enable tests for cross-built targets. Each case rerun uses binary_id(=<id>) & test(=<name>), so a passing case whose name contains the failed case's name is left alone. The first run uses --no-fail-fast, including when the native profile enables fail-fast. A requested case missing from the rerun report remains failed and reports TEST_RERUN_INCOMPLETE; an empty native selection cannot repair a failure. When .config/nextest.toml configures retries in the default profile or its per-test overrides, nextest owns those retries and Oyzu adds none of its own. JUnit flakyFailure/flakyError and rerunFailure/rerunError entries retain the native attempt history in order. Assertion failures, execution errors, timeouts and process aborts retain distinct failure kinds. A persistent failure keeps the original nextest exit status (100). These rules also apply with --no-cache. Set retries = 0 under [tests] in oyzu.toml to disable Oyzu retries, or flaky = "fail" to make a recovered flake block an enforced or required check. Flaky units cannot be reused as clean cache results; independently passing units keep their normal reuse. See test retries for completion guards, context defaults and native retry settings. Rust 0.1.0-preview.6 lacks rerun-cases. It can stop before tests with version control changed after preparation: Cargo.lock when used with a newer driver's version projection, including with version.strategy = "native". Preparation failure produces no retry evidence; select a compatible newer package. Older drivers do not gain Oyzu retries by installing a newer plugin; a package requiring an unsupported engine feature is refused with PLUGIN_ENGINE_REQUIREMENT before it runs. Plugins without rerun-cases that complete preparation and the required report checks use whole-unit fallback: the driver retries every case in the failed unit, including previously passing siblings, and reports TEST_RETRY_UNIT. Attempts and recovered flakes are still recorded. Exact case retries require both the 0.4.0 CLI release and a published Rust package containing the case-selection and attempt-reporting adapter. The package must advertise rerun-cases in describe; the first-party manifest also requires that engine feature. Updating the CLI alone leaves existing plugin locks unchanged. Once a compatible signed package is published and catalogued, select its exact version with oyzu plugins update rust/app@<version> (or rust/library@<version>). This verifies the release and updates oyzu.lock; no unpublished version or digest can be pinned in advance. Test failures and coverage failures are reported separately. A missing or invalid required report fails collection. oyzu inspect dist checks the bundle's integrity. The Cobertura report omits per-function records and keeps line and branch details to reduce its size. The report limit is 64 MiB per file and 2,000,000 XML nodes; a larger report fails the build. Oyzu's coverage gate uses covered and valid source-line counts. Cargo doctests run as part of the same test gate, since nextest doesn't run them. Oyzu runs cargo test --doc --locked --offline --package <name> for each workspace package that has a doctest-enabled target (doctest = false is honored). Binary-only targets and registry dependencies don't run doctests. doctest.xml has one case per package invocation, not per documentation example. A package with doctests enabled but no examples still passes. A non-zero Cargo exit is a failure and a launch error is an error. Output streams live, and the report keeps the start of each diagnostic. All selected packages run even if one fails. A failed doctest blocks artifact collection even when nextest passes. Coverage covers nextest runs only. It doesn't include doctests or individual doctest cases. Build tests inherit the default nextest profile; selecting alternate profiles isn't supported.

oyzu run test produces nextest JUnit, LLVM Cobertura coverage and doctest reports, and you can follow it with oyzu inspect dist. It's supported on Windows (MSVC) and Linux. See direct tests for the bundle layout.

Rust with the llvm-tools-preview component and the compiler's profiler runtime, cargo-nextest 0.9.146 and cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1. On Windows, use an MSVC or windows-gnullvm compiler with its linker and SDK. The windows-gnu compiler isn't supported for coverage because it lacks profiler_builtins (see native build prerequisites). Dependencies must already be installed so Cargo can resolve them offline with --locked. This task doesn't install tools. If the LLVM tools are missing, it fails before llvm-cov tries to download them. LLVM_COV and LLVM_PROFDATA can point at installed copies. When invoking coverage directly with the portable windows-gnullvm Rust archive's bare rust-lld, cargo-llvm-cov's gnullvm workaround uses the Clang-driver spelling -C link-arg=-Wl,--no-gc-sections. Bare lld needs -C link-arg=--no-gc-sections instead. Use cargo llvm-cov show-env --sh --no-rustc-wrapper, translate that argument in the returned coverage environment, run cargo test --tests --locked --offline with that environment, then run cargo llvm-cov report --json --output-path coverage.json with the same environment. Keep the other returned flags and variables, including instrumentation and profile paths. This applies to direct bare-linker use; a Clang driver accepts -Wl,.

Cargo's metadata --no-deps --locked --offline supplies the workspace members and doctest-enabled packages. oyzu run list never runs Cargo. The default cargo test --locked --workspace task is instrumented automatically. A task you replace keeps its own command and still has to produce the JUnit, coverage and doctest reports. No Oyzu configuration is needed for the default. A temporary nextest profile inherits your default profile and writes fresh JUnit output. Your .config/nextest.toml isn't edited. Compilation and coverage use private temporary target directories, so project build state isn't reused. Extra command arguments go to nextest. Alternate nextest profiles, arbitrary cargo test arguments and filtered doctest selection aren't supported here. The task runs nextest, generates coverage even if tests failed, and runs doctests. Any failing phase fails the task. Build scripts and proc macros run normally. Cargo's offline flags aren't a network sandbox on the host. See direct tests.

With the default with.artifacts: all, an isolated build produces <package>-<selected-version>.crate for each publishable workspace package, plus <binary>-<selected-version>-<compiler-host> for each enabled binary. with.artifacts: binaries selects only executables and fails if there are none. The selected version is normally a projected snapshot. See Registry backreferences for the exception. Manifest names use the crate- and bin- prefixes. A publishable library-only package gets a crate archive and no invented executable. Duplicate binary names fail planning.

Cargo's resolved features decide whether a binary with required-features exists. A binary whose features aren't on is left out. Turn the features on through Cargo's defaults or with.features to include it.

Oyzu reads Cargo's JSON compiler messages and matches each expected binary by its manifest path and target name. It takes the executable path from Cargo's own compiler-artifact events rather than guessing filenames, and never publishes test binaries. Cached results count as well as fresh compilation. A missing, unexpected or conflicting output, a failed Cargo process, or an executable outside the target root fails the build. Oyzu clears its staging directory before each Cargo run, so an old executable can't stand in for a disabled feature or a failed compile. A task you replace must still produce the planned artifacts. This builder doesn't publish, sign or promote anything. Crate archives don't include Oyzu's private .oyzu-build files.

Cargo package verification re-resolves through a private registry. A projected prerelease version of a member can then conflict with a registry dependency of the same name. When the resolved graph has a registry dependency named after a workspace member, Oyzu keeps that member's declared version, and local path requirements use it. Only affected members keep declared versions. Others get snapshot versions. An inactive dependency declaration doesn't count. These artifacts are still snapshots. oyzu.dev/versioning records reason: cargo-registry-backreference, the source digest, intent: snapshot and productionEligible: false, even if the version looks like a release. Use the bundle's source identity and artifact digest to tell apart snapshots with the same version.

A [tools] rust = "1.95.0" declaration in oyzu.toml, installed into oyzu.lock, selects the compiler for isolated builds. The container worker uses the linux/<architecture>/gnu installation from the project's .oyzu/tools store. That's the compiler's own platform. Artifact platforms in build.yaml don't change it. Only a Rust-only tool selection works this way. Before any package is downloaded or Cargo runs, Oyzu verifies the lock, the installer, the installation receipts and the payload. It copies the installation into the private dependency snapshot while holding a lease, and verifies the copy. The build uses that copy's Cargo, rustc and rustdoc. The live tool store is not mounted into containers. The dependency record keeps the identities of the request, the installation, the lock and the copy. If anything is missing or stale, the build fails: a missing or stale lock, a missing worker distribution, an absent installation, an unsupported layout or a changed payload. Install the matching compiler first. Oyzu doesn't resolve versions, edit the lock or use the network to restore the compiler. oyzu install provisions only its own host, so installing a Linux compiler from a Windows host isn't supported yet. The base image has no Rust, so an isolated build without a locked compiler stops with a message that names oyzu pin. The image provides only OS prerequisites and a C toolchain. Formatting, lint and test tools come from the lock too.

Build manifests list oyzu.dev/tool-requirements for each Rust target. Oyzu reads literal package.rust-version values and Rust toolchain channel constraints, with their source files and locations, in every form rustup accepts (details). It lists compiler components, standard libraries for the platforms you build, and the formatting, lint and test tools that the selected stages need. Fast builds leave out the quality tools they don't run. Components named in your toolchain file stay required. A rust-version inherited from the workspace needs workspace metadata. Without it, the build fails with a clear message instead of ignoring the value. For a locked compiler, isolated builds choose their recipe from the same build-stage requirements as oyzu pin. A build with tests selected therefore needs the locked llvm-tools-preview component, even if the lock also holds a smaller recipe for fast builds. An incomplete lock stops the build. An environment override doesn't replace it. The helper tools cargo-nextest and cargo-llvm-cov are restored from the lock as stage tools.

Declaring artifact platforms in build.yaml runs isolated builds on the execution image with the pinned cross linkers listed under the isolated-build image. Supported platforms are linux/x86_64, linux/arm64, darwin/x86_64, darwin/arm64, windows/x86_64 and windows/arm64. Linux builds musl and Windows builds gnullvm. Other ABIs are refused. Baselines: musl for Linux, Apple Darwin with a macOS 13 deployment target, and LLVM MinGW for Windows. They don't guarantee compatibility with older operating systems. The locked compiler and target standard libraries are restored separately from the linkers.

Declare the compiler in oyzu.toml and install it into oyzu.lock. On Windows, oyzu install also fetches the Linux compiler when the project declares a Rust build. Equivalent locked selections in one build share one verified compiler extraction per archive digest and worker image. It's mounted read-only. Cargo homes, outputs and workspaces stay private. The extraction is released when the build ends. The persistent oyzu-tools-* volumes are reused by identity, and superseded ones are pruned (see build logging). The build runs without network access. Compiler sharing is automatic and adds no build.yaml options. It doesn't deduplicate crate downloads or preparation, and it isn't a persistent compiler cache.

Each cross-platform Rust action reserves 8 GiB of memory and may run up to two hours. Oyzu limits concurrent targets by Docker's available memory and keeps 25% as headroom. A Docker engine needs about 11 GiB to run one such action. Preparing the locked compiler reserves 4 GiB. Tests and coverage run on the Linux worker. Cross-compiled executables are checked for the right binary format and architecture, but not run on the target OS. Cargo extraction and Git checkouts use a private Linux scratch filesystem of at least 2 GiB that grows with larger memory reservations. Only the Git object databases are copied back, which keeps registry extraction and symlinks off Windows host mounts. Build inputs and workspaces live under the project's .oyzu directory on the same volume as the project, not in the system temp folder. They're private, and excluded from source snapshots and bundles. cargo fmt runs with the same locked compiler and never receives feature arguments.

Rust compilation stages declare OYZU_RELEASE_COMMIT and SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH as environment inputs, so their values affect cache keys. Native builds inherit them from the invocation; isolated builds require values in the configured environment, as with other build-script environment inputs. For Oyzu's own CLI, set both to a full commit ID and Unix build seconds to produce the explicit release label; leaving the commit unset produces the development display label. This does not authenticate a release or grant publication. Native host builds retain a local Cargo producer evidence record in the build bundle. It binds the compiler identity, selected sysroot, original Cargo metadata, captured source inventory, final native command controls and original build streams. Restored actions retain their original record. Older cached actions without this completion contract are rebuilt once; the native Cargo compiler cache remains usable. The record contains private build paths and is local engineering evidence, with no release or legal approval. Core oyzu/plugin-package declarations have no external builder or additional native tools. oyzu exec, installation and pinning resolve the executable producer's tools while keeping package declarations available for reference validation. Isolated builds support single packages and local workspaces, including libraries, binaries, proc macros and build scripts. Only crates.io registry dependencies and public GitHub Git dependencies work. Private or alternate registries, private Git and Git LFS don't. Isolated Rust builds run on Linux with Docker. Cross-compiling needs the platform's linker or the container executor (see above). Alternate nextest profile selection, doctest coverage and individual doctest cases aren't supported. Release and registry publication aren't done by the Rust builder.

Local builds, build tasks and build bundles for the shared build model and output. Version inference, direct tests and Docker images for adjacent behavior. Rust installation for provisioning the compiler. Private Cargo registries for private sparse registries on the host.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/scan.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu scan runs security and quality scanners against a build you already made: Gitleaks, Trivy, Grype and SonarQube. It checks the same source files and artifacts that oyzu build recorded in dist/, and tells you whether the result passes the thresholds you set. No platform account is needed. Note: oyzu scan is experimental and has been tested on Windows only (native Gitleaks, and container scanners through Docker Desktop with Linux containers). oyzu build oyzu scan oyzu scan --json scan never rebuilds, runs tests or publishes. Each call starts a new scan.

There are two ways to choose scanners: Method Scanners Where Project settings Gitleaks, run natively [scan.gitleaks] in oyzu.toml Administrator policy SonarQube, Trivy, Gitleaks, Grype, run in Docker scan.policy in administrator configuration only If no scanner is selected, you get SCAN_SELECTION_REQUIRED with the setting to add.

[scan.gitleaks] enabled = true failOnFindings = true Setting Values Default Meaning scan.gitleaks.enabled boolean false Run Gitleaks natively on the recorded source. scan.gitleaks.failOnFindings boolean false Fail the scan if Gitleaks finds anything. When false, findings are recorded but don't fail the scan; Gitleaks errors still fail it. These settings follow the normal configuration cascade and its constraints. They can't replace or loosen an administrator's container selection; failOnFindings can only make it stricter. Oyzu installs Gitleaks like any other tool: from your [tools] request if there is one, otherwise a compatible pin or the default version. It doesn't edit your configuration or oyzu.lock, and it never falls back to a Gitleaks on PATH or a container.

Option Meaning --store <DIR> Use this native tool store instead of the shared user store. A relative path is resolved from the project root. --offline Use only tools, images and inputs already on this machine. See offline scans. --json Print only the result on standard output; progress events go to standard error. Works before or after scan.

Only administrator configuration can set scan.policy. In the protected admin-settings.json file: { "schemaVersion": 1, "kind": "local-admin-policy", "settings": { "scan.policy": { "locked": true, "value": { "sonar": { "image": "sonarsource/sonar-scanner-cli@sha256:a3f4215076706c95a17a68c19322ee916e40a3acd081a8c1a1e839e0194afa57", "endpoint": "https://sonarqube.example.com", "projectKey": "example", "sources": ["app/src/main/java", "library/src/main/java"], "requireClasses": true }, "trivy": { "image": "aquasec/trivy@sha256:af6acf9a6b85dfe389a1941505c0ce9efef52a4719635e1a962f022a3d855daa", "maximumFindings": 0 }, "requireQualityGate": true } } }, "profiles": {}, "requiredCapabilities": [] } Each scanner (sonar, trivy, gitleaks, grype) is optional, but at least one is required. Images must be pinned by digest. Oyzu pulls missing images through Docker before scanning and reuses ones you already have. Private tool catalogs and custom registry routes aren't supported for scanner images. Key Meaning <scanner>.image The scanner image, by digest. <scanner>.maximumFindings The most findings allowed before the scan fails. Omit for no limit. (Trivy, Gitleaks, Grype.) requireQualityGate Require a passing SonarQube quality gate. Needs sonar. Default false. sonar.endpoint, sonar.projectKey The SonarQube server and project. sonar.sources Source folders to analyze, relative to the project. sonar.requireClasses Give SonarQube compiled classes taken from the build's JAR artifacts. trivy.rules Extra Trivy secret rules; see Trivy. gitleaks.config Gitleaks TOML rules; see Gitleaks. Container scanners need Docker on the machine running oyzu scan. Scanners never get the Docker socket. For SonarQube, set up the SonarQube server and project yourself, and put SONAR_TOKEN in the environment (never in the policy file). The token needs permission to submit analysis and read tasks, quality gates and project issues. endpoint may use HTTP for a local server. Tool versions belong under [tools] or in the policy image, not in other scanner settings.

scan rebuilds the exact list of source files the build recorded, and their digest must match the build's. It doesn't rediscover inputs or reread ignore files, and a Git commit alone isn't enough. If source changed since the build, the scan fails with SCAN_SOURCE_MISMATCH before any scanner runs. Restore the files or build again. A bundle without a recorded source selection fails with SCAN_SOURCE_SELECTION_MISSING; a malformed one with SCAN_SOURCE_SELECTION_INVALID. Build again with the current CLI. For Cargo, adding an ignored release.toml or a file that could become a workspace member can make the scan refuse even if the recorded digest still matches. Declare the file as a build input or fix the workspace members, then build again. Differences between machines' filesystems can prevent a match. They aren't smoothed over. Artifacts are copied and digest-checked for the scan. The original dist/ is checked before and after and never changed. Source isn't fetched from Git and remote bundles aren't downloaded.

Each scan is saved under .oyzu/scans/<run-id>/: File Contents manifest.json The final result, with digests of the other files. plan.json The policy, tool versions and inputs used. events.jsonl Progress events. <scanner>/report.json The scanner's own JSON report (Trivy, Gitleaks, Grype). <scanner>/native.log The scanner's own output. sonarqube/provider.json The SonarQube server's response. grype/database.log Grype database download output. Each check records whether its tool was installed or reused, and the exact image or native tool version. If a scan fails partway, a failure manifest names the phase. A configuration error caught before the scan starts writes nothing. Scanning never pins tools or writes oyzu.lock. Reports can include secrets or source text, so protect .oyzu/scans. Human output shows only counts, never matched text.

The terminal view follows the build layout: a Preflight phase (install or reuse each scanner), a Scan phase with each scanner's progress, then a table of scanner, analysis type, subject, result and duration. Details below list findings, quality gates, the pass or fail decision, report links and the result path. NO_COLOR turns color off and --quiet hides progress, not the result.

Exit Meaning 0 Every check ran and the result passes. 1 A scanner failed, a threshold or quality gate failed, or SCAN_SOURCE_MISMATCH. 2 Invalid flags or input. 3 Configuration or policy errors (CONFIG_*, POLICY_*). If one scanner fails, the others still run and keep their reports, but the overall pass/fail decision is skipped. Findings by themselves never count as a scanner failure; they're compared with the threshold afterwards. A nonzero scanner exit or a malformed report is a failure.

A successful scanner exit only means the analysis was submitted. Oyzu then waits up to three minutes for the server to finish and reads that analysis's quality gate. The dashboard and issue links in the result show the project's current state, not a snapshot of this analysis; the result says so and keeps the analysis and task IDs. Issue snapshots are cut off at 500 issues and don't affect the result. A passing quality gate doesn't mean zero findings or permission to publish.

Trivy runs secret detection on the recorded source only. It has no vulnerability database, network, credentials or Docker socket. Repository trivy.yaml, ignore files and secret rules are ignored. Administrators can add trivy.rules: an array of custom secret rules with id, title, regex and severity (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH or CRITICAL). Built-in rules stay on. An invalid regex fails the check.

Add gitleaks to scan.policy, alone or with other scanners: { "gitleaks": { "image": "zricethezav/gitleaks@sha256:691af3c7c5a48b16f187ce3446d5f194838f91238f27270ed36eef6359a574d9", "maximumFindings": 0 } } This selects Gitleaks 8.30.0. It scans the recorded source files (gitleaks dir), not Git history. gitleaks.config can supply Gitleaks TOML rules. Without it, Gitleaks' default rules apply. Project .gitleaks.toml, .gitleaksignore and gitleaks:allow comments are ignored. A config error fails the check. Source is mounted read-only. There's no network, credentials or Docker socket. Gitleaks redacts matches in its report, but treat reports as sensitive anyway. See the Gitleaks documentation for rule syntax.

Add grype to scan.policy to check the build's JAR artifacts (application/java-archive) for known vulnerabilities: { "grype": { "image": "anchore/grype@sha256:af65fbc0c664691067788fe95ff88760b435543e45595eb2ca6f102fc476fbe1", "maximumFindings": 0 } } This selects Grype 0.110.0. Each scan downloads a fresh vulnerability database into the scan folder, then analyzes the JARs with networking off. This uses disk space and bandwidth on every run. Project Grype configuration is ignored. Grype's own database age and hash checks stay on. Findings count vulnerability matches, not unique CVEs. Only packages Grype finds in the recorded JARs are checked. Container images, SBOMs, lock files and other artifacts aren't. A clean result isn't a full dependency audit. See Grype database behavior and the Grype CLI reference.

Concurrency. scan.jobs (1 to 65535, default 2) sets how many scanners run at once. Set 1 for one at a time, or 4 to run all four together. A failed scanner doesn't stop the others. Results keep plan order. Offline scans. oyzu scan --offline works when tools, images and inputs are already on the machine. A missing image fails with TOOL_OFFLINE, native Gitleaks without a recorded installation or pin fails before resolving a version, SonarQube fails with SCAN_OFFLINE and Grype with SCAN_DB_OFFLINE. Checks are never skipped to make an offline scan pass. Scanners are never run during oyzu build, and scan never runs Maven or other build tools. Native installation is available for Gitleaks only. Trivy, Grype and SonarQube run in Docker. Grype's database isn't cached between scans. Results prove the files weren't changed; they aren't signed provenance. Docker administrators on the machine can see scanner environment variables, including SONAR_TOKEN. Missing JAR artifacts for Grype fail with SCAN_INPUT_MISSING. For nested projects, inputs from sibling folders outside the project are checked against the build but may not be passed to scanners.
Build bundles Configuration

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/secrets.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu secrets manages the secrets your Oyzu platform account keeps for the account, one of its organizations or one of its projects. A secret is either a token a build job receives (build exposure) or a webhook secret the platform uses to check incoming deliveries (internal exposure). Values are write-only. You can set or replace a value, but no command or API ever shows a stored value back to anyone, including account owners. Note: This command is experimental and hasn't been tested against a live platform yet. Everything else Oyzu does is local and works without an account. oyzu secrets create release-webhook --exposure internal --description "Release tool deliveries" oyzu secrets set release-webhook --generate oyzu secrets list

platform.url and platform.account in your configuration, usually at user scope: oyzu config set --global platform.account payments. A platform credential: an oyzu auth login session (used at a terminal, or when platform.authentication.provider is session) or a token in OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. See which credential a command uses. Unattended runs need an explicit provider or token and never use your stored session. Don't copy a browser session into a token. Permission for the operation on the platform. Having a credential isn't enough on its own. You don't need a Git checkout.

Command What it does oyzu secrets list Lists the account's secrets: name, type, exposure, value version and description. oyzu secrets create <name> --exposure build|internal Creates a secret with no value. Add --type file for exact bytes such as a key file (default text) and --description. oyzu secrets set <name> < value.txt Sets or replaces the value from standard input. oyzu secrets set <name> --file key.pem Sets or replaces the value with a file's exact bytes. oyzu secrets set <name> --generate Generates a value, sets it and prints it once. oyzu secrets set <name> ... --overlap 24h Keeps the replaced value valid for this long, up to 168h. Units: h, m, s. oyzu secrets rm <name> --previous Ends an overlap now, for example if the old value leaked. oyzu secrets rm <name> Deletes the secret and all its values. Add --org <org> or --project <project> to any command to work in that scope; without them, commands act on the account. Use the organization's or project's identifier. set and rm accept a secret's name or id. set never creates a secret; if it doesn't exist you get SECRETS_NOT_FOUND with the create command to run. Exposure, type and scope are fixed when you create a secret. To change one, create a new secret.

oyzu secrets set release-webhook --generate --overlap 24h # update the sender with the new value oyzu secrets rm release-webhook --previous Both values are accepted during the overlap, so no deliveries are dropped.

Values come from standard input, --file or --generate, never from a command-line argument, so they don't end up in shell history or process listings. Standard input must be piped or redirected. If it's a terminal, set fails with SECRETS_VALUE_REQUIRED rather than echo what you type. Bytes are sent exactly as read. echo token | oyzu secrets set x stores a trailing newline; use printf '%s' "$TOKEN" or a file without one. A value can't be empty and can be at most 64 KiB. A text value must be UTF-8. --generate takes 32 bytes from the operating system's secure random source and uses them as 64 lowercase hex characters, which webhook senders accept. The value is printed once, after the platform has stored it. If the platform refuses, the value is thrown away and never shown.

A listing is a table. The Value column shows the version (and, during an overlap, when the old one stops working) or not set: Secrets · project web of payments Name Type Exposure Value Description npm-token text build version 2 (version 1 valid until 2026-10-11T09:05:00Z) hook text internal not set Release tool Values are write-only: no command shows a stored value. Replace one with `oyzu secrets set <name>`. A generated value is shown once: ✓ Set the value of release-webhook (version 1) Generated value 3f9c…(64 hexadecimal characters) Copy it into the sender's webhook settings now. It cannot be shown again; if it is lost, set a new one. With --json, standard output holds one record with kind, account and scope: kind Extra fields secrets secrets (metadata only) secret-created, secret-overlap-ended secret secret-value-set secret, and generated_value for --generate only secret-deleted name, id The JSON from --generate contains the value, so treat it as sensitive.

Exit status is 0 on success and 2 on any failure. Platform errors keep the platform's code with a SECRETS_ prefix, plus the platform request id. Code Cause Fix SECRETS_NOT_CONFIGURED platform.url or platform.account is missing. Set them. SECRETS_UNAUTHENTICATED No credential, or it was refused. Run oyzu auth login, or set a current OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. SECRETS_PERMISSION_DENIED You can't do this in that scope. Ask for access. SECRETS_NOT_FOUND No secret with that name in that scope. Check the scope, or create it first. SECRETS_RESOURCE_CONFLICT Name already taken, no previous value to end, or a sign-only secret. Pick another name, or leave platform-managed secrets alone. SECRETS_VALIDATION_FAILED The platform rejected a field (named in the error). Correct that field. SECRETS_VALUE_REQUIRED, SECRETS_VALUE_EMPTY, SECRETS_VALUE_TOO_LARGE, SECRETS_VALUE_UNREADABLE No usable value. Pipe the value, use --file or --generate. SECRETS_OVERLAP_INVALID Bad --overlap duration. Use a value like 24h, at most 168h. SECRETS_UNREACHABLE The platform couldn't be reached. Retry later. SECRETS_RESPONSE_INVALID The platform's reply was malformed. Run oyzu secrets list to see what happened before retrying. Check CLI and platform compatibility. list retries a 503 or network failure with backoff. create, set and rm are sent once, because retrying a value could create an extra version and, with an overlap, retire the value you meant to keep. If one fails in transit, run oyzu secrets list to check before trying again.

No command reads a value back. Values never come from arguments, are never logged and are never written to disk by the CLI. The credential is sent only to platform.url, using your proxy and trust settings. Redirects aren't followed. A reply that contains a secret value is rejected, not printed. sign-only secrets (the platform's own integration keys) are listed but can't be created or changed here.
There is no hidden prompt for typing a value. Pipe it or use --file.
Platform sign-in Remote runs

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/self-update.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu self keeps the oyzu you installed up to date. It follows a release channel (stable, beta or nightly), installs the newest version of that channel, installs one exact version on request, and rolls back to the version you had before. Every download is checked against the signed evidence oyzu's own releases carry before it replaces anything. Note: Releases are previews. They are published on the public oyzuai/oyzu-releases repository, which oyzu self reads by default, so you need no account or token. The unsigned internal dev-YYYYMMDD archives and latest-green pointer use a separate dev channel, outside oyzu self. Their publication requires successful Linux and opt-in Windows jobs; disabling Windows leaves latest-green unchanged. Pull request builds are not published through self-update. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Released 0.3.8 reports FILE_READER_TOO_OLD (exit status 3) when an Oyzu-owned file declares a min_oyzu_version newer than that reader. Its error names the file, required version and reader version. Newer readers can continue with a FILE_READER_NEWER upgrade notice when they understand the content; unsupported required features and replacements that would lose newer data still refuse. Keep the marker: removing it can make an old reader misinterpret configuration. Run these commands in PowerShell, cmd or Git Bash, then retry the project: oyzu self update oyzu --version Self commands work even when the current project's configuration needs a newer reader. If the installation is pinned, use oyzu self channel stable to follow stable releases again. The required version must already be published on the selected channel; an up-to-date older release cannot read a future project. For a CLI without self, use the Windows install script. After a successful self-update, oyzu self status names the previous version. To undo it in any of the three shells, run oyzu self rollback, then oyzu --version. This pins the restored version. A project requiring the newer reader will refuse again after rollback; use a compatible project revision or return to the newer channel. Running programs continue with their original CLI until restarted. If another executable shadows the updated one, open a new terminal and check Get-Command oyzu (PowerShell), where oyzu (cmd), or type -a oyzu (Git Bash).

documents.t: Command What it does oyzu self or oyzu self status The installed version, channel or pin, whether updates are automatic, the install folder, the last check and the previous version. Uses no network. oyzu self update Installs the newest version of your channel, including after rolling back to a local build when a channel is recorded. Prints that you are up to date when you are. oyzu self update --check Only reports whether a newer version is available. oyzu self channel Shows the channel and mode. oyzu self channel beta Follows beta from now on and installs its newest version. Also clears a pin. Moving to a narrower channel (nightly to stable) may install an older version; that is the only time an update goes backwards. oyzu self channel --manual / --auto Switches between notices only and automatic updates. Combine with a channel name to do both. oyzu self versions The newest version in each channel, and which channel you follow. --all adds every recent version with its channel, date and whether it has an executable for your platform. --all --channel beta filters that history by exact channel. oyzu self install 0.2.1 Installs exactly that version and pins it, so automatic updates stop until you run oyzu self channel <name>. oyzu/v0.2.1 and v0.2.1 work too. oyzu self rollback Swaps back the binaries you had before the last change and pins that version. Running it again swaps forward. Every command supports --json. In JSON mode the result is one record with an operation field (status, update, channel, versions, install or rollback) and the same facts the human view shows. To list recent releases of one kind (illustrative): oyzu self versions --all --channel beta oyzu self versions --all --channel nightly --json oyzu --json self versions --all --channel stable Versions option Accepted values Default Meaning --all flag off Add history from up to 100 recent releases instead of reading 30 for channel summaries. --channel <name> stable, beta, nightly no filter Requires --all. Keep only history rows with this exact classification. --json flag, before or after the subcommand off Return the same facts as JSON. The history filter keeps channel summaries unchanged and never changes the followed channel, pin or files on disk. Filtering for beta excludes stable and nightly history, even though beta updates may select a stable release. An empty match succeeds with versions: []; human output explains that no matching versions are in the recent release list. This is a bounded recent list, not a search through all release history. An invalid channel or a filter without --all exits 2 before opening configuration or contacting the network; use oyzu self versions --help for accepted options. Filtered JSON adds channelFilter with the requested name; channel continues to mean the installation's followed channel. channels retains all summaries, and versions contains the filtered rows. Unfiltered output keeps its existing fields. For example, a nightly filter with no matching release returns "channelFilter": "nightly" and "versions": []. Illustrative output (values and timings vary): Updating oyzu linux/x86_64 · stable · 0.2.1 → 0.2.2 ── Download ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ oyzu oyzu-linux-x86_64 · 12.0 MB · verified 1.1s ✓ Shim oyzu-shim-linux-x86_64 · 0.4 MB · verified 0.2s ── Install ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ✓ Swap oyzu replaced · 0.2.1 kept for rollback 0.1s ✓ Shims unchanged (links to oyzu) 0.1s ✓ oyzu updated: 0.2.1 → 0.2.2 (stable) · 1.8s Release oyzu/v0.2.2 · sha256:1836d82c…09c1 Verified digest · release provenance · publication to oyzuai/oyzu-releases Runs oyzu 0.2.2 (release; x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) Folder /home/you/.oyzu/bin Next: oyzu self rollback undoes this. Running programs keep the old version until they restart. Human output shares the sectioned step view used by oyzu build, at 80 columns or the terminal's narrower width. Downloads name each member, its downloaded size and verification result. Install rows report actual work; Linux needs no separate Linux engine. Live terminals show running rows; redirected output prints start and completion lines without redraws. A non-fatal Linux-engine or shim failure has a warning row and a Warnings section with the reason, a short cause and a recovery command. The update stays installed. -v includes the complete child cause and full digests; ordinary human output abbreviates digests. --json keeps the original records and full values, with the additive previous.runs status field described below. Untrusted terminal controls are escaped in human output. oyzu self status groups Installation and Updates, shows the last check as an age, and adds its absolute timestamp with -v. oyzu self versions marks the followed channel with both a symbol and a word; a pinned install shows its pin instead of a followed-channel mark. --all also reports whether each recent version is installed, available, or has no asset for this OS. With NO_COLOR, TERM=dumb, or no color capability, marks become words (ok, warn, FAIL) and rules use dashes. Tables become labelled records without color or when they do not fit, preserving every value. Status names a previous local build as, for example, Previous local build (0.2.2-dev.gabc…) · oyzu self rollback. In oyzu --json self, previous.version remains null for a local build; previous.runs contains that previous binary's complete --version line, in the same form as an update result's runs. Status identifies the previous file on disk as rollback does, then reads its version only when it matches the recorded digest. This stays offline. runs is null if the file is missing, no longer matches, or its version cannot be read; the other status fields are unchanged.

A version's channel comes from its version string. GitHub's prerelease flag is ignored, so the 0.2.0 Preview is a stable version. The existing GitHub release list supplies tag_name, optional published_at and assets (name, id, optional digest). Additional release and asset fields are ignored; missing dates and assets remain readable. Draft releases, unrecognized version kinds and tags for other packages are excluded. There is no separate channel manifest, schema revision or minimum-reader gate for this metadata. Listing availability means the executable and its two evidence files are present; installation still verifies their signatures and bytes. Channel Contains Release tags stable releases without a prerelease part oyzu/v0.2.1 beta stable releases plus release candidates and betas oyzu/v0.3.0-rc.1, oyzu/v0.3.0-beta.2 nightly all of the above plus nightly builds oyzu/v0.2.2-alpha.0.nightly.20261027, oyzu/v0.3.0-rc.1.nightly.20261028 A wider channel never runs behind a narrower one: beta takes 0.3.0 as soon as it is stable. oyzu self decides the newest version by semantic version order of the signed tag, and a release counts only when it has the executable for your platform and both of its evidence files. A nightly's version names the release it was built after, so version order matches build order. After a stable 0.2.1, nightlies are 0.2.2-alpha.0.nightly.<date>, below any alpha, beta, candidate or release of 0.2.2. After a prerelease such as 0.3.0-rc.1, they are 0.3.0-rc.1.nightly.<date>, above rc.1 and below rc.2. A nightly follower therefore moves to each new prerelease or release and to every later nightly, in the order they were built: 0.2.1 < 0.2.2-alpha.0.nightly.20261027 < 0.2.2-beta.1 < 0.2.2-beta.1.nightly.20261028 < 0.2.2 < 0.3.0-rc.1 < 0.3.0-rc.1.nightly.20261029 < 0.3.0

Installs made by the install scripts or by oyzu self update themselves by default. At most once every 24 hours, an ordinary command you run in a terminal starts a background oyzu self update and carries on without waiting. The background run downloads, verifies and swaps in the newest version of your channel, or with --manual only records that one is available. The next command you run in a terminal then prints one line on standard error: ✓ oyzu updated 0.2.0 → 0.2.1 (stable) · undo: oyzu self rollback ! oyzu 0.2.1 is available on stable · run oyzu self update Nothing is checked, started or printed when any of these is true: OYZU_SELF_UPDATE=off is set, or the CI variable is set (to anything except false). The version is pinned. Standard error is not a terminal, or the command runs with --json. The command is help, --version, a tool shim, shell activation or the prompt hook, oyzu env, oyzu exec, oyzu run, oyzu which, oyzu shell or oyzu self itself. The folder has no install receipt, or the running binary is not the release the receipt records (a local build). OYZU_SELF_UPDATE=off only turns off the automatic check; the oyzu self commands still work when you run them. A swap never interrupts work: programs that are running keep the binary they started with, and the next start gets the new one.

Before a downloaded binary can replace anything, all of these must hold. Otherwise the command stops with SELF_UPDATE_UNVERIFIED or SELF_UPDATE_DIGEST_MISMATCH, and nothing in the folder changes. Its SHA-256 matches the digest the release reports for the asset. <asset>.provenance.sigstore.json is signed by oyzu's release builder key, names the release builder, and covers exactly that digest. <asset>.publication.sigstore.json is signed by oyzu's release publisher key, covers that digest, places it in oyzuai/oyzu-releases at this tag under this asset name, and names the provenance from step 2. An old signed binary moved under a newer tag or another name is refused. The new binary runs --version before it is swapped in. The two public keys are built into oyzu; they are the ones in the [publish.requirements] of the repository's oyzu.toml. There is no option to skip a check. The same checks cover oyzu-shim and, on macOS and Windows, the Linux oyzu used for isolated builds.

oyzu self only changes the folder that holds the running oyzu, links resolved: File Purpose oyzu, oyzu-shim (.exe on Windows) The installed binaries. oyzu.previous, oyzu-shim.previous (oyzu.previous.exe, oyzu-shim.previous.exe on Windows) The binaries from before the last change, for oyzu self rollback. One generation is kept. .oyzu-install.json The install receipt: channel, pin, mode, repository, version, tag and digest, the previous version, the last check and a pending notice. .oyzu-self.lock Locked by the operating system while a change runs, so two never overlap. Normal completion or failure releases it even when an unrelated child retains a descriptor. A competing foreground change reports SELF_UPDATE_BUSY immediately; a busy background update is skipped. The operating system also closes the process's handle if it crashes. The file stays. .oyzu-update/ Downloads before the swap. Removed afterwards. Receipt readers tolerate descriptive additions; channel and mode values remain closed, and a matching receipt digest is still required to recognize the running binary as a managed installation. A newer minimum-reader marker is advisory. If a receipt rewrite would discard unknown data from a newer-marked record, Oyzu refuses with FILE_READER_TOO_OLD and leaves the receipt intact. Update Oyzu before changing its mode or channel. Published 0.3.8 accepts baseline descriptive receipt additions but still refuses higher minimum-reader markers. The swap renames instead of overwriting: the old oyzu becomes oyzu.previous and the verified download takes its name. Every platform allows renaming a running executable, which is why this works on Windows too. If a rename fails, the binaries already swapped are put back. After the swap: On Windows, the new oyzu reshim runs (after a rollback too), because Windows shims are hard links to the old oyzu-shim.exe. It runs only when the shared shims folder is new, has no owner record, or is already owned by the Oyzu being replaced. If another Oyzu owns the shims (for example when you install into a scratch folder or an older version), the install leaves them alone and reports unchanged (shims belong to another Oyzu; run oyzu reshim to take them); taking them over stays the explicit oyzu reshim. On Linux and macOS, shims are links to oyzu and already reach the new binary. On macOS and Windows, the new oyzu engine install --linux registers the release's Linux oyzu for isolated builds, as the install scripts do. A failure there is reported, and oyzu stays updated.

A folder whose oyzu matches no release, such as one built with oyzu build cli or installed by oyzu run bootstrap -- --source, is a local build. It is never updated automatically. When self-update settings record a channel, oyzu self update follows it again, just as oyzu self channel <that channel> would. This includes returning to a release after oyzu self rollback restored a local build; following the channel clears a pin and enables automatic updates. oyzu self update --check reports the available release without replacing the local build or changing its settings. With no recorded channel, oyzu self update refuses with SELF_UPDATE_LOCAL_BUILD and Next: oyzu self channel stable. That command records stable and installs its newest release. oyzu self install <version> or oyzu self channel <name> also replaces a local build when you ask, keeping it as oyzu.previous. An install from before oyzu self existed has no receipt. The first oyzu self update adopts it, as a stable install with automatic updates, when the running binary's digest equals a published asset's digest.

oyzu self reads the same variables as the install scripts: Variable Default Meaning OYZU_RELEASE_REPO the receipt's repository, else oyzuai/oyzu-releases Repository whose releases are read OYZU_API_BASE https://api.github.com GitHub API base, for GitHub Enterprise or a test server OYZU_DOWNLOAD_BASE https://github.com Base of anonymous release downloads GH_TOKEN, then GITHUB_TOKEN none Sent only to the API origin, to lift the anonymous limit of 60 requests an hour or to read a private mirror A mirror must serve the same signed evidence as oyzuai/oyzu-releases; the publication signature still has to name that repository. Downloads go through the proxy and certificate settings other oyzu downloads use. Plain HTTP is allowed only for loopback test servers. An unpublished source candidate cannot be installed by self update through a local channel: changing these bases does not authorize new signing keys or unsigned provenance. Use the install script's local-channel route to exercise candidate installation separately. That route checks the advertised digest only and does not prove signed self-update, retention of the previous version, or self rollback. Those checks still require an admitted signed release. Never disable verification to make a candidate pass.

Code Cause Recovery SELF_UPDATE_LOCAL_BUILD self update has no recorded channel for the local build oyzu self channel stable SELF_UPDATE_PINNED oyzu self update while a version is pinned oyzu self channel <name> to follow a channel again SELF_UPDATE_VERSION_UNAVAILABLE No such release, no release of that channel for your platform yet, or a PR build was requested oyzu self versions --all SELF_UPDATE_VERSION_INVALID The version is not a release version Use a version such as 0.2.1 or 0.3.0-rc.1 SELF_UPDATE_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE The release has no executable for this platform Choose another version SELF_UPDATE_UNVERIFIED, SELF_UPDATE_DIGEST_MISMATCH A check in Verification failed Don't use that release; report it. Nothing was changed SELF_UPDATE_UNRUNNABLE The downloaded binary does not run on this host Choose another version. Nothing was changed SELF_UPDATE_HTTP, SELF_UPDATE_NETWORK The release repository could not be read Check the connection, HTTPS_PROXY or GH_TOKEN, then retry SELF_UPDATE_WRITE The install folder is not writable, the filesystem cannot lock .oyzu-self.lock, or a rename failed Check the folder's permissions; a package manager's folder is updated by that manager SELF_UPDATE_BUSY Another oyzu self operation holds the lock; reported immediately (a background update skips as busy instead) Wait a minute and retry SELF_UPDATE_NO_PREVIOUS oyzu self rollback with no oyzu.previous Nothing to roll back All of them exit with status 1.

Linux, macOS and Windows on x86_64 use the same rename swap. Unpublished source builds still require explicit installation; API overrides do not admit unsigned updates. ARM64 hosts, including x64 executables running under emulation, are unsupported. Existing architecture detection and old release assets do not establish support. The channel list reads the newest 30 releases (100 with versions --all). Release signing uses oyzu's self-managed release keys, not keyless Sigstore. Changing those keys needs a release, signed with the old keys, whose binary carries the new ones. oyzu 0.2.0 predates oyzu self, so after installing it the command is missing. Run oyzu.previous self rollback (Windows: oyzu.previous.exe self rollback) from the same folder to go back, or reinstall with the install script. Unsigned internal dev builds and pull request builds are not available through self-update. Organization policy over the channel or automatic updates is not available yet.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/shell-activation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Shell activation puts a project's tools and [env] settings into your terminal as you cd into it, and puts your environment back when you leave. Use it for everyday work in an interactive shell. For a single command, use oyzu exec; to see what would be applied, use oyzu env. Supported shells: Bash and Zsh on Linux and macOS, and PowerShell 7.5 or newer on Windows. Git Bash on Windows uses Bash activation. Windows cmd.exe does not support activation or the activation-provided oyzu-dev command; use PowerShell or Git Bash for that workflow. Ordinary oyzu commands can still run from cmd.exe with an external driver on PATH. oyzu activate cmd (also cmd.exe, including --shims) exits 2 without applying an environment. Its error gives the activation commands for PowerShell and Git Bash. Open PowerShell 7.5+ and run oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression, or open Git Bash and run eval "$(oyzu activate bash)". Activate in the Oyzu checkout to get oyzu-dev; typing oyzu-dev in cmd.exe does not define the launcher.

Bash or Zsh: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" # or: oyzu activate zsh cd ./project-a cd ../project-b oyzu deactivate PowerShell: oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression Set-Location ./project-a Set-Location ../project-b oyzu deactivate Entering a project applies its environment and tools. Moving to another project or leaving restores what you had before. The first time, a project's [env] values may be skipped until you trust the folder. To set up every supported shell and keep oyzu and the shims on the persistent PATH, run oyzu shell install (the install scripts do); for one shell, run oyzu shell install SHELL --rc-file PATH. See installing activation in a shell profile. If activation fails with unknown field strength, the executable predates the installed receipts. Select a current Oyzu executable and activate again, keeping the receipts and installed tools intact. See receipt compatibility and recovery.

Activate from Oyzu’s own checkout to define oyzu-dev, which runs the latest dist/cli/<os>/<arch>/oyzu[.exe] without changing the everyday oyzu on PATH. Run oyzu build cli first. The function retains that checkout path when you change to another project; deactivation removes it. It refuses to drive builds of its own checkout. See the source development loop and explicit promotion.

A project that only sets environment variables needs no tools, lock file, install or account. [env] APP_MODE = "development" _.path = ["./bin", "./node_modules/.bin"] _.path adds directories to the front of PATH, in order. To add some to the end as well: [env] _.path = { prepend = ["./bin"], append = ["./scripts"] } Shell activation, oyzu exec and shims apply these values once the folder is trusted. oyzu run and oyzu build always apply them.

env._ is reserved for settings like _.path. It's never exported as a variable. Values are literal. There's no variable expansion, scripts, .env loading or command substitution. Setting env.PATH directly is an error. Use _.path. Relative paths are relative to the file that declares them (including local and profile files), not to your current folder. Use "." for the declaring folder. Directories don't have to exist. Empty entries, NUL, control characters and an embedded PATH separator are errors.

Normal configuration precedence applies. The winning _.path replaces any inherited one entirely. [] clears project additions. The final PATH order is: tool shims, project prepends, your existing PATH, then project appends. Directories already on your PATH stay where they are.

Inside Git, the project root is the repository root unless you pass --root. Outside Git, it's the outermost folder with Oyzu configuration. Nested files affect only their own subtree. Installed tools live in the shared user store, not in the project. oyzu activate --store <dir> uses a different store. A relative path is resolved from where you run the command. Use the same store for install and activate.

oyzu run <task> --store <path> runs a task with tools from that store. The path is resolved from where you run the command, and applies to the whole task, including hooks and prerequisites. Missing tools aren't installed and there's no fallback to another store. oyzu run list --store <path> only lists tasks; it doesn't open or create the store. Put task arguments after --. A --store after -- goes to the task.

You can activate outside any project. Starting PowerShell in an unconfigured directory such as Windows System32 keeps activation ready for the next directory change. Unrelated files there are not stored in the shell session's input inventory. Changing folder applies the new environment before your next command. Edits to configuration are picked up at the next prompt. Run _oyzu_hook to refresh by hand. Hooks never install tools, run tasks or use the network. Tools in [tools] must already be installed and locked. Each terminal keeps its own state. A nested shell can activate and change projects without affecting its parent. oyzu deactivate restores the environment the shell started with. Ordinary oyzu commands in an activated shell run the first oyzu on PATH (so a project-local build of oyzu takes over). Activation hooks keep using the oyzu that activated the shell. For activation fixes, update the installed CLI named by the shell profile and start a new shell or reactivate. Rebuilding only a project-local CLI does not replace the frontend already running its hooks. Bash has no native folder-change hook, so Bash activation defines cd, pushd and popd functions that call the builtin with the same arguments. A failed change returns the builtin's status and runs no hooks. After a successful change, a defined chpwd function runs first, then each defined function named in the chpwd_functions array, in order, stopping at the first failing hook; the change still succeeds. Oyzu adds its own _oyzu_hook_chpwd entry, keeps entries other tools registered and works under set -u; oyzu deactivate removes only Oyzu's entry. Activation replaces a cd, pushd or popd function of your own. Zsh uses its native chpwd hook. PowerShell 7 uses its native location-changed event. Windows PowerShell 5.1 has no such event, so there the new environment is applied at the next prompt: cd .\project; node -v typed on one line still runs with the previous folder's variables. Removing the profile block affects new shells only. Run oyzu deactivate in the current one.

Switching projects first undoes the previous project's changes. A variable is restored only if it still has the value Oyzu set. If you edited or unset it, your change is kept. A new project's value can override your edit temporarily; your edit comes back when you leave. An empty variable and an unset one are treated as different. PATH restoration keeps directories you added and removes the ones Oyzu added, even if they were reordered. If a duplicate makes that ambiguous, the entry is kept and you get a message. To unset a variable inside a project: [overrides] remove = ["env.APP_MODE"] It's restored when you leave, unless you changed it.

If configuration is invalid or a required tool isn't available, the previous project's changes are undone and OYZU_TOOL_STATUS is set to unavailable. Nothing from the failing project is half-applied. Fix the configuration or install the tools; the next prompt tries again. A working environment sets ready. Managed environment values and secret references aren't supported and fail with an error. Hooks never sign in or refresh credentials.

Environment variables can make shells, loaders and interpreters run code, so Oyzu won't apply a checkout's [env] and _.path in your shell until you say you trust it. Review the settings, then: Command Effect oyzu trust [path] Trust the project root (the current project if no path). oyzu trust --revoke [path] Remove the trust record. oyzu trust --list List trusted folders. All forms support --json. Trust is tied to the folder's real path (symlinks resolved) and survives edits to oyzu.toml. It never writes into the checkout or contacts a service. Records live under trusted-projects in the user state directory.

Tools still work. Only project and local [env], _.path and their removals are skipped. Your user-level environment values still apply. Prompt hooks, shims, exec and oyzu env --shell follow the same rule. A short hint about oyzu trust is printed once per command, or once per activated shell. oyzu run, oyzu build and build planning always apply project environment settings, trusted or not, so they match CI. oyzu config also shows them.

Setting Where Default Effect [trust] enabled = false User or administrator configuration true Turns the check off. [trust] parents = ["/absolute/projects"] User or administrator configuration none Trusts every project under these folders (for example E:\\projects on Windows). OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST=false Environment, one command Turns the check off. OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST=true Environment, one command Turns the check on, overriding files. CI (including CI=true) Automatic Trusted. Platform executors count as CI. Project and local files can't change these settings. Local coding agents get no exemption. --revoke removes only the explicit record. A parent rule, a disabled check or CI can still trust the folder.

oyzu env shows configuration sources, the resulting variables and the selected executables in separate tables. It doesn't change your shell. Sources show which file and profile won for each value, including oyzu.local.toml and _.path. PATH entries are listed in search order. Tool-provided variables and your existing PATH are included. In an untrusted folder, project entries are marked skipped until trusted. The PATH shown is the configured one, not what activation has applied. oyzu env --json lists the values and selected commands, with sources in the configuration array. projectEnvironmentSkipped says whether project values are being held back, and affected rows carry the same skipped until trusted status.

Ordinary values are shown in human and JSON output. Values with credential-like names (token, secret, password, API key, auth, private key) are redacted, as are values that look like credentials. This is a best-effort guess. Don't put secrets in innocently named variables.

oyzu exec -- program runs a command with the trust-filtered environment, including unsets, without changing your shell. A bare command name must be a declared tool; use an absolute path for anything else. oyzu env --shell SHELL prints one-time changes with no hooks. Use activate if you want them undone when you leave. _.path isn't passed to tasks as a variable and isn't a build input.

Directories Oyzu adds to PATH use normal drive or UNC paths, without \\?\ prefixes. Your existing entries keep their original spelling. Windows PowerShell 5.1 activates and switches environments when you change folder, applying the change at the next prompt rather than mid-line. Keeping empty variables needs PowerShell 7.5 or newer.

Supported shells are Bash, Zsh and PowerShell 7.5+. PowerShell before 7.5 can't keep empty environment values (Microsoft documentation). Other shells, managed values and secret references aren't supported.
Configuration for the cascade and the user state directory. Tool shell environment for oyzu env details, shims and profile installation. Tool commands for installing a project's tools.

Run oyzu shell check in the process environment you want to verify. It lists commands that resolve before Oyzu's shims, the winning executable, its PATH source and a suggested fix. Exit status is 0 with no shadowing commands, or 1 when any are found. --json returns a shadowed array. The check is read-only, lists only the shims folder, and needs no network or project configuration. A missing or empty shims folder has no shadowing commands; this does not prove a tool is installed. oyzu shell install also reports shadowing, but still succeeds when setup succeeds. Windows combines the machine Path before the user Path for new processes. A system Node installation can therefore win over shims on the user Path, even when an interactive PowerShell profile puts the shims first. The check reports both registry-based new-process PATH and current-process PATH separately. Restart programs after changing persistent PATH; existing processes keep their old environment. Linux and macOS checks inspect only the current process PATH, not a prediction of login-shell or GUI environments. To verify Windows lookup without a PowerShell activation profile, open a new Command Prompt and run where node followed by oyzu shell check. The first where result should be the shim. A successful machine installation can still report current-process shadowing until that terminal is restarted. On a single-user Windows machine, run these in an elevated terminal: oyzu shell install --machine oyzu shell check # Undo the machine entries added by Oyzu: oyzu shell remove --machine --machine puts the per-user shims folder and the folder holding oyzu first on the machine Path. This suits single-user machines. On shared machines, remove or reorder the system copy instead: other users should not run tools from your writable folder. It does not elevate automatically or edit shell profiles. On Linux and macOS there is no machine Path; use the login profile and oyzu shell check instead. If a Unix startup line (nvm, Homebrew shellenv or pyenv, for example) prepends PATH after Oyzu's block, move the block marked # >>> oyzu below that line or rerun oyzu shell install. Reinstallation moves a recognized, unmodified login-profile PATH block to the end. Modified blocks are refused and preserved for manual repair. Services, scheduled tasks, launchd jobs and systemd units read no shell profile. Set the job's own PATH to start with the shims folder, or invoke a shim by its absolute path, for example <shims folder>/node (<shims folder>\node.exe on Windows). Obtain the folder with oyzu reshim, and run oyzu shell check with the job's environment to verify precedence. Oyzu installs no service or scheduled task and does not configure launchd or systemd for you.

documents.t: CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/stage-reuse.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Stage reuse restores an earlier build action's outputs when its admitted inputs still match. Use this page to check which builders can reuse stages, which commands run again, and why an unchanged build can refuse reuse. crun is the container runtime Oyzu uses to run isolated Linux actions without a Docker daemon. Status: experimental. Complete-read lifecycle reuse is available for Maven, Gradle, Ant, npm, Helm, eligible go/app stages and conventional .NET compile/test/pack on Linux crun. Compatible Java plugins reuse eligible Maven modules and Gradle projects independently. Generated pip python/app builds reuse on Linux crun with a current plugin package; other Python lanes do not yet. Windows Rust compilation can still report incomplete reads on unchanged builds. Native Windows stages with incomplete reads run again.

Illustrative commands, run from a project with a build target named app: oyzu build app --explain oyzu cache explain app oyzu cache explain app:build The build explanation reports reuse decisions for the current run. Cache explanation reads recorded key history for a target or action. Replace app:build with the action named by your builder. A reused action is labelled as reused; its tests and reports were not executed now.

A matching key is necessary, but reuse also requires admitted reads, bounded outputs and a valid stored result. The key binds source inputs, command and environment, admitted tools and dependencies, execution identity and producer outputs. Restored artifacts and required reports still pass the current checks. On the native host, reads must be complete through admitted native observations or fixed command semantics. A predicted source list or a private source copy alone does not establish completeness. Missing dep-info, unresolved runtime reads or unbounded outputs can require execution even when source is unchanged. Docker and crun share results keyed on the whole target: a stage that one isolated backend ran is reused by the other. Results keyed on enforced runtime reads exist only on crun, and a Docker result never satisfies one. An incomplete native stage cannot fall back to a whole-source key or be skipped by whole-target restoration. Other independently admitted stages can still hit. Adding inputs covers known files; it does not prove that a script, plugin or test reads nothing else. Authored tasks with cache = true and declared outputs follow the same rule: only complete reads of that action admit reuse. Supported native Node commands on Linux can use crun per action with frozen source, bounded producer outputs, the locked native tool and an identified runtime root. Captured isolated Node targets retain their own complete-read path. Unsupported commands and native Windows/macOS actions rerun with a named explanation. An inherited builder contract cannot admit an authored replacement. See authored tasks for prerequisites, source visibility, output bounds, diagnostics and the author's ambient output-independence obligation. An admitted native authored action keeps its lookup when a companion lacks a stage contract. The companion executes each time and no whole-target group can skip it. Only separately bounded, frozen producer bytes are visible to the consumer; equal hook output can hit and changed consumed bytes miss. Required checks still run or reparse restored reports. --no-cache preserves the selected read view, including denied outside reads, while disabling lookup, storage and history. On native Windows, Maven/Gradle lifecycles and arbitrary npm scripts run again because their runtime reads are incomplete. build --explain and cache explain app name the refusal: native reads are incomplete on this host. Windows has no merged complete-read backend for Vite or uv lifecycles. An unchanged source tree or a private source copy cannot make them reusable. The explanation points to the isolated Linux crun path for supported builders; run that command on a Linux host. It does not enable native Windows reuse. Clearing the cache does not fix missing read admission. --no-cache executes the same native commands without action-cache reads or writes; an external input change must affect both ordinary and uncached builds. See native Windows refusal. The experimental Windows ETW complete-read pipeline remains disabled by default. Capture and decoding exist, but live ETW coverage is unproven without an elevated validation run. Each capture retains at most 262,144 events and 64 MiB of event metadata plus payload bytes (allocator overhead is additional). Exceeding either limit permanently marks the capture incomplete, refusing reuse and publication. Malformed Close events also refuse. Path canonicalization refuses case-sensitive ancestor directories and unavailable case-sensitivity attributes, so distinct absence probes cannot be merged by case folding. There is no user-facing switch to enable this path. Stage reuse is separate from Cargo incremental state, individual compiler-result caching, tool downloads and prepared dependencies. A stage that executes again may still benefit from those caches. See action-cache controls for disabling reuse or selecting local and remote storage. No account is needed for local reuse.
documents.s: When can a stage reuse a result?

documents.t: The table describes successful unchanged builds with compatible CLI/plugin versions, caching enabled and no overriding hooks or tasks. A changed admitted input or rejected result can rerun any eligible stage. “Always reruns” means whenever that stage is selected. Preparation and validation can still run on a hit. Builder Path What can reuse What always reruns How to see why Rust Native host Compilation and Clippy with complete Cargo observations; fixed-read rustfmt Unbounded test/coverage stages; compile or lint with incomplete reads build --explain; cache explain <target> Java: Maven/Gradle Isolated Linux crun Coupled lifecycle per admitted module/project, including compilation, archives and validated test/coverage evidence; separate archive exports Preparation and current report validation still apply; unbounded module views retain the whole lifecycle build --explain; cache explain <target> Java: Maven/Gradle Native host Fixed-read formatter, with a compatible plugin Lifecycle and Checkstyle: incomplete reads/unbounded outputs build --explain; cache explain <target> Java: Ant Isolated Linux crun Coupled build/test/JAR target lifecycle and validated test/coverage reports; archive exports Preparation, separate quality actions and current report/artifact validation; compound authored commands retain conservative reads build --explain; cache explain <target> Java: Ant Native host Archive export when its producer workspace is unchanged Build/test/archive and quality actions: incomplete reads/unbounded outputs build --explain; cache explain <target> Node: npm/pnpm/Yarn Classic Isolated Linux crun Script-free shared install and independent member build/test actions; contained direct workspace links can restore Install with lifecycle/environment-read uncertainty or unsupported links; aggregate root dispatch retains workspace scope build --explain; cache explain <target>:<stage> Node: npm Native host Independently admitted bounded helpers; download caches remain separate Arbitrary build/package lifecycle scripts; bounded install selectors alone do not admit install reuse build --explain; cache explain <target> Helm Isolated Linux crun Packaging/rendering, lint, validation and helm-unittest with the enforced input view and locked tools Preparation and current artifact/report validation still apply; outputs remain location sensitive unless declared relocatable build --explain; cache explain <target>:<stage> Helm Native host No complete runtime read guarantee from chart predictions Incomplete chart stages rerun build --explain;
