cache explain <target> Go Native host Build, vet and format-check with complete admitted reads Stages whose read/output contracts are not admitted build --explain; cache explain <target> Python application Native host No complete backend/runtime read guarantee Preparation, application assembly and packaging without complete native admission build --explain; cache explain <target> Python application Captured Linux crun pip and uv distribution applications: preparation, assembly, generated pytest tests and packaging under their captured source contracts; a source edit does not rerun preparation Requirements applications and authored build or test tasks use the whole target as their read set. Poetry preparation always reruns build --explain; cache explain <target>:<stage> Go: go/app Isolated Linux crun Stages with complete admitted reads: compilation, generated test preparation, test results and exports Stages whose read/output contracts are not admitted; current report validation still applies build --explain; cache explain <target>:<stage> .NET Native host No native stage reuse: NuGet/MSBuild reads are unbounded Native restore, build, tests and packaging when selected build --explain; cache explain <target> .NET Isolated Linux crun Deterministic compile, test and pack per project for admitted literal reference graphs; otherwise conventional solution stages Offline restore regenerates local assets; publish and unknown/unbounded customizations rerun build --explain; cache explain <target> Rust's Windows x64/MSVC compile stage can report incomplete reads even on an unchanged build. Expect execution in that case. Fixed-read rustfmt, retained Cargo state and eligible individual compiler results have separate admission. Linux compilation can reuse when its observations are complete. See Rust native host builds for the current limits, including the distinction between declared-version compilation and full-build inferred-version finalization. Java reuse keeps Maven's verify or Gradle's coupled lifecycle together inside each module/project, with a compatible Java plugin. Native models supply module membership and dependency edges; no additional configuration is needed. For a → b → c (each module depends on the one before it), an unchanged rebuild reuses all modules, a c source edit reruns only c, and an a source edit invalidates the chain. Module keys include their sources, shared native build definitions, declared producers and admitted tool/dependency identities. Reports retain module ownership and reused evidence is labelled reused. Ant keeps its selected target set together. This does not cache every native task or test class separately. Maven dependency preparation still runs on warm lifecycle hits. Plain Java builds remain native. See Maven, Gradle and Ant. Ant's coupled lifecycle changes captured planning from 0.3.x, which planned build, test and archive as separate actions. oyzu build --isolated now runs the selected tests even without --full, and a failing test blocks the JAR, matching Maven and Gradle in 0.4.0. To retain separate Ant stages, use oyzu build --full without --isolated on the native host, with the native prerequisites. Plain oyzu build keeps native fast-mode check selection. There is no switch to restore split planning on the captured path; native host stages retain their incomplete-read limits and run without container isolation. Node's package-local workspace actions use native package-manager membership and dependency edges. An unchanged rebuild reuses every admitted member. Editing a leaf's source reruns its build/tests; editing a shared member's source also reruns its native dependents. Each member follows its own version output and required workspace producers. All member manifests key shared installation. For a metadata-only member package.json edit, npm and Yarn Classic can reuse an untouched leaf's build/tests when installation output stays identical; the edited member and its native dependents rerun. pnpm changes shared installation bookkeeping and reruns every member, even when package code stays identical. This accepted precision limit retains all readable installation bytes in keys. --explain names a stored result matches this key for npm/Yarn leaf hits and the changed app:prepare-dependencies output for pnpm reruns. Changed shared installation output invalidates all members for any manager. Named JUnit/LCOV reports retain reused producer labels. Shared root configuration keeps the whole workspace visible and refuses member reuse with node-member-shared-configuration. Non-crun executors refuse it with node-member-reuse-requires-crun. pnpm hooks/patches and active Yarn rc configuration refuse manifest-only install narrowing. A failed command that names a hidden path can report confined-read-outside-contract; optional probes that succeed are not diagnosed. This does not trace every read. Root aggregate scripts and opaque root dispatch keep their whole-workspace boundary. See Node workspace reuse. Helm retains the plugin's chart read bounds for bounded stages. Suites without complete observations use the entire admitted source view. Helm and helm-unittest bind their current locked tool identities, so a selected release or archive change invalidates reuse. oyzu install adopts the helm-unittest requirement without deleting existing installations. See Helm isolated reuse. Go's isolated go/app path can reuse stages with complete admitted reads. Build-phase generated test manifests and compiled tests are explicit outputs, consumed as identified inputs in test-stage read sets and keys. A changed manifest invalidates reuse; undeclared carried files are refused. Runtime tests include the whole admitted source view, so source edits can invalidate additional tests. See Go isolated stage reuse. Go's native build/vet read observations remain separate: incomplete native reads still refuse stage and whole-target reuse on Linux, Windows and macOS. Windows and macOS have no complete Go runtime-read enforcement backend. .NET's captured stage reads admit conventional compile/test/pack under Linux crun, including cross-root reuse when their retained bytes are location-free. Native host execution still refuses incomplete reads; other executors do not gain this complete boundary. With a compatible plugin, eligible multi-project solutions reuse compile, test and pack per project along literal reference edges. Unchanged projects reuse their results; a source edit reruns its project and reference dependents. Shared configuration changes invalidate all affected projects. Failed actions execute again on repeated failing builds and never become reusable successes. Shared or nested project folders, solutions containing applications and unknown customizations retain the solution-wide path. See .NET project reuse. Module splitting retains the whole Maven reactor or Gradle lifecycle when the source inventory contains links, exceeds the selector limit, has an invalid module graph, or contains module-local control files outside src/ and the native build definitions. This conservative fallback lets configurations share files such as build-tools/checkstyle.xml or x/version.txt on every captured executor, including Docker. It does not grant native-host reuse or relax isolated read enforcement. Runtime reads of sibling sources remain outside a split module's admitted view.
documents.s: What can reuse for each builder?

documents.t: For Maven, Gradle, Ant, npm, Helm, eligible go/app stages and .NET, select the existing Linux crun path: oyzu build app --isolated --no-docker --explain This requires the builder's locked tools, prepared dependencies, admitted base execution image and an available Linux crun runtime. See the execution image for provisioning. No extra reuse setting is needed. Docker, other executors and native Windows/macOS execution do not inherit this complete-read guarantee. The executor enforces the identified source, dependency, tool/runtime and producer-output view. Live /proc and /sys data and undeclared host files are hidden except the closed startup allowance below; network access is denied. Private output state and validated phase handoffs prevent an action from reading unrelated bundle output. A handled file absence is stable within this view. A failed unsupported read stores no reusable success. This is enforcement, rather than a syscall trace. The closed non-keying device allowance is /dev/random, /dev/urandom, /dev/null and /dev/zero. The closed self-proc startup allowance also supplies read-only files for the requesting process and its actual executable readlink, without exposing other processes' entries. Facts record self-proc presence only, never contents. These ambient values do not enter keys. Entropy must not affect retained outputs; workloads that embed random or ambient values are outside this reuse contract. Completion records retain these allowance facts under oyzu.dev/ambient-reads; they describe permitted reads, not observed syscalls. CPU count remains a separate keyed boundary fact. --no-cache executes under the same isolation and report checks. It does not make an unsupported workload admissible. Offline execution still requires previously acquired tools, images and dependencies; stage reuse does not supply missing prerequisites.

Native actions receive private TEMP, TMP and TMPDIR paths allocated by Oyzu. Inherited, configured and builder-declared values for those three names are replaced before launch and excluded from native action keys. Changing only those overwritten values does not invalidate an otherwise reusable action. Environment policy still validates authored values and the final environment. This exception applies only to those executor-owned temporary variables. Passed HOME, USERPROFILE, APPDATA and LOCALAPPDATA values remain keyed. A configuration file read as ordinary program data also remains an input: editing its bytes can invalidate the stage. Private scratch does not establish complete reads or add host isolation. See native environment inputs and temporary directories.
documents.s: Do temporary-directory changes invalidate native reuse?

documents.t: Typed locked-tool external inputs bind runtimes outside the source tree to core-admitted identities from oyzu.lock, such as Java's JDK, Node's runtime, Helm and its helm-unittest plugin, or the .NET SDK. Core resolves these identities before lookup; a missing binding fails admission. A changed identity invalidates its consumers. Naming a tool does not establish complete reads or grant arbitrary external file access. Prepared native builds project mandatory oyzu.lock source/version identity to the selected closure: selected tool recipes, plugin pins and transitive tool dependencies. Unrelated toolsets, unused plugin pins and valid unused current resolutions do not themselves invalidate that identity. Selected tool or builder changes still do. The whole lock remains structurally validated. This projection does not discard raw bytes when the lock is an authored input or read explicitly as program data. Unknown reads, incomplete tool declarations or missing preparation retain conservative fallbacks. See native cache keys for the full rules.
documents.s: Which tool and lock changes invalidate reuse?

documents.t: A bounded single-root npm or script-free workspace install keys its manifests/lockfile, npm configuration, tool identity and other admitted execution inputs. Only the generated OYZU_VERSION default is omitted when the admitted model establishes that installation cannot read it. Build and test stages always keep their version input, and explicit environment values remain keyed. Workspace installation uses native membership and checks admitted registry archive manifests for lifecycle or implicit native-compilation uncertainty. It keys every member manifest and manager control. On Linux, relative workspace links can restore when they stay inside the workspace and point directly to ordinary files or directories. Escapes, indirect links and unsupported file types refuse restoration. Ordinary source edits leave this install key unchanged. Root or dependency install scripts, implicit native compilation, incomplete lock facts, interpolated manager configuration and runtime-loading hooks keep the version input and refuse install reuse. Reviewed dependency file-read allowances do not prove unread environment values. Arbitrary lifecycle code conservatively reads the whole admitted source view. See Node stage reads for configuration and package-manager limits.
documents.s: When does npm installation survive a source edit?

documents.t: oyzu build --explain reports refusals as well as key changes. A typical refusal is native stage has no complete observed reads; native stage reuse requires complete reads. A whole-target refusal names the stage that needs complete reads and bounded outputs. An incomplete-read refusal means the stage executes again; it is not a failed test or a corrupt cache entry. Read the named stage and reason; use oyzu cache explain <target> or the action ID for recorded decisions. Clearing the cache cannot supply missing read admission. Keep executing the stage, or update to a compatible builder/CLI when support is available. For ordinary misses, compare the named source, tool, builder, command/environment or producer input. See explaining reuse and failure recovery.
documents.s: Why did unchanged inputs still run?

documents.t: CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/target-workspaces.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A native oyzu build gives each target its own private copy of its source before it prepares dependencies. The target's hooks and stages share that copy, but other targets can't see the files it generates. To pass files from one target to another, use materialize. This page covers which source goes into a target's workspace, how artifacts are passed between targets, and how Python wheels and Docker images fit in. Note: Private workspaces keep targets apart; they aren't a sandbox. Native processes still have your user's access to files and the network. oyzu run tasks run in your checkout as usual. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.
documents.s: Host target workspaces and artifact inputs

documents.t: Each target's folder is copied with your current edits and untracked files, minus the usual exclusions (.git, .oyzu, dist, target, node_modules, virtual environments). Files outside the target's folder must be listed in inputs, unless they already belong to the same native project: builds: api: uses: node/app path: api inputs: [../../shared/schemas] inputs is a list of file or folder paths relative to the build.yaml that declares them, not to the target's path. Paths must stay inside the Git repository, or inside the build root when there is no repository. Absolute paths and paths that escape fail. On the container path, an input must stay under the folder holding build.yaml and match at least one captured file. It becomes part of the target's cache scope (declared inputs). Declared inputs also join each stage's source read set, including stages with explicit captured-provider contracts. A declaration such as inputs: [docs/data] keeps that folder visible to a confined stage and includes its files in the stage's key. Paths remain relative to build.yaml even for a target in a subfolder. Declarations add reads; they cannot make an unbounded stage confined. Copies keep the repository-relative layout. Each target gets its own copy. Symlink and reparse-point restrictions still apply. Only selected targets and their dependencies need their inputs. For example, oyzu build cli doesn't need the docs target's inputs, but oyzu build docs and a full build do. A missing input of a selected target fails before anything runs. Use artifact relationships, not inputs, for another build's generated output. Oyzu doesn't infer what a script reads.

Private workspaces live in .oyzu/host-workspaces and persist between builds: Each build updates them in place. Files whose size, modification time and read-only flag match aren't rewritten; others are copied again, and files no longer selected are removed. A source file is read and hashed only when it changed. Oyzu remembers each file's digest with its size, modification time and file identity in .oyzu/source-stat-cache.json; while those still match and the private copy is current, the remembered digest is used without opening the file. Builds with --require-release read and hash every file. Like Git's index, this trusts file metadata. On Linux and macOS the status-change time catches a rewrite that keeps the size and restores the modification time; on Windows such a rewrite isn't noticed. Delete .oyzu/source-stat-cache.json to make the next build read everything. The build's source revision, recorded for verification evidence, hashes each file with line endings normalised. Oyzu remembers that hash by the file's content digest in .oyzu/source-revision-digests.json, so only content it hasn't seen is read again. Its time is part of the Source evidence step. Builds with --require-release read every file for it too. Between builds the copies are parked outside the checkout (see source parking). At the end of a build, files the build generated inside the workspace are removed. An interrupted build leaves state that the next build cleans up. Copies keep modification times, and paths stay the same between builds, so native tools can stay incremental. Rust compiler caches stay in the original project's .oyzu/native/rust, under the cache budget. Cleaning workspaces never removes bundles, installed tools or compiler caches.

builds: server: uses: rust/app path: server consumer: uses: node/app path: consumer materialize: - from: server to: inputs/server - from: server into: inputs/original Field Meaning from The producer target. Required. artifact The producer's logical output name. Optional when the producer has one primary artifact. to Exact destination for a file, or the folder to fill with a directory artifact's contents. into Folder to place a file in, keeping its file name. If the file name is only known after the build (a native wheel), the real name is used; see file name discovery. Directory artifacts use to. usage runtime (default), build or data; see artifact compatibility. runtime A local image that must accept a native Python wheel; see native wheels. Only with usage: runtime. Set exactly one of to and into. Destinations are relative to the consumer target. Archives aren't extracted, source files aren't overwritten, and destinations can't overlap. materialize already orders the targets; don't add depends_on as well. Platform compatibility and artifact identity are checked. Artifacts are passed after all of the producer's actions and required reports succeed, and before the consumer's first action. Each consumer gets its own copy, checked against the collected digest, and the manifest records each handoff. Inputs that the consumer needs during dependency preparation (for example, files npm ci reads) aren't supported. The producer's pre_build, build and post_build actions share its workspace, so changes a post-hook makes to the output are included. A failure in any of them means no artifact is passed, even if output files were written. A failed producer blocks its consumers; independent artifacts can still appear in the failed bundle. A host-built Python output is a wheel folder named primary, so use to. A python/package built in a worker image (--image pip=<image>) exports files named wheel and sdist; choose one with artifact: wheel and into.

materialize.usage says how the consumer uses the artifact: usage Compatibility checked against runtime (default) The consumer artifact's platform. build The platform the consumer's build runs on, for a tool that runs during the build. The producer must be unambiguous. data Nothing: the bytes are included without any runtime claim. The output must still be unique, the producer successful and the bytes verified. Artifacts carry oyzu.dev/artifact-compatibility: Value Meaning target Built for a specific platform. pending Must be inspected by the builder before use. independent Runs anywhere, such as a pure Python wheel. native Bound to one platform, and checked against the consumer's runtime. unknown Compatibility can't be established. pending and unknown artifacts can't be used at runtime. The handoff record notes the consumer's platform and usage under oyzu.dev/artifact-consumer. These checks don't certify arbitrary binaries or ABIs. When a consumer has several platforms, each gets the producer variant built for its platform. A producer with no platforms that outputs a python/package wheel can serve several consumer platforms: pure wheels are shared, native wheels go through the runtime check. A plain native build always uses host outputs; for a native binary feeding an image for another platform, use --all-platforms.

A native build can also include docker/image targets. Images build in a rootless BuildKit worker, while the other targets still run on the host. Docker is needed only when an image target is selected. No build container gets the host Docker socket, and no nested Docker daemon is started. Note: Image workers in native builds are experimental and tested on Windows. Image targets need the base execution image and, for RUN steps, the pinned rootless BuildKit worker; the Docker plugin package supplies the helpers. Oyzu pulls both by pinned digest on first use. Base images must already be in the Docker daemon. Preparation records their identities, and worker actions run offline. Your docker.apparmorProfile setting still applies. An image tag doesn't satisfy a tool pin. A Linux producer and image: builds: package: uses: python/package path: package image: uses: docker/image path: image materialize: - from: package to: payload oyzu build image --plan shows the producer, the artifact edge and each target's executor without contacting Docker. oyzu build image runs it. The Dockerfile can use COPY payload/ /wheels/ without knowing the wheel's versioned name. Installing the wheel into the image is up to the Dockerfile. The image's build context follows its source selection and .dockerignore, plus the materialized artifacts. Files your hooks generate don't join the context unless they were already part of it. Named image platforms must include the worker's platform. Use --all-platforms for several platforms. Fast builds assemble and verify the image. --full adds image assertions, lint and formatting. Image content and platform are always verified before publication. --isolated builds the whole graph in containers instead. Host Python wheel folders are inspected after collection. A wheel tagged pure Python and none-any can go to any platform. A host-built wheel whose tags all name one Linux x86_64 or aarch64 platform (linux_*, manylinux*, musllinux_*) is native and goes through the runtime check below. Other native tags, such as Windows or macOS, fail the handoff, even on the same OS.

Before a native wheel enters the consumer's workspace, Oyzu runs pip install --dry-run --no-index --no-deps for it in the consumer's runtime image, with networking off. pip decides whether the Python version, ABI and wheel tag fit. The runtime image is: the input's runtime: <image>, a local image (never pulled) that must match the consumer's platform; else the consumer's pip dependency base image (a requirements.txt used with a pinned base; see Docker images). materialize: - from: package to: inputs runtime: registry.example/python:3.12-slim # only needed without a pip base A consumer with neither, such as a plain COPY into scratch, can't receive a native wheel. Use usage: data to include it without the check. For generic linux_x86_64 and linux_aarch64 wheels, Oyzu also checks: libc. Oyzu inspects the wheel's .so files and the consumer's Python. A clear glibc/musl mismatch is refused before the image builds, naming the wheel, file, linkage and image. If it can't tell, it reports NATIVE_WHEEL_LIBC_UNVERIFIED and lets pip decide. Extension suffix. For a *.cpython-<version>-<platform>.so file, Oyzu compares the suffix with the consumer Python's supported suffixes. A mismatch, or a consumer that can't report them, gives the warning NATIVE_WHEEL_EXTENSION_SUFFIX_UNVERIFIED. The build continues. If you see it, check that the module imports in the final image; if not, build the wheel with that image's Python. Plain .so and .abi3.so files aren't compared. manylinux* and musllinux_* wheels skip these extra checks; pip decides. A rejection fails the consumer with the wheel name, the image and the libc mismatch or pip's message. It appears as an ERROR line, in diagnostics with --json, and in full in the action log. Wheels built for a version (cp313-cp313-linux_x86_64) are accepted only by the matching Python; abi3 wheels are accepted by any compatible Python. Host-built native wheels need a Linux host. Windows and macOS hosts build win_*/macosx_* wheels, which a Linux consumer refuses.
documents.s: Native wheels and the consumer runtime

documents.t: To get a Linux native wheel from any host with Docker, build it in a container with oyzu build --image pip=<image>. Use an image with a C compiler (not -slim) that meets the bring-your-own requirements; Oyzu mounts its engine, so the image needs no Oyzu worker. The wheel's tag comes from the Python that runs the build, the locked CPython when there is one, for example cp313-cp313-linux_x86_64. Oyzu finds the file (below), reads its tags from the wheel's WHEEL metadata and records it as native for the image's platform, so the consumer check applies.
documents.s: Wheels built in a worker image

documents.t: A planned output normally has an exact file name. The one exception is when a builder can only know the name after building: Python's python/package wheel output: if no file exists at the planned path, Oyzu looks for the single file {name}-{version}-*.whl next to it. No match fails with missing bundle path; several matches fail and name them. A file at the planned name, such as a pure py3-none-any wheel, is always used as is. Symlinks are ignored, and the usual containment, regular-file, digest and size checks apply. The bundle records the real file. The plan and --plan keep the planned name, so the two can differ for a native wheel. materialize with into writes the real name. to needs an exact name, so use into for a discovered file. An existing file is never overwritten. sdist, applications and other builders don't use discovery. This also applies to an older setup.py wheel whose planned tag is missing: a different tag is collected and classified from its metadata.

oyzu build --plan shows declared inputs and artifact relationships without installing, copying or building. During a build, Ctrl+C on Windows or SIGINT/SIGTERM on Unix cancels it. Oyzu stops starting actions, stops running processes and workers, keeps available logs and a failed bundle, blocks pending dependents, and exits with code 130. Post-hooks aren't guaranteed to run. After a forced kill (SIGKILL), check for leftover processes and build files yourself. To recover from an invalid input path, artifact selector, collision or failed command, fix it and rebuild. You never need to copy files into a consumer by hand. Each rebuild starts from a fresh private copy of the source.

Private workspaces are separation, not sandboxing, and don't make a build eligible for production publication. Native workspaces support Linux and Windows x86-64. macOS support is limited to the Zig path. Image-worker limits depend on the builder. The usage: build path is tested on Linux x86-64. Native wheel handling supports Linux x86_64 tags. ARM64 consumers, deeper libc version checks and Windows or macOS tags are unsupported. Choosing a build tool from a producer with several platform variants isn't supported.
Native local builds for the native build path. Directory artifacts and build bundles for artifact layout. Docker images for image builds.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-aqua.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Registry packages are command-line tools described by the aqua registry, the same catalog mise's aqua backend reads. Oyzu installs them with an oyzu: tool ID and verifies each download against the publisher's SHA-256. Use them for tools Oyzu doesn't provide itself, such as terraform, gh or ripgrep. Note: Experimental. Error codes, field names and the pinned registry snapshot may change. Supported on Linux x86-64; Windows and macOS are not supported yet. When a tool index is configured (the default), packages it lists install from the index. The rest of this page describes what Oyzu does when it resolves a recipe from the registry itself. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.
documents.s: Registry packages (oyzu: ids, from the aqua registry)

documents.t: oyzu install terraform@1.9.8 # a curated name oyzu install gh@2.49.2 # a catalog short name, stored as oyzu:gh oyzu install oyzu:burntsushi/ripgrep@14.1.1 oyzu install aqua:go-task/task@3.54.0 # mise spelling, rewritten to oyzu:task gh --version # runs the installed binary oyzu tools info oyzu:gh # provider, source, commands, platforms, verification oyzu tools versions oyzu:gh # releases, newest first, with excluded ones explained oyzu uninstall oyzu:gh In an activated shell, which the install script sets up, the plain tool commands run the pinned versions. Where a shell isn't activated, prefix them with oyzu exec --. Configuration stores the tool's canonical ID: [tools] "oyzu:task" = "3.54.0" "oyzu:gh" = "2.49.2" terraform = "1.9.8" # curated names can be written bare All tool commands work (scopes, --dry-run, --frozen, --offline, update, tools current, tools list). No account and no mise executable are needed.

mise's table form of a [tools] entry is accepted for every tool, with one option, version. It means the same as the plain string: [tools] "oyzu:gh" = { version = "2.49.2" } [tools."oyzu:jq"] version = "1.7.1" oyzu install gh@2.50.0 changes only version inside the table, keeping its form and comments. A table under an aqua: or core: key is replaced by a plain entry under the new key. Other options (os, exe, bin, asset_pattern, install_env, postinstall, ...) are ignored with a warning. They never run hooks or change the installation. oyzu config validate --strict turns the warnings into errors. A table without a valid version string is refused (CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE). Arrays of versions aren't supported.

Every spelling of a package resolves to one canonical ID, and configuration and the lock store that ID, so how you typed it never changes the lock. IDs never carry an aqua: prefix. Package Canonical ID Also accepted In the curated set (for example hashicorp/terraform) oyzu:<name> (oyzu:terraform) terraform, oyzu:hashicorp/terraform, aqua:hashicorp/terraform Any other registry package oyzu:<owner>/<repo>[/<name>], lowercased (oyzu:burntsushi/ripgrep) aqua:BurntSushi/ripgrep; a catalog short name (ripgrep) with oyzu install A GitHub repository's release assets github:<owner>/<repo> Oyzu's own providers (Node, Go, Rust, ...) oyzu:<name> (oyzu:go) go, and the older core:go Curated names are built into Oyzu, so they resolve without the network. Each is the package's primary name in mise's catalog, except cli/cli, which is oyzu:gh (mise's github-cli also works). Names that would clash with an Oyzu provider (kubectl, helm, k3d) or a Cargo helper aren't curated; those packages keep their owner/repo ID. aqua: is accepted as input wherever an ID is (commands, [tools] keys, policy) and rewritten. Oyzu never writes it. Installing a tool declared under an aqua: or core: key moves the declaration to the new key. The lock records the origin. Each lock entry lists the registry package in components (package:<owner>/<repo>), next to registry: and tag:. Older locks with aqua: or core: IDs are stale. oyzu install reports TOOL_LOCK_STALE naming the rename, and oyzu install --frozen fails. Run oyzu update to re-lock the same versions under their oyzu: IDs (same archives and digests). [tools] keys written as aqua: keep working and aren't rewritten. Unused current IDs do not require migration. A correctly identified oyzu: resolution without an environment root does not block build preparation. Legacy-ID migration removes legacy resolutions while preserving unrelated current-format resolutions. All resolution identities are still verified, including unused ones; changing a selected tool still invalidates its build cache entries.

As in mise, oyzu install gh@2.49.2 looks up a short name that Oyzu neither provides nor curates in mise's name catalog, expands it to the first backend Oyzu supports (aqua:cli/cli) and stores the canonical ID (oyzu:gh). oyzu:gh is looked up the same way. $ oyzu install gh@2.49.2 $ cat oyzu.toml [tools] "oyzu:gh" = "2.49.2" The catalog is the registry/*.toml data from the mise crate release 2026.10.5. Oyzu downloads it from static.crates.io, checks it against a pinned SHA-256 and caches it as <store>/catalogs/mise-registry-<digest>.crate. Once cached, it works offline. No mise code is run. A name Oyzu provides itself (node, go, ...) always resolves to Oyzu's provider. Short names work with oyzu install only. Other commands and [tools] keys need a curated name or the canonical ID. Situation Result Unknown name TOOL_NAME_UNKNOWN, suggesting the oyzu:<owner>/<repo> spelling. Only available through backends Oyzu lacks (cargo:, npm:, asdf:, ...) TOOL_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED, listing them. Catalog can't be fetched, or its digest differs TOOL_REGISTRY_UNAVAILABLE or TOOL_REGISTRY_DIGEST_MISMATCH.

Request Meaning Needs the GitHub release list 3.54.0 or v3.54.0 Exactly this release. No latest Newest stable release the recipe covers. Yes 2.49 Highest stable 2.49.x the recipe covers. Yes An exact version tries the tag spellings <version_prefix>v<version> and <version_prefix><version>, and uses the first whose checksum file exists. Pinned installs make no GitHub API request, so they can't hit its rate limit. latest and prefixes read GitHub's releases API (the newest 300 releases). Set GITHUB_TOKEN to raise the anonymous limit; it's sent to api.github.com only. Drafts are never offered. Pre-releases are only used when named exactly. The lock keeps your request and the exact release. A latest lock stays valid without re-reading the release list.

Registry. One pinned snapshot, aqua-registry v4.573.0, downloaded from raw.githubusercontent.com, checked against its SHA-256 and cached in the tool store as catalogs/aqua-registry-<digest>.yaml. Each Oyzu build uses a fixed snapshot. Resolution. Declaring or updating a tool evaluates its recipe for each default platform (linux/amd64/gnu, darwin/amd64/native, windows/amd64/msvc) with the recipe evaluator, reads the publisher's checksum file and writes one lock entry per platform. A platform with no build is recorded as unavailable. Recipe types. github_release (a GitHub release asset) and http (a direct download URL, such as https://releases.hashicorp.com/...). Other types (go_install, cargo, github_content, ...) are refused with SOURCE_KIND. Formats. The recipe's format decides how the download is unpacked: format Installed as tar.gz, tgz gzip tar tar.xz, txz xz tar tar.zst zstd tar tar plain tar zip ZIP raw (or an asset with no archive extension) The file is the executable. It's stored under the first command's name (<name>.exe on Windows) and every declared command runs it. Other formats (tar.bz2, tbz, single-file gz, bz2, xz or zst, 7z, dmg, pkg) fail with TOOL_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED. Archives are unpacked with limits on entries, size, depth and expansion ratio. The lock is the pin. Each lock entry holds the archive URL, its SHA-256, and in components what install needs: kind:, bin:<command>=<path in the archive>, tag: and registry:. A locked tool installs without the registry, and oyzu install --frozen into an empty store needs only the locked URLs. Download. Only the host archive is downloaded, and its SHA-256 must match the lock. GitHub's release hosts are always allowed. A recipe that downloads from elsewhere is allowed that host only over HTTPS on port 443, with a public DNS name (no IP address, single-label or .local-style name) and no credentials in the URL. Tool routes for registry packages aren't supported (TOOL_ROUTE_UNSUPPORTED). Commands. The executables a recipe declares (files) become the tool's commands. Without files, the command is the last part of the package name (kubectl for kubernetes/kubernetes/kubectl). On Windows, .exe is added as the registry specifies. With several commands, each is available through oyzu exec -- <command>, and each command's folder is added to PATH for child processes. When several names share one file (superfly/flyctl declares flyctl and fly), each works through oyzu exec, but a child process searching PATH only finds the file's own name.
documents.s: What is installed, and from where

documents.t: Install checks the publisher's SHA-256: the lock records the checksum from the recipe's checksum file for each platform, and the download must match it. A checksum file whose body is a single digest with no file name (like dl.k8s.io's kubectl.sha256) is read as that asset's digest. Recipes can also declare GitHub artifact attestations, cosign, SLSA provenance or minisign. Oyzu doesn't check those yet, and they don't stop an install. For example, oyzu install oyzu:gh@2.102.0 installs on its checksum even though the recipe declares an attestation. tools info says so. A successful install means the archive matches the checksum the publisher listed when you resolved it. It doesn't prove the publisher or the checksum file is authentic. Code Cause TOOL_CHECKSUM_MISSING The recipe declares no checksum, and the package isn't on the GitHub-reported digest list. TOOL_CHECKSUM_UNSUPPORTED The checksum isn't SHA-256, or the checksum file uses the regexp format. TOOL_CHECKSUM_UNVERIFIABLE The checksum file doesn't list the archive, or lists conflicting values.

A recipe without a checksum normally can't be locked. For a short, reviewed list of packages, Oyzu instead locks the SHA-256 that GitHub reports for the release asset in the package's own repository. The list currently holds protocolbuffers/protobuf/protoc. It isn't open to every checksum-less recipe, because that would weaken checks for tools nobody reviewed. Any other checksum-less package reports TOOL_CHECKSUM_MISSING. For a tool a builder detected, that's a warning row and the build continues; for a tool you pinned, it's an error.

Code Cause and fix TOOL_ALIAS_UNSUPPORTED Another backend (asdf:, vfox:, ...) isn't supported. The message lists what is. TOOL_SPEC_INVALID Not oyzu:<name>, oyzu:<owner>/<repo> (or <owner>/<repo>/<name>), github:<owner>/<repo> or the aqua: alias. TOOL_NAME_UNKNOWN oyzu:<name> isn't curated. Use oyzu:<owner>/<repo>, or oyzu install <name>. TOOL_NOT_IN_REGISTRY The package isn't in the pinned snapshot. Check the spelling. TOOL_VERSION_NOT_FOUND No such release, or nothing matches a prefix in the newest 300 releases. Run oyzu tools versions. TOOL_RATE_LIMITED GitHub refused the release list (anonymous limit or access policy). Set GITHUB_TOKEN, or request an exact version. TOOL_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED The format isn't in the format table. CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE A [tools] table has no valid version string. See option tables. TOOL_RECIPE_UNSUPPORTED The recipe uses something the evaluator doesn't support. See recipe resolution. TOOL_REGISTRY_UNAVAILABLE, TOOL_REGISTRY_DIGEST_MISMATCH The pinned snapshot couldn't be fetched, or doesn't match its digest.

oyzu tools versions oyzu:<name> lists releases, newest first, for this host. A release the recipe doesn't cover, with no build for this platform, or whose verification Oyzu can't perform appears under excluded with the reason, so the list shows what install would accept. oyzu tools info shows the provider, source, commands (once locked), platforms, eligibility under tools.allowed, declarations and the verification rule. Both support --json.

Supported on Linux x86-64 only. Formats: tar.gz, tar.xz, tar.zst, tar, zip and raw executables only. Only SHA-256 checksum files. Attestations, cosign, SLSA and minisign aren't checked. A command name that differs from its file's name (such as flyctl's fly) works through oyzu exec but isn't on the child PATH. Option tables honor only version. Other mise backends aren't supported (github: is separate; see the github: backend). A hand-written declaration with no lock entry needs oyzu install <id> or oyzu update; plain oyzu install reports TOOL_LOCK_STALE. The registry snapshot is fixed per Oyzu build. Your own registries and a floating registry aren't supported. Tool routes aren't supported for registry packages, and version listing needs GitHub's API. Recipe vars and musl builds aren't supported. tools.allowed matches the canonical oyzu: ID.
Tool index Resolving recipes into artifact sets The github: backend Tool commands

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-catalog.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. An organization tool catalog lists the tools and versions your organization approves. Set toolCatalog when your organization runs a delivery edge (the server that publishes the catalog and serves approved downloads): Oyzu then installs registry packages and Oyzu's own providers (oyzu:java, oyzu:node, ...) only from that signed catalog. Note: Experimental. Setting names, error codes and the catalog format may change. Supported on Linux x86-64 and Windows x86-64; macOS is not supported yet. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Point Oyzu at the signed tool index and the delivery edge, and pin the edge's public signing key: # ~/.config/oyzu/config.toml [toolIndex] url = "https://index.example.test/" [toolCatalog] url = "https://dl.example.test/" keys = ["ed25519:7sb4o1W0lRKR712+E7DQ8uYEeTX2sUXSzJMTpKc0lzI="] Put the organization token in OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN. Then: oyzu tools versions <tool> lists the versions your organization approves. oyzu tools check --catalog checks the declared tools the way an install would. oyzu tools request <tool>@<version> asks for a version the catalog doesn't offer yet.

The catalog is the signed public tool index, narrowed to the approved versions, with each version's state and how its files are delivered. With a catalog configured: Only approved versions resolve. Any other version fails before anything is downloaded. A blocked or quarantined version fails with your organization's reason. Oyzu only uses a catalog signed by a key in toolCatalog.keys. The catalog can only narrow the index. An entry whose SHA-256 differs from the signed index is refused, so the edge can't substitute other files. Files the catalog marks proxy download from the edge with the organization token. Files marked direct (for licenses that forbid redistribution) download from the publisher, and Oyzu still checks the catalog's SHA-256. Oyzu doesn't fall back to local recipes, registry files, GitHub release lists or publisher APIs. If the edge is unreachable, Oyzu uses the last good catalog for a limited time (toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge) and warns you.

The signed tool index doesn't yet carry Node's LTS markers. Under a catalog, node@lts fails with TOOL_LTS_METADATA_UNAVAILABLE, and tools check --catalog reports it unavailable. Use an approved exact version or a named line such as lts/krypton. Without a catalog, an unpinned Node requests lts, even when engines.node is set. Oyzu picks the newest stable LTS release that satisfies every engine constraint, or, if none does, the newest stable release that does. The build plan explains which rule applied. Explicit latest, major, exact and named LTS requests keep their meaning and must satisfy the engines. A locked lts version installs offline without refreshing.

A signed tool index (toolIndex.url). The catalog approves versions from the index; it isn't an index by itself. An organization token from the edge's operator. The edge's catalog signing public key (ed25519:<base64>), from the edge's operator.

Setting or variable Values Default Meaning toolCatalog.url HTTPS URL (HTTP only on loopback) unset Base URL of the delivery edge. Unset means registry packages resolve from the index or locally. toolCatalog.keys One to eight ed25519:<base64> public keys unset Keys the catalog must be signed with. Required when toolCatalog.url is set. Pin two while the edge rotates its key. User or machine configuration only. toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge 0, <n>h or <n>d (up to 366d) 7d How long after the edge built it the last good catalog can be used while the edge is unreachable. 0 turns this off. User or machine configuration only. toolCatalog.adminUrl HTTPS URL (HTTP only on loopback) unset Delivery admin API, used by tools request. Also OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL. Can't be set in a project file, because your sign-in token is sent there. OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN environment variable unset Organization token, sent as Authorization: Bearer. It is never a setting, so it can't end up in a committed file. Settings marked "user or machine configuration only" fail with CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file. Oyzu fetches <url>v1/catalog once per command, with the ETag of its saved copy, so an unchanged catalog isn't downloaded again. Proxied files are fetched from <url>v1/upstream/<host><path>.

To make the catalog mandatory on a machine, set it as a locked setting in the machine's protected admin-settings.json (see configuration). User and project files can then neither remove nor change it: { "schemaVersion": 1, "kind": "local-admin-policy", "settings": { "toolCatalog.url": { "locked": true, "value": "https://dl.example.test/" }, "toolCatalog.keys": { "locked": true, "value": ["ed25519:7sb4o1W0lRKR712+E7DQ8uYEeTX2sUXSzJMTpKc0lzI="] }, "toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge": { "locked": true, "value": "3d" }, "toolIndex.url": { "locked": true, "value": "https://index.example.test/" } }, "profiles": {}, "requiredCapabilities": [] } Pair it with a network allowlist that permits the edge and the index host but not the publishers' hosts. Distribute both through device management.

For an aqua: package: The index picks the version from those the catalog approves on any platform, so every platform in the lock gets the same version. Each platform's entry must be approved for that platform, not refused, and carry the index's SHA-256. A version approved only for other platforms is treated like a release with no build for this one, and that platform is left out of the lock. The download follows the catalog's delivery for that URL: proxy through the edge, direct from the publisher. A URL the catalog doesn't list is refused. Reinstalls and the lock: Reinstalling from a cached archive still checks the current catalog first. A cached, verified archive isn't downloaded again. install --offline uses the saved catalog (under the rules in When the edge is unreachable) and never contacts the edge. Both the catalog and the archive must be available locally. The lock is the same as without a catalog: the publisher URL and SHA-256, never the edge's host or the token. github: packages are refused under a catalog, because the catalog doesn't list their files.

A version withdrawn from the signed index (see the index) stays in the catalog with state withdrawn, and the edge won't serve it. Oyzu refuses it with TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN, the reason and the newest version the catalog serves for your platform: TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN: oyzu:golang-migrate 4.20.0 was withdrawn from the tool index: upstream release assets were deleted (404). The newest version the acme tool catalog serves for linux/amd64/gnu is 4.19.1. If nothing else is available, the message suggests oyzu tools request. A prefix or latest skips withdrawn versions. A lock that names one is refused on the next install. tools versions lists it under excluded, and tools check --catalog reports it as withdrawn.

Oyzu's archive providers (Java, Node, Go, Python, Maven, Gradle, kubectl, k3d, Helm, Liquibase, Tailscale, npm and pnpm) follow the same three steps under a catalog, instead of reading the publisher's live metadata. The index lists them under their oyzu: ID (for example oyzu:java, from core:java). The catalog can use either name. The version and SHA-256 come from the index as narrowed by the catalog. The lock records oyzu:java, the publisher URL and the SHA-256, the same as without a catalog. Accepted requests: An exact release (21.0.8), a release-line prefix (21, 1.25) or latest. For Java, lts and * pick the newest approved LTS release (8, 11, 17, 21, 25, ...). Node's named lines (lts/jod, lts-iron). The moving lts alias is refused, as described above. A range (^20, ~1.24, >=3.12 <3.14) picks the newest approved release it matches. Native constraints (>=17) narrow every request. Tools the index doesn't carry: A provider missing from the index fails with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX. oyzu:rust installs from an approved Rust channel manifest in the index, and each download is verified. See indexed Rust. An unapproved version fails with TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG. cargo: helpers (cargo:cargo-nextest, cargo:cargo-llvm-cov) are refused with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX.

With toolCatalog.url set, oyzu tools check --catalog fetches the catalog (or reads the saved copy with --offline) and judges each declared tool as an install would. The selected version must be approved for the host and for every platform listed in tools.lockPlatforms. Other default lock platforms are optional. Status Meaning Refused approved Installs version through the catalog. no not-in-catalog No approved release matches the request. Also every github: package. yes refused Your organization refuses version (with its reason), or the catalog names different files than the index. Also cargo: helpers and Rust missing from the index. yes withdrawn The version was withdrawn from the index. The reason names the newest available one. yes not-in-index The index doesn't carry the tool. yes unavailable No approved build for the host or a required platform. yes excluded, blocked, unknown Same as without a catalog. yes The command exits 1 if anything would be refused. JSON adds catalog (org, built, source and any saved-copy warning).

oyzu tools versions <tool> lists, newest first, the versions the catalog approves and serves for your platform. A version your organization refused appears under excluded with TOOL_REFUSED and the reason, in a "Refused by the catalog" table. A version whose catalog SHA-256 disagrees with the index shows TOOL_CATALOG_MISMATCH. A withdrawn one shows TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN. Versions never approved aren't shown. A tool the catalog doesn't list fails with TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG. In JSON, source is organization catalog, and catalog shows org, built and whether the copy was fetched or cached.

oyzu tools request <tool>@<version> [--reason TEXT] asks your organization's administrators to approve a version. The version can be a prefix (kubectl@1.31). oyzu tools request yq@4.44.3 oyzu tools request kubectl@1.31 --reason "cluster upgrade" oyzu tools request --status 7 oyzu tools request --cancel 7 oyzu tools requests What you need: toolCatalog.adminUrl (or OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL). Without it the command fails with TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL_MISSING. A personal sign-in: oyzu auth login (with platform.url and platform.account) or OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. Your personal token is sent to the admin URL, not the organization token. You need the catalog.request permission. OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN, to read the catalog. What it reports: The request's id, state and what to do next. The state is pending, or approved if one of your organization's auto-approve rules accepts it immediately. Asking again for the same tool and version returns the pending request. A version the catalog already serves reports served. A tool missing from the index, or a version with no verified download, fails with TOOL_REQUEST_INVALID. A request stays pending until an administrator approves or denies it, you cancel it, or it expires after 30 days (unless your organization sets another limit). An expired or cancelled request can be asked for again. --status ID shows a request's state (pending, approved, denied, cancelled or expired), when it was made and expires, who asked, who decided and why. --cancel ID cancels your own pending request. Only the person who asked can cancel it. oyzu tools requests lists the newest 50 requests made from this machine with the current organization token, with their state read now. Oyzu remembers only the IDs, tools and versions, in the default store under state/tool-catalog/. A request the edge no longer has shows as unknown. Neither command waits for a decision. Run it again later.

The edge serves the catalog as a DSSE envelope with payload type application/vnd.oyzu.tool-catalog+json. Each signature is Ed25519, and its keyid is the hex SHA-256 of the public key. Oyzu accepts the catalog when one signature verifies with a pinned key; anything else fails with TOOL_CATALOG_UNTRUSTED. Payload field Meaning org The organization the token belongs to. revision SHA-256 of the catalog's content; changes whenever the catalog does. index {serial, sha256} of the signed index the catalog was built from. policy_revision Revision of the organization's policy. built, expires When the edge signed it, and when a fetched copy stops being accepted (24 hours later by default). entries Approved entries: ID, aliases, version, platform, sha256, delivery, state, refusal and upstream URL. Oyzu checks, in order: The signature. For a fetched copy, that it hasn't expired (TOOL_CATALOG_STALE; also check your clock). If Oyzu's index has the same serial as the catalog's index, that both have the same SHA-256 (TOOL_CATALOG_MISMATCH). A catalog built from a neighboring index release is accepted, since the edge and Oyzu update on their own schedules. Every entry is still checked against Oyzu's own index.
To rotate keys, the edge's operator adds the new key next to the old one (the edge signs with both), you update toolCatalog.keys to the new key, and the operator removes the old key.

Oyzu keeps each verified catalog in the default tool store under catalogs/tool-catalog/<key>/catalog.json (~/.local/share/oyzu/tools/... on Linux), exactly as the edge sent it. The signature is checked every time the copy is read. An edited copy, or one signed by a key you no longer pin, is refused. The <key> comes from the catalog URL and a hash of the token, so switching edges or organizations never reads another catalog's copy. Only a newer catalog replaces the saved copy. When fetching fails with a network error or HTTP 5xx: The saved copy is used if the edge built it no more than toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge ago, and you see TOOL_CATALOG_CACHED with its age. Its expires time doesn't apply offline. Entries are still checked against the signed index. An older copy fails with TOOL_CATALOG_STALE. A refused token (401, 403), a missing catalog (404), a bad signature or a malformed document is never replaced by the saved copy. When less than a quarter of maxOfflineAge remains (under 42 hours at the default 7d), you also see TOOL_CATALOG_EXPIRING. Oyzu also records when the newest catalog it ever fetched was built. A saved copy older than that fails with TOOL_CATALOG_STALE, so restoring an old backup can't bring back a version your organization has since withdrawn. oyzu tools versions --offline uses the saved copy and the cached index without contacting the edge. oyzu install --offline replays the lock.

Oyzu accepts index records for Linux amd64 and arm64 (GNU), macOS arm64 and Windows amd64 (MSVC). macOS amd64 records in the index aren't installable. Tailscale has Linux archives only. Someone who can write to your own tool store can put back an older genuine catalog and use a withdrawn version offline, but only until maxOfflineAge after that copy was built. Someone between you and the edge with a valid token can replay a genuine catalog until its expires (24 hours by default). While offline, a withdrawal made after the last fetch isn't seen until the next fetch.

Code Cause Fix TOOL_CATALOG_UNAUTHENTICATED OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN is empty or the edge rejected it. Get a current token from your administrator. TOOL_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE The catalog couldn't be fetched and there is no usable saved copy, or the edge has no catalog for your organization (404). Check the network path to the edge. TOOL_CATALOG_STALE The saved copy is older than maxOfflineAge or than the newest one fetched, or the edge sent an expired catalog. Reconnect to the edge; check your clock. TOOL_CATALOG_UNTRUSTED toolCatalog.keys is missing, or the catalog isn't signed by a pinned key. Pin the edge's current public key; report a bad signature to the edge's operator. TOOL_CATALOG_CACHED (warning) The edge is unreachable; the saved copy was used. None while it's recent enough. TOOL_CATALOG_EXPIRING (warning) The saved copy has less than a quarter of maxOfflineAge left. Reconnect before it runs out. TOOL_CATALOG_INVALID The catalog is malformed. Report it to the edge's operator. TOOL_CATALOG_MISMATCH The catalog names different files than the signed index, or a different index with the same serial. Nothing was installed. Report it to the edge's operator. TOOL_CATALOG_NOT_CONFIGURED tools request or tools requests without toolCatalog.url. Requests only work with a catalog. TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL_MISSING tools request without toolCatalog.adminUrl. Set it to the delivery admin API URL. TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX The index doesn't carry the tool, a cargo: helper, Rust missing from the index, or no index configured. Ask an administrator. TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG Your organization hasn't approved this tool or version, or the download URL isn't listed. oyzu tools request <tool>@<version>. TOOL_REFUSED The version is blocked, quarantined or otherwise refused (with the reason), or the edge refused the download. Use another approved version. TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN The version was withdrawn from the index. Use the version the message names, for example with oyzu update <tool>. TOOL_REQUEST_INVALID Not <tool>@<version>, or the edge refused the request. Fix the spec or pick an indexed version. TOOL_REQUEST_UNAVAILABLE The admin API has no such organization or route (404), or the edge takes no requests. Check toolCatalog.adminUrl; ask an administrator directly. TOOL_REQUEST_UNAUTHENTICATED No personal sign-in, or it was refused (401). oyzu auth login. The organization token isn't accepted here. TOOL_REQUEST_NOT_CONFIGURED platform.url or platform.account isn't set. Set them. TOOL_REQUEST_UNKNOWN --status or --cancel with an ID your organization doesn't have. oyzu tools requests shows the IDs made here. TOOL_REQUEST_FORBIDDEN You lack catalog.request, or tried to cancel someone else's request (403). Ask an administrator, or the requester. TOOL_REQUEST_NOT_PENDING --cancel on a request that's already decided, cancelled or expired (409). Nothing to cancel; --status shows it.
Tool index Tool commands Configuration

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-commands.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Use these commands to add, lock, install, update and inspect the tools a project or your user account needs. Each command changes the declaration ([tools] in configuration) and the lock (oyzu.lock) together, so the two never drift apart. Use them instead of editing oyzu.toml and oyzu.lock by hand. Note: These commands are experimental, and their syntax and error codes may change. They are fully tested on Linux x86-64; Windows x86-64 works with less test coverage, and macOS isn't supported yet. No account is needed. oyzu install go@1.26 # this project: declare, lock, install oyzu install -g node@22 # your user configuration, all projects oyzu install go # declared: make sure it is installed; undeclared: go@latest oyzu update go # newer version within the requirement; config untouched oyzu uninstall go # remove the project declaration and lock entry oyzu tools current # what is in effect here oyzu tools list # what is in the store, and what uses it oyzu tools prune # preview unreferenced store content oyzu tools versions go # what could be installed oyzu tools info go # provider, verification, eligibility Supported tools: Archive providers: node, go, python, java, maven, gradle, helm, kubectl, k3d, liquibase, tailscale, npm, pnpm, yarn. Rust: rust and the Cargo helpers cargo-nextest and cargo-llvm-cov. Experimental registry packages: aqua:<owner>/<repo> (see the aqua: backend) and github:<owner>/<repo> (see the github: backend). Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.
documents.s: Tool commands: install, update, uninstall and inspection

documents.t: Each command acts on one scope. The default is the current project. Flag Configuration written Lock written none, inside a project project oyzu.toml (created if missing) project oyzu.lock -g, --global your user configuration file (OYZU_USER_CONFIG or the platform default) the oyzu.lock next to it --local oyzu.local.toml project oyzu.lock --toolset NAME (global option) [toolsets.NAME.tools] in oyzu.toml, or in oyzu.local.toml with --local that toolset's entries in oyzu.lock; [tools] entries are untouched (toolsets) The project is --root, or the workspace root when it holds oyzu.toml, oyzu.local.toml, build.yaml or a Git marker. Outside a project, a command without -g fails with TOOL_NO_PROJECT and writes nothing. -g ignores project files, even when you run it inside a project. --global and --local can't be combined, and --toolset can't be used with --global. Profiles never hold tools. --profile with install SPEC or uninstall fails with TOOL_PROFILE_DECLARATION. If the same tool is declared in another scope, the command prints a note.

oyzu install with no arguments installs configured tools and the native tool requirements of the project containing the current directory. A conventional project needs no oyzu.toml, build.yaml or existing oyzu.lock: installation selects its builder plugin, discovers tool requests from native files, and records the verified tools in oyzu.lock. It does not install application dependencies; the builder prepares those during oyzu build. It accepts --frozen (require matching tool and plugin locks), --offline (use only locks, installations and cached archives) and --store DIR. First-time plugin acquisition needs network access and an eligible published plugin; Preview plugins require the Preview opt-in. Existing locked tool versions are retained. Global installation uses only global tool declarations. An online, non-frozen install in a project with builds also records the project's captured build requirements through the same resolution and lock transaction as bare oyzu pin. Installation records alone cannot restore a tool in a captured build worker. An image-and-chart project can run oyzu install, then oyzu build, without a separate pin step. This records requirements for the project's builds; host installation still follows the selected tools. The human result reports Recorded build requirements for N build(s).; JSON includes recordedBuildRequirements with that build count. These are omitted for tools-only folders, global installs and frozen/offline installs. Repeating an install with unchanged inputs and a complete lock keeps the lock byte-identical and retains selected versions. Online installation can still refresh signed tool-index and catalog metadata for current admission; captured resolution reuses complete locked recipes. --frozen never adds missing recipes, and --offline never resolves them from publisher metadata. If a captured build has installation records but lacks its tool recipe, it stops during preparation, before build actions, with TOOL_LOCK_MISSING. Run oyzu pin online in the project, then retry. Global installs do not resolve project build requirements. Captured requirement resolution follows verified host installation. If that final resolution fails, installed tools and their installation records remain available; correct the reported requirement and rerun oyzu pin or oyzu install online. oyzu install --global installs your global tools using your user configuration and its oyzu.lock, independent of the current project. oyzu install --global --frozen --offline restores a locked global selection from local data. A missing lock fails with TOOL_LOCK_MISSING.

A spec is [provider:]name[@version], split at the last @. Spec Meaning go@1.26 Newest version starting with 1.26. go@1.26.8 Exactly this version. go@latest Newest eligible version. go Keep the declared requirement and make sure it is installed; if undeclared, use latest. Several specs are applied together or not at all. Naming a tool twice fails with TOOL_SPEC_INVALID. Configuration stores what you typed ("1.26"). The lock stores the exact version. Core tools (node, go, python, java, maven, gradle, rust) are written under the name you typed. Other tools are written under their full ID (for example "cargo:cargo-nextest"). An existing declaration keeps its spelling. An ambiguous bare name fails and lists the exact spellings to retry with. Replacing a requirement prints Replaced "1.25" (1.25.9) -> "1.26" (1.26.8) and reuses an installation already in the store. Other declared tools in the same lock that aren't locked yet are locked and installed in the same run, keeping their current versions. What install does, in order: Parses the specs. Checks tools.allowed. Resolves lock entries for every platform your builds declare, plus the host. tools.lockPlatforms replaces the inferred platform list (the host is always kept). Downloads and installs only the host archive. Writes configuration and lock in one transaction. Any failure leaves both files unchanged. A concurrent edit fails with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT.

--dry-run resolves versions (reading publisher catalogs) and reports versions, files, platforms and acquisition changes. It downloads no archive and writes nothing. Specs with --frozen, --offline or --update fail with TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT, as do --dry-run and --local without specs. Archive tools and Rust tools can't be mixed in one command (TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT). Run two commands.

✓ Installed go 1.26.8 Declared "1.26" in ./oyzu.toml (project) Locked in ./oyzu.lock for 3 platforms (darwin/arm64/native, linux/amd64/gnu, windows/amd64/msvc) With --json the result has tools[] (tool, key, request, version, previous, status, platforms, otherScopes) plus configuration, lock, scope, store and recipeChanges. Acquisition changes retain complete before/after recipes, including platform/components, provider identity, input URLs/checksums and verification evidence. Human output shows Tool acquisition changes; see reviewing acquisition changes.

If the publisher has no artifact for a platform, that platform is left out of the lock and reported as unavailable (a warning in human output, unavailablePlatforms in JSON). The other platforms lock and the host installs normally. Selecting the unavailable platform later fails. For example, oyzu install node@14 locks Linux and Windows only, because Node 14 has no macOS arm64 build. This applies when a tool is first declared or its request changes, and only for Node, Go and Java. update uses current lock coverage (the declared build platforms, or tools.lockPlatforms, plus the host). Platforms left over from an earlier default or declaration do not become new requirements. A tool with no artifact on any platform fails, as does any other resolution problem (for example a missing checksum file).

oyzu install oyzu:NAME@VERSION --artifact-set FILE [--artifact-set-digest sha256:D] installs a tool from a resolved artifact set instead of a built-in provider. This is experimental, works in the project scope only, and doesn't yet make the tool runnable. See artifact sets.

oyzu update [TOOL...] moves locked versions forward within each existing requirement, locks the result for all platforms and installs the host selection. It never edits configuration. With no arguments it updates every tool in the scope. It takes names, not versions. In a project without --toolset, it also updates every toolset: [tools] first, then each toolset. The Set column (toolset in JSON) shows which one each row belongs to. A named tool is updated wherever [tools] or a toolset declares it. --dry-run reports versions and the complete acquisition changes that would be locked. An unchanged version with changed source, checksum or backend identity is reported as updated, rather than current. Tools you removed from configuration by hand aren't pruned from the lock. Only selected tools are re-resolved for current platform coverage. Valid recipes for unselected tools stay unchanged; unreferenced recipes are pruned without fetching their metadata again. install --update still works but is deprecated.

oyzu uninstall TOOL... removes the declaration and every lock entry for the tool in the selected scope, in one transaction. Comments elsewhere in the file are kept. Installed files stay in the store and show as unreferenced in oyzu tools list. A tool that the scope doesn't declare fails with TOOL_NOT_DECLARED, naming the scope that does. --dry-run writes nothing.

oyzu pin kubectl@1.34 helm@3.22.0 adds the requests to the project's [tools] and locks their exact archives for the configured platforms, in one transaction. It installs nothing. Run oyzu install --frozen afterward to install. --dry-run previews the result. Specs can't be combined with --refresh or --offline. Bare oyzu pin locks what your builds need, and accepts --refresh and --offline. Bare oyzu pin covers every toolset. oyzu --toolset NAME pin locks only that toolset. Pin removes recipes no request set references, including with --offline. Recipes still referenced by other sets stay unchanged. This cleanup does not require refreshing their versions or resolving their platforms again. A separate bare oyzu pin is optional after an online, non-frozen project install. It remains useful for reviewing a resolution without installing, and for preparing a lock before oyzu install --frozen. Configuration precedence and policy still apply. A request that another scope overrides fails without changing files. oyzu --json pin ... returns the same facts with status: "pinned". Rust pinning reads publisher manifests, checksum metadata or the tool index without downloading compiler, component or installer payloads. A backend that cannot provide a metadata-only artifact identity cannot satisfy that portable-lock path; it must report the limitation. Pin uses the current platform coverage. Inferred foreign platforms the provider doesn't publish are left out and reported. Bare pin and targeted pin/update previews share recipeChanges before/after facts. Ordinary pin retains helper recipes only when they match the built-in table, including their sources and checksums. Drift refuses with TOOL_RECIPE_MISMATCH and leaves the lock unchanged. Review oyzu pin --refresh --dry-run, then apply oyzu pin --refresh to refresh their acquisition identity while keeping selected versions. Targeted update can also refresh acquisition identity. Bare pin leaves authored TOML unchanged; a targeted version edit preserves known options in an existing tool table, including Rust's Windows ABI selection.

Node, Java and Docker default quality tools are exact stage-tool selections in oyzu.lock, under quality.node, quality.java and quality.docker. Bare oyzu pin records the sets your enabled checks need. It records versions, upstream URLs, upstream integrity and SHA-256 values together with support files such as Node's package lock and Java's default rules. Commit the lock; do not edit versions or hashes by hand. The pin result lists each locked quality set's name, version and snapshot digest in the Locked quality sets table. A dry run labels these as proposed sets. --json exposes the same metadata in qualitySets, an array of {name, version, digest} records. These describe the lock snapshot; they do not claim the tools are installed or available on the current platform. pin selects metadata. Before a quality task runs, preparation installs its locked bundle in the shared tool store if needed. Local builds, isolated builds and oyzu run use the same set. Downloads are admitted and verified at install; installed payloads are trusted on reuse. Native project tools and authored task replacements retain their documented precedence. No separate checker-home environment variable or repository provisioner is required. Concurrent tasks needing the same bundle share its installation. In a cold store, one caller publishes the verified bundle while others wait and then reuse it. Active consumers can keep using it while later callers acquire it. A caller waits up to 30 minutes for another publisher; acquisition and task execution retain their own limits. Malformed installed metadata is refused and retained unchanged. New default sets ship with Oyzu releases. Ordinary builds, runs and oyzu pin keep an existing exact selection. Two explicit operations adopt the current CLI's defaults: oyzu pin --refresh refreshes default quality sets required by the selected build scope while preserving selected native runtime versions. oyzu update with no tool names in the project scope refreshes its already locked quality sets, including Docker projects with no runtime declaration. Named tool updates, global updates and toolset-only updates leave them alone. Both update the lock; the next task installs any newly selected quality bundle. oyzu update --dry-run reports the proposed set versions without writing or installing them. Checker eligibility and source restrictions remain binding. Offline operation requires the exact lock and the needed installation or admitted cached inputs in the same store. Run an online check first to populate it. Missing quality pins report QUALITY_LOCK_REQUIRED; run oyzu pin and retry. An unavailable complete tool pair reports QUALITY_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE rather than taking a tool from ambient PATH. Versions, project-tool precedence and platform limits are described in Node quality, Java quality and Docker quality.

Repository maintainers regenerate defaults with the compiled tooling/refresh-quality-tools operation. Activate Oyzu's checks toolset first; its npm verifies registry signatures and available package provenance without running lifecycle scripts. Refresh, reports and the GitHub bot live in the repository-only oyzu-quality-tools binary; they are not shipped with the CLI or plugins. Build the non-default target first. Set OYZU_QUALITY_TOOLS to a specific maintenance executable when testing a resolver change. eval "$(oyzu --toolset checks activate bash)" oyzu build quality-tools tooling/refresh-quality-tools --update tooling/refresh-quality-tools --check tooling/refresh-quality-tools --report --json --update (the default) selects stable versions in each currently allowed major, with a seven-day publication cooldown. Maven formatter selection also preserves the existing Java 17 runtime baseline: base classes requiring a newer JVM are excluded, while optional multi-release classes do not raise the baseline. This bytecode check limits candidate selection but cannot establish compatibility with the JDK's compiler APIs. The formatter remains capped below 1.29 on its Java 17-compatible line; 1.28.0 is the default. The native Java acceptance suite still verifies the selected formatter on Java 17. Freshness reports continue to show newer minor and major releases for maintainer review; the cap does not declare those releases current or compatible. Raising the baseline or cap requires an explicit compatibility change. --regenerate verifies the versions in the native inputs and regenerates their pin records and hashes without selecting new versions. --set node|java|docker restricts the refresh; the default is all three. --check is an offline consistency gate and directs manual pin/hash drift back to this command. It does not download tools or prove upstream freshness. Refresh verifies npm SHA-512, Maven checksums and detached OpenPGP signatures, and GitHub release SHA-256 values and available artifact attestations. Published proofs that cannot be verified fail the operation. Maven signer continuity is anchored in the previously pinned artifact and retained signer fingerprint; a signer change requires maintainer investigation. npm's native signature audit also covers optional platform packages, without executing their binaries. All verification completes before generated source files are replaced. Project locks are never changed by this maintainer operation. --security may bypass cooldown only when the currently pinned set has an affecting advisory and every changed release younger than seven days fixes an advisory affecting its prior version. The resulting set must be clear of known advisories. A missing date, unavailable advisory service, unsupported proof or remaining advisory fails visibly; it is not treated as a clean result. The report compares every pinned asset with upstream stable releases, including new majors, after checking native-pin consistency. It counts current, held and stale rows, plus affecting advisories. A row is held when newer releases exist but none is permitted by all applicable constraints. Reasons come from the recorded native lock's parent dependency ranges (including optional and peer requirements) and the explicit compatibility policies: Checkstyle major 10, google-java-format below 1.29 for Java 17, and TypeScript major 6 while the quality root pins that line. Other direct version pins do not themselves justify holding an update. Held rows do not fail the report. Each run recomputes their reasons: widening a parent range or lifting a compatibility cap makes newly permitted updates actionable. The report still shows unrestricted upstream lag from the earliest newer stable release. Its actionable lag starts at the earliest newer release permitted by every constraint, even if a later release is blocked. More than 60 days of actionable lag makes the row stale and fails the report. An affecting advisory always fails, including on held and transitive packages. Advisory coverage includes npm packages, Maven coordinates, Dockerfmt's Go module and the release repositories' published advisories; this is not a complete inventory of dependencies embedded inside upstream executable or all-dependencies JARs. A completed --report prints the full report on stdout and exits 0 when the check passes, or 1 when actionable lag or an advisory fails it. Human output shows the counts, held rows grouped by reason (one line per tool), and freshness and affecting-advisory tables. --json includes counts, the same reason groups in held, and each tool's status, heldReason, actionableLagDays and firstAllowedNewerPublishedAt. It preserves every tool observation and advisory in the structured result, including status: "failed".
