A transport, metadata or advisory-service error remains a failing diagnostic, rather than an incomplete report presented as a completed check. Dependabot watches the Node native lock on the repository's weekly cadence. The existing scheduled tool-management job runs this same verifier and opens a draft refresh PR, and regenerates hashes for eligible same-repository Dependabot PRs targeting dev. The draft refresh PR also bases on and targets dev. It executes trusted main code and reads only allowlisted PR data. Delivery needs a GitHub App installed on this repository only, with Contents and Pull requests permissions set to write. Configure the repository variable QUALITY_TOOLS_APP_CLIENT_ID and secret QUALITY_TOOLS_APP_PRIVATE_KEY. Token creation and refresh delivery skip when the client-ID variable is absent; the independent freshness report still runs. The bot adds no CI label and grants no release or compliance approval. --pull-request is the automation entry point and requires that App's token and bot identity. Source files, workflows and scripts from the proposed PR are never executed.

oyzu tools list --details includes Publisher evidence for each stored installation. The JSON row uses evidenceStrength, with digest-only, checksum-file, signature or provenance. These are receipt facts, not a fresh integrity check. An older receipt without a strength reports digest-only. See publisher evidence and release age for pin-time verification, the seven-day default cool-down, security exceptions and explicit early-version warnings. Human and JSON modes use the same facts. These commands are read-only. They install nothing, don't re-check installed files (tools are verified when installed, then trusted) and print the store path. All accept --store DIR. Command Shows oyzu tools current [-g] [--all] [--details] One row per tool in effect: requested and selected versions, scope and status. -g shows only global declarations; --all adds declarations a closer scope overrides. oyzu tools list [--details] Installations in the store, with size and what uses each: global, project or unreferenced. oyzu tools versions TOOL [--offline] Versions you can install, newest first. oyzu tools info TOOL Provider, accepted names, commands, platforms, verification, eligibility, declarations by scope and current state. oyzu tools check --catalog, oyzu tools migrate [--write] Check declarations against the tool index, or move mise.toml tools to Oyzu names. See tool index. Statuses in tools current: Status Meaning ok Installed and locked. not installed Locked but not in the store. Run oyzu install. blocked Excluded by tools.allowed; the rule is named. stale lock No lock, or no entry for this tool, platform or provider. Run oyzu pin. ambiguous Conflicting lock entries or names. Notes: tools list only knows about the global lock and the current project. An "unreferenced" installation may still be used by another project. tools versions reads the publisher's catalog, or the tool index when it lists the package (which also works offline). Otherwise it needs the network and fails with TOOL_OFFLINE under --offline. Pre-release and nightly versions aren't offered. A version blocked by tools.allowed says why. Rust and the Cargo helpers have no version catalog (TOOL_VERSIONS_UNSUPPORTED).

oyzu tools prune [--store DIR] previews unreferenced tool installations, blobs and plugins. Add --apply to remove eligible entries. Human and --json output include sizes and retention reasons. It keeps recorded lock/receipt references, recent use and active leases; uncertainty retains content. See store reclamation for platform limits and the conservative retention rules. tools list has a narrower reference view and does not establish collection eligibility.

Supported on Linux x86-64 only. Archive and Rust tools need separate commands. Installing one tool also installs the other declared tools in its lock. These commands don't run in managed (enrolled) mode.

Code Cause and fix TOOL_SPEC_INVALID Unparseable spec, empty version or a tool named twice. TOOL_NO_PROJECT No project here. Run inside a project or use --global. TOOL_NOT_DECLARED uninstall or update of a tool this scope doesn't declare. TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT Flags that don't combine, archive and Rust tools mixed, or a declaration overridden in this invocation. CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED tools.allowed excludes the tool. The rule is named; nothing is written. TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT A configured version is below the minimum in Go's go.mod or go.work. Both sources are named. Exit status 3. See Go version selection. TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_CONFLICT A [tools] value in the pin file's folder or nearer the build, or set by policy, names a different version than a native pin file (rust-toolchain.toml, .nvmrc, .node-version, .python-version, packageManager). Exit status 3. See native pin files. TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_INVALID A native pin file holds a value [tools] doesn't accept (an alias such as lts/* or nightly, a range, several versions, or a Rust toolchain.path). The file and a fix are named. Exit status 3. TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_OVERRIDDEN Warning: oyzu.local.toml overrides a native pin. oyzu pin locks the pin, not the override. TOOL_LOCK_STALE The lock has no entry for a request, or a native pin or minimum changed (for example go get rewrote go.mod). Run oyzu pin. PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT Another process changed the files at the same time. Retry.

If a configuration and lock write was interrupted, the next oyzu install, oyzu update, oyzu uninstall or oyzu pin finishes or rolls it back before doing anything else. Read-only commands report PIN_RECOVERY_REQUIRED with the affected folder and the command to run. If the files were edited by something else in the meantime, recovery stops with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT and leaves its journal for you to inspect. A concurrent edit while a command reads configuration reports CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT. Retry the command.

If installation recipes are out of date, the error names the tool, version and lock. Run oyzu pin --refresh (keeps selected versions), then oyzu install. Tool preparation failures name the tool, version, store path and the command to recover. Windows paths in errors use the plain C:\... or \\server\share\... form.
Shell activation to use installed tools in your shell. Configuration for [tools], toolsets and native pin files. Tool index and tool catalog for where tools come from and organization policy.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-github.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. github:<owner>/<repo> installs a program from a GitHub repository's release assets. It uses the same [tools] syntax as mise's github: backend. No account and no mise executable are needed. Note: Experimental. Tested on Intel macOS with Pandoc 3.12.1 and Poedit GettextTools 1.0. Linux, Windows and Apple Silicon are not supported yet. $ oyzu install github:cli/cli@2.49.2 $ cat oyzu.toml [tools] "github:cli/cli" = "2.49.2" You need network access to api.github.com, github.com and GitHub's release-asset host. The lock attempts coverage for every platform your builds declare, plus the current host. When a release has no matching artifact, inferred foreign coverage is omitted and reported in platformsNotLocked (human output: Inferred platforms not locked). The host and explicit tools.lockPlatforms entries remain required. See which platforms are locked.

An exact MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH request reads the release tagged v<version> or <version>. oyzu tools versions github:owner/repo lists releases. Moving requests (latest and prefixes such as 2.49) fail with TOOL_RELEASE_AGE_UNAVAILABLE: this direct adapter has no signed-index publication dates to enforce the release cool-down. Select an exact version explicitly. For each platform, Oyzu picks the asset whose name best matches the OS, architecture and libc. Assets identified as belonging to another platform are excluded; the Darwin-only GettextTools xcframework cannot be selected for Linux or Windows. A wrong architecture is never used as a fallback. Checksums, signatures, packages (.deb, .rpm, .msi) and source archives are never picked. The SHA-256 is the digest GitHub reports for the asset, or one from a checksum file published next to it. Oyzu downloads the asset once per platform, checks it against that digest and finds the command: the file named after the repository, or else the only executable. The lock records the asset URL, its SHA-256 and the command path. oyzu install --frozen doesn't need the GitHub API again. Only the publisher's SHA-256 is checked. Attestations, signatures and SLSA provenance are not verified.
documents.s: How a release is chosen and pinned

documents.t: github:poedit/gettext-tools version 1.0 installs the GNU msgfmt from Poedit's GettextTools.xcframework.zip on macOS (11.5 or newer). Oyzu runs Versions/A/Helpers/msgfmt from the unmodified framework, so its bundled libraries load without extra settings. The package version (1.0) is separate from the gettext version the binary prints. [tools] lockPlatforms = ["darwin/amd64/native"] "github:poedit/gettext-tools" = "1.0" Oyzu only uses this command path for that exact archive (SHA-256 04dcba5b92ad8d0ff475e29baee72180f096431af220a858f0d29a9ec8988dcd). Other packages use the normal command detection, which refuses archives with more than one candidate.

Code Cause and fix TOOL_RATE_LIMITED GitHub refused the request (anonymous rate limit or access policy). Set GITHUB_TOKEN; it is sent to api.github.com only. TOOL_VERSION_NOT_FOUND No release matches the request. TOOL_CHECKSUM_MISSING The release publishes no SHA-256 for the chosen asset. Nothing is installed. TOOL_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH The download doesn't match the published digest. TOOL_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED The chosen asset isn't tar.gz or zip (for example a bare binary or tar.xz). TOOL_RECIPE_UNSUPPORTED The archive has no single identifiable command. TOOL_SPEC_INVALID The ID isn't github:<owner>/<repo>.

Supported on Intel macOS only. Not supported: bare-binary assets, tar.xz and tar.zst, options such as asset_pattern, bin and version_prefix, private repositories and GitHub Enterprise hosts. tools versions lists releases without looking at their assets, so a listed version may have no build for your platform. Resolving downloads each platform's asset once, which can be large.
Tool commands The aqua: backend

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-go-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can install the official Go distribution for your project and run go and gofmt from it, so you don't need Go installed on the machine. The exact release and archive digest are recorded in oyzu.lock. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Declare a version in oyzu.toml: [tools] go = "1.24.13" Then install and run it: oyzu install oyzu which go go version gofmt -l main.go go run ./main.go In an activated shell, which the install script sets up, the plain tool commands run the pinned versions. Where a shell isn't activated, prefix them with oyzu exec --. gofmt -l main.go prints the file name when the file needs formatting and nothing when it's already formatted. With oyzu exec --json, the command's output is in the stdout field. To reinstall later without changing anything or touching the network: oyzu install --frozen --offline

Source Role [tools] go in oyzu.toml The request, when set go.mod / go.work The Go minimum (the newer of the go and toolchain lines). It becomes the request when [tools] go is unset, and an incompatible [tools] go is rejected oyzu.lock The exact release, reused until you update it See Go version selection for how builds use this. To move to a newer release that matches your request, run oyzu update go (oyzu install --update go does the same). --frozen and --offline commands never pick a new version.

oyzu exec, shims and activated shells: put the installed Go bin directory first on PATH; set GOROOT to the installation; set GOTOOLCHAIN=local so Go uses the locked compiler instead of downloading another one. You can override this with an environment setting in oyzu.toml. Module downloads are still done by Go itself, using your normal Go proxy settings. When you activate a shell, oyzu creates go and gofmt shims. A shim runs the Go selected for the current directory and refuses commands that aren't part of that selection. oyzu env --json shows the selected tool.
documents.s: What oyzu sets when Go runs

documents.t: oyzu reads the release list from https://go.dev/dl/?mode=json&include=all and downloads archives from https://dl.google.com/go/. Before installing, it checks that the archive's size and SHA-256 match the release list and its .sha256 file. The lock records the digest. Go releases have no publisher signature to check.

An administrator can send downloads through a mirror with a tools route scoped to go, oyzu:go or * (see proxy acquisition). The mirror serves the original paths and queries: /dl/?mode=json&include=all for metadata and /go/<archive> for archives and checksum files. Host routes can select go.dev and dl.google.com separately. When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.

Installations made by older oyzu versions keep working for go, but may not expose gofmt. Run oyzu update go once to refresh the installation for the same Go version, then use frozen commands as usual. oyzu pin --refresh updates lock metadata only, not the installed files.

Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Windows x86-64 Supported macOS Intel Installs from an exact version or version line; automatic default pinning isn't available yet macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Recorded in the lock, not supported yet Linux musl Not supported

oyzu selects the compiler only. Module downloads and proxies are Go's own behavior, and choosing a compiler doesn't make a build hermetic. --offline needs the tool installed or its archive already cached.
Go applications Tool commands Organization tool catalog

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-helm-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can pin and install helm, so a project that packages or deploys Helm charts doesn't need Helm installed on the machine. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

[tools] helm = "3.16.2" # exact release # helm = "latest" # the publisher's current stable release oyzu install helm@3.16.2 # declares, locks every platform, installs for this one helm version --short oyzu which helm In an activated shell, which the install script sets up, the plain tool commands run the pinned versions. Where a shell isn't activated, prefix them with oyzu exec --. The installed command is helm (helm.exe on Windows).

Request Result 3.16.2 or v3.16.2 That release latest The release named by the publisher's helm-latest-version marker Ranges, minor lines such as 3.16 and pre-releases are refused, because the Helm download site has no list of releases. For the same reason oyzu tools versions helm fails. latest currently points at a Helm 4 release. Pin an exact version if your project depends on Helm 3 behavior. The lock keeps the resolved version until you run oyzu update.

oyzu downloads the release archive for each platform from https://get.helm.sh/ (.tar.gz on Linux and macOS, .zip on Windows) and checks it against the SHA-256 in the publisher's .sha256sum file on the same site. The digest is recorded in the lock. No publisher signature is checked. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to helm, oyzu:helm or * (see proxy acquisition). When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.
Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Windows x86-64 Supported macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Recorded in the lock, not supported yet macOS Intel, Linux musl Not supported
--offline needs the tool installed or its archive already cached.
Tool commands Organization tool catalog

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-index.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The tool index is a public, signed list of every registry package's versions, with per-platform download URLs and the SHA-256 Oyzu verified for each file. oyzu install and oyzu tools versions read it instead of asking GitHub or each publisher, so only the download itself goes to the vendor. You don't need to configure anything to use it. Note: Experimental. Settings, error codes and exit statuses may change. Supported on Linux x86-64; Windows and macOS are not supported yet. By default Oyzu reads the index published as GitHub releases of oyzuai/tool-index, refreshed daily. The file format is tool-index.schema.json. Versions may carry evidence (strength, mechanism and publisher identity), platform_evidence (per-artifact verdicts and optional Sigstore bundles), and advisory_fixes (advisory ids mapped to affected exact pins). Missing evidence on an older index means digest-only. Defaults observe the release cool-down. OpenPGP verification belongs to the non-shipping producer; signing an index alone does not upgrade publisher evidence. The public producer must integrate the publisher-verification step and publish those verdicts before clients can claim stronger evidence for its records. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.
documents.s: The public tool index (toolIndex, tools check --catalog, tools migrate, tools trust)

documents.t: The index can carry Oyzu's own providers: Java, Node, Go, Python, Maven, Gradle, Helm, kubectl, k3d, Liquibase, Tailscale, npm, pnpm, Yarn and Rust. Archive records name the exact download URL the provider uses. Rust records approve a channel manifest and carry its component digests; see Rust installation. Without an organization catalog, a provider request uses the newest verified index record that matches and has completed the cool-down. It can read live publisher metadata for an explicit exact version when the index has nothing for it; a moving default without signed publication dates fails with TOOL_RELEASE_AGE_UNAVAILABLE. Once an indexed version is selected, a platform it has no record for is unavailable; Oyzu doesn't look it up at the publisher. Under a catalog, a tool missing from the index fails with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX, and an unapproved version with TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG. Cargo helpers aren't available under a catalog. Index records are produced with oyzu --json tools evidence --provider <name> --version <exact-release>. See provider records for the publisher sources and checksum formats. The default matrix is Linux amd64 and arm64 (GNU), macOS arm64 and amd64, and Windows amd64 (MSVC). macOS amd64 records exist for Rust, Node, Go, Python, npm, pnpm, Yarn and Zig when the publisher provides them; other providers report it unsupported. Tailscale reports macOS and Windows as unsupported.

Setting Values Default Meaning toolIndex.url HTTPS URL (HTTP only on loopback), or false https://github.com/oyzuai/tool-index/releases/latest/download/ Where the index is. false reads no index, and registry packages are resolved locally from their recipes (refused under managed configuration). toolIndex.trustedRoot Absolute path Sigstore's production trusted root (built in, or newer from oyzu tools trust refresh) A Sigstore trusted_root.json to verify against instead, for a private Sigstore deployment. User or machine configuration only. toolIndex.identity https: URI https://github.com/oyzuai/tool-index/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main The signing identity the index must have, for an index you sign yourself. User or machine configuration only. Settings marked "user or machine configuration only" fail with CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file. # ~/.config/oyzu/config.toml [toolIndex] # A mirror instead of the public index (or `false` for no index): url = "https://index.example.test/" # Only for an index signed by another workflow or another Sigstore instance: # identity = "https://github.com/example/tool-index/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main" # trustedRoot = "/etc/oyzu/sigstore-trusted-root.json" The URL can point at a GitHub release directory, an Oyzu host or your own mirror. Trust comes from the signature and the pinned identity, not from the host. The default URL redirects to the newest release (releases/download/index-v<serial>/) and then to release-assets.githubusercontent.com. If your network blocks that host, use a mirror.

Each index release has three files: index.json, index.json.zst (the same content compressed, used only for transfer) and index.json.sigstore.json, a Sigstore bundle. The index is signed keylessly by the index repository's GitHub Actions release workflow, and the signature is recorded in the public Rekor transparency log. Oyzu verifies the bundle itself, offline, against the trusted root (no cosign and no extra network call). It checks that: the bundle has exactly one log entry and one signature; the log entry is signed by a Rekor key that was valid at signing time (Rekor v1 signed entry timestamps and Rekor v2 inclusion proofs with RFC 3161 timestamps are both accepted); the certificate chains to a Sigstore Fulcio CA valid at signing time; the certificate names toolIndex.identity, the GitHub Actions OIDC issuer and a GitHub-hosted runner (an index signed on a self-hosted runner is refused); the signed statement names the SHA-256 of the exact index.json bytes. Oyzu doesn't check certificate transparency timestamps, the Rekor v1 inclusion proof, or the timestamp authority's signing-certificate attribute. Only ECDSA (P-256 or P-384) timestamp authorities are supported. Then the document itself: Unknown fields are refused, tools must be sorted with lowercase oyzu: IDs, and every record's digests must recompute. expires must be in the future. serial can't go below the highest one accepted before, and the same serial can't have different content (rollback protection). The signed index and its recipe records have no free-form annotation slot. Unknown members can change acquisition or verification and remain errors even when a file is otherwise well formed. Refused documents do not advance the accepted serial. Signature verification covers the original index bytes; removing an unfamiliar member also invalidates that signature. Update Oyzu or obtain a compatible signed index from its publisher instead of editing it. Oyzu downloads index.json.zst (up to 256 MiB uncompressed), or index.json if the server returns 404 for the compressed file. The signature is checked on the uncompressed bytes.

An index refresh has one 30-second download budget shared by the compressed index, any uncompressed fallback and index.json.sigstore.json, including redirects and response bodies. Each asset gets at most four attempts. Each HTTP request is limited to five seconds or the remaining budget. Transient failures (HTTP 5xx, 408, 429, timeouts and connection failures) retry after 1, 2 and 4 seconds. This allows short outages to recover without holding a CI step indefinitely. Retry-After seconds and HTTP dates can lengthen that delay. If the requested wait would exhaust the remaining budget, Oyzu stops instead of retrying early. Other HTTP 4xx errors are permanent and stop immediately; only a 404 for the optional compressed index selects index.json. Signature, digest, decoding, expiry and rollback failures never trigger a download retry. Every completed pair still passes the verification checks above before it can be used or cached. If downloads fail, the diagnostic names the asset and distinguishes transient from permanent errors. A transient failure includes attempts, elapsed time, the total budget and the last error, for example after 4 attempts over 7.0 seconds (30 seconds total budget); last error HTTP 504 (transient). The existing verified-cache rules below still apply; without a valid copy the command fails with TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE.

The last verified index is kept under <store>/catalogs/tool-index/<key>/. The highest accepted serial is kept separately in <store>/state/tool-index/<key>.json, so deleting the cache doesn't reset rollback protection. Each store has its own history. A copy fetched less than an hour ago is used without a request (index.source is recent). After an hour, Oyzu checks for a new one. If a newer copy can't be fetched or fails verification, the cached copy is verified again and used while it hasn't expired. index.source is cached and index.warning says why. With --offline (tools versions, tools check --catalog, tools migrate), only the cached copy is read. install --offline replays the lock and doesn't read the index. With no valid copy, the command fails with TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE, naming the fetch failure and the cache state.

For a registry package (oyzu: IDs and their aqua: aliases, not github:), after checking the lock: The index. The package matches an index tool by ID (oyzu:terraform) or by its origin package (oyzu:hashicorp/terraform, aqua:hashicorp/terraform), ignoring case. The request (1.16.5, v1.16.5, 1.16 or latest) picks a version with a record for the platform. Prefixes and latest skip pre-releases. The lock gets the record's URL and verified SHA-256. Local recipe evaluation (standalone only), when the index doesn't list the package, has no matching release, or has no verified SHA-256 for it. Under managed configuration, step 2 never runs; a miss fails with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX. A tool the index lists as excluded fails with TOOL_EXCLUDED. A listed version with no build for the platform fails as an unavailable platform. A configured index that can't be verified is always an error, never a silent fallback. With an organization tool catalog, step 1 considers only approved versions, and step 2 never runs.

The index can withdraw a version, for example when its upstream files were deleted or the release was broken. The version keeps its records, so a lock still matches it by name, and gains a reason (1 to 512 characters): { "version": "4.20.0", "released": {...}, "sets": [...], "withdrawn": { "reason": "upstream release assets were deleted (404)" } } A prefix or latest skips withdrawn versions, for registry packages and for the providers that read the index (Java, Node, Go, Python). An exact request for a withdrawn version, a prefix whose every match is withdrawn, and an existing lock entry for one are all refused: TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN: oyzu:golang-migrate 4.20.0 was withdrawn from the tool index: upstream release assets were deleted (404). The newest available version is 4.19.1. The last sentence names the newest stable version with a build for your platform, if there is one. A lock is checked against whatever index the install can read (fetched, or cached with --offline). If no index is readable, a locked install proceeds. tools versions lists a withdrawn version under excluded with the reason, and tools check --catalog reports it as withdrawn. Under an organization catalog, the message names the newest version the catalog serves; see the catalog reference.

oyzu tools versions aqua:owner/repo lists an indexed package's versions, newest first, with tags, release time (publisher or first-seen) and versions excluded for this platform. With --offline it reads only the cached copy. It needs no GITHUB_TOKEN. In JSON, source is tool index, and index gives the URL, version (the serial), expires and whether the copy was fetched or cached.

Checks every tool declared here (the project, or your global configuration outside a project) against the index. It installs and writes nothing. With toolCatalog.url set, it checks against the organization catalog instead (see the catalog statuses). Availability is judged for this host plus any platforms listed in tools.lockPlatforms. Missing records for other default lock platforms don't count against a tool. oyzu tools check --catalog Status Meaning Refused indexed Installs from the index at version for the host and every tools.lockPlatforms entry. no local Not in the index (or no matching release); would be resolved locally from its recipe. no (standalone) refused Same as local, under managed configuration. yes direct A github: package, or one of Oyzu's own providers (uses the index when it has a record, the publisher otherwise). no unavailable Listed, but no build for the host or a required platform. yes withdrawn The version was withdrawn; reason gives the reason and the newest available version. yes excluded The index excludes the tool. yes blocked tools.allowed doesn't list it. yes unknown Not a tool Oyzu recognizes. yes Exit status: 0 when nothing is refused, 1 when something is, 2 when toolIndex.url is false (TOOL_INDEX_NOT_CONFIGURED). JSON has tools[], the refused count, outcome and index.

Moves tool declarations from mise.toml (or .mise.toml) into oyzu.toml under Oyzu names. By default it's a dry run that shows every change and the complete proposed oyzu.toml (after). --write replaces oyzu.toml atomically, keeping comments and formatting. mise.toml is never changed. oyzu tools migrate # show what would change oyzu tools migrate --write # apply it mise spelling Becomes node, go, ... and core:<name> The bare name. A short name for a supported backend (gh, terraform) Unchanged; bare names resolve against the index. aqua:owner/repo (also when already in oyzu.toml) The tool's index name (terraform), or oyzu:owner/repo (lowercased) if the index doesn't list it. github:owner/repo Unchanged. ubi:owner/repo github:owner/repo. asdf:, vfox: and short names only available through them Left out, with the reason. Other backends (npm:, pipx:, cargo:, go:, ...) Left out, with the reason. A version array keeps its first entry, and a table keeps its version. Anything dropped is noted. A tool oyzu.toml already declares is reported as a conflict, and the existing declaration is kept. Running it again after --write reports no change. Short names are resolved from mise's name list, downloaded once into the store. --offline reads only the cached index.

Oyzu ships with a copy of Sigstore's production trusted_root.json. When Sigstore rotates a key or adds a log, oyzu tools trust refresh fetches the newer root without waiting for an Oyzu release: oyzu tools trust refresh # from https://tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev/ oyzu tools trust refresh --from /media/sigstore # from a copy, on a machine without network oyzu tools trust status # which root verifies the index now --from takes an HTTPS URL of a TUF repository mirror or a directory. The directory can hold the repository files as Sigstore serves them (16.root.json, timestamp.json, 166.snapshot.json, 14.targets.json, targets/<sha256>.trusted_root.json) or be a checkout of github.com/sigstore/root-signing. The refresh runs the standard TUF client checks, starting from the TUF root built into Oyzu (or the last refresh): each newer root must be signed by the previous and its own root keys; the timestamp, snapshot and targets files must be properly signed, unexpired and not older than before; and trusted_root.json must match the length and SHA-256 the targets file lists. The result is saved in <store>/state/sigstore-root.json and verified again, offline, every time it's read. An edited file fails with TOOL_TRUST_INVALID; delete it to go back to the built-in root. A refreshed root is used only while it's newer than the built-in one. A later Oyzu release with a newer built-in root takes over. toolIndex.trustedRoot, when set, wins over both. Expiry is only checked when refreshing. Sigstore's timestamp expires within about a week, so an offline copy must be recent. The saved refresh record has a closed field set: unknown wrapper fields fail with TOOL_TRUST_INVALID, even if intended only for display. Signed TUF metadata keeps its own verification rules. Root, timestamp, snapshot and targets versions track trust freshness and rollback protection; they are not file-format versions to rename or reset for compatibility. refresh reports status (refreshed or unchanged), the TUF root and targets versions with their expiry, the trusted root's SHA-256, and inUse (refreshed or built-in). status reports inUse (built-in, refreshed or configured), the built-in root and the saved refresh. While the TUF root Oyzu starts from expires within 30 days (or has expired), commands that load the index warn with TOOL_TRUST_ROOT_EXPIRING. Index verification still works; run oyzu tools trust refresh to clear it. The built-in TUF root (version 16) expires on 2027-04-22.
documents.s: oyzu tools trust refresh and status

documents.t: Code Cause and fix TOOL_INDEX_UNTRUSTED The toolIndex.trustedRoot file can't be read or isn't a trusted root. Inside a TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE reason: the signature didn't verify. TOOL_INDEX_URL_INVALID The URL isn't HTTPS (or loopback HTTP). TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE No verified, unexpired copy could be obtained. TOOL_INDEX_INVALID The signed document is malformed (wrong format, no serial or expires, unsorted, digests don't match). TOOL_INDEX_NOT_CONFIGURED tools check --catalog with toolIndex.url = false. TOOL_INDEX_EXPIRING (warning) The index expires within three days, so publishing has stalled. After it expires, commands that need it fail with TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE. TOOL_TRUST_ROOT_EXPIRING (warning) The TUF root expires within 30 days. Run oyzu tools trust refresh. TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX Managed configuration, and the index lacks the package or release. TOOL_EXCLUDED The index lists the tool as excluded. TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN The requested or locked version was withdrawn. Install the version the message names, or run oyzu update <tool> for a lock. TOOL_MIGRATE_NOTHING tools migrate found nothing to migrate. TOOL_MIGRATE_INVALID A TOML file can't be parsed. TOOL_TRUST_REFRESH_FAILED tools trust refresh couldn't fetch or verify the TUF repository. The reason names the file and the check. TOOL_TRUST_SOURCE_INVALID --from is neither an HTTPS URL nor a directory. TOOL_TRUST_INVALID The saved refresh no longer verifies. Delete it or refresh again.

A release published in the last hour may not be seen until the hour is up. There is no flag to force a fetch. If a new release is published between Oyzu's two downloads, they won't verify together, and the cached copy is used (with a warning) until the next run. The built-in trusted root is never refreshed automatically. Update Oyzu or run oyzu tools trust refresh. tools evidence always uses the built-in root. Moving defaults use a release cool-down. Exact versions can be selected explicitly; see release age. Supported on Linux x86-64 only.
Organization tool catalog Resolving recipes and recording evidence Tool commands

A Sigstore publisher record carries identity (the exact certificate SAN), issuer (the OIDC issuer) and runner_environment when the provider has that claim. The signed index supplies these values; the client re-verifies them against the bundle at pin time. Oyzu's reviewed issuer allowlist currently admits https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com and its github-hosted or self-hosted runner claims. A different issuer, absent required identity fact, or a certificate mismatch refuses the pin with TOOL_PUBLISHER_UNTRUSTED. The record shape is provider neutral; an additional OIDC issuer needs an Oyzu trust-list review, not a new index version. Non-Sigstore evidence omits OIDC facts. An older index without publisher evidence continues to mean digest-only.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-java-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can install a JDK, Maven and Gradle itself, so a fresh checkout of a Maven or Gradle project builds without any of them on the machine. See native host builds for which projects build this way. Note: Supported on Linux x86-64 only.

Pinning is optional. For a Maven project that builds natively, oyzu build picks a JDK and Maven (or Ant 1.10.18 for a build.xml project), writes oyzu.lock, installs them into the shared tool store and builds: oyzu build # no Java or Maven on PATH, no pin needed oyzu pin --dry-run # preview: oyzu:java 17 and oyzu:maven 3.9, with where each came from mvn -version In an activated shell, which the install script sets up, the plain tool commands run the pinned versions. Where a shell isn't activated, prefix them with oyzu exec --. To choose versions yourself, set them in oyzu.toml. This takes precedence: [tools] java = "21" # latest 21.x; also "lts" or an exact "21.0.8" maven = "3.9" # latest 3.9.x; any Maven release range

Tool Default Override JDK The root Maven compiler floor described below, raised to 17 if lower. Otherwise a literal java.version default hint, or lts: the newest long-term-support release [tools] java Maven 3.9, which supports Java 8 and newer [tools] maven Gradle Gradle 8, or Gradle 9 when the root script or native daemon criteria declares a Java level above 24 [tools] gradle For Maven, Oyzu reads direct root maven-compiler-plugin configuration and root maven.compiler.release, maven.compiler.source, maven.compiler.target and maven.compiler.testRelease properties. Configuration wins over its corresponding property; release then overrides both source and target. Without release, both source and target floors are retained. A separate testRelease floor is retained alongside the production compiler facts; their highest floor chooses the default JDK. For example, production release 17 with testRelease 25 selects JDK 25 or newer, while a lower test release does not lower the production requirement. Values must be literal Java levels (1.8 means 8). A configuration reference to its corresponding literal root property, such as ${maven.compiler.release}, also works. An invalid or unresolved winning value stops discovery instead of falling back to a lower level. Literal release/testRelease configuration requires an explicit literal compiler-plugin 3.x version of at least 3.6. The plugin must have artifact ID maven-compiler-plugin and group org.apache.maven.plugins (or omit the group). Foreign literal groups are ignored; ambiguous identities and duplicate compiler entries are refused. Root java.version alone is a legacy default hint, not a compiler compatibility constraint: it can be overridden by [tools] java. This is partial root discovery, not Maven's effective model. Relevant profiles, executions, other test-specific levels (testSource/testTarget), executable/toolchain/compiler overrides and configuration merge directives need native evaluation and stop inference with their location. Managed compiler parameters that could supply or mask a level also stop inference, even without a direct plugin declaration. Make the compiler parameters explicit in a supported root declaration to resolve the diagnostic. The main release does not shadow a managed testRelease; only a direct testRelease declaration makes that managed value irrelevant. An inherited=false compiler entry in a pom root without executions is inactive and supplies no module floor. Parent and module POMs are not evaluated here; existing literal root-property facts remain available for parent-based projects. Unknown or older release-configuration semantics and Maven 4 are outside this inference subset. Maven still owns its effective configuration and compilation. The compiler level is a minimum, not the newest JDK: a project declaring 21 gets JDK 21. A project declaring 8, 9 or 11 gets JDK 17, the oldest JDK that Maven, Gradle and oyzu's Java support run on. JDK 17 still compiles for older levels correctly (--release 8 checks against the Java 8 API). Gradle projects follow the same rule. The lock records the exact versions. Gradle's static startup requirements come only from the root script and native daemon JVM criteria. Native preparation checks the effective compiler providers of standard Java tasks in nested members; see Gradle compiler availability. Unregistered sibling scripts do not select the JDK. Isolated (Docker) builds use the same locked JDK instead of the image's (see Maven). An explicit [tools] java below 17 still installs for use on your machine, but an isolated build refuses it with TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION.

Tool Source Check JDK Eclipse Temurin, found through the Adoptium API and downloaded from the adoptium GitHub organization SHA-256 published by the Adoptium API Maven The Apache distribution server (maven-3 and maven-4 listings) The publisher's SHA-512; the lock records the SHA-256 of the checked bytes Gradle The catalog at services.gradle.org/versions/all; the zip is served from Gradle's GitHub releases SHA-256 from the catalog Maven and Gradle use one archive for every platform. Downloads are fetched in 2 MiB pieces, each with its own 45-second timeout, so a slow server makes the first build slower but doesn't make it fail. Checksums come from the publisher; no signatures are checked. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to java, maven, oyzu:java, oyzu:maven or * (see proxy acquisition). When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install. Maven and Gradle dependency downloads use the JVM's trust configuration, not Oyzu's. Behind a TLS-inspecting proxy, set SSL_CERT_FILE to a PEM bundle holding your organization's CA, the same variable Oyzu's own downloads honor. For a java/app build, Oyzu passes that path to the Java builder's worker at launch. It is not part of the build's environment inputs, so it never changes a cache key, and it is used only by java/app. The worker runs one short JVM to write a PKCS12 truststore holding the JDK's own cacerts (JKS or PKCS12) plus every certificate of the bundle, then starts Maven, Gradle and everything they fork with it through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. That includes test forks and Gradle daemons. The JDK's cacerts is never modified, and the store lives in a worker-private temporary directory deleted when the worker ends. If JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS already names a -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore for the worker, that store is the base instead of the JDK's, and the three trust-store properties are replaced by the merged store, so your roots stay trusted and the CA is added. The worker fails closed like Oyzu's own downloads: an unreadable bundle, or one with no importable certificate, stops the build with TRUST_BUNDLE_UNREADABLE or TRUST_BUNDLE_INVALID under JVM_TRUSTSTORE_UNAVAILABLE. OpenSSL TRUSTED CERTIFICATE blocks can't be imported; the worker reports each one as JVM_TRUSTSTORE_SKIPPED (convert with openssl x509). A native PKIX path building failed error means the CA isn't in the bundle. Proxy host and port settings are separate: Oyzu does not translate HTTPS_PROXY into JVM properties.

JAVA_HOME points at the installed JDK (on macOS, its Contents/Home). Build tasks see JAVA_HOME, MAVEN_HOME and GRADLE_HOME from the installed tools. Values already set on your machine are ignored, so a machine-wide JDK can't change which Java a build uses. Shims are provided for java, javac, mvn and gradle.
documents.s: What oyzu sets when Java runs

documents.t: If the project commits mvnw or gradlew, oyzu runs the wrapper instead of mvn or gradle and installs only the JDK. The wrapper downloads its own Maven or Gradle: The Maven wrapper in bin form needs Java plus unzip or tar. The only-script form also needs curl or wget on PATH. That download is the wrapper's own, so oyzu's mirror routes, credentials and checksum checks don't apply. Set distributionSha256Sum in gradle-wrapper.properties or maven-wrapper.properties to have the wrapper verify it.

Maven runs verify, so tests run as part of the build. Each module with Java sources under src/test/java must produce Surefire XML in target/surefire-reports. Results show as Tests N passed · M failed. A failing test fails the build and no artifacts are published. Files under src/test/resources alone do not require Surefire or JaCoCo reports. Java files stored as resources do not count as test sources. JaCoCo 0.8.13 runs around verify, and each tested module's target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml is collected as coverage. A module that declares maven-failsafe-plugin and has an IT*, *IT or *ITCase Java test class under src/test/java must also produce target/failsafe-reports, collected as integration tests. Automatic host report discovery covers this conventional Java test directory. Custom test source roots and other JVM languages need an authored build task with explicit reports. Custom report directories aren't collected. An authored build command supplies its own reports. Gradle runs gradle --no-daemon --console=plain build. oyzu adds an init script that reads Gradle's own model to find each project's archive and test tasks. It publishes the jar and archive outputs, collects JUnit XML and build/reports/oyzu/<test task>/jacoco.xml (JaCoCo 0.8.13). Archive types oyzu doesn't recognize are refused with a reason. Archives with the same name are told apart by project path. Integration-test source sets are collected only when Gradle reports them as Test tasks. Coverage tools are downloaded by Maven or Gradle from Maven Central, so a failed or throttled download fails the build, and offline builds need them cached. --full lint and format checks need Checkstyle and google-java-format provisioned separately (see Java quality); the error says how.
documents.s: What a native Maven or Gradle build runs

documents.t: Native Maven builds need every jar's name to be readable from the POMs: literal or inherited versions, jar packaging, no finalName or classifier. Other projects use the isolated (Docker) build. Ant isn't built natively. oyzu doesn't install Ant. Without Docker, oyzu build stops before doing any work and says it needs the isolated Docker executor (see native host builds). With Docker and the base execution image, the isolated build works. Maven still downloads your project's dependencies from Maven Central, which can throttle shared IP addresses. Pinning records Java requirements for every Maven target, including ones that build in Docker. Windows (including mvn.cmd and the Windows JDK zip) and macOS aren't supported yet.
Maven Gradle Native host builds Liquibase installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-k3d-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can pin and install k3d, so a project that runs a local Kubernetes cluster in Docker doesn't need k3d installed on the machine. oyzu installs only the k3d binary; creating clusters still needs a running Docker engine. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

[tools] k3d = "5.7.4" oyzu install k3d@5.7.4 # declares, locks every platform, installs for this one k3d version In an activated shell, which the install script sets up, the plain tool commands run the pinned versions. Where a shell isn't activated, prefix them with oyzu exec --. The installed command is k3d.

Only exact versions are accepted: 5.7.4 or v5.7.4. Ranges, minor lines such as 5.7, latest and pre-releases are refused, because oyzu doesn't query GitHub for a list of releases. For the same reason oyzu tools versions k3d fails.

oyzu downloads the binary for each platform from the k3d GitHub release (https://github.com/k3d-io/k3d/releases/download/v<version>/k3d-<os>-<arch>, with .exe on Windows). It checks the binary against the SHA-256 listed in the release's checksums.txt and records that digest in the lock. No publisher signature is checked. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to k3d, oyzu:k3d or * (see proxy acquisition). When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.
Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Windows x86-64, macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Recorded in the lock, not supported yet macOS Intel, Linux musl Not supported
oyzu doesn't install or start Docker. --offline needs the tool installed or its binary already cached.
Tool commands kubectl installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-kubectl-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can pin and install kubectl, so a project that deploys to Kubernetes doesn't need kubectl installed on the machine. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

[tools] kubectl = "1.31.2" # exact release # kubectl = "1.31" # newest stable 1.31 patch # kubectl = "latest" # current stable release oyzu install kubectl@1.31 # declares, locks every platform, installs for this one kubectl version --client oyzu which kubectl In an activated shell, which the install script sets up, the plain tool commands run the pinned versions. Where a shell isn't activated, prefix them with oyzu exec --. The installed command is kubectl (kubectl.exe on Windows). oyzu sets no environment variables for it.

Kubernetes doesn't publish a list of every release, so oyzu can't resolve ranges. Use one of these forms: Request Resolved through 1.31.2 or v1.31.2 Used as is 1.31 https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable-1.31.txt latest or * https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt Ranges such as >=1.30, channels and pre-releases are refused, and oyzu tools versions kubectl fails. The lock keeps the exact version, so 1.31 stays on the patch it resolved to until you run oyzu update.

oyzu downloads the binary from https://dl.k8s.io/release/v<version>/bin/<os>/<arch>/kubectl (the site redirects to cdn.dl.k8s.io) and checks it against the .sha256 file published beside it. The digest is recorded in the lock. No publisher signature is checked. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to kubectl, oyzu:kubectl or * (see proxy acquisition). When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.
Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Windows x86-64, macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Recorded in the lock, not supported yet macOS Intel, Linux musl Not supported
--offline needs the tool installed or its binary already cached.
Tool commands Helm installation k3d installation

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-liquibase-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can pin and install liquibase, so a project that applies database changelogs doesn't need Liquibase installed on the machine. Liquibase runs on Java, so pin a JDK beside it (see Java installation). The JDK oyzu installs sets JAVA_HOME, which the Liquibase launcher uses, so no machine-wide Java is involved. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

[tools] java = "21" liquibase = "5.0.4" # exact release # liquibase = "latest" # newest stable release oyzu install java@21 oyzu install liquibase@5.0.4 # declares, locks every platform, installs for this one liquibase --version liquibase --url=jdbc:h2:file:./db/app --username=sa --changelog-file=changelog.xml update In an activated shell, which the install script sets up, the plain tool commands run the pinned versions. Where a shell isn't activated, prefix them with oyzu exec --. The installed command is liquibase (run through liquibase.bat on Windows).

Request Result 5.0.4 or v5.0.4 That release latest The newest GitHub release that isn't a draft or pre-release Ranges, minor lines such as 5.0 and pre-releases are refused, and oyzu tools versions liquibase fails because oyzu doesn't list releases. The lock keeps the resolved version until you run oyzu update. Only releases 4.33.0 and later can be installed (see below).

Liquibase publishes no checksum file. oyzu reads the release from the GitHub API (api.github.com/repos/liquibase/liquibase/releases/) and uses the SHA-256 digest GitHub records for the archive: liquibase-<version>.zip on Windows and liquibase-<version>.tar.gz on Linux and macOS. It checks the download against that digest and records it in the lock. The digest is computed by GitHub when the file is uploaded; it isn't a signature from the Liquibase project. GitHub records these digests only for recent uploads. Releases from 4.33.0 have one; 4.32.0 and earlier don't. oyzu refuses a release without a digest rather than install it unchecked. Unauthenticated GitHub API requests are limited to 60 per hour per IP address, and an install reads the release once per platform. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to liquibase, oyzu:liquibase or * (see proxy acquisition). When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.
Liquibase 5.x is source-available under FSL-1.1-ALv2, not an open-source license. Check that it fits your use before you adopt it.
Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Windows x86-64 Supported macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Recorded in the lock, not supported yet macOS Intel, Linux musl Not supported

On Windows, run liquibase.bat from a normal Windows shell. It calls find /i and fails in a shell that puts a POSIX find ahead of find.exe on PATH. --offline needs the tool installed or its archive already cached.
Java installation Tool commands

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-lock-inspection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu.lock records the exact tool versions, download URLs and digests a project uses. This page describes what the lock contains, how oyzu pin decides which platforms to lock, and how to check a lock file with oyzu tools inspect-lock. Status: experimental. The lock format may change. Native Windows GNU/LLVM qualification for the explicit ABI path is pending. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

The lock envelope and nested tool, plugin, engine, resolution, quality and verification records are security-strict. There is no free-form descriptive field in this format: a newer marker never permits unknown lock members. Readers validate the complete lock before projecting selected tools, and typed writers cannot silently discard unknown newer lock data because decoding refuses it first. All tool locks use format = 1. Writers optionally set the top-level min_oyzu_version to the minimum reader the owner declares for the content, written only when the content requires a reader newer than the marker baseline (0.3.5) (a semantic version such as 0.3.6). Rewrites retain a higher existing minimum; changing the writer's release version alone does not change the marker. Existing unmarked developer-reuse snapshots remain reusable after lock validation; reuse retains their immutable bytes. This is independent of format, which remains 1. Before decoding the lock records, Oyzu validates the marker locally. A newer marker produces one compatibility notice per command, including on failure: this project uses newer features; run oyzu self update Inspection leaves the lock unchanged and needs no network; updating Oyzu requires access to its release source. Missing markers are accepted for existing files. Malformed markers fail with FILE_READER_INVALID. Unknown fields in otherwise readable locks fail with FILE_UNKNOWN_FIELD, name the field and suggest oyzu self update before correcting a possible spelling mistake. With a newer marker, strict unknown-field or unknown-variant failures also name the file-declared minimum in the error and recovery guidance. The declared release is conservative advice; an old reader cannot know the first supporting release for a future semantic field. Without a newer marker, the update hint does not invent an exact minimum. These failures retain exit status 3 and code FILE_UNKNOWN_FIELD. The diagnostic is available from Oyzu 0.3.5 onward. Released 0.3.4 and older binaries cannot acquire it without updating and may still report an unknown field. A marker grants no permission to skip lock validation or publisher verification. Warnings go to stderr as JSON Lines in --json mode, code FILE_READER_NEWER, without changing a successful exit status. Published 0.3.8 still refuses higher markers; this behavior requires an updated reader. Lock records retain strict field validation: unknown verification, package and engine-selection semantics still refuse. A higher marker never permits ignored security data. Do not remove verification fields to make inspection succeed. Installation receipts, quality-bundle receipts, locked quality assets and package-content inventories keep their admission fields closed. A newer marker alone is advisory; unknown fields in these records still refuse because they can change executable content, launch behavior or placement. Publisher evidence also keeps its identity, issuer, strength and verification checks. Updating Oyzu is the recovery path; do not edit away unfamiliar trust data. When reinstalling an engine or plugin whose release directory is missing, Oyzu checks stale package-content metadata before publishing the release. A replacement retains a readable record's higher minimum reader, or refuses with FILE_READER_TOO_OLD if newer unknown data would be lost. Refusal leaves the existing bytes intact and the release uninstalled, so retries cannot reuse a partially installed release. Corrupt JSON, oversized records, permission-denied reads and non-directory stale entries (including Unix symlinks and FIFOs) can be repaired when the filesystem permits unlinking the entry. Symlink targets are never followed or modified. Other read failures, such as resource exhaustion or device errors, stop installation before removing the existing metadata. A directory, Windows directory symlink or junction at the receipt path is not removed. Windows read-only files or sharing locks can also prevent removal. These failures stop before publishing the release; correct the receipt path or its access restrictions, then retry once any sharing lock is released. One file can hold two kinds of records, and neither implies the other: resolved_environment and resolution records: what oyzu pin or an online, non-frozen project install resolved (versions, URLs and digests per platform). environment and tool records: verified installations. It can also hold optional [[requirements]] records, which list what Oyzu discovered your builds need. Their resolved and installed fields are always false. oyzu pin updates resolution records and keeps installation records. An online, non-frozen project install also records captured build requirements through pin's resolution path, retaining selected versions. Frozen installs keep the lock unchanged; offline installs consume existing recipes. Any other format value fails. A set locked for a toolset carries toolset = "NAME". Sets for [tools] carry none. The label only decides which sets a command changes; the same requests get the same identity in every toolset. Entries have no scope or profile field. The format is described by the lock JSON schema. If Oyzu rejects a lock written by an older development build, run oyzu pin --refresh, then oyzu install. Existing installed files are kept.

New resolution records carry evidence.strength; installed distributions and receipts carry verification.strength. The values describe the publisher evidence actually verified: Strength Meaning digest-only Pinned SHA-256, with no authenticated publisher identity. checksum-file The digest agrees with a publisher checksum file. A file from the same origin is not proof of publisher identity. signature A publisher signature, including a signed checksum list or an authenticated checksum-database entry, binds the selected bytes. provenance Verified publisher build provenance binds the selected bytes. If activation reports unknown field strength while reading an installed-tool receipt, the affected bootstrap 0.2.1-local.aab8c60e967a cannot be repaired by this change or by changing its input. The base verification type already accepts strength; the observed stale-bootstrap failure requires upgrading that binary. Run oyzu self update through a current installed executable, then run oyzu shell install through that executable to refresh the profile's absolute CLI path and guarded activation block. Restart the shell or rerun oyzu activate pwsh (PowerShell) or oyzu activate bash (Bash) through the current executable. Keep receipts and installed tools intact; no reinstall is needed. Receipt readers from this version onward ignore unknown descriptive members inside verification.annotations, reporting one debug note per command, without rewriting receipts. activate, which and shell share these readers. The verification kind, strength, required digests and all other admission fields remain strict; annotations cannot grant trust or change a launch. Unknown fields outside this descriptive object still require a reader that understands them. Existing old binaries cannot gain this behavior without upgrading. Adding a new flat verification field, as happened earlier with strength, will still break older readers. Signed publisher evidence and lock records retain their closed contracts. Receipt writers MUST put new descriptive verification data under verification.annotations. Adding a flat member to the verification record is a breaking change for older readers and requires the must-understand process: justify the security or integrity semantics explicitly and update the owning contract, producers, consumers, fixtures and compatibility guidance together. Never put trust-gating data in annotations. Lock verification records remain closed and do not accept annotations. Flat verification writer allowlist: strength, kind, evidence_digest, verifier_digest, subject_digest. strength is optional and omitted when absent. The signed tool index records the verdict for a version; it is the weakest strength among its resolved platforms. OpenPGP verification happens in index production, outside the shipping CLI. At pin time, a supplied Sigstore bundle is also verified by the CLI against its subject, certificate identity and trust root. A wrong signer or digest fails with TOOL_PUBLISHER_UNTRUSTED. An index signature authenticates the index publisher, not the tool publisher. Older index/lock records without a strength remain readable and count as digest-only; refreshing does not invent signature evidence. Unchanged frozen locks retain their identities. Installs consume recorded evidence and check the locked archive digest and layout; they do not re-verify publisher signatures or scan previously installed payloads. Moving default selections wait at least seven days after the index's released.time. tools.minimumReleaseAgeDays can lengthen that delay; values below seven are invalid, and organizational minimum constraints remain binding. An exact earlier version is allowed and emits TOOL_RELEASE_COOLDOWN. Only a signed index's security-release reason, or an advisory fix naming the current exact pin, can bypass the delay. The selected reason is frozen in evidence.security_exception; there is no user bypass flag. If every matching indexed version is too young, selection fails with TOOL_RELEASE_COOLDOWN. Moving default selections require publication dates from the signed index. Without suitable index metadata they fail with TOOL_RELEASE_AGE_UNAVAILABLE; configure an index or request an exact version explicitly. Offline operation reuses existing resolution records or a previously verified, unexpired index; it does not contact publishers. The direct github: adapter has no signed-index release dates and therefore requires an exact request. An explicit unindexed version has no authenticated publication date to compare; its weaker evidence remains visible. oyzu pin --dry-run previews what would be locked, and oyzu pin writes it without installing. See requirement discovery.

Human previews include Tool acquisition changes. JSON includes recipeChanges[]: each entry has tool, change (added, removed or changed), and complete before/after recipes; the absent side is null. The comparison includes execution platform, components, canonical tool/provider identity, input URLs/checksums and publisher evidence. A source or checksum change is visible even when the version stays the same. Ordinary pin preserves compatible versions and complete compiler/helper recipes. Before reusing a selected locked Cargo helper recipe, plain pin compares its complete recipe identity with the built-in table, including URLs and checksums. A mismatch refuses with TOOL_RECIPE_MISMATCH and leaves the lock unchanged, including during offline pin. Review oyzu pin --refresh --dry-run to see the replacement in recipeChanges, then apply oyzu pin --refresh deliberately. Adding execution coverage keeps unrelated request sets and existing platform installation identities. oyzu pin --refresh --dry-run deliberately refreshes metadata while retaining selected versions; inspect its proposal before applying oyzu pin --refresh. Targeted pin/update previews expose the same recipe facts, and an explicit update reports an acquisition change as updated even at the same version. A frontend rebuild alone does not invalidate the semantic provider identity. Missing required coverage or incompatible backend semantics fail explicitly; pin never publishes an incomplete proposal.

oyzu tools inspect-lock [PATH] checks that a lock file is well formed. It doesn't resolve, download, install or run anything, and it doesn't check that the tools are installed. oyzu -C /path/to/project tools inspect-lock oyzu tools inspect-lock path/to/oyzu.lock PATH defaults to oyzu.lock in -C, then --root, then the current directory. An absolute path also works. Output is readable text by default; --json returns the structured result. Exit 0 on success, 2 on a validation or read error. The file must be a regular UTF-8 TOML file of at most 8 MiB. Symlinks to a regular file are followed; FIFOs are refused. It doesn't read project configuration or mise files, make network requests or change the lock. The whole file is checked, whatever profile or toolset is selected.

The command rejects: unknown or duplicate fields, an unsupported format and malformed digests; record keys that don't match their content, and verification subjects that differ from artifact digests; duplicate sets, missing dependencies, cycles, unreachable tools, conflicting IDs in one set and missing platform entries; source or artifact identifiers containing colons, path separators or control characters. Limits: 1,024 environments, 4,096 tools, 64 platform entries per tool, 16,384 dependency edges, depth 64 and 256 roots per environment.

The format, environment and tool counts, and the sorted list of platforms. A selection digest for each environment and platform. It covers every tool in the set, including dependencies, their file digests, verification and layout. Comments and ordering don't affect it; changing any dependency's file changes it. installation_keys, mapping each tool to the identity of its installation. Changing a dependency changes its key and the keys of tools that depend on it. Adding a platform leaves the existing keys unchanged. These keys name intended content; they don't mean the installation exists. The result says validation: "structure-and-identity-only". A pass means the file is consistent. It doesn't prove the publisher is authentic, that policy allows the tools, or that installed files are intact. A carefully crafted malicious lock can pass. Request digests are checked for shape, not recomputed against your configuration. If the check fails, fix the records or restore a known good lock (or regenerate it with oyzu pin). Don't edit digests to make it pass. The command never repairs files.

Node and Go projects can run oyzu pin --dry-run, oyzu pin, then oyzu install --frozen: Set node or go in [tools]. For Go, the minimum in go.mod or go.work (the newer of the go and toolchain lines) is a request by itself when [tools] go is unset; see Go version selection. Node also checks engines.node in package.json. Neither tool is run to find this out. If a configured version is missing, the preview is incomplete, explains why and exits 2. It never writes an empty lock. Pin records the selected version, the archive URL and its SHA-256. It doesn't download the archive. Node and Go entries keep your request (including prefixes and ranges) next to the exact version. Validation checks that the version satisfies the request, using the provider's rules (including Node aliases). --frozen doesn't re-read the publisher's catalog. Rust accepts an exact stable release, or stable selected through eligible signed-index metadata. An existing compatible lock retains its exact selection. Cargo helper requests are exact versions.

ARM64 is unsupported. A project may retain ARM64 metadata in an existing lock without installing it. The Oyzu repository requires x64 Linux, Intel macOS and Windows lock coverage; updating this scope does not delete old lock records or installations. By default, the lock covers the platforms declared by every build in the project, plus the host, whatever command you run. Inferred platforms without a matching provider artifact are listed in platformsNotLocked (human output: Inferred platforms not locked). This includes a GitHub release whose only applicable asset belongs to another platform, such as the reviewed Darwin gettext xcframework when Linux coverage is inferred. The host and any platform you list explicitly must be covered. Oyzu never borrows another platform's artifact. Missing coverage is optional only for inferred foreign platforms. Checksum, archive-layout and ambiguous-command failures still fail pin instead of becoming an omission. Offline pin needs existing matching entries; it may leave other inferred platforms unlocked. oyzu install installs the host entry and keeps the rest of the lock. A repeat offline install reuses the verified copy in your store. To lock platforms explicitly, for example for another machine that runs your builds, set tools.lockPlatforms: [compatibility] requires = ["tools.rust-windows-abi"] [tools] rust = { version = "1.95.0", windowsAbi = "gnullvm" } lockPlatforms = ["windows/amd64/gnullvm", "linux/amd64/gnu"] The list must not be empty and must use exact supported platforms. The host is always included. Coverage does not select the invocation's Rust ABI. The example's windowsAbi selects GNU/LLVM on a Windows x64 host; the same declaration leaves Linux execution unchanged. tools.platforms is no longer accepted. Remove it, or rename it to lockPlatforms. See mapping and migration.

Rust uses the current lock coverage, rather than every platform an older lock recorded. Current x64 execution tuples are linux/amd64/gnu, darwin/amd64/native, windows/amd64/msvc and windows/amd64/gnullvm; native installation limits still apply. ARM64 tuples remain readable as metadata, but ARM64 installation and execution are unsupported regardless of retained metadata. Windows GNU/LLVM entries also lock the rust-mingw component. Windows x64 defaults to MSVC; tools.rust = { version = "1.95.0", windowsAbi = "gnullvm" } selects the GNU/LLVM compiler context explicitly. On other Windows host architectures this request refuses with TOOL_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED, naming the host and requested ABI. Listing GNU/LLVM in lockPlatforms alone requests its metadata and does not switch the host compiler. Pin resolves every requested platform and its components before writing. Missing publisher data fails without writing a partial lock. Offline pin needs existing matching entries for every required platform. A locked stable request reuses its exact stable release without resolving a newer version. The Cargo helpers are cargo-nextest 0.9.146 and cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1, with URLs and SHA-256 digests from their GitHub releases. Only these two helpers may use Windows x64 MSVC artifacts in a GNU/LLVM execution context; all other tools require an exact platform match. macOS cargo-nextest is a universal binary. Always pair the ABI option with [compatibility] requires = ["tools.rust-windows-abi"]. A client without that capability then refuses the configuration instead of ignoring the optional field. The complete winning Rust declaration supplies version and ABI together, including when input aliases are used. Supported ABI values are msvc and gnullvm; an invalid known value or windowsAbi on a non-Rust tool fails. Unrecognized future optional fields warn and are ignored; --strict makes those warnings fatal. The experimental pure-Rust GNU/LLVM path uses the locked Rust 1.95.0 compiler and rust-mingw, with explicit selection of bundled rust-lld from the admitted compiler sysroot, for example through CARGO_TARGET_X86_64_PC_WINDOWS_GNULLVM_LINKER. Compiler ABI selection alone does not configure a linker. C/C++ dependencies may require an externally provisioned compatible LLVM/MinGW toolchain. Oyzu does not provision Windows OS components or SDKs. Frozen installation consumes only the selected execution closure; native Windows Cargo helpers remain MSVC binaries. The tool qualification harness builds this checkout's native Rust adapter with oyzu build qualification-rust-plugin and accepts it through --rust-plugin. It creates an isolated user configuration with an explicit development binding; the committed fixture still owns the shared tool recipes. The published Rust builder package currently has no Windows payload, so this source qualification does not establish availability of a released Windows builder package. Locking a platform does not establish native execution support. Current Windows GNU/LLVM native installation/build/report qualification remains pending. Intel macOS metadata is not native macOS qualification. ARM64 installation and execution remain unsupported.

Store inspection Tool commands Configuration For Sigstore evidence, locks preserve the signed index's issuer and runner_environment next to the exact signer identity. Pinning checks the issuer against Oyzu's allowlist and matches all supplied claims to the signing certificate; omission never creates authenticated evidence. Offline inspection reads the frozen facts and does not run a producer verifier. To impose a fourteen-day organizational minimum, policy uses the existing numeric constraint contract: [constraints."tools.minimumReleaseAgeDays"] minimum = 14 A corporate policy constraint wins over a user's tools.minimumReleaseAgeDays = 7; inspection, moving selections and replacement suggestions use that resolved minimum. Values below seven are invalid in settings and policy alike. Exact pins retain the documented early-selection warning and signed-index security exceptions.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-npm-pnpm-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can pin and install npm, pnpm and Yarn as their own tools (oyzu:npm, oyzu:pnpm and oyzu:yarn), separate from the npm bundled with Node. Choose a release in [tools] or with packageManager in package.json; the lock records it with the registry's integrity hash. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

[tools] node = "22.12" npm = "11.6.2" # exact release, a range such as "11", or "latest" # pnpm = "10.20.0" oyzu install npm@11.6.2 # declares, locks, installs npm --version npx --version oyzu install pnpm@10.20.0 pnpm --version In an activated shell, which the install script sets up, the plain tool commands run the pinned versions. Where a shell isn't activated, prefix them with oyzu exec --. oyzu tools versions npm and oyzu tools versions pnpm list the registry's stable releases.

Selecting Node also gives you its bundled npm and npx, through oyzu exec, activated shells and shims, with no separate npm declaration. Both run on the selected Node. Declare npm only when you want a different npm release; its npm and npx then take precedence over the bundled copy. npm needs Node: when oyzu:npm is selected, select oyzu:node too. A lifecycle script that calls npm through PATH during oyzu exec still finds Node's bundled npm; in an isolated build it finds the locked one. After upgrading oyzu, run oyzu reshim to refresh existing shims. A shim doesn't pick a version itself: it uses the project or global selection each time it runs.

pnpm releases combine the older platform packages and the pnpm 12 packages. latest follows the pnpm package's latest tag. If that release isn't available for your platform, latest fails, but exact pins and ranges still work.

A Node build uses the nearest package.json with a packageManager field, searched from the build folder up to the project root (as Corepack does). If it names an exact stable npm or pnpm release, such as "packageManager": "pnpm@10.20.0", that release becomes a tool requirement: It's a native pin file. When the project has no oyzu.lock, the build locks it beside Node. A [tools] npm or [tools] pnpm value must agree. A disagreeing value in the same folder or nearer the build fails with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_CONFLICT; one further away loses to packageManager. A Corepack hash suffix (+sha512.<hex>) is accepted but not compared. The lock records the registry's integrity hash instead. A range, tag, bare major, pre-release or URL fails with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_INVALID. Write an exact stable release, or remove the field and set [tools]. If oyzu.lock already exists without that release, add it with oyzu install npm@<version> or oyzu install pnpm@<version>. When there's no packageManager, an exact devEngines.packageManager version with onFail: "error" is the request. For Yarn, see Managed Yarn. engines.node constrains Node's version instead; see Node selection.

Isolated builds use the locked release instead of the copy in the build image, for dependency installation and every action: pnpm is placed at /scratch/pnpmtool and comes first on PATH. npm is placed at /scratch/npmtool. Dependency installation writes npm and npx launchers to /dependencies/manager/bin, which comes first on PATH for every action. The build's dependency record lists the locked release under the oyzu.dev/locked-manager extension. A changed digest in oyzu.lock is refused. Isolated builds run on linux/amd64 workers only, and an offline build needs the archive already cached. On a Windows machine, pnpm workspace links stay inside the Linux build workspace. oyzu reads them without following them on the host, and doesn't restore cached action results that contain links.
