Note: Managed Yarn is experimental. It supports Classic 1.22.22 and Berry 4.17.1 with Node 22.23.3 for single-package applications on Linux and Windows (x86-64). Isolated builds don't support Yarn yet. oyzu installs Classic Yarn from the yarn package and modern Yarn from @yarnpkg/cli-dist on the npm registry. latest follows the modern package's tag. Both yarn and yarnpkg run bin/yarn.js on the selected Node. Declare Node too: Yarn doesn't install its own runtime or use Corepack. [tools] node = "22.23.3" yarn = "4.17.1" oyzu pin oyzu install --frozen yarn --version yarnpkg --version Both commands print 4.17.1. Use yarn = "1.22.22" for Classic.

Yarn builds go through the Node plugin with a declared node/app target and a yarn.lock generated by Yarn. A full frozen build exports fresh dist output with JUnit and LCOV reports. A failed test or missing required report blocks the export. To run tests directly, install dependencies first (for Berry, yarn install --immutable). Requirements: packageManager names exactly yarn@1.22.22 or yarn@4.17.1. Berry needs a .yarnrc.yml with nodeLinker: node-modules (or the quoted "node-modules"). oyzu never converts a Plug'n'Play project. Berry needs Node >=18.12.0 as well as the project's engines.node. Workspaces, Yarn plugins, yarnPath, custom registries and Git, file or patch dependencies aren't supported. Dependency installation needs yarn.lock. Classic runs install --frozen-lockfile (plus --offline for offline builds). Berry runs install --immutable, with YARN_ENABLE_NETWORK=0 for offline builds. Offline builds need the tools and Yarn's cache already present. A failed install stops dependent actions and artifact collection.

Before running Yarn, oyzu checks the project, parent-folder and home rc files. For native Berry, the admitted settings are nodeLinker: node-modules (including the quoted linker value) and YAML boolean enableTelemetry: false: nodeLinker: "node-modules" enableTelemetry: false The opt-out alone does not select a linker; the project must still select node-modules. Other telemetry values, including the string "false", and other settings remain refused. The opt-out works for native single-root applications on Linux x86_64 (GNU) with Berry 4.17.1 and Node 22.23.4. Classic and isolated Berry configuration keep their existing rules. For Classic, oyzu also checks .config/yarn/config, .config/yarn, .yarn/config, the XDG or Windows config location, /etc/yarn/config, /etc/yarnrc and npm's global npmrc under the selected Node's prefix. Directories at those paths are ignored, as Classic does. Any other setting, an unusual or oversized rc file, or an environment override of the registry or linker (including YARN_CONFIG, YARN_REGISTRY, an alternate npm user config or DESTDIR) fails with YARN_CONFIG_UNSUPPORTED before Yarn runs. Remove the setting, then retry.

Each tarball is checked against the registry's SHA-512 integrity and the original files and notices are kept. Classic includes a BSD-2-Clause LICENSE file. The Berry package has its bundled notices but no standalone LICENSE; its source license is BSD-2-Clause.

All three tools come from https://registry.npmjs.org/. oyzu reads the package's metadata and refuses a release whose tarball isn't at <registry>/<package>/-/<file>-<version>.tgz or that has no SHA-512 integrity. It downloads the tarball, checks it against that integrity and locks the SHA-256 of the checked bytes. Tool Releases up to 11 Releases from 12 Commands npm npm, one tarball for every platform Same package npm and npx, run on the selected Node pnpm on Linux x86-64 @pnpm/linux-x64 @pnpm/exe.linux-x64 pnpm pnpm on Linux ARM64 @pnpm/linux-arm64 @pnpm/exe.linux-arm64 pnpm pnpm on macOS Apple silicon @pnpm/macos-arm64 @pnpm/exe.darwin-arm64 pnpm pnpm on Windows x86-64 @pnpm/win-x64 @pnpm/exe.win32-x64 pnpm.exe npm's own bin/npm and bin/npx launchers (and their .cmd and .ps1 forms) run Node's bundled npm, so oyzu leaves them out and runs bin/npm-cli.js and bin/npx-cli.js directly. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to npm, oyzu:npm, pnpm, oyzu:pnpm or * (see proxy acquisition). Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.

pnpm is supported on Windows x86-64 for isolated builds. Other platforms for the dedicated npm and pnpm tools aren't supported yet, and neither is offline dependency installation. Nested npm calls from lifecycle scripts inside builds aren't supported yet. Linux ARM64 is recorded in the lock but not supported yet; musl isn't supported.
Node applications pnpm Yarn Tool commands

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-proxy-acquisition.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Administrative tool routes send tool archives and metadata through an approved mirror or proxy. The acquisition owner uses the same route rules for built-in providers, registry recipe tools, the pinned short-name catalog, artifact sets, recipe evidence and tool-index metadata. Routing applies on Linux, Windows and macOS and does not depend on standalone or managed configuration. Each provider's supported installation platforms and managed admission requirements still apply. Routes change the source of bytes. They do not grant approval or replace digest, publisher evidence, tool-index admission, layout or installation checks.

An administrator adds routes to the protected admin-settings.json, inside its settings object, or supplies them through managed policy: "registries.routes": { "locked": true, "value": [ {"protocol": "tools", "scope": "node", "connectorId": "corp-node"}, {"protocol": "tools", "scope": "static.rust-lang.org", "connectorId": "corp-rust"} ] } The scope is an exact lowercase host (optionally including a port), or a tool family such as node, go, rust or oyzu:node. Built-in oyzu: and core: spellings are aliases of the bare family name. A recipe's canonical aqua: ID can select that recipe's downloads. * supplies a fallback route. For a family's own release metadata, checksums and archives, a matching family scope takes precedence over a matching host scope. Node headers prepared for node-gyp use the Node family route too; their declared-fetch source admission and pinned digest checks still apply. Tool-index and organization-catalog requests, including catalog edge delivery, use their service's host route, then *. Selecting Node never sends those requests through the Node family mirror. A host scope takes precedence over *. Two rules for the same scope, including family aliases, fail with ROUTE_RULE_CONFLICT; configuration order does not choose a winner. With no tools routes, providers download directly using their reviewed upstream host lists. Redirects outside that provider's hosts are refused; registry recipes may additionally admit their pinned public download hosts. Index/catalog metadata retains its own service hosts. Artifact sets retain their standalone direct behavior, including open HTTPS redirect hops. Once any tools route exists, each download must match a family, host or fallback rule. Otherwise it fails before download with ROUTE_UNROUTABLE. Only protocol tools participates. Routes cannot appear in project TOML, oyzu.local.toml or profiles.

The caller explicitly supplies a host binding file; Oyzu does not discover one in the project: format = 1 [connectors.corp-node] base_url = "https://mirror.example/node/" authorization_env = "CORPORATE_NODE_AUTHORIZATION" redirects = "server" [connectors.corp-rust] base_url = "https://mirror.example/rust/" redirects = "client" oyzu install --connector-bindings /absolute/path/to/host-bindings.toml oyzu tools evidence --provider node --version 22.20.0 --connector-bindings /absolute/path/to/host-bindings.toml oyzu tools trust refresh --connector-bindings /absolute/path/to/host-bindings.toml Key Meaning base_url HTTPS destination and fixed path prefix. Plain HTTP is permitted only for loopback fixtures. No credentials, query, fragment, dot segments or encoded path separators. authorization_env Optional environment variable holding the complete Authorization header value. redirects "client" (default): the client follows redirects and resolves each new host through the same table. "server": the destination must follow redirects itself; a 3xx reply fails. The destination is base_url without its trailing slash, followed by the original URL's path and query. For example, Node's /dist/index.json goes to https://mirror.example/node/dist/index.json. This replaces Node's earlier special mapping, which removed /dist/; existing Node mirrors must serve the full upstream path. Go, Rust and every other family use the same rule. A family route also applies to that family's own download redirect hops. A host-only client route requires a rule for each redirected host; an unlisted hop fails with ROUTE_REDIRECT_UNROUTABLE. Server routes reject redirects with ROUTE_REDIRECT_UNEXPECTED. Redirect targets and credentials are never recorded in locks or printed. The metadata commands tools versions, tools check --catalog and tools migrate also accept --connector-bindings. Keep credentials in secret provisioning, outside project files, binding files and arguments. Publisher credentials are not forwarded to a configured mirror; its binding supplies its authorization.

Missing bindings or credentials, denied requests and failed verification are terminal; Oyzu does not retry through an alternative public source. Fix the administrative rule or binding and retry. Removing every tools route restores direct acquisition without changing locked content identities. The lock keeps logical source URLs and digests, never mirror destinations or credentials. Offline acquisition uses only already available store inputs and verified metadata; missing inputs fail without contacting a mirror. A cached provider installation needs no connector credentials. An online acquisition loads its binding table once and reuses its HTTP client while the destination origin and connector stay the same. Changes to bindings take effect in a new acquisition. Managed catalog approval, index withdrawal and publisher verification remain binding. A route cannot make an unapproved tool installable. The sandbox runtime and Sigstore trust refresh also consult host routes. Plugin package downloads (OCI and HTTPS) use their separate catalog routing contract; these administrative tool routes do not redirect them.
Artifact sets Configuration Tool commands Tool index and tool catalog

Check the route scope, binding path, mirror certificate chain and the authorization variable before retrying. The mirror must preserve the complete upstream path, including prefixes such as /dist/ for Node. Use oyzu tools evidence with the same connector bindings to inspect a selected download's verification inputs. An existing installed tool is trusted and does not test mirror connectivity.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-python-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can install CPython itself for a Python build, so a fresh checkout builds without Python on the machine. See native host builds for which projects build this way. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Pinning is optional. For a Python project that builds natively, oyzu build picks a CPython release, writes oyzu.lock, installs it into the shared tool store and builds with it: oyzu build # no Python on PATH, no pin needed oyzu pin # optional: preview or refresh the selection python --version In an activated shell, which the install script sets up, the plain tool commands run the pinned versions. Where a shell isn't activated, prefix them with oyzu exec --. To choose a version yourself, set it in oyzu.toml: [tools] python = "3.12" # latest 3.12.x; ranges such as ">=3.11 <3.14" also work

Source Role .python-version (one release such as 3.12 or 3.12.4), the nearest one from the build folder up to the project root The request. It's a native pin file [tools] python in oyzu.toml The request when no .python-version applies. Otherwise it must agree with the file (3.12 agrees with 3.12.4). A disagreeing value further from the build than the file loses to it; one in the same folder or nearer fails with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_CONFLICT [project] requires-python in pyproject.toml A constraint every selection must meet [tool.poetry.dependencies] python in pyproject.toml, using supported PEP 440 comparisons An additional constraint every selection must meet None of these The newest stable release oyzu picks the newest stable CPython that meets the request and every constraint. Pre-releases, free-threaded and debug builds are never picked. A .python-version holding anything other than one CPython release (system, pypy3.10, 3.13t, several versions) fails with TOOL_NATIVE_PIN_INVALID. Blank lines and # comments are ignored. requires-python follows PEP 440: <=3.12 means at most 3.12.0, and ~=3.10 means >=3.10, <4. !=, === and local or pre-release specifiers can't be used as a tool range and fail with the specifier named. Use a supported native range; a configured tool pin does not bypass an unsupported declaration. When nothing matches, the error names the request, each constraint and the file it came from. Poetry's native Python declaration accepts the same expressible PEP 440 comparison form, for example python = ">=3.12,<3.13". When it accompanies project.requires-python, both declarations apply; conflicting ranges fail selection. The error identifies tool.poetry.dependencies.python and the source file. A configured interpreter never overrides either native constraint. Poetry-only ^, ~, bare wildcards (* or 3.12.*) and union forms are not translated. Rewrite an unsupported declaration using equivalent supported comparisons before pinning; the error includes an example. Oyzu does not run Poetry or install a manager to read this declaration.

oyzu installs the install_only builds from Python Build Standalone. It reads the publisher's latest-release.json and that release's SHA256SUMS, then records the archive URL and digest in oyzu.lock. Downloads are checked against that digest; no signatures are checked. With a lock in place, oyzu doesn't need to read the release list again. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to python, oyzu:python or * (see proxy acquisition). The mirror serves the original upstream paths and queries for metadata and release archives; host routes can select their upstream hosts separately. When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install. If the signed tool index marks a platform unsupported, installation fails with TOOL_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE even when the publisher has an archive.

python runs the real interpreter (python.exe on Windows, bin/python3.X on Unix). python3 and python3.X also work through oyzu exec and shims. When pip is included, pip, pip3 and pip3.X run python -m pip on the selected interpreter. You don't need to declare pip separately. The distribution's bundled terminfo database (share/terminfo) is left out, because it contains file names that differ only by letter case. Python's curses module uses the system's terminfo instead. After upgrading oyzu, run oyzu reshim to refresh an existing shims directory.

oyzu checks the archive digest and layout when it installs Python and trusts the installation after that. Builds, tasks, oyzu exec and shells don't re-check it, so Python can write __pycache__ files next to its standard library as usual. If an installation is damaged or edited, oyzu doesn't notice in advance; the interpreter fails when it runs. Delete that tool installation to reinstall it.

Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported, including native wheel builds macOS Intel Installing and running the interpreter (Python 3.11) Windows x86-64 Native pip applications with an admitted managed CPython and matching native plugin; tool-index platform availability still applies macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Not supported yet Linux musl Not supported

Native builds cover pip wheels and static PEP 621 applications from pyproject.toml. Isolated builds with pip, uv, Poetry and other managers use the same locked Python in Docker; see interpreter selection. pip downloads the project's build backend from the package index during the wheel build, so --offline builds fail unless it's already cached. With nothing declared, oyzu picks the newest stable CPython, which may be very recent. Declare requires-python or pin a version to avoid surprises.
Python preparation Native pin files Tool commands

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-resolve.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Many tools are single-binary releases described only by community recipes (the public aqua registry). These two commands turn a recipe into a file that lists exactly what to download for each version and platform, and then check those downloads against what the publisher published. Use them to build or audit an artifact set or tool index records. Neither command installs anything. Note: Experimental. Command and field names, exit code 3 and limit values may change. Supported on Linux x86-64; Windows and macOS are not supported yet. oyzu tools resolve evaluates a recipe snapshot offline and writes one record per tool, version and platform (the discovery tier). It reads only the snapshot file you name and its flags, and writes to stdout. oyzu tools evidence takes that output, downloads each artifact and its checksum file from the publisher, records the SHA-256 and size, compares them with the published checksum and fills in the verified tier. With --provider, it first builds the records for one of Oyzu's own providers from the publisher's listing. tools resolve reads only its explicit local inputs. tools evidence reads effective configuration to enforce administrative tool routes and accepts --connector-bindings FILE for host endpoints and credentials. Neither command changes configuration, locks or installed tools, and neither requires an account in standalone mode. Paths resolve from the invocation directory, including -C; managed configuration retains its normal access rules. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.
documents.s: Recipe resolution and evidence (oyzu tools resolve, oyzu tools evidence)

documents.t: # 1. Download a registry snapshot yourself (resolve never fetches one) curl -sSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquaproj/aqua-registry/v4.573.0/registry.yaml # 2. Evaluate offline, pinned to the snapshot digest oyzu --json tools resolve --registry registry.yaml \ --registry-digest sha256:52a43b0b2817a56fe7566625809d7cca41a1178ccae2b152941221b516e70228 \ --snapshot-tag v4.573.0 \ --tool hashicorp/terraform --version v1.16.5 > terraform.discovery.json # 3. Download and check the real files (needs the network) oyzu --json tools evidence --set terraform.discovery.json > terraform.verified.json Without --json, both commands print a summary: the outcome, a table of records, unsupported platforms and errors with reasons, and next steps.

Flag Meaning --registry FILE The merged registry.yaml. A directory (the per-package tree form) is rejected with SNAPSHOT_INVALID. --registry-digest sha256:HEX Reject the snapshot unless its SHA-256 matches (SNAPSHOT_DIGEST_MISMATCH). --snapshot-tag, --snapshot-commit Labels recorded in the output. Not checked. --tool NAME (repeatable), --tools-file FILE Registry package names such as hashicorp/terraform. The file has one name per line; # starts a comment. --version V (repeatable) Exact upstream version as the recipe sees it, including any prefix (v1.16.5). Required. --platform OS/ARCH/ABI (repeatable) Default: linux/amd64/gnu, darwin/amd64/native, windows/amd64/msvc, whatever the host. OS: linux, darwin, windows. Architecture: amd64, arm64. Other ABIs (for example musl) give an error record, PLATFORM_ABI_UNSUPPORTED. --limit NAME=VALUE (repeatable) Lower a limit: recipe_nodes, recipe_bytes, recipe_depth, recipe_overrides, string_bytes, expression_steps, url_bytes, record_urls, regex_bytes, snapshot_bytes, output_bytes. Limits can't be raised. Every tool and version is evaluated for every platform. The output is sorted by tool ID, version and platform, so flag order doesn't matter. Tool IDs are aqua:<package> (for example aqua:cli/cli), the same spelling mise uses.

Packages of type github_release and http. Oyzu has its own evaluator for the registry's data format, which supports: Version selection: version_constraint, the first matching version_overrides entry, version_prefix and version_filter. The record's version.branch is top-level, override[N], or null when no branch applied. Expressions: Version, SemVer, string and list literals, semver("..."), ==, !=, in, matches, startsWith, endsWith, contains, not/!, and/&&, or/||. semver() is false for a non-semver version. Pre-release versions only satisfy constraints that name a pre-release. Templates: {{.Version}}-style fields, pipes, parentheses, if/else/end, and the functions trimV trimPrefix trimSuffix replace title semver regexFind index splitList eq ne. supported_envs (with rosetta2 and windows_arm_emulation), replacements, platform overrides (first match), no_asset, error_message, complete_windows_ext, files, checksum, cosign, minisign, slsa_provenance, github_artifact_attestations. Anything else (a loop, an unknown function, recipe vars) is reported as RECIPE_FEATURE_UNSUPPORTED for that record, never guessed.

One JSON document (format: 1, kind: "artifact-sets") matching artifact-set.schema.json. It holds the engine, the snapshot (its digest plus your labels), the limits used and the records. Each record has a status: Status Meaning Exit resolved URLs (artifact, checksum, signatures, ...), archive facts and declared evidence. 0 unsupported A normal result: PLATFORM_EXCLUDED, NO_ASSET, RECIPE_MESSAGE, SOURCE_KIND (build-from-source packages), VERSION_NOT_COVERED, PRIVATE_PACKAGE. 0 error Couldn't decide: LIMIT_EXCEEDED, RECIPE_INVALID, RECIPE_FEATURE_UNSUPPORTED, RENDER_FAILED, URL_NOT_HTTPS, PLATFORM_ABI_UNSUPPORTED. 3 Each record carries digests.declared (the record without its verification results) and digests.full (everything except digests), computed over canonical JSON (RFC 8785). The output contains no time, host, user or path, so the same inputs always produce identical output. GitHub release downloads are stored as the recipe renders them (github.com/...). Redirect targets are never stored.

Exit Meaning 0 Complete; every record is resolved or unsupported. 1 Bad input, no records: SNAPSHOT_INVALID, SNAPSHOT_DIGEST_MISMATCH (and for evidence: SET_INVALID, SET_SCHEMA_INVALID, SET_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED, SET_DIGEST_MISMATCH). With --json, the standard error object (error, code, nextStep, exitCode) is on stdout. 2 Usage problem, no records: FLAGS_CONFLICT, REQUEST_EMPTY. 3 Complete, but at least one record is error (resolve) or a resolved record stayed at the discovery tier (evidence). 5 Not found, no records: TOOL_NOT_IN_SNAPSHOT. A process killed by the system (memory, time limit) writes nothing. Run one tool per process if you need to contain that.

Flag Meaning --set FILE or - A tools resolve document (or standard input). Every record's digests are checked first; a mismatch is SET_DIGEST_MISMATCH and nothing is downloaded. --connector-bindings FILE Host binding file for administrative tool routes; never discovered in the project. --allow-host HOST (repeatable) Allow a host beyond those in the set's own URLs. --verify METHOD (repeatable) Run only these methods; others are reported not-run. --provider NAME Build the records for one of Oyzu's providers from its publisher instead of reading a set, then verify them the same way. Can't be combined with --set. --version V (repeatable, with --provider) Exact provider release, such as 21.0.8. Required with --provider. --platform OS/ARCH/ABI (repeatable, with --provider) Default: linux/amd64/gnu, darwin/amd64/native, windows/amd64/msvc. Platforms the provider doesn't install get an unsupported record.

For each resolved record, evidence downloads the artifact (hashed as it streams, never stored, up to 2 GiB) and the checksum file (up to 4 MiB, once per URL), and records verified.artifact (digest, size, publisher_digest, agree). Up to five redirects are followed. Each hop must be an allowed host, or github.com to release-assets.githubusercontent.com. The hosts seen are listed in verified.observed_redirect_hosts. --connector-bindings FILE supplies host bindings for administrative tool routes. HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY and SSL_CERT_FILE are honored (see acquisition transport). Each download is retried up to twice on network errors and HTTP 408, 429 and 5xx. Credentials are never sent to publisher hosts. GITHUB_TOKEN, if set, goes to api.github.com only. Each evidence entry gets an outcome in verified.results[].outcome: Outcome Meaning verified For checksum: the checksum file lists the artifact's name with a matching sha256 or sha512. For attestations and provenance: see below. failed The checksum file lacks the name, has conflicting or malformed values, couldn't be fetched, or doesn't match; or no attestation or provenance verifies. The detail says which. verifier-unavailable Oyzu has no verifier for the method (cosign, minisign, openpgp), or the algorithm (md5, sha1) or format (regexp) isn't supported. Never counted as verified. not-run Excluded by --verify. A record becomes tier: verified only when at least one entry verified and none failed. verified.lock then holds the strongest result: attestation when a GitHub attestation or SLSA provenance verified, otherwise digest-only. Otherwise the record stays discovery with verified.status: failed, and the command exits 3. What a result means: A checksum-verified record means these bytes match what the publisher's checksum file listed when fetched. It doesn't prove the checksum file is authentic, that a signature holds, or that you're allowed to use the tool. An attestation-verified record also means a GitHub Actions workflow in the release's repository attested these exact bytes, or, for SLSA provenance, that a slsa-github-generator release built them from that repository. It says nothing about whether the workflow's source is trustworthy.

For github-attestation evidence (aqua's github_artifact_attestations), Oyzu asks GitHub for the attestations of the artifact's digest (GET https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/attestations/sha256:<digest>?predicate_type=https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1). The repository comes from the artifact's GitHub release URL; other URLs fail. Set GITHUB_TOKEN to raise GitHub's anonymous limit of 60 requests an hour. Each Sigstore bundle is verified offline against Sigstore's public-good trusted root built into Oyzu. A bundle verifies when: its Rekor entry timestamp is signed by a trusted Rekor key, and its certificate chains to a Fulcio CA valid at that time; the certificate's issuer is GitHub Actions, its source repository is https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>, and, if the recipe names a signer_workflow, the certificate names that workflow (like gh attestation verify --repo --signer-workflow); the signature verifies and the signed statement names the artifact's SHA-256 with an SLSA v1 provenance predicate. The first bundle that verifies wins; identity shows its signing workflow and verifier is sigstore-public-good. Not checked: certificate transparency timestamps, inclusion proofs, RFC 3161 timestamps (so bundles from GitHub's private Sigstore instance, used for private repositories, don't verify), the runner environment and the provenance contents.

For slsa-provenance evidence (aqua's slsa_provenance, typically {{.Asset}}.intoto.jsonl), Oyzu downloads the provenance file published by slsa-github-generator (up to 4 MiB, same host rules as checksum files). As slsa-verifier does, it finds the matching log entries in Rekor's public API by the artifact's digest (rekor.sigstore.dev, at most 16 entries, no credentials sent). Everything Rekor returns is verified offline against the built-in trusted root: the file is an in-toto statement with an SLSA v0.2 or v1 provenance predicate naming the artifact's file name and SHA-256; a Rekor entry with a trusted signed timestamp records this envelope; the certificate chains to a Fulcio CA and was valid at that time; the issuer is GitHub Actions, the certificate names a slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator workflow at a v* release tag, and the source repository is the recipe's source_uri (or the release's repository); with source_tag, the source ref must be refs/tags/<source_tag>; the signature verifies. identity shows the builder workflow. Not checked: certificate transparency timestamps, inclusion proofs and the provenance contents (builder ID, build type, materials). Any generator workflow at a v* tag is accepted, and for delegated (BYOB) builds the delegated builder isn't checked.

For Java (Eclipse Temurin), Oyzu reads the publisher's GA release list for each feature release once (api.adoptium.net, the newest 20 releases) and writes one record per version and platform: tool.id is core:java (the index tool oyzu:java lists it as its origin). The version is the release (21.0.8). A resolved record names the archive and its .sha256.txt file on github.com/adoptium/temurin<feature>-binaries, the same archive the Java provider installs. release carries the publisher's release time when known. A platform the provider doesn't install is unsupported (PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED); a release with no build for the platform is unsupported (NO_PLATFORM_ARTIFACT); a release not in the list is an error (VERSION_NOT_FOUND); an unreadable list gives error records (SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE). oyzu --json tools evidence --provider java --version 21.0.8 --version 17.0.16 > java.verified.json Only Temurin JDK builds are recorded, and only the newest 20 GA releases of a feature; an older release is VERSION_NOT_FOUND.

These follow the same rules (tool.id is core:<name>, the same status codes, and each record names the archive the provider installs): Node reads nodejs.org/dist/index.json for the release and its date, then the release's SHASUMS256.txt. Go reads go.dev/dl/?mode=json&include=all. The release must be stable and list the platform's archive. The checksum is the archive's .sha256 file on dl.google.com. Python reads python-build-standalone's latest-release pointer, then that release's SHA256SUMS. Only versions that release ships as install_only builds for all four install platforms are recorded; any other is VERSION_NOT_FOUND. The archive URL includes the release tag, so a lock doesn't depend on the pointer.

--provider also accepts maven, gradle, helm, kubectl, k3d, liquibase, tailscale, zig, npm, pnpm, yarn and rust (optionally prefixed with oyzu: or core:). Versions must be exact stable three-part releases. Without --platform, all five index platforms are recorded. Intel macOS records are produced for Rust, Node, Go, npm, pnpm, Yarn and Zig when the publisher supports that release; other providers record it as unsupported. Provider Source and check Maven Apache archive listing, binary tarball and SHA-512 file. Gradle services.gradle.org release list's SHA-256 and binary ZIP. Zig ziglang.org stable index's tar.xz URL and SHA-256. Helm get.helm.sh archive and its SHA-256 file. kubectl dl.k8s.io binary and its SHA-256 file. k3d GitHub release binary and its checksums.txt entry. Liquibase The digest GitHub's release API reports for the asset (no publisher checksum file). Tailscale pkgs.tailscale.com stable Linux tarball and its SHA-256 file. npm, pnpm, Yarn npm registry tarball metadata and SHA-512, converted to SHA-256 after the archive is verified. Rust static.rust-lang.org channel manifest and its SHA-256 file, every available component URL and digest, plus a checksum-verified rustup bootstrap. Registry metadata is limited to 64 MiB; checksum files to 4 MiB. Liquibase 5.x records carry params.license = "FSL-1.1-ALv2", a source-available license. This records the license; it isn't a legal approval. For Rust, the artifact is dist/channel-rust-<version>.toml. Its checksum entry's params.rust_distribution lists each component and target with its URL and digest, plus the rustup bootstrap. evidence verifies the manifest checksum, checks the component list against the manifest and verifies the bootstrap. Component tarballs are checked when installed, not downloaded here. An unreachable publisher produces error or discovery records, never a verified result. oyzu --json tools evidence --provider kubectl --version 1.34.1 oyzu --json tools evidence --provider helm --version 3.22.0 oyzu --json tools evidence --provider rust --version 1.95.0

tools resolve makes no network calls, starts no processes and writes no files. It doesn't add an operating-system sandbox; run it in one (for example an empty network namespace) if you need that. Recipes are untrusted data. Recipe text in human output has control characters escaped. The evaluator contains no registry data or code from another project. Credentials are never sent to publisher hosts.

Only merged-file snapshots are supported, not the per-package tree form. Checked: checksums, GitHub artifact attestations and SLSA provenance. Not checked: cosign, minisign and OpenPGP. Rekor's search is best effort; an artifact whose entries it doesn't list fails. evidence runs downloads one at a time, has no stall timeout, and doesn't refuse private or loopback addresses after DNS resolution. Its allowed hosts come from the set's own URLs. On Windows, .exe is only added for raw assets, not for files entries. Edge cases of pre-release and build-metadata versions in semver() may differ from the registry's own engine. Duplicate YAML keys fail the whole snapshot. version.branch is null when no branch was selected (PLATFORM_ABI_UNSUPPORTED, a limit hit on the whole entry, or VERSION_NOT_COVERED). Supported on Linux x86-64 only.
Installing from resolved artifact sets Tool index Registry packages

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-rust-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can install the Rust toolchain for your project (rustc, Cargo, rustdoc, rustfmt, Clippy and the LLVM coverage tools) and the Cargo helpers the Rust builder uses, so you don't need rustup or Rust installed on the machine. The exact release is recorded in oyzu.lock. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Pinning is optional. With nothing declared, oyzu pin or your first oyzu build picks the newest stable Rust and records it in oyzu.lock. To choose a version, set it in oyzu.toml or in rust-toolchain.toml: [tools] rust = "1.95.0" oyzu install rust oyzu which cargo rustc --version cargo build oyzu install rust --frozen --offline In an activated shell, which the install script sets up, the plain tool commands run the pinned versions. Where a shell isn't activated, prefix them with oyzu exec --. oyzu install rust checks that rust is configured, then installs the project's whole tool selection into one lock. Bare oyzu install does the same for every configured tool. On Windows, new installs use the compact tool-store layout. Running oyzu install upgrades physical placement without changing the pinned compiler identity or deleting existing installations. A sufficiently deep profile or explicit store can still exceed MSVC's library path limit; see Windows library paths for admission and recovery.

Source Role rust-toolchain.toml or rust-toolchain, the nearest one from the build folder up to the project root The request. It's a native pin file; see Rust toolchain files [tools] rust (or [tools]."oyzu:rust") The request when no toolchain file applies. Otherwise it must agree with the file rust-version in Cargo.toml A minimum every selection must meet None of these stable: the newest stable release Accepted requests are an exact stable version (1.95.0) or stable. oyzu resolves stable to one exact release and keeps it in the lock; offline commands and oyzu pin --refresh don't move it. oyzu install rust and oyzu update rust need an exact version in configuration. Beta, nightly, partial versions such as 1.95, dated channels and ranges aren't supported. A fresh stable request needs the network. Offline, it works only when the lock already has the selection.

When it installs Rust, oyzu: Downloads the official channel manifest for the exact release and its published SHA-256, and checks that every needed component has a URL and digest. Looks up every pinned input (components, channel manifest and fixed rustup installer) in the shared tool store by its locked SHA-256 before creating the private distribution mirror. Missing inputs are downloaded and verified before entering blobs/sha256; unchanged inputs are reused when one component changes. Runs rustup against a private local copy of those files, with its own private Cargo and rustup homes, a minimal profile, the listed components and targets, and self-update turned off. Nothing outside those files is downloaded. Stores the finished toolchain as an archive in oyzu's tool store, with its license files. The completed archive is also indexed by the full locked recipe: provider, version, execution platform, components and every input URL/digest. With that archive available, preparation skips component downloads, rustup staging and repacking, and proceeds to the normal final installation. Native installs and captured Rust builds use the same resolution index and content-addressed store. A changed input or component set cannot select the previous completed archive; only missing input digests need downloading. A missing or corrupt cached blob is not reused; online acquisition can replace it. Installation logs use the same phase names for acquired and reused archives: Rust component download, Rust digest verification, Rust install into staging, Rust repack, Rust archive store, Rust archive verification, and Rust final install. A complete-archive hit explicitly marks component download, staging installation, repacking and archive storage as skipped. Archive verification and final installation still run. Newly materialized captured Linux compilers also pass the Linux restoration step, which stages a candidate and obtains its verified installation lease before handoff to the build. Skipped work is named explicitly. Input verification includes content-store admission and publication. Cached archives are verified before extraction; installed payloads remain trusted without re-hashing on reuse. Current catalog admission and final archive-layout checks still apply to a cache hit. Reinstalling from the lock (--frozen) restores an available completed archive without running rustup. Portable input recipes can recreate a missing completed archive from their exact inputs. Offline acquisition still refuses missing input bytes; it never falls back to the network. For older locks that record only the finished archive digest, if both the installation and that archive are gone, run an online update: oyzu won't substitute different bytes for an existing digest. The default profile also installs the standard libraries for the targets the Rust builder supports. Having a target's standard library doesn't mean you have a linker for it.

The toolchain's bin directory goes first on PATH. RUSTC and RUSTDOC point at the installed binaries. RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN points at the installed toolchain, so Cargo subcommands from your own Cargo home can't pick a different global Clippy or rustfmt. Cargo still downloads crates and Git dependencies itself, and your Cargo cache and configuration are separate from the installed toolchain.
documents.s: What oyzu sets when Rust runs

documents.t: oyzu doesn't install system linkers or SDKs: Platform You need Windows (MSVC) Visual Studio Build Tools with the C++ workload and a Windows SDK. The IDE isn't needed macOS Apple Command Line Tools, which provide the SDK, linker and Git (oyzu uses Git to infer versions). Check with xcode-select -p, xcrun --show-sdk-path and git --version; install with xcode-select --install. Some builders may need full Xcode GNU or LLVM targets LLVM or MinGW installed yourself, if you select those toolchains CMake and other build tools your crates need are also up to you.

On Windows x86-64, for a Rust-only project: oyzu pin oyzu install oyzu run install oyzu run install runs the Rust builder's executable installation task; it doesn't install tools. The compiler platform is windows/amd64/msvc. If an installation was made by an older oyzu or for a different pin, run oyzu install --update rust. oyzu run uses tools from the default user-level tool store. It puts them on PATH (and sets RUSTC/RUSTDOC) for the whole task and its hooks. If a needed tool isn't installed, the task fails before any hook runs and tells you to run oyzu install. Listing tasks and help don't need tools. To use a custom store, use oyzu exec --store; oyzu run doesn't accept one.
documents.s: Pinned native Rust and task execution

documents.t: The Rust builder needs cargo-nextest 0.9.146 for tests and cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1 for coverage. You don't have to list them: after oyzu pin, oyzu install installs everything the enabled build stages need; oyzu build --full installs and runs the quality stages; plain oyzu build installs only what compiling needs, unless configuration turns on more checks; oyzu run test uses the pinned helpers but needs them installed first. You can also set them in [tools] as cargo:cargo-nextest and cargo:cargo-llvm-cov (short names work too). Other versions fail with a clear error. oyzu never runs cargo install or builds helpers from source. oyzu tools current, oyzu which, oyzu exec and activated shells use the selection of the nearest build target. Child targets don't change a parent shell's tools. If pins are missing, run oyzu pin; oyzu build never re-pins on its own. If installations are missing, run an online install; --offline reuses installed tools and cached archives only. Installations live in the shared user store and are reused across projects; the project lock stays portable.

When toolCatalog.url is set (see organization tool catalog), pin, install and build only use an approved release from the signed index: The downloaded channel manifest must match the index's SHA-256, and its full component list must match the indexed one. Every component selected by rust-toolchain.toml and the rustup installer must match an indexed URL and digest. There's no fallback to the public site. Locked selections are checked against the current catalog before install or reuse. Error Cause TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG The release isn't approved TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX The tool isn't indexed, or its record has no component list TOOL_CATALOG_MISMATCH The indexed and locked inputs differ A downloaded file with the wrong digest fails before rustup starts. cargo: helpers are refused under a catalog. Rust metadata, rustup and component archives use the shared administrative tool routes: a rust family route takes precedence over host routes, and the mirror serves the original upstream paths. The native rustup child still reads only the verified local distribution staged by the acquisition owner. To see what an index entry would contain, run oyzu tools evidence --provider rust --version 1.95.0 (see tools evidence).

All tool selections live in one oyzu.lock (see lock inspection). oyzu pin updates what's selected; oyzu install records what's installed. Neither edits oyzu.toml or native files. Command What it does oyzu pin Resolves every tool the project needs, on every platform it builds for, and writes oyzu.lock. Doesn't install anything oyzu pin --dry-run Shows the result without writing. With --json, the proposed lock is in proposed_files. Exits 0 when complete, 2 when something couldn't be resolved oyzu pin --refresh Re-fetches installation details for the versions already selected, without upgrading. Needs the network oyzu pin --refresh --dry-run Previews the refresh A failed or incomplete pin doesn't replace the lock. If two sources disagree on a version, the error names both files and versions and confirms nothing changed. oyzu writes the lock and related files through a recovery journal (.oyzu-pin-journal.json). If a pin is interrupted, the next pin finishes it. Commands that read tools refuse to run while the journal is unfinished. If a file was changed by something else in the meantime, pin keeps the journal and fails with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT.

Isolated builds use the locked compiler too. With no oyzu.lock, the first build resolves and writes one before it starts. Linux ARM64 builds use the arm64 execution image, oyzu-execution/base:1-linux-arm64 until the image is published. oyzu checks its architecture but doesn't install emulators. oyzu install never sets up a Linux worker just because build.yaml declares Rust targets. The installer container gets 6 GiB of scratch space, 8 GiB of memory and two CPUs, with no network and a read-only root. Make sure Docker allows that much.

oyzu build --offline needs an existing lock and a cached compiler. It doesn't resolve versions or change the lock, and it fails without running an installer if the compiler is missing. Offline builds work only for projects whose Cargo.lock has no registry or Git dependencies (local workspace packages are fine). Otherwise the build fails before fetching, because cached crate replay isn't available yet.

Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Windows x86-64 (MSVC) Supported macOS Intel Supported with an existing lock; automatic default pinning isn't available yet Windows ARM64 (MSVC) Unsupported; retained lock metadata is not native installation qualification macOS Apple silicon, Linux ARM64 Not supported yet Helper installation (cargo-nextest, cargo-llvm-cov) is supported on Windows x86-64; on other platforms it isn't supported yet.

If a failed Rust command reports a missing component of its selected Oyzu installation, TOOL_COMPONENT_MISSING names Rust's version, the component and the install folder. Remove that folder and run the exact install command shown in the diagnostic; do not use rustup component add on the custom sysroot. Cargo's missing-Clippy command error is also diagnosed when the selected payload's Clippy executable is absent. Native action logs retain the tool's output. See missing installed executables and components for recovery, offline requirements and failure-path-only detection.
Rust toolchain files Lock inspection Tool commands Organization tool catalog

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-shell-environment.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. This page covers the ways to put a project's locked tools on PATH outside oyzu run and oyzu build: a one-time oyzu env --shell, an activated shell that switches tools as you change directory, a shell profile block, and a shims folder for IDEs and scheduled jobs. It also lists the settings that control when tools install themselves on first use. For the overall model (provenance, PATH views, nested shells), see shell activation. Note: Activation and env --shell are supported in Bash and Zsh on Linux and macOS, and in PowerShell 7 on Windows. Writing a shell profile with oyzu shell install is supported for Bash and Zsh on Linux; macOS and PowerShell profiles are not supported yet.

oyzu env shows the selected tools' executables and the effective environment variables. oyzu env --json returns the same as JSON. Credential-like fields and values that look sensitive are redacted. Tools that aren't installed are left out; env never installs anything. Invalid locks, damaged install records and policy denials still fail. The environment is the same one oyzu exec uses: the literal values from [env] in your configuration, plus the selected tools' folders added to the front of your PATH. To apply the environment to your current shell once, pick a shell: # Bash (use --shell zsh for Zsh) eval "$(oyzu env --shell bash)" node --version oyzu env --shell pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression node --version With --json, the code is returned in a script field next to the shell name. No network access and no installs. Values stay literal: quotes, dollar signs and shell metacharacters are escaped, never interpreted. Values must be valid UTF-8. If you installed into a shared store, pass the same --store here. This changes the current shell once. It doesn't add a prompt hook, switch on cd or restore old values. Use activation for that.

Activation, env --shell, prompt hooks, shims and oyzu exec only apply a project's [env] and PATH additions after you trust the project folder, because those values end up executed by your shell. An untrusted project still gets its selected tools, without those additions and without a prompt. oyzu env marks such entries skipped until trusted. oyzu run, oyzu build and build planning always apply those settings.

oyzu exec -- COMMAND runs a command with the project's environment. Put Oyzu flags before --. By default the command's output passes straight through; with --json, Oyzu captures it in stdout and stderr fields next to exitCode.

Activate a Bash or Zsh session from a project with installed tools: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" # use zsh for Zsh node --version cd ../another-installed-project node --version # the other project's Node oyzu deactivate In PowerShell: oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression. --store /absolute/store uses a shared store. Without it, the default user store is used. --root, --profile and --toolset given to activate stay in effect for the session. On every prompt, Oyzu checks whether the directory, relevant environment variables or configuration and lock files changed. If nothing changed, it does nothing. If something changed, it applies the new project's locked tools and [env] values. The prompt hook never uses the network, installs tools or runs project tasks. cd alone never installs anything or writes a lock. Running a missing command may install it, depending on the invocation controls. In PowerShell, missing-command installs only trigger for a command you typed in the interactive session, not for lookups inside scripts. The prompt check looks at file metadata only. Installed tools aren't re-checked on each prompt: they were verified when installed and are trusted afterward. oyzu env can take longer than oyzu config show because it fully reads the selection.

Invalid configuration or a denied tool clears the previous project's changes, sets OYZU_TOOL_STATUS=unavailable and prints a message once. Missing installations don't stop a valid environment from applying. OYZU_TOOL_STATUS=ready means the environment was composed, not that every tool is installed. Check with oyzu tools current. A trusted project's PATH additions come before the selected tool folders.
documents.s: When the selection fails or is incomplete

documents.t: Oyzu saves what it changed in a private per-user shell-sessions folder so oyzu deactivate can undo it. The shell holds only a random token. On Unix the folder is private (0700) and linked directories are refused. On Windows it lives under your LocalAppData and reparse points are refused. oyzu deactivate restores a variable only if it still has the value Oyzu set, so your own edits survive. An unchanged PATH is restored exactly. Entries Oyzu added are removed even if you added or reordered others; ambiguous duplicates are kept with a message. oyzu --json deactivate only previews; the session stays active. If the record is missing or unreadable, you get a warning and the hooks are removed, but old values can't be recovered. Open a new terminal or activate again. Activation cleans up records at most once a day: a record older than a day whose shell has exited, and any record unused for a week. An open shell marks its record as in use at its first prompt each day, so a terminal left without a prompt for more than a week loses its record; activate it again. Activation adds the Oyzu executable's folder to PATH if it isn't there. That entry stays after deactivation. The oyzu shell function that activation defines evaluates the output of oyzu deactivate for you. Running the binary by full path with deactivate only prints the code. Global flags such as oyzu -q deactivate work. --log-level and -q can't be combined; a rejected command leaves the session active.

oyzu shell install with no shell is the machine-level setup that the install scripts run. It does not install tools or use the network. It edits, once: the activation block of each supported shell found: bash (login shell, or ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile exists, including Git Bash on Windows), zsh (login shell, or $ZDOTDIR/.zshrc or ~/.zshrc exists) and PowerShell 7 (when pwsh is on PATH or in %ProgramFiles%\PowerShell\7); the persistent PATH, with the fixed shims folder (STORE/shims/bin, refreshed first as oyzu reshim does) ahead of the folder holding the running oyzu. On Windows that is the user Path value in HKCU\Environment: entries such as %USERPROFILE%\bin keep their raw spelling, the value kind is kept (REG_EXPAND_SZ for a new value), entries already present are not duplicated (compared after expanding variables, ignoring case and a trailing separator) and WM_SETTINGCHANGE is broadcast so programs started afterwards, such as IDEs, see it. On Linux and macOS it is a marked PATH block in the login profile: the first existing of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login and ~/.profile (~/.profile when none exists), and $ZDOTDIR/.zprofile or ~/.zprofile when zsh is set up. oyzu shell remove with no shell reverses it: it removes intact blocks from those files and the two folders from the user Path, and leaves other content. Only entries spelled exactly as install wrote them (the running oyzu and its store folders) are removed, so entries added by an oyzu installed in another location, and your own %USERPROFILE%\bin-style spelling of a folder, stay. A block that was edited is refused as below. Reports list each file or the registry value under entries with changed. Windows PowerShell 5.1 and fish are not configured. Programs already running keep the PATH they started with. Checked by unit tests for planning, PATH list editing and (on Linux) install, repeat and remove over a temporary home, a unit test of the registry code on a scratch key, and the compiled CLI on Windows. macOS and fish are not checked.
documents.s: Set up all shells and PATH

documents.t: oyzu activate never edits files. To activate in every new shell, add a block to your startup file: oyzu shell install bash oyzu shell remove bash --rc-file ~/.bashrc oyzu shell install pwsh --rc-file $PROFILE oyzu shell remove pwsh --rc-file $PROFILE Default startup files: Shell Default bash ~/.bashrc zsh $ZDOTDIR/.zshrc, or ~/.zshrc pwsh PowerShell 7's current-user console profile: Documents/PowerShell/Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1 on Windows, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/powershell/Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1 on Unix (falling back to ~/.config/powershell/...) --rc-file PATH picks another file. A relative path resolves against the current directory (or -C). For another PowerShell host or version, pass --rc-file $PROFILE. The global --profile option selects an Oyzu configuration profile, not a shell file. Oyzu creates missing folders and files, appends one marked block and leaves the rest of the file and its permissions unchanged. The block calls the oyzu executable by its full path. If you move or upgrade it, run oyzu shell install again to update the block. Running it again with the same executable changes nothing. If activation fails when a shell starts (for example, a configuration file can't be read), oyzu prints the error and the rest of the startup file still runs. The PowerShell block runs the activation code only when oyzu activate printed some. The block uses the default store and configuration. It doesn't include a project, profile, credentials or store path. For a custom store, add your own oyzu activate <shell> --store PATH line outside the block. Install the project's tools before opening a new shell. Editing the profile itself uses no network. --json reports changed, shell, profile_path, installed, shims, activation, check and nextStep. Install and remove refuse a block that is modified, incomplete, duplicated or written by a different oyzu. Fix or restore the block by hand first. A symlinked profile needs the real target path, and a non-UTF-8 profile must be converted first. oyzu shell remove deletes only the intact block and leaves the rest of the file byte for byte. A file Oyzu created stays as an empty file. Removing the block affects new shells; run oyzu deactivate to end the current session.
documents.s: Install activation in a shell profile

documents.t: oyzu install and oyzu activate create a launcher (shim) for every command of every installed tool, including companions such as npm, npx, kubectl and helm. Each shim works out the project, configuration and lock from the directory it runs in. Concurrent shim refreshes serialize their writes. A finished refresh releases its publication lock without waiting for unrelated child processes; readers continue to see complete records. On Unix, shims are symbolic links to oyzu. On Windows, oyzu-shim.exe is a small launcher that delegates tool execution to oyzu.exe. Install or copy both into the same folder. Published shims find the frontend through the adjacent .oyzu-frontend pointer; a launcher without a pointer looks for oyzu.exe beside itself. If that frontend is missing or invalid, restore the pair and run oyzu reshim. Shims for activated shells live under STORE/shims/native/. Run oyzu install, oyzu activate or oyzu reshim to refresh them; oyzu install also refreshes shims in already activated shells, so newly installed commands appear there. A shim keeps the command's arguments, exit status and signals unchanged. On Windows x64 in PowerShell 7 and CMD, both fixed-folder and activated-session exe shims let the foreground child handle Ctrl-C. A handler that exits 42 reports 42; an unhandled Ctrl-C reports Windows -1073741510 (0xC000013A). The prompt returns after the child exits, and Oyzu closes its owned child job. These are console statuses, not Unix signal conversions. A tool can call another shim (for example, a Node script starting another Node process); each call selects its tool again. Prompt hooks don't create shims. Oyzu doesn't delete old shim folders automatically, since running shells may still use them.

IDEs, CI jobs and scheduled tasks never run a prompt hook. For them, put the store's shims folder on PATH. It holds one launcher for each installed command, and each launcher picks the right tool for the project it runs in: oyzu reshim # refresh launchers and print the folder eval "$(oyzu activate bash --shims)" # put it first on PATH in this shell oyzu shell install bash --shims --rc-file ~/.bash_profile oyzu shell install zsh --shims --rc-file ~/.zprofile On Windows, add it to your user PATH: $shims = (oyzu reshim --json | ConvertFrom-Json).directory [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('Path', "$shims;" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path', 'User'), 'User') The folder is STORE/shims/bin. The PATH line removes any existing copy of the folder and puts it first, so an unmanaged copy of a tool earlier on PATH can't win. A store path containing the PATH separator (:, or ; on Windows) fails with SHIMS_PATH_INVALID. On Windows, Bash and Zsh lines use Git Bash or MSYS/Cygwin path spelling (/c/Users/...). Generate Cygwin profiles from inside Cygwin. activate --shims only prints the PATH line. Run oyzu reshim once first, and again after moving or upgrading oyzu. shell install --shims runs that refresh for you. If a shim has no selected tool, it falls back to the next matching command on PATH, unless you turn that off (see invocation controls). oyzu reshim refreshes the shims folder and the activation shims owned by the running oyzu, using local install records only. It downloads nothing and edits no startup file. --json reports the folder as directory and the command names as commands. On Windows, run it after updating both executables.

These settings control when a tool installs itself the first time you use it. They go in the usual configuration files (including profiles), and administrators can constrain them. The values shown are the defaults: [settings] auto_install = true offline = false exec_auto_install = true not_found_auto_install = true not_found_auto_install_registry = false not_found_system_fallback = true auto_install_disable_tools = [] windows_executable_extensions = ["exe", "bat", "cmd", "com", "ps1", "vbs"] windows_shim_mode = "exe" [settings.task] run_auto_install = true Setting Meaning auto_install Master switch. false turns off the exec, missing-command and task installs below. offline Use only cached downloads; never fetch. Same as oyzu exec --offline. exec_auto_install oyzu exec installs configured tools that are missing. not_found_auto_install A shim, or a command your shell couldn't find, installs its configured tool. not_found_auto_install_registry A command the shell couldn't find, and that no configuration declares, is looked up in Oyzu's tool list, installed and added to your global configuration as latest. not_found_system_fallback A shim with no selected tool runs the next matching command on PATH. auto_install_disable_tools Tools (short or full IDs) that never install themselves. oyzu install still works for them. windows_executable_extensions Extensions treated as executable on Windows. windows_shim_mode How shims are created on Windows (below). task.run_auto_install oyzu run installs missing tools for the task. How they behave: A compatible lock entry always wins. Running a command never upgrades a locked version, and a missing locked tool isn't replaced by another installed version. In a project with no compatible lock entry, shells, exec, tasks, env and which can reuse a matching version you already installed. This writes no lock. A command may create a missing lock when it installs a configured tool. With not_found_auto_install_registry, a name that matches more than one tool is skipped. A project declaration still overrides the global entry. Progress goes to stderr, so the command's stdout is unchanged. To make unresolved shims fail instead of running a system command, set both not_found_system_fallback and not_found_auto_install to false. Fallback skips Oyzu shim folders and keeps PATH order. A failed install, invalid lock, denied tool or unavailable managed integration is an error. It never silently falls back to a system command. Prompt hooks, env, which and oyzu build --plan never install tools. which shows the selected tool; a shim on PATH doesn't mean the tool is installed. oyzu build ignores these settings. It requires the full locked selection, and never accepts a system command in place of a locked tool or a denied tool.

For each target, oyzu build prepares the tools its builder needs for the selected steps, plus the tools pinned in the oyzu.toml files from the project root down to that target's folder. A root pin reaches every target; a pin in docs-site/ reaches only targets in that folder. So oyzu build cli doesn't download a tool only docs uses. oyzu exec, shells and oyzu install still provide every pinned tool. Host prerequisites are checked, never installed.

Node provides node, npm and npx. A separately configured npm takes over npm and npx. On Windows, PATH lookup follows PATHEXT order. PowerShell and VBScript files run with their own interpreters. Bare bash and sh resolve to Git for Windows; WindowsApps aliases are skipped. Unix commands get interrupts forwarded and keep terminal control. --json reports the numeric exit status.

windows_shim_mode Behavior exe A small native launcher (oyzu-shim.exe) per command, delegating to the frontend with native arguments and exit status. Default. hardlink Hard links to oyzu. Needs a filesystem that supports them, on the same volume. symlink Symbolic links to oyzu. Needs symlink permission (usually Developer Mode). file CMD and Git Bash forwarder scripts. CMD's own rules apply: PowerShell's default argument passing can change empty arguments and embedded quotes, and delayed expansion changes ^ and !. After changing the mode, run oyzu reshim (with the same --store). If the mode isn't available (missing permission or unsupported filesystem), Oyzu reports it instead of picking another mode. Other platforms always use symbolic links.
Shell activation Tool commands Configuration

Use oyzu shell check (or oyzu shell check --json) to find commands that win over the shims. It is read-only and exits 1 when shadowed, 0 otherwise. The no-argument shell install also reports findings without failing setup. Windows machine Path comes before user Path in new processes; an elevated oyzu shell install --machine puts the per-user shims and Oyzu folders first on machine Path. Undo newly added machine entries with elevated oyzu shell remove --machine. Use this on single-user machines; on shared machines remove or reorder the system tool instead. Unix hosts have no machine Path. Rerunning shell install moves an unmodified login PATH block to the end, after later PATH-prepending lines. User-modified blocks remain protected. Services, scheduled tasks, launchd jobs and systemd units need the absolute shim path (for example <shims folder>/node) or the shims folder first on their own PATH. Verify with oyzu shell check in that environment. Oyzu installs no such jobs. See PATH checks and platform limits.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-store-inspection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The tool store is the folder where Oyzu keeps downloaded archives and installed tools. Every project, shell and build on your machine shares it, so a tool version is downloaded and installed once. This page explains what's in the store, what Oyzu checks when it installs a tool, how concurrent installs and running tools are kept safe, and how to inspect an installed tool's files. Note: Experimental. The store layout may change.

Platform Default Linux $XDG_DATA_HOME/oyzu/tools, or ~/.local/share/oyzu/tools macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/tools Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Oyzu\tools Most tool commands accept --store DIR to use another store. A relative path is resolved from the current directory. Pass the same --store to install, inspect and activate. oyzu tools list --json shows the store in use. Archive providers, registry packages and Rust all use the same store.

Folder Contents installs/<key>/ One installed tool: payload/ (its files) and receipt.json (what was installed, from where, and its commands). i/<key>/ Compact Windows installations: p/ holds the payload and receipt.json retains its logical paths. The key encodes the complete SHA-256 in lowercase base32. blobs/sha256/<digest> Downloaded archives, named by their SHA-256. staging/ Installs and downloads in progress. quarantine/ Cached archives that failed their digest check, kept for you to inspect. locks/ Lock files that coordinate concurrent installs and running tools. Never delete these while Oyzu is running. leases/ Records of which installations are in use. catalogs/, state/ Cached tool index, catalogs and trust state. shims/ Command launchers (see using tools in your shell).

New Windows installations use i/ and p/ to leave more room for native library paths. Existing installs/ entries remain usable. The next oyzu install populates the compact location through normal archive and receipt verification; it never deletes or moves the older installation. Lock identities and lease identities do not change. Use oyzu tools list --details to find the selected physical paths instead of constructing paths from the lock. Oyzu checks a tool thoroughly when it installs it, and trusts it afterward: Every download must match the SHA-256 from the lock, index or publisher before it is used. A new installation's files are checked against its receipt before it is committed. Later commands, shells and builds check that the installation exists and that its receipt matches the lock. They don't re-hash the files. A tool that is damaged or edited after install simply fails when it runs. An organization catalog or the tool index can still refuse an unapproved or withdrawn version when you install or reuse it. Tool installation receipts have no free-form annotation slot. Unknown receipt, verification, command or environment fields are rejected even when the receipt declares a newer minimum reader. The error says to reinstall the tool and retains the file unchanged. Run oyzu self update before retrying; do not remove unfamiliar fields to activate a tool. The self-install receipt has a separate compatibility contract. Current readers understand the optional verification.strength field, including receipts that omit it. The field records publisher evidence and participates in verification identity; it is not an inert annotation. Historical readers that predate it can reject a shared store before selecting any tool. Use a current driver with current receipts. If an experiment must retain a historical driver, select a separately provisioned compatible store with --store; do not delete strength, rewrite receipts or change a lock to make the old reader accept them.

Archives are downloaded to a temporary file, checked and then moved into blobs/. Memory use doesn't grow with archive size. A download is limited to 8 GiB and must be exactly the expected size. A short, long or mismatched download stores nothing. A cached archive is checked again whenever it is used. If it no longer matches, it is moved to quarantine/ and downloaded again (online) or reported as missing with its path (offline). If a lock records a digest but no size, Oyzu uses the cached archive's size. Offline installs need the archive already in the cache. The error names the missing digest; retry online.

Installs unpack tar, tar.gz, tar.xz, tar.zst, ZIP and single-file (raw) downloads, within these limits: Limit Value Entries 200,000 Total size 8 GiB Single file 1 GiB Path depth 64 Expansion ratio 200:1 (some reviewed tools allow up to 1024:1) Paths that escape the folder, absolute paths, Windows device names, names that differ only by case, and conflicting entries are refused. Tar archives can contain files, directories and relative symbolic links. Hard links and sparse files aren't supported. ZIP archives can contain stored or deflated files, directories and Unix relative symbolic links. Encrypted, multi-volume and ZIP64 archives aren't supported. Symbolic links are created after all files are written, and must stay inside the tool's folder. This keeps macOS framework layouts intact. Symbolic links inside archives aren't supported on Windows. Ownership, set-ID bits and the archive's directory permissions aren't applied. Files are private to you, and Unix executable bits are kept.

Before an installation is committed, Oyzu prepares it in staging/ and checks it: The archive layout (how it's unpacked, which prefix is stripped, which files are commands) must match the layout recorded in the lock. Every command file must exist. On Unix, declared executables are set to mode 0700. Commands and environment values may only refer to files in the tool itself or its direct dependencies. The receipt is written last, with the digests of the final files. Nothing in the tool is run during this step, and oyzu.lock isn't changed. If a step fails, the staging folder is discarded and no installation is created.
documents.s: Checking an installation before it is committed

documents.t: Each installation is moved into installs/ in one atomic step, and never replaces an existing one. When a tool has dependencies, each one is committed separately. If a later one fails, earlier ones stay as valid, unreferenced installations. The lock is never edited. An existing valid installation is reused. A damaged one fails; Oyzu doesn't replace it or fall back to another download. Windows supports long store paths, including UNC paths.

Tool installation for the same tool on the same platform takes turns across oyzu install, builds, developer commands and operation tools. A later caller prints that it's waiting, waits without a timeout, then reuses the installation the first one published instead of installing a second copy. The OS releases the install lock if its holder exits or crashes. Publishing an installation or archive waits up to 30 seconds for another process publishing the same one. If a store already holds several installations of one recipe with identical installed files, for example from older concurrent installs, Oyzu uses one of them. Installations of one recipe with different files still fail with TOOL_LOCK_AMBIGUOUS. While a command, shell or build uses a tool, it holds a shared lock on the installation, so it can't be removed underneath it. Each such use writes a small record in leases/ with its process ID, start time and installation keys. It contains no paths, environment values or credentials. The record is removed when the command ends. A crash can leave a record or a .pending file behind. Oyzu cleans these up when it next starts an install, but only once their locks show nobody is using them. It never deletes an installation during cleanup. Records it can't verify are left for manual review. Lease records also reject unknown fields. Recovery retains such a record and counts it under unverified_or_failed; it does not interpret the extra data as permission to remove the record or an installation. The recorded process ID and creation time must match the lease ID; OS locks determine whether a lease is still in use.
documents.s: Concurrent installs and tools in use

documents.t: Give each container or sandbox its own store with --store DIR; use the same directory for installation and execution inside that environment. Avoid bind mounting a host store into a container, bwrap or Flatpak sandbox that has a different PID or mount namespace. An unrestricted /proc mount (hidepid=0) only exposes processes visible in its PID namespace. Another namespace can hide a tool holder or show its files under different paths. A scan that finds no holder therefore does not prove a shared installation is unused. Keep shared installations until all environments using that store have stopped; do not manually remove them while tools run. The collector must have Linux's initial PID namespace inode (4026531836); another or unrecognized value retains entries even if the collector and its PID 1 have matching namespaces. It compares PID and mount namespaces for same-user processes and processes with root UIDs or effective DAC capabilities. Nested or unknown NSpid information for privileged or foreign-user processes also retains entries, including a missing, empty or malformed field. Bind/subtree mounts, overlay mounts, visible store aliases and mounts receiving propagation (master: or propagate_from:) retain entries. A store device that differs from the collector's root device also retains entries. Missing namespace or mount information, including unreadable /proc/1/ns, prevents collection. These conservative checks can retain an entire private store on an unrestricted host, a separate filesystem or a filesystem subvolume. These are process and mount observations, not an inventory of every store export. User namespace identities are not compared. Use separate stores for containers and sandboxes. A foreign-user process with a single valid NSpid and no current root UID or effective DAC capability is excluded from holder inspection. It may still hold files opened before dropping privileges or received through descriptor passing (SCM_RIGHTS). This host-PID case, including a container using the host PID namespace, remains a gap even if it uses another mount namespace. To reclaim an existing shared store, stop every environment using it and run oyzu tools prune on the host with unrestricted procfs access, then apply the preview. Keep locks and lease records intact.

Installs work in their own folder under staging/. If an install is interrupted, the next install removes abandoned staging folders, but only when no other install is running. Older leftover staging files (.tmp* and top-level blob-*) and quarantined archives are kept for you to inspect and delete.

oyzu tools inspect-tree lists the files of an installed tool, with their digests, so you can compare or audit an installation. It's a diagnostic command; Oyzu never runs it automatically. oyzu tools list --details # find installation paths oyzu tools inspect-tree <store>/installs/<id>/payload Payload inspection Bytes: 3 Digest: sha256:79a94bbfa8c76fb62b27ce178116533fb1e8239516c2015be5e8e8123793b851 Entries: Digest Executable Path Size Target Type not specified 73 bin not specified not specified directory sha256:98ea6e4f216f2fb4b69fff9b3a44842c3 73 bin/x 3 not specified file 8686ca685f3f55dc48c5d3fb1107be4 Manifest digest: sha256:7a8aea237bd28004828e36b056b48fbdb164f8c7dd1cb244c288f9111ad1a718 Validation: payload-observation-only --json returns bytes, digest, entries[] (path, type, size, digest, executable, target), manifest_digest and validation. Each file's entry has its digest, size and Unix executable bits (always zero on Windows). Directories and relative symbolic link targets are listed. Timestamps, owners and ACLs aren't included. It never runs files, follows links inside the tree or changes anything. Exit 0 on success, 2 on error. A relative path is resolved from -C, --root or the current directory. The path must not contain .. or pass through a symbolic link. Hard links to files outside the tree, special files and files that change during the scan fail. Limits: 200,000 entries, 8 GiB in total, 1 GiB per file, path depth 64 and 64 link hops. validation: "payload-observation-only" means this is a snapshot of what was on disk when read. It doesn't prove the files are authentic or haven't been changed by another process at the same time.

oyzu tools prune previews eligible tool installations, downloaded blobs and plugin installations, with their logical file size and a reason for every entry. Only --apply removes content. It runs offline and needs no account. Illustrative usage: oyzu tools prune oyzu tools prune --store /path/to/private-store oyzu tools prune --store /path/to/private-store --apply oyzu --json tools prune --store /path/to/private-store Option Default Meaning --store DIR Shared user store above Inspect or clean this store; relative to the invocation directory. --apply Off Remove eligible entries instead of previewing. --json Off Return the same entries, states, byte counts and reasons as JSON.

There is no index of other projects' current paths. Collection keeps everything named by the current project lock, the global lock next to the selected user configuration, and every recorded developer-selections lock snapshot.
