Snapshots are conservative historical references, so uninstalling a declaration may not make its installation eligible. Collection never scans your disk for projects. Every installed tool receipt also protects the archive, installer and dependency installations it names. Installed plugins protect their archive blobs. Archive blobs protected by a removed receipt may become eligible on a later invocation. Action results remain owned by oyzu cache clear; collection leaves caches, engines, trust state, shims, staging, quarantine and permanent locks alone. Active use leases and lease journals retain installations. Concurrent Oyzu commands keep their referenced installations while they run; collection holds the entry’s mutation and exclusive use locks through removal. Entries whose permanent mutation or use lock is missing or busy stay. The last recorded store access or use lease within 30 days also retains an entry, as does an uncertain timestamp. Store access refreshes lock-file timestamps without reading installed payloads. Older clients did not record every use this way; their lock-file timestamps only record creation. Known locks, receipts and active leases still protect them. Linux additionally checks the current user's executable, working-directory, open-file and mapped-file process references through /proc, including readable /proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/fd tables for threads with separate file descriptors. An unreadable live thread table retains the entry; scanning continues to find definite holders in other readable tables. A missing table is ignored only when the thread is confirmed gone. The leader alias and kernel-confirmed shared tables are read once after successful inspection; unsupported or denied sharing checks fall back to independent scans. Collection requires a private store owned by that user (mode 0700). Before trusting the process listing, it checks /proc/self/mountinfo. A restricted mount (hidepid other than 0/off, or a subset option), unreadable mount information or an unrecognized procfs root prevents reclamation: the listing may omit a live holder entirely. This conservatively applies even to namespace root or callers with a mount's privileged group; prune does not attempt to prove a privilege bypass. It also checks namespace identities and the store's mounts as described under containers and sandboxes. Observed namespace sharing or unavailable evidence prevents reclamation even when hidepid=0. On an unrestricted mount, a process is excluded only when its real, effective, saved and filesystem UIDs all belong to other users and are nonzero, and its readable CapEff has neither CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE nor CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH, and NSpid contains exactly one valid positive process ID. Missing or malformed CapEff for a non-root foreign process retains entries. Missing, nested or invalid NSpid for that process also retains entries. A private store limits new opens; it cannot rule out previously opened or passed descriptors, as described under containers and sandboxes. Root UIDs and these capabilities can bypass a private store's permissions, so those processes remain subject to namespace and holder inspection. An unreadable identity or undecidable same-user process retains candidates, including a zombie whose descriptor directory cannot be read. Inspection continues after an undecidable process so a positively observed running-tool reference can still be reported. Permission errors identify the process path that could not be inspected. If the store is not private, it retains candidates because other users' process use cannot be established. On CI container runners, a restricted /proc or an unreadable same-user process, including a zombie with an inaccessible descriptor directory, may therefore retain every candidate and reclaim nothing. Retention is the safe result: prune cannot establish that a hidden or unreadable process holds no file, mapping, working directory or executable in the store. For zombie retention, rerun after the parent has reaped the exited process. For a restricted mount, use a host with unrestricted procfs visibility. Do not remove locks or retention records to force cleanup. Windows preflights every file with exclusive access: in-use or mapped files stay, without forced deletion. On macOS, direct process use cannot yet be established, so candidates stay. Unreadable locks, snapshots, receipts or journals inhibit removal and appear in entry reasons. Unknown entry names, links, hardlinked files and layouts exceeding inspection bounds stay for manual inspection. Collection reads metadata and file sizes; it never hashes or re-verifies installed payloads.

Human output leads with the result, then lists kind, path, size, state and reason. JSON returns store, apply, bytes, entries, locksChecked, recentDays and note. Each entry has kind, path, bytes, state and reason; an unmeasured entry has bytes: null (shown as unknown in human output). bytes at the result root sums eligible or completely removed entries; it is a logical size, not a guarantee of filesystem space freed. State Meaning eligible Preview found this entry removable; no files changed. removed Apply completed removal. retained Referenced, recently used, busy, or uncertain; entry kept. incomplete Removal started but an OS error stopped it; some files may be gone. Exit 0 means observation completed, including deliberate retention; exit 1 means an incomplete removal; exit 2 means a command/input/store access error. Resolve reported permissions, busy processes or filesystem errors, then preview again before applying. Do not delete permanent locks or retention records to force eligibility. Keep project lock files available when collecting; projects with no recorded snapshot and no visible lock cannot be discovered by this command. Process visibility can change between entries and invocations. A preview's eligibility is an observation, not a promise that a later apply will remove the entry; apply checks the same safeguards again.

Collection is explicit; there is no automatic or background cleanup. Recorded lock snapshots can keep older versions indefinitely. Locks coordinate Oyzu processes. They don't protect the store from other programs running as your user.
Tool lock files and inspection Tool commands Using tools in your shell

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-tailscale-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can pin and install tailscale and tailscaled on Linux, so a project or CI job that joins a tailnet doesn't need Tailscale installed on the machine. oyzu installs the two binaries only. It doesn't start the daemon, log in or grant any network capability. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

[tools] tailscale = "1.78.1" # exact release # tailscale = "latest" # newest version on the stable track oyzu install tailscale@1.78.1 # declares, locks, installs on Linux tailscale version tailscaled --version In an activated shell, which the install script sets up, the plain tool commands run the pinned versions. Where a shell isn't activated, prefix them with oyzu exec --. tailscaled usually needs root or a TUN device, or its userspace-networking mode. How you run it is up to you.

Platform Status Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Linux ARM64 (glibc) Recorded in the lock, not supported yet macOS No download: Tailscale ships only a GUI app and a .pkg installer Windows No download: Tailscale ships only .exe and .msi installers Other Linux architectures, musl Not supported Platforms without a download are left out of the lock, and oyzu install prints a warning naming them. Running oyzu install tailscale on macOS or Windows fails with TOOL_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE and changes nothing. A lock created on Linux still works for Linux CI.

Request Result 1.78.1 or v1.78.1 That release latest The TarballsVersion in https://pkgs.tailscale.com/stable/?mode=json Ranges, minor lines and pre-releases are refused, and oyzu tools versions tailscale fails because oyzu doesn't list releases. The lock records the resolved version.

oyzu downloads https://pkgs.tailscale.com/stable/tailscale_<version>_<arch>.tgz (arch is amd64 or arm64) and checks it against the .sha256 file on the same site. The digest is recorded in the lock. No publisher signature is checked. The installed commands are tailscale and tailscaled; the systemd unit files in the archive aren't installed as services. An administrator can route downloads through a corporate mirror with a tools route scoped to tailscale, oyzu:tailscale or * (see proxy acquisition). When a route is set, oyzu never falls back to the public site. Under an organization tool catalog, only approved releases install.
oyzu doesn't run or configure tailscaled. --offline needs the tool installed or its archive already cached.
Tool commands

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-zig-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu can install a stable Zig compiler from the official download index and run it for your project, with no existing Zig installation or account. The exact archive is recorded in oyzu.lock. Note: Zig installation is experimental and currently supported on Intel macOS and Linux x86-64 (glibc). Windows x86-64 ZIP installation recipes are available, but selection also requires a resolved Windows record in the signed tool index. The default index currently reports PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED for Zig 0.15.2 on Windows.

Create oyzu.toml in your project: [tools] zig = "0.15.2" oyzu pin zig@0.15.2 oyzu install --frozen oyzu which zig zig version In an activated shell, which the install script sets up, the plain tool commands run the pinned versions. Where a shell isn't activated, prefix them with oyzu exec --. $ zig versionCopy 0.15.2 Commit oyzu.toml and oyzu.lock. Later, oyzu install --frozen --offline reinstalls without the network. oyzu install zig@0.15.2 declares and installs in one step. oyzu pin zig@0.15.2 works before the project has any discovered build; plain oyzu pin needs one. The names zig, oyzu:zig and core:zig all select the same tool. The installed command is zig. Setting Meaning [tools] zig An exact stable version, a release line, latest or a semver range tools.lockPlatforms Optional list of platforms to lock oyzu.lock The exact version, platform, archive URL and SHA-256 oyzu doesn't read a compiler version from build.zig.zon. A minimum version there is a constraint for the Zig builder, not a pin.

oyzu reads the official index and picks stable releases only (no master or nightly builds). It downloads the archive, checks it against the SHA-256 the index publishes, and installs the full distribution, including libraries and license files. Zig releases are checked by digest; no publisher signature is verified. Under an organization tool catalog, only an approved release can be selected, and a missing record fails instead of falling back to the public index. Frozen installs rebuild the download from the URL in the lock without reading the index again. --offline needs the tool installed or its archive cached. Zig's own package fetching is separate: pinning the compiler doesn't make package downloads offline.

Platform Status macOS Intel Supported Linux x86-64 (glibc) Supported Windows x86-64 Official ZIP layout with zig.exe; blocked by the default signed index's unresolved Windows record Other architectures, musl Not supported

Failure Cause and recovery TOOL_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE The platform isn't supported. Use a supported platform No stable version matches Choose a published stable version that fits your constraints. Master and nightly builds aren't supported Invalid or missing archive or checksum Nothing is installed. Check the official release before retrying Archive URL doesn't match the expected layout Restore the original lock or update the selection. Use administrative routes for mirrors; keep the locked logical upstream URL and archive name TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX / TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG Ask your organization to approve that release and platform TOOL_LOCK_STALE Run the suggested oyzu update or oyzu pin command. Frozen commands never change the selection
Zig builds Tool commands Organization tool catalog

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/toolchain-platforms.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Container builds run each language build on the base execution image, with the language's tools restored from oyzu.lock for the action's platform. The supported worker platform is linux/amd64; ARM64 workers and targets are unsupported. No project configuration is needed. Language builders need an image whose OS and architecture match the target platform, because they run tests and other target code. The Docker image builder can assemble images for another platform on its usual worker when it doesn't run target code. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Oyzu looks up the base image oyzu-execution/base:1 and inspects its platform. If the platform matches, that image is used. Otherwise it looks for a sibling named oyzu-execution/base:1-<os>-<arch>, such as oyzu-execution/base:1-linux-arm64, and checks that the image really has that platform (a matching tag isn't enough). A missing image or sibling is pulled from the pinned index for that architecture. Running another architecture's image still needs emulation in Docker; Oyzu doesn't install emulators. Illustrative retained platform-selection contract (ARM64 execution is unsupported): oyzu build image oyzu inspect dist When an image target declares two platforms and copies in a Go binary, Oyzu builds two Go producers, each running its build, tests and checks on the base image for its platform with the Go locked for that platform. Docker then assembles both images and Oyzu writes an OCI index for them.

For a locally provisioned multi-platform index, Oyzu asks Docker for the requested child with docker image inspect --platform. It checks the child descriptor's OS and architecture and any top-level config facts Docker returns. Docker's containerd store can leave top-level Os and Architecture empty when the selected child's config is not downloaded; a matching descriptor alone does not make that content available. Provision the target child explicitly, for example docker pull --platform linux/amd64 alpine:3.22, before building. Oyzu still verifies exported manifest/config bytes and rejects a different platform or an attestation in place of a runnable image. It never pulls Dockerfile bases itself.

--image manager=reference sets the image for every selected variant that uses that manager. Oyzu uses it as given and doesn't look for siblings. An override with the wrong platform fails before preparation, so one override generally can't serve both sides of a platform matrix. oyzu run tasks use host tools and never pick container images.

Plans and dependency records include the image identity and the platform it ran on, separately from the artifact's target platform. Canonical platform identities are JSON strings such as "linux/x86_64" or "linux/arm64". Go preparation also checks that Go's OS and architecture match the image. Old core platform objects are not decoded as strings. Cache results and key history containing them are treated as misses and retained on disk. Unreadable tool receipts and installed engine metadata name the affected file and request reinstallation; an unreadable oyzu.lock requests explicit re-locking. Oyzu does not delete these records. Plugin payload descriptors and native OCI descriptors keep their separate structured contracts, including in oyzu.lock.

A missing sibling, a sibling with the wrong platform, or an execution failure stops the build. Oyzu never silently builds on the wrong architecture. For supported x64 builds, provision the right image or fix the --image override, then rebuild. ARM64 is unsupported; do not provision emulation as a support workaround.

The container executor accepts Linux images only. Every ecosystem uses the same image lookup. ARM64 execution is unsupported. Records don't say whether a build ran on native hardware or under emulation. Your Docker host provides any emulation; Oyzu never installs it. See Docker's multi-platform guide. Cross-compilation alone does not establish that an artifact runs on its target. Dockerfiles that RUN commands for another platform have separate rules; see Docker platform admission. Image selection only uses the local daemon. Remote worker pools aren't discovered.

Default recipe resolution and provider-evidence requests select Linux x86-64 (GNU), Intel macOS and Windows x86-64 (MSVC): linux/amd64/gnu, darwin/amd64/native and windows/amd64/msvc. Tool-lock coverage follows the actual host, build inventory and tools.lockPlatforms; the Oyzu repository explicitly requires these three x64 tuples. A provider with no matching release reports it as unavailable; for example, Tailscale has Linux archives only. ARM64 tool hosts and targets are unsupported. Explicit metadata queries and existing locks can retain ARM64 records without installing or running them. Native installation support remains specific to each provider; Intel macOS metadata coverage alone does not establish native installation support.
Native local builds for platforms and executors. Verification toolsets and platform matrices for how producers are matched to platforms. Docker images and OCI indices.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/version-inference.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build works out a version for every artifact from your native version declarations, your Git tags and your Conventional Commit messages. You don't configure anything: build as usual and each artifact gets a version that says which release it's heading for and exactly which source it came from. Supported builders: Cargo, Node (npm, pnpm, Yarn), Helm, Go, Docker, Python, Maven, Gradle and Ant. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

A single-package repository declares version 1.4.2, has the tag v1.4.2, and one newer commit feat: add endpoint. oyzu build resolves the next version to 1.5.0, and artifacts get: 1.5.0-dev.g<12-character-source-hash> The suffix comes from the content of the build's source files, not the Git commit SHA. There's no counter or timestamp, so the same source always gives the same version. The suffix is the same on every platform. It covers file paths and contents but not the executable bit, which Windows can't see, so a Windows build and a Linux build of one commit get the same version. (Action-cache keys still include the bit, because changing it can change what a command does.) Artifact digests, not version strings, identify the exact bytes. Every ordinary build produces a snapshot version like this. Only release staging produces exact release versions.

Run oyzu build in a supported project. No Oyzu configuration is needed. Git must be on the host. Oyzu reads your repository before the build starts. If history is missing (for example in a shallow CI clone), Oyzu can fetch it read-only. A folder exported without Git uses the native version, or 0.0.0 when the builder has no native version, plus the source suffix. Oyzu never edits your checkout. Inferred versions are written only into the private copies of manifests used for the build.

Choose a strategy in oyzu.toml if the default doesn't suit you: [version] strategy = "tags" Strategy How the base version is chosen auto (default) Combine the native version, exact tags, the nearest stable tag and commit impacts. Fall back to the native version or 0.0.0 when history can't supply a baseline. native Use the native version. Ignore tags and commit bumps. Fails if there's no native version. tags Use an exact tag on the commit, otherwise the nearest stable tag. No bump is inferred and the native version doesn't have to match. conventional Like auto, but requires complete history and a baseline or exact tag, and rejects relevant commits that aren't Conventional Commits. Native snapshot encodings retain their original source scope when a shared source refinement cannot preserve that encoding. In particular, a PEP 440 Python snapshot is never replaced with a SemVer snapshot spelling. Every strategy still produces snapshot versions, and none changes who may publish or sign. The setting follows the normal configuration cascade, including profiles and administrative constraints. Unknown values fail validation.

The first stable tag that applies to the package, walking first-parent history, is the baseline. Commits after it (including merged ones) bump the version once, by the largest impact: a breaking change bumps major, feat bumps minor, fix bumps patch. Other Conventional Commit types don't bump. A native version already ahead of the baseline is kept if it's at least the computed minimum. An RC tag matching a stable native version keeps its prerelease label in the snapshot.

An exact tag on the built commit still produces a snapshot version and doesn't allow publishing by itself. It does name the release: oyzu publish uses the exactTags a build records as its GitHub release tag, so the version and the release tag always agree. Builds for one destination must agree, and oyzu publish --tag overrides it. See which release. Only tags that apply to the package are recorded (see tag names). For example, an unscoped v1.4.0 on a member of a multi-package Cargo workspace records nothing, so publishing it needs --tag. Artifacts from the Rust builder and Node workspace packages carry extensions["oyzu.dev/versioning"].package, naming the package their version came from.

Each target in dist/plan.json and dist/manifest.json has extensions["oyzu.dev/versioning"] with the native version, resolved base and version, source digest, commit, baseline tag and commit, exact tags, contributing and unclassified commits, whether history was complete, the reason, the strategy used and the configured requestedStrategy. Cargo keeps unselected workspace entries as native facts; they have no inferred tag or minimum-version obligation. When release subjects are recorded, selectedPackages identifies the selected scope, including complete fixed groups. extensions["oyzu.dev/version-history"] records the Git facts each decision used: HEAD, the repository prefix, shallow status, tags (names, object IDs and commits), and the commits read (parents, messages, paths). Decisions point to it with historyDigest, and record baselineDistance and analyzedCommits. These are local observations. They aren't authenticated source-control facts and don't make a build releasable. History records include commit messages and paths, so treat bundles as repository information when you share them.

Code Cause Fix version-needs-native The strategy needs a native version and there isn't one. Declare the version natively, or pick another strategy. version-needs-tags, version-needs-history The strategy needs tags or complete history. Fetch complete history and tags, or pick another strategy. version-unclassified-commits conventional found relevant commits that aren't Conventional Commits. Reword the commits' intent, or pick a less strict strategy. unsupported-version-strategy tags or conventional on a native version scheme Oyzu can't map. (auto and native keep a native snapshot instead.) Use auto or native. version-conflict, ambiguous-version-tags An exact tag conflicts with the native version, one commit has two version tags, or the native version is too low. Fix the native declaration or the tags and rerun.

Oyzu reads Git history once per repository per build. How much it reads depends on the build: Build What is read CI, --full, a ci profile, or the tags / conventional strategy Commit messages and changed paths back to each package's nearest stable tag. Older history can't change the result. If an origin is configured and the build is online, Oyzu also fetches complete ancestry and a fresh tag list first. Local fast build with auto, or native Only the head commit, shallow state and tag list. No commit messages. So in a local fast build with auto, an exact tag can still set the version, but otherwise the version falls back to the native version (or 0.0.0) plus the source suffix, with reason native-fallback-local-history-skipped and historyComplete: false. A local artifact's version can therefore differ from CI's for the same commit. Use --full, the CI context or the tags/conventional strategy to get the version a release build would use.
documents.s: What history is read, and when

documents.t: When a build needs history it doesn't have, Oyzu can fetch it read-only from a public https://github.com/owner/repository origin. Acquisition for the same origin and captured HEAD uses a nonblocking lock. An active acquisition reports that history acquisition is already in progress. The lock is released on completion or failure; unrelated child processes do not keep a finished acquisition locked. Credentials, SSH and file URLs, queries and fragments are refused. Plain HTTP is allowed only for loopback hosts. The administrative fetches.sources allowlist also applies. Fetching is refused whenever organization management or registries.routes is in effect. Authenticated or managed Git connections aren't supported; provide complete history locally instead. History is fetched into a private store under cache/git-history in the user data directory. Your checkout's refs, tags, index and commit are never touched. A checkout that moves during the build, or a local tag that disagrees with the remote one, stops the build. Fetched tags never grant release permission. --offline never fetches, but reuses earlier fetched history for the same origin and HEAD. Local fast auto builds, native and --plan never fetch. If history can't be fetched, auto keeps its snapshot fallback; tags and conventional stop before any build actions if their inputs are still missing. Diagnostic Cause Fix SOURCE_DENIED The origin URL or fetches.sources doesn't allow this source. Use a credential-free HTTPS GitHub origin, or ask your administrator to allow it. CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED Organization management or registry routing is in effect. Provide complete history and tags locally. HISTORY_INPUT_MISSING Offline, with no earlier fetch for this origin and HEAD. Run once online, or provide complete history. HISTORY_ACQUISITION_UNAVAILABLE The source couldn't be reached or exceeded its limits. Restore access or provide complete history. HISTORY_INTEGRITY_CONFLICT Fetched or stored history failed validation. The build stops. Investigate, remove the bad stored copy and retry. version-conflict Local and remote tags disagree, or the checkout moved. Reconcile the tags and retry from a stable checkout. The manifest records fetch outcomes and times in extensions["oyzu.dev/history-acquisition"]; they don't affect the version. Each online fetch currently downloads a full fresh copy, even if an earlier one had the same objects, and old copies aren't cleaned up. This can add network and disk use to full builds.

For Cargo builds, with.packages limits version inference and release staging to the named workspace packages. An unselected package's inferred minimum cannot block the build. Its native version remains unchanged in the private workspace; the complete workspace inventory still determines tag ownership and dependency input paths. Omitting with.packages selects the whole workspace. Changes to an unselected local dependency still contribute to the selected consumer's inferred minimum. That dependency keeps its native coordinate rather than acquiring a snapshot or release version from the consumer's build. Selecting one member of an explicitly declared fixed release group selects that whole release subject and preserves its common-version requirements. Independent packages outside the selection are not staged, even if the event tag names one of them. A selected independent package uses its own native version and package tag, such as oyzu-plugin-go/v0.1.0; selecting it alone does not admit root tags. A standalone package at the repository root, or a single-package Cargo workspace, uses unscoped tags such as v1.4.2. Independent Cargo and Node members use package-name tags. Maven modules use the artifact ID (or groupId.artifactId when IDs collide). Gradle projects use the project name (or directory path when names collide). Multi-project builds need scoped tags such as library/v1.4.2. Go workspace modules use directory-scoped tags. Equal native versions never imply that packages are released together. For that, see Cargo fixed release subjects.

Within a workspace, a change to a package also bumps the packages that depend on it. For example, with app -> bridge -> shared and a separate independent package, a feat that changes only shared moves the first three from 1.4.2 to 1.5.0; independent stays at 1.4.2. Each package is compared with its own tag, and each consumer's metadata gets its dependencies' chosen versions. Dependencies come from the native model (Cargo and Node local dependency edges, Maven's reactor, Gradle's resolved project graph, Go imports). Development, build, optional and peer dependencies count. This is a cautious view of build inputs, not a claim about public API changes. A changed file belongs to the most specific member folder that contains it. Files outside every member (workspace manifests, lock files, root build inputs) count for all members. inputScope in each decision records the directories and workspaceDirectories used. Oyzu doesn't guess undeclared imports between members.

Separate targets can depend on each other through depends_on, tasks and artifact relationships, and through inputs paths in build.yaml (including paths outside the producer's folder). A change in a producer can then bump its consumer's version against the consumer's own tag, without bumping unrelated targets. Changed paths are matched against the build's recorded source selection, including your ignore overrides. Deleted paths count too. Git paths are relative to the repository root, even in a nested workspace. Decisions record inputScope.declaredPaths. Inputs in a different Git repository fail with version-inputs-outside-repository. This works for Node (isolated builds), and for native Go and Rust builds.

For isolated builds on Unix, Oyzu can narrow a target's source suffix to the files its shipping commands actually read, so an unrelated shared file doesn't change every target's version. It applies only to per-action eligible targets, where every selected action has a contract and execution can enforce the shipping read bounds. It applies when every version-carrying command (build, package, export, or an artifact producer) has a complete, confinable stage contract and stays cacheable. An unbounded version-carrying command keeps the wider source hash. Test, lint and format commands may keep whole-target read keys without widening the development version only when their complete write bounds cannot feed shipping. An incomplete write bound on any command retains the wider version. The scope includes files the shipping commands read, declared inputs, and the configuration, build and lock files. Files only checks read are left out when the checks' outputs can't reach a shipping command. An optional file that a command would read stays in scope while absent, so creating it changes the version. A source projection's selected file list is a membership input alongside those reads. Adding or removing a selected file changes the version; an ignored file outside the shipping reads does not. Artifact inputs are admitted only when their producers also belong to the same confined shipping closure. Windows, native host builds, cross-target prerequisites, hooks, custom replacements and artifact inputs from outside that closure keep the full source scope. So does any target whose command details are incomplete. The final scope is computed from the frozen plan, then the core version decisions and accepted captured command strings are rebound together before action keys are computed. This applies to captured plugins through one shared mechanism, including Node. Complete core versions embedded in argv, environment, native payloads and artifact filenames follow the rebound version only when the old value contains its recorded per-build source hash. An unmarked plain version (for example 1.0.0) retains the whole-target version and plan, preserving equal dependency versions and path fragments. oyzu cache explain reports why this narrowing was skipped. Native version declaration files remain inputs even when the shipping commands do not read them directly. An unstable read/write boundary retains the original wider version. Native formats without a supported SemVer rebind retain their provider's conservative decision. Non-check steps with other names (for example generate, compile or dependency staging) join the shipping scope whenever their writes can feed a shipping read, transitively. Unknown writes, including those of checks, keep the whole-target version. An unrelated step is excluded only when its complete write bound proves it cannot feed shipping. Upstream-only shipping actions include the reads of all their transitive data predecessors, following produced-output edges, native workspace sequences and explicit dependencies. Order-only edges and incidental task prerequisites do not add source reads. An unrelated non-shipping upstream-only action does not widen the scope. The planner makes native sequencing after a check with complete empty workspace writes order-only and passes through its data predecessors. This same graph defines cache inputs; version inference adds no separate check exclusion. A Helm chart's README ships unless .helmignore excludes it, so editing that README changes its development version. A README outside a nested chart, or one excluded by a supported positive literal .helmignore rule, is outside the shipping version scope. The ignore control remains in scope. See Helm documentation inputs. Helm staging reads the keyed prepared chart, not source. Its native version stays unchanged in preparation; the captured stage projects the final core version into its private chart. Cache narrowing also requires complete read declarations and dependency views that hide unselected prepared files. See Helm source reads.

For isolated Node builds, a pre_build hook that declares outputs counts as a generator. The version hash covers the target's source without the hook's own script, plus the files the hook wrote to its declared outputs. Editing the script without changing what it writes keeps the version; changing what it writes changes it. The script stays in the hash if a build stage reads or writes it, or if it isn't an argument of the hook's command. plan.json records the version before the hook runs; the final version is in plans/<target>.post-hooks.json and the manifest. See hooks as always-run actions. --no-cache gives the same version. Other builders and hook phases use the plain source hash.

Isolated captured Cargo builds retain the conservative version chosen during preparation: that version is already frozen into the admitted metadata, manifest overlay and lockfile. Later read-scope refinement keeps the matching version decision and reports why it cannot change those prepared bytes. Source, metadata and artifact validation still apply. Native host version behavior below is unchanged. Inferred versions and local package references are written only into Cargo's private build copy. Host compile, test, lint and format stages use declared Cargo versions. Those stages do not receive the injected OYZU_VERSION default; the final stage does, and explicit environment values remain keyed. There is no substituted package-wide or action-wide default. Plain local development builds, including shared-cache readers, may export that declared-version binary directly. Their decision records the actual compiledVersion separately from the inferred artifact version. Full, CI, optimized, shared-cache writer, handed-off, packaged and release builds retain a final Cargo stage with inferred package versions, including the real CARGO_PKG_VERSION. Explicit tag/history strategies also require projection. That final stage binds its version map and projected-control digests. Development results do not satisfy its cache key or stamped packaging, publication and release gates. Those consumers refuse a compiledVersion marker with VERSION_STAMP_REQUIRED; rebuild with --full or --optimized. Restored compile outputs do not include Cargo compiler state. Final projection changes Cargo package identities and can recompile workspace crates even when they read neither version environment variable. See local builds. Executable names don't change.

The native package name and version from package.json drive the version, for isolated and native host builds alike. With native, a package without a version fails before the build; add the version to package.json. Native host builds never change package.json. Isolated builds write the version into private copies of the root and member manifests and their local references. Native Node facts and host policy​ Node plugins report the native package name and version with their source path and digest. A target's alias is separate from the package name. The decision sets the plan version, the artifact file name and version, and the default OYZU_VERSION. The native compiled version may differ from the artifact's snapshot; both are recorded.
The root chart version is written into the private build copy. appVersion and dependency chart versions keep their native meaning.

Go uses the version in artifact names and the manifest. It doesn't inject a version into compiled code. Docker uses it in the OCI archive name, image reference and manifest. Both record nativeVersion: null. An exact tag supplies the base; otherwise an ancestor tag is the baseline for commit impact, or 0.0.0. Go resolves each workspace module separately, using imports and test imports. Module zip, mod and info outputs keep native v prefixes and RC qualifiers. See Go native module artifacts.

Native PEP 440 versions are normalized by Python's packaging library. Stable versions with up to three components, and alpha, beta and RC versions, take part in tag inference. For example, base 1.5.0-rc.2 becomes 1.5.0rc2.dev0+g<source-hash>. Epochs, post-releases, existing dev versions and longer version tuples keep a native snapshot (reason native-ecosystem-source). The .dev0+g<source-hash> suffix always comes from the current captured inputs. A version stamped during an earlier acquisition does not fix that suffix for a later build. Static PEP 621 projects (pip, uv, Poetry) get the version in their private pyproject.toml. Projects with a dynamic version take it from tags (or 0.0.0); see dynamic versions. Legacy setuptools projects get the version through their distribution metadata. The source archive includes a generated setup.py wrapper so rebuilding it keeps the version. Custom distribution code beyond standard setuptools and distutils entry points isn't supported. Requirements-only applications have no native version and use SemVer application versions. Recreate dependency captures made by older Oyzu versions.

A trailing -SNAPSHOT is removed when the rest is SemVer. Other forms keep their value and get a native snapshot. Gradle's unspecified lets tags set the base. Ant falls back to 0.0.0 when there's no version property. Maven and Gradle read native models in an isolated step, then apply the chosen versions in the private workspace. Maven writes module, parent and dependency versions; Gradle archive tasks use the chosen versions; Ant records it in the JAR manifest. Requires the Gradle 8.14.3 profile and a current Maven image. Reprovision an older Maven image if reactor dependencies are missing. Recreate older dependency captures. Releasing inherited Maven versions together isn't supported.

Cargo workspaces can declare packages that always share one version, using cargo-release's shared-version setting: shared-version = true joins the shared group. A string names a separate group. false opts out of an inherited group. See Rust fixed version groups for an example, field precedence, and the supported tag-prefix and tag-name forms. Membership comes from all packages in the workspace, including private and unselected ones. Other ecosystems don't support fixed groups. A change to any member bumps the whole group once, by the largest impact. A package that depends on a member sees that change too, while keeping its own tag. Every member must declare the same native version, including qualifiers. Strategy Group behavior auto, fast local Common native snapshot, with exact group tags. No commit history read. auto, full or CI Common exact tag or nearest stable baseline, and the combined commit impact. native Common native snapshot. Ignores tags and commits. tags Needs a declared tag prefix and enough tags. conventional Needs a tag prefix, complete history and Conventional Commits. If no member declares a tag prefix, auto and native record a native snapshot with reason native-group-missing-namespace, and strict strategies refuse. A prefix on only some members is refused. Non-native strategies reject conflicting per-package tags on HEAD or the baseline commit. Private Cargo manifests, local requirements and the lock get the chosen versions. Your checkout isn't changed. Host binaries are compiled with the final inferred version. extensions["oyzu.dev/version-subjects"] records the group, members, tag prefixes and resolution; each member's oyzu.dev/versioning entry points to it with releaseSubject. --plan never runs Cargo or fetches history to fill in missing facts. Fixed groups are supported on Linux x86_64.

Release staging builds exact release-candidate or stable versions, instead of snapshots, in a CI job triggered by a tag push. Request it explicitly with --require-release; ordinary builds retain snapshot coordinates. Note: Release staging is experimental. It supports only a GitHub Actions job triggered by a tag push in the same repository. Cargo targets support Linux x86_64/arm64 (GNU or musl), Darwin x86_64/arm64 and Windows x86_64 MSVC. Plugin packages inherit their executable's staging. Staged versions are never marked production-eligible. Other builders and providers are unsupported. oyzu -C app build app --require-release --full The native version and the tag together choose the version. Native 1.5.0-rc.1 with a matching exact tag stages a release candidate; native 1.5.0 with its tag stages a stable release. Each needs a fresh build: renaming an RC archive doesn't make it stable. A native/tag conflict fails, and native doesn't let a tag override the native version. Option Behavior (none) Keeps snapshot versions, including in a tag-event job. --require-release Missing, offline, unsupported or contradictory evidence refuses the build before any build, check or package action runs. --release-profile FILE Accept only the exact reusable workflow and source in this release profile. --context release, OYZU_CONTEXT Only set the context. They never authenticate a release. --optimized Only chooses the build profile. --plan Read-only preview. Shows what evidence is missing. --check --require-release Reports missing release evidence as a blocking finding. A staged build always runs every required check, including real test and coverage reports. A nested target can't turn those off.

Job permissions: contents: read, actions: read and id-token: write. Oyzu requests a fresh GitHub OIDC token and checks the signed repository, ref, commit, workflow, run attempt and job against GitHub's API (using the job's GITHUB_TOKEN). CI variables, a local tag, a JWT file or OYZU_ID_TOKEN can't stand in for this. The built files must match the tagged commit byte for byte, and the tag must stay the same until the build finishes. Unix also compares executable bits. Windows has no POSIX executable bit: the immutable Git tree supplies that identity, recorded as sourceFileModes: git-tree-no-posix-mode. Git's CRLF conversion is not applied to the comparison; use a byte-preserving checkout. Refused: uncommitted changes, forks, the wrong job or attempt, a moved tag, repository hooks, Git symlinks or submodules in the selected source, and inputs outside the repository. Reusable workflows need --release-profile, and both signed workflow claims must match. When staging is requested, the manifest records GitHub's answers and any unresolved reasons in extensions["oyzu.dev/release-staging"]. Ordinary Cargo snapshots omit that extension and don't request GitHub release evidence, including when CI variables describe a tag event. Those hints alone cannot create staging observations or classifications. If a check fails, or the source or tag changes before the end, no final output is accepted. A job token proves the job's identity and event. It doesn't prove where Oyzu ran, who built the artifact, that checks were correct, or that the build was isolated.

Required tests and coverage run for the same selected Cargo packages and features on the prepared compiler's host triple, in the same build invocation. A positive passing native test result and all mandatory reports remain required; missing, skipped or failing checks refuse staging. Format and lint remain mandatory. --require-release disables action-result reuse so earlier runs' reports cannot satisfy this invocation. Native compiler caches can still accelerate the work; the test and check commands execute again. The staging record's testEvidence names the packages, host and target triples, and report IDs. For a cross build, targetRuntimeTested is false. These host tests do not establish target-specific behavior, linking at runtime, or tests behind target-only conditional compilation. Run the artifact's tests on its target platform separately.

An oyzu/plugin-package member takes the exact version only from its staged executable artifact and package decision. Build each member with --require-release --full in the matching package tag event. For a Cargo workspace member, use its package tag namespace, for example oyzu-plugin-go/v0.1.0. Composition with --compose ... --require-release needs every admitted member's staging record to agree on repository, tag, peeled commit, package and version. The current composing job must independently authenticate that same tag and source; saved member records never replace fresh GitHub evidence. The root records the exact version in its artifact, plugin metadata and OCI version annotation. Composition still enforces ordinary provenance, content integrity and platform completeness. Without --require-release, composition produces a snapshot and does not carry release staging.

If GitHub is unavailable or permissions are missing, a build without --require-release keeps snapshot versions. With --require-release it fails, naming the missing fact. Retry online in the matching job after fixing access. Saved manifests and earlier attempts can't authenticate a new invocation, and offline builds can't stage. Admitted staged members can be composed only after fresh authentication of the composing job. Error Recovery release-profile-unsupported Select a supported Cargo platform and remove repository hooks. release-member-unstaged Rebuild every executable and plugin member with --require-release --full. release-member-mismatch Rebuild members for one repository, package tag, commit and version. release-required-check Restore all mandatory checks and positive passing host test evidence in this invocation. release-source-mismatch, release-tag-mismatch Use the members' unchanged tagged commit in the matching tag-event job.

Release staging is limited as described above. No other CI providers, events, builders or platforms are supported. Fixed release groups are Cargo-only. Native version schemes Oyzu can't map to SemVer (some Python, Maven and Gradle forms) keep native snapshots and don't get tag or commit bumps. History can be fetched only from public GitHub HTTPS origins.
Rust, Go, Python preparation Publishing Release provenance verification

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/yarn.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu builds and tests Node projects that use Yarn. Yarn Classic (1.22.22) projects and workspaces are discovered from native manifests and the lock with no Oyzu build file. Single-root applications also work with Yarn Berry 4.17.1. Note: Yarn support is experimental. Each setup below lists the exact versions and platforms it supports. Anything not listed there is not supported yet. Builds use the Node builder plugin, which must be installed and selected (see plugin packages). Native Yarn always owns dependency layout, peer behavior and lifecycle scripts. Platform scope: Use an x64 host and supported x64 build targets. ARM64 is unsupported. Feature-specific limits are listed in the support matrix.

Setup Yarn Platforms Section Isolated Classic builds (package archives, workspaces) Classic 1.22.22, Node 22 Isolated Linux amd64 worker (not fully tested yet) Capture and installation, Workspace builds Isolated single-root application Classic 1.22.22, Node 22.23.3 Windows x64 coordinator with Linux amd64 worker External captured Classic application Isolated single-root application Berry 4.17.1, Node 22.23.3 Windows x64 coordinator with Linux amd64 worker Captured Berry application Native single-root application Classic 1.22.22 or Berry 4.17.1, Node 22.23.3 Windows x64 and Linux x64 Managed Yarn Native single-root telemetry opt-out Berry 4.17.1, Node 22.23.4 Linux x86_64 (GNU) Yarn configuration checks Native workspace packages Classic 1.22.22 Linux x86_64 (GNU) Native Classic workspace packages Native workspace packages Berry 4.17.1 Windows x64 Native Berry workspace package continuation Berry setups need an existing nodeLinker: node-modules in .yarnrc.yml. Isolated builds require the literal declaration. Native configuration also admits the quoted linker value and YAML boolean enableTelemetry: false; see Yarn configuration checks. The telemetry opt-out works for native single-root applications on Linux x86_64 (GNU) with Berry 4.17.1 and Node 22.23.4. Yarn Plug'n'Play is not supported.

The tested profile is Yarn Classic 1.22.22 on Node 22. Isolated builds run on the base execution image with Docker. Node and Yarn both come from oyzu.lock, so pin Node in [tools] and Yarn with an exact packageManager (or yarn in [tools]). oyzu --root path/to/project run list oyzu --root path/to/project build oyzu --root path/to/project inspect dist Oyzu never installs a replacement package manager during a build. --image yarn=<image> runs Yarn's isolated actions on an image of your own. Its immutable identity is recorded, and the locked Node and Yarn still run. The @yarnpkg/lockfile 1.1.0 parser ships in the Node plugin package, and the default quality tools are restored from their pinned lock, so no image needs either. An exact packageManager declaration must agree with native Yarn's version. A Corepack suffix such as yarn@1.22.22+sha512.<hex> is accepted and ignored in that comparison. Incompatible Node engine requirements fail. Your native scripts appear as tasks. During isolated builds, the conventional build and test work and read-only lint and format checks run. oyzu run uses host tools, and explicit formatting can modify your source (build format checks cannot). Node test scripts produce JUnit and LCOV. See Node quality.

Oyzu reads Yarn Classic v1 lock syntax with Yarn's own parser, including grouped selectors. It needs a lock that parses, current direct dependency selectors, conventional HTTPS registry archive URLs and an integrity value for every entry. SHA-512 is the normal form. Older Classic locks also carry integrity sha1-... values for packages locked before the registry published SHA-512. Those are accepted only when the SHA-1 value matches the #<sha1> fragment of the resolved URL. They are verified against that SHA-1 and named in the dependency record. SHA-1 is weaker, so regenerate those entries with native Yarn if you need SHA-512 throughout. Several selectors for one archive share its captured identity. Conflicting identities and ambiguous offline-mirror file names fail. Every locked archive is captured, including optional and transitive ones. Git, file and other non-registry resolutions are refused. Preparation uses the scoped broker routes for https://registry.npmjs.org/ and https://registry.yarnpkg.com/, recorded as npm-public and yarn-public. Redirects stay subject to broker authorization. Your lock keeps its original URLs and hashes. The archive inventory strips URL fragments from transport addresses and verifies the lock's SHA-512 before installation. Credentials never enter the inventory or mirror. The snapshot holds content-addressed archives and an inventory, not Yarn's extracted cache. Each install creates a fresh private mirror and cache and a temporary Yarn configuration outside your source. Installation uses the mirror, includes development dependencies, and has no network in the worker. Before lifecycle scripts are allowed, Oyzu runs yarn install --offline --ignore-scripts --force in the private tree and compares the resulting lock with the captured one. Any change in dependency resolution fails. Cosmetic serialization changes are discarded, so your lock bytes stay as they were. During execution, yarn install --offline --frozen-lockfile --force runs the lifecycle without a broker. Acquisition never enables scripts. Native Yarn and Node versions must match the captured versions. The comparison matters because suppressing lock writes alone doesn't show that changed resolutions agree with the lock. Registry version overrides in package.json resolutions are supported, including a different transitive version alongside a direct one: { "dependencies": {"is-odd": "3.0.1", "is-number": "6.0.0"}, "resolutions": {"is-odd/is-number": "7.0.0"} } Generate and commit the matching lock with native Yarn first (see the yarn-resolutions example). Yarn's own warnings and selective-resolution limits apply. File, Git, URL and alias-protocol resolution values are rejected before any native invocation. See Yarn's selective resolutions. Oyzu uses Yarn's offline mirror and does not reimplement package resolution or Yarn's cache layout.

Yarn Classic reads native project and user registry settings. Authenticated private registries use .npmrc as described in private registry configuration. Oyzu handles registry and authentication settings before source capture and removes them from the captured copy. Remaining settings cannot redirect archive sources or supply credentials during captured metadata queries. Other captured settings remain limited to the following list: File Accepted settings .yarnrc ignore-engines, save-prefix, save-exact, disable-self-update-check, version-tag-prefix, version-git-message, version-git-tag, version-sign-git-tag .npmrc registry, @scope:registry, //host/path/:_authToken, always-auth; legacy capture also accepts package-lock, loglevel, progress, save-exact, save-prefix, fund, audit, update-notifier For example, webpack's .yarnrc has ignore-engines true and its .npmrc has package-lock=false. Both are accepted and Yarn applies them. Any other key fails acquisition before native installation. Refused settings include yarn-path, yarn-offline-mirror, cache-folder and ---prefixed command-line settings. The message names the key, not its value. .yarnrc is read with Yarn's lock parser. .npmrc is read as key=value lines, and an ini section header is rejected as an unknown key. Settings files inside workspace members are not supported. .yarnrc.yml is Yarn Berry configuration. In a Classic build it fails with a message saying Berry needs its own setup.

To test other Node versions, use verification toolsets in oyzu.toml. matrix.node in build.yaml is refused. Toolset verification runs on the native host executor, and isolated Yarn builds use the isolated executor, so a build with verification runs fails with VERIFICATION_RUN_UNSUPPORTED. A successful build emits snapshot .tgz packages with normalized archive metadata. The embedded package version matches the artifact version. dist/manifest.json lists artifacts, tests and coverage, with dependency snapshots and native logs beside it. Failed tests keep their reports and block packaging. oyzu inspect dist checks content integrity, not release trust. Dependency records use adapter layout 2. They list names, versions, source IDs, SHA-256 digests and sizes. The oyzu.dev/yarn extension records lockfile-sha512 integrity and the all-locked-registry-tarballs inventory. If any archive was verified by a legacy SHA-1 value, integrity is lockfile-sha512-or-legacy-sha1 and legacySha1Packages lists those archives as name@version. Packages are classed as build inputs. Registry dependency edges and runtime or test classification aren't recorded, so this is not a runtime SBOM. Workspace captures also keep local package edges for build ordering and version projection. Failure Recovery Stale or conflicting lock Fix it with native Yarn and commit the result. Corrupt archive, missing captured input, disallowed source or runtime mismatch Fails instead of downloading a replacement during execution. Fix the cause and rebuild. Layout-1 dependency-free capture Capture again. It can't be replayed as layout 2. Unsupported source configuration Rejected before any native invocation, including version queries.

A Yarn Classic workspace has a private native root, a committed Classic lock and locally linked packages (see the Yarn Classic workspace example). Run the commands above from that root with no Oyzu configuration. oyzu run list includes build, test, lint and format-check. A plain oyzu run build runs yarn workspaces run build when there is no root script, so every member needs a build script. The isolated oyzu build also handles packages without build scripts. Acquisition asks Yarn for its workspace list after lock validation. Member locations and local dependency edges become captured facts. Oyzu does not read Yarn's workspace globs itself. Oyzu orders members by those edges, assigns snapshot versions and declares each package's reports. It rewrites versions and matching local references only in the private tree, before a fresh offline install. Your manifests and lock are unchanged. An explicit root script owns its stage once. Otherwise build scripts run in dependency order, and tests and read-only quality checks combine member scripts with inferred defaults. JUnit and LCOV are collected per package. yarn pack --ignore-scripts creates each archive. Oyzu normalizes archive metadata and publishes the packages to dist only after the required stages pass. Failed assertions or quality checks block artifact collection and keep the failure evidence. Hooks and overrides follow the shared task and report rules. For a coarse root build, Oyzu checks the concrete public JavaScript entries selected by Node's import and require conditions before packing. It also checks declaration files selected by the types condition and literal legacy declaration paths. Existence is checked, not TypeScript validity. Missing regular files fail. Null exclusions and conditional alternatives are left to Node. The check doesn't look inside Yarn's archive, and skips browser or custom conditions and wildcard paths. Limits: Classic needs a private workspace root. Cyclic local graphs, custom registry configuration, affected selection and member task groups are not supported. Direct host build and quality composition is less complete than the isolated build. Direct tests use the workspace report integration. Workspaces with external dependencies and broader framework setups aren't covered beyond a linked two-package project.

A single-root application with Yarn Classic 1.22.22 and Node 22.23.3 builds into an application directory plus Node-test JUnit and LCOV. It runs on a Linux amd64 worker, driven from a Windows x86_64 coordinator. Workspaces, other versions and other platforms are not supported. Select node/app and keep the package manager declaration: builds: app: {uses: node/app} {"packageManager":"yarn@1.22.22","dependencies":{"semver":"7.7.2"}} You need: A current Classic yarn.lock. Tool selections in oyzu.toml and oyzu.lock. An installed Node plugin package that supports multiple platforms (see plugin packages). Ordinary native build, test and quality scripts, an exact packageManager, public HTTPS registry dependencies with supported lock integrity, and no workspaces, project plugins, yarnPath or non-comment rc settings. oyzu -C path/to/app --json build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --frozen --no-cache --image yarn=<image> oyzu -C path/to/app inspect dist The plugin and tool selections and your lock must already be in oyzu.lock for --frozen. On first adoption a normal build creates them. Don't delete an existing oyzu.lock to retry a failed build. You don't need installed project dependencies or a Yarn lock parser in the image. Oyzu orchestrates, and native Node and Yarn do installation and scripts. Acquisition captures authorized registry archives with their original integrity data and without lifecycle scripts, then validates the lock with scripts off. Execution installs from the private mirror with network disabled, then runs lifecycle, build, test and quality steps. --frozen freezes selections but doesn't make acquisition offline. On success, dist holds a versioned application directory and fresh required reports, with dependency and tool identity and action logs in the manifest. Failed assertions keep available reports and block export. A test that exits zero but writes no JUnit and LCOV still fails the build. Problem Recovery Stale lock Run native Yarn to generate the intended lock, and keep it with the manifest. Missing yarn.lock Restore it. Admission can report the generic PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED: no owned captured dependency provider. A selected tool was lost during the build Retry with the corrected coordinator. Don't purge caches by hand. Both lock problems fail before lifecycle scripts run.

An isolated Berry build needs exact packageManager: yarn@4.17.1, Node 22.23.3, a current lock and an existing literal nodeLinker: node-modules: nodeLinker: node-modules It handles a single root with public registry dependencies. Plug'n'Play, child workspaces, yarnPath and project plugins are not supported. It runs on a Linux amd64 worker, driven from a Windows x86_64 coordinator. Other combinations, macOS, Windows ARM64 and Linux ARM64 are not supported yet. Use the same node/app declaration and isolated command as above. Oyzu prefetches public-registry metadata and archives through the broker, with SHA-512 checks, and serves only those fixed local GET and HEAD routes. Yarn creates and validates its own ZIP cache with install --immutable --mode=skip-build. Execution copies that cache into private scratch and runs install --immutable --immutable-cache with network disabled, before your commands run. Your .yarnrc.yml, package.json and lock are not rewritten. Archive integrity and Yarn's ZIP checksums are separate checks. The worker also gets an executable alias archive for yarn and yarnpkg, bound to the selected Node and Yarn. Executable modes survive Windows coordination, and the files are read-only for every action, including your commands and their child processes. The image's own Yarn is never used. Problem Recovery Lock drift (YN0028) Regenerate the lock with the selected Yarn only when you intend to change dependencies. Missing lock Restore it. Plug'n'Play project Fails admission. Oyzu doesn't convert PnP projects. Stale or missing lock, a checksum failure, or a request outside the prefetched routes Fails preparation. Fix the lock or dependency and rebuild. Child workspaces, yarnPath, project plugins, custom sources or extra rc settings Refused.

Note: Experimental. Supported on Linux x86_64 (GNU) only. Windows, macOS and ARM64 are not supported for this setup. A native build (without Docker) of a Classic workspace into package archives, using Node 22.23.3, Yarn Classic 1.22.22 and node/package. Your project needs: A named, semver-versioned private coordinator (root) with two publishable members. A genuine Classic yarn.lock, and local references such as *. Flat cp source.cjs dist.cjs builds and implicit package-owned Node tests. Select tools through normal configuration and the lock, and declare the output: builds: package: uses: node/package oyzu --json build package --full --no-cache --jobs 1 How it works: Oyzu runs the selected yarn install --frozen-lockfile task, after a script-free preparation with --ignore-scripts. Yarn's workspaces info supplies member links, and installed links confirm local targets. The private root is a build, test and report owner even though Classic leaves it out of its membership map. Oyzu rewrites versions and local references to exact versions in the private tree only. Classic packs each publishable member with --filename. Your manifests and lock keep their bytes. First adoption may add plugin and tool selections to oyzu.lock. The output is two TGZ archives and six JUnit/LCOV reports. A failing root assertion blocks both member archives and all export. A replaced install task is refused before any action. Native build scripts and helpers keep their implicit pre/post lifecycle and the protected-path rules. Not supported: pack hooks, peer dependencies and their metadata, active rc overrides, private members, aggregate builds and isolated Yarn workspaces. Empty or comment-only rc files are accepted.

Note: Experimental. Supported on Windows x64 with Node 22.23.3 and Yarn 4.17.1 only. A native build of a Berry workspace into package archives. It needs an existing literal nodeLinker: node-modules, a named and versioned root, publishable app and shared members, literal workspace:* local dependencies, recognized package-local build bodies and implicit package-owned Node tests. Declare the output in build.yaml, keep the genuine yarn.lock, and select tools through configuration and the lock: builds: package: {uses: node/package} oyzu --json build package --full --no-cache { "status": "succeeded", "runId": "45292-1792727760814863500" } Output shortened. A root, app and shared project produces three .tgz archives and six owner reports. Oyzu runs the ordinary immutable install, does a script-free preparation, fixes native membership, links and versions, then builds and tests in the private tree. Yarn packs the archives. Private version projection leaves the lock untouched and lets Yarn translate workspace:* when packing.

A root with "private": true still builds, runs implicit tests and writes its JUnit/LCOV, using its Oyzu-resolved version. Only publishable members get archives. Two members mean two archives and six reports. A failing root assertion blocks member export. Keep the root named and semver-versioned. Private members are not supported.

Authored install replacements are refused. prepack and postpack bodies are accepted only when Oyzu can show they have package-local effects before preparation or your commands. Recognized copy bodies and local Yarn helpers keep the protected-path rules. Coarse JavaScript bodies and foreign writes are refused. The whole script and helper map must match its analyzed value just before packing. Yarn runs each accepted hook in one native pack. prepack can generate archive content. postpack runs after the archive is made and can't change it. A postpack failure blocks export of the target, including archives packed earlier. Yarn's own postinstall stays ordinary native behavior. Berry doesn't run arbitrary pre and post build hooks automatically the way npm does.

Active .yarnrc.yml files in member directories and parents must be absent, comments, or the same node-modules setting. Other or malformed active settings fail before preparation. Settings changed by installation fail the frozen-facts comparison before member execution. Managed environment admission also applies to the install task. An alternate rc file name doesn't bypass it. Explicit npm or pnpm helper delegation is refused. Yarn options before a helper's selected script that can change script or binary ownership, such as -T/--top-level and -B/--binaries-only, are refused. Arguments after the script or -- are forwarded. Not supported: Classic, Plug'n'Play, isolated Yarn workspaces, aggregate scripts and other platforms.

Supported versions and platforms are in Supported setups. Modern Yarn (Berry) is not supported for isolated workspace builds. Isolated Berry configuration remains limited to literal nodeLinker: node-modules. Native configuration also admits the quoted linker and boolean enableTelemetry: false; other settings and telemetry values remain refused. Custom registry layouts, member settings files and other .yarnrc or .npmrc settings are not supported. Classic private registries use the native configuration described above; Berry private registries remain unsupported. Lifecycle scripts that need external downloads fail in the isolated worker. Yarn Plug'n'Play and project plugins are not supported.
Node applications, npm workspace builds and pnpm builds Managed Yarn for tool selection and direct-test preparation Workspace test bundles and Node quality

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/zig.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The zig/project builder runs a native Zig project's build.zig and collects what it installs. Use it when your build.zig defines the programs, libraries and resources you want in the build bundle. Note: Experimental. Zig 0.15.2 is the supported compiler. Native builds are supported on Intel macOS and, for projects without build.zig.zon dependencies, on Linux (x86-64, GNU) and Windows x86-64. Dependency-free Windows executable builds and native tests with test-step JUnit are verified. Isolated builds with dependencies run on Linux (x86-64, GNU). Without a [tools].zig entry, Oyzu selects Zig 0.15.2. A version prefix such as zig = "0.15" also works. Other compiler versions and platforms aren't supported yet. Dependency-free native tests and isolated Linux tests, including projects with dependencies, produce JUnit at test-step granularity. Coverage is not available. Windows compiler recipes exist, but selection also requires a resolved Windows record in the signed tool index. Until the default Zig installation index publishes one, pinning Zig 0.15.2 on Windows reports PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED; an existing Zig executable on PATH does not replace that record. Native Windows builds additionally require a Zig plugin package with a Windows payload.

Dependency-free native builds require a compatible Zig plugin declaring native-cache; native JUnit additionally requires zig-native-test-report. For a source build without a published compatible Windows package, use a local development binding to the compiled Zig plugin. On Windows x86-64, compiler acquisition also needs a resolved Windows record in the signed tool index. The default index currently rejects Zig 0.15.2 with PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED, before compilation. Default Windows acquisition awaits a signed index release containing that record. Dependency-bearing Windows projects, Windows isolated execution and coverage are not supported. The signed oyzu/zig package is available from the official plugin catalog. Enable preview selection in your user configuration: oyzu config set --global plugins.preview true Create build.yaml beside your build.zig: builds: hello: uses: zig/project Run oyzu build. The first build installs the selected plugin and records it in oyzu.lock; commit that file. Without a compiler pin, Oyzu selects Zig 0.15.2. The installation tree is collected as the install directory artifact in dist/manifest.json. Check the manifest for its path before running install/bin/hello. See plugin selection and build bundles.

Native Debug artifacts are not currently reproducible across independent clean source and cache roots. Zig 0.15.2 embeds absolute workspace and compiler-cache roots in DWARF debug information and has no remapping flag. This is an upstream compiler limitation. --no-cache disables Oyzu action-result reuse; it does not normalize those embedded paths. Equal source contents alone therefore do not guarantee equal install artifact digests. Keep debug information enabled when diagnosing this limitation; stripping it or selecting release optimization does not establish reproducible Debug builds. This limitation does not change release modes or captured execution. Select a native release mode explicitly in build.zig, for example by setting a module's .optimize = .ReleaseFast. with.definitions cannot override the reserved optimize control. Release mode alone is not a guarantee of reproducibility: native build programs can still embed paths or other changing inputs. ReleaseFast can retain DWARF with absolute workspace paths too, making its binaries location-sensitive across clean roots. Captured builds retain their existing fixed worker paths and isolation; Oyzu does not force local Debug builds into captured execution. Managed Zig acquisition currently supports Intel macOS and Linux x86-64 GNU. Windows native builder admission does not provide a Windows compiler acquisition recipe; automatic acquisition on Windows fails with TOOL_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED.

Input Meaning build.yaml with uses: zig/project Required. Zig targets aren't detected automatically. [tools] zig and oyzu.lock The compiler request and the exact installation Oyzu selected. build.zig The native build program. Only Zig runs it, during the build. build.zig.zon Optional. Oyzu reads the package name, version and minimum Zig version from it. with.steps Native build steps to run. with.definitions Project options passed to zig build as -Dname=value. with.install-format directory (default) or tar.gz. .minimum_zig_version in build.zig.zon is a minimum, not a pin. Choose a compiler that satisfies it through [tools]. Manifest fields, package enum names and dependency names can use native Zig quoted identifiers, such as .name = .@"hello-world" and .@"local-dep" = .{ .path = "local" }. Oyzu preserves the decoded name when reading package and dependency facts. Metadata must remain literal; expressions and duplicate fields, including a quoted spelling of an existing bare name, are refused at their source location. Quoted names do not change dependency source admission or the supported execution platforms. Task Command Notes build zig build --summary all Oyzu uses a fresh install prefix in its own output directory. Dependency-free host builds retain native compiler caches separately in core-managed disposable storage; other builds redirect both caches into the output directory. test zig build test --summary all Dependency-free native builds and isolated Linux builds produce JUnit with one case for the native test step. Coverage is not available. format zig fmt . Changes your source. format-check zig fmt --check . Read-only. A build task you write yourself keeps its own command and working directory, and must produce the install artifact itself. Oyzu doesn't add arguments to it. Build options (with.steps, with.definitions, with.install-format) only work with the conventional build, so combining them with your own build task fails before anything runs.

oyzu cache explain <target> --json distinguishes source changes from command changes. When the source projection digest and a native action's source-scope metadata equal the source input already in its key, that digest is counted once as source. Selection rules and captured file membership remain key inputs; distinct projection or source-scope digests remain bound separately. Adding a document can still change Zig build and test source keys and the inferred target version. Conventional commands exclude Oyzu's default inferred version from their environment, but their filesystem reads and writes remain unbounded, so those stages must run. Compiler cache manifests and an inventory of .zig/.zon files do not establish a complete boundary for arbitrary build programs or runtime tests.

These reports require a plugin that declares zig-native-test-report and the native-process effect for its compiled test worker. The catalog's 0.1.0-preview.3 does not declare it. Use a compatible package before requiring JUnit from this path. Define a test step in build.zig, then run oyzu build --full. Oyzu's compiled Rust adapter runs the conventional zig build test, keeps native stdout/stderr in JUnit, and collects junit.xml in the build bundle's reports. Check dist/manifest.json for the collected path. A failed assertion, compile error or crash fails the step and the build; a missing test step also fails. Zig 0.15.2 has no JUnit reporter. Its build runner consumes the per-test binary protocol internally, and the build summary does not expose every test case. The JUnit case therefore represents the complete native test step, not each Zig test function. A successful step with zero native tests is still a successful step; individual pass/skip counts are not claimed. Native test reads remain unbounded. Oyzu uses separate task-owned Zig caches for the report invocation. Authored replacement test commands are refused by this adapter. For isolated Linux builds, run oyzu build --isolated --full. Tests use the build's prepared packages/p tree through --system, with serial -j1 and separate writable task-owned caches. No second dependency fetch occurs, and the executor continues to deny network access. This includes contained local path dependencies. Offline runs need the same packages and tools prepared by an earlier online build. Native Linux builds with dependencies remain unsupported; use isolated execution. Dependent native macOS test reports also remain unavailable. Coverage remains unavailable in every mode. Set checks.coverage = "off" when requesting only test reports; required coverage checks remain binding and cannot be satisfied by this report.

For dependency-free native builds, the conventional test task emits one unit named zig.build.test through the public plugin protocol. With tests.retries enabled, a retry runs the complete zig build test step in a fresh native process. Individual Zig test functions cannot be selected. The adapter requests --summary all --color off from Zig 0.15.2. A failure is eligible only when the complete summary tree agrees with its aggregate counts, every compile/install step succeeded or was cached successfully, and the only failed steps are recognizable native test runs with reported test failures. Compilation and setup failures, missing targets, leaked memory, omitted or ambiguous steps, additional pending steps, and unparseable summaries are never retried. An otherwise zero exit without a complete parseable summary fails as incomplete evidence. Native test-run failures without enough completion facts also remain failed.
