Every attempt retains its native stdout/stderr, JUnit and completion facts in the build bundle. A fail-then-pass unit is reported as flaky and cannot be stored as a reusable pass. Consistent failures keep their original native exit. A requested synthetic case missing on a rerun stays failed. --no-cache disables reuse without changing these retry rules. Direct oyzu run test remains a single native invocation and applies the same completion/report validation. Zig has no native retry setting for this conventional command. Retry loops implemented in arbitrary build programs or custom test runners are not inferred from the summary and remain a detection limit. See test retry configuration for settings and shared guards. Dependent and isolated Zig test execution remains unsupported.

Stage Source boundary build Unbounded: build.zig is a program and may read arbitrary files or launch other programs. Zig 0.15.2's compiler dependency files and cache manifests do not account for all of those reads. An authored build command is likewise unbounded. test Unbounded: zig build test runs the build program and tests may read files at run time. JUnit reports the native step outcome, not a complete source read set. format-check Fixed: planning inventories regular .zig and .zon files under non-dot directories, then zig fmt --check receives those explicit file paths. It does not evaluate imports or build programs, or follow symlink entries. Formatting declares the inventoried file contents. Adding or removing a source file changes its arguments and invalidates it. Adding an unrelated README, or editing one, changes neither its arguments nor its read set. An incomplete, empty or non-portable formatting inventory stays unbounded with a reason. When explicit file arguments exceed the portable command-line budget, formatting falls back to zig fmt --check . and whole-target keying. The formatter's own rules establish this fixed boundary; no runtime observation is claimed. Build cache manifests are not treated as complete observed reads. Artifact collection consumes the build's installation tree, without a separate Zig export command. See native read admission for cache admission and version-related misses. For dependency-free native targets, format-check opts into a private source workspace with no retained output files. Its edges to build and test are order-only, so those unbounded stages do not enter its cache dependency closure. With core private-stage admission, formatting reuses independently when its source and command identity stay unchanged. A README content edit leaves the formatter's source key unchanged, as does adding an unrelated file. Zig commands exclude the engine's inferred OYZU_VERSION default from their environment, so the version no longer changes command identity; build scripts that read OYZU_VERSION must not rely on it. Changing a formatted source file reruns it. Dependency-bearing native targets on Intel macOS keep formatting in the shared workspace with whole-target keying. This preserves the source path bound by the prepared dependency launcher; independent private formatting is not supported for these targets. Captured builds retain their existing formatting plan. Build and test remain shared with whole-target source scope; their unbounded output contracts currently make them run on every invocation. The install prefix identifies the artifact to collect; it does not bound every file a build program or its children can write. Private-stage admission requires an exact list of retained regular files, so naming the installation directory alone does not make the build reusable. An incomplete formatter inventory also retains whole-target keying. Hooks, replacements and materialized inputs retain the target-wide fallback described in the action cache reference. The Zig plugin using this opt-in requires a core release with native-read and private-stage admission support. These declarations do not add a Zig test report adapter.

Oyzu reads build.zig.zon without running Zig. It accepts strings, enum package names, fingerprints, comments, literal containers, package versions, minimum compiler versions and string paths. A root .description string is accepted as plain metadata. Duplicate fields, expressions, other unknown fields and unsupported escapes are errors, reported with file, line and column. A package .version is a semantic version such as 1.0.0, 0.5.0-dev or 1.0.0-rc.1+build.1. It is limited to 32 bytes; major, minor, patch and numeric prerelease identifiers must fit unsigned 64-bit integers. Original spelling, including prerelease/build identifier case and build leading zeros, is preserved in package facts. Invalid versions are errors; correct the manifest before retrying. Minimum compiler versions must still be stable major.minor.patch releases, without prerelease or build identifiers. A package version does not select or pin the compiler. The manifest is limited to 1 MiB, 32 nesting levels and 20,000 values.

Tools pinned in the target folder's oyzu.toml apply to every selected build in that folder. The Zig compiler stays first on PATH, and other tool directories follow it. For example, a build that runs Pandoc needs the GitHub provider named explicitly: [tools] zig = "0.15.2" "github:jgm/pandoc" = "3.12.1" Then pin, install and build: oyzu pin zig@0.15.2 oyzu pin 'github:jgm/pandoc@3.12.1' oyzu install --frozen oyzu build --isolated This works with Pandoc 3.12.1 on Linux x86-64 GNU. Plain pandoc has no entry in the tool index, so the GitHub provider is the way to ask for it. Oyzu accepts complete publisher tar.gz or tar.xz trees. Interpreter commands, command aliases, partial payloads and other archive types are refused. Oyzu never changes file modes on downloaded bytes to make an archive executable. Normal tool-index and download policy checks apply before a cached tool is reused. A missing tool or platform fails. The image or host never substitutes for a pin. Offline builds need the tools prepared by an earlier online build, including the exact cached archives. An installed executable alone isn't enough, and TOOL_OFFLINE asks you to prepare online first. Isolated builds run with the network denied. If the build step fails, nothing is exported. Pandoc runs during the build but isn't part of the collected installation tree.

with.steps selects native build steps and with.install-format: tar.gz collects the install tree as one archive. This works at an ordinary checkout root. Keep your build.zig and tracked files in place and move the bundle out of the way in oyzu.toml: [tools] zig = "0.15.2" [build] bundleDirectory = ".oyzu/bundle" builds: ghostty: uses: zig/project inputs: [dist] with: steps: [lib-vt] install-format: tar.gz Evidence and collected files go in .oyzu/bundle, and the native dist directory comes in as a declared source input. oyzu inspect picks that bundle by default. Git and source containment checks still apply, and an unowned destination is refused. Oyzu doesn't translate your Zig build graph into YAML. build.zig owns the compile, documentation and install steps. The YAML says what to collect and which native entry point to run. Option Values Default Effect steps 1 to 16 distinct names. Each starts with an ASCII letter and has at most 64 letters, digits, _ or -. Zig's default install step Selects native build steps. Flags, paths, shell text and an empty list are refused. definitions Map of up to 16 option names to strings, booleans or signed 64-bit integers Empty Each entry becomes one -Dname=value argument. install-format directory, tar.gz directory tar.gz packs the install tree into install.tar.gz before collection. Definitions let you set project-defined Zig options: builds: ghostty: path: ghostty uses: zig/project inputs: [ghostty/dist] with: definitions: xcframework-target: native install-format: tar.gz The project decides what an option means. Here xcframework-target: native tells Ghostty to build only its host Mac application. Keep tool versions in oyzu.toml. Don't put ordered actions or commands in definitions. Rules for definitions: Names follow the same grammar and 64-byte limit as steps. String values can be up to 1,024 UTF-8 bytes with no control characters. Empty strings are fine. Booleans become true or false, and integers become decimal numbers. The rendered arguments total at most 4,096 bytes and are sorted by name. Spaces and punctuation stay inside one argument and are never run through a shell. Null, floats, nested objects and arrays are refused. Names that control the compiler, target and CPU, optimization, release or version, install prefix and caches, toolchain, system packages, fetching or job count are reserved (including case and underscore variants). Any other option goes to your project's own build.zig, and its failures show up normally. Oyzu owns the Zig binary and the prefix, cache and --system paths. Steps and definitions don't grant tool, source, network or credential access. Native build exit codes stay separate from JUnit and coverage, and required-report checks still apply.
documents.s: Native steps and linked installation archives

documents.t: After the native build succeeds, Oyzu writes install.tar.gz and collects it as a regular file. It keeps relative links inside the tree and executable bits, and refuses links that escape, dangle or loop, and unsupported file types. Limits are 100,000 entries, 10 GiB of file content, and 64 nested link expansions. Plain directory collection rejects links, so use tar.gz for trees that contain them. oyzu inspect checks the archive's bytes. It doesn't unpack it.

On Intel macOS, a Zig project with dependencies is prepared before the build, using the Oyzu-managed compiler. Oyzu downloads each original archive through its broker, checks the archive hash and Zig's package hash, and then builds with --system pointing at its prepared package tree and -j1. A build task you wrote yourself doesn't get this preparation. Required isolated execution is refused on this path. Native builds run with your account's access. oyzu build --offline fails with OFFLINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE. The prepared packages aren't kept between builds, so dependency builds need to be online. Preparation runs in a macOS sandbox with network and host-read access denied, a private HOME, and no registry credentials or inherited environment. If your project refers to installed resources through zig-out, the build keeps zig-out available in its private workspace as a view of the real install prefix. An existing path or a case collision is refused, and your checkout is not changed. XZ package metadata is checked with Apple's system liblzma from the selected SDK. If the SDK can't provide it, the build fails. There is no other decoder. An Xcode flow is also supported for a nested project, limited to Xcode 26.3 (build 17C529), Apple Swift 6.2.4 and a finite Sparkle 2.9.0 binary package recipe on Intel macOS. One canonical Package.resolved is recognized. Unknown pins, manifests, layouts and multiple resolutions are refused, and arbitrary SwiftPM projects aren't supported. Packages come from the broker through a separate swiftpm route, SwiftPM runs with its network denied, and its caches stay private. Only TZ=UTC, LC_ALL=C and the selected DEVELOPER_DIR are accepted as explicit environment for this flow. Other task environment values or PATH changes are refused before anything downloads. Xcode tools write to temporary files under your user's Darwin temp root. Oyzu allows only the specific paths Xcode's tools use, on top of a sandbox that still denies network and unrelated reads. Other builds by the same user can share those temporary files, and Oyzu doesn't delete them. Required stronger isolation is refused. Authored Swift or Xcode arguments for CLANG_MODULE_CACHE_PATH are refused, because Oyzu sets it.

This configuration builds the installed documentation and C library of Ghostty (tested with upstream v1.3.1) as one native build: [tools] zig = "0.15.2" "github:jgm/pandoc" = "3.12.1" [build] bundleDirectory = ".oyzu/bundle" builds: ghostty-docs: uses: zig/project inputs: [dist] with: definitions: emit-docs: true emit-exe: false install-format: tar.gz oyzu build ghostty-docs runs the project's default install step. There is no separate docs step. The tree has section 1 and 5 Markdown, standalone HTML, man pages, and the VT library with headers and pkg-config files. It leaves out the application resources that belong to the executable. The project's native build graph decides all of that. The output keeps the version fallback 1.3.1-dev+0000000 and the pkg-config build prefix. pkg-config paths aren't relocated. Two builds in one folder can't own the same native build unit, so a library build and a docs build need separate configurations. The build reserves 4,096 MiB for its native action, so Docker needs more than its 4 GiB default. A 6 GiB Docker budget on an 8 GiB machine worked, with jobs set to 1. Keep at least 2 GiB of disk free.

Use the native steps example to select lib-vt and collect the public headers and versioned shared library in install.tar.gz. Set steps: [lib-vt, test-lib-vt] to require Ghostty's native VT tests as part of the same build. The test-lib-vt step fails in unmodified upstream v1.3.1; it needs native repairs before that combined build can succeed. The native command produces no test totals or reports. Library installation does not include the Linux or macOS application.

Select Ghostty's native Linux application installation in build.yaml: builds: ghostty-linux: uses: zig/project inputs: [dist] with: definitions: gtk-wayland: false gtk-x11: true emit-docs: false emit-terminfo: true strip: true install-format: tar.gz The native default install owns the executable, VT library and headers, compiled terminfo, shell integration, completions, themes, desktop metadata, icons and localizations. The native default is Debug; strip=true strips the executable without selecting an optimization profile. App metadata therefore uses the native com.mitchellh.ghostty-debug identifier. Documentation conversion and the required VT test suite use their own build configurations. This configuration targets Debian 13 on Linux amd64 GNU. The image needs GTK 4.14 or newer, libadwaita 1.5 or newer, Blueprint compiler 0.16 or newer, glib-compile-resources, gettext, tic, pkg-config, a C/C++ toolchain, the X11 SDK, the Oniguruma development library and xmllint for XML resource preprocessing. These native prerequisites must be provisioned in the image before the build. oyzu build ghostty-linux --isolated --jobs 1 --image zig=your-compatible-linux-image Oyzu collects the installation archive; it does not launch a graphical session. Embedded version metadata can use Ghostty's no-Git fallback 1.3.1-dev+0000000. Wayland, desktop service activation, distribution packaging, musl and other Linux distributions are outside the supported scope of this configuration.

For the conventional build, Oyzu runs zig build --summary all --prefix <output>/install --cache-dir <cache>/cache --global-cache-dir <cache>/global-cache and exports only the install directory, keeping the executable bits of installed files. Dependency-free host builds keep <cache> under the target's .oyzu/native/zig, outside private source projections and fresh artifact output, subject to the existing native cache retention budget. Unchanged source reuses Zig's native compilation results; editing source rebuilds affected output. Captured and dependency-bearing builds keep invocation-local caches. The installation directory isn't promoted into .oyzu/bin; Windows executables retain their .exe suffix. The plugin reads static source metadata and plans the build. It doesn't launch the compiler, download anything or use observation tools. Oyzu selects the compiler, verifies archives, runs the build, applies policy and reports, and collects the bundle. The plugin can't waive required checks. Native host builds refuse declared dependencies (including path and lazy ones), except in the Intel macOS flow above. Use an isolated build, described below, for projects with dependencies on Linux. Dependent native test reports, coverage and app packaging aren't supported. Dependency-free native and isolated Linux JUnit reports use the adapter described above. A fast build proves only that it built and collected its artifacts. A tree with links fails directory collection. Use install-format: tar.gz. A build that installs nothing fails artifact collection. A failed Zig command never produces a successful artifact. Fix invalid metadata at the reported location. Choose a compiler that satisfies the minimum, and keep the real failures from your build.zig. Don't replace them with an ambient compiler or remove required checks.

Collection preserves native .pc files, including their producer installation prefix. To use a collected library from another directory, point pkg-config at the collected metadata and override its standard prefix variable: install_dir=/absolute/path/to/collected/install metadata_dir="$install_dir/lib/pkgconfig" PKG_CONFIG_LIBDIR="$metadata_dir" \ pkg-config --define-variable=prefix="$install_dir" --cflags --libs your-library Set metadata_dir to the actual collected .pc directory. Packages may install it under lib/pkgconfig or share/pkgconfig; Ghostty uses share/pkgconfig. Pass the resulting compiler and linker flags to your native C consumer. The override applies to that pkg-config invocation; it does not modify the collected files or require the producer workspace. A package can instead emit relocatable metadata using prefix=${pcfiledir}/../.. when its .pc file is installed under lib/pkgconfig or share/pkgconfig. This works when the native metadata derives its paths from prefix. Other hard-coded producer paths need a correction in the native package; Oyzu does not rewrite them. If the metadata names dependencies, provide their corresponding metadata directories and libraries too. Preserve the native toolchain, ABI and runtime-library requirements of the collected library.

Isolated builds prepare every URL, transitive, contained path and lazy dependency before build.zig runs. This needs a Linux amd64 GNU compiler and a multi-platform Zig plugin build. A single local plugin binding can't do captured planning. Oyzu's broker downloads the archives and records each archive's SHA-256 separately from Zig's package hash. Zig sees only local files. The build uses the prepared packages/p tree through --system with separate writable caches and serial -j1. Your own build task doesn't receive these arguments.

HTTPS archives: the URL can't contain user information, queries, fragments, percent encoding, control characters, backslashes or path traversal. Archive types are .tar, .tar.gz (.tgz), .tar.xz, .tar.zst and .zip, or their media types. Other types fail with ZIG_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED. GitHub commits: git+https://github.com/<owner>/<repository>#<40-hex-commit>. Oyzu downloads the commit tarball over HTTPS, with no Git executable and no branch or tag lookup, and the compiler must produce the exact hash you declared. Credentials, queries, abbreviated commits, .git suffixes, extra path segments and other hosts are refused. A matching native hash doesn't verify a Git object or signature. Registry routes: registries.routes with protocol zig maps a source host[:port]/prefix/ (HTTPS implied) to an administrator-configured connector. Once any Zig route exists, all package routing is closed. A missing source or connector, an overlap, an unapproved redirect or an unavailable mirror is refused with no public fallback. Project and user configuration can't grant route authority. The connector's credentials stay in Oyzu and Zig never sees them. Authenticated downloads aren't reused from the cache.

A dependency normally has a regular build.zig.zon. A dependency without one is accepted only after Zig's hash check and a bounded scan of the original archive proves no build.zig.zon appears anywhere in it. This works for gzip and XZ tars. The scan has limits of 64 MiB compressed, 256 MiB decoded and 10,000 members, runs in a separate worker for XZ (4,096 MiB and 120 seconds), and fails closed. Code Meaning and fix ZIG_SOURCE_INVALID The dependency declaration isn't a supported exact source. Fix it. SOURCE_DENIED The download or a redirect isn't on an approved route. ZIG_HASH_MISMATCH The downloaded bytes don't produce the declared hash. Oyzu doesn't substitute another source. ZIG_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED The archive type isn't supported. ZIG_MANIFEST_UNAVAILABLE Oyzu can't prove the dependency's manifest. Keep a regular build.zig.zon or use a supported original archive. ZIG_CACHE_INVALID Reused data no longer matches its recorded receipt. Prepare again online.

Linux dependency package trees keep regular filenames that end in a dot, such as ._., and direct symlinks from one regular file to a sibling regular file (the target is a single portable name). Chains, directory links, dangling links and absolute or traversing links aren't supported. Project sources, build artifacts, directories, trailing spaces and other filename rules are unchanged. Packaging for Docker image dependency contexts still applies portable names and can refuse these trees.

Reuse needs identical dependency contents, compiler and plugin identities, and source mapping, and checks current routes again. Offline builds replay prepared dependencies from an earlier online build. Required test reports need a compatible plugin declaring zig-native-test-report; older packages are refused before preparation. Isolated Linux tests use the same prepared package tree as the build. Coverage is not available and remains refused before preparation. Private connector sessions and live organization endpoints aren't supported. Zig's native caches are fresh for each executed isolated build, so native incremental compile speed isn't available there.

The Zig plugin accepts optional annotations only in the designated plugin protocol containers. Native commands, target paths, prepared digests, identities and signed manifests remain strict. Missing request capabilities direct you to oyzu plugins update zig/project; missing engine support in a manifest directs you to oyzu self update. Unknown reply security fields and undeclared required reply features are plugin contract violations and direct you to update the plugin. Development bindings require rebuilding and rebinding instead. No remedy changes locks or bypasses package admission automatically. Source adoption requires a new normally admitted Zig plugin release; updating the CLI alone does not change installed plugin readers. Writers omit annotations unless the peer advertises support, including the initial describe exchange. The existing v1alpha1 contract remains in place.

Oyzu is an early release. The core local workflow works without an account; some areas are experimental or limited to certain platforms. This page is a summary; each linked reference page has the details. Area Status Help and machine-readable output Every command has offline --help and --json output Discovery, tasks and local builds Available for the supported ecosystems. Support for each builder varies by platform; see ecosystem support Tool management Available. Fully supported on Linux x86-64 Build bundles and history Available: every build writes a bundle you can inspect, and recent builds are kept Local action cache On by default. Experimental Remote OCI cache Experimental. Supported on Linux Isolated (container) builds Experimental. Supported on Linux hosts Publishing Experimental. OCI registries Remote builds Experimental. Needs an Oyzu platform account See Known limitations for the details behind each experimental area.
CLI output Local builds Action cache Remote runs
Read this before you choose Oyzu for a project. Each section links to the page with the full details.

Every release so far is a preview. The install script downloads from the public oyzuai/oyzu-releases repository without a token. There is no Linux musl executable; build from source on those systems. The install script checks the release's SHA-256 digest but not its provenance files. There is no package-manager distribution.

Support for tool versions, operating systems, builders and dependency handling varies. See ecosystem support, local builds and tool commands. Tool management is fully tested on Linux x86-64. Windows x86-64 works with less test coverage, and macOS isn't supported yet. Isolated (container) builds are experimental and supported on Linux hosts.

The local action cache is on by default and experimental. The remote OCI cache is experimental and supported on Linux. Entries are not signed, and entries larger than 256 MiB are not pushed. Native stages without complete admitted reads or bounded outputs rerun, even with unchanged source. This also prevents whole-target reuse. Windows Rust compile observations can currently remain incomplete; see native read coverage. Complete-read stage reuse for supported Go, Node, Helm, .NET and Maven/Gradle stages requires isolated Linux crun. Docker and native Windows/macOS do not inherit that guarantee. Native Windows Vite/uv enforcement is pending; refusal remains the supported outcome for incomplete reads. Python complete-read stage reuse is not yet available. Maven/Gradle module, Node workspace-member and .NET project reuse require supported project shapes and compatible plugins. See the stage-reuse table. See Cache build results.
Publishing is experimental. OCI registry publication is supported. See Publish artifacts.

Remote builds are experimental and need a platform account or access to a standalone pool. Standalone pools support pushed commits and, on snapshot-capable servers, local changes through --worktree. Output downloads are not available. See Remote builds.
The site uses the Segoe UI font when it is installed on your system and a fallback font otherwise.
If something on this site doesn't match your installed CLI, include oyzu --version, your platform, the command you ran, its full output (with -v) and the relevant --help output when you report it.

Website privacy Updated October 21, 2026. This page covers docs.oyzu.ai. Your choice We use free Google Analytics to understand visits to the documentation and clicks to GitHub or downloads. Google loads only after you choose Allow analytics. No thanks leaves every page and local search available without sending analytics requests to Google. With JavaScript disabled, analytics does not load. Use Analytics settings at the bottom of any page to change your choice. This browser remembers it for 180 days on the docs site, separately from the marketing site. If storage is unavailable, your choice applies only to the current document. Rejecting after acceptance stops measurement, clears the docs analytics cookies and reloads the page. It does not delete data already collected by Google. What is collected After acceptance, Google receives page visits, GitHub and download click events, browser and device information, approximate geographic information, and cookie identifiers. Your IP address reaches Google through the network connection. Analytics cookies expire after 180 days; visits can renew them. A download click does not prove installation or use of Oyzu. We remove query strings and fragments from reported page addresses and report only the referring website’s origin. Valid campaign labels may be included; do not put personal information or secrets in campaign links. We do not send search terms, copied code, user IDs or link addresses in action events. Google Signals and advertising personalization are disabled. Our setup uses explicit events rather than automatic enhanced measurement. Google processes analytics data under its terms. Read Google’s Privacy Policy and how Google uses information from sites using its services. Hosting and contact GitHub Pages hosts the documentation and processes requests to deliver it even when analytics is rejected. See GitHub’s privacy statement. Search Console supplies search-performance reports independently of the optional visitor tag. For website privacy questions, email hello@oyzu.ai.
